Initially created: 2025-12-17T20:46:05.435+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Principal Records of Liáng, Part 1 (The
Principal Records,
following the old style for naming, originally recorded the origin of the beginnings and then chronologically ordered the events.
Before the enthronement,
the events are detailed,
tracing back to their origins,
thus they are recorded comprehensively and thoroughly,
showing that his rise had both gradual and sudden aspects.
After the enthronement,
the events are summarized.
Residing in a position of honor and bearing heavy responsibility,
what was demanded was great,
thus what was recorded was brief,
for only brevity could establish the legal framework.
Tàizǔ Shénwǔ Yuánshèng Xiàohuángdì,
whose surname was Zhū,
was a native of Wǔgōulǐ, Dàngshān, Sòngzhōu.
His father, Chéng,
taught the Five Classics in the local area.
He had three sons,
named Quányù, Cún, and Wēn.
When Chéng died,
the three sons were poor
and could not earn a living.
They and their mother worked as laborers for Liú Chóng, a native of Xiāoxiàn.
Quányù had no special talent,
but he was quite respectable in character.
Cún and Wēn were brave and strong,
but Wēn was especially fierce and violent.
The tabooed name is changed to ‘a certain name’ in the text;
the meaning is in the note on ‘claiming kingship.’
In the fourth year of Qiánfú of Táng Xīzōng [877 CE],
Huáng Cháo rose up in Cáo and Pú.
Cún and Wēn fled into the rebel ranks.
When Cháo attacked Lǐngnán,
Cún died in battle.
When Cháo captured the capital,
he appointed Wēn as the Vanguard Commissioner of the Campaigning Army for the Southeast Circuit.
Wēn captured Tóngzhōu
and was appointed as the Defense Commissioner of Tóngzhōu.
At this time,
the Son of Heaven was in Shǔ,
and the various circuits gathered troops to suppress the rebels.
Wēn was repeatedly defeated by Wáng Chóngróng of Hézhōng
and frequently requested reinforcements from Cháo,
but Cháo's Court Supervisor Mèng Kǎi suppressed the requests and failed to communicate them.
Wēn's advisor Xiè Tóng persuaded Wēn, saying:
“The Huáng family arose from the grass roots,
and by exploiting the decline and disorder of the Táng,
they directly seized the opportunity to take power,
they do not possess the achievements and virtues necessary for establishing a royal lineage.
How can they be relied upon to accomplish great things together!
Now the Son of Heaven is in Shǔ,
and the troops of the various circuits gather daily to plan the restoration;
this shows that the virtue of Táng is not yet exhausted in the eyes of the people.
Furthermore, you, General, fight hard on the outside,
while mediocre people control things on the inside.
This is why Zhāng Hán turned his back on Qín and submitted to Chǔ.”
Wēn agreed,
and subsequently killed his Supervising Army Officer Yán Shí.
He submitted himself to Hézhōng
and surrendered through Wáng Chóngróng.

Commander-in-Chief Wáng Duó, acting under imperial mandate, appointed Wēn as Grand General of the Left Gold Scabbard Guard and Deputy Commissioner of Campaigning and Suppression for the Hézhōng Circuit.
The Son of Heaven bestowed the name Quánzhōng upon Wēn.
“Various circuits”
records the terminology used at the time.
The Táng referred to the military prefectures governed by the Jìdùshǐ as Fānzhèn (vassal circuits),
hence the terms 'proceeding to the circuit' and 'moving the circuit'.
In the third month of the third year of Zhōnghé [883 CE],
Quánzhōng was appointed Prefect of Biànzhōu and Jìdùshǐ of Xuānwǔ Commandery.
In the fourth month,
the troops of the various circuits defeated Cháo
and recovered the capital.
Cháo fled to Lántián.
On the day Dīngmǎo in the seventh month,
Quánzhōng returned to Xuānwǔ.
In this year,
Huáng Cháo exited the Lántián Pass,
captured Càizhōu.
The Jìdùshǐ Qín Zōngquán rebelled and joined Cháo,
then besieged Chénzhōu.
Shí Pǔ of Xúzhōu was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Campaigning Army for the Southeast Circuit,
and gathered troops from the eastern circuits to relieve Chén.
Zhào Chōu, the Prefect of Chénzhōu, also requested troops from Quánzhōng.
Although Pǔ was the Commander-in-Chief, he did not personally command the troops.
In the fourth year [884 CE],
Quánzhōng personally led troops to rescue Chōu,
and commanded the forces of the various circuits to defeat Cháo's generals Huáng Yè, Shàng Ràng, and others.
Chōu regarded Quánzhōng favorably
and first submitted his allegiance.
At this time,
Lǐ Kèyòng of Hédōng led his troops across the Tàiháng Mountains,
crossed the river (the Yellow River),
emerged at Luòyáng,
and joined the eastern forces to attack Cháo.
Cháo had already been defeated and fled.
Quánzhōng and Kèyòng pursued and defeated him at Yǎnchéng.
Cháo fled to Zhōngmóu,
where they defeated him again at Wángmǎn.
Cháo fled to Fēngqiū,
and was again greatly defeated.
Cháo broke through and fled eastwards.
Upon reaching Lánghǔ Gǔ (Wolf and Tiger Valley) in Tàishān,
he was killed by Shí Pǔ's pursuing troops.
In the ninth month,
the Son of Heaven appointed Quánzhōng as Verified Minister of Works and Concurrent Chancellor,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Pèijùn.
In the third month of the second year of Guāngqǐ [886 CE],
he was advanced in rank to Prince (Wáng).
The Yìchéng Commandery mutinied,
drove out its Jìdùshǐ Ān Shīrú,
and recommended the camp general Zhāng Xiāo as acting commander.
Shīrú came seeking refuge,
and was killed.
Zhū Zhēn and Lǐ Tángbīn were dispatched to capture Huázhōu,
and Hú Zhēn was appointed as acting commander.
In the twelfth month,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Prince of Wúxīng Jùn.
Whenever someone is referred to by "a certain person of a certain prefecture/commandery,"
it means their Jìdùshǐ.
After Huáng Cháo died,
Qín Zōngquán declared himself emperor,
and captured Shǎn, Luò, Huái, Mèng, Táng, Xǔ, Rǔ, and Zhèng prefectures.
He dispatched his generals Qín Xián, Lú Táng, and Zhāng Ào to attack Biàn.
Xián's army was at Bǎnqiáo,
Ào's army was in the northern suburbs,
and Táng's army was at Wànshèng.
They encircled Biàn with thirty-six stockades.
The King, seeing his troops were few,
dared not sally forth.
So he sent Zhū Zhēn to recruit soldiers in the east,
and sought aid from Yǎn and Yùn.
In the spring of the third year,
Zhēn returned with ten thousand men and several hundred horses.
He then attacked Xián at Bǎnqiáo,
capturing four of his stockades.
He also attacked Táng at Wànshèng;
Táng was defeated
and threw himself into the water and died.
When Zōngquán heard of Táng and others' defeat,
he personally led several thousand elite soldiers
and set up a stockade in the northern suburbs.
In the fifth month,
Zhū Jǐn of Yǎnzōu and Zhū Xuān of Yùnzhōu came to provide aid.
The King held a feast in the army camp.
In the middle of the feast,
the King ostensibly rose to go to the latrine,
and with light troops, sallied out from the northern gate to raid Ào,
while the music did not stop.
Ào did not expect the arrival of the troops,
and the Yǎn and Yùn armies then joined in the attack,
completely defeating them,
beheading more than twenty thousand.
Zōngquán and Ào fled by night,
passing through Zhèng,
they massacred its city before leaving.
Zōngquán reached Cài,
and again sent Zhāng Ào to attack Biàn.
When the King heard Ào was returning,
he ascended the ridge behind Fēngchán Sì,
observed Ào's troops passing,
and sent Zhū Zhēn to follow them,
cautioning him:
"When Ào sees our troops,
he will surely stop.
When you see him stop,
you should return quickly,
do not fight him."
Soon after, Ào saw Zhēn behind him,
and indeed stopped.
Zhēn immediately galloped back.
The King ordered Zhēn to lead his troops to hide behind a large forest,
and he himself led elite cavalry out from its east,
lying in ambush between large mounds.
Ào stopped and ate.
After eating,
he raised his banners
and galloped to attack Zhēn.
Zhēn's troops retreated a little,
then the King led his hidden troops to emerge from the side,
cutting Ào's army into three and attacking them.
Ào was greatly defeated
and escaped.
Zōngquán was enraged
and beheaded Ào.
The troops from Héyáng, Shǎn, and Luò who were guarding for Zōngquán,
hearing that all of Cài's elite soldiers had been annihilated at Biàn,
then dispersed.
Therefore, Zhūgě Shuǎng's general Lǐ Hǎnzhī took Héyáng, and Zhāng Quányì took Luòyáng and came to submit.
In the tenth month,
the Son of Heaven sent an envoy,
bestowing upon the King a stele commemorating his achievements.
Zhū Xuān and Zhū Jǐn's armies, after assisting Biàn
and defeating Zōngquán, returned east.
The King then sent a manifesto to Yǎn and Yùn,
falsely accusing them of enticing Biàn's runaway soldiers to the east,
and then dispatched troops to attack them,
capturing their Cáo Prefecture and Pú Prefecture.
He then sent Zhū Zhēn to attack Yùnzhōu,
but he was greatly defeated and returned.
In the twelfth month,
the Son of Heaven sent an envoy,
bestowing upon the King an iron certificate and a stele of virtuous governance.
Initially, he was referred to by name;
later, by his noble title;
later still, he was referred to as emperor;
this was a gradual process.
It was only after reaching the title of King that he was referred to as such,
indicating his imminent rise.
It is customary in the common usage that
"Xuān"
follows
"Wáng"
is incorrect.
After Huáinán Jìdùshǐ Gāo Pián died,
Yáng Xíngmì entered Yángzhōu.
The Son of Heaven appointed the King concurrently as Huáinán Jìdùshǐ.
The King then memorialized Yáng Xíngmì as Deputy Envoy,
and appointed Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Lǐ Fán as Acting Governor (Liúhòu).
When Fán went to Yángzhōu,
Xíngmì did not receive him.
In the first month of Wéndé First Year,
the King went to Huáinán,
reaching Sòngzhōu and then returned.
At this time,
Qín Zōngquán captured Xiāngzhōu,
and appointed Zhào Déyīn as Jìdùshǐ.
Déyīn rebelled against Zōngquán and came to submit.
The Son of Heaven then appointed the King as Càizhōu Sìmiàn Xíngyíng Dūtǒng,
with Déyīn as his deputy.
On the Gēngzǐ day of the third month,
Xīzōng died.
Tiānxíong Jūn rebelled,
imprisoning their Jìdùshǐ Lè Yànzhēn.
His son, Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Cóngxùn, attacked Wèi
and came to request troops.
Zhū Zhēn was dispatched to assist Cóngxùn in attacking Wèi.
However, the Wèi army killed Yànzhēn,
Cóngxùn died in battle,
the Wèi people enthroned Luó Hóngxìn,
so Zhēn returned.
Zhāng Quányì took Héyáng,
expelling Lǐ Hǎnzhī.
Hǎnzhī fled to Hédōng.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent troops to besiege Héyáng,
Quányì came to seek aid.
Dīng Huì and Niú Cúnjié were dispatched to rescue him,
defeating the Hédōng troops at Yǎnhé.
In the fifth month,
the Xíngyíng attacked Càizhōu,
besieging it for over a hundred days,
but failed to capture it.
At this time,
Shí Pǔ had already been appointed Dōngnánmiàn Dūtǒng,
and the King was again appointed to command the Xíngyíng while Pǔ still retained the title of Dūtǒng.
The King then submitted a memorial,
arguing that Pǔ had achieved nothing in attacking Cài and yet had not lost his Dūtǒng title,
also intending to provoke Pǔ to initiate military action.
Earlier,
when Gāo Pián died,
Huáinán fell into chaos.
Chǔzhōu Cìshǐ Líu Zàn came to defect,
and was accepted.
When the King's forces attacked Cài unsuccessfully,
they returned,
intending to attack Xú.
So Zhū Zhēn was dispatched with several thousand troops to the east,
ostensibly to escort Zàn back to Chǔzhōu.
Pǔ was angered by the criticism of himself,
and upon hearing that Zhēn was coming with troops,
indeed sent out troops to resist him.
Zhēn fought at Wúkāng,
greatly defeating them,
and took their two counties of Fēng and Xiāo.
He then attacked Sùzhōu
and captured it.
Zhēn garrisoned Xiāoxiàn,
and separately sent Páng Shīgǔ to attack Xúzhōu.
In the first month of Lóngjì First Year,
Shīgǔ defeated Pǔ at Lǚliáng.
Huáixī Yájiàng Shēn Cóng captured Qín Zōngquán,
broke his legs,
and was about to cage him and send him to the capital;
another general Guō Fán killed Cóng,
usurped Zōngquán, and offered him (as a captive).
The King sent Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Lǐ Fán to present the captive to the capital,
and memorialized Guō Fán as Huáixī Liúhòu.
In the third month,
the Son of Heaven enfeoffed the King as Dōngpíng Wáng.
In the seventh month,
Zhū Zhēn killed Lǐ Tángbīn.
The King went to Xiāoxiàn,
seized Zhēn and killed him,
and then attacked Xúzhōu.
In winter,
there was heavy rain
and floods,
so he could not campaign and returned.
Initially,
Qín Zōngquán sent his younger brother Zōnghéng to plunder territory in Huáinán.
In this year,
Zōnghéng was killed by his general Sūn Rú,
and Rú attacked Yáng Xíngmì at Yángzhōu.
Huáinán fell into great chaos,
Xíngmì fled to Xuānzhōu,
and Rú entered Yángzhōu.
In the spring of Dàshùn First Year,
Páng Shīgǔ was dispatched to attack Sūn Rú in Huáinán,
but was greatly defeated and returned.
In the fourth month,
Sùzhōu general Zhāng Yún returned Sùzhōu to Shí Pǔ.
The King personally led an attack on it,
but failed to capture it.
Initially,
Huáng Cháo was defeated and fled.
Lǐ Kèyòng pursued him,
reaching Yuānqú,
but failed to catch him and returned.
Passing Biàn,
he stationed his troops in the northern suburbs.
The Wáng invited Kèyòng and held a banquet at Shàngyuán Yì.
That night, he attacked him with soldiers.
Kèyòng escaped by scaling the city wall,
and reported the matter to Jīngshī.
The Son of Heaven knew the fault lay with Biàn and mediated a reconciliation.
By this time,
Chancellor Zhāng Jùn secretly communicated with Biàn,
and the Wáng offered him generous bribes.
Jùn, on behalf of Biàn, requested an attack on Hédōng.
All the ministers of Táng believed it was inappropriate to raise an army.
Jùn, relying on Biàn's strength,
made his request even firmer.
The Son of Heaven had no choice,
and granted it.
In the fifth month,
Jùn was made the Commander-in-Chief of the Four Directions Campaign Army of Tàiyuán,
and the Wáng was made the Commissioner for Pacification of the Southeast Front.
However, the Wáng did not personally lead the troops,
but merely assigned two thousand soldiers to Jùn.
Jùn garrisoned his troops at Yīndì.
Hédōng rebel general Féng Bà killed the Lùzhōu garrison commander Lǐ Kègōng and came to surrender,
and [the Wáng] sent Gě Cóngzhōu into Lùzhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent Kāng Jūnlì to attack him,
and Cóngzhōu fled to Héyáng.
In the ninth month,
the Wáng proceeded to Héyáng.
In the tenth month,
the Son of Heaven appointed the Wáng concurrently as Xuānyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and he subsequently went to Huázhōu,
requesting passage through Wèi,
in order to attack Hédōng.
He also demanded military supplies from them,
which was also intended to anger Wèi and provide a pretext for war.
The Wèi people indeed believed that this was not the route troops should take,
and declined, citing a shortage of provisions.
They refused all his requests.
Thereupon, he attacked Wèi.
In the eleventh month,
Zhāng Jùn's army was utterly defeated at Yīndì.
In the first month of the second year,
the Wáng fought the Wèi people at Nèihuáng,
and routed them,
massacring the former Yuánchéng,
and Luó Hóngxìn came to submit terms.
In the tenth month,
Sùzhōu was captured.
In the eleventh month,
Cáozhōu general Guō Shàobīn killed his prefect Guō Ráo and came to surrender.
In the twelfth month,
Dīng Huì defeated Zhū Jǐn at Jīnxiāng.
In the second month of the first year of Jǐngfú,
he attacked Yùnzhōu.
The vanguard, led by Zhū Yǒuyù, was defeated at Dǒumén,
the Wáng's army arrived later,
was also defeated, and retreated.
In winter,
Yǒuyù took Púzhōu,
and then attacked Xúzhōu.
In the fourth month of the second year,
Páng Shīgǔ captured Xúzhōu,
and killed Shí Pǔ.
The Wáng proceeded to Xúzhōu,
made Shīgǔ the Acting Military Governor,
and then attacked Yǎn and Yùn.
In the second month of the first year of Qiánníng,
the Wáng fought Zhū Xuān at Yúshān,
and routed him.
In the eighth month of the second year,
he again defeated Xuān at Liángshān.
In the eleventh month,
he again defeated him at Jùyě.
Yǎn and Yùn sought help from Hédōng,
Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched troops to relieve them,
requesting passage through Wèi.
Subsequently, the Wèi people attacked him,
Kèyòng became furious,
and launched a major offensive against Wèi.
Luó Hóngxìn came to ask for help,
and [the Wáng] sent Gě Cóngzhōu to aid Wèi.
That same year,
Lǐ Kèyòng was enfeoffed as Jìn Wáng.
In the fifth month of the third year,
they fought at Huánshuǐ,
captured Kèyòng's son, Luòluò,
sent him to Wèi,
and killed him.
In the seventh month,
Lǐ Màozhēn of Fèngxiáng violated Jīngshī.
The Son of Heaven left and resided in Huázhōu.
The Wáng requested to lead troops to address the crisis,
but the Son of Heaven issued a gracious decree instructing him to desist.
He also requested to move the capital to Luòyáng,
but this was not granted.
In the first month of the fourth year,
Páng Shīgǔ captured Yùnzhōu,
the Wáng proceeded to Yùnzhōu,
and made Zhū Yǒuyù the Acting Military Governor.
Then he attacked Yǎnzhōu.
Zhū Jǐn fled to Huáinán,
and [the Wáng] made Gě Cóngzhōu the Acting Military Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
In the ninth month,
he attacked Huáinán.
Páng Shīgǔ advanced through Qīngkǒu,
Gě Cóngzhōu advanced through Ānfēng,
and the Wáng's army garrisoned at Sùzhōu.
Yáng Xíngmì sent Zhū Jǐn to first attack Qīngkǒu,
and Shīgǔ was defeated and killed.
Cóngzhōu quickly turned back his troops,
reaching Bī Hé,
where Jǐn again defeated him.
The Wáng was alarmed,
and galloped back.
In the third month of the first year of Guānghuà,
the Son of Heaven appointed the Wáng concurrently as Tiānpíng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the fourth month,
he sent Gě Cóngzhōu to attack Jìn's Shāndōng,
and captured the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
Zhào Kuāngníng of Xiāngzhōu had been attached [to the Wáng] since the time of his father Déyīn,
but Kuāngníng also secretly communicated with Yáng Xíngmì and Lǐ Kèyòng,
and the matter was exposed.
In the seventh month,
he sent Shì Shūcóng and Kāng Huáiyīng to attack Kuāngníng,
and took his three prefectures of Bì, Suí, and Dèng.
Kuāngníng requested peace, and the attack ceased.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī surrendered Lùzhōu.
In the second year,
Liú Rén'gōng of Yōuzhōu attacked Wèi.
Luó Shàowēi came to ask for help.
The Wáng rescued Wèi,
and defeated Rén'gōng at Nèihuáng.
In the fourth month,
he sent Shì Shūcóng to attack Jìn's Tàiyuán,
but failed to capture it.
In the seventh month,
Lǐ Kèyòng seized Zé and Lù.
In the eleventh month,
Bǎoyì Jūn mutinied,
killed its Military Governor Wáng Gǒng,
and supported their headquarters general Lǐ Fán as Acting Military Governor.
Their general Zhū Jiǎn killed Fán and came to surrender.
Jiǎn was appointed Bǎoyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the fourth month of the third year,
he sent Gě Cóngzhōu to attack Liú Rén'gōng's Cāngzhōu,
captured his Dézhōu,
and fought Rén'gōng at Lǎofù Dī,
routing him utterly.
In the eighth month,
Jìn took Míngzhōu.
The Wáng proceeded to Míngzhōu,
and retook it.
At this time,
Zhèn and Dìng had both submitted to Jìn.
Consequently, he attacked Zhènzhōu,
defeated Línchéng,
and Wáng Róng came to submit terms.
He advanced to attack Dìngzhōu,
Wáng Gào fled to Jìn,
and his general Wáng Chǔzhí surrendered Dìngzhōu.
Zēng Sānyì revised and determined: Sānyì notes that,
in the Geographical Monograph of the Táng History, Tángzhōu,
in the third year of Tiānyòu, Zhū Quánzhōng moved the administrative seat to Bìyáng,
and memorialized to rename it Bìzhōu.
Therefore, in the second year of Tiānyòu, the old name Tángzhōu was still in use,
and it was only in the third year that it was changed to Bì.
In the beginning of Guānghuà,
the name Bìzhōu should not yet have existed.
Now that the text records Bì,
it is an error.
eunuch Liú Jìshù staged a rebellion,
and the Son of Heaven was imprisoned in the Dōnggōng (Eastern Palace).
In the first month of the first year of Tiānfù (901 CE),
Sūn Dézhāo, the Commander of the Imperial Guard, executed Jìshù,
and the Son of Heaven was restored to his position.
Wáng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Liáng (Liáng Wáng).
[He] dispatched Zhāng Cúnjìng to attack Wáng Kē in Hézhōng,
exiting Hánshān,
and capturing the two prefectures of Jìn and Jiàng.
Wáng Kē sought aid from Jìn,
but Jìn could not save him,
so he came and surrendered.
In the third month,
[Wáng] launched a major campaign against Jìn.
Shì Shūcóng exited Tàiháng,
and captured Zé and Lù.
The armies of Gě Cóngzhōu, Zhāng Cúnjìng, Hóu Yán, Zhāng Guīhòu, and the troops from Zhèn and Dìng,
all assembled at Tàiyuán,
besieging it,
but they did not overcome it,
and returned upon encountering rain.
In the fifth month,
the Son of Heaven appointed Wáng concurrently as the Magistrate of Hézhōng (Hézhōng Yǐn) and Jiedushi of Hùguó Army (Hùguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
In the sixth month,
Jìn captured Cí and Xí.
Since the execution of Liú Jìshù and his cohorts,
Chancellor Cuī Yìn, outwardly allied with Liáng,
wished to borrow Liáng's forces to execute all the eunuchs.
However, Lǐ Màozhēn of Fèngxiáng and Wáng Xíngyú of Bīnníng, among others, all dispatched their sons and younger brothers with elite troops to guard the Son of Heaven overnight,
and the eunuchs Hán Quánhuì and others relied on this for support.
When the Son of Heaven discussed matters with Yìn,
the eunuchs kept an ear open,
and heard much of the discussion.
They then selected beautiful women
and brought them into the palace,
secretly ordering them to investigate the true situation.
After a long time,
they indeed obtained Yìn's memorial detailing the plot to execute the eunuchs.
Quánhuì and the others were terrified,
weeping together day and night,
thinking how to plot against Yìn in order to save themselves.
Yìn knew the plot had leaked,
and the situation was desperate.
He immediately forged an imperial decree
summoning the Liáng army to enter and execute the eunuchs.
In the tenth month,
Wáng took 70,000 troops from Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, Tiānpíng, and Hùguó,
arrived at Hézhōng,
captured Tóngzhōu,
and subsequently attacked Huàzhōu.
Hán Jiàn came out and surrendered.
Quánhuì and the others heard that the Liáng Wáng's troops were about to arrive,
and immediately used the night guard troops of Qí and Bīn to seize the Son of Heaven and flee to Fèngxiáng.
Wáng then submitted a memorial explaining Yìn's intention in summoning him.
The Son of Heaven was angry,
dismissed Yìn from chancellorship,
punished him by appointing him Shàngshū of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū),
and decreed that the Liáng troops should return to their garrisons.
Wáng led his troops away,
attacked Bīnzhōu,
and garrisoned at Sānyuán.
Yáng Chóngběn, the Jiedushi of Bīnzhōu, surrendered with the four prefectures of Bīn, Níng, Qìng, and Yǎn.
Cuī Yìn fled to Huàzhōu.
In the spring of the second year (902 CE),
Wáng withdrew his army to Hézhōng.
Jìn attacked Jìn and Jiàng.
[Wáng] dispatched Zhū Yǒuníng to defeat the Jìn army at Púxiàn,
capturing Fén, Cí, and Xí,
and subsequently besieged Tàiyuán.
[He] did not overcome it and returned,
and Fén, Cí, and Xí returned to Jìn's control.
In the fourth month,
Yǒuníng led troops west,
reaching Xīngpíng,
and fought Lǐ Màozhēn at Wǔgōng,
completely defeating him.
Wáng's troops encroached upon Fèngxiáng,
Màozhēn repeatedly went out to fight,
but was invariably defeated,
and [Wáng] then besieged the city.
In the eleventh month,
Lǐ Zhōuyí of Fūfāng led troops to rescue Fèngxiáng.
Wáng dispatched Kǒng Qíng to raid Fūzhōu,
capturing Zhōuyí's family,
and relocating them to Hézhōng.
Zhōuyí subsequently surrendered.
At this time,
the Qí troops had been repeatedly defeated,
and the siege was prolonged.
Food was exhausted within the city,
and from the Son of Heaven down to the rear palace,
everyone suffered from cold and starvation.
In the first month of the third year (903 CE),
Màozhēn killed Hán Quánhuì and twenty others,
bagged their heads,
showed them to the Liáng army,
and negotiated the release of the Son of Heaven to conclude the matter.
On *jiǎ* day, the Son of Heaven left the city and proceeded to the Liáng camp.
[Wáng] dispatched envoys to swiftly summon Cuī Yìn,
but Yìn pleaded illness and did not come.
Wáng sent a person to mock Yìn, saying:
"I have not yet seen the Son of Heaven
and fear that he may not be genuine.
Please come and identify him for me."
When the Son of Heaven returned to Xīngpíng,
Yìn led the officials to respectfully welcome him.
Wáng personally held the reins for the Son of Heaven,
walking and weeping,
proceeding for more than ten *lǐ*,
before stopping.
Those who witnessed it
all believed him to be loyal.
On *jǐsì* day,
the Son of Heaven arrived from Fèngxiáng,
wore plain robes, wept at the Tàimiào (Grand Ancestral Temple), and only then entered the palace,
and executed over seven hundred eunuchs.
On *jiǎxū* day in the second month,
the Son of Heaven bestowed upon Wáng
the meritorious title, "Meritorious Official Who Turned Heaven, Reconstructed, Exhausted Loyalty, and Maintained Righteousness" (Huítiān Zàizào Jiézhōng Shǒuzhèng Gōngchén).
[He] appointed Huī Wáng Zuò as the Grand Marshal of All Circuits (Zhūdào Bīngmǎ Yuánshuài),
and Wáng as the Vice Marshal (Fù Yuánshuài).
Wáng then left his son Yǒulún as Commander of the Imperial Guard (Hùjià Zhǐhuīshǐ),
to serve as the Son of Heaven's guard,
and led his army eastward to return home.
The Son of Heaven held a farewell feast for him at Yánxǐlóu,
and presented him with five songs of "Willow Branches" (Yángliǔzhī).
Zēng Sānyì revised and determined: Sānyì notes:
Family traditions say that Yǒulún was the son of Wáng's elder brother, Cún.
Later, when the Secretariat (Zhōngshū) submitted a discussion,
they also universally referred to him as the Imperial Nephew (Huángzhí).
Earlier,
when the Liáng army had already gone west,
Wáng Shīfàn of Qīngzhōu dispatched his general Liú Mǒu to raid and occupy Liáng's Yǎnzhōu.
After Wáng had returned to Liáng,
in the fourth month,
[he] went to Yùnzhōu,
and dispatched Zhū Yǒuníng to attack Qīngzhōu.
Shīfàn defeated him at Shílóu,
and Yǒuníng died.
In the ninth month,
Yáng Shīhòu defeated the Qīng people at Línqú,
and captured their Dìzhōu.
Shīfàn surrendered with Qīngzhōu,
and Mǒu also surrendered.
Yǒulún was playing polo (jījū)
when he fell from his horse and died.
Wáng was enraged,
believing that Cuī Yìn had killed him,
and dispatched Zhū Yǒuqīan to kill Yìn in the capital (Jīngshī).
Those who had played polo with Yǒulún
were all killed.
Zēng Sānyì revised and determined: Sānyì notes:
Family traditions say that the one who killed Cuī Yìn was Zhū Yǒumóu,
not Yǒuqīan.
Since the Son of Heaven fled to Huàzhōu,
the Wáng requested to move the capital to Luòyáng.
Although this was not granted,
the Wáng commanded Zhāng Quányì of Hénán to repair the Luòyáng palace in anticipation.
In the first month of Tiānyòu 1 (904 CE),
the Wáng went to Hézhōng.
He sent the commander Kòu Yànqīng to the capital,
requesting the capital be moved to Luòyáng,
and also moving the residents of Cháng'ān eastward.
When the Son of Heaven traveled to Shǎnzhōu,
the Wáng paid court at the temporary residence (Hángzài),
but first proceeded to the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū).
At this time,
the soldiers of the Six Armies and various guards had already scattered and perished.
Those who followed him eastward included
about ten junior eunuchs,
and over two hundred people, including polo attendants and palace garden boys.
When they reached Gǔshuǐ,
the Wáng instructed the physician Xǔ Zhāoyuǎn to accuse them of plotting rebellion,
had them all killed and replaced them,
and then reported the matter.
Because of this,
all those around the Son of Heaven were Liáng men.
On the day Jiǎchén in the fourth month,
the Son of Heaven arrived from the Western Capital (Xīdū).
At this time,
Jìn Wáng Lǐ Kèyòng, Qí Wáng Lǐ Màozhēn, Chǔ Wáng Zhào Kuāngníng, Shǔ Wáng Wáng Jiàn, and Wú Wáng Yáng Xíngmì, hearing that Liáng had moved the Son of Heaven to Luòyáng,
all wanted to raise troops to punish Liáng.
The Wáng was greatly frightened.
In the sixth month,
Yáng Chóngběn again defected to Qí.
The Wáng then took troops to Hézhōng,
claiming to attack Chóngběn,
but sent Zhū Yǒugōng, Shì Shūcóng, and Jiǎng Xuánhuī to carry out the regicide.
Emperor Zhāozōng died.
In the tenth month,
the Wáng paid court at the capital (Jīngshī),
and killed Zhū Yǒugōng and Shì Shūcóng.
In the eleventh month,
he attacked Huáinán.
He captured Guāngzhōu,
attacked Shòuzhōu,
but did not conquer it and returned.
In the second month of the second year (905 CE),
he sent Jiǎng Xuánhuī to kill Dè Wáng Yù and eight other princes (nine princes in total) at Jiǔqǔ Chí.
In the sixth month,
he killed Sīkōng Péi Zhì and over one hundred other people.
In the seventh month,
the Son of Heaven sent an envoy,
bestowing upon the Wáng
the "Monument Recording Merits of Welcoming the Imperial Carriage."
Zēng Sānyì revised and determined: Sānyì observes,
the Basic Annals of Kèyòng and the Biography of Màozhēn,
and the Hereditary Houses of Jiàn and Xíngmì,
all record the titles they were granted during Táng.
Only Kuāngníng does not have his Táng title recorded;
this is a textual omission.
The Wáng wished to replace Táng,
and sent people to instruct the various garrisons.
Zhào Kuāngníng of Xiāngzhōu deemed it unacceptable.
[The Wáng] sent Yáng Shīhòu to attack him,
capturing seven prefectures: Táng, Dèng, Fù, Yǐng, Suí, Jūn, and Fáng.
The Wáng went to Xiāngzhōu,
encamping north of the Hàn River.
In the ninth month,
Shīhòu defeated Xiāngzhōu,
and Kuāngníng fled to Huáinán.
Shīhòu captured Jīngnán,
and Zhào Kuāngmíng, the Military Governor of Jīngnán, fled to Shǔ.
[The army] then marched out from Guāngzhōu,
to attack Shòuzhōu,
but failed.
The Son of Heaven decided by divination to perform the suburban sacrifice to Heaven in the south.
The Wáng was enraged,
believing that Jiǎng Xuánhuī and others wished to pray to Heaven to prolong the life of Táng.
The Son of Heaven, frightened,
changed the divination for the suburban sacrifice.
On the day Xīnsì in the eleventh month,
the Son of Heaven enfeoffed the Wáng as Wèi Wáng and Xiàngguó (Chancellor),
overseeing all government affairs.

Twenty-one armies—Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, Tiānpíng, Hùguó, Tiānxíong, Wǔshùn, Yòuguó, Héyáng, Yìwǔ, Zhāoyì, Wǔníng, Bǎoyì, Zhōngyì, Wǔzhāo, Wǔdìng, Tàiníng, Pínglú, Kuāngguó, Zhènguó, Jīngnán, and Zhōngwǔ—were designated as the State of Wèi,
and he was granted the Nine Distinguished Gifts (Jiǔ Xī).
The Wáng was angry
and refused to accept.
In the twelfth month,
the Son of Heaven appointed the Wáng as Commander-in-Chief of All Armed Forces in the Realm.
The Wáng grew even angrier.
He sent men to accuse the Commissioner of Military Affairs Jiǎng Xuánhuī of having an illicit relationship with Empress Dowager Hé Tàihòu,
killed Xuánhuī and burned his body,
and then assassinated the Empress Dowager in Jīshàn Gōng.
He also killed the Chancellor Liǔ Càn,
and the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Zhāng Yánfàn was torn apart by chariots as a public warning.
The Son of Heaven issued an edict suspending the suburban sacrifice due to the Empress Dowager's death.
In the spring of the third year (906 CE),
Luó Shàowēi of Wèizhōu planned to kill his Yájūn troops,
and came to borrow troops [from the Wáng] in case of disturbances.
The Wáng dispatched troops northward to attack Liú Rén'gōng's Cāngzhōu,
but before the troops passed Wèi, Shàowēi had already killed the Yájūn.
Those of his soldiers who were outside all rebelled,
occupying Bèi, Wèi, Chán, and Bó prefectures.
The Wáng used his troops to kill all of them.
He then attacked Cāngzhōu,
encamping at Chánglú.
Liú Rén'gōng sought aid from Jìn.
The Jìn people captured Lùzhōu,
so the Wáng withdrew his army.
Basic Annals of Liáng, Volume Two
In the spring, the first month, on the day Rén'yín, of Kāipíng 1 (907 CE),
the Son of Heaven sent the Grandee Secretary Xuē Yíjǔ to console the army.
The Chancellor Zhāng Wénwèi led the various officials to encourage the Wáng to ascend the throne.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Rénxū,
[The Wáng] changed his given name to Huǎng.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor ascended the throne.
On the day Wùchén,
there was a great amnesty,
the era name was changed,
and the state was titled Liáng.
The former Lord of Táng was enfeoffed as Jìyīn Wáng.
Biànzhōu was elevated to Kāifēng Fǔ,
established as the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū).
The former Táng Eastern Capital was made the Western Capital (Xīdū).
Jīngzhào Fǔ was abolished and became Yōngzhōu.
The residents of the Eastern Capital were granted a feast day.
Ābǎojī of Qìdān sent Páo Hùméilǎo to come.
Since the accession to the throne,
major events are recorded;
changes to ancient institutions are recorded;
extraordinary occurrences are recorded;
those that convey meaning are recorded;
those that have later implications are recorded.
If not among these five,
they are omitted.
Amnesty documents usually state "Great Amnesty Under Heaven."
This record uses the character "great" (dà),
showing the intention to extend its reach widely,
but does not say "Under Heaven,"
indicating that in reality, some areas were not reached.
Calling the Son of Heaven the Lord of Táng
records the original wording as such.
The abolishing and establishment of prefectures and counties,
can be seen in the Records of Geography (Zhífāng Kǎo);
only those related to the capital are recorded here.
When barbarians (Yídí) came,
we do not use the word "pay tribute" (cháo),
so as not to demand their rituals;
we do not use the word "offer tribute" (gòng),
so as not to value their goods.
Therefore, the record simply says "came" (lái).
During the chaotic era of the Five Dynasties,
recording their repeated arrivals
shows that the arrival or non-arrival of the Yídí
is not determined by whether the era is peaceful or chaotic.
And the repeated arrivals during a chaotic era
are not worth valuing.
In the fifth month, on Dīngchǒu (the first day of the month),

the Táng Chancellors Zhāng Wénwèi and Yáng Shè were appointed Vice Ministers of the Chancellery (Ménxià Shìláng), and the Grandee Secretary Xuē Yíjǔ was appointed Vice Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng): all holding the title Concurrent Manager of Affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
On the day Wùyín,
Bóhǎi and Qìdān sent envoys to come.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
his elder brother Quányù was made Wáng of Guǎng,
his son Yǒuwén was Wáng of Bó,
Yǒuguī was Wáng of Yǐng,
Yǒuzhāng was Wáng of Fú,
Yǒuzhēn was Wáng of Jūn,
Yǒuhuī was Wáng of Jiàn,
his nephew Yǒuliàng was Wáng of Héng,
Yǒunéng was Wáng of Huì,
and Yǒuhuì was Wáng of Shào.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Yuàn) was renamed the Bureau of Venerated Governance (Chóngzhèng Yuàn),
and the Minister of the Court of the Treasury Jìng Xiáng was made its commissioner (Shǐ).
In this month,
Lǐ Sī'ān, Commander-in-Chief of the Lùzhōu Field Headquarters (Xíngyíng), battled the Jìn people,
and suffered a defeat.
The names and titles of the rulers and officials of the Yídí
are sometimes recorded and sometimes not;
completeness is not necessary.
Sometimes this depends on the level of detail in their own former histories.
We merely record their arrival to convey the meaning.
Yǒuwén was not a son but is recorded as a son;
the explanation is found in the Biography of Family Members (Jiārén Zhuàn).
If we are defeated, we use the term bàijī;
if they are defeated, we use the term bàizhī.
This is appropriate usage.
Since the Field Headquarters (Xíngyíng) has already been mentioned,
the place of battle is not stated.
In the sixth month, on the day Jiǎyín,
Hán Jiàn, Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú Army, was appointed provisional Minister of Education (Shǒu Sītú),
and Concurrent Manager of Affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the day Jǐhài,
he posthumously honored his ancestors and grandfathers as Huángdì,
and his grandmothers as Hòuhòu: His Imperial Great-Great-Grandfather Àn was given the posthumous title Xuānyuán,
his temple name Sùzǔ,
and his Great-Great-Grandmother, née Fàn, was given the posthumous title Xuānxī;
his Great-Grandfather Mào-lín was given the posthumous title Guāngxiàn,
his temple name Jìngzǔ,
and his Great-Grandmother, née Yáng, was given the posthumous title Guāngxiào;
his Grandfather Xìn was given the posthumous title Zhāowǔ,
his temple name Xiànzǔ,
and his Grandmother, née Liú, was given the posthumous title Zhāo-yì;
his Father Chéng was given the posthumous title Wénmù,
his temple name Lièzǔ,
and his Mother, née Wáng, was given the posthumous title Wénhuì.
In the eighth month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
in Tóngzhōu, a noxious insect was killed and appeared.
The Huánghé River in Xízhōu became clear.
In this writing,
the mention of [these things] shows they were not treated as auspicious omens.
In the ninth month,
horses were registered.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day Jǐwèi,
military exercises were conducted at Fántái.
In the eleventh month, on the day Rén-yín,
an amnesty was granted to fugitives who had deserted the army and to convicts serving the tattooing and penal servitude sentence.
In a generation fond of killing,
a small amnesty must be recorded,
showing that he also had the intention to love the people.
In the second year, on the day Dīngyǒu of the first month of spring,
Bóhǎi sent envoys to come.
On the day Jǐhài,
divination was performed for the suburban sacrifice at the Western Capital.
Jìnyīn Wáng was assassinated.
Assassination (shì)
is the greatest wickedness of a minister or son;
recording Jìnyīn Wáng
follows the reality of the situation;
recording the assassination (shì)
corrects the name of Liáng's crime.
In the second month, on the day Xīnwèi,
Ābǎojī of Qìdān sent envoys to come.
In the third month, on the first day Rén-shēn,
he went to the Western Capital.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
he went to Huáizhōu.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
he went to Zézhōu.
On the day Wùyín,
Lǐ Sōng, Minister of the Court of Dependencies (Hónglú Qīng), was enfeoffed as Lái Guó Gōng,
to serve as a successor to the Two Kings.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Liú Zhījùn, Military Governor of the Kuāngguó Army, was made Commander of the Lùzhōu Operational Camp (Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ).
On the day Guǐsì,
the location for the suburban sacrifice was changed by divination.
Zhāng Wénwèi passed away.
Xìng (to be present)
means he had already arrived.
Rú (to go to)
is the term for travelling but not yet arriving.
Recording rú
means he was on the road.
If there was an event,
it could be recorded.
During the chaotic Five Dynasties period,
there was never a day without war,
which cannot all be recorded.
Therefore, battles without victory or defeat,
and sieges without capture or loss,
are not recorded.
The appointment of a great general or the Emperor's journey to a place
is by itself a major event.
This journey to Huái and Zé
was because the army was attacking Lùzhōu.
Liáng once changed
Wù
to
Wǔ,
but the old histories completely restored it to
Wù.
In the fourth month of summer, on the day Guǐmǎo,
Yáng Shè was dismissed.
Yú Jīng, Vice Minister of Personnel, was made Vice Minister of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng);
Zhāng Cè, Hanlin Academician Compiler-in-Chief and Vice Minister of Rites, was made Vice Minister of Punishments: both serving concurrently as Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
On the day Rénzǐ,
he arrived at Zézhōu.
In the fifth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
Kāng Huái-yīng, Deputy Commander of the Lùzhōu Operational Camp, fought the Jìn forces at Jiāchéng,
and was defeated.
On the day Wùxū,
the Three Temples of Táng were established.
Qìdān sent envoys to come.
Building a wall to besiege Lù,
and fighting inside the city,
is why the location is recorded.
In the sixth month, on the day Rén-yín,
Liú Zhījùn, Military Governor of the Zhōngwǔ Army, was made Commander of the Western Route Operational Camp (Xīlù Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ),
to attack Qí.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Wáng Shīfàn, General-in-Chief of the Right Army of the Imperial Insignia (Yòujīnwèi Shàngjiāngjūn), was killed,
and his clan was exterminated.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Liú Zhījùn fought the Qí forces at Mògǔ,
and defeated them.
There are four terms for military operations: two sides attacking each other is called gōng (attack);
a large force acting against a smaller one is called fá (punitive expedition);
acting against the guilty is called tǎo (suppression);
the Son of Heaven going himself is called zhēng (campaign).
The text is structured according to the event,
and must therefore differ;
there is no implied praise or blame.
When they ought to be killed, it is written as fúzhū (executed);
when they ought not to be killed,
it is recorded using language indicating mutual killing.
In the ninth month of autumn, on the day Dīngchǒu,
he went to Shǎnzhōu.
Bó Wáng Zhū Yǒuwén was left to guard the Eastern Capital.
This was because the Jìn forces were attacking Jìn and Jiàng.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day Dīngwèi,
he arrived back from Shǎnzhōu.
In the eleventh month, on the day Guǐsì,
Zhāng Cè was dismissed,
and Yáng Shè, Left Grandee Secretary, served concurrently as Grand Chancellor.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jǐhài,
the Duke of Jiè was appointed as one of the Three Revered Vassals (Sān Kè),
and the Dukes of Xié and Lái were appointed as successors to the Two Kings.
In the third year, on the day Jiǎxū of the first month of spring,
he went to the Western Capital.
The custom of lighting lanterns to pray for blessings was resumed.
On the day Gēngyín,
a sacrifice was offered at the Supreme Ancestral Temple.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
rites were performed at the Southern Suburb,
and a great amnesty was proclaimed.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the officials presented the honorable title Ruìwén Shèngwǔ Guǎngxiào Huángdì.
Lighting lanterns
was a custom passed down through society,
from the Son of Heaven down to the common people;
the whole realm shared this extravagance and enjoyment,
and it was a major factor in the collapse of societal morality.
Therefore, the meaning of the imperial edict is recorded,
so that its fault can be known.
Sacrificing to Heaven at the Southern Suburb is recorded as 'rites were performed' (yǒu shì),
recording the language of the time.
In the second month, on the day Rénxū,
military exercises were conducted at the Western Apricot Garden.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Gāo Wànxīng of Yánzhōu rebelled against Qí and came to surrender.
During the chaos at the end of Táng,
the strong annexed the weak,
and people sometimes left one side for another,
which was not constant [behavior]
and hard to immediately judge harshly.
The fact that it is now recorded as 'rebelled' (pàn)
marks the beginning of correcting their established status.
In the third month, on the day Xīnwèi,
Dà Yīnxuǎn, King of Bóhǎi, sent envoys to come.
On the day Jiǎxū,
he went to Hézhōng.
Yáng Shīhòu, Military Governor of the Shānnán Dōngdào circuit, was made Commander of the Four Routes Operational Camp at Lùzhōu.
Liú Zhījùn captured Dānzhōu.
This was because Gāo Wànxīng had surrendered,
and Liú Zhījùn's forces were attacking Fū and Yán.
In the fourth month of summer, on the day Bǐngwǔ,
Zhījùn conquered the three prefectures of Yán, Fū, and Fāng.
Something easy to obtain is recorded as qǔ (capture),
something difficult to obtain is recorded as kè (conquer);
this is appropriate according to the literary principle.
In the fifth month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
he arrived back from Hézhōng,
and killed Wáng Chóngshī, Military Governor of the Yòuguó Army.
In the sixth month, on the day Gēngxū,
Liú Zhījùn arrested Liú Hàn, Military Governor of the Yòuguó Army,
rebelled, and defected to Qí.
On the day Xīnhài,
he went to Shǎnzhōu.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Jì Wáng Zhū Yǒuqīan was made Commander of the Eastern Route Operational Camp at Tóngzhōu.
Liú Zhījùn fled to Qí.
The Dānzhōu army mutinied,
expelling its Prefect Sòng Zhīhuǐ.
Returning oneself is called jiàng (surrender),
returning land is called fù (defect);
this is also appropriate according to the literary principle.
Zhījùn was the Military Governor of the Zhōngwǔ Army.
When he defected to Qí from Tóngzhōu,
it is simply recorded here that Zhījùn rebelled,
without mentioning the place,
as Zhōngwǔ was already mentioned in the preceding text.
This was because Liú Zhījùn had rebelled.
In autumn, the seventh month,
the troops of Shāngzhōu mutinied,
expelling their Prefect, Lǐ Chóu.
Chóu fled to Qí.
On Yǐchǒu,
Dānzhōu was conquered,
and its chief villain, Wáng Xíngsī, was captured.
On Yǐhài,
arrived from Shǎnzhōu.
On Jiǎshēn,
the troops of Xiāngzhōu mutinied,
killing their Acting Military Governor, Wáng Bān.
Yáng Qián, the Prefect of Fángzhōu, rebelled and defected to Shǔ.
Initially, the identities of the chief villains were unknown,
so it was simply called a troop mutiny.
They were identified after the conquest and investigation.
In the conquest of Dānzhōu,
the name of the principal commander is absent;
Xíngsī held no official title or rank,
nor is the date of his execution recorded.
All these details were lost in the old histories.
When one's wisdom is insufficient to protect oneself,
and one's talent is insufficient to govern the multitude, leading to one's death by murder,
we do not record the death;
instead, we use the phrasing "was killed."
To see death being attained by those who earned it (a noble death),
is a great principle for a scholar,
and is not lightly bestowed upon others.
In the eighth month, on Xīnhài,
death row prisoners were reprieved.
On Xīnyǒu,
Zhāng Jìngfāng, Prefect of Jūnzhōu, conquered Fángzhōu,
and captured Yáng Qián.
In the intercalary month, on Guǐyǒu,
the Qìdān sent envoys to come.
On Jǐmǎo,
the harvest was reviewed at the Western Park.
In the ninth month, on Rén'yín,
Chén Huī, Commander of the Field Army and General-in-Chief of the Left Guard, conquered Xiāngzhōu,
and captured its chief villain, Lǐ Hóng.
On Dīngwèi,
Wáng Tán, Military Governor of Bàoyì Command, was appointed Commander of the Eastern Field Army for Lùzhōu.
On Xīnhài,
Hán Jiàn and Yáng Shè were dismissed.

Zhào Guāngfèng, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery; Dù Xiǎo, Chamberlain of the Hanlin Academy and Vice Minister of Works, was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue: both were given the title Concurrent Manager of Affairs in the Chancellery and the Department of State Affairs.
On Xīnyǒu,
Lǐ Hóng and Yáng Qián were executed.
The order for Huī to suppress the rebellion
was lost and not recorded in the old histories;
it first appears here.
Since the chief villain was identified only after the conquest and investigation,
initially, it was also recorded simply as a troop mutiny.
In winter, the eleventh month, on Jiǎwǔ,
the sun reached its southernmost point (winter solstice),
and thanks were offered at the Southern Suburbs.
On Jǐyǒu,
the search for worthy and virtuous men began.
Kāng Huáiyīng, Military Governor of Zhènguó Command, attacked Qí.
The winter solstice does not necessarily need to be recorded;
it is recorded because thanks were offered on that day.
The offering of thanks primarily uses the solstice date,
thus it is recorded.
We do not say "performed ritual affairs at the Southern Suburbs,"
but follow the original wording.
This is perhaps because it was slightly simpler than the main Southern Suburb ritual.
In the twelfth month,
Huáiyīng conquered the three prefectures of Níngzhōu, Qìngzhōu, and Yǎnzhōu.
When Láu Zhījùn battled at Shēngpíng,
they were defeated.
In the fourth year, spring, the first month, on Rénchén (the first day of the month),
music was used for the first time.
On Dīngwèi,
military exercises were held at Yúlín.
Since the chaos at the end of the Táng dynasty,
rituals and music had been lost;
music was used for the first time now,
thus it is recorded.
In the second month, on Jǐchǒu,
the harvest was reviewed at Gǔshuǐ.
In autumn, the eighth month, on Bǐngyín,
went to Shǎnzhōu.
Zhāng Zōngshì, Magistrate of Hénán, remained to guard the Western Capital.
On Xīnwèi,
Yáng Shīhòu, Military Governor of Hùguó Command, was appointed Commander of the Western Route Field Army to attack Qí.
This was because the people of Qí and the people of Jìn were attacking Xiàzhōu.
In the ninth month, on Jǐchǒu,
arrived from Shǎnzhōu.
On Xīnhài,
the search for worthy and virtuous men began.
In winter, the eleventh month, on Jǐchǒu,
Wáng Jǐngrén, Military Governor of Níngguó Command, was appointed Commander of the Northern Field Army to attack Zhào.
Wáng Róng, Prince of Zhào, and Wáng Chǔzhí, Prince of Běipíng, rebelled and defected to Jìn.
The people of Jìn aided Zhào.
In the twelfth month, on Guǐyǒu,
statutes, ordinances, and precedents were promulgated.
In the first year of Qiānhuà, spring, the first month, on Dīnghài,
Wáng Jǐngrén battled the people of Jìn at Bǎixiāng,
and was defeated.
On Gēngyín,
prisoners sentenced to banishment or lesser punishments were pardoned,
and dangerous speech and righteous counsel were sought.
On Guǐsì,
Yáng Shīhòu, Military Governor of Tiānxíong Command, was appointed Commander of the Northern Field Army.
In summer, the fourth month, on Rénshēn,
Ābǎojī of the Qìdān sent envoys to come.
In the fifth month, on Jiǎshēn (the first day of the month),
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the reign title was changed.
On Guǐsì,
visited Zhāng Zōngshì’s residence.
In autumn, the eighth month, on Wùchén,
the harvest was reviewed at Yúlín.
Bóhǎi sent envoys to come.
On Wùyín,
a grand review was held at Xīng'ān Ball Field.
In the ninth month, on Xīnsì (the first day of the month),
attended the Wénmíng Hall,
and entered the Inner Chamber.
On Gēngzǐ,
went to Wèizhōu.
Zhāng Zōngshì remained to guard the Western Capital.
Attending the Hall and then saying "entered the Inner Chamber"
records the original wording.
It is recorded to show the loss of ritual propriety.
The event is found in the biography of Lǐ Qí.
This ritual,
was performed repeatedly afterward,
but none are recorded,
recording it once is sufficient to show its impropriety.
This was because the people of Jìn were attacking Wèi.
In winter, the tenth month, on Bǐngzǐ,
a grand review was held in the eastern suburbs of Wèi.
In the eleventh month,
Gāo Wànxīng captured Yánzhōu.
On Rénchén,
arrived from Wèizhōu.
On Yǐwèi,
the Huíghé and Tǔbō sent envoys to come.
In the second year, spring, the second month, on Dīngsì,
Lú Pín, Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, was sent as envoy to Shǔ.
On Jiǎzǐ,
went again to Wèizhōu.
Zhāng Zōngshì remained to guard the Western Capital.
Upon reaching Báimǎ,
Sūn Zhì, Permanent Attendant on the Left, Zhāng Yǎn, Grand Master of Remonstrance on the Right, and Zhāng Jùn, Minister of the Board of War, were killed.
On Wùyín,
went to Bèizhōu.
This was also because the people of Jìn and Zhènzhōu and Dìngzhōu were attacking Xiāngzhōu and Wèizhōu.
In the third month, on Bǐngxū,
Zǎojùn was massacred.
On Dīngwèi,
returned again to Wèizhōu.
The writing of
"massacred" (Tú),
marks the severity of the brutality.
In summer, the fourth month, on Jǐsì,
arrived from Wèizhōu.
On Wùyín,
went to the Western Capital.
The subsequent entry
"went to the Western Capital" (Rú Xīdū),
allows us to know that he arrived here (earlier) at the Eastern Capital.
In the fifth month, on Dīnghài,
a benevolent decree reprieved prisoners sentenced to death or lesser punishments.
Corvée laborers were dismissed,
and the slaughter of animals and capture of living creatures were forbidden.
Bóhǎi sent envoys to come.
In this month,
Xuē Yíjǔ died.
A "benevolent decree" (Déyīn)
is a minor amnesty.
We follow its original name
to establish the facts.
In the sixth month,
the illness was critical,
and Yǐng Wang Yǒu-guī rebelled.
On *wù-yín*,
the Emperor collapsed (died).
A rebel (*pàn* 叛)
is one who turns their back on this and attaches to that,
like a retainer serving another person.
Revolt (*fǎn* 反)
is plotting against the superior from below,
the greatest of heinous crimes and perversities.
The reason the day and month are not recorded
is that although there is no fixed principle for this omission,
there are events for which the exact day cannot be determined.
A revolt is not the work of a single morning or evening;
one cannot determine its exact day,
thus, the day is omitted for all who revolt.
He was sixty-one years old.
The place of his collapse is not recorded
to distinguish it from those who met their proper end.
In the eleventh month of Qiánhuà 2nd year (912),
Yǒu-guī buried him in Yīquè County, Hénán,
titling it Xuānlíng.
Because he did not meet a natural death,
the burial is not recorded.
Alas!
The world had long hated Liáng!
Since the Later Táng (Hòutáng),
everyone regarded it as illegitimate.
When I came to compile and organize the Five Dynasties (Wǔdài),
I alone did not delegitimize Liáng,
and some commentators criticized me for greatly losing the meaning of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
saying:
“Liáng bore a great evil;
it ought to have been utterly condemned and destroyed,
yet you advanced it instead.
This encourages usurpation,
which is not the aim of the *Chūnqiū*.”
I replied:
“This is precisely the aim of the *Chūnqiū*.
Lǔ Huán-gōng assassinated Yǐn-gōng and established himself;
Xuān-gōng assassinated Zǐ-chì and established himself;
Zhèng Lì-gōng expelled Crown Prince Hū and established himself;
Wèi Gōngsūn Piǎo expelled his ruler Kàn and established himself.
The Sage (Confucius), in the *Chūnqiū*,
never failed to recognize them as rulers.
This is why I do not delegitimize Liáng;
I use the method of the *Chūnqiū*.”
“If so, does the *Chūnqiū* also encourage usurpation?”
I replied:
“It is precisely by recognizing those four men as rulers
that the intention of the *Chūnqiū* is revealed.
The Sage, concerning the *Chūnqiū*,
used profound intention,
thus he could offer sharp encouragement and warnings,
and his words were trustworthy.
Only then are good and evil made clear.
If one wishes to record their crimes for later generations,
it lies in not obscuring the facts.
The fact is that he had once been ruler;
record him as ruler.
The fact is that it was usurpation;
record the usurpation.
By transmitting the facts accurately
and making later generations trust them,
the crimes of those four rulers
cannot be covered up.
If those who become rulers cannot cover up their evil,
then people will know that an evil reputation cannot be escaped,
and thus those who commit evil may perhaps cease their actions.
This is called profound intention resulting in sharp encouragement and warnings,
and trustworthy words resulting in clear good and evil.
Jié and Zhòu,
do not require their royalty to be disparaged
for them to be universally hated throughout the ages.
The reason the *Chūnqiū* does not utterly condemn rulers of great evil
does not harm its aim of praising good and condemning evil.
It is solely by not obscuring the facts to make their crimes known,
and to be trusted by later generations,
that those who are rulers cannot conceal their evil,
thereby halting men from committing evil.
If one can understand this intent of the *Chūnqiū*,
only then will they understand my reason for not delegitimizing Liáng.”
Basic Annals of Liáng, Part III
The Last Emperor (Mòdì)
was Yǒu-zhēn, the third son of Tàizǔ.
He was handsome in appearance,
profound and silent,
and sincerely fond of Confucian scholars.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Jūn Wang
and served as the Commissioner of the Left Tiānxīng Army and Overall Commander of the Metropolitan Cavalry and Infantry.
“Mò” (Last)
is not a posthumous title (*shìhào*),
but follows his actual designation.
In the sixth month of Qiánhuà 2nd year (912),
Tàizǔ was assassinated.
Yǒu-guī established himself
and killed Bó Wang Yǒu-wén,
imputing the crime of regicide to him.
He made the Prince (Yǒu-zhēn) Retainer-in-Chief of the Eastern Capital and Governor of Kāifēng,
Jìng Xiáng Minister of the Secretariat and Concurrent Chancellor (*Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*),
and Lǐ Zhèn, Minister of Revenue, as Commissioner of the Chóngzhèng Academy.
The following year,
Yǒu-guī changed the reign title to Fèng-lì.
In the second month,
the Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant Zhào Yán arrived at the Eastern Capital.
The Prince secretly conferred with him
and dispatched Mǎ Shè-jiāo to Wèizhōu
to meet Yáng Shī-hòu and discuss affairs.
Shī-hòu sent Junior Officer Wáng Shùn-xián to Luòyáng
to inform Yuán Xiàng-xiān, the Commander of the Left Lónghǔ Guard, to suppress the traitor.
At that time, the troops stationed at Huáizhōu Lóngxiāng had mutinied,
and they were currently being pursued and captured.
The Prince then forged an imperial edict from Yǒu-guī,
ordering all troops of the Left and Right Lóngxiāng Guards who were in the Eastern Capital to return to Luòyáng,
and then incited their anger, saying:
“Because the garrison troops in Huáizhōu have rebelled,
the Son of Heaven is recalling you all to bury you completely!”
All the generals wept,
not knowing what to do.
The Prince said:
“The former Emperor worked for the royal enterprise for over thirty years,
yet today he was killed by Yǒu-guī.
How can you expect to escape death!”
He then took out a portrait of Tàizǔ and showed it to the generals, weeping, and saying:
“If you can rush to Luòyáng and capture the rebel,
you will turn misfortune into blessing.”
The soldiers all shouted “Long live the Emperor!”
and asked the Prince to be their master.
The Prince then sent men to urge Xiàng-xiān and the others.
On *gēng-yín*,
Xiàng-xiān and the others used the palace guards to suppress the traitor.
Yǒu-guī died,
and Dù Xiǎo was killed.
Xiàng-xiān sent Zhào Yán to carry the Imperial Seal to the Eastern Capital
and request the Prince to enter Luòyáng.
The Prince replied:
“Yímén
was where Tàizǔ began his royal enterprise.
It faces the north against Bīng and Fén,
extends east to the Huái and the sea.
The nation’s frontier garrisons
are mostly in the east.
Deploying generals and dispatching armies
is more convenient from here.”
That month,
the Emperor was inaugurated in the Eastern Capital,
and the reign title was restored to Qiánhuà 3rd year.
The official titles and rank of Bó Wang Yǒu-wén were restored.
For the major event of the inauguration,
the day is missed and recorded only as
“that month,”
showing the extremity of the turmoil.
“In the Eastern Capital”
concludes the previous text.
On *dīng-mǎo* in the third month,
his name was changed to Huáng.
In the fifth month of summer,
Yáng Shī-hòu took Cāngzhōu.
On *jiǎ-chén* in the ninth month of autumn,
Yáo Jì, Grandee Remonstrant, became Minister of the Secretariat and Concurrent Chancellor.
In the twelfth month of winter,
the Jìn people took Yōuzhōu.
On *dīng-chǒu* in the fourth month of summer of the 4th year,
Yú Jīng was demoted to Vice Administrator of Láizhōu.
Jiǎng Yīn, Military Governor of Wǔníng Circuit, rebelled.
Niú Cún-jié, Military Governor of Tiānpíng Circuit, was dispatched to suppress him.
In the first month of spring of Zhēnmíng 1st year (915),
Cún-jié conquered Xúzhōu.
Jiǎng Yīn immolated himself,
thus it is not recorded that he was executed.
On *dīng-mǎo* in the third month,
Zhào Guāng-fēng was dismissed.
Hè Dé-lún, Military Governor of Pínglú Circuit, was appointed Military Governor of Tiānxíong Circuit.
Xiāng, Chán, and Wèi Prefectures were separated from his territory to form the Zhāodé Circuit,
and Zhāng Jūn, Commissioner of the Palace, was appointed its Military Governor.
On *jǐ-chǒu*,
the Tiānxíong army mutinied,
and Hè Dé-lún rebelled and defected to Jìn.
Lǐ Bǎo-héng of Bīnzhōu rebelled against Qí
and came to defect to us.
Appointments of officials are not recorded [unless]
they are extraordinary or have a specific cause, in which case they are recorded.
This entry (of the appointments) serves as a prelude to the Tiānxíong army mutiny.
The army mutiny is recorded,
but the principal offender is not recorded; instead, Hè Dé-lún’s rebellion is recorded.
This shows profound censure for those of high status.
Dé-lún cannot be designated the principal offender,
but he can be censured for not dying but defecting.
Zhāng Yàn-shí was the principal offender,
but he is barely mentioned.
Yàn
was of low status.
Dé-lún could have been executed but was not,
thus Dé-lún alone is made to bear the responsibility.
Jìn Wáng Lǐ Cūnxù entered
Wèizhōu,
and subsequently took Dézhōu.
In winter, the tenth month, day *Xīnhài*,
Kāng Wáng Yǒuzī rebelled
and was executed.
Those who rebelled are not recorded by date;
those who executed the rebels are recorded by date,
hence the record.
In the eleventh month, day *Yǐchǒu*,
the reign title was changed.
Wēn Zhāotú of Yàozhōu rebelled against Qí
and came to join us.
In this year,
[The Emperor] changed his name to Zhèn.
The old histories lost the specific month and day for this.
Second year, spring, the second month, day *Bǐngshēn*,
Yáng Shè was dismissed.
The third month,
Liú Mó (or Liú Zhuăn), Jìedùshǐ of Zhènnán Jūn, fought the Jìn people at the former Yuánchéng,
suffered a great defeat,
and fled to Huázhōu.
The Jìn people took Wèizhōu and Huìzhōu.
Zuōshēng Dūjiāng Lǐ Bà rebelled
and was executed.
Summer, the sixth month,
Zuōshēng Dūjiāng Zhāng Wēn defected and surrendered to Jìn.
Autumn, the seventh month,
The Jìn people took Xiāngzhōu.
Zhāng Jūn fled to the capital.
Yán Bǎo, Jìedùshǐ of Ānguó Jūn, rebelled and joined Jìn.
The eighth month, day *Dīngyǒu*,
Zhào Guāngféng, retired Tàizǐ Tàibǎo, was appointed Sīkōng concurrently Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
The ninth month,
The Jìn people took Cāngzhōu.
Dài Sīyuǎn, Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi Jūn, fled to the capital.
The Jìn people conquered Bèizhōu.
The defending general Zhāng Yuándé died there.
Recording
"died"
means his death was earned.
Winter, the tenth month, day *Dīngyǒu*,
Zhèng Jué, Zhōngshū Shìláng, was appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Third year, summer, the fourth month, day *Xīnmǎo*,
Liú Qú, Yòuqianniúwèi Dàjiāngjūn, was sent as an envoy to the Qìdān.
Winter, the twelfth month,
Hè Guī, Jìedùshǐ of Xuānyì Jūn, was appointed Commander of the Northern Campaign Army (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ).
Day *Jǐsì*,
[The Emperor] went to the Western Capital (Xīdū) to perform the suburban sacrifice divination.
The Jìn people took Yángliú.
Fourth year, the first month,
[The Emperor] was unable to perform the sacrifice.
Day *Jǐmǎo*,
he arrived back from the Western Capital.
Summer, the fourth month, day *Jǐyǒu*,
Xiāo Qǐng, Shàngshū Lìbù Shìláng, was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Day *Jǐsì*,
Zhào Guāngféng was dismissed.
Winter, the twelfth month, day *Gēngzǐ* (the new moon),
Hè Guī killed his generals Xiè Yànzhāng, Mèng Shěnchéng, and Hóu Wēnyù.
Day *Guǐhài*,
Guī fought the Jìn people at Húliǔ
and suffered a great defeat.
In this year,
Zhāng Shǒujìn, Jìedùshǐ of Tàiníng Jūn, rebelled and joined Jìn.
Liú Mó, Tuánliànshǐ of Bózhōu, was appointed Yǎnzhōu Ānfǔ Zhìzhìshǐ to suppress him.
The old histories did not record this,
and the month and day are lost,
so it is recorded at the end of the year
as preparation for the conquest of Yǎnzhōu the following year.
Fifth year, spring, the first month,
The Jìn army stationed itself at Déshèng.
When troops are used without victory or defeat, it is not recorded,
but this event concerned the gains and losses between Liáng and Jìn,
hence the record.
Autumn, the eighth month, day *Yǐwèi* (the new moon),
Wáng Zàn, Yǐn of Kāifēng, was appointed Commander of the Northern Campaign Army.
Winter, the tenth month,
Liú Mó conquered Yǎnzhōu,
and Zhāng Shǒujìn was executed.
The twelfth month,
The Jìn people took Púyáng.
Huò Yànwēi, Jìedùshǐ of Tiānpíng Jūn, was appointed Commander of the Northern Campaign Army.
Sixth year, summer, the fourth month, day *Jǐhài*,
[The Emperor] pardoned prisoners sentenced to death and below.
Day *Yǐsì*,
Lǐ Qí, Shàngshū Zuǒchéng, was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Zhū Yǒuqīan, Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng, attacked Tóngzhōu,
killed its Jìedùshǐ Chéng Quánhuī,
rebelled, and joined Jìn.
Liú Mó, Jìedùshǐ of Tàiníng Jūn, was ordered to suppress him.
Autumn, the seventh month,
The rebel sorcerer Wú Yǐ of Chénzhōu proclaimed himself Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
The ninth month, day *Gēngyín*,
Láng Gōngyuǎn, a Gòngfèng Officer, was appointed Envoy for Friendly Relations with the Qìdān.
Winter, the tenth month,
Wú Yǐ was executed.
Lóngdé first year, spring,
Zhāng Wénlǐ, a general of Zhào, killed his lord Róng and came requesting aid (from Liáng),
but this was refused.
Wénlǐ was initially Róng’s adopted son,
named Wáng Démíng.
Recording him here as Zhāng Wénlǐ
follows the old histories.
The third month, day *Dīnghài* (the new moon),
the private ordination of Buddhist monks and nuns was prohibited.
Huì Wáng Yǒunéng, Prefect of Chénzhōu, rebelled.
Summer, the fifth month, day *Bǐngxū* (the new moon),
an Imperial Edict proclaimed a change of reign title
and pardoned prisoners sentenced to exile and below.
Autumn,
Yǒunéng was pardoned,
and demoted to be the Marquis of Fánglíng.
Dài Sīyuǎn, Jìedùshǐ of Tiānpíng Jūn, was appointed Commander of the Northern Campaign Army.
Winter, the tenth month,
Sīyuǎn fought the Jìn people at Qīchéng
and suffered a great defeat.
Second year, spring, the first month,
Sīyuǎn attacked Wèizhōu
and took Chéng'ān.
Autumn, the eighth month,
Duàn Níng, Bīngmǎ Liúhòu of Huázhōu, attacked Wèizhōu
and captured its Prefect, Lǐ Cúnrú.
Dài Sīyuǎn conquered Qímén, Gòngchéng, and Xīnxiāng.
Third year, spring, the third month,
Lǐ Jìtāo of Lùzhōu rebelled against Jìn
and came to join us.
Summer, intercalary fourth month,
The Táng people took Yùnzhōu.
Jìn had not yet ascended the throne,
but already regarded itself as an enemy state of Liáng.
When they established their title (Tang),
it brought no particular advantage or disadvantage to Liáng,
hence it is not recorded.
The reason the Táng established their title is recorded, and the term
"Táng people"
is used
because it arose directly from the event.
The fifth month, day *Gēngshēn*,
Wáng Yànzhāng, Jìedùshǐ of Xuānyì Jūn, was appointed Commander of the Northern Campaign Army,
and he took the southern city of Déshèng.
Autumn, the eighth month,
Duàn Níng was appointed Commander of the Northern Campaign Army.
The vanguard general Kāng Yánxiào rebelled and surrendered to Táng.
Winter, the tenth month, day *Jiǎxū*,
Wáng Yànzhāng, Jìedùshǐ of Xuānyì Jūn, fought the Táng people at Zhōngdū,
suffered a great defeat,
and died there.
The Táng people took Cáozhōu.
A thief stole the Imperial Seal (Chuánguó Bǎo) and fled to Táng.
Day *Wùyín*,
The Emperor died.
Liáng perished.
Generally, official titles are not repeated,
but recording the title here
is to prevent the misunderstanding that Yànzhāng was already dismissed as Commander of the Northern Campaign Army when he fought Táng.
In fact, he was dismissed as Commander but led troops to battle as a general.
[The Emperor] was thirty-six years old.
The record states
"Liáng perished,"
to show how quickly Táng Zhuāngzōng established himself.
In the fourth month,
Zhuāngzōng was established,
proclaiming Táng,
and in the tenth month,
Liáng finally perished,
showing that Táng established itself without waiting to destroy Liáng.
Basic Annals of Táng, IV
Zhuāngzōng Guāngshèng Shénmǐn Xiàohuángdì,
his ancestors were originally titled Zhūyé,
likely descending from the Western Tujue (Tūjué).
Later generations
separately titled themselves Shātuó,
and used Zhūyé as their surname.
During the time of Táng Dézōng,
there was Zhūyé Jìnzhōng,
who lived in Jīnmǎnzhōu in Běitíng.
During the Zhēnyuán period,
the Zànpǔ of Tǔbō (Tibetans) attacked and captured Běitíng,
relocating Jìnzhōng to Gānzhōu and enslaving him.
Afterwards, the Zànpǔ was defeated by the Huíhú (Uighurs).
Jìnzhōng and his son Zhíyí fled eastward.
The Zànpǔ grew angry
and pursued them,
catching them at Shíménguān.
Jìnzhōng died in battle,
and Zhíyí alone fled back to Táng,
where he was settled in Yánzhōu
and placed under the command of Fàn Xīcháo, Jìedùshǐ of Héxī.
When Xīcháo moved his garrison to Tàiyuán,
Zhíyí followed him
and was settled in Xīnchéng in Dìngxiāng Shénwǔchuān.
His tribe consisted of ten thousand cavalrymen,
all fierce, brave, and skilled at mounted archery.
They were called
the "Shātuó Army."
Zhí Yí died.
His son was named Chìxīn.
In the tenth year of Xiántōng
of Yìzōng, the Grand General of the Shéncè Army, Kāng Chéngxùn, commanded eighteen generals to attack Páng Xūn in Xúzhōu,
appointing Zhūxié Chìxīn as the Commander of the Shātuó Three Tribes for the Tàiyuán Temporary Headquarters Pacification Campaign.
For his service in defeating Xūn,
he was appointed Grand Protector-General of the Chányú and Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhènwǔ Army,
and was granted the name Lǐ Guóchāng,
thereby being registered among the Han lineage.
The Shātuó had always been strong,
and Guóchāng, relying on his merits, became increasingly arrogant and lawless.
Yìzōng worried about this.
In the thirteenth year,
Guóchāng was transferred to be the Prefect of Yúnzhōu and Defense Commissioner of the Dàtóng Army.
Guóchāng claimed illness and refused the order.
Guóchāng’s son, Kèyòng,
was especially skilled in archery on horseback,
able to shoot two wild ducks in flight,
and served as the Garrison Commander of Yúnzhōu.
Since Guóchāng had already refused the order,
Kèyòng then killed Duàn Wénchǔ, the Defense Commissioner of the Dàtóng Army,
occupied Yúnzhōu,
and proclaimed himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
The Táng appointed Lú Jiǎnfāng, the Minister of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Qīng), as the Military Governor of Zhènwǔ,
and mustered troops from Yōu and Bīng to attack them.
When Jiǎnfāng traveled as far as Lánzhōu,
his army scattered.
Consequently, the Shātuó invaded and plundered Dàiběi, becoming a border threat.
The following year,
Xīzōng ascended the throne.
Believing that the former Military Governor of Tàiyuán, Lǐ Yè, had shown kindness to the Shātuó,
but Yè was already deceased,
he appointed Yè’s son Jūn as Military Governor of Língwǔ and Envoy to Comfort and Recruit the Shātuó Six Circuits and Three Tribes,
in order to bring them back.
Kèyòng was appointed Defense Commissioner of the Dàtóng Army.
The names of the Six Circuits and Three Tribes
are nowhere to be seen;
according to the Táng History, the appointment of the envoy included this phrasing.
After residing there for a long time,
Guóchāng went out to attack the Dǎngxiàng.
The Tǔhún Hèlián Duó attacked and destroyed Zhènwǔ.
When Kèyòng heard this,
he went from Yúnzhōu to welcome Guóchāng,
but the people of Yúnzhōu also closed the gates and resisted him.
Guóchāng and his son had nowhere to go,
so they plundered the region between Wèizhōu and Shuòzhōu,
gained three thousand soldiers,
and Guóchāng entered and secured Wèizhōu.
Kèyòng returned and occupied Xīnchéng.
Xīzōng then appointed Duó as Commander of the Dàtóng Army,
and made Lǐ Jūn the Pacification Commissioner of Dàiběi,
in order to attack the Shātuó.
In the fifth year of Qiánfú,
the Shātuó defeated the Zhēlǔ Army,
and then defeated the Kělán Army.
The Táng forces suffered numerous defeats,
and the Shātuó thus grew stronger.
They occupied Wèi and Shuò in the north,
and invaded Xīn, Dài, Lán, and Shí in the south,
reaching as far as Tàigǔ.
In the first year of Guǎngmíng,
Pacification Commissioner Lǐ Zhuó joined forces with Lǐ Kějǔ of Yōuzhōu and Hèlián Duó of Yúnzhōu to attack the Shātuó.
Kèyòng and Kějǔ faced off at the Xióngwǔ Army barracks.
His uncle Yǒujīn surrendered Wèi and Shuò Circuits to Zhuó.
Kèyòng, hearing this,
hastily returned.
Kějǔ pursued him to Yào'ér Lǐng
and heavily defeated him.
Zhuó's army attacked simultaneously,
defeating him again at Wèizhōu.
The Shātuó suffered a massive rout,
and Kèyòng and his father fled into Dádá.
Kèyòng was heroic and brave in his youth.
In the army, he was called
"Lǐ Bù'ér."
He was blind in one eye,
and when he achieved prominence,
he was also called
"The One-Eyed Dragon."
His prestige and fame covered Dàiběi.
While he was in Dádá,
after a long time,
he was despondent and frustrated.
He also constantly feared that they were plotting against him,
so he would often join the local magnates in shooting and hunting.
Sometimes he would hang a needle on a tree,
or set up a horsewhip,
and when he shot at it from a hundred paces, he always hit the target.
All the magnates submitted to him, considering him a god.
Huáng Cháo had already captured the capital.
In the first year of Zhōnghé,
Chén Jǐngsī, the Commander of the Dàiběi Rising Army, mobilized those Shātuó who had previously surrendered,
along with ten thousand Tǔhún and Ānqìng troops, to rush to the capital.
Upon reaching Jiàngzhōu,
the Shātuó army mutinied,
plundered heavily, and returned.
Jǐngsī recognized that the Shātuó could not be commanded without Kèyòng,
so he used an imperial decree to summon Kèyòng from Dádá,
and by imperial mandate appointed him Prefect of Dàizhōu and Military Governor of the Temporary Headquarters North of Yànmén.
Kèyòng led ten thousand barbarian and Han soldiers out through Shílǐng Guān,
passed Tàiyuán,
and requested the disbursement of military funds.
Military Governor Zhèng Cóngdǎng gave him one thousand strings of cash and one thousand *shi* of rice.
Kèyòng was enraged,
let his soldiers loose to plunder heavily, and returned.
In the eleventh month of the second year,
Jǐngsī and Kèyòng once again rushed to the capital with seventeen thousand infantry and cavalry.
In the first month of the third year,
they emerged at Hézhōng,
and advanced to camp at Qiánkēng.
Huáng Cháo's followers exclaimed in alarm:
"Bù'ér's army has arrived!"
In the second month,
they defeated Huáng Yè, Huáng Cháo's general, at Shídī Gǔ.
In the third month,
they defeated Zhào Zhāng and Shàng Ràng at Liángtián Pō,
leaving corpses strewn for thirty *lǐ*.
At that time,
the troops from all circuits gathered at Cháng'ān
and fought a great battle at Wèiqiáo.
The rebels were defeated and fled back into the city.
Kèyòng pursued them, capitalizing on the victory.
Entering first through Guāngtài Mén,
he fought at Wàngchūn Gōng and Shēngyáng Diàn.
Huáng Cháo was defeated
and fled south out of Lántián Guān.
The capital was pacified,
and Kèyòng's merit was the greatest.
The Son of Heaven appointed Kèyòng Acting Minister of Works (Jiǎnxiào Sīkōng), Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì), and Military Governor of Hédōng,
and made Guóchāng the Military Governor of the Temporary Headquarters North of Yànmén.
In the tenth month,
Guóchāng died.
In the eleventh month,
Kèyòng dispatched his younger brother Kèxiū to attack Mèng Fānglì of Zhāoyì,
capturing the two circuits of Zé and Lù.
Fānglì fled to Shāndōng,
and used the three circuits of Xíng, Míng, and Cí to independently establish the Zhāoyì Army.
Huáng Cháo fled south until he reached Càizhōu,
surrendered to Qín Zōngquán,
and subsequently attacked Chénzhōu.
In the fourth year,
Kèyòng brought fifty thousand troops to rescue Chénzhōu.
He exited Tiānjǐng Guān
and requested passage through Héyáng,
but Zhūgě Shuǎng refused permission,
so he crossed the river from Hézhōng.
In the fourth month,
he defeated Shàng Ràng at Tàikāng,
and then defeated Huáng Yè at Xīhuá.
Huáng Cháo both fled and fought,
reaching Zhōngmóu.
He was nearing the river but had not yet crossed,
when Kèyòng caught up with him.
The rebel masses scattered in panic.
By the time they reached Fēngqiū,
he was defeated again.
Huáng Cháo escaped and fled.
Kèyòng pursued him,
galloping two hundred *lǐ* day and night,
reaching Yuānqú,
but failed to catch him and returned.
During the Táng era, the Zhāoyì Army
spanned Shāndōng and Shānxī, governing five circuits.
By this time, Zé and Lù had fallen to Jìn,
while the Mèng clan occupied Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
Therefore, there were two Zhāoyì regions at that time.
Passing Biànzhōu,
Kèyòng rested his army at Fēngchán Sì.
Zhū Quánzhōng hosted Kèyòng at Shàngyuán Yì.
That night,
after the wine,
Kèyòng lay down intoxicated.
The ambushing troops were launched,
and a fire broke out.
The attendant Guō Jǐngzhū extinguished the candle,
hid Kèyòng beneath the bed,
sobered his face with water, and informed him of the danger.
Coincidentally, heavy rain extinguished the fire.
Kèyòng, with his followers Xuē Tiěshān and Hè Huíhú,
followed the lightning flashes,
rappelled out through the gate of Wèishì, and returned to his army camp.
In the seventh month,
he reached Tàiyuán.
He reported the incident to the capital,
requesting to launch an attack on Biàn,
and dispatched his brother Kèxiū to camp ten thousand troops at Hézhōng to wait.
Xīzōng reconciled the matter.
For his service in defeating Huáng Cháo,
Kèyòng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lǒngxī Commandery.
In the first year of Guāngqǐ,
Wáng Chóngróng of Hézhōng had a falling out with the eunuch Tián Lìngzī.
Chóngróng was transferred to Yǎnzhōu,
and Wáng Chǔcún of Dìngzhōu was made the military commissioner (Jiédù Shǐ) of Hézhōng.
An imperial edict ordered Kèyòng to use troops to escort Chǔcún to his post.
Chóngróng sent someone to deceive Kèyòng, saying:
“The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) decreed that Chóngróng,
upon Kèyòng’s arrival,
should cooperate with Chǔcún to execute him.”
Then he forged an imperial edict and showed it to Kèyòng, saying:
“This is Zhū Quánzhōng’s plot.”
Kèyòng believed it,
and submitted eight memorials requesting permission to attack Zhū Quánzhōng,
but Emperor Xīzōng refused.
Kèyòng was greatly angered.
Kèyòng did not usurp the imperial title,
thus he did not call himself king.
Since Chóngróng refused to move,
Emperor Xīzōng sent Zhū Méi of Bīnzhōu and Lǐ Chāngfú of Fèngxiáng to attack him.
Kèyòng, contrarily, used his troops to aid Chóngróng,
defeating Méi at Shāyuàn,
and subsequently attacking the Capital (Jīngshī),
setting fires and plundering widely.
The Son of Heaven went out to reside at Xīngyuán.
Kèyòng retreated and stationed his forces at Hézhōng.
Zhū Méi also rebelled and pursued the Son of Heaven with troops.
Failing to catch him,
he seized Prince of Xiāng (Xiāng Wáng) Yūn,
forced him to proclaim himself Emperor,
and stationed himself at Fèngxiáng.
Emperor Xīzōng thought that only Kèyòng could defeat Méi but that he could not be commanded.
When Cháng'ān was broken by Huáng Cháo,
Yáng Fùgōng, the Supreme Inspector of the World’s Armies and Horses, was friendly with Kèyòng.
So, he dispatched the Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū) Liú Chóngwàng with an imperial edict to summon Kèyòng,
and also convey Fùgōng’s intention,
to make him advance troops to attack Méi and the others.
Kèyòng pretended to agree but did not act.
The following year,
Mèng Fānglì died,
and his younger brother Mèng Qiān was established.
In the first year of Dàshùn,
Kèyòng attacked and defeated Mèng Qiān,
taking the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
He then dispatched Ān Jīnjùn to attack Hèlián Duó at Yúnzhōu.
Lǐ Kuāngwēi of Yōuzhōu came to rescue Duó,
and they fought at Wèizhōu.
Jīnjùn was utterly defeated.
Thereupon, Kuāngwēi, Duó, and Zhū Quánzhōng all requested permission to use this defeat as an opportunity to attack Kèyòng.
Emperor Zhāozōng considered that Kèyòng’s merit in defeating Huáng Cháo was great,
and that he should not be attacked.
He submitted the matter to the discussion of the four-rank officials of the Censorate and the Ministries.
Most of the discussants said it should not be done.
Only the Chancellor Zhāng Jùn argued that the Shātuó had previously forced Emperor Xīzōng to flee to Xīngyuán,
and that the crime warranted execution,
and thus they should be attacked.
