The Director of Military Affairs Yáng Fùgōng,
who was friendly with Kèyòng,
also strongly remonstrated against it, deeming it impossible.
Emperor Zhāozōng agreed with him,
and issued an edict reassuring Quánzhōng and the others.
Quánzhōng secretly bribed Jùn,
making him hold his position even more firmly.
Emperor Zhāozōng, having no choice,
made Jùn the Commander-in-Chief of the Four-Front Campaign Armies and Horses of Tàiyuán,
with Hán Jiàn as his Deputy.
At this time,
Féng Bà, a general in Lùzhōu, rebelled and defected to Liáng.
Liáng sent Gě Cóngzhōu into Lùzhōu.
The Táng appointed Sūn Kuí, the Governor of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào Yǐn), as the military commissioner of Zhāoyì Jūn.
Kèyòng sent Lǐ Cúnxiào to capture Kuí at Chángzǐ,
and also sent Kāng Jūnlì to take Lùzhōu.
In the eleventh month,
Jùn fought Kèyòng at Yīndì.
Jùn’s army was defeated three times in three battles.
Jùn and Jiàn fled back.
Kèyòng’s troops widely plundered Jìn and Jiàng,
reaching Hézhōng,
leaving the land devastated for a thousand *lǐ*.
Kèyòng submitted a memorial pleading his case,
the language of which was arrogant and disrespectful.
The Son of Heaven accepted the blame himself
and responded with a gracious edict.
In the second month of the second year (891),
Kèyòng was again appointed Military Commissioner of Hédōng and Prince of Lǒngxī,
and was given the added titles of acting Grand Preceptor and concurrent Director of the Secretariat.
In the fourth month,
he attacked Hèlián Duó at Yúnzhōu,
besieging him for over a hundred days,
after which Duó fled to Tǔhún.
In the eighth month,
he held a grand review at Tàiyuán,
went out through Jìn and Jiàng,
plundered Huái and Mèng,
reaching Xíngzhōu,
and then attacked Wáng Róng at Zhènzhōu.
Kèyòng barricaded the west of Chángshān,
and crossed the Hūtuó River with a dozen riders to spy on the enemy.
He encountered heavy rain,
and the water depth reached several feet on level ground.
The people of Zhèn attacked him.
Kèyòng hid in the forest,
and prayed to his horse, saying:
“If my family is destined to hold Tàiyuán for generations, let the horse not neigh.”
The horse happened not to neigh, and he escaped.
The vanguard, Lǐ Cúnxiào, captured Línchéng,
and advanced to attack Yuánshì.
Lǐ Kuāngwēi came to aid Róng,
and Kèyòng returned his army to Xíngzhōu.
In the first year of Jǐngfú,
Wáng Róng attacked Xíngzhōu.
Lǐ Cúnxìn, Lǐ Sìxūn, and others defeated Róng at Yáoshān.
In the second month,
Kèyòng met Wáng Chǔcún to attack Róng,
fighting at Xīnshì,
but they were defeated by Róng.
In the eighth month,
Lǐ Kuāngwēi attacked Yúnzhōu,
in order to divert Kèyòng’s troops.
Kèyòng secretly entered Yúnzhōu,
then turned and came out to attack Kuāngwēi.
Kuāngwēi was defeated and fled.
In the tenth month,
Lǐ Cúnxiào rebelled with Xíngzhōu.
In the second year (893),
Cúnxiào sought aid from Wáng Róng.
Kèyòng led troops out through Jǐngxíng to attack Róng,
and also sent a letter inviting Róng,
while rapidly attacking his Píngshān.
Róng became frightened
and subsequently made peace with Kèyòng,
offering 500,000 bolts of silk
and dispatching troops to aid in the attack on Xíngzhōu.
In the third month of the first year of Qiánníng,
Cúnxiào was captured
and executed.
In the winter,
Kèyòng attacked Yōuzhōu.
Lǐ Kuāngchóu abandoned the city and fled.
He was pursued to Jǐngchéng
and killed.
Liú Réngōng was installed as the caretaker (Liúhòu).
In the second year,
Wáng Chóngyíng of Hézhōng died.
His sons Kē and Gǒng fought over the succession.
Kèyòng requested that Kē be established.
Lǐ Màozhēn of Fèngxiáng, Wáng Xíngyú of Bīnníng, and Hán Jiàn of Huázhōu requested that Gǒng be established.
Emperor Zhāozōng initially found both difficult (to choose),
and so made the Chancellor Cuī Yìn the Military Commissioner of Hézhōng.
Subsequently, however, he permitted Kèyòng to establish Kē.
Màozhēn and the others were enraged,
and the armies of the three commanderies violated the Capital.
Hearing that Kèyòng had also mobilized his troops,
they all withdrew.
In the sixth month,
Kèyòng attacked Jiàngzhōu,
and executed the Prefect Wáng Yáo.
Yáo was
Gǒng’s younger brother,
who had helped Gǒng in the dispute.
In the seventh month,
Kèyòng reached Hézhōng.
Wáng Xíngyuē of Tóngzhōu fled to the Capital,
falsely announcing:
“Ten thousand Shātuó troops have arrived!”
He plotted to escort the Son of Heaven to Bīnzhōu.
Yán Guī, an adopted son of Màozhēn, also plotted to seize and escort him to Fèngxiáng.
The Capital fell into great chaos,
and Emperor Zhāozōng went out to reside at Shímén.
army remained for more than a month without advancing.
Emperor Zhāozōng dispatched Yán Wáng Jièpī and Dān Wáng Yǔn to serve Kèyòng as elder brothers,
and also reported the urgent situation.
In the eighth month,
Kèyòng advanced his army to Wèiqiáo,
and was made Commander-in-Chief of the Four-Sided Campaigning Armies of Bīnníng.
Emperor Zhāozōng returned to the capital (Jīngshī).
In the eleventh month,
Kèyòng attacked and defeated Bīnzhōu.
Wáng Xíngyú fled to Qìngzhōu,
where he was killed.
Kèyòng returned his army to Yúnyáng,
and requested permission to attack Mào Zhēn.
Emperor Zhāozōng consoled and rewarded Kèyòng,
urging him to resolve the enmity with Mào Zhēn in order to relieve the difficulties.
Kèyòng was appointed
"Loyal and Upright Meritorious Official Who Pacified the Troubles" (Zhōngzhèng Píngnàn Gōngchén),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng).
At this time,
the Jìn army was north of the Wèi River (Wèiběi).
They encountered sixty days of continuous rain.
Some advised Kèyòng to enter the court,
but Kèyòng was undecided.
The Grand Deputy Guard Gài Yù said:
"The Son of Heaven has returned from Shímén;
his sleeping mat is not yet secure.
If the Jìn soldiers cross the Wèi River,
how can the populace feel secure again?
It is enough merely to support the Emperor;
why must you necessarily attend the court?"
Kèyòng laughed and said:
"Even Gài Yù does not trust me,
how much less will the rest of the world!"
Thereupon, he withdrew his troops and returned.
In the first month of the third year,
Emperor Zhāozōng again appointed Zhāng Jùn as Chancellor (Xiàng).
Kèyòng said:
"This is a plot by Zhū Quánzhōng."
He then submitted a memorial, saying:
"If Your Majesty appoints Jùn as Chancellor in the morning,
then I will arrive at the palace gate in the evening!"
The capital (Jīngshī) was greatly terrified,
and the order concerning Jùn was immediately stopped.
When Zhū Quánzhōng attacked Yǎnzhōu and Yùnzhōu,
Kèyòng dispatched Lǐ Cúnxìn, borrowing passage through Wèizhōu, to rescue Zhū Xuān and others.
Cúnxìn was stationed at Shēnxian.
The soldiers plundered and invaded the territory of Wèi.
Luó Hóngxìn ambushed and attacked them.
Cúnxìn was defeated and fled to Míngzhōu.
Kèyòng personally led an attack on Wèi,
fighting at Huánshuǐ.
He lost his son Luòluò.
In the sixth month,
he defeated Wèi and captured more than ten towns, including Chéng'ān, Huánshuǐ, and Línzhāng.
In the tenth month,
he again defeated the Wèi forces at Báilóngtán,
and advanced to attack Guānyīnmén.
Quánzhōng's relief force arrived,
whereupon he withdrew.
In the fourth year,
Liú Rén'gōng rebelled against Jìn.
Kèyòng led fifty thousand troops to attack Rén'gōng,
fighting at Ānsài.
Kèyòng suffered a great defeat.
In the first year of Guānghuà,
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched Gě Cóngzhōu to attack and capture Xíngzhōu, Míngzhōu, and Cízhōu.
Kèyòng dispatched Zhōu Déwēi, who marched out from Qīngshānkǒu.
He encountered Cóngzhōu at Zhānggōngqiáo,
and Déwēi was greatly defeated.
In winter,
Xuē Zhìqín, the defending general of Lùzhōu, died.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī occupied Lùzhōu,
rebelling and defecting to Zhū Quánzhōng.
In the second year,
Quánzhōng dispatched Shì Shūcóng to attack and defeat Chéngtiānjūn,
and then defeated Liáozhōu.
They reached Yúcì.
Zhōu Déwēi defeated them at Dòngwō.
In autumn,
Lǐ Sìzhāo recaptured Zézhōu and Lùzhōu.
In the third year,
Sìzhāo defeated the Biàn army at Shāhé,
and recaptured Míngzhōu.
Zhū Quánzhōng personally led forces to besiege it.
Sìzhāo fled,
and upon reaching Qīngshānkǒu,
encountered the Biàn ambush troops.
Sìzhāo was greatly defeated.
In autumn,
Sìzhāo captured Huáizhōu.
That year,
the Biàn forces attacked Zhènzhōu and Dìngzhōu.
Both Zhènzhōu and Dìngzhōu severed ties with Jìn and defected to Zhū Quánzhōng.
In the first year of Tiānfù,
Quánzhōng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Liáng (Liáng Wáng).
The Prince of Liáng attacked and captured Jìnzhōu, Jiàngzhōu, and Hézhōng,
capturing Wáng Kē and taking him back.
Jìn lost three allied prefectures.
They then condescended to send letters and gifts to invite peace with Liáng.
The Prince of Liáng believed that Jìn was weak and could be taken.
He then said:
"Although Jìn requested an alliance,
the language of their letter was disrespectful."
Consequently, he launched a major campaign against Jìn.
In the fourth month,
Shì Shūcóng entered Tiānjǐng.
Zhāng Wénjìng entered Xīnkǒu.
Gě Cóngzhōu entered Tǔmén.
Wáng Chǔzhí entered Fēihú.
Hóu Yán entered Yīndì.
Shūcóng captured Zézhōu and Lùzhōu.
His subordinate general Bái Fèngguó defeated Chéngtiānjūn.
Zhāng È, the defending general of Liáozhōu, and Lǐ Táng, the defending general of Fénzhōu, both welcomed the Liáng army and surrendered.
The people of Jìn were greatly terrified.
Coincidentally, there was heavy and prolonged rainfall.
Many Liáng soldiers fell ill,
and they all withdrew.
In the fifth month,
Jìn recaptured Fénzhōu,
and executed Lǐ Táng.
In the sixth month,
Zhōu Déwēi and Lǐ Sìzhāo captured Cízhōu and Xízhōu.
In the second year,
they advanced to attack Jìnzhōu and Jiàngzhōu,
but suffered a major defeat at Púxiàn.
The Liáng army exploited the victory to defeat Fénzhōu, Cízhōu, and Xízhōu.
They then besieged Tàiyuán.
Kèyòng was greatly afraid.
He plotted to flee to Yúnzhōu,
and also considered fleeing to the Xiōngnú,
but had not decided yet.
The Liáng army suffered a major epidemic,
and withdrew.
Zhōu Déwēi subsequently recaptured Fénzhōu, Cízhōu, and Xízhōu.
In the fourth year,
Liáng moved the Táng capital to Luòyáng,
and changed the reign title to Tiānyòu.
Kèyòng held that it was Liáng who had coerced the Son of Heaven and moved the capital.
Tiānyòu was not a Táng reign title
and should not be used.
He therefore continued to use Tiānfù.
In the fifth year,
he met Qìdān Ābǎojī at Yúnzhōng,
and they swore an oath to be brothers.
In the sixth year,
Liáng attacked Yān's Cāngzhōu.
Liú Rén'gōng, the Prince of Yān, came to beg for troops.
Kèyòng resented Rén'gōng's repeated treachery
and wanted to refuse him.
His son Cúnxù remonstrated, saying:
"This is the time for us to recover our power.
Currently, of all the powerful factions under Heaven,
seventeen or eighteen out of twenty belong to Liáng.
Powerful states like Zhào, Wèi, and Zhōngshān
all obey his orders.
This means that north of the [Yellow] River,
there are none who pose a threat to Liáng,
except for us and Rén'gōng.
If Yān and Jìn combine forces,
it will not be a blessing for Liáng.
A man who seeks to rule the world does not dwell on minor grievances.
Furthermore, while he constantly troubled us, we rush to aid him in his crisis;
we can thus use this virtue to win his loyalty.
This is what is called achieving two gains with one action.
This opportunity must not be missed."
Kèyòng agreed with this view.
He then deployed troops on behalf of Yān and attacked and captured Lùzhōu.
The Liáng siege was thus lifted,
and Lǐ Sìzhāo was made Acting Administrator of Lùzhōu.
In the seventh year,
the Liáng army of one hundred thousand attacked Lùzhōu,
surrounding it with a double wall (jiāchéng).
Zhōu Déwēi was dispatched to relieve Lùzhōu,
and stationed his army at Luànliǔ.
In winter,
Kèyòng fell ill.
That year,
Liáng destroyed Táng.
Kèyòng reverted to calling the year Tiānyòu Fourth Year.
On the *xīnmǎo* day of the first month of the fifth year,
Kèyòng died,
at the age of fifty-three.
His son Cúnxù succeeded him,
and buried Kèyòng at Yànmén.
Alas!
As ages pass, many have lost their tradition,
is this mistake solely that of the historians!
The ancestors of the Lǐ shì,
probably originated from the Xī Tūjué,
originally bearing the name Zhūyé.
In later generations,
they independently adopted the name Shātuó,
and took Zhūyé as their surname,
naming Báyěgǔ as their progenitor.
Their own account says: Shātuó
is the desert of Běitíng.
During the time of Táng Tàizōng,
when the various tribes of the Xī Tūjué were defeated,
he settled the people of Tóngluó and Púgǔ in this desert,
establishing the Shātuó Fǔ,
and making their progenitor Báyěgǔ the Dūdū (Military Governor).
His descendants,
for several generations, all served as the Dūdū of Shātuó,
hence their later generations adopted the name Shātuó.
However, when I examine the historical records,
all these claims are incorrect.
Barbarian tribes (Yídí) do not have surnames;
Zhūyé
was merely the name of a tribal division.
Báyěgǔ was a contemporary of Zhūyé,
not their progenitor,
and during the time of Táng Tàizōng,
there was never a Shātuó Fǔ.
When Táng Tàizōng defeated the Xī Tūjué,
he divided their various tribes
and established thirteen prefectures (zhōu).
He made the Tóngluó the Guīlín Dūdū Fǔ,
the Púgǔ the Jīnwēi Dūdū Fǔ,
and the Báyěgǔ the Yōulíng Dūdū Fǔ.
There was never a Shātuó Fǔ.
At that time,
among the Xī Tūjué were the Tiělè,
Yántuó, and Āshǐnà tribes, which were the largest;
their separate divisions included Tóngluó, Púgǔ, Báyěgǔ, and others, numbering over ten,
which were generally smaller tribes;
there were also the Chǔyuè and Chǔmì tribes,
which were smaller still.
Zhūyé
was merely the designation for a separate division of the Chǔyuè.
In the 22nd year of Tàizōng
the Báyěgǔ had already submitted.
In the following year,
Āshǐnà Hèlǔ rebelled.
By the second year of Gāozōng’s Yǒnghuī era (651 CE),
Zhūyé Gūzhù of the Chǔyuè followed Hèlǔ and fought at Láoshān.
They were defeated by Qìbì Hélì
and subsequently disappeared from history.
One hundred and fifty or sixty years later,
during the time of Xiànzōng,
Zhūyé Jìnzhōng and his son Zhíyí appeared in China
and called themselves Shātuó,
taking Zhūyé as their surname.
Shātuó
was simply the name of a great desert,
located on the south side of Jīnshā Shān
and east of Púlèi Hǎi.
Since the time of the Chǔyuè, tribes had resided in this desert,
and were called Shātuó Tūjué.
But since the Yídí had no written records or traditions,
and the Zhūyé tribe was too insignificant to be recorded,
their later generations consequently lost their own history.
It was not until the grandson of Jìnzhōng that they were first bestowed the surname Lǐ shì.
The Lǐ shì later rose to prominence,
and thus the barbarian people (Yídí) claimed Shātuó was a noble lineage.
Táng Běnjì, Chapter 5
Cúnxù
was the eldest son of Kèyòng.
Initially,
after Kèyòng defeated Mèng Fānglì at Xíngzhōu,
he returned his army to Shàngdǎng
and hosted a feast at Sānchuígǎng.
An actor performed the “Song of a Hundred Years.”
When the song reached the part concerning old age and decay,
the sound was extremely mournful,
and everyone seated became sad and distressed.
At that time, Cúnxù was by his side,
being only five years old.
Kèyòng stroked his beard with emotion,
pointed at him, and laughed, saying:
“I am growing old now.
This is a remarkable child.
In twenty years,
will he be able to fight in my place here!”
When Cúnxù was eleven years old,
he followed Kèyòng to defeat Wáng Xíngyú,
and was sent to present the victory report to the Jīngshī (Capital).
Zhāozōng was struck by his appearance
and bestowed upon him a Xīshī Zhī cup and a jade plate (fěicuì pán),
patting his back and saying:
“This child has a remarkable presence;
he will surely achieve wealth and honor in the future.
Do not forget my house (the Táng dynasty).”
When he grew up,
he excelled at horsemanship and archery,
and his courage surpassed ordinary men.
He studied the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) slightly,
and understood general principles.
He was particularly fond of music, singing, dancing, and theatrical performances (bāiyōu).
In the first month of the fifth year of Tiānyòu (908 CE),
he ascended the position of Prince (wáng) in Tàiyuán.
His uncle Kèníng killed the Commander of the Guards, Lǐ Cúnzhì.
The favored official Shǐ Jìngróng accused Kèníng of plotting rebellion.
In the second month,
he was captured and executed.
Cúnxù then informed Zhōu Déwēi of the funeral of the previous Prince and the calamity involving his uncle.
Déwēi returned his troops from Luànliǔ to Tàiyuán.
The Liáng troops at the fortified encampment (jiāchéng) heard that Jìn was undergoing a great funeral
and that Déwēi’s forces were departing,
and consequently became rather lax.
The Prince (wáng) addressed his generals, saying:
“The Liáng people are taking advantage of our great mourning
and think that since I am young and newly established,
I will be unable to act.
We should seize their moment of complacency and attack them.”
Thereupon, he marched his troops toward Shàngdǎng.
When they reached Sānchuígǎng,
he sighed, saying:
“This is where the former Prince hosted his feast!”
Coincidentally, a great fog caused the day to grow dark.
The troops advanced through the fog,
attacked the fortified encampment,
and destroyed it.
The Liáng army suffered a great defeat,
and the Prince returned victorious to report to the ancestral temple.
In the ninth month,
Shǔ Wáng Wáng Jiàn, Qí Wáng Lǐ Màozhēn, and Yáng Chóngběn attacked Liáng at Dà'ān.
Jìn also dispatched Zhōu Déwēi to attack Jìnzhōu,
defeating the Liáng army at Shénshān.
In the sixth year (909 CE),
Liú Zhījùn defected from Liáng
and came to request aid.
The Prince personally led forces to Yīndì Guān,
and sent Zhōu Déwēi to attack Jìnzhōu,
defeating the Liáng army at Méngkēng.
In the winter of the seventh year (910 CE),
Liáng sent Wáng Jǐngrén to attack Zhào.
Zhào Wáng Wáng Róng came to request aid.
The generals all suspected Wáng Róng of treachery
and advised against sending troops immediately,
but the Prince did not listen,
and went to rescue Zhào.
In the first month of the eighth year (911 CE),
the Liáng army was defeated at Bǎixiāng,
20,000 heads were cut off,
and 300 officers and officials were captured,
along with 3,000 horses.
He advanced and attacked Xíngzhōu,
but failed to take it.
He left troops to besiege it,
and then departed
to attack Wèi.
He separately dispatched Zhōu Déwēi to raid the Liáng territories of Xiàjīn and Gāotáng,
attack Bózhōu,
and destroy Dōngwǔ and Cháochéng.
They then struck Líyáng, Línhé, and Qímén,
and plundered Xīnxiāng and Gòngchéng.
Yān Wáng Liú Shǒuguāng heard that Jìn was attacking deeply into Liáng territory,
so he greatly prepared his military,
ostensibly claiming he would assist Jìn.
The Prince worried about this,
and therefore turned his army back.
In the seventh month,
he met with Zhào Wáng Wáng Róng at Chéngtiān Jūn.
Liú Shǒuguāng proclaimed himself Emperor in Yān.
In the first month of the ninth year (912 CE),
he sent Zhōu Déwēi to join Zhèn and Dìng to attack Yān.
Shǒuguāng sought aid from Liáng.
The Liáng army attacked Zhào
and massacred Zǎoqiáng.
Lǐ Cúnshěn attacked and drove them away.
In the eighth month,
Zhū Yǒuqiān, based in Hézhong, rebelled against Liáng and submitted to Jìn.
Liáng sent Kāng Huáiyīng to suppress Yǒuqiān.
Yǒuqiān subsequently pledged allegiance to Liáng again,
but secretly remained aligned with Jìn.
In the tenth month of the tenth year (913 CE),
Liú Shǒuguāng requested surrender.
The Prince proceeded to Yōuzhōu.
Shǒuguāng broke his promise and did not surrender,
so the Prince attacked and defeated him.
In the eleventh year (914 CE),
Yān Wáng Liú Shǒuguāng was executed at Tàiyuán,
and his father, Rén'gōng, was put to death at Yànmén.
At this time, Zhào Wáng Wáng Róng and Běipíng Wáng Wáng Chùzhí respectfully presented a document recommending the Prince to be Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs),
and he began establishing a Xíngtái (Temporary Seat of Government).
In the seventh month,
he attacked Liáng at Xíngzhōu.
They fought at Zhānggōng Qiáo,
and the Jìn army suffered a great defeat.
He cut open his heart to offer sacrifice at the grave.
In the twelfth year,
the Wèizhōu (魏州) army mutinied.
Hè Délún (賀德倫) rebelled against Liáng (梁) with Wèi (魏) and Bó (博) prefectures and defected.
The Wáng (王) entered Wèizhōu (魏州).
When he reached Yǒngjì (永濟),
he executed Zhāng Yàn (張彥), the leader of the mutiny,
and took his five hundred soldiers as his personal guards,
calling them the Zhàngqián Yínqiāng Jūn (帳前銀槍軍) (Silver Spear Army of the Tent).
In the sixth month,
the Wáng (王) concurrently held the title of Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wèibó (魏博).
Dézhōu (德州) was taken.
In the seventh month,
Chánzhōu (澶州) was taken.
Liú Kuài (劉●) encamped at Huánshuǐ (洹水).
The Wáng (王) led one hundred cavalry to scout his camp.
He encountered Kuài's (●) ambushers, who surrounded him in several layers.
He broke through the encirclement,
losing seven or eight cavalrymen.
In the eighth month,
Liáng (梁) retook Chánzhōu (澶州).
The Jìn (晉) army and Kuài (●) faced each other at Shēn (莘).
The Jìn (晉) army repeatedly challenged them,
but Kuài (●) remained behind his fortifications.
In the first month of the thirteenth year,
the Wáng (王) left Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) at Shēn (莘),
announcing his intention to return west.
When Kuài (●) heard that the Jìn Wáng (晉王) was about to leave,
he immediately led his troops to attack Wèi (魏),
attacking the east of the city.
The Wáng (王), having reached Bèizhōu (貝州),
turned back to attack Kuài (●),
soundly defeating him.
He pursued him to Gù Yuánchéng (故元城),
defeated him again,
and Kuài (●) fled to Líyáng (黎陽).
In the third month,
he attacked Liáng's (梁) Wèizhōu (衞州),
and its Cìshǐ (刺史) Mǐ Zhāo (米昭) surrendered.
Cízhōu (磁州) was captured,
and its Cìshǐ (刺史) Jìn Zhāo (靳昭) was killed.
In the fourth month,
Míngzhōu (洺州) was captured.
In the eighth month,
Xíngzhōu (邢州) was besieged,
and its Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Yán Bǎo (閻寶) surrendered.
Zhāng Jūn (張筠) of Liáng (梁) abandoned Xiàngzhōu (相州) and Dài Sīyuǎn (戴思遠) abandoned Cāngzhōu (滄州) and fled.
The two prefectures were then taken.
The people of Bèizhōu (貝州) killed the Liáng (梁) commandant Zhāng Yuándé (張源德)
and surrendered the city.
The Qìdān (契丹) raided Wèizhōu (蔚州),
capturing Zhènwǔ Jìedùshǐ (振武節度使) Lǐ Sìběn (李嗣本).
In the fourteenth year,
the Qìdān (契丹) raided Xīnzhōu (新州),
and then Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) attacked and drove them away.
In winter,
Xiè Yànzhāng (謝彥章) of Liáng (梁) encamped at Yángliú (楊劉).
In the twelfth month,
Yángliú (楊劉) was attacked.
The Wáng (王) personally carried fodder to fill the moats,
and thus breached it.
In the first month of the fifteenth year,
Liáng (梁) and Jìn (晉) confronted each other at Yángliú (楊劉).
Yànzhāng (彥章) diverted the river water to separate the Jìn (晉) army.
In the sixth month,
they crossed the water to attack Yànzhāng (彥章),
destroying four of his camps.
In the eighth month,
a grand review was held at Wèi (魏).
The armies of Lúlóng (盧龍), Hénghǎi (橫海), Zhāoyì (昭義), Ānguó (安國), as well as Zhèn (鎮) and Dìng (定), totaling one hundred thousand men and ten thousand horses, were assembled.
They encamped at Májiādù (麻家渡).
Xiè Yànzhāng (謝彥章) encamped at Xíngtái (行臺).
In the twelfth month,
the army advanced to Línpú (臨濮).
The Liáng (梁) army pursued them,
and they battled at Húliǔ (胡柳).
The Jìn (晉) army suffered a great defeat,
and Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) died.
The Liáng (梁) army rested at dusk on a dirt mound.
The Jìn (晉) army attacked again,
soundly defeating them.
They then encamped at Déshèng (德勝),
forming a double stockade.
In the first month of the sixteenth year,
the Wáng (王) concurrently held the title of Lúlóng Jūn Jìedùshǐ (盧龍軍節度使).
Wáng Zàn (王瓚) of Liáng (梁) attacked the southern city of Déshèng (德勝),
but did not conquer it.
In the tenth month,
the northern city of Déshèng (德勝) was expanded.
In the twelfth month,
the Liáng (梁) army was defeated north of the Hé (河) (Yellow River).
In the seventeenth year,
Zhū Yǒuqīan (朱友謙) raided Tóngzhōu (同州).
Liáng (梁) dispatched Liú Kuài (劉●) to attack Yǒuqīan (友謙).
Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) defeated the Liáng (梁) army at Tóngzhōu (同州).
In the first month of the eighteenth year,
a monk named Chuánzhēn (傳真) from Wèizhōu (魏州) presented a Tang (唐) imperial seal of mandate.
Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮), a general of Zhào (趙), assassinated his lord Róng (鎔).
Wénlǐ (文禮) came to request a commission.
In the second month,
Wénlǐ (文禮) was appointed Zhènzhōu Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (鎮州兵馬留後).
In the third month,

Zhū Yǒuqīan (朱友謙), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hézhōng (河中); Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhāoyì Jūn (昭義軍); Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hénghǎi Jūn (橫海軍); Wáng Chǔzhí (王處直), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yìwǔ Jūn (義武軍); Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Ānguó Jūn (安國軍); Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮), Zhènzhōu Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (鎮州兵馬留後); Yán Bǎo (閻寶), concurrently Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Tiānpíng Jūn (天平軍); Lǐ Cúnzhāng (李存璋), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Dàtóng Jūn (大同軍); Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènwǔ Jūn (振武軍); and Zhū Lìngdé (朱令德), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Kuāngguó Jūn (匡國軍),
requested the Wáng (王) to ascend the imperial throne.
The Wáng (王) declined thrice.
Yǒuqīan (友謙) and others requested thrice more.
The Wáng (王) said,
"I shall ponder this."
In the eighth month,
the Wáng (王) dispatched Fú Xí (符習), a former general of Wáng Róng (王鎔), the Wáng (王) of Zhào (趙), along with Yán Bǎo (閻寶) and Shǐ Jiàntáng (史建瑭), to attack Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮) at Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
Jiàntáng (建瑭) took Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮) died,
and his son Chǔjǐn (處瑾) closed the city gates and resisted.
In the ninth month,
Jiàntáng (建瑭) died in battle.
In the tenth month,
Dài Sīyuǎn (戴思遠) of Liáng (梁) attacked the northern city of Déshèng (德勝).
Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) defeated him at Qīchéng (戚城).
Wáng Chǔzhí (王處直) rebelled and defected to the Qìdān (契丹).
His son Dū Yōu (都幽) held Chǔzhí (處直) captive and came to defect.
In the twelfth month,
the Qìdān (契丹) raided Zhuōzhōu (涿州),
and then Dìngzhōu (定州).
In the first month of the nineteenth year,
the Qìdān (契丹) were defeated at Xīnchéng (新城) and Wàngdū (望都).
The pursuit continued to Yōuzhōu (幽州).
In the third month,
Yán Bǎo (閻寶) was defeated at Zhènzhōu (鎮州),
and Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) replaced him.
In the fourth month,
Sìzhāo (嗣昭) died in battle,
and Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進) replaced him.
In the eighth month,
Liáng (梁) took Wèizhōu (衞州).
In the ninth month,
Cúnjìn (存進) defeated the Zhèn (鎮) people at Dōngyuán (東垣),
and Cúnjìn (存進) died in battle.
In the tenth month,
Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) captured Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
The Wáng (王) concurrently held the title of Chéngdé Jūn Jìedùshǐ (成德軍節度使).
In the spring, third month of Tóngguāng (同光) first year,
Lǐ Jìtāo (李繼韜) rebelled with Lùzhōu (潞州) and defected to Liáng (梁).
In summer, fourth month, on the Jǐsì (己巳) day,
the Emperor ascended the throne.
A general amnesty was declared,
the era name was changed,
and the dynastic name was Táng (唐).
Dòu Lúgé (豆盧革), Left Prime Minister of the Xíngtái (行臺), became Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎).
Lú Chéng (盧程), Right Prime Minister, became Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎), both holding the concurrent title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (同中書門下平章事).
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜), Zhōngmén Shǐ (中門使), and Zhāng Jūhàn (張居翰), Jiānjūn (監軍) of Zhāoyì (昭義), became Shūmì Shǐ (樞密使).
Wèizhōu (魏州) was designated as Dōngjīng (東京),
Tàiyuán (太原) as Xījīng (西京),
and Zhènzhōu (鎮州) as Běidū (北都).
The Shūmì Shǐ (樞密使)
in the former Táng (唐) was held by eunuchs.
Its position was very minor.
It was from this time that scholars were first included
and their power and authority became equal to that of the Zǎixiàng (宰相).
Therefore, they are recorded together with the Zǎixiàng (宰相).
In the intercalary month,
the imperial ancestors were posthumously honored as Huángdì (皇帝) and
their consorts as Huánghòu (皇后): Great-grandfather Zhíyí (執宜) and great-grandmother Cuī Shì (崔氏) were both given the posthumous title Zhāoliè (昭烈),
with the temple name Yìzǔ (懿祖).
Grandfather Guóchāng (國昌) and grandmother Qín Shì (秦氏) were both given the posthumous title Wénjǐng (文景),
with the temple name Xiànzǔ (獻祖).
Father was given the posthumous title Wǔ (武),
with the temple name Tàizǔ (太祖).
Temples were established in Tàiyuán (太原),
with seven temples from Táng Gāozǔ (唐高祖), Tàizōng (太宗), Yìzōng (懿宗), and Zhāozōng (昭宗) downwards.
On the Rén Yín (壬寅) day,
Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) took Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
As the imperial ancestors were posthumously honored,
it is implied that temples were established for them.
Therefore, the word
"temple" is not written in most cases.
Here it is written
because four temples from Gāozǔ (高祖) downwards were established.
This is a major event,
but the old histories lost the date.
Later, Táng Tàizǔ (後唐太祖) established a large number of adopted sons' armies, such as Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) and others.
Initially, all were given surnames and given names,
but they were not fully treated as sons.
Therefore, Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) is written as such,
recording the surname and given name he was bestowed,
not as a son.
This is different from Yǒuwén (友文) and Cóngkē (從珂).
On the fifth month, Xīnyǒu (辛酉) day,
the Liáng (梁) people took the southern city of Déshèng (德勝).
In the sixth month,
they battled Wáng Yànzhāng (王彥章) at Xīnlěi (新壘),
defeating him.
In this month,
Lú Chéng (盧程) was dismissed.
In the eighth month of autumn,
the Liáng people overcame Zézhōu;
the defending general Péi Yuē died there.
At the end of the Táng Dynasty,
Zé and Lù both belonged to Jìn.
In the early period of Liáng, Zézhōu was already obtained,
but by this time it belonged to Jìn again,
and then Liáng overcame it.
In the interval, the month and year when Jìn obtained Zézhōu are not seen;
this is likely due to omissions in the old histories.
During the chaos of the Five Dynasties,
wars, attacks, and seizures
meant that gains and losses between rivals were not constant,
and many instances are like this.
On the day Wùchén in the ninth month,
Lǐ Sìyuán and Wáng Yànzhāng fought at Dìfāng,
and defeated him.
On the day Rénshēn in the tenth month of winter,
he went to Yùnzhōu to launch a surprise attack on Liáng.
On the day Jiǎxū,
he captured Zhōngdū.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
he captured Cáozhōu.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Liáng was extinguished.
Jìng Xiáng committed suicide.
On the day Bǐngxū,
Zhèng Yù was demoted to Administrative Aide of the Bureau of Households in Láizhōu,
and Xiāo Qǐng to Administrative Aide of the Bureau of Households in Dēngzhōu;
Lǐ Zhèn, Zhào Yán, Zhāng Hànjié, and Zhū Guī were killed,
and their clans were exterminated.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
a gracious decree was issued: those sentenced to death were pardoned,
and those sentenced to exile or lesser punishments were forgiven.
By exploiting their lack of preparation
and rapidly driving in and entering,
it is therefore called
"surprise attack" (xí);
this is appropriate according to the context of the text,
and contains neither praise nor censure.
Xiáng was a minister of Liáng.
The reason Liáng destroyed Táng
was largely due to Xiáng's strategies.
When Liáng perished,
although Xiáng died for it,
it is not written
"died" (sǐ)
but written
"committed suicide" (zìshā).
Death (sǐ)
concerns a great matter of principle (dàjié),
showing that it is not lightly granted to others.
On the day Yǐsì in the eleventh month,
Běidū was restored as Zhènzhōu,
and Tàiyuán became Běidū.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Biànzhōu was restored as Xuānwǔ Jūn.
On the day Dīngsì,
Zhào Guāngyìn, Left Policy Monitor of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
and Wěi Shuō, Attendant-in-ordinary of the Board of Rites: both given the concurrent title Co-administrator of the Affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Korei's king Jīn Pòyīng sent an envoy to come.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Yǒngpíng Jūn was restored as Xīdū.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
he went to Luòjīng.
Luòjīng
follows the terminology of the time.
On the first day of the twelfth month, Gēngwǔ,
he arrived from Biànzhōu.
On the day Xīnsì,
Lǐ Jìtāo was executed.
Jìtāo's younger brother Jìdá killed his elder brother Jìchóu in Lùzhōu.
On the day Rénchén,
he hunted at Yīquè.
Jìchóu is recorded as having been killed (bèishā),
not because his death is denied,
but because Jìdá killed his elder brother,
which naturally serves to record his crime.
This is the same as the recording style for regicides.
In the first month of spring in the second year,
Zhāng Quányì, Administrator of Hénán, and the various governors presented gifts for the warm hall.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
eunuchs of Táng were sought.
On the day Gēngxū,
Korei's king Jīn Pòyīng and his Military Commissioner of Quánzhōu, Wáng Fēngguī, both sent envoys to come.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
King Dà Yīnxuàn of Bóhǎi sent Dà Yǔmó to come.
On the day Gēngshēn,
he went to Héyáng.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
he arrived from Héyáng.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
the spirit tablets of the Seven Ancestral Temples arrived from Tàiyuán,
and were interred in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Morning sacrifices were offered at the Tàiwēi Palace.
On the day Wùchén,
sacrifices were offered at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Whenever writing about mistakes or wicked deeds without satire or censure,
it is simply to record the facts and let them speak for themselves.
This refers to welcoming the Empress Dowager.
Empress Dowager Cáo Shì
was Zhuāngzōng's mother.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he sent Lú Chéng to present the official patent appointing her as Empress Dowager.
The old histories and official records both lack the month and day of the presentation of the patent,
therefore it is not recorded.
On the first day of the second month, Jǐsì,
rites were performed at the Southern Suburb,
and a general amnesty was granted.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
the officials presented the honorable title Zhāowén Ruìwǔ Guāngxiào Huángdì.
On the day Wùyín,
he visited Lǐ Sìyuán's residence.
On the day Guǐwèi,
Lady Liú Shì was established as Empress.
Among the thirteen rulers of the Five Dynasties,
seven established empresses.
The wording differs: for those correctly established,
it says
"Empress [surname] Shì, formerly [title] such-and-such concubine/lady, was established as Empress";
for those incorrectly established,
it simply says
"Lady [surname] Shì was established as Empress."
It is feared that it might be mistaken for a correctly established one,
containing neither praise nor censure.
On the day Jǐyǒu in the third month,
the Dǎngxiàng came.
On the day Gēngxū,
rewards were bestowed upon the meritorious officials and soldiers who participated in the pacification of Biànzhōu and the Southern Suburb parade in Luòyáng.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Lǐ Tú, Director in the Board of Works, was appointed Inspector of the Imperial Tombs.
Yáng Lì, a general in Lùzhōu, revolted.
These were the tombs of the Táng emperors.
On the day Rén'yín in the fifth month of summer,
Chén Jùn, Director of the Imperial Music Bureau, was appointed Prefect of Jǐngzhōu;
Chǔ Déyuán, Director of Grafting and Planting in the Imperial Garden, was appointed Prefect of Xiànzhōu.
On the day Bǐngchén,
King Dà Yīnxuàn of Bóhǎi sent an envoy to come.
On the day Bǐngyín,
Lǐ Sìyuán captured Lùzhōu.
Appointments of officials are not recorded,
but this is recorded because of its importance.
The appointment of the general is not recorded;
this is an omission in the old histories.
On the day Bǐngzǐ in the sixth month,
Yáng Lì was executed.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
King Rénměi of the Huíhé was enfeoffed as Yīngyì Kèhán.
On the day Jǐyǒu in the seventh month of autumn,
he went to Léishān to make sacrifices to the Heaven Spirits.
This is an act of the northern barbarians (Yídí).
In the eighth month,
there was heavy, continuous rain,
and the river overflowed.
On the day Rénzǐ in the ninth month,
water was placed at the city gates
to ward off Huòxīng (Mars).
On the day Jiǎyín,
he visited Guō Chóngtāo's residence.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Hēishuǐ sent an envoy to come.
The Basic Annals record calamities but not anomalies.
Placing water for Huòxīng
is not according to the rites for recording,
but shows his intention to fear misfortune
without knowing how to revere Heaven and cultivate virtue.
Calamities are things that harm beings, like floods, droughts, winds, and locusts,
and are therefore calamities (zāi),
thus they are recorded;
anomalies are changes that violate normal principles and whose cause is unknown,
and are therefore anomalies (yì).
Since they cannot be known,
they are not recorded.
On the day Guǐwèi in the tenth month of winter,
the wife of Zhào Huī, General of the Left Xióngwēi Army, gave birth to three boys in one labor.
This is also an anomaly,
but it is recorded
because human affairs are given importance,
thus it is treated carefully.
Later generations took this as a good omen,
so it is recorded during a period of chaos
to show that it is not so.
On the day Guǐmǎo in the eleventh month,
he hunted at Yīquè.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
he arrived from Yīquè.
On the day Dīngsì,
the Huíhú envoy, Commandant Ān Qiānxiǎng, came.
Recording
"arrived" (zhì)
shows that he stayed for four days and indulged excessively.
On the day Gēngwǔ in the twelfth month,
he and the Empress visited Zhāng Quányì's residence.
On the day Gēngzǐ in the first month of spring in the third year,
he went to Dōngjīng,
and destroyed the altar of accession to create a ball game field.
In the second month, on the *jǐsì* day,
they played *jū* (ball game) at Xīnchǎng.
On the *yǐhài* day,
they shot wild geese at the Wángmǎng Hé.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Húnjiělóu of the Tūjué and Dàyīnzhàn, King of the Bóhǎi State, both sent envoys to come.
They shot wild geese in the Northern Suburbs.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
they shot ducks at Guōpō.
On the *gēngyín* day,
they shot wild geese in the Northern Suburbs.
In the third month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
(during) the Cold Food Festival (*Hánshí*),
a distant sacrifice (*wàngjì*) was offered in the Western Suburbs.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
(the Emperor) arrived from Dōngjīng.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Dōngjīng was renamed Yèdū,
and Luòjīng was made Dōngdū.
This was a sacrifice of the common custom,
not in accordance with ritual (*lǐ*),
thus it is recorded.
In summer, the fourth month, on the *yǐhài* day,
the Emperor and the Empress visited the residences of Guō Chóngtāo and Zhū Hànbīn.
There was a drought.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Zhào Guāngyìn died.
In the fifth month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
the Imperial Consort Dowager (*Huáng Tàifēi*) died,
and court was suspended for five days.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Hēishuǐ and Nǚzhēn both sent envoys to come.
She was the principal wife of Tàizǔ,
and thus the legal mother (*dímǔ*) of Zhuāngzōng.
The record of
"Tàifēi"
and
"suspending court" (instead of the proper Empress Dowager rites),
shows that in this chaotic era, ritual (*lǐ*) had decayed and affection was shallow.
In the sixth month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
Lǐ Shū, the Minister of the Imperial Clan Court (*Zōngzhèng Qīng*), was made the commissioner to select new sites for the tombs and mausolea of Zhāozōng and the Young Emperor (*Shàodì*).
Horses were requisitioned.
The Young Emperor (*Shàodì*),
was the Prince of Jìyīn.
Liáng had previously given him the posthumous title
"Ái Huángdì" (Mournful Emperor),
but the Táng people called him
"Shàodì" (Young Emperor),
following their original terminology.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the *rényín* day,
the Empress Dowager (*Huáng Tàihòu*) died.
The omission of recording
"installation of the Empress Dowager" (or similar ceremony),
is already explained in the note above.
In the eighth month, on the *guǐwèi* day,
Luó Guàn, the magistrate of Hénán County, was killed.
In the ninth month, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
Jì Jí, the Prince of Wèi, was made the Supreme Commander of the Field Army in the Four Directions of Xīchuān,
and Guō Chóngtāo was made the Commissioner for Pacification and Attack, in order to campaign against Shǔ.
It rained continuously from the sixth month until this month.
On the *dīngsì* day,
they shot wild geese at Jiānshān.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
the Xī, Tǔhún, and Tūjué all sent envoys to come.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Empress Dowager Zhēnjiǎn was buried at Kūnlíng.
In the eleventh month, on the *dīngwèi* day,
Gāolì sent envoys to come.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Wáng Yǎn surrendered.
Guō Chóngtāo killed Wáng Zōngbì and his younger brothers Zōng Wò and Zōng Xùn,
exterminating their clan.
The Táng troops entered Shǔ,
neither attacking nor fighting.
The ruler and his ministers welcomed them and surrendered,
thus the fact is directly recorded,
so that the later record
"killed Yǎn"
is seen as killing those who surrendered.
In the twelfth month, on the *jǐmǎo* day,
they hunted at Báishā.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
(the Emperor) arrived from Báishā.
In the intercalary month, on the *xīnhài* day,
his younger brother Cúnměi was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yōng;
Cúnbà as the Prince of Yǒng;
Cúnlǐ as the Prince of Xuē;
Cúnwò as the Prince of Shēn;
Cúnyì as the Prince of Mù;
Cúnquè as the Prince of Tōng;
and Cúnjì as the Prince of Yǎ.
In the fourth year, spring, the first month, on the *rénxū* day,
pardons were granted to prisoners sentenced to death and below.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Jì Jí, the Prince of Wèi, killed Guō Chóngtāo and his two sons in Shǔ
On the *wùyín* day,
Měilǎo Xiélǐ, an envoy from the Qìdān, arrived.
On the *gēngchén* day,
(the Emperor) killed his younger brother Cúnyì, the Prince of Mù, and Lǐ Jìlín, the Military Governor (*Jiédùshǐ*) of the Hùguó Army in Hézhōng,
exterminating their clans.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Cáo Yìjīn of Shāzhōu sent envoys to come.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Āduōyù of the Huíhú sent envoys to come.
On the *dīnghài* day,
(the Emperor) killed Lǐ Jìlín's generals Shǐ Wǔ, Xuē Jìngróng, Zhōu Tángyīn, Yáng Shītài, Wáng Jǐng, Lái Rén, and Bái Fèngguó,
exterminating all their clans.
In reality, Empress Liú had issued an instruction to Jì Jí to have Chóngtāo killed,
but the record states
"Jì Jí killed him"
because
Jì Jí was leading troops externally,
the Empress’s instruction was not an imperial decree,
and he could have stopped it but did not.
In the second month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
Lǐ Shàohóng, the Commissioner of the Southern Court of the Bureau of Palace Affairs (*Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ*), was made the Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Shūmì Shǐ*).
On the *guǐsì* day,
Zhào Zàilǐ, a general of the Yèdū army, rebelled in Bèizhōu.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
they hunted at Lěngquán.
Zhào Zàilǐ captured Yèdū,
and Lǐ Shàoróng, the Military Governor of the Wǔníng Army, was sent to suppress him.
Zhào Tài, a general of the Xíngzhōu army, rebelled,
and Lǐ Shàozhēn, the Commissioner for Pacification and Attack in the Northeast, was sent to suppress him.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Lǐ Sìyuán, the Military Governor of the Chéngdé Army, attacked Zhào Zàilǐ.
The day of the other rebellions was not recorded,
only Zàilǐ's day is recorded.
By examining his intent, this can be understood.
The full details are in his biography.
Probably Zàilǐ initially had no intention of rebellion,
but was forced to rebel on that day.
Although he is charged with the name of a great evildoer,
his original intention is spared and treated differently from other rebels.
From this, it is seen that when recording people's good and evil,
titles are not arbitrarily added.
In the third month,
Zhào Tài was executed.
Lǐ Sìyuán rebelled.
Zhái Jiàn, the defender of Bózhōu, proclaimed himself Prefect (*Cìshǐ*).
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Wáng Yǎn was killed,
and his clan was exterminated.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
(the Emperor) went to Biànzhōu.
On the *rénshēn* day,
(the Emperor) stopped at Xíngzé.
Yáo Yànwēn, Commander of the Lóngxiāng Command, mutinied with the Vanguard Army and surrendered to Lǐ Sìyuán.
Sìyuán entered Biànzhōu.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
(the Emperor) arrived from Wànshèng.
Guō Cóngqiān, Commander of the Cavalry Guard (*Cóngmǎ Zhí*), rebelled.
(The Emperor) had promised him that he would not be killed,
but after he surrendered, he was killed,
and his clan was also exterminated.
This was the worst instance of killing the innocent,
but the record uses no distinctive language (from other executions).
Because the earlier entry stated
"Yǎn surrendered,"
the meaning is implicitly clear.
The Emperor reached Wànshèng Garrison,
heard that Sìyuán had already entered Biànzhōu,
and thus returned.
In summer, the fourth month, on the *dīnghài* day, the first day of the month (*shuò*),
the Emperor died.
He was forty-three years old.
The Emperor's corpse was burned by actors (*língrén*).
Míngzōng entered Luò,
and recovered his bone ashes.
In the seventh month of the first year of Tiānchéng,
he was buried in Xīn'ān County, Hénán,
named Yōnglíng.
Later, during the Jìn dynasty, to avoid an imperial taboo name,
it was renamed Yīlíng.
The omission of recording the
"burial,"
is the same as that for Liáng Tàizǔ.
Basic Annals of Táng, Chapter Six:
Emperor Míngzōng Shèngdé Héwǔ Qīnxiào.
His lineage was originally barbarian (*yídí*),
without a surname.
His father, Ní,
was a tribal general in Yànmén.
He bore a son, Miǎojíliè,
who served Tàizǔ with his skill in riding and archery.
He was inherently honest, sincere, and reserved in speech,
performing his duties respectfully and cautiously.
Tàizǔ adopted him as a son,
and granted him the name Sìyuán.
Liáng (梁) attacked Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆).
Zhū Xuān (朱宣) and Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾) came to beg for troops.
Tàizǔ (太祖) dispatched Lǐ Cúnxìn (李存信) leading thirty thousand troops to rescue them.
Cúnxìn (存信) remained in Shēnxiàn (莘縣) and did not advance,
ordering Sìyuán (嗣源) to separately lead three thousand troops to first attack the Liáng (梁) forces.
The Liáng (梁) forces dispersed and left.
Cúnxìn (存信) remained in Shēnxiàn (莘縣) for a long time.
He was attacked by Luó Hóngxìn (羅弘信).
Cúnxìn (存信) was defeated and fled.
Sìyuán (嗣源) alone covered the rear guard and returned.
Tàizǔ (太祖) named the five hundred cavalry led by Sìyuán (嗣源)
the "Héngchōng Dū" (橫衝都, Charging Column).
In the third year of Guānghuà (光化, 900 CE),
Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) attacked Xíng (邢) and Míng (洺) held by Liáng (梁).
He emerged from Qīngshān (青山),
and encountered the troops of Gé Cóngzhōu (葛從周).
Sìzhāo (嗣昭) was greatly defeated and fled.
The Liáng (梁) forces pursued him.
Sìyuán (嗣源) arrived later via a side path
and said to Sìzhāo (嗣昭):
"I will fight one battle for you, Sir."
Thereupon, he dismounted, sharpened his arrowheads,
and established a formation atop high ground.
He directed his troops left and right.
The pursuing Liáng (梁) troops looked at this, unable to gauge his strength.
Sìyuán (嗣源) shouted urgently, saying:
"I will take Gé Gōng (葛公, Gé Cóngzhōu).
The officers and soldiers must not move!"
Then he galloped his cavalry and charged them,
fighting fiercely, in and out.
Sìzhāo (嗣昭) followed and advanced.
The Liáng (梁) forces dispersed and left.
Sìyuán (嗣源) was struck by four arrows.
Tàizǔ (太祖) took off his own robes and bestowed medicine upon him to reward him.
From this, the reputation of Lǐ Héngchōng (李橫衝) became great throughout the land.
Liáng (梁) and Jìn (晉) faced off against each other at Bǎixiāng (柏鄉).
The Liáng (梁) Lóngxiāng Army (龍驤軍) formed two battle lines using red horses and white horses,
with banners, armor, and weapons all matching the color of the horses.
The Jìn (晉) troops looked upon them and were all afraid.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) raised a wine cup and offered a drink to Sìyuán (嗣源), saying:
"Do you fear the red and white horses of the House of Liáng (梁)?
Even I feel timid about them."
Sìyuán (嗣源) laughed and replied:
"They are only showy appearance.
Tomorrow they will belong to my stables."
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) was greatly pleased and said:
"You should swallow them with your spirit."
He then took the cup and drank it dry,
and Sìyuán (嗣源) brandished his whip, galloped his horse,
and charged their white horses.
He returned holding two subordinate generals captive.
The Liáng (梁) forces were defeated.
For this merit, he was appointed Dàizhōu Cìshǐ (代州刺史, Prefect of Dàizhōu).
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) attacked Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光).
Sìyuán (嗣源) and Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) led thirty thousand troops and separately emerged via Fēihú (飛狐).
They pacified the region behind the mountains,
and captured the three prefectures of Wǔ (武), Guī (媯), and Rú (儒).
After Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) had pacified Wèizhōu (魏州),
he subsequently campaigned and took Cí (磁) and Xiāng (相) prefectures.
Sìyuán (嗣源) was appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (相州刺史, Prefect of Xiāngzhōu) and Jìedùshǐ (節度使, Military Governor) of the Zhāodé Army (昭德軍).
After a long time,
he was transferred to govern Ānguó (安國).
The Qìdān (契丹) attacked Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) dispatched Sìyuán (嗣源) along with Yán Bǎo (閻寶) and others to attack and drive them off.
In the first year of Tóngguāng (同光, 923 CE),
he was transferred to govern Hénghǎi (橫海).
At that time,
Liáng (梁) and Táng (唐) were facing off against each other on the Yellow River.
Lǐ Jìtāo (李繼韜) rebelled with Lùzhōu (潞州) and defected to Liáng (梁).
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) showed worry.
He summoned Sìyuán (嗣源) to his tent
and said:
"Jìtāo (繼韜) has defected to Liáng (梁) with Shàngdǎng (上黨).
And Liáng (梁) is currently urgently attacking Zézhōu (澤州).
If I unexpectedly attack Yùnzhōu (鄆州)
to sever Liáng's (梁) right arm,
is that feasible?"
Sìyuán (嗣源) replied:
"The forces arrayed along the river have been there a long time.
Unless we employ a brilliant surprise move,
the grand strategy will not be settled.
I request permission, your subject, to undertake this alone."
He then took five thousand infantry and cavalry, crossed the river,
and arrived at Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
The people of Yùn (鄆) were unprepared.
He consequently launched a surprise attack and defeated them.
He was immediately appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使, Military Governor) of the Tiānpíng Army (天平軍) and Deputy Supreme Commander (Fù Dū Zǒngguǎn, 副都總管) of the Barbarian and Han Cavalry and Infantry Forces.
The Liáng (梁) army attacked and destroyed the Southern Stockade of Déshèng (德勝).
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) retreated and secured Yángliǔ (楊劉).
Wáng Yànzhāng (王彥章) urgently attacked Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) deployed all his troops to rescue it.
Sìyuán (嗣源) served as the vanguard and attacked the Liáng (梁) army.
He pursued them to Zhōngdū (中都),
capturing Yànzhāng (彥章) and Zhāng Hànjié (張漢傑), the Liáng (梁) Supervisor of the Army.
Although Yànzhāng (彥章) was defeated,
Duàn Níng (段凝) commanded all the Liáng (梁) forces and stationed them along the river.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) did not know which direction to proceed.
Many generals argued that they should use the victory to capture Qīng (青) and Qí (齊) prefectures.
Sìyuán (嗣源) said:
"Níng (凝) does not yet know of the defeat of Yànzhāng (彥章).
If he hears of it,
and hesitates in deciding strategy,
it will still require three days.
Even if he estimates our target direction
and urgently sends reinforcements,
they must cross Líyáng (黎陽).
Tens of thousands of troops
will require more than a day to gather boats.
From here to Biànzhōu (汴州),
is not many hundreds of miles.
There are no obstacles ahead.
Marching in square formation,
we can reach it in two nights.
If Biànzhōu (汴州) is already captured,
how can Duàn Níng (段凝) be worth worrying about!"
And Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) also advised Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) to enter Biàn (汴).
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) deemed it correct.
He dispatched Sìyuán (嗣源) with a thousand cavalry to first reach Biànzhōu (汴州),
and attack Fēngqiūmén (封丘門, Fēngqiū Gate).
Wáng Zàn (王瓚) opened the gate and surrendered.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) arrived later.
Seeing Sìyuán (嗣源), he was extremely happy.
He personally grasped his clothes
and bumped him with his head, saying:
"The world will be shared with you."
Sìyuán (嗣源) was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令, Director of the Chancellery).
In the second year (924 CE),
when Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) performed the Sacrifice to Heaven at the Southern Suburb,
he bestowed upon him an Iron Charter (tiě juàn).
In the fifth month,
Yáng Lì (楊立) was defeated at Lùzhōu (潞州).
In the sixth month,
he was transferred to govern Xuānwǔ (宣武),
concurrently serving as Supreme Commander (Zǒngguǎn, 總管) of the Barbarian and Han Internal and External Cavalry and Infantry Forces.
In winter,
the Qìdān (契丹) raided Yúyáng (漁陽).
Sìyuán (嗣源) defeated them at Zhuōzhōu (涿州).
In the third year (925 CE),
he was transferred to govern Chéngdé (成德).
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) visited Yè (鄴),
Sìyuán (嗣源) requested an audience at the interim court (xíng zài, 行在),
but this was not permitted.
When Empress Dowager Zhēnjiǎn (貞簡太后) became ill,
he requested to enter and attend to her,
but again, this was not permitted.
When the Empress Dowager passed away,
he requested to attend the funeral preparations (shānlíng, 山陵).
This was permitted,
but because the Qìdān (契丹) invaded the border,
he stopped.
In the twelfth month,
he finally had an audience at Luòyáng (洛陽).
Regarding
Tiānchéng Yuánnián (天成元年, the first year of Tiānchéng):
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) and Zhū Yǒuqiān (朱友謙) both died due to slander.
Sìyuán (嗣源), due to his high rank and reputation,
was also viewed with suspicion and envy.
Zhào Zàilǐ (趙在禮) rebelled in Wèi (魏).
The high ministers all requested that Sìyuán (嗣源) be dispatched to suppress the rebels.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) did not permit it.
The officials repeatedly requested,
and Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) had no choice but to
dispatch him.
This was actually the fourth year of Tóngguāng (同光),
but the text writes
“Tiānchéng Yuánnián.”
The reason for this
is understandable from the subsequent document regarding the general amnesty and change of reign title.
The Basic Annals of Zhuāngzōng (莊宗 Běnjì, 本紀) itself writes
“Tóngguāng Sìnián.”
Each follows what it refers to;
since it mentions changing the reign title,
there is no issue with having two names.
On the Rénzǐ (壬子) day of the third month,
Sìyuán (嗣源) arrived at Wèi (魏).
He encamped south of the Yùhé (御河) river.
Zàilǐ (在禮) climbed a tower and apologized for his crimes.
On the Jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
the army mutinied.
Sìyuán (嗣源) entered Wèi (魏),
and joined forces with Zàilǐ (在禮).
That evening he departed,
stopping at Wèixiàn (魏縣).
On the Dīngsì (丁巳) day,
he marched his troops south,
dispatching Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) to lead three hundred cavalry as vanguard.
As Sìyuán (嗣源) passed Jùlù (鉅鹿),
he seized two thousand horses from the small farms to augment his army.
On the Rénshēn (壬申) day,
he entered Biànzhōu (汴州).
In the fourth month, on the *dīnghài* day,
Zhuāngzōng died.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
he entered Luòyáng.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
he oversaw the state,
holding court with the assembled ministers at the Xīngshènggōng Palace.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
the Internal Gate Commissioner, Ān Chónghuǐ, was made Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Shūmìshǐ*).
Yuán Xíngqīn and the Commissioner of Taxes and Levies, Kǒng Qiān, were killed.
On the *rén'yín* day,
Kǒng Xún, Great General of the Left Swift Cavalry Guard (*Zuǒ Xiāowèi Dàjiàngjūn*), was made Commissioner of Military Affairs.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the preliminary offering was first made at the Western Palace,
and the Emperor ascended the throne before the coffin,
exchanging the coarse mourning garment (*zhǎncuī*) for the imperial robe and crown (*gǔnmiǎn*).
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Jì Jí, Prince of Wèi, died.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign title was changed.
Dà Chénlín came as an envoy from Dà Yīnchuàn, King of the Bóhǎi State.
In this month,
Zhāng Jūhàn was dismissed.
Recording
"the preliminary offering"
shows the delay.
From the *jǐchǒu* day when he entered Luò [Luòyáng],
twenty days had passed until this time.
Ascending the throne before the coffin
is the rite of a successor ruler.
For a rebellious subject to establish himself,
yet use the rites of a successor ruler—
the recording follows the reality without altering the text
because his rebellion had already been recorded previously,
confirming his crime.
Recording the reality here
shows that he still retained a sense of shame,
and wished to escape the name of a great evildoer.
Having already used the rites of a successor ruler,
he immediately abandoned the mourning clothes and donned the crown;
therefore, it is recorded to show his deceptive nature.
The deaths of various princes are not usually recorded,
but this recording
shows that Míngzōng's deployment of troops was truly rebellion,
coupled with Cóng Qiān's regicide and treason;
he then falsely claimed the name of rushing to aid the crisis.
At the time of his enthronement,
Zhuāngzōng's eldest son was still alive,
thus his justification was weak.
In the fifth month, on the first day (*shuò*), which was *bǐngchén*,

Zhèng Yù, Guest of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Bīnkè*), and Rèn Huán, Minister of Works (*Gōngbù Shàngshū*), were made Central Secretariat Vice Ministers (*Zhōngshū Shìláng*) and concurrently Managers of Affairs with the Central Secretariat and Chancellery (*Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*).
On the *wùchén* day,
Zhào Zàilǐ was made Military Governor (*Jiédùshǐ*) of the Yìchéng Army.
Zàilǐ should have been executed for starting the disturbance,
but Míngzōng relied on him to rebel,
and appointed him to a regional command
to reward his merit;
therefore, it is recorded.
In the sixth month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
the Crane Control Army (*Kònghè Jūn*) in Biànzhōu revolted.
The Commander (*Zhǐhuīshǐ*), Zhāng Jiàn, killed Gāo Tì, who was provisionally managing the affairs of the prefecture.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Jiàn was executed.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
Ān Chónghuǐ killed Mǎ Yán, a Palace Attendant (*Diànzhí*), at the gate of the Censorate (*Yùshǐ Tái*).
Méilǎo Shùgǔ came as an envoy from the Qìdān.
Dà Zhāozuǒ came as an envoy from Bóhǎi.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Dòu Lúgé was demoted to Prefect (*Cǐshǐ*) of Chénzhōu,
and Wéi Shuō was demoted to Prefect of [Shuō]zhōu.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Lúgé was banished to Língzhōu,
and Shuō was banished to Hézhōu.
The Censorate is meant to impeach illegal actions by all officials;
killing a person at the Censorate gate
marks this as an extreme evil.
In the eighth month, on the first day (*shuò*), which was *yǐyǒu*,
Gāo Cún's wife, a commoner in Xiáshí County, Shǎnzhōu, gave birth to three boys at once.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
thirty-two ivory tablets (*hù*) were bestowed upon those officials who lacked them.
The crops were inspected at the Lěngquángōng Palace.
On the *jǐhài* day,
the Qìdān violated the border.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Huò Yànwēi, Military Governor of the Pínglú Army, killed his Prefect of Dēngzhōu, Wáng Gōngyǎn.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Zhāng Zhìzhōng, a Medical Official (*Yīguān*), was made Vice Prefect (*Shǎoyǐn*) of Tàiyuán.
At this time, the court was extremely weak;
therefore, this is recorded.
In the ninth month, on the *jǐwèi* day,
[The Emperor] visited the Zhìdégōng Palace and Yuán Jiànfēng’s residence.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *dīnghài* day,

Fù Nénghéhuá, the Great Ghost Master (*Dà Guǐzhǔ*), came as an envoy from Lǐ Bēiwǎn, Chief Ghost Master of the Two Forests and Hundred Barbarians Behind the Mountains of Yúnnán, and Great General of the Right Martial Guard (*Yòu Wǔwèi Dàjiàngjūn*).
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Mògǔněi came as an envoy from the Qìdān to announce the mourning for Ābǎojī;
court was suspended for three days.
There was a drought.
On the *xīnhài* day, it rained.
In the second year, spring, the first month, on the first day (*shuò*), which was *guǐchǒu*,
his name was changed to Dǎn.
On the *guǐhài* day,

Féng Dào, Academician of the Duānmíng Hall (*Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì*) and Vice Minister of War (*Bīngbù Shìláng*), and Cuī Xié, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Qīng*), were made Central Secretariat Vice Ministers and concurrently Managers of Affairs with the Central Secretariat and Chancellery.
In the second month, on the first day (*shuò*), which was *rénwǔ*,
Zhāng Fēn came as an envoy from Sīllá.
Mèng Zhīxiáng, Military Governor of Xīchuān, killed Lǐ Yán, his Commissioner Overseeing the Armies and Horses (*Bīngmǎ Dūjiān*).
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
prisoners in the capital were pardoned.
Guō Cóngqiān was made Prefect of Jǐngzhōu,
and subsequently killed.
On the *wùxū* day,
Liú Xùn, Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào, was made Southern Pacification Commissioner (*Nánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ*),
to attack Jīngnán.
Cóngqiān committed regicide;
Míngzōng did not punish him but appointed him to office,
therefore, it is recorded.
He committed the same crime as Zàilǐ and deserved execution,
but the recording
"killed"
means that
Míngzōng was also equally guilty,
and could not carry out the execution;
therefore, it is recorded as the two killing each other.
At this time,
Jīngnán had cut itself off from the Central Plains and attached itself to Wú.
This was not sufficient to hold them guilty [of treason against the dynasty],
so instead of recording it as "punishing" (*tǎo*), it is recorded as
"attacking" (*fá*),
showing that since they were not internal subjects,
they were not blamed for rebellion.
In the third month, on the first day (*shuò*), which was *rénzǐ*,
[The Emperor] visited the Huìjiéyuán Garden,
and the assembled ministers paid for a banquet.
Lútái was in disorder,
and its general, Wū Zhèn, was killed.
Lín Yàn came as an envoy from Sīllá.
If the imperial excursions and visits were not excessive,
they would be minor affairs,
and generally not recorded.
They were only recorded during the reigns of Zhuāngzōng and Jìn Chūdì,
to emphasize their excessiveness.
Míngzōng was a diligent and thrifty ruler among the Five Dynasties;
his excursions were not excessive.
This record, detailing the paid banquet,
shows the lapse of conduct between the ruler and his ministers.
Summer, the fourth month, on the *gēngyín* day,
Lóng Zhǐ and other generals of the Lútái army were executed.
The sixth month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Rèn Huán was dismissed.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
[The Emperor] visited Báisīmǎpō,
and sacrificed to the Tūjué deities.
This is a matter related to the barbarians.
Autumn, the seventh month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Xīfāng Yè, Prefect of Suízhōu, captured Kuízhōu, Zhōngzhōu, and Wànzhōu.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
Dòu Lúgé and Wéi Shuō were killed.
The eighth month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
Sòng Cháohuà came as an envoy from Zāngkē, along with envoys from Kūnmíng.
The ninth month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
Rú Liánshān came as an envoy from the Dǎngxiàng.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Méilǎo came as an envoy from the Qìdān.
Winter, the tenth month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
[The Emperor] proceeded to Biànzhōu.
Zhū Shǒuyīn, Military Governor of the Xuānwǔ Army, rebelled,
and Mǎ Yànchāo, Grand Commander of the Cavalry and Infantry (*Mǎbù Jūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ*), died for him.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Shǒuyīn committed suicide.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
Rèn Huán, Junior Mentor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo*) who had retired, was killed.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
a benevolent decree pardoned the imprisoned.
In this month,
the tally arrow was passed to Huò Yànwēi.
The reason for not recording the capture (*kè*) of Biànzhōu
is that the Son of Heaven personally led the army to suppress the rebellion;
there was no siege or battle,
he simply entered the city directly.
In other cases,
"committed suicide"
is not recorded,
because the capture of the prefecture is recorded instead;
since the capture of the prefecture is not recorded here,
therefore,
"committed suicide" is recorded.
In reality, Ān Chónghuǐ falsely issued an imperial decree and killed him,
but the reason for not recording Chónghuǐ's killing
is that Míngzōng knew of it but did not hold him responsible,
and moreover issued an edict falsely incriminating Huán;
therefore, it is recorded as Míngzōng [ordering him to] commit suicide.
This is a matter related to the barbarians.
In the eleventh month, on the *yǐhài* day,
Méilǎo came as an envoy from the Qìdān.
In the twelfth month, on the day *jǐchǒu* (己丑),
Tuyǔhún (吐蕃) from the western border of Huíhú (回鶻) dispatched an envoy to come.
On *jiǎchén* (甲辰),
hunted in the eastern suburbs.
On *bǐngwǔ* (丙午),
honored his deceased ancestors as Emperors
and his deceased grandmothers as Empresses: His Great Ancestor Yù (聿) was posthumously titled Xiàogōng (孝恭),
with the temple name Huìzǔ (惠祖).
His Great Ancestress, née Liú (劉氏), was posthumously titled Xiàogōngzhāo (孝恭昭);
His Great Grandfather Áo (敖) was posthumously titled Xiàozhì (孝質),
with the temple name Yìzǔ (毅祖).
His Great Grandmother, née Zhāng (張氏), was posthumously titled Xiàozhìshùn (孝質順);
His Grandfather Yǎn (琰) was posthumously titled Xiàojìng (孝靖),
with the temple name Lièzǔ (烈祖).
His Grandmother, née Hé (何氏), was posthumously titled Xiàojìngmù (孝靖穆);
His Father was posthumously titled Xiàochéng (孝成),
with the temple name Dézǔ (德祖).
His Mother, née Liú (劉氏), was posthumously titled Xiàochéngyì (孝成懿).
A temple was established in Yìngzhōu (應州).
Third year, spring, first month, on *dīngsì* (丁巳),
the Qìdān (契丹) captured Píngzhōu (平州).
Second month, on *xīnsì* (辛巳),
Lǐ Shàolǔ (李紹虜), the Area Commander (Dūdu) of the Tǔhún (吐渾), came.
On *yǐwèi* (乙未),
Kǒng Xún (孔循) was dismissed.
On *wùxū* (戊戌),
Lǐ Āshān (李阿山), an envoy from Huíhú (回鶻), came.
Third month, on *dīngwèi* (丁未), the first day of the month (*shuò*),
an Imperial Edict sought frank criticism.
On *jǐwèi* (己未),
Zhèng Yù (鄭[⿰王玉]) was dismissed.
On *guǐhài* (癸亥),
Wáng Jiànlì (王建立), Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Chéngdé Army (成德軍), was made Right Vice Director (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè) and Manager of Affairs (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Xīfāng Yè (西方鄴) captured Guīzhōu (歸州).
On *wùchén* (戊辰),
Fàn Yánguāng (范延光), Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of Palace Affairs (Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ), was made Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ).
Summer, fourth month, on *wùyín* (戊寅),
Yánguāng (延光) was dismissed.
On *yǐyǒu* (乙酉),
the Dádá (達靼) dispatched an envoy to come.
Wáng Dū (王都), Military Governor of Yìwǔ Army (義武軍), rebelled.
On *rényín* (壬寅),
Wáng Yànqiú (王晏球), Military Governor of Guīdé Army (歸德軍), was made Mobilization Commissioner of the Northern Front Campaign Headquarters (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ).
Fifth month,
the Qìdān (契丹) general Tūněi (禿餒) entered Dìngzhōu (定州).
On *xīnyǒu* (辛酉),
Zhào Jìngyí (趙敬怡), General-in-chief of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn), was made Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ).
Wáng Rényù (王仁裕), the Khagan (Kèhán) of the Huíhú (回鶻), was enfeoffed as Shùnhuà Kèhán (順化可汗).
Autumn, seventh month, on *jǐwèi* (己未),
Cáo Tíngyǐn (曹廷隱), the Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Qízhōu (齊州), was executed.
Eighth month,
Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞), Military Governor of Lúlóng Army (盧龍軍), captured the Qìdān (契丹) leader Tǎngyǐn Hèmò (愓隱赫邈).
Dòu Tíngwǎn (竇廷琬), Defense Commissioner of Qìngzhōu (慶州), rebelled.
Winter, tenth month,
Lǐ Jìngzhōu (李敬周), Military Governor of Jìngnán Army (靜難軍), campaigned against him.
On *dīngsì* (丁巳),
Zhāng Mùjìn (張慕晉), an envoy from the Tūjué (突厥), came.
Eleventh month, on *rénwǔ* (壬午),
Niànjiǔ (念九), an envoy from the Tǔhún (吐渾), came.
On *jiǎwǔ* (甲午),
Wáng Jiànlì (王建立) was dismissed.
Twelfth month,
Lǐ Jìngzhōu (李敬周) captured Qìngzhōu (慶州),
and Dòu Tíngwǎn (竇廷琬) suffered the death penalty.
On *xīnhài* (辛亥),
the Emperor visited Kāng Yìchéng's (康義誠) residence.
Fourth year, spring, first month, on *rénchén* (壬辰),
Chèbō Dūdu (掣撥都督), an envoy from Huíhú (回鶻), came.
Second month, on *guǐmǎo* (癸卯),
Wáng Yànqiú (王晏球) captured Dìngzhōu (定州).
On *xīnyǒu* (辛酉),
Yànqiú (晏球) presented the severed heads and captives.
Zhào Jìngyí (趙敬怡) passed away.
On *dīngmǎo* (丁卯),
Cuī Xié (崔協) passed away.
On *gēngwǔ* (庚午),
arrived from Biànzhōu (汴州).
Wáng Dū (王都) immolated himself,
therefore it is not recorded that he suffered the death penalty.
Third month, on *bǐngxū* (丙戌),
his nephew Cóng Càn (從璨) was executed.
Summer, fourth month,
the Qìdān (契丹) raided Yúnzhōu (雲州).
On *guǐchǒu* (癸丑),
Liáoguā Méilǐ (撩括梅里), a Qìdān (契丹) envoy, came seeking Tūněi (禿餒),
and was executed.
On *jiǎyín* (甲寅),

Zhào Fèng (趙鳳), Scholar of the Duānmíng Hall (Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì) and Vice Minister of the Ministry of War (Shàngshū Bīngbù Shìláng), was made Vice Minister of the Chancellery (Ménxià Shìláng) concurrently Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū) and Manager of Affairs (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Fifth month, on *jǐsì* (己巳),
held court with the assembled officials,
celebrating the new moon (*Hè Shuò*).
On *yǐyǒu* (乙酉),
the Young Emperor (Shàodì) was posthumously titled Zhāoxuān Guāngliè Xiàohuángdì (昭宣光烈孝皇帝).
The Qìdān (契丹) raided Yúnzhōu (雲州).
It is not recorded as "attending court,"
but rather as
"celebrating the new moon" (*Hè Shuò*).
This shows it was an act of impropriety (*fēilǐ*).
Attending court is a routine matter,
and thus generally not recorded.
Celebrating the new moon in the fifth month
originated from Dàoist (Dàojiā) theories.
It has been practiced since the Táng (唐) Dynasty.
Recording it shows that in troubled times, people prioritize minor improprieties.
This rite was performed repeatedly thereafter,
but was no longer recorded,
similar to the custom of entering the inner court (*rùgé*).
Autumn, seventh month, on *rénshēn* (壬申),
Máo Zhāng (毛璋), General-in-chief of the Right Military Guard (Yòu Jīnwú Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn), was executed.
Eighth month, on *yǐsì* (乙巳),
Gǔzhì (骨至), an envoy from Hēishuǐ (黑水), came.
On *dīngwèi* (丁未),
Niàngōngshān (念公山), a leader of the Tǔhún (吐渾), came.
On *yǐmǎo* (乙卯),
Shé Yùmíng (折遇明) of the Dǎngxiàng (党項), came.
On *jǐwèi* (己未),
Zhāng Bīn (張彬), an envoy sent by Wáng Jiàn (王建), King of Gāolì (高麗), came.
Ninth month, on *guǐsì* (癸巳),
Wū Zhāoyù (烏昭遇), an attendant official (Gòngfèngguān), was executed.
Winter, twelfth month, on *xīnchǒu* (辛丑),
Lǐ Shāng (李商), Magistrate of Xīpíng County (Xīpíng Xiàn Lìng), was executed.
Chángxīng (長興) first year, spring, first month, on *dīngmǎo* (丁卯),
reviewed horses in the Imperial Park.
On *xīnmǎo* (辛卯),
Zhū Hóngzhāo (朱弘昭), Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of Palace Affairs, was made Keeper of the Grand Palace (Dànèi Liúshǒu).
Second month,
on *wùxū* (戊戌),
the Wùér (兀兒) of Hēishuǐ (黑水) dispatched an envoy to come.
On *yǐsì* (乙巳),
Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭), Military Governor of Tiānxíong Army (天雄軍), was made Commissioner of the Imperial Camp (Yùyíngshǐ).
On *guǐchǒu* (癸丑),
performed the morning offering at the Tàiwēi Palace (Tàiwēi Gōng).
On *jiǎyín* (甲寅),
performed the sacrifice at the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào).
On *yǐmǎo* (乙卯),
performed the rites in the Southern Suburbs (Nánjiāo).
A general amnesty was issued,
and the era name was changed.
Third month, on *gēngyín* (庚寅),
Consort Shū (Shūfēi), née Cáo (曹氏), was established as Empress (Huánghòu).
Summer, fourth month, on *wùxū* (戊戌),
Ān Chónghuǐ (安重誨) ordered Yáng Yànwēn (楊彥溫), Commander of the Headquarters Guard in Hézhōng (Hézhōng Yánèi Zhǐhuīshǐ), to expel his Military Governor Cóng Kē (從珂).
On *rényín* (壬寅),
Suǒ Zìtōng (索自通), Resident General of the Western Capital (Xījīng Liúshǒu), and Yào Yànchóu (藥彥稠), Commander of the Palace Guard Infantry (Shìwèi Bùjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ), campaigned against him.
On *xīnhài* (辛亥),
Zìtōng (自通) captured Yànwēn (彥溫) and executed him.
On *wùwǔ* (戊午),
the assembled officials presented the honorific title Shèngmíng Shénwǔ Wéndé Gōngxiào Huángdì (聖明神武文德恭孝皇帝).
On *xīnyǒu* (辛酉),
Yú Bōgě (于撥葛), a leader of the Tǔfān (吐蕃), came.
Although Yànwēn (彥溫) was guilty,
there was an order to capture him but not execute him.
Zìtōng (自通) arbitrarily executed him.
Therefore, the text does not record
"suffered the death penalty" (*zhū*)
but records
"executed" (*shā*).
Fifth month, on *dīngchǒu* (丁丑),
Nièlìzǔ (孽栗祖), an envoy from Huíhú (回鶻), came.
On *gēngchén* (庚辰),
Ān Hēilián (安黑連), an envoy from Huíhú (回鶻), came.
Autumn, seventh month, on *rénwǔ* (壬午),
searched for the burial place of Zhuāngzōng's (莊宗) descendants.
That the burial place of Zhuāngzōng's (莊宗) descendants was unknown
shows the calamity suffered by those
who were involved when Míngzōng (明宗) raised troops disobediently. This is lamentable.
To search for it only now
shows that the matter was treated lightly and without compassion.
Eighth month, on *yǐwèi* (乙未),
Zhāng Yánlǎng (張延朗), Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ Army (忠武軍), was made Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsīshǐ).
On *rényín* (壬寅),
Lǐ Xíngdé (李行德), Army Commander of the Běngshèng Capital (Běngshèng Dū Jūnshǐ), and Zhāng Jiǎn (張儉), a Section Commander (Shíjiāng), were executed,
and their clans annihilated.
The Tǔhún (吐渾) came to submit.
His son Cóngróng (從榮) was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín (Qínwáng).
On *wùshēn* (戊申),
Wáng Chuánjí (王傳極), a general in Hǎizhōu (海州), executed its Prefect Chén Xuān (陳宣),
defected from Wú (吳), and surrendered.
On *yǐmǎo* (乙卯),
Kāng Hébì (康合畢) of the Tǔhún (吐渾) came.
On *bǐngchén* (丙辰),
His son Cónghòu (從厚) was enfeoffed as the Prince of Sòng (Sòngwáng).
The position of Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsīshǐ) began here,
and is consequently maintained today.
Ninth month, on *rénxū* (壬戌),
Wáng Mǎnrú (王滿儒), an envoy from the Tǔfān (吐蕃), came.
Dǒng Zhāng (董璋), Military Governor of Dōngchuān (東川), rebelled.
On *jiǎshēn* (甲申),
Fàn Yánguāng (范延光), Military Governor of Chéngdé Army (成德軍), was made Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ).
On *dīnghài* (丁亥),
Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) was made Mobilization Commissioner-in-Chief of the Dōngchuān Campaign Headquarters (Dōngchuān Xíngyíng Dū Zhāotǎoshǐ).
In winter, the tenth month, on the *Dīngyǒu* day,
storage of ice began.
On the *Jiǎchén* day,
Zhāng Jūn (張筠), Senior General of the Valiant Guard (Xiāowèi Shàng Jiāngjūn), who had retired (*zhìshì*), presented military grain.
On the *Yǐsì* day,
Dǒng Zhāng (董璋) captured Làngzhōu (閬州),
and killed the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ), Lǐ Rénjù (李仁矩).
Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ) Yáo Hóng (姚洪) died there.
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) rebelled.
The eleventh month, on the *Gēngshēn* new moon day,
Cóng Róng (從榮), Prince of Qín (Qín Wáng), received the official investiture scroll
and paid respects at the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tài Miào).
On the *Bǐngxū* day,
Tūyù (突欲), Prince of Dōngdān (Dōngdān Wáng) of the Qìdān (契丹), came to defect.
The ceremony of investiture had been neglected during times of chaos,
and was only now carried out for the first time;
therefore, it is recorded.
The barbarians cannot be judged by the standards of rites and righteousness (lǐyì),
therefore, it is not recorded that he "rebelled against the Qìdān."
The twelfth month, on the *Dīngwèi* day,
Yáng Rénjù (楊仁矩), Duke of Xī (Xīguó Gōng), Palace Secretary (Mìshū Chéng), and descendant of the Two Former Dynasties (Èr Wáng Hòu), died.
The court was suspended for one day.
On the *Dīngsì* day,
Zhái Mòsī (翟末斯), envoy of Wáng Rénwáng (王仁裕), the Shùnhuà Khaghan (Shùnhuà Kèhán) of the Huíhú (回鶻), arrived.
Ān Chónghuǐ (安重誨) led an expedition against Dǒng Zhāng (董璋).
Cáo Yìjīn (曹義金) of Shāzhōu (沙州) sent an envoy to arrive.
The name of the general was not given;
the Chief Military Commissioner (Shūmìshǐ) simply proceeded.
The second year, in spring, the first month, on the *Wùchén* day,
Zhé Qīyí (折七移), envoy of the Dǎngxiàng (党項), arrived.
On the *Gēngchén* day,
Liè Liùxuēnángjū (列六薛孃居), envoy of the Dádá (達靼), arrived.
The second month, on the *Dīngyǒu* day,
His Majesty visited Ān Yuánxìn's (安元信) residence.
On the *Wùxū* day,
Dù Āshú (杜阿熟), envoy of the Tūjué (突厥), and Kāng Wànlín (康萬琳), envoy of the Tǔhún (吐渾), arrived.
On the *Xīnchǒu* day,
Ān Chónghuǐ (安重誨) was dismissed.
The third month,
Zhào Fèng (趙鳳) was dismissed.
On the *Dīnghài* day,
Lǐ Yú (李愚), Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng), became Vice Director of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Summer, the fourth month, on the *Jiǎchén* day,
Zhào Yánshòu (趙延壽), Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of Palace Affairs (Xuānhuī Běiyuàn Shǐ), became Chief Military Commissioner (Shūmìshǐ).
On the *Jiǎyín* day,
Dǒng Zhāng (董璋) captured Suízhōu (遂州).
Xià Lǔqí (夏魯奇), Military Commissioner of Wǔxìn Army (Wǔxìn Jūn Jiédùshǐ), died there.
On the *Yǐmǎo* day,
due to drought, prisoners sentenced to exile and lesser crimes were pardoned.
Intercalary fifth month, on the *Dīngyǒu* day,
Ān Chónghuǐ (安重誨), retired Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàishī), along with his wife, Lady Zhāng (Zhāng Shì), and his sons, Chóngzàn (崇贊) and Chóngxù (崇緒), were executed.
Autumn, the eighth month, on the *Jǐwèi* day,
Xiégū'ér (邪姑兒), envoy of the Qìdān (契丹), arrived.
The ninth month, on the *Dīnghài* day,
the eagles and falcons of the Five Bureaus (Wǔ Fāng) were released.
Winter, the eleventh month, on the *Wùshēn* day,
the Tǔfān (吐蕃) sent an envoy.
On the *Xīnchǒu* day,
the household gate of Xíng Zhāo (邢釗), a commoner from Dìzhōu (棣州), was publicly commended and marked.
In an era of war and weapons,
the Kingly Way (Wáng Dào) had ceased and rites and righteousness (lǐyì) were destroyed,
yet the common people still knew how to practice filial piety and fraternity,
and the ruler of the time commended and marked it;
this still served the purpose of encouraging the people,
therefore, because both things were good, it is recorded.
The twelfth month, on the *Jiǎyín* new moon day,
the ban on iron was lifted,
and tax money was newly levied on farm implements.
On the *Jǐwèi* day,
Xīliáng Fǔ (西涼府) sent an envoy.
On the *Jǐsì* day,
Ān Qiúsī (安求思), envoy of the Huíhú (回鶻), arrived.
On the *Xīnwèi* day,
Wénchéng Jué (文成角), envoy of Bóhǎi (渤海), arrived.
The Dǎngxiàng (党項) raided Fāngqú (方渠).
This practice has continued until today;
therefore, it is recorded.
The third year, in spring, the first month, on the *Gēngzǐ* day,
Zhuàigǔ (拽骨), envoy of the Qìdān (契丹), arrived.
On the *Jǐyǒu* day,
both Bóhǎi (渤海) and Huíhú (回鶻) sent envoys.
The second month, on the *Jǐmǎo* day,
Yào Yànchóu (藥彥稠), Military Commissioner of the Jìngnán Army (Jìngnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ), fought the Dǎngxiàng (党項) at Niú'érgǔ (牛兒谷),
and defeated them.
The third month, on the *Jiǎshēn* day,
the Qìdān (契丹) sent an envoy.
Summer, the fourth month, on the *Gēngshēn* day,
Xīnluó (新羅) sent an envoy.
The fifth month, on the *Jǐchǒu* day,
Yáng Yánshào (楊延紹), Palace Steward and Director of the Court (Zhānshì Sīzhí) and descendant of the Two Former Dynasties (Èr Wáng Hòu), inherited the title Duke of Xī (Xīguó Gōng).
On the *Bǐngwǔ* day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) attacked Dǒng Zhāng (董璋),
and captured Miánzhōu (綿州).
The sixth month, on the *Jiǎyín* day,
Wáng Jiàn (王建) was enfeoffed as King of Gāolì (Gāolì Guówáng) and Military Commissioner of the Dàyì Army (Dàyì Jūn Shǐ).
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) killed Dǒng Zhāng (董璋),
and captured Dōngchuān (東川).
Xiégē (頡哥), leader of the Dádá (達靼), arrived with his tribe to submit.
Autumn, the eighth month, on the *Jǐmǎo* day,
the Tǔfān (吐蕃) sent an envoy.
Winter, the tenth month, on the *Gēngshēn* day,
His Majesty visited Shí Jìngtáng's (石敬瑭) residence.
The fourth year, in spring, the first month, on the *Gēngyín* day,

Liú Xù (劉昫), Academician of the Duānmíng Hall (Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì) and Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng), became Vice Director of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōng Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
The second month, on the *Wùwǔ* day,
Zhū Huàng (朱滉), envoy of Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥), arrived.
The Ten Kingdoms (Shí Guó) are treated as outside states and are generally not recorded,
but this entry is recorded because
Zhīxiáng (知祥) was originally a subject of Táng (唐) who rebelled,
and now repented and submitted himself.
To refuse him would suggest that he was not allowed to reform,
but to record it means there was still hope that he might turn toward goodness.
However, when he came,
the protocol for a subject was not fully observed,
therefore, it is recorded in the manner of treating an internal envoy as a barbarian (Yídí).
The third month, on the *Jiǎchén* day,
Lady Xià (Xià Shì), Madame of Jìn (Jìn Guó Fūrén), was posthumously invested as Empress (Huánghòu).
Summer, the fifth month, on the *Wùyín* day,
his son Cóng Kē (從珂) was enfeoffed as Prince of Lù (Lù Wáng),
Cóng Yì (從益) as Prince of Xǔ (Xǔ Wáng),
his nephew Cóng Wēn (從溫) as Prince of Yǎn (Yǎn Wáng),
Cóng Zhāng (從璋) as Prince of Yáng (Yáng Wáng),
and Cóng Mǐn (從敏) as Prince of Jīng (Jīng Wáng).
On the *Bǐngxū* day,
Shùgǔ Qīng (述骨卿), envoy of the Qìdān (契丹), arrived.
Cóng Kē (從珂) was not his son,
yet he is recorded
as "son,"
which is the same as the case of Yǒuwén (友文), Prince of Bó (Bó Wáng) of Liáng (梁).
