Autumn, the seventh month, on the *Yǐwèi* day,
Lǐ Mò (李末), Governor-General (*dūdū*) of the Huíhú (回鶻), arrived.
He presented a white falcon (báihú);
an order was given to release it.
The eighth month, on the *Wùshēn* day,
a general amnesty was issued.
The ninth month, on the *Wùxū* day,
Zhào Yánshòu (趙延壽) was dismissed.
Zhū Hóngzhāo (朱弘昭), Military Commissioner of Shānnán Dōng Dào (Shānnán Dōng Dào Jiédùshǐ), became Chief Military Commissioner (Shūmìshǐ).
Winter, the tenth month, on the *Gēngshēn* day,
Fàn Yánguāng (范延光) was dismissed.
Féng Yūn (馮贇), Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī Shǐ), became Chief Military Commissioner (Shūmìshǐ).
On the *Rénshēn* day,
His Majesty visited Shìhétíng (士和亭),
and became ill.
The record
of "became ill"
provides detail regarding Cóng Róng's (從榮) affair.
The eleventh month, on the *Rénchén* day,
Cóng Róng (從榮), Prince of Qín (Qín Wáng), entered the Xīngshèng Palace (Xīngshèng Gōng) with troops,
failed to succeed,
and was executed.
On the *Yǐwèi* day,
Kāng Yìchéng (康義誠), Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Army (Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ), killed Sūn Yuè (孫岳), Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī Shǐ).
On the *Wùxū* day,
the Emperor died in the Yōnghé Palace (Yōnghé Diàn).
When the sovereign was ill, he did not attend him,
but sought to install himself using military force.
His crime warranted execution,
therefore, it is recorded
as "was executed."
The intent [of Cóng Róng] was likely that he believed the Emperor had already died,
and fearing he would not be enthroned,
he raised troops to help himself;
this was not rebellion,
therefore, the word "rebelled" is not recorded.
He was sixty-seven years old.
In the first year of Qīngtài (清泰),
he was buried in Luòyáng County (Luòyáng Xiàn), Hénán (河南),
and his tomb was named Huī Líng (徽陵).
Although he met his natural death,
he was buried by the traitors;
therefore, the burial is also not recorded [as an official rite].
Alas!
Since ancient times, periods of good governance have been few and periods of chaos many!
Among the kings of the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài) who possessed the world,
all reigned for several hundred years,
yet those who are worthy of mention
are but a few sovereigns;
how much more so in later ages!
How much more so during the Five Dynasties (Wǔ Dài)!
I heard an elder tell me:
“Míngzōng, although of barbarian origin,
was pure and simple in character,
magnanimous and kind to people.”
Among the rulers of the Five Dynasties,
he is worthy of praise.
He once burned incense at night,
looked up to Heaven and prayed, saying:
“I am but a barbarian,
how am I fit to govern the world!
The world has been in chaos for a long time,
I pray that Heaven will soon give birth to a sage.”
From the beginning of his reign,
he reduced and dismissed palace women and musicians;
he abolished the imperial treasury,
and all tribute from the four quarters
was handed over to the relevant authorities.
When Guǎngshòu Diàn suffered a fire,
the authorities dealt with it,
and requested to add paint and vermilion.
He sighed profoundly and said:
“Heaven uses fire to warn me,
how can I increase extravagance and debauchery!”
One year it was drought,
and then it snowed.
He sat exposed in the courtyard,
and ordered the Wǔdé Sī that no snow should be swept in the palace,
saying:
“This is what Heaven has bestowed upon me.”
He frequently asked Prime Minister Féng Dào and others about the people's hardships.
When Dào and others said that grain and silk were cheap,
and the people suffered no epidemics,
he rejoiced and said:
“How can I bear this,
I should do good deeds with you,
to repay Heaven above.”
If an official committed embezzlement,
he would immediately put him to death,
saying:
“These are the pests of the people!”
He issued an imperial edict to commend honest officials like Sūn Yuè,
to serve as an example for the world.
His love for people and care for all creatures
indeed showed his intention to govern well.
When he ascended the throne,
he was already advanced in years,
not indulging in music and women,
nor enjoying hunting.
He reigned for seven years,
among the rulers of the Five Dynasties,
it was the longest reign.
Military conflicts largely ceased,
and the years saw abundant harvests,
the common people truly relied on this for peace and recovery.
However, being of barbarian nature, he was resolute,
benevolent but not discerning,
repeatedly executing ministers and subordinates without just cause.
As for the relationship between Cóngróng and his father,
he failed to foresee danger and take precautions,
and a sudden upheaval arose,
ultimately trapping him in a great evil,
and the Emperor also died with regret because of this.
At that time,
Kāng Chéng, the Junior Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, submitted a memorial on current affairs.
His words were:
“For those who govern a nation, there are five things not to fear,
and six things to greatly fear: The misalignment of the three luminaries is not to be feared;
the manifestation of celestial anomalies is not to be feared;
the misleading rumors of petty people are not to be feared;
mountain collapses and rivers drying up are not to be feared;
droughts, floods, insects, and locusts are not to be feared;
but the hiding of worthy scholars is deeply to be feared;
the change of occupation of the four classes of people is deeply to be feared;
collusion between superiors and subordinates is deeply to be feared;
the decline of integrity and shame is deeply to be feared;
the confusion of true and false by praise and blame is deeply to be feared;
and the unheard straight words are deeply to be feared.”
Those with insight all praised Chéng's words as sharply hitting the ailments of the time.
Such as the rebellion of Cóngróng,
and the deaths of Rèn Yuán, Ān Chónghuì, and others,
can be called the弊 of superiors and subordinates colluding,
and praise and blame confusing true and false.
However, Chéng's words
are not just about the ailments of one era;
for all who govern a nation,
how can they not take heed!
Collation Notes
The Tǔhún Dūdū Lǐ Shàolǔ: Volume 74 of the main history, in the appendix on the Four Barbarians, records: There was a Tǔhún chieftain named Bái Chéngfú,
whom Táng Zhuāngzōng appointed as Dūdū of the Níngshuò and Fènghuà Prefectures,
and bestowed upon him the surname and given name Lǐ Shàolǔ.
Xué Shǐ, volume 39, the Chronicle of Táng Míngzōng, also states
“appointed Lǐ Shàolǔ, the Dū Zhī Bīngmǎ Shǐ of the Tǔhún Níngshuò and Fènghuà Prefectures, as the Tǔhún Níngshuò Fǔ Dūdū.”
This is presumably the same person.
Chronicle of Táng, Part Seven
Emperor Mǐn,
Míngzōng's fifth son, Cónghòu.
He was of ample physique,
spoke little, and was fond of propriety.
Míngzōng particularly loved him because his appearance resembled his own.
In Tiānchéng second year,
he was appointed Hénán Yǐn and concurrent judge of the affairs of the Six Armies and all Guards, with the title of Jiǎnjiào Sītú,
and later promoted to Jiǎnjiào Tàibǎo and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Cónghòu's consort
was the daughter of Kǒng Xún.
Ān Chónghuì was angry at Xún for giving his daughter to Cónghòu as wife.
In the third year,
Xún was dismissed as Pímìshǐ,
and Cónghòu was sent out as the Jiédùshǐ of Xuānwǔ Jūn.
The following year,
he was moved to govern Hédōng.
In Chángxīng first year,
Cónghòu was enfeoffed as Sòng Wáng,
and moved to govern Chéngdé.
In the second year,
he was moved to govern Tiānxíong,
and repeatedly promoted to concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year,
Qín Wáng Cóngróng was executed.
Míngzōng was gravely ill
and sent the eunuch Mèng Hànqióng to summon the King at Yè,
but Míngzōng died,
and his death was kept secret for six days.
On the first day of the twelfth month, Guǐmǎo,
the mourning was announced at the West Palace,
and the Emperor ascended the throne before the coffin,
the officials paid homage from the east steps,
and then returned to their mourning positions.
On Bǐngwǔ,
the mourning attire was completed at the West Palace.
On Gēngxū,
he ascended the Guāngzhèng Mén tower
to inquire after the well-being of the military and civilians.
On Xīnhài,
he executed Sīyī Wáng shì.
On Guǐchǒu,
he began to attend to government affairs.
On Yǐmǎo,
he executed Sīyí Kāng shì.
On Dīngsì,
Féng Dào was appointed as the mountain tomb commissioner for the late Emperor,
Hùbù Shàngshū Hán Yànhùn as deputy,
Zhōngshū Shèrén Wáng Yán as registrar,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Wáng Quán as ceremonial commissioner,
Bīngbù Shàngshū Lǐ Lín as imperial carriage commissioner,
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Lóng Mǐn as ceremonial guard commissioner,
and Zuǒ Púyè, acting Hénán Fǔ magistrate Lú Zhì, as bridge and postal relay commissioner.
On Dīngmǎo,
the final mourning rites were performed.
Among the five rulers of the Second Dynasty,
this is the first instance of a successor ascending the throne and observing mourning rites.
The late sovereign achieved his end,
and the successor attained his beginning,
thus averting disaster and rebellion among ministers and common people.
In an era of usurpation and chaos,
such events are rarely seen,
hence they are specifically detailed here.
In the spring, the first month, Rénshēn, the first day of Yìngshùn first year,
he held court at Guǎngshòu Diàn.
On Yǐhài,
the Qìdān envoy Dūdū Mòlàwū came.
On Wùyín,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
the era name was changed,
and music was used.
The Uighur Khagan Wáng Rénměi sent envoys.
Shāzhōu and Guāzhōu sent envoys.
On Yǐwèi,
Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yún offered money to assist in building the imperial tomb.
This is recorded as improper.
In the intercalary month, Bǐngwǔ,
the Empress Dowager was formally invested.
On Jiǎyín,
Consort Wáng shì was formally invested.
Běijīng Liúshǒu Shí Jìngtáng offered silver and silk to assist in building the imperial tomb.
The text does not state the family name
nor explicitly say "invested so-and-so as Empress Dowager"
because the mother's dignity forbids direct mention,
and the event is self-evident in the chronicles.
In the second month, Gēngyín,
he inspected the construction of the imperial tomb.
Lù Wáng Cóngkē, Jiédùshǐ of Fèngxiáng, rebelled.
On Xīnmǎo,
Wáng Sītóng, Liúshǒu of Xījīng, was appointed Dū Bùshǔ of the Western Campaigning Army,
and Yào Yànchóu, Jiédùshǐ of Jìngnán Jūn, as his deputy.
On the day bingchén in the third month,
Sī-Tóng's army collapsed.
Yán Wèi Circulatory Commissioner Yǐn Huī and Yǔ Lín Circulatory Commissioner Yáng Sī-Quán rebelled with their troops and surrendered to Cóng-Kē.
On the day xīnyǒu,
Zhu Hóng-Shí, Commissioner-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards, was killed.
On the day guǐhài,
Kāng Yì-Chéng, Jìedùshǐ of Heyang San Cheng, was made Commissioner-in-Chief of the Fèngxiáng Expeditionary Army,
and Wáng Sī-Tóng was made his deputy.
Liú Suì-Yǒng, Vice Left-overseer of Xījīng, rebelled and surrendered to Cóng-Kē.
Sī-Tóng fled back to the capital,
but did not succeed,
and died there.
On the day dīngmǎo,
Ān Cóng-Jìn, Inspector of the Capital City, rebelled,
killed Féng Yūn,
and Zhū Hóng-Zhāo committed suicide.
Cóng-Jìn sent their two heads to Cóng-Kē.
On the day wùchén,
[the Emperor] went to Wèizhōu.
The Emperor's collapse is not recorded here
because the assassination of Èwáng should be recorded in the Annals of the Deposed Emperor.
The Deposed Emperor
was from Píngshān, Zhènzhōu.
His original surname was Wáng.
His family was of humble origin.
His mother, Lady Wèi,
became a widow young.
Míngzōng, then a cavalry general,
passed through Píngshān
and captured her.
Lady Wèi had a son, Āsān,
already over ten years old.
Míngzōng adopted him as his son,
and named him Cóng-Kē.
When he grew up,
he was imposing in appearance,
cautious and reticent,
but brave and skilled in battle.
Míngzōng loved him very much.
From the time the Jìn army fought the Liáng at the river,
Cóng-Kē often achieved military success.
Zhuāngzōng called him by his childhood name, saying:
"Āsān not only is my age,
but his bravery in battle is also like mine."
In the second year of Tóngguāng,
he became the Cìshǐ and Tuqí Commander of Wèizhōu,
stationed at Shímén.
When Míngzōng was campaigning against Zhào Zài-Lǐ,
and rebelled from Wèi to the south,
Cóng-Kē led his garrison troops from Qǔyáng and Méngxiàn to Chángshān to pursue Míngzōng.
When Míngzōng moved south,
his troops were few.
With Cóng-Kē's troops following,
the army's morale greatly improved.
When Míngzōng entered and ascended the throne,
he appointed Cóng-Kē as Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng,
and enfeoffed him as Lùwáng.
At this time,
Míngzōng was already advanced in age,
and the Prince was the eldest among his sons.
Pīmìshǐ Ān Chóng-Huì was concerned about this,
so he forged an imperial edict to Yang Yàn-Wēn, a subordinate general in Hézhōng, to plot against him.
When the Prince was reviewing horses at Huánglóngzhuāng,
Yàn-Wēn immediately closed the gates and resisted him.
The Prince stopped at Yúxiāng and reported this.
Míngzōng summoned the Prince back to the capital,
and housed him in his residence in Qīnghuàlǐ.
Chóng-Huì repeatedly requested that military law be applied,
but Míngzōng did not listen.
Later, Chóng-Huì was killed,
and then the Prince was appointed as Grand General of the Left Guard and Left-overseer of Xījīng.
In the third year of Chángxīng,
he was made Jìedùshǐ of Fèngxiáng.
The Prince's son, Chóng-Jí, had commanded imperial guards since Míngzōng's time,
serving as Kònghè Circulatory Commissioner.
When Mǐndì ascended the throne,
Zhū Hóng-Zhāo and Féng Yūn gained power,
and so Chóng-Jí's military post was removed,
and he was sent out as Tuánliànshǐ of Bózhōu.
The Prince was also transferred to be Left-overseer of Běijīng,
but the imperial edict was not issued, only proclaimed.
Lǐ Cóng-Zhāng was then made his replacement.
Originally,
when Ān Chóng-Huì fell into disgrace and was dismissed from Hézhōng,
Cóng-Zhāng was made his replacement.
And Chóng-Huì was killed.
Therefore, the Prince grew increasingly suspicious,
and consequently occupied the city and rebelled.
Mǐndì dispatched Wáng Sī-Tóng to assemble troops from various garrisons to suppress him.
Sī-Tóng was defeated and fled,
and all the garrison troops collapsed.
On the day dīngsì in the third month of the first year of Qīngtài,
the Prince marched his army east.
On the day gēngshēn,
he reached Cháng'ān.
Liú Suì-Yǒng, Vice Left-overseer of Xījīng, rebelled against Táng
and surrendered.
On the day jiǎzǐ,
he reached Huázhōu,
and arrested Yào Yàn-Chóu.
On the day bǐngyín,
he reached Língbǎo.
Ān Yàn-Wēi of Hézhōng and Kāng Sī-Lì of Shǎnzhōu rebelled against Táng
and surrendered.
On the day jǐsì,
he reached Shǎn.
Kāng Yì-Chéng rebelled against Táng
and surrendered.
Xuānhuīshǐ Mèng Hàn-Qióng was killed.
Mǐndì moved to Wèizhōu.
On the day rénshēn in the fourth month of summer,
[the Prince] entered the capital.
Féng Dào led the hundred officials to welcome the Prince at Jiǎngqiáo,
but the Prince declined to see them.
He entered and wept in the Western Palace,
then met with the officials.
Dào bowed,
and the Prince returned the bow.
He moved into the Zhìdé Palace.
On the day guǐyǒu,
by order of the Empress Dowager, the Son of Heaven was demoted to Èwáng,
and the Prince was ordered to supervise the state.
On the day yǐhài,
the Emperor ascended the throne.
On the day bǐngzǐ,
wealth from the people of Hénán was used to reward the army.
On the day dīngchǒu,
a five-month tax on people's rental properties was borrowed to reward the army.
On the day wùyín,
Èwáng was assassinated.
Sòng Lìng-Xún, Cìshǐ of Cízhōu, died.
On the day yǐyǒu,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
On the day wùzǐ,
Kāng Yì-Chéng and Yào Yàn-Chóu were killed.
The meaning
is the same as "assassinated the King of Jìnyīn."
Yì-Chéng rebelled against Mǐndì,
so his crime should be described as "executed."
However, the Deposed Emperor killed a fellow evil-doer,
so it is recorded as "killed."
On the day bǐngwǔ in the fifth month,
Hán Zhāo-Yìn, Scholar of the Duānmíng Hall and Left Remonstrance Official, was made Pīmìshǐ.
Liú Yán-Lǎng, Zhūangzhái Envoy, was made Deputy Pīmìshǐ.
On the day gēngxū,
Féng Dào was dismissed.
Fàn Yán-Guāng, Jìedùshǐ of Tiānxíong Commandery, was made Pīmìshǐ.
On the day jiǎyín,
officials were granted to those who urged the Emperor to ascend and to imperial clan members.
On the day gēngchén in the sixth month,
[the Emperor] visited the residences of Fàn Yán-Guāng and Suǒ Zì-Tōng.
On the day xīnhài in the seventh month of autumn,
Lú Wén-Jì, Táicháng Qīng, was made Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì.
On the day dīngsì,
Lady Liú of Pèiguó was established as Empress.
On the day xīnwèi in the eighth month,
Yáo Yǐ, Shàngshū Zuǒchéng, was made Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì.
Permission was granted for imperial appointment of officials.
"Imperial appointment of officials"
likely refers to officials appointed by the Deposed Emperor when he first raised his army.
Since they were not officially appointed by the Ministry of Personnel,
an imperial decree was required for them to be eligible for selection.
This has no encouraging or admonishing significance for historical events
and need not be recorded.
However, since older histories are unclear,
what is unknown is preserved
to transmit doubts cautiously.
In the ninth month,
the Qìdān raided the border.
On the day wùyín in the tenth month of winter,
Lǐ Yú and Liú Xù were dismissed.
On the day yǐhài in the twelfth month,
Zhāng Yán-Lǎng, Jìedùshǐ of Xióngwǔ Commandery, was made Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì.
The Qìdān raided Yúnzhōu.
On the day gēngyín,
[the Emperor] visited Lóngmén.
There was a drought.
On the day jiǎxū in the second month of spring in the second year,
Fàn Yán-Guāng was dismissed.
On the day jǐchǒu,
Lady Wèi, Grand Madam of the State of Lǔ, was posthumously honored as Empress Dowager.
As she was not his biological mother,
her title and surname are detailed.
On the day xīnchǒu in the third month,
Zhào Yán-Shòu, Jìedùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ Commandery, was made Pīmìshǐ.
On the day xīnmǎo in the fifth month of summer,
Liú Yán-Hào, Xuānhuī Southern Court Envoy, was made Pīmìshǐ.
The Qìdān raided the border.
On the day guǐwèi in the sixth month,
officials presented additional horses for the army.
"Dū"
refers to a military unit.
Fèidì (The Deposed Emperor)
was a person from Píngshān, Zhènzhōu.
His original surname was Wáng.
His lineage was humble and lowly.
His mother, née Wèi,
became a widow early.
When Míngzōng was a cavalry general,
he passed Píngshān
and seized her (Wèi Shì).
Wèi Shì had a son, Āsān,
who was already over ten years old.
Míngzōng adopted him as his son
and named him Cóngkē (Lǐ Cóngkē).
When he grew up,
his appearance was imposing and majestic.
He was cautious, trustworthy, and spoke little,
but he was fierce, brave, and good at fighting.
Míngzōng loved him greatly.
Since the Jìn army fought the Liáng along the river,
Cóngkē constantly established military achievements.
Zhuāngzōng called him by his nickname, saying:
"Āsān is not only the same age as I,
but his daring in battle is also like mine."
In Tóngguāng 2nd year (924 CE),
he served as the Commander of Elite Cavalry and Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Wèizhōu,
garrisoned at Shímén.
When Míngzōng attacked Zhào Zàilǐ,
and his soldiers at Wèi mutinied and went south,
Cóngkē led his garrison troops from Qǔyáng and Yùxiàn, speeding out of Chángshān to pursue Míngzōng.
When Míngzōng went south,
his troops were few.
When he gained Cóngkē's troops in the rear,
his military prestige greatly increased.
When Míngzōng entered and established himself (as emperor),
he appointed Cóngkē as Jiedushi of Hézhōng,
and enfeoffed him as King Lù (Lù Wáng).
At that time,
Míngzōng was already advanced in years,
and the King was the eldest among the sons (in order of birth).
The Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ), Ān Chónghuǐ, worried about this,
and therefore falsely issued an edict to Yáng Yànwēn, the Deputy General of Hézhōng, ordering him to plot against him (the King).
When the King was reviewing his horses at Huánglóngzhuāng,
Yànwēn immediately closed the gates and resisted him.
The King stopped at Yúxiāng and reported the situation.
Míngzōng summoned the King back to the capital
and had him reside at the Qīnghuàlǐ residence.
Chónghuǐ repeatedly requested the execution of military law (against the King),
but Míngzōng did not consent.
Later, Chónghuǐ was killed.
Subsequently, the King was raised to be Grand General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Dàjiāngjūn) and Resident Commissioner of the Western Capital (Xījīng Liúshǒu).
In Chángxīng 3rd year (932 CE),
he became Jiedushi of Fèngxiáng.
The King's son, Chóngjí, had commanded the Imperial Guards since Míngzōng’s time,
serving as Commander of the Crane-Controlling Guards (Kònghè Zhǐhuīshǐ).
When Mǐndì (The Lamented Emperor) ascended the throne,
Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yūn held power.
They subsequently dismissed Chóngjí from his military post
and sent him out to be the Commandant (Tuánliànshǐ) of Bózhōu.
Furthermore, they moved the King to be Resident Commissioner of the Northern Capital (Běijīng Liúshǒu).
They did not issue an imperial edict but merely declared the appointment,
and further appointed Lǐ Cóngzhāng as his replacement (at Fèngxiáng).
Previously,
when Ān Chónghuǐ incurred guilt and was dismissed from Hézhōng,
Cóngzhāng was appointed as his replacement,
and later Chónghuǐ was killed.
Therefore, the King became increasingly suspicious of himself (his fate),
and consequently seized the city and rebelled.
Mǐndì sent Wáng Sītóng to gather the troops of various circuits to attack him.
Sītóng was defeated in battle and fled,
and the troops of all the circuits scattered.
In Qīngtài 1st year (934 CE), 3rd month, on the Dīngsì day,
the King marched his troops east.
On the Gēngshēn day,
he reached Cháng’ān.
Liú Suìyōng, the Deputy Resident Commissioner of the Western Capital, rebelled against the Táng
and surrendered.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
he reached Huàzhōu
and arrested Yào Yànchóu.
On the Bǐngyín day,
he reached Língbǎo.
Ān Yànwēi of Hézhōng and Kāng Sīlì of Shǎnzhōu rebelled against the Táng
and surrendered.
On the Jǐsì day,
he reached Shǎn.
Kāng Yìchéng rebelled against the Táng
and surrendered.
Mèng Hànqióng, the Commissioner of Palace Affairs (Xuānhuīshǐ), was killed.
Mǐndì departed to reside at Wèizhōu.
In summer, 4th month, on the Rénshēn day,
he entered the capital.
Féng Dào led the numerous officials to welcome the King at Jiǎngqiáo,
but the King declined to meet them.
He entered and wept at the Western Palace,
and then met the officials.
Dào bowed,
and the King returned the bow.
He entered and resided in Zhìdé Palace.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
by order of the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu), the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) was demoted to King È (È Wáng),
and the King (Lǐ Cóngkē) was ordered to oversee the state.
On the Yǐhài day,
the Emperor ascended the throne.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
the wealth of the people of Hénán was commandeered to reward the army.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
the tax revenues from civilian housing were appropriated for five months to reward the army.
On the Wùyín day,
King È was assassinated.
Sòng Lìngxún, the Prefect of Cízhōu, died (with him).
On the Yǐyǒu day,
there was a general amnesty
and the reign title was changed.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Kāng Yìchéng and Yào Yànchóu were killed.
The meaning is the same as
"assassinated the King of Jìnyīn (Jìyīn Wáng)."
Yìchéng rebelled against Mǐndì,
so the offense ought to be called
"execution" (zhū).
However, Fèidì killed a fellow wrongdoer,
thus the record states
"killed" (shā).
5th month, on the Bǐngwǔ day,
Hán Zhāoyìn, Grand Academician of the Duānmíng Hall and Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left, was made Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Liú Yánlǎng, Commissioner of Palaces and Residences (Zhuāngzháishǐ), was made Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs.
On the Gēngxū day,
Féng Dào was dismissed.
Fàn Yánguāng, Jiedushi of Tiānxíong Army, was made Commissioner of Military Affairs.
On the Jiǎyín day,
officials were granted to those selected for their efforts in urging the Emperor to advance (to the throne) and to members of the imperial clan (Zōngzǐ).
6th month, on the Gēngchén day,
the Emperor visited the residences of Fàn Yánguāng and Suǒ Zìtōng.
Autumn, 7th month, on the Xīnhài day,
Lú Wénjì, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng), was made Vice Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
On the Dīngsì day,
Madame Liú of Pèiguó was established as Empress (Huánghòu).
8th month, on the Xīnwèi day,
Yáo Yǐ, Left Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng), was made Vice Director of the Chancellery and Grand Councilor.
Approval was granted for selecting officials appointed by imperial signature (Yùshǔ Guān).
"Yùshǔ Guān" (Officials appointed by imperial signature),
is likely an official position established by Fèidì when he first raised his army.
Because these were not officially conferred by the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù),
a special decree was required before they could be selected (for regular posts).
This matter offers neither encouragement nor warning,
and does not necessarily need to be recorded.
However, as the older histories are not detailed (on this point),
what is unknown is preserved,
so as to be careful in transmitting doubts.
9th month,
the Qìdān plundered the frontier.
Winter, 10th month, on the Wùyín day,
Lǐ Yú and Liú Xù were dismissed.
12th month, on the Yǐhài day,
Zhāng Yánlǎng, Jiedushi of Xióngwǔ Army, was made Vice Director of the Chancellery and Grand Councilor.
The Qìdān plundered Yúnzhōu.
On the Gēngyín day,
the Emperor visited Lóngmén.
There was a drought.
2nd year (935 CE), spring, 2nd month, on the Jiǎxū day,
Fàn Yánguāng was dismissed.
On the Jǐchǒu day,
Madame Wèi, Grand Madam of the State of Lǔ (Lǔguó Tàifūrén), was posthumously honored as Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
She was not the legal wife (Dímǔ),
hence her title and clan name are detailed.
3rd month, on the Xīnchǒu day,
Zhào Yánshòu, Jiedushi of Zhōngwǔ Army, was made Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Summer, 5th month, on the Xīnmǎo day,
Liú Yánhào, Commissioner of the Southern Division of Palace Affairs (Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ), was made Commissioner of Military Affairs.
The Qìdān plundered the frontier.
6th month, on the Guǐwèi day,
the officials presented Tiāndū horses.
Dū
refers to
a name used in the military ranks.
Autumn, 7th month, on the Dīngyǒu day,
Wáng Rénměi, the Khagan of the Huíhú (Uygurs), sent his Commander (Dūdu) Chén Fúhǎi to come (as envoy).
Liú Yánhào was dismissed.
9th month, on the Jǐyǒu day,
Fáng Gǎo, Minister of the Board of Punishments (Xíngbù Shàngshū), was made Commissioner of Military Affairs.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
Bóhǎi sent an envoy to come.
3rd year (936 CE), spring, 1st month, on the Yǐwèi day,
Bǎijì (Baekje) sent an envoy to come.
On the Dīngwèi day,
his son, Chóngměi, was enfeoffed as King Yōng (Yōng Wáng).
3rd month, on the Bǐngwǔ day,
Mǎ Yìnsūn, Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of the Board of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng), was made Vice Director of the Chancellery and Grand Councilor.
Shí Jìngtáng, Jiedushi of Hédōng, rebelled.
In the summer, the fifth month, on the *Yǐmǎo* day,
Zhāng Jìngdá, Jìanxióng Jūn Jìedùshǐ, was appointed Supreme Commander of the Four Fronts of Tàiyuán,
with Yáng Guāngyuǎn, Yìwǔ Jūn Jìedùshǐ, as his deputy.
On the *Wùshēn* day,
Ān Shěn Xìn, Commander of the Vanguards, defected and surrendered to Shí Jìngtáng.
On the *Jǐyǒu* day,
Ān Chóngróng, Garrison General of Zhènwǔ, defected and surrendered to Shí Jìngtáng.
On the *Rénzǐ* day,
Zhāng Lìngzhāo, Commander of the Běngshèng Capital Vanguard stationed in Tiānxíong Jūn, drove out his Jìedùshǐ, Líu Yánhào.
In the sixth month, on the *Gǔihài* day,
Lìngzhāo was made Yòu Qiānniú Wèi Jīangjūn,
temporarily overseeing the affairs of Tiānxíong Jūn.
On the *Jǐaxū* day,
Fàn Yánguāng, Xuānwǔ Jūn Jìedùshǐ, was made Supreme Commander of the Four Fronts of Tiānxíong Jūn.
When appointing other officials, the character
‘*yǐ*’ (to appoint) is not written.
That it is written
here,
makes clear that Lìngzhāo was still considered fit
to be ‘*yǐ*’ (appointed).
In autumn, the seventh month, on the *Wùshēn* day,
Wèizhōu was conquered.
On the *Rénzǐ* day,
Zhāng Lìngzhāo was executed.
On the *Gǔichǒu* day,
Zhāng Wàndí, Commander of Zhāngshèng, defected and surrendered to Shí Jìngtáng.
In the eighth month, on the *Wùmǎo* day,
Mèilí, an envoy from Qìdān, arrived.
In the ninth month, on the *Jǐachén* day,
Zhāng Jìngdá fought against Qìdān at Tàiyuán.
He suffered a complete defeat,
and Qìdān besieged Jìngdá at Jìn’ān.
On the *Wùshēn* day,
went to Héyáng.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *Rénxū* day,
horses were requisitioned,
and common people were registered for military service.
In the eleventh month, on the *Wùzǐ* day,
Zhào Déjūn, Lúlóng Jūn Jìedùshǐ, was made Supreme Commander of the Field Army.
On the *Dīngyǒu* day,
Qìdān established Jìn.
In the intercalary month, on the *Jǐazǐ* day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn killed Zhāng Jìngdá,
and defected with his army to Qìdān.
On the *Jǐaxū* day,
Qìdān and the Jìn people arrived at Lùzhōu.
On the *Dīngchǒu* day,
arrived from Héyáng.
On the *Xīnsì* day,
The Emperor died.
Regarding Jìngdá, that it does not record his death but records
“killed”
is because,
Jìngdá was a great general.
It was proper to hold Guāngyuǎn accountable by justice and execute him,
but although this was not carried out and he was killed,
it was still considered an honorable death.
He thus hinted for Guāngyuǎn to kill him in order to defect,
so it is recorded according to his wish.
He was fifty-one years old.
The Emperor immolated himself and died.
Jìn Gāozǔ ordered his cremated remains to be buried within the precinct of Huī Líng.
Alas!
The relationship between ruler and minister,
can truly be called difficult!
For the wise foresee the danger before it sprouts and know it beforehand,
while the foolish, though warned that calamity approaches, are not afraid.
Therefore, if one speaks before the event occurs,
although loyal, one is not believed.
If one repents when the event arrives,
how can it be remedied?
Chónghuǐ alone clearly saw the disaster involving the Prince of Lù,
but his plan was not good,
leading to his own death and the extermination of his clan.
The rift began here.
When Emperor Mǐn died,
he was interred in a pit at Huī Líng,
with a single mound of earth.
Passersby who saw it
all grieved for him.
If Míngzōng possessed awareness (in the afterlife),
he would surely be ashamed before Chónghuǐ.
How sorrowful!
Basic Annals of Jìn, Part Eighth
Gāozǔ Shèngwén Zhāngwǔ Míngdé Xiào Huángdì,
his father was Nìelì Jī.
He originally came from the Western Barbarians.
When Zhū Yé submitted to Táng,
he followed Zhū Yé and settled in Yīnshān.
Afterwards,
Lǐ Kèyòng, the Prince of Jìn, rose up in the area between Yún and Shuò.
Nìelì Jī, being skilled in horsemanship and archery,
often followed the Prince of Jìn on campaigns and achieved merit.
His office reached the level of Míngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Nìelì Jī begat Jìngtáng.
His surname was Shí.
The origin of how he acquired this surname is unknown.
Jìngtáng was a man of profound gravity and few words.
Míngzōng loved him,
and gave him his daughter as wife.
She was Yǒngníng Gōngzhǔ.
Consequently, he was always attached to Míngzōng’s command,
known as Zuǒshè Jūn (Left Archery Army).
When Zhuāngzōng had already secured Wèi,
Líu Xún, a general of Líang, urgently attacked Qīngpíng.
Zhuāngzōng rushed to relieve it,
but before his troops could form a line of battle,
they were ambushed by Xún.
Jìngtáng, with about ten cavalrymen, rode forward, leveled his lance, and attacked fiercely,
then snatched back the position and returned.
Zhuāngzōng clapped him on the back and praised his valor,
and personally fed him *sū* (ghee/butter).
Feeding *sū*
was highly valued by the Yi-Di (Barbarians).
From this, his reputation spread throughout the army.
In the fifteenth year,
when Zhuāngzōng fought at Húliǔ,
Zhōu Déwēi, the vanguard, was killed in battle.
Jìngtáng, leading the Zuǒshè Jūn under Míngzōng, counterattacked and defeated the Líang forces.
When Míngzōng fought at Húlútào and Yángcūn,
he was defeated by the Líang forces,
but Jìngtáng constantly rescued Míngzōng from danger.
During the rebellion of Zhào Zàilǐ,
Míngzōng campaigned against him.
When he reached Wèi, the soldiers mutinied.
Míngzōng initially wished to return himself to the Son of Heaven,
to prove that he had not intended to rebel.
Jìngtáng offered a strategy, saying:
“How can a military mutiny occur outside,
and the Supreme General alone be spared?
Moreover, hesitation is the greatest taboo in warfare.
It is better to act quickly.
I request three hundred cavalry to first attack Bìanzhōu.
Yímén is a vital strategic point in the realm;
if we secure it, we can achieve success.”
Míngzōng agreed,
and gave him three hundred elite cavalry.
He crossed Líyáng as the vanguard.
Míngzōng then entered Bìan.
Zhuāngzōng arrived later from Luò,
but could not enter,
and all his troops scattered and fled.
As Zhuāngzōng returned west,
Míngzōng made Jìngtáng the vanguard to proceed quickly to Sìshuǐ,
and also to gather the scattered soldiers.
Zhuāngzōng was assassinated.
Míngzōng entered and ascended the throne.
He appointed Jìngtáng Bǎoyì Jūn Jìedùshǐ,
and granted him the title
“Meritorious Official Who Exerted Loyalty, Proposed Strategy, and Restored the State,”
concurrently serving as Deputy Commissioner of the Six Armies and Various Guards.
While governing Shǎn, he became renowned for his integrity.
At this time,
many regional commanders disregarded the law.
Táo of Dèngzhōu and Lǐ Yè of Bózhōu were both sentenced to death for corruption.
Míngzōng issued an imperial edict commending honest officials like Ān Chóngruǎn of Pǔzhōu, Zhāng Wànjìn of Míngzhōu, and Sūn Yuè of Yàozhōu, to serve as a cautionary example to the realm,
and designated Jìngtáng as the foremost example.
In the tenth month of Tiānchéng second year (927 CE),
he accompanied the Emperor to Bìanzhōu.
He was made Imperial Camp Commissioner,
appointed Xuānwǔ Jūn Jìedùshǐ, and Supreme Commander of the Cavalry and Infantry of the Imperial Guards;
his post as Deputy Commissioner of the Six Armies remained as before.
His granted title was changed to
“Meritorious Official Who Displayed Loyalty, Aided Stability, and Maintained Integrity.”
In the fourth month of the third year (928 CE),
he was transferred to govern Tiānxíong,
and appointed Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì and Xīngtáng Yǐn.
In the fifth month,
he was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (Son-in-law Commandant).
When Dǒng Zhāng rebelled in Dōngchuān,
Jìngtáng was made Supreme Commander of the Field Army for the Campaign,
but returned without success.
He resumed his concurrent post as Deputy Commissioner of the Six Armies and Various Guards.
He was transferred to govern Hèyáng Sānchéng,
but before he departed,
Qìdān, Tǔhún, and Tūjué all invaded.
At this time,
Qín Wáng Cóngróng commanded the Six Armies.
Jìngtáng suspected that Cóngróng would inevitably face disaster,
and did not wish to serve as his deputy,
so he personally requested permission to proceed (to Hèyáng).
When the edict was issued,
the title of Deputy Commissioner was not dropped.
He promptly declined the transfer again.
Míngzōng repeatedly questioned his senior officials, asking who could take the post.
Fàn Yánguāng, Zhào Yánshòu, and others eventually nominated Jìngtáng for the request.
He was then appointed Hédōng Jìedùshǐ, and Supreme Commander of the Barbarian and Han Cavalry and Infantry of the Dàtóng, Zhāngguó, Zhènwǔ, and Wēisài Armies,
and the post of Deputy Commissioner of the Six Armies was dropped.
Then he departed.
The following year,
Míngzōng died,
Mǐndì ascended the throne,
and conferred the title of Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat).
In the third month,
he was transferred to govern Chéngdé.
In the fifth month of Qīngtài first year (934),
he was again stationed at Tàiyuán,
and came to pay respects to the capital (Jīngshī).
Lù Wáng Cóngkē rebelled at Fèngxiáng,
Mǐndì fled,
and met Jìngtáng on the road.
Jìngtáng killed over a hundred of the emperor's followers,
and detained the emperor at Wèizhōu before leaving.
Fèidì (The Deposed Emperor) ascended the throne,
and suspected that Jìngtáng would certainly rebel.
In the fifth month of Tiānfú first year (936),
he was transferred to govern Tiānpíng.
Jìngtáng consequently refused to obey the order,
and said to his subordinates:
"The former emperor (Xiāndì) granted me Tàiyuán so that I might retire here.
Now, to be transferred without cause,
is to suspect me of rebellion.
Moreover, Tàiyuán is a strategically dangerous place and has abundant grain.
I ought to internally issue a summons to all garrisons
and externally seek aid from the Qìdān.
Is this acceptable?"
Sāng Wéihàn, Liú Zhìyuǎn, and others jointly agreed.
They then submitted a memorial arguing that Fèidì should not have been established,
and requested that Xǔ Wáng Cóngyì be established as the heir to Míngzōng.
Fèidì issued an edict stripping Jìngtáng of his official ranks and titles,
and ordered Zhāng Jìngdá and others to suppress him.
Jìngtáng sought aid from the Qìdān.
In the ninth month,
Yèlǜ Déguāng of the Qìdān entered through Yànmén,
and fought the Táng troops.
Jìngdá was utterly defeated.
Jìngtáng left the north gate at night to meet Yèlǜ Déguāng,
and pledged a father-son relationship.
On the *dīngyǒu* day of the eleventh month,
the Emperor (Jìngtáng) ascended the throne,
with the state title Jìn.
He ceded the prefectures of Yōu, Zhuó, Jì, Tán, Shùn, Yíng, Mò, Wèi, Shuò, Yún, Yīng, Xīn, Guī, Rú, Wǔ, and Huán to the Qìdān.
On the *jǐhài* day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign title was changed.
The Secretary (Zhǎng Shūjì) Sāng Wéihàn was made Hánlín Xuéshì (Academician of the Hanlin Academy) and Shàngshū Lǐbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites),
and took charge of the affairs of the Privy Council (Zhī Shūmì Shǐ Shì).
In the Basic Annals of Fèidì, it is written:
"The Qìdān established Jìn."
This is based on what was seen.
In this record, it is written:
"The Emperor ascended the throne."
This uses his self-establishment as the phrasing,
to trace his original intent.
Jìn Gāozǔ’s rebellion,
even without the aid of the Qìdān,
would certainly have led to his self-establishment,
for his ambition lay in becoming emperor.
Thus, he must take responsibility for his own misdeeds.
On the *bǐngyín* day of the intercalary month,

Zhào Yíng, Hánlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ (Academician-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy) and Shàngshū Hùbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue), was made Ménxià Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Chancellery).
Sāng Wéihàn was made Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Secretariat). Both received the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Jointly Manager of Affairs in the Secretariat and Chancellery),
and concurrently Shūmì Shǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs).
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Zhào Déjūn and his son Yánshòu rebelled against Táng and came to surrender.
The Qìdān detained them and took them back.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
he arrived at Héyáng.
The Jiédù Shǐ (Military Governor) Cháng Cóngjiǎn rebelled against Táng and came to surrender.
On the *xīnsì* day,
he arrived from Tàiyuán.
Lú Wénjì and Yáo Yǐ were dismissed.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Zhāng Yánlǎng and Liú Yánlǎng were executed.
Fáng Gǎo was pardoned.
On this day, Fèidì was still alive.
On the *yǐyǒu* day of the twelfth month,
he went to Héyáng.
Wáng Cóngkē was posthumously demoted to commoner status.
On the *dīnghài* day,
Sīkōng (Minister of Works) Féng Dào concurrently served as Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Shí Zhònglì, Commandant of Cáozhōu, killed its Cìshǐ (Prefect) Zhèng Wán.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
an imperial mandate was issued seeking frank criticism.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Mì Qióng, Yánèi Dū Yúhòu (Commandant of the Inner Encampment) of Zhènzhōu, drove out Lǐ Yànqí, the Deputy Jiédù Shǐ.
Mén Duó, a staff officer of Tóngzhōu, killed his general Yáng Hànbīn.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Wáng Jiànlì, Jiédù Shǐ of Tiānpíng Commandery, killed his deputy Lǐ Yànrūn.
There was a drought.
"Wáng Cóngkē,"
follows the original terminology used by the Jìn people.
In the spring, the first month, on the *guǐhài* day of the second year (937),
Lú Wénjìn, Jiédù Shǐ of Ānyuǎn Commandery, rebelled and defected to Wú.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Fàn Yánguāng, Jiédù Shǐ of Tiānxíong Commandery, killed Mì Qióng, the Fángyù Shǐ (Defense Commissioner) of Qízhōu.
On the *wùyín* day,
Lǐ Sōng, Bīngbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Ministry of War), was made Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì, and Shūmì Shǐ.
A son of the Táng imperial clan was enfeoffed as a Duke (Gōng),
and the Duke of Xī (Xī Gōng) of Suí was established as a successor to the Two Kings (Èr Wáng Hòu).
The Duke of Jiè (Jiè Gōng) of Zhōu was prepared for the position of the Three Revered Guests (Sān Kè).
The historians failed to record the name
of the son of the Táng imperial clan.
This is recorded to show that the structures of the Two Kings’ Successors and the Three Revered Guests were still maintained,
and it is not necessary to specify the individual.
In the second month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Xièlǐ, the Crown Prince of the Qìdān, came as an envoy.
In the third month, on the *gēngchén* day,
he went to Biànzhōu.
In summer, the fourth month, on the *dīnghài* day,
prisoners were pardoned,
and the people's rents and taxes were abolished.
Zhào Yíng was sent as an envoy to the Qìdān.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn, Jiédù Shǐ of Xuānwǔ Commandery, presented money to aid the state.
Lǐ Kěxīng, Gōngyuàn Shǐ (Director of the Palace Parks) of the Qìdān, came as an envoy.
In the fifth month, on the *rénxū* day,
an imperial mandate was issued seeking frank criticism.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
his ancestors and father were posthumously honored as emperors,
and his ancestresses and mother as empresses. His great-great-grandfather Jǐng was given the posthumous title Xiào'ān,
with the temple name Jìngzǔ.
His great-great-grandmother, née Qín, was given the posthumous title Xiào'ān Yuán.
His great-grandfather Chēn was given the posthumous title Xiàojiǎn,
with the temple name Sùzǔ.
His great-grandmother, née Ān, was given the posthumous title Xiàojiǎn Gōng.
His grandfather Yù was given the posthumous title Xiàopíng,
with the temple name Ruìzǔ.
His grandmother, née Lái, was given the posthumous title Xiàopíng Xiàn.
His father Shàoyōng was given the posthumous title Xiàoyuán,
with the temple name Xiànzǔ.
His mother, née Hé, was given the posthumous title Xiàoyuán Yì.
In the sixth month, on the *guǐwèi* day,
an Yílíbì (Qìdān official title) envoy came from the Qìdān.
Fàn Yánguāng, Jiédù Shǐ of Tiānxíong Commandery, rebelled.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
an arrow (token of command) was transmitted to Fú Yànráo, Jiédù Shǐ of Yìchéng Commandery.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn was made Dū Bùshǔ (Commander-in-Chief) of the Four Fronts Field Army of Wèifǔ.
Zhāng Cóngbīn, Patrol Inspector (Xúnjiǎn) of the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū), rebelled.
Lǐ Xiá, Registrar (Pànguān) of the Garrison, died in the incident.
Hóu Yì, Fèngguó Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Loyal Guard), and Dù Zhòngwēi, Hùshèng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guard), were ordered to suppress him.
Cóngbīn invaded Héyáng
and killed the Imperial son Zhòngxìn;
he invaded Hénán
and killed the Imperial son Zhòngyì.
In autumn, the seventh month,
Cóngbīn captured Sǐshuǐ Pass
and killed Sòng Tínghào, the Patrol Inspector.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Yǐn Huī, Yòuwèi Dà Jiàngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Right Guard), rebelled and fled to Wú.
He failed,
and was executed.
Lóu Jìyīng, Yòu Jiānmén Wèi Dà Jiàngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Right Gate Guard), rebelled and defected to Zhāng Cóngbīn.
Yìchéng Commandery was in disorder;
the garrison commander Bái Fèngjìn, Shìwèi Mǎbù Jūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Cavalry and Infantry Forces), was killed.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Mǎ Wàn, Fèngguó Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commandant of the Loyal Guard) of the garrison, seized Fú Yànráo and returned to the capital (Jīngshī).
He was ordered to be executed at Chìgāng.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn was made Dū Zhāotǎo Shǐ (Commander-in-Chief of Pacification) of the Wèifǔ Field Army.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Dù Zhòngwēi conquered Sǐshuǐ Pass.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn conquered Bózhōu.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Wáng Huī, Túfáng Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commandant of Garrison Defense) of Ānzhōu, killed his Jiédù Shǐ Zhōu Guī.
Lǐ Jīnquán, Yòuwèi Dà Jiàngjūn, was ordered to suppress him.
Although Yànráo was guilty of allowing his troops to run wild,
he was falsely accused of rebellion and executed.
Therefore, the text does not record 'executed' (*zhū*),
but says
"ordered to be executed,"
to avoid the implication that Mǎ Wàn executed him without authorization.
Zhāng Cóngbīn threw himself into the river and died,
therefore, the text does not record his execution.
Jīnquán had not yet arrived when Huī fled
and was killed.
Therefore, the text does not record Huī's rebellion,
does not record the conquest of Ānzhōu,
and does not record his execution.
In the eighth month, on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Ān Shūqiān, Jiédù Shǐ of Jìngnán Commandery, presented additional horses for the capital.
On the *yǐsì* day,
prisoners not sentenced to death, along with the remaining partisans of Zhāng Cóngbīn, Fú Yànráo, and Wáng Huī, were pardoned.
In the ninth month,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn presented grain.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *xīnsì* day,
the manufacture of armor and weapons was prohibited.
In the third year, spring, second month, day Wùxū,
all the various *Zhèn* presented goods to aid the state.
They oppressed the people to offer to their superiors.
Rulers and ministers shared the same desires,
and bribery was openly practiced.
By this time, the number [of presented items] was overwhelmingly large!
Therefore,
"the various *Zhèn*"
is mentioned summarily and will not be recorded again hereafter.
Third month, day Rénxū,
Wáng Rénměi (王仁美), the Khagan of Huíhú (回鶻), sent Zhái Quánfú (翟全福) to come.
Day Dīngchǒu,
the private manufacture of copper vessels was prohibited.
Autumn, seventh month, day Xīnyǒu,
the *Huángyè qián* (皇業錢) were used to create the Seal of Receiving the Mandate (*Shòumìng Bǎo*).
The making of the seal is not necessarily recorded;
the *Huángyè qián*
were private coins.
The Son of Heaven kept private money,
hence this is recorded.
Eighth month, day Wùyín,
Fēng Dào (馮道) and the Left Grand Minister Liú Xù (劉昫) were appointed Envoys for the Qìdān (契丹) Investiture Ceremony.
Day Rénwǔ,
Fēng Huī (馮暉), Prefect (*Cìshǐ*) of Chánzhōu (澶州), surrendered.
Day Bǐngxū,
selection of officials by Imperial endorsement was permitted.
Day Jǐchǒu,
taxes for people affected by floods and droughts were remitted.
Day Xīnchǒu,
the musicians/entertainers (*líng guān*) were returned to Qìdān.
Since Gāozǔ (高祖) served Qìdān as a father,
when they requested something, it was not said "to give" but
"to return"
implying it was a tribute delivery.
Ninth month, day Jǐyǒu,
Fàn Yán'guāng (范延光) was pardoned.
Day Jǐwèi,

Liú Shǒuwēi (劉守威), an official of the Whip of Silence; Wáng Yīn (王殷), an official verifying imperial tallies of the Jīnwú Guard; and Yīn Huī (殷暉), a student of the Cock-Crowers in the Directorate of Astronomy, were returned to Qìdān.
Mǎ Jìróng (馬繼榮), envoy of Yútián (于闐), came;
Lǐ Wànjīn (李萬金), envoy of Huíhú, came.
Day Jǐsì,
Wèizhōu (魏州) was pardoned,
and the people's taxes were remitted.
In this month,
Liú Chùràng (劉處讓), Commissioner of the Southern Court of the Bureau of Military Affairs (*Xuān Huī Nán Yuàn Shǐ*), was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Shūmì Shǐ*).
Initially,
Yán'guāng requested surrender,
but Gāozǔ did not permit it.
Yán'guāng then held his defenses firmly.
[The Imperial army] attacked him,
but for a long time could not defeat him.
Eventually, [the court] regretted this and pardoned him,
hence his surrender is not recorded.
Winter, tenth month, day Wùyín,
Hán Jiá (韓頰), Grand Councillor of the Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Lìng*) and envoy of Qìdān, came to present the imperial edict, addressing [the Jin ruler] as Emperor Yīngwǔ Míngyì (英武明義皇帝).
Day Gēngchén,
Biànzhōu (汴州) was elevated to Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng),
Luòyáng (洛陽) was made Western Capital (Xījīng),
and Yōngzhōu (雍州) was made Jìnchāng Jūn (晉昌軍).
Day Wùzǐ,
Mǎ Cóngbīn (馬從斌), Grand General of the Right Jīnwú Guard, was sent as envoy to Qìdān.
Day Jǐwèi,
Méilǐ (梅里), envoy of Qìdān, came.
Day Wùxū,
a general amnesty was granted.
Day Gēngzǐ,
Lǐ Shèntiān (李聖天) was enfeoffed as King of the Great Treasure Yútián Kingdom.
Eleventh month, day Xīnhài,
Guǎngshēng Fǔ (廣晉府) was elevated to Yèdū (鄴都).
Day Rénxū,
the prohibition on coining money was abolished.
Twelfth month, day Bǐngzǐ,
his son Chóngguì (重貴) was enfeoffed as Prince of Zhèng (*Zhèng Wáng*).
Fourth year, spring, first month,
robbers opened the tomb of Emperor Mǐn (愍皇帝) of Táng.
Day Xīnhài,
Zhāng Cóng'ēn (張從恩), Defense Commissioner of Chánzhōu, was appointed Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Shūmì Fùshǐ*).
The gate and neighborhood of Lǐ Zìlún (李自倫), a commoner of Shēnzhōu (深州), were commended and honored.
The Emperor [Mǐn] was interred in the grounds of Míngzōng's (明宗) Huīlíng Tomb,
but had no tomb name,
therefore it is referred to
as a "tomb."
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted the title Emperor Mǐn.
The posthumous titles of the various Emperors of the Five Dynasties cannot serve as a standard,
and are generally not worth mentioning;
only Emperor Mǐn's is recorded [here]
because he was once demoted to Prince of È (*È Wáng*).
However, because the dynasty fell and the rites were incomplete,
neither the Old History nor the Veritable Records (*Shílù*) contain the date he was memorialized, given the posthumous title, and presented in the imperial register.
Therefore, although it should have been recorded, it could not be,
and is only mentioned here incidentally.
Third month, day Yǐsì,
Huíhú sent its Commander-in-Chief (*Dūdu*) Zhuāilǐdūn (拽里敦) to come.
Day Bǐngchén,
the *Tiáo Yuán Lì* (調元歷) calendar was promulgated.
Wáng Yànzhōng (王彥忠), the garrison commander of Língzhōu (靈州), rebelled at Huáiyuǎn Chéng (懷遠城).
Day Jǐwèi,
Yànzhōng surrendered.
Qí Yánzuò (齊延祚), an official of the Imperial Household, killed him.
Summer, fourth month, day Xīnsì,
Wáng Rénměi, the Khagan of Huíhú, was enfeoffed as Fènghuà Khagan (奉化可汗).
Day Jiǎshēn,
the post of Commissioner of Military Affairs was abolished.
Autumn, seventh month, day Bǐngchén,
the coining of money was prohibited again.
Intercalary month, day Rénshēn,
Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) was dismissed.
Eighth month, day Jǐhài (the first day of the month),
the Yellow River breached its banks at Bópíng (博平).
The Western Róng (戎) raided Jìngzhōu (涇州).
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤), Military Governor of Zhāngyì Army, defeated them,
capturing their leader Yělíluóxiādú (野離羅蝦獨).
Ninth month, day Dīngchǒu,
Niánmùgū (粘木孤), envoy of Qìdān, came.
Day Guǐwèi,
Lǐ Cóngyì (李從益) was enfeoffed as Duke of Xún (郇國公) to maintain the Táng imperial lineage.
Day Bǐngxū,
Wáng Jiàn (王建), King of Gāolì (高麗), sent his Grand Advisor (*Guǎng Píng Shìláng*) Xíng Shùn (邢順) to come.
Winter, eleventh month, day Yǐhài,
temples were established for Táng Gāozǔ, Tàizōng (太宗), Zhuāngzōng (莊宗), Míngzōng, and Emperor Mǐn in the Western Capital.
Day Wùzǐ,
Yáozhé (遙折), envoy of Qìdān, came.
Bàyánzú (罷延族) of Tǔfān (吐蕃) came to join [the court].
Fifth year, spring, first month, day Dīngmǎo (the first day of the month),
an edict of grace cancelled public and private debts owed by the people.
Day Jǐchǒu,
Shí Hǎijīn (石海金), envoy of Huíhú, came.
Summer, fourth month, day Jiǎzǐ,
Xīnghuà Wáng (興化王), a prince of Qìdān, came.
Fifth month, day Bǐngxū,
Lǐ Jīnquán (李金全), Military Governor of Ānyuǎn Army, rebelled and defected to Táng.
Sixth month, day Guǐmǎo,
Lǐ [name unknown] sent his general Lǐ Chéngyù (李承裕) to enter Ānzhōu (安州).
Jīnquán fled to Táng.
Mǎ Quánjié (馬全節), Military Governor of Ānyuǎn Army, fought Chéngyù
and defeated him.
Day Dīngsì,
Ānzhōu was captured.
Chéngyù fled to Yúnmèng (雲夢).
Quánjié captured and killed him.
Autumn, eighth month, day Dīngyǒu,
[The Emperor] inspected the crops in the western suburbs.
Day Jǐwèi,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠), Resident Commissioner of the Western Capital, killed Fàn Yán'guāng, Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Ninth month, day Dīngmǎo,

Hé Níng (和凝), Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Draftsman and Vice Minister of Revenue, was made Grand Councillor of the Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Shìláng*) and concurrently Chief Minister (*Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì*).
Day Xīnsì,
[The Emperor] inspected the crops at Shā Tái (沙臺).
Winter, tenth month, day Dīngwèi,
Shèlì (舍利), envoy of Qìdān, came.
Eleventh month, day Bǐngzǐ,
on the Winter Solstice,
the Two Dances (*èr wǔ*) were performed for the first time.
Sixth year, spring, first month, day Wùyín,
Táng Shūyú (唐叔虞) was enfeoffed as Prince of Xīng'ān (興安王).
Tái Dài (臺駘) was enfeoffed as Duke of Chāngníng (昌寧公).
Second month, day Wùshēn,
the buying of banquet money was halted.
Third month,
taxes owed by the people from the second year to prior to the fourth year were cancelled.
The current collections were heavy and the people could not bear them.
Summer, fourth month, day Jǐwèi,
Shùkuò (述括), envoy of Qìdān, came.
Fifth month,
Bái Chéngfú (白承福), the chieftain of Tǔhún (吐渾), came.
Autumn, seventh month, day Rénwǔ,
Xuē Tónghǎi (薛同海), envoy of the Tūjué (突厥), came.
Eighth month, day Rénchén,
[The Emperor] went to Yèdū.
Prince of Zhèng Chóngguì, Prefect of Kāifēng, was appointed Resident Commissioner of the Eastern Capital.
Zhāng Cóng'ēn, Commissioner of the Southern Court, was appointed Overall Overseer of the Internal and External Military Forces of the Eastern Capital.
Day Rén'yín,
a general amnesty was granted.
Day Jiǎyín,
Zhāng Chéng (張澄), Minister of the Imperial Household, was sent as envoy to Qìdān.
Ninth month, day Yǐhài,
Yáng Yànxún (楊彥詢), former Military Governor of Ānguó Army, was sent as envoy to Qìdān.
Day Dīngchǒu,
Bái Kějiǔ (白可久), envoy of Tǔhún, came.
The Yellow River breached its banks at Zhōngdū,
flowing into Tǎ Hé (沓河).
Winter, tenth month,
the Yellow River breached its banks in Huá (滑), Pú (濮), Yùn (鄆), and Chánzhōu.
Ān Cóngjìn (安從進), Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào, rebelled.
Eleventh month, day Dīngchǒu,
Gāo Xíngzhōu (高行周), Resident Commissioner of the Western Capital, was made Overall Commander of the Southern Front Army to suppress him.
The twelfth month, *bǐngxū* (day 1 of the lunar month).
Zhèng Wáng Chóngguì was made the Yǐn (Administrator) of Guǎng Jìn,
and subsequently transferred his enfeoffment as Qí Wáng (King of Qí).
Guō Jīnhǎi, the Commander of the Vanguard, and Ān Cóngjìn fought at Táng Zhōu,
and defeated them.
Ān Chóngróng, the Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor) of Chéngdé Jūn, rebelled.
Dù Chóngwēi, the Jiédùshǐ of Tiānpíng, was made the Commander of the Campaigning Forces (Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ) at Zhèn Zhōu.
*Bǐngshēn* (day).
The Qìdān sent an envoy to come.
*Wùxū* (day).
Dù Chóngwēi and Ān Chóngróng fought at Zōngchéng,
and Dù Chóngwēi defeated him.
The seventh year, spring, first month, *dīngsì* (day).
Zhèn Zhōu was conquered,
Ān Chóngróng was executed,
and an amnesty was granted to Guǎng Jìn.
*Gēngwǔ* (day).
Dálà, an envoy of the Qìdān, arrived.
The third month.
Ān Yànwēi, the Jiédùshǐ of Guīdé Jūn, stopped the breach in the river at Huá Zhōu.
The intercalary month.
Heaven produced locusts which ate the wheat.
Summer, fifth month, *yǐsì* (day).
Imperial Consort Liú Shì was honored as the Tàihòu (Empress Dowager).
She was the birth mother of Gāozǔ (Founding Ancestor).
Sixth month, *bǐngchén* (day).
Niànchǒu Hàn, an envoy of the Tǔhún, arrived.
*Yǐchǒu* (day).
The Emperor died at the Bǎochāng Diàn (Baochang Palace).
He was fifty-one years old.
Basic Annals of Jìn, Volume Nine.
The father of Chū Dì (Deposed Emperor) was Jìngrú,
who was the elder brother of Gāozǔ.
He served as a cavalry general under Táng Zhuāngzōng,
but died early.
Gāozǔ adopted Jìngrú’s son, Chóngguì, as his own son.
Gāozǔ had six sons;
five all died young,
and Chóngruì was still a child,
therefore Chóngguì was able to succeed to the throne.
When Chóngguì was young, he was cautious and sincere,
and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
Gāozǔ ordered the scholar Wáng Zhèn to teach him the *Lǐ Jì* (Classic of Rites).
After a long time,
Chóngguì could not grasp the main concepts,
and he said to Zhèn:
“This is not a concern for my family.”
Gāozǔ was placed on the throne by the Qìdān.
He planned to leave one son to guard Tàiyuán.
The Qìdān envoy ordered all the sons to come forth so he could choose himself.
Pointing to Chóngguì, he said:
“This one with the large eyes will do.”
He was then appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of the Radiant Luster, Gold and Purple),
acting Yǐn of Tàiyuán and Liúshǒu (Resident Retainer) of Běijīng,
and administrator of the affairs of the Hédōng Jiédù (Military Command).
In the ninth month of Tiānfú second year (937),
he was summoned and appointed General-in-Chief of the Left Guard of the Jinwu (Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn).
In the winter of the third year,
he was made Yǐn of Kāifēng,
enfeoffed as Zhèng Wáng (King of Zhèng),
given the additional title of Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant),
and conferred the rank of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Concurrently Manager of Affairs for the Central Secretariat and Chancellery).
In the sixth year,
Gāozǔ proceeded to Yè,
and Chóngguì remained to guard Dōngjīng (Eastern Capital).
Afterward, he was made Yǐn of Guǎng Jìn,
and transferred his enfeoffment as Qí Wáng (King of Qí).
The seventh year, sixth month, *yǐchǒu* (day).
Gāozǔ died,
and the Emperor immediately ascended the throne before the coffin.
*Gēngwǔ* (day).
He ordered Shí Déchāo, General of the Right Valiant Guard (Yòu Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn), to use two imperial horses
to perform a ritual sacrifice (*pǔjì*) on the Western Mountain of Xiāng Zhōu.
Lǐ Rénkuò, the Envoy to the Capital, was sent on a mission to the Qìdān.
Méi Lǐ, an envoy of the Qìdān, arrived.
*Bǐngzǐ* (day).
Féng Dào was made the Commissioner for the Mountain Mausoleum of the Recently Deceased Emperor (Dàxíng Huángdì Shānlíng Shǐ).
Dòu Zhēngù, Attendant Gentleman of the Chancellery (Ménxià Shìláng), was made the Deputy.
Cuī Zhuō, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng), was made the Commissioner for Rites.
Lǚ Qí, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng), was made the Commissioner for Imperial Guard of Honor.
Wáng Yìjiǎn, Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), was made the Commissioner for Ceremonial Guards.
*Jǐmǎo* (day).
Zhū Chóngjié, Envoy of the Sīfāng Guǎn (Four Directions Hostel), and Liáng Yán, General-in-Chief of the Right Jinwu Guard (Yòu Jīnwú Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn), were sent on a mission to the Qìdān.
This was a custom of the Yi and Di (barbarians).
The Old Histories and Veritable Records make no mention of the Commissioner of Bridges and Couriers (*Qiáodào Dùndì Shǐ*).
It is suspected that the position was not established,
or perhaps the record is missing.
Hàn Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn) also acted similarly.
Autumn, seventh month, *rénchén* (day).
Imperial Grandmother Liú Shì died,
and court sessions were suspended for three days.
*Dīngyǒu* (day).
Shí Déchāo was sent to perform the horse sacrifice (*pǔmǎ*) on the Western Mountain of Xiāng Zhōu.
*Gēngzǐ* (day).
A great amnesty was granted.
*Jiǎchén* (day).
A translator (Tōngshì) envoy of the Qìdān arrived.
She was the birth mother of Gāozǔ.
During Gāozǔ’s reign, she had been honored as Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager).
When she died,
her funeral and burial did not follow the rites appropriate for an Empress,
showing the meagerness of the favor and respect granted.
The reason the record does not refer to her as Huáng Tàihòu
is that for the Emperor (Chū Dì), she was the grandmother.
The use of the word
“bēng” (died/collapsed)
is to properly define her status.
As this has already been fully seen earlier,
the text is brief here.
Eighth month, *wùwǔ* (day).
Gāo Xíngzhōu conquered Xiāng Zhōu.
*Gēngshēn* (day).
Jǐng Yánguǎng, Jiédùshǐ of Tiānpíng Jūn; Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, Jiédùshǐ of Yìchéng Jūn; and Guō Jǐn, Jiédùshǐ of Zhāngdé Jūn,
contributed cash and grain to assist in the construction of the mountain mausoleum.
*Jiǎzǐ* (day).
Láng Wǔ, an envoy of the Qìdān, arrived.
*Gēngwǔ* (day).
The Imperial Grandmother was buried in Wèi Xiàn.
*Guǐyǒu* (day).
Zhāng Jiǔsī, the Commissioner of the Ministry for Guest Affairs (Kèshěng Shǐ), an envoy of the Qìdān, arrived.
Ān Cóngjìn burned himself to death,
hence the record does not state that he was executed.
Ninth month, *xīnchǒu* (day).
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn was made the Overall Director for the Mountain Mausoleum of the Recently Deceased Emperor (Dàxíng Huángdì Shānlíng Dū Bùshǔ).
Winter, tenth month, *jǐwèi* (day).
Shèlì, an envoy of the Qìdān, arrived.
*Gēngwǔ* (day).
The Huíghú (Uighurs) sent an envoy to come.
Eleventh month.
Dàqīng (Grand Minister), an envoy of the Qìdān, arrived.
*Gēngyín* (day).
The Shèngwén Zhāngwǔ Xiào Huángdì (Holy and Cultivated, Brilliant and Martial, Filial Emperor—Gāozǔ) was buried at Xiǎnlíng Mausoleum.
*Jǐhài* (day).
Dǒng Yīn, the Commissioner of Cattle and Sheep (Niúyáng Shǐ), was sent on a mission to the Qìdān.
*Gēngzǐ* (day).
Gāozǔ’s spirit tablet was enshrined in the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple).
*Xīnchǒu* (day).
Half of the taxes owed by the common people through whose area Gāozǔ’s funerary carriage passed were remitted.
The mausoleum is located in Shòu'ān Xiàn, Hénán.
During the disorder of the Five Dynasties,
up to this point there had been seven rulers,
five of whom did not die a natural death.
Although Míngzōng ended his life well,
Mǐn Dì (Emperor Mǐn) could not be buried,
and was only able to be buried during the time of Fèi Dì (Deposed Emperor).
Therefore, these events were not fully recorded (in the previous annals).
Only now does it first appear that a son was able to bury his father,
thus the burial and the enshrinement in the temple are recorded in detail.
Twelfth month, *gēngwǔ* (day).
Liú Zhīyuǎn, the Liúshǒu of Běijīng, presented one hundred yurts (*qiónglú*).
Lìng Gǔzhī, the Yuyue (Grand Regent) envoy of the Qìdān, arrived.
*Xīnwèi* (day).
Yělǐ Sì, another envoy, arrived.
*Bǐngzǐ* (day).
Liú Zàishēng, the Dū Dū (Commander-in-Chief) envoy of Yútián, arrived.
Cáo Yuánshēn of Shā Zhōu and Cáo Yuánzhōng of Guā Zhōu both sent envoys to accompany Zàishēng on his journey.
There was a drought.
Locusts appeared.
The *Qiónglú* (yurts)
are used by the Yi and Di (barbarians).
The eighth year, spring, first month.
Wūduō Ào, the Yuyue (Grand Regent) envoy of the Qìdān, arrived.
Second month, *rénzǐ* (day).
Jǐng Yánguǎng was made the Commissioner of the Imperial Camp (Yùyíng Shǐ).
*Jǐwèi* (day).
He proceeded to Dōngjīng
and pardoned the prisoners in Guǎng Jìn Fǔ.
*Gēngshēn* (day).
He stopped at Chán Zhōu
and pardoned prisoners.
*Yǐchǒu* (day).
He arrived back from Yè Dū.
*Gēngwǔ* (day).
It was Hánshí (Cold Food Festival).
The ceremonial distance sacrifice (*wàngjì*) was offered toward Xiǎnlíng at Nánzhuāng,
and imperial robes and paper money were burned.
Acts like burning clothing and offering sacrifices in the fields
are affairs of common villagers.
Their use by the Son of Heaven
shows how badly the rites and music had deteriorated.
Third month, *jǐmǎo* (day 1 of the lunar month).
Zhào Yíng was dismissed.
Sāng Wéihàn, the Jiédùshǐ of Jìnchāng Jūn, was made Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor).
*Xīnchǒu* (day).
Mèng Chénghuì, the Commissioner of Presentation (Yǐnjìn Shǐ) and Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng), was sent on a mission to the Qìdān.
Locusts appeared.
Summer, fourth month, *gēngwǔ* (day).
Dǒng Yīn was sent on a mission to the Qìdān.
Zhāng Fú, an official of the Palace Attendants, led the Wēishùn Jūn (Weishun Army) to catch locusts at Chén Zhōu.
Fifth month,
Ān Shěn Xìn (Military Governor of Tàiníng Jūn) caught locusts at Zhōngdū.
Dīnghài (day),
the Emperor’s uncle, Jìng Rú, was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Sòng (Sòng Wáng).
Guǐmǎo (day),
Féng Dào was dismissed.
Jiǎchén (day),
due to drought and locusts, a general amnesty was declared.
Sixth month, Gēngxū (day),
sacrifices were offered to the locusts at Gāomén.
Guǐhài (day),
seven Gòngfèng Guān (Attending Officials) led the Fèngguó Jūn army to catch locusts in the Jīngjī (Capital Region).
Xīnwèi (day),
people's grain was requisitioned and borrowed;
those who hoarded grain were executed.
Autumn, seventh month, Jiǎwǔ (day),
the Empress Dowager was formally invested.
Dīngyǒu (day),
(the Emperor) held an archery practice at Nánzhuāng.
Měilǐ and others, envoys from the Qìdān, arrived.
Jiǎchén (day),
Lǐ Hànchāo (Gòngfèng Guān) led the Fèngguó Jūn army to catch locusts in the Jīngjī (Capital Region).
Eighth month, Dīngwèi (first day of the month),
people were recruited to catch locusts,
compensated with grain.
Xīnhài (day),
the people's green shoots (crops) were inspected.
Ninth month, Wùyín (day),
Lady Ān of Qín Guó was honored as the Imperial Consort (Huáng Tàifēi).
Bǐngshēn (day),
(the Emperor) visited Dànián Zhuāng and Jǐng Yán Guǎng's residence.
Winter, tenth month, Wùshēn (day),
Lady Féng was established as Empress (Hòuqīn).
Rénzǐ (day),
(the Emperor) hunted in the near suburbs,
and visited Shātái.
Bǐngyín (day),
Liú Yìn, the interpreter envoy from the Qìdān, arrived.
Gēngwǔ (day),
people's grain was requisitioned and borrowed.
Lady Féng was the Emperor’s paternal aunt by marriage (Shūmǔ).
Eleventh month, Jǐmǎo (day),
Dǒng Yīn was sent as an envoy to the Qìdān.
Jiǎshēn (day),
(the Emperor) visited Bājiǎo,
and inspected the horse pastures.
Yǐwèi (day),
Měilǐ, an envoy from the Qìdān, arrived.
Wùxū (day),
Yáng Chéngzuò (Prefect of Qí Zhōu) fled to Qīng Zhōu.
Xīnchǒu (day),
Gāolì (Goryeo) sent its Guǎngpíng Shìláng (Assistant Minister of Deliberations), Jīn Rénfēng, to arrive.
Twelfth month, Guǐchǒu (day),
Biān Guāngfàn (Gěishì Zhōng) and Guō Yànwēi (Prefect of Dēng Zhōu) were sent as envoys to the Qìdān.
Jiǎyín (day),
an envoy (Tàixiàng) from Gāolì arrived.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn (Military Governor of Pínglú Jūn) rebelled;
Zhái Jìnzōng (Prefect of Zī Zhōu) died resisting him.
Chūn, first month of the first year of Kāiyùn, Jiǎxū (first day of the month),
the Qìdān raided Cāng Zhōu.
Jǐmǎo (day),
Bèi Zhōu fell.
Gēngchén (day),
Gāo Xíngzhōu (Military Governor of Guīdé Jūn) was appointed Supreme Commander of the Northern Field Headquarters (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Dū Bùshǔ).
The Qìdān entered Yànmén,
and raided Dài Zhōu.
Xīnsì (day),
Wáng Bān (Diànzhí) was sent as an envoy to the Qìdān,
reached Yèdū,
but was unable to proceed further and returned.
There was a great famine.
Rénwǔ (day),
Lǐ Zhōu (former Military Governor of Jìngnàn Jūn) was appointed Acting Defender of Dōngjīng (Eastern Capital),
and Jǐng Yán Guǎng was made Imperial Camp Commissioner (Yùyíng Shǐ).
Yǐyǒu (day),
(the army began) the Northern Expedition.
Bǐngxū (day),
the Qìdān raided Líyáng.
Xīnmǎo (day),
military exercises were held at Chán Zhōu.
The Qìdān camped at Yuánchéng,
Zhào Yánshòu raided Nánlè.
Jiǎwǔ (day),
Liú Zhīyuǎn was appointed Pacification Commissioner of the Yōuzhōu Circuit Field Headquarters.
Horses were requisitioned.
Bǐngshēn (day),
the Qìdān raided Líyáng.
Xīnchǒu (day),
Liú Zhīyuǎn fought the Qìdān Prince Wěi (Wěi Wáng) at Xiùróng,
and defeated him.
Zhōu Rú (Prefect of Bó Zhōu) rebelled and defected to the Qìdān.
Since Gāozǔ of Jìn treated the Qìdān with great deference, like a son serving a father,
and sent envoys seasonally,
the former histories and Veritable Records did not record it.
When Chū Dì (the Abdicated Emperor) ascended the throne,
envoys came continuously and thickly,
too numerous to count.
Therefore, those whose rank was low were generally omitted and not recorded.
Wáng Bān was recorded
because he was unable to proceed further.
Second month, Wùshēn (day),
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn (former Commander of the Palace Army) fought the Qìdān at Mǎjiādù,
and defeated them.
Guǐchǒu (day),
Mǎ Quánjié (Commander of the Northern Field Headquarters) fought the Qìdān at Běipíng,
and defeated them.
Third month, Guǐyǒu (day),
(the army) fought the Qìdān at Qīchéng,
and the Qìdān departed.
Jǐchǒu (day),
Bái Cónghuī (Prefect of Jì Zhōu) fought the Qìdān at Héngshuǐ,
and defeated them.
Guǐsì (day),
people were registered to form the Wǔdìng Jūn army.
Both sides suffered casualties in the battle,
(the Qìdān) withdrew their troops and slowly departed.
Jìn (forces) could not pursue them,
thus the wording "departed by themselves" is used.
Summer, fourth month,
the Qìdān captured Dé Zhōu.
Liáng Jìn (Inspector Commissioner along the River) defeated them,
and recovered Dé Zhōu.
Jiǎyín (day),
(the Emperor) arrived from Chán Zhōu,
and pardoned the capital (Jīngshī).
Jǐwèi (day),
Mǎ Quánjié fought the Qìdān at Dìngfēng,
and defeated them.
Xīnyǒu (day),
ordered the requisitioning and borrowing of civilian assets.
Fifth month, Wùyín (day),
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn campaigned against Yáng Guāngyuǎn.
Dīnghài (day),
Zhāng Cóng'ēn (Acting Defender of Yèdū) was appointed Supreme Commander of the Bèi Zhōu Field Headquarters.
Xīnmǎo (day),
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn was appointed Supreme Commander of the Qīng Zhōu Field Headquarters.
Sixth month,
Zī Zhōu was captured.
Bǐngwǔ (day),
the office of Shūmì Shǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs) was restored.
Dīngwèi (day),
Sāng Wéihàn (Shìzhōng) was made Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat),
and additionally served as Shūmì Shǐ.
Bǐngchén (day),
the river (Yellow River) breached at Huá Zhōu,
circled Liáng Shān,
and flowed into the Wèn and Jǐ Rivers.
Autumn, seventh month, Xīnwèi (first day of the month),
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
Jǐchǒu (day),

The Qìdān extinguished Jìn.
Generals who perish in battle or commanders who die defending a city are not recorded simply as having "died"
because their true intentions are not yet knowable.
They might have wanted to flee but couldn't,
or wanted to surrender but had no time,
and were suddenly killed.
If they neither fled nor surrendered and clearly died upholding their loyalty,
then we record
"died,"
as in the case of [Wánɡ] Qīnɡ.
Although Emperor Chūdì was still alive,
Jìn was already destroyed,
therefore we record
"extinguished."
Alas!
When I recorded
"enfeoffed his son Chónɡɡuì as Prince of Zhènɡ,"
and also recorded
"posthumously enfeoffed the Imperial Elder Uncle Jìnɡrú as Prince of Sònɡ,"
was this
without reason?
The Rites state:
"The son of a brother is considered as one's own son."
Recording Chónɡɡuì as
"son"
is acceptable.
But Jìnɡrú
was the father of Emperor Chūdì;
why is he recorded as
"Imperial Elder Uncle"?
Emperor Chūdì ascended the throne improperly,
and thus repudiated his birth father.
Now, Emperor Chūdì could be considered the son of [Emperor] Gāozǔ but could not be considered the heir,
because Gāozǔ had his own son.
When Gāozǔ was critically ill,
he held his son Chónɡruì and placed him in Fénɡ Dào's arms, entrusting him [to Fénɡ Dào].
How could Emperor Chūdì have been allowed to ascend?
The ministers of Jìn,
having violated the Rites and ignored the mandate by installing him,
believed that if Emperor Chūdì was considered Gāozǔ's son, he could stand,
but if he was considered Jìnɡrú's son, he could not stand.
Therefore, they deeply concealed and repudiated his birth father,
in order to deceive the world into thinking he was truly Gāozǔ's son.
The Rites state:
"He who becomes the heir of another
offers sacrifices for his birth parents."
Had Gāozǔ been without a son,
Emperor Chūdì could have become the heir and ascended properly;
in that case, there would have been no need to repudiate his birth father in order to deceive others.
Therefore, when I recorded
"posthumously enfeoffed the Imperial Elder Uncle Jìnɡrú as Prince of Sònɡ,"
it was
to show that his ascension was improper,
that he destroyed natural bonds of kinship,
and that he treated his own father as a subordinate official to be granted a title,
thereby deceiving the world.
