The Qìdān destroyed Jìn.
If a general died in battle or a commander died defending a city and their death is not recorded,
it is because their intentions are not clear.
Perhaps they wanted to flee but could not,
or they wanted to surrender but had no time,
and were simply killed.
If someone did not flee, did not surrender, and clearly died for their principles,
it is recorded as
"died",
as in the case of Wáng Qīng.
Although Chūdì was still alive,
Jìn was already destroyed,
thus it is recorded as
"destroyed".
Emperor Gāozǔ Ruìwén Shèngwǔ Zhāosù Xiàohuángdì,
whose surname was Liú,
originally named Zhīyuǎn,
his ancestors were people of the Shātuó tribe.
His descendants subsequently lived in Tàiyuán.
Zhīyuǎn, when young, disliked playing games;
he was serious and spoke little.
His face was purple,
and his eyes had much white,
inspiring awe.
He and Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn both served Míngzōng as subordinate generals.
When Míngzōng and the Liáng people fought at Déshèng,
the horse armor of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn broke,
and the Liáng soldiers were close to catching him.
Zhīyuǎn gave him the horse he was riding,
and then, taking Gāozǔ's horse, guarded the rear and returned.
Gāozǔ appreciated this favor.
When Gāozǔ was stationed as the Acting Administrator of Běijīng,
Zhīyuǎn served as Yāyá (Chief Clerk).
When Lù Wáng Cóngkē rebelled,
Emperor Mǐn fled.
Gāozǔ traveled from Zhènzhōu to the capital for an audience,
and met Emperor Mǐn at Wèizhōu.
They stopped at a courier station.
Zhīyuǎn sent the brave warrior Shí Gǎn to attend Gāozǔ, hiding an iron hammer in his sleeve, fearing sudden danger.
Gāozǔ and Emperor Mǐn were discussing matters that remained unresolved.
The attendants wished to attack Gāozǔ.
Zhīyuǎn escorted Gāozǔ into a room.
Gǎn fought the attendants and died.
Zhīyuǎn immediately led his troops and killed all of Emperor Mǐn’s attendants,
leaving the Emperor at the courier station and departing.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) ascended the throne,
Gāozǔ was again stationed at Hédōng.
After a while, a rift appeared,
and Gāozǔ intended to raise an army.
Zhīyuǎn and Sāng Wéihàn secretly planned the strategy for Gāozǔ
and helped him succeed.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne at Tàiyuán,
he made Zhīyuǎn the Commander of the Imperial Guard (Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūyúhòu),
concurrently holding the title of Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Bǎoyì Circuit.
Yēlǜ Déguāng of Qìdān escorted Gāozǔ to Lùzhōu.
Just before parting,
he pointed to Zhīyuǎn and said:
“This Commander of the Army (Dū Jūn) is very *cāolà* (fierce and brave);
do not abandon him without a great reason.”
Common speech calls bravery and fierceness
“cāolà”;
this records the original phrase.
In Tiānfú 2 (937),
he was promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry Imperial Guard (Shìwèi Mǎbù Jūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ),
concurrently holding the title of Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ Circuit.
After a while, Dù Chóngwēi replaced Zhīyuǎn as Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ,
and Zhīyuǎn was transferred to lead Guīdé Circuit.
Zhīyuǎn was ashamed to be under the same system as Chóngwēi,
and kept his door shut, refusing to go out.
Gāozǔ was angry,
and wanted to dismiss him from his military post.
The Chancellor Zhào Yíng thought this should not be done.
Gāozǔ then sent the Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, Hé Níng, to his residence to convey the imperial command.
Zhīyuǎn then accepted the order.
In the 5th year (940),
he was transferred to be the Acting Administrator of Yèdū.
In the ninth month,
he had an audience at the capital.
Gāozǔ visited his residence.
In the 6th year (941),
he was appointed Military Governor of Hédōng Circuit and Acting Administrator of Běijīng.
In the 7th year (942),
Gāozǔ died.
Zhīyuǎn followed Gāozǔ from the time he arose in Tàiyuán,
and had the merit of assisting in the founding of the dynasty.
Since Emperor Chū (Chūdì) ascended the throne,
he broke the alliance with Qìdān,
and campaigned militarily in the north.
He often suspected that, since Zhīyuǎn’s achievements and position were already high,
he might take advantage of the Jìn dynasty's many troubles and harbor rebellious intentions,
so he always treated him with exceptional respect.
Zhīyuǎn was appointed Director of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
ennobled as Prince of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán Wáng), and made Commissioner for Campaigns in Yōuzhōu Circuit (Yōuzhōu Dào Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ).
He was also appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Front Campaigns (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Dūtǒng).
In Kāiyùn 2 (945), fourth month,
he was ennobled as Prince of Běipíng (Běipíng Wáng).
In the third year (946), fifth month,
he was given the concurrent title of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
However, the Prince never led troops out.
The Qìdān attacked Chánzhōu,
and separately sent Wěi Wáng to attack Yànmén.
They were defeated at Xiùróng.
Eighth month,
Zhīyuǎn killed Bái Chéngfú and others of the Tǔhún tribe,
seized immense wealth,
and several thousand fine horses.
In the fourth year (947),
Qìdān encroached upon the capital.
Emperor Chū was relocated north.
The Prince sent his Ya General Wáng Jùn to present a memorial to Qìdān.
Yēlǜ Déguāng addressed him as "my son,"
and bestowed upon him a wooden staff.
In the barbarian custom, this was valued like the official staff in the Central States,
and could only be obtained by highly favored ministers.
Jùn returned holding the staff.
When the barbarian people saw it, they all avoided his path.
Upon Jùn's return,
he told the Prince that Qìdān certainly could not hold the Central States,
and so they discussed establishing a state.
In the second month, on the day Wùchén,
Zhāng Yànwēi, the Director of Campaign Administration of Hédōng, and others, presented a petition urging him to ascend the throne.
On the day Xīnwèi,
the Emperor ascended the throne,
and proclaimed the year as Tiānfú 12.
Liáng Huī, the bandit leader from Cízhōu, captured Xiāngzhōu and came to submit.
Shǐ Hóngzhào, the Commander-in-Chief of the Wǔjié Corps, captured Dàizhōu,
and killed its Prefect (Cìshǐ) Wáng Huī.
The Jìnzhōu General Yào Kěchóu killed its garrison commander Luò Cónglǎng, as well as Zhào Xī, the Money Collection Commissioner and Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū), and came to submit.
On the day Xīnsì,
Zhào Huī, the Acting Administrator of Shǎnzhōu, and Wáng Shǒu'ēn, the Acting Administrator of Lùzhōu, came to submit.
Tiānfú
was the reign title of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn.
Tiānfú only ran for eight years before the reign title was changed to Kāiyùn.
It has been four years since then.
Although Hàn had established a state,
it did not yet have a state name.
Furthermore, it used the Jìn reign title,
abandoning Kāiyùn and retroactively continuing Tiānfú as the 12th year.
Initially, there was no logical rationale
—we simply record the reality of the situation.
The phrase used when they changed sides and surrendered is
“lái guī” (came to submit).
We pity these people.
At that time, the world was without a ruler.
If they found a ruler, they went and submitted to him.
This is different from those who rebelled against one side to join another.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn was not a virtuous ruler,
but the desperate people who had nowhere to turn
still found refuge in him.
Therefore, we say
“guī” (submit/return).
Third month, on the first day, Bǐngxū,
miscellaneous taxes in Hédōng were waived.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
the Yánzhōu army rioted,
driving out its Military Governor Zhōu Mì.
On the day Rénchén,
Gāo Yànxún, the Commander of Dānzhōu, came to submit with his prefecture.
On the day Rényín,
Qìdān retreated (dùn),
leaving its general Xiāo Hàn as the Military Governor of Xuānwǔ Circuit to guard Biànzhōu.
Hearing that Hàn had risen in Tàiyuán,
they were afraid and left.
Therefore, the wording used here is different from simply "left by themselves."
Dùn
means
a term for retreating and avoiding.
Summer, fourth month, on the day Jǐwèi,
Yáng Bīn, the Right Chief Yāyá, was made Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ).
Guō Wēi, the Chief Clerk of Fānhàn Cavalry and Infantry, was made acting Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ).
Qìdān captured Xiāngzhōu
and killed Liáng Huī.
On the day Guǐhài,
Lady Lǐ of the State of Wèi was established as Empress.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,

Sū Féngjí, the Secretary to the Hédōng Military Governor, and Sū Yǔguī, the Investigator of the Surveillance Commission, were made Vice Directors of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilors (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Shǐ Hóngzhào, the Commander-in-Chief of the Infantry of the Imperial Guard, captured Lùzhōu.
On the day Wùchén,
Wǔ Xíngdé, the Commander of Fèngguó, came to submit with Héyáng.
Shǐ Hóngzhào captured Zézhōu.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Yēlǜ Déguāng of Qìdān died at Luánchéng.
The Qìdān entered Zhènzhōu.
Fifth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Liú Chóng, the Administrator of Tàiyuán, was made Acting Administrator of Běijīng.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the Emperor went to the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng).
Xiāo Hàn retreated and returned to Qìdān,
leaving Lǐ Cóngyì, Duke of Xún State, in charge of military and state affairs of the Southern Court.
On the day Wùshēn,
the Emperor arrived at Jiàngzhōu.
The Prefect Lǐ Cónglǎng came to submit.
Sixth month, on the day Bǐngchén,
the Emperor arrived at Héyáng.
Lǐ Cóngyì and his mother were killed in the capital.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor arrived from Tàiyuán.
On the day Wùchén,
the state name was changed to Hàn.
Criminals were pardoned, and people’s taxes were waived.
Yútián sent an envoy to arrive.
When Gāozǔ first established the state, there was no state name.
Perhaps because his imperial decrees and edicts contained no clear declaration,
it is omitted and not recorded here.
However, since he proclaimed the year Tiānfú 12,
it can be known that the state was still called Jìn.
But since there is no clear evidence,
we are cautious about what is doubtful.
This text records
“changed the state name to Hàn,”
so before the change, there must have been an existing designation;
this can be inferred.
That summer,
Liú Xù died.
In autumn, the intercalary seventh month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
the manufacture of Qìdān clothing and utensils was prohibited.
Dù Chóngwēi, Military Governor of Tiānxíong Commandery, rebelled.
Gāo Xíngzhōu, Military Governor of Tiānpíng Commandery, was appointed Chief Commander of the Field Headquarters at Yè Dū to suppress him.
On the day Gēngchén,
the imperial ancestors and grandparents were posthumously honored as emperors,
and their wives as empresses: Great-great-grandfather Tuān was given the posthumous name Míngyuán,
with the temple name Wénzǔ,
and Great-great-grandmother Lady Lǐ was given the posthumous name Míngzhēn;
Great-grandfather Áng was given the posthumous name Gōngxī,
with the temple name Dezǔ,
and Great-grandmother Lady Yáng was given the posthumous name Gōnghuì;
Grandfather Zuàn was given the posthumous name Zhāoxiàn,
with the temple name Yìzǔ,
and Grandmother Lady Lǐ was given the posthumous name Zhāomù;
Father Diǎn was given the posthumous name Zhāngshèng,
with the temple name Xiǎnzǔ,
and Mother Lady Ān was given the posthumous name Zhāngyì.
Hàn Gāo Huángdì was designated the High Progenitor (Gāozǔ),
and Guāngwǔ Huángdì the Venerated Ancestor (Shìzǔ),
and neither was subject to removal from the ancestral temple.
Dù Chóngwēi, during the reign of Jìn Chū Dì, had avoided the emperor’s personal name by removing
“Chóng,”
but restored it upon the rise of Hàn.
In the eighth month,
Bái Zàiróng, Commander of the Hùshèng Command, drove out the Qìdān
and returned with Zhènzhōu.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Xuē Huáiràng, Military Governor of Ānguó Commandery, killed the Qìdān general Liú Duó,
and entered Xíngzhōu.
In the ninth month, on the day Jiǎxū,
Dòu Zhēngù, Minister of Personnel, was made Minister of Works and concurrently Attendant Counselor of the Gate of the Palace (Ménxià Shìláng),
while Lǐ Tāo, Academician of the Hanlin Academy

and Draftsman in the Central Secretariat, was made Attendant Counselor of the Central Secretariat: both were given the title Concurrent Manager of Affairs of the Central Secretariat and the Gate of the Palace (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
On the day Gēngchén,
the northern campaign began.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
the emperor arrived at Wéichéng,
and granted a general amnesty to Hébĕi.
In the eleventh month, on the day Rénshēn,
Dù Chóngwēi surrendered.
In the twelfth month, on the day Kuǐsì,
the emperor returned from Yè Dū.
The first year of Qiányòu, spring, the first month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the reign title was changed.
On the day Jǐwèi,
the emperor’s name was changed to Gǎo.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
the emperor died at the Wànsuì Palace.
He was fifty-four years old.
Yǐndì
was Chéngyòu, the second son of Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Chéngyòu was appointed Upper General of the Right Guard and Commander-in-Chief of the Inner Palace.
Wèi Wáng Chéngxùn was older and virtuous.
Gāozǔ loved him,
and was about to designate him as heir,
but Chéngxùn died.
Gāozǔ fell ill,
and, grieving intensely,
entrusted Chéngyòu to his generals and ministers.
Sū Féngjí, the Chancellor, said:
“Imperial Prince Chéngyòu has not yet been enfeoffed as a king.
I request that he be swiftly enfeoffed.”
Before he could be enfeoffed, Gāozǔ died.
The death was kept secret,
and Dù Chóngwēi was executed.
The first year of Qiányòu, second month, on the day Xīnsì,
Chéngyòu was enfeoffed as King of Zhōu.
On that same day,
the emperor ascended the throne before the coffin.
On the day Rénchén,
Wáng Jǐngchóng, Major General of the Right Guard and Patrol Commissioner of Fèngxiáng, fought the Shǔ people at Dàsànguān,
and defeated them.
On the day Kuǐsì,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
In the third month, on the day Rénxū,
Dòu Zhēngù was appointed Director of the Imperial Mausoleum for the Late Emperor,
Duàn Xīyáo, Attendant Counselor of the Ministry of Personnel, was made Deputy Director,
Zhāng Zhāo, Grand Minister of Ceremonies, was made Director of Rituals,
Lú Jià, Attendant Counselor of the Ministry of War, was made Director of Imperial Equipage,
and Biān Wèi, Censor-in-Chief, was made Director of Imperial Guards and Banners.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Lǐ Tāo was dismissed.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, Military Governor of Hùguó Commandery, rebelled
and captured Tóngguān.
Summer, the fourth month, on the day Xīnsì,
Wáng Yù, Grand Army Monitor of Shǎnzhōu, captured Tóngguān.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Zhào Sīwǎn, a general of Yǒngxīng Commandery, rebelled and defected to Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
Wáng Jùn, Commissioner of Guests, commanded troops and stationed them west of the pass.

Yáng Bīn was appointed Attendant Counselor of the Central Secretariat and concurrently Minister of Personnel, with the title Concurrent Manager of Affairs of the Central Secretariat and the Gate of the Palace.
Guō Wēi was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Guō Cóngyì, Military Governor of Zhènníng Commandery, was appointed Grand Army Commander of Yǒngxīng Commandery.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Bái Wénkē, Military Governor of Bǎoyì Commandery, was appointed Grand Army Commander of Hézhōng.
The Yellow River breached its bank at Yuánwǔ.
Wáng Jùn was not appointed a general,
nor was he ordered to suppress the rebels,
but merely directed to reinforce the area west of the pass with troops.
The appointment of generals is recorded in the text below.
The fifth month, on the day Jǐwèi,
the Uighurs sent envoys to come.
On the day Yǐhài,
Wǔ Jìn, a commoner of Nèihuáng in Wèizōu, had a wife who gave birth to three boys at once.
The Yellow River breached its bank at Yúchí in Huázhōu.
There was drought
and locusts.
Autumn, the seventh month, on the day Wùshēn, the first day of the month,
Wáng Jìhóng, Military Governor of Zhāngdé Commandery, killed his judicial assistant Zhāng Yì.
Jays and mynas consumed the locusts.
On the day Bǐngchén,
the capture of jays and mynas was prohibited.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Guō Wēi was appointed Concurrent Manager of Affairs of the Central Secretariat and the Gate of the Palace.
On the day Kuǐhài,
Wáng Yànhuī, Qìdān Prefect of Màozhōu, defected.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Zhāng Péng, Vice Commissioner of Chéngdé Commandery, was executed.
On the day Yǐhài,
Wáng Jǐngchóng rebelled and defected to Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
The eighth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Guō Wēi suppressed Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
In the ninth month,
Shàng Hóngqiān, Grand Provisioning Commander of the Western Field Headquarters, fought Zhào Sīwǎn
and was defeated.
Winter, the tenth month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
the Tibetan envoy Sīmàndǔ Lìnzhānyàosī arrived.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jiǎyín,
Lǐ Sōng, Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, was executed
and his clan was exterminated.
On the day Rénshēn,
Ruìwén Shèngwǔ Zhāosù Xiào Huángdì was buried at Ruìlíng.
The mausoleum is in Gàochéng County, Hénán.
The twelfth month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
Gāo Yǔnquán, Military Governor of Zhāngwǔ Commandery, killed Liú Jǐngyán, Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, who had retired from office.
The second year, spring, the first month, on the day Yǐsì, the first day of the month,
prisoners were pardoned.
From the time Yǐndì ascended the throne until now,
the reign title should have been changed but was not;
this is detailed in the note for the second year of Zhōu Xiǎndé.
And yet, the emperor’s personal name was Chéngyòu,
and the era name was Qiányòu;
the entire nation’s officials and populace commonly used both without changing them to observe avoidance.
This was the greatest fault of that time,
and the Basic Annals make no criticism,
but merely record the facts,
leaving it for later generations to judge.
The second month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the tax on paired households (niǔpèi zū) was exempted for the populace.
Summer, the fifth month,
Zhōu Guāngxùn, a general under Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, surrendered.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Zhào Sīwǎn surrendered.
The sixth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
Yáng Yànxún, a leader of the Uighurs, arrived.
An envoy was sent from Xīliáng Fǔ.
There were locusts.
Autumn, the seventh month, on the day Dīngsì,
Guō Wēi executed Zhào Sīwǎn, Surveillance Commissioner of Huázhōu, in Jīngzhào.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Hézhōng was captured.
Shǒuzhēn burned himself to death,
so it is not recorded that he was executed.
The eighth month,
Guō Cóngyì killed Qiáo Shǒuwēn, former Patrol Commissioner of Yǒngxīng.
On the day Bǐngxū,
Guō Wēi sent an envoy to present the captives.
Winter, the tenth month,
the Qìdān plundered Zhào and Wèi.
The assembled ministers presented additional horses for the capital.
The Qìdān captured Nèiqiū.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Guō Wēi and Wáng Jùn, Commissioner of the Southern Chancellery of the Palace Secretariat, attacked the Qìdān.
The eleventh month,
the Qìdān fled.
The third year, spring, the first month,
Zhào Huī, Grand Army Commander of the Western Field Headquarters, captured Fèngxiáng.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Guō Wēi presented additional horses for the capital.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Zhào Huī presented the heads of the slain and the captives.
Jǐngchóng burned himself to death,
so it is not recorded that he was executed.
The second month, on the day Jiǎxū,
the household of Qǔ Wēn, a commoner of Rǔyīn in Yǐngzhōu, was publicly honored.
The third month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
during the Cold Food Festival,
the sacrifice to the spirits was made at the Southern Imperial Garden.
Summer, the fourth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Guō Wēi, Commissioner of Military Affairs, was made Military Governor of Tiānxíong Commandery.
The sixth month, on the day Kuǐmǎo,
the Yellow River breached its bank at Yuánwǔ.
Autumn, the eighth month,
the Tatars came to submit.
In the winter, the eleventh month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào (the Commissioner of Palace Guards), and Wáng Zhāng (the Commissioner of the Three Bureaus) were executed,
and their clans were exterminated.
Guō Wēi rebelled.
On the day Gēngchén,
Sòng Yánwò, the Military Governor of Yìchéng Commandery, defected and joined Wēi.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Wēi invaded Fēngqiū,
and Mùróng Yànchāo, the Military Governor of Tàiníng Commandery, camped at Qīlǐ Diàn.
On the day Guǐwèi,
the troops were rewarded in the Northern Suburbs.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
the troops were rewarded at Liúzipō.
Mùróng Yànchāo and Guō Wēi fought,
and were defeated.
Hóu Yì, the Prefect of Kāifēng, defected and surrendered to Wēi.
Guō Yǔnmíng rebelled.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
the Emperor passed away.
Sū Féngjí committed suicide.
Hàn perished.
He was twenty years old.
He was buried in Yángzhái County, Xǔ Prefecture, in the first year of Guǎngshùn of Zhōu,
and his tomb was named Yǐng Líng.
Since he was buried by the rebels,
this is therefore not recorded.
Forty-two days after the passing of Emperor Yǐndì,
Zhōu Tàizǔ first ascended the throne,
yet (the text) cut off the record immediately upon the Emperor's passing, writing
"Hàn perished."
This shows
that when the Emperor passed away, Hàn collapsed and perished.
That the Empress Dowager held court,
and that the Duke of Xiāngyīn succeeded to the throne,
were all pretexts fabricated by Zhōu,
and were not true facts.
To expose this deception,
the text therefore states:
"Hàn perished."
This also shows that the establishment of Zhōu was delayed;
since it was delayed and difficult to establish itself independently,
it suggests that they still felt some shame.
Alas!
When a sovereign ascends the throne and names the first year 'Yuánnián,'
it is an ordinary matter,
and the ancients did not consider it serious or important.
Before Kǒngzǐ compiled the *Chūnqiū*,
things were already thus,
and even if they were tyrannical rulers, foolish sovereigns,
or arrogant and mediocre historians,
in recording events, whether near or far, in order,
they all counted them using the sequence of years and months (one, two, etc.);
this is simply the natural order of things.
That 'one' is called 'Yuán' (beginning/first)
was also never based on a specific rule;
it was simply the phrasing used by the ancients.
But later scholars who twisted their learning,
began to claim that Kǒngzǐ recording
'Yuánnián'
was the great fundamental principle of the *Chūnqiū*,
and consequently regarded changing the reign title as a serious matter.
The ancients referred to the first month of the year
and did not call it 'one,'
but called it 'Zhēngyuè.'
The *Guóyǔ* discusses the six *Lǚ* pipes, saying that 'Yuán' is paired with Dà Lǚ.
The *Zhōu Yì* lists the six lines (Yáo) saying 'Chūjiǔ' (initial nine).
Generally, when the ancients spoke of numbers, they often did not use 'one,'
and this was not restricted to calling the year 'Yuán.'
Since the Hàn dynasty,
they further named years by establishing reign titles (Jiànyuán),
and orthodox and spurious reigns became entangled,
so the titles became numerous,
too many to record completely.
The Wǔdài
was an age of chaos.
Many of its affairs lacked method and did not conform to reason,
and are generally not worth mentioning.
However, regarding the errors and discrepancies in their reign titles, which confuse later generations,
these must be clarified.
Liáng Tàizǔ was assassinated in the second year of Qiánhuà.
The next year,
Mòdì had already executed Yǒuguī,
rejected his reign title Fèng Lì,
and reverted to calling it the third year of Qiánhuà.
This can still be explained.
But when Hàn Gāozǔ established his state,
why did he reject Jìn Chūdì's fourth year of Kāiyùn,
and revert to calling it the twelfth year of Tiānfú?
Why was this?
It was probably due to his private feelings of love and hatred.
When Chūdì was in power,
Hàn Gāozǔ resided in Tàiyuán,
and often looked down upon Jìn with great resentment,
while Jìn outwardly treated him with special courtesy,
fortunately without yet showing any weakness.
When the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
Hàn never intended to rush to its aid.
After Chūdì had been taken north,
(Hàn Gāozǔ) merely pretended to use military might to claim pursuit,
reaching Tǔmén before returning.
When he ascended the throne and changed the reign title,
and rejected the title Kāiyùn,
his intentions become clear.
Essentially, he no longer held the righteous principles of sovereign and minister toward Chūdì,
but rather sought advantage by rejoicing in disaster—
this was his long-held ambition.
What a cause for lamentation!
Indeed, what is said to be present within must manifest outwardly;
this is evidenced here!
Annals of Zhōu, Chapter 11
Emperor Tàizǔ Shèngshén Gōngsù Wénwǔ,
whose surname was Guō,
was a native of Yáoshān, Xíng Prefecture.
His father, Jiǎn,
served Jìn as the Prefect of Shùn Prefecture.
Liú Róngōng attacked and captured Shùn Prefecture,
and Jiǎn was killed.
His son, Wēi, was orphaned young,
and depended on a member of the Cháng clan from Lù Prefecture.
Lǐ Jìtāo, the acting governor of Lù Prefecture, recruited brave and capable men as soldiers.
Wēi was eighteen years old,
and volunteered due to his strength and courage.
He was high-spirited,
and fond of aggressive drunken behavior.
Jìtāo especially valued him.
Wēi once wandered through the marketplace.
There was a butcher in the market
who habitually dominated the market people with his bravery.
Wēi, being drunk,
called the butcher,
asked him to bring forward a table and cut meat.
When the cutting did not meet his standard,
he shouted at him.
The butcher bared his abdomen and showed it to Wēi, saying:
"You claim to be a brave man.
Can you kill me?"
Wēi immediately stepped forward, took a knife, and stabbed him to death.
The entire market was alarmed,
but Wēi remained quite composed.
He was seized by the officials.
Jìtāo regretted losing his courage,
and secretly allowed him to escape.
Later, he recalled him and placed him under his command.
Jìtāo rebelled against Jìn and defected to Liáng.
Later, when Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
Jìtāo was executed.
All the soldiers under Jìtāo were assigned to the Mounted Cavalry Guards.
Wēi, being proficient in writing and arithmetic, was appointed as a military clerk.
He enjoyed reading military classics,
and had a general understanding of military strategy.
Later, he became a Palace Guard clerk.
When Hàn Gāozǔ was the Commander of the Palace Guards,
he especially cherished and favored Wēi.
Afterward, whenever Gāozǔ governed a commandery,
he always had Wēi accompany him.
When the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
Hàn Gāozǔ raised troops in Tàiyuán,
and ascended the imperial throne.
He appointed Wēi as Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
In the first month of the first year of Qiányòu (948),
Gāozǔ's illness worsened significantly.
He entrusted Emperor Yǐndì to Wēi, Shǐ Hóngzhào, and others.
When Emperor Yǐndì ascended the throne,
Wēi was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs.
In the third month of that year,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn in Hézhōng, Zhào Sīwǎn in Yǒngxīng, and Wáng Jǐngchóng in Fèngxiáng rebelled successively.
Emperor Yǐndì dispatched Bái Wénkē, Guō Cóngyì, Cháng Sī, and others to suppress them separately,
but for a long time, none of them achieved success.
Emperor Yǐndì said to Wēi:
"I wish to trouble you, sir. Is that permissible?"
Wēi replied:
"Your subject dares not request it,
nor dares he decline.
I await only Your Majesty's command."
Wēi was then additionally granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì (Chancellor),
and sent west to supervise the various generals.
When Wēi stayed in the army camps,
hosting and meeting with guests,
he wore wide robes and broad belts.
But when facing the enemy or setting up camp,
he wore a simple cloth cap and short tunic,
indistinguishable from the common soldiers.
Of the gifts bestowed by the Emperor,
he would hold an archery contest with his generals,
allowing them to take whatever they won.
All the remainder he distributed among the officers and soldiers.
All the officers and men were delighted.
Wēi arrived at Hézhōng,
and personally palisaded the east of that city.
Sī palisaded the south,
Wén Kē palisaded the west,
and twenty thousand able-bodied men from five counties were mobilized to construct connecting barricades to protect the three palisades.
All the generals asserted that Shǒuzhēn was a desperate bandit,
and his defeat was imminent,
so it was improper to exhaust the men in this manner.
Wēi did not listen.
Afterward, Shǒuzhēn repeatedly sent troops out to attack and damage the connecting barricades.
Wēi immediately repaired them.
Shǒuzhēn repeatedly went out again to attack,
and every time he went out, there were casualties and losses.
After a long time,
both troops and food supplies within the city were exhausted.
Wēi said:
"It is done!"
He then prepared siege equipment,
set an appointed day,
and attacked it from four sides.
They breached the outer city wall (luó chéng).
Shǒuzhēn and his wife and children burned themselves to death.
Sī Wǎn and Jǐng Chóng subsequently surrendered.
Emperor Yǐn rewarded Wēi with a jade belt,
and added the titles Examiner Grand Preceptor (Jiǎnjiào Tàishī) and concurrent Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Wēi declined, saying:
"Your servant served the former emperor (Xiān Dì),
and saw many meritorious ministers.
None were ever bestowed a jade belt."
He continued, saying:
"Your servant was fortunate to lead the ranks,
and relying on the awe and might of the Hàn [dynasty], was able to defeat the rebels.
How can this be solely the achievement of your servant?
It is due to the wisdom of the generals and chancellors,
who managed to stabilize the imperial court,
and soothe those within and without,
and supplied provisions on time.
Therefore, your servant was able to focus entirely on the campaign."
Emperor Yǐn considered Wēi virtuous.
Thereupon, he summoned Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào, Sū Féngjí, Yǔ Guī, Dòu Zhēngù, Wáng Zhāng, and others, and bestowed upon all of them jade belts.
Only then did Wēi accept.
Wēi further attributed the credit to the high officials,
and requested increases in their titles and rewards.
Thereupon, Dòu Zhēngù was promoted to Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
Féngjí to Minister of Instruction (Sītú),
and Yǔ Guī and Bīn to Left and Right Directors of the Affairs of the Secretariat (Púshè).
Afterward, he further said:
"These are merely the close ministers of the Hàn court!
The various imperial relatives of Hàn and the regional commanders (fāngzhèn) throughout the realm,
as well as those outwardly connected to Jīng, Zhè, and Húnán,
have not yet been reached."
Because of this, excessive rewards spread throughout the realm.
That winter,
the Qìdān invaded the border.
Wēi, as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ), led a northern campaign.
When he reached Wèizhōu,
the Qìdān fled.
In the second month of the third year,
the army returned.
In the fourth month,
Wēi was appointed Commissioner of Defense of Yèdū (Yèdū Liúshǒu) and Military Governor of Tiānxióng Command (Tiānxióng Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
He was still to hold his post as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) while commanding the region.
Chancellor Sū Féngjí argued that the Commissioner of Military Affairs should not concurrently hold the office of a regional military commander (fānzhèn),
and strongly disputed this with Shǐ Hóngzhào and others.
After a long time,
Wēi finally proceeded to his post while retaining the title of Commissioner of Military Affairs.
An imperial edict ordered that all prefectures north of the Yellow River (Héběi) be subject to Wēi's command.
Emperor Yǐn plotted with Lǐ Yè and others.
They had already killed Shǐ Hóngzhào and others.
An edict ordered Lǐ Hóngyì, the Military Governor of Zhènníng Command, to kill Wáng Yīn, the Commander of the Imperial Infantry Guard, at Chánzhōu.
Another edict ordered Guō Chóng, the Commander of the Imperial Cavalry Guard, to kill Wēi and Xuānhuī Envoy Wáng Jùn at Wèi.
The edict first reached Chánzhōu.
Hóngyì feared the matter would not succeed,
and instead showed the edict to Yīn.
Yīn and Hóngyì sent men to inform Wēi.
Soon after, the envoy carrying the edict to kill Wēi and Jùn also arrived at a gallop.
Wēi concealed the edict,
and summoned Wèi Rénpǔ, a clerk in the Bureau of Military Affairs, to plot with him in his private chambers.
Rénpǔ advised Wēi to revolt.
He instructed Wēi to use the seal of the Commissioner of Defense upside down,
and counterfeit a new imperial edict,
ordering Wēi to execute various generals and officers to incite their anger.
The generals and officers were all enraged and eagerly offered their service.
On the dīngchǒu day of the eleventh month,
Wēi then raised troops and crossed the Yellow River.

Emperor Yǐn sent Hóu Yì, the Prefect of Kāifēng, Zhāng Yànchāo, the Military Governor of Bǎodà Command, and Yán Jìnqīng, the Director of the Guest Hall, along with others, to lead troops to resist Wēi.
He also sent the palace eunuch Tuō to secretly observe Wēi's movements.
Tuō was captured by Wēi.
Wēi then used Tuō to submit a memorial requesting that Lǐ Yè and others be bound and sent to the army camp.
When Emperor Yǐn received Wēi's memorial,
he showed it to Yè and the others.
Yè and the others all stated that Wēi's intent to rebel was now manifest.
They then executed all of Wēi's family members in the capital.
On the gēngchén day,
Wēi arrived at Huázhōu.
Sòng Yánwò, the Military Governor of Yìchéng Command, defected from Hàn and surrendered.
On the rénwǔ day,
he violated Fēngqiū.
On the jiǎchén day,
he fought with Mùróng Yànchāo, the Military Governor of Tàiníng Command, at Liúzǐpí.
Yànchāo was defeated
and fled to Yǎnzhōu.
Guō Yǔnmíng revolted
and assassinated Emperor Yǐn at Zhàocūn.
On the bǐngxū day,
Wēi entered the capital,
setting fires and looting extensively.
On the wùzǐ day,
he led all the officials to pay respects to the Empress Dowager at Míngdé Gate,
requesting that an heir be enthroned.
The Empress Dowager issued an order: all civil and military officials and generals and officers of the Six Armies
should deliberate on selecting a wise and sagacious person
to inherit the great lineage (the throne).
On the gēngyín day,
Wēi led all officials to the Míngdé Gate,
requesting that Yūn, the Military Governor of Wǔníng Command, be enthroned as the heir.
He sent Grand Preceptor Féng Dào to welcome Yūn from Xúzhōu.
On the xīnmǎo day,
he requested the Empress Dowager preside over the court and attend to state affairs.
Wáng Jùn was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs,
and Fàn Zhì, Academician of the Hanlin Academy and Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, was appointed Deputy Commissioner.
On the jiǎwǔ day, the first day of the twelfth month,
Wēi campaigned north against the Qìdān.
He stationed his army at Huázhōu.
On the guǐchǒu day,
he reached Chánzhōu and then returned.
Wáng Jùn sent Guō Chóng with seven hundred cavalry to intercept Liú Yūn at Sòngzhōu.
They killed him.
His generals, Gǒng Tíngměi and Yáng Wēn, were defending Xúzhōu for Yūn.
On the wùwǔ day,
Wēi arrived at the Palace Gate (Zhǎi Mén).
The former Hàn Chancellors Dòu Zhēngù and Sū Yǔguī came to urge him to ascend the throne.
On the gēngshēn day,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict making Wēi Regent (Jiānguó).
In the first month of spring of the first year of Guǎngshùn (951), on the dīngmǎo day,
the Emperor (Wēi) ascended the throne,
granted a general amnesty,
changed the reign title,
and named the state Zhōu.
On the jǐsì day,
he conferred the honorary title Zhāoshèng Huáng Tàihòu (Illustrious Sage Imperial Empress Dowager) upon the Hàn Empress Dowager.
On the wùyín day,
Liú Chóng of Hàn established himself [as Emperor] at Tàiyuán.
On the jǐmǎo day,
Féng Dào was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
The various states of Wú and Shǔ established themselves,
and all broke off [relations] and are not recorded here.
This record,
and their failure to submit to Zhōu,
is mentioned in the discussion section of the Chronological Tables of the Ten Kingdoms (Shí Guó Niánpǔ Lùn).
In the second month, on the xīnchǒu day,
an envoy, a Dūdu (Commander), came from the Xīzhōu Uighurs (Huíhú).
On the dīngwèi day,
Wùyù of Qìdān sent the envoy Dìgǔzhī.
On the guǐchǒu day,
during the Cold Food Festival,
he performed a remote sacrifice (wàng jì) at Púchí.
On the dīngsì day,
Tián Mǐn, Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs, was sent as envoy to the Qìdān.
An envoy, Mó Ní, came from the Huíhú.
Púchí
is the name of a Buddhist monastery.
In the third month, on the jiǎxū day,
Wáng Yànchāo, the Military Governor of Wǔníng Command, conquered Xúzhōu.
That Gǒng Tíngměi and Yáng Wēn died is not recorded here;
the account is found in the Biography of Yūn.
In the fourth month of summer, on the jiǎwǔ day,
Lady Dǒng was established as Virtuous Consort (Défēi).
In the fifth month, on the xīnwèi day,
he posthumously honored his ancestors and father as Emperors,
and their wives as Empresses: Great-Great-Grandfather Jǐng was given the posthumous title Ruìhé (Sagacious and Harmonious),
with the temple name Xìnzǔ;
Great-Great-Grandmother, Lady Zhāng, was given the posthumous title Ruìgōng (Sagacious and Respectful);
Great-Grandfather Chén was given the posthumous title Míngxiàn (Luminous and Illustrious),
with the temple name Xīzǔ;
Great-Grandmother, Lady Shēn, was given the posthumous title Míngxiào (Luminous and Filial);
Grandfather Yùn was given the posthumous title Yìshùn (Assisting and Compliant),
with the temple name Yìzǔ;
Grandmother, Lady Hán, was given the posthumous title Yìjìng (Assisting and Respectful);
Father was given the posthumous title Zhāngsù (Illustrious and Solemn),
with the temple name Qìngzǔ;
Mother, Lady Wáng, was given the posthumous title Zhāngdé (Illustrious and Virtuous).
In the sixth month, on the xīnhài day,

Fàn Zhì and Lǐ Gǔ, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue and Director of the Three Bureaus (Pàn Sānsī), were appointed Vice Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
Dòu Zhēngù and Sū Yǔguī were dismissed.
On the guǐchǒu day,
Fàn Zhì participated in administering the affairs of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Cān Zhī Shūmìyuàn Shì).
On the dīngsì day,
Zhái Guāngyè, Envoy of the Northern Bureau of the Court of Review, was appointed Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the wùyín day,
the Emperor visited Wáng Jùn's residence.
In the eighth month, on the rényín day,
the Qìdān returned the remains of Zhào Yíng.
, the Hàn people
came to punish [us],
attacking from Jìnzhōu. The punishment was levied upon the guilty.
Regarding Hàn toward Zhōu
, righteousness dictates that they deserved execution (or punishment).
That it states
"from Jìnzhōu"
means that the Hàn troops, who ought to have executed the criminals in the capital (Jīngshī)
, merely entered from Jìnzhōu.
Attacks on the city that involved neither gain nor loss are not recorded.
This recording
permits (or acknowledges) the Hàn coming to punish.
The eleventh month
, Wáng Jùn
and Wáng Yànchāo, the Jìedùshǐ of the Jiànxíong Army, repelled them.
The twelfth month, Mùróng Yànchāo
rebelled. Second year, spring, the first month, on the day Jiǎzǐ
, Cáo Yīng, the Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard Infantry
, was made the General Commander of the Yǎnzhōu Mobile Camp.
On the day Gēngwǔ, King Zhāo of Gāolì
sent his Guǎngpíng Shìláng Xú Féng to come.
Second month, on the day Gēngyín, Zhé Déyǐ, the Defense Commissioner of Fǔzhōu
, captured Kělán Garrison.
Third month, on the first day Dīngsì, during the Cold Food festival (Hánshí)
, the distant sacrifices were offered in the suburbs (jiāo).
On the day Wùchén
, Zhèng Rénhuì, the Director of the Inner Guest Hall
, was made Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ). Zhái Guāngyè
was dismissed. Summer, fifth month, on the day Gēngshēn
, the Eastern Campaign
began. Lǐ Gǔ
was left behind to govern the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū), and Zhèng Rénhuì
was made Grand Palace Inspector (Dànèi Dōu Diǎnjiǎn).
On the day Guǐhài, they reached Cáo zhōu
, and prisoners sentenced to exile and lesser crimes were pardoned.
On the day Yǐhài
, Yǎnzhōu
was captured.
On the day Rénwǔ, Yǎnzhōu
was pardoned. Yànchāo
threw himself into a well and died, thus it is not recorded that he was executed (fúzhū).
Sixth month, on the first day Yǐyǒu
, the Emperor traveled to Qūfù
and offered sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ (Confucius).
On the day Gēngzǐ
, they returned from Yǎnzhōu.
Autumn, ninth month, on the day Yǐchǒu
, Wáng Yǎn
, the Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud (Dàpú Shàoqīng), was sent as envoy to Gāolì.
The Qìdān raided the borders.
Third year, spring, first month, on the day Yǐmǎo, Yáng Chóngxùn
, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Línzhōu, rebelled against Hàn
and came to defect.
Intercalary month, on the day Bǐngxū, the Huíhú
envoy Dúchéng Xiāngwēn came.
Second month, on the day Jiǎzǐ, Wáng Jùn
was demoted to Sheriff (Sīmǎ) of Shāngzhōu.
Third month, on the day Jiǎshēn, Róng
was enfeoffed as Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng).
On the day Bǐngxū, Zhèng Rénhuì
was dismissed.
On the day Jǐchǒu, Wáng Rénhào

, the Commander (Tuánliànshǐ) of Dìzhōu, was made General-in-Chief of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Dàjiāngjūn) and Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ). The reason why the word "son" (zǐ) is not written
is that according to ritual (lǐ), Róng
could not be considered a son. If "son" is not written, then his original surname should have been written
. The reason it is not written
is that it was a taboo shared by the Zhōu people.
Summer, sixth month
, heavy rain
and flooding.
Autumn, seventh month
, Zhāng Zàngyīng
, the Military Commissioner of the Lú tái Army for the Qìdān, came to defect.
Ninth month, Tǔhún Dǎng Fùdá
and others came.
Winter, tenth month, on the day Gēngshēn, Fèng Dào
was made Commissioner for Offering and Welcoming the Spirit Tablets.
Eleventh month, on the day Guǐwèi, the Dǎngxiàng
envoys Wú Tiēmó Wǔ and others came.
Twelfth month, on the day Wùshēn, the spirit tablets of the Four Temples
arrived from the Western Capital (Xījīng).
They were welcomed in the western suburbs
and installed in the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào).
On the day Rénshēn, Wáng Yīn
, the Jìedùshǐ of the Tiānxíong Army, was executed.
On the day Yǐhài, sacrifices were offered in the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Xiǎndé first year, spring, first month, on the first day Bǐngzǐ
, rites were performed in the southern suburbs (Nánjiāo)
. A great amnesty was declared
, and the reign title was changed
. The officials submitted the honorific title: Shèngmíng Wénwǔ Réndé Huángdì (Holy, Bright, Cultured, Martial, Benevolent, and Virtuous Emperor).
On the day Wùyín
, Yèdū
was abolished.
On the day Bǐngxū, Zhèng Rénhuì
, the Jìedùshǐ of the Zhènníng Army, was made Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ).
On the day Rénchén, Wáng Pǔ

, Academian of the Duānmíng Hall and Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng), was made Vice Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councillor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì). Wáng Rénhào
was dismissed.
On this very day, the Emperor passed away (bēng) in the Zīdé Palace.
He was fifty-one years old.
Recording
"this very day"
connects the entry to the preceding text
, preventing the suspicion that there was no day recorded for the passing.
Annals of Zhōu, Volume Twelve Emperor Shìzōng Ruìwǔ Xiàowén
, whose original surname was Chái
, was a native of Lónggāng
in Xíngzhōu. A daughter of the Chái clan
married Tàizǔ (Grand Progenitor);
she became Empress Shèngmù. The son of the Empress's elder brother, Shǒulǐ, named Róng
, followed his paternal aunt and grew up in Tàizǔ's household
. He was loved for his diligence and sincerity
, and Tàizǔ subsequently adopted him as his son.
Later, Tàizǔ gradually rose in status
. Róng was also fully grown
, possessing an extraordinary and heroic appearance
. He was skilled in horsemanship and archery
, had a basic understanding of books, history, and the Huang-Lao philosophies
, and his disposition was serious and reserved.
When Tàizǔ was the Hàn Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ)
, Róng
was the General-in-Chief of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Jiānménwèi Dàjiāngjūn). When Tàizǔ governed Tiānxíong
, Róng concurrently held the posts of Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Guìzhōu and Commander-in-Chief of the Headquarters (Yánèi Dōu Zhǐhuīshǐ) of the Tiānxíong Army.
In the winter of Qiányòu third year
, the Zhōu troops rose up in Wèi
and invaded the capital (Jīngshī)
. Róng
was left behind to guard Wèi. When Tàizǔ entered and was established [as emperor]
, Róng was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Chánzhōu, Jìedùshǐ of the Zhènníng Army
, Acting Grand Tutor (Jiǎnxiào Tàifù), and Grand Councillor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Róng
had always been viewed with suspicion by Wáng Jùn, the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ). In the first month of Guǎngshùn third year
, when Róng came to court,
he was not allowed to stay. Subsequently, Jùn
was found guilty and executed. In the third month
, Róng
was appointed Prefect (Yǐn) of Kāifēng,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng). That winter
, divination was performed to hold the Rites of the Southern Suburbs (Nánjiāo) on the first day of the first month of the following year
. However, Tàizǔ fell ill
and was unable to hold court for a long time.
In Xiǎndé first year, first month, on the day Bǐngzǐ
, the suburban sacrifices were held
, barely completing the ceremony
. Immediately, the Prince (Wáng) was tasked with overseeing all military affairs, internal and external.
On the day Rénchén
, Tàizǔ passed away (bēng)
, but the death was kept secret and not officially announced.
On the day Bǐngshēn
, the death was announced
, and the Emperor immediately ascended the throne before the coffin.
Wèi Rénpǔ
, the General-in-Chief of the Right Guard (Yòu Jiānménwèi Dàjiāngjūn), was made Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ). The record of enfeoffing him as Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng)
rectifies the fact that he was not the [biological] son.
The remaining instances where he usurped the rites of a legitimate successor
are evident without waiting for criticism or censure
; therefore, no differing words are used for them.
Second month, on the day Gēngxū
, the Huíhú
sent envoys to come.
On the day Dīngmǎo, Fèng Dào
was made Commissioner for the Mountain Mausoleum of the Late Emperor (Dàxíng Huángdì Shānlíng Shǐ). Tián Mǐn
, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng), was made Commissioner of Rites and Ceremonies. Zhāng Zhāo
, the Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū), was made Commissioner for Imperial Carriages and Standards. Zhāng Xù
, the Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), was made Commissioner for Ceremonial Guards. Wáng Mǐn
, the Deputy Prefect (Shàoyǐn) of Kāifēng who provisionally managed the Prefectural Affairs, was made Commissioner for Bridges, Roads, and Courier Stations. The Hàn people
came to punish,
attacking from Lùzhōu.
a general amnesty was granted. On the day Guǐwèi
Zhèng Rénhuì was appointed Resident Grandee (Liúshǒu) of Dōngjīng. On the day Yǐyǒu
[the Emperor] went to Lùzhōu to attack Hàn. On the day Rénchén
[the army] arrived at Zézhōu,
and reviewed troops in the northern suburbs. On the day Guǐsì
[they] fought Liú Mín at Gāoyuán,
defeating him,
pursuing him to Gāopíng,
and defeating him again. On the day Dīngyǒu
[the Emperor] visited Lùzhōu. On the day Jǐhài
Fán Àinéng, Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry of the Imperial Guard (Shìwèi Mǎjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ), and Hé Huī, Commander-in-Chief of the Infantry (Bùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ), were executed. On the day Rén'yín
Fú Yànqīng, Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Tiānxióng Command, was appointed Overall Commander of the Hédōng Field Army (Hédōng Xíngyíng Dū Bùshǔ).
It does not state "attack" (fá),
because the fault lies with Zhōu,
and the matter cannot be determined by size [of the states];
therefore, the text uses "two attacking each other."
Since he (Liú Mín) refused to submit to Zhōu,
and since he claimed the title of Emperor,
his personal name (Xìngmíng) is recorded. In summer, the fourth month, on the day Yǐmǎo
Shénshèng Wénwǔ Gōngsù Xiàohuángdì was buried at Sōnglíng.
Dǒng Xīyán, Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Fénzhōu, rebelled against Hàn and defected [to Zhōu]. On the day Bǐngchén
Zhāng Hànchāo, Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Liáozhōu, rebelled against Hàn and defected [to Zhōu]. On the day Xīnyǒu
Ānzhōu and Xiànzhōu were captured. On the day Rénxū
Lady Fú of Wèiguó was installed as Empress (Huánghòu).
Shízhōu and Qìnzhōu were captured. On the day Yǐchǒu
Féng Dào died. On the day Gēngwǔ
prisoners in Lùzhōu convicted of exile (liú zuì) or lesser crimes were pardoned.
[The Emperor] went to Tàiyuán.
Lǐ Qíng, Supervisor of the Army (Jiānjūn) of Xīnzhōu, killed its Prefect Zhào Yīn,
rebelled against Hàn and defected [to Zhōu].
[This event occurred] in Xīnzhèng County, Zhèngzhōu. In the fifth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ
Zhèng Chǔqiān, the defending general of Dàizhōu, rebelled against Hàn and defected [to Zhōu];
the Qìdān rescued Hàn. On the day Dīngyǒu
the Uyghur envoy Yīnnándílüè arrived.
Fú Yànqīng fought the Qìdān at Xīnkǒu,
suffering a great defeat;
Shǐ Yànchāo, Commander-in-Chief of the Vanguard (Xiānfēng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ), died there. In the sixth month, on the day Yǐsì
the army returned to the capital. On the day Yǐchǒu
[the Emperor] arrived at Xīnzhèng,
and subsequently offered sacrifices at Sōnglíng. On the day Gēngwǔ
[the Emperor] arrived from Tàiyuán. In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Gēngchén
[the Emperor] inspected the crops at the Southern Imperial Estate (Nán Yùzhuāng). On the day Guǐsì

Jǐng Fàn, Direct Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Yuàn Zhí Xuéshì) and Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng), was appointed Vice Minister of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì);
Wèi Rénpǔ was appointed Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ). In winter, the tenth month, on the day Jiǎchén
Mèng Hànqīng, Grand General of the Left Yǔlín Guard, was executed. In the second year [of Xiǎndé], spring, the second month
an imperial edict sought forthright counsel.
During the chaotic era of the Five Dynasties,
there were five cases of succession by the designated heir,
and four instances where the era name (gǎiyuán) was not changed according to ancient practice.
The Last Emperor of Liáng (Liáng Mòdì) and the Deposed Emperor of Jìn (Jìn Chūdì) both ascended the throne and ruled for more than a year;
they ought to have changed the era name but did not,
only changing it in the subsequent year.
The Emperor Yǐndì of Hàn and Emperor Shìzōng of Zhōu
both continued to use the era name of the previous emperor,
and did not change it throughout their reigns.
The imperial annals (Běnjì) contain no censure of this,
only recording the facts,
allowing the fault to be recognized spontaneously. In summer, the fifth month, on the day Xīnwèi
Xiàng Xùn, Commissioner of the Southern Court of Palace Affairs (Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ), and Wáng Jǐng, Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng, attacked Shǔ. On the day Jiǎxū
Buddhist monasteries were greatly destroyed,

and common people whose parents had no attendance or support were prohibited from becoming monks or nuns, as were those who privately ordained themselves. In autumn, the ninth month, on the first day (Shuò) Bǐngyín
a copper prohibition was issued. In the intercalary month, on the day Guǐchǒu
Xiàng Xùn captured Qínzhōu.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Xīnwèi
Tàixiāng Róng, a prince and envoy from Gāolì (Goryeo), arrived.
Jiēzhōu was captured. In the eleventh month, on the first day Yǐwèi
Lǐ Gǔ was appointed Overall Commander of the Huáinán Circuit Field Army (Huáinán Dào Xíngyíng Dū Bùshǔ) to attack Táng. On the day Wùshēn
Wáng Jǐng captured Fèngzhōu. In the twelfth month, on the day Bǐngxū
Zhèng Rénhuì died. In the third year, spring, the first month
the capital city wall was extended and strengthened. On the day Gēngzǐ
Xiàng Xùn was appointed Resident Grandee (Liúshǒu) of Dōngjīng. On the day Rén'yín

defeating them. On the day Jiǎyín
Chóngjìn was appointed Grand Commander of the Huáinán Circuit Field Army (Huáinán Dào Xíngyíng Dū Zhāotǎoshǐ). In the second month, on the day Bǐngyín

Jǐng sent his minister Zhōng Mó to present a memorial. On the day Bǐngxū
Yángzhōu was captured. On the day Xīnmǎo
Tàizhōu was captured. In the third month, on the day Gēngzǐ
Yuán Yàn, Grand Marshal of the Inner and Outer Cavalry and Infantry (Nèiwài Mǎbùjūn Dū Jūntóu), was appointed Overall Commander of the Zhúlóng Corps (Zhúlóng Dū Bùshǔ).
In this month,
Guāngzhōu, Shūzhōu, and Chángzhōu were captured.
Writing
"In this month"
shows that the three prefectures were captured on different days. In summer, the fourth month
Chángzhōu and Tàizhōu reverted to Táng control. In the fifth month, on the day Yǐmǎo
[the Emperor] arrived from Huáinán,
and pardoned the prisoners in the capital. In the sixth month, on the day Rénshēn
a gracious edict pardoned the prisoners in Huáinán. In autumn, the seventh month
the Empress died.
Yángzhōu, Guāngzhōu, Shūzhōu, and Chúzhōu reverted to Táng control. In the eighth month, on the day Yǐchǒu
the people were instructed to plant trees and leeks.
In the ninth month, on the day Bǐngwǔ

, Wáng Pǔ, Academician of the Duānmíng Hall (Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì) and Left Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì), was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue (Shàngshū Hùbù Shìláng) and Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Fùshǐ). In winter, the tenth month, on the day Xīnyǒu
Empress Xuānyì was buried at Yìlíng. In the eleventh month, on the day Gēngyín
all shrines not included in the official sacrificial canon (Sìdiǎn) were abolished. On the day Yǐsì

Writing
"killed Jǐng's minister"
without recording Shèng's death [in detail]
implies profound censure of Zhōu for killing a loyal official;
thus, Shèng's demonstration of loyalty through death becomes self-evident. In the fourth year, spring, the first month, on the first day Jǐchǒu
prisoners convicted of crimes not punishable by death were pardoned. In the second month, on the day Jiǎxū
Wáng Pǔ was appointed Resident Grandee (Liúshǒu) of Dōngjīng. On the day Yǐhài

Shòuzhōu was captured.
It does not record Liú Rénshàn's surrender;
the details are found in the Biographies of Those Who Died for Loyalty (Sǐjié Zhuàn).
This is because Rénshàn truly did not surrender,
therefore the text merely records that Zhōu captured it.
The term "captured" (kè)
signifies difficulty in taking;
since Shòu [zhōu] was difficult to take,
it shows Rénshàn's loyalty was manifest.
Not recording
"died there"
is because
Rénshàn died of illness,
but because he guarded his loyalty until death,
he is placed in the Biographies of Those Who Died for Loyalty. In summer, the fourth month, on the day Jǐsì
[the Emperor] arrived from Shòuzhōu. On the day Jǐmǎo
eight hundred Shǔ prisoners of war were released and sent back to Shǔ. On the day Guǐwèi

Táizhōu (泰州) was taken.
Those who were occupying their land and came to surrender are recorded as

Although Zàiyù (再遇) and Tíngwèi (廷謂) surrendered with territory,

Tíngwèi (廷謂) is not recorded as
"rebelled" (pàn);

Chǔzhōu (楚州) was overcome,

It had been under attack since the fourth year, twelfth month, on the day Xīnyǒu (辛酉),

That they neither fled nor surrendered is evident,
therefore their death is recorded.
In the Basic Annals, those recorded as
"died" (sǐ)
number more than ten people.
Sòng Lìngxún (宋令詢), Lǐ Xiá (李遐), Yànqīng (彥卿), and Zhāoyè (昭業) all could not have biographies written due to incomplete records of their deeds.
However, what is valued is their death,
and it is sufficient for the Basic Annals to record their great integrity.

This is recorded

Shìzōng (世宗) captured three passes:
Wǎqiáo (瓦橋) and Yìjīn (益津) were established as prefectures and are thus seen (recorded);

hence the date of its capture is not seen.
This is now Xìn’ānjūn (信安軍).

"Qìdān" (契丹) is not written.

Fú Shì (符氏) had no rank of state (Guójúe),
so it is not written "established Fú Shì (符氏) as Empress,"
lest it suggest she was improperly established.
Presumably, her position was settled before marriage,
therefore the record states,
"established the Empress Fú Shì (符氏)."
The literary structure must be so,
without praise or censure.
He was thirty-nine years old.
Emperor Gōng (恭皇帝)
was Zōngxùn (宗訓), the fourth son of Shìzōng (世宗).
When Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne,
the great ministers requested that the imperial sons be enfeoffed as princes,
but Shìzōng (世宗) was humble and declined for a long time.
When he captured the three passes in the north,
he fell ill and returned to the capital (Jīngshī).
Only then was Zōngxùn (宗訓) finally enfeoffed as the Prince of Liáng (Liáng Wáng);
he was seven years old at the time.
Xiǎndé (顯德) six years, sixth month, on the day Guǐsì (癸巳),
Shìzōng (世宗) passed away.
On the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
the Emperor ascended the throne before the coffin.

and Zǎn Jūrùn (昝居潤), Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of Palace Affairs (Xuānhuī Nányuànshǐ) and Magistrate of Kāifēng Fǔ (Kāifēng Fǔ Shì), was appointed Commissioner of Roads and Relays (Qiáodào Dùndì Shǐ).
Autumn, seventh month, on the day Dīngwèi (丁未),

and Lú Yì (盧億), Director in the Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī Lángzhōng), was appointed Judicial Officer (Pànguān).
Eighth month, on the day Gēngyín (庚寅),

Emperor Ruìwǔ Xiàowén (睿武孝文皇帝) was buried at Qìnglíng (慶陵).
Gāolì (高麗) sent envoys to come.
[The tomb] is located in Guǎnchéng Xiàn (管城縣) of Zhèngzhōu (鄭州).
In the seventh year, Spring, the first month, *jiǎchén*
, abdicated the throne.
The Sòng arose.
Regarding the downfall of the Five Dynasties,
the way it is recorded is different,
merely composing the text according to the specific circumstances.
Recording "The Liáng perished"
shows the swiftness of Táng's establishment;
recording "The Hàn perished"
shows the delay of Zhōu's establishment.
The Táng deceived the world by claiming to suppress rebels,
and the Zhōu deceived the world by establishing Rùn (Yūn)
. Therefore, recording
"The Liáng perished"
shows the swiftness of Táng's establishment,
thus knowing that its intention was not truly to suppress rebels;
recording "The Hàn perished"
shows the delay of Zhōu's establishment,
thus knowing that the one establishing Rùn (Yūn) was false.
The Táng perished without an explicit declaration of demise.
When Zhuāngzōng was assassinated
, the Táng had already perished
, yet Míngzōng still claimed the Táng title.
When Mǐndì fled
, the Táng perished again
, yet Fèidì still claimed the Táng title.
Its perishing could not be recorded repeatedly
, therefore it is not recorded.
Regarding the downfall of Jìn, it says
, "The Qìdān destroyed Jìn,"
stated clearly for profound warning.
Regarding Zhōu, it says
, "abdicated the throne."
*Xùn*
means compliance,
meaning being able to comply with the Mandate of Heaven.
Alas
, the Basic Annals of the Five Dynasties is complete!
The relationship between ruler and minister
—how can it be fully recounted?
Yǒuguī of Liáng rebelled
. Táng mutilated Kèníng and killed Cúnyì and Cóngcàn
. Thus, how little remains of the affection between father and son, of flesh and blood, that it did not cease entirely.
When the Grand Consort died, court was suspended
; when Lady Liú and Lady Féng were established as Empresses
, how little remains of the righteousness between husband and wife that it did not become perverse and lead them toward becoming mere beasts.
Offering sacrifices in the fields and burning paper money during the Cold Food Festival
, changing the era name and using music while in mourning
, killing Mǎ Yán and Rèn Huán
—thus, how little remains of ritual, music, punishment, and administration that it did not collapse entirely.
As for sacrificing at Léishān, passing the arrow, and clubbing the horses
—how little remains of Zhōngguó that it did not become entirely barbarian!
Can this be called an age of chaos!
Yet Shìzōng, in the mere five or six years
, took Qínlǒng
, pacified Huáiyòu
, and recovered the Three Passes
. The sound of his martial might terrified the barbarians and the Huáxià
. Moreover, within the realm, he invited Confucian scholars and literary gentlemen
, examined institutions and regulations, revised the general rites, established the corrected music, and discussed the laws and penal code
. The methods of governance he instituted could all be applied by later generations.
As a person, he was intelligent, penetrating, heroic, and decisive
. His discussions and deliberations were impressive.
Immediately in the year after his enthronement
, he abolished 3,336 Buddhist monasteries across the realm.
At this time, Zhōngguó lacked currency
. He thus issued an edict to utterly destroy all bronze Buddha images in the world to mint coins.
He once said
: "I have heard that the Buddha taught that the body and the material world are illusory
, and benefiting humanity is paramount.
If his true body were still here
, if it would benefit the world
, he would still desire to sever and cut it up
. How much less, then, these bronze images
? How could they be cherished by him?"
Because of this, none of the officials dared to speak.
Once, reading late at night
, he saw the Equal Field Diagram of Táng's Yuán Zhěn
. He sighed with deep emotion, saying
: "This is the foundation for achieving good governance
! The policy of a true king begins with this!"
He then issued an edict distributing the diagrams and methods
, ordering officials and common people to first study and understand them
, planning within one year to carry out a great equalization of all land under Heaven
. How could his scope and ambition be considered small!
When he attacked Southern Táng
, he asked the Chancellor Lǐ Gǔ for strategy
. Later, after conquering Huáinán
, he brought out Gǔ's memorial
, commanded the scholar Táo Gǔ to compose a eulogy for it
, placed it in a brocade pouch
, and often kept it by his seat
. His talent for heroism and martiality can truly be called exceptional.
Furthermore, in his open-mindedness to listen and accept advice
, and his trust in utilizing people without suspicion
—is he not what is called a worthy ruler!
When he campaigned north and took the Three Passes
, the soldiers did not shed blood
. Yet historians still criticize him for treating the importance of the altars of the State lightly
and relying on a single, lucky victory achieved hastily
. They are profoundly unaware that he assessed strengths and weaknesses, compared himself to the enemy, and took advantage of Shùlǜ's exhaustion
, seizing an opportunity that could not be missed
. If this was not someone enlightened in deciding victory
, who could achieve it?
Truly, this is beyond the grasp of historians!
*Bèi* (complete)
means that the events of disaster and chaos
were completely present.
The Liáng Family Biography, Number One
Alas
, the wickedness of the Liáng reached its extreme!
From the time he arose as a bandit
, until the demise of Táng
, his lingering poison spread throughout the world.
Heroes and exceptional men throughout the realm
rose up on all four sides
—who did not desire to plunge a weapon into his chest?
Yet, ultimately, they were unable to blunt his edge even slightly and achieve their aims.
The Liáng's lack of rivals under Heaven
can be called the strength of a tiger or a wolf.
Yet when he was defeated
, it was due to the pleasures derived from one or two women
, leading to a pierced chest and flowing intestines
, being carved up like sheep or pigs
. Calamity arose between father and son
. Thus we know the power of feminine beauty to ruin a man.
Since ancient times, the calamities caused by women
: the greatest destroy the realm
; the next destroy the family
; the next destroy the body
. Even if the body manages to escape
, the harm still reaches the descendants
. Although the speed of arrival varies
, none are without calamity.
However, tracing its origin and culmination
, it never fails to begin from minute and negligible things.
The *Yì* (*I Ching*), under *Kūn*, *chū liù* says
: "Treading upon frost
, hard ice arrives."
The *Jiārén* (Family) hexagram, *chū jiǔ* says
: "Guarding the family
, remorse vanishes."
These words are profound
—should one not be warned!
The family affairs of the Liáng
are what the *Shī* (Odes) calls
"things that cannot be spoken of"
Furthermore, after the Táng and the Jìn
, the relationships of close and distant kin, and legitimate and illegitimate heirs, became chaotic
! Therefore, the Family Biographies are composed.
Empress Wénhuì, née Wáng
The mother of Liáng Tàizǔ was called Empress Wénhuì, née Wáng
. She was a person from Shànfù in Shānzhōu.
She bore three sons:
the eldest was Quányù, Prince Guǎng; the second was Cún, Prince Lǎng
; the youngest was Tàizǔ.
The Empress became a widow young.
Her three sons worked for wages at the house of Liú Chóng, a man from Xiāoxiàn.
When Tàizǔ grew up, he was reckless
, and everyone in the county disliked and resented him.
Chóng worried about Tàizǔ's laziness and failure to work
, and frequently disciplined and punished him.
Only Chóng's mother pitied him
. She often personally combed his hair and bathed him
, and instructed her family members, saying
: "Zhū Sān is no ordinary person
; you must treat him well!"
When Huáng Cháo rebelled
, Tàizǔ and Cún both fled and became bandits.
They followed Huáng Cháo to attack Guǎngzhōu
, where Cún died in battle.
After several years
, Tàizǔ abandoned Cháo and surrendered to Táng
. He then turned around and defeated Cháo
, subsequently becoming the Military Governor of Xuānwǔ.
He then sent someone with carriages and horses to Xiāoxiàn
to welcome the Empress from Chóng's home.
When the envoy arrived at the gate
, the Empress fled in terror to hide
, saying to Lady Liú (Chóng's mother)
: "Zhū Sān was wretched and immoral
, and must have died as a bandit
. Why are they here!"
The envoy fully explained the circumstances of Tàizǔ
. The Empress was then startled, overjoyed, and wept
. She rode back together with Chóng's mother
, and was enfeoffed as the Grand Lady of Jìn State.
Tài Zǔ set out wine before the Tài Fūrén,
raised his cup to wish her longevity,
and was extremely joyous.
Tài Zǔ began by saying:
“Zhū Wǔjīng studied throughout his life,
but never attained a single degree.
To have a son become a military commissioner (Jiédùshǐ),
is not to bring shame upon our ancestors.”
The Empress Dowager felt deeply sympathetic for a long time and said:
“That you could reach this point,
can be called heroic and exceptional;
however, your conduct in righteousness may not be like that of your ancestors! ”
Tài Zǔ did not know the reason,
and the Empress Dowager said:
“Zhū Èr and you both followed Huáng Cháo,
but he died alone at Mán Lǐng.
His orphans are all in Wǔgōu.
Now that you are rich and honored,
do you not remember them?”
Tài Zǔ wept, confessed his fault, and apologized.
He then summoned all the surviving children and brought them home.
Tài Zǔ was violent and often ordered killings,
but the Empress Dowager frequently cautioned him,
and many relied on her intervention to save their lives.
In the autumn of Dàshùn 2 (911 CE),
the Empress Dowager fell ill.
The diviner said:
“She should return to her ancestral home.”
Thereupon she returned.
She died in Wǔgōu.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he established the Four Ancestral Temples,
and posthumously honored his deceased father as Mù Huángdì,
and the Empress Dowager as Wén Huì Huánghòu.
Yuánzhēn Huánghòu Zhāng Shì
Tài Zǔ’s Yuánzhēn Huánghòu Zhāng Shì,
was the daughter of a wealthy family from Qútíng Lǐ, Dàngshān Xiàn, Shàn Zhōu.
When Tài Zǔ was young, she was engaged to him as his wife,
and she bore Mò Dì.
When Tài Zǔ became noble,
she was enfeoffed as Wèi Guó Fūrén.
The Empress was virtuous, intelligent, and resolute;
her actions always followed ritual propriety.
Even though Tài Zǔ was violent,
he sometimes feared her.
Tài Zǔ often consulted her on external affairs,
and her advice was usually correct.
When Tài Zǔ occasionally flew into a murderous rage,
the Empress often saved and protected people,
who relied on her to gain their complete preservation.
Tài Zǔ once dispatched troops,
but halfway through the journey,
the Empress felt that the action was ill-advised.
She immediately dispatched an attendant to recall them,
and they arrived back on schedule.
Chēn Wáng Yǒuyù attacked Xú Zhōu
and defeated Zhū Jǐn at Shífó Shān.
Zhū Jǐn fled,
but Yǒuyù did not pursue him.
Tài Zǔ was furious,
and stripped him of his command.
Yǒuyù, terrified,
fled into the mountains with a few horsemen.
After a long time,
he secretly hid himself with Guǎng Wáng.
The Empress secretly sent someone to instruct Yǒuyù to leave his hiding place and return to confess his crime.
Yǒuyù rushed back at dawn to see Tài Zǔ,
prostrating himself in the courtyard,
weeping and begging to be executed.
Tài Zǔ’s rage was extreme,
and he ordered his attendants to drag him out,
intending to behead him.
When the Empress heard this,
she did not even have time to put on her shoes.
She ran into the courtyard, grasped Yǒuyù, and wept, saying:
“You presented yourself to confess your fault;
is it not because you wanted to prove you were not rebelling?”
Tài Zǔ’s anger subsided,
and Yǒuyù was spared.
After Tài Zǔ defeated Zhū Jǐn,
he took Zhū Jǐn’s wife and brought her back.
The Empress welcomed Tài Zǔ at Fēngqiū,
and Tài Zǔ informed her.
The Empress hastily met Zhū Jǐn’s wife.
Zhū Jǐn’s wife bowed twice,
and the Empress also bowed,
and sadly wept, saying:
“Yǎn Yùn and Sīkōng are nations of the same surname,
yet between brothers,
a small conflict leads to war,
causing my sister-in-law to reach this point.
If by misfortune Biàn Zhōu were to fall,
I would also be like this!”
Having said this, she wept again.
Tài Zǔ was moved by this,
and sent Zhū Jǐn’s wife away to become a Buddhist nun,
and the Empress often provided her with clothing and food.
Sīkōng
was Tài Zǔ’s acting official title at that time.
In the first year of Tiānyòu (904 CE),
the Empress died of illness.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
she was posthumously titled Xián Fēi.
She was initially buried in Rùnsè Xiāng, Kāifēng Xiàn.
When Mò Dì ascended the throne,
she was posthumously given the title Yuánzhēn Huáng Tàihòu,
and interred next to the emperor at Xuānlíng.
After the Empress died,
Tài Zǔ began to indulge in debauchery,
which ultimately led to disaster.
Zhāoyí Chén Shì
Zhāoyí Chén Shì,
was a native of Sòng Zhōu,
who gained entry [to the palace] in her youth due to her beauty.
When Tài Zǔ became noble,
he had hundreds of concubines,
but Zhāoyí received exclusive favor.
Tài Zǔ once fell ill,
and Zhāoyí and several dozen nuns practiced Buddhist rites day and night,
without ever resting.
Tài Zǔ believed she loved him,
and favored her even more.
In the third year of Kāipíng (909 CE),
she was ordained as a nun,
and lived in a Buddhist temple in Sòng Zhōu.
Zhāoróng Lǐ Shì
Zhāoróng Lǐ Shì
also gained entry due to her beauty.
She was especially careful and compliant,
and never left his side.
When Tài Zǔ was ill,
he was sleeping soundly during the day.
A beam broke,
and only Lǐ Shì was attending him nearby.
She quickly pulled Tài Zǔ’s sleeve,
Tài Zǔ, startled, ran out.
The beam broke right above the bed.
Tài Zǔ appreciated her virtue,
and elevated her to Zhāoróng.
The fate of both [Chén Shì and Lǐ Shì] is unknown.
Défēi Zhāng Shì
Mò Dì’s Défēi Zhāng Shì,
her father, Guī Bà,
served Tài Zǔ and was a meritorious official of the Liáng.
When the Emperor was still a prince (Wáng),
she was engaged to him as his wife.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he planned to elevate the consort (Fēi) to Empress (Hòu),
but the consort requested to wait until the Emperor had performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven (Jiāotiān),
but the Emperor ultimately never managed to perform the sacrifice.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng (915 CE),
the consort became gravely ill.
The Emperor hastily elevated her to Défēi,
but she passed away that same night,
aged twenty-four.
Cì Fēi Guō Shì
Cì Fēi Guō Shì,
her father, Guī Hòu,
served Liáng as the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Dēng Zhōu.
The consort gained entry in her youth due to her beauty.
When Liáng fell,
Táng Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn.
The former consorts and concubines of Liáng
all wept and knelt to greet him.
Hè Wáng Yǒuyōng’s consort, Shí Shì, was beautiful.
Zhuāngzōng summoned her,
but Shí Shì cursed him arrogantly,
so Zhuāngzōng killed her.
Next, he summoned the consort (Guō Shì).
The consort, afraid, obeyed the order.
Afterward, she was ordained as a nun,
given the name Shìzhèng,
and resided in Luòyáng.
Previously,
when Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
Mò Dì ascended the Jiànguó Lóu,
and said to the Kòng Hè Zhǐhuīshǐ Huángpǔ Lín:
am the ancestral enemy of Jìn.
I cannot wait for their executioner’s blade.
Sir, please end my life completely;
do not let me fall into the hands of my enemy!”
Lín and the Emperor embraced and wept loudly.
That evening,
Lín drew his sword upon the Emperor,
and Lín also committed suicide by slitting his own throat.
When Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
he ordered Zhāng Quányì of Hé Nán to bury the bodies,
and store the head in the Tài Shè.
In the third year of Tiānfú of Jìn (938 CE),
an imperial edict allowed relatives to collect and bury [heads of] criminals previously stored in the Tài Shè.
Thus,
Mò Dì’s head was released,
and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Ān Chóngruǎn was dispatched to bury it alongside the consort (Guō Shì).
The consort died in Luòyáng.
Tài Zǔ had two elder brothers: one named Quányù,
the other named Cún.
He had eight sons: the eldest was Yǒuyù,
followed by Yǒuguī, Yǒuzhāng, Yǒuzhēn, Yǒuyōng, Yǒuhuī, and Yǒuzī.
The eighth was an adopted son named Yǒuwén.
In the fifth month, *yǐyǒu* day, of the first year of *Kāipíng* [907 AD],
Yǒuwén was enfeoffed as the Prince of Bó, Yǒuguī as the Prince of Yǐng, Yǒuzhāng as the Prince of Fú, Yǒuzhēn as the Prince of Jūn, Yǒuyōng as the Prince of Hè, and Yǒuhuī as the Prince of Jiàn.
Yǒuyù had died prior to the enthronement,
and was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Chēn.
As for Kāng Wáng Yǒuzī,
he was enfeoffed upon the accession of the Last Emperor (*Mòdì*).
Yǒuzhāng initially served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Shòuzhōu, Director of the Imperial Guards on Duty, and Superintendent of the Fēngdé Treasury.
During Yǒuguī’s reign,
he was Acting Military Governor of Yùnzhōu.
During the Last Emperor’s reign,
he became the Military Governor of the Zhōngwǔ Army,
and was later transferred to govern Wǔníng.
As for Yǒuyōng and Yǒuhuī, their end is unknown.
Guǎng Wáng Quányù
Guǎng Wáng Quányù,
was enfeoffed when Tàizǔ ascended the throne.
Tàizǔ and his middle elder brother Cún both fled and became bandits.
Quányù alone, with their mother, was still living as a dependent in the household of Liú Chóng.
When Tàizǔ gained high status,
he and their mother returned to Xuānwǔ.
He was made the Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào.
He retired with the rank of Grand Preceptor.
When Tàizǔ was about to accept the abdication,
the relevant departments prepared the ceremonies in the front hall.
Quányù looked at them,
turned to Tàizǔ, and said:
"Zhū Sān,
can you pull this off?"
Tàizǔ was feasting in the palace,
drinking and gambling with the Prince.
When Quányù was drunk,
he picked up the dice, struck the basin, and shattered it.
He yelled at Tàizǔ, saying:
"Zhū Sān,
you were a commoner from Dàngshān.
You were fortunate enough to have the Son of Heaven appoint you Military Governor of four circuits.
What offense did he commit against you?
Yet you destroy the three-hundred-year dynastic stability of the Táng family.
I expect to see your clan massacred soon.
Why waste time gambling!"
Tàizǔ was displeased,
and ended the gathering.
Quányù was also unhappy staying in the capital,
and frequently resided in his old home in Dàngshān.
His three sons were all enfeoffed as princes: Yǒuliàng as the Prince of Héng,
Yǒunéng as the Prince of Huì,
and Yǒuhuì as the Prince of Shào.
In the first year of *Qiānhuà*,
Sòngzhōu was elevated to the Xuānwǔ Army,
and Yǒuliàng was appointed Military Governor.
Yǒuliàng presented auspicious wheat—one stalk bearing three heads.
Tàizǔ angrily said:
"Sòngzhōu suffered massive flooding this year,
what is the point of this!"
Yǒuliàng was then dismissed
and ordered to reside in the capital.
When Tàizǔ was ill in bed,
Quányù came to visit him.
He and Tàizǔ held onto each other and wept grievously.
Tàizǔ then released Yǒuliàng
and allowed him to return eastward with Quányù.
In the second year of *Zhēnmíng*,
Quányù died of illness.
Héng Wáng Yǒuliàng was transferred to succeed him as the Prince of Guǎng.
Yǒunéng served as the Acting Military Governor of Sòngzhōu and Huázhōu, and the Prefect of Chénzhōu.
Wherever he went, he acted lawlessly,
and many wicked people depended on him.
The customs in Chénzhōu favored licentious shrines and heterodox practices.
Those who studied Buddhism
established a separate doctrine,
which they called
the "Supreme Vehicle."
They gathered secretly day and night,
men and women mingling indiscriminately.
The evil practitioners Mǔ Yǐ and Dǒng Yǐ gathered a crowd and proclaimed themselves the Son of Heaven,
establishing officials and staff.
Yǒunéng initially permitted them to operate freely.
Yǐ and his followers attacked and plundered prefectures and counties.
The Last Emperor dispatched troops and annihilated them.
Ever since Kāng Wáng Yǒuzī plotted rebellion and was executed,
the Last Emperor began to alienate and reject the imperial clan.
All imperial relatives felt restless.
In the fourth year of *Zhēnmíng*,
Yǒunéng rebelled with the Chénzhōu forces,
attacking the capital.
Upon reaching Chénliú,
his army was defeated.
He fled back to Chénzhōu.
Several months later, he surrendered.
The Last Emperor pardoned him
and demoted him to the Marquis of Fánglíng.
Yǒuhuì, serving as the Military Governor of Shǎnzhōu,
intended to cause chaos with the prefectural troops.
The Last Emperor summoned him back to the capital,
and he, Yǒuliàng, and Yǒunéng were all confined.
When the Liáng Dynasty perished,
Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
and they were all killed.
Lǎng Wáng Cún (Sons: Yǒuníng, Yǒulún)
Lǎng Wáng Cún,
initially followed Huáng Cháo along with Tàizǔ to attack Guǎngzhōu.
Cún died in battle.
Cún's sons were Yǒuníng and Yǒulún.
Yǒuníng, courtesy name Ānrén,
was quick-witted and intelligent in his youth,
showing neither joy nor displeasure on his face.
Tàizǔ made him a military officer.
He was skilled in the use of the bow and sword.
He was promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Victorious Troops of the Palace Guard and Prefect of Gōngzhōu.
When Tàizǔ besieged Fèngxiáng,
he dispatched Yǒuníng eastward to guard against Xuānwǔ.
Wáng Shīfàn attacked the Liáng forces,
besieging Qízhōu.
Yǒuníng led troops to strike him,
seizing one thousand horses
and killing several thousand men.
Tàizǔ escorted Zhāozōng back to the capital.
Yǒuníng was appointed Military Governor of the Jiànwǔ Army,
and granted the title
"Meritorious Minister for Escorting the Emperor, Brave and Resolute."
Tàizǔ again sent him to attack Shīfàn,
besieging Bóchāng.
They slaughtered its inhabitants,
causing the Qīng Hé River to stop flowing.
They fought at Shílóu,
where his army was defeated.
Yǒuníng fell from his horse and was killed.
Yǒulún was also bright and quick-witted in childhood.
He was familiar with the *Lúnyǔ* and the *Xiǎoxué*,
and understood musical temperament.
Since Cún had died,
Tàizǔ made Yǒulún Commander of the Vanguard Cavalry,
and reported him as General of the Right Wēiwǔ.
When the Yān forces attacked Nèihuáng in Wèi,
Yǒulún, leading the vanguard, crossed the river at night
and captured a thousand horses.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī surrendered Lùzhōu to the Liáng.
The Jìn forces attacked Lù.
Yǒulún entered Lùzhōu with troops
and brought Hǎnzhī back.
He was repeatedly promoted to Inspector of Works,
and served as Prefect of Téngzhōu.
When Tàizǔ besieged Fèngxiáng,
the Jìn forces attacked the Liáng.
Yǒulún brought 30,000 troops to Fánshān.
The Jìn forces then retreated.
Yǒulún traveled west to meet Tàizǔ at Fèngxiáng.
When Zhāozōng returned to Cháng’ān,
Yǒulún was appointed Military Governor of the Níngyuǎn Army.
When Tàizǔ returned east,
he left Yǒulún on night guard duty,
