to secretly observe Zhāozōng’s actions.
Yǒulún died after falling from his horse while playing polo.
Tàizǔ was furious,
and brought 70,000 troops to Hézhōng.
Zhāozōng wept,
not knowing what course of action to take.
He planned to flee to Tàiyuán,
but was unable to do so.
Prime Minister Cuī Yìn sent someone to restrain Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ believed that Yìn and his associates had killed Yǒulún,
and submitted a petition requesting the execution of Yìn and the others.
Zhāozōng did not immediately comply.
Tàizǔ then dispatched Yǒuliàng to the capital,
who surrounded the Kāihuà Ward with troops,

killing Yìn, along with Zhèng Yuánguī, the Mayor of Jīngzhào; Wáng Jiànxūn, the Commissioner of the Imperial City; Chén Bān, the Commissioner of the Flying Dragon Guard; Wáng Jiànxí, the Commissioner of the Palace Gate; Wáng Jiànyì, the Commissioner of the Guest Department; and the former Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Zhāng Jùn.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he had already enfeoffed the imperial clan.
The Secretariat submitted a proposal that
the late imperial elder brother Cún,
and the imperial nephews Yǒuníng, Military Governor of the Jiànwǔ Army, and Yǒulún, Military Governor of the Níngyuǎn Army,
should all be enfeoffed.
Consequently, Cún was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Lǎng, Yǒuníng as the Prince of Ān, and Yǒulún as the Prince of Mì.
Chēn Wáng Yǒuyù
Chēn Wáng Yǒuyù, courtesy name Duānfū,
was skilled in riding and archery in his youth.
He followed Tàizǔ on military campaigns.
He was able to win the loyalty of the officers and soldiers through his generosity and tolerance.
Tàizǔ, along with Jìn, besieged Huáng Yè at Xīhuá.
Yè's soldiers carried spears, climbed the wall, and cursed the enemy.
Jìn Wáng sent Hu cavalry to shoot continuously, but they could not hit them.
Tàizǔ looked back at Yǒu Yù,
who struck them with a single shot.
The entire army shouted loudly.
Jìn Wáng was pleased,
and presented Yǒu Yù with a fine bow and a hundred arrows.
Tàizǔ governed Xuānwǔ,
making him Yánèi Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the first year of Jǐngfú,
Tàizǔ attacked Yùn.
Yǒu Yù, serving as the vanguard, halted at Dǒumén.
The Yùn soldiers attacked him by night,
and Yǒu Yù was defeated and fled.
Tàizǔ followed behind later,
unaware of Yǒu Yù's defeat.
The vanguard encountered the enemy and many died.
When Tàizǔ reached the villages,
he finally linked up with Yǒu Yù.
At that time,
Zhū Xuān was in Púzhōu.
Tàizǔ then sent Yǒu Yù forward first with two hundred cavalry.
Tàizǔ arrived later,
and became separated from Yǒu Yù.
Tàizǔ unexpectedly met the enemy,
was defeated, and fled.
The enemy troops pursued him very closely.
They arrived before a great ditch
and nearly failed to escape.
Fortunately, there was piled firewood in the ditch,
allowing the horses to cross.
More than ten people, including the Liáng general Lǐ Fán, died.
In winter,
Yǒu Yù captured Púzhōu,
and then besieged Shí Pǔ at Xúzhōu.
Zhū Jǐn led twenty thousand troops to rescue Pǔ.
Yǒu Yù defeated Jǐn at Shífóshān,
and Jǐn fled.
Dū Yúhòu Zhū Yǒu Gōng slandered him to Tàizǔ,
claiming that Jǐn could have been pursued, but Yǒu Yù failed to do so.
Tàizǔ became greatly enraged,
stripped him of his troops and transferred them to Páng Shīgǔ.
Yǒu Yù was handed over to the clerks.
The messenger mistakenly delivered the order (for execution) to Yǒu Yù.
Yǒu Yù was terrified,
and did not know what to do.
Fortunately, Empress Zhāng instructed him,
and he was spared.
He was provisionally put in charge of Xǔzhōu.
Xǔzhōu was near Cài,
and suffered greatly from major banditry.
The residents were ravaged and broken.
Yǒu Yù recruited and pacified the scattered population,
increasing the registered households by more than thirty thousand.
He was promoted to Zhūjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ,
participated in pacifying Yǎn and Yùn,
and returned to govern Xǔzhōu.
When Cuī Hóng fled to Huáinán,
Yǒu Yù led troops to stabilize Càizhōu;
markets did not change their places of business.
When Tàizǔ concurrently governed Hùguójūn,
he made Yǒu Yù the Liúhòu.
He was promoted to Zhōngwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
Tàizǔ attacked Fèngxiáng,
but failed to take it,
and left to attack Bīnzhōu.
Yǒu Yù crushed Língtái and Liángyuán,
and captured Lǒngzhōu.
Yáng Chóngběn subsequently surrendered Bīnzhōu.
Later, Chóngběn rebelled again.
Tàizǔ sent Yǒu Yù to attack him;
he camped at Yǒngshòu.
Yǒu Yù died of illness.
Bó Wáng Yǒu Wén.
Bó Wáng Yǒu Wén, courtesy name Démíng,
originally had the surname Kāng and the personal name Qín.
As a child, he had beautiful demeanor,
loved learning,
was skilled in conversation,
and was quite capable of writing poetry.
Tàizǔ adopted him as a son.
When Tàizǔ governed the four circuits,
he made Yǒu Wén the Dùzhī Yántiě Zhìzhìshǐ.
As Tàizǔ campaigned everywhere,
Yǒu Wén levied taxes and gathered resources to supply the army.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he established tax levies for the four circuits he had previously governed—Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, Tiānpíng, and Hùguó.
He established the Jiànchāng Palace to manage them overall,
and made Yǒu Wén the commissioner.
He was enfeoffed as Bó Wáng.
When Tàizǔ visited the Western Capital,
Yǒu Wén remained to guard the Eastern Capital.
Regarding the Commoner Yǒu Guī:
When Tàizǔ first governed Xuānwǔ,
he was surveying territory between Sòng
and Bó,
and was born from a casual union with a woman at an inn.
When grown, he was eloquent, clever, and cunning.
Bó Wáng Yǒu Wén possessed many talents and skills,
and Tàizǔ loved him.
Moreover, he was older,
and when Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
the legitimate heir had not yet been established.
He had always privately intended to entrust the succession to Yǒu Wén.
Since Empress Zhāng died,
Tàizǔ had taken no subsequent wife.
When his sons were governing circuits,
they all invited their wives to enter and attend upon him.
Yǒu Wén’s wife, Madame Wáng, was beautiful,
and Tàizǔ especially favored her.
Tàizǔ had been ill for a long time.
Madame Wáng and Yǒu Guī’s wife, Madame Zhāng,
regularly monopolized his chamber while attending to his illness.
When Tàizǔ’s illness slightly improved,
he said to Madame Wáng:
“I know I will ultimately not recover.
You must go to the Eastern Capital,
and summon Yǒu Wén to come.
I will decide matters with him.”
This clearly meant he privately intended to entrust the succession to him.
He then said to Jìng Xiáng:
“Yǒu Guī can be given one prefecture;
hurry and send him to his post.”
Consequently, Yǒu Guī was made the Prefect of Láizhōu.
Tàizǔ was normally rigid and violent,
and having fallen ill, his moods became unpredictable.
At that time, those who were demoted
were invariably followed by orders for execution.
Yǒu Guī was greatly fearful.
His wife, Madame Zhāng, said:
“His Majesty gave the Imperial Seal to Madame Wáng,
sending her to the Eastern Capital to summon Yǒu Wén.
You are now surely doomed!”
The couple faced each other and wept.
His attendants advised Yǒu Guī, saying:
“When matters are urgent, action must be taken to survive.
Why don’t you plan for yourself early?”
Yǒu Guī then changed his clothes,
and secretly entered the Zuǒ Lónghǔ Army camp,
meeting with Commander Hán Qíng to plan the affair.
That night, Qíng gave five hundred Yábīng to accompany Yǒu Guī.
Mixing in with the Kònghè guards, they entered.
At the third night watch,
they broke the barrier and entered Wànchūn Mén,
reaching the Emperor’s sleeping quarters.
All those attending the sick ruler fled.
Tàizǔ arose in panic and fear, shouting:
“I have suspected this villain for a long time!
I regret not killing him sooner!
Rebellious thief, do you dare kill your father?”
Féng Tíng'è, Yǒu Guī’s trusted aide, attacked Tàizǔ with a sword.
Tàizǔ circled a pillar while fleeing.
The sword struck the pillar three times.
Tàizǔ became exhausted
and fell onto the couch.
Tíng'è stabbed him with the sword,
piercing his abdomen.
His intestines and stomach spilled out.
Yǒu Guī wrapped him in a quilt and mat inside the chamber,
keeping the death a secret for four days.
He then opened the government treasuries
and heavily rewarded the assembled ministers and the various armies.
He dispatched Dīng Zhāopǔ, who had received his command, to gallop to the Eastern Capital with a false edict,
and kill Yǒu Wén.
He further issued an imperial edict stating:
“We arduously founded this dynasty,
spanning more than thirty years.
Entrusted to rule over the people,
it has been six years in a flash.
With coordinated efforts both inside and outside the court,
we aimed for minor prosperity.
How could I have expected Yǒu Wén to secretly harbor illicit plans,
and intend to commit great rebellion?
Last night, the second day,
armored soldiers burst into the Great Palace.
Thanks to Yǒu Guī’s loyalty and filial piety,
he led troops to suppress and execute them,
preserving Our person.
However, due to illness and severe shock,
Our condition is extremely precarious.
Yǒu Guī successfully pacified the fierce rebels.
His achievements are unmatched.
It is proper to delegate him the authority to manage military and state affairs.”
Only then was the mourning publicly announced.
On the day after the full moon of the sixth month of Qiánhuà 2,
Yǒu Guī ascended the imperial throne before the coffin.
He appointed Hán Qíng as Zhōngwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He made the Last Emperor the Liúhòu of Biànzhōu,
and Zhū Yǒuqiān of Hézhōng the Zhōngshū Lìng.
Yǒuqiān refused the appointment.
Meanwhile, three thousand troops of the Lóngxiāng Army in Huáizhōu,
kidnapped their general, Liú Zhòngbà,
occupied Huáizhōu,
and declared themselves to be punishing the traitor.
In the first month of the third year,
Yǒu Guī performed the Sacrifice to Heaven in the southern suburbs of Luòyáng,
and changed the era name to Fènglì.
Tàizǔ’s maternal grandson, Yuán Xiàngxiān,
along with the imperial son-in-law and commandant Zhào Yán, and others,
planned to seek out the last emperor to punish the traitor.
In the second month,
Xiàngxiān led the palace guards into the palace.
Yǒu Guī and his wife, Lady Zhāng, hurried toward the base of the northern curtain wall tower,
intending to climb the wall and flee,
but failed.
He ordered Fēng Tíng’ě to strike his wife and himself with a blade,
and Tíng’ě also committed suicide.
The last emperor (Mò Dì) ascended the throne,
restored the official ranks and titles of Yǒu Wén,
and demoted Yǒu Guī to commoner status.
Kāng Wáng Yǒu Zī.
Kāng Wáng Yǒu Zī
had double pupils in his eyes
and often secretly prided himself,
believing he was destined to be the Son of Heaven.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng (915 CE),
Mò Dì’s Consort Dé died.
Just before the burial,
Yǒu Zī sent an assassin to enter the sleeping quarters at night.
Mò Dì was asleep.
He dreamt that someone was trying to harm him.
Upon waking,
he heard his precious sword on the couch clang loudly.
He leaped up,
drew his sword, and said:
"Is there going to be a disturbance?"
He then searched the sleeping quarters,
found the assassin,
killed him with his own hand,
and subsequently executed Yǒu Zī.
The next day,
he said to Zhào Yán and Zhāng Hànjié:
"I almost never saw you gentlemen again."
Consequently, he became distant from the weak imperial clan
and relied on Zhào and Zhāng,
which ultimately led to ruin and demise.
Alas!
The principles of the Chūn Qiū (Spring and Autumn Annals),
concerning the determination of right and wrong, and granting or denying legitimacy,
are truly difficult!
Someone asked:
"Liáng Tàizǔ assassinated his sovereign as a subject,
and Yǒu Guī assassinated his father as a son;
they are the same.
After usurping the throne,
Yǒu Guī changed the era name the following year.
According to the principles of the Chūn Qiū,
both should be recorded using the sovereign’s style of writing,
but Yǒu Guī was not listed in the Basic Annals (Běnjì).
Why is this?
Moreover, the wickedness of father and son is equal,
yet by denying the son,
one is supporting the father.
How can this be the intent of the Chūn Qiū?"
I replied:
"The matter of Liáng is already well established!
The wickedness of his father
does not need the denial of his son to be made manifest.
However, the resolve of Mò Dì
cannot be left unexpressed.
According to the principles of the Chūn Qiū,
when a sovereign is assassinated and the criminal is not punished,
the ministers and sons of the state bear the responsibility.
In the matter of Yǒu Guī,
my purpose is to express the resolve of those who punished the traitor."
The Family Biographies of Táng Tàizǔ, Second: The Primary Wife, Lady Liú; The Secondary Consort, Lady Cáo.
Tàizǔ’s primary wife, Lady Liú,
was from the north of Dài.
His secondary consort, Lady Cáo,
was from Tàiyuán.
When Tàizǔ was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìn,
Lady Liú was enfeoffed as the Lady of Qín State.
From the time Tàizǔ raised troops north of Dài,
Lady Liú often accompanied him on campaigns.
She was intelligent, quick-witted, and rich in strategic knowledge,
and quite familiar with military mechanisms.
She often taught her maidservants riding and archery,
to assist Tàizǔ.
When Tàizǔ pursued Huáng Cháo eastward
and returned his army, passing through Liáng,
he was quartered at Fēngchán Temple.
The Prince of Liáng invited Tàizǔ into the city
and hosted a feast at Shàngyuán Post Station.
In the middle of the night, he attacked him with troops.
Some of Tàizǔ’s attendants managed to escape first
and reported the danger to the Lady.
The Lady’s demeanor remained unshaken.
She immediately executed the informant,
and secretly summoned the chief generals to plan the army’s safe return.
When dawn broke,
Tàizǔ returned.
He and the Lady wept toward each other.
Consequently, he wanted to raise troops to attack Liáng.
The Lady said:
"You originally raised arms to punish the rebels for the country.
Now, the affair of Liáng has not yet been exposed,
and if you abruptly turn your troops to attack them,
when the world hears of it,
no one will be able to distinguish right from wrong.
It is better to collect the army and return to the garrison,
and appeal to the court yourself."
Tàizǔ followed her advice.
Afterward,
Tàizǔ attacked Liú Réngōng
and returned defeated.
Liáng sent Shì Shūcóng, Kāng Huái Yīng, and others to repeatedly attack Jìn for years,
besieging Tàiyuán.
Jìn forces were defeated repeatedly,
and Tàizǔ was worried and distressed,
not knowing what to do.
Chief General Lǐ Cúnxìn and others advised Tàizǔ to flee into the northern regions,
gather troops, and plan for a future resurgence.
Tàizǔ agreed with this.
He entered and told the Lady.
The Lady asked who had proposed this plan.
He replied:
"It was Cúnxìn."
The Lady cursed, saying:
"Cúnxìn
is merely a shepherd boy from north of Dài.
How can he be relied upon to strategize success or failure!
Moreover, you once laughed at Wáng Xíngyú for abandoning Bīnzhōu and fleeing,
only to be captured in the end.
Are you doing this yourself now?
In the past, when you were stranded in Dádá,
you almost couldn’t escape,
and it was only thanks to the many troubles across the land
that you managed to return south.
Now, the repeatedly defeated troops
are scattered, with few survivors.
If you abandon your defense,
who will follow you?
Can the northern regions even be reached?"
Tàizǔ greatly understood and stopped.
Soon after, the scattered troops gradually regrouped.
The Lady had no son,
but was virtuous by nature
and not jealous.
She often told Tàizǔ:
"Lady Cáo is destined to give birth to a noble son;
you should treat her well."
And Lady Cáo, in turn, was modest and yielding,
so they got along very happily.
Lady Cáo was enfeoffed as the Lady of Jìn State,
and later bore a son,
who became Zhuāng Zōng.
Tàizǔ considered this extraordinary,
and Lady Cáo consequently received exclusive favor.
Tàizǔ was violent by nature
and often killed people in anger.
No one around him dared to speak,
but Lady Cáo would offer gentle admonitions and analogies,
which were often heeded.
When Zhuāng Zōng ascended the throne,
he served Lady Cáo with extreme reverence.
When he rescued Zhào, defeated Yān, and captured Wèibó,
and fought Liáng on the river for over ten years,
he would still rush back to visit his mother three or four times a year.
Everyone praised his filial piety.
When Zhuāng Zōng ascended the throne,
he honored Lady Cáo with the title Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
and designated his legal mother, Lady Liú, as Imperial Consort Dowager (Huáng Tàifēi).
The Consort Dowager went to thank the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager showed a look of shame.
The Consort Dowager said:
"I wish that my son may rule the nation without end,
and that I may be allowed to die in this land to follow the late sovereign.
That would be fortunate;
what more can I say!"
When Zhuāng Zōng destroyed Liáng and entered Biàn,
he sent someone to welcome the Empress Dowager back to Luò,
where she resided in Chángshòu Palace,
while the Consort Dowager alone remained in Jìnyáng.
In the fifth month of the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE),
the Consort Dowager died.
In the seventh month,
the Empress Dowager died,
receiving the posthumous title Zhēnjiǎn,
and was buried at Kūnlíng.
The Consort Dowager received no posthumous title
and was buried in Wèi County.
The Consort Dowager and the Empress Dowager loved each other deeply.
When she sent the Empress Dowager off to Luò,
they parted tearfully.
Upon returning, she missed her so much
that she subsequently fell ill and could not recover.
When the Empress Dowager heard this,
she wanted to rush to Jìnyáng to see her illness.
When she died,
she again wanted to go personally to bury her.
Zhuāng Zōng tearfully advised against it,
and the ministers unanimously requested she remain,
so she stopped.
But after the death of the Consort Dowager, the Empress Dowager
grieved and refused food and drink,
and collapsed (died) the following month.
Empress Liú.
Empress Shénmǐnjìng, Liú Shì, of Zhuāngzōng,
was a native of Chéng'ān, Wèizhōu.
Zhuāngzōng's official principal wife was Lady Hán of Wèiguó,
next was Lady Yī of Yānguó,
and next was the Empress (Liú Shì).
She was initially enfeoffed as Lady of Wèiguó.
The Empress's father, Liú Sǒu,
had a yellow beard,
was skilled in medicine and divination,
and styled himself Liú Shānrén.
When the Empress was five or six years old,
the Prince of Jìn attacked Wèi,
and plundered Chéng'ān.
The adjutant Yuán Jiànfēng captured her,
and presented her to the Jìn Palace.
Empress Dowager Zhēnjiǎn taught her to play the sheng (reed pipe), sing, and dance.
When she reached adulthood,
she was very beautiful.
Zhuāngzōng saw her and was delighted.
When Zhuāngzōng had already become the Prince of Jìn,
the Empress Dowager visited his palace.
She arranged a banquet to wish him longevity.
She personally rose to sing and dance.
The Empress Dowager was extremely joyful,
and ordered Liú Shì to play the sheng to accompany the wine.
When the banquet ended, she departed,
leaving Liú Shì behind as a gift to Zhuāngzōng.
Previously,
when Zhuāngzōng attacked the Liáng army at Jiāchéng,
he captured Hóu Shì, the wife of Fú Dàozhāo.
Her favor dominated the entire palace,
and those in the palace called her
"Lady of the Entrenched Camp" (Jiāzhài Fūrén).
When Zhuāngzōng led armies to various regions,
Hóu Shì always accompanied the army.
Subsequently,
Liú Shì gave birth to his son Jìjí.
Zhuāngzōng believed the child resembled him,
and loved him.
From this point, Liú Shì's favor became even more singular.
For more than ten years, spanning the conquest of Wèibó and the battles along the Héshàng (Yellow River),
only Liú Shì accompanied him.
Liú Shì was very intelligent,
and excelled at anticipating his wishes and obeying his commands.
None of the other concubines or consorts could gain an audience.
When her father heard that Liú Shì had become noble,
he went to the Wèi Palace to request an audience.
Zhuāngzōng summoned Yuán Jiànfēng and questioned him.
Jiànfēng replied:
“I first found Liú Shì at the northern mound of Chéng'ān.
At that time, there was an old man with a yellow beard protecting her.”
When Liú Sǒu was brought out and shown to Jiànfēng,
Jiànfēng said:
“It is he.”
However, Liú Shì was currently competing for favor with the other ladies,
and was trying to elevate her family status.
She became extremely angry and said:
“When I left my village,
I remember vaguely:
My father unfortunately died at the hands of rebellious soldiers.
I wailed around his corpse and then departed.
How dare this rustic old man reach this place!”
She then ordered Liú Sǒu to be whipped at the palace gate.
When Zhuāngzōng had already ascended the throne as Emperor,
he wished to establish Liú Shì as Empress.
But Lady Hán was the principal wife,
and Lady Yī's rank was above Liú Shì.
For this reason, the matter was difficult and had not been announced.
The Chancellor Dòulú Gé and the Commissioner of Military Affairs Guō Chóngtāo sought to please the Emperor,
and submitted a memorial arguing that Liú Shì ought to be established.
Zhuāngzōng was greatly pleased.
In the Guǐwèi year, the second year of Tóngguāng (924 CE),
the Emperor presided over the Wénmíng Hall,
and dispatched an envoy to formally install Liú Shì as Empress.
The Empress received the mandate,
rode the pheasant carriage,
with her ceremonial guard (lǔbù) and musicians (gǔchuī),
and paid respects at the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào).
Lady Hán and the others were all resentful about this.
So Hán Shì was enfeoffed as Consort Shū,
and Yī Shì as Consort Dé.
After Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
his ambition waned and he became arrogant and neglectful.
Eunuchs and performers disrupted governance,
and the Empress particularly wielded power within the palace.
As she came from humble origins
and was established (as Empress) out of rank order,
she attributed it to the power of the Buddha.
She also loved to accumulate wealth.
She secretly dispatched people to act as merchants and traders,
such that in the marketplace,
firewood, fodder, fruits, and vegetables,
were all claimed to be sold by the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng).
Tribute from all four directions,
was necessarily divided into two parts:
one for the Son of Heaven (the Emperor),
and one to enter the Central Palace.
Goods and bribes piled up like mountains in the palace.
She only spent money on copying Buddhist scriptures
and giving gifts and bribes to monks and nuns.
Zhuāngzōng, consequently, also became a devout Buddhist.
There was a Hu monk who came from Yútián (Khotan).
Zhuāngzōng led the Empress and his various sons to welcome and bow before him.
When the monk traveled to Mount Wǔtái,
imperial eunuchs were sent to provide lodging and provisions.
Wherever he went, cities and towns were greatly moved.
There was also a monk named Chénghuì,
who claimed he could subdue dragons.
He once passed through Zhènzhōu.
Wáng Róng did not treat him with courtesy.
Chénghuì angrily said:
“I have five hundred venomous dragons.
If I were to send one dragon to lift a single stone slab,
the people of Chángshān (a region including Zhènzhōu),
would all become fish and turtles (drowned).”
Coincidentally, the following year, the Hūtuó River flooded severely,
destroying the walls and gates of Zhènzhōu.
Everyone believed it was miraculous.
Zhuāngzōng and the Empress led their sons and consorts to bow before him.
Chénghuì sat upright and did not rise.
Consequently, all officials, regardless of rank, bowed to him.
Only Guō Chóngtāo did not bow.
At this time,
the Empress Dowager and the Empress communicated extensively with the regional governors (fānzhèn).
The Empress Dowager's orders were called
"Gàolìng" (Imperial Command),
and the Empress's orders were called
"Jiàomìng" (Instructional Mandate).
The envoys of the two palaces thronged the roads.
Wēn Tāo, the Military Governor of Xǔzhōu, knowing the Empress favored Buddhism,
requested permission to convert his private residence into a Buddhist temple,
in order to pray for blessings for the Empress.
Zhuāngzōng frequently visited the private residences of Guō Chóngtāo, Yuán Xíngqīn, and others,
often accompanied by the Empress.
Subsequently,
he visited Zhāng Quányì's residence.
During the height of the drinking,
he ordered the Empress to bow to Quányì as her foster father.
Quányì daily sent concubines and maids to enter and leave the Central Palace,
and gifts never ceased.
Zhuāngzōng had a beloved concubine,
who was very beautiful and had borne him a son.
The Empress was inwardly worried about her.
Once, when Zhuāngzōng was casually residing in the palace,
Yuán Xíngqīn was attending nearby.
Zhuāngzōng asked:
“You recently lost your wife.
Will you marry again?
I will help you find a bride.”
The Empress pointed to the beloved concubine and requested:
“Since Your Majesty takes pity on Xíngqīn,
why not bestow her upon him?”
Zhuāngzōng had no choice
and pretended to consent.
The Empress hurried Xíngqīn to bow in thanks.
Xíngqīn bowed twice.
When he stood up and looked back at the beloved concubine,
her sedan chair had already been carried out of the palace.
Zhuāngzōng was unhappy
and claimed illness, refusing to eat for several days.
In the autumn of the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE), there was a great flood.
The people of the two Hé (Yellow River) regions
were displaced and wandered the roads.
Taxes and levies in the capital were insufficient.
Soldiers of the Six Armies
often starved and collapsed dead.
They therefore preemptively borrowed the summer and autumn taxes for the following year.
The common people were distressed and suffering,
wailing and weeping on the roads,
while Zhuāngzōng and the Empress indulged recklessly in hunting and excursions.
On the Jǐmǎo day of the Làyuè (twelfth lunar month),
he hunted at Báishā.
The Empress led the imperial sons and the entire harem to follow.
They traveled past Yīquè,
and stayed overnight at Kānjiàn.
They only returned on the Guǐwèi day.
At this time there was heavy snow.
The soldiers suffered from cold and freezing.
The ten thousand cavalry of the Jīnqiāng Guards,
demanded provisions from the populace wherever they went.
They destroyed household goods,
pulled down houses and burnt them.
The county officials were fearful,
and fled, hiding in the mountains and valleys.
In the third month of the following year,
a guest star encroached upon the Tiānkù (Celestial Treasury),
and a star streaked towards the Tiānpèi (Celestial Cudgel).
The astrologer said:
"There will surely be urgent military trouble before the sovereign.
It is fitting to disperse accumulated wealth to ward it off."
The Chancellor requested to take goods from the treasury to supply the army.
Zhuāngzōng permitted it,
but the Empress refused,
saying:
"My husband and I obtained the realm;
although it was due to military prowess,
fundamentally, it was also due to the Mandate of Heaven (Tiānmìng).
Since the Mandate resides in Heaven,
what can men do to me!"
The Chancellor discussed this in the Yányīng Hall.
The Empress, from behind the screen, listened intently.
Thereupon, she took her burial valuables and the Emperor’s youngest son, Mǎnxǐ, placed them before the Emperor, and said:
"The tribute presented by the vassal lords,
and the gifts provided, are already exhausted.
All that remains in the palace is only this.
I request that they be sold to supply the army!"
The Chancellor, terrified, withdrew.
Subsequently, when Zhào Zàilǐ rebelled
and troops were dispatched to suppress Wèi,
goods were finally brought out to bestow upon the army.
The soldiers carried them away and cursed, saying:
"My wife and children have already starved to death!
What use is getting this now!"
Zhuāngzōng traveled east to Biànzhōu,
accompanied by 25,000 troops.
When they reached Wànshèng,
they could not advance and returned.
The soldiers dispersed,
and more than half were lost.
When they arrived at Yīngzǐ Gǔ,
where the road was narrow and constricted,
Zhuāngzōng saw the attendant officials carrying weapons,
and comforted them all with kind words, saying:
"I just received word that the King of Wèi (Wèi Wáng) pacified Shǔ.
He obtained 500,000 measures of Shǔ’s gold and silver,
which should all be given to you."
[They] replied:
"Your Majesty gives this too late,
and those who receive it will not be grateful."
Zhuāngzōng wept.
Thereupon, he looked at Zhāng Rónggē, the Director of the Internal Treasury, and requested robes and belts to bestow upon them.
Rónggē replied:
"They are all gone."
The soldiers shouted angrily at Rónggē, saying:
"Bringing our Lord to this pass
is all due to your sort!"
Thereupon, they drew their knives and chased him.
His attendants saved him, and he escaped.
Rónggē said:
"The Empress hoards goods
and refuses to give them to the army,
yet assigns blame to me.
If the situation becomes unforeseen,
my body will be torn into ten thousand pieces!"
He then jumped into the water and died.
Guō Cóngqiān rebelled.
Zhuāngzōng was struck by a stray arrow;
the injury was severe.
He lay under the corridor of the Jiàngxiāo Hall,
thirsty and wishing for a drink.
The Empress ordered a eunuch to bring koumiss,
but she did not personally attend to him.
Zhuāngzōng died.
The Empress, along with Lǐ Cúnwò and others, burned the Jiāqìng Hall,
and, guarded by a hundred cavalrymen, exited the Shīzǐ Gate.
On horseback, the Empress used bags to carry gold vessels and jeweled belts,
intending to establish a temple in Tàiyuán and become a nun.
While on the road, she committed adultery with Cúnwò.
When they reached Tàiyuán,
she then shaved her head and became a nun.
Míngzōng entered and took the throne,
and sent someone to grant the Empress death.
In the fifth year of Tiānfú of Jìn,
she was posthumously granted the title Shénmǐnjìng Huánghòu.
Since the devastating chaos at the end of the Táng dynasty,
the system governing empresses and consorts was incomplete.
By the time of Zhuāngzōng,
the number of occupants in the imperial harem was particularly high.
There were Zhāoróng, Zhāoyí, Zhāoyuàn, Chūshǐ, Yùzhèng, Shìzhēn, Yìcái, Xiányī, Yáofāng, Yìdé, Xuānyī, and others;
the remaining titles
are too numerous to record fully.
When Zhuāngzōng was assassinated,
the imperial harem scattered and fled.
Zhū Shǒuyīn entered the palace
and selected over thirty women.
Because Lady Xià, the Lady of Guó State (Guóguó Fūrén), had previously been favored by Zhuāngzōng,
Shǒuyīn dared not keep her.
When Míngzōng was established,
he released all the palace women from Zhuāngzōng’s time to return to their homes.
Only Lady Xià had nowhere to return.
Since Xià Lǔqí, the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Héyáng, shared the same surname,
she was therefore entrusted to him.
Later, she married Lǐ Zànhuá (Qìdān Túyù).
Zànhuá was cruel and malicious by nature
and enjoyed killing people.
If maids or concubines made slight mistakes,
he often inflicted cuts and burns.
Lady Xià was afraid
and sought divorce.
She then shaved her head, became a nun, and died.
Furthermore, Consort Hán Shūfēi and Consort Yī Défēi both resided in Tàiyuán.
When Jìn Gāozǔ rebelled,
they were captured by the Qìdān.
The Táng dynasty originated from the Zhūxié tribe, adopted the surname Lǐ;
gained a state and became Jìn;
gained the empire and became Táng.
Their origin was barbarian (Yídí),
and they ultimately perished in chaos.
Therefore, their generational lineage cannot be fully detailed.
Those who are known
are Tàizǔ’s four younger brothers, eight sons, and five grandsons,
and the line ended after three generations.
Tàizǔ’s four younger brothers were Kèràng, Kèxiū, Kègōng, and Kèníng.
The names or titles of their parents are unknown.
Kèràng
Kèràng,
in his youth, excelled at riding and archery.
He served as an officer (Jūnxiào) in the Zhènwǔ Army
and followed the expedition to suppress Wáng Xiānzhī.
Based on his merit, he was appointed General of the Jīnwú Guard,
and remained in the capital (Jīngshī).
Since the time of Emperor Xiànzōng, the Lǐ clan had brought their tribe and submitted to the Táng.
The Táng settled them in Héxī.
They habitually sent one son
to serve as a guard in the capital (Jīngshī), and granted him a residence in the Qīnrén Quarter.
After that, Tàizǔ raised troops in Yúnzhōng
and killed the Táng defending general, Duàn Wénchǔ.
Táng dispatched troops to attack Tàizǔ
and sent Wáng Chǔcún with soldiers to surround the Qīnrén Quarter,
seeking to capture Kèràng, the guard son.
Kèràng, along with his servants Hé Xiāngwēn and Shí Dìlì, and more than ten riders,
drew their bows and leaped on their horses,
breaking through the encirclement and escaping.
Chǔcún pursued them with over a thousand men as far as Wèiqiáo.
Kèràng and his group shot and killed over a hundred men.
The pursuing troops then halted,
and Kèràng fled to Yànmén.
The following year,
Tàizǔ again submitted to the Táng,
and Kèràng returned to serve as a guard in the capital (Jīngshī).
When Huáng Cháo attacked Cháng'ān,
Kèràng defended Tóngguān.
He was defeated by the rebels,
fled to Nánshān,
hid in a Buddhist temple,
and was killed by the temple monks.
Kèxiū
Kèxiū, courtesy name Chóngyuǎn,
followed the expedition against Páng Xūn.
Based on his merit, he was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Shuòzhōu.
When Tàizǔ garrisoned Yànmén,
he made him Commander (Jūnshǐ) of Fèngchéng.
He followed [Tàizǔ] in entering the Pass
to campaign against Huáng Cháo,
serving as the vanguard.
He was promoted to Commander of the Left Camp.
When Mèng Fānglì of Lùzhōu moved to Xīngzhōu,
Jìn captured Lùzhōu,
and Kèxiū was recommended as the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhāoyì Army.
He frequently went out to Shāndōng to attack Fānglì,
and also, together with Lǐ Hǎnzhī, attacked and raided the region between Huái and Mèng.
After that,
Tàizǔ personally led troops to attack Fānglì.
When the army returned and passed through Lù,
Kèxiū was frugal and stingy by nature,
and the provisions he offered were very meager.
Tàizǔ was greatly enraged,
reviled him, and struck and whipped him.
Kèxiū, ashamed and angry,
fell ill and died.
He had two sons: Sìbì and Sìgōng.
Sìbì was the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Zhuōzhōu.
In the nineteenth year of Tiānyòu,
the Qìdān attacked and destroyed Zhuōzhōu,
and Sìbì died in captivity.
The Táng (唐) dynasty, from the time Zhūyé (朱邪) acquired the surname and became Lǐ (李) clan,
acquired a state and became Jìn (晉),
acquired the empire and became Táng (唐).
Its origin was among the barbarians,
and it ended in chaos and collapse.
Therefore, its lineage cannot be clearly seen.
What can be seen
are four younger brothers, eight sons, and five grandsons of Tàizǔ (太祖),
whose line ended in three generations.
Tàizǔ's (太祖) four younger brothers were named Kèlìang (克讓), Kèxiū (克脩), Kègōng (克恭), and Kèníng (克寧).
The names of their parents are all unknown.
Kèlìang (克讓)
Kèlìang (克讓),
from a young age, was skilled in archery and horsemanship.
He served as a military officer in the Zhènwǔ (振武) Army.
He followed in the campaign against Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝),
and for his merits, was appointed General of the Jīnwú (金吾) Guard,
remaining in the capital.
The Lǐ (李) clan, since the time of Xiànzōng (憲宗), returned to Táng (唐) with their tribe.
Táng (唐) settled them in Héxī (河西).
They once sent a son to guard the capital,
and bestowed upon him a residence in Qīnrén Fāng (親仁坊).
Later, Tàizǔ (太祖) raised an army in Yúnzhōng (雲中),
and killed the Táng (唐) commander Duàn Wénchǔ (段文楚).
Táng (唐) dispatched troops to attack Tàizǔ (太祖),
sending Wáng Chǔcún (王處存) with troops to besiege Qīnrén Fāng (親仁坊),
to capture Kèlìang (克讓), the son on duty.
Kèlìang (克讓), with his servants Hé Xiāngwēn (何相溫) and Shí Dìlì (石的歷) and more than ten cavalrymen,
drew their bows and spurred their horses,
breaking out of the siege.
Chǔcún (處存) pursued them with over a thousand men to Wèiqiáo (渭橋).
Kèlìang (克讓) and his men shot and killed over a hundred men,
and the pursuing troops then stopped.
Kèlìang (克讓) fled to Yànmén (鴈門).
The next year,
Tàizǔ (太祖) again submitted to Táng (唐),
and Kèlìang (克讓) returned to guard the capital.
When Huáng Cháo (黃巢) attacked Cháng'ān (長安),
Kèlìang (克讓) defended Tóngguān (潼關).
He was defeated by the rebels
and fled to Nánshān (南山),
hiding in a Buddhist temple.
He was killed by a temple monk.
Kèxiū (克脩)
Kèxiū (克脩), courtesy name Chóngyuǎn (崇遠),
followed in the campaign against Páng Xùn (龐勛),
and for his merits, was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ, 刺史) of Shuòzhōu (朔州).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) was stationed in Yànmén (鴈門),
he appointed Kèxiū (克脩) as Fèngchéng (奉誠) Army Commander.
He followed Tàizǔ (太祖) into the pass,
campaigned against Huáng Cháo (黃巢),
served as vanguard,
and was promoted to Commander of the Left Camp.
When Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) of Lùzhōu (潞州) moved to Xíngzhōu (邢州),
Jìn (晉) took Lùzhōu (潞州),
and appointed Kèxiū (克脩) as Jiedushi (節度使) of the Zhāoyì (昭義) Army.
He repeatedly went out to the east of the mountains to attack Fānglì (方立),
and also, with Lǐ Hǎnzhī (李罕之), attacked and plundered between Huái (懷) and Mèng (孟).
Afterwards,
Tàizǔ (太祖) personally led an attack on Fānglì (方立).
On his return journey, passing through Lù (潞),
Kèxiū (克脩) was by nature frugal and stingy,
and his provisions were very meager.
Tàizǔ (太祖) was greatly angered,
cursed and flogged him.
Kèxiū (克脩), shamed and indignant,
fell ill and died.
He had two sons: Sìbì (嗣弼) and Sìgōng (嗣肱).
Sìbì (嗣弼) was Governor of Zhuōzhōu (涿州).
In the 19th year of Tiānyòu (天祐)
the Qìdān (契丹) attacked and broke through Zhuōzhōu (涿州),
and Sìbì (嗣弼) died at the hands of the barbarians.
Sìgōng (嗣肱)
was brave and resourceful from a young age.
He followed Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) and repeatedly achieved military success,
becoming the Supreme Commander of Infantry and Cavalry.
When Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) defeated the Liáng (梁) army at Húbì (胡壁),
Sìgōng (嗣肱) captured one Liáng (梁) general.
When Liáng Tàizǔ (梁太祖) besieged Tiáoxiàn (蓨縣),
Sìgōng (嗣肱) followed Cúnshěn (存審) to relieve Tiáo (蓨).
The Liáng (梁) army withdrew,
and Sìgōng's (嗣肱) contribution was significant.
He was promoted exceptionally to Governor of Wèizhōu (蔚州) and Commander of All Infantry and Cavalry North of Yànmén (鴈門).
He was successively promoted to Governor of Zé (澤) and Dài (代) prefectures.
When Wáng Yù (王郁) of Xīnzhōu (新州) rebelled against Jìn (晉)
and fled to the Qìdān (契丹),
all the prefectures north of the mountains rebelled.
Sìgōng (嗣肱) retook Guī (媯), Rú (儒), and Wǔ (武) prefectures,
and was appointed Governor of Xīnzhōu (新州) and Commander of All Militias North of the Mountains.
In the spring of the first year of Tóngguāng (同光),
he died in office.
Kègōng (克恭)
Kègōng (克恭)
was initially the Commander of the Juéshèng (決勝) Army.
When Kèxiū (克脩) died,
Kègōng (克恭) was appointed in his place as Jiedushi (節度使) of the Zhāoyì (昭義) Army.
Kèxiū (克脩) was simple and frugal in character,
and the people of Lù (潞) had always been content with his governance,
and moreover, pitied his death by flogging.
Kègōng (克恭) was violent and unlawful,
and also inexperienced in military affairs.
Because of this, the people of Lù (潞) all resented him.
Kègōng (克恭) selected five hundred elite soldiers from his rear quarters
and presented them to Tàizǔ (太祖).
When they reached Tóngdī (銅鞮),
their general Féng Bà (馮霸) rebelled with his followers.
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Lǐ Yuánshěn (李元審) to suppress them.
They fought at Qìnshuǐ (沁水),
where Yuánshěn (元審) was greatly defeated and wounded,
fleeing into Lùzhōu (潞州).
The deputy general Ān Jūshòu (安居受) also rebelled,
killing Kègōng (克恭) and Yuánshěn (元審).
He sent someone to summon Bà (霸),
but Bà (霸) refused the order.
Jūshòu (居受) became frightened and fled.
When he reached Chángzǐ (長子),
he was killed by commoners,
and his head was sent to Bà (霸).
Bà (霸) then entered Lùzhōu (潞州),
declared himself Acting Jiedushi (Liúhòu, 留後),
and allied himself with Liáng (梁).
Kèníng (克寧)
Kèníng (克寧)
was benevolent and filial,
the most virtuous among all his brothers.
He served Tàizǔ (太祖) with caution and diligence.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) fought against Hèlián Duó (赫連鐸) and Lǐ Kějǔ (李可舉) between Yún (雲) and Wèi (蔚),
later fled to Dádá (達靼),
and entered to defeat Huáng Cháo (黃巢),
Kèníng (克寧) never failed to accompany him.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) was stationed in Tàiyuán (太原),
he appointed Kèníng (克寧) as Grand Commander of all Barbarian and Han Troops for Internal and External Administration,
acting Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo, 太保) and Jiedushi (節度使) of the Zhènwǔ (振武) Army.
All matters of the army,
great or small, were decided by Kèníng (克寧).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) fell ill,
he summoned Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) to his side,
and entrusted him to Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業) and Kèníng (克寧), saying:
"I entrust the second son to you all."
When Tàizǔ (太祖) passed away,
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) said to Kèníng (克寧):
"I am young and inexperienced,
and not yet familiar with general administration.
Although there is the late king's command,
I fear it is insufficient to handle important matters.
Uncle's merits and virtues are both high,
and the late king once entrusted you with administration.
I dare to burden my youngest uncle with the military and government affairs,
awaiting my establishment."
Kèníng (克寧) said:
"My elder brother's command
entrusted his son to me.
Who would dare to change it!"
He then bowed down facing north and made two prostrations to offer congratulations.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) then ascended the throne as King of Jìn (晉).
Initially,
when Tàizǔ (太祖) rose in the region between Yún (雲) and Shuò (朔),
many of the brave and fierce men he acquired
were adopted as sons.
And in his wars against heroes,
he ultimately achieved his hegemonic enterprise.
The adopted sons' contributions were numerous,
so he particularly favored and loved them.
Their clothing and ritual ranks were like those of嫡 (dí) legitimate sons.
The adopted sons each had elite soldiers under their command.
Relying on their merits, they acted wantonly,
and had often been shown leniency even in the late king's time.
When the new king ascended,
being young,
some feigned illness and did not attend court,
or appeared but did not bow.
The adopted sons Cún Hào (存顥) and Cún Shí (存實) told Kèníng (克寧):
"When an elder brother dies, a younger brother succeeds him;
this is the ancient way.
How can it be right for an uncle to bow to a nephew?
One's wealth and status in life
should be seized for oneself."
Kèníng (克寧) said:
"In our family for three generations,
fathers have been kind and sons filial.
If the late king's territory
has a rightful heir,
what more do I seek!"
Sìgōng,
when young, had boldness and strategy.
Following Zhōu Déwēi, he frequently established military merits,
and was made Commander of the Imperial Vanguard of the Infantry and Cavalry (Mǎbùjūn Dū Yúhòu).
When Lǐ Cúnshěn defeated the Liáng army at Húbì,
Sìgōng captured one Liáng general.
When the Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) of Liáng besieged Xiānxuàn County,
Sìgōng followed Cúnshěn to relieve Xiānxuàn.
The Liáng army withdrew.
Sìgōng’s merit was considered great,
and he was promoted exceptionally to Prefect of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ) and Military Commissioner of the Northern Yànmén Region (Yànmén Yǐ Běi Dū Zhī Bīngmǎshǐ).
He was successively transferred to serve as Prefect of Zézhōu and Dàizhōu.
When Wáng Yù of Xīnzhōu rebelled against Jìn
and fled into Qìdān territory,
all the prefectures in the region north of the mountains (Shānhòu) revolted.
Sìgōng seized Guīzhōu, Rúzhōu, and Wǔzhōu,
and was appointed Prefect of Xīnzhōu and Circuit Commandant of the Northern Mountains (Shānběi Dū Tuánliànshǐ).
In the spring of the first year of the Tóngguāng reign period (923 CE),
he died while in office.
Kègōng
Kègōng,
was initially the Commissioner of the Juéshèng Army (Juéshèng Jūnshǐ).
When Kèxiū died,
Kègōng was appointed to replace him as Regional Governor of the Zhāoyì Circuit (Zhāoyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
Kèxiū was known for his simplicity and thrift,
and the people of Lùzhōu had long been content with his governance,
and they also grieved that he was flogged to death.
Kègōng was tyrannical, violent, and lawless,
and furthermore, he was unfamiliar with military affairs.
Consequently, all the people of Lùzhōu resented him.
Kègōng selected five hundred elite soldiers from the Rear Compound (Hòuyuàn)
to present to the Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ).
When they arrived at Tóngdī,
their commander, Féng Bà, rebelled with his followers.
The Grand Progenitor sent Lǐ Yuánshěn to suppress them.
They fought at Qìnshuǐ,
where Yuánshěn suffered a great defeat and was wounded,
fleeing into Lùzhōu.
The Headquarters Guard Commander (Yájiàng), Ān Jūshòu, also rebelled,
killed Kègōng and Yuánshěn,
and sent someone to summon Bà.
Bà did not accept the order.
Jūshòu became afraid and fled.
When he reached Chángzǐ,
he was killed by local commoners,
and his head was sent to Bà.
Bà then entered Lùzhōu,
declared himself Acting Regional Governor (Liúhòu),
and submitted to the Liáng [Dynasty].
Kèníng
Kèníng
was benevolent and filial.
Among his brothers, he was the most worthy,
and he served the Grand Progenitor with cautious devotion.
When the Grand Progenitor fought Hèlián Duó and Lǐ Kějǔ between Yúnzhōu and Wèizhōu,
later fled to the Dádá,
and entered to defeat Huáng Cháo,
Kèníng never failed to accompany him.
When the Grand Progenitor was stationed in Tàiyuán,
he made Kèníng the Commissioner of all Military Affairs, Both Barbarian and Chinese, Inside and Outside the Domain (Nèiwài Zhìzhì Fānhàn Dū Zhī Bīngmǎshǐ),
Acting Grand Mentor (Jiǎnxiào Tàibǎo), and Regional Governor of the Zhènwǔ Circuit (Zhènwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
All military matters,
regardless of importance, were decided by Kèníng.
When the Grand Progenitor became ill,
he summoned Zhuāngzōng to his side,
and entrusted him to Zhāng Chéngyè and Kèníng, saying:
“I entrust my second son (yàzǐ) to you all.”
When the Grand Progenitor died,
Zhuāngzōng addressed Kèníng, saying:
“I am young and orphaned,
and not yet versed in state affairs.
Although I have the command of the late King,
I fear I am insufficient to handle major matters.
My uncle’s merit and virtue are both exalted,
and the late King frequently entrusted him with governance.
I dare to trouble my paternal younger brother with the military administration,
awaiting the time when I become capable.”
Kèníng replied:
“My elder brother’s command
entrusted his son to me.
Who dares to disregard it!”
He then knelt down, faced north, bowed twice, and offered congratulations.
Zhuāngzōng then ascended the throne as the King of Jìn (Jìn Wáng).
Initially,
when the Grand Progenitor arose in the region between Yúnzhōu and Shuòzhōu,
the courageous and valiant men he acquired
were often adopted as sons.
In his battles against heroes and powerful men,
he ultimately achieved his hegemony.
The adopted sons contributed greatly to his success,
and therefore he especially favored and loved them.
Their clothing, rites, and rank were like those of his legitimate sons.
All the adopted sons had elite troops under their command.
Relying on their achievements, they indulged themselves,
and had often been shown great leniency since the time of the late King.
When the new King was established,
being young,
some feigned illness and did not attend court,
or when they saw him, they did not bow.
The adopted sons Cún Hào and Cún Shí reported to Kèníng, saying:
“When an elder brother dies, a younger brother succeeds—
this is the ancient way.
Is it proper in principle [lǐ] for an uncle to bow to a nephew?
When a man achieves wealth and high rank,
he should seize it himself.”
Kèníng said:
“For three generations in my family,
the fathers have been kind and the sons filial.
As long as the territory of the late King
has a designated successor,
what else do I seek!”
Kèníng’s wife, Madame Mèng, was inherently stern and fierce.
Cún Hào and the others each sent their wives to persuade Madame Mèng.
Madame Mèng repeatedly pressured Kèníng with this.
Kèníng was benevolent but lacked resolve,
and was confused by the multiple voices,
which ultimately led to disaster.
The Commander of the Imperial Vanguard (Dū Yúhòu), Lǐ Cúnzhì, incurred Kèníng’s displeasure.
Kèníng killed him,
and thereby created a rift with Zhāng Chéngyè and Lǐ Cúnzhāng.
He also requested to concurrently hold the position of Regional Governor of the Dàtóng Army (Dàtóng Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
At this point, the favored attendant Shǐ Jìngróng saw the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu),
and accused Kèníng of plotting with Cún Hào to seize the King and the Empress Dowager and surrender to Liáng.
Zhuāngzōng summoned Chéngyè and Cúnzhāng and told them:
“My paternal younger brother is acting like this.
What should be done?
However, kin should not consume each other.
I should avoid the path of the worthy (bì xián lù) to relieve my family of misfortune.”
Chéngyè and the others requested that Kèníng be executed.
They then concealed soldiers in the administrative headquarters (fǔ),
prepared a great banquet.
When Kèníng arrived,
he was seized and killed.
Sons of the Grand Progenitor (Cúnměi, Cúnbà, Cúnlǐ, Cúnwò, Cúnyì, Cúnquè, Cúnjì)
The Grand Progenitor had eight sons: Zhuāngzōng was the eldest son;
the others were named Cúnměi, Cúnbà, Cúnlǐ, Cúnwò, Cúnyì, Cúnquè, and Cúnjì.
In the twelfth month, on the day Xīnhài, of the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE),
an edict formally invested Cúnměi and the other seven men as Kings.
Cúnbà, Cúnwò, and Cúnjì shared the same mother as Zhuāngzōng,
but the names, lineage, titles, and ranks of the mothers of Cúnměi, Cúnyì, Cúnquè, and Cúnlǐ are unknown.
Cúnměi was enfeoffed as the King of Yōng (Yōng Wáng),
Cúnbà as the King of Yǒng (Yǒng Wáng),
Cúnlǐ as the King of Xuē (Xuē Wáng),
Cúnwò as the King of Shēn (Shēn Wáng),
Cúnyì as the King of Mù (Mù Wáng),
Cúnquè as the King of Tōng (Tōng Wáng),
and Cúnjì as the King of Yǎ (Yǎ Wáng).
Cúnyì successively served as Regional Governor of the Jiànxióng and Bǎodà Circuits.
He married the daughter of Guō Chóngtāo.
At that time,
the charlatan Yáng Qiānláng from Wèizhōu was influential.
He claimed to possess the arts of Mòzǐ,
able to command ghosts and spirits,
and transmute cinnabar and mercury.
Zhuāngzōng greatly revered him.
Qiānláng was appointed Acting Director of the Department of State Affairs (Jiǎnxiào Shàngshū Láng)
and bestowed with purple robes.
His wife frequently entered and left the imperial palace,
receiving favor and affection.
Scholars often sought official positions or ranks through him.
Cúnyì, Cúnwò, and others frequently indulged in dissolute behavior with their families.
When Chóngtāo and his clan were executed,
Zhuāngzōng sent eunuchs to secretly observe and inquire about public opinion regarding the matter.
The eunuchs, wanting to exterminate all of Chóngtāo’s relatives and followers to eliminate future trouble,
then falsely reported:
“Cúnyì visited Qiānláng,
and in his cups,
he rolled up his sleeves and wept aloud,
crying out for the injustice suffered by his father-in-law,
and expressed great resentment and discontent.”
Zhuāngzōng was enraged.
He surrounded Cúnyì’s residence with soldiers and executed him,
and also executed Qiānláng.
Cún Bà successively served as Jiédùshǐ of the three armies: Zhāoyì, Tiānpíng, and Hézhōng.
Cún Wò served as Jiédùshǐ of the two armies: Yìchéng and Tiānpíng.
Both resided in the capital,
and merely received their salaries and emoluments.
When Zhào Zàilǐ rebelled,
Cún Bà was then dispatched to Hézhōng.
When Lǐ Sīyuán’s army mutinied
and headed toward the capital,
Zhuāngzōng again took refuge in Sìshuǐ.
He transferred Cún Bà to be the Liúshǒu of Běijīng,
and Cún Wò to be the Jiédùshǐ of Hézhōng.
Before the imperial edict was fully proclaimed,
Guō Cóngqiān rebelled,
attacking the Xīngjiào Gate.
Cún Wò followed Zhuāngzōng and resisted the rebels.
Zhuāngzōng was struck by a stray arrow and collapsed (died).
Cún Wò fled together with Empress Liú toward Tàiyuán.
When they reached Fēnggǔ,
he was killed by his subordinates.
Cún Bà, hearing of the chaos in the capital,
also fled from Hézhōng toward Tàiyuán.
By the time he arrived,
all his immediate followers had scattered and fled,
only the subordinate official Kāng Cóngbiàn remained.
Cún Bà then cut his hair and dressed in monastic robes,
and went to see Fú Yànchāo, saying:
“I wish to become a mountain monk;
I hope Your Excellency will grant me protection.”
Yànchāo wanted to keep him,
but he was killed by the soldiers.
Cún Jì and Cún Què, hearing that Guō Cóngqiān had rebelled,
fled to Nánshān,
hiding in a commoner's home.
Míngzōng decreed to Hénán Fǔ and all circuits:
“If any princes flee,
wherever they are, send them to the court;
if they unfortunately perish,
collect and bury them, and report it.”
The commoner family where Cún Jì and the others were hiding reported it to Ān Zhònghuǐ.
Zhònghuǐ said to Huò Yànwēi:
“The two princes are fleeing danger,
and the sovereign is searching for them,
fearing they might lose their place.
Now that the present Emperor is acting as regent and overseeing the funeral rites,
what is the proper ceremony for this?”
Yànwēi said:
“The Emperor’s nature is benevolent and compassionate,
it is inappropriate to report this (to him).
It is appropriate to deal with them secretly,
in order to reassure the people.”
They then immediately killed them at the commoner’s house.
Cún Měi had always suffered from wind disease,
and lived in Tàiyuán.
Neither he nor Cún Lǐ are known as to their ultimate fates.
Zhuāngzōng’s Five Sons (Jìjí, Jìtóng, Jìsōng, Jìchán, Jìyáo)
Zhuāngzōng had five sons: the eldest was named Jìjí;
the next were Jìtóng, Jìsōng, Jìchán, and Jìyáo.
Jìjí’s mother was Empress Liú;
the names and titles of the mothers of the other four are not recorded.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
Jìjí was made Liúshǒu of the Northern Capital,
overseeing the affairs of the Six Armies and various Guards.
He was promoted to Acting Tàiwèi and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
When Dòulú Gé became Chancellor,
he proposed: according to Táng precedents,
imperial sons all served as Palace Envoys.
Consequently, the Yè Palace was established as the Xīngshèng Palace,
and Jìjí was made its Envoy.
In the third year of Tóngguāng,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wèi.
That year, Shǔ was attacked,
and Jìjí was appointed Supreme Commander of the Southwest Mobile Headquarters (Xīnnán Xíngyíng Dūtǒng).
Guō Chóngtāo was appointed Chief Pacification Commissioner,
while Rèn Yuán, Minister of Works, and Lǐ Yú, Hanlin Academician, both served as military advisors.
In the ninth month, on the *wùshēn* day,
he led 60,000 troops from Fèngxiáng and entered the Dàsàn Pass.
The army had less than ten days' provisions,
but every prefecture and garrison they reached welcomed them and surrendered,
and thus they lived off their stores.
Upon reaching Xīngzhōu,
the Shǔ general Chéng Fèngliǎn surrendered with five hundred cavalry.
Consequently, his troops were used to repair the gallery roads,
allowing the Táng army to cross.
Wáng Yǎn commanded ten thousand troops garrisoned at Lìzhōu.
He detached half of them to resist battle at Sānquán,
but they were defeated by the vanguard Kāng Yánxiào.
Yǎn became fearful,
cut the pontoon bridge over the Jíbǎi River,
and fled back to Chéngdū.
The Táng army entered via side roads from Wénzhōu.
In the tenth month, on the *jǐyǒu* day,
Jìjí arrived at Miánzhōu.
Yǎn presented a memorial requesting surrender.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
they entered Chéngdū.
Wáng Yǎn rode a bamboo carriage to Shēngxiān Bridge,
dressed in plain clothes and leading a sheep,
a grass rope tied around his neck,
his upper body bared, holding a jade disk in his mouth, and carrying a coffin.
His ministers wore mourning clothes,
and surrendered barefoot.
Jìjí dismounted and accepted the jade disk.
Chóngtāo removed the restraints,
and burned the coffin.
From the time the army was dispatched until Yǎn’s surrender,
it took a total of seventy-five days.
The troops achieved this without bloodshed,
The ease of warfare since antiquity
has never been matched like this.
However, although Jìjí was the Supreme Commander,
the military administration, orders, and commands all issued solely from Chóngtāo.
Previously,
Zhuāngzōng had dispatched the palace eunuch and Gōngfèng Guān, Lǐ Cóngxí, to supervise the central army,
and the high-ranking eunuchs Lǐ Tíng'ān and Lǚ Zhīróu to serve as Court Ushers.
Cóngxí and the others had long disliked Chóngtāo.
Furthermore, seeing Chóngtāo monopolize the military affairs,
they became increasingly indignant.
When Shǔ was conquered,
the noble officials and great generals of Shǔ,
starting with Wáng Zōngbì,
all competed to present Shǔ treasures, goods, singing girls, and musicians to Chóngtāo and his son.
But what the Prince of Wèi received
was merely a single horse, a bundle of silks, a spittoon, and a duster handle.
Chóngtāo managed military affairs daily,
and generals, officials, and guests flocked to his courtyard.
However, at the Supreme Commander’s headquarters, only the major generals paid morning respects,
and the main gate was utterly quiet.
For this reason, Cóngxí and the others could not suppress their indignation.
Shortly thereafter, Zōngbì led the people of Shǔ to see Jìjí,
requesting that Chóngtāo remain to govern Shǔ.
Cóngxí and the others took this opportunity to say that Chóngtāo had ulterior motives,
and advised Jìjí to make preparations.
Jìjí said to Chóngtāo:
“His Majesty relies on the Shìzhōng as heavily as Mount Héng and Mount Huà,
honoring him highly in the halls of government,
expecting him to unify the realm and control the four quarters,
and he will certainly not abandon a veteran statesman in this land of the barbarians.
This matter is not something I dare to know.”
Zhuāngzōng, hearing that Chóngtāo wanted to stay in Shǔ,
was also displeased.
He dispatched the eunuch Xiàng Yánsì to urge Jìjí to return the army.
When Yánsì arrived in Chéngdū,
Chóngtāo did not come out to welcome him.
And when they finally met,
his courtesy was extremely lax.
Yánsì became angry.
Cóngxí and the others consequently informed Yánsì that Chóngtāo had ulterior motives,
and feared danger for the Prince of Wèi.
Yánsì returned,
and reported everything in detail.
Empress Liú wept and pleaded for the protection of Jìjí.
Zhuāngzōng dispatched the eunuch Mǎ Yànguī to observe whether Chóngtāo intended to stay or leave.
At this time,
the Two Chuān regions had just been pacified.
Mèng Zhīxiáng had not yet arrived.
Bandits were gathering in the mountains and forests everywhere.
Chóngtāo was currently dispatching Rèn Yuán and others to go out and pacify and recruit them,
fearing that trouble might arise later,
thus the army had not immediately returned.
But when Yànguī was about to depart,
he saw Empress Liú and said:
“I heard Yánsì say that the state of affairs in Shǔ is already untenable.
The seeds of disaster are forming,
there is no room for delay.
How can I travel three thousand *lǐ* to report back and await orders?”
Empress Liú reported Yànguī’s words to Zhuāngzōng.
Zhuāngzōng said:
“The reports are unverified;
how can we immediately issue a definitive order?”
The Empress, failing to obtain approval,
personally wrote an instruction to Jìjí,
ordering him to kill Chóngtāo.
In the first month of the following year,
Chóngtāo left Rèn Yuán to guard Shǔ,
to await Zhīxiáng’s arrival.
Chóngtāo had set a date for the army’s return.
Yànguī arrived in Shǔ,
and presented the Empress’s instruction to Jìjí.
Jìjí said:
“The main army is about to depart,
and there is no cause for suspicion yet.
How can we commit such a treacherous act!”
Cóngxí and the others wept and said:
“There is a secret imperial decree here.
If Your Highness fails to act,
and Chóngtāo finds out,
then none of us will survive!”
Jìjí said:
“The Emperor has no imperial decree;
it is only the Empress’s personal instruction.
How can I kill the Chief Pacification Commissioner?”
Cóngxí and the others argued vehemently,
and Jìjí reluctantly complied.
The next morning,
Cóngxí used the Supreme Commander’s authority to summon Chóngtāo.
Jìjí ascended a tower to avoid him.
Chóngtāo entered,
and ascended the steps.
Lǐ Huán, Jìjí’s attendant, smashed his head with a baton.
Jìjí then withdrew his army.
In the second month,
the army reached Níxī.
The vanguard commander Kāng Yánxiào rebelled
and occupied Hànzhōu.
Jìjí sent Rèn Huán to suppress and pacify him.
In the fourth month, on the Xīnmǎo day,
upon reaching Xīngpíng,
he heard that Míngzōng had rebelled
and that the troops had entered the capital.
Jìjí wanted to retreat and secure Fèngxiáng.
When they arrived at Wǔgōng,
Lǐ Cóngxí urged Jìjí to hasten toward the capital
to resolve the internal crisis.
Traveling to the Wèihé River,
Zhāng Jiān, the Resident Commissioner of the Western Capital, cut the pontoon bridge.
Jìjí was unable to cross.
He then followed the river eastward
to Wèinán,
where all his attendants scattered.
Cóngxí said to Jìjí:
"The great matter is over.
Fortune cannot be repeated.
Your Highness ought to make plans for yourself."
Jìjí paced in tears
and said to Lǐ Huán:
"My way is finished and my road is exhausted.
You must kill me."
Huán hesitated for a long time
and said to Jìjí's wet nurse:
"I cannot bear to look upon His Highness.
If His Highness has no way to seek survival,
he should lie face down and await it."
Jìjí faced the bed and lay down.
Huán strangled him to death.
Rèn Huán arrived later
and buried Jìjí southwest of Huàzhōu.
Jìjí was sickly and castrated from youth
and had no sons.
Míngzōng had already ascended the throne.
Huán led the twenty thousand troops who had campaigned against Shǔ to the capital.
Míngzōng comforted and reassured him for a long time
and asked Huán where Jìjí was.
Huán reported the circumstances of Jìjí’s death in full detail.
In the third year of Tóngguāng,
an imperial decree appointed the imperial sons Jìsōng, Jìtóng, Jìchán, and Jìyáo all as Grand Masters of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Dàfū)
and Provisional Ministers of Instruction (Jiǎnxiào Sītú).
This was probably because they were all young,
and thus not enfeoffed with titles.
When Zhuāngzōng was assassinated,
there were eleven surviving descendants of Tàizǔ.
When Míngzōng took the throne,
four of them were killed,
and the remaining ones were all of unknown fate.
Thus, the lineage of Tàizǔ was cut off.
In the Family Biographies (Jiārén Chuán) of Liáng and Táng,
brothers are always placed before sons.
The sons of brothers
are appended to their respective fathers.
This is the standard principle.
As for the accounts of Zhuāngzōng’s seven younger brothers,
they are not ranked by age,
but are recorded according to the sequence of their deaths,
merely for the convenience of narration,
not due to any fixed rule.
Family Biographies of Táng Míngzōng, Part Three: Empress Cáo Shì, Empress Xià Shì.
Míngzōng had three Empresses and one Consort: Empress Héwǔxiàn Cáo Shì bore the Princess of Jìnguó;
Empress Zhāoyì Xià Shì bore the Prince of Qín, Cóngróng, and Emperor Mǐn;
Empress Xuānxiàn Wèi Shì
was the mother of the Prince of Lù, Cóngkē;
Consort Shú Wáng Shì
was the nurturing mother of the Prince of Xǔ, Cóngyì.
The detailed lineage of both Cáo Shì and Xià Shì is not recorded.
Xià Shì had no official title
and died before Míngzōng ascended the throne.
In the first year of Tiānchéng of Míngzōng,
Lady Cáo Shì, Lady of Chǔguó, was enfeoffed as Consort Shú,
and Lady Xià Shì was posthumously enfeoffed as Lady of Jìnguó.
In the first year of Chángxīng,
Consort Shú was established as Empress.
Because the two sons born to Xià Shì had both become Princes,
she was posthumously invested as Empress
with the posthumous name Zhāoyì.
Empress Wèi Shì
Wèi Shì
was a native of Píngshān in Zhènzhōu.
She was originally married to a commoner named Wáng Shì from Píngshān
and had a son who was ten years old.
When Míngzōng was a cavalry general,
he pillaged Píngshān
and took the mother and son back.
After several years,
Wèi Shì died
and was buried in Tàiyuán.
Her son was the later Prince of Lù, Cóngkē.
During Míngzōng's reign,
Cóngkē was already a Prince,
so Wèi Shì was posthumously enfeoffed as Lady of Lǔguó.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored Wèi Shì as the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
Discussions were held about building a mausoleum,
but Shí Jìngtáng rebelled in Tàiyuán.
Therefore, a memorial hall was established east of Hénán Fǔ in the capital.
On the Bǐngyín day in the sixth month of the third year of Qīngtài,
the Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū) Cuī Jiǎn was dispatched to present the ceremonial scroll to the Empress Dowager,
and she was given the posthumous name Xuānxiàn.
Consort Shú Wáng Shì
Consort Shú Wáng Shì
was the daughter of a pastry maker in Bīnzhōu.
She was beautiful
and was nicknamed
"Flower-Shamer" (Huā Jiàn Xiū).
In her youth, she was sold to the deceased Liáng general Liú Mǒu as a maidservant.
When Mǒu died,
Wáng Shì had nowhere to go.
At this time,
Míngzōng’s Lady Xià had already died,
and he was looking for a new concubine.
Someone spoke about Wáng Shì to Ān Chónghuǐ.
Chónghuǐ reported this to Míngzōng, and Míngzōng received her.
Wáng Shì had previously obtained a great amount of gold.
She gave it all to Míngzōng's attendants and the wives of his sons.
Everyone spoke highly of Wáng Shì,
and Míngzōng favored her increasingly.
But Lady Cáo Shì was simple and modest in character
and often avoided official duties.
Consequently, Wáng Shì enjoyed exclusive favor.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
there was deliberation about establishing an Empress.
Cáo Shì was the proper person to be established.
Cáo Shì said to Wáng Shì:
"I have always been prone to illness,
and my nature cannot bear bother.
Sister, you should take my place."
Wáng Shì said:
"The Empress
is the Emperor's match.
It is a position of ultimate veneration.
Who would dare interfere with it!"
Cáo Shì was then established as Empress,
and Wáng Shì as Consort Shú.
The Consort also served the Empress very respectfully.
Whenever the Emperor rose in the morning,
the washing, combing, dressing, and serving
were all duties the Consort personally managed at his side.
And when court was dismissed,
when the Emperor ate with the Empress,
the Consort attended,
only withdrawing when the meal was concluded.
She never showed the slightest lack of diligence,
and the Empress increasingly loved her in her heart.
However, the affairs within the palace
were all controlled by the Consort.
When Míngzōng was ill,
the Consort and the eunuch Mèng Hànqióng managed all matters around him,
and consequently monopolized power.
They were involved in the killings of Ān Chónghuǐ and the Prince of Qín, Cóngróng.
All the sons of Liú Mǒu
were appointed to official ranks and titles because of the Consort.
When Emperor Mǐn ascended the throne,
he formally honored the Empress as Empress Dowager,
and the Consort as Grand Consort (Huáng Tàifēi).
Earlier,
a son had been born to one of Míngzōng's palace women,
and the Consort was ordered to act as his mother.
This was the Prince of Xǔ, Cóngyì.
Cóngyì's wet nurse, Superintendent of Wardrobe (Sīyī) Wáng Shì,
seeing that Míngzōng was old and the Prince of Qín held military power,
secretly intended to rely on him and make plans for her future.
She then said:
"The child misses the Prince of Qín."
At that time, Cóngyì was four years old,
and she repeatedly taught Cóngyì to say that he wanted to see the Prince of Qín.
Míngzōng sent the wet nurse with the child back and forth to the Prince of Qín's residence (Qínfǔ).
She subsequently had a secret affair with Cóngróng.
Cóngróng then used Wáng Shì to secretly observe the activities inside the palace.
After Cóngróng was killed,
Sīyī Wáng Shì believed that the Prince of Qín had actually entered the palace with troops to guard the Son of Heaven,
but had been executed as a rebel,
and she uttered words of resentment.
Emperor Mǐn heard of this
and was greatly enraged.
He ordered Sīyī Wáng Shì to commit suicide.
Since the affair implicated the Grand Consort,
he was displeased with her.
He wanted to move her to the Zhìdégōng Palace,
but because the Empress Dowager was always kind to the Consort,
he feared hurting her feelings and abandoned the plan.
However, he treated her very coldly.
He once held a feast in the *Fēi*'s residence.
The *Fēi* raised her cup and said:
"I wish to resign from serving the Emperor and become a Buddhist nun (*bǐqīuní*)."
The Emperor was startled,
and asked her reason.
She replied:
"The youngest son was only accidentally spared.
If the eldest son is not tolerated,
then on the day I die,
how can I face the late Emperor (*Xiāndì*)?"
Thereupon, tears fell.
*Fèidì* (Li Cóngkē) was also deeply saddened by this
and treated her quite kindly.
When Shí Jìngtáng's troops invaded the capital (*Jīngshī*),
*Fèidì* (Li Cóngkē) gathered his relatives intending self-immolation.
The *Fēi* said to the Empress Dowager (*Tàihòu*):
"The situation is critical.
It is advisable to step away for a while
to await your maternal uncle/aunt's husband."
The *Tàihòu* replied:
"My house has come to this;
how can I bear to live alone?
Sister, take care of yourself!"
The *Tàihòu* then burned herself to death along with the Emperor,
while the *Fēi*, along with Xǔ Wáng (Prince of Xu) Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì) and his younger sister, hid in the ball court (*jūyuàn*) and escaped death.
When Jìn Gāozǔ (Shí Jìngtáng) ascended the throne,
the *Fēi* personally requested to become a nun.
This was not permitted.
She was then moved to the Zhìdé Gōng Palace.
When Jìn moved the capital to Biàn,
the *Fēi* and her son were moved east together,
and placed inside the palace.
Gāozǔ's Empress served the *Fēi* as if she were her own mother.
In the fourth year of Tiānfú (939 CE), on the *guǐwèi* day of the ninth month,
an edict granted three thousand households in Xún Guó (Xun State) to the Táng Prince of Xǔ, Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì), making him Xún Guó Gōng (Duke of Xun State),
in order to maintain the sacrifices of the Táng dynasty.
Their clothing, colors, banners, and flags all followed the former system.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (*Tàicháng*) proposed establishing three ancestral temples for Zhuāngzōng (Lǐ Cúnxù), Míngzōng (Lǐ Sīyuán), and Mǐndì (Lǐ Cónghòu),
using the Zhìdé Gōng Palace as the temple.
An edict was issued establishing temples for Gāozǔ and Tàizōng (Lǐ Sìshì),
making five temples in total,
and making Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì) responsible for presiding over the seasonal sacrifices.
When Chūdì (Shí Chóngguì) ascended the throne,
the *Fēi* and her son both returned to Luòyáng.
When the Qìdān invaded the capital (*Jīngshī*),
the Míngzōng Gōngzhǔ (Princess of Mingzong) whom Zhào Yánshòu had married had already died.
Yēlǜ Déguāng then arranged for Yánshòu (Zhao Yanshou) to marry Cóngyì's younger sister,
who became Yǒng'ān Gōngzhǔ (Princess Yong'an).
The Princess did not know who her mother was,
having always been raised by the *Fēi*.
The *Fēi* traveled to the capital to preside over the wedding ceremony.
Déguāng (Yelü Deguang) saw the portrait of Míngzōng (Li Siyuán),
burned incense, and bowed twice.
He looked at the *Fēi* and said:
"Míngzōng and I pledged to be brothers,
therefore you are my sister-in-law (*sǎo*)."
Afterward, he teased her, saying:
"But today, she is my daughter-in-law (*fù*)."
He then appointed Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì) as Zhāngxìn Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of the Zhangxin Army).
Cóngyì declined
and did not take up the post,
returning to Luòyáng with the *Fēi*.
When Déguāng (Yelü Deguang) returned north,
he left Xiāo Hàn to guard Biànzhōu.
When Hàn Gāozǔ (Liú Zhīyuǎn) arose in Tàiyuán,
Hàn (Xiao Han) wished to leave for the north.
He therefore sent men to summon Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì),
entrusting the Central Plains (*Zhōngguó*) to him.
Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì) and his mother fled and hid within the area of Huī Líng (Hui Mausoleum)
to evade the envoys.
The envoys pressured them eastward,
and thus Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì) was temporarily placed in charge of the military and state affairs of the Southern Court (*Náncháo*).
Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì) presided at the Chóngyuán Diàn Hall.
Hàn (Xiao Han), leading the various Qìdān generals, bowed above the hall,
and the Jìn officials bowed below the hall.
The officials entered to pay respects to the Grand *Fēi* (*Tàifēi*).
The *Fēi* said:
"My son and I are orphaned and weak.
We were pressured by Hàn (Xiao Han).
How can this be a blessing?
Disaster is surely imminent!"
She then appointed Wáng Sōng and Zhào Shàngjiāo as Left and Right Chéngxiàng (Chancellors),
Lǐ Shì and Zhái Guāngyè as Shūmìshǐ (Commissioners of Military Affairs),
and the Yān general Liú Zuò as Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guard).
Hàn (Xiao Han) left a thousand Qìdān soldiers under Zuò (Liu Zuo) and departed.
Hàn Gāozǔ (Liú Zhīyuǎn) led his troops south.
Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì) sent men to summon Gāo Xíngzhōu, Wǔ Xíngdé, and others to resist,
but Xíngzhōu (Gao Xingzhou) and the others all failed to arrive.
He then planned with Wáng Sōng to use the Yān soldiers to close the city and defend themselves.
The *Fēi* said:
"My family are the remnants of a fallen state.
How dare we contend for the empire (*tiānxià*) with others!"
She then sent someone to submit a letter welcoming Hàn Gāozǔ (Liú Zhīyuǎn).
Gāozǔ (Liu Zhiyuan), upon hearing that they had previously summoned Xíngzhōu (Gao Xingzhou) who failed to arrive,
sent Guō Cóngyì ahead to enter the capital and kill the *Fēi* and her son.
As the *Fēi* faced death, she cried out:
"What crime have my son and I committed?
Why not spare my son,
so that every year during the Cold Food Festival (*Hánshí*), he can take a bowl of rice and sprinkle it over Míngzōng's (Li Siyuán) tomb."
Those who heard this were saddened.
Cóngyì (Li Cóngyì) was seventeen years old when he died.
Empress Kǒng Shì
Mǐndì's Lamentable Empress, Kǒng Shì.
Her father was Xún (Kǒng Xún),
Military Commissioner of the Hénghǎi Army.
The Empress possessed virtuous conduct
and bore four sons.
When Mǐndì (Li Cónghòu) ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
Before the official installation ceremony could be held, the rebellion broke out.
Mǐndì (Li Cónghòu) fled.
The Empress was ill, and her sons were young,
so none could follow him.
When *Fèidì* (Li Cóngkē) entered and ascended the throne,
the Empress and her four sons were all killed.
When Jìn Gāozǔ (Shí Jìngtáng) ascended the throne,
she was posthumously granted the honorific name Āi (Lamentable).
Míngzōng's son, Cóngjǐng
Míngzōng (Li Siyuán) had four sons:
namely Cóngjǐng (Lǐ Cóngjǐng), Cóngróng (Lǐ Cóngróng), Cónghòu (Lǐ Cónghòu), and Cóngyì (Lǐ Cóngyì).
Cóngjǐng's original name was Cóngshěn (Li Cóngshěn).
As a person, he was brave, fierce, and skilled in battle,
yet humble, reserved, and cautious.
He fought alongside Zhuāngzōng (Lǐ Cúnxù)
and repeatedly achieved merit.
He served as Jīnqiāng Zhīhuīshǐ (Commander of the Golden Spear Guard).
When Míngzōng's (Li Siyuán) army rebelled at Wèi,
Zhuāngzōng (Li Cúnxù) said to Cóngjǐng (Li Cóngjǐng):
"Your father has great accomplishments for the state.
His loyalty and filial devotion
I clearly trust.
Now he is being pressured by rebellious troops.
You ought to go yourself and convey My intent,
so that he does not doubt himself."
Cóngjǐng (Li Cóngjǐng) galloped to Wèizhōu,
where he was seized by Yuán Xíngqīn,
who was about to kill him.
Cóngjǐng (Li Cóngjǐng) cried out:
"My father was pressured by rebellious troops.
Since you gentlemen do not understand his true feelings,
I also cannot reach Wèi.
I wish to return to serve the Son of Heaven (*Tiānzǐ*)."
Xíngqīn (Yuan Xingqin) released him.
Zhuāngzōng (Li Cúnxù) pitied his words,
granted him the name Jìjǐng (Lǐ Jìjǐng),
and adopted him as his own son.
He followed Zhuāngzōng (Li Cúnxù) to Biànzhōu.
Many officers and soldiers deserted along the way,
but Cóngjǐng (Li Cóngjǐng) alone did not leave.
His attendants sometimes urged him to flee the disaster,
but Cóngjǐng (Li Cóngjǐng) did not listen.
Zhuāngzōng (Li Cúnxù), hearing that Míngzōng (Li Siyuán) had already crossed Líyáng,
again wanted to send Cóngjǐng (Li Cóngjǐng) to relay a message.
Xíngqīn (Yuan Xingqin) believed this was unacceptable
and consequently killed him.
When Míngzōng (Li Siyuán) ascended the throne,
he was posthumously appointed Tàibǎo (Grand Tutor).
Alas!
How can one live without a father?
How can one live without a lord?
Yet the sayings of the world state:
"One who practices loyalty (zhōng) and filiality (xiào) cannot achieve both completely."
How could that be true?
The lord and the father
are the great foundation of human relationships;
loyalty and filiality
are the great virtues of ministers and sons.
How could they fail to support each other
and instead cause harm to each other?
Rather, it depends only on selfishness (sī) or righteousness (yì).
If one proceeds by selfishness, both are harmed;
if one proceeds by righteousness, both are achieved.
If his father uses troops to attack his lord,
the son,
should he follow his father?
Should he follow his lord?
I say:
"The person follows where he resides,
the will follows righteousness,
this is permissible."
If the person resides in the lord's location, then he follows the lord;
if he resides in the father's location, then he follows the father.
He who follows the lord
must excuse himself to his lord, saying:
"A son cannot shoot his father;
I wish not to participate in the conflict!"
Then he should wail and weep and call to his father, saying:
"Why not lay down your arms and return to submission to our lord?"
If the lord is defeated, he dies for him;
if the father is defeated, he completes the mourning ritual and then serves the lord.
He who follows the father
must inform him, saying:
"The lord must not be shot;
why not lay down your arms and return to submission to my lord?"
If the lord is defeated, he dies for him;
if the father is defeated, he awaits punishment from the lord;
if he is pardoned, then he completes the mourning ritual and serves him.
Among the ancients, none understood filiality better than Shùn,
and none understood righteousness better than Kǒng and Mèng.
Their understanding of the relationship between lord and minister, father and son, was exhaustive.
Should they have unluckily encountered such a situation,
they would have acted exactly like this!
Cóng Jǐng, regarding Zhuāng Zōng,
knew whom to follow and thereby obtained his death.
What sorrow!
Qín Wáng Cóng Róng
Qín Wáng Cóng Róng.
In the first year of Tiānchéng (926 CE),
holding the concurrent titles of *Jiǎnjiào Sītú* and *Yùshǐ Dàfū*,
he was appointed *Tiānxióng Jūn Jiédùshǐ* and *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*.
In the third year (928 CE),
he was moved to govern Hédōng.
In the first year of Chángxīng (930 CE),
he was appointed *Hénán Yǐn*,
concurrently managing the affairs of the Six Armies and various Guards.
When Cóng Jǐng died,
Cóng Róng was the eldest among all the imperial sons,
and furthermore held military authority.
However, his character was frivolous and boastful, with an ambitious gaze.
He quite liked Confucian scholars,
learned to compose songs and poems,
and frequently recruited literary men.
He composed poetry and drank wine.
Therefore, later generations of shallow and frivolous individuals
daily offered flattery and deceit, thereby inflating his arrogance.
Generals, ministers, and high officials were all concerned about him.
Míng Zōng somewhat recognized his faults but was unable to restrain him.
Cóng Róng once attended him at his side.
Míng Zōng asked:
"After your military administration duties,
what activities do you practice?"
He replied:
"When I have leisure, I read books
and discuss the meanings of the Classics with various Confucian scholars."
Míng Zōng said:
"The Classics contain the Way of the lord and minister, father and son.
However, one must approach
established scholars and upright gentlemen to learn it.
I saw the former emperor (Xiān Dì) enjoy composing songs and poems,
which was utterly meaningless.
You are the son of a general's house (a military background),
literary composition is not your lifelong practice,
so you surely cannot excel at it.
If it is spread among the people,
it will merely invite ridicule.
I am old;
although I cannot comprehend the meaning of the Classics,
I still like to hear them often.
Other things are not worth learning."
In the autumn of this year,
Cóng Róng was invested as Qín Wáng.
According to previous precedent,
