princes who received investiture did not pay respects at the ancestral temple.
However, the responsible officials, seeking to please the emperor,
wished to make the ceremony grander.
They thus proposed, saying:
"In ancient times, titles and emoluments were conferred during the *dì* and *cháng* sacrifices,
demonstrating that the ruler dared not act arbitrarily.
Now, receiving a grand investiture without announcing it at the temple
is not the way of respect and obedience."
Thereupon, Cóng Róng donned court robes,
rode in the state carriage,
arranged the imperial guard,
proceeded to the court hall to receive the document of appointment,
and left.
He loaded the document onto the carriage,
and paid respects at the Supreme Ancestral Temple (Tài Miào).
All the people in the capital considered this an honor.
Three years later (933 CE),
he was given the additional concurrent title of *Zhōngshū Lìng*.
The responsible officials again argued:
"According to precedent,
imperial princes ranked below the Chief Ministers (*Zǎixiàng*).
Now Qín Wáng's position is high, yet he ranks lower,
which is inappropriate."
Consequently, he ranked separately from the Chief Ministers, taking the right side.
In the fourth year (934 CE),
he was given the additional title of *Shàngshū Lìng*,
with an income fief of ten thousand households.
Hé Zé, the Vice Minister of the Imperial Stud, submitted a memorial
requesting that Cóng Róng be established as Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
At this time, Míng Zōng was already ill.
Upon receiving Hé Zé’s letter, he was displeased.
He looked around at his attendants and said:
"If the officials wish to establish a Crown Prince,
I should retire to Hédōng to spend my final years."
He then summoned his high officials to discuss the establishment of the Crown Prince.
None of the high officials dared to agree or disagree.
Cóng Róng entered and reported:
"Your servant has heard malicious people suggesting
they wish to establish your servant as Crown Prince.
Your servant truly does not desire this."
Míng Zōng said:
"This is what the officials desire."
Cóng Róng exited,
met Fàn Yán'guāng, Zhào Yánshòu, and others, and said:
"These gentlemen are deliberating establishing me as Crown Prince.
This is merely intended to seize my military authority and confine me in the Eastern Palace."
Yán'guāng and the others were troubled by this,
and consequently granted Cóng Róng the title of Grand Marshal of All Military Forces in the Realm (*Tiānxià Bīngmǎ Dà Yuánshuài*).
The responsible officials then stated:
"A Marshal either commands various circuits
or is dedicated to a single front.
Since ancient times, there has been no title of Grand Marshal of All Military Forces in the Realm.
The appropriate protocol for this office cannot be determined by research.
We request that from the *Jiédùshǐ* down,
all who hold military positions
should wear quivers and bowcases and pay respects at court using military rites.
For those who also hold the concurrent title of *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*,
the initial audience should also follow this;
subsequently, they may be permitted to use the rites for visiting dignitaries.
All documents and decrees issued by the Marshal’s Headquarters
throughout the realm shall use official notifications.
Furthermore, he shall rank higher than the Chief Ministers."
Cóng Róng held a grand banquet at the Marshal’s Headquarters.
All the generals received grants: Commanders of the Kònghè, Fèngshèng, and Yánwèi Guards,
one horse and ten bolts of silk per man;
the commanders of the other armies
received ten bolts of silk per man.
From the Dōutóu rank down,
they received seven down to three bolts of silk.
He further requested one thousand men from the Yánwèi and Pěngshèng Guards to serve as his headquarters troops.
Whenever he entered court,
he used several hundred cavalrymen preceding and following him.
They drew their bows and held arrows,
galloping along the road.
Those who saw them were all terrified.
Cóng Róng also commanded his staff and wandering scholars from the four directions to try writing a Proclamation for the Campaign against Huái,
setting forth his own intentions for unifying all the realm.
Those who spoke on affairs of state requested that tutors be selected for the various princes
to provide further instruction and guidance.
The Chief Ministers found the matter difficult,
and therefore requested that Cóng Róng select them himself.

Cóng Róng then requested that Cuī Zhuó, Academician of the Hànlín Academy, and Rèn Zàn, Vice Minister of the Board of Punishments, be appointed as Judicial Administrators for the Marshal’s Headquarters.
Míng Zōng said:
"Academicians speak on my behalf;
it is impermissible."
Cóng Róng left in anger and said:
"To be appointed Marshal but not be allowed to request subordinate officials,
this is incomprehensible to me."
The generals, Chief Ministers, and high officials, seeing Cóng Róng's authority and status constantly rising,
yet behaving with such arrogance and flippancy,
all knew his downfall was imminent, but none dared to speak.
Only Yán'guāng and Yánshòu secretly intended to avoid disaster.
They frequently visited Míng Zōng
and tearfully requested to resign their positions in the Bureau of Military Affairs.
Both men withdrew,
and Cóng Róng’s disaster began.
it snowed.
Míngzōng visited the Shìhétíng pavilion west of the palace,
and contracted a typhoid fever illness.
On the day *Jǐchǒu*,
Cóngróng, accompanied by the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yūn, entered to inquire about the Emperor's health at Guǎngshòu Diàn.
The Emperor could not recognize people.
Consort Wáng Shūfēi informed him, saying:
"Cóngróng is here."
She then said:
"Hóngzhāo and the others are here."
The Emperor did not respond to any of them.
After Cóngróng and the others left,
the Emperor was moved to Yōnghé Diàn.
Everyone in the palace wept bitterly.
After midnight,
the Emperor suddenly rose from his couch,
and all those attending to his illness had left.
He looked at the court ladies guarding the water clock in the hall and asked:
"How late is the night?"
They replied:
"It is the fourth watch!"
The Emperor immediately spat out several pieces of flesh resembling lung tissue
and passed more than a *dǒu* of thick saliva/phlegm.
The guards of the clock asked:
"Has Your Majesty recovered consciousness?"
He replied:
"I do not know."
After a moment,
the ladies of the inner courts all arrived,
saying:
"Your Majesty’s spirit has returned!"
Consequently, they brought him a bowl of congee.
By dawn,
his illness was slightly better,
but Cóngróng claimed illness and did not attend court.
Earlier,
Cóngróng had always envied Sòng Wáng Cónghòu for being more virtuous than himself,
and feared he would not become the heir.
Normally, he was arrogant, self-satisfied, and pompous.
But whenever he heard people speak of Sòng Wáng's goodness,
he would look gloomy and discontented.
When he entered to inquire about the illness,
he saw the Emperor could no longer recognize people.
After he left,
and heard the sounds of weeping in the palace,
he believed the Emperor had already died,
and therefore plotted to enter the palace with troops.
He sent his *yāyá* Mǎ Chǔjūn to inform Hóngzhāo and the others
that he wished to enter the palace guard with his personal soldiers,
and asked where he might reside.
Hóngzhāo and the others replied:
"The entire palace is available for the Prince's residence;
the Prince should choose for himself."
They then privately told Chǔjūn:
"His Imperial Majesty is in good health (*Wànfú*).
The Prince should exert all his efforts in loyalty and filial piety;
he must not act carelessly."
Chǔjūn reported everything to Cóngróng.
Cóngróng immediately sent Chǔjūn back to tell Hóngzhāo and the others:
"Do you fellows not think of your families?"
Hóngzhāo, Yūn, and the Commissioner of Palace Affairs (Xuānhuīshǐ) Mèng Hànqióng, along with others, entered and informed Consort Wáng Shūfēi of the plot,
saying:
"For this matter, we must obtain the assistance of the palace guard troops."
They then summoned the Commander of the Palace Guards (Shìwèizhǐhuǐshǐ) Kāng Yìchéng
and plotted beneath the bamboo grove.
Yìchéng had a son in the Qín Wáng Fǔ (Prince of Qín’s Residence),
and did not dare to commit to the plot.
He said to Hóngzhāo:
"I am merely a general officer,
I only follow your orders!"
Hóngzhāo was greatly alarmed.
The next day,
Cóngróng sent Mǎ Chǔjūn to inform Féng Yūn, saying:
"I shall enter and reside in Xīngshèng Gōng today."
He also informed Yìchéng,
and Yìchéng consented.
Yūn immediately rode quickly into the palace
and found Yìchéng, Hóngzhāo, Hànqióng, and others sitting in the hall of Zhōngxīng Diàn discussing the matter.
Yūn rebuked Yìchéng, saying:
"The reason the Sovereign has supported and maintained us
is for this day!
Now the moment of crisis, danger or safety,
is separated by a hair's breadth.
How can you hesitate because of your son,
allowing the Prince of Qín to reach this gate?
Where will the Sovereign find refuge?
Will any of us survive?"
Hànqióng said:
"My worthless life is not worth preserving.
I will personally lead troops to resist him."
He immediately went in to see the Emperor and said:
"Cóngróng has rebelled;
his troops are already attacking the Duānmén (Gate of Correctness)."
Those in the palace looked at each other and cried bitterly.
Míngzōng asked Hóngzhāo and the others:
"Is this true?"
They replied:
"It is true."
Míngzōng pointed to Heaven and wept,
and after a long time said:
"Let Yìchéng handle the situation himself;
do not let there be turmoil in the capital (Jīngshī)."
The son of the Prince of Lù, Zhòngjí, was by his side.
Míngzōng said:
"Your father and I rose from humble origins
and succeeded in taking the empire,
often rescuing me from peril and distress.
What strength does Cóngróng possess
that he commits such an evil act!
You must immediately take troops to guard all the gates."
Zhòngjí immediately used the Kònghè troops to guard the palace gates.
That day,
Cóngróng came forth from Hénán Fǔ leading a thousand troops.
Cóngróng had many subordinates and associates,
but honest and upright officials were often disliked by him.
Those he particularly hated were Liú Zàn and Wáng Jūmǐn,
while those he was intimate with were Liú Zhì and Gāo Niǎn.
When Cóngróng’s troops came out,
he rode alongside Zhì and Niǎn, whispering into their ears.
Traveling until they reached the south of Tiānjīn Qiáo (Tianjin Bridge),
he pointed at the sun and said to Niǎn:
"Tomorrow, at this time,
Wáng Jūmǐn will be executed!"
He then arrayed his troops north of the bridge,
dismounted, took a folding stool, and sat down,
sending someone to summon Kāng Yìchéng.
But the Duānmén was already shut.
He knocked on the Zuǒyèmén (Left Flank Gate),
which was also shut,
and through the gate crack, they saw the Commander of the Imperial Escort (Pěngshèng Zhǐhuǐshǐ), Zhū Hóngshí, leading cavalry coming from the north,
and immediately galloped back to inform Cóngróng.
Cóngróng was startled and terrified.
He sought the *tiěyànxīn*,
and personally prepared his bow and arrows.
The Commissioner of the Imperial City (Huángchéngshǐ), Ān Cóngyì, led three hundred cavalry to charge them.
Cóngróng's troops shot arrows at them,
and Cóngyì slightly retreated.
Hóngshí's five hundred cavalry emerged from the Zuǒyèmén.
Just as they were crossing the river,
a large number of reinforcements arrived.
Cóngróng then fled back to Hénán Fǔ.
His administrator, Rèn Zàn, and all his subordinates fled out of Dìngdǐngmén (Dingding Gate).
His personal guards plundered Jiāshàn Fāng (Jiashan Ward) and dispersed.
Cóngróng and his wife hid under a bed,
and Cóngyì killed them.
When Míngzōng heard that Cóngróng was dead,
he wept mournfully and nearly fell off his couch,
losing consciousness and reviving twice.
Féng Dào led the hundreds of officials to enter and pay their respects.
Míngzōng said:
"My family affairs have come to this;
I am ashamed to face my ministers!"
The Emperor and the officials looked at each other,
their weeping soaking their robes.
Cóngróng's two sons were still young,
and were all killed with him.
Six days later, Míngzōng died.
Míngzōng's nephew Cóngcàn
Míngzōng's brothers are not mentioned in the hereditary records,
but he had four nephews,
named Cóngcàn, Cóngzhāng, Cóngwēn, and Cóngmǐn.
Cóngcàn was initially the Grand General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Dàjiāngjūn).
When Ān Zhònghuǐ held power,
all the princes, generals, and chancellors deferred to him.
Cóngcàn was resolute and fierce,
unable to yield even slightly,
and his nature was unconventional;
he valued wealth lightly and enjoyed giving alms.
Zhònghuǐ was jealous of him.
When Míngzōng visited Biànzhōu,
he appointed Cóngcàn as Commissioner of the Imperial City of the Great Interior (Dànèi Huángchéngshǐ).
Once, during a feast in Huìjié Yuán (Huijie Garden),
when drunk,
he playfully climbed onto the imperial couch.
Zhònghuǐ reported the incident,
and Cóngcàn was demoted to Administrative Aide (Sīhù Cānjūn) of Fángzhōu,
and granted death.
After Zhònghuǐ was executed,
an imperial edict restored Cóngcàn's official rank,
and posthumously appointed him Grand Preceptor (Tàibǎo).
Cóngzhāng
, courtesy name Zǐliáng
. In his youth, he excelled at riding and archery.
During the reign of Zhuāngzōng
, he led troops to guard Chángshān.
Hearing that Míngzōng's army had mutinied in Wèi
, he also raised troops and occupied Xíngzhōu.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Pěngshèng Zuǒxiāng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ,
then changed to Huángchéngshǐ,
concurrently serving as the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Ráozhōu,
and was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Zhāngguójūn.
He was later transferred to govern Yìchéng.
When Míngzōng visited Biànzhōu,
Cóng Zhāng wished to lead the people in presenting tributes.
His subordinate advisor remonstrated, believing this was improper.
Cóng Zhāng became enraged,
drew his bow, and intended to shoot him.
Due to this incident, he was dismissed and made Yòuxiāowèi Shàng Jiāngjūn.
After residing there for a long time,
he was sent out to govern Bǎoyì,
and then transferred to Hézhōng.
In the summer of Chángxīng Fourth Year,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yáng.
When Jìn Gāozǔ was established,
he was transferred to govern Wēishèng,
and his title was demoted to Duke of Lǒngxī Commandery.
Cóng Zhāng was inherently greedy and vulgar.
Since governing Bǎoyì,
he began to humble himself and reform.
While in Nányáng, he left behind considerable affection among the people.
He died in Tiānfú Second Year,
at the age of fifty-one.
Cóng Wēn
. Cóng Wēn's courtesy name was Déjī
. He initially served as the Deputy Resident Governor (Fù Liúshǒu) of Běijīng.
He subsequently held positions as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of five circuits: Ānguó, Zhōngwǔ, Yìwǔ, Chéngdé, and Wǔníng.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yǎn.
When Jìn Gāozǔ was established,
he was reinstated as the Military Governor of Zhōngwǔjūn.
Cóng Wēn was greedy and vulgar.
He frequently made imperial ritual vessels and robes in an act of usurpation.
Though his relatives and guests remonstrated with him
, he would not listen.
His wife, née Guān, shouted loudly at the headquarters gate,
saying: "Cóng Wēn intends to rebel,
having manufactured the robes and vessels of the Son of Heaven!"
Cóng Wēn was greatly alarmed
, and subsequently destroyed all of them.
Míngzōng had eight sons.
By the time of Jìn Chūdì, six had already died
, leaving only Cóng Wēn and Cóng Mǐn.
The Empress Dowager often said:
"I have only one brother remaining;
how can he be constrained by law!"
Due to this, Cóng Wēn became even more arrogant.
He once falsely accused his personal officer Xuē Rénsì of being a thief
, and confiscated all of his family's property, amounting to tens of millions.
Rénsì and others went to the palace gate to plead their case.
The matter was handed over to the relevant authorities,
and Cóng Wēn fully confessed.
Chūdì, fearing he would offend the Empress Dowager
, released him without further investigation.
In Kāiyùn Second Year,
he was transferred to Hèyáng Sānchéng,
and died in office.
At that time, Cóng Zhāng's son, Chóngjùn, was the Prefect of Guózhōu.
When he was implicated in a corruption case
, due again to the Empress Dowager
, only his judicial administrator, Gāo Xiàn, was punished.
Chóngjùn was reinstated as the Prefect of Shāngzhōu.
He was implicated in committing incest with his sister, murdering his servant Sūn Hànróng, and raping the servant's wife.
He was given death by imperial decree.
Cóng Mǐn
. Cóng Mǐn's courtesy name was Shúdá
. He was reserved and spoke little
, and excelled at riding and archery.
He initially served Zhuāngzōng as the Grand Commander of the Cavalry and Infantry (Mǎbùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ) concurrently holding the title of Administrative Controller (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
When Míngzōng entered and took the throne,
he was promoted to Huángchéngshǐ and Military Governor of Bǎoyìjūn,
and participated in suppressing Wáng Dū.
He successively governed Hénghǎi, Yìwǔ, Chéngdé, Guīdé, Bǎoyì, Zhāoyì, and Hèyáng.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jīng.
During the time of Hàn Gāozǔ,
he served as the Resident Governor of Xījīng,
and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Qínguó.
He died in Zhōu Guǎngshùn First Year.
He was posthumously granted the title Zhōngshū Lìng,
and his posthumous name was Gōnghuì.
The Biography of the Family of Táng Fèidì Part Four: Empress Liú.
Fèidì's Empress, née Liú
, had a father named Mào Wēi
, a native of Húnyuán, Yìngzhōu.
The Empress was a strong and fierce person
, and Fèidì always feared her.
She was initially enfeoffed as the Lady of Pèiguó.
When Fèidì ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
Her younger brother, Yán Hào
, served Fèidì as a staff officer (Yájiàng) when he was young.
When Fèidì ascended the throne
, he was appointed Palace and Garden Commissioner (Gōngyuànshǐ) and Director of the Southern Bureau of Military Affairs (Xuānhuī Nányuànshǐ).
In Qīngtài Second Year,
he became Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) and Military Governor of Tiānxióngjūn.
Yán Hào was fundamentally cautious and generous
, but changed his principles upon becoming powerful.
Because of the Empress, he handled affairs recklessly
, accepted bribes,
seized people's gardens and residences.
While stationed in Yèxià, he failed to care for his soldiers
, and all the soldiers resented him.
Zhāng Lìngzhāo, the Commandant of the Pěngshèng Capital Garrison (Dū Yúhòu), used his garrisoned troops to drive out Yán Hào.
Yán Hào fled to Xiāngzhōu.
At this time
, Shí Jìngtáng had already rebelled
and was employing his army
, and Lìngzhāo's rebellion began.
Lìngzhāo then sealed the city
and sent his deputy, Biān Rénsì, to request that he himself be appointed Military Governor.
Fèidì appointed Lìngzhāo as Yòuqianniúwèi Jiāngjūn,
provisionally managing the affairs of the Tiānxióngjūn headquarters.
Soon after, he dispatched Fàn Yánguāng to suppress him.
Lìngzhāo was defeated and fled to Xíngzhōu.
He was pursued to Shāhé
and executed.
Over three thousand rebellious soldiers from the garrisons were killed.
The relevant authorities requested that Yán Hào be punished according to military law.
Fèidì
, on account of the Empress, merely stripped him of his official titles and ranks.
Fèidì had two sons
, named Chóngjí and Chóngměi,
and one daughter who became a Buddhist nun
, named Yòuchéng.
The identity of their birth mothers is unknown.
When Fèidì governed Fèngxiáng
, Chóngjí was the Commander of the Kònghè Troops,
and he remained in the capital along with the nun.
The Kònghè
were imperial personal guards.
When Mǐndì ascended the throne
, he did not wish for Chóngjí to command the personal guards.
Therefore, he sent Chóngjí out to serve as the Commissioner of Regional Militias (Tuánliànshǐ) of Bózhōu
, housed Yòuchéng within the palace
, and transferred Fèidì to Běijīng.
Fèidì grew suspicious
, and subsequently rebelled.
Mǐndì sent men to kill Chóngjí in Sòngzhōu.
Yòuchéng also died.
Chóngměi
. Chóngměi
, though young, was bright and quick-witted, like an adult.
When Fèidì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Zǔowèi Shàng Jiāngjūn, concurrently serving as Military Governor of Chéngdéjūn, Mayor of Hénányǐn, and administrator of the Six Armies and various guards.
He was later changed to hold the title of Military Governor of Tiānxióngjūn, and Associate Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yōng.
When Shí Jìngtáng rebelled
, Fèidì intended to march north.
Chóngměi advised him that caution was necessary
and repeatedly pleaded with him not to go.
Fèidì inwardly feared Jìngtáng
and initially did not wish to go.
Hearing Chóngměi's words
, he thought they were correct.
However, Liú Yán Hào and Liú Yán Lǎng and others incessantly pressured him.
Fèidì subsequently went to Hèyáng
, leaving Chóngměi to guard the capital.
The capital was seized by panic
, and the residents all fled the city to hide
, but the gatekeepers forbade them.
Chóngměi said:
"The state is experiencing great difficulty,
and we cannot provide safety for the people.
Is it right
to prohibit them from escaping disaster?"
He consequently allowed the people to leave.
When the Jìn army was about to arrive
, Empress Liú piled firewood on the ground
, intending to burn down the palace buildings.
Chóngměi said:
"When the new Son of Heaven arrives
, he certainly will not sit in the open.
But later, it will only exhaust the strength of the people
and cause resentment after we are gone!"
The Empress thought this was correct.
Fèidì immolated himself
, and the Empress and Chóngměi died along with him.
Alas!
The way of the family and the state (jiārén zhī dào),
must not be incorrect.
Rites (lǐ),
are what distinguish doubt and illuminate the subtle.
It is extreme!
During the period of the Five Dynasties (Wǔ Dài),
the ways of ruler-as-ruler, minister-as-minister, father-as-father, and son-as-son became perverse (guāi),
and in the ancestral temples (zōngmiào) and the imperial court (cháotíng),
humans and spirits alike lost their proper order.
This may truly be called a time of disorder (luàn shì)!
From antiquity, there has never been such a thing.
The Táng [Dynasty] (Táng) had one title (hào) but three surnames (xìng);
the Zhōu [Dynasty] (Zhōu) had one title but two surnames.
Táng Tàizǔ (Táng Tàizǔ) and Zhuāngzōng (Zhuāngzōng) were one family;
Míngzōng (Míngzōng) and Mǐndì (Mǐndì) were one family;
the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) was one family;
Zhōu Tàizǔ (Zhōu Tàizǔ) was one family;
Shìzōng (Shìzōng) was one family.
Why is it that their families are distinguished (bié qí jiā) but their titles are the same?
What is the reason?
The Táng followed the title [because]
they recognized that it was seized by a usurper (dào) and held;
the Zhōu followed the title [because]
it was conferred (yǔ zhī).
And the reason their families are distinguished
is that the ancestral ranking (zhāomù) and the proximity or distance of kinship (qīnshū) must not be confused.
The titles may be the same,
but the families cannot fail to be distinguished;
this is what distinguishes doubt and illuminates the subtle.
Why was Bówáng Yǒuwén (Bówáng Yǒuwén) of the Liáng [Dynasty] (Liáng) not distinguished?
What is the reason?
It is to make manifest the root of calamity (huò běn).
The calamity of Liáng Tàizǔ (Liáng Tàizǔ)
began with Yǒuwén (Yǒuwén);
preserving this record is meant as a warning.
The Jìn Family Tradition (Jìn Jiārén Chuán) 5: Empress Lǐ (Lǐ Shì), Consort of Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ Huánghòu)
Empress Lǐ (Lǐ Shì), Consort of Gāozǔ,
was the daughter of Emperor Míngzōng (Míngzōng Huángdì) of the Táng.
The Empress was initially titled Princess Yǒngníng (Yǒngníng Gōngzhǔ);
in the second year of Qīngtài (Qīngtài), she was invested as Grand Princess of Wèiguó (Wèiguó Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ).
After the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) ascended the throne,
he constantly suspected that Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) would certainly rebel.
In the third year,
the Princess came to the court from Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán) for the Qiānchūn Festival (Qiānchūn Jié).
She bid farewell to return,
but he could not detain her.
The Deposed Emperor, being drunk,
said to the Princess:
“Why do you return so quickly?
Do you wish to rebel with Shí Láng (Shí Láng)?”
After he sobered up,
his attendants informed him of what he had said,
and the Deposed Emperor greatly regretted it.
The Princess returned,
and related this to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ, from this, became increasingly uneasy.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
the Princess was entitled to become Empress (Huánghòu).
In the third month of the second year of Tiānfú (Tiānfú),
the competent officials reported:
“The honored title of the Imperial Dowager Consort (Huáng Tàifēi) has been formally established.
We request presenting the treasured seals (bǎocè).”
The Dowager Consort (Tàifēi)
was Gāozǔ’s secondary mother (shùmǔ), Lady Liú (Liú Shì).
Gāozǔ, believing the Ancestral Temple (Zōngmiào) had not yet been established,
modestly deferred the matter of the Empress.
In the fifth month of the summer of the seventh year,
Gāozǔ was already ill.
He then decreed that the Dowager Consort (Tàifēi) be honored as Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
However, the seals were ultimately not presented before Gāozǔ died,
thus the Empress (Hòu) also received no official investiture during Gāozǔ’s lifetime.
In the seventh month of the eighth year of Tiānfú (Tiānfú), during the reign of Chūdì (Chūdì),
the Empress (Huánghòu) was formally invested and honored as Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) was known for her strength and sharpness;
Gāozǔ often held her in awe and dread.
When Empress Féng (Féng Huánghòu), Consort of Chūdì (Chūdì), held sway over affairs,
the Empress Dowager repeatedly admonished and warned her,
but Chūdì did not comply,
and consequently suffered defeat.
In the twelfth month of the third year of Kāiyùn (Kāiyùn),
Yēlǜ Déguāng (Yēlǜ Déguāng) having already defeated the Jìn (Jìn) forces,
sent Zhāng Yànzé (Zhāng Yànzé) to first attack the capital (jīngshī).
He sent a letter to the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu),
fully detailing the surrender of the Jìn army,
and furthermore said:
“I had a maid who dressed my hair (shūtóu nīzi) who stole a medicine pouch (yàonáng) and fled to Jìn.
Are they all still here?
When I fought at Yángchéng (Yángchéng),
I lost one Khitan cart (xī chē).
Is it still here?”
He also asked about the whereabouts of the Khitan (Qìdān) soldiers previously captured by Jìn, and Jǐng Yánguǎng (Jǐng Yánguǎng), Sāng Wéihàn (Sāng Wéihàn), and others.
When the Empress Dowager and the Emperor (Dì) heard of Yànzé’s arrival,
they intended to immolate themselves.
The favored minister Xuē Chāo (Xuē Chāo) advised them to stop.
When they received the letter from Déguāng (Déguāng),
they extinguished the fire and came out into the Upper Garden (Shàngyuàn).
The Emperor summoned the attending academician Fàn Zhì (Fàn Zhì),
and said:
“How did Dù Láng (Dù Láng) betray me?
Formerly, when the Late Emperor (Xiāndì) rose up in Tàiyuán,
he intended to select one son to remain as garrison commander (liúshǒu).
He consulted the Emperor of the Northern Court (Běi Cháo Huángdì),
and the Emperor entrusted this matter to me.
I had always thought he was aware of this.
You must draft a memorial for me detailing this clearly,
hoping that it may save my son and myself.”
Zhì drafted a memorial of surrender for the Emperor, which read: Your Imperial Grandson and Subject Chóngguì (Chóngguì) states: Recently, the Táng destiny came to an end,
and the Central Plains (Zhōngyuán) lost governance.
Fate reached its limit, misfortune reached its extreme;
the heavens collapsed and the earth tilted.
My ancestor had a field of one chéng (a small estate),
and
a troop (lǚ) of men.
War broke out and calamities accumulated,
strength was exhausted and influence isolated.
You, the August Grandfather Emperor (Wēng Huángdì), rescued us from trouble and crushed the powerful,
promoting benefit and eliminating harm.
You personally donned armor,
and penetrated deep into the battlefield of the enemy.
Braving
dew and enduring frost,
you crossed the dangers of Yànmén (Yànmén);
Riding the wind and striking like lightning,
you executed judgment in the lands of Jì (Jì).
With a single wave of the yellow battle-axe (huáng yuè),
the world was greatly pacified.
Your power overwhelmed the universe,
and your righteousness moved
gods and spirits.
Achieving success without claiming credit,
you then established the Jìn mandate (Jìn zuò).
Thus, the August Grandfather Emperor conferred great creation upon the Shí clan (Shí Shì).
Soon thereafter, the heavens sent down great misfortune,
and my late father passed away.
Your subject followed and inherited his dying command,
and succeeded to the former foundation.
At the beginning of the period of mourning (liàng'àn),
I was confused and lost the proper sequence.
In all important affairs of the military
and state,
I entrusted everything to the generals, chancellors, and great ministers.
As for daring to succeed to the ancestral lineage (zōngtiāo) without authorization,
this was already not done by received command;
lightly issuing documents,
and repeatedly daring to defy Your Dignity.
I personally initiated the conflict,
and consequently incurred your terrible wrath.
When calamity arrived, my spirit was confused;
when fortune was exhausted, heaven destroyed us.
Ten myriad troops
surrendered immediately upon seeing the wind [of your power];
the countless common people
stretched their necks and turned their hearts toward you.
Your subject carried the burden of unrighteousness
and shame,
craving life and enduring disgrace.
I brought ruin upon myself,
and furthermore implicated my ancestors,
hastily passing the days and nights,
merely existing and breathing.
If the August Grandfather Emperor would kindly remember the past,
and slightly dispel
Your thunderous rage,
not bestow Your divine execution,
and not cut off the ancestral sacrifices (xiān sì),
then one hundred mouths would bear the virtue of new life,
and the whole family would cherish gratitude that can never be repaid.
Although this is what we wish,
we do not dare
hope for it.
Your subject, together with the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) and my wife, Lady Féng (Féng Shì), is now bound in the outskirts, awaiting punishment.

He also drafted a memorial for the Empress Dowager, which read: Lǐ Shì (Lǐ Shì), your daughter-in-law (xīnfù) and concubine (qiè), the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) of the Jìn House (Jìn Shì), states: Zhāng Yànzé (Zhāng Yànzé), Fù Zhù'ér (Fù Zhù'ér), and others have arrived.
I humbly received the letter sent down by the August Father Emperor (Huángdì Āwēng) to calm and soothe us.
I humbly
reflect that the Late Emperor (Xiān Huángdì), when he was formerly in Bīng (Bīng) and Fén (Fén),
happened upon hardship and distress;
the danger was like stacked eggs,
the urgency like hanging upside down.
Both wisdom and courage were exhausted,
and safety could not be guaranteed from one morning to the next.
The August Father Emperor (Huángdì Āwēng)
set out from the north of Jì (Jì Běi),
and personally arrived at Hédōng (Hédōng).
You crossed mountains and rivers,
and overcame dangers and obstacles.
You immediately pacified Jùlù (Jùlù),
and consequently secured the Central Plains (Zhōngyuán),
saving the Shí clan (Shí Shì) from ruin,
and establishing the altars of state (shèjì)
of the Jìn
dynasty.
Unfortunately, the Late Emperor passed away,
and his heir succeeded to the ancestral line (chéngtiāo).
He could not continue friendly relations and grant peace to the people,
but instead diminished grace and betrayed righteousness.
We repeatedly agitated military conflict,
Regretful!
Misery is truly self-inflicted;
who shall hold the blame?
Now the Vast Heaven trembles with rage,
the capital and the regions are separated,
the supreme general is led like a captive ram,
the six armies have laid down their armor.
I, your servant, and my whole clan bear the offense,
viewing our circumstances and stealing a meager life.
In the midst of fear and confusion,
this solace and inquiry arrived,
clearly proclaiming the benevolent decree,
specially showing inclusion and tolerance,
and giving repeated comforting instructions.
My spirit soared beyond the heavens.
How could I have expected a life already hanging
by a thread,
suddenly to receive the grace of renewed life?
Examining my crime and reproaching myself,
even nine deaths would not repay it.
Now I dispatch my grandsons Yánxù and Yánbǎo,
to present a memorial requesting punishment,
setting forth my gratitude for you to hear.
Déguāng replied:
"You can be without worry;
I guarantee you a place to eat."
In the first month of the fourth year, on the *dīnghài* day, the first day of the month,
Déguāng entered the capital city.
The Emperor and the Empress Dowager went by palanquin to the suburbs,
but Déguāng refused to see them.
They were housed at Fēngchán Sì,
and he dispatched his general Cuī Yánxūn with troops to guard them.
At this time, it was snowing and bitterly cold,
and everyone suffered from hunger.
The Empress Dowager sent someone to tell the temple monks:
"I once provided food here for tens of thousands of monks.
Today, can you not take pity on us?"
The temple monks excused themselves, saying that the intentions of the barbarians were hard to predict,
and they dared not offer food.
The Emperor secretly appealed to the guards,
and thus they gradually obtained some food.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Déguāng demoted the Emperor to Guānglù Dàfū and Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi,
sealing him as
the "Fùyì Hóu,"
and relocating him to Huánglóng Fǔ.
Déguāng sent someone to tell the Empress Dowager:
"I hear that Chóngguì reached this state because he did not follow his mother's teachings.
You may seek convenience for yourself
and do not need to go with him."
The Empress Dowager replied:
"Chóngguì served me, your servant, with great respect.
His failing was
violating the will of the late sovereign
and breaking the harmony between the two nations.
However, as Chóngguì departs now,
fortunately receiving great favor,
preserving his life and protecting his family,
if the mother does not follow the son,
where can she go?"
Thereupon, the Empress Dowager, along with Empress Féng, the Emperor’s younger brother Chóngruì, the imperial sons Yánxù and Yánbǎo, and the entire family followed the Emperor north.

They were accompanied by fifty palace maids, thirty eunuchs, fifty officials of the East and West Ranks, one medical official, four Kònghè officials, seven imperial cooks, three officials of the Tea and Wine Department, three officials of the Yíluán Department, and twenty soldiers of the Six Armies.
They were escorted by three hundred cavalry troops.
The prefectures and districts they passed through
were all governed by former Jìn generals and officials.
When they had provisions and food to offer,
they were not allowed to deliver them.
The elderly people along the road
scrambled to bring mutton and wine as offerings,
but the guards pushed them away and prevented them from seeing the Emperor.
They all departed weeping.
After traveling for more than ten days from Yōuzhōu,
they passed Píngzhōu,
exited Yúguān,
and traversed the sandy wastes.
Starving, they could not obtain food.
They dispatched palace maids and attending officials
to gather tree nuts and wild vegetables to eat.
After traveling another seven or eight days,
they reached Jǐnzhōu.
The barbarians forced the Emperor and the Empress Dowager to bow before the portrait of Ābǎojī.
The Emperor could not bear this humiliation,
and weeping, he cried out:
"Xuē Chāo misled me
and prevented me from dying!"
After traveling another five or six days,
they passed Hǎiběi Zhōu,
and arrived at the tomb of the Dōngdān Wáng.
They sent Yánxù to bow before it.
After traveling another ten or more days,
they crossed the Liáoshuǐ,
and arrived at Tiězhōu in the Bóhǎi Guó.
After traveling another seven or eight days,
they passed Nánhǎi Fǔ,
and finally reached Huánglóng Fǔ.
In the sixth month of that year,
the Qìdān Empress Dowager moved the Emperor and the Empress Dowager to Huáimì Zhōu,
which lay one thousand five hundred *lǐ* northwest of Huánglóng Fǔ.
They had traveled past Liáoyáng by two hundred *lǐ*
when the Qìdān Empress Dowager was imprisoned by the Yǒngkāng Wáng.
The Yǒngkāng Wáng sent the Emperor and the Empress Dowager back to stay in Liáoyáng,
and provided them with some supplies.
In the fourth month of the following year,
the Yǒngkāng Wáng arrived at Liáoyáng.
The Emperor, dressed in white clothes and a gauze cap,
went with the Empress Dowager and the Empress to the tent to pay respects,
but the Yǒngkāng Wáng stopped the Emperor and instructed him to appear in ordinary clothes.
The Emperor prostrated himself on the ground, weeping heavily,
and confessed his faults and guilt.
The Yǒngkāng Wáng ordered someone to help him up,
gave him a seat,
and served wine and music.
However, the performers and accompanying officials under the Yǒngkāng Wáng’s command,
seeing their former lord,
all shed tears,
overcome with grief.
They vied with one another to give him clothes and medicine as gifts.
In the fifth month,
the Yǒngkāng Wáng went up to Xíng.
He took fifteen eunuchs and fifteen officials of the East and West Ranks who were accompanying the Emperor, as well as the imperial son Yánxù, and departed.
The wife's elder brother of the Yǒngkāng Wáng, Chánnú, desired the Emperor's youngest daughter.
He requested her,
but the Emperor declined, stating she was still too young.
The Yǒngkāng Wáng quickly dispatched a horseman to take her
and bestow her upon Chánnú.
Xíng
is barbarian territory,
extremely high and cool.
The barbarians usually went up to Xíng in the fifth month to escape the heat,
and descended in the eighth month.
When the eighth month arrived,
the Yǒngkāng Wáng descended from Xíng.
The Empress Dowager personally rode quickly to Bàzhōu to see the Yǒngkāng Wáng,
requesting land near Hàn'ér Chéng to farm and raise livestock for their sustenance.
The Yǒngkāng Wáng took the Empress Dowager with him
for more than ten days of travel,
and then sent her and Yánxù back to Liáoyáng together.
The following year, which was the second year of Hàn Gānyòu,
in the second month,
the Emperor and the Empress Dowager were moved to Jiànzhōu.
Traveling one thousand two hundred *lǐ* southeast from Liáoyáng to Jiànzhōu,
the Military Commissioner Zhào Yánhuī vacated his main residence to house them.
They obtained fifty *qǐng* of land dozens of *lǐ* outside Jiànzhōu.
The Emperor sent his attendants to cultivate it for their food.
In the third month of the following year,
the Empress Dowager fell ill.
Without medicine or doctors,
she often looked up to heaven and wept.
Facing south, she pointed her finger like a halberd and cursed Dù Chóngwēi, Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, and others, saying:
"If the dead have no knowledge, so be it!
But if they do have knowledge,
I shall never forgive you in the underworld!"
In the eighth month, her illness became critical.
She said to the Emperor:
"When I die,
burn my bones and send them to a Buddhist temple in Fànyáng.
Do not let me become a ghost in barbarian territory!"
Then she died.
The Emperor, along with the Empress, palace women, eunuchs, and officials of the East and West Ranks,
all disheveled their hair and went barefoot,
carrying her coffin to the assigned land.
They burned her bones,
dug a hole in the ground, and buried them there.
During the Zhōu Xiǎndé era,
a Chinese person who had fled from Qìdān and returned
reported having seen the Emperor, the Empress, and all the imperial sons, all of whom were well.
Afterwards, it is unknown what became of them.
Consort Dowager Ān
Consort Dowager Ān
was a native of Dàiběi.
Her family lineage is unknown.
She was the wife of Jìngrú,
and mother of the Later Emperor (Chū Dì).
She was titled Qínguó Fūrén.
When the Later Emperor ascended the throne,
she was honored as Imperial Consort Dowager.
The Consort Dowager grew old and lost her sight.
She followed the Later Emperor in the northern relocation.
While being moved from Liáoyáng to Jiànzhōu,
she died on the way.
Before her death, she said to the Emperor:
"You must burn me to ashes,
and scatter them facing south.
Perhaps then my remaining spirit can return to Zhōngguó."
After she died,
since there were no plants or trees in the sandy wastes,
they dismantled a Xī carriage and burned it [to cremate her].
They carried her ashes to Jiànzhōu.
Empress Dowager Lǐ also died,
and they were then buried together.
The Later Emperor’s Empress, Féng Shì.
FÉNG Shì, the consort of Emperor Chū (Chūdì),
was a native of Dìngzhōu.
Her father, MÓNG,
served as a Provincial Presenting Clerk (zhōu jìnzòu lì).
While residing in the capital (Jīngshī),
he used his cunning and flattery to please Ān Zhònghuǐ,
who made him Vice Resident Commissioner of Yèdū (Yèdū Fù Liúshǒu).
When Gāozǔ served as the Resident Commissioner in Yèdū,
he greatly enjoyed MÓNG's company,
and thus married MÓNG's daughter to Zhòngyìn.
Later, she was enfeoffed as the Lady of Wú State (Wúguó Fūren).
Zhòngyìn died young,
and the Lady lived as a widow.
She was attractive,
and Emperor Chū was pleased by her.
When Gāozǔ died,
and his coffin was lying in state,
Emperor Chū, while observing the period of mourning,
took her as his Empress (Hòu).
On that day,
using the guards of the Six Armies and the music of the Grand Court Sacrifices (Tàicháng Gǔchuī),
he commanded the Empress to proceed to the Western Imperial Manor (Xī Yùzhuāng)
and present herself at the portrait hall of Gāozǔ.
All the officials offered congratulations.
The Emperor turned and said to FÉNG Dào and the others:
“By order of the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
I cannot, along with you gentlemen, proceed with great celebration.”
When the officials withdrew,
the Emperor and the Empress drank heavily, sang, and danced.
Passing in front of the coffin,
he poured a libation and announced:
“By order of the Empress Dowager,
I cannot, along with the former Emperor (Xiāndì), proceed with great celebration.”
All his attendants burst into laughter,
and the Emperor himself fell over laughing,
turning to his attendants and saying:
“Today I am acting as a new son-in-law (nǚxù).
How does that look?”
The Empress and the attendants all laughed loudly,
their voices heard outside.
Once the Empress was installed,
she monopolized imperial favor.
She enfeoffed and appointed palace officials—such as the Palace Attendants (Shànggōng) and the Managers of Guests (Zhīkè)—all as Ladies of Commanderies (Jùn Fūren).
She also employed the male Lǐ Yànbì as the Chief Commander of the Empress’s Palace (Huánghòu Gōng Dū Yāyá).
Her elder brother, YÙ, held political power,
wielding authority both internally and externally.
Thus, Jìn fell into disorder.
When the Qìdān invaded the capital (Jīngshī),
they publicized the Emperor’s offenses to the world, saying:
“He took his uncle’s wife (shūmǔ) into the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng),
disrupting the great standards of human relations.”
The Empress followed the Emperor in his northern exile.
Grieving the Emperor’s disgrace,
she repeatedly sought poison,
wishing to drink it with the Emperor and die,
but the poison could not be obtained.
Her end is unknown.
The Jìn clan (Jìn Shì) initially rose from the barbarians (yídí) and then declined,
and finally was destroyed by the barbarians.
Therefore, the complete order and history of their imperial lineage cannot be fully known.
Those who can be seen are: Gāozǔ’s two paternal uncles (shúfù),
one elder brother and six younger brothers,
seven sons and two grandsons.
Some accounts are brief and some are detailed.
It is not only because of frequent disasters and turmoil that the facts are lost,
but also because some were not worth mentioning.
Nevertheless, we have roughly preserved those who are known,
in order to fill in the gaps.
The two paternal uncles are WÀNYǑU and WÀNQUÁN.
The elder brother is JÌNGRÚ.
The younger brothers are JÌNGWĒI, JÌNGDÉ, JÌNGYĪN, JÌNGYŪN, JÌNGHUĪ, and ZHÒNGYÌN.
The sons are ZHÒNGGUÌ, ZHÒNGXÌN, ZHÒNGYÌ, ZHÒNGYĪNG, ZHÒNGJÌN, ZHÒNGRUÌ, and ZHÒNGGǍO.
The grandsons are YÁNXÙ and YÁNBǍO.
Emperor Xiàopíng (Xiàopíng Huángdì) fathered Emperor Xiàoyuán (Xiàoyuán Huángdì), WÀNYǑU, and WÀNQUÁN.
Emperor Xiàoyuán fathered Gāozǔ.
WÀNYǑU fathered JÌNGWĒI and JÌNGYŪN.
WÀNQUÁN fathered JÌNGHUĪ.
However, it is unknown whether JÌNGRÚ, JÌNGDÉ, JÌNGYĪN, and ZHÒNGYÌN were closely or distantly related to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ
was the second son of Emperor Xiàoyuán (Xiàoyuán Huángdì).
Since JÌNGRÚ was his elder brother,
it is suspected that JÌNGRÚ was the eldest son,
and thus senior and close to Gāozǔ.
However, the posthumous title bestowed upon him was actually the latest among all the younger brothers,
and during Gāozǔ’s reign, he alone did not receive a posthumous enfeoffment.
This is also suspicious.
ZHÒNGYÌN
was Gāozǔ’s younger brother,
and it is also unknown whether they were closely or distantly related.
However, Gāozǔ loved him
and raised him as his own son.
Therefore, his given name was preceded by
“Zhòng,”
and he was ranked below the other sons.
Gāozǔ’s uncles, elder brother, and younger brother JÌNGYĪN, along with his son ZHÒNGJÌN,
all died before Gāozǔ took the throne.
However, JÌNGWĒI, JÌNGDÉ, ZHÒNGYÌN, and ZHÒNGYĪNG
died when Gāozǔ rebelled.
Gāozǔ’s youngest son was named FÉNGLIÙ,
who died before being officially named.
The old accounts which take ZHÒNGRUÌ as the youngest son
are incorrect.
The Shí clan (Shí Shì) had been active in the military for generations,
but WÀNYǑU and WÀNQUÁN held humble positions and were not often seen.
In the first month of the second year of Tiānfú,

WÀNYǑU was posthumously granted the title Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), having formerly been Grand Master of Imperial Splendor (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū), Acting Minister of the Multitude (Jiǎnjiào Sītú) concurrently Grand Censor (Yùshǐ Dàfū), and Pillar of the State (Shàng Zhùguó).

WÀNQUÁN likewise was posthumously granted the title Grand Mentor (Tàifù), having formerly been Grand Master of Imperial Splendor, Acting Minister of Works (Jiǎnjiào Sīkōng) concurrently Grand Censor, and Pillar of the State.
In the fifth month of the eighth year of Tiānfú during Emperor Chū’s reign,
His Imperial Grand-Uncle WÀNYǑU was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín (Qín Wáng).
WÀNQUÁN was additionally granted the title Grand Preceptor (Tàishī)
and posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Zhào (Zhào Wáng).
JÌNGWĒI.
JÌNGWĒI’s courtesy name was FÈNGXÌN.
During the reign of the Deposed Emperor of Táng (Táng Fèidì), he served as the Commander-in-Chief of the Third Right Regiment of Zhāngshèng (Zhāngshèng Yòu Dì Sān Dū Zhīhuǐshǐ),
holding the position of Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Cángzhōu.
When he heard that Gāozǔ had raised troops in Tàiyuán,
he said to people:
“Life inevitably leads to death.
Who among men can avoid it?
My brother is currently undertaking a great endeavor,
and I cannot cling to life, inviting disgrace,
and be laughed at by my contemporaries.”
Thereupon, he committed suicide.
JÌNGDÉ was then serving as the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry (Mǎbùjūn Zhīhuǐshǐ) of Yízhōu.
He was executed because of Gāozǔ’s rebellion.
In the first month of the second year of Tiānfú,
JÌNGWĒI and JÌNGDÉ were both posthumously granted the title Grand Mentor (Tàifù).
JÌNGYĪN was concurrently granted the title Acting Guest of the Crown Prince (Jiǎnjiào Tàizǐ Bīnkè),
and also Grand Mentor,
but JÌNGRÚ was excluded.
In the first month of the seventh year,
JÌNGWĒI was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Guǎng (Guǎng Wáng),
JÌNGDÉ as the Prince of Fú (Fú Wáng),
and JÌNGYĪN as the Prince of Tōng (Tōng Wáng).
They were all granted the posthumous title Grand Commander (Tàiwèi).

JÌNGRÚ was initially granted the posthumous title Grand Mentor (Tàifù), having formerly been Grand Master of Imperial Splendor, Acting Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Jiǎnjiào Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè) concurrently Grand Censor, and Pillar of the State,
but he alone did not receive an enfeoffment.
In the fifth month of the eighth year of Tiānfú during Emperor Chū’s reign,
the three Imperial Uncles were additionally all granted the title Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
And Imperial Elder Brother JÌNGRÚ was finally posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Sòng (Sòng Wáng),
and also additionally granted the title Grand Preceptor.
JÌNGYŪN.
JÌNGYŪN’s courtesy name was DÉHÉ.
When young, he was a rascal,
hiding among the common people.
Gāozǔ sent men to find him,
and appointed him a Garrison General of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán Yájiàng).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he made him Commissioner of the Flying Dragon Palace City (Fēilóng Huángchéng Shǐ),
and he was subsequently promoted to Defense Commissioner of Cáozhōu (Cáozhōu Fángyùshǐ).
In the winter of the fifth year of Tiānfú,
he was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Three Prefectures of Héyáng (Héyáng Sānchéng).
JÌNGYŪN was naturally greedy and brutal.
Gāozǔ selected virtuous assistants and clerks to support him,
and JÌNGYŪN, fearing Gāozǔ’s strictness,
never dared to violate the law.
After more than a year,
he was transferred to garrison Bǎoyì.
During Emperor Chū’s reign,
he was additionally granted the title Grand Administration Assistant (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
and gradually began to act arrogantly and wantonly.
When the Emperor occasionally sent envoys,
JÌNGYŪN invariably asked:
“How is my nephew doing?”
The people of Shǎn suffered from his tyranny.
He was recalled to the capital (Jīngshī).
Because he was an Imperial Uncle (Huángshū), the Emperor could not directly reprimand him.
Instead, he dismissed JÌNGYŪN’s original Chief Commanders (Yuáncóng Dū Yāyá), SŪ YÀNCÚN and ZHÈNG WĒNYÙ, to warn him.
When the Qìdān invaded the frontier,
JÌNGYŪN followed Emperor Chū on his trip to Chányuān.
He was ordered to use his troops to prepare defenses at Wènyáng,
and guard Mǎjiādù.
He never encountered the enemy,
and achieved no merit.
In the seventh month of the first year of Kāiyùn,
he was again sent out to serve as the Military Governor of Wēishèng Army (Wēishèng Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
After more than a year,
Emperor Chū renamed Cáozhōu as Wēixìn Army (Wēixìn Jūn),
and appointed JÌNGYŪN as the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ).
While in Cáo, his greed and brutality were particularly excessive.
After a long period,
he was recalled.
When ZHĀNG YÀNZÉ’s troops invaded the capital (Jīngshī),
JÌNGYŪN fled by night,
climbing over the eastern wall of the city.
He fell into the moat (shā háo) and drowned,
aged forty-nine.
JÌNGHUĪ, Prince of Hán (Hán Wáng).
JÌNGHUĪ’s courtesy name was DÉZHĀO.
He was a man of integrity, gravity, and strong rectitude,
courageous and highly intelligent.
Gāozǔ especially loved him.
During Gāozǔ’s reign, he served as Defense Commissioner of Cáozhōu (Cáozhōu Fángyùshǐ).
He was praised for his honesty and frugality.
He died while in office
and was posthumously granted the title Grand Mentor (Tàifù).
In the eighth year of Tiānfú,
he was additionally granted the posthumous title Grand Preceptor (Tàishī)
and posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Hán (Hán Wáng).
His son XĪ succeeded him.
Gāozǔ's [Gāozǔ] Empress Lǐ [Lǐ Huánghòu] bore Chǔ Wáng Chóngxìn [Chǔ Wáng Chóngxìn].
The mothers of his other sons were all unknown.
When Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán [Tàiyuán],
Chóngyīng [Chóngyīng] was Yòu Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn.
Gāozǔ expressed grief for the two sons
and both were posthumously awarded the title Tàibǎo.
Furthermore, Chóngjìn [Chóngjìn] was posthumously awarded the title Tàibǎo, replacing his former title of Zǔo Jīn Wǔ Wèi Jiāngjūn.
In the first month of the seventh year,
all were additionally awarded the title Tàifù.
Chóngyīng was posthumously enfeoffed as Guó Wáng,
Chóngyìn [Chóngyìn] as Tán Wáng,
and Chóngjìn as Kuí Wáng.
In the fifth month of Chū Dì's [Chū Dì] Tiānfú [Tiānfú] eighth year,
all were additionally awarded the title Tàishī.
Chǔ Wáng Chóngxìn.
Chǔ Wáng Chóngxìn, courtesy name Shǒufú [Shǒufú],
was quick-witted, highly intelligent, and fond of rites.
In the second month of Tiānfú second year,
based on his position as Zǔo Xiāowèi Shàng Jiāngjūn, he was appointed Governor (Jié dù shǐ) of Hèyáng [Hèyáng] Three Cities.
He implemented good governance,
and Gāozǔ issued an imperial decree commending him.
That year, Fàn Yánguāng [Fàn Yánguāng] rebelled.
An edict ordered Zhāng Cóngbīn [Zhāng Cóngbīn], the former Governor of Língwǔ [Língwǔ], to deploy the Hèyáng troops to suppress Yánguāng.
Cóngbīn also rebelled,
and Chóngxìn was killed.
He was twenty years old at the time.
Gāozǔ wished to posthumously award Chóngxìn the title Tàiwèi.
The ministers cited the precedent of the Hàn [Hàn] dynasty, stating
that imperial sons should not hold the title of Sān Gōng (Three Dukes).
Gāozǔ said:
"This child, having done good, suffered misfortune.
My sorrow for him is profound.
This is done by myself alone;
how can precedent restrict it!"
Thus, he was posthumously awarded Tàiwèi.
In the first month of the seventh year,
he was additionally awarded the title Tàishī,
and posthumously enfeoffed as Yí Wáng.
In the fifth month of Chū Dì's Tiānfú eighth year,
his title was changed back to Chǔ Wáng.
Shòu Wáng Chóngyì [Shòu Wáng Chóngyì].
Shòu Wáng Chóngyì, courtesy name Hónglǐ [Hónglǐ],
was a scholar, fond of learning,
and quite knowledgeable about military strategy.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Zǔo Xiāowèi Dà Jiāngjūn.
When Gāozǔ traveled to Biànzhōu [Biànzhōu],
he made him the Defender of the Eastern Capital.
Zhāng Cóngbīn rebelled,
attacked Hénán [Hénán],
and Chóngyì was killed.
He was nineteen years old at the time,
and was posthumously awarded Tàifù.
In the first month of Tiānfú seventh year,
he was additionally awarded the title Tàiwèi,
and posthumously enfeoffed as Shòu Wáng.
In the fifth month of Chū Dì's Tiānfú eighth year,
he was additionally awarded the title Tàishī.
Neither had sons.
Chóngruì [Chóngruì].
Chóngruì resembled Gāozǔ in appearance.
When Gāozǔ lay ill,
the Chancellor Féng Dào [Féng Dào] entered to visit him in his chamber.
Chóngruì was still young.
Gāozǔ called him out and made him bow to Dào in front of him,
then had a eunuch hold the child and place him in Dào's embrace.
Although Gāozǔ did not speak,
everyone around him knew that he was entrusting Chóngruì to Dào.
When Gāozǔ died,
the ministers of Jìn [Jìn], considering the many difficulties facing the state,
debated establishing an adult ruler.
Jǐng Yánguǎng [Jǐng Yánguǎng] had already secretly agreed to enthrone Chū Dì,
so Chóngruì was ultimately not enthroned.
Chū Dì appointed Chóngruì as Jiǎnxiào Tàibǎo and Prefecture Chief (Yǐn) of Kāifēng [Kāifēng],
and made Biān Wèi [Biān Wèi], Zǔo Sǎn Qí Cháng Shì, temporarily oversee the affairs of the Kāifēng Prefecture.
In the fifth month of Kāiyùn [Kāiyùn] second year,
Chóngruì was appointed Governor (Jié dù shǐ) of Xióngwǔ [Xióngwǔ] Army.
After more than a year,
he was transferred to command Zhōngwǔ [Zhōngwǔ] Circuit.
He never went to take up either post.
When the Qìdān [Qìdān] destroyed Jìn,
Chóngruì followed Chū Dì in the northern migration.
His subsequent fate is unknown.
Chónggǎo [Chónggǎo].
Chén Wáng Chónggǎo [Chén Wáng Chónggǎo]
was Gāozǔ's youngest son.
His nickname was Féngliù [Féngliù].
He died before receiving a formal name,
and was posthumously awarded Tàifù,
posthumously enfeoffed as Chén Wáng,
and granted the name Chónggǎo.
In the fifth month of Chū Dì's Tiānfú eighth year,
he was additionally awarded the title Tàishī.
Yánxù [Yánxù] and Yánbǎo [Yánbǎo].
Yánxù and Yánbǎo
were Gāozǔ's grandsons,
whom Chū Dì adopted as his own sons.
In the autumn of Kāiyùn second year,
Yánxù was made Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Zhèngzhōu [Zhèngzhōu].
Yánxù was young
and unable to manage the affairs of government,
so a eunuch was assigned to accompany him,
and Lù Háng [Lù Háng], Shàngshū Láng, was selected to assist in overseeing the prefectural matters.
The eunuch consequently monopolized the political affairs
and frequently insulted Háng.
Chū Dì then recalled Háng.
Subsequently, Yánxù was transferred to be the Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Qízhōu [Qízhōu].
In the third year (of Kāiyùn),
he was appointed Governor (Jié dù shǐ) of Zhènníng [Zhènníng] Army.
At this time,
there was fighting north of the Yellow River (Héběi),
and the entire land suffered drought and locust plagues.
The starving population was numbered in the millions.
Yet, the various circuits competed to hoard wealth.
Zhào Zàilǐ [Zhào Zàilǐ] amassed huge fortunes,
the greatest among the vassal lords.
Chū Dì desired this wealth,
so he arranged for Yánxù to marry Zàilǐ's daughter.
Zàilǐ presented three thousand rolls of silk as tribute.
The tributes presented before and after this event were countless.
In the fifth month of the third year,
the Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Qīng), Shí Guāngzàn [Shí Guāngzàn], was dispatched with one hundred and fifty chests of wedding gifts to welcome the bride at Zàilǐ's residence.
Chū Dì hosted a banquet for Zàilǐ in the Wànsuì Diàn Hall.
The gifts bestowed were extremely generous.
Ruler and subject indulged in ultimate extravagance;
people at the time regarded this as an honor.
Zàilǐ said to people:
"This single marriage for me
cost 100,000 [in currency units]."
In the eleventh month,
Yánxù was transferred to command Bǎoyì [Bǎoyì] Circuit.
When Yánxù became the Defense Commissioner of Qízhōu,
Yánbǎo replaced him as Prefect of Zhèngzhōu.
When the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
Chū Dì and the Empress Dowager sent Yánxù and Yánbǎo to deliver the surrender memorial, the Imperial Jade Seal, and the Golden Seal to the Qìdān.
Yánbǎo at that time had also become the Governor of Wēixìn [Wēixìn] Army.
When the Qìdān received the seal,
they judged that the craftsmanship was crude
and different from what previous histories described.
They ordered Yánxù and the others to return and request the genuine Imperial Seal.
Chū Dì replied with a detailed explanation:
"Previously, Lù Wáng Cóngkē [Lù Wáng Cóngkē] immolated himself at Luòyáng [Luòyáng].
The whereabouts of the Imperial Jade Seal is unknown,
and it is suspected to have been burned.
When the former Emperor received the Mandate,
he ordered jade craftsmen to create this seal.
All the officials currently in office are aware of this."
The Qìdān then dropped the matter.
Afterwards, Yánxù and the others followed Chū Dì in the northern migration.
Their subsequent fate is unknown.
Alas!
In antiquity, if one was unfortunate enough to have no son,
and adopted a son from the same clan as an heir,
the sages permitted this
and recorded it in the canons of rites without concealment.
However, later generations of common, rustic people conceal it.
If they conceal it, they cannot avoid deceit and falsehood.
Thus, they secretly and illicitly take babies in swaddling clothes,
conceal their true parents,
and deceive themselves into believing that the child is born to them,
saying:
"If we do not do this,
then the child cannot be single-minded in their devotion and complete love for us,
and their heart will surely be divided."
And the adopted child,
likewise conceals his origins,
cutting off his natural ties,
and instead treats his birth parents as paternal uncles.
By doing this, they deceive their entire extended clan,
and confuse the proper relationship between human and spirit, near and distant.
Every creature born with consciousness
loves its parents.
If this child
can endure this and truly sever his natural affinity,
then he is worse than birds and beasts.
If he cannot endure it but outwardly pretends to sever it,
this is a great falsehood.
Truly, the considerations of these common, rustic people concerning this matter
are quite profound!
However, secretly deceitful and false practices cannot be taken as law;
this is the affair of the petty person.
The sages, however, are not like this.
They consider that nothing in the Way of Man is greater than carrying on the line which has ended.
This is a universal system for ten thousand generations and a public practice throughout the world;
why must it be concealed?
Regarding those called sons,
there are none who are not born by parents.
Therefore, one who becomes an heir
must have a father who begot him,
and a father whose line he continues.
This is the natural order of things;
why must it be concealed?
What is simple and clear,
not reckless or illicit,
not deceitful or false,
and can be a universal system and public practice,
is the law of the sages.
Moreover, they held that those who act as heirs (Wèirén Hòuzhě) bear the heaviest responsibility (suǒ chéng zhòng),
thus increasing their mourning observance (fú) to the rank of Zhǎn.
The reason they do not completely sever relations with the biological parent (suǒ shēng zhī qīn)
is that natural affection (tiānxìng) cannot be severed.
However, affection (ēn) must yield to righteousness (yì);
therefore, their mourning observance is lowered to Qī (one year).
Mourning observance (Fú)
is an external thing;
it can be lowered.
But the name of 'father and mother' (fù mǔ zhī míng) cannot be changed,
thus it is recorded in the Classic (Jīng), saying:
"He who acts as an heir (Wèirén Hòuzhě)
mourns for his original father and mother (fù mǔ bào)."
Since the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài),
those possessing the realm and the state (tiān xià guó jiā) all utilized this,
but the Jìn Shì (House of Jìn) did not use it.
Chū Dì (Shì Chóngguì), regarding Jìngrú (Shì Jìngrú),
severed the path of fatherhood (fù dào),
treating him as a minister and conferring titles upon him.
This was not merely because in righteousness (yì) he should not have been established [as heir],
and that this severance was unavoidable;
rather, it was likely due to frequently witnessing the conduct of commoners (lǘ yán bǐ lǐ).
The Five Dynasties (Wǔ Dài)
was an era of weapons, wars, and rebellion (gān gē zéi luàn).
The rites and music (lǐ yuè) collapsed and were destroyed,
the Way of the Three Bonds and Five Constants (Sān Gāng Wǔ Cháng zhī Dào) was severed,
and the governmental systems and cultural achievements (zhì dù wén zhāng) of the former kings (xiān wáng) were entirely swept away!
Acts such as offering sacrifices in the fields on the Cold Food Festival (Hán Shí Yě Jì) and burning paper money (zhǐ qián) —
many were the actions of commoners (lǘ yán bǐ lǐ) performed even by the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ)!
Furthermore, the Jìn Shì (House of Jìn) arose from the barbarians (Yídí),
gained the realm through usurpation and rebellion (cuàn nì).
Gāozǔ (Shì Jìngtáng) treated Yēlǜ Déguāng as his father,
and Chū Dì (Shì Chóngguì), regarding Déguāng, treated him as a grandfather and called himself a grandson.
Yet, regarding his biological father (suǒ shēng fù), he referred to him as a minister and named him.
How can one judge this by human principle (rén lǐ)!
Han Family Records, Biography Six: Empress Lǐ
Empress Lǐ (Lǐ Shì), the Empress of Gāozǔ (Liú Zhīyuǎn),
was a native of Jìnyáng.
Her father was a farmer.
When Gāozǔ was young and serving as a soldier (jūn zú),
he pastured horses in Jìnyáng.
He entered her house at night and abducted her.
After Gāozǔ achieved prominence,
she was enfeoffed as the Lady of Wèiguó.
She gave birth to Yǐndì (Liú Chéngyòu).
In the fourth year of Kāiyùn (947 CE),
Gāozǔ raised troops in Tàiyuán.
When rewarding the soldiers (jūn shì),
the treasury stores (táng cáng) were insufficient.
He wanted to levy taxes on the people.
The Empress (Hòu) remonstrated, saying:
"We are currently beginning this enterprise,
proclaiming ourselves a righteous army (yì bīng).
If the people have not yet received kindness (huì) but we first seize their wealth,
this is probably not the intention of the new Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) in saving the people.
All that the Inner Palace (hòu gōng) possesses,
I request that it all be released.
Even if it is insufficient,
the soldiers (shì) will not bear resentment."
Gāozǔ changed his demeanor and apologized to her.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress (Huánghòu).
When Gāozǔ died,
Yǐndì (Liú Chéngyòu) conferred upon her the title of Grand Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
The Emperor was young.
He often played games within the palace with petty men like Guō Yǔnmíng, Hòu Zàn, and Lǐ Yè.
The Empress Dowager frequently criticized him sternly.
The Emperor said:
"Regarding the affairs of the state,
there is the Imperial Court (cháo tíng) outside;
these are not matters that the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) should discuss."
When Zhāng Zhāo, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng), heard this,
he submitted a memorial advising the Emperor,
requesting:
"Draw near to teachers and mentors (shī fù),
invite and consult with upright men (zhèng rén),
in order to open your intelligence."
The Emperor paid even less heed.
Later,
the Emperor eventually plotted with Yǔnmíng (Guō Yǔnmíng) and the others,
which ultimately led to his downfall.
Initially,
the Emperor plotted with Yǔnmíng (Guō Yǔnmíng) and others to execute Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào, and their associates.
Once the plan was settled,
he entered the palace to inform the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihòu).
The Grand Empress Dowager said:
"This is a great affair;
you should discuss it with the Chancellor (Zǎixiàng)."
Lǐ Yè, who was nearby, countered:
"The Former Emperor (Xiān Huángdì) often said,
regarding major affairs of the court,
do not consult bookish scholars (shū shēng)."
The Grand Empress Dowager firmly believed this was unacceptable,
but the Emperor brushed his sleeves and departed,
saying:
"Why must I seek counsel within the women's quarters (guī mén)!"
After Bīn (Yáng Bīn) and the others were killed,
Zhōu Tàizǔ (Guō Wēi) raised troops and marched toward the capital (Jīngshī).
When Mùróng Yànchāo was defeated at Liú Zǐ Pī,
the Emperor wished to go out himself to oversee the troops.
The Grand Empress Dowager stopped him, saying:
"Guō Wēi was originally one of our household members.
If he were not in dire peril and doubt,
how would he consent to do this?
If we now restrain the troops and make no movement,
and send an imperial decree to placate Wēi (Guō Wēi),
Wēi will certainly have something to say.
Then the relationship between sovereign and minister (jūn chén zhī jì)
might perhaps still be preserved."
The Emperor did not follow this advice and went out,
thus encountering disaster.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ (Guō Wēi) entered the capital (Jīngshī),
all his actions were conducted under the proclamation (gào) of the Grand Empress Dowager.
Shortly thereafter, there was discussion about establishing Xiāngyīn Gōng Yūn (Liú Yūn) as the Son of Heaven.
Before Yūn arrived,
Tàizǔ (Guō Wēi) invited the Grand Empress Dowager to oversee the court (lín cháo).
Soon after, Tàizǔ marched out to campaign against the Qìdān.
The soldiers surrounded him and brought him back [to assume the throne].
Tàizǔ requested to serve the Grand Empress Dowager as his mother.
The Grand Empress Dowager proclaimed in reply:
"The achievements and merit of the Court Attendant (Shì Zhōng, i.e., Guō Wēi) are exalted and lofty,
his virtuous reputation is widely known.
He has eliminated calamity and rebellion,
bringing stability to the state and the household.
The songs of praise gravitate toward him,
the Mandate of Heaven (lì shù) belongs to him.
Therefore, the military and the people support and sustain him,
and the myriad millions share this joy.
This aged person (Lǎoshēn) has not yet finished her remaining years,
caught amidst these many troubles,
and relying only on my aging frailty,
I entrust myself to the beginning and the end [of this transition].
Having reviewed the document (jiān) that came,
I see that I am treated like a mother.
I am moved, acknowledging your profound intent,
and tears flow horizontally."
Thereupon, the Empress Dowager was moved to Tàipíng Gōng,
and the honorable title Zhāoshèng Huáng Tàihòu was conferred upon her.
She died in the spring of the first year of Xiǎndé (954 CE).
Yǐndì (Liú Chéngyòu):
Both the Old History (jiù shǐ) and the Veritable Records (shí lù) state that he had no Empress (Huánghòu).
The Emperor reigned for three years and died,
at the age of twenty.
Therefore, he never established an Empress.
Gāozǔ's Two Younger Brothers (Chóng, Xìn) and Gāozǔ's Three Sons (Chéngxùn, Chéngyòu, Chéngxūn)
Gāozǔ (Liú Zhīyuǎn) had two younger brothers and three sons: The brothers were named Chóng (Liú Chóng) and Xìn (Liú Xìn).
The sons were named Chéngxùn, Chéngyòu, and Chéngxūn.
Chóng's son was named Yūn (Liú Yūn).
Gāozǔ loved him,
treating him as his own son.
In the first year of Qiányòu (948 CE),
Yūn was appointed Jìedùshǐ (Military Governor) of Xúzhōu.
Chéngxùn died early,
and was posthumously titled Prince of Wèi (Wèi Wáng).
Chéngyòu was next established [as successor],
who is called Yǐndì.
Chéngxūn was made the Prefect (Yǐn) of Kāifēng.
Zhōu Tàizǔ had already defeated the Hàn army at the northern suburbs,
Emperor Yǐn was assassinated.
Tàizǔ entered the capital,
thinking that the Hàn great ministers would surely mutually recommend and support him,
but when he met the Chancellor Féng Dào and others,
Dào showed no intention of doing so.
Tàizǔ had no choice;
upon seeing Dào, he still bowed down.
Dào received Tàizǔ’s bow as if it were peacetime,
and slowly consoled him, saying:
“Your Excellency’s journey must have been arduous!”
Tàizǔ’s spirits and countenance were both disheartened.
He realized that the Hàn officials did not yet have the intention of supporting him,
and it was difficult to establish himself unilaterally.
Therefore, he reported to the Hàn Grand Empress Dowager, asking her to select and establish a Hàn successor.
Among the imperial clan members present were four individuals, including Chóng, the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Hédōng.
Then they drafted an edict for the Grand Empress Dowager, which read:
“Chóng, the Military Commissioner of Hédōng,
Xìn, the Military Commissioner of Xǔzhōu,
are both younger brothers of Gāozǔ.
Yūn, the Military Commissioner of Xúzhōu,
and Chéngxūn, the Prefect of Kāifēng,
are both sons of Gāozǔ.
Let the civil and military officials, the hundred dignitaries,
select a successor sovereign to inherit the heavenly mandate.”
Thereupon, Zhōu Tàizǔ and Wáng Jùn entered to see the Grand Empress Dowager,
and said:
“Chéngxūn, the Prefect of Kāifēng,
is the son of Emperor Gāozǔ,
and ought to be established.”
The Grand Empress Dowager believed that Chéngxūn had been ill for a long time,
and was unfit to be the successor.
Tàizǔ and the assembled ministers requested to see Chéngxūn to observe his condition.
The Grand Empress Dowager ordered that Chéngxūn be carried out on a bed to meet the ministers.
The ministers observed him, and it was indeed true,
so they jointly submitted a memorial, saying:
“Yūn, the Military Commissioner of Xúzhōu,
was beloved by Gāozǔ,
who adopted him as a son.
He ought to be established as the successor.”
Thereupon, the Grand Preceptor Féng Dào was dispatched to lead the ministers to welcome Yūn.
Dào surmised that Zhōu Tàizǔ's true intention was not centered on Yūn.
He said to Tàizǔ:
“Is this action of Your Excellency truly sincere?”
Tàizǔ pointed to Heaven and swore an oath.
After Dào had departed,
he said to others:
“I have never in my life spoken falsely to people,
but now I have spoken falsely!”
Dào met Yūn,
and conveyed the Grand Empress Dowager's intention to summon him.
When Yūn traveled until he reached Sòngzhōu,
Tàizǔ, having been coerced by the soldiers at Chánzhōu, was escorted back to the capital.
Wáng Jùn worried that Yūn's attendants might cause trouble,
so he sent Guō Chóng, the Commander of the Palace Cavalry, with seven hundred horsemen to guard Yūn.
When Chóng arrived at Sòngzhōu,
Yūn ascended a tower and asked Chóng the reason for his arrival.
Chóng replied:
“There was a military mutiny at Chánzhōu.
Fearing that you might not be aware of it,
I was sent to protect you.
There is no ill intent.”
Yūn summoned Chóng,
but Chóng dared not advance.
Féng Dào came out and spoke with Chóng.
Only then did Chóng ascend the tower to see Yūn.
Soon afterward, he seized the troops serving under Yūn.
Tàizǔ sent a letter summoning Dào to return first,
leaving his deputies Zhào Shàngjiāo and Wáng Dù to escort Yūn to pay respects to the Grand Empress Dowager.
Dào thus returned first.
Yūn said to Dào:
“When I came here,
what I relied upon was Your Excellency, the elder chancellor of thirty years.
That is why I had no doubt.”
Dào remained silent.
Jǐa Zhèng and others, Yūn's guest generals, repeatedly eyed Dào,
intending to harm him.
Yūn said:
“Do not be hasty.
How could this matter stem from His Excellency?”
After Dào had left,
Guō Chóng imprisoned Yūn in an outer residence,
and killed Jǐa Zhèng, the Administrator Dǒng Yì, the Palace Military Inspector Liú Fú, and the Clerk Xià Zhāodù, among others.
Tàizǔ had already assumed the regency.
The Grand Empress Dowager then issued an edict, saying:
“Recently, Guō Wēi, the Commissioner of Military Affairs,
intended to stabilize the imperial ancestral shrine,
and proposed establishing a senior sovereign.
Since Yūn, the Military Commissioner of Xúzhōu, is a close relative of Gāozǔ,
he was established as the Hàn successor,
and summoned from his frontier command to the capital.
Although the imperial decree had been issued,
the sentiment of the army was not supportive.
Heaven’s Way lies to the North,
the people’s hearts did not incline to the East.
Since this is the initial period of changing the succession,
let him receive the mandate of being assigned a fiefdom.
Yūn shall be demoted to receive the titles of Minister who Establishes a Government (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
Acting Grand Preceptor, and Supreme Pillar of the State (Shàng Zhùguó),
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Xiāngyīn.”
Yūn died while imprisoned.
Initially,
when Yūn entered (the capital) from Xúzhōu,
he left Gǒng Tíngměi, the Deputy Commander, and Yáng Wēn, the Training Commissioner, to guard Xúzhōu.
When Tíngměi and the others heard that Yūn was not established,
they sealed the city gates and resisted the command.
Tàizǔ appointed Wáng Yànchāo as Military Commissioner of Xúzhōu,
and issued an imperial decree persuading Tíngměi and the others, offering them the post of Prefect (Cìshǐ),
and also decreed that Yūn pardon Tíngměi and the others.
In the third month of Guǎngshùn First Year,
Yànchāo conquered Xúzhōu,
and Tíngměi and the others were all killed.
Chéngxūn,
died of illness in Guǎngshùn First Year,
and was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Chén.
Alas!
I mourn the affair of the Duke of Xiāngyīn, Yūn,
and also praise the actions of Tíngměi and Yáng Wēn.
Yūn was neither the primary son nor the eldest son of Hàn,
but merely because the Zhōu clan was transferring the state,
they feared the world and found it difficult (to usurp immediately),
and thus they used Yūn as a pretext to watch for an opportunity.
At that time,
everyone under Heaven knew that Yūn would certainly not be established,
Yet Tíngměi and Wēn earnestly guarded the isolated city for Yūn and died doing so.
Their record, from beginning to end,
how is it inferior to that of a scholar who dies for loyalty!
However, when I examined the verifiable records,
the manner of these two men’s deaths is unclear.
The deeds of these two men,
while known to be unsuccessful,
what is valued is their death.
But the historians did not record it clearly;
we do not know how they died.
When Wáng Yànchāo was attacking Xúzhōu,
Zhōu once sent someone to recruit Tíngměi and the others.
I obtained four imperial edicts regarding this.
All of them stated that Tíngměi and the others had previously submitted their surrender to Zhōu,
but later feared punishment and rebelled again.
However, the original petition of surrender from Tíngměi and the others is also not seen.
These things are all unknowable.
The omissions in historical writing,
how can one not be cautious!
If one is suspicious, and transmits it as suspicious,
then what is certain will be believed.
I certainly praise the loyalty of these two men and mourn their resolution,
but for them not to be included among the scholars who died for loyalty,
is a pity!
Cài Wáng Xìn
Cài Wáng Xìn,
was a younger paternal cousin of Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ commanded at Tàiyuán,
he made Xìn the Commander-in-Chief of the Xīngjié Army, holding the title of Military Commissioner of the Yìchéng Army.
He was later transferred to govern Xǔzhōu.
When Gāozǔ became gravely ill,
and Emperor Yǐn was due to be established as successor,
Yáng Bīn and others received the dying injunction,
and did not want Xìn to be in the capital.
They therefore dispatched Xìn to his command post.
Xìn left weeping.
Wherever Xìn went, he defiled (his position) with greed,
and loved to carry out massacres.
If a soldier violated the law,
Xìn would summon his wife and children,
and in front of them, he would slice and dismember (the offender),
forcing the family members to eat the flesh.
With blood streaming everywhere before him,
Xìn would order music and drink wine as if nothing were happening.
When Yáng Bīn and the others died,
Xìn was greatly pleased.
He said to his subordinates:
“I used to think Heaven had no eyes,
and had caused me to be depressed here for three years!
The Sovereign above is isolated,
and almost fell into the hands of villains.
Gentlemen, you may encourage me with a cup of wine.”
Soon afterwards, when he heard that trouble had arisen,
Xìn was so worried he could not eat.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ's army mutinied at Chánzhōu,
Wáng Jùn sent Mǎ Duó, the former Prefect of Shēnzhōu, with troops to patrol and inspect Xǔzhōu.
Xìn then committed suicide.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed him as the Prince of Cài.
In this biography,
Yūn is placed before Xìn,
which merely facilitates the narration of the events.
Zhōu Tàizǔ's Family Biography Seventh: Empress Chái.
Cài Wáng Xìn
was Gāo Zǔ's paternal cousin.
When Gāo Zǔ garrisoned Tàiyuán,
he appointed Xìn as Commander-in-Chief of the Xīngjié Army and Military Governor of Yìchéng Command,
then transferred him to command Xǔzhōu.
When Gāo Zǔ fell ill,
and Yǐn Dì was to be established as heir,
Yáng Bīn and others, who had received the dying command,
did not want Xìn to be in the capital.
So they sent Xìn to his post.
Xìn wept and departed.
Wherever Xìn went, he was greedy for bribes
and fond of killing.
When a soldier committed an offense,
Xìn would summon his wife and children,
and in front of them, he would disembowel, carve, and dismember the offender,
forcing them to eat his flesh.
Blood would flow abundantly before him,
while Xìn would command music and drink wine as if nothing was amiss.
When Yáng Bīn and the others died,
Xìn was greatly pleased.
He said to his subordinates:
"I once thought that Heaven had no eyes,
and it has kept me here in melancholy for three years!
The emperor is isolated
and almost fell into the hands of bandits.
Gentlemen, you may encourage me with a cup!"
After a while, hearing that troubles had broken out,
Xìn was too worried to eat.
When Zhōu Tài Zǔ's army mutinied at Chánzhōu,
Wáng Jùn sent former Shēnzhōu Prefect Mǎ Duó with troops to patrol and inspect Xǔzhōu.
Xìn then committed suicide.
When Zhōu Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed him as Cài Wáng.
The biography
places Yūn before Xìn;
this is merely for convenience in narrating events.
Zhōu Tài Zǔ's Family Biographies, Seventh, Empress Chái
Tài Zǔ had one empress and three consorts.
Empress Shèngmù Chái Shì
was from Yáoshān, Xíngzhōu.
She was from the same village as Tài Zǔ,
and thus returned to him.
When Tài Zǔ was humble,
he was fond of drinking, gambling, and acting as a knight-errant,
disregarding minor conduct.
The empress often advised him to stop.
Tài Zǔ's appearance was extraordinary and magnificent,
and the empress inwardly knew he was a distinguished person.
She served him with great prudence.
By the time Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
the empress had already passed away.
So he issued an edict:
"The late Lady Chái Shì
is posthumously honored as empress,
