with the posthumous title Shèngmù."
Consort Shū Yáng Shì
Consort Shū Yáng Shì
was from Zhēndìng, Zhènzhōu.
Her father, Hóngyù,
was the Junior Administrator of Zhēndìng.
As a child, the consort was chosen for her beauty and entered the palace of Zhào Wáng,
serving Wáng Róng.
When Róng was killed by Zhāng Wénlǐ,
Zhènzhōu was in chaos,
and the consort also became a refugee among the common people.
Later, she married Shí Guāngfǔ, a villager.
After several years,
Guāngfǔ died.
When Tài Zǔ's Lady Chái died,
he heard that the consort was beautiful and virtuous,
so he married her as his second wife.
Tài Zǔ was serving Hàn Gāo Zǔ in Tàiyuán at the time.
The consort died during the Tiānfú reign
and was buried in the near suburbs of Tàiyuán.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
in the ninth month of the first year of Guǎngshùn,
she was posthumously honored as Consort Shū.
He appointed the consort's younger brother, Tíngzhāng, as Right Fēilóng Envoy.
Tíngzhāng declined, saying:
"My father is old,
I wish to bestow it upon him."
Tài Zǔ said:
"I am thinking about it,
how could I forget your father!"
He immediately summoned Hóngyù.
Hóngyù was too old to travel,
so he was appointed Grand Master of Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon and Junior Administrator of Zhēndìng at his home.
When Tài Zǔ died,
he was buried in Sōnglíng.
The one empress and three consorts were all to be interred with him,
but Tàiyuán had not yet been conquered.
Shì Zōng ordered the officials to construct an empty tomb next to Sōnglíng to await them.
In the first year of Xiǎndé,
after Shì Zōng defeated Liú Mín at Gāopíng,
he then attacked Tàiyuán.
Tàiyuán closed its gates and was besieged,
so the consort's remains were moved and buried.
Consort Guì Zhāng Shì
Consort Guì Zhāng Shì
was from Zhēndìng, Zhènzhōu.
Her grandfather, Jì,
was the Judicial Commissioner of Chéngdé Army and Provisional Minister of War.
Her father, Tóngzhī,
served Zhào Wáng Wáng Róng as Counselor,
reaching the rank of Provisional Minister of Works.
When Róng died,
Zhènzhōu was in chaos.
Zhuāng Zōng sent Fú Cúnshěn of Yōuzhōu with troops to suppress Zhāng Wénlǐ.
His subordinate general, Wǔ Cóngjiàn, stayed at the consort's home
and saw that the consort was still young.
He pitied her,
and since Cóngjiàn's family was in Tàiyuán,
he took the consort back with him
to be his son's wife.
After a long time,
Tài Zǔ served Hàn Gāo Zǔ in Tàiyuán,
Lady Yáng died,
and Wǔ's son also died.
So he took the consort as his second wife.
When Tài Zǔ became noble,
she was repeatedly enfeoffed as Lady of Wú.
When Tài Zǔ entered the capital with his army,
Hàn sent Liú Zhū to slaughter his family,
and the consort and all her sons died.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
she was posthumously honored as Consort Guì.
Consort Dé Dǒng Shì (Sons Dǒng, Xìn; Nephews Shǒuyuàn, Fèngchāo, Xùn)
Consort Dé Dǒng Shì
was from Língshòu, Zhènzhōu.
Her grandfather, Wénguǎng,
was the Registrar of Shēnzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
Her father, Guāngsì,
was the Commandant of Zhāoqìng in Zhàozhōu.
As a child, the consort was intelligent and discerning.
As soon as she could speak,
she knew the musical scales upon hearing music.
At the age of seven,
Zhènzhōu was in chaos,
and her family lost her.
She was found by a staff officer from Lùzhōu,
who placed her in a basket and took her home.
The Lùzhou officer's wife had previously given birth to daughters
who did not survive.
She pitied the consort when she found her,
raised her as her own child,
loving her more than her biological children.
After five or six years,
the consort's family grieved and longed for her.
Her brother, Yǔ, searched for her among the people,
but no one knew her whereabouts.
The Lùzhōu officer served in the capital,
met Yǔ,
and happily returned her to him when she was thirteen years old.
Yǔ married her to Liú Jìnchāo, a villager.
Jìnchāo also served Jìn in an internal office.
When the Qìdān attacked the capital,
Jìnchāo died among the captives.
The consort lived as a widow in Luòyáng.
When Hàn Gāo Zǔ entered the capital from Tàiyuán,
Tài Zǔ followed.
Passing through Luòyáng,
he heard that the consort had virtuous conduct
and married her.
When Tài Zǔ established his state,
the central palace position was vacant,
so he appointed her as Consort Dé.
She died in the third year of Guǎngshùn
at the age of thirty-nine.
The consort had three elder brothers:
Yǔ reached the rank of Right Zànshàn Dàfū of the Crown Prince;
Xuánzhī and Zìmíng both reached the rank of Prefect.
Previously,
when the Emperor raised troops in Wèi,
Hàn sent troops to besiege the Emperor's residence.
At that time, Consort Guì Zhāng Shì and her sons Qīnggē, Yìgē,
and nephews Shǒuyún, Fèngchāo, Dìnggē
were all executed.
The mothers of Qīnggē and Yìgē
are unknown.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he decreed that his second son, Qīnggē, be posthumously appointed Grand Tutor
and granted the name Dǒng;
his third son, Yìgē, be posthumously appointed Minister of Works
and granted the name Xìn;
his imperial nephew, Shǒuyún, be posthumously appointed General of the Left Leader of the Army Guard.
As the sound "Yún" was close to "Róng,"
to avoid Shì Zōng's taboo,
his name was changed to Shǒuyuàn;
Fèngchāo was posthumously appointed General of the Left Jìanmén Guard;
Dìnggē was posthumously appointed General of the Left Qiānniú Guard
and granted the name Xùn.
Tàizǔ had one Empress and three Consorts.
Shèngmù Huánghòu, née Chái,
was a person from Yáoshān in Xíngzhōu.
She was from the same village as Tàizǔ,
and thus married him.
When Tàizǔ was still obscure,
he enjoyed drinking, gambling, and acting as a chivalrous man (rènxiá),
and was not restricted by minor conduct.
The Empress often admonished him to stop.
Tàizǔ’s appearance was extraordinary and imposing.
The Empress inwardly knew he was a noble person,
and served him with great deference.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
the Empress had already died beforehand.
He then issued an edict saying:
“The late Madame Chái
is posthumously titled Empress
with the posthumous name Shèngmù.”
Shū Fēi Yáng shì
Shū Fēi Yáng shì
was a person from Zhēndìng in Zhènzhōu.
Her father, Hóngyù,
was the Vice Magistrate (Shàoyǐn) of Zhēndìng.
When the Consort was young, she was selected for her beauty and entered the palace of the Prince of Zhào.
She served Wáng Róng.
When Róng was killed by Zhāng Wénlǐ,
Zhènzhōu fell into chaos,
and the Consort also wandered and lived among the common people.
Later, she married Shí Guāngfǔ, a man from the village.
After living together for several years,
Guāngfǔ died.
When Tàizǔ’s Madame Chái died,
he heard that the Consort was beautiful and virtuous,
and subsequently married her as his second wife (jìshì).
Tàizǔ was then serving Hàn Gāozǔ in Tàiyuán.
The Consort died during the Tiānfú period
and was buried in the nearby suburbs of Tàiyuán.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
in the ninth month of Guǎngshùn first year (951 CE),
she was posthumously titled Shū Fēi.
He appointed the Consort’s younger brother, Tíngzhāng, as Right Fēilóng Envoy.
Tíngzhāng declined, saying:
“My father is elderly.
I wish for this position to be conferred upon him.”
Tàizǔ said:
“I am currently considering that matter.
How could I forget your father!”
He immediately summoned Hóngyù.
Hóngyù was too old to travel,
so Tàizǔ sent an official to his home to appoint him as Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū and Vice Magistrate (Shàoyǐn) of Zhēndìng.
When Tàizǔ died
and was buried at Sōnglíng,
the one Empress and three Consorts were all supposed to be interred alongside him.
However, since Tàiyuán had not yet been subdued,
Shìzōng ordered the relevant department to construct an empty tomb beside Sōnglíng to wait.
In Xiǎndé first year (954 CE),
Shìzōng had already defeated Liú Mín at Gāopíng,
and subsequently attacked Tàiyuán.
While Tàiyuán was closed off and besieged,
he moved the Consort’s remains and buried them.
Guì Fēi Zhāng shì
Guì Fēi Zhāng shì
was a person from Zhēndìng in Zhènzhōu.
Her grandfather, Jì,
was the Advisor (Pànguān) to the Military Governor of Chéngdé Army and Provisional Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū).
Her father, Tóngzhī,
served the Prince of Zhào, Wáng Róng, as the Cīchéng Official,
and his office reached the rank of Provisional Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū).
When Róng died
and Zhènzhōu was in chaos,
Zhuāngzōng sent Fú Cúnshěn of Yōuzhōu with troops to punish Zhāng Wénlǐ.
The Deputy General Wǔ Cóngjiàn stayed at the Consort’s family home.
He saw that the Consort was still young
and pitied her.
Since Cóngjiàn’s family was in Tàiyuán,
he took the Consort back
to be his son's wife.
After a long time,
Tàizǔ served Hàn Gāozǔ in Tàiyuán.
When Madame Yáng died,
and the son of Wǔ shì also died,
Tàizǔ married the Consort as his second wife (jìshì).
As Tàizǔ rose in prominence,
she was repeatedly titled Madame of Wú State.
When Tàizǔ entered the capital with troops,
Hàn (the Han dynasty) sent Liú Zhū to execute her family.
The Consort and her various sons all died.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
she was posthumously titled Guì Fēi.
Dé Fēi Dǒng shì (Sons: Dòng, Xìn; Nephews: Shǒuyuàn, Fèngchāo, Xùn)
Dé Fēi Dǒng shì
was a person from Língshòu in Zhènzhōu.
Her grandfather, Wénguǎng,
was the Registrar and Staff Supervisor (Lùshì Cānjūn) of Shēnzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Her father, Guāngsì,
was the Sheriff (Wèi) of Zhāoqìng in Zhàozhōu.
The Consort was intelligent and perceptive when young.
As soon as she could speak,
upon hearing music, she understood its pitch and rhythm (lǜlǚ).
At the age of seven,
Zhènzhōu fell into chaos,
and her family lost track of her.
She was obtained by a Headquarters General (Yájiàng) from Lùzhōu,
who put her in a sack and took her home.
The wife of the Lù General had often given birth to daughters
who never survived.
When she obtained the Consort, she cherished her,
raising her as her own child,
even more so than her birth children.
After five or six years,
the Consort’s family lamented and searched for her.
Her elder brother, Yǔ, searched for her everywhere,
but did not know her location.
The Lù General served in the capital (Jīngshī).
He met Yǔ
and gladly returned her to him.
She was thirteen years old.
Yǔ married her to Liú Jìnchāo, a man from the village.
Jìnchāo also served the Jìn (Jin dynasty) as an official in the inner court.
When the Qìdān violated the capital,
Jìnchāo perished among the captives.
The Consort lived as a widow in Luòyáng.
When Hàn Gāozǔ entered the capital from Tàiyuán,
Tàizǔ accompanied him.
Passing through Luòyáng,
he heard that the Consort possessed virtuous conduct
and sought her hand in marriage.
When Tàizǔ established his state,
the central palace position (Empress) was vacant,
and she was subsequently titled Dé Fēi.
She died in Guǎngshùn third year (953 CE),
at the age of thirty-nine.
The Consort had three elder brothers: Yǔ reached the rank of Right Chancellor of the Heir Apparent;
Xuánzhī and Zìmíng both reached the rank of Prefect (Cìshǐ).
Initially,
when the Emperor raised troops at Wèi,
Hàn (the Han dynasty) used troops to surround the Emperor’s residence.
At that time, Guì Fēi Zhāng shì, along with her sons Qīnggē and Yìgē,
and his nephews Shǒuyún, Fèngchāo, and Dìnggē,
were all executed.
Regarding Qīnggē and Yìgē,
it is unknown who their mother was.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he issued an edict granting his deceased second son, Qīnggē, the title of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
and bestowed upon him the name Dòng;
his third son, Yìgē, was granted the title of Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
and bestowed upon him the name Xìn;
his imperial nephew Shǒuyún was granted the title of General of the Left Leader Guard,
but since the sound of Yún was close to Róng,
in order to observe the naming taboo for Shìzōng,
the name was changed to Shǒuyuàn;
Fèngchāo was granted the title of General of the Left Gate Guard;
Dìnggē was granted the title of General of the Left Qiānniú Guard,
and bestowed upon him the name Xùn.
On the day Guǐwèi in the fourth month of summer of Xiǎndé fourth year (957 CE), Shìzōng
issued an edict saying:
“Rites originate from human feelings,
and grace serves to mourn the departed.
Especially regarding those in the ranks of kinship,
feelings of sorrow and pity particularly arise.
The late Imperial younger brother Dòng, granted the title Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo),
and Xìn, granted the title Minister of Works (Sīkōng)—
Their splendid destinies had just begun,
but their great years were not attained.
That I was permitted to be the sole survivor
truly pains my heart.
Dòng shall be granted the title Grand Tutor (Tàifù)
and posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Tán;
Xìn (shall be granted the title) Minister of Education (Sītú),
and (posthumously enfeoffed as) the Prince of Shí.”
Another edict stated:

“The late Imperial cousins, Shǒuyuàn, granted the title General of the Left Leader Guard; Fèngchāo, granted the title General of the Left Gate Guard; and Xùn, granted the title General of the Left Qiānniú Guard, and others—
In the recent tumultuous era,
they did not enjoy long lives.
Every time I think of their innocence,
it is difficult to forget my grief.
Shǒuyuàn shall be granted the title Grand General of the Left Guard,
Fèngchāo (shall be granted the title) Grand General of the Right Guard,
and Xùn (shall be granted the title) Grand General of the Right Martial Guard.”
Biography Eight: Family of Zhōu Shìzōng: Chái Shǒulǐ
Zhōu Tàizǔ’s Shèngmù Huánghòu Chái shì
had no sons.
She adopted the son of her elder brother, Shǒulǐ, as her own son;
this was Shìzōng.
In the fourth year of Xiǎndé of Shìzōng, in the summer, fourth month, on the day Kuǐwèi,
an edict stated:
“Ritual arises from emotion,
and grace from grieving for the departed.
How much more so for those in the ranks of brothers,
upon whom profound sorrow falls.
Thus, the imperial younger brother, the posthumously granted Tàibǎo, Tóng
and the posthumously granted Sīkōng, Xìn,
whose grand fortunes were just beginning,
did not attain a great age.
This leaves me forever desolate,
and truly troubles my heart.
Tóng is to be posthumously granted Tàifù
and posthumously enfeoffed as Tán Wáng;
Xìn as Sītú
and Suī Wáng.”
Another edict stated:

Biographies of Liáng Ministers, Chapter Nine
Alas!
Méngzǐ (Mencius) said:
"In the Springs and Autumns there are no righteous wars."
I likewise say that during the Five Dynasties there were no complete ministers (i.e., those of perfect loyalty).
To say there were none,
does not mean literally not one person,
but rather that they were merely few.
I found three scholars who died for their integrity.
As for those who served no more than two dynasties,
they are grouped under their respective states,
forming the Biographies of Liáng, Táng, Jìn, Hàn, and Zhōu Ministers.
The rest, who served multiple dynasties,
and cannot be grouped under one state,
form the Miscellaneous Biographies (Zá Chuán).
Indeed, to be included in the Miscellaneous section
is truly a source of shame for a gentleman.
However, the ministers of a single dynasty are not necessarily all worthy of respect;
may readers examine their good and evil deeds carefully.
Jìng Xiáng
Jìng Xiáng, courtesy name Zǐzhèn,
was a native of Féngyì in Tóngzhōu.
He claimed to be a descendant of Huī, Prince of Píngyáng (Píngyáng Wáng Huī) of the Táng Dynasty.
In his youth, he loved learning
and excelled at writing documents and manifestos.
During the Qiánfú period, he failed the imperial examination (Jìnshì).
He then traveled to Dàliáng.
Wáng Fā, who was from the same neighborhood as Xiáng, served as the Assistant Observer (Guānchá Zhīshǐ) of Biànzhōu.
Xiáng subsequently went to rely on him.
After a long time,
Fā did not recommend or promote him.
Xiáng’s condition as a visitor became increasingly distressed.
He wrote petitions and messages for others,
circulating them among the army.
Tàizǔ (Zhū Wēn) was fundamentally illiterate.
Xiáng’s writings were all in colloquial and vernacular language.
Tàizǔ liked them
and said to Fā:
"I hear you have an old acquaintance;
bring him with you when you come."
Xiáng met Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ asked:
"I hear you read the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū).
What kind of events does the Chūnqiū record?"
Xiáng replied:
"Merely the affairs of contention and warfare among the feudal lords."
Tàizǔ said:
"Can its methods of warfare be used by me?"
Xiáng replied:
"Warfare
relies on responding to change and using surprise to achieve victory.
The Chūnqiū records ancient methods,
which cannot be applied today."
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased
and appointed him to a military position,
which was not to his liking.
Tàizǔ then made him Director of Post Stations (Guǎnyì Xúnguān).
When Tàizǔ fought the people of Cài on the outskirts of Biàn,
Xiáng often provided strategies and plans for Tàizǔ,
many of which proved accurate.
Tàizǔ was delighted,
regretting that he had met Xiáng so late,
and constantly consulted him on all activities.
Tàizǔ escorted Zhāozōng from Qí back to Cháng’ān.
Zhāozōng summoned Xiáng and Lǐ Zhèn, having them ascend the Yánxǐ Lóu (Tower of Prolonged Joy) to reward and comfort them.
Xiáng was appointed Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng).
Previously,
Tàizǔ often attended the emperor in the hall.
Zhāozōng intended for the Imperial Guards to capture him.
He pretended that his shoelace had come undone
and looked toward Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ knelt down and tied it.
However, none of the attendants dared to move.
Tàizǔ was drenched in sweat.
After this, he rarely requested an audience again.
Zhāozōng moved to Luòyáng
and held a banquet in the Chóngxūn Diàn Hall.
He rose halfway through the drinking
and sent someone to summon Tàizǔ into the inner palace hall,
intending to entrust him with something.
Tàizǔ became increasingly fearful
and declined, citing illness.
Zhāozōng said:
"If you do not wish to come,
then send Jìng Xiáng to come."
Tàizǔ quickly motioned for Xiáng to leave
and also pretended to be drunk and departed.
Tàizǔ had already defeated Zhào Kuāngníng,
capturing Jīng and Xiāng,
and then proceeded to attack Huáinán.
Xiáng strongly remonstrated,
arguing that newly victorious troops
should maintain a weighty posture to cultivate their prestige.
Tàizǔ did not listen.
When the troops exited Guāngzhōu,
they encountered torrential rain,
almost failing to advance.
They proceeded to attack Shòuzhōu,
but did not conquer it,
and suffered great losses.
Tàizǔ then felt great remorse and regret.
Upon returning, he became enraged and restless,
killing almost all of the Táng ministers.
Nevertheless, he increasingly considered Xiáng trustworthy.
In the usurpation and regicide of the Liáng (Hòu Liáng),
Xiáng’s strategies were numerous.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
because the Táng Dynasty’s Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Yuàn) typically used eunuchs,
he changed it to the Chóngzhèng Yuàn (Council for Esteeming Government),
appointing Xiáng as its commissioner (Shǐ).
He was promoted to Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū) and Grand Academician of the Jīnluán Diàn Hall.
Xiáng was a deep and reserved man possessing great strategy.
He followed Tàizǔ in military campaigns for more than thirty years,
and all matters, great and small, were connected to him.
Xiáng also devoted his heart and worked diligently,
staying awake day and night,
saying himself that only on horseback could he find rest.
However, Tàizǔ was harsh, violent, and difficult to approach.
If there was something inappropriate,
Xiáng never spoke of it overtly,
but subtly initiated the subject.
Tàizǔ would then understand the implication,
and often change his course accordingly.
Tàizǔ (太祖) defeated Xúzhōu (徐州),
obtaining the favored concubine, Lady Liú (劉氏), of Shí Pǔ (時溥).
He loved and favored her.
Lady Liú was formerly the wife of Shàng Ràng (尚讓).
Tàizǔ then gave her as a wife to Xiáng (翔).
Although Xiáng had achieved high status,
Lady Liú still served Tàizǔ,
entering and leaving his private chambers as usual.
Xiáng was rather troubled by this.
Lady Liú rebuked Xiáng, saying:
"Do you think that I lost my virtue to bandits?
Shàng Ràng
was the Prime Minister of the Huáng (黃) house;
Shí Pǔ
was a loyal minister of the state.
Given your family's standing,
you still disgrace me.
I request that we part ways from this point!"
Because of Tàizǔ,
Xiáng apologized and stopped her.
Lady Liú’s carriages and attire were extravagant and luxurious.
She established her own attendants and heralds.
She associated with the regional governors (fānzhèn).
Powerful and influential figures often attached themselves to her,
and the favor and trust given to her comments on affairs of state were no less than that given to Xiáng.
At that time, noble families
often imitated her.
After Tàizǔ collapsed (died),
Yǒuguī (友珪) ascended the throne.
Since Xiáng was the deceased emperor’s strategizing minister,
Yǒuguī feared that he would plot against him.
He did not want Xiáng to hold an internal court position.
He therefore appointed Lǐ Zhèn (李振) to replace Xiáng as the Administrator of the Affairs of State (Chóngzhèng Shǐ),
and appointed Xiáng as Deputy Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Xiáng, knowing that Yǒuguī feared him,
often claimed illness,
and never attended to official duties.
When the Last Emperor (Mòdì) ascended the throne,
Zhào Yán (趙巖) and others took charge of government,
frequently alienating the old ministers.
Xiáng became increasingly depressed and frustrated.
After that,
Liáng (梁) completely lost Hébĕi (河北),
and was locked in a standoff with Jìn (晉) at Yángliú (楊劉).
Xiáng said:
"In former times, half of Héshuò (河朔) was still ours.
With the martial prowess of the previous emperor,
and ministers who commanded fierce troops,
we still could not prevail against Jìn.
Now Jìn daily grows stronger,
and Liáng daily diminishes.
Your Majesty resides deep within the palace,
and those with whom you scheme
are either your close servants
or merely private relatives.
How can you hope to succeed?
I heard that when Jìn attacked Yángliú,
Lǐ Yàzǐ (李亞子) carried firewood and crossed the water,
leading the soldiers.
Your Majesty merely follows prescribed rules,
taking pleasure in refined scholarly behavior,
and you send Hè Guī (賀瓌) to be the general.
Is he sufficient to withstand their remaining sharp edges (forces)?
Although I am worn out,
I have received deep grace from the state.
Even if I lack ability,
I wish to be allowed to exert myself."
Yán and the others considered Xiáng's words to be expressions of resentment,
and consequently did not use him.
After that,
Wáng Yànzhāng (王彥章) was defeated at Zhōngdū (中都).
Mòdì was terrified,
and summoned Duàn Níng (段凝) from the riverbank.
At this time,
all of Liáng’s elite troops were in Níng’s army.
Níng had different intentions,
hesitating and not coming.
Mòdì urgently called for Xiáng and said:
"I usually ignored your words.
Now it is critical.
Do not hold it against me.
Please instruct me on where I should retreat?"
Xiáng replied:
"I followed the previous emperor for more than thirty years.
Although I am now a chief minister,
in reality I am just an old servant of the Zhū (朱) family,
serving Your Majesty as my young master.
With my feelings,
how dare I conceal anything?
When Your Majesty first employed Duàn Níng,
I already argued against it.
Now Níng is not coming,
and the enemy forces are pressing close.
If I try to plan for Your Majesty,
the petty men will slander me,
and my advice certainly won't be listened to.
I request to die first;
I cannot bear to witness the destruction of the imperial ancestral shrine!"
The sovereign and the minister faced each other and wept bitterly.
Xiáng and Lǐ Zhèn were both trusted by Tàizǔ.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) entered Biàn (汴),
an imperial edict pardoned the Liáng officials.
Lǐ Zhèn happily said to Xiáng:
"There is an edict clearing our names;
we are going to pay court to the new sovereign."
He invited Xiáng, wanting to go together to meet him.
Xiáng stopped overnight at Gāotóu Chēfāng (高頭車坊).
Just before dawn,
his attendants reported:
"Administrator Lǐ (Lǐ Gōng) has gone to court!"
Xiáng sighed, saying:
"Lǐ Zhèn wrongly presumes himself a true man!
What face do I have left to enter the Jiànguó Mén (建國門) of Liáng?"
Thereupon, he hanged himself and died.
Zhū Zhēn (朱珍) (Attached Biography of Lǐ Tángbīn [李唐賓])
Zhū Zhēn
was a man from Fēng (豐) in Xúzhōu.
In his youth, he and Páng Shīgǔ (龐師古) and others followed Tàizǔ of Liáng as bandits.
As a general,
Zhēn was skilled at managing armies and selecting officers.
When Tàizǔ first garrisoned Xuānwǔ (宣武),
Zhēn established the military system for Tàizǔ.
He was highly methodical in selecting commanders and training soldiers.
The troops Tàizǔ obtained, whether recruited by other generals or surrendered troops from elsewhere,
were all entrusted to Zhēn.
Zhēn selected more than fifty generals,
all of whom were capable.
In Liáng’s defeats of Huáng Cháo (黃巢), the breaking of Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權), and the eastward annexation of Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆),
Zhēn was never absent from the battles,
and his courage always surpassed the other generals.
Tàizǔ and the King of Jìn (Jìn Wáng) were pursuing Huáng Cháo eastward.
When they returned and passed through Biàn,
the King of Jìn was lodged at Shàngyuán Yì (上源驛).
Tàizǔ ordered Zhēn to attack him with troops that night.
The King of Jìn escaped,
and Zhēn killed all the soldiers under his command.
When the Yìchéng (義成) army mutinied
and expelled Ān Shīrú (安師儒),
Shīrú fled to Liáng.
Tàizǔ sent Zhēn with troops to hasten toward Huázhōu (滑州).
On the way, they encountered heavy snow.
Zhēn urged his troops to hasten rapidly.
Within one night, they arrived below the city,
and immediately scaled the city walls.
The Yìchéng army, thinking it was still snowing,
did not expect Liáng troops to arrive
and had not prepared,
so the city was taken.
Qín Zōngquán sent Lú Táng (盧瑭), Zhāng Zhì (張晊), and others to attack Liáng.
At this time, Liáng’s forces were still few,
and were repeatedly besieged by Zōngquán.
Tàizǔ therefore appointed Zhēn as the Prefect of Zīzhōu (淄州),
commissioning him to recruit soldiers in Zīqīng (淄青).
Zhēn's subordinate general, Zhāng Rén’yù (張仁遇), reported to Zhēn, saying:
"If anyone in the army violates an order,
I request to execute them first and report afterward."
Zhēn said:
"Does a subordinate general intend to monopolize execution power?"
He immediately executed Rén'yù and displayed the body to the army.
The army was all deeply moved and pleased.
Zhēn returned with more than ten thousand recruited soldiers.
Tàizǔ was overjoyed and said:
"The bandits are at our suburban borders.
If they trample our wheat,
what shall we do!
Now that Zhēn has arrived,
our affairs are settled!
Moreover, the bandits are currently resting their troops and bolstering their courage,
assuming our troops are few
and unaware that Zhēn has arrived.
They believe we will do no more than hold fast defensively.
We should strike them unexpectedly."
Tàizǔ then sent out troops and defeated Zhì and the others.
Zōngquán was consequently defeated and perished,
and the military might of Liáng greatly increased,
all thanks to obtaining Zhēn's soldiers.
Zhēn followed Tàizǔ in attacking Zhū Xuān (朱宣),
capturing Cáozhōu (曹州),
and seizing its Prefect, Qiū Hónglǐ (丘弘禮).
He also captured Púzhōu (濮州).
The Prefect, Zhū Yù (朱裕), fled to Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
Tàizǔ then returned to Biàn,
leaving Zhēn to attack Yùnzhōu.
When Zhēn was twenty lǐ away from Yùn,
he sent elite soldiers to provoke them,
but the people of Yùn did not come out.
Zhū Yù deceitfully wrote a letter of surrender,
secretly sending someone to summon Zhēn,
and promising to open the gates to provide internal assistance.
Zhēn believed him,
and at night led his troops to knock on the Yùn city gate.
Zhū Yù ascended the battlements,
opened the gate, and allowed Zhēn’s army in.
When Zhēn’s army had already entered the barbican (wèngchéng), the portcullis dropped.
The people of Yùn threw large stones down from the city walls.
Zhēn’s soldiers all died inside the barbican.
Zhēn barely escaped with his life, Tàizǔ did not blame him for this.
Wèibó Jūn rebelled,
and imprisoned Yuè Yànzhēn.
Tàizǔ dispatched Zhēn to rescue Wèi.
Zhēn defeated Líyáng, Línhé, and Lǐ Gù,
and separately sent Niè Jīn, Fàn Jūshí, and others to raid Chánzhōu,
killing two thousand soldiers of the Wèi Bàozǐ Jūn at Línhuáng.
Zhēn's might shook Héshuò.
The Wèi people killed Yànzhēn,
and Zhēn then returned.
Liáng attacked Xúzhōu,
sending Zhēn first to attack and capture Féng Xiàn.
He also defeated Shí Pǔ at Wúkāng
and garrisoned Xiāoxiàn together with Lǐ Tángbīn and others.
Tángbīn
was a person from Shǎn.
Initially, he was a subordinate general under Shàng Ràng.
He fought Tàizǔ at Wèishì Mén.
He was defeated by Tàizǔ,
and Tángbīn then surrendered to Liáng.
As the Liáng army attacked and plundered everywhere,
Tángbīn was often together with Zhēn.
His prestige and fame were roughly equal to Zhēn's,
but his valor surpassed him.
Whenever Zhēn fought and slightly retreated,
Tángbīn would assist him, resulting in a great victory.
Zhēn once secretly brought his family into the camp.
Tàizǔ suspected Zhēn harbored treacherous designs
and sent Tángbīn to spy and observe him.
Zhēn and Tángbīn did not get along.
Tángbīn could not bear it
and fled back to Xuānwǔ by night.
Zhēn pursued him alone on horseback
and they exchanged accusations before Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ valued the talent of both of them
and reconciled the dispute.
Zhēn was garrisoned at Xiāoxiàn.
Hearing that Tàizǔ was about to arrive,
he ordered the army to prepare lodging to wait.
Yán Jiāo, a subordinate general of Tángbīn, missed the deadline for preparation.
A military clerk pressed him,
and Jiāo complained to Tángbīn.
Tángbīn relayed the complaint to Zhēn.
Zhēn became furious,
drew his sword, and stood up.
Tángbīn smoothed his robes and approached Zhēn.
Zhēn immediately executed him
and sent an envoy to report that Tángbīn had rebelled.
The envoy arrived in Liáng in the morning.
Jìng Xiáng feared Tàizǔ's sudden wrath would be unpredictable,
so he concealed the envoy,
waiting until night to present him,
saying that although something had happened,
they must wait until the next morning,
hoping to slightly delay the matter and plan accordingly.
When evening came,
he then led Zhēn's envoy in for an audience.
Tàizǔ was greatly startled,
but since it was already night,
he could not immediately take action.
Xiáng then calmly laid out a strategy for Tàizǔ.
The next day,
[Tàizǔ] pretended to arrest Tángbīn's wife and children and throw them into prison.
Then he proceeded to Zhēn's army.
One *shè* away from Xiāo,
Zhēn came out to welcome and greet him.
Tàizǔ ordered the guards to seize him.
Generals including Huò Cún, more than ten men, kowtowed to plead for Zhēn's life.
Tàizǔ grew greatly enraged,
lifted his camp stool and hurled it at them, saying:
"When Zhēn killed Tángbīn,
why did none of you save him?!"
Cún and the others withdrew.
Zhēn was then forced to hang himself.
Páng Shīgǔ
Páng Shīgǔ,
was a person from Nánhuá in Cáozhōu.
His initial name was Cóng.
When Liáng Tàizǔ governed Xuānwǔ,
he first acquired five hundred horses for cavalry.
He then made Shīgǔ their commander.
[Shīgǔ] followed [him] in defeating Huáng Cháo and Qín Zōngquán,
all achieving merit.
Tàizǔ attacked Shí Pǔ but had not yet subdued him.
He left troops assigned to Shīgǔ to hold the position.
Shīgǔ captured Sùqiān
and advanced to garrison Lǚliáng.
Pǔ led twenty thousand troops out to fight.
Shīgǔ defeated him,
beheading two thousand men.
Sūn Rú drove out Yáng Xíngmì
and took Yángzhōu.
Huáinán fell into great chaos.
Tàizǔ dispatched Shīgǔ to cross the Huai River and attack Rú.
He was defeated by Rú.
At this time,
Zhū Zhēn and Lǐ Tángbīn were already dead,
and Shīgǔ and Huò Cún divided command of their troops.
Chēn Wáng Yǒu Yù attacked Xúzhōu.
Zhū Jǐn led troops to rescue Shí Pǔ.
Yǒu Yù defeated Pǔ at Shífó Shān.
Jǐn gathered the remaining troops and departed.
Tàizǔ believed Yǒu Yù failed to pursue [the enemy] when he could have,
and stripped him of his troops, assigning them to Shīgǔ.
Shīgǔ attacked and captured Xúzhōu,
executing Pǔ.
Tàizǔ memorialized [the court] to appoint Shīgǔ as the Resident Administrator (*Liúhòu*) of Xúzhōu.
The Liáng army attacked Yùnzhōu,
approaching the Jì Shuǐ.
Shīgǔ dismantled timber to build a bridge,
and crossed first at night with the central army.
Zhū Xuān fled to Zhōngdū,
where he was killed.
After Tàizǔ subdued Yǎn and Yùn,
he then sent Shīgǔ and Gě Cóngzhōu to attack Yáng Xíngmì in Huáinán.
Shīgǔ marched out via Qīngkǒu;
Cóngzhōu marched out via Ānfēng.
Shīgǔ had served Tàizǔ since the time he was humble.
He was extremely cautious as a person,
and never left [Tàizǔ's] immediate presence.
When he became a general leading troops,
he must receive the strategy before departing.
In the army, unless ordered by Tàizǔ,
he would not move rashly.
Shīgǔ set up camp at Qīngkǒu.
The terrain was low-lying.
Someone requested moving to higher ground to build a stockade.
Shīgǔ refused, citing that it was not Tàizǔ's order.
The Huai people diverted water to flood the area.
The person who had requested [the move] reported, saying:
"The Huai people have broken the river banks!
The upstream floodwaters are arriving!"
Shīgǔ believed this would panic the soldiers
and immediately executed him.
Soon after, the water arrived.
The troops could not fight,
and consequently, [Shīgǔ] was killed.
Alas!
The victory or defeat of war,
how can it be easily determined!
The Liáng army was the strongest in the world,
yet the Wú people were regarded as insignificant and weak.
However, Shīgǔ twice launched campaigns to attack Wú,
and twice was defeated and died.
Afterward,
Tàizǔ personally commanded a march out of Guāngshān,
attacking Shòuchūn.
However, he was also defeated.
Since Gāo Pián died,
the Táng had appointed Liáng to concurrently govern Huáinán.
Consequently, [Liáng] contended with Sūn and Yáng.
In the space of thirty years,
[Liáng] launched three campaigns and suffered three defeats.
That the supremely strong encountered the supremely weak and ended up like this—
this cannot be explained by reason.
Military strategy certainly includes situations where the few defeat the many, and the weak conquer the strong.
But how could Wú possibly have understood this?
Was it not merely that the opportunity presented itself to them?
Therefore it is said:
"Weapons are instruments of ill omen;
battle is a perilous affair."
How can one not be cautious!
Gě Cóngzhōu
Gě Cóngzhōu, courtesy name Tōngměi,
was a person from Zhēnchéng in Púzhōu.
In his youth, he followed Huáng Cháo.
After defeat, he surrendered to Liáng.
[He] followed Tàizǔ in attacking Càizhōu.
Tàizǔ fell from his horse.
Cóngzhōu helped Tàizǔ remount.
While fighting the enemy on foot, [he] suffered a face wound,
and his body sustained several injuries.
Subordinate General Zhāng Yánshòu struck [the enemy] from the side,
and Cóngzhōu was able to depart together with Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ dismissed all the other generals,
using only Cóngzhōu and Yánshòu as major generals.
Qín Zōngquán plundered the lands of Yǐng and Bó.
When the Liáng forces fought at Jiāoyí,
Cóngzhōu captured one of their generals, Wáng Juān.
He followed Zhū Zhēn to gather troops in Zīqīng.
Whenever they met the eastern armies, they immediately fought.
Zhēn was able to return with his troops,
and Cóngzhōu's contribution was the greatest.
Zhāng Quányì attacked Lǐ Hǎnzhī at Héyáng.
Hǎnzhī fled to Jìn.
He summoned Jìn forces to attack Quányì.
Quányì begged for aid from Liáng.
Tàizǔ sent Cóngzhōu, Dīng Huì, and others to rescue him,
defeating the Jìn forces at the Yǎnhé.
In Lùzhōu, Féng Bà killed the Jìn defending general Lǐ Kègōng and surrendered to Liáng.
Tàizǔ sent Cóngzhōu to enter Lùzhōu.
Jìn forces attacked him.
Cóngzhōu could not defend it
and fled to Héyáng.
Tàizǔ attacked Wèi.
Cóngzhōu and Dīng Huì first captured Líyáng and Línhé,
meeting Tàizǔ at Nèihuáng,
and defeated the Wèi forces at Yǒngdìng Qiáo.
Following Dīng Huì, he attacked Sùzhōu.
They flooded the city with water,
and subsequently captured it.
Tàizǔ attacked Zhū Jǐn at Yǎnzhōu.
Having not yet taken it,
he left Cóngzhōu to surround it.
Jǐn kept the fortifications closed and did not come out.
Cóngzhōu falsely claimed that relief forces had arrived,
pretending to withdraw to Gāowú.
At midnight, he secretly returned beneath the city walls.
Jǐn believed that Cóngzhōu had already left,
and therefore sent troops out to clear the outer moat.
Cóngzhōu ambushed and attacked them,
killing over a thousand men.
Jìn attacked Wèi.
The Wèi people requested aid.
Tàizǔ sent Hóu Yán to rescue Wèi.
Yán built ramparts at the Huán Shuǐ.
Tàizǔ was angry that Yán did not go out to fight,
and sent Cóngzhōu to replace him.
When Cóngzhōu arrived at the army,
he further closed the ramparts and did not come out,
but dug three hidden gates and waited.
When the Jìn forces attacked,
Cóngzhōu led elite troops out from the hidden gates to strike,
defeating the Jìn King's army.
The Jìn King was furious,
and personally led the attack against Cóngzhōu.
Although Cóngzhōu was heavily defeated,
the Liáng forces captured his son Luòluò,
sent him to Wèi,
and executed him.
They then moved to attack Yùnzhōu,
capturing Zhū Xuān at Zhōngdū.
They also attacked Yǎnzhōu
and drove off Zhū Jǐn.
Tàizǔ memorialized Cóngzhōu as the Acting Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
Using the armies of Yǎn and Yùn, he attacked Huáinán.
He advanced through Ānfēng,
and was supposed to meet Páng Shīgǔ at Qīngkǒu.
Cóngzhōu marched until he reached Háozhōu.
Hearing that Shīgǔ had died,
he quickly returned.
When he reached Bēi Hé and was about to cross, the Huái forces pursued him.
Cóngzhōu was also heavily defeated.
At this time,
the Jìn forces emerged from Shāndōng to attack Xiāng and Wèi.
Tàizǔ sent Cóngzhōu to seize territory in Shāndōng.
He captured Míngzhōu
and executed its Inspector, Xíng Shànyì.
He also captured Xíngzhōu
and drove off its Inspector, Mǎ Shīsu.
He further captured Cízhōu
and killed its Inspector, Yuán Fèngtāo.
In five days, he captured three prefectures.
Tàizǔ then memorialized Cóngzhōu to concurrently serve as the Acting Governor of Xíngzhōu.
Liú Rén'gōng attacked Wèi.
He had already massacred Bèizhōu.
Luó Shàowēi requested aid from Liáng.
Cóngzhōu joined Tàizǔ to rescue Wèi
and entered Wèizhōu.
The Yān forces attacked Guǎntáo Gate.
Cóngzhōu led five hundred cavalry out to fight.
He said:
"With a great enemy right ahead,
how can we look back?"
He ordered the gates closed before engaging in battle.
He broke through eight of their stockades.
The Yān forces fled.
He pursued them to Línqīng,
herding them into the Yù Hé.
The number of those who drowned was extremely high.
Tàizǔ appointed Cóngzhōu as the Provisional Military Administrator of Xuānyì Command.
Tàizǔ sent Cóngzhōu to attack Liú Shǒuwén at Cāngzhōu,
appointing Jiǎng Huī to supervise his army.
Shǒuwén requested aid from his father, Rén'gōng.
Rén'gōng sent Yān forces to rescue him.
Huī spoke to the generals, saying:
"Our King appointed me to supervise the generals.
Now that the Yān forces have come,
we should not meet them in battle.
We should let them enter the city,
gather food from the granaries,
and then seize them after both sides are exhausted."
The generals largely agreed with this assessment.
Cóngzhōu angrily said:
"Authority over the army rests with the chief general!
How can the Military Supervisor speak in this way?
Moreover, Huī's words are merely conventional talk.
The critical moment for victory or defeat rests in my heart.
How could Huī possibly understand it?"
He then marshaled his troops and met Rén'gōng at Qiánníng,
fighting at Lǎobù Dī.
Rén'gōng was heavily defeated,
with more than thirty thousand enemy heads taken.
He captured over a hundred generals, including Mǎ Shènjiāo,
and three thousand horses.
At this time,
Shǒuwén also requested aid from Jìn.
Jìn attacked Xíng and Míng prefectures to distract him.
Cóngzhōu quickly returned
and defeated the Jìn forces at Qīngshān.
He subsequently followed Tàizǔ to attack Zhènzhōu.
Línchéng was captured.
Wáng Róng requested a treaty.
Tàizǔ memorialized Cóngzhōu as Military Commissioner of Tàiníng Command.
He followed Shì Shūcóng to attack Jìn's Tàiyuán,
but was unsuccessful.
The Liáng forces attacked Fèngxiáng to the west.
Wáng Shīfàn of Qīngzhōu sent his general Liú Hán to raid Yǎnzhōu.
Cóngzhōu's family members were captured by Hán,
who treated them kindly and did not kill them.
Tàizǔ returned from Fèngxiáng,
and then sent Cóngzhōu to attack Hán.
Cóngzhōu eventually convinced Hán to surrender.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Senior General of the Left Metropolitan Guard.
Due to illness, he retired from office,
but was appointed Senior General of the Right Guard,
residing at Yǎnshī.
When Mòdì ascended the throne,
he appointed him Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì Command and Prince of Chénliú,
drawing his salary while staying at home.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Commandant.
Huò Cún
Huò Cún,
was a native of Qǔzhōu, Míngzhōu.
When young, he followed Huáng Cháo.
When Cháo was defeated,
Cún then surrendered to Liáng.
Cún was a valiant and courageous general,
skilled in horsemanship and archery.
When Qín Zōngquán attacked Biàn,
Cún led three thousand men to break through Zhāng Ào's stockade at night.
He also used cavalry to defeat Qín Xián,
killing three thousand men,
and defeated Ào at Chìgāng.
Following Zhū Zhēn in raiding Zīqīng, and Páng Shīgǔ in attacking Shí Pǔ,
he achieved merit in all engagements.
Zhū Zhēn and Lǐ Tángbīn both died.
Therefore, Páng Shīgǔ replaced Zhēn, and Cún replaced Tángbīn to attack Pǔ.
They captured Dàngshān.
Cún captured fifty people, including his general Shí Jūnhé.
When Liáng attacked Sùzhōu,
Gě Cóngzhōu diverted water to flood it.
Dīng Huì and Cún fought beneath the city walls,
and subsequently took it.
Following the attack on Lùzhōu,
they encountered the Jìn people.
Fighting at Mǎláo Chuān,
when Cún advanced, he led the vanguard;
when he retreated, he formed the rearguard.
The Jìn people were repulsed.
He then attacked Wèi to the east,
taking Qímén
and killing three thousand men.
When Liáng gained Cáozhōu,
Tàizǔ made Cún the Inspector,
concurrently serving as Supreme Commander of All Forces.
Liáng attacked Yùnzhōu,
Zhū Jǐn came to the rescue.
Some of Liáng's commanders advised Tàizǔ to allow Jǐn to enter Yùn,
exhausting their supplies,
maintain a firm siege without fighting,
and thus both sides would be weakened.
Tàizǔ said:
"If Jǐn comes, he must come together with Shí Pǔ.
It is better to dispatch Cún to ambush them."
Cún hid troops in Xiāoxiàn.
Soon after, Jǐn and Pǔ indeed came out together at Mílí.
Cún launched the ambush and attacked them.
Subsequently, he defeated Jǐn and the others at Shífóshān.
Cún died after being struck by a stray arrow.
After Tàizǔ had ascended the throne,
he reviewed the cavalry at Fántái,
and looking at his generals, he said:
"If Huò Cún were still alive,
why would I labor to review them myself?
Gentlemen, do you ever think of him?"
On another day, he spoke similarly.
Zhāng Cúnjìng
Zhāng Cúnjìng was
a native of Qiáojùn.
He was inherently firm, upright, courageous, and daring.
When young, he served Liáng Tàizǔ as a commander,
excelling at producing brilliant strategies when in danger or distress.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī and the Jìn forces attacked Zhāng Quányì at Héyáng.
Tàizǔ dispatched Cúnjìng along with Dīng Huì and others to rescue him,
and Hǎnzhī lifted the siege and departed.
Tàizǔ appointed Cúnjìng as Dū Yúhòu of all armies.
When Tàizǔ attacked Xú and Yǎn,
he made Cúnjìng the Xíngyíng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
He followed Gě Cóngzhōu to attack Cāngzhōu
and defeated Líu Rónggōng at Lǎobǔdī.
Returning, he attacked Wáng Róng at Zhènzhōu,
entering his city
and seizing ten thousand head of horses and cattle.
He was promoted to Cìshǐ of Sòngzhōu.
He later followed the commanders to attack Yōuzhōu.
Cúnjìng captured the four prefectures of Yíng, Mò, Qí, and Jǐng.
When Liáng attacked Dìngzhōu,
he fought Wáng Chǔzhí at Huáidéyì,
utterly defeating him,
with corpses piled up over ten *lǐ*.
After Liáng had subdued Zhèn and Dìng,
they sent Cúnjìng to attack Wáng Kē at Hézhōng.
Cúnjìng marched out of Hánshān
and captured Jìn and Jiàng prefectures.
Kē surrendered to Liáng.
Tàizǔ memorialized that Cúnjìng be made Hùguójūn Líuhòu,
then transferred him back to Cìshǐ of Sòngzhōu.
Before reaching the post,
he died at Hézhōng.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàifù.
Cúnjìng’s sons were Rén Yǐng and Rén Yuàn.
Rén Yuàn was known for his filial conduct.
After Cúnjìng died,
he served his elder brother Rén Yǐng:
he would certainly inform him before leaving,
and report back upon returning,
following the rites due to a father.
Rén Yuàn understood laws and regulations.
He served Liáng, Táng, and Jìn,
always holding the position of Dàlǐ Qīng.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title of Mìshūjiān.
Fú Dàozhāo
Fú Dàozhāo was
a native of Càizhōu.
He served Qín Zōngquán as a cavalry commander.
When Zōngquán was defeated,
Dàozhāo drifted without a place to settle.
Later, he attached himself to Lǐ Màozhēn of Fèngxiáng.
Màozhēn loved him
and adopted him as a son,
naming him Jìyuǎn.
When Liáng attacked Màozhēn,
Dàozhāo fought the Liáng troops.
He was repeatedly defeated,
and subsequently surrendered to Liáng.
Tàizǔ memorialized Dàozhāo as Jié Dùshǐ of Qínzhōu,
but due to the turmoil, he did not take up the post.
When Tàizǔ became Marshal,
and first established his administration,
Lǐ Zhōu Yí surrendered with Fūzhōu,
and was made Zuǒ Sīmǎ.
It was difficult to select the right person for Yòu Sīmǎ.
When Dàozhāo was found,
he was immediately appointed to the role.
Luó Shàowēi was planning to execute his elite guard troops (Yá Bīng),
but feared the strength of the Wèi troops
and did not dare to proceed,
so he sought aid from Liáng.
Tàizǔ then mobilized all the Wèi troops and sent them to attack Yān,
and dispatched Mǎ Sìxūn to help Shàowēi execute the Yá Bīng.
After the Yá Bīng were executed,
the Wèi troops who were deployed outside all became rebellious.
The Wèi commanders Zuǒ Xíngqiān occupied Lìtíng, and Shǐ Rén Yù occupied Gāotáng in rebellion.
Dàozhāo and others followed Tàizǔ and completely defeated them.
As a commander, Dàozhāo
was brave in attacking the enemy but lacked thorough planning.
In every battle, he was the first to attack,
often resulting in defeat,
but Zhōu Yí and others would follow up and secure the victory.
In the first year of Kāipíng, he, along with Kāng Huái Yīng and others, attacked Lùzhōu.
They constructed supporting ramparts and a segmented trench (Yóuyántiàn) to besiege it.
After more than a year, they could not take it.
The Jìn troops attacked and broke through the supporting ramparts,
and Dàozhāo died in battle.
Líu Hàn
Líu Hàn was
a native of Kāifēng.
He was intelligent, quick-witted, and possessed imposing ceremonial dignity.
He excelled at protocol and ushering (*bīnzàn*).
When Tàizǔ first took control of Xuānwǔ,
he appointed him as Kè Jiàng,
sending him to recruit soldiers in Zīqīng alongside Zhū Zhēn.
When Tàizǔ attacked Zhènzhōu in the north
and made peace with Wáng Róng,
he sent Hàn to meet Róng.
Róng's army did not yet know Liáng’s intentions
and was enforcing strict military discipline.
Hàn rode a single horse into the city
and conveyed Tàizǔ’s intentions to Róng.
Róng then accepted the command.
When the Liáng troops attacked Dìngzhōu
and Wáng Chǔzhí surrendered,
Hàn again entered the city alone on horseback to reassure the populace.
When Tàizǔ besieged Fèngxiáng,
he sent Hàn to meet Lǐ Màozhēn to discuss matters.
Emperor Táng Zhāozōng summoned him
and asked about affairs in the Liáng army.
He spoke in a manner that pleased the emperor's will,
and was granted a brocade robe.
He was appointed Cìshǐ of Dēngzhōu
and bestowed the title
"Yíngluán Yìyǒng Gōngchén."
When the Liáng troops attacked Huáinán,
Hàn was sent ahead to Huáikǒu
to build a pontoon bridge below Mǎtóu to allow the Liáng troops to cross.
When Tàizǔ marched out of Guāngshān to attack Shòuzhōu,
Hàn was again tasked with building a pontoon bridge north of the Huái River
to allow the returning army to cross.
He was appointed Cìshǐ of Sòngzhōu.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Tiānwǔ Zhǐhuīshǐ, Yuáncóng Qīnjūn Dū Yúhòu, and Zuǒ Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn,
and then sent out as Hùguójūn Líuhòu.
Líu Zhījùn of Tóngzhōu rebelled.
He used bribes to entice Hàn's subordinate officials,
seized Hàn, and departed.
Zhījùn shackled him
and sent him to Lǐ Màozhēn,
who executed him.
Tàizǔ mourned him
and posthumously granted Hàn the title of Tàifù.
Kòu Yànqīng
Kòu Yànqīng, courtesy name Jùnchén,
was a native of Kāifēng.
For generations, his family had served the Xuānwǔ military command as Yá Jiàng.
When Tàizǔ first took control of the command,
he made him Tōngyǐn Guān,
and he was successively promoted to Yòu Chángzhí Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ,
also holding the post of Cìshǐ of Míngzhōu.
When Luó Shàowēi was about to execute his guard army (Yájūn),
Tàizǔ sent Yànqīng to Wèi to plan the matter.
Yànqīng secretly planned the strategy for Shàowēi,
and subsequently the entire guard army was executed.
Yànqīng was eight *chǐ* tall,
with a high nose and square face,
and his voice resonated like a bell.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
fond of books and history,
and excellent at anticipating Tàizǔ’s intentions.
All his actions were in accordance with the emperor's will.
Tàizǔ once said:
"Jìng Xiáng, Líu Hàn, and Kòu Yànqīng were all born for me by Heaven."
Such was his love for them.
He gifted him the beloved horse he rode,
"Yī Zhàng Wū" (One Zhang Black).
When Tàizǔ besieged Fèngxiáng,
he made Yànqīng the Dū Páizhèn Shǐ.
Yànqīng rode Wū as he charged and assaulted the front lines.
Tàizǔ looked at him and said:
"He is truly a divine general!"
Initially,
Tàizǔ planned with Cuī Yìn,
wishing to move the capital to Luòyáng,
but Zhāozōng did not permit it.
Afterward, Zhāozōng fled to Fèngxiáng,
Tàizǔ surrounded it with troops,
and when Zhāozōng finally departed,
the following year,
Tàizǔ reached Hézhōng with troops,
and dispatched Yànqīng bearing a memorial to compel the request to move the capital.
Yànqīng consequently drove and relocated all the residents of Cháng'ān eastward,
all houses were dismantled for lumber,
which was floated down the Wèi River.
Along the roads, they wailed loudly,
looking up to heaven and cursing vehemently, saying:
“The national villains Cuī Yìn and Zhū Wēn have caused me to reach this point!”
Zhāozōng also looked back at the imperial tombs and ancestral temples,
wandering reluctantly, unable to bear leaving,
and said to his attendants in a folksy manner:
“Sparrows frozen dead atop Hégān Shān,
why not fly away to a joyous living place?”
They wept together, soaking their lapels.
When Zhāozōng traveled to Huàzhōu,
he sent a person to inform Tàizǔ that Empress Hé was pregnant,
wishing to remain in Huàzhōu and depart after winter.
Tàizǔ became furious,
and looked at Yànqīng, saying:
“Go and hurry His Majesty here;
he cannot remain even for a single day.”
Yànqīng immediately galloped back to Huà,
and on that very day compelled Zhāozōng to start the journey.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Yànqīng as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Gǎnhuà Commandery.
After more than a year,
he was summoned to become General-in-Chief of the Left Army of the Metropolitan Prefecture (Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi Dàjiāngjūn),
serving as the Envoy for Street Patrols of the Metropolitan Prefecture (Jīnwú Jiēzhàng Shǐ).
Yànqīng arrived at Tiānjīn Qiáo during the morning court session,
and the commoner Liáng Xiàn did not yield the path.
The advance guard seized Xiàn and threw him onto the stone railing of the bridge, causing his death.
Yànqīng went to see Tàizǔ and confessed,
Tàizǔ cherished him,
and decreed that Yànqīng should compensate Xiàn’s family with money to atone for the crime.
Cuī Yí, the Supervising Censor and Chief Justice, impeached Yànqīng in a memorial,
requesting judgment according to the law.
Tàizǔ, having no alternative,
demoted Yànqīng to Commandant (Zhōnglángjiāng) of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi).
He was later re-appointed as Defender (Fángyù Shǐ) of Xiàngzhōu,
and transferred to Military Commissioner of Héyáng.
When Tàizǔ was assassinated,
Yànqīng brought out Tàizǔ’s portrait and served him as if he were alive.
Whenever he spoke to guests about the former court,
tears and snot would stream down.
When Mòdì ascended the throne,
he was relocated to govern Wēishèng.
Yànqīng was bright, sharp, and good at serving others,
but he relied on favor to exert tyranny,
liked executions,
and was full of suspicion and jealousy.
He died while governing the circuit,
at the age of fifty-seven.
Biography of Subjects of the Liáng, Tenth: Kāng Huáiyīng
Kāng Huáiyīng
was a native of Yǎnzhōu.
He served Zhū Jǐn as a personal guard general (Yájiàng).
When Liáng troops attacked Jǐn,
Jǐn went out to forage for food between Fēng and Pèi.
He left Huáiyīng to defend the city.
Huáiyīng immediately surrendered the city to the Liáng,
and Jǐn consequently fled to Wú.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased upon obtaining Huáiyīng.
Later, he followed Shì Shūcóng to attack Zhào Kuāngníng,
capturing Dèngzhōu.
Liáng troops attacked Lǐ Màozhēn at Qí,
using Huáiyīng as the vanguard.
Arriving at Wǔgōng,
they struck and killed over ten thousand Qí soldiers.
Tàizǔ rejoiced and said:
“The town is named Wǔgōng (Military Merit),
it truly is military merit.”
He bestowed a famous horse upon him.
At this time,
Lǐ Zhōuyí brought Fūfāng troops to aid Qí,
and encamped on the borders of Sānyuán.
Huáiyīng attacked and routed them,
and consequently took their Dízhōu before returning.
Qí troops were encamped at Fèngtiān,
and Huáiyīng barricaded their northeast.
In the middle of the night,
Qí troops attacked him.
Huáiyīng believed it was nighttime and did not wish to startle the other armies,
so he alone went out to battle with two thousand men.
When dawn approached,
the Qí troops dispersed and left.
He himself sustained more than ten wounds.
Lǐ Màozhēn made peace with the Liáng,
and Zhāozōng returned to the capital.
Huáiyīng was granted the title
“Meritorious Subject, Resolute and Brave, Who Welcomed the Imperial Chariot” (Yíngluán Yìyǒng Gōngchén).
Yáng Xíngmì attacked Sùzhōu.
Tàizǔ dispatched Huáiyīng to attack and repulse him,
and memorialized to appoint him Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Sùzhōu.
He was transferred to Military Commissioner of Bǎoyì Commandery.
Dīng Huì rebelled against the Liáng with Lùzhōu and surrendered to the Jìn.
Tàizǔ ordered Huáiyīng to be the Commander of Pacification (Zhāotǎo Shǐ).
As he was about to depart,
Tàizǔ warned him,
speaking very sharply.
Huáiyīng was terrified.
He believed that Lùzhōu was definitely within his grasp,
so he built a double wall to surround it.
The Jìn dispatched Zhōu Déwēi to encamp at Luànliǔ,
and he repeatedly attacked the double wall.
Huáiyīng did not dare to leave and fight.
Tàizǔ then replaced Huáiyīng with Lǐ Sī'ān as general,
demoting Huáiyīng to Inspector-General (Dū Yúhòu).
After a long time,
Sī'ān also achieved nothing.
Tàizǔ was greatly enraged,
dismissed Sī'ān,
and appointed Liú Zhījùn of Tóngzhōu as the Commander of Pacification.
Before Zhījùn reached the army,
Tàizǔ personally arrived at Zézhōu,
to serve as reinforcements for Huáiyīng’s army and others,
and also to supervise them.
Soon thereafter, Prince of Jìn Lǐ Kèyòng died,
and Zhuāngzōng summoned Zhōu Déwēi back.
Tàizǔ heard that the Jìn had a mourning period,
and that Déwēi had left,
so he also returned to Luòyáng,
and the various generals also relaxed slightly.
Zhuāngzōng said to Déwēi:
“The reason the Jìn has been able to oppose the Liáng,
and the one they fear,
is the late King.
Now that they have heard of the mourning for our King,
they suppose that I have just ascended the throne
and cannot yet deploy troops,
so their intent must be lax.
It is fitting to strike them when they least expect it.
Not only will this lift the siege,
but it will also be sufficient to secure our hegemony.”
Thereupon, he and Déwēi rapidly traveled for six days until they reached Běi Huángniǎn.
Coincidentally, the sky was very dark and foggy.
They hid troops on Sānchuí Gāng,
marched straight toward the double wall,
and attacked and breached it.
Huáiyīng was utterly defeated,
losing three hundred major generals.
Huáiyīng fled back with one hundred cavalry,
and presented himself at the palace gate to request death.
Tàizǔ said:
“When we raised troops last year,
the moon was eclipsed (Tàiyīn Kuīshí).
Diviners considered it unfavorable.
I alone disregarded this, leading to defeat.
This is not your fault.”
He released him,
and appointed him General-in-Chief of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn).
Liú Zhījùn rebelled,
fleeing to Qí.
Huáiyīng was appointed Military Commissioner of Bǎoyì Commandery and Deputy Commander of Pacification for the Western Route (Xī Lù Fù Zhāotǎo Shǐ).
Zhījùn used Qí troops to surround Língwǔ.
Tàizǔ dispatched Huáiyīng to attack Bīnnìng to divert him.
Huáiyīng took Níngzhōu, Qìngzhōu, and Yǎnzhōu—three prefectures.
Upon returning to Shēngpíng,
Zhījùn ambushed and attacked him.
Huáiyīng was utterly defeated.
He was relocated to govern Gǎnhuà.
Afterward, Zhū Yǒuqīan rebelled and defected to the Jìn.
Huáiyīng was ordered to suppress him.
He fought the Jìn forces at Báijìng Lǐng,
and Huáiyīng suffered another great defeat.
He was relocated to govern Yǒngpíng,
and died while governing the circuit.
Liú Quán
Liú Quán,
was a native of Ānqīu, Mìzhōu.
In his youth, he served Wáng Jìngwǔ of Qīngzhōu.
When Jìngwǔ died,
his son Shīfàn was established.
Zhāng Chán, Prefect of Dìzhōu, rebelled.
Shīfàn dispatched Commander Lú Hóng to suppress Chán.
Hóng also rebelled.
Shīfàn falsely extended kind words to summon Hóng.
When Hóng arrived,
he was welcomed outside the city,
and Shīfàn ordered Quán to behead him while seated.
He then made Quán attack Zhāng Chán,
and defeated him.
Shīfàn memorialized to appoint Quán as Prefect of Dēngzhōu,
and made him Adjutant of the Field Army (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
Liáng Tàizǔ marched west to attack Fèngxiáng.
Shī Fàn took advantage of Liáng's weakness,
secretly sending men to separately assault Liáng's various prefectures and counties.
The plans of his other envoys were often leaked,
and they failed.
Only **Liú Shǒng** had always been fond of military treatises,
and possessed strategic ingenuity.
At this time,
Liáng had already defeated Zhū Jǐn and others,
and completely occupied Yǎn and Yùn prefectures.
Gé Cóngzhōu was made the Jiédùshǐ of Yǎnzhōu.
Cóngzhōu was leading troops outside.
**Liú Shǒng** then sent men carrying oil to sell inside the city,
who observed all the weak points of the city and the places where people entered and exited.
The oil sellers discovered a water conduit beneath the outer city wall through which they could enter.
**Liú Shǒng** then took five hundred infantry through the water conduit and successfully attacked the city.
He moved Cóngzhōu’s family to an outer residence,
and personally bowed to his mother,
treating her with great kindness and courtesy.
Tàizǔ had already extracted Zhāozōng from Fèngxiáng,
and led his troops back east.
He sent Zhū Yǒuníng to attack Shī Fàn, and Cóngzhōu to attack **Liú Shǒng**.
**Liú Shǒng** placed Cóngzhōu’s mother on a palanquin atop the city wall.
His mother called out to Cóngzhōu, saying:
“General Liú treats me extremely well,
no different than you do.
Every subject serves his own lord;
you must observe this!”
Cóngzhōu consequently slowed his attack.
**Liú Shǒng** then selected all the women and the citizens who were old, sick, or unfit for battle, and sent them out,
remaining only with the young and strong to share the hardships,
distributing clothing and food,
and holding firm in defense to wait.
External aid did not arrive,
and morale began to weaken considerably.
The Deputy Envoy, Wáng Yànwēn, climbed over the wall and fled.
Many of those guarding the battlements ran away.
**Liú Shǒng** then sent a man to speak openly to Yànwēn, saying:
“Deputy Envoy, do not bring out too many people;
those I did not originally send out,
you must not let them leave.”
He also issued an order within the city saying:
“Only those whom I allowed to follow the Deputy Envoy may leave;
otherwise, the whole clan will be executed.”
Everyone in the city was confused,
and those fleeing then stopped.
Soon after, the Liáng forces heard this,
and indeed suspected that Yànwēn was not a genuine surrenderer.
They executed him below the city wall.
Because of this, the city's defense became even stronger.
Shī Fàn’s forces were already exhausted.
Cóngzhōu tried to persuade **Liú Shǒng** by discussing the consequences of failure and success.
**Liú Shǒng** replied:
“Wait until my sovereign surrenders,
then I will return the city to Liáng.”
Shī Fàn was defeated
and surrendered to Liáng.
**Liú Shǒng** then also surrendered.
Cóngzhōu prepared the necessary traveling gear for him,
sending **Liú Shǒng** back to Liáng.
**Liú Shǒng** said:
“It is fortunate that a surrendered general has received Liáng's grace and was not executed!
It is lucky!
How dare I ride a horse and wear furs?”
He then wore plain clothes and rode a donkey back to Liáng.
Tàizǔ bestowed upon him a hat and belt,
and offered him wine.
**Liú Shǒng** declined, citing his low capacity for drink.
Tàizǔ said:
“When you captured Yǎnzhōu,
how great was your capacity then?”
Tàizǔ appointed him as Yuáncóng Dūyāyá (Chief Commander of the Imperial Retinue).
At this time,
Tàizǔ had already commanded four Circuits (Zhèn),
and his generals and officials were all veterans who had rendered meritorious service.
**Liú Shǒng**, a surrendered general, suddenly ranked above them.
When the various generals met **Liú Shǒng**,
they all treated him according to military etiquette.
**Liú Shǒng** behaved naturally.
Tàizǔ admired him even more.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
**Liú Shǒng** was repeatedly promoted to Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn (Commander of the Left Dragon Martial Army).
Liú Zhìjùn rebelled,
capturing Cháng'ān.
Tàizǔ sent **Liú Shǒng** and Niú Cúnjié to suppress him.
Zhìjùn fled to Fèngxiáng.
Tàizǔ then established Cháng'ān as Yǒngpíng Jūn,
and appointed **Liú Shǒng** as Jiédùshǐ.
When Mò Dì ascended the throne,
**Liú Shǒng** held the title of Zhènnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and served as Kāifēng Yǐn (Prefect of Kāifēng).
Yáng Shīhòu died.
Xiàng and Wèi prefectures were divided into two circuits.
Mò Dì feared that the Wèi troops would revolt,
so he sent **Liú Shǒng** with troops to garrison Wèixiàn (Wèi County).
The Wèi troops indeed revolted,
seizing Hè Délún and forcing him to surrender to Jìn.
Zhuāng Zōng entered Wèi.
**Liú Shǒng** believed that all the Jìn troops were following Zhuāng Zōng to Wèi,
and that Tàiyuán could be attacked.
He then tied straw to form human figures,
holding flags and banners,
and had donkeys carry them moving back and forth on the city wall.
Meanwhile, he secretly led his army out through Huángzé Guān to attack Tàiyuán.
The Jìn troops watched the Liáng ramparts where flags and banners moved back and forth,
unaware that he had left,
and therefore did not pursue him.
**Liú Shǒng** reached Lèpíng,
encountering rain,
and could not advance and thus returned.
He rushed quickly toward Línqīng,
attempting to seize the stored grain supplies in Wèi.
However, Zhōu Déwēi had already arrived first.
**Liú Shǒng** then established a garrison at Shēnxian,
building a covered walkway that reached the river to supply his army.
After a long time,
Mò Dì sent a letter criticizing **Liú Shǒng**, saying:
“All matters outside the palace walls were fully entrusted to the General,
yet all the prefectures north of the Yellow River have suddenly been lost.
Now the granaries are exhausted,
and transport by fast wagons is insufficient.
Since the General shares the nation's concerns,
you should devise an excellent plan!”
**Liú Shǒng** replied:
“The Jìn troops are extremely sharp;
they should not be attacked yet.
It is best to wait.”
Mò Dì again sent an envoy to ask **Liú Shǒng** for a guaranteed winning strategy.
**Liú Shǒng** said:
“I have no secret techniques.
I request that each man be supplied with ten *hú* of rice.
When the rice is finished, the enemy will be defeated!”
Mò Dì was greatly angered.
He reproached **Liú Shǒng**, saying:
“General, are you hoarding rice
to cure hunger,
or to defeat the enemy?”
He then sent an inspector to oversee the army.
**Liú Shǒng** summoned his generals to consult, saying:
“The Sovereign remains deep inside the forbidden palace,
consulting with 'white-faced youths' (courtiers),
which is certain to ruin our affairs.
Now the enemy is powerful;
we cannot act rashly.
What do you gentlemen think?”
All the generals wanted to fight.
**Liú Shǒng** then summoned all the generals to sit at the camp gate,
and gave each man a cup of river water to drink.
The generals were bewildered.
Some drank, some declined.
**Liú Shǒng** said:
“If the difficulty of [drinking] a single cup is like this,
can the surging river be drained dry?”
All the generals turned pale.
At this time,
Zhuāng Zōng was in Wèi,
repeatedly pressing **Liú Shǒng**’s camp with strong forces.
**Liú Shǒng** refused to engage.
But Mò Dì repeatedly urged **Liú Shǒng**,
ordering him to go out and fight.
Zhuāng Zōng discussed the matter with his generals, saying:
“Liú Shǒng studied the *Six Strategies* (Liù Tāo),
and likes to employ troops using unexpected stratagems.
He originally intended to show weakness in order to ambush us.
Now that he is being pressured,
he will certainly seek a quick battle.”
Zhuāng Zōng then publicly announced that he was returning to Tàiyuán,
ordered Fú Cúnshěn to guard Wèi,
feigned a retreat west,
and secretly stationed troops in Bèizhōu.
**Liú Shǒng** indeed reported to Mò Dì, saying:
“The Prince of Jìn has returned west.
Wèi is unprepared;
we can attack it.”
He then led ten thousand troops to attack the east side of the city of Wèi.
Zhuāng Zōng returned rapidly from Bèizhōu and attacked him.
**Liú Shǒng** suddenly saw the Jìn army
and cried out in alarm:
“Is the Prince of Jìn here!”
His troops gradually fell back.
They were pursued to Gù Yuánchéng.
Zhuāng Zōng and Fú Cúnshěn formed two square formations and pressed him from both sides.
**Liú Shǒng** formed a circular formation to defend against the Jìn forces.
When the armies clashed again,
**Liú Shǒng** was utterly defeated.
He fled south,
crossed the river from Líyáng,
and secured Huázhōu.
Mò Dì appointed him Yìchéng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
The following year,
all the lands north of the Yellow River fell to Jìn,
and **Liú Shǒng** was demoted to Bózhōu Tuánliànshǐ (Commander of Regional Militias of Bózhōu).
Zhāng Wànjìn of Yǎnzhōu rebelled.
He was appointed Pacification and Control Commissioner (Ānfǔ Zhìzhìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu.
Wànjìn was defeated and killed,
whereupon he was appointed Jiedushi of the Tàiníng Army (Tàiníngjūn Jiédùshǐ).
Zhū Yǒuqīan rebelled
and captured Tóngzhōu.
Emperor Mò (Mòdì) appointed him Pacification and Suppression Commissioner (Zhāotǎoshǐ) of the Hédōng Circuit.
When he reached Shǎnzhōu,
he wrote a letter to entice Yǒuqīan (to surrender).
Yǒuqīan did not respond,
so he remained there for more than a month waiting for him.
Yǐn Hào, Duàn Níng, and others had long disliked him,
so they slandered him,
claiming that he was related to Yǒuqīan by marriage (qīnjiā),
and therefore he was delaying in order to nurture the rebel.
Later, his troops were repeatedly defeated,
so he was dismissed and returned to Luòyáng.
He was poisoned and killed,
at the age of sixty-four.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Secretary (Zhōngshū Lìng).
His sons, Suìníng and Suìyōng,
both served the Táng as Prefects (Cìshǐ).
His concubine, Lady Wáng (Wáng Shì), was beautiful.
After his death,
she entered the palace of Emperor Míngzōng,
and became Consort Shū Wáng (Wáng Shūfēi).
In the later years of Emperor Míngzōng,
Consort Shū wielded influence,
and his two sons were thus favored.
When the Prince of Lù, Lù Wáng Cóngkē, rebelled at Fèngxiáng,
Suìyōng was then the Deputy Resident Administrator (Fù Liúshǒu) of the Western Capital (Xījīng).
Wáng Sītóng, the Resident Administrator, led the troops of various circuits to suppress Fèngxiáng.
They were defeated in battle and returned eastward,
but Suìyōng closed the city gates and refused to admit them.
He sealed all the government treasuries to await the Prince of Lù.
When the Prince of Lù’s vanguard arrived,
he gave them all gold and silk.
When the Prince of Lù met Suìyōng,
he clasped his hand and wept.
Thereafter, regardless of the importance of the matter, he consulted with Suìyōng.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) ascended the throne,
he appointed Suìyōng Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Zīzhōu,
and replaced Suìyōng as Deputy Resident Administrator of the Western Capital with Suìqīng, the son of his elder brother Qí.
Suìqīng subsequently served as Prefect of five prefectures, including Yì and Dì.
In all cases, he governed well.
He was promoted to Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Fèngzhōu and Commissioner of the Northern Department of the Court of Transmission (Xuānhuī Běiyuàn Shǐ),
and managed the Three Departments (Sānsī).
During the Kāiyùn reign of the Jìn dynasty, he died while serving as Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Ānzhōu.
Suìqīng possessed utmost filial piety.
During the mourning period for his father, he was devastated by grief,
and his community praised him for it.
Once, while serving as Prefect of Zīzhōu,
he welcomed his mother.
When his mother reached the suburbs,
Suìqīng held the reins for his mother and walked several dozen *lǐ*.
The people of the prefecture all considered this an honor.
Niú Cúnjié
Niú Cúnjié, courtesy name Zànzhèng,
was a native of Bóchāng in Qīngzhōu.
His original name was Lǐ.
He served Zhūgě Shuǎng at Héyáng.
When Shuǎng died,
Cúnjié looked at his followers and said:
“The world is in chaos;
we should find a great hero to serve.”
He then led his followers, numbering more than ten men, to submit to Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng.
Cúnjié was simple, resolute, loyal, and cautious.
Tàizǔ loved him,
bestowed upon him his current name and courtesy name,
and made him a junior officer.
When Zhāng Zhì attacked Biàn,
Cúnjié destroyed two of his fortified camps.
When Liáng attacked Púzhōu,
fighting at Nánliúqiáo and Fànxiàn,
Cúnjié achieved great merit.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī besieged Zhāng Quányì at Héyáng.
Quányì requested troops from Liáng.
Tàizǔ, knowing that Cúnjié had previously served at Héyáng
and was familiar with the secret routes,
ordered him to lead the troops as the vanguard.
At that time, there was a famine.
The army lacked food during the march.
Cúnjié traded gold and silk with the people for dried mulberries (gān shèn) to feed the troops,
and attacked and drove away Hǎnzhī.
Tàizǔ attacked Wèi.
Cúnjié captured Líyáng and Línhé in Wèi,
killed twelve thousand Wèi soldiers,
and met Tàizǔ at Nèihuáng.
He was promoted to Commander of the Rear Guard of the Fortress City of Huázhōu (Huázhōu Láochéng Èhòu Zhǐhuīshǐ).
When the Liáng troops attacked Yùn,
Cúnjié ordered the Regional Commander Wáng Yán to hide boats in the moat at the northwest corner of Yùn.
He set a deadline for noon to cross the troops over the moat and launch a swift assault.
Coincidentally, a fire broke out in the camp.
The people of Yùn climbed the wall to look at the fire.
Yán hid and dared not move,
missing the appointed time with Cúnjié.
Cúnjié alone breached the barbican gate on the west side of Yùn
and seized the moat bridge.
The Liáng troops were thus able to advance together,
and consequently defeated Zhū Xuān.
He followed Gě Cóngzhōu in the attack on Huáinán.
Cóngzhōu was defeated at the Bēi River.
Cúnjié gathered his eight thousand scattered soldiers and returned.
He was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Bó and Sù Prefectures.
Zhū Jǐn fled to Wú
and summoned Wú forces to attack Xú and Sù.
Cúnjié planned, saying:
“The Huái troops will certainly not attack Sù first.
However, Sù’s ditches and ramparts are already solid,
and can be used to resist the enemy.”
So he rushed his troops to Xúzhōu by night.
By the time he reached the foot of the Xú city wall,
Jǐn’s troops were just arriving.
Seeing the dust rise,
they were shocked and said:
“The Liáng troops have already come!
How fast they are!”
They were unable to launch an attack and retreated.
Soon after, Tàizǔ’s envoy arrived,
bearing military plans for Cúnjié.
These plans were entirely consistent with Cúnjié’s own intentions,
and because of this, the various generals admired his ability even more.
He was promoted to Commander-in-Chief (Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ) of Lùzhōu.
When Tàizǔ attacked Fèngxiáng,
he sent for Cúnjié.
As a general, Cúnjié’s
laws and orders were strict and orderly, yet he was skilled at winning the hearts of the soldiers.
Those from Lùzhōu who came to send him off all wailed and wept.
He was repeatedly promoted to Militia Commissioner (Tuánliànshǐ) of Xíngzhōu and Chief Patrol Inspector of the Left in the Marshal's Residence (Yuánshuàifǔ Zuǒ Dū Yāyá).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Supreme General of the Right Qiānniú Guard (Yòu Qiānniúwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn).
He followed Kāng Huáiyīng to attack Lùzhōu,
serving as Commander for Arraying Troops in the Mobile Camp (Xíngyíng Páizhènshǐ).
The Jìn forces had already breached the outer city wall.
Cúnjié and others returned with their remaining troops.
When they marched to Tiānjǐng Pass,
they heard that the Jìn forces were attacking Zézhōu.
Cúnjié looked at the generals and said:
“Although I have not received orders for this action,
Zézhōu is a crucial location
and cannot be lost.”
The other generals all did not want to rescue it.
Cúnjié ordered his officers and soldiers to rest well.
Afterwards, he said to them:
“If we do not respond when the situation is urgent,
how can we call ourselves brave?”
He raised his whip and advanced first,
and the soldiers followed him.
By the time they reached Zézhōu,
the people of the prefecture had already burned the outer wall
and were about to surrender to Jìn.
Hearing of Cúnjié’s arrival,
they gradually stabilized.
Cúnjié entered the city
and helped the people of Zézhōu defend it.
The Jìn forces dug tunnels to attack.
Cúnjié selected several dozen brave soldiers,
who also dug tunnels to meet them.
They fought inside the tunnels.
The enemy could not enter,
and the Jìn forces withdrew.
He was promoted to Commander of the Left Dragon and Tiger Guard (Zuǒ Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn), Commander-in-Chief of the Six Armies (Liùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ), and Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Jiàngzhōu.
He was subsequently transferred to Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu) of Fūzhōu.
When Liú Zhījùn of Tóngzhōu rebelled
and fled to Fèngxiáng,
Cúnjié was then transferred and appointed Jiedushi of the Kuāngguó Army (Kuāngguójūn Jiédùshǐ).
When Zhū Yǒuguī ascended the throne,
Zhū Yǒuqīan rebelled and allied himself with Jìn.
To the west, he connected with Fèngxiáng,
leaving Cúnjié exposed to attacks from both the east and the west.
The water in Tóngzhōu was salty and there were no wells.
When Zhījùn had rebelled against Liáng,
he had fled because he could not hold the city due to thirst.
Therefore, Yǒuqīan combined with the Qí forces to maintain a persistent siege,
hoping to exhaust them through thirst.
Cúnjié prayed, selected locations, and dug eighty wells.
The water in all of them was sweet and drinkable.
Yǒuqīan was eventually unable to take the city.
When Mòdì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì,
and transferred to govern Tiānpíng.
When Jiǎng Yīn rebelled in Xúzhōu,
Cúnjié was sent to attack and defeat him.
For this achievement, he was promoted to Tàiwèi.
As Liáng and Jìn confronted each other on the river,
Cúnjié fell ill with dysentery.
While Liáng and Jìn were locked in bitter struggle,
Cúnjié's loyalty and indignation were greatly roused.
He managed the army and supervised his officers,
never once mentioning his illness.
When his illness became critical,
he was summoned back to the capital.
Before he died,
he said to his son Zhīyè:
"Loyalty and filial piety
are what my son should embody."
He did not speak of anything else.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī.
Zhāng Guībà (younger brothers Guīhòu, Guībiàn)
Zhāng Guībà
was a native of Qīnghé.
Mòdì married his daughter,
who became Dèfēi.
Guībà, when young, and his younger brothers Guīhòu and Guībiàn all followed Huáng Cháo.
When Cháo was defeated and fled east,
the Guībà brothers surrendered to Liáng.
When Qín Zōngquán attacked Biàn,
Guībà distinguished himself in several battles.
Zhāng Zhì's army was stationed at Chìgāng.
When Zhì challenged with cavalry,
an arrow struck Guībà.
Guībà pulled it out
and shot it back at the enemy.
With one shot, he killed him,
seized his horse, and returned.
Tàizǔ, observing from Gāoqiu,
was greatly impressed,
rewarding him with gold and silk,
and also giving him the horse.
He sent Guībà with five hundred archers to lie in ambush in Huáng,
while Tàizǔ led several hundred cavalry as skirmishers.
Passing Zhì's palisade,
Zhì's troops came out to pursue Tàizǔ.
Guībà sprang his ambush,
killing a thousand of Zhì's soldiers
and capturing dozens of horses.
When Tàizǔ attacked Càizhōu,
Cài general Xiāo Hào fiercely attacked Tàizǔ's camp.
Guībà, without waiting to ask permission,
divided his forces with Xú Huáiyù and sallied out from the southeast wall gate.
They jointly attacked and defeated them,
allowing Tàizǔ to withdraw his camp.
Tàizǔ attacked Yǎn and Yùn,
and captured Cáozhōu.
He ordered Guībà to guard it with several thousand troops.
They fought against Zhū Jǐn at Jīnxiāng,
and thoroughly defeated him.
He also broke Púzhōu.
When the Jìn people attacked Wèi,
Guībà followed Gé Cóngzhōu to relieve Wèi.
Fighting at Huánshuǐ,
Guībà captured Kèyòng's son Luòluò and handed him over to the Wèi people.
He also defeated Liú Rén'gōng at Nèihuáng,
his achievements surpassing those of all other generals.
In the second year of Guānghuà (904 CE),
he temporarily governed Xíngzhōu.
He was transferred to be the Prefect of Láizhōu,
and appointed Zuǒwèi Shàngjiāngjūn and Cáozhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Kāipíng (907 CE),
he was appointed Yòu Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn and Zuǒ Xiāowèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
In the second year (908 CE),
he was appointed Héyáng Jiédùshǐ,
and died of illness.
His son, Hànjié,
served Mòdì as a high official,
and held power due to Zhāng Dèfēi.
When Liáng fell,
Táng Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
and Hànjié's entire clan was executed.
His younger brother Guīhòu,
courtesy name Dékūn.
As a general, he was skilled with bow and spear,
and capable of defeating many with few.
When Zhāng Zhì was stationed at Chìgāng,
Guīhòu fought Zhì alone in front of the formation.
Zhì, exhausted, retreated,
and the other generals pressed the attack.
Zhì was then utterly defeated.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased
and appointed him Qíjǐng.
When Liáng attacked Shí Pǔ,
Guīhòu led his subordinates to advance first to Jiǔlǐshān.
They encountered Xú soldiers and fought.
The former Liáng general Chén Fán had rebelled and was in Xú.
Guīhòu recognized him upon sight,
glared and cursed loudly,
then galloped directly towards him to capture him.
An arrow struck his left eye.
When Chēn Wáng Yǒuyù attacked Yùn
and was stationed in Púzhōu,
Tàizǔ arrived later.
Yǒuyù moved his palisade,
and Tàizǔ lost track of him.
Tàizǔ eventually encountered Yùn's troops.
Tàizǔ ascended a high point to observe.
The Yùn troops numbered only about a thousand.
Tàizǔ and Guīhòu, with the Tīngzǐ Army, charged directly at them.
As the battle joined,
a large force of Yùn troops arrived.
Guīhòu judged they could not hold,
and with several dozen cavalry, escorted Tàizǔ back first.
Guīhòu's horse was struck by an arrow and collapsed,
so he fought on foot with his spear.
Tàizǔ returned to the army camp
and sent Zhāng Jūn to gallop back to rescue him,
believing he was surely dead.
Guīhòu had been struck by more than ten arrows.
He returned on Jūn's horse.
When Tàizǔ saw him,
