he wept and said:
"With you alive,
what is the loss of an army to count?"
He ordered him to be carried back to Xuānwǔ.
He was promoted to Yòu Shénwǔ Tǒngjūn,
and successively served as Prefect of Míng, Jìn, and Jiàng prefectures.
He fought repeatedly against the Jìn people and never yielded.
In the first year of Gānhuà (911 CE),
he was appointed Zhènguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and died of illness.
His son was Hànqīng.
Guībiàn,
as a general, was also skilled in battle.
In the early Kāipíng era, he was Huázhōu Chángjiàn Zhǐhuīshǐ.
His son was Hànróng.
When Liáng fell,
they were all executed with their clans.
Wáng Chóngshī
Wáng Chóngshī
was a native of Chángshè, Xǔzhōu.
He was a taciturn man, full of wisdom,
and skilled with sword and spear.
When Qín Zōngquán captured Xǔzhōu,
Chóngshī escaped and returned to Liáng.
He followed Tàizǔ to pacify Cài,
and attacked Yǎn and Yùn,
serving as Bášān Jūn Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Chóngshī fought bitterly between Qí and Lǔ,
and his might shook his enemies.
He was promoted to Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Tàizǔ attacked Púzhōu.
After it was breached,
the people of Pú piled up straw and set it on fire,
preventing the Liáng army from entering.
At this time,
Chóngshī was suffering from a metal-wound,
lying in his tent.
When the generals urged him,
Chóngshī immediately rose,
took all the felt blankets in the army, soaked them with water,
and covered the fire with them.
He led elite soldiers with short weapons to storm in.
The Liáng army followed them all in,
and thus Púzhōu was captured.
Chóngshī sustained eight or nine wounds,
and his soldiers carried him back.
When Tàizǔ heard of it,
he exclaimed in surprise:
"How can I gain Púzhōu and lose Chóngshī!"
He had doctors treat him,
and he recovered after more than a month.
When Wáng Shīfàn surrendered,
he presented Chóngshī as the Acting Administrator of Qīngzhōu.
He was successively promoted to Yòuguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
He held this position for several years,
and had great prestige and benevolence.
Chóngshī had an old grudge with Liú Hàn.
Hàn often sowed discord about him with Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ became suspicious of him.
Chóngshī sent his general Zhāng Jūnliàn to attack Bīn and Fèng to the west without asking for permission first.
Jūnliàn's troops suffered a minor defeat.
Tàizǔ, because he had unilaterally launched troops
and thereby diminished the nation's prestige,
was about to summon and punish him.
He sent Liú Hàn to replace Chóngshī.
Chóngshī did not know Tàizǔ was angry with him.
When Hàn arrived,
Chóngshī did not go out to welcome him,
meeting him at the Green Gate.
His礼 (decorum/etiquette) was also arrogant.
Hàn then rushed to inform Tàizǔ,
claiming that Chóngshī had rebellious intentions.
Tàizǔ became even angrier.
He demoted Chóngshī to Xīzhōu Cìshǐ,
then again to Yázhōu Sīhù Cānjūn.
Before he could depart,
he was granted death.
Xú Huáiyù
Xú Huáiyù,
was a person from Jiāoyí, Bózhōu.
In his youth, he served Liáng Tàizǔ (Founding Emperor of the Liáng),
and rose with Tàizǔ from humble origins.
Huáiyù served as a general,
taking upon himself the role of a hero and champion,
and was brave in battle formations.
He followed Tàizǔ to garrison Xuānwǔ,
and became the defense commander of Yǒngchéng.
Qín Zōngquán attacked Liáng,
encamping at Jīntī, Língchāng, and Suānzǎo.
Huáiyù used light cavalry to repeatedly attack and defeat them,
capturing and killing over five thousand men.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Chángjiàn Dū Yúhòu (Commander of the Palace Guards).
He again defeated Zōngquán at Bǎnqiáo and Chìgāng,
destroying eight of his fortified camps (zhà).
He followed Tàizǔ eastward to attack Yǎn and Yùn,
and defeated Xú and Sù.
Huáiyù was covered in metal wounds (serious wounds),
and in battle, he always achieved victory and success.
The rewards and gifts he received,
he often distributed to his officers and soldiers.
He became a famous general of Liáng.
His original name was Cóng;
Tàizǔ bestowed upon him the name Huáiyù.
He followed Tàizǔ to attack Wèi,
defeating the Wèi troops at Líyáng.
He then attacked Yǎn eastward,
defeating Zhū Jǐn at Jīnxiāng.
He again followed Páng Shīgǔ to attack Yáng Xíngmì.
When Shīgǔ was defeated at Qīngkǒu,
Huáiyù alone maintained the integrity of his division.
He subsequently collected over ten thousand scattered soldiers and returned.
He was promoted to Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yízhōu.
As the region enjoyed frequent bumper harvests,
he repaired his weapons and fortified his walls,
preparing equipment for offense and defense.
Soon after, Wáng Shīfàn rebelled against Liáng,
attacking the eastern border.
Huáiyù repeatedly used the provincial troops to attack and defeat him.
He was promoted to Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Qízhōu.
In the fourth year of Tiānfù (904 CE),
he led his provincial troops westward to welcome Shāozōng to the capital Luòyáng.
He was promoted to Acting Surveillance Commissioner (Guānchá Liúhòu) of Huàzhōu,
and stationed his troops in Yōngzhōu.
He was promoted to Commander of the Right Yǔlín Army (Yòu Yǔlín Tǒngjūn).
He was stationed at Zézhōu.
The Jìn troops attacked it,
digging a tunnel to enter.
Huáiyù struck them within the tunnel,
and the Jìn forces retreated.
During the time of Tàizǔ,
he successively served as Prefect of Cáozhōu and Jìnzhōu.
Jìn repeatedly attacked these,
but Huáiyù held firm in defense,
defeating the Jìn army at Hóngdòng.
He was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Bǎodà Army.
When Tàizǔ died,
Yǒuguī established himself [as emperor].
Zhū Yǒuqiān defected to Jìn,
using this allegiance to attack Fūzhōu.
He captured Huáiyù and killed him.
Biography 11 of the Ministers of Liáng: Yáng Shīhòu.
Yáng Shīhòu,
was a person from Jīngōu, Yǐngzhōu.
In his youth, he served Lǐ Hǎnzhī of Héyáng.
When Hǎnzhī surrendered to Jìn,
he selected a hundred stout soldiers from his command to present to the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng).
Shīhòu was among those listed.
While Shīhòu was in Jìn,
he achieved no fame.
Later, due to a crime, he fled to Liáng.
Tàizǔ appointed him Deputy Commander (Yāyá) of the Xuānwǔ Army and Prefect of Cáozhōu.
When Liáng attacked Wáng Shīfàn,
Shīhòu fought at Línqú,
capturing over eighty of Shīfàn's subordinate generals.
He captured Dìzhōu,
and for his merit was appointed Prefect of Qízhōu.
When Tàizǔ attacked Zhào Kuāngníng at Xiāngyáng,
he sent Shīhòu as the vanguard.
Shīhòu used wood from Tóngshān west of Gǔchéng to construct a pontoon bridge,
crossed the Hàn River,
attacked Kuāngníng,
and defeated him.
Kuāngníng abandoned the city and fled.
Shīhòu advanced to attack Jīngnán,
and also drove away Kuāngníng's younger brother, Kuāngmíng.
His achievements were numerous,
and he was appointed Military Governor of the Shānnán Dōngdào circuit and Concurrently Manager of Affairs (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Liú Zhījùn rebelled,
capturing Cháng'ān.
Liú Yuè, Niú Cúnjié, and others attacked him,
but for a long time could not overcome him.
Shīhòu led out surprise troops,
moving along the South Mountains (Nánshān) and entering through the west gate.
He forced the defenders to surrender,
and thus captured the city.
Zhōu Déwēi of Jìn attacked Jìnzhōu in response to Zhījùn.
Shīhòu defeated him at Méngkēng.
For this merit, he was promoted to Military Governor of the Bǎoyì Army,
and later transferred to govern Xuānyì.
At this time,
the Liáng army had attacked Zhào for a long time without success.
Tàizǔ was ill and bedridden in Luòyáng.
When he slightly recovered,
he personally led a force northward to attack Zhào.
Shīhòu followed Tàizǔ to Huánshǔi.
Traveling at night, they lost their way.
The next morning,
they reached Wèixiàn.
Hearing that the enemy was approaching,
the Liáng troops scattered in uncontrollable chaos.
After a long while, realizing there was no enemy,
they settled down.
Soon after, Tàizǔ's illness flared up,
and so they returned.
The following year, his health improved slightly.
Since the Jìn army was attacking Yān,
Liú Shǒuguāng, the Prince of Yān, requested aid from Liáng.
Tàizǔ, in order to divert Jìn, attacked Zhào.
He garrisoned at Lónghuā,
and sent Shīhòu to attack Zǎoqiáng.
After three months, it could not be taken.
Tàizǔ was enraged,
and went himself to supervise the troops in battle.
They then breached the city,
massacred the inhabitants,
and advanced to besiege Tiáoxiàn.
Shǐ Jiàntáng of Jìn used light cavalry to attack the Liáng army at night.
The Liáng army was greatly thrown into disorder.
Both Tàizǔ and Shīhòu abandoned their baggage trains and fled south.
Tàizǔ returned to the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū).
Shīhòu remained, garrisoning Wèizhōu.
The following year,
Tàizǔ was assassinated,
and Yǒuguī established himself.
Shīhòu seized the opportunity to kill the Wèi camp generals Pān Yàn, Zāng Yánfàn, and others,
and drove out the Military Governor Luó Zhōuhàn.
Yǒuguī then appointed Shīhòu as the Military Governor of the Tiānxíong Army.
From the time Tàizǔ fought Jìn north of the Yellow River (Héběi),
Shīhòu always served as the Commissioner of Pacification and Mobilization (Zhāotǎoshǐ),
taking command of all the crack troops of Liáng.
When Tàizǔ died,
Shīhòu then drove out his superior,
and became increasingly arrogant and difficult to control.
At that time, Wèi relied on its resident army (yá bīng),
allowing its governors to be stubbornly independent.
In the time of Luó Shàowēi,
the resident army had been wiped out.
Wèi's power became isolated,
and it began to be controlled by Liáng.
Once Shīhòu had achieved his goal,
he re-established the Silver Spear Loyal Service Army (Yínqiāng Xiàojié Jūn).
Yǒuguī secretly planned against him,
summoning Shīhòu to the capital to discuss matters.
His subordinates, Tián Wēn and others, advised Shīhòu not to go.
Shīhòu said:
"I have not betrayed the Zhū clan for twenty years.
If I do not go now,
I will be suspected and trouble will arise.
However, I know the character of the sovereign,
and even if I go,
he can do nothing against me."
He then led twenty thousand crack troops to the capital (Jīngshī) for the audience,
leaving his army outside the city.
Taking only ten or so followers,
he entered to meet Yǒuguī.
Yǒuguī became increasingly frightened,
bestowed enormous gifts upon him, and Shīhòu returned.
Soon after, the Last Emperor (Mòdì) planned to eliminate Yǒuguī.
He inquired of Zhào Yán.
Yán said:
"The success or failure of this matter
rests entirely with Commissioner Yáng (Yáng Gōng).
If we can get him to give a single command to instruct the Forbidden Army (Jìnjūn),
our affair will be settled immediately."
Mòdì then sent Mǎ Shènjiāo to secretly meet Shīhòu,
and reveal his innermost thoughts.
Shīhòu hesitated and could not decide.
He said to his subordinates:
"When the Prince of Yǐng (Yǐng Wáng) committed regicide,
I was unable to immediately suppress him.
Now the distinction between sovereign and subject is already settled.
If I change my plans without reason,
what will people say about me?"
One of his subordinates said:
"Yǒuguī murdered his father and lord,
which is a universal evil.
The Prince of Jūn (Jūn Wáng) relies on great righteousness to execute the rebel;
this matter will be easily accomplished.
If he defeats the rebel one morning,
how will you place yourself?"
Shīhòu was greatly enlightened.
He then sent his general Wáng Shùnxián to Luòyáng
to meet Yuán Xiàngxiān and plan the affair,
and arranged for Zhū Hànīn to garrison troops in Huázhōu as a supporting move.
The Last Emperor subsequently allied with Xiàngxiān and killed Yǒuguī.
When Mòdì ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Shī Hòu (師厚) as Yè Wáng (鄴王, Prince of Yè).
Imperial edicts did not refer to him by name,
and he consulted him on matters great and small.
However, Mòdì increasingly envied and feared him in his heart.
Soon after, Shī Hòu died from a severe abscess.
Mòdì received congratulations for this inside the palace.
From this time onward, Xiàng (相) and Wèi (魏) were first divided into two garrisons (zhèn).
The Wèi army revolted,
and they surrendered Wèibó (魏博) to Jìn (晉).
The loss of Hébĕi (河北) by Liáng (梁) started from this event.
Wáng Jǐngrén (王景仁)
Wáng Jǐngrén,
was a native of Héféi (合淝), Lúzhōu (廬州).
His initial name was Mào Zhāng (茂章).
When young, he followed Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) when he rose in Huáinán (淮南).
Jǐngrén, as a general, was swift, brave, resolute, and fierce.
His manner was crude and lacked solemn demeanor.
Facing the enemy, he made it his duty to lead his soldiers personally.
Xíngmì admired him.
Liáng Tàizǔ (梁太祖) dispatched his son Yǒu Níng (友寧) to attack Wáng Shīfàn (王師範) at Qīngzhōu (青州).
Shīfàn begged Xíngmì for troops.
Xíngmì sent Jǐngrén with seven thousand infantry and cavalry to rescue Shīfàn.
Shīfàn used his troops to form two stockades with the city behind them.
Yǒu Níng attacked one of the stockades at night.
Those inside the stockade sent an urgent message,
urging Jǐngrén to go out and fight.
Jǐngrén held his troops and did not move.
After Yǒu Níng had broken one stockade,
the continuous fighting did not cease.
When dawn approached,
Jǐngrén calculated that Yǒu Níng’s troops must be exhausted.
He then went out to fight,
and severely defeated them.
He subsequently beheaded Yǒu Níng,
and reported Xíngmì with his head.
At this time,
Liáng Tàizǔ was attacking Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
When he heard that his son Yǒu Níng was dead,
he brought two hundred thousand troops, traveling double speed (forced march), and arrived.
Jǐngrén closed his camp and displayed cowardice,
watching for the Liáng troops to become negligent.
He destroyed the stockades and emerged.
He charged swiftly into battle.
When the battle was intense, he withdrew and sat down,
summoning his generals to drink wine.
Afterward, he fought again.
Tàizǔ climbed a height and watched him.
He captured a surrendered man from Qīngzhōu,
and asked:
"Who is the one drinking wine?"
The man replied:
"It is Wáng Mào Zhāng."
Tàizǔ sighed, saying:
"If only I could obtain this man to be my general,
the world would not be difficult to pacify!"
The Liáng troops were defeated again.
When Jǐngrén’s army returned,
the Liáng troops chased them urgently.
Jǐngrén judged that they could not simply flee.
He sent his second-in-command, Lǐ Qiányù (李虔裕), with one brigade (lǚ) of troops to set up an ambush at the base of the mountain to await them.
He kept his main army back and did not proceed,
dismounted his saddle, and slept.
Qiányù hastily shouted, saying:
"The pursuing troops are arriving!
You should flee quickly.
I, Qiányù, will stop them, even if it means death!"
Jǐngrén replied:
"I shall fight here too."
Qiányù pleaded three times.
Jǐngrén then proceeded,
and Qiányù finally died in battle.
For this reason, the Liáng troops could not catch up,
and Jǐngrén returned with his entire army intact.
Jǐngrén served Xíngmì,
and became the Military Commissioner (Tuánliànshǐ) of Rùnzhōu (潤州).
When Xíngmì died,
his son Wò (渥) entered from Xuānzhōu (宣州) and was installed.
He appointed Jǐngrén to take his place and govern Xuānzhōu.
After Wò was installed,
he demanded the return of old items from Xuānzhōu.
Jǐngrén regretted them and did not hand them over.
Wò grew angry,
and attacked him with troops.
Jǐngrén fled to Qián Liú (錢鏐).
Liú nominated Jǐngrén to govern as the Jìedùshǐ (節度使, Military Governor) of Xuānzhōu.
Liáng Tàizǔ had long known Jǐngrén.
He therefore sent men to summon him.
Jǐngrén returned to Liáng via a secluded path.
He was retained as the Jìedùshǐ of the Níngguó Army (寧國軍),
and given the additional title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì (同中書門下平章事).
For a long time,
he was not utilized in any capacity.
He was allowed to participate in the ranks of the Chancellors (Zǎixiàng),
and merely served as an attendant during court sessions.
In the fourth year of Kāipíng (開平, 910 CE),
Jǐngrén was appointed Northern Commander of Pacification (Běimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ).
Leading the troops of Hán Qíng (韓勍) and Lǐ Sī’ān (李思安), he marched to attack Zhào (趙).
When they traveled to Wèizhōu,
the Director of the Astronomical Bureau (Sītiān Jiān) said:
"The Moon is obscured (wanes/eclipsed).
It is unfavorable for launching troops."
Tàizǔ urgently summoned Jǐngrén and the others to return.
Soon after, he sent them out again.
When Jǐngrén had already departed,
Tàizǔ recalled the words of the diviner (shùzhě).
He swiftly dispatched an envoy to stop Jǐngrén at Wèi (魏) and wait.
Jǐngrén had already passed Xíng (邢) and Míng (洺).
The envoy caught up to him.
Jǐngrén did not comply with the edict,
and advanced his camp to Bǎixiāng (柏鄉).
In the first month, on the day Gēng Yín (庚寅), of the first year of Qiánhuà (乾化, 911 CE),
there was an eclipse of the sun.
Jìng Xiáng (敬翔), the Administrator of the Bureau of High Governance (Chóngzhèng Shǐ), reported to Tàizǔ, saying:
"The troops cause worry!"
Tàizǔ ate late (out of anxiety) because of this.
On that same day,
Jǐngrén fought against the Jìn people,
suffering a great defeat at Bǎixiāng.
Jǐngrén returned and complained to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ said:
"I already know this.
It must be that Hán Qíng and Lǐ Sī’ān treated you lightly as an outsider,
and failed to obey your command (Jiédù)."
He then dismissed Jǐngrén and sent him to his residence.
A few months later,
he fully restored his offices and titles.
When Mòdì was installed,
he appointed Jǐngrén as the Huáinán Commander of Pacification.
He attacked Lú (廬) and Shòu (壽).
When the army passed Dúshān (獨山),
there was a shrine to Yáng Xíngmì on the mountain.
Jǐngrén prostrated twice, wailed, and departed.
They fought at Huòshān (霍山).
The Liáng troops were defeated and fled.
Jǐngrén stayed behind to cover the rear and fought fiercely.
Because of this, the Liáng army was not severely routed.
Jǐngrén returned to the capital.
He died from a carbuncle.
He was posthumously granted the title Tàiwèi (太尉).
Hè Guī (賀瓌)
Hè Guī, courtesy name Guāngyuăn (光遠),
was a native of Púzhōu (濮州).
He served Zhū Xuān (朱宣) of Yùnzhōu as the Overall Commander (Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ).
Liáng Tàizǔ attacked Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾) at Yănzhōu (兗州).
Xuān sent Guī, along with Hé Huáibǎo (何懷寶) and Liŭ Cún (柳存), leading ten thousand troops to rescue Yănzhōu.
Guī hastened toward Dàibīnguăn (待賓館),
intending to cut off the Liáng supply route.
Liáng Tàizǔ was campaigning and advancing to Zhōngdū (中都).
He captured a surrendered soldier,
who reported that Guī’s troops were advancing toward Dàibīnguăn.
He divined using Liù Rén (六壬) methods.
He obtained
"Zhǎn Guān" (斬關, Breaking the Pass),
and considered it auspicious.
He then selected elite troops and rode swiftly for a hundred lĭ (里) overnight,
planning to arrive at Dàibīn first to intercept Guī.
But the night was dark,
and the troops lost their way.
At dawn, they arrived east of Jùyě (鉅野),
where they encountered Guī’s troops.
They attacked them.
Guī and the others were severely defeated.
Guī fled.
The Liáng troops urgently pursued him.
Guī realized his road was blocked.
He climbed a height and shouted loudly, saying:
"I am Hè Guī!
Do not kill me!"
Tàizǔ rode swiftly to capture him,
and simultaneously captured Huáibǎo and several tens of others.
They forced over three thousand of their soldiers to surrender.
On that day,
a great wind carried sand, obscuring the sky.
Tàizǔ said:
"Is Heaven angry because I killed too few people?"
He immediately killed all three thousand surrendered soldiers.
He then bound Guī, Huáibǎo, and the others, bringing them below the walls of Yănchéng (兗城) to entice Jǐn.
Jǐn did not accept the offer.
Tàizǔ consequently executed Huáibǎo and more than ten others,
but spared Guī alone.
Guī was deeply moved that Tàizǔ had not killed him,
and swore to dedicate his life in service.
He followed Tàizǔ in pacifying Qīngzhōu,
and was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Cáozhōu (曹州).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was successively promoted to Prefect of Xiāngzhōu (相州).
During Mòdì’s reign,
he was promoted to Commander of the Left Dragon and Tiger Guards (Zuǒ Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn),
and Jìedùshǐ of Xuānyì Army (宣義軍).
The name of the divination figure (guà).
In the first year of Zhēnmíng,
the Wèi troops revolted.
Hè Délún surrendered to Jìn.
The King of Jìn entered Wèizhōu.
Liú Yè was defeated at the old Yuánchéng,
fleeing to Líyáng.
Bèi, Wèi, Míng, and Cí prefectures all submitted to Jìn.
The Jìn army captured Yángliú.
Emperor Mò then appointed Guī as the Commander-in-Chief for Pacification and Investigation (Zhāotǎoshǐ),
and he garrisoned at the Traveling Palace (Xíngtái) with Xiè Yànzhāng and others.
The Jìn army pressed Guī, setting up a stockade ten *lǐ* away,
and they held their ground against each other for over a hundred days.
Guī and Yànzhāng had a rift,
so he ambushed and killed him with armed soldiers.
Zhuāngzōng was delighted and said:
"When commanders are not in harmony,
the downfall of Liáng is imminent!"
He then ordered his army to send their old and sick back to Yè,
and with light troops, he attacked Púzhōu.
Guī pursued him from the Traveling Palace,
and they fought at Húliǔ Pō.
The Jìn people's baggage train was west of the formation.
Guī's army was about to close in on it;
the Jìn army fell into disarray.
(Guī's forces) killed their general Zhōu Déwēi
and seized all their baggage train.
Although the army had won,
the battleground had no Shi Mountain (Shí Shān).
At dusk,
the Jìn troops attacked it uphill.
Guī's army came down the hill to attack the Jìn troops.
Guī was utterly defeated.
Jìn then captured Púzhōu,
fortified Déshèng,
and set up stockades flanking the river.
Guī attacked the southern stockade with naval forces,
but could not succeed.
He returned his army to the Traveling Palace,
and died there of illness.
He was sixty-two years old.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shìzhōng.
He had a son, Guāngtú.
All those mentioned as having a son named "so-and-so"
served the Imperial Dynasty and were renowned.
Wáng Tán
Wáng Tán, courtesy name Zhòngměi,
was a man from Jīngzhào.
In his youth, he served Liáng Tàizǔ as a junior officer.
When Shàng Ràng attacked Liáng,
they fought at the Wèishì Gate.
Tán displayed bravery superior to all the other generals.
Tàizǔ thought highly of him,
and promoted him to Deputy Commander of the Vanguard (*Tàbái Fù Zhǐhuīshǐ*).
He followed Zhū Zhēn in recruiting soldiers in the eastern region,
and was successful in several battles.
When Liáng fought the Cài troops at Bǎnqiáo,
Lǐ Chóngyì’s horse stumbled
and he was captured by the Cài troops.
Tán raced to rescue him
and captured one of their generals as well.
He followed Tàizǔ in defeating Wèi at Nèihuáng
and was promoted to Commander of the Assault Vanguard (*Chōngshān Dū Yúhòu*).
He again followed Zhū Zhēn in attacking Xúzhōu,
where Tán captured one of their generals.
When the Liáng troops attacked Wáng Shīfàn,
Tán, with a single detachment, defeated Mìzhōu
and was appointed Prefect of Mìzhōu (*Cǐshǐ*).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Military Commissioner of the Bǎoyì Army (*Bǎoyìjūn Jiédùshǐ*),
and Commander-in-Chief for Pacification and Investigation of the Northeast Sector of Lùzhōu (*Lùzhōu Dōngběimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ*).
Wáng Jǐngrén was defeated at Bǎixiāng,
and the Jìn troops besieged Xíngzhōu.
Tàizǔ was greatly afraid
and wanted to personally lead the rescue effort.
Tán stopped Tàizǔ
and requested to personally resist the enemy.
He fought fiercely
and ultimately saved Xíngzhōu.
For his achievements, he was additionally given the title of Concurrent Chancellor (*Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*),
and advanced to be enfeoffed as Prince of Lángyá Commandery (Lángyá Jùnwáng).
When Yǒuguī was enthroned,
he was moved to govern Xuānhuà.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng, he was again moved to Kuāngguó.
At this time,
Zhuāngzōng had captured Wèibó.
Tán believed that all Jìn troops were in the region north of the Yellow River (Héběi),
so he led specialized troops westward out of Yīndì to attack Tàiyuán.
He failed and returned.
He was moved to govern Tiānpíng.
Tán once harbored vagrants and bandits under his command.
The troops under his command mutinied
and broke in and killed Tán.
He was fifty-eight years old.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor (*Tàishī*)
and given the posthumous name Zhōngyì.
Mǎ Sìxūn
Mǎ Sìxūn
was a man from Zhōnglí, Hāozhōu.
In his youth, he served the prefecture as a guest general (*Kèjiàng*).
He was talented, martial, and articulate.
When Liáng Tàizǔ attacked Hāozhōu,
the Prefect Zhāng Suì sent Sìxūn with the official seals and credentials to surrender to Liáng.
Yáng Xíngmì attacked Suì,
and Suì again sent Sìxūn to request troops from Tàizǔ.
Before the Liáng troops arrived,
Hāozhōu had already fallen.
Sìxūn had nowhere to go,
so he stayed and served Liáng.
Tàizǔ made him Commander of the Original Escort of the Xuānwǔ Army (*Xuānwǔjūn Yuáncóng Yāyá*).
When Tàizǔ marched west to attack Fèngxiáng,
he reached Huàzhōu
and sent Sìxūn to persuade Hán Jiàn.
Jiàn immediately surrendered.
In the second year of Tiānyòu,
Luó Shàowēi, intending to execute the garrison army (*Yájūn*),
requested troops from Liáng.
The daughter of Liáng, who was married into Wèi,
had just died.
Tàizǔ then sent Sìxūn with a thousand Imperial Guards (*Chángzhí*) as a ceremonial carriage procession to enter Wèi,
placing weapons within the carriages,
ostensibly to assist with the funeral.
Sìxūn was quartered at Tóngtái.
At night, he attacked the Shízhù Gate with troops from Xīnxiāng Town in Wèi,
entered, and welcomed Shàowēi's family
and guarded them.
He then gathered more Wèi armored troops and attacked the garrison army (*Yájūn*).
The garrison army did not know where the soldiers had come from
and could not prepare defenses.
Over eight thousand of them were killed.
By daybreak, they were all wiped out.
Sìxūn died from severe wounds.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian (*Tàibǎo*).
Wáng Qiányù
Wáng Qiányù
was a man from Línyí, Lángyá.
He was robust, courageous, and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He made a living by hunting.
In his youth, he followed Zhūgě Shuǎng in the region between Qīng and Dì.
Later, Shuǎng became the Defense Commissioner of Rǔzhōu (*Fángyùshǐ*).
He led troops north to attack the Shātuó,
returned, entered Cháng'ān, and attacked Huáng Cháo.
Shuǎng's troops were defeated and surrendered to Cháo.
Cháo made Shuǎng the Military Commissioner of Héyáng (*Jiédùshǐ*).
In the third year of Zhōnghé,
Sūn Rú captured Héyáng,
and Qiányù followed Shuǎng, fleeing to Liáng.
At that time,
Tàizǔ had newly established his administration.
The forces of Huáng Cháo, Qín Zōngquán, and others were flourishing.
Tàizǔ was frequently hard-pressed by them,
and Liáng did not yet have other commanders.
Therefore, he appointed Qiányù to lead the cavalry.
He always served as the vanguard to attack Cháo between Chén and Cài.
He captured several of his stockades.
Cháo fled.
The Liáng troops pursued him
and fought at Wànshèng Post (*Wànshèng Shù*).
The bandits were defeated and went east.
Qiányù's merit was considerable,
so (Tàizǔ) memorialized that Qiányù be made Prefect of Yìzhōu (*Cǐshǐ*).
After Huáng Cháo had left,
Qín Zōngquán attacked Xǔ and Zhèng,
becoming an enemy territory to Liáng.
In over a hundred battles, both large and small,
Qiányù consistently achieved merit.
Qín Zōngxián attacked the southern border of Biàn.
Tàizǔ sent Qiányù to resist Xián at Wèishì.
(Qiányù) was defeated in battle
and lost a deputy general.
Tàizǔ was enraged
and detained Qiányù in the army camp.
Mèng Qiān of Xíngzhōu surrendered to Liáng
but was besieged by the Jìn people.
Tàizǔ sent Qiányù with a hundred elite soldiers to rush quickly.
At night, they broke the Jìn siege
and entered Xíngzhōu.
At daybreak,
Liáng banners and standards were erected atop the city wall.
The Jìn people thought that relief troops had arrived
and consequently retreated.
Subsequently, the Jìn troops returned.
Qiān seized Qiányù and surrendered to Jìn.
(Qiányù) was killed.
Xiè Yànzhāng
Xiè Yànzhāng,
was a man from Xǔzhōu.
When young, he served Gě Cóngzhōu.
Cóngzhōu, pitying his quick intelligence and kindness,
raised him as a son,
and taught him military strategy.
Cóngzhōu used a thousand coins placed in a large tray
to represent the formation of ranks, units, and detachments,
showing him the principles of advancing, retreating, entering, and exiting.
Yànzhāng mastered all of it.
When he grew up,
he served Liáng Tàizǔ as a cavalry general.
At that time,
Hè Guī was skilled at deploying infantry,
while Yànzhāng, along with Mèng Shěnchéng and Hóu Wēnyù, were all skilled at leading cavalry.
Shěnchéng and Wēnyù commanded no more than three thousand men,
but Yànzhāng, having more troops, was even more capable.
Yànzhāng served Mòdì,
and was successively promoted to Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Kuāngguó Army.
In the fourth year of Zhēnmíng (918 CE),
Jìn attacked Héběi.
Hè Guī was the Commissioner of Northern Campaigns (Běimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ),
and Yànzhāng was the Commissioner of Arraying Ranks (Páizhèn Shǐ),
stationed at Xíngtái.
As a general,
Yànzhāng treated Confucian scholars courteously.
Although residing in the army camp,
he often wore Confucian attire.
When facing the enemy and commanding the troops,
he possessed the solemn dignity of a commander,
and galloped back and forth,
swift as wind and rain.
When the Jìn men saw his ranks were neat and orderly,
they said among themselves:
"Xiè Yànzhāng must be here!"
Such was the esteem he held among the enemy.
Guī inwardly resented him.
Yànzhāng accompanied Guī on a scouting trip outside the camp.
Guī pointed to a place and said to Yànzhāng:
"This ground has high ridges and mounds,
but the center is flat and open.
It is a suitable place for an entrenched camp."
Soon after, the Jìn troops established a camp there.
Guī suspected Yànzhāng had secretly informed Jìn,
and disliked him even more.
Yànzhāng already had a feud with Zhū Guī, the Deputy Commander of Cavalry and Infantry (Mǎbù Dū Yúhòu).
Guī wished to fight quickly,
but Yànzhāng requested to maintain a secure defense to wear out the enemy.
Guī then falsely accused Yànzhāng of planning rebellion.
Guī hosted a feast for the officers the next morning,
and had Guī conceal armored men to kill him.
Shěnchéng and Wēnyù were also harmed.
Biography Twelve of the Táng Officials: Guō Chóngtāo
Guō Chóngtāo,
was a man from Yànmén, Dàizhōu,
and served as the Commissioner of Training (Jiàoliàn Shǐ) for Hédōng.
He was intelligent and quick-witted,
good at responding to situations,
and praised for his competence.
When Zhuāngzōng was the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng),
Mèng Zhīxiáng was the Palace Gate Commissioner (Zhōngmén Shǐ),
and Chóngtāo was the Deputy Commissioner.
The role of the Palace Gate Commissioner
involved participating in managing critical affairs.
Previously,
Wú Gǒng, Zhāng Qiánhòu, and others had all subsequently incurred guilt while serving as Palace Gate Commissioners.
Zhīxiáng was afraid
and requested an external appointment.
Zhuāngzōng said:
"If you wish to avoid this responsibility,
you should recommend someone who can replace you."
Zhīxiáng then recommended Chóngtāo as Palace Gate Commissioner,
and he became greatly trusted and favored.
The Jìn troops besieged Zhāng Wénlǐ at Zhènzhōu,
but failed to take it for a long time.
Meanwhile, Wáng Dū of Dìngzhōu brought in the Qìdān to invade.
When the Qìdān reached Xīnlè,
all the Jìn men were afraid
and wanted to lift the siege and depart.
Zhuāngzōng had not yet decided.
Chóngtāo said:
"The Qìdān came
not to save Wénlǐ;
they were merely tempted by Wáng Dū with promises of profit.
Moreover, Jìn has recently defeated the Liáng army;
we should capitalize on our renewed momentum
and must not suddenly retreat out of fear."
Zhuāngzōng agreed with him,
and consequently defeated the Qìdān.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Chóngtāo as Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū) and Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ).
The Liáng general Yànzhāng defeated Déshèng.
The Táng army retreated east to defend Yángliǔ,
and Yànzhāng besieged it.
Zhuāngzōng ascended the rampart
and saw that Yànzhāng had constructed deep trenches to cut off the Táng army.
He treated it lightly,
and laughed, saying:
"I know his intent.
He wishes to prolong the conflict to exhaust us."
He immediately led close-combat troops out to fight,
but was shot at by Yànzhāng's concealed forces,
and returned in heavy defeat.
Zhuāngzōng asked Chóngtāo:
"What strategy should we employ?"
At this time,
Táng had already captured Yùnzhōu.
Chóngtāo therefore said:
"Yànzhāng is besieging us here,
but his true goal is to capture Yùnzhōu.
I request several thousand troops
to occupy the lower reaches of the river,
and construct a fort at a strategically vital location,
under the pretext of reinforcing Yùnzhōu.
Yànzhāng will certainly come to contest it.
Once his troops are divided,
we can then plan our move.
However, the work of building with rammed earth is difficult to complete quickly.
Your Majesty should daily challenge the enemy with elite troops,
to prevent Yànzhāng's forces from moving east.
In ten days, the fort will be complete."
Zhuāngzōng agreed that this was sound.
He then dispatched Chóngtāo and Máo Zhāng, leading several thousand men, to travel by night.
Wherever they passed, they drove off and plundered the inhabitants,
destroyed houses, and cut down trees.
They crossed the river and constructed a fort east of Bózhōu.
They supervised the work day and night,
and the fort was completed in six days.
Yànzhāng indeed led his troops to attack it urgently.
The weather was extremely hot at the time,
and Yànzhāng's soldiers died from the heat.
They failed to take the fort in the assault,
losing more than half of their men.
They returned, hurrying toward Yángliǔ.
Zhuāngzōng met and attacked them,
and subsequently defeated them.
Kāng Yánxiào fled from Liáng to Táng.
He first met Chóngtāo.
Chóngtāo invited him into his inner chamber,
and learned everything about the strengths and weaknesses of Liáng.
At this time,
Zhuāngzōng’s army was at Cháochéng,
and Duàn Níng’s army was facing the river (Lín Hé).
Since Táng lost Déshèng,
Liáng troops constantly plundered Chán and Xiāng [prefectures],
and captured Líyáng and Wèizhōu.
Furthermore, Lǐ Jìtāo rebelled with Zé Lù and joined Liáng.
The Qìdān repeatedly violated Yōu and Zhuō.
When they also heard Yánxiào say that Liáng was calling up troops from all the circuits to launch a major campaign,
all the Táng generals were worried and confused,
believing that success or failure was unpredictable.
Zhuāngzōng was troubled by this,
and asked his generals.
The generals all said:
“Táng captured Yùnzhōu,
but it is difficult to hold across the river.
It would be better to abandon Yùn and give it to Liáng,
and instead take Wèizhōu and Líyáng to the west.
Use the river as the boundary,
and arrange a truce with Liáng,
so that we do not attack each other.
Perhaps this will allow us to plan for the future.”
Zhuāngzōng was displeased.
He retired to his tent,
summoned Chóngtāo, and asked for a plan.
Chóngtāo said:
“Your Majesty raised troops for a righteous cause.
Generals and soldiers are exhausted by warfare, and the populace suffers from providing transport.
This has gone on for more than ten years.
Moreover, the great standard has now been raised.
North of the river,
everyone stretches their necks, hoping for success and anticipating peace.
Now we have acquired a single Yùnzhōu;
if we cannot hold it and abandon it,
even if you wish to set the river as the boundary,
who will guard it for Your Majesty?
Furthermore, before Táng lost Déshèng,
merchants and traders from all directions,
and tribute supplies would surely gather there.
Firewood, fodder, rations, and provisions
were accumulated like mountains.
Since losing the southern wall
and securing Yángliú,
the roads have shifted,
and more than half [of the supplies] have been consumed or lost.
The five prefectures of Wèi and Bó,
had poor autumn harvests.
If we exhaust the people to collect taxes,
it will not sustain us for several months.
How can this be a time to restrain the army and prolong the conflict?
Since Kāng Yánxiào arrived,
I have completely grasped the reality of Liáng.
This is truly the time Heaven wills their destruction!
I ask Your Majesty to divide your troops to guard Wèi,
fortify Yángliú,
and drive straight from Yùn [zhōu] to smash their nest.
In less than half a month,
the realm will be settled!”
Zhuāngzōng was greatly delighted and said:
“This is the endeavor of a true hero!”
He then consulted the office of Si Tiān.
The Si Tiān official reported:
“The year is not favorable for employing troops.”
Chóngtāo said:
“In ancient times, when commissioning a general,
they would cut through the ‘Inauspicious Gate’ to depart.
Moreover, the strategy for victory has already been determined;
how can mere trivial conventional talk
be trusted?”
Zhuāngzōng immediately issued an order to the army,
sent their families back to Wèi,
crossed Yángliú that night,
entered from Yùnzhōu, and attacked Biàn.
It took eight days to destroy Liáng.
Zhuāngzōng credited the achievement,
bestowed an iron certificate upon Chóngtāo,
appointed him Shìzhōng and Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Chéngdé Army,
and maintained his previous position as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Pīmìshǐ).
Zhuāngzōng and the generals had conquered the realm with military force,
but Chóngtāo had never been on the battlefield.
He was merely ranked first among those who aided the foundation of the state through strategic counsel,
holding positions both military and civil.
Consequently, he took the affairs of the realm upon himself,
and avoided nothing when encountering difficult matters.
However, the eunuchs and performers who held influence
found him particularly inconvenient.
Initially,
Chóngtāo and the eunuch Mǎ Shàohóng both served as Zhōngmén Shǐ,
and Shàohóng ranked above him.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
both men were due to become Pīmìshǐ.
But Chóngtāo did not want Shàohóng to be ranked above him,
so he made Zhāng Jūhàn Pīmìshǐ,
and Shàohóng Xuānhuī Shǐ.
Shàohóng felt wronged by the loss of position and held resentment.
Chóngtāo then established the Internal Audit Commissioner (Nèi Gōu Shǐ),
and put Shàohóng in charge of it.
All the money and grain of the realm that passed through the Tax and Treasury office,
went through the Nèi Gōu office.
Soon after, the paperwork became excessively complicated,
causing corruption in the prefectures and counties.
The office was abruptly abolished,
and Shàohóng regarded [Chóngtāo] with even more hostility.
Chóngtāo grew quite fearful.
He spoke to the sons and younger relatives of his old friends, saying:
“I assisted the Son of Heaven in taking the realm.
Now that the great task is complete,
minor factions are rising up together.
I wish to avoid them,
return and guard Zhènyáng,
and perhaps escape disaster.
Would this be possible?”
The sons and younger relatives of his old friends replied:
“The vulgar saying goes: ‘The one who rides the tiger,
cannot dismount due to circumstances.’
Now your authority and position are already immense,
and many below you harbor resentment and jealousy.
If you lose your position for a moment,
how can you keep yourself safe?”
Chóngtāo said:
“What should I do?”
They replied:
“The Empress has not yet been established,
but Lady Liú is favored.
You should request that Lady Liú be established as Empress,
and also propose many reforms beneficial to the people regarding the realm’s governance.
Only then should you step back and ask to retire.
The Son of Heaven knows that you have great merit and no fault,
and will certainly not permit you to leave.
In this way, outwardly you will have the reputation of shunning power,
and inwardly you will have the aid of the Empress.
Moreover, you will be beloved by the people of the realm.
Even if there are slanders or intrigues,
how can they move you?”
Chóngtāo thought this was wise.
He then submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of Lady Liú as Empress.
Chóngtāo was usually honest.
Only since entering Luò [yáng],
did he begin to accept bribes and gifts from all directions.
The sons and younger relatives of his old friends spoke to him about this.
Chóngtāo said:
“My position encompasses both military and civil leadership,
and my salary and gifts amount to millions.
How could I lack these amounts?
Now the Regional Commanders
are mostly former Liáng generals,
and all of them are the sovereign’s ‘cut-sleeve and hooked-arrow’ men.
If I refuse them all outright,
will they not feel uneasy?
Moreover, if it is stored in private homes,
how is it different from the public treasury?”
The following year,
when the Son of Heaven was to perform the sacrifice in the Southern Suburb,
he presented all that he had stored,
to aid in rewards and supplies.
After Zhuāngzōng performed the sacrifice,
he then established Lady Liú as Empress.
Chóngtāo repeatedly submitted memorials expressing his situation,
requesting that according to the old Táng regulations,
the position of Pīmìshǐ be returned to the inner officials (eunuchs),
and concurrently resigning from the Zhènyáng governorship.
Favorable imperial edicts did not permit this.
Chóngtāo said again:
“When your servant followed Your Majesty’s army to Cháochéng,
we fixed the plan to defeat Liáng.
Your Majesty patted my back and promised, saying: ‘When the affair is settled,
I will grant you one circuit.’
Now the realm is unified,
and talented men are advancing together.
Your servant is weary.
I request to retire according to that promise.”
Zhuāngzōng summoned Chóngtāo and said:
“The promise at Cháochéng
was to grant you one circuit,
not to permit you to leave.
If you wish to abandon Us,
where shall We be safe?”
Chóngtāo then proposed twenty-five points concerning the realm’s governance,
and they were put into practice.
Lǐ Sìyuán became the Military Governor of Chéngdé Army,
and Chóngtāo was transferred to Zhōngwǔ.
Chóngtāo consequently reported that his authority and position had reached their peak,
speaking with great earnestness.
Zhuāngzōng said:
“How can I, who occupy the highest position in the realm,
allow you to have no land of your own?”
Chóngtāo’s repeated resignations did not cease,
so [Zhuāngzōng] withdrew the transfer order,
and he remained Shìzhōng and Pīmìshǐ.
In the summer of the third year of Tóngguāng,
continuous heavy rain did not cease,
a great flood damaged the people’s fields,
and many people were swept away and died.
Zhuāngzōng worried that the palace was hot and humid and uninhabitable,
and contemplated acquiring a high tower to escape the summer heat.
A eunuch stepped forward and said:
"I saw that when Cháng'ān was in its prime,
Dàmíng and Xīngqìng Palaces had hundreds of towers and pavilions.
Now the Great Palace is inferior to the homes of former high officials and chancellors."
Zhuāngzōng said:
"I possess the wealth of the realm;
how can I not be able to construct one tower?"
So he sent the Commissioner of Palaces and Parks, Wáng Yǔnpíng, to supervise its construction.
The eunuch said:
"Guō Chóngtāo’s brow is never relaxed;
he constantly grudges expenditure for the sake of taxes and levies.
Even if Your Majesty wishes to undertake construction,
how can it be achieved?"
Zhuāngzōng then sent someone to ask Chóngtāo, saying:
"Previously, when I faced Liáng across the river Hé,
even in bitter cold or intense heat,
wearing armor and mounting a horse,
I did not find it tiring.
Now I reside deep within the palace,
shaded by vast halls,
yet I cannot endure the heat.
Why is this?"
Chóngtāo replied:
"Formerly, Your Majesty took the entire realm to heart,
but now you concern yourself only with your personal self.
Hardship and ease—
the nature of your concerns is different.
This situation is naturally so.
I hope Your Majesty does not forget the hardship of founding the dynasty,
and remains always as you were by the river Hé,
then even the most oppressive heat can instantly change to refreshing coolness."
Zhuāngzōng was silent.
Ultimately, he sent Yǔnpíng to begin building the tower,
and Chóngtāo indeed strongly remonstrated against it.
A eunuch said:
"Chóngtāo’s mansion
is no different from the Imperial Residence;
how could he know Your Majesty suffers from the heat!"
Consequently, slander and malicious rumors penetrated even deeper.
The magistrate of Hénán County, Luó Guàn,
was a firm and straightforward man,
and was quite known to Chóngtāo.
Guàn maintained his integrity and upheld the law.
He did not accept requests or influence from powerful magnates.
When eunuchs and court performers had requests,
the letters piled up on his desk,
but he did not reply to a single one.
He showed all of them to Chóngtāo.
Chóngtāo frequently spoke of this to the Emperor,
causing the eunuchs and performers to gnash their teeth in hatred.
Ever since the time of the former Táng dynasty, when Zhāng Quányì was Governor of Hénán,
many county magistrates came from his faction,
and Quányì treated them like personal servants and dependents.
When Guàn took the post,
he served Quányì without subservience.
County residents who relied on Quányì to act unlawfully
were all investigated and executed.
Quányì was furious,
and once sent someone to inform Empress Liú,
asking her to subtly report on Guàn’s actions.
Meanwhile, the attendants collaborated day and night to expose Guàn’s shortcomings.
Zhuāngzōng had not yet found an opportunity to act.
When the Empress Dowager died,
and was buried at Kūnlíng.
The mausoleum was in Shòu'ān.
Zhuāngzōng traveled to the site of the mausoleum's construction,
but the roads were muddy,
and the bridges were broken.
Zhuāngzōng stopped his carriage and asked:
"Who is the responsible official?"
A eunuch said:
"It falls under Hénán's jurisdiction."
He immediately summoned Guàn.
When Guàn arrived,
he replied:
"I initially did not receive an imperial decree;
I request that the responsible official be questioned."
Zhuāngzōng said:
"This is within your jurisdiction;
whom else should I ask again?"
He immediately placed Guàn in prison.
The jailers beat and tortured him,
leaving his body entirely covered in wounds.
The next day,
an edict was issued to execute him.
Chóngtāo remonstrated, saying:
"Guàn’s offense is minor;
for failing to repair bridges and roads,
the law does not warrant the death penalty."
Zhuāngzōng angrily said:
"The Empress Dowager’s hearse is about to depart,
the Son of Heaven’s carriage travels back and forth,
yet the bridges and roads are not repaired.
If you claim he is innocent,
that shows you are forming a clique!"
Chóngtāo said:
"Although Guàn has committed an offense,
he should have been fully investigated and the law carried out by the proper authorities.
Your Majesty, holding the prestige of the sovereign of the ten thousand chariots,
is angry at a single county magistrate,
causing the people of the realm
to say that Your Majesty administers justice unfairly.
This is the fault of your servants."
Zhuāngzōng said:
"Guàn
is the one you favor.
I authorize you to make the final decision!"
Then he rose and entered the palace.
Chóngtāo followed him,
continuing his argument without stop.
Zhuāngzōng personally closed the palace gates,
and Chóngtāo was unable to enter.
Guàn was subsequently executed.
The following year, Shǔ was invaded.
They discussed choosing a commanding general.
At that time, Míngzōng was the Zǒngguǎn,
and was expected to lead the campaign.
But Chóngtāo was endangered by slander,
and planned to achieve great merit as a strategy for his own security.
So he said:
"The Qìdān are causing trouble on the northern frontier,
and they cannot be repelled without the Zǒngguǎn.
Wèi Wáng Jìjí,
is the heir apparent of the state,
but he has not yet established great merit.
Furthermore, a Prince serving as Yuánshuài
is customary from the Táng dynasty."
Zhuāngzōng said:
"Jìjí
is a mere boy;
how can he be entrusted with such a great undertaking?
You must select his deputy for me."
Before Chóngtāo could speak,
Zhuāngzōng said:
"I have found him.
No one can replace you."
He then appointed Jìjí as the Xīnán Miàn Xíngyíng Dūtǒng (Commander-in-Chief of the Southwest Campaigning Army),
and Chóngtāo as the Zhāotǎo Shǐ (Pacification Commissioner).
All military and political decisions rested with Chóngtāo.
When the Táng army entered Shǔ,
every place they passed surrendered.
Wáng Yǎn’s younger brother, Zōngbì,
secretly offered surrender terms to Chóngtāo,
requesting to be the Xīchuān Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (Interim Military Governor of Xīchuān).
Chóngtāo promised him the rank of Jiédù Shǐ.
When the army reached Chéngdū,
Zōngbì moved Yǎn to the western palace,
took all of Yǎn’s concubines, performers, and treasures, and presented them to Chóngtāo and his son Tínghuì.
He also submitted petitions along with the people of Shǔ to Wèi Wáng,
requesting that Chóngtāo remain to govern Shǔ.
Jìjí became quite suspicious of Chóngtāo.
Chóngtāo had no way to clear his name,
so he used this incident as a pretext to execute Zōngbì along with his younger brothers, Zōngwò and Zōngxūn.
He confiscated their family wealth.
The people of Shǔ were greatly frightened.
*Chóng Tāo* had always intensely disliked eunuchs,
and once said to *Jì Jí*:
"The Prince has the merit of having conquered *Shǔ*.
When the army returns,
you will certainly be made Crown Prince.
Wait until after His Majesty enjoys ten thousand years [i.e., dies],
and you should remove all the eunuchs.
As for the fanned horses (*shàn mǎ*),
they also must not be ridden."
*Jì Jí*'s Supervising Officers *Lǐ Cóngxí* and others saw that *Chóng Tāo* monopolized military affairs,
and their hearts were already discontented.
When they heard these words,
they all gnashed their teeth,
thinking how they might scheme against him.
When *Zhuāng Zōng* heard of the conquest of *Shǔ*,
he sent the eunuch *Xiàng Yánsì* to console the army.
*Chóng Tāo* did not go out to the suburbs to receive him,
and *Yánsì* was greatly angered.
Consequently, he conspired with *Cóngxí* and the others to frame *Chóng Tāo*.
When *Yánsì* returned,
he presented the registers of *Shǔ*,
listing 300,000 soldiers,
9,500 horses,
7,000,000 weapons,
2,530,000 *shí* of grain,
1,920,000 *mín* of cash,
220,000 *liǎng* of gold and silver,
20,000 units of pearls, jade, rhino horn, and ivory,
and 500,000 bolts of patterned silks, damasks, and gauze.
*Zhuāng Zōng* said:
"People said *Shǔ* was the richest state under Heaven,
is this all that was obtained?"
*Yánsì* then stated that the treasures of *Shǔ* had all gone to *Chóng Tāo*,
and further falsely accused him of harboring rebellious intentions,
and planning to endanger the Prince of *Wèi*.
*Zhuāng Zōng* was enraged,
and sent the eunuch *Mǎ Yànguī* to *Shǔ*
to observe *Chóng Tāo*'s behavior and intentions.
*Yànguī* reported this to Empress *Liú*,
and Empress *Liú* instructed *Yànguī* to forge an imperial edict for the Prince of *Wèi* to execute *Chóng Tāo*.
*Chóng Tāo* had five sons.
Two of them followed him to their deaths in *Shǔ*,
and the rest were all killed.
Everything acquired from the conquest of *Shǔ*
was confiscated.
When *Míng Zōng* ascended the throne,
he decreed that *Chóng Tāo* be allowed to be buried,
and granted his old residence in *Tàiyuán* to his two grandsons.
When *Chóng Tāo* was in power,
even high officials like Chancellor *Dòu Lú Gé* and *Wéi Yuè* all eagerly attached themselves to him.
The personal name of *Chóng Tāo*'s father was *Hóng*.
*Gé* and the others immediately took advantage of another matter
and proposed changing the *Hóngwén* Hall to the *Chóngwén* Hall.
Because his surname was *Guō*,
people therefore assumed he was a descendant of *Zǐyí* [Guō Zǐyí],
and *Chóng Tāo* subsequently believed it to be true.
When he marched to attack *Shǔ*,
passing by *Zǐyí*'s tomb,
he dismounted, wailed loudly, and then departed.
Those who heard of it found it quite laughable.
However, *Chóng Tāo* was completely loyal to the state,
and possessed great strategic vision.
After he had already conquered *Shǔ*,
he sent envoys to issue an admonition, based on the power and virtue of the *Táng* (Dynasty), to *Nánzhào* and the various *Mán* tribes,
intending to use this opportunity to pacify and attract them.
This can be called having ambition!
*Ān Chónghuǐ*
*Ān Chónghuǐ*
was a man from *Yìngzhōu*.
His father, *Fúqiān*,
served the *Jìn* state as a general,
and was famous for his bravery and skill.
When *Liáng* attacked *Zhū Xuān* in *Yùnzhōu*,
the *Jìn* troops went to rescue *Xuān*.
*Xuān* was defeated,
and *Fúqiān* died in battle.
*Chónghuǐ* served *Míng Zōng* from a young age,
and he was intelligent, quick-witted, cautious, and respectful.
When *Míng Zōng* was stationed at *Ānguó*,
he made *Chónghuǐ* the Chamberlain of the Middle Gate (*Zhōngmén Shǐ*).
When the military mutiny occurred at *Wèi*,
all major plans and strategies discussed
were decided by *Chónghuǐ* and *Huò Yànwēi*.
When *Míng Zōng* ascended the throne,
*Chónghuǐ* was appointed General-in-Chief of the Left Guard (*Zuǒ Lǐng Jūn Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn*) and Commissioner of Military Affairs (*Shūmì Shǐ*),
concurrently holding the position of Military Governor (*Jiédù Shǐ*) of *Shānnán Dōngdào*.
He firmly declined the appointments.
He was then changed to Minister of War (*Bīngbù Shàngshū*),
retaining his former responsibilities.
He held office for six years,
and was progressively promoted to Grand Councilor (*Shìzhōng*) concurrently serving as Director of the Chancellery (*Zhōngshū Lìng*).
From the time *Chónghuǐ* was Chamberlain of the Middle Gate,
he was already deeply trusted,
and as a founding meritorious official,
he held positions of military and secret importance.
Matters, regardless of size,
were all subject to his participation and decision,
and his power shook the whole realm.
Although he was completely loyal and worked diligently,
sometimes providing benefits and improvements,
he relied on his achievements and boasted of imperial favor,
wielding authority and reward/punishment independently.
Without the help of wise gentlemen around him,
his own singular considerations
resulted in the creation of calamity and discord,
eventually leading to harm for both minister and ruler,
and almost exterminating his own clan.
This is indeed deplorable.
Once, when *Chónghuǐ* was going out,
and passed the gate of the Censorate (*Yùshǐ Tái*),
*Diànzhí* officer *Mǎ Yánwù* rushed past his vanguard.
*Chónghuǐ* became angry,
and immediately executed *Yánwù* at the gate of the Censorate before submitting a report to the throne.
At that time,
*Sāng Hóngqiān*, a soldier of the *Suíjià Tīngzi* Army,
beat and injured the Recorder and Staff Supervisor (*Lùshì Cānjūn*) of *Xiāngzhōu*;
the Attendant Commander of Horses and Troops (*Qīncóng Bīngmǎshǐ*) *Ān Qián*
galloped his horse and rushed past the Chancellor's vanguard.
*Hóngqiān* was executed for his crime,
but *Qián* merely suffered a beating with the rod.
Because *Chónghuǐ* had executed *Yánwù*,
he requested that an imperial decree be issued concerning the disposal of the matter.
*Míng Zōng* had no choice but to comply,
and from then on, no Censor or Remonstrance Official dared to speak up.
Chancellor *Rèn Huán*, presiding over the Three Offices (*Sānsī*),
disputed with *Chónghuǐ* over their respective duties,
but could not prevail.
*Huán* grew angry,
pleaded illness,
and retired to *Cízhōu*.
When *Zhū Shǒuyīn* rebelled in *Biànzhōu*,
*Chónghuǐ* immediately sent someone to ride to *Huán*'s home with a forged edict,
executed *Huán*, and only then reported the matter.
He falsely accused *Huán* of conspiring with *Shǒuyīn*,
and *Míng Zōng* was unable to challenge any of these actions.
However, *Chónghuǐ* feared that the world would criticize him,
so he took the accumulated debts owed to the Three Offices, amounting to over 2,000,000 [cash/units],
and requested that they be waived.
He hoped to please the people and thereby silence criticism.
*Míng Zōng* had no choice
but to issue an edict pardoning and eliminating these debts.
His independent wielding of authority and reward/punishment
often involved incidents of this nature.
At this time,
when officials from all quarters presented memorials,
they first reported to *Chónghuǐ* before submitting them to the Emperor.
*Hénán* County presented auspicious grain (*jiā hé*),
having five ears on one stalk.
*Chónghuǐ* looked at it and said:
"It is fake."
He flogged the presenter and sent him away.
*Lǐ Rénfú* of *Xiàzhōu* presented a white eagle.
*Chónghuǐ* rejected it,
and the next day,
he reported:
"Your Majesty issued a decree forbidding the presentation of eagles and hawks throughout the realm,
yet *Rénfú* violated the decree by presenting an eagle.
Your servant has already rejected it."
When *Chónghuǐ* was gone,
*Míng Zōng* secretly sent someone to retrieve the eagle and bring it in.
Another day,
he was exercising the eagle in the western suburbs,
and instructed his attendants:
"Do not let *Chónghuǐ* know!"
*Sùzhōu* presented a white rabbit.
*Chónghuǐ* said:
"Rabbits are secretive and sly,
even if they are white, what good are they?"
He thus rejected it without reporting it [to the Emperor].
Although *Míng Zōng* was generally generous and magnanimous,
his nature was that of a barbarian (*Yídí*),
and he was decisive in execution.
The horses overseen by *Tián Lìngfāng*, Commander of the Horse Pastures,
were thin and many had died.
He was impeached and sentenced to death.
*Chónghuǐ* remonstrated, saying:
"If the world hears that a military commander was killed
merely because of horses,
this is called valuing animals and degrading human beings."
*Lìngfāng* was consequently spared the death penalty.
*Míng Zōng* sent *Hóu Sān* of the *Huíhú* (Uighur) people with a hasty diplomatic dispatch to his nation.
When *Hóu Sān* reached *Lǐquán* County,
the county was normally isolated,
and had no relay horses.
Furthermore, the magistrate, *Liú Zhīzhāng*, was out hunting,
and the horses were not supplied promptly.
*Hóu Sān* hastily reported this to the Emperor.
*Míng Zōng* was furious.
He chained *Zhīzhāng* and brought him to the capital,
intending to execute him.
*Chónghuǐ* spoke on his behalf in a measured way,
and *Zhīzhāng* consequently avoided execution.
These instances of his complete loyalty and beneficial advice
were also of this nature.
Chóng Huǐ, having already taken the world as his own responsibility,
thereupon desired internally to plan for the state (shè jì),
and externally to restrict the power of the various feudal lords (zhū hóu).
However, he lightly believed the slanders of Hán Méi,
and severed relations with Qián Liú, who was a vassal;
he merely caused Yàn Wēn to fall to death,
but he could not remove the threat posed by Lù Wáng;
Lǐ Yán was sent out, and Zhī Xiáng became disloyal;
Rén Jǔ had not yet arrived when Dǒng Zhāng rebelled;
the four quarters were disturbed and agitated,
and armies simultaneously arose,
like throwing fat onto a fire to stop it,
which only served to accelerate the trouble.
This is what is called planning based on singular insight,
the very source from which misfortune arises.
Qián Liú occupied the two Zhè regions (Liǎng Zhè),
and was titled as the King covering Wú and Yuè (Wú Yuè),
from the time of the Liáng dynasty up to Zhuāng Zōng,
his ritual treatment was always exceptional,
merely keeping him loosely controlled (jī mí) as a vassal.
When Míng Zōng ascended the throne,
Liú sent an envoy to pay respects at the capital (Jīng Shī),
and sent a message to Chóng Huǐ,
but the etiquette was disrespectful.
Chóng Huǐ was angry,
but had not yet found a way to act,
so he dispatched his favored official Hán Méi and Deputy Attendant Officer Wū Zhāo Yù to serve as envoys again to Liú.
Méi, relying on Chóng Huǐ's power,
repeatedly insulted and humiliated Zhāo Yù,
and taking advantage of intoxication and rudeness,
struck him with a horsewhip.
Liú wanted to report this matter (to the throne),
but Zhāo Yù believed this would disgrace the state,
and firmly stopped him.
When Méi returned,
he slandered back to Chóng Huǐ, saying:
“When Zhāo Yù met Liú,
he bowed and danced, proclaiming himself a subject (of Liú),
and privately informed Liú of affairs of the imperial court.”
Zhāo Yù was implicated and died in the censor's prison (Yù Shǐ Yù),
then an edict was issued stripping Liú of his official ranks and titles,
and making him retire as Grand Preceptor (Tài Shī).
Consequently, the Qián clan was completely cut off from the Táng dynasty!
Lù Wáng Cóng Kē was the Military Commissioner (Jié Dù Shǐ) of Hé Zhōng,
Chóng Huǐ considered that Cóng Kē was not a son of the Lǐ clan (the imperial family),
and would surely become a threat to the state later,
so he secretly planned against him.
When Cóng Kē was reviewing his cavalry at Huáng Lóng Zhuāng,
his Internal Headquarters Commander Yáng Yàn Wēn sealed the city gates and rebelled.
Cóng Kē sent someone to speak to Yàn Wēn, saying:
“I treated you generously,
why must you rebel?”
The reply was:
“Yàn Wēn is not rebelling;
I received a declaration from the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shū Mì Yuàn),
requesting you, sir, to quickly return to the imperial court!”
Cóng Kē fled to Yú Xiāng,
and rode swiftly to report the change (up to the capital).
Míng Zōng suspected the matter was unclear,
and wished to investigate the reasons behind it.
Therefore, he sent Fàn Yūn, the Commander-in-chief of the Palace Directorate (Diàn Zhí Dū Zhī), to bestow upon Yàn Wēn a golden belt, official robes, and a horse with a golden saddle and bridle,
and appointed Yàn Wēn as the Prefect (Cì Shǐ) of Jiàng Zhōu,
in order to lure and bring him in.
Chóng Huǐ firmly requested the use of military force.
Míng Zōng, having no choice,
dispatched the Palace Guard Commander Yào Yàn Chóu and the Western Capital Resident Administrator Suǒ Zì Tōng to lead troops and suppress him,
but strictly warned them, saying:
“Bring Yàn Wēn to me alive,
I will personally interrogate him regarding this matter.”
Yàn Chóu and the others attacked and captured Hé Zhōng,
hoping to comply with Chóng Huǐ's unspoken desire,
and executed Yàn Wēn to silence him.
Chóng Huǐ led the assembled officials in offering congratulations.
Míng Zōng became greatly enraged and said:
“Since Our family matter is unresolved,
it is improper for you gentlemen to offer congratulations!”
Cóng Kē was dismissed from his post as commander,
and resided in his mansion in Qīng Huà Lǐ.
Chóng Huǐ repeatedly hinted to the Chief Ministers (Zǎi Xiàng),
saying that since Cóng Kē had failed to hold his defense,
he ought to be punished.
Féng Dào consequently presented a memorial requesting that the law be applied.
Míng Zōng angrily said:
“My son was victimized by treacherous people,
and the matter has not been fully clarified.
For you gentlemen to utter these words,
is it because you do not wish My son to remain among the living?”
Zhào Fèng then stated:
“The principle of the *Chūn Qiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) regarding censuring commanders,
is intended to encourage those who serve as ministers.”
Míng Zōng said:
“This is not truly the intention of you gentlemen!”
Dào and the others retreated in fear and trembling.
A few days later,
Dào and the others requested the same thing again.
Míng Zōng looked around at his attendants and spoke of other matters.
The next day,
Chóng Huǐ then personally presented his arguments.
Míng Zōng said:
“How do you, sir, wish to deal with him?
I will follow your suggestion!”
Chóng Huǐ said:
“This is a matter between father and son,
it is improper for a subject to speak upon it;
Your Majesty alone must decide!”
Míng Zōng said:
“When I was a petty officer,
I could not provide enough clothing and food for myself.
This boy carried lime for me,
and picked up horse manure,
in order to support and sustain us.
Now that I am honored as the Son of Heaven (Tiān Zǐ),
can I alone not shelter him?
Even if I allow him to stay confined to his private residence,
how does this affect public affairs!”
Chóng Huǐ consequently did not dare to speak of it again.
Mèng Zhī Xiáng governed Xī Chuān,
Dǒng Zhāng governed Dōng Chuān.
Both men harbored rebellious intentions.
Chóng Huǐ restricted and suppressed them in every matter,
striving to control their treacherous hearts.
Whenever the defending commanders of the two Chuān regions were replaced,
he often employed those close to him and whom he trusted,
and they were always accompanied by elite troops,
gradually ordering them to divide and garrison the various prefectures,
in anticipation of any emergency.
The two men perceived this,
believing they were being plotted against,
and became increasingly uneasy.
Subsequently, Lǐ Yán was sent to be the Army Supervisor (Jiān Jūn) of Xī Chuān.
Zhī Xiáng was greatly enraged,
and executed Yán.
Furthermore, Làng Zhōu was split off to become the Bǎo Níng Commandery,
and Lǐ Rén Jǔ was made the Military Commissioner (Jié Dù Shǐ) to restrict Zhāng,
and also to reduce his territory.
Zhāng used his troops to attack and kill Rén Jǔ.
Consequently, both men rebelled.
The Táng troops garrisoned in Shǔ,
accumulated to thirty thousand men.
Later, Zhī Xiáng killed Zhāng,
and jointly occupied the two Chuān regions,
and the elite troops of the Táng were all trapped in Shǔ.
Initially,
when Míng Zōng visited Biàn Zhōu,
Chóng Huǐ proposed,
that they should seize the opportunity to attack Wú,
but Míng Zōng considered it difficult.
Later, Lǐ Lín, the Minister of Revenue (Hù Bù Shàng Shū), received word from a Wú spy:
“Xú Zhī Gào wishes to offer the state of Wú to declare vassalage (chēng fān),
and requests a single word from Lord Ān (referring to Chóng Huǐ) as a token of sincerity.”
Lín immediately brought the spy to meet Chóng Huǐ.
Chóng Huǐ was greatly pleased and believed the story,
and thus gave a jade belt to the spy,
ordering him to deliver it to Zhī Gào as a token of trust,
which was worth a thousand strings of cash (mín).
Initially, he did not report this matter (to the emperor).
More than a year later,
no inquiry or message arrived from Zhī Gào,
so he finally memorialized to have Lín demoted to Army Commander (Xíng Jūn Sī Mǎ).
Subsequently, Lǐ Xíng Dé, Commander of the Běng Shèng Division, and Zhāng Jiǎn, a Decarch (Shí Jiàng), reported a treachery,
stating:
“Lǐ Qián Huī, the Vice Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shū Mì Chéng Zhǐ), told his retainer Biān Yàn Wēn that: ‘Chóng Huǐ is secretly hiring soldiers and gathering troops,
repairing armor and weaponry,
wishing to personally attack Wú.
Moreover, he has private dealings with spies.’”
Míng Zōng questioned Chóng Huǐ about this.
Chóng Huǐ was terrified,
and requested a thorough investigation of the matter.
Míng Zōng initially had some doubts about Chóng Huǐ,
but all the high ministers and attendants spoke up in his defense.
Afterward, his suspicion lessened.
He then informed Chóng Huǐ of Yàn Wēn's words,
and subsequently interrogated Yàn Wēn in court,
who fully confessed to his falsehood.
Thereupon, the Emperor and his minister looked at each other and wept.
Yàn Wēn, Xíng Dé, and Jiǎn were all punished by having their clans executed.
Chóng Huǐ consequently requested to be relieved of his position.
Míng Zōng comforted him, saying:
“The matter has been clarified;
be sure not to dwell on it in your heart!”
Chóng Huǐ continued to argue for and request dismissal without cease.
Míng Zōng angrily said:
“If I let you, sir, leave,
We shall not worry about having no one (to replace you)!”
He ordered the Wǔ Dé Envoy Mèng Hàn Qióng to go to the Central Secretariat (Zhōng Shū),
and urge Féng Dào and the others to discuss Chóng Huǐ’s replacement.
Féng Dào said:
“If the gentlemen truly care for Lord Ān (Chóng Huǐ),
and allow him to resign and leave,
this would be alleviating his misfortune.”
Zhào Fèng believed that a high minister should not be lightly moved (from office).
Consequently, Fàn Yán Guāng was made the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shū Mì Shǐ),
but Chóng Huǐ remained in his office as before.
Dǒng Zhāng and others rebelled.
Shí Jìngtáng was dispatched to suppress them.
However, the road to Chuān was treacherous and difficult,
and transporting grain was extremely hard.
For every *shí* expended,
only one *dǒu* arrived.
West of the passes (Guān),
the people suffered greatly from these transport duties,
and frequently fled to gather in the mountains and forests, becoming bandits.
Míngzōng said to Chónghuǐ:
"Since the situation is like this,
I must go myself."
Chónghuǐ said:
"This is the responsibility of your subject."
Thereupon, he requested permission to go.
When the people of Guānxī (west of the passes) heard that Chónghuǐ was coming,
they were already agitated with fear.
But Chónghuǐ traveled several hundred *lǐ* a day,
alarming and shocking people far and wide.
He urgently supervised the grain transport,
which continued ceaselessly day and night.
Those who collapsed and died on the roads
were countless.
When Chónghuǐ passed through Fèngxiáng,
the Jìedùshǐ Zhū Hóngzhāo welcomed him into his private chamber,
and ordered his wife and children to attend to him with great care.
When Chónghuǐ was drunk,
he spoke to Hóngzhāo, saying:
"Yesterday, I was slandered and framed,
almost failing to preserve myself.
Relying on the enlightened sagacity of the sovereign,
I was able to protect my family."
Thereupon, he sighed emotionally and wept.
After Chónghuǐ departed,
Hóngzhāo immediately rode to submit a memorial (to the emperor), saying:
"Chónghuǐ harbors resentment and grudges.
He must not be allowed to reach the field headquarters (Xíngyíng),
lest he cause trouble."
Meanwhile, Mèng Hànqióng, the Xuānhuī Envoy, returned from serving at the field headquarters,
and also spoke of the shocked and terrified state of the western people,
and consequently described Chónghuǐ’s transgressions and wickedness.
Chónghuǐ traveled as far as Sānquán,
when he was recalled.
Passing through Fèngxiáng,
Hóngzhāo refused to receive him.
Chónghuǐ, fearing (for his life),
quickly hurried toward the capital (Jīngshī).
Before he arrived,
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng.
Once Chónghuǐ had been dismissed,
those seeking favor with the emperor vied to find fault with him.
The eunuch Ān Xīlún,
because he had secretly associated with Chónghuǐ,
and had often stealthily monitored the affairs and activities inside the palace with Chónghuǐ,
was arrested and executed in the marketplace when the matter came to light.
Chónghuǐ became even more fearful,
and consequently submitted a memorial requesting retirement due to old age.
He retired with the title of Tàizǐ Tàishī (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince).
However, Lǐ Cóngzhāng was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng,
and Yuè Yànchóu was sent to lead troops to Hézhōng to guard against trouble.
Chónghuǐ’s sons, Chóngxù and Chóngzàn,
who were guarding the capital,
heard the imperial decree was issued,
and immediately ran to their father.
When Chónghuǐ saw them,
he cried out in surprise:
"How did you manage to come here!"
After a moment, he said:
"This is not your own intention;
you have been sent by others.
I will repay the state with my death.
What else is there to say!"
Thereupon, he had his two sons shackled and sent to the capital.
When they reached Shǎnzhōu,
they were imprisoned.
Míngzōng further sent Zhái Guāngyè to Hézhōng
to observe Chónghuǐ’s actions and intentions,
instructing him:
"If he harbors rebellious intentions,
then conspire with Cóngzhāng to handle it."
He also sent a eunuch as an envoy to Chónghuǐ.
When the envoy saw Chónghuǐ,
he wept and wailed incessantly.
Chónghuǐ asked the reason,
and the envoy said:
"People say you have rebellious intentions,
and the court has sent Yuè Yànchóu to lead troops here!"
Chónghuǐ said:
"Even my death would not fully discharge my responsibility.
How could I abruptly burden the court by raising an army,
thus increasing the worries of the enlightened sovereign?"
When Guāngyè arrived,
Cóngzhāng led troops to surround Chónghuǐ’s residence,
and entered to bow in the courtyard.
Chónghuǐ descended and returned the bow.
Cóngzhāng used a staff to strike him on the head.
Chónghuǐ’s wife rushed forward, embraced him, and cried out:
"It is not too late for the Grand Duke (Lìng Gōng) to die;
why act so hastily!"
Cóngzhāng struck him again on the head.
The husband and wife both died,
and blood filled the courtyard.
Cóngzhāng inspected and searched his family's wealth;
it amounted to less than a few thousand *mín*.
Míngzōng issued an imperial decree,
citing his severance of relations with Qián Liú,
which led to the rebellions of Mèng Zhīxiáng and Dǒng Zhāng,
and also his plan to attack Wú,
as his crimes.
His two sons were also executed,
but his remaining descendants were spared.
When Chónghuǐ was convicted,
knowing he was certain to die,
he sighed and said:
"I certainly deserve to die,
but I regret that I could not, along with the state, eliminate the Prince of Lù (Lù Wáng)!"
This was his regret.
Alas!
Officials have long lost their proper functions!
When I read the archives of the Liáng (Dynasty),
I saw Jìng Xiáng and Lǐ Zhèn serving as Chóngzhèngyuàn Envoys.
Whenever they received the sovereign's command,
they would proclaim it to the Chief Ministers (Zǎixiàng) who would then execute it.
If the Chief Ministers had matters that were not currently visible (i.e., not urgent) but required the sovereign's decision,
or if they had received a decree and needed to request clarification again,
they would prepare a written memorandum (*jìshì*) and enter (the palace).
They presented it through the Chóngzhèng Envoy to be heard (by the sovereign).
Upon receiving the decree, the envoy would again proclaim it and leave.
The Chóngzhèng Envoy of Liáng
held the duties of the Púmì (Bureau) in Táng.
This was essentially the responsibility of managing input and output (of documents/decrees).
In Táng, this position was usually held by eunuchs.
When it came to Liáng, in order to guard against the dangers (of eunuch power),
they began to use educated men (shìrén) instead.
It included providing advice and participating in strategy discussions within the court,
but they never exclusively executed external affairs.
It was not until Chóng Tāo and Chónghuǐ held the post
that the name Púmì (Bureau) of Táng was revived.
However, their power became equal to that of the Chief Ministers.
Later generations followed this,
and consequently split the administration into two:
civil affairs were entrusted to the Chief Ministers (Zǎixiàng),
and military affairs were entrusted to the Púmì (Bureau).
Since the responsibilities of the Púmì became heavy,
the Chief Ministers lost their proper functions from that time on.
The term *Jìshì*
is like the current submission and report system used in the Academy of Scholars (Xuéshìyuàn).
Today, written correspondence between scholar-officials is called
*jiăntiě* (memos/notes),
but the common populace still refers to it as
*jìshì*
Biography of Táng Subjects, Chapter 13: Zhōu Déwēi.
Zhōu Déwēi, courtesy name Zhènyuăn,
was a man from Măyì, Shuòzhōu.
As a person, he was brave and highly intelligent,
capable of judging the number of enemy troops by observing the dust they raised.
His appearance was magnificent and imposing;
his expression did not change even when he smiled.
People who saw him
found him composed.
He served the Prince of Jìn as a cavalry general,
gradually advancing to Commander of the Tiělín Army.
He followed (the Prince) in defeating Wáng Xíngyú,
and for his merit, he was promoted to Commander within the Headquarters (Yánèi Zhǐhuīshǐ).
His childhood name (xiăozì) was Yángwǔ.
During the era between Liáng and Jìn,
the bravery of Zhōu Yángwǔ was renowned throughout the land.
When the Liáng army besieged Tàiyuán of Jìn,
(the Liáng commander) ordered his troops, saying:
"Whoever can capture Zhōu Yángwǔ alive will be made an Inspector (Cìshǐ)."
There was a fierce general named Chén Zhāng,
nicknamed "Chén the Wild Ogre" (Chén Yěyì).
He habitually rode a white horse and wore vermilion armor to distinguish himself.
He charged in and out of the ranks,
seeking Zhōu Yángwǔ,
determined to capture him alive.
The Prince of Jìn warned Déwēi, saying:
"Chén the Wild Ogre wants to capture you to gain the post of Inspector.
When you see the white horse and vermilion armor,
you must prepare carefully!"
Déwēi laughed and said:
"Chén Zhāng merely likes to boast.
How does he know that the Inspector post won't be made by your subject?"
He then instructed his troops, saying:
"When you see the white horse and vermilion armor,
you should feign retreat and avoid him."
Both armies formed ranks.
Déwēi disguised himself in humble clothing and mingled among the common soldiers.
Chén Zhāng came out to challenge,
and when the armies first engaged,
Déwēi’s troops saw the man on the white horse with vermilion armor,
and consequently retreated.
Chén Zhāng indeed brandished his spear and chased them hard.
Déwēi waited until Zhāng had passed,
and swung an iron hammer to strike him.
He hit Zhāng, who fell off his horse,
and was then captured alive.
Liáng attacked Yān.
Jìn dispatched Déwēi, leading fifty thousand men, to attack Liáng on behalf of Yān.
He captured Lùzhōu,
and was transferred to be Dàizhōu Cìshǐ and Nèi Wài Fān Hàn Mǎ Bù Jūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (Area Commander-in-Chief of the Internal and External Barbarian and Han Cavalry and Infantry Forces).
The Liáng army abandoned Yān and attacked Lù,
surrounding it with a double enclosure (jiāchéng).
The defending general of Lùzhōu, Lǐ Sìzhāo, shut the gates and held firm,
while Déwēi and the Liáng army held a stalemate outside for over a year.
Sìzhāo and Déwēi had long held a grudge against each other.
When the Jìn Wáng (Prince of Jìn) was gravely ill,
he said to Zhuāngzōng:
“The Liáng army has besieged Lù,
and Déwēi and Sìzhāo have enmity.
I worry deeply about this!”
After the Wáng's funeral rites were being held in the coffin chamber,
Zhuāngzōng had just ascended the throne.
He killed his uncle Kèníng,
and the state had not yet stabilized.
Moreover, Jìn’s heavy forces
were entirely under Déwēi outside.
All the Jìn people were afraid.
Zhuāngzōng sent someone to inform Déwēi of the mourning and the difficulty concerning Kèníng,
and to recall his army.
When Déwēi heard the command,
he returned his army to Tàiyuán that very day,
leaving his soldiers outside the city walls.
He entered on foot
and prostrated himself before the coffin, weeping bitterly, almost collapsing.
Only then did the Jìn people feel secure.
He subsequently followed Zhuāngzōng and again attacked the Liáng army,
breaking the double enclosure,
and his relationship with Lǐ Sìzhāo became as friendly as before.
For the merit of breaking the double enclosure,
he was appointed Zhènwǔ Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
In the autumn of the seventh year of Tiānyòu,
Liáng dispatched Wáng Jǐngrén, leading seventy thousand troops from Wèi, Huá, Biàn, and Sòng, to attack Zhào.
Zhào Wáng Wáng Róng begged Jìn for aid.
Jìn sent Déwēi to first garrison Zhàozhōu.
In winter,
the Liáng army arrived at Bǎixiāng.
The Zhào people reported the emergency.
Zhuāngzōng personally led the troops out of Zànhuáng
and met Déwēi at Shíqiáo.
They advanced to five *lǐ* from Bǎixiāng
and encamped north of the Yěhéběi River.
The Jìn forces were few,
but the armies led by Jǐngrén—Shénwēi, Lóngxiāng, and Gǒngchén—
were all Liáng elite troops.
Their men, horses, armor, and helmets were decorated with woven silk, embroidery, gold, and silver.
Their brilliance illuminated the sun;
the Jìn army was unsettled just by looking at them.
Déwēi encouraged his multitude, saying:
“These are merely mercenaries and vendors from Biàn and Sòng,
who have only decorated their exteriors.
There is nothing inside them to fear!
One suit of their armor is worth tens of thousands of cash.
Capturing them is simply accumulating resources for us.
Do not merely gaze upon them and cherish them.
You must exert yourselves and go seize them.”
He then withdrew and reported to Zhuāngzōng, saying:
“The Liáng troops are very sharp.
We should not contend with them yet.
It is advisable to retreat a little and wait for them.”
Zhuāngzōng said:
“I have led a solitary army out a thousand *lǐ*;
it is advantageous for us to fight quickly.
