If we do not seize this opportunity to attack them immediately,
allowing the enemy to realize the size of our forces,
then we will have no strategy left to employ!”
Déwēi said:
“That is not so.
The Zhào people can defend cities but cannot fight in the field.
Our advantage in achieving victory
lies in cavalry.
Flat plains and wide fields
are where cavalry excels.
Now we are encamped beside the river,
pressing against the enemy’s camp gate.
This is not a place where we can use our strengths.”
Zhuāngzōng was displeased
and retired to sleep in his tent.
None of the generals dared to enter and see him.
Déwēi said to the Jiānjūn Zhāng Chéngyè:
“The Prince is angry at this old soldier.
The reason for not fighting immediately
is not cowardice.
Moreover, our army is small, and we are right next to the enemy’s camp gate.
What we rely on
is merely the separating river.
If Liáng manages to cross the river by boat,
we will be wiped out!
It is better to retreat the army to Guōyì,
luring the enemy out of their camp.
By harassing and tiring them out,
we can achieve victory through strategy.”
Chéngyè went in and reported:
“Déwēi is an experienced general who understands military affairs.
Please do not disregard his words!”
Zhuāngzōng immediately rose and said:
“I was just thinking about it.”
Shortly thereafter, Déwēi captured a Liáng scouting troop
and asked them what Jǐngrén was doing.
They replied:
“He is preparing several hundred boats
to use as a pontoon bridge.”
Déwēi led them to see Zhuāngzōng,
who laughed and said:
“It turned out just as you predicted, Duke.”
Accordingly, they retreated the army to Guōyì.
In the morning, Déwēi sent three hundred cavalry to knock on the Liáng camp and issue a challenge,
while he personally followed up with three thousand elite troops.
Jǐngrén was enraged
and led out his entire army.
He fought skirmishes with Déwēi over dozens of *lǐ*,
reaching Guō Nán.
Both armies deployed their formations.
The Liáng army stretched horizontally for six or seven *lǐ*.
The armies of Biàn and Sòng were on the west,
and the armies of Wèi and Huá were on the east.
Zhuāngzōng spurred his horse and climbed a high point,
looked down, and happily said:
“This flat plain with shallow grass,
where we can advance or retreat,
is truly our place of victory!”
He then sent someone to inform Déwēi, saying:
“I shall lead the way for you,
and you may follow up the advance.”
Déwēi remonstrated, saying:
“The Liáng army came out lightly and traveled far.
They fought skirmishes with us.
They must not have had time to carry provisions,
and even if they were able to carry them,
they would not have had time to eat.
Before noon
both men and horses will be hungry.
If we attack them when they are about to retreat, we will win.”
All the other generals also agreed with this.
By the time of the *wèi* and *shēn* hours,
dust rose from the eastern flank of the Liáng army.
Déwēi advanced with drums beating and shouts,
waving his banner toward their western flank and saying:
“The Wèi and Huá armies are running!”
He then waved his banner toward their eastern flank and said:
“The Liáng army is running!”
The Liáng formation shifted
and could not be reorganized.
They all subsequently fled
and suffered a massive defeat.
They were pursued from Guō all the way to Bǎixiāng,
with corpses stretching for dozens of *lǐ*.
Jǐngrén barely escaped with only ten-odd cavalrymen.
Since Liáng and Jìn began their struggle,
they had fought dozens of battles,
but never suffered such a great defeat.
Liú Shǒuguāng usurped the title of Emperor in Yān.
Jìn sent Déwēi, leading thirty thousand men, to exit Fēihú and attack him.
Déwēi entered Qígōu Guān,
captured Zhuōzhōu,
and subsequently besieged Shǒuguāng in Yōuzhōu,
breaching the outer city wall.
Shǒuguāng shut the gates and held the defense.
The Jìn army had conquered all the states and districts of Yān,
but Yōuzhōu alone had not fallen.
It was besieged for over a year before it was finally broken.
For this merit, he was appointed Lúlóng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Although Déwēi was a great general,
he always personally rode among the soldiers amidst the arrows and stones.
Shǒuguāng’s fierce general, Shàn Tíngguī,
saw Déwēi in the formation
and said:
“That is Zhōu Yángwǔ!”
He then brandished his spear, spurred his horse, and chased him.
Déwēi feigned retreat.
Calculating that Tíngguī was about to reach him,
he turned sideways and slightly withdrew.
Tíngguī’s horse was currently charging
and could not be stopped.
Allowing him to pass slightly,
Déwēi furiously wielded his bludgeon and struck him.
Tíngguī fell from his horse
and was subsequently captured.
Zhuāngzōng and Liú Xún were stalemated at Wèi.
Liú Xún secretly led his army out through Huángzé Guān by night to raid Tàiyuán.
Déwēi, with a thousand cavalry from Yōuzhōu, entered Tǔmén to track him.
Liú Xún reached Lèpíng
but, encountering rain, could not advance and returned.
Déwēi and Liú Xún both moved east,
racing toward Línqīng.
Línqīng had grain stockpiled,
and was also the supply route for the Jìn army.
Déwēi raced ahead and occupied it first,
which is why Zhuāngzōng was ultimately able to corner Liú Xún’s army and defeat it.
Zhuāngzōng was brave and loved warfare,
especially eager to encounter the enemy.
Zhōu Déwēi was an old general,
who always sought to maintain gravity to blunt the enemy's edge;
therefore, when he deployed troops,
he constantly sought the enemy's weak points to achieve victory.
In the fifteenth year (of Tiānyòu, 918 CE),
Zhōu Déwēi led thirty thousand Yān soldiers,
and along with the armies of Zhèn, Dìng, and others, followed Zhuāngzōng at the Héshàng (Yellow River bank).
They advanced from Mǎjiādù and proceeded toward Línpú,
heading toward Biànzhōu.
The army encamped at Húliǔpō.
At dawn,
a scout reported,
“The Liáng army has arrived!”
Zhuāngzōng asked Zhōu Déwēi for advice on fighting.
Déwēi replied,
“This place is close to Biànzhōu,
only two nights' rest away.
The parents, wives, and children of the Liáng army are all within it,
and the fate of the Liáng state and its people depends on this single action.
We are an army deep in enemy territory,
facing troops fighting a battle of certain death.
We can win by strategy,
but it is difficult to contend with their brute force.
Moreover, our army arrived here first;
our provisions are prepared and our camp defenses are complete.
This is called 'using rest to await the weary army.'
Your Majesty should hold the army steady without moving,
and I request to use the cavalry to harass them,
preventing them from completing their camp defenses
and having no time to prepare firewood and meals.
By taking advantage of their exhaustion and fatigue to strike them,
we can achieve victory.”
Zhuāngzōng said,
“Our army has been at the Héshàng,
waiting for the enemy all day long.
Now that we see the enemy, if we do not attack,
what is the purpose of this campaign?”
He looked at Lǐ Cúnshěn and said,
“You, sir, take the baggage train first;
I shall protect your rear.”
He immediately urged the army forward and went out.
Zhōu Déwēi said to his son,
“I do not know where I will die!”
He advanced and formed a battle line upon meeting the Liáng army: the King stood in the center,
the armies of Zhèn and Dìng were on the left,
Zhōu Déwēi’s army was on the right,
and the baggage train was positioned west of the right flank.
Once the fighting began,
Zhuāngzōng led the Silver Lance Army and charged into the Liáng formation.
The Liáng army suffered a minor defeat,
but then they breached the Jìn baggage train.
When the baggage train saw the Liáng vermilion banners,
they all panicked and fled into Zhōu Déwēi’s army.
Déwēi’s army fell into disorder,
and the Liáng army pressed their advantage.
Zhōu Déwēi and his son were both killed in battle.
Zhuāngzōng and his generals stood together and wept, saying,
“I did not heed the words of the old general,
causing his father and son to meet this end!”
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted Déwēi the title Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
During Míngzōng’s reign,
the title was further elevated to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
and he was enshrined with Zhuāngzōng in the ancestral temple.
Jìn Gāozǔ later posthumously enfeoffed Zhōu Déwēi as the Prince of Yān.
His son, Guāngfǔ,
held the office of Administrator (Cìshǐ).
Fú Cúnshěn (Sons Yànchāo, Yànráo, Yànqīng)
Fú Cúnshěn, courtesy name Déxiáng,
was a native of Wǎnqiū, Chénzhōu.
His original name was Cún.
When young, he was lowly and poor.
He once violated the law and was condemned to death.
When facing execution,
he pointed to a collapsing wall nearby and looked at the officer in charge, saying,
“I wish to be executed there,
hoping to get wall earth to cover my corpse.”
The officer felt pity and granted his request,
moving him beneath the wall.
At that time, the commanding general was drinking wine.
He looked at his favorite courtesan
and thought of getting a good singer to accompany the wine.
The courtesan said,
“Fú Cún often sang for me,
and he is very good.”
The commanding general sent a rider to summon Cúnshěn.
Because Cúnshěn had been moved beneath the wall,
the execution had not yet been carried out.
He consequently went to answer the summons
and sang, which pleased the general,
and thus Cúnshěn was spared death.
Later, he served Lǐ Hǎnzhī.
He followed Hǎnzhī and submitted to Jìn.
The King of Jìn made him Commander of the Adopted Sons Army (Yì’ér Jūnshǐ),
granted him the surname Lǐ,
and named him Cúnshěn.
He followed the King of Jìn to attack Lǐ Kuāngchóu,
serving as the vanguard,
and defeated them at Jūyōng Pass.
He also followed the attack on Wáng Xíngyǔ,
and breached the Luóngquán Stockade.
For his merit, he was promoted to Provisional Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Jiǎnjiào Zuǒ Púshè).
He followed Lǐ Sìzhāo to attack Fénzhōu,
capturing Lǐ Táng,
and was promoted to Commander of the Foot Soldiers of the Left and Right Wings.
He then followed Sìzhāo to attack Lùzhōu,
receiving the surrender of Dīng Huì.
He followed Zhōu Déwēi to defeat the Liáng forces at Jiāchéng,
and was promoted to Administrator of Xīnzhōu and Commander of the Horse and Foot Soldiers of the Fān and Hàn.
When Jìn and Zhào attacked Yān,
Liáng came to Yān’s rescue,
attacking Zhào at Shēnzhōu
and besieging Tiáoxiàn.
Cúnshěn and Shǐ Jiàntáng’s forces were stationed at Xiàbó,
where they defeated and drove away the Liáng army.
He was promoted to concurrently hold the post of Commissioner of Militia for Xíngzhōu.
When Wèibó rebelled against Liáng and surrendered to Jìn,
Cúnshěn served as the vanguard,
stationed at Línqīng.
When Zhuāngzōng entered Wèi,
Cúnshěn protected the rear at Wèixiàn,
facing Liú Tàn at Xīnzī.
He followed Zhuāngzōng to defeat Tàn at the former Yuánchéng.
Yán Bǎo surrendered Xíngzhōu,
and Cúnshěn was appointed Military Governor of Ānguó Command (Jiédùshǐ).
When Máo Zhāng surrendered Cāngzhōu,
Cúnshěn was transferred to Hénghǎi
and additionally granted the title of Grand Councillor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
When the Qìdān besieged Yōuzhōu,
at that time Jìn and Liáng were confronting each other at the Héshàng.
If they mobilized troops,
they would be short of soldiers;
if they did not rescue it,
they feared losing it.
Zhuāngzōng was doubtful
and asked his generals for advice.
Only Cúnshěn believed they should rescue it,
saying,
“I only request the loan of five thousand cavalry, and that will be sufficient!”
Thereupon, Cúnshěn was dispatched to lead a detachment of troops to rescue the city,
and ultimately defeated and drove away the Qìdān.
He participated in the battle of Húliǔpō.
The Jìn army was initially defeated in the morning,
losing Zhōu Déwēi.
Cúnshěn and his son Yàntú fought bravely,
and in the evening they again defeated the Liáng army at Tǔshān.
They then took Déshèng
and built two cities on the north and south banks of the river.
The Jìn people called them
“The Twin Stockades” (Jiāzhài).
He was promoted to Grand Commander of the Horse and Foot Soldiers of the Domestic and Foreign Fān and Hàn.
When Zhū Yǒuqīan of Liáng surrendered Hézhōng and Tóngzhōu to Jìn,
Liáng sent Liú Tàn to attack Tóngzhōu.
Yǒuqīan requested aid,
so Cúnshěn and Lǐ Sìzhāo were dispatched to rescue him.
The Hézhōng troops were few and weak,
and the Liáng people usually treated them lightly,
and furthermore did not anticipate the speed of the Jìn army’s arrival.
Cúnshěn selected two hundred elite cavalry and mixed them with the Hézhōng soldiers to sally out and attack Tàn’s ramparts.
They feigned defeat and fled.
Tàn’s soldiers pursued them,
but the Jìn cavalry turned back and counterattacked,
capturing fifty of their cavalry.
The Liáng people realized they were Jìn troops
and were greatly astonished.
However, Hézhōng was short on provisions and had recently surrendered;
the people were somewhat ambivalent.
The Jìn army encamped at Cháoyì.
All the generals wanted a quick battle.
Cúnshěn said,
“If the Liáng army knows that we favor a swift battle,
they will encamp along the Wèi River,
cut off our supply route,
and try to wear us down by prolonging the conflict.
Then, we will be unable to advance or retreat,
which is the way to defeat.
It is better to relax our forces and show weakness,
awaiting an opportunity to launch a surprise attack.
This way we can achieve victory.”
So, he held the army steady and did not move.
After about ten days,
an observer of atmospheric signs reported:
“There is black vapor,
shaped like fighting chickens.”
Cúnshěn said,
“We can fight one battle now!”
He then advanced his troops to attack Tàn
and thoroughly defeated him.
Tàn closed his ramparts and did not venture out again.
Cúnshěn said,
“Tàn’s army is already defeated.
It is better to let them relax.”
He then rested his soldiers
and sent his subordinate general Wáng Jiànjí to graze horses in Shāyuàn.
Tàn assumed the Jìn army was becoming complacent,
and fled away by night.
Cúnshěn pursued and attacked him at the Wèi River,
again inflicting a major defeat.
Zhāng Wénlǐ assassinated Zhào Wáng Wáng Róng.
Jìn sent Yán Bǎo, Lǐ Sìzhāo, and others to attack him.
They often died in battle upon arrival.
Finally, [Jìn] sent Cúnshěn to defeat him.
Cúnshěn, as a general,
possessed strategy and cunning.
He fought over a hundred battles, large and small,
and never suffered a defeat.
He was equally famous as Zhōu Déwēi.
When Déwēi died,
Cúnshěn was the only one remaining among the old generals of Jìn.
When the Qìdān attacked Zhēlǔ,
Cúnshěn was then made Lúlóng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
At that time, Cúnshěn was already ill
and declined, refusing to go.
Zhuāngzōng sent someone to comfort and instruct him,
and forcefully ordered him to depart.
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng and entered Luò[yáng],
Cúnshěn considered that, being a great general,
he had not been able to participate in the meritorious deed of destroying Liáng.
He was resentful and depressed,
and his illness worsened.
He therefore requested to attend court at the Jīngshī.
At this time,
Guō Chóngtāo’s authority and position were already significant.
However, his fame and reputation had always been inferior to Cúnshěn’s,
and he was unhappy that Cúnshěn might come and surpass him.
He therefore obstructed the matter.
Cúnshěn's wife, Guō Shì, tearfully pleaded with Chóngtāo, saying:
“My husband has rendered service to the state,
and is an old acquaintance from your hometown.
How can you bear to let him die abandoned in a desolate field?”
Chóngtāo grew even angrier.
Cúnshěn submitted memorials repeatedly,
but they were always disallowed.
Cúnshěn lay on his pillow and sighed, saying:
“I, an old man, have served two lords for forty years.
Today, the world is unified as one family.
Even people from the remote lands of the four barbarians,
and down to generals of defeated states and men who shot the hook or cut the sleeve,
all can personally see the Son of Heaven
and present a cup [of wine] for his longevity.
Yet I alone am abandoned here to die.
Is this not fate?”
Chóngtāo estimated that Cúnshěn’s illness was already critical,
and then requested permission for him to come to court.
Cúnshěn was transferred to Xuānwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and he died in Yōuzhōu.
On his deathbed,
he admonished his sons, saying:
“When I was young, I left my hometown carrying a single sword.
In forty years, I attained the ranks of general and minister.
However, I achieved this by stepping on sharp points, braving blades, and passing through death to life.”
He then brought out over a hundred arrowheads that had struck his body throughout his life and showed them, saying:
“You must strive hard!”
Cúnshěn had three sons: Yànchāo, Yànráo, and Yànqīng.
Yànchāo was Fénzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Guō Cóngqiān assassinated Zhuāngzōng,
Míngzōng entered Luòyáng.
At this time,
Yànchāo was the Běijīng Inspector.
Yǒng Wáng Cúnbà fled to Tàiyuán.
Yànchāo met with the Garrison Commander, Zhāng Xiàn, to plan [Cúnbà’s fate].
Xiàn,
being a scholar,
and having served Zhuāngzōng the longest,
could not bear to betray the kindness [shown to him].
He wished to take Cúnbà in,
but Yànchāo did not agree.
Cúnbà was consequently killed.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
Yànchāo came to court.
Míngzōng valued his virtue
and praised him, saying:
“The peace in Hédōng,
relied on your strength.”
He appointed him Jiànxióng Jūn Liúhòu.
He was promoted to Běijīng Garrison Commander,
then transferred to govern Zhāoyì,
and later dismissed to serve as Shàng Jiāngjūn.
He was again appointed Tàiníng Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and then transferred to Ānyuǎn.
Wáng Xīquán, a slave in charge of Yànchāo’s treasury, stole his assets.
Yànchāo gradually confronted him about it.
The slave, in fear,
knocked on his gate at night,
claiming there was an emergency.
Yànchāo came out
and was killed.
He was posthumously granted the title Tàiwèi.
The second son, Yànráo,
was Biànzhōu Mǎbù Jūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
In the first year of Tiānchéng,
when 3,000 Biàn soldiers were sent to garrison Wǎqiáo Guān,
the Kònghè Commander, Zhāng Jiàn, rebelled.
He killed the Acting Prefect, Gāo Tì,
and forced Yànráo to become their commander.
Yànráo pretended to agree, saying:
“If you wish me to be your commander,
you must cease burning and looting.
Tomorrow, meet me at the Southern Headquarters with military rites.”
He secretly conspired with Páng Qǐ, the Gǒngyá Commander, to conceal armored troops within the headquarters.
The next day,
Jiàn and the others all gathered.
The hidden troops were deployed,
executing Jiàn and his group,
killing over four hundred people.
That same day, he transferred the affairs of the prefecture to the Judicial Inspector Wéi Yǎn.
Míngzōng issued an edict praising his loyalty and strategy.
Subsequently, he was repeatedly promoted to Zhāngshèng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ,
and served successively as Cìshǐ of the three prefectures: Cáo, Yí, and Ráo.
In the third year of Qīngtài,
he was appointed Zhōngzhèng Jūn Jiédùshǐ and Shìwèi Mǎbù Jūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ from his position as Ráo Zhōu Cìshǐ.
When Jìn Gāozǔ raised troops in Tàiyuán,
Yànráo accompanied Fèi Dì with the Imperial Guard troops to Héyáng.
When Fèi Dì was defeated,
Jìn Gāozǔ replaced Yànráo with Yáng Guāngyuǎn to command the imperial troops.
Yànráo was transferred to Yìchéng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Fàn Yánguāng rebelled,
Bái Fèngjìn stationed 3,000 Imperial Guard troops in Huázhōu.
Some soldiers committed crimes.
Fèngjìn arrested five men;
three of them were Yìchéng soldiers.
He executed them all together.
Yànráo was enraged.
The next day,
Fèngjìn, accompanied by a few riders, passed by Yànráo to apologize for executing the men without first informing him.
Yànráo said:
“Soldiers belong to their respective divisions.
How can Yìchéng soldiers be executed by you, sir?
Why is there no courtesy between host and guest?”
Fèngjìn became angry and said:
“When soldiers violate the law,
how can there be any distinction between ‘us’ and ‘them’?
Moreover, I have already apologized for my fault,
yet your anger does not subside.
Do you wish to join Yánguāng in rebellion?”
He brushed his sleeves and rose to leave.
Yànráo did not try to detain him.
Yànráo's subordinates raised a great clamor,
chased Fèngjìn, and killed him.
Yànráo did not stop them.
Soon after, the generals of the stationed army, Mǎ Wàn and others, heard of the disturbance.
They used their troops to capture Yànráo and send him to the Jīngshī,
and reported that Yànráo had consequently joined Yánguāng’s rebellion.
While traveling to Chìgāng,
Gāozǔ sent men to kill him.
An edict was issued stripping him of all his existing official ranks and titles.
Yànráo had no previous grudge against the founding of Jìn;
due to a sudden burst of anger,
he failed to control his troops.
The killing of Fèngjìn was already contrary to his original intention.
To be executed for rebellion
was not his crime!
Shǐ Jiàntáng (His son was Kuānghàn).
Shǐ Jiàntáng
was a man of Yànmén.
When the Jìn Wáng was Yànmén Jiédùshǐ,
his father, Jìngsī, was a Jiǔfǔ Dūdū.
He followed the Jìn Wáng into the Pass to defeat Huáng Cháo,
recapture the Jīngshī,
and strike Qín Zōngquán at Chénzhōu.
He often commanded cavalry as the vanguard.
When the Jìn Wáng pursued Huáng Cháo eastward to Yuānqú,
they returned via Liáng,
and encamped north of its city walls.
The Liáng Wáng hosted a feast at Shàngyuán Yì.
Only Jìngsī, Xuē Tiěshān, Hè Huíhú, and about ten others attended.
The Jìn Wáng became drunk,
and remained to spend the night at the Liáng postal station.
Liáng troops surrounded and attacked the station that night.
Jìngsī ascended the station tower,
shooting and killing more than ten Liáng soldiers.
Coincidentally, there was a heavy rain.
The Jìn Wáng was able to leave along with his attendants,
letting themselves down by rope from the gate of Wèishì to exit.
Jìngsī, however, was captured by the pursuing Liáng troops
and was killed.
In his youth, Jiàntáng served in the army as a staff officer.
From the time Jìn forced Dīng Huì to surrender,
and battled Liáng at Lùzhōu,
Jiàntáng was already the vanguard of the Jìn army.
Liáng soldiers were frequently killed by Jiàntáng,
and they cautioned each other always to avoid "Vanguard Shǐ."
When Liáng sent Wáng Jǐngrén to attack Zhào,
the Jìn army rescued Zhào.
Jiàntáng led the vanguard troops out through Jǐngxíng,
and fought at Bǎixiāng.
The Liáng army formed a square formation,
dividing its troops into two: the forces of Biàn and Sòng were on the left,
and the forces of Wèi and Huá were on the right.
Zhōu Déwēi attacked their left,
and Jiàntáng attacked their right.
The Liáng armies all fled,
and [Jìn] achieved a great victory.
For this merit, he was granted the title Jiǎnxiào Zuǒ Púshè.
In the ninth year of *Tiānyòu* (912),
*Jìn* attacked *Yān*.
*Yān* King *Liú Shǒuguāng* requested aid from *Liáng*.
*Liáng Tàizǔ* personally led troops to attack *Zhào*,
besieging *Zǎoqiáng* and *Tiáoxiàn* County.
At this time, all of *Jìn*'s elite troops were attacking *Yān* in the north;
only *Fú Cúnshěn* and *Jiàntáng* were stationed at *Zhàozhōu* with three thousand cavalry.
The *Liáng* army had already defeated *Zǎoqiáng*;
*Cúnshěn* secured the *Xiàbó* Bridge.
*Jiàntáng* divided five hundred cavalry under his command into five squads: one went to *Héngshuǐ*,
one to *Nángōng*,
one to *Xìndū*,
one to *Fùchéng*,
and he personally led the last one.
They were instructed to each capture ten *Liáng* foragers and meet at *Xiàbó*.
By dusk,
they had captured several dozen *Liáng* soldiers,
and killed them all.
They spared one person from each captured group,
allowed them to flee,
and instructed them:
"The *Jìn* King's army is about to arrive in great force."
The next day,
*Jiàntáng* led a hundred cavalry displaying *Liáng* banners,
mixing them with the foragers.
At dusk, they knocked on the gates of the *Liáng* camp,
killed the gate guards,
set fires and shouted loudly,
striking down several hundred people.
Furthermore, the *Liáng* foragers who had set out
had encountered *Jìn* soldiers in various places
and suffered losses.
Those whom *Jiàntáng* had spared and not killed
returned and all reported that the *Jìn* army was about to arrive.
*Liáng Tàizǔ* broke camp and departed that night.
The people of *Tiáoxiàn* pursued and attacked them.
The *Liáng* army abandoned an incalculable amount of supplies, equipment, and armor.
*Liáng Tàizǔ* was already ill,
and this incident made his condition worse.
The reason the *Jìn* army was subsequently able to consolidate its strength to conquer *Yān*
was due to the efforts of these two men.
Later, he followed *Zhuāngzōng* into *Wèibó*,
defeating *Liú Mǒu* at the old *Yuánchéng*.
Due to accumulated merit, he successively served as the Prefect (*cìshǐ*) of *Bèi* and *Xiāng* Prefectures.
In the eighteenth year (921),
the *Jìn* army attacked *Zhāng Wénlǐ* at *Zhènzhōu*.
*Jiàntáng*, leading the vanguard, took *Zhàozhōu*,
capturing its prefect, *Wáng Chán*.
When the troops reached *Zhènzhōu*,
*Jiàntáng* attacked the city gate,
was hit by a stray arrow and died,
at the age of forty-two.
*Jiàntáng*'s son was *Kuānghàn*.
He married the daughter of *Jìn Gāozǔ*,
who was known as the Eldest Princess of *Lǔguó*.
*Kuānghàn* served as a general,
being profound, resolute, and strategic.
He treated subordinates with courtesy,
and when speaking with his immediate troops (*bùqǔ*), he never failed to address them by name.
He successively held the posts of Overall Commander (*Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ*) of the Infantry of the *Tiānxíong* Army and Overall Commander of the Cavalry of the *Zhāngshèng* Army.
Serving *Jìn*, he was Prefect (*cìshǐ*) of *Huái* and *Hé* Prefectures, Defense Commissioner (*fángyùshǐ*) of *Zhèngzhōu*, and Military Governor (*Jiédùshǐ*) of the *Yìchéng* Army.
Wherever he went, the soldiers and populace praised and admired him.
The *Shǐ* clan served as generals for generations,
but *Kuānghàn* loved reading,
especially enjoying the *Chūnqiū Sān Zhuàn* (Three Commentaries on the Spring and Autumn Annals).
He lectured and discussed with scholars,
without tiring all day long.
*Guān Chè*, an administrator (*cóngshì*) of the *Yìchéng* Army, was especially fond of wine.
He once cursed *Kuānghàn* while drunk, saying:
"I recently heard that *Zhāng Yànzé* sliced *Zhāng Shì* (to death),
but I haven't seen *Shǐ Kuānghàn* behead *Guān Chè*.
Those who speak of the world have yet to pair these incidents!"
*Kuānghàn* was not angry.
He poured himself a full cup as a self-imposed penalty and comforted and encouraged *Chè*.
Everyone admired his magnanimity.
He died at the age of forty.
*Wáng Jiànjí*
*Wáng Jiànjí*
was a man from *Xǔzhōu*.
When young, he served *Lǐ Hǎnzhī*.
He followed *Hǎnzhī* when he defected to *Jìn*,
becoming Commander of the *Kuāngwèi* Guard.
When *Liáng* and *Jìn* fought at *Bǎixiāng*,
they faced off along the wild river above *Guōyì*.
The *Zhèn* and *Dìng* armies secured the river bridge.
The *Liáng* troops attacked them aggressively.
*Zhuāngzōng* climbed a high platform and saw that the *Zhèn* and *Dìng* armies were about to be defeated.
He looked at *Jiànjí* and said:
"If the bridge is seized by *Liáng*,
then our army will be in danger.
What should be done?"
*Jiànjí* selected two hundred men and rode rapidly to attack the *Liáng* troops.
The *Liáng* troops were defeated
and withdrew.
He followed in the battles at *Shēnxuàn* and the old *Yuánchéng*.
In all cases, he was the first to scale the ramparts and breach the enemy lines.
Due to accumulated merit, he was appointed Prefect (*cìshǐ*) of *Liáozhōu*,
and commanded the Silver Spear Loyalty Guard (*Yínqiāng Xiàojié Jūn*).
When *Jìn* attacked *Yángliú*,
*Jiànjí* personally carried reeds and rushes to fill the trenches,
and was the first to storm and capture it.
He followed in the battle of *Húliǔ*.
The *Jìn* troops had already been defeated.
They fought *Liáng* for a dirt hill.
The *Liáng* troops arrived first,
climbed the hill, and deployed their formation.
*Zhuāngzōng* reached the foot of the hill, saw that the *Liáng* formation was firm and orderly,
and called out to his army:
"In today's battle,
those who gain the hill will win."
He then charged forward on horseback to challenge them.
*Jiànjí* followed closely with the Silver Spear Army.
The *Liáng* troops ran downhill
and arrayed themselves west of the hill.
The *Jìn* army thus captured the dirt hill.
All the generals said:
"The scattered troops have not yet gathered;
we cannot fight immediately."
*Yán Bǎo* said:
"When they were arrayed on the hill
and we were below them,
we were still able to attack them.
How much more so when attacking down from the high ground?
This opportunity must not be lost."
*Jiànjí* agreed with this,
and therefore reported to *Zhuāngzōng*, saying:
"I request that you ascend the height and watch your servant destroy the enemy!"
He immediately shouted to the multitude:
"All the supplies and equipment we lost today are west of the hill!
Why not go and retrieve them?"
He immediately charged against the *Liáng* formation.
The *Liáng* army was completely defeated.
*Jìn* subsequently camped at *Déshèng*,
building north and south cities along the river.
The *Liáng* general *Hè Guī* attacked the south city,
securing his warships in the river using bamboo cables.
*Jìn* troops could not cross,
and the south city was in extreme peril.
*Zhuāngzōng* accumulated gold and silk outside the camp gate,
recruiting those who could destroy the *Liáng* warships.
People practicing everything from fire-breathing to using forbidden spells were among them.
*Jiànjí*, clad in heavy armor and holding his spear, shouted:
"*Liáng* and *Jìn* are separated only by a stretch of water!
Why must we rely on clever methods?
I shall now destroy them."
He immediately took large ceramic jars, piled them with firewood,
and set fire to them from upstream, burning the *Liáng* warships.
*Jiànjí* followed with two boats loaded with armored soldiers,
chopping the bamboo cables.
The *Liáng* soldiers all fled.
The *Jìn* army was then able to cross,
rescue the south city,
and *Guī*'s* siege was lifted.
Since *Zhuāngzōng* gained *Wèibó*,
*Jiànjí* commanded the Silver Spear Loyalty Guard.
When *Jiànjí* served as a general,
he liked to distribute his personal wealth among the officers and soldiers.
*Zhuāngzōng* sent the eunuch *Wéi Língtú* to supervise his army.
*Língtú* remarked:
"*Jiànjí* has won the hearts of the troops.
I fear he harbors unusual ambitions.
He should not be allowed to command the palace guards (*yábīng*)."
He was immediately made Prefect (*cìshǐ*) of *Dàizhōu*.
*Jiànjí* died feeling frustrated and resentful,
at the age of fifty-seven.
*Yuán Xíngqīn*
*Yuán Xíngqīn*
was a man from *Yōuzhōu*.
He was a subordinate general under *Liú Shǒuguāng*.
When *Shǒuguāng* usurped his father *Réngōng*,
he ordered *Xíngqīn* to use troops to attack *Réngōng* at *Dà'ānshān* and subdue him.
He also ordered *Xíngqīn* to harm *Shǒuguāng*'s brothers.
Afterwards, when *Jìn* attacked *Yōuzhōu*,
*Shǒuguāng* sent *Xíngqīn* to recruit soldiers between *Yún* and *Shuò* Prefectures.
At this time, *Míngzōng* was raiding territory north of the mountains,
and faced *Xíngqīn* at *Guǎngbiānjūn*.
In eight battles,
*Míngzōng* hit *Xíngqīn* seven times with arrows.
*Xíngqīn* pulled out the arrows and continued fighting.
He also shot *Míngzōng*, hitting him in the thigh.
*Xíngqīn* was repeatedly defeated
and then surrendered.
*Míngzōng* patted his back, gave him wine to drink, and said:
"A brave man indeed!"
He subsequently adopted him as a son.
He constantly fought alongside *Míngzōng*
and repeatedly established merit.
After *Zhuāngzōng* conquered *Wèi*,
he increasingly selected fierce generals for his own guard.
Hearing of *Xíngqīn*'s fierceness and bravery,
he took him and made him Overall Commander of Scattered Personnel (*Sànyuán Dū Bùshǔ*),
and bestowed upon him the name *Lǐ Shàoróng*.
Zhuāngzōng loved war and lightly regarded his enemies,
and fought the Liáng army at Pānzhāng,
where his army was defeated and scattered.
Zhuāngzōng escaped with three or four horsemen, riding off swiftly.
Several hundred Liáng soldiers pursued and caught up,
surrounding him with gathered spears.
Xíng Qīn sighted his banner and recognized him.
He galloped forward on one horse,
brandished his sword and cut down two of their spears,
and chopped off one head.
The Liáng soldiers dispersed and left.
Zhuāngzōng returned to the camp,
grasped Xíng Qīn and wept, saying:
“Wealth and status, I shall share them with you!”
From this, his favor exceeded that of all other generals.
He was appointed Cìshǐ of Xīnzhōu,
and later promoted to Jiédùshǐ of the Wǔníng Army.
Zhuāngzōng hosted a banquet for his officials in the inner palace hall.
When the wine was flowing and the music was playing,
he recounted his life's battle experiences for amusement,
but was surprised that Xíng Qīn was not present.
He then looked around and said:
“Where is Shàoróng?”
The relevant official reported:
“By imperial decree, only envoys and chancellors were summoned for the banquet.
Shàoróng holds a rank without substantive post,
so he was not permitted to attend.”
Zhuāngzōng ended the gathering, displeased.
The next day,
he immediately appointed Xíng Qīn as Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
From then on, he did not summon all officials into the inner palace hall;
he only hosted banquets for military officials.
Zhào Zàilǐ rebelled at Wèi.
Zhuāngzōng was currently selecting a great general to attack him.
Empress Liú said:
“This is a minor matter.
You can quickly order Shàoróng to command it.”
Thus, he was appointed Yèdū Xíngyíng Zhāofǔshǐ,
leading two thousand men to suppress the rebellion.
Xíng Qīn attacked the south gate of Yè,
using an imperial edict to persuade Zàilǐ to surrender.
Zàilǐ sent sheep and wine to reward the army,
and climbed the city wall to address Xíng Qīn, saying:
“The officers and soldiers have been separated from their parents for a year.
They ran back without receiving an imperial decree,
causing worry for the Sage (Emperor) above.
What good is regret now?
If you, sir, can skillfully intercede for them,
they may still be able to change their ways and renew themselves.”
Xíng Qīn said:
“The Son of Heaven considers that you all have merits in serving the state.
Minor offenses will certainly be forgiven.”
Zàilǐ bowed twice,
and displayed the imperial edict to the various armies.
Huángfǔ Huī suddenly snatched the edict and tore it up.
The soldiers erupted in clamor.
Xíng Qīn reported the entire matter.
Zhuāngzōng was furious,
and decreed to Xíng Qīn:
“On the day the city is breached,
leave no seed (i.e., kill everyone)!”
Subsequently, he summoned troops from various circuits to reinforce,
all placed under Xíng Qīn's command.
Xíng Qīn stationed his forces at Chánzhōu,
dividing the troops from the circuits into five routes.
He destroyed the civilian population's cartwheels, doors, and roof rafters to make rafts.
He crossed the Chángqìng River and attacked the Guānshì Gate,
but could not succeed.
At this time,
Xíng and Míng prefectures,
rebelled one after another.
Since Xíng Qīn’s attack on Yè was unsuccessful,
Zhuāngzōng wanted to lead the army there himself.
All the officials advised against it,
so he dispatched Míngzōng to suppress the rebellion.
When Míngzōng arrived at Wèi,
he stationed his army west of the city.
Xíng Qīn’s army was stationed south of the city.
However, Míngzōng's army mutinied,
entered Wèi,
and joined Zàilǐ.
Xíng Qīn heard of this,
retreated and stationed himself at Wèizhōu,
and reported Míngzōng’s rebellion.
Zhuāngzōng sent Lǐ Cóngjǐng, Commander of the Gold Spears, with an urgent decree to Míngzōng to discuss the situation.
Cóngjǐng
was Míngzōng's son.
When he traveled to Wèizhōu,
Míngzōng had already rebelled.
Xíng Qīn thus seized Cóngjǐng,
and was about to kill him.
Cóngjǐng requested to return to the capital,
and he was permitted to do so.
Míngzōng led his troops south from Wèixiàn.
Xíng Qīn led his troops to hurry back to the capital.
He followed Zhuāngzōng on an imperial progress to Biànzhōu.
When they reached Xíngzé,
they heard Míngzōng had already crossed Lìyáng.
Zhuāngzōng again dispatched Cóngjǐng to communicate with Míngzōng.
Xíng Qīn thought this was inappropriate,
and immediately struck and killed Cóngjǐng.
Míngzōng entered Biànzhōu.
Zhuāngzōng reached Wànshèngzhèn but could not advance further.
He climbed a mound beside the road with Xíng Qīn,
set out wine,
looked at each other, and wept.
A local offered a pheasant,
and asked the name of the mound.
The local said:
“It is Chóutái (Sorrow Terrace).”
Zhuāngzōng became even more displeased,
and consequently stopped drinking and left.
They traveled west to Shíqiáo,
and set out wine in a makeshift camp.
Zhuāngzōng said to Xíng Qīn:
“You gentlemen have followed me for a long time.
We have shared wealth and status, and faced difficulties together.
Now we are in distress and danger,
yet you are silent, saying nothing,
merely sitting and watching success and failure unfold.
When I reached Xíngzé,
I wanted to cross the river alone on horseback,
and personally seek out Zǒngguǎn.
You gentlemen each presented the advantages and disadvantages (of that plan).
Since today you have caused me to reach this point,
what course of action do you gentlemen suggest now?”
Xíng Qīn wept and replied:
“I was originally a common person,
but I received Your Majesty’s care and cultivation,
rising to the rank of general and chancellor.
In this time of danger,
I have been unable to repay the state.
Even if I die, I cannot fulfill my duty.”
Consequently, he, along with more than a hundred other generals,
all untied their topknots and cut their hair,
placing it on the ground.
They swore to repay the Emperor with their lives.
The ruler and his ministers held onto each other and wept bitterly.
Zhuāngzōng returned to Luòyáng.
After a few days,
he again traveled to Sìshuǐ.
Guō Cóngqiān rebelled,
and Zhuāngzōng died.
Xíng Qīn fled.
When he reached Pínglù,
he was captured by a local,
and sent to Guózhōu.
Shí Tán, the Cìshǐ, broke both his legs,
placed him in a cage-cart,
and sent him to the capital.
Míngzōng saw him
and cursed, saying:
“What wrong did my son commit against you?”
Xíng Qīn glared back with wide eyes and said:
“What wrong did the Former Emperor commit against you?”
He was then executed in the marketplace of Luòyáng.
The market people all shed tears for him.
Alas!
The reason death is precious
is that one's integrity does not allow a shameful survival.
Therefore, it is said: those who exist when the lord exists,
and perish when the lord perishes,
are true ministers of the state.
When Míngzōng's army mutinied at Wèi,
the various generals did not know whether to stay or leave,
but Xíng Qīn alone reported the rebellion.
Furthermore, he killed Míngzōng's son, Cóngjǐng,
and even went so far as to cut his hair and swear an oath.
His sincerity and integrity are certainly commendable.
However, upon the death of Zhuāngzōng,
he could not make his own decision,
but instead fled death seeking survival,
and ended up being captured and killed.
Although his words were not subservient (when facing Míngzōng),
his death was not according to his will.
How can this be considered precious?
Ān Jīnquán
Ān Jīnquán
was a man from Dàiběi.
He was courageous and resolute,
skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He was known for being able to capture rebels alive and overrun hidden enemy positions.
Serving Jìn, he became a cavalry general,
and repeatedly followed Zhuāngzōng in military campaigns, earning merit.
His official position reached that of Cìshǐ.
Due to illness, he resided in Tàiyuán.
After Zhuāng Zōng subdued Wèibó,
he confronted Liáng across the river.
The Liáng general Wáng Tán attacked Tàiyuán.
As all Jìn troops were following Zhuāng Zōng on the river,
Tàiyuán was unprepared.
The Supervisory Commissioner Zhāng Chéngyè was greatly alarmed.
He led the artisans and craftsmen of the various offices to climb the city walls and defend.
Meanwhile, the attack from outside was very urgent.
Jīn Quánqiáng rose up and said to Chéngyè:
"Tàiyuán
is the root of Jìn.
If it fails to hold one day,
then the great enterprise will be lost!
This old man is truly exhausted,
but I can still defeat the bandits for you, sir."
Chéngyè was delighted
and granted him armor and weapons.
Jīn Quán donned his armor and mounted his horse.
He summoned and led his sons, younger brothers, and former officers and clerks, obtaining more than a hundred men.
They went out the North Gate at night
and struck Tán inside the yángmǎ chéng (sheep-and-horse enclosure).
Tán's army panicked and scattered,
and Jìn relief troops gradually arrived.
However, Zhuāng Zōng did not consider Jīn Quán capable,
and throughout his reign, he never recorded his merit.
Jīn Quán had a past relationship with Míng Zōng.
When Míng Zōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Jīn Quán as Zhènwǔjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ Commandery) and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Chancellor).
He served at the commandery for two years,
was recalled to the capital,
and died of illness.
Yuán Jiànfēng
The ancestral family background of Yuán Jiànfēng
is unknown.
When the Prince of Jìn campaigned against Huáng Cháo and reached Huàyīn,
he happened upon him by chance.
At that time, he was only nine years old.
Liking his quick wit and clarity,
he took him in and raised him.
When he grew up, he practiced horsemanship and archery.
He became Tiělín Dōu Yúhòu (Commander of the Tiělín Guards).
He followed in the attacks against Wáng Xíngyú and Lǐ Kuāngwēi.
For his merits, he was promoted to Tūzhèn Zhǐhuīshǐ (Assaulting Vanguard Commander).
He followed Zhuāng Zōng in defeating Jiáchéng
and fighting at Bǎixiāng,
and was promoted to Zuǒxiāng Mǎjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ (Left Wing Cavalry Commander).
Míng Zōng was the Yánèi Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander of the Inner Palace Guards),
and Jiànfēng was the Deputy Commander.
He followed Zhuāng Zōng in entering Wèi,
capturing the three prefectures of Wèi, Cí, and Míng,
and was appointed Míngzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Míng Prefecture).
He attacked the Liáng general Wáng Qiān,
beheaded over a thousand men,
and captured more than seventy of their officers and commanders.
He was promoted to Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Xiāng Prefecture).
He followed in the Battle of Húliǔ.
When the commander Mèng Qiān seized Xiāng Prefecture and rebelled,
Jiànfēng returned and suppressed the rebellion.
He was transferred to Xízhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Xí Prefecture),
but was disabled by wind illness.
When Míng Zōng ascended the throne,
due to their old friendship, he summoned him back to the capital.
He personally visited his residence
and offered very generous comfort and assurance.
He was given the honorary title Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi (Supervisory Grand Commandant),
nominally appointed Zhènnánjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Zhènnán Commandery),
and allowed to draw his salary until he died.
He was posthumously granted the title Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant).
Xīfāng Yè
Xīfāng Yè
was a native of Mǎnchéng, Dìngzhōu.
His father, Zàiyù,
was a military officer in Biànzhōu.
Yè lived among the troops
and was known for his courage and strength.
At the age of twenty,
he crossed the river southward and served in Liáng,
but was not utilized.
He returned to Zhuāng Zōng on the riverfront.
Zhuāng Zōng appointed him Xiàoyì Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander of the Xiàoyì Guards).
He frequently accompanied campaigns and earned merits.
During the Tóngguāng reign period, he became Cáo Zhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Cáo Prefecture).
He garrisoned Biànzhōu with his prefectural troops.
Míng Zōng rebelled from Wèi,
and his troops crossed the Hé southward.
Meanwhile, Zhuāng Zōng traveled east to Biànzhōu.
Kǒng Xún, the Jiédùshǐ of Biànzhōu, harbored dual intentions.
He sent men out the north gate to welcome Míng Zōng
and out the west gate to welcome Zhuāng Zōng.
The provisions and supplies were identically prepared,
and he said:
"Whichever arrives first shall enter."
Yè thereupon rebuked Xún, saying:
"Our Lord subdued Liáng and thereby obtained you, sir.
He showed the favor of not killing you.
How can you now wish to receive the General Commander and betray the state!"
Xún did not reply.
Yè judged that Xún could not be reasoned with.
Shí Jìngtáng's wife,
who was Míng Zōng's daughter,
was currently in Biàn.
Yè wanted to kill her
in order to solidify morale.
Xún learned of his plan
and took her and hid her in his own residence.
Yè could do nothing about it.
Since Míng Zōng had already reached Biàn,
Yè then took five hundred cavalry and rode west to meet Zhuāng Zōng at Sìshuǐ.
He sobbed, weeping bitterly.
Zhuāng Zōng also sighed with grief because of him,
and subsequently made his troops the vanguard.
Zhuāng Zōng reached the west of Biàn,
but was unable to enter.
He returned to Luòyáng
and was assassinated.
When Míng Zōng entered Luò,
Yè requested death before his horse.
Míng Zōng praised and admired him for a long time.
The following year,
Gāo Jìxīng of Jīngnán rebelled.
Míng Zōng dispatched Liú Xùn, the Jiédùshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, and others to campaign and suppress the rebellion.
He appointed Dǒng Zhāng of Dōngchuān as Xīnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ (Campaign Commissioner for the Southwest Region).
He then appointed Yè as Kuízhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Kuí Prefecture),
to assist Zhāng and lead troops out through the Sānxiá (Three Gorges).
Soon after, Xùn and the others were dismissed without having achieved merit.
All the generals were disbanded.
Although Zhāng had also led troops out,
only Yè alone captured three prefectures.
Consequently, Kuí Prefecture was established as Níngjiāng Commandery,
and Yè was appointed Jiédùshǐ.
Soon after, he also captured Guī Prefecture
and repeatedly defeated Jìxīng's troops.
Yè,
being a military man,
often acted outside legal norms and regulations.
His Adjutant, Tán Shàndá, repeatedly remonstrated with him about this.
Yè became angry
and sent men to accuse Shàndá of receiving bribes (gold),
throwing him into prison.
Shàndá was naturally resolute;
his language became increasingly disrespectful,
and he subsequently died in prison.
Yè fell ill
and saw Shàndá as an avenging ghost.
He died while serving at his post.
Biographies of Táng Subjects, Chapter Fourteen: Fú Xí
Fú Xí
was a native of Zhāoqìng, Zhàozhōu.
In his youth, he served Wáng Róng, the Prince of Zhào, as a military officer.
Since Jìn had saved Zhào
by defeating the Liáng army at Bǎixiāng,
Zhào consistently sent Xí to lead troops and follow Jìn.
When the Jìn army reached Déshèng,
Zhāng Wénlǐ killed Wáng Róng, the Prince of Zhào.
He submitted a memorial to Zhuāng Zōng
requesting that Xí be returned to Zhào.
Zhuāng Zōng sent him back.
Xí wailed and wept, saying:
"My family has served Zhào for generations.
I received favor from the Prince of Zhào.
The Prince once gave me a sword and commanded me to prove my worth.
Now that I hear the Prince is dead,
I wished to use the sword to take my own life,
but I realized that in the end, it would be pointless.
I request permission to attack Zhào, defeat the bandits,
and avenge the Prince."
Zhuāng Zōng admired his spirit,
and subsequently dispatched Yán Bǎo, Shǐ Jiàntáng, and others to assist Xí in attacking Wénlǐ.
He appointed Xí as Zhènzhōu Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (Acting Military Administrator of Zhèn Prefecture).
Xí attacked Wénlǐ but could not overcome him.
Zhuāng Zōng used other generals to defeat him.
Xí was appointed Chéngdējūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Chéngdé Commandery).
Xí declined, not daring to accept.
Consequently, the two prefectures of Xiāng and Wèi were established as Yìníng Commandery,
and Xí was made the Jiédùshǐ.
Xí declined again, saying:
"The six prefectures of Wèibó
are the domain of the Hegemon-King.
It is not appropriate to divide it and show weakness.
I wish Your Majesty would grant me a commandery in Hénán
which I can capture myself."
He was then appointed Xí as Tiānpíngjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng Commandery) and Dōngnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ (Campaign Commissioner for the Southeast Region).
Xí, however, never campaigned and conquered the territory.
Afterwards, he was transferred to Zhèn'ānguó Commandery,
and later transferred again to Pínglú.
raised a rebellion,
sending Xí with garrison troops to suppress the bandits.
Before Xí arrived at Wèi,
Míngzōng's troops mutinied,
and Xí dared not advance.
Míngzōng sent a messenger to recruit him,
and Xí met Míngzōng at Zuòxiàn.
However, because Míngzōng's rising up in arms was illegitimate,
Xí's intention regarding whether to leave or join was unresolved.
Huò Yànwēi deceived Xí, saying:
"The sovereign has killed ten people,
and you were involved in four of those incidents.
Why do you still hesitate?"
Xí's intention was then decided.
Yáng Xīwàng, the Supervisor of the Army at Pínglú, heard that Xí had been summoned by Míngzōng,
so he used troops to surround Xí's family,
intending to kill them.
Wáng Gōngyǎn, a Commander, had always been trusted by Xīwàng.
He deceived Xīwàng, saying:
"The Palace Attendant is devoting loyalty to the court.
Who would dare not follow orders when the families of rebels are being executed!
Who would dare not offer their life in service!
It is advisable to divide the troops to guard the city,
in case of external threats,
Xí's family is not worth worrying about."
Xīwàng believed him,
and therefore divided all his troops to guard the city.
Gōngyǎn consequently captured Xīwàng and executed him.
Xí's family members were thus saved from harm.
However, Gōngyǎn declared that the people of Qīng (Pínglú) disliked Xí's severe and urgent rule,
and did not want Xí to return.
He then sought the position of Jiédùshǐ for himself.
Míngzōng then used Fáng Zhīwēn to replace Xí as garrison commander at Pínglú,
and appointed Gōngyǎn as the Cìshǐ of Dēngzhōu.
Gōngyǎn did not accept the command immediately.
Zhīwēn captured and killed him.
Xí returned to command at Tiānpíng,
and was later transferred to command at Xuānwǔ.
Xí had always been disliked by Ān Zhònghuǐ.
Those who sought to please Ān Zhònghuǐ reported that Xí heavily taxed the people of Biàn,
so he was made *Tàizǐ Tàishī* and retired from service.
He returned to his former village, Zhāoqìng.
Míngzōng appointed his son, Lìngqiān, as the Cìshǐ of Zhàozhōu so that he could provide for Xí.
Xí, believing himself to be innocent,
was resentful and miserable about losing his post.
He indulged in hunting and heavy drinking to amuse himself.
After living there for more than a year,
he died from a stroke,
and was posthumously granted the title *Tàishī*.
Xí had two sons: Lìngqiān and Méng.
Lìngqiān,
possessed great courage and strength,
and was skilled in archery from horseback.
He became a general due to his father's position,
and his official rank reached Cìshǐ of Zhàozhōu.
He governed well,
and died while in the prefecture.
Several thousand people from the prefecture wept and wailed while seeing his funeral off.
At the time, he was called a virtuous Cìshǐ.
Méng,
loved learning since youth,
and was by nature firm and upright.
He served as the Deputy Jiédùshǐ of the Chéngdé Army.
Later, he served the Jìn,
and his official rank reached *Lǐbù Shìláng*.
Wū Zhèn
Wū Zhèn,
was a man from Xìndū in Jìzhōu.
In his youth, he served Wáng Róng, the Prince of Zhào, as a soldier.
Gradually, due to his merits, he was promoted to a junior officer,
and was attached to Fú Xí's army.
When Xí followed Zhuāngzōng to the area along the river,
Róng was assassinated by Zhāng Wénlǐ.
Zhèn followed Xí to suppress Wénlǐ,
but his family was in Zhào.
Wénlǐ seized Zhèn's mother, wife, and over ten children to entice Zhèn,
but Zhèn paid no heed.
Wénlǐ then ordered them to cut off their hands and noses,
maiming them but not executing them,
and released them to reach Xí's army.
Everyone in the army could not bear to look directly at them.
Zhèn wailed once and then stopped,
feeling enraged and encouraging himself.
He personally led the charge ahead of the troops.
When the Jìn army broke through and captured Zhènzhōu,
Zhèn was appointed Cìshǐ due to his merits,
serving successively in Shēn and Zhào prefectures.
Zhèn was a man of simple and honest character.
He loved learning in his youth,
and was conversant with the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū*.
He enjoyed writing poetry,
and was skilled in calligraphy.
When he became Cìshǐ,
he gained renown for governing with integrity and impartiality.
He was promoted to Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu,
and concurrently served as the Commissioner of Water and Land Transport for the Northern Front.
Míngzōng heard of his reputation,
and promoted him to Deputy Pacification Commissioner of Héběidào,
leading the Jiédùshǐ post of the Níngguó Army,
replacing Fáng Zhīwēn in the Lútái Army garrison.
Immediately upon his arrival, the garrison soldiers, led by Lóng Zhǐ and others, rebelled.
He was killed,
and posthumously granted the title *Tàishī*.
Alas!
Loyalty and filial piety, if based on righteousness, can both be achieved.
I have already spoken of this.
As for a man like Wū Zhèn,
can he be called loyal?
How extreme
that Zhèn did not consider this.
Now, if one accepts a man's emolument and undertakes a man's duty,
where the duty is inherent,
and the responsibility is focused solely on oneself,
and the profit or harm to the state
depends entirely on whether oneself acts or does not act—
even if acting benefits the state
but harms one's parents,
one should still resign the emolument and leave.
How much more so when the matter is something that everyone can do,
and the responsibility is not exclusive to oneself,
and furthermore, whether one acts or does not act,
the profit or harm of the state is not dependent upon it!
To be thus and yet disregard one's parents,
even if one does not seek profit thereby,
is still called unfilial;
how much worse if one profits from it!
One who can serve their parents with filial piety,
only then can serve their sovereign with loyalty.
As for a man like Wū Zhèn,
he can be called greatly unfilial;
what loyalty can he possibly possess?
Kǒng Qiān
Kǒng Qiān,
was a man from Wèizhōu.
He served as a *Kǒngmùguān* in Wèizhōu.
When Wèibó submitted to Jìn,
Zhuāngzōng made him *Dùzhīshǐ*.
Qiān was a diligent and keen man,
but also cunning and skilled at serving people.
Zhuāngzōng and his entourage were all pleased with him.
Having served as a clerk since youth,
he was adept at writing and calculating,
and quite knowledgeable about matters of finance, grain, and taxation.
The Jìn and the Liáng opposed each other along the river for more than ten years,
fighting over a hundred battles, both large and small.
Qiān managed the requisitioning and provision of supplies,
never allowing shortages.
The accomplishment of Zhuāngzōng's endeavor
was largely due to Qiān's efforts.
However, the people also suffered immensely from his harshness.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng initially established his grand title,
and [Kǒng] Qiān personally believed he ought to be the Commissioner of Taxes and Levies (Zūyōngshǐ),
but Guō Chóngtāo employed Zhāng Xiàn, the Adjutant (Pànguān) to the Military Governor (Guānchásǐ) of Wèibó, as the Commissioner,
making Qiān the Deputy.
Qiān was already resentful.
Afterward, when Zhuāngzōng destroyed [Later] Liáng,
Qiān followed him into Biàn,
and said to Chóngtāo:
“Yè,
is the Northern Capital (Běidū).
It ought to be governed by a highly respected person,
and no one but Zhāng Xiàn will do.”
Chóngtāo agreed,
and consequently assigned Xiàn to be the Resident General (Liúshǒu) of the Northern Capital,
and appointed the Chancellor (Zǎixiàng) Dòulú Gé to supervise the Zūyōng.
Qiān was even more disappointed.
He then secretly sought out Gé’s transgressions.
Gé had once used a handwritten note to borrow 100,000 in Zūyōng funds.
Qiān then used this note to show Chóngtāo,
and subtly leaked the matter,
ensuring Gé heard about it.
Gé, afraid,
consequently asked to resign his post in favor of Chóngtāo.
Chóngtāo also refused to accept the position.
Zhuāngzōng asked:
“Who is capable?”
Chóngtāo replied:
“Although Kǒng Qiān is skilled in finance (jīngǔ),
public opinion suggests he is not yet fit for a great responsibility.
It is better to re-employ Zhāng Xiàn.”
He then quickly summoned Xiàn.
Xiàn was intelligent and articulate,
and many people were quite jealous of him.
Qiān seized the opportunity and said to Gé:
“Taxes, levies, money, and grain (Zūyōng qiángǔ)
are all right at hand;
entrusting them to a minor official is sufficient.
Yèdū is critically important to the whole empire,
and it cannot be lightly entrusted to anyone.”
Gé relayed this to Chóngtāo.
Chóngtāo dismissed the idea of summoning Xiàn,
and appointed Wáng Zhèngyán, the Prefect (Yǐn) of Xīngtáng, as the Commissioner of Taxes and Levies (Zūyōngshǐ).
Qiān became increasingly resentful,
and therefore requested to resign his post.
Zhuāngzōng was angered by his evasion of duty,
and wanted to punish him according to the law.
Thanks to the palace entertainer (língguān) Jǐng Jìn who interceded for him,
the matter was stopped.
After a while, Zhèngyán suffered from paralysis (bìngfēng),
and could not manage affairs.
Jǐng Jìn repeatedly spoke about this,
so Zhèngyán was dismissed,
and Qiān was made the Commissioner of Taxes and Levies (Zūyōngshǐ).
He was bestowed
the title "Meritorious Official Who Enriches Finances and Sustains the State" (Fēngcái Shànguó Gōngchén).
Qiān had no other talent;
he simply made concentration of wealth and extortion his business.
When Zhuāngzōng first ascended the throne,
he extended grace across the empire,
abolishing the field taxes of the common people,
and pardoning those who were in arrears regarding duties or profits owed to various government agencies (chǎngwù).
Qiān violated all these imperial edicts and rigorously pursued collection.
According to established regulations: matters pertaining to the prefectures governed by the Military Governor (Guānchásǐ)
could not be reported directly [to the throne].
Imperial levies and taxes (fùdiào)
were also issued through the Guānchásǐ for implementation.
However, Qiān directly used Zūyōng warrants (tiè) to assign tasks and issue levies to various prefectures,
bypassing the Guānchásǐ.
The Guānchásǐ submitted memorials arguing the principles,
stating:
“Imperial orders and edicts (zhìchì) are not sent directly to sub-prefectures,
and Prefects (Cìshǐ) cannot memorialize independently;
this is the institutional rule of Táng (Tang Dynasty).
The direct Zūyōng warrants (zhítiè)
follow the corrupt practices of the spurious Liáng,
and cannot be adopted as standard practice.
Now that the fortunes of Táng are revived,
we request a return to the old system.”
An imperial edict approved their request,
but Qiān did not obey the edict,
and ultimately continued issuing direct warrants.
He further requested a reduction in the stipends (fèngqián) of all officials,
and the dismissal and reduction of the number of staff, such as Adjutants (Pànguān) and Reviewing Officials (Tuīguān), under the Jìedùshǐ and Guānchásǐ.
Furthermore, he blocked off mountain valleys and pathways throughout the empire,
prohibiting travelers,
in order to collect taxes and levies from merchants and travelers.
He dispatched major taxation officials (Dà Chéngguān) to seize pigs, sheep, firewood, and charcoal,
and took possession of (or sheltered) households.
He revised the pole and ruler used for measuring fields (kuòtián gānchǐ).
He completely seized all public funds (gōngxiè qián) held by prefectural officials.
Because of this, everyone in the empire resented and suffered under him.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict proclaiming Qiān’s crimes,
and had him executed in the marketplace of Luò[yáng],
confiscating his property.
The office of the Commissioner of Taxes and Levies (Zūyōngshǐ) was then abolished,
and the Salt and Iron, Treasury (Dùzhī), and Revenue (Hùbù) offices were divided into the Three Offices (Sānsī).
Zhāng Yánlǎng.
Zhāng Yánlǎng,
was a native of Kāifēng, in Biànzhōu.
He served [Later] Liáng,
and, as a Zūyōng clerk, became the Commissary Official (Liángliàosǐ) of Yùnzhōu.
When Míngzōng captured Yùnzhōu,
he acquired Yánlǎng,
and reappointed him as Commissary Official.
Later, he was transferred to the commands of Xuānwǔ and Chéngdé,
serving as a Primary Staff Official (Yuáncóng Kǒngmù Guān).
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,

he served as the Director of Palaces and Residences (Zhuāngzháishǐ), Commissioner of the Northern Court of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Xuānhuī Běiyuànshǐ), and Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Zhōngwǔ Command.
In the first year of Chángxīng [930 CE], he was appointed Commissioner of the Three Offices (Sānsīshǐ).
The Táng system decreed: the Revenue (Hùbù) and Treasury (Dùzhī) affairs were supervised by the Director (Lángzhōng) and Vice-Minister (Shìláng) of those respective offices,
and there was the Commissioner of Salt and Iron Monopolies (Yántiě Zhuǎnyùnshǐ).
Later, during military campaigns,
because national finance (guójì) became critical,
Chancellors (Zǎixiàng) were consequently appointed to lead these duties.
After Qiánfú [874-879 CE],
the empire descended into chaos and turmoil,
and the national treasury became increasingly depleted.
The office of Commissioner of Taxes and Levies (Zūyōngshǐ) was first established,
and during intermittent warfare,
taxes and levies were adjusted as needed;
when military activities ceased, the office stopped.
When [Later] Liáng arose,
they first established the Zūyōngshǐ,
to govern all money and grain in the empire,
abolishing the offices of Salt and Iron, Revenue (Hùbù), and Treasury (Dùzhī).
Zhuāngzōng destroyed [Later] Liáng,
and maintained this system without change.
When Míngzōng took the throne,
he executed the Zūyōngshǐ Kǒng Qiān and abolished that commission,
appointing one high official to supervise the Revenue (Hùbù), Treasury (Dùzhī), and Salt and Iron offices,
which was termed the Supervisor of the Three Offices (Pàn Sānsī).
Yánlǎng then requested the establishment of the Commissioner of the Three Offices (Sānsīshǐ).
The matter was forwarded to the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū).
The Zhōngshū, following the precedents of Táng,
appointed Yánlǎng as Grand Master of Court Discussion (Tèjìn) and Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū),
and designated him Commissioner for Salt and Iron Transport, etc., across all circuits,
concurrently supervising the affairs of the Revenue (Hùbù) and Treasury (Dùzhī) offices.
An edict designated Yánlǎng as the Commissioner of the Three Offices (Sānsīshǐ).
His rank was placed below that of the Commissioners of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Xuānhuīshǐ).
The establishment of the Sānsīshǐ began with this appointment.
Yánlǎng was known to be meticulous and calculating,
and took the Sānsī as his personal responsibility,
yet he achieved nothing constructive regarding the empire’s finance and grain.
Míngzōng often went out on imperial tours,
and summoned Yánlǎng to share a meal.
Yánlǎng did not come,
sending a reply through the messenger, saying:
“The Sānsī affairs are busy;
I have no time.”
Those who heard this laughed at him.
He successively held the post of Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Tàiníng and Xióngwǔ commands.
The Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) appointed him Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) concurrently Administrator of the Affairs of the Central Secretariat and Chancellery (Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
and Supervisor of the Three Offices (Pàn Sānsī).
When Jìn Gāozǔ harbored unorthodox ambitions,
Yánlǎng mobilized and confiscated all the wealth and goods of the Sānsī that were stored in Tàiyuán.
Gāozǔ deeply resented this.
[Omitted by translator; continuation of 157]
When the Jìn troops rose in revolt,
the Deposed Emperor wanted to personally lead the campaign,
but inwardly feared Gāozǔ,
and hesitated, unable to decide.
Yánlǎng, along with Liú Yánlǎng and others, advised the Emperor that he must proceed.
Yánlǎng registered the people of all circuits as able-bodied men (dīng) and confiscated their horses.
Before the men and horses arrived,
the Jìn troops entered the capital.
Gāozǔ captured Yánlǎng,
and executed him.
Lǐ Yán.
Lǐ Yán,
was a native of Yōuzhōu.
His initial name was Ràngkūn.
He served Liú Shǒuguāng as a Prefect (Cìshǐ).
Later, he served Zhuāngzōng as the Commissioner of Guests (Kèshěngshǐ).
Yán was intelligent, astute, and possessed many skills.
He practiced horsemanship and archery,
was quite literate, and articulate.
third year, he was sent as an envoy to Shǔ
, where he explained to Wáng Yǎn
the greatness of the achievements and virtue resulting from the restoration of the Táng dynasty
. His voice and diction were clear and resonant
, and all the Shǔ people who listened were awestruck.
Wáng Yǎn's Privy Councilor (Shūmìshǐ), Sòng Guāngsì
, invited Yán to a feast, and casually asked about matters in the Central Plains (Zhōngguó)
. Yán replied:
"The year before last, the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) established his great title at the Yè Palace
, rushed from Yùn to Biàn
, and pacified the world in less than ten days
. Yet, the surrendered troops of Liáng still numbered three hundred thousand
. Eastward, reaching the sea
; westward, extending to Gān and Liáng
; northward, aweing Yōu and Líng
; and southward, crossing the Mǐn Ridge
—in the four directions, covering ten thousand *lǐ*
, none failed to submit as subjects
. Furthermore, the Yáng clan of Huáinán
, inheriting the strength of successive generations, and Lord Lǐ of Fèngxiáng
, relying on his status from the former court, both sent their sons to serve at court
and bowed their heads declaring vassalage
. As for Jīng, Hú, and Wúyuè
, those who presented tribute and tax
, offered rare treasures
, and wished to compare themselves to ordinary prefectures
, did so without a single month passing empty
. The Son of Heaven is now embracing them with virtue
and shaking them with power
. The trend of All Under Heaven
inevitably leads to unification."
Guāngsì said:
"Jīng, Hú, and Wúyuè are unknown to us
. As for Fèngxiáng, they are Shǔ's in-laws
. Since their people are fickle
, can they be trusted
? Also, we hear that the Qìdān are growing stronger daily
. Should the great state (Táng) not be concerned?"
Yán said:
"How does the strength of the Qìdān
compare to that of the False Liáng (Wěi Liáng)
?" Guāngsì said:
"They are slightly inferior to Liáng
Yán said:
"Táng destroyed Liáng as easily as pulling apart rotten wood
. What need is there to mention those who are inferior to Liáng
? Táng troops are spread throughout the world
. Deploying the forces of just one garrison (zhèn)
would be sufficient to annihilate the barbarians (lǔ) until none remain
. However, Heaven created the Four Barbarians
, and since they are not within the Nine Provinces (Jiǔzhōu)
, the kings of ancient times
have all let them exist without discussing action against them
. This is likely because they did not wish to exhaust their military resources and engage in excessive warfare
When the Shǔ people heard Yán's replies
, they were increasingly impressed by him
. At this time
, the ruler and officials of Shǔ were all mediocre and unenlightened
. They relied on their difficult terrain for safety
and indulged in the height of extravagance and excess
When Yán returned from Shǔ
, he reported fully on the situation suggesting it could be conquered
. Previously
, Zhuāngzōng had sent Yán into Shǔ with famous horses
, intending to purchase rare treasures to supply the rear palace
. However, Shǔ law strictly prohibited rare goods from being taken out through the Jiàn Gate (Jiànmén)
. Items that were not rare goods but were taken out
were called
"Grass-Entered Goods" (*Rùcǎo wù*)
. Consequently, Yán returned having obtained nothing
, except for two hundred *liǎng* of gold, floor coverings (*dìyī*), and woolen cloth (*máobù*)
Zhuāngzōng heard this
and was furious, saying
: "Things returned to the Central Plains (Zhōngguó)
are called 'Grass-Entered'
—how can Wáng Yǎn
avoid becoming a 'Grass-Entered Person' (*Rùcǎo rén*)
?" Thereupon
, the decision to attack Shǔ was finalized
, Wáng Yǎn sent word, saying
: "If Lǐ Yán comes, I will surrender immediately
." Everyone felt that since the plan to attack Shǔ had originated with Yán
, and since Wáng Yǎn deeply resented Yán
, it was inappropriate for Yán to go
. Yán heard this and rejoiced
, immediately riding into Yìzhōu
. Wáng Yǎn met Yán
, entrusted his wife and mother to him
, and surrendered Shǔ that same day
. Yán returned
, and Míngzōng appointed him Defense Commissioner of Sìzhōu (Sìzhōu Fángyùshǐ)
, retaining his position as Commissioner of the Guest Department (Kèshěngshǐ)
. Later
, since Mèng Zhīxiáng was obstinate in Shǔ
, Ān Zhònghuǐ gradually suppressed and restrained him
. Thinking of someone who could control Zhīxiáng, Yán then requested to be made the Supreme Inspector of Military Affairs for Xīchuān (Xīchuān Bīngmǎ Dūjiān)
. When he was about to depart
, his mother said
: "You previously initiated the scheme to destroy Shǔ
. If you go now
, you will certainly repay the Shǔ people with your death
!" Yán did not listen
. Initially
, Yán and Zhīxiáng had served Zhuāngzōng together
. At that time, Zhīxiáng was the Chamberlain for Palace Communications (Zhōngménshǐ)
. Yán once committed a fault
. Zhuāngzōng was extremely angry
and ordered him executed
. Zhīxiáng secretly instructed the executioners to delay slightly
, went in to report to Zhuāngzōng, and said
: "Yán's offense is small
. It is inappropriate to kill a man based on happiness or anger
, lest we lose the loyalty of the officials and scholars (shìdàfū)
." Zhuāngzōng's anger slightly subsided
, and he ordered Zhīxiáng to supervise the caning of Yán twenty times and then release him
. Although Zhīxiáng had previous kindness toward Yán
, he was displeased by his arrival
. When the Shǔ people heard Yán was coming
, they also all resented him
. When Yán arrived
, Zhīxiáng prepared a feast and casually asked Yán
: "Did the Imperial Court (Cháotíng) send you
, or did you wish to come of your own accord
?" Yán replied
: "It is the Emperor's command
." Zhīxiáng erupted in anger, saying
: "None of the various regional commands (fānzhèn) in the realm have a Military Inspector (Jiānjūn)
. How is it that you alone come here
? This is simply an attempt by a mere child (meaning Ān Zhònghuǐ) to confuse the Imperial Court
!" He immediately seized and executed him
. Míngzōng was unable to investigate the matter
, and Zhīxiáng consequently rebelled because of this
. Lǐ Rénjǔ
. The ancestry of Lǐ Rénjǔ
is unknown
. When he was young, he served Míngzōng as a guest general (kèjiàng)
. When Míngzōng ascended the throne
, he appointed him Commissioner of the Guest Department (Kèshěngshǐ) and General-in-Chief of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Dàjiāngjūn)
. When Míngzōng performed the Heaven Sacrifice in the Southern Suburbs (Nánjiāo)
, the Eastern and Western Chuān (Dōng-Xī Chuān)
were due to contribute money for the ceremony, and Rénjǔ was sent to hurry the collection
. Rénjǔ relied on the emperor's favor to be arrogant and presumptuous
, and he did not treat the regional officials (fānchén) with propriety
. Dǒng Zhāng
, the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Dōngchuān, held a feast and summoned Rénjǔ
. Rénjǔ declined, claiming he was drunk and would not go. Instead, he drank with courtesans in the relay post (zhuǎnshè)
. Zhāng was enraged
. He led his headquarters troops (yábīng) with unsheathed blades to the relay post
. Rénjǔ was terrified
. He ran around the courtyard wearing only his boots, without socks
. Zhāng rebuked him, saying
: "Because Xīchuān was able to execute Lǐ Yán
, do you think I alone cannot execute you
?" He looked at his attendants and ordered them to drag him out and behead him
. Rénjǔ wept, knelt, and prostrated himself, begging forgiveness
. Only then did Zhāng stop
. The next day
, Zhāng held a feast and summoned Rénjǔ
, meeting with his wife and children
, and offered him generous gifts
. When Rénjǔ returned
, he stated that Zhāng would certainly rebel
. Rénjǔ had always been trusted by Ān Zhònghuǐ
. Since Zhāng showed signs of rebellion
, Zhònghuǐ sought a way to control him
. He therefore partitioned Làngzhōu from Dōngchuān
, establishing it as the Bǎoníng Command
, appointed Rénjǔ as the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ)
, and sent Yáo Hóng to command troops to garrison it
. Zhāng sent a letter to the capital informing his son Guāngyè
, saying
: "The Imperial Court has severed my subordinate prefecture
, separately established a Military Governor there
, and also garrisoned troops
. This means they intend to kill me
. If Táng again sends even a single horseman into the Xié Valley
, my rebellion will be certain
! I am deciding this matter starting now with you
." Guāngyè privately showed the letter to the Privy Council Official Lǐ Qiánhuī
arrived at the garrison, observing Dǒng Zhāng's
activities and reporting everything he learned. Dǒng Zhāng
grew increasingly suspicious and fearful, and
consequently decided to revolt. Ān Chónghuǐ
again dispatched Xún Xián-yì to lead troops and reinforce the defense of Lǎngzhōu. Guāngyè
urgently argued that this should not be done, but Ān Chónghuǐ
did not listen. Before Xián-yì
arrived, Dǒng Zhāng
had already revolted. He attacked Lǎngzhōu.
Rénjǔ
summoned the generals and officers to ask for advice. They all
said: "Dǒng Zhāng
has harbored rebellious intentions for a long time. He constantly
uses benefits to entice our soldiers. Our troops
are not yet ready for use, and the rebels'
edge is currently sharp. We should
strengthen our walls to frustrate them. If we hold
for ten days, the main army
will surely arrive, and the rebels
will naturally retreat." Rénjǔ
said: "Shǔ
is weak; how can they
withstand my elite troops!" He immediately
drove them out to battle. The troops
collapsed before engagement, and Rénjǔ
was captured. Both
he and his family members were killed. Máo Zhāng
Máo Zhāng
was a native
of Cāngzhōu. Late in the Liáng
period, Dài Sīyuǎn
served as the Jiédùshǐ of the Hénghǎi Army. Máo Zhāng
served Sīyuǎn as a military officer. After Jìn
had subjugated Wèibó, Sīyuǎn
abandoned Cāngzhōu and fled. Máo Zhāng
surrendered Cāngzhōu to Jìn. For his service,
he was made Prefect of Bèizhōu. Máo Zhāng
was a man of courage and valor. From the time Jìn
and Liáng faced each other across the river, Máo Zhāng
repeatedly gained merit in battle. When Zhuāngzōng
destroyed Liáng, Máo Zhāng
was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Huàzhōu. While at
the garrison, he committed many unlawful acts. Commentators suspected
he harbored ulterior motives. Therefore, Máo Zhāng
was transferred to garrison Zhāoyì. Máo Zhāng
initially wanted to refuse the order. His Aide, Biān Wèi,
strongly remonstrated with him and advised him. Only then
did he comply. Máo Zhāng
had served successively in various regional commands (Fānzhèn). Moreover, while in Huàzhōu,
he acquired the surplus wealth from Wèi Wáng Jìjí's campaign against Shǔ. Being both
wealthy and arrogant, he indulged
increasingly in extravagance and dissipation. He once
wore an ochre robe while drinking wine, and ordered the Shǔ courtesans he had acquired
to perform the court entertainment of Wáng Yǎn before him. Míngzōng
heard of this and disliked him. He was summoned
and appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Jīnwǔ Guards. Dǒng Zhāng
of Dōngchuān submitted a memorial claiming that Máo Zhāng had sent his son Tíngyūn with a letter to Xīchuān, suggesting
suspicious activity. Míngzōng
therefore sent men to recall Tíngyūn, and Máo Zhāng
was imprisoned in the Censorate jail. Tíngyūn
confessed, stating that he was actually Máo Zhāng’s adopted son, that he had
an uncle in Shǔ, and that he wished
to visit him, but there
was no private correspondence. Máo Zhāng
had no formal charges against him. The relevant authorities
deliberated, saying: "Máo Zhāng,
when formerly serving in a Fānzhèn, secretly
nurtured disloyal plans, and when he
held a court position, he did not
conduct himself carefully." Therefore, Máo Zhāng
was stripped of his current office and ordered
to return to his private residence. Previously,
when Tíngyūn
went to Shǔ, he was accompanied
by his retainer, Zhào Yánzuò. When
Máo Zhāng was summoned and imprisoned, Yánzuò
gathered many of Máo Zhāng's secret deeds and intended to report them. Máo Zhāng
promised Yánzuò a heavy bribe to silence him. After being released,
Yánzuò demanded the bribe from Máo Zhāng, but Máo Zhāng
refused to give it. Yánzuò
then went to the Censorate himself to confess, and Máo Zhāng
was again imprisoned. The interrogation,
however, revealed no solid evidence. The Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǚ Mèngqí
argued: "Máo Zhāng
was previously investigated and impeached, but has already
been exonerated. Now Yánzuò,
due to his demand for a bribe, has again fabricated
charges." Máo Zhāng
was then slightly pardoned. When Máo Zhāng
made his confession, an informer alleged
that Mèngqí had accepted a bribe and had not fully investigated the case. The case
was then transferred to the military authorities for review. The prison officials,
eager to please the emperor, fabricated
the facts of the case. Máo Zhāng
fully confessed: he had promised Yánzuò a bribe but had not yet given it, and he had once
lent Mèngqí a horse, but Mèngqí had not accepted a bribe (in exchange for official action). Máo Zhāng
was sentenced to permanent exile in Rúzhōu. Later,
an order was issued for him to be granted self-execution wherever he was located. Biographies of Táng Officials,
Chapter 15: Zhū Hóngzhāo (with an appendix on Féng Yūn) Zhū Hóngzhāo
was a native
of Tàiyuán. When he was young,
he served Míngzōng as a retainer general. When Míngzōng
ascended the throne, he was made
Director of the Wénsī Bureau. Because he
had a rift with Ān Chónghuǐ, he was often
sent out of the capital on missions. When Dǒng Zhāng
became the Jiédùshǐ of Dōngchuān, Hóngzhāo
was appointed his Deputy. Mèng Zhīxiáng
of Xīchuān killed his Surveillance Commissioner, Lǐ Yán. Hóngzhāo
was greatly alarmed and sought
to return to the capital. Dǒng Zhāng
refused permission. Consequently,
mutual suspicion arose. Hóngzhāo
increasingly treated Dǒng Zhāng openly and without suspicion, and Dǒng Zhāng
rather respected his character. Later, Dǒng Zhāng
had military business, and dispatched
Hóngzhāo to the court. Hóngzhāo
was thus relieved of his post. He was promoted
to General-in-Chief of the Left Guard, Director of the Inner Retainers' Bureau, Director of the Southern Bureau of Palace Announcements, and Jiédùshǐ of Fèngxiáng. When Mèng Zhīxiáng
rebelled, Shí Jìngtáng
campaigned against Shǔ. Since there
had long been no success, Míngzōng
sent Ān Chónghuǐ to supervise the troops. At this time,
Chónghuǐ was already subject to estrangement (from the emperor). When Chónghuǐ
arrived at Fèngxiáng, Hóngzhāo
welcomed and paid respects to him, showing
extreme deference. He invited
Chónghuǐ into his home, and had his wives
and concubines attend to his meal and drinks. Chónghuǐ,
believing Hóngzhāo treated him generously, when the wine
was flowing freely, fully expressed
how much kindness he had received from the Son of Heaven, but also revealed the source
of the slanders and estrangement, and consequently
shed tears. Hóngzhāo
immediately memorialized that Chónghuǐ was resentful and held grudges. He also secretly
dispatched a messenger to rush a warning to Shí Jìngtáng, telling him
to refuse to submit to Chónghuǐ. Coincidentally,
Jìngtáng, due to a shortage of provisions, hastily
burned his camps and retreated. Chónghuǐ
was also recalled due to slanders against him. When he passed
Fèngxiáng, Hóngzhāo
closed the gates and refused him entry. Chónghuǐ
incurred the emperor’s wrath and died because of this. Fàn Yánguāng,
the Commissioner of Military Affairs, especially disliked Hóngzhāo’s character. Hóngzhāo was dismissed
as General-in-Chief of the Left Wǔwèi Guard and Director of the Southern Bureau of Palace Announcements. After a long
time, he was made
Jiédùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào. At this
time, Míngzōng
was already ill, and the crisis involving Qín Wáng Cóngróng
was starting to brew. All the major ministers
of Táng wished to resign and avoid the impending trouble. Fàn Yánguāng
