and Zhào Yánshòu, Commissioners of Military Affairs, visited the emperor day and night, weeping
and begging to leave their posts. Míngzōng
was angry and refused permission. Yánshòu
sent his wife, Princess Xīngpíng, to speak for him inside the palace. Yánguāng
also used Mèng Hànqióng and Consort Wáng to present his case. Therefore,
they were both allowed to resign. Hóngzhāo
and Féng Yūn replaced Yánshòu and Yánguāng. Hóngzhāo
came for an audience and declined,
saying: "I possess
merely the talent of a slave or retainer, and am not
fit to bear such a great responsibility." Míngzōng
shouted at him, saying: "Do you
all refuse to remain before me? What good is it
for me to employ and sustain you!" Hóngzhāo
was terrified and
took up his duties. As for Féng Yūn,
he was
also a native of Tàiyuán. His father,
Zhāng, served
Míngzōng as a gatekeeper. When Yūn
was a child, he was intelligent
and cunning, and thus beloved by Míngzōng. When Míngzōng
was Jiédùshǐ, he appointed
Yūn as Communications Officer. When Míngzōng
ascended the throne, Yūn was immediately
made Director of the Retainers' Bureau and Director of the Northern Bureau of Palace Announcements. He successively served
as Jiédùshǐ of Hédōng and Zhōngwǔ, and Commissioner of Finance (Sānsī Shǐ).
Míngzōng’s illness was severe,
and high ministers rarely came forward for audiences.
Méng Hànqióng and Empress Dowager Wáng Shúfēi held power,
while Hóngzhāo and Yūn jointly managed state affairs from within,
with major decisions all being settled by these four people.
After they killed the Prince of Qín and installed Emperor Mǐn,
they increasingly regarded this as their achievement.
Moreover, many of the people they employed were unsuitable.
Chén Yì, the Gěishìzhōng (Attendant Gentleman of the Palace Gate),
was insidious and treacherous
and fond of intrigue.
He had previously served Zhāng Hànjié of Liáng
and later served Guō Chóngtāo,
and both men subsequently failed and died.
Nevertheless, Hóngzhāo brought him in as a Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì (Direct Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs)
and utilized his counsel.
At this time,
Hóngzhāo and Yūn sent Hànqióng to Wèi,
to summon Emperor Mǐn to enter and ascend the throne,
and left Hànqióng temporarily in charge of posthumous affairs.
In the first month of the following year,
Hànqióng requested permission to enter the court.
Hóngzhāo and Yūn then discussed transferring Fàn Yán’guāng of Chéngdé to replace Hànqióng,
Shí Jìngtáng, the Commander of Běijīng (Northern Capital), to replace Yán’guāng,
and Lùwáng Cóngkē of Fèngxiáng to replace Jìngtáng.
These three men were all high ministers of Táng (Later Tang),
and due to Hànqióng,
their posts were lightly and easily changed.
Furthermore, no imperial decree was issued;
only envoys were sent to supervise them to set out on the journey.
Cóngkē, consequently, rebelled because of this.
Once Cóngkē’s army had advanced eastward,
Emperor Mǐn became greatly alarmed
and sent someone to summon Hóngzhāo to discuss the situation.
Hóngzhāo said to his retainer Mù Yánhuī:
“The Emperor summons me urgently,
intending to punish me.
My son’s wife
is your daughter;
she should return to you,
to prevent her from being caught in the disaster.”
He then drew his sword and wept loudly,
intending to kill himself,
but his family stopped him.
The envoy urgently pressed Hóngzhāo to enter and have an audience.
Hóngzhāo cried out,
“Misfortune has reached this point!”
and threw himself into a well and died.
Ān Cóngjìn heard of this
and also killed Yūn at his home.
Yūn’s mother had just died,
and the corpses of both mother and son were abandoned on the road;
his wife and children were all killed.
Yūn had a son who was three years old;
his former clerk, Zhāng Shǒusù, concealed him, allowing him to escape.
After Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn (Later Han) ascended the throne,
Hóngzhāo was posthumously granted the title of Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs),
and Yūn, Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Central Secretariat).
Liú Yánlǎng
Liú Yánlǎng
was a native of Yúchéng in Sòngzhōu.
Previously,
when the Deposed Emperor (Cóngkē) rose up in Fèngxiáng,
there were five people who worked with him: Hán Zhāoyìn, the Jiéduàn Pànguān (Military Governor’s Aide);
Lǐ Zhuānměi, the Zhǎng Shūjì (Chief Secretary);
Sòng Shěnqián, the Yájìang (Camp General);
Fáng Gǎo, the Kèjiàng (Guest General);
and Yánlǎng served as the Kǒngmù Guān (Clerical Officer).
Initially,
when Emperor Mǐn ascended the throne,
he moved the Deposed Emperor to serve as the Commander of Běijīng.
He did not issue an imperial decree,
but sent the Gòngfèng Guān (Service Official) Zhào Chǔyuàn to urge the Emperor to set out on the journey.
The Emperor was suspicious
and summoned Zhāoyìn and others to discuss the plan.
Zhāoyìn and the others all encouraged the Emperor to rebel.
Consequently, regardless of whether the matter was large or small,
these five people planned it all.
Gǎo was also fond of sayings about ghosts, spirits, shamans, and diviners.
There was a blind man named Zhāng Méng,
who claimed to serve the god of Mount Tàibái.
The god,
he said, was Cuī Hào of Wèi,
and his predictions of fortune and misfortune were invariably accurate.
Gǎo had always believed in him.
He once brought Méng to see the Emperor.
When the Emperor heard his voice,
he exclaimed in surprise,
“This is no subject!”
Gǎo had Méng ask the god,
and the god relayed the message:
“Three pearls combine into one pearl;
donkeys and horses are driven by men.
The year is Jiǎ-wǔ or Gēng-wǔ,
the restoration is Wù-jǐ Tǔ (Earth).”
Gǎo did not understand the meaning,
so he asked Méng,
Méng said,
“The god spoke thus.
I can relay it,
but I cannot interpret it.”
The Emperor then appointed Méng as a Guǎnyì Xúnguān (Inspector of Post Stations).
The Emperor was about to rebel,
but his army was small
and lacked provisions.
He was consequently very fearful.
He sent Gǎo to ask Méng,
and Méng relayed the god’s message:
“The King shall possess the world.
You may have no worries!”
Thereupon, the decision to rebel was made.
He had Zhuānměi draft the declaration,
which stated:
“Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yūn took advantage of Míngzōng’s illness,
killed the Prince of Qín, and installed Emperor Mǐn.
The Emperor is young,
and petty men hold power,
sowing discord among kin.
We shall call the court to account!”
Envoys were dispatched to rush the news to various circuits,
but none responded.
Only Xiānglǐ Jīn, the Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner) of Lǒngzhōu, sent his Pànguān (Aide) Xuē Wén’yù to discuss the situation.
When the Emperor received Wén’yù,
he was greatly pleased.
Yánlǎng mobilized the wealth and resources of the city residents to supply the army.
Wáng Sītóng led the armies of various circuits to surround Fèngxiáng.
The Deposed Emperor was fearful,
and again sent Gǎo to ask the god.
The god said:
“The King’s army is small.
The eastern army is coming
to welcome the King.”
Afterwards, the eastern army indeed defected and surrendered to the Emperor.
When the Emperor entered the capital,
on the day of his enthronement,
he received the investiture scroll before Míngzōng’s coffin.
The scroll read:
“In the first year of Yìngshùn (Corresponding Harmony),
the cyclical designation is Jiǎ-wǔ,
the fourth month, on the Gēng-wǔ first day of the lunar cycle.”
The Emperor looked back at Gǎo and said,
“How could the prediction of Zhāng Méng’s god
not be confirmed!”
Because of this, Gǎo was increasingly trusted and relied upon,
and he governed affairs purely through shamanism and divination.
After the Emperor was established,
he appointed Zhāoyìn as Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū (Grandee Remonstrant on the Left) and Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì (Academician of the Duānmíng Hall),
Zhuānměi as Bǐbù Lángzhōng (Director of the Bureau of Comparison) and Shūmìyuàn Zhí Xuéshì (Direct Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs),
Shěnqián as Huángchéng Shǐ (Commissioner of the Imperial City),
Gǎo as Xuānhuī Běiyuàn Shǐ (Commissioner of the Northern Court of the Bureau of Palace Affairs),
and Yánlǎng as Zhuāngzhái Shǐ (Commissioner of Palaces and Residences).
After a long time,
Zhāoyìn and Gǎo became Shūmìshǐ (Commissioners of Military Affairs),
Yánlǎng became their Fùshǐ (Vice-Commissioner),
Shěnqián became Shìwèi Bùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (Supreme Commander of the Palace Guard Infantry),
and Xuē Wén’yù also became Zhífāng Lángzhōng (Director of the Bureau of Census) and Shūmìyuàn Zhí Xuéshì.
From then on, Shěnqián commanded the troops,
Zhuānměi and Wén’yù were in charge of strategy and deliberation,
while Zhāoyìn, Gǎo, and Yánlǎng managed confidential affairs.
Initially,
the Emperor and Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn (Later Jin) both served Míngzōng,
but their hearts were not pleased with each other.
After the Emperor entered and was installed,
Gāozǔ had no choice but to come to court.
However, he felt quite self-suspicious
and wished to request permission to return to his circuit,
but found it difficult to speak of.
So, he pretended to be frail and ill,
with moxa burns covering his whole body,
hoping the Emperor would take pity and send him away.
Yánlǎng and many others said that Jìngtáng should be kept in the capital.
Zhāoyìn and Zhuānměi said,
“Jìngtáng and Zhào Yánshòu are both married to Táng princesses,
so we cannot keep one but not the other.”
Thus, Gāozǔ was restored to Hédōng and sent away.
At this time,
the Qìdān frequently raided the northern border.
Gāozǔ was appointed Dàtóng, Zhènwǔ, Wēisài, Zhāngguó, and other military commands’ Fānhàn Mǎbùjūn Dū Zǒngguǎn (Supreme Commander of the Barbarian and Han Cavalry and Infantry),
and stationed at Xīnzhōu.
But the stationed troops suddenly mutinied,
surrounding Gāozǔ and shouting
“Long Live!”
Gāozǔ was frightened,
and only stopped the unrest after executing more than thirty people.
The Emperor was subsequently even more suspicious of him.
At this time,
Gāozǔ held all the elite troops in the north,
transporting provisions and fodder,
which caused hardship and exhaustion far and wide.
The Dì and Yánlǎng daily consulted and deliberated,
while Zhuānměi and Wényù lodged alternately in the Zhōngxīng Diànlú,
being summoned for interviews and discussions,
often concluding only at midnight.
At this time,
Gāozǔ’s younger brother Chóngyìn served as Huángchéng Fùshǐ (Vice Administrator of the Imperial City),
and Cáo Tàihòu (Empress Dowager Cáo), mother of the Shí family princess, resided in the palace.
She was thus able to monitor the Dì’s movements and words and report them to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ increasingly felt endangered and fearful.
Whenever the Dì sent envoys to comfort the troops,
Gāozǔ would feign illness and inability to cope,
and repeatedly request to be relieved of the post of Zǒngguǎn (Commander-in-Chief) to gauge the Dì's feelings.
At this time,
the Dì's mother, Wèi Shì, was posthumously honored as Xuānxiàn Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager Xuānxiàn),
and since her tomb was in Tàiyuán,
officials proposed establishing an imperial funerary palace there.
Gāozǔ advised that the mausoleum was intermixed with commoners' graves,
and a palace should not be established.
The Dì suspected that Gāozǔ wanted to destroy the commoners' graves
and bring resentment upon the state.
The Dì was thus angered,
dismissed Gāozǔ as Zǒngguǎn,
and exiled him to Yùnzhōu.
Yánlǎng and others mostly protested that this was unacceptable,
and Zhào Yányì, the Sītiān (Observatory Official), also stated that the celestial phenomena were disturbed,
and that quietude was necessary to avert disaster.
The matter was thus halted.
More than a month later,
Wényù was on duty alone.
The Dì summoned him at night
and discussed the matter of Jìngtáng.
Wényù said:
“I have heard the saying, 'Building a house by the roadside,
three years and it is not complete.'
The affairs of the state
must be decided by Your Majesty (Bìxià).
Jìngtáng will rebel whether he is moved
or not moved;
it is merely a matter of sooner or later.
It is better to plan against him preemptively.”
The Dì was greatly pleased and said:
“The prognosticators said I would gain a wise assistant this year to stabilize the realm—
are you that man?”
He then ordered Wényù to write out the appointments himself,
and had the draft edict sent down to the Xuéshì Yuàn (Academy of Scholars) at midnight.
The next day, when the decree was proclaimed,
both civil and military officials turned pale.
Five or six days later,
news arrived that Jìngtáng had revolted.
Jìngtáng submitted a memorial,
stating that the Dì was not the son of Míngzōng,
and that Xǔwáng Cóngyì was next in line to the throne.
The Dì received the letter and grew furious,
crumpling it with his hands and throwing it away.
He summoned the Xuéshì Mǎ Yìnsūn to draft a reply,
saying:
“You should use harsh words to slander him.”
Yánlǎng and others urged the Dì to personally lead the campaign.
The Dì was worried and fearful in his heart,
always speaking ill of Jìngtáng’s affairs,
and constantly warned people, saying:
“You must not speak of Shíláng (Sir Shí),
it makes my heart sink to the ground!”
Because of this, he did not want to leave.
But Yánlǎng and others repeatedly pressured him,
so he departed.
Arriving at Huáizhōu,
the Dì summoned Lǐ Sōng at night to ask for strategies.
Wényù, unaware, arrived immediately afterward.
When the Dì saw him, his expression changed,
and Sōng stepped on his foot,
so Wényù went out.
The Dì said:
“When I saw Wényù, I trembled,
and wanted to draw my sword and stab him.”
Sōng said:
“Wényù is a small-minded man.
Killing him would only worsen the great affair;
stabbing him would only increase the ugliness.”
The Dì stopped.
At this time,
the Qìdān had already installed Jìngtáng as the Son of Heaven,
and were marching south with their troops.
The Dì was distraught and did not know where to go.
He sent Shěnqián with a thousand cavalry to Báimǎ Pō to scout the battlefield.
Shěnqián said:
“What ground is unsuitable for battle?
Even if there were such ground,
which men would be willing to stand here?
It is better to return.”
The Dì then returned
and immolated himself.
When Gāozǔ entered the Jīngshī (Capital),
Yánlǎng and the other six men were all stripped of their offices and reduced to commoners.
Originally,
Yánlǎng and Gǎo were jointly in charge of confidential affairs,
but Yánlǎng monopolized the handling of matters.
When generals were due to receive prefectures,
he did not prioritize them according to merit or rank:
those who offered large bribes received good prefectures,
while those who offered few or no bribes received poor prefectures,
or sometimes went long periods without receiving anything.
Due to this, everyone complained.
Gǎo worried about this in his heart,
but could not dispute it,
and merely ate his fill and slept soundly every day.
Whenever Yánlǎng discussed affairs,
Gǎo would lower his head, pretend to sleep, and not attend to the matter.
When the Jìn army invaded,
Yánlǎng fled alone on horseback toward the Southern Mountains.
Passing his home,
he pointed and sighed:
“I stored three hundred thousand cash here,
I wonder who will take it!”
He was subsequently killed by the pursuing troops.
Jìn Gāozǔ heard that Gǎo had always distanced himself from Yánlǎng’s affairs,
felt pity for him,
and later reinstated him as a general.
He died more than a year later.
Zhuānměi served the Jìn dynasty as Dàlǐ Qīng (Minister of the Court of Judicial Review),
and died during the Kāiyùn reign period.
When the Jìn dynasty was about to rise,
the Fèidì appointed Zhāoyìn as Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice Director of the Chancellery) and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (De Facto Chancellor),
and later sent him out as the Héyáng Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Héyáng).
The final fates of him, Shěnqián, and Wényù are all unknown.
Alas,
the principles of fortune and misfortune, success and failure—
must one not be warned?
Zhāng Méng’s divine words proved true,
yet how could one know that they would not lead to disaster?
The events I have recorded
are generally thus;
those who peruse this may reflect deeply.
When the Fèidì rose,
those with whom he planned and deliberated
were merely these five or six men.
Considering the principles of loyalty and rebellion,
even if a wise man had advised him,
he might not necessarily have avoided defeat,
let alone with five or six men such as these!
Therefore, I have included their stories and appended them to the biography of Yánlǎng,
to show the conclusion of their careers.
Kāng Sīlì
Kāng Sīlì
was originally a man from the various tribes of Shānyīn.
In his youth, he was a cavalry commander,
following Zhuāngzōng to defeat the Jiāchéng of the Liáng,
and fighting at Bǎixiāng.
He was repeatedly promoted for merit until he became Tūqí Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander of the Elite Cavalry).
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,

he successively held the posts of Cìshǐ (Prefect) of the two prefectures of Yīng and Lán, Sùzhōu Tuánliànshǐ (Regulator of Militia in Sùzhōu), and Zhāowǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the Zhāowǔ Army).
He was then transferred to garrison Bǎoyì,
and in all these posts, he governed well.
When Lùwáng Cóngkē rebelled in Fèngxiáng,
Mǐndì dispatched Wáng Sītóng and others to suppress him.
Sīlì had 1,500 garrisoned Pěngshèng and Yǔlín troops.
He then assigned a thousand Yǔlín troops to Sītóng.
When Sītóng reached Fèngxiáng,
his army mutinied
and surrendered to Cóngkē.
When Sīlì heard this,
he wanted to execute the families of all thousand Yǔlín soldiers.
Before he could carry this out,
Cóngkē's troops had already arrived.
Sīlì then used the Pěngshèng troops to defend the city.
Cóngkē's troops approached the city walls
and shouted:
“Ten thousand western troops support the new Son of Heaven!
How can you five hundred men resist?
You are merely leading the people of Shǎn to their deaths!”
When the Pěngshèng troops heard this,
they all laid down their armor,
and Sīlì subsequently opened the gates and welcomed Cóngkē.
When the Fèidì ascended the throne,
because Sīlì had initially shown no intention of surrendering,
the Dì was rather displeased with him.
He was transferred to Ānyuǎn,
and then transferred again to Ānguó.
Due to old age, he was dismissed and made Yòu Shénwǔ Tǒngjūn (Commander of the Right Divine Martial Guard).
When Shí Jìngtáng rebelled in Tàiyuán,
the Fèidì appointed Sīlì as Běimiàn Xíngyíng Mǎjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (Supreme Commander of Cavalry for the Northern Expeditionary Camp).
When the Fèidì traveled to Huáizhōu,
he ordered Sīlì to lead the imperial cavalry out through Tuánbǎigǔ to rescue Zhāng Jìngdá.
Before he arrived,
Jìngdá was killed,
and Yáng Guāngyuǎn surrendered to Jìn.
Sīlì fell ill
and died on the road.
After Jìn Gāozǔ entered and established himself,
he was posthumously granted the title Tàizǐ Shàoshī (Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent).
Kāng Yìchéng
Initially,
Yánlǎng and Gǎo jointly managed confidential matters.
Yánlǎng took sole charge of affairs.
Among the generals who were to receive a prefecture,
their merits and seniority were not prioritized.
Those who gave more bribes received good prefectures;
those who gave few or no bribes received bad prefectures,
or were delayed indefinitely.
Because of this, everyone resented him.
Gǎo was inwardly troubled by this,
but could not contend with him.
He merely ate his fill and rested high on his pillow every day.
Whenever Yánlǎng discussed matters,
he would hang his head and feign sleep, paying no attention.
When the Jìn troops entered,
Yánlǎng fled alone on horseback to Nánshān.
Passing his home,
he pointed and sighed, saying:
"I accumulated three hundred thousand *qián* here;
I wonder who will take it!"
He was then killed by the pursuing soldiers.
Jìn Gāozǔ heard that Gǎo had always avoided Yánlǎng's affairs,
and pitied him.
Later, he reinstated him as a general.
He died more than a year later.
Zhuānměi served Jìn as Dàlǐ Qīng [Grand Judge],
and died during the Kāiyùn reign.
When Jìn was about to rise,
the Deposed Emperor appointed Zhāoyìn as Zhōngshū Shìláng [Secretary of the Central Secretariat] and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì [Chancellor].
He was sent out as Háyáng Jiédù Shǐ [Military Governor of Háyáng].
He, Shěnqián, and Wényù, all met unknown ends.
Alas,
the principles of fortune and misfortune, success and failure,
how can one not be cautious!
Zhāng Méng's divine words proved true,
but how could he know that they would not lead to disaster!
What I have recorded
is largely like this.
Readers can ponder deeply.
When the Deposed Emperor rose,
those with whom he plotted and deliberated
were merely these five or six people.
Considering the principles of their rebellion and loyalty,
even if there were wise men to advise them,
they might not necessarily avoid defeat,
much less these five or six people!
Therefore, I have included this narrative and appended it to Yánlǎng's account,
to show the beginning and end of their situation.
Kāng Sīlì
Kāng Sīlì
was originally a native of various tribes in Shānyīn.
As a youth, he was a cavalry commander,
and followed Zhuāngzōng to defeat the Liáng forces at Jiāchéng,
and fought at Báixiāng.
He was repeatedly promoted for his merits to Túqí Zhǐhuīshǐ [Commander of Elite Cavalry].
After Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he successively served as Cǐshǐ [Prefect] of Yìng and Lán prefectures, Sùzhōu Tuánliàn Shǐ [Militia Commissioner of Sùzhōu], and Zhāowǔ Jūn Jiédù Shǐ [Military Governor of Zhāowǔ Army].
He was then moved to command Bǎoyì,
and in all these posts, he governed well.
When Lùwáng Cóngkē rebelled at Fèngxiáng,
Mǐndì dispatched Wáng Sītóng and others to suppress him.
Sīlì had a thousand five hundred soldiers of the Pěngshèng and Yǔlín divisions.
He then assigned a thousand Yǔlín soldiers to Sītóng.
When Sītóng reached Fèngxiáng,
his army mutinied
and surrendered to Cóngkē.
Upon hearing this, Sīlì
wanted to execute all the families of the thousand Yǔlín soldiers,
but before he could,
Cóngkē's troops had already arrived.
Sīlì then garrisoned the city with his Pěngshèng troops.
Cóngkē's troops pressed against the city,
shouting:
"Ten thousand Western soldiers are supporting the new emperor.
Can you five hundred men resist?
You will only doom the Shǎnxī people to death!"
Hearing this, the Pěngshèng soldiers
all laid down their armor.
Sīlì then opened the gates and welcomed Cóngkē.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was quite displeased with Sīlì because he initially had no intention of surrendering.
He was moved to Ānyuǎn,
then to Ānguó,
and due to old age, was dismissed as Yòu Shénwǔ Tǒngjūn [Commander of the Right Divine Martial Army].
When Shí Jìngtáng rebelled at Tàiyuán,
the Deposed Emperor appointed Sīlì as Běimiàn Xíngyíng Mǎjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ [Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry for the Northern Campaign].
The Deposed Emperor went to Huáizhōu,
and sent Sīlì to lead the cavalry accompanying him to Tuanbó Gǔ to relieve Zhāng Jìngdá.
Before he arrived,
Jìngdá had died,
and Yáng Guāngyuǎn had surrendered to Jìn.
Sīlì fell ill
and died on the way.
When Jìn Gāozǔ entered and ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted him the title of Tàizǐ Shàoshī [Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince].
Kāng Yìchéng
Kāng Yìchéng,
courtesy name Xìnchén,
was a native of the Three Tribes north of Dài.
He served the Jìn king with his archery and horsemanship.
During Zhuāngzōng's time, he was Túqí Zhǐhuīshǐ [Commander of Elite Cavalry].
He followed Míngzōng to suppress Zhào Zàilǐ.
When they reached Wèi, the army mutinied.
Yìchéng stepped forward to enumerate Zhuāngzōng's mistakes,
and advised Míngzōng to head south.
After Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Pěngshèng Zhǐhuīshǐ [Commander of the Pěngshèng Division],
and concurrently served as Fénzhōu Cǐshǐ [Prefect of Fénzhōu].
He followed in the defeat of Zhū Shǒuyīn,
and was promoted to Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎbùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ [Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards' Cavalry and Infantry],
concurrently serving as Háyáng Sānchéng Jiédù Shǐ [Military Governor of the Three Prefectures of Háyáng].
He was sent out as Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédù Shǐ [Military Governor of the Eastern Shānnán Circuit],
then returned to be Qīnjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ [Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards],
concurrently serving in Háyáng,
and was granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì [Chancellor].
Qínwáng Cóngróng was always arrogant.
He served as Hénán Yǐn [Prefect of Hénán],
commanded the Six Armies,
and was appointed Dà Yuánshuài [Grand Marshal].
All the Tang ministers feared disaster would strike them,
and sought to distance themselves.
Only Yìchéng was wholeheartedly devoted to him,
and sent his son to serve in Qínwáng's residence.
When Míngzōng fell ill,
Cóngróng planned to enter the palace with troops.
Tang ministers Zhū Hóngzhāo, Féng Yūn, and others all deemed it impermissible,
but Yìchéng alone played both sides.
Cóngróng had already raised troops
and reached Tiānjīn Qiáo.
Hóngzhāo and others entered
and reported his rebellion.
Míngzōng tearfully summoned Yìchéng
and ordered him to handle the situation himself,
but Yìchéng ultimately did not dispatch troops.
Mǎjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ [Cavalry Commander] Zhū Hóngshí attacked Cóngróng with his troops.
Cóngróng was defeated and fled,
and was killed.
Sānsī Shǐ [Commissioner of Finance] Sūn Yuè had once spoken to Féng Yūn about Cóngróng's inevitable defeat.
Yìchéng heard of this and was displeased.
When Cóngróng died,
Yìchéng then led his troops into Hénán Fǔ [Hénán Prefecture],
and summoned Yuè to inspect Cóngróng's family assets.
When Yuè arrived,
Yìchéng, amidst the chaos,
ordered men to shoot him.
Yuè fled to Tōnglì Fāng where he was killed.
Míngzōng could not investigate the matter.
After Yìchéng killed Yuè,
and also because of Cóngróng,
he had a rift with Hóngshí.
When Mǐndì ascended the throne, Hóngshí often prided himself on his achievement of executing Cóngróng, and Yìchéng grew even more resentful.
, courtesy name Xìnchén,
was a man from the Three Tribes north of Dài.
He served the Prince of Jìn through his skill in mounted archery.
During Zhuāngzōng's time, he became the Commander of the Tūqí (Elite Cavalry).
He followed Míngzōng to suppress Zhào Zàilǐ
. When they reached Wèi, the army mutinied.
Yìchéng stepped forward and enumerated Zhuāngzōng's errors
, advising Míngzōng to turn south.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne
, he was promoted to Commander of the Běngshèng (Guarding the Sage)
, and concurrently held the post of Governor (Cìshǐ) of Fénzhōu.
He followed in defeating Zhū Shǒuyīn
, and was promoted to Supreme Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry
, concurrently holding the title of Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Héyáng Sānchéng.
He was posted out as the Military Governor of Shānnán Dōngdào
, and later returned to be Supreme Commander of the Imperial Guard
, concurrently governing Héyáng
, and was granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Qín Wáng Cóngróng was naturally arrogant.
After he became the Magistrate (Yǐn) of Hénán
, oversaw the Six Armies
, and was appointed Grand Marshal (Dà Yuánshuài)
, all the great ministers of Táng feared that disaster would strike them
, and sought to extricate themselves.
Only Yìchéng privately allied himself with him
, sending his son to serve in the residence of the Prince of Qín.
When Míngzōng fell ill
, Cóngróng planned to enter the palace with troops.
The Táng ministers, Zhū Hóngzhāo, Féng Yūn, and others, all believed this was unacceptable
, but Yìchéng alone held ambiguous positions.
When Cóngróng finally raised his troops
, and reached Tiānjīn Bridge
, Hóngzhāo and others entered the palace
, and reported the rebellion.
Míngzōng tearfully summoned Yìchéng
, ordering him to handle the situation himself
, but Yìchéng ultimately did not mobilize troops.
Zhū Hóngshí, the Commander of the Cavalry
, attacked Cóngróng with his troops. Cóngróng was defeated and fled
, and was killed.
Sūn Yuè, the Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī Shǐ), had previously told Féng Yūn that Cóngróng was certain to fail
. Yìchéng heard this and was displeased.
After Cóngróng died
, Yìchéng finally led troops into Hénán Prefecture
, and summoned Yuè to inspect Cóngróng's household assets.
When Yuè arrived
, Yìchéng took advantage of the chaos
, and ordered men to shoot him.
Yuè fled to Tōnglì Fāng where he was killed
. Míngzōng could not investigate this.
After Yìchéng had killed Yuè
, and also because of Cóngróng
, he had a feud with Hóngshí.
When Mǐndì ascended the throne
, Hóngshí often prided himself on the merit of executing Cóngróng
, and Yìchéng grew increasingly discontented.
Lù Wáng Cóngkē rebelled at Fèngxiáng
. Wáng Sītóng led the troops from various garrisons to surround him
. The troops of Zhāng Qiánzhāo from Xīngyuán mutinied and surrendered to Cóngkē
. Sītóng fled
, and the troops of all the garrisons dispersed.
Mǐndì was greatly enraged
, and said to Zhū Hóngzhāo and others
: "I have just ascended the throne
, and the affairs of the realm are all managed by you gentlemen
. However, regarding how I treated my older brother
, I have not yet lost my principles
. You gentlemen pressed me with grand strategy
, and I could not alone oppose it.
Now that events have reached this point
, how can we avert this disaster?
I should lead my attendants to go and welcome my elder brother
, and yield the throne to him
. If he does not trust me
, I will die there!"
Hóngzhāo and the others were terrified and could not respond
. Yìchéng stepped forward and said
: "The western army panicked and dispersed
. The commander was merely fearful
. Currently, the capital still has many troops
. I request permission to lead them all west
, to defend the passes
, recruit the scattered survivors
, and plan for the future."
Mǐndì thought this was correct
. He personally visited the Zuǒzàng Treasury
, and personally bestowed upon the officers and soldiers twenty bolts of silk per man
, and five thousand cash.
At this time
, Míngzōng's imperial tomb ceremony had not yet been completed
, and the imperial treasury was depleted.
The soldiers, carrying their rewards, openly declared
: "When we reach Fèngxiáng, we will demand another portion."
Zhū Hóngshí saw that the soldiers lacked morale
, and since Yìchéng was leading all the troops west
, he suspected him of disloyalty.
He said to Yìchéng
: "Now the western army has suffered a slight defeat
, but not a single horseman has fled eastward
. The sentiment of the people is thus clear
. It would be better to use the available troops to guard the capital and secure ourselves
. Although they enjoyed a victory
, they merely gained Qiánzhāo's single army
. The troops of the various garrisons are behind them
. Dare they come straight here?"
Yìchéng angrily replied
: "If you say such a thing
, Hóngshí is the rebel!"
Hóngshí retorted
: "Who do you suppose wishes to rebel, sir?"
His voice was stern and loud.
Mǐndì summoned the two men
. They argued before him
. The Emperor could not decide
, and consequently executed Hóngshí
. He appointed Yìchéng as the Commissioner of Pacification and Mobilization (Zhāotǎoshǐ)
, leading all the Forbidden Armies westward.
Mǐndì fled to Wèizhōu.
Yìchéng marched until he reached Xīn'ān
, and surrendered to Cóngkē.
In the fourth month of Qīngtài first year (934 CE)
, he was executed outside the Xīngjiào Gate
, and his clan was exterminated.
Alas!
The Five Dynasties, in establishing their states
, rose and fell by means of their armies
, yet their military system
, is not worth mentioning to later generations.
Only the title, Imperial Guard (Shìwèi Qīnjūn)
, is still retained today and is held in great importance
. This is a legacy institution of the Five Dynasties.
However, tracing its origins, it started out insignificantly
, but by the time it reached its zenith
, it could truly be called grand!
During the late Táng era
, there were many troops belonging to the regional commands (Fāngzhèn)
. Every single army had one Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ)
, and for all the armies within a prefecture (zhōu) combined
, there was also one Supreme Commander of Cavalry and Infantry
. This was generally the leader of the soldiers and ranks.
When the Liáng dynasty established its state based on the Xuānwǔ Army
, it followed their old system
, having the Supreme Commander of Metropolitan Cavalry and Infantry.
The Later Táng dynasty adopted this
. By the time of Míngzōng
, the title was first changed to Supreme Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry.
At that time
, the Son of Heaven naturally held authority over the positions of the Six Armies and various Guards
. The Six Armies had the Tǒngjūn (Army Controllers)
, and the various Guards had Generals (Jiāngjūn)
. Furthermore, one great minister or imperial relative would be appointed to oversee the affairs of the Six Armies and various Guards
. This was the old system whereby the court's Grand General commanded the nation's army on behalf of the Son of Heaven
. As for the Imperial Guard (Shìwèi Qīnjūn)
, it was the private army personally commanded by the Son of Heaven
. This can be inferred from its title.
Since the Son of Heaven was the commander himself
, the Supreme Commander was merely the general leader of his ranks and soldiers.
However, since the Hàn and Zhōu dynasties
, that office became increasingly important.
In Hàn, there was the Shìwèi Sīyù (Imperial Guard Judicial Office)
, and all major court affairs were decided by the Imperial Guard Judicial Office.
At that time
, Shǐ Hóngzhào served as the Supreme Commander
, and held state power alongside the Chancellor (Zǎixiàng) and the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ)
. Hóngzhào was especially entrusted with authority
, leading to the dynasty's ruin.
As the saying goes
: "If trickles are not cut off
, they flow into rivers and seas
. If faint flames are not extinguished
, what can be done against roaring conflagrations?"
Should one not be warned!
However, at that time
, the regional commands each had their own troops
, and the Son of Heaven's Imperial Guard amounted to no more than the troops stationed in the capital
. Now, the regional commands exist in name but are defunct in reality
. The Six Armies and various Guards have furthermore been abandoned
. The court lacks the office of the Grand General
, and all the armies of the realm, both internal and external, belong to the Imperial Guard Bureau (Shìwèi Sī)
. In this case, for the one who holds the post of Supreme Commander
, how could his power not be increasingly significant!
The title 'Imperial Guard' (Qīnjūn)
, began with Míngzōng
. Afterward, there was also the Supreme Commander of the Palace Front (Diànqián Dūzhǐhuīshǐ)
, who was also an Imperial Guard commander
. The exact beginning of this restructuring is unknown.
Today, the armies of the realm
, are divided under these two Bureaus.
Yuè Yànchóu
Yào Yànchóu
was a person of the Three Shātuó Tribes.
Initially, he served as a cavalry general.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Cénɡzhōu Cìshǐ.
He followed Wánɡ Yànqiú in defeating Wánɡ Dū at Dìnɡzhōu,
and was promoted to Shìwèi Bùjūn Dū Yúhòu,
and concurrently held the title of Shòuzhōu Jiédùshǐ.
Ān Chónɡhuǐ falsely issued an edict sending Yánɡ Yànwēn, Commander of Hèzhōnɡ, to expel the Jiédùshǐ, Lù Wánɡ Cónɡkē.
Yànchóu was made the Commander for the Campaign (Zhāotǎoshǐ).
Míngzōnɡ suspected that Yànwēn might have something to say,
and instructed Yànchóu not to kill Yànwēn if he captured him,
intending to question him.
Yànchóu sought to comply with Chónɡhuǐ's wishes,
and killed Yànwēn to silence him.
Míngzōnɡ was furious,
but did not punish him for this crime.
During the Chánɡxīnɡ era, he served as Jìnɡnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
The Dǎnɡxiànɡ tribes, led by Āmái and Qūxībǎo, raided Fānɡqú,
and ambushed and killed the Huíhú envoy.
Míngzōnɡ sent Yànchóu to join forces with Kānɡ Fú of Línɡwǔ to attack them.
Āmái and the others fled and hid in the valleys.
Míngzōnɡ believed that the Dǎnɡxiànɡ knew fear,
and that constraints should be imposed upon them, followed by conciliation and comfort.
Before the envoy arrived,
Yànchóu and his men entered Báiyú Gǔ from Niú'ér Tribe,
and completely exterminated their tribe.
They captured their great leader Lián Xiānɡ and others,
and sent men to report the victory.
Míngzōnɡ said to the envoy:
"My reason for executing the Dǎnɡxiànɡ
was not for profit.
Whatever the army captures,
must all be distributed among the soldiers.
Do not use the pretense of 'tribute presentation' (jìnfènɡ)
to heavily tax the troops."
Later, Yànchóu presented, as tribute, two jade spheres that the Dǎnɡxiànɡ had stolen from the Huíhú, and a gold-fitted *húgē* dedicated to Qín Wánɡ.
Míngzōnɡ said:
"I have already instructed Yànchóu;
I cannot break my word."
Therefore, he bestowed all of it upon Yànchóu.
He also drove out the various Rónɡ tribes of Yánzhōu,
and recovered more than a thousand men and women they had seized.
When Lù Wánɡ Cónɡkē rebelled,
Yànchóu served as Deputy Commander for the Campaign (Zhāotǎo Fùshǐ).
Wánɡ Sītónɡ's army was defeated and scattered.
Yànchóu fled east together with Sītónɡ.
They were captured by Lù Wánɡ's forces,
and imprisoned in the jail at Huàzhōu.
Afterwards, they were killed.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Shìzhōnɡ.
Yànchóu and Sītónɡ both fled following their defeat.
At that time, Mǐndì was still alive,
and the Tánɡ dynasty had not yet fallen.
The two men fled back toward the country;
regarding integrity, they had not failed,
which made their flight different from that of Yuán Xínɡqīn.
However, Sītónɡ's words and righteousness were unyielding;
his death is commendable.
Yànchóu was merely captured and executed,
and nothing else worthy of praise remains.
Therefore, he is not listed among those who died for the state.
Biography of Tánɡ Ministers, Chapter 16: Dòulú Gé
Dòulú Gé.
His father, Zàn,
was the Tánɡ Cìshǐ of Shūzhōu.
The Dòulú clan was a prominent family throughout the generations.
Late in the Tánɡ dynasty, when the world was in chaos,
Gé fled to Zhōnɡshān.
When Tánɡ perished,
he became Wánɡ Chǔzhí's Chief Secretary (Zhǎnɡshūjì).
When Zhuānɡzōnɡ was in Wèi,
discussions were held about establishing the Tánɡ state.
Since almost all of the noble families and high officials of the former Tánɡ had been lost in the chaos,
and Gé was a son of a prominent family,
he was summoned to serve as Acting Left Chancellor (Xínɡtái Zuǒ Chénɡxiànɡ).
When Zhuānɡzōnɡ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Tónɡ Zhōnɡshū Ménxià Pínɡzhānɡ Shì.
Although Gé belonged to a famous Tánɡ family,
he had no learning in his nature.
When appointing officials,
he often failed to follow the proper procedure,
and was frequently corrected by Shànɡshū Lánɡ Xiāo Xīfǔ.
Gé was quite troubled by this.
After Zhuānɡzōnɡ destroyed Liánɡ,
Gé recommended Wéi Yuè to be Chancellor (Xiànɡ).
Yuè,
late in the Tánɡ dynasty, had been Diànzhōnɡ Shì Yùshǐ,
but was demoted to Nánhǎi due to an incident.
Later, he served Liánɡ as Lǐbù Shìláng.
Gé considered that Yuè was knowledgeable about the affairs of the previous dynasty,
and therefore brought him in to assist himself.
However, Yuè also lacked scholarship;
he merely acted superior due to his social standing.
At this time,
Zhuānɡzōnɡ feared Empress Liú internally,
and was externally misled by eunuchs and entertainers.
Although Guō Chónɡtāo was completely loyal to the state,
he also lacked scholarship.
Gé and Yuè passively accepted matters and did nothing,
only giving their assent to Chónɡtāo.
At the juncture between the Tánɡ and Liánɡ dynasties,
officials encountered chaos and fled,
and the Ministry of Personnel's records (quánwénshū) were incomplete.
People used this opportunity for illicit gain.
This extended to secretly selling official certificates (gàochì),
and confusing the seniority order (zhāomù),
leading to paternal uncles and maternal uncles bowing to their nephews and sons-in-law.
Chónɡtāo requested that they be judged according to the law.
At this time, Tánɡ had just destroyed Liánɡ,
and court discipline had not yet been established.
Commentators thought reforms should be gradual,
but Chónɡtāo abhorred evil too much,
and was resolute in enforcing the law strictly.
Yuè and Gé knew in their hearts that this was improper,
but they were unable to offer any proposals.
In the winter of that year,
Wú Yánhào, an examinee, altered the certificate (gàoshēn) of his deceased uncle to carry out official duties.
When the matter was discovered,
Yánhào and the selecting official Yǐn Méi were both condemned to death.
Cuī Yí, the Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shànɡshū Zuǒ Chénɡ) overseeing the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Quán), and others were all demoted.
Yuè and Gé went to the Palace Gate (Gémén) to await punishment.
Consequently, all affairs were conducted according to the new law.
Those who were rejected for being fake or excessive, and who died in exile or cried lamenting in the streets,
were countless.
When Chónɡtāo died,
Yuè instructed his disciples to submit memorials discussing this matter,
and commentators also blamed Yuè for it.
That year,
there was a great flood,
and earthquakes continuously shook the lands in all four directions.
Tens of thousands of displaced persons starved to death,
and the soldiers' wives gathered wild plants for food.
Zhuānɡzōnɡ daily reprimanded Kǒnɡ Qiān, the Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī Shǐ).
Qiān did not know what to do.
Duàn Huái, a minor official in the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì), said: "I have seen precedents from the former dynasty:
when the state faces a great calamity,
the Son of Heaven (Tiānzi) uses an imperial decree written in vermillion to question the Chancellors (Zǎixiànɡ).
Floods and droughts
are the responsibility of the Chancellors."
Zhuānɡzōnɡ then ordered the Academicians (Xuèshì) to draft an edict,
wrote it out himself,
and used it to question Gé and Yuè.
Gé and Yuè could not reply,
only stating: "Your Majesty's imposing virtue is manifest throughout the four seas.
Now, the Western army has defeated Shǔ,
gaining countless treasures,
which can supply the army.
Floods and droughts
are the constant way of Heaven;
they are nothing to worry about."
Since Gé became Chancellor,
he encountered many troubles in the realm,
yet he was engaged in consuming cinnabar (dānshā) and practicing *liànqì* (energy cultivation) to seek immortality.
He once vomited blood for several days,
nearly dying.
Both men made their sons Shíyí (Corrector),
placing father and son in the same department.
People considered this improper,
so they quickly changed their posts to other offices.
Gé made Yuè's son Hónɡwén Guǎn Xuéshì,
and Yuè made Gé's son Jíxián Yuàn Xuéshì.
When Zhuānɡzōnɡ died,
Gé served as the Commissioner of the Imperial Mausoleum (Shānlínɡ Shǐ).
After Zhuānɡzōnɡ was interred in the ancestral temple,
Gé returned to his private residence.
After several days, he had not yet received a new appointment,
but his old friends and guests urged him to attend court.
Ān Chónɡhuǐ, the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ), denounced him in court, saying: "The title of Commissioner of the Imperial Mausoleum is still active!
Without waiting for a change of appointment,
you rushed to take part in the new court.
Do you think we military men
can be fooled?"
submitted memorials falsely accusing Gé of allowing his tenants to commit murder,
and Yuè was accused of arguing with a neighbor over a well.
Consequently, both were dismissed.
Gé was demoted to Cìshǐ of Chénzhōu,
and Yuè to Cìshǐ of Mǎnɡzhōu.
They were dispatched urgently via post horses to their posts.
The Chancellors Zhènɡ Yù and Rèn Huán submitted memorials three times,
requesting that the subsequent sentences not be carried out,
but they received no response.
Gé was again condemned for privately taking his requested salary,
and Yuè for selling offices to examinees.
Gé was demoted to Sīhù Cānjūn of Fèizhōu,
and Yuè to Sīhù Cānjūn of Yízhōu.
Both were given the concurrent title of Yuánwài Zhì Tónɡzhènɡ Yuán.
Afterwards, Gé was exiled to Línɡzhōu,
and Yuè to Hézhōu,
both permanently relocated as commoners.
Initially,
Shuō had once been exiled to Nánhǎi due to an offense.
He received amnesty,
and returned to reside temporarily in Jiānglíng.
He became acquainted with Gāo Jì Xīng,
and when he (Shuō) became chancellor,
they constantly exchanged correspondence and gifts.
When the Táng army attacked Shǔ,
Jì Xīng requested to lead troops into the Sānxiá (Three Gorges).
Zhuāngzōng permitted this,
allowing Jì Xīng to independently seize Kuí, Zhōng, Wàn, Guī, and Xiá prefectures, etc., as dependent commanderies.
When Shǔ was defeated,
Jì Xīng achieved no merit,
and the Táng used other generals to capture the five prefectures.
When Míngzōng first ascended the throne,
Jì Xīng repeatedly requested the five prefectures,
claiming that the late emperor had granted permission,
so the imperial court had no choice but to concede them.
When Gé and Shuō were demoted again,
he consequently blamed the matter on the two men.
In the summer of Tiānchéng second year (927 CE),
an imperial edict commanded the prefects of Líng and Hé Prefectures to supervise their forced suicides.
Gé's son, Shēng,
and Shuō's son, Tāo,
both reached the rank of Shàngshū Láng (Secretary of the Department of State Affairs),
but were dismissed due to their fathers.
Later, at the beginning of Jìn Tiānfú (936 CE),
Tāo served as Yuánwàiláng (Supernumerary Secretary) in the Department of Provisions (Shàngshū Zhànbù),
and died.
Lú Chéng
Lú Chéng,
it is unknown what family he descended from.
During the reign of Táng Zhāozōng,
Chéng passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and served as an Investigating Official (Xúnguān) attached to the Salt and Iron Commission.
When Táng fell,
he fled the chaos to Yān and Zhào,
changed his clothes to resemble a Dàoshì (Daoist priest),
and wandered among the feudal lords.
Dòu Lú Gé served as Wáng Chǔ Zhí's Adjutant (Pànguān),
and Lú Rǔ Bì served as Deputy Military Governor (Jiédù Fùshǐ) of Hédōng.
Both men were famous clansmen from the former Táng era,
and their social standing was equal to Chéng's.
They consequently jointly recommended him to be Hédōng Military Governor's Commissioner of Judgment (Tuīguān).
Zhuāngzōng once summoned Chéng to draft documents,
but Chéng declined, saying he was unable.
Afterwards, during the Battle of Húliǔ,
the Chief Secretary (Zhǎngshūjì), Wáng Jiān, died in battle.
Zhuāngzōng returned his army to Tàiyuán,
hosted a banquet, and said to the Supervising Official (Jiānjūn), Zhāng Chéng Yè: "I shall use this goblet of wine to summon a secretary to the assembly.
" He then raised the goblet and presented it to the Investigating Official (Xúnguān), Féng Dào.
Chéng's rank was higher than Dào's,
but because he had previously declined, stating inability,
he was not chosen,
but Chéng was promoted to Administrative Assistant (Zhīshǐ).
Chéng was greatly resentful and said: "Do you employ men without considering pedigree, and prioritize a country bumpkin instead!
When Zhuāngzōng had already ascended the throne,
deliberation was made on selecting chancellors.
Lú Rǔ Bì and Sū Xún were already dead,
and next in line was Military Governor's Adjutant (Jiédù Pànguān) Lú Zhì, who was due for appointment.
But Zhì was not happy taking on responsibility,
so he said that Dòu Lú Gé and Chéng were both famous clansmen from the former Táng era
and could serve as chancellors.
Zhuāngzōng appointed Chéng as Chieftain Administrator (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Chancellor (Tóng Píngzhāng Shì).
At this time,
the imperial court had just been established,
and the hundred systems were incomplete.
On the day Chéng and Gé accepted their appointments,
they used sedan chairs and large retinues,
shouting loudly along the roads.
Zhuāngzōng heard the noise and asked those around him.
They replied: "The chancellors' palanquins are entering the gate.
Zhuāngzōng climbed the tower to watch them,
and laughed, saying: "This is what is called ‘seeming right but being wrong.'
from Wèi to Tàiyuán.
Traversing mountains and dangerous terrain,
wherever he went in prefectures and counties,
he conscripted laborers.
When officials came to welcome and bow to him,
Chéng sat in his sedan chair as usual,
and if anyone slightly displeased him,
he would certainly flog and humiliate them.
Someone requested the loan of donkey drivers from Chéng.
Chéng issued a directive to Xīngtáng Prefecture to provide them.
The prefectural clerk reported that there was no precedent (for this request).
Chéng, in anger, flogged the clerk on the back.
The Vice Prefect (Shàoyǐn), Rèn Huán,
who was Zhuāngzōng's brother-in-law (husband of his sister),
went to Chéng to protest that this was unacceptable.
Chéng wore a Huáyáng headscarf,
donned a crane-feather cloak (*hèchǎng*),
leaned on a desk, and decided affairs.
He looked at Huán and cursed: "What creature are you,
relying on the power of your wife's family!
Chancellors draw provisions from prefectures and counties—
why should this be unacceptable!
Huán did not reply and departed,
riding rapidly that night to Bózhōu to see Zhuāngzōng.
Zhuāngzōng was furious,
and said to Guō Chóng Tāo: "We mistakenly appointed this foolish creature as chancellor.
How dare he insult my Nine Ministers!
" He immediately ordered him to commit suicide.
Chóng Tāo also wanted him executed,
but thanks to Lú Zhì's strong intervention,
he was instead dismissed and made Right Privy Counselor (Yòu Shùzǐ).
When Zhuāngzōng entered Luò,
Chéng fell off his horse on the road,
suffered a stroke, and died.
He was posthumously granted the title Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū).
Rèn Huán
Rèn Huán,
was a man from Sānyuán in Jīngzhào.
He was clear-headed and quick-witted,
and skilled in speech and debate.
Those who saw him admired his appearance and demeanor,
and upon hearing his brilliant and wide-ranging discourse,
they were further moved with awe.
Lǐ Sì Zhāo was the Military Governor of Zhāoyì,
and invited Huán to be his Investigating Administrative Assistant (Guānchá Zhīshǐ).
The Liáng army built a double wall and besieged Lùzhōu.
After more than a year, the Prince of Jìn died,
and the Jìn soldiers who were relieving Lù all disbanded and left.
Sì Zhāo was in extreme danger
and asked Huán for advice on whether to stay or leave.
Huán advised Sì Zhāo to hold firm and wait,
and not to harbor disloyal thoughts.
Soon after, Zhuāngzōng attacked and broke the Liáng double wall.
Hearing that Huán had devised the defense plan for Sì Zhāo,
he greatly praised him,
and thus Huán became even more famous.
Later, Sì Zhāo had a rift with Zhuāngzōng.
Huán frequently traveled back and forth as an envoy,
clarifying the fabricated slanders.
Sì Zhāo ultimately avoided disaster,
which was due to Huán's efforts.
Sì Zhāo followed Zhuāngzōng in the Battle of Húliǔ
and defeated the Liáng army.
Huán had considerable merit.
Zhuāngzōng praised him, saying: "Can a scholar also suffer bodily harm?
The courage of the benevolent,
how magnificent it is!
Zhāng Wén Lǐ assassinated Wáng Róng,
and Zhuāngzōng sent Sì Zhāo to suppress him.
Sì Zhāo died in battle,
and Huán took command of his army in his place.
His orders and commands were strict and solemn.
However, Wén Lǐ's son, Chǔ Qiú, and others closed the city and defended firmly,
making it impossible to capture.
Huán repeatedly explained the consequences (of fortune and misfortune) to the garrison people,
and the garrison people trusted him.
Huán once led his troops to the base of the city wall.
Chǔ Qiú climbed the wall and called out to Huán: "The provisions and troops inside the city are both exhausted,
yet we have resisted the royal army for a long time.
If we surrender ourselves now,
I fear there is no way to escape responsibility.
I hope you will show pity,
and point out a path to survival.
" Huán told him: "Given the deeds of your father,
it is truly difficult to forgive or pardon.
However, punishment does not usually extend to descendants;
you might receive lighter treatment.
But having resisted and defended for a year,
injuring our great general,
and then, only upon sudden exhaustion,
expressing sincerity—
judged by this standard,
you too will be difficult to spare.
Nevertheless, sitting still and waiting for ruin,
how does that compare to submitting and awaiting the mandate?
Chǔ Qiú wept and said: "Your words are correct!
" He then sent his son with a formal petition begging for surrender.
Everyone praised Huán, saying his words were not deceptive.
Soon afterward, another general attacked and breached Zhènzhōu.
were mostly able to preserve their families.
Zhènzhōu was designated Běijīng.
Huán was appointed Shàngshū of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū),
concurrently holding the posts of Yǐn of Zhēndìng, Vice Resident (Fù Liúshǒu) of Běijīng, acting as the Resident (Zhī Liúshǒu Shì).
His governance was beneficial and beloved.
The next year,
Guō Chóngtāo concurrently became Jiedushi of the Chéngdé Army.
Huán was reassigned as Sīmǎ of the Traveling Army (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ),
still holding the office of Zhī Zhēndìng Fǔ Shì.
Huán and Chóngtāo had always been on good terms,
and Huán was also his Sīmǎ.
Chóngtāo therefore entrusted him with the affairs of Zhènzhōu,
but Huán often disagreed or handled things differently.
Previously,
Huán's Assistant Judge (Tuīguān), Zhāng Péng, was treacherous, dangerous, greedy, and corrupt.
Huán failed to perceive this,
trusted him,
and was often betrayed by him.
When Chóngtāo took charge of Zhèn,
Péng plotted for Huán to conceal public office funds.
Zhuāngzōng sent eunuchs to select over a hundred palace women from the time of the former Prince Zhào.
There was a woman of the Xǔ clan who was particularly beautiful.
Péng bribed the guards to hide her.
Later, the matter came to light.
Péng was summoned to the capital (Jīngshī)
to be punished.
Péng became frightened
and presented all the account books for the public funds he had previously hidden to Chóngtāo.
Chóngtāo felt deeply indebted to Péng
and did not kill him.
Consequently, a rift formed between Chóngtāo and Huán.
In the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE),
Huán was dismissed as Sīmǎ
and retained the post of Gōngbù Shàngshū.
When Prince Wèi, Jìjí, and Chóngtāo attacked Shǔ,
they feared Huán might attack them from the rear,
so they appointed Huán to assist in the military affairs of Prince Wèi.
When Shǔ was destroyed,
they recommended Huán for the post of Jiedushi of Qiánnán.
Huán earnestly declined the appointment.
Jìjí killed Chóngtāo
and used Huán to replace him in commanding his army for the return journey.
Kāng Yánxiào rebelled.
Jìjí sent Huán leading three thousand men
to join the forces of Dǒng Zhāng and Mèng Zhīxiáng,
and they defeated Yánxiào at Hànzhōu.
However, Prince Wèi had already reached Wèinán
and committed suicide.
Huán took command of the entirety of his army and marched eastward.
Míngzōng commended his achievements
and appointed Huán Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì,
concurrently presiding over the Three Offices (Pàn Sānsī).
At this time,
Míngzōng had recently executed Kǒng Qiān.
Huán selected and appointed talented and distinguished individuals,
suppressed all avenues for opportunism and undue influence.
Public and private finances were sufficient,
and the entire realm found this convenient.
That autumn,
Wéi Shuō and Dòu Lú Gé were dismissed from the Chancellorship.
Huán, Án Chónghuǐ, Zhèng Yù, and Kǒng Xún debated selecting suitable candidates for Chancellor.
Huán favored Lǐ Qí,
but Yù and Xún intrinsically did not want Qí to be Chancellor.
They told Chónghuǐ: "Lǐ Qí is not without literary skill,
but he is simply not incorruptible!
The Chancellor
must be upright and possess great capacity;
Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng) Cuī Xié would be suitable."
Chónghuǐ agreed with this assessment.
Another day,
Míngzōng asked who was suitable for the Chancellorship.
Chónghuǐ immediately nominated Xié in response.
Huán stepped forward and argued: "Chónghuǐ is not yet familiar with the personnel of the imperial court
and has been misled by others.
Everyone knows that Cuī Xié is illiterate,
possessing only an empty bearing;
he is nicknamed the 'Stele Without Inscription' (Méizì Bēi).
I worry Your Majesty may mistakenly promote and appoint
those who gain advancement without merit.
If this man, who knows no letters,
is enough to make a laughingstock of me alone, that is sufficient.
How many Chancellorships are there?
How can we tolerate adding further causes for mockery?"
Míngzōng said: "The Chancellorship is a weighty position.
You gentlemen should deliberate further yourselves.
However, when I was in the provinces,
I knew Wéi Sù, the Prefect of Yìzhōu.
People say Sù is a son of a noble family,
and moreover, he treated me very kindly.
Would it be permissible to place him in this position?
If Sù is perhaps unsuitable,
then Secretary Féng,
who was an Assistant Official (Pànguān) in the previous dynasty,
is called a virtuous elder (Zhǎngzhě),
and can be Chancellor!"
Secretary Féng
was Dào.
As the discussion was undecided,
Chónghuǐ and the others retired to the corridor outside the Zhōngxīng Hall.
Kǒng Xún refused to bow,
brushed his sleeves, and departed,
walking and cursing, saying: "In matters of state, first there is Rèn Huán,
and second, Rèn Huán!
Who exactly is Huán?"
Huán said to Chónghuǐ: "Lǐ Qí's talent and skill
are superior to a hundred men of his generation,
but slanderers cunningly obstruct him
and are jealous of his ability.
If we abandon Qí and appoint Xié as Chancellor,
it is like discarding the pill of *sūhé* (storax) and picking up the dung rolled by a beetle!"
Chónghuǐ smiled and stopped the debate.
Nevertheless, Chónghuǐ ultimately believed Xún's words.
After more than a month,
both Xié and Féng Dào were appointed Chancellor.
Xié held the Chancellorship for several years,
and many people ridiculed his actions,
but the deterioration of relations between Huán and Chónghuǐ started with Xié.
Traditionally, when imperial envoys traveled to the four directions,
their credentials (quàn) were all issued by the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù).
Chónghuǐ memorialized, requesting they be issued by the Inner Court (Nèi).
Huán argued based on precedent,
but could not succeed.
He then debated Chónghuǐ before the Emperor,
and Huán's tone and expression were both severe.
When Míngzōng adjourned court,
the imperial consorts and attendants of the inner palace came forward and asked: "Who was the person arguing with Chónghuǐ?"
Míngzōng replied: "It was the Chancellor (Zǎixiàng)."
The women of the palace submitted: "When I was in Cháng'ān,
I saw Chancellors reporting on affairs,
but never like this.
He must surely hold Your Majesty in slight regard!"
Míngzōng was displeased by this,
and the envoys' credentials were ultimately issued by the Inner Court.
Huán became increasingly frustrated and discouraged.
Chónghuǐ once visited Huán.
Huán brought out a courtesan
who was skilled in singing and beautiful.
Chónghuǐ desired her,
but Huán refused to give her up.
From this point on, the two men increasingly disliked each other.
Huán then immediately requested to resign his position,
and was dismissed to become Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo).
Huán did not feel secure,
so he requested retirement (Zhìshì)
and moved to live in Cízhōu.
When Zhū Shǒuyīn rebelled at Biànzhōu,
Chónghuǐ falsely accused Huán of conspiring with Shǒuyīn
and sent men falsely claiming an imperial decree to kill him.
Huán accepted the order calmly,
gathered his family, drank heavily, and then died.
Míngzōng knew about it but did not inquire further.
He issued an edict
condemning Huán for corresponding with Shǒuyīn and speaking words involving resentment and ill-will.
When Emperor Mǐn (Mǐn Dì) ascended the throne,
Huán was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
Zhào Fèng.
Zhào Fèng
was a man from Yōuzhōu.
In his youth, he was well known for his Confucian scholarship.
During the time of Liú Shǒuguāng, the Prince of Yān,
all the people of Yān were tattooed and made soldiers.
Fèng was afraid,
so he shaved his head and became a monk,
hiding himself by relying on Shǒuguāng's younger brother, Shǒu Qí, the Prince of Yān.
Shǒu Qí fled to Liáng,
and Liáng made Shǒu Qí the Prefect of Bózhōu.
Fèng became his Assistant Official (Pànguān).
When Shǒu Qí died,
Fèng left to become the Jiedushi's Assistant Official (Jiédù Pànguān) of Yùnzhōu.
Jìn captured Yùnzhōu.
Zhuāngzōng heard of Fèng's reputation,
was pleased to acquire him,
and made him Scholar Attending the Imperial Carriage (Hù Luán Xuéshì).
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
Fèng was appointed Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén) and Hanlin Academician (Hànlín Xuéshì).
Zhuāngzōng and Empress Liú visited the residence of Zhāng Quányì, the Administrator (Yǐn) of Hénán.
While thoroughly enjoying the wine,
the Emperor ordered the Empress to bow to Quányì as her father.
The next day,
eunuchs were sent to order the Academicians to write a memorial (jiān) to Quányì,
treating him as a father.
Fèng submitted a letter arguing strongly against the propriety of this action.
Zhāng Quányì's adopted son, Hǎo Jìsūn, committed a crime and was executed.
The eunuchs and court entertainers hoped to seize his property
and earnestly requested the confiscation of his assets.
Fèng again submitted a letter, saying: "Jìsūn was Quányì's adopted son.
It is inappropriate for him to have separate registered wealth.
Moreover, according to law, the crime does not warrant confiscation.
To execute a man and profit from his wealth
cannot be demonstrated to the world."
At this time,
the Empress and various petty individuals held sway, and Fèng's recommendations were all disregarded.
Míngzōng was a martial ruler,
unversed in literature.
The memorials and reports from all quarters
were usually assigned to Ān Zhònghuǐ to read.
Zhònghuǐ also did not know letters,
and his readings of the memorials often did not suit the emperor's intentions.
Kǒng Xún instructed Zhònghuǐ to seek out Confucian scholars to keep at his side.
Since neither of them understood the precedents of the Táng dynasty,
they established the post of Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì (Academician of the Hall of Luminous Beginnings),
appointing Féng Dào and Fèng to these positions.
Fèng enjoyed frank speech and was of a firm character.
He had always been friendly with Rèn Huán.
After Huán became Prime Minister,
he recommended Fèng quite frequently.
Originally,
the rank of Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì was below that of Hànlín Xuéshì (Academician of the Hànlín Academy),
and the official title was also listed below the main office designation.
The following year,
Fèng was promoted to Lǐbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites).
He subsequently persuaded Huán to raise the status of the Academician above the official designation,
and an edict also ranked the position above that of Hànlín Xuéshì.
Huán was killed by Zhònghuǐ
under the false charge of plotting rebellion.
At that time,
Zhònghuǐ held great power,
and even Míngzōng could not question him.
Fèng alone wept loudly and shouted at Zhònghuǐ, saying:
"Rèn Huán was an upright scholar of the entire realm!
How could he possibly plot rebellion?
If you kill him,
how will you show justice to the world?"
Zhònghuǐ was ashamed and unable to reply.
The diviner Zhōu Xuánbào used physiognomy to predict human affairs, often accurately.
Zhuāngzōng particularly trusted and valued him,
appointing him as the Patrol Officer of Běijīng.
When Míngzōng was Nèiyá Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander of the Inner Court Guard),
Zhònghuǐ wanted to test Xuánbào.
He had another person exchange clothes with Míngzōng
and seated Míngzōng in the lower seat.
He summoned Xuánbào to read the fortune of the disguised person.
Xuánbào said:
"The Commander
is a noble general,
this man is not worthy of the title."
He then pointed at Míngzōng in the lower seat and said:
"This is the one!"
He then informed Míngzōng that his future nobility would be ineffable.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he recalled Xuánbào, believing him divine,
and planned to summon him to the capital.
Fèng remonstrated, saying:
"Preferences and dislikes
are things the sovereign must be cautious about.
If Your Majesty now deifies his art and summons him,
then the people of the entire country
will all chase after pronouncements of fortune and misfortune,
leading to mutual confusion and chaos,
which will become a serious disaster."
Míngzōng consequently stopped the plan to summon him.
When Zhū Shǒuyīn rebelled,
Míngzōng proceeded to Biànzhōu.
After Shǒuyīn was executed,
an edict further ordered a progression to Yè.
At this time,
the armies accompanying the carriage had just moved their families from Hénán to Biàn,
and they did not want to travel north.
The troops were agitated by this.
Meanwhile, Wáng Dū of Dìngzhōu believed that the Emperor’s visit to Biànzhōu was to execute Shǒuyīn,
and that the subsequent visit to Yè was aimed at him,
causing him to feel insecure and suspicious.
The Prime Ministers led the hundreds of officials to the imperial chamber
to request the cancellation of the progression to Yè.
Míngzōng did not heed them.
Public sentiment was greatly alarmed,
and the assembled officials no longer dared to speak.
Fèng personally wrote a memorial criticizing Ān Zhònghuǐ,
speaking with great sincerity and directness.
Zhònghuǐ reported this [to the Emperor],
and the progression was subsequently canceled.
There was a monk who traveled to the Western Regions
and obtained a Buddha’s tooth relic to present [to the court].
Míngzōng showed it to his high officials.
Fèng said:
"It is traditionally believed that a Buddha’s tooth cannot be harmed by water or fire.
I request that we verify its authenticity."
He then chopped it with an axe,
and it shattered immediately.
At that time,
the court had already been donating thousands of objects [to religious institutions],
but due to Fèng shattering the tooth, this activity ceased.
In the summer of Tiānchéng 4 (929 CE),
he was appointed Ménxià Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Chancellery) and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Concurrently Director of the Chancellery).
Yú Qiáo, the Bìshū Shàojiān (Assistant Director of the Palace Library),
had been a Hànlín Xuéshì alongside Fèng since the time of Zhuāngzōng.
Qiáo was also harsh, frank, and dared to speak out,
and had always been friendly with Fèng.
When Fèng became noble,
Qiáo had not been promoted for a long time.
Believing that his talent and reputation surpassed Fèng’s but that he was unused,
he consequently joined Xiāo Xīfǔ in frequently criticizing current government policies,
especially denigrating Fèng.
Fèng resented this deeply
but had not yet found a way to act upon it.
Then Qiáo had a dispute with a neighbor over a water channel,
which angered Ān Zhònghuǐ.
Fèng immediately had Qiáo demoted to Bìshū Shàojiān.
Qiáo, being drunk, went to see Fèng.
Fèng knew that Qiáo would surely be disrespectful,
so he excused himself, claiming he was washing his hair.
Qiáo then insulted the duty officers,
and then urinated in the barracks of Fèng's attendants before leaving.
A ministry official reported to Fèng
that Qiáo had urinated in the waiting hall
and had also insulted Fèng.
Fèng reported the incident [to the throne].
Míngzōng issued an edict stripping Qiáo of his offices,
exiling him permanently to Wǔzhōu as a commoner,
and later banishing him again to Zhènwǔ.
The entire realm felt he had been wronged.
Afterward, Ān Zhònghuǐ was accused of treason by Biān Yànwēn and others.
Míngzōng summoned Yànwēn and the others to be interrogated in court.
They fully confessed their deceit,
and were immediately executed.
A few days later,
Fèng presented a memorial in the Zhōngxīng Diàn (Hall of Central Revival).
He began by saying: "I have heard that wicked people have falsely accused Zhònghuǐ."
Míngzōng said: "This is a trivial matter.
I have already dealt with it.
You do not need to ask about it."
Fèng said: "What I have heard
pertains to the national interest.
Your Majesty cannot treat it as trivial."
He then pointed to the roof of the hall and said: "The reason this hall is majestic, solemn, and grand
is that it is supported by its ridgepoles, beams, pillars, and stones.
If one ridgepole were broken,
or one pillar removed,
it would collapse into danger.
High officials
are the ridgepoles, beams, pillars, and stones of the state.
Moreover, Zhònghuǐ rose from humble status,
endured hardships and dangers,
and enabled Your Majesty to become a restorer of the dynasty.
How can wicked individuals be allowed to destabilize him?"
Míngzōng changed his expression and apologized, saying: "Your words are correct."
Consequently, the three clans of Yànwēn and the others were exterminated.
Afterward, when Zhònghuǐ incurred guilt,
none of the officials dared to speak up,
but Fèng alone repeatedly insisted that Zhònghuǐ had been utterly loyal.
Míngzōng considered Fèng to be part of a faction,
and dismissed him to become the Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor) of Ānguó Commandery.
The stipends Fèng received while governing the commandery
were all distributed among his generals, officers, and retainers.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
Fèng was recalled to serve as Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince).
Suffering from a foot illness, he remained at home.
When his sickness became critical,
he performed divination for himself.
He cast the yarrow stalks and sighed, saying: "None in my family lineage have ever lived past fifty,
and all were poor and humble.
I have now surpassed that number in age and achieved wealth and nobility.
What more could I ask for?"
He died at home in Qīngtài 2 (935 CE).
Lǐ Xíjí
Lǐ Xíjí's
father was Tú.
He was a native of Luòyáng.
Some say he was a descendant of the Táng Prime Minister Línfǔ.
During the Qiánfú era (874–879 CE),
Xíjí successfully passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and served as the Tuōyán Pànguān (Salt Monopoly Judicial Officer) for Lǐ Dū, the Jiédùshǐ of Hézhōng.
Later, he departed for Jìn.
The Prince of Jìn appointed him as the Magistrate of Yúcì,
and subsequently he became the Zhǎngshūjì (Chief Secretary).
Xíjí was extensively learned
and knew many precedents of the Táng dynasty.
He was promoted to Jiédù Fùshǐ (Vice Military Governor),
and his highest office reached Jiànyì Dàfū (Grand Master Remonstrant).
The Prince of Jìn had conflict with Liáng,
and they engaged in years of fighting.
Later, the Prince of Jìn was repeatedly in difficulty
and wished to establish peace with Liáng.
He ordered Xíjí to compose a letter to Liáng,
the language of which was highly articulate and beautiful.
The Grand Ancestor of Liáng had someone read it.
When they reached the lines, "Poisoned hands and esteemed fists
exchanged blows in the dark of night,
Golden halberds and iron steeds
trampled during daylight hours,"
he sighed and said: "Although Lord Lǐ is secluded in a corner,
he has a scholar like this!
If I could acquire him,
it would be like giving wings to a tiger!"
He turned to his attendant Jìng Xiáng and said:
"Reply well to this for me."
However, Xiáng's reply
was not skillfully written,
and Xíjí's letter was widely circulated in the world.
Xí Jí (Xí Jí) was a tranquil and indifferent person,
amusing himself with literature and poetry.
He died in the third year of Tiānyòu (906 CE).
Lú Rǔbì (Lú Rǔbì) replaced him as Deputy Envoy.
Rǔbì was skilled in calligraphy and painting,
but his literary ability was inferior to Xí Jí’s.
His father, Jiǎnqiú (Jiǎnqiú), served as the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Hédōng,
and was a renowned figure during the Táng dynasty.
Therefore, Rǔbì also knew many historical precedents of the Táng dynasty.
When the Prince of Jìn died,
Zhuāngzōng (Zhuāngzōng) succeeded him as the Prince of Jìn.
The imperial mandates for conferring titles and appointing officials all came from Rǔbì.
In the eighteenth year (of Tiānyòu),
he died.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted Xí Jí the title of Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) and Rǔbì the title of Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū).
Zhāng Xiàn
Zhāng Xiàn, courtesy name Yǔnzhōng,
was a person from Jìnyáng.
He was a quiet, tranquil, and temperate person,
studious since youth,
and skilled at playing the zither and drinking wine.
Zhuāngzōng, who already knew of his literary talent,
made him Private Secretary (Zhǎngshūjì) to the Military Governor of Tiānxióng Command.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng) and Commissioner of Taxes (Zūyōngshǐ).

He was promoted to Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng), Manager of Personnel Selection for the Ministry of Personnel (Pàn Lìbù Quán), and Deputy Resident of the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū Fùliúshǒu).
Xiàn was highly proficient in administrative affairs,
and his governance was very effective.
When Zhuāngzōng visited the Eastern Capital,
Wáng Dū (Wáng Dū) of Dìngzhōu came to pay homage.
Zhuāngzōng ordered Xiàn to prepare a polo field,
to play polo with Dū.
Previously,
when Zhuāngzōng established his reign title in the Eastern Capital,
he had used the polo field as the Altar of Accession (Jìwèitán).
Therefore, Xiàn argued: "The Altar of Accession
is where the ruler rises to power.
The Altar south of Gāo in the Hàn Dynasty and the Fányáng Altar in the Wèi Dynasty
are still standing today and
should not be destroyed."
Thus, he prepared a separate polo field west of the palace.
Before the field was completed,
Zhuāngzōng became angry,
and ordered two palace attendants (Yúhòu) to immediately tear down the altar to make the field.
Xiàn withdrew and sighed, saying: "This is an inauspicious omen!
Originally,
when Míngzōng (Míngzōng) campaigned against the Qìdān in the north,
he took armor and weapons from Wèi (Wèizhōu) to supply the army.
There were five hundred suits of fine armor.
Xiàn distributed them but failed to report it.
When Zhuāngzōng arrived at Wèi,
he was furious,
and ordered Xiàn to hasten to fetch the armor himself.
He only stopped after his attendants intervened.
He then asked Xiàn how much money was in the treasury.
Xiàn submitted the treasury ledger, which showed thirty thousand *mín* of cash.
Zhuāngzōng became even angrier.
He told his favored actor, Shǐ Yànqióng (Shǐ Yànqióng): "I am gambling with my officials
and I need over a hundred thousand [mín],
yet Xiàn deceives me with old paper (ledgers).
Before I crossed the Yellow River,
the treasury usually held a million *mín*.
Where is it now?
" Yànqióng defended Xiàn, and the matter subsided.
When Guō Chóngtāo (Guō Chóngtāo) campaigned against Shǔ,
he recommended Xiàn as suitable for the position of Prime Minister.
However, the eunuchs and actors did not want Xiàn serving in court.
Duàn Huái (Duàn Huái), the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Chéngzhǐ), said: "If a Prime Minister is before the Son of Heaven,
and there is something wrong with his affairs,
it can still be corrected.
But if a person is appointed to govern a region,
and he is not the right man,
the resulting trouble will not be small.
Xiàn's talent is certainly useful,
but it is better to appoint him to govern a region."
Consequently, he was appointed Magistrate of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán Yǐn) and Resident of Běijīng (Běijīng Liúshǒu).
When Zhào Zàilǐ (Zhào Zàilǐ) revolted,
Xiàn's family was in Wèizhōu.
Zàilǐ treated his family well,
and sent a messenger with a letter to entice Xiàn.
Xiàn executed the messenger,
sealed the letter unopened, and submitted it [to the throne].
Zhuāngzōng was assassinated.
Míngzōng entered the capital (Jīngshī).
Tàiyuán had not yet heard the news,
when Yǒngwáng Cúnbà (Yǒngwáng Cúnbà) fled to Tàiyuán.
Xiàn’s staff told him: "Now the Wèi troops are moving south,
and the fate of the Emperor is uncertain.
Cúnbà arrived without an imperial edict,
and the crupper (qiū) of his horse is broken.
Is he not a defeated person fleeing battle?
We should restrain him and await orders."
Xiàn said: "I am fundamentally a scholar,
without any merit whatsoever,
yet the Emperor treated me extremely well.
How could I harbor disloyalty and seek advantage from this change?
I can only die along with him!
" Xiàn's subordinate, Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn (Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn), instructed Xiàn to present a memorial to Míngzōng urging him to ascend the throne.
Xiàn refused tearfully.
Soon after, Cúnbà shaved his head,
met with Fú Yànchāo (Fú Yànchāo), the Patrol Inspector of Běijīng,
and requested to become a monk to save his life.
The soldiers under Yànchāo’s command raised a great clamor,
and killed Cúnbà.
Xiàn fled to Yízhōu,
where he was also killed.
Alas!
Among those who died for their loyalty,
I have gained three and lost three.
The deaths of Gǒng Tíngměi (Gǒng Tíngměi) and Yáng Wēn (Yáng Wēn),
I have already mourned.
As for the affair of Zhāng Xiàn,
I feel particular sorrow and regret for him.
I examined the facts concerning Xiàn in the old histories,
but the accounts written about Yǒngwáng Cúnbà, Fú Yànchāo, and Xiàn differ entirely in their details,
and I cannot verify and correct them.
This is probably because during the chaos and urgency of the rebellion,
the reports were mistaken.
Nevertheless, looking at his greater principle of loyalty,
it can still be discerned:
Xiàn's integrity and sincerity can certainly be called loyalty.
When he disregarded his family,
spurned Zàilǐ, and executed his messenger,
and tearfully refused Zhāoyuǎn's suggestion,
his resolve was very clear.
Regarding his desire to die together with Cúnbà,
and then, when Cúnbà was killed,
he instead abandoned Tàiyuán and fled,
I still do not know what his true intention was.
The old history states that Xiàn was put to death for abandoning the city,
but I believe that is incorrect.
While I certainly wish to affirm Xiàn’s noble resolve,
the main point is that Xiàn abandoned his post and the circumstances of his death are unclear.
Therefore, he cannot be listed among those who died for their loyalty.
Xiāo Xīfǔ
Xiāo Xīfǔ,
was a person from Sòngzhōu.
He possessed sharp rhetoric and debating skills,
and was often extravagant and unrestrained.
In his youth, he passed the Imperial Examination (Jìnshì)
and served as Private Secretary to Yuán Xiàngxiān (Yuán Xiàngxiān), the Magistrate of Kāifēng for the Liáng Dynasty.
When Xiàngxiān became the Military Governor of Qīngzhōu,
he made Xīfǔ a Circuit Inspector (Xúnguān).
Xīfǔ was unhappy [with this position],
so he abandoned his mother and wife,
changed his name,
and fled to Zhènzhōu.
He claimed to be the Private Secretary of Qīngzhōu
and sought an audience with Wáng Róng (Wáng Róng), the Prince of Zhào.
Róng appointed Xīfǔ as an aide (Cānjūn).
Xīfǔ was still very unhappy,
and after residing there for over a year,
he fled again to Yìzhōu,
shaved his head to become a monk,
and lived on Mount Bǎizhàng.
When Zhuāngzōng was about to establish his state in Wèi,
and appoint various officials,
he sought out secluded scholars throughout the realm.
Lǐ Shàohóng (Lǐ Shàohóng) of Yōuzhōu recommended Xīfǔ as the Judicial Officer (Tuīguān) of Wèizhōu.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the imperial throne,
he wished to appoint him Compiler of Imperial Edicts (Zhī Zhìgào).
There was an imperial edict to fix the protocol for imperial banquets.
He asked Xīfǔ:
"Are the Commissioners of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) permitted to sit?
" Xīfǔ thought they should not be permitted.
Zhāng Jūhàn (Zhāng Jūhàn), the Commissioner of Military Affairs, heard this and was angry.
He said to Xīfǔ:
"I have served three generations of Emperors,
and have seen hundreds of imperial banquets.
You are fundamentally a peasant boy—
how can you know the affairs of the inner court?
" Xīfǔ could not reply.
From then on, all the influential eunuchs gnashed their teeth [in hatred].
The Chancellor Dòulú Gé (Dòulú Gé) and others sought to please the eunuchs,
and jointly sought to exclude him.
He was made Director of the Bureau of Equipage (Jiàbù Lángzhōng).
Xīfǔ lost his ambition,
and was particularly discontented.
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed the Liáng Dynasty,
he sent Xīfǔ to pacify the Qīng and Qí regions.
