Xīfǔ then first learned that his mother had died,
and his wife, née Yuán (Yuán Shì), had also remarried.
Xīfǔ expressed his sorrow and observed mourning rites,
residing in Wèizhōu.
Someone quoted a letter by Lǐ Líng (Lǐ Líng) of the Hàn dynasty to mock him, saying:
"The aged mother has died in the hall;
the living wife has left the house."
Everyone at the time circulated this and laughed about it.
Míngzōng ascended the throne,
and summoned him to be the Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū).
At this time,
the Complaint Box (Guǐ Hán) was reestablished,
and Xīfǔ was made the commissioner.
Xīfǔ proposed, saying:
"Since the military disturbances have multiplied,
the royal order (Wáng Gāng) is completely ruined.
Usurpation, deception, bullying, and plundering abound,
and those with power prevail.
Those who seize other people's wives and daughters,
occupy others' fields and residences,
corrupted and avaricious officials,
and those wronged in criminal cases
are too numerous to count.
When the Complaint Box is opened,
the submitted grievances will certainly be many,
reaching to meritorious ministers and imperial relatives,
whom it might be impossible to prosecute according to the law."
Therefore, everything that occurred before dawn on the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month of the first year of Tiānchéng
which involved crimes warranting the death penalty (Dà Pì) or higher,
was all pardoned and abolished.
Only then was the Complaint Box opened to the public.
Initially,
Míngzōng intended to make Xīfǔ a Grand Master Remonstrant,
but Dòulú Gé and Wéi Shuō strongly opposed and obstructed it.
Afterward, Gé and Shuō were hated by Ān Zhònghuǐ.
Xīfǔ, anticipating the emperor's wishes,
falsely accused them in a memorial,
claiming that "Gé allowed his farm tenant to commit murder,
and Shuō disputed a well with his neighbor,
claiming the well contained treasure."
The relevant authorities investigated,
finding only a broken cauldron in the well,
but Gé and Shuō were both eventually demoted and died.
Míngzōng bestowed upon Xīfǔ one hundred bolts of silk and three hundred *shi* of grain and wheat,
and appointed him Regular Attendant in the Left (Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì).
Xīfǔ was narrow-minded and eager for advancement.
He once sent a man at night to knock on the palace gate and report a sudden change,
saying that Lǐ Jūn, a staff officer at the river weir, reported his own army was plotting rebellion.
The next morning,
upon investigation, the claim was found baseless,
Jūn was executed,
and the soldiers went to Ān Zhònghuǐ demanding that Xīfǔ be given to them to be eaten.
At this time,
Míngzōng was about to perform the ritual sacrifice at the Southern Suburb (Nán Jiāo).
The day before the fast,
the assembled ministers practiced the ceremonies in the palace courtyard.
The Chancellors Féng Dào and Zhào Fèng,
the Prefect of Hénán, Prince of Qín, Cóngróng,
and the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ), Ān Zhònghuǐ, waited for their place in the procession outside Yuèhuá Gate.
Xīfǔ and the officials of the Two Bureaus entered first.
Dào and the others remained seated under the corridor and did not rise.
When Xīfǔ came out,
he summoned the officials who managed the internal affairs of the government hall,
and reprimanded them, asking why the Chancellors and the Commissioner of Military Affairs dared not rise when they saw the officials of the Two Bureaus,
and proceeded to curse and revile them loudly.
That night,
he claimed illness and returned to his residence.
After more than a month,
because the matter of denouncing Lǐ Jūn had agitated the troops,
he was demoted to Administrator of Households (Sīhù Cānjūn) of Lán Zhōu,
and died in the place of banishment.
Liú Zàn
Liú Zàn
was a man from Wèizhōu.
His father, Pín, was a County Magistrate (Xiàn Lìng).
When Zàn first began his studies,
he was dressed in a blue cloth jacket and tunic.
Whenever they ate, Pín would eat meat himself,
but served Zàn vegetarian food separately below the couch,
saying to him: "Meat eating
is the salary (lù) of a gentleman.
If you desire it,
then diligently pursue learning to obtain a salary.
My meat
is not your food."
Because of this, Zàn studied even harder
and passed the civil service examination (Jìnshì).
He served as Rō Shàowēi's Staff Supervisor (Pànguān),
then left to become Zhào Yán's Circuit Inspector (Xúnguān) under the Commissioner of Revenue (Zūyōng Shǐ),
and later served as Kǒng Qiān's Salt and Iron Supervisor (Yántiě Pànguān).
During Míngzōng's reign,
he was successively promoted to Palace Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén), Imperial Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), and Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng).
He administered his office according to the law,
and the powerful and wealthy could not approach him with personal requests.
At this time,
Prince of Qín, Cóngróng, held military power and was arrogant,
committing many errors.
Those who spoke on affairs of state requested that a tutor (shīfù) be established to assist and guide him.
The great ministers feared the Prince
and dared not make the decision,
so they requested that the Prince be allowed to choose himself.
The Prince of Qín immediately requested Zàn,
so Zàn was appointed Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān)
and Tutor to the Prince of Qín (Qín Wáng Fù).
Zàn wept and said: "Calamity is about to arrive!"
The officials and staff Cóngróng requested for the Prince's headquarters, totaling more than ten people,
were mostly frivolous, deceptive, and reckless individuals,
who daily offered flattery to indulge the Prince's arrogance.
Only Zàn subtly remonstrated with him in a relaxed manner,
consistently guiding him toward the correct path.
The Prince of Qín once ordered his guests to compose essays in his presence.
Zàn, considering himself the tutor,
felt ashamed to be ranked alongside the common rabble.
Although he reluctantly took up his brush,
he showed signs of displeasure.
The Prince of Qín resented this.
Later, he instructed his attendants not to announce Zàn when he came.
Zàn also stopped going,
only visiting the headquarters once a month,
and when he returned, he shut his gate and avoided social interaction.
Soon after, the Prince of Qín was indeed defeated and killed.
The ministers of Táng debated which officials affiliated with the Prince should be held responsible.
Féng Dào said:
and had held his post for less than a month.
Wáng Jūmǐn, the Chamberlain, and Liú Zàn were both hated by the Prince for their uprightness.
Sītú Xǔ, the Staff Supervisor of the Hénán Prefecture, had been home on sick leave for a long time.
All of them should be considered not involved in the conspiracy.
However, Gāo Niǎn, the Consulting Staff Officer, was closest to the Prince.
Niǎn legally deserves death,
but the others can be pardoned or reduced in sentence sequentially."
Zhū Hóngzhāo said:
If the Prince of Qín had succeeded in entering Guāngzhèng Gate,
how would he have treated Zàn and the others?
Would we (or our families) have survived?
Moreover, the law distinguishes between leaders and followers.
Now the Prince of Qín, his wife, and his sons and daughters are all dead.
Zàn and the others are fortunate just to save their own lives!"
Dào and the others found this difficult to refute.
However, Féng Yūn also argued strongly against it,
and Zàn and the others were spared death.
Consequently, Gāo Niǎn was sentenced to death,
and Rèn Zàn and seventeen others were all exiled permanently.
Initially,
when Zàn heard of the Prince of Qín's defeat,
he immediately dressed in plain white clothes and rode a donkey, awaiting his fate.
Someone informed him that he had merely been stripped of his office.
Zàn said:
"How can the Emperor's eldest heir be executed
while his subordinate officials are only stripped of office?
Not dying is fortunate enough!"
Eventually, Zàn was permanently exiled to Lán Zhōu as a commoner.
In the second year of Qīngtài (935 CE),
an imperial edict allowed him to return to his hometown,
but he fell ill and died
while traveling, reaching Shíhuì Pass.
Hé Zàn
Hé Zàn
was a man from Mǐn.
He passed the imperial examination during the late Táng dynasty.
When Zhuāngzōng was the Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of Tàiyuán,
he recruited him as a Staff Supervisor.
Whenever Zhuāngzōng went out on campaign,
he left Zhāng Chéngyè to guard Tàiyuán.
When Chéngyè died,
Zàn took his place overseeing the retention of the defense post.
Zàn was intelligent and sharp,
proficient in official duties,
seemingly careless and brief externally, but quite thorough internally.
When Zhuāngzōng established his imperial title at Yè Dū,
Zàn was appointed Grand Master Remonstrant.
Zàn worried that Zhuāngzōng's undertaking would not succeed,
and requested to remain as the Resident Administrator (Liúshǒu) of Běijīng.
Zàn had a prior relationship with Míngzōng.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he summoned him back.
He was received in the inner palace,
and Míngzōng consoled and questioned him for a long time.
Afterward, Zàn was made Deputy Military Governor (Jiédù Fùshǐ) of Xīchuān.
At this time,
Mèng Zhīxiáng already harbored rebellious intentions,
and was employing Deputy Military Governor Zhào Jìliáng as his confidant.
Hearing that Zàn was replacing him,
he urgently submitted a memorial requesting Jìliáng be retained,
so Zàn was instead changed to Marshal of the Military Headquarters (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
Zàn was too ashamed to resign himself,
and had no choice but to go.
Míngzōng gave him generous gifts.
Previously,
Zhīxiáng had been the Commander of the Metropolitan Cavalry and Infantry (Mǎbù Jūn Dū Yúhòu) in Běijīng,
while Zàn was the Resident Administrator of Tàiyuán.
Zhīxiáng had treated Zàn with military courtesy,
but Zàn consistently restrained him with the law.
Initially, Zhīxiáng was displeased.
When Zàn became the Marshal (Sīmǎ),
Zhīxiáng still forced himself to treat Zàn very generously.
When Zhīxiáng rebelled,
he dismissed Zàn as Marshal,
confining him to a private residence.
Zàn drank his sorrow and died.
Biography of Jìn Ministers, Chapter 17. Sāng Wéihàn
Xīfǔ's nature was narrow-minded and impetuous.
He once sent someone at night to knock on the palace gate to report a serious matter,
saying that Lǐ Jūn (李筠), the Yágūan (牙官) of the river weir, had reported the current army's intention to rebel.
The next morning,
an investigation revealed it to be groundless,
so Jūn was executed.
The soldiers went to Ān Chónghuì (安重誨) to demand Xīfǔ (希甫) be handed over to them.
At that time,
Míngzōng (明宗) was about to perform rituals at the Southern Suburb.
The day before the fasting,
all the officials practiced the ceremony in the palace hall.
The chancellors Féng Dào (馮道) and Zhào Fèng (趙鳳),
Qínwáng (秦王) Cóngróng (從榮), the Hénán Yǐn (河南尹),
and the Shūmìshǐ (樞密使) Ān Chónghuì (安重誨) awaited their turn outside the Yuèhuá Mén (月華門).
Xīfǔ (希甫) and the officials of the two departments entered first.
Dào (道) and the others sat under the corridor and did not rise.
After Xīfǔ (希甫) came out,
he summoned the Tángtóu Zhíshěng Cháotáng Qūshǐguān (堂頭直省朝堂驅使官)
and reprimanded them, asking why the chancellors and Shūmì (樞密) did not rise upon seeing the officials of the two departments.
He then launched into a great tirade.
That night,
he feigned illness and returned to his residence.
More than a month later,
for causing unrest among the troops with the false accusation against Lǐ Jūn (李筠),
he was demoted to Sīhù Cānjūn (司戶參軍) of Lánzhōu (嵐州),
and died at the place of his demotion.
Liú Zàn
Liú Zàn (劉贊)
was a native of Wèizhōu (魏州).
His father, Pín (玭), was a county magistrate.
When Zàn (贊) first began his studies,
he wore a blue cloth shirt and jacket.
Whenever they ate, Pín (玭) would eat meat himself,
but would serve Zàn (贊) vegetables separately at the foot of the bed,
telling him: "Meat
is the stipend of a gentleman.
If you desire it,
then study diligently to attain a stipend.
My meat
is not your food."
From then on, Zàn (贊) studied even harder
and passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination.
He became the Pànguān (判官) for Luó Shàowēi (羅紹威),
then left to become the Xúnguān (巡官) for Zūyōngshǐ (租庸使) Zhào Yán (趙巖),
and later the Yántiě Pànguān (鹽鐵判官) for Kǒng Qiān (孔謙).
During Míngzōng's (明宗) reign,
he was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人), Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞), and Xíngbù Shìláng (刑部侍郎).
He administered his office according to law,
and the powerful and influential could not bribe him for personal favors.
At that time,
Qínwáng (秦王) Cóngróng (從榮) held military power and was arrogant,
making many mistakes.
Those who spoke on affairs of state requested that a tutor be appointed to guide him.
The great ministers feared the king
and dared not decide the matter themselves,
so they asked the king to choose for himself.
Qínwáng (秦王) then requested Zàn (贊).
Zàn (贊) was consequently appointed Mìshū Jiān (祕書監)
and tutor to Qínwáng (秦王).
Zàn (贊) wept and said: "Calamity is about to befall us!"
Qínwáng (秦王) had requested over ten officials for his princely mansion,
most of whom were frivolous and treacherous individuals,
who daily offered flattery to inflate the king's ego.
Only Zàn (贊) calmly offered remonstrance,
always according to the correct path.
Qínwáng (秦王) once ordered his guests to compose essays in his presence.
Zàn (贊), considering himself a tutor,
was ashamed to be grouped with such petty individuals.
Although he reluctantly took up his brush,
he showed displeasure.
Qínwáng (秦王) disliked this.
Later, he instructed his attendants not to admit Zàn (贊) when he came.
Zàn (贊) also stopped going,
only visiting the mansion once a month.
After retiring, he would close his door and avoid all social contact.
Shortly thereafter, Qínwáng (秦王) indeed suffered defeat and died.
When the Táng (唐) ministers discussed which of the king's subordinate officials should be implicated,
Féng Dào (馮道) said: "Yuánshuài Pànguān (元帥判官) Rèn Zàn (任贊) and Qínwáng (秦王) were not previously close,
and he was in office for less than a month.
Zhànshì (詹事) Wáng Jūmǐn (王居敏) and Liú Zàn (劉贊) were both disliked by the king for their uprightness.
Hénánfǔ Pànguān (河南府判官) Sītú Xǔ (司徒詡) had been home on sick leave for a long time.
All of them should be deemed not privy to the conspiracy.
However, Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍) Gāo Niǎn (高輦) was closest to the king.
Niǎn (輦) should legally be put to death;
the rest can be gradually pardoned or have their sentences reduced."
Zhū Hóngzhāo (朱弘昭) said: "You gentlemen do not understand his true intention.
If Qínwáng (秦王) had managed to enter the Guāngzhèng Mén (光政門),
how would he have treated Zàn (贊) and the others?
Would we still have our families?
Moreover, the law distinguishes between principals and accessories.
Now that Qínwáng (秦wáng), his wife, sons, and daughters are all dead,
Zàn (贊) and the others are fortunate to merely keep their lives!"
Dào (道) and the others found it difficult to argue.
And Féng Yūn (馮贇) also strongly argued against it.
Zàn (贊) and the others were then spared death.
Thereupon, Gāo Niǎn (高輦) was sentenced to death,
and Rèn Zàn (任贊) and seventeen others were all exiled for life.
At first,
when Zàn (贊) heard of Qínwáng's (秦王) defeat,
he immediately donned white clothes and rode a donkey, awaiting his fate.
Someone told Zàn (贊) that he would merely be dismissed from office.
Zàn (贊) said:
"How can the emperor's heir be slain
while his retainers merely lose their offices?
Not to die is already fortunate!"
Afterwards, Zàn (贊) was exiled to be a commoner in Lánzhōu (嵐州).
In the second year of Qīngtài (清泰),
an imperial edict ordered his return home.
He fell ill and died
at Shíhuì Guān (石會關) while en route.
Hé Zàn
Hé Zàn (何瓚)
was a native of Mǐn (閩).
At the end of the Táng (唐) dynasty, he passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) was Jìdùshǐ (節度使) of Tàiyuán (太原),
he was appointed Pànguān (判官).
Whenever Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) went on military campaigns,
he left Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業) to guard Tàiyuán (太原).
After Chéngyè (承業) died,
Zàn (瓚) took his place as acting Liúshǒushì (留守事).
Zàn (瓚) was bright and astute,
skilled in official matters.
He appeared outwardly relaxed and simple, but was inwardly quite thorough and meticulous.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) established his grand title in Yèdū (鄴都),
Zàn (瓚) was appointed Jiàn Yì Dàfū (諫議大夫).
Zàn (瓚), fearing that Zhuāngzōng's (莊宗) endeavor would not succeed,
requested to remain as Liúshǒu (留守) of Běijīng (北京).
Zàn (瓚) had old ties with Míngzōng (明宗).
When Míngzōng (明宗) ascended the throne,
Zàn (瓚) was summoned back
and met in the inner palace.
Míngzōng (明宗) inquired about him for a long time,
and then appointed Zàn (瓚) as Xīchuān Jìdù Fùshǐ (西川節度副使).
At this time,
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) already harbored ambitions.
He was treating his Fùshǐ (副使) Zhào Jìliáng (趙季良) as his confidant.
Hearing that Zàn (瓚) was to replace him,
he urgently memorialized to retain Jìliáng (季良).
Consequently, Zàn (瓚) was reassigned as Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬).
Zàn (瓚) was ashamed to decline the position himself,
so he went reluctantly,
with Míngzōng (明宗) giving him generous gifts.
Initially,
Zhīxiáng (知祥) was Mǎbùjūn Dōu Yúhóu (馬步軍都虞候) in Běijīng (北京),
while Zàn (瓚) was Liúshǒu (留守) of Tàiyuán (太原).
Zhīxiáng (知祥) treated Zàn (瓚) with military deference,
and Zàn (瓚) always kept him to the law.
Zhīxiáng (知祥) was initially displeased.
But when Zàn (瓚) became Sīmǎ (司馬),
Zhīxiáng (知祥) still grudgingly treated him very well.
When Zhīxiáng (知祥) rebelled,
he dismissed Zàn (瓚) from his Sīmǎ (司馬) post
and confined him to his private residence.
Zàn (瓚) died consumed by resentment.
Jiàokān Jì (校勘記)
Jìn Chén Zhuàn (晉臣傳) Volume 17 Sāng Wéihàn
Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰), courtesy name Guóqiáo (國僑),
was a native of Hénán (河南).
He was ugly,
short in stature with a long face.
He often looked at himself in a mirror and remarked with self-admiration:
"A seven-foot body
is not as good as a one-foot face."
He harbored great ambitions of becoming a high-ranking official.
When he first sat for the Jìnshì (進士) examination,
the chief examiner disliked his surname,
because
"Sāng" (桑)
and "Sàng" (喪)
were homophones.
Someone advised him not to necessarily take the Jìnshì (進士) exam,
suggesting he could seek office through other means.
Wéihàn (維翰) responded with emotion,
then wrote the essay "Rì Chū Fúsāng Fù" (日出扶桑賦) to express his ambition.
He also cast an iron inkstone and showed it to people, saying:
"When this inkstone is worn out, then I will change my ambition and seek office otherwise."
Ultimately, he passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination.
Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) appointed him Zhǎng Shūjì (掌書記) of Héyáng Jìdù (河陽節度),
and thereafter he always kept him by his side.
, courtesy name Guóqiáo
, was a native of Hénán.
His appearance was ugly and grotesque;
his body was short while his face was long.
He often looked into a mirror, considering himself extraordinary, and said:
"A seven-chǐ body
is inferior to a one-chǐ face."
He was deeply motivated to achieve a position as a high official.
When he first attempted the *jìnshì* examination,
the officials in charge disliked his surname
because
*sāng* (mulberry)
and *sāng* (mourning/loss)
were homophones.
Someone advised him that he did not necessarily need to attempt the *jìnshì*,
and could seek office through other means.
Wéihàn was resolute,
and subsequently wrote the *Fù* (Rhapsody) on "The Sun Rises from the Fúsāng" (Rì Chū Fúsāng Fù) to demonstrate his resolve.
He also forged an iron inkstone and showed it to people, saying:
"If this inkstone wears out, then I will change and seek office elsewhere."
Eventually, he passed the *jìnshì* examination.
Jìn Gāozǔ appointed him as the Chief Secretary (Zhǎng Shūjì) to the Hèyáng Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ).
Thereafter, Gāozǔ always kept him close.
When Gāozǔ moved from Tàiyuán to Tiānpíng,
he refused the imperial order
and harbored rebellious intent.
He consulted his generals and aides,
who were all fearful and dared not speak.
Only Wéihàn and Liú Zhīyuǎn approved of the plan.
Consequently, Wéihàn was tasked with writing a letter seeking aid from the Qìdān.
Yēlǜ Déguāng had already consented,
but Zhào Déjūn also tempted Déguāng with heavy bribes,
asking for help to usurp the Táng dynasty himself.
Gāozǔ feared the plan would fail,
so he dispatched Wéihàn to meet Déguāng.
Wéihàn argued the advantages and disadvantages very persuasively,
and Déguāng's decision was finalized.
Ultimately, the destruction of the Táng and the rise of the Jìn
were due to Wéihàn's effort.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Wéihàn as Grand Academician (Hànlín Xuéshì), Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng), and Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Zhī Shūmì Yuàn Shì).
He was promoted to Vice Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì),
concurrently serving as the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ).
In the fourth year of Tiānfú,
he was sent out to be the Military Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
After more than a year,
he was transferred to govern Tàiníng.
Bái Chéngfú of the Tǔhún was pressed by the Qìdān,
and attached himself to Ān Chóngróng at Zhènzhōu to defect to the Jìn.
Chóngróng thereupon requested breaking relations with the Qìdān
and using the Tǔhún to attack them.
Gāozǔ was reluctant to offend Chóngróng
and was undecided.
Wéihàn submitted a memorial listing seven reasons why conflict with the Qìdān should be avoided.
Gāozǔ summoned Wéihàn's messenger into his private chamber
and said:
"The matter regarding the northern direction
has been troubling my mind.
Having received your memorial,
my plan is decided.
There is no need to worry."
Wéihàn also advised Gāozǔ to visit Yèdū.
In the seventh year,
Gāozǔ was in Yè.
Wéihàn came for an audience
and was transferred to govern Jìnchāng.
Chū Dì ascended the throne,
and summoned and appointed Wéihàn as Chamberlain (Shìzhōng).
However, Jǐng Yánguǎng held power
and broke the alliance with the Qìdān.
Wéihàn's warnings were unheeded.
So, he secretly sent someone to persuade the Emperor, saying:
"To control the Qìdān and pacify the realm,
it is imperative to employ Wéihàn."
Consequently, Yánguǎng was dismissed to Hénán.
Wéihàn was appointed Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Lìng),
reinstated as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ),
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Wèiguó.
Regardless of the importance of the affair,
everything was entrusted to him.
Within a few months,
the functions of the government gradually became orderly.
Initially,
Lǐ Hàn was a Grand Academician (Hànlín Xuéshì).
He liked drinking and frequently made mistakes while drunk,
so Gāozǔ considered him frivolous.
In the ninth month of the fifth year of Tiānfú,
an edict abolished the position of Grand Academician,
restoring its duties, according to the *Six Statutes of Táng* (Táng Liù Diǎn), to the Chancellery Drafters (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
The positions of Academician of the Duānmíng Hall (Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì) and Academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Yuàn Xuéshì) were also abolished.
When Wéihàn became the Commissioner of Military Affairs,
he successfully memorialized for the reinstatement of the Academician posts,
and filled them all with his relatives and old friends.
Wéihàn's authority and power became extensive.
Bribes and gifts from all directions
accumulated to enormous amounts yearly.
Lǐ Yàntāo, the Director of the Palace Guest Department (Nèi Kèshěng Shǐ), and Féng Yù, the Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, held influence
and jointly slandered him.
The Emperor wished to suddenly dismiss Wéihàn,
but the great ministers Liú Xù and Lǐ Sōng both argued against it.
Eventually, Yù was made Commissioner of Military Affairs,
and later made Chancellor (Xiàng).
Wéihàn was increasingly alienated.
The Emperor fell ill from excessive drinking.
Wéihàn secretly sent someone to inform the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu),
requesting tutors be appointed for the Emperor’s younger brother, Chóngruì.
When the Emperor recovered from his illness,
he found this out,
became angry,
and dismissed Wéihàn, making him the Governor of Kāifēng (Kāifēng Yǐn).
Wéihàn consequently claimed a foot ailment
and rarely attended court thereafter.
The Qìdān stationed troops at Zhōngdù
and broke through Luánchéng.
The main army under Dù Chóngwēi and others was cut off.
Wéihàn said:
"The situation is desperate!"
He then met with Féng Yù and others to plan,
but their strategies did not agree.
He also requested an audience with the Emperor,
but the Emperor was busy training hawks in the imperial garden
and had no time to see him.
Wéihàn retreated and sighed, saying:
"The Jìn will no longer receive ancestral sacrifices!"
The alliance between the Qìdān and the Jìn
began with Wéihàn
and ultimately failed because of Jǐng Yánguǎng.
Therefore, since the start of hostilities,
every proclamation written by the Qìdān
invariably mentioned these two men.
When Yēlǜ Déguāng invaded the capital,
he sent Zhāng Yànzé with a letter for the Empress Dowager,
asking if these two men were present
and instructing that they be sent to him first.
However, the Emperor did not want Wéihàn to see Déguāng, because Wéihàn had advised against breaking the alliance and the Emperor had ignored him.
Consequently, the Emperor hinted to Yànzé to deal with him,
and Yànzé was also covetous of Wéihàn's wealth.
Wéihàn's appearance was unusual,
and he usually maintained an air of prestige and strictness.
The elderly generals and high ministers of the Jìn,
when they met him, all submitted.
Yànzé prided himself on his bravery and aggressiveness,
yet every time he went to visit Wéihàn,
even in winter, he inevitably sweated.
Initially,
when Yànzé entered the capital,
Wéihàn's staff urged him to flee the danger.
Wéihàn said:
"I am a high minister.
Since the state has reached this point,
where can I flee from death?"
He sat calmly in his official residence and did not move.
Yànzé entered with troops
and asked:
"Where is Wéihàn?"
Wéihàn loudly declared:
"I
am a high minister of Jìn.
I ought to die for the state.
How dare you be disrespectful!"
Yànzé trembled and dared not look up.
He retreated and said to others:
"I did not know what kind of man Sāng Wéihàn was,
but seeing him today
still makes a person this terrified.
How could I see him again?"
He then used the Emperor’s order to summon Wéihàn.
As Wéihàn was leaving,
he met Lǐ Sōng.
They stopped their horses and talked.
A military official stepped forward to address Wéihàn,
requesting him to proceed to the prison of the Palace Guards Command (Shìwèi Sī Yù).
Wéihàn knew he could not escape.
He looked at Sōng and said:
"Since you, Prime Minister (Xiànggōng), are in charge of the state,
will you allow Wéihàn to die alone?"
Sōng was ashamed and could not reply.
That night,
Yànzé ordered men to strangle him to death.
He placed a silk cord around Wéihàn's neck
and reported to Déguāng, saying:
"Wéihàn hanged himself."
Déguāng said:
"I originally had no intention of killing Wéihàn.
Why did Wéihàn have to kill himself?"
When Déguāng arrived at the capital,
he sent men to examine the body
and believed he had indeed died by hanging.
He then bestowed the corpse upon Wéihàn's family,
but all of Wéihàn's assets were plundered by Yànzé.
Jǐng Yánguǎng
Jǐng Yán'guǎng (景延廣), courtesy name Hángchuān (航川),
was a man from Shǎnzhōu (陝州).
His father, Jiàn (建), was skilled at archery.
He once taught Yán'guǎng (延廣), saying:
"If an arrow cannot penetrate iron,
it is better not to shoot it."
Because of this, Yán'guǎng (延廣) became known for his powerful draw (of the bow).
He served Shàowáng Yǒuhuì (梁邵王友誨) of Liáng (梁).
When Yǒuhuì (友誨) plotted rebellion and was imprisoned,
Yán'guǎng (延廣) fled.
Later, he followed Wáng Yànzhāng (王彥章) to fight at Zhōngdū (中都).
Yànzhāng (彥章) was defeated,
and Yán'guǎng (延廣) suffered several wounds,
barely escaping with his life.
During Míngzōng's (明宗) reign,
Zhū Shǒuyīn (朱守殷) rebelled in Biànzhōu (汴州).
Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) was Deputy Commissioner of the Six Armies (Liùjūn Fùshǐ, 六軍副使),
primarily responsible for executing those who followed Shǒuyīn (守殷) in rebellion.
Yán'guǎng (延廣), being a military officer in Biànzhōu (汴zhou), was scheduled for execution.
Gāozǔ (高祖), regretting the loss of his talent,
secretly allowed him to escape.
Later, he recruited him as a retainer general (Kèjiàng, 客將).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
he appointed him Grand Commander of the Palace Army Infantry (Shìwèi Bùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ, 侍衞步軍都指揮使),
concurrently holding the position of Commandant of the Militia of Guǒzhōu (Guǒzhōu Tuánliànshǐ, 果州團練使).
He was transferred to concurrently hold the position of Military Commissioner of the Níngjiāng Army (Níngjiāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ, 寧江軍節度使).
In the fourth year of Tiānfú (天福) [939 CE],
he was sent out to govern Yìchéng (義成).
He was then transferred to Bǎoyì (保義).
He was recalled to serve as Grand Marshal of the Palace Army Cavalry and Infantry (Shìwèi Mǎbùjūn Dōu Yúhòu, 侍衞馬步軍都虞候).
He was transferred to govern Hèyáng Sānchéng (河陽三城),
and promoted to Grand Commander of the Cavalry and Infantry (Mǎbùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ, 馬步軍都指揮使),
concurrently holding Tiānpíng (天平).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) died,
Chūdì (出帝) was established.
Yán'guǎng (延廣) had played an influential role
and greatly boasted of his achievement.
Initially,
when Chūdì (出帝) was established,
the Jìn (晉) ministers debated notifying the Qìdān (契丹) [court],
submitting a memorial to declare themselves subjects (chēngchén, 稱臣).
Yán'guǎng (延廣) alone refused,
only submitting a letter referring to the emperor as a grandson (chēng sūn, 稱孫).
Although the high ministers knew this was inappropriate, they could not overrule him.
The Qìdān (契丹) were indeed enraged
and repeatedly reproached Jìn (晉) for this.
Yán'guǎng (延廣) said to the Qìdān (契丹) envoy, Qiáo Yíng (喬瑩):
"The former emperor was established by the Northern Court,
but the Son of Heaven today was installed by the Central States themselves.
He can be considered a grandson,
but he cannot be considered a subject.
Furthermore, Jìn (晉) possesses 100,000 great swords polished crosswise (Héngmó Dàjiàn, 橫磨大劍).
If the Elder (Wēng, 翁) wants war,
then let him come.
Should he fail to restrain his grandson later,
he will be ridiculed by all under Heaven."
Yíng (瑩) knew that these words would certainly spark conflict between the two nations,
and feared that he would later be unable to prove their source.
He therefore requested that the statement be written down on paper,
in case of forgetfulness.
Yán'guǎng (延廣) ordered an official to fully record it and hand it to Yíng (瑩).
Yíng (瑩) concealed the document in the collar of his robe and returned [home].
He fully reported Yán'guǎng's (延廣) words to the Qìdān (契丹),
and the Qìdān (契丹) became even angrier.
In the autumn of the eighth year of Tiānfú (天福) [943 CE],
Chūdì (出帝) returned after visiting the Great Year Manor (Dànián Zhuāng, 大年莊),
and held a banquet at Yán'guǎng's (延廣) residence.
The vessels, garments, saddles and horses, tea tables, and chairs presented by Yán'guǎng (延廣) were all covered in gold and silver,
and decorated with dragons and phoenixes.
Furthermore, he presented 5,000 bolts of silk,
1,400 taels of floss,
22 horses,
jade saddles, ceremonial robes, rhinoceros horn, jade, and gold belts, etc.
He requested that these be bestowed upon the attending officials,
starting from the Emperor's brother, Chóngruì (重睿),
down to the escorting prefects (bànshí cìshǐ) and Chóngruì's (重睿) followers, each receiving gifts according to their rank.
The Emperor also bestowed appropriate gifts upon Yán'guǎng (延廣), his mother, wife, subordinates (cóngshì), marshals (yāyá), and accounting officials (kǒngmùguān), etc.
At that time, the empire suffered from drought and locusts,
and hundreds of thousands of people starved to death every year,
yet the ruler and his minister pursued the utmost extravagance, boasting to one another in this manner.
In the spring of the following year,
the Qìdān (契丹) invaded.
Yán'guǎng (延廣) accompanied Chūdì (出帝) on the northern campaign as the Commissioner of the Imperial Camp (Yùyíng Shǐ, 御營使),
and they held the line between Chán (澶) and Wèi (魏).
The vanguard commander, Shí Gōngbà (石公霸), encountered the invaders at Qīchéng (戚城).
Gāo Xíngzhōu (高行周) and Fú Yànqīng (符彥卿), having too few troops, were unable to rescue him.
They rode quickly to urge Yán'guǎng (延廣) to send reinforcements.
Yán'guǎng (延廣) held his troops and did not move.
The three generals were surrounded several deep.
The Emperor personally led the army to rescue them.
The three generals managed to escape
and tearfully reported [Yán'guǎng's failure].
However, Yán'guǎng (延廣) commanded the imperial troops (qīnbīng),
relied on his achievements, and acted with reckless arrogance.
All the generals followed his command,
and the Emperor himself could not control him.
The Qìdān (契丹) often called out to the Jìn (晉) people, saying:
"Jǐng Yán'guǎng (景延廣) summoned us here,
why doesn't he hurry up and fight?"
At this time,
all the other generals fought fiercely,
but Yán'guǎng (延廣) never faced the enemy.
After the Qìdān (契丹) had departed,
Yán'guǎng (延廣) alone stayed behind closed walls, not daring to venture out.
Since Yán'guǎng's (延廣) single statement caused the deterioration of relations between the Qìdān (契丹) and Jìn (晉),
all orders regarding military campaigns and expeditions originated solely from Yán'guǎng (延廣).
None of the Jìn (晉) high ministers were allowed to participate [in decision-making].
Therefore, in all the written dispatches sent by the Qìdān (契丹),
Yán'guǎng (延廣) was always mentioned.
When the Qìdān (契丹) left,
Chūdì (出帝) returned to the capital.
He then sent Yán'guǎng (延廣) out to serve as Administrator of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn, 河南尹)
and Garrison Commissioner of the Western Capital (Xījīng, 西京).
The following year,
Chūdì (出帝) visited Chányuān (澶淵),
taking Yán'guǎng (延廣) with him,
but achieved nothing.
Yán'guǎng (延廣), residing in Luòyáng (洛陽),
was depressed and unfulfilled.
Seeing that Jìn (晉) was deteriorating daily,
and estimating that it definitely could not withstand the Qìdān (契丹),
he indulged in endless nighttime drinking,
greatly renovating his residence,
installing courtesans and musicians in the gardens,
and acting entirely as he pleased.
Later, the Emperor also regretted [his actions].
He dispatched the Court Attendant Zhāng Huī (張暉) to present a memorial declaring Jìn a subject (chēngchén, 稱臣) in order to seek peace.
Déguāng (德光) replied, saying:
"If you send Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) and Jǐng Yán'guǎng (景延廣) here,
and cede Zhèn (鎮) and Dìng (定) to us,
then peace is possible."
Jìn (晉) knew this was impossible,
and thus stopped.
When the Qìdān (契丹) reached Zhōngdù (中渡),
Yán'guǎng (延廣) was garrisoned at Hèyáng (河陽).
Upon hearing that Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威) had surrendered,
he retreated.
When Déguāng (德光) approached the capital,
and reached Xiāngzhōu (相州),
he dispatched several thousand cavalry mixed with Jìn (晉) troops to cross the river and head toward Luò[yáng] (洛),
in order to capture Yán'guǎng (延廣).
He gave strict orders, saying:
"If Yán'guǎng (延廣) flees south to Wú (吳),
or runs west to Shǔ (蜀),
you must pursue and capture him."
But Yán'guǎng (延廣) worried about his family
and was unable to make a quick decision.
The enemy cavalry suddenly arrived.
He and his subordinate, Yán Pī (閻丕), rode quickly to meet Déguāng (德光) at Fēngqiū (封丘).
Pī (丕) was also immediately shackled.
Yán'guǎng (延廣) said:
"Pī (丕)
is my subordinate.
He followed me only because of his duties.
What crime has he committed that he should be shackled?"
Pī (丕) was then released.
Déguāng (德光) reproached Yán'guǎng (延廣), saying:
"The breakdown of good relations between the North and South
is entirely due to you."
He summoned Qiáo Yíng (喬瑩) to verify Yán'guǎng's (延廣) earlier statement.
Yán'guǎng (延廣) initially denied it,
but Yíng (瑩) produced the document he had concealed in his robe collar.
Yán'guǎng (延廣) then admitted the truth.
Déguāng (德光) proceeded to accuse Yán'guǎng (延廣) of ten offenses.
For every offense he admitted,
he was given an ivory tally (yáchóu, 牙籌).
When he had been given eight tallies,
Yán'guǎng (延廣) lay face down on the ground,
unable to look up.
Déguāng (德光) then shouted at him and had him shackled.
As he was being sent north,
he reached Chénqiáo (陳橋)
and stopped at a commoner's house.
In the middle of the night,
Yán'guǎng (延廣) waited until the guards were exhausted,
and used his hands to strangle himself to death.
He was fifty-six years old at the time.
During the time of Hàn Gāozǔ (漢高祖) [Liu Zhiyuan],
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Mentor (Shìzhōng, 侍中).
Among the principles of misfortune and fortune, success and failure since ancient times,
none is as clearly proven as that of the Jìnshì (House of Jìn)!
It initially rose through the Qìdān,
and was finally destroyed by the Qìdān.
However, at the time when he resisted the legitimate power with rebellion,
and the great undertaking had not yet coalesced,
his isolated city was besieged,
without outside rescue,
yet merely relying on the life of a single emissary,
and wielding the power of a tiny tongue,
he was able to make the Qìdān empty their state and raise an army,
responding as if matching a tally,
saving them from danger and resolving their difficulties,
thereby establishing the Jìnshì.
At that time,
the power of Wéihàn was greatest.
When the young ruler was newly established,
grievances formed and fighting ensued,
breaking treaties and starting conflict,
which originated with Yánguǎng.
Therefore, regarding the affairs of the Jìnshì,
Wéihàn accomplished them,
and Yánguǎng ruined them.
Although the intentions of these two men were different,
they received the same misfortune.
Why was this so?
It is generally because those who violate the proper order (of ruler and subject) and cooperate with foreign barbarians
usually see misfortune,
and never see fortune.
How can one not be cautious!
How can one not be cautious!
Wú Luán.
Wú Luán, courtesy name Bǎochuān,
was a man from Lúxiàn, Yùnzhōu.
When young, he failed the examination for the Classicists (Míngjīng).
During the Qīngtài era, he served as the Commissioner (Jiédu Pànguān) under Shā Yànxún of Dàtóng.
When Jìn Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán,
he summoned the Qìdān for support.
When the Qìdān passed through Yúnzhōu,
Yànxún left the city to welcome and pay respects,
but was captured by the Qìdān.
The people in the city elected Luán to manage the prefecture’s affairs.
Luán immediately closed the gates and resisted the siege.
The Qìdān surrounded it with troops.
Gāozǔ entered the capital and ascended the throne,
ceding Yúnzhōu to the Qìdān.
But Luán still held the city and refused to surrender.
The Qìdān besieged it for seven months in total.
Gāozǔ honored Luán’s actions
and consequently sent a letter to the Qìdān,
asking them to lift the siege and leave.
Gāozǔ summoned Luán
and appointed him Deputy Commissioner of Wǔníng Commandery (Wǔníng Jūn Jiédu Fùshǐ), Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū), and Defender of Fùzhōu (Fùzhōu Fángyùshǐ).
When Chūdì ascended the throne,
he broke the alliance with the Qìdān.
All the prefectures north of the Yellow River (Héběi) were put on alert.
They considered Bèizhōu to be a critical junction for both water and land routes,
where supplies could be transported quickly in an emergency.
Consequently, they accumulated hundreds of thousands of bundles of hay and grain,
and appointed Wáng Lìngwēn as Military Commissioner of Yǒngqīng Commandery (Yǒngqīng Jūn Jiédu Shǐ).
Lìngwēn’s staff officer, Shào Kē,
had always been arrogant and difficult to control,
so Lìngwēn stripped him of his position.
Kē, bored in idleness,
secretly sent a person to defect to the Qìdān,
stating that Bèizhōu had a large stockpile of grain but lacked defending troops,
and could be taken.
Lìngwēn went to the capital (Jīngshī) for an audience concerning official matters.
He was quite suspicious of Kē in his heart,
so he detained Kē’s son, Chóngfàn, to accompany him.
The ministers of Jìn, noting that Luán had previously defended Yúnzhōu for seven months
without the Qìdān being able to take it,
dispatched Luán via post-horse to replace Lìngwēn in defending Bèizhōu.
Luán was skilled at treating his soldiers kindly.
As it happened to be extremely cold,
he tore up his own tents and curtains to clothe the troops.
The soldiers all loved him.
Kē consequently sought an audience with Luán,
requesting to offer his services.
Luán trusted him wholeheartedly.
In the first month of the first year of Kāiyùn (944 CE),
the Qìdān invaded the south
and besieged Bèizhōu.
Luán ordered Kē to guard the South Gate.
The Qìdān besieged the city for three days,
assaulting it fiercely from all four sides.
Luán threw firewood and brush from the top of the wall, burning up almost all of the enemy’s siege ladders and rams.
Soon after, Kē led the Qìdān into the city through the South Gate.
Luán was defending the East Gate and fighting,
when his attendants reported that Kē had rebelled.
Luán looked around and saw that the city was already in chaos,
and immediately threw himself into a well and died.
Lìngwēn’s family members were captured by the Qìdān.
Chūdì pitied him,
and appointed Lìngwēn as Military Commissioner of Wǔshèng Commandery (Wǔshèng Jūn Jiédu Shǐ).
Later, he successively held several regional commands (fāngzhèn),
and died during the Xiǎndé era of Zhōu.
Lìngwēn
was a native of Héjiān, Yíngzhōu.
Wáng Lìngwēn suspected Shào Kē and detained his son,
but Luán was unable to perceive his treachery,
and instead entrusted him with troops.
When the Qìdān entered Bèizhōu,
he did not refuse battle,
but immediately threw himself into a well and died.
His death is not worthy of honor,
therefore he is not listed among those who died for the state.
Biography of Ministers of Hàn, Chapter 18: Sū Féngjí
Sū Féngjí
was a native of Cháng'ān, Jīngzhào.
When Hàn Gāozǔ governed Hédōng,
his father, Yuè, served as Gāozǔ’s staff member.
Féngjí often wrote official memoranda (zòujì) on Yuè’s behalf,
and Yuè consequently spoke of him to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ summoned and received Féngjí.
Seeing his sharp and elegant demeanor,
he took a liking to him
and appointed him Commissioner’s Aide (Jiédu Pànguān).
Gāozǔ was naturally rigid and severe,
and his retainers and aides rarely gained an audience.
Féngjí alone was permitted entry,
and attended Gāozǔ in his study all day long.
The documents from the two agencies accumulated heavily,
and no one dared to present them.
Féngjí would take them and put them inside his robes,
waiting for a moment when Gāozǔ seemed approachable to present them.
Gāozǔ often approved them,
and for this reason, loved him very much.
However, Féngjí was greedy, deceitful, immoral,
and fond of killing.
Gāozǔ once, on his birthday, sent Féngjí to streamline the administration of prisons and prisoners to pray for fortune,
calling it
"Silencing the Prison" (Jìng Yù).
Féngjí entered the prison to review the inmates,
and killed them all, regardless of whether their crimes were minor or major, or whether they were wrongfully accused or guilty.
He reported, saying:
"The prison is silenced."
When Gāozǔ established his dynastic title,
he appointed Féngjí Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Minister of State (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
At that time,
institutions were newly founded,
and all major court affairs originated with Féngjí.
Féngjí took this upon himself as his duty.
However, he was fundamentally unlearned.
He decided matters as they arose,
based purely on his own opinion.
Consequently, the Hàn dynasty especially lacked legal structures
and failed to implement benevolent governance,
and the people had nothing to praise.
After Gāozǔ settled in the capital (Jīngshī),
Féngjí and Sū Yǔguī were together in the Secretariat,
and most appointments of officials violated old regulations.
Féngjí especially accepted bribes and gifts,
trading power and selling offices.
Those who condemned him were clamorous.
However, Gāozǔ greatly relied upon and trusted the two men,
so no one dared to report them.
When Lǐ Yǒngjí of Fèngxiáng first paid court to the capital (Jīngshī),
Féngjí believed that since Yǒngjí was the son of the former Prince of Qín, Cóngyǎn,
and his family had been princes and marquises for generations,
he must possess rare valuables.
He sent a person to notify Yǒngjí,
promising him a prefecture
in exchange for his late father's jade belt.
Yǒngjí pleaded that he did not have it.
Féngjí then ordered someone to purchase a jade belt,
worth several thousand strings of cash,
and demanded Yǒngjí pay for it.
Wáng Yún, the former Director of the Bureau of Guest Reception (Kèshěng Shǐ), had been an envoy to Chǔ since the end of Jìn.
By this time, he returned.
Féngjí suspected that Yún had received a large bribe from the King of Chǔ,
and sent people to request it,
promising him a prefecture.
Yún was resentful,
but presented half of his travel funds to him.
Yet, neither of them received a prefecture.
Lǐ Sōng, the Jìn Chancellor, had gone north with the Qìdān.
When Gāozǔ entered the capital (Jīngshī),
Sōng’s residence was granted to Féngjí.
Sōng had separate fields and residences in the Western Capital (Xījīng),
which Féngjí subsequently seized entirely.
When Sōng returned from the north,
he presented the title deeds for the residence to Féngjí.
Féngjí was displeased,
and Sōng's sons and younger relatives often uttered complaints.
After this,
Féngjí enticed someone to accuse Sōng, along with his younger brother Yǔ and ● others,
resulting in their imprisonment.
Sōng confessed, falsely incriminating himself:
"I plotted rebellion
with twenty household servants, intending to use Gāozǔ’s burial rites as an opportunity."
The prison records were submitted to the Secretariat (Zhōngshū).
Féngjí changed
"twenty men"
to
"fifty men,"
and subsequently exterminated Sōng’s entire clan.
At that time,
the world was full of robbers.
Féng Jí personally drafted imperial edicts and sent them down to the prefectures and counties,
stating that where a robber lived, both their immediate family and their neighbors were to be executed as a clan.
Someone said to Féng Jí:
"Executing a robber's entire clan
is already contrary to royal law,
how much more so the neighbors!"
Féng Jí was startled and realized this was true;
having no choice,
he merely removed the clause about executing the clan.
Thereupon, Zhāng Lìngróu, the commissioner for catching bandits in Yùn Zhōu, killed several hundred villagers from seventeen villages in Píngyīn Xiàn.
Yè Rénlǔ, the Prefect of Wèi Zhōu, heard there were bandits in his department,
and personally led troops to capture them.
At that time, ten or so villagers were jointly pursuing the bandits,
entering into the mountains,
and the bandits all dispersed and fled.
Rénlǔ arrived afterwards,
saw the villagers who were pursuing the bandits,
mistook them for rebels,
captured them all,
cut their Achilles tendons,
and exposed them on the mountainside.
Twisting and crying out,
they died after several days.
Those who heard this could not bear the injustice,
but Féng Jí considered Rénlǔ capable.
Because of this, the killing of people throughout the land in connection with banditry became increasingly excessive.
Féng Jí, having already become distinguished,
became even more extravagant and luxurious.
He claimed that the food served in the dining hall of the Central Secretariat was inedible,
so he ordered his personal chef to present delicacies,
which were daily extremely rare and fine.
When his stepmother died,
he did not wear mourning clothes.
When his wife, Lady Wǔ Shì, died,
he suggested that all civil and military officials and regional governors should contribute damask and silk for the mourning attire.
Before the first anniversary of Wǔ Shì's death,
he appointed her various sons to official posts.
A paternal elder half-brother came from outside.
Before reporting to Féng Jí, he saw Féng Jí's sons.
Féng Jí was enraged,
and using a pretext about another matter, reported it to Gāozǔ,
and had the brother beaten to death with a staff.
Féng Jí once followed Gāozǔ in the campaign against Yè,
and frequently, while drunk, insulted Zhōu Tàizǔ in the military camp.
Tàizǔ resented this.
Later, when Yǐndì ascended the throne,
Féng Jí was always friendly with Lǐ Tāo.
He persuaded Tāo to request the dismissal of Tàizǔ and Yáng Bīn from their positions as military commissioners.
Empress Dowager Lǐ Tàihòu was angered that Tāo was alienating high officials,
so she dismissed Tāo from his position as Chancellor.
She appointed Yáng Bīn to concurrently hold the title of *Píngzhāngshì* (Flatting Affairs),
and all matters were submitted to him for decision.
Féng Jí and Yǔguī merely filled their posts thereafter.
In the second year of Qiányòu (949 CE),
he was additionally granted the title of Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
When Zhōu Tàizǔ governed Yè,
he did not lose the position of Military Commissioner.
Féng Jí believed that the post of Military Commissioner,
when held concurrently by a regional governor, was inconvenient,
and he argued with Shǐ Hóngzhào over this.
In the end, the matter was resolved according to Hóngzhào's suggestion.
Hóngzhào resented Féng Jí for opposing him.
Later, they met at Wáng Zhāng's residence.
Féng Jí used the occasion to get drunk in their presence,
and Hóngzhào became extremely angry.
Féng Jí plotted to request a post as a regional governor to avoid him.
But then he stopped midway.
When people asked him the reason,
Féng Jí said:
"If I leave this place,
one order from Lord Shǐ,
and I will be minced meat!"
At that time,
Emperor Yǐndì was young,
and petty people were by his side.
Hóngzhào and others dominated the Emperor,
and the Emperor and his close attendants, Lǐ Yè, Guō Yǔnmíng, and others, were all troubled by this.
Whenever Féng Jí met Yè and the others,
he incited them with his words.
Yè and the others eventually killed Hóngzhào,
and immediately appointed Féng Jí to provisionally take charge of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
Just as they ordered the drafting of the edict,
they heard that Zhōu Tàizǔ had raised troops,
and so they stopped.
Féng Jí spent the night in the East Chamber of the Jīnxiáng Diàn.
He said to Wáng Chùnè, the Director of the Summer Office of the Bureau of Astronomy:
"Before I fell asleep last night,
I already saw Lǐ Sōng standing nearby.
When the living communicate with the dead,
it portends no good fortune."
Zhōu Tàizǔ reached the northern suburbs.
The imperial army was defeated at Liúzǐ Pí.
Féng Jí stayed overnight at Qī Lǐ.
That night, he drank heavily with his roommates.
He asked for a knife intending to commit suicide,
but was stopped by his attendants.
The next day, he fled with Emperor Yǐndì to Zhào Cūn,
and committed suicide in a common dwelling.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ secured the capital,
he displayed Féng Jí's head on a stake,
which happened to be right at the spot where Lǐ Sōng had been executed.
In the beginning of the Guǎngshùn era (951 CE),
his son was granted an estate and a residence complex in the Western Capital (Xījīng).
Shǐ Hóngzhào
Shǐ Hóngzhào, courtesy name Huàyuán,
was a native of Xíngzé, Zhèng Zhōu.
He was brave and fierce in character;
he could run as fast as a galloping horse.
In the late period of the Liáng dynasty,
when the people were mobilized so that seven households provided one soldier,
Hóngzhào became a soldier,
assigned to the Kāidào Command,
and was selected to be part of the Imperial Guard.
When Hàn Gāozǔ commanded the Imperial Guard,
Hóngzhào was a military officer.
Subsequently,
when Hàn Gāozǔ governed Tàiyuán,
he made Hóngzhào the commander of the Left and Right Wǔjié Commands,
and appointed him Prefect of Léi Zhōu.
When Gāozǔ proclaimed his authority in Tàiyuán,
Wáng Huī of Dài Zhōu resisted the order.
Hóngzhào attacked and defeated him,
and for this merit, he was appointed Military Governor of the Zhōngwǔ Jūn and Commander-in-Chief of the Metropolitan Infantry.
At this time, the Qìdān retreated north,
leaving Gěng Chóngměi to attack Wáng Shǒu'ēn in Lù Zhōu.
Gāozǔ sent Hóngzhào ahead to attack them.
Chóngměi was defeated and fled,
and Shǒu'ēn surrendered the city to the Hàn.
Wǔ Xíngdé of Héyáng and Zhái Lìngqí of Zé Zhōu, among others,
all welcomed Hóngzhào and surrendered themselves.
Hóngzhào entered Héyáng.
Gāozǔ arrived shortly after,
and subsequently entered the capital.
As a general, Hóngzhào
was severe, stern, and taciturn.
If anyone under his command slightly displeased him,
he would immediately beat them to death with a rod.
The army trembled with fear.
Therefore, at the beginning of Gāozǔ's uprising,
wherever Hóngzhào marched his troops,
not a single hair was harmed,
and the two capitals were settled.
He was promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Metropolitan Cavalry and Infantry of the Imperial Guard,
and concurrently held the titles of Military Governor of the Guīdé Jūn and *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì* (Chancellor).
When Gāozǔ was critically ill,
he was entrusted with the dying instructions along with Yáng Bīn, Sū Féngjí, and others.
One source reads *shòu* (received).
During the time of Emperor Yǐndì,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn of Hézhōng, Wáng Jǐngchóng of Fèngxiáng, and Zhào Sīwǎn of Yǒngxīng all rebelled.
Troops were deployed west of the Pass (Guānxī),
people's hearts were fearful,
and the citizens of the capital
used rumors to frighten each other.
Hóngzhào dispatched troops for policing,
and made it his business to carry out mass killings;
all crimes, great or small, incurred the death penalty.
At this time, the planet Venus (Tàibái) was visible in the daytime.
If a citizen looked up at it,
they would immediately be cut in half at the waist in the marketplace.
In the marketplace, a drunken man offended a soldier.
The soldier falsely accused him of spreading rumors,
and the man was executed in the marketplace.
Whenever a citizen committed a crime,
the officials reported it to Hóngzhào,
who merely pointed three fingers at them,
and the officials immediately cut the person in half at the waist.
He also implemented punishments such as cutting out the tongue, slicing the mouth, severing tendons, and breaking feet.
Lǐ Sōng was executed along with his clan because his slave reported a rebellion.
Hóngzhào took Lǐ Sōng's young daughter as a maidservant.
Consequently, the families of former officials and retired generals who had lost their posts
pampered their domestic servants and slaves,
and this class of bondservants
often threatened and controlled their masters.
Xiè Huī, an administrative clerk in the Imperial Guard, was cunning and cruel.
He took advantage of circumstances to commit corrupt acts,
and the citizens whom he punished
dared not appeal.
Hé Fújìn, a man from Yān, had a jade pillow
worth 140,000 cash.
He sent a servant to sell it in Huáinán in order to trade for tea.
The servant hid the money.
Fújìn flogged him for it.
The servant then falsely accused Fújìn of having acquired Zhào Yánshòu's jade pillow
and giving it to a Wú person.
Hóngzhào arrested and prosecuted him.
Fújìn was executed in the marketplace.
Those under Hóngzhào's command divided his wife and children among themselves,
and confiscated his household wealth.
Hóngzhào did not like receiving guests.
He once said:
"Literati are intolerable;
they call me a mere soldier."
Shǐ Hóngzhào led Guīdé,
and his deputy envoys, etc., would contribute a thousand *mín* of private money monthly as tribute.
Qū Wēn, the official in charge of the yeast brewery in Yǐngzhōu, quarreled over official business with the military commander Hé Zhěng.
They brought the dispute to the Sānsī (Three Offices),
and the Sānsī ruled in favor of Wēn.
Zhěng appealed the case to Hóngzhào.
Hóngzhào considered Yǐng to be his subordinate prefecture,
but Wēn had not first reported to him.
So he summoned Wēn and killed him,
and several dozen people were implicated.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ pacified Lǐ Shǒuzhēn,
he praised the merits of the officials.
Hóngzhào was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (Minister of the Central Secretariat).
When Yǐn Dì (the Hidden Emperor) returned his troops from Guānxī,
he gradually drew close to sycophants,
and indulged excessively in pleasure with Hòu Zàn, Lǐ Yè, and others.
Furthermore, the relatives of the Empress Dowager often sought influence and favors.
Hóngzhào and Yáng Bīn somewhat restrained them.
The Empress Dowager had the son of an old acquaintance who sought appointment to a military post.
Hóngzhào immediately had him executed.
The Emperor began to listen to music,
and bestowed jade belts and brocade robes upon the officials of the Jiàofāng (Imperial Music Bureau).
They went to thank Hóngzhào.
Hóngzhào angrily said:
“The brave men who fight campaigns for the state have not yet received special rewards.
What merit do you fellows possess,
that you dare receive this?”
He took all the gifts they had received and returned them to the court.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ went out to govern Wèizhōu,
Hóngzhào proposed that he assume the duties of the Shūmì (Military Commissioner).
Sū Féngjí and Yáng Bīn thought it improper,
and Hóngzhào resented them for it.
The next day,
they gathered to drink at Dòu Zhēngù’s residence.
Hóngzhào raised his cup and loudly addressed Tàizǔ, saying:
“Yesterday in the court discussion,
why were there conflicting opinions?
Today, let us drink this together.”
Féngjí and Bīn also raised large cups and said:
“This is a matter for the state.
Why must you take offense?”
Thereupon, they all drained their cups.
Hóngzhào said:
“To stabilize the court,
and settle disorder and chaos,
one simply needs long spears and great swords.
As for ‘hair brushes’
how are they worth using?”
Wáng Zhāng, the Sānsī Commissioner, said:
“Without ‘hair brushes,’
where would the military revenues come from?”
The ‘hair brush’
was a metaphor for the writing brush.
Hóngzhào fell silent.
Another day,
they gathered to drink at Zhāng’s residence.
When the drinking was festive,
they played the finger-guessing game.
Hóngzhào could not play it.
Yán Jìnqīng, the Commissioner of the Reception Hall, sat next to Hóngzhào,
and repeatedly instructed him.
Sū Féngjí joked, saying:
“Since there is a person named Yán sitting here,
why worry about having to drink a penalty cup!”
Hóngzhào’s wife was named Yán,
and she was a singing girl from a tavern.
Hóngzhào thought this was mocking him,
and became greatly enraged.
He insulted Féngjí with vulgar language.
Féngjí did not retaliate.
Hóngzhào wanted to strike him.
Féngjí left first.
Hóngzhào stood up, sought his sword, and wanted to pursue him.
Yáng Bīn wept and said:
“Lord Sū
is the Chancellor of the Hàn dynasty.
If you kill him,
where will you put the Son of Heaven?”
Hóngzhào galloped away on his horse.
Bīn escorted him to his residence and then returned.
From this point on, the generals and chancellors were like fire and water.
Yǐn Dì sent Wáng Jùn to set up a feast at Gōngzǐ Tíng (The Young Lord’s Pavilion) to reconcile them.
At that time,
Lǐ Yè, Guō Yǔnmíng, Hòu Zàn, Niè Wénjìn, and others held power,
and disliked the high officials who governed the court.
Although Yǐn Dì was gradually growing older,
he was controlled by the great ministers,
and frequently uttered angry words.
Yè and the others seized the opportunity to slander them,
claiming that Hóngzhào’s might intimidated the sovereign,
and if he were not eliminated, he would surely cause trouble.
Yǐn Dì was quite inclined to eliminate them.
One night, hearing the sound of armor being forged in the workshops,
he thought troops had arrived,
and stayed awake until dawn.
Therefore, he plotted secretly with Yè and the others within the Forbidden Palace.
On the thirteenth day of the tenth month in the winter of Qiányòu 3 (950 CE),
Hóngzhào, along with Yáng Bīn, Wáng Zhāng, and others, entered the court.
They sat in the eastern gallery of Guǎngzhèng Diàn (Guangzheng Hall).
Several dozen armored soldiers emerged from the interior,
captured Hóngzhào, Bīn, and Zhāng, and executed them,
and exterminated their three families simultaneously.
After Hóngzhào had died,
the Emperor sat in Chóngyuán Diàn (Chongyuan Hall) and summoned the officials,
announcing that Hóngzhào and the others had plotted rebellion.
None of the officials could respond.
He then summoned all the military officers to see him at Wànsuì Diàn (Wansui Hall).
The Emperor said:
“Hóngzhào and the others usurped authority,
making you men constantly fear an untimely death.
Today, I have finally been able to become your true lord!”
The military officers all bowed.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously titled Hóngzhào as Zhèng Wáng (Prince of Zheng),
and buried him according to proper rites.
Yáng Bīn
Yáng Bīn
was a native of Guànshì in Wèizhōu.
When he was young, he served as a document clerk for the prefecture.
When Kǒng Qiān, the Commissioner of Rent and Taxation, governed the Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī),
he appointed Bīn as a Gōuyā official.
He successively served as the Director of the Provisioning Bureau in the three prefectures of Mèng, Huà, and Yùn.
He served Hàn Gāozǔ as the Right Commander of Military Headquarters (Yòu Dū Yāyá).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Shūmì Shǐ (Military Commissioner).
Bīn originated from the low-ranking bureaucracy,
and disliked literary scholars.
He and Sū Féngjí, etc., engaged in mutual political exclusion.
Féngjí implicitly encouraged Lǐ Tāo to submit a memorial calling for Bīn and Zhōu Tàizǔ to be dismissed as Military Commissioners.
Bīn tearfully appealed before Empress Dowager Lǐ.
The Empress Dowager was angered,
dismissed Tāo from his chancellorship,
and promoted Bīn to Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat) concurrent with Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel) and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì (Executive Director).
At that time,
Féngjí and Yǔ Guī frequently appointed officials based on private bribes,
and many errors resulted.
When Bīn became chancellor,
regardless of the importance of the matter,
it had to be shown to Bīn first.
If Bīn deemed it acceptable,
it was then submitted to the Emperor.
He profoundly reformed the practices introduced by Féngjí.
All those who entered office through hereditary privilege (Mènyìn),
or who were appointed clerks by various bureaus,
were entirely dismissed.
Although Bīn was skilled in bureaucratic affairs,
he did not grasp the larger principles of governance.
He believed that for the state,
as long as the treasuries and granaries were full,
and the armor and weapons complete—that was sufficient.
Rites, music, literature, and culture were all merely superficial tools.
Therefore, while holding high political power, he focused on minute and harsh details.
He decreed that all former officials were forbidden to reside outside the capital,
and all travelers in the realm
must be issued a travel permit (*guòsuǒ*) before being allowed to proceed.
Within ten days,
public sentiment was greatly disturbed.
Bīn realized it could not be implemented and stopped.
Bīn often discussed affairs with Wáng Zhāng before the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
“After the policy has been carried out,
do not let there be any dissenting comments!”
Bīn quickly replied:
“Your Majesty, just prohibit speech.
Your servant is here.”
Those who heard this trembled in fear.
Lǐ Yè, the younger brother of Empress Dowager Lǐ, sought the position of Xuānhuī Shǐ (Commissioner of the Palace Affairs).
The Emperor and the Empress Dowager privately asked Bīn about it.
Bīn simply said it was unacceptable.
The Emperor wanted to establish his favorite, Lady Gěng, as Empress.
Bīn again deemed it unacceptable;
when Lady Gěng died,
the Emperor intended to bury her with the rites due an Empress.
Bīn again deemed it unacceptable.
Because of this, Yǐn Dì became extremely angry,
and his attendants took the opportunity to sow discord.
He was killed on the same day as Shǐ Hóngzhào and the others.
Bīn was generally frugal and quiet.
Although he did not refuse bribes from all corners of the land,
he often presented them to the Emperor.
At home, he refused to receive guests.
In his later years, he gradually interacted with gentry officials,
and welcomed guests at his gate.
Knowing that historical writings were useful,
he instructed clerks to copy them.
Not long after,
he met disaster.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously titled him Hóngnóng Wáng (Prince of Hongnong).
Wáng Zhāng
Zhōu Tàizǔ went out to govern Wèizhōu.
Shǐ Hóngzhào proposed taking the Bureau of Military Affairs position with him,
but Sū Féngjí and Yáng Bīn thought it was not permissible.
Shǐ Hóngzhào resented this.
The next day,
they met for a drink at Dòu Zhēnggù’s residence.
Shǐ Hóngzhào, raising his goblet with a stern voice, toasted Zhōu Tàizǔ, saying:
“Yesterday in the court discussion,
why was there disagreement?
Today I drink this with you.”
Féngjí and Bīn also raised large goblets, saying:
“This is a matter of the state,
why must you take it to heart!”
And they all drank their cups dry.
Shǐ Hóngzhào said:
“To bring peace to the court,
and settle chaos,
one simply needs long spears and great swords.
How can ‘hairy cones’
be of any use?”
The Three Department Commissioner, Wáng Zhāng, said:
“Without ‘hairy cones’,
how would the military tax be collected?”
“Hairy cones”
referred to writing brushes.
Shǐ Hóngzhào fell silent.
Another day,
they met for a drink at Wáng Zhāng’s residence.
When the wine was flowing freely,
they played a hand gesture game.
Shǐ Hóngzhào couldn’t play it.
Yán Jìnqīng, the Commissioner of the Guest Bureau, who sat next to Shǐ Hóngzhào,
repeatedly taught him.
Sū Féngjí joked:
“With someone named Yán sitting here,
why worry about a penalty drink!”
Shǐ Hóngzhào’s wife was named Yán,
and she was a singing girl from a tavern.
He took this as a jab at himself
and became furious,
cursing Féngjí with foul language.
Féngjí did not respond.
Shǐ Hóngzhào wanted to strike him,
but Féngjí left first.
Shǐ Hóngzhào rose, grabbing a sword, wanting to pursue him.
Yáng Bīn tearfully said:
“Sū Gōng
is a prime minister of Hàn.
If you kill him,
where would you place the Son of Heaven?”
Shǐ Hóngzhào galloped away on his horse,
and Bīn saw him to his residence and returned.
From then on, the generals and ministers were like fire and water.
Yǐndì sent Wáng Jùn to host a banquet at Gōngzǐ Tíng to reconcile them.
At this time,
Lǐ Yè, Guō Yǔnmíng, Hòu Zàn, Niè Wénjìn, and others were in power,
and disliked the executive officials.
As Yǐndì grew older,
he was controlled by his powerful ministers
and often expressed resentment.
Lǐ Yè and others seized the opportunity to slander them,
claiming that Shǐ Hóngzhào’s power intimidated the emperor,
and that if he were not eliminated, he would surely cause trouble.
Yǐndì greatly desired to eliminate them.
At night, he heard the sound of armor being forged in the workshops,
and thought that soldiers had arrived.
He did not sleep until dawn.
Because of this, he secretly conspired with Lǐ Yè and others within the palace.
On the thirteenth day of the tenth month of the third year of Qiányòu,
Shǐ Hóngzhào, Yáng Bīn, Wáng Zhāng, and others entered the court.
They sat in the east corridor of Guǎngzhèng Diàn.
Dozens of armed guards emerged from within the palace,
captured Shǐ Hóngzhào, Bīn, and Zhāng, and beheaded them,
and also exterminated their three clans.
After Shǐ Hóngzhào’s death,
the Emperor sat in Chóngyuán Diàn and summoned his officials,
informing them that Shǐ Hóngzhào and the others had plotted rebellion.
None of the officials could respond.
He then summoned the various military commanders to Wànsuì Diàn.
The Emperor said:
“Shǐ Hóngzhào and the others wielded exclusive power,
causing you all to constantly worry about violent death.
Today I can be your lord!”
All the military commanders bowed.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed Shǐ Hóngzhào as Prince Zhèng
and buried him with due rites.
Yáng Bīn
Yáng Bīn was
a native of Guànshì in Wèizhōu.
In his youth, he served as a record-keeping clerk in the prefecture.
When Kǒng Qiān, the Commissioner of Taxation, was in charge of the Department of State Finance,
he appointed Bīn as a supervising official.
He successively served as manager of the provisioning office in the three prefectures of Mèng, Huá, and Yùn.
He served Hàn Gāozǔ as the Right Capital Overseer.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Bīn came from a humble background as a minor official,
and disliked literati.
He and Sū Féngjí and others were in mutual contention within the court.
Féngjí prompted Lǐ Táo to submit a memorial to dismiss Bīn and Zhōu Tàizǔ from their positions as Commissioners of Military Affairs.
Bīn tearfully pleaded before Empress Dowager Lǐ.
The Empress Dowager was angered
and dismissed Lǐ Táo from his prime ministership,
and promoted Bīn to Grand Secretary of the Central Secretariat, concurrently Minister of Personnel, and Co-equal with the Grand Administrator.
At this time,
Féngjí and Yǔ Guī often appointed officials through private bribery,
making many errors.
When Bīn became prime minister,
all matters, large or small,
had to be presented to Bīn first.
Only if Bīn approved
would they be reported to the emperor.
He deeply reformed Féngjí’s practices.
All officials who gained office through family influence
or were appointed as clerks by various departments
were dismissed without exception.
Although Bīn was skilled in official affairs,
he lacked a grand vision.
He believed that for the state,
the granaries should be full,
and the army strong and complete,
and that ritual, music, and cultural artifacts were all empty formalities.
Thus, holding great political power, he focused on petty details.
For example, former officials were not allowed to reside outside the capital,
and all travelers in the realm
had to be issued travel permits before they could proceed.
Within a few days,
public sentiment was greatly disturbed,
and Bīn, realizing it was impractical, stopped.
Bīn often discussed matters with Wáng Zhāng before the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
“After the matter is put into practice,
do not allow anyone to speak ill of it!”
Bīn quickly said:
“Your Majesty need only silence your voice,
your humble servant is here.”
Those who heard it trembled.
Empress Dowager Lǐ’s younger brother, Lǐ Yè, sought to become Commissioner of the Palace Gate.
The Emperor and Empress Dowager privately consulted Bīn about this.
Bīn simply said it was not permissible.
The Emperor wished to make his beloved Lady Gěng Empress,
but Bīn again said it was not permissible.
When Lady Gěng died,
the Emperor planned to bury her with the rites of an empress,
but Bīn again said it was not permissible.
Because of this, Yǐndì was greatly angered,
and his attendants seized the opportunity to sow discord.
He was killed on the same day as Shǐ Hóngzhào and the others.
Bīn was a rather frugal and quiet person.
Although he did not refuse bribes from all corners,
he often presented them to the Emperor.
At home, he refused all guests,
but in his later years, he gradually interacted with literati
and invited guests to his residence.
Knowing the utility of historical records,
he instructed his clerks to copy them.
Not long after,
he met with disaster.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed him as Prince Hóngnóng.
Wáng Zhāng
Wáng Zhāng was
a native of Nánlè in Wèizhōu.
He served as a secretary in the prefecture.
When Zhāng Lìngzhāo expelled the military governor Liú Yánhào,
Wáng Zhāng served Lìngzhāo.
When Lìngzhāo was defeated,
Wáng Zhāng’s father-in-law, Bái Wénkē, was on good terms with the Deputy Commander Lǐ Zhōu,
and entrusted Wáng Zhāng to Lǐ Zhōu.
Lǐ Zhōu hid Wáng Zhāng in a box
and carried him on a camel to Luòyáng,
where he concealed him in his residence.
When the Táng dynasty fell,
Wáng Zhāng emerged
and became the provisions manager for Héyáng.
When Hàn Gāozǔ commanded the imperial guards,
he appointed Wáng Zhāng as a secretary
and Wáng Zhāng followed him to Tàiyuán.
Wáng Zhāng
was a man of Nánlè, Wèizhōu.
He served as the Kǒngmùguān (Registrar) of the prefecture.
Zhāng Lìngzhāo expelled Jiéduànshǐ Liú Yánhào,
and Zhāng served Lìngzhāo.
When Lìngzhāo was defeated,
Zhāng's father-in-law, Bái Wénkē, was close with the Deputy Commander Lǐ Zhōu.
He then entrusted Zhāng to Zhōu.
Zhōu hid Zhāng within a cloth sack,
carried him on a camel to Luòyáng,
and concealed him in Zhōu's residence.
When Táng was destroyed,
Zhāng emerged,
becoming the Liángliàoshǐ (Quartermaster) of Héyáng.
Gāozǔ of Hàn commanded the Imperial Guards,
appointed Zhāng as Kǒngmùguān,
and Zhāng followed him to Tàiyuán.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Sānsīshǐ (Commissioner of Finance) and concurrently Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi (Acting Grand Commandant).
When Gāozǔ passed away,
Yǐndì ascended the throne,
and he was promoted to Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Chancellor).
At this time,
the Hàn dynasty was newly established,
succeeding the Qìdān.
The capital was empty and impoverished.
Furthermore, the three rebellions in Guānxī occurred,
and Zhōu Tàizǔ was campaigning in the west.
Zhāng supplied provisions to the troops,
and they never ran out.
However, he sought profit and exploited the common people,
who suffered greatly from this.
Previously, for every *shí* of grain rent, the people surrendered two *shēng* as the
"Sparrow and Rat Tax" (Quèshǔ Hào).
Zhāng then increased it to two *dǒu* per *shí* as the
"Provincial Loss Tax" (Shěng Hào).
For strings of cash being paid in or out,
they all previously counted eighty coins as one *mò* (string).
Zhāng reduced the amount paid out by three coins per *mò*.
When people in the prefectures and counties complained about land,
he would have the entire prefecture and county reviewed,
in order to ferret out hidden fields.
The entire realm suffered heavily because of this.
Moreover, he particularly disliked scholars (literary officials).
He once said to people:
"Give these types an abacus,
and they won't even know how to use it properly.
How can they benefit the state!"
For the salaries and stipends of all officials, he took surplus items unfit for military use,
commanded the relevant authorities to overestimate their price,
and after the assessment was fixed, he increased it again,
calling this
the "Inflated Assessment" (Yì Gū).
Zhāng often still felt unsatisfied,
and would frequently increase the price yet again.
If citizens committed offenses related to salt, alum, or yeast (jiǔqǔ),
regardless of the quantity, they were all sentenced to death.
Officials used this as an opportunity for corruption,
and the people found life unbearable.
Later, he was killed on the same day as Shǐ Hóngzhào and others.
Liú Zhū
Liú Zhū
was a man of Shǎnzhōu.
In his youth, he served as a commander (Yájiàng) for the Prince of Shào of Liáng.
He was an old acquaintance of Gāozǔ of Hàn.
When Gāozǔ was stationed at Tàiyuán,
he made Zhū the Zuǒ Dū Yāyá (Left Chief Military Attendant).
Zhū was a cruel man who delighted in killing.
Gāozǔ believed his decisive bravery resembled his own,
and especially trusted him.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Jiéduànshǐ of Yǒngxīng Commandery.
He was transferred to command Pínglú,
promoted to Jiǎnxiào Tàishī (Acting Grand Tutor) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (Chancellor),
and further granted the title Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
At this time,
the Jiānghuái region was inaccessible,
and envoys from Qián Liú of Wúyuè often traveled by sea to reach the Central Plains (Zhōngguó).
All the coastal prefectures had established Trading Offices (Bóyì Wù)
to conduct commerce with the people.
If a person fell into debt or missed a deadline,
the office clerks would arbitrarily arrest and punish them,
establishing their own prisons,
without consulting the prefectures or counties.
Furthermore, former officials
accepted hefty bribes
and let the offenders go unpunished.
The people were quite distressed by this,
so Zhū prohibited all these practices entirely.
However, Zhū's application of the law
was also inherently severe.
If a citizen committed an offense,
he would ask their age.
If they answered "so many years,"
he would immediately beat them with that number of strokes,
calling it
the "Age-Appropriate Beating" (Suí Nián Zhàng).
Every time he beat someone,
he insisted that two rods must strike simultaneously,
calling it
the "Joyous Union Beating" (Héhuān Zhàng).
He also requested an increase in the land tax,
requiring thirty cash per *mǔ* for public use,
which the people could not bear.
Yǐndì worried about Zhū's harshness and violence,
and summoned him,
but Zhū was afraid and did not come.
At this time,
Guō Huái of Yízhōu returned after attacking Nántáng,
and stationed his troops at Qīngzhōu.
Yǐndì then sent Fú Yànqīng to replace Zhū.
Zhū realized the Imperial Guards were present,
and no one dared to harbor dissenting views,
so he accepted the replacement and returned to the capital.
Zhū had always gnashed his teeth in hatred toward Shǐ Hóngzhào, Yáng Bīn, and others.
When Hóngzhào and the others were eventually killed,
Zhū said to Lǐ Yè and his associates:
"Gentlemen, you may now be called true scoundrels (Lóuluō Er)."
He temporarily managed Kāifēng Prefecture.
When the troops of Zhōu Tàizǔ invaded the capital,
Zhū executed the entire family of Tàizǔ, Wáng Jùn, and others.
When Tàizǔ entered the capital,
Zhū's wife, naked and exposed, covered herself with a mat,
and was captured along with Zhū.
Zhū said to his wife:
"I am certainly going to die,
you will probably become a slave for someone else."
Tàizǔ sent someone to rebuke Zhū, saying:
"You and I served the Former Emperor together.
Do you not harbor any feeling for an old acquaintance?
My family was massacred and exterminated.
Although there was an imperial command,
applying such severe cruelty—
how could you bear to do it?
Now you also have a wife and children.
Do you not think of them?"
Zhū replied:
"I executed the rebellious subjects for Hàn,
how could I know anything else?"
At this time,
Tàizǔ was seeking to gain the hearts of the people,
so he discussed it with his officials, saying:
"Shìzhōng Liú fell from his horse and was severely injured,
and the soldiers pressed and humiliated him.
Since he still holds a sliver of life,
I wish to petition the Empress Dowager
to spare his family.
What do you think?"
All the officials thought this was good.
So he ceased the execution of Zhū,
and along with Lǐ Yè and others, they were publicly exposed in the marketplace (their heads were displayed),
but their wives and children were pardoned.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he granted one estate and one residence in Shǎnzhōu to each family.
Lǐ Yè
Lǐ Yè
was the younger brother of Gāozǔ's Empress.
The Empress had seven siblings,
and Yè was the youngest,
thus he was especially cherished.
During Gāozǔ's reign,
he was made Wǔdéshǐ (Commander of the Martial Virtue Guard).
When Yǐndì ascended the throne,
because of the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
Yè gained even more power
and acted without restraint.
At the time, the realm suffered from drought and locusts,
the Yellow River breached its banks,
and a great wind in the capital uprooted trees
and destroyed city gates.
In the palace, monstrous phenomena were often seen throwing tiles and stones and shaking the doors.
Yǐndì summoned the Astronomer (Sī Tiān), Zhào Yán'yì, and asked about methods of exorcism.
Yán'yì replied:
"My duty is the celestial phenomena and the calendar,
to observe their changes
and examine conformity, rebellion, good fortune, and bad fortune—that is all.
Matters of exorcism
are not within my knowledge.
However, what I have heard
suggests they are mountain demons (Shānxiāo)."
The Empress Dowager then summoned Buddhist nuns (ní) to recite scriptures for exorcism.
One nun went to the lavatory,
and after returning,
wept mournfully, remaining unconscious for several days.
When she awoke and was questioned,
no one knew the reason why.
Meanwhile, the Emperor was intimate with Yè, Niè Wénjìn, Hòu Zàn, Guō Yǔnmíng, and others.
They frequently engaged in riddles and satirical games,
and flew paper kites inside the palace.
