The Empress Dowager frequently warned the Emperor about the disasters and anomalies,
but he refused to listen.
At that time, the position of Xuānhuī Shǐ (Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs) was vacant.
Lǐ Yè wanted to obtain it.
The Empress Dowager also sent people to suggest this to the chief ministers.
The chief ministers, Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào, and others, all believed it was unacceptable.
Lǐ Yè was consequently resentful and disgruntled,
plotting to murder Bīn and the others.
After Bīn and the others had died,
he further sent the Attendant Official Mèng Yè with an imperial decree to kill Guō Wēi in Wèizhōu.
Wēi raised an army and rebelled.
Emperor Yǐn sent Yuán Kè (Yuan ●), the Supreme Commander of the Left Shénwǔ Army, and Yán Jìnqīng, the Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Cavalry, and others to lead troops to resist Wēi at Chányuān.
Before the troops had departed,
Wēi had already reached Huázhōu.
The Emperor was greatly afraid,
and said to his ministers:
"Yesterday things were too hasty!"
Lǐ Yè requested to open the imperial treasury to reward the army.
The Chancellor Sū Yǔguī thought this was not yet appropriate.
Lǐ Yè bowed to Yǔguī before the Emperor and said:
"Prime Minister, please, for the sake of the Imperial Family, do not begrudge the treasury."
Thereupon, an imperial decree was issued bestowing ten thousand cash per person upon the capital troops and the Wèi troops who had followed Wēi southward,
and ordering their sons and younger brothers to write letters
to inform those northern troops who were approaching.
When the Hàn army was defeated in the Northern Suburbs,
Lǐ Yè took gold and valuables from the inner treasury,
concealed them, and fled to his elder brother, Hóng Xìn, the Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor) of the Bǎoyì Army.
Hóng Xìn refused to admit him.
Lǐ Yè fled until he reached Jiàngzhōu,
where he was killed by people.
Niè Wénjìn.
Niè Wénjìn
was a native of Bìngzhōu.
When young, he was a soldier.
He was skilled in writing and calculation,
serving in the tent of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
When Gāozǔ was stationed in Tàiyuán,
he made him Yāsī Guān (Administrative Officer).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he successively received appointments as General of the Lǐngjūn Garrison and Commissioner of the Privy Council (Shūmìyuàn Chéngzhǐ).
When Emperor Tàizǔ of Zhōu was Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs),
he relied on and trusted him greatly.
Wénjìn gradually became arrogant and unrestrained.
He was promoted to Grand General of the Right Lǐngjūn Army.
When he entered the court to offer thanks,
he summoned various generals to a banquet in the court hall.
The Yíluán Bureau, the Hànlín Academy, and the Imperial Kitchen supplied the tents, provisions, and food.
Wénjìn acted as he pleased,
and the relevant authorities did not dare impeach him.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of Zhōu was stationed in Yè,
Wénjìn and others held power within the court.
When they planned to murder Yáng Bīn and the others,
Wénjìn drafted the imperial decree at night,
regulating (or imposing control over) internal and external affairs.
After Bīn and the others had died,
Wénjìn checked the military registers,
directed the killings,
treating it as his own responsibility.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of Zhōu, being in Yè, heard that Bīn and the others had been murdered,
he initially thought Wénjìn was not involved.
But when the imperial decree was issued,
it was all in Wénjìn's handwriting,
and Tàizǔ greatly reviled him.
When the Zhōu troops reached the capital,
Emperor Yǐn was defeated in the Northern Suburbs.
The Empress Dowager was afraid,
and sent someone to tell Wénjìn to guard the Emperor well.
He replied:
"With your subject here,
what harm can a hundred Guō Wēi’s do!"
Mùróng Yànchāo was defeated and fled.
The Emperor lodged at Qīlǐ.
That night, Wénjìn drank wine with his followers,
singing and shouting, acting as if nothing was wrong.
The next morning,
Emperor Yǐn was assassinated.
Wénjìn also committed suicide.
Hòu Zàn.
Hòu Zàn
was a native of Xiáqiū, Yǎnzhōu.
His mother
was a courtesan.
Zàn was skilled at singing when young,
and served Zhāng Yánlǎng.
When Yánlǎng died,
Zàn switched to serving Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
Gāozǔ favored him
and made him a Yájiàng (Aide).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Fēilóng Shǐ (Director of the Flying Dragon Bureau).
Emperor Yǐn especially favored and relied on him.
When Yáng Bīn and the others held political power,
Zàn was long unable to get promoted,
so he conspired with others to murder Bīn and the others.
After Bīn and the others died,
Emperor Yǐn regretted it.
Zàn and Yǔnmíng, among others, took turns attending the Emperor during breaks,
not wishing for those around the Emperor to speak ill of themselves.
When Emperor Yǐn’s troops were defeated in the Northern Suburbs,
Zàn fled to Yǎnzhōu.
Mùróng Yànchāo arrested him and sent him to the capital,
where his head was displayed in the marketplace.
Guō Yǔnmíng.
Guō Yǔnmíng,
when young, was a servant of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
Gāozǔ favored him
and made him Director of Tea and Wine of the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Chájiǔ Shǐ).
Emperor Yǐn especially indulged and favored him.
Yǔnmíng became increasingly arrogant and unrestrained, showing no fear or avoidance,
and the chief ministers could not restrain him.
Yǔnmíng was sent on a mission to Gāo Bǎoróng in Jīngnán.
His carriages, attire, escort, and entourage were like those of a Jiédùshǐ.
Bǎoróng treated him extremely generously.
Yǔnmíng secretly ordered people to pace out and measure the height of their city walls and moats,
as if devising a plan for attack and capture,
in order to alarm him.
The people of Jīng were all terrified.
Bǎoróng gave him a lavish bribe and sent him away.
He was promoted to Fēilóng Shǐ.
Subsequently, Lǐ Yè and Yǔnmíng conspired to murder Yáng Bīn and the others.
That day was cloudless but dark,
with mist and rain like weeping.
At noon,
more than ten corpses of Bīn and the others were loaded onto carts and exposed in the marketplace.
Yǔnmíng personally killed the sons of Bīn and the others in the West Gallery of the court hall.
The blood of Zhāng Yísù, the son-in-law of Wáng Zhāng, flowed backward (upward).
When Emperor Yǐn was defeated in the Northern Suburbs,
he returned to Fēngqiū Gate,
but was unable to enter.
The Emperor fled to Zhàocūn.
Yǔnmíng pursued him from behind,
assassinated the Emperor in a civilian house,
and then committed suicide.
Biographies of Zhōu Officials, Chapter 19: Wáng Pǔ.
Wáng Pǔ, courtesy name Wénbó,
was a native of Dōngpíng.
When young, he passed the Imperial Examination (Jìnshì).
He served as Archivist (Jiàoshū Láng),
relying on Yáng Bīn, the Shūmìshǐ of Hàn.
Bīn had friction with Wáng Zhāng, Shǐ Hóngzhào, and others.
Pǔ saw that the Hàn dynasty had been established only recently,
Emperor Yǐn was young and feeble,
and he employed petty men.
Furthermore, Bīn, as a chief minister,
was on bad terms with the generals and chancellors.
Pǔ knew that chaos was inevitable,
so he left Bīn and returned east.
Later, Lǐ Yè and others instructed Emperor Yǐn to execute the powerful ministers.
Bīn, Zhāng, and Hóngzhào were all killed.
Many retainers of the three families were implicated,
but Pǔ, for this reason, was the only one spared.
When Emperor Shìzōng of Zhōu was stationed in Chányuān,
Pǔ served as the Jiédù Zhǎngshūjì (Secretary to the Military Governor).
When Shìzōng became the Prefect of Kāifēng (Kāifēng Yǐn),
he appointed Pǔ to the Censorate (Yòu Shíyí)
and made him an Investigating Official (Tuīguān).
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Pǔ was promoted to Bǐbù Lángzhōng (Director of the Bureau of Accounts).
He presented a strategy for pacifying the borders,
saying: "The Táng lost the Way and consequently lost Wú and Shǔ.
The Jìn lost the Way and consequently lost Yōu and Bìng.
Observing the reasons for their loss,
one can understand the methods required for pacification.
At the time
of those losses,
the ruler was unenlightened and governance was chaotic,
the military was arrogant, and the populace was distressed.
Those nearby committed treason internally,
and those far away rebelled externally.
Minor issues were not restrained, leading to usurpation;
major issues were not restrained, leading to
excess.
The hearts of the people under Heaven were alienated,
and men would not obey orders.
Wú and Shǔ seized the opportunity of the chaos to usurp titles,
while Yōu and Bìng took advantage of the rift to occupy their territories.
The technique for pacification
lies simply in reversing the errors of the Táng and Jìn.
We must first promote the worthy and dismiss the unworthy,
thereby purifying the administration;
employ the capable and dismiss the incapable,
thereby judging their talents;
use favor and trust
in issuing commands,
thereby winning their hearts;
reward merit and punish crime,
thereby ensuring they exert their utmost strength;
be reverent, frugal, and moderate in expenditure,
thereby enriching the national wealth;
and ensure labor service is seasonal,
thereby fostering the people.
We must wait until the granaries are full, equipment is ready, and men are fit for service before undertaking the action.
The people of those regions,
knowing that our benevolent governance is widely implemented,
that superiors and subordinates share one heart,
that our military strength is high and our wealth is abundant,
that the people are secure and the generals are harmonious,
and that we possess the assured momentum to seize the lands,
then those who know their conditions will wish to act as our spies,
and those who know their mountains and rivers will wish to act as our guides.
Those people and
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Sānsīshǐ and Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi.
When Gāozǔ passed away,
Yǐndì ascended the throne,
and Zhāng was promoted to Tàiwèi and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
At this time,
the Hàn dynasty had just been established,
inheriting from the Qìdān.
The capital was impoverished,
and three rebellions broke out in Guānxī.
Zhōu Tàizǔ was campaigning in the west,
and Zhāng supplied the army
without ever running short.
However, he profited from exploiting the lower classes,
which caused great suffering to the people.
Previously, for every shí of grain rent, two shēn were paid as
"quèshǔhào" (sparrow and rat loss);
Zhāng increased this to two dòu per shí as
"shěnghào" (provincial loss).
For money in strings,
all transactions used eighty coins as a mò,
but Zhāng reduced the outgoing amount by three per mò.
When people in the prefectures and counties complained about land,
the entire prefecture and county would be scrutinized
to uncover hidden land.
The empire was thus heavily burdened.
Furthermore, Zhāng particularly disliked scholars.
He once said to someone:
"If you give this sort of person an abacus,
they won't even know how to use it upside down;
what good are they to the country!"
The stipends for all officials were taken from the remnants of military supplies that were unusable.
He ordered the relevant authorities to value them highly,
and after the valuation was set, he would increase it again,
calling it
"yìgū" (forced valuation).
Zhāng was still not satisfied,
and often increased it further.
If people violated laws concerning salt, alum, or yeast,
regardless of the amount, they were sentenced to death.
Officials exploited this for corruption,
and the people could not endure it.
Later, he was killed on the same day as Shǐ Hóngzhào and others.
Liú Zhū
Liú Zhū,
was from Shǎnzhōu.
In his youth, he served as a yájiàng for Liáng Shàowáng.
He had an old acquaintance with Hàn Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ was stationed in Tàiyuán,
he made him Zuǒ Dū Yāyá.
Zhū was cruel and fond of killing.
Gāozǔ considered him brave and decisive, like himself,
and particularly trusted and employed him.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Zhū was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Yǒngxīng Commandery.
He was then transferred to Pínglú,
promoted to Jiǎnjiào Tàishī and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and further granted Shìzhōng.
At this time,
the Jianghuai region was inaccessible,
so emissaries from Wúyuè Qián Liú often traveled by sea to reach the central plains.
In all coastal prefectures, Bóyìwù (trade offices) were established
to trade with the people.
If people defaulted or missed deadlines,
the office clerks would arbitrarily arrest and punish them,
setting up their own prisons,
without involving the prefectures or counties.
However, former officials
would accept generous bribes
and let them go unpunished.
The people suffered greatly from this,
so Zhū banned it all.
Nevertheless, Zhū's application of the law
was also excessively harsh.
When people committed an offense,
he would ask their age.
If they answered a certain number,
he would cane them with that many strokes,
calling it
"suíniánzhàng" (age-based caning).
For each person caned,
he would always use two canes simultaneously,
calling it
"héhuānzhàng" (joyful union caning).
He also requested to increase land rent,
charging thirty coins per mù for public use,
which the people could not bear.
Yǐndì was troubled by Zhū's rigidity and violence,
and summoned him,
fearing he would not come.
At this time,
Guō Huái of Yízhōu had returned from attacking Southern Táng
and stationed his troops in Qīngzhōu.
Yǐndì then sent Fú Yànqīng to replace Zhū.
Zhū saw that the imperial guards were present,
and no one dared to have dissenting thoughts,
so he accepted the replacement and returned to the capital.
Zhū had always harbored a bitter grudge against Shǐ Hóngzhào, Yáng Bīn, and others.
Later, when Hóngzhào and the others were killed,
Zhū said to Lǐ Yè and others:
"You gentlemen can truly be called 'lǒulúo'ér' (lowly subordinates)."
While acting as the Prefect of Kāifēng,
Zhōu Tàizǔ's troops invaded the capital.
Zhū executed all the family members of Tàizǔ and Wáng Jùn.
When Tàizǔ entered the capital,
Zhū's wife, naked and covered with a mat,
was captured along with Zhū.
Zhū said to his wife:
"I am going to die,
you will probably become someone's slave."
Tàizǔ sent someone to rebuke Zhū, saying:
"You served the former emperor with me,
do you have no feeling for old friends?
My family was slaughtered and annihilated.
Although it was an imperial command,
the cruelty and venom you added to it,
how could you bear it?
Now you also have a wife and children,
do you think of them?"
Zhū replied:
"I was executing rebellious subjects for Hàn,
I knew nothing else."
At this time,
Tàizǔ was seeking to win over the hearts of the people,
so he discussed with his officials:
"Liu Shìzhōng fell from his horse and was severely injured,
and the soldiers insulted him.
If there is still a slight chance of life,
I wish to propose to the Empress Dowager
to spare his family.
What do you think?"
All the officials thought it was a good idea.
So they ceased killing Zhū,
and impaled his head along with Lǐ Yè and others in the marketplace,
pardoning his wife and children.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he bestowed upon Shǎnzhōu one estate and one residence each.
Lǐ Yè
Lǐ Yè
was the younger brother of Gāozǔ's empress.
The empress had seven siblings,
and Yè was the youngest,
thus particularly beloved.
During Gāozǔ's reign,
he was made Wǔdéshǐ.
When Yǐndì ascended the throne,
due to being the Empress Dowager's relative,
Yè gained even more power
and acted without scruples.
At that time, there was drought and locusts throughout the land,
the Yellow River burst its banks,
and the capital experienced strong winds that uprooted trees
and damaged city gates.
Within the palace, monsters were often seen throwing tiles and stones, and shaking doors.
Yǐndì summoned the Director of Astronomy Zhào Yányì and asked about methods for exorcism.
Yányì replied:
"My duty is to observe celestial phenomena and times,
to notice their changes,
and to examine auspiciousness or inauspiciousness, and nothing more.
Matters of exorcism
are not within my knowledge.
However, what I have heard
is probably the mountain demon (shānxiāo)."
The Empress Dowager then summoned Buddhist nuns to chant scriptures for exorcism.
One nun went to the latrine,
and upon her return,
wept uncontrollably for several days, unaware of people around her.
When she awoke and was questioned,
no one knew the reason.
Meanwhile, the Emperor was close with Yè, Niè Wénjìn, Hòu Zàn, Guō Yǔnmíng, and others,
often exchanging riddles and teasing each other,
and flying paper kites in the palace.
The Empress Dowager repeatedly warned the Emperor about the calamities,
but he did not listen.
If the minds of the people are united,
this is consistent with the will of Heaven;
when consistent with the will of Heaven,
then there is no achievement that cannot be accomplished.
The way of offensive campaigns
begins with the easiest target.
Currently, only Wú
is easy to subdue.
Eastward to the sea
and southward to the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
it has two thousand *lǐ* of territory that can be harassed.
Begin by harassing
the areas with the fewest preparations.
If they prepare the east, harass the west;
if they prepare the west, harass the east.
They will surely rush about to remedy the situation,
and during their rushing,
we can discern their strengths and weaknesses,
the vigor and feebleness of their forces.
Attacking the weak and striking the feeble,
our advance will be unstoppable.
Do not launch a major invasion;
simply use light troops to harass them.
Their people are timid and weak.
Knowing that our forces have entered
their territory,
they will surely launch a major mobilization to respond.
If they mobilize greatly multiple times, the people will be exhausted and the state depleted.
If they fail to mobilize greatly even once, we will seize the advantage.
When they are depleted and we are advantaged,
then the various prefectures north of the Jiāng
will belong to the state.
Once the north of the Jiāng is secured,
then using their people
and deploying our troops,
the south of the Jiāng will also not be difficult to pacify.
If this is done,
the effort will be minimal while the achievement will be great.
Upon taking Wú,
both Guì and Guǎng will become interior vassals,
and Mín and Shǔ can be summoned by merely sending a letter.
If they do not comply,
then
we will advance simultaneously from four directions,
and Shǔ will be swept clean and pacified.
Once Wú and Shǔ are pacified,
Yōu can be expected to submit at the mere sight of our prestige.
Only Bì, the death-defying brigands,
cannot be persuaded by kindness and trust.
They must be attacked with strong forces.
Once their strength is exhausted
and their morale is lost,
they will not be sufficient to cause border trouble
and can be dealt with later.
Currently, our armed forces are skilled and well-trained,
military supplies are fully prepared,
all subordinates understand the laws,
and the generals follow orders.
After one year of harvest,
the borders can be pacified.
I am merely a scholar,
insufficient to discuss grand affairs.
Should I fail to grasp the big picture
or miss the shifting strategies,
I beg Your Majesty to be lenient!”
He was transferred to be Zuo Jiànyì Dàfū
and was appointed manager of the affairs of Kāifēng Fǔ.
Mid-year,
he was transferred to be Zuo Sànqí Chángshì,
and appointed Scholar of the Duānmíng Diàn.
At that time,
Shìzōng had newly ascended the throne
and was intent on military campaigns,
having already overruled all dissenting opinions
and personally defeated Liú Mín at Gāopíng.
He returned and further managed the military,
feeling deeply the ambition to unify the entire realm.
He frequently sought out high officials to ask about governance,
and selected scholars of literature like Xú Táifú and twenty others,
instructing them to compose essays on the difficulty of being a ruler and the challenge of being a minister, as well as strategies for pacifying the borders.
Piáo was among those selected.
However, the literati at the time generally did not want the Emperor to be hasty in using military force,
arguing that the priority for pacifying the usurpers and rebels
lay in cultivating civil virtue.
Only Grand Academician Táo Gǔ, Dòu Yí, Censor-in-Chief Yáng Zhāojiǎn, and Piáo all presented military strategies.
Piáo argued that Jiānghuái should be conquered first.
Shìzōng already had a good impression of Piáo,
and upon seeing his excellent proposals,
he considered him even more remarkable.
He invited him to discuss and consult on the affairs of the realm,
and they agreed on everything.
Consequently, the Emperor resolved to utilize him.
In the third year of Xiǎndé (956 CE),
when campaigning against Huái,
Piáo was appointed Deputy Resident-General of Dōngjīng.
Upon returning,
he was appointed Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue and Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs,
and later promoted to Commissioner of Military Affairs.
In the fourth year (957 CE),
when campaigning against Huái again,
Piáo was left behind to guard the capital (Jīngshī).
During Shìzōng’s reign,
he engaged in external military campaigns
while domestically reforming laws and regulations.
Piáo was a person of great intelligence and versatility.
Not only was he adept at the duties of the time,
but he was also knowledgeable about
the methods of *yīnyáng* and calendar studies.
In the second year of Xiǎndé (955 CE),
an edict ordered Piáo to revise and fix the Dàlì (Great Calendar).
He excised the modern superstitious and heterodox theories of *Fútiān Liúsú*,
established the three methods of *Tōng*, *Jīng*, and *Tǒng*,
and used the numbers derived from the cycle of the annual track, the lunar nodal cycle, and the synodic cycle
to calculate the movements of the sun, moon, and five planets,
creating the Qīntiān Lì (Reverent Heaven Calendar).
In the sixth year (959 CE),
Piáo was again ordered by edict to examine and correct the court music (*yǎyuè*).
Piáo believed that the pitch pipes of the Twelve Tones (*shí’èr lǜ*) were difficult to calibrate accurately when blown in succession,
so
he followed Jīng Fáng’s method to create a pitch standard (*lǜ zhǔn*).
He used thirteen nine-foot strings,
set frets according to the measured lengths of the pitch pipes,
and employed the seven sounds (*qī shēng*) for the tuning.
The resulting music was harmonious.
Piáo’s character was resolute,
and he was also trusted by Shìzōng.
Whatever he did,
no one dared to oppose him at the time,
though no one could surpass him either.
When Shìzōng campaigned against Huái,
Piáo remained in the capital,
enlarging the new city walls
and improving the roads.
The construction was grand and magnificent.
Much of the layout of the current capital
was based on his planning.
The music he composed
is still used today and cannot be altered.
His strategic plan for military engagement
was not merely a temporary measure.
Regarding the order in which the various states would rise and fall, he said:
“Huáinán can be conquered first,
and Bì, the death-defying brigands,
will be the last to fall.”
Later, when the Sòng Dynasty arose
and pacified the four directions,
only Bì submitted last,
all exactly as Piáo had predicted.
In the spring of the sixth year (959 CE),
Shìzōng sent Piáo to inspect the mouth of the Biàn River
and construct pound locks (*dǒumén*).
Upon returning,
while passing by the residence of former Prime Minister Lǐ Gǔ,
he fell ill,
collapsed in his seat,
was carried home, and died,
aged fifty-four.
Shìzōng attended his funeral,
striking the ground with a jade battle-ax (*yù yuè*),
and wept bitterly several times.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shìzhōng.
Zhèng Rénkuì
Zhèng Rénkuì, courtesy name Rìxīn,
was a native of Tàiyuán Jìnyáng.
Initially,
he served Chén Shàoguāng, a general of Táng.
Shàoguāng was fierce and brave but fond of heavy drinking.
Once, in a drunken rage, he became angry with Rénkuì,
drew his sword intending to kill him.
All the attendants ran away,
but Rénkuì stood still,
showing no fear.
Shàoguāng threw the sword to the ground
and patted Rénkuì, saying:
“You possess great capacity.
You will certainly become wealthy and noble,
which is beyond my reach.”
Rénkuì later left Shàoguāng,
returned to his hometown,
and was renowned for his filial piety towards his mother.
was the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng,
Zhōu Tàizǔ served under his command,
often going to visit Rén Huǐ,
and they spoke very happily.
Whenever there was doubt about a matter,
he immediately questioned Rén Huǐ,
and Rén Huǐ’s replies were never sycophantic.
Zhōu Tàizǔ valued him even more highly.
When Hàn arose,
Zhōu Tàizǔ became the Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs).
He then summoned Rén Huǐ and employed him.
He was successively promoted until he reached the office of Nèikèsěngshǐ.
When Tàizǔ defeated Lǐ Shǒuzhēn at Hézhōng,
in the strategies and planning of the army,
Rén Huǐ participated and resolved much.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Rén Huǐ as Dànèi Dūdiǎnjiǎn, Tuánliànshǐ of Ēnzhōu, and Shūmì Fùshǐ (Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs).
He was successively promoted to Xuānhuī Běiyuànshǐ,
and was later sent out to serve as Jìedùshǐ of Zhènníng Jūn.
In Xiǎndé first year (954),
he was appointed Shūmìshǐ.
When Shìzōng attacked Hédōng,
Rén Huǐ remained behind to guard Dōngdū (the Eastern Capital).
In the winter of the following year,
he died of illness.
Shìzōng intended to attend his funeral,
but the officials concerned stated that the year was inauspicious for attending funerals.
Shìzōng ignored them,
and first attended the rite using a peach wand and calamus grass (to ward off evil).
Rén Huǐ, even from the time when he was obscure,
often planned strategies for Tàizǔ.
Yet, when he occupied a high position,
he was never heard to boast of this;
but Tàizǔ and Shìzōng both personally valued him highly.
Moreover, he was able to remain humble, prudent, and fond of propriety,
never boasting of his own achievements.
He was praised by the officials and scholars.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhōngshū Lìng,
posthumously enfeoffed as Hánguó Gōng,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngzhèng.
Hù Zǎi
Hù Zǎi, courtesy name Zhòngxī,
was a man of Běiyān.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was skilled at composition.
In the early Guǎngshùn period (951-953),
he achieved the highest grade in the *jìnshì* examination.
He was appointed Jiàoshū Láng,
and served in the Historiography Institute.
He was twice promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
In his literary compositions,
he often took pleasure in his rich vocabulary.
He compiled the records of the rise, fall, order, and disorder of successive dynasties
into the *Yùnyuán Fù* (Rhapsody on the Origin of Fate), which was extremely detailed.
Once, while visiting Xiàngguó Sì,
he saw that the courtyard bamboo was lovely,
so he composed the *Bìxiān Fù* (Rhapsody on Verdant Freshness),
inscribing it on the wall.
Shìzōng heard about it,
and sent a minor court attendant to copy it directly from the wall.
After reading it, he praised it as excellent.
He was consequently appointed Shuǐbù Yuánwàiláng and Zhī Zhìgào.
He was promoted to Hànlín Xuéshì,
and bestowed a crimson robe,
but Zǎi was already ill
and unable to attend court to give thanks.
After more than a hundred days,
he forced himself, despite his illness, to enter and serve in the Hall of Academicians.
Shìzōng took pity on him,
granted him leave to return home,
and sent imperial physicians to attend to his illness.
Previously,
Zǎi was famous at the time for his writing.
The Shūmìshǐ Wáng Pǔ especially valued his talent
and recommended him to the Chancellor Lǐ Gǔ.
After a long time, he was still not employed.
Pǔ asked Gǔ:
"Why is Hù Zǎi not made a Shèrén?
What is the reason?"
Gǔ replied:
"It is not that I do not recognize his talent,
but Zǎi’s fortune is thin (short-lived),
and I fear he cannot endure it."
Pǔ said:
"As Chancellor,
your duty is to promote the worthy and dismiss the unworthy.
Why speak of destiny?"
Shortly thereafter, he was summoned and appointed Zhī Zhìgào.
When he became an Academician,
he died of illness within the year,
at the age of thirty-six.
Commentators believed that Gǔ was capable of judging character, and Pǔ was capable of recommending scholars.
At that time,
the Son of Heaven (Shìzōng) was heroic and martial,
delighting in attracting exceptional talents from all corners,
and especially courteous to literary men.
Zǎi, along with Zhāng Zhāo, Dòu Yǎn, Táo Gǔ, Xú Táifú, and others, were all promoted and employed.
Among these men, Gǔ
had the weakest literary style
and was particularly lacking in conduct.
Zhāo and Yǎn frequently engaged in discussions,
and their writings were brilliant.
But Gǔ was only skilled at anticipating the ruler’s wishes
and advancing flattery to please the sovereign.
Regardless of the significance of the matter,
he always offered high praise and eulogies.
Even concerning things like expanding the capital city, creating wooden farming figures, or matters of purple fungus and white rabbits,
he composed eulogies and presented them.
His prose was generally like that of an entertainer.
Zǎi, due to his misfortune of dying early,
though his discourse may not have equaled Zhāo and Yǎn,
he did not resort to Gǔ’s flattery.
Alas!
A maker of vessels
may lack excellent material yet possess an excellent craftsman;
a ruler who governs the state
may lack capable ministers yet possess a capable sovereign.
This is because the material relies on the craftsman to be completed,
and the minister relies on the sovereign to be employed.
Therefore, it is said,
governing a state is like playing *wéiqí* (Go):
the one who knows the value of the pieces and places them correctly wins;
the one who does not know their value and places them incorrectly loses.
The loser stares at the board,
toiling and stressing all day long.
If one were to let a skilled player look at it,
and simply re-place the pieces, he would win.
Those employed by the winner
are the same pieces used by the loser;
those employed by a rising state
are the same ministers used by a doomed state.
The talent of Wáng Pǔ
can truly be called capable.
Had he not met Shìzōng,
where could he have applied himself?
During the time of Shìzōng,
externally, he managed military campaigns and expeditions,
conquering and winning battles;
internally, he reformed institutions,
deliberated on penal laws,
fixed the calendar,
and thoroughly studied the surviving texts on rites and music.
Those whom he employed were the scholars of the Five Dynasties period.
Were they all foolish and cowardly during Jìn and Hàn,
but talented and wise during Zhōu?
It was only a matter of knowing how to employ them.
Truly, the ruler of a chaotic state
constantly places the foolish and unworthy in high positions,
forcing them to do what they cannot,
thereby exposing their shortcomings and flaws.
He places the worthy and wise in low positions,
causing their talents and abilities to be submerged,
making both the *jūnzǐ* (gentlemen) and the *xiǎorén* (petty men) lose their proper place,
leading himself into danger and ruin.
The ruler of a well-governed state
is able to place the worthy and wise nearby,
and place the foolish and unworthy far away,
allowing the *jūnzǐ* and the *xiǎorén* each to fulfill their role,
and thus enjoying peace and glory himself.
Although the difference between order and chaos is vast,
the means by which they are achieved are not numerous:
simply reversing the placement of personnel.
Alas,
since antiquity, wise rulers have been few and chaotic rulers many.
How much more so during the Five Dynasties period!
The scholars who met with success or failure—
how sorrowful they must have been!
Biographies of Those Who Died for Integrity, Chapter 20
The saying goes:
"In times of chaos, loyal ministers are recognized."
How true!
During the Five Dynasties period,
it cannot be said there were no capable men.
I have found three men who maintained their integrity whole,
for whom I compose the Biographies of Those Who Died for Integrity.
Wáng Yànzhāng (with Péi Yuē and Líu Rénshàn appended)
Wáng Yànzhāng, courtesy name Zǐmíng,
was a native of Shòuzhāng in Yùnzhōu.
In his youth, he became a soldier,
serving Liáng Tàizǔ.
He served as Yāyá of Kāifēng Fǔ, Zuǒ Qīncóng Zhǐhuīshǐ, and Xíngyíng Xiānfēng Mǎjūnshǐ.
When the Last Emperor (Mòdì) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Cìshǐ of Púzhōu,
and later transferred to Cìshǐ of Chánzhōu.
Yànzhāng was naturally valiant, fierce, and strong.
He could walk a hundred paces barefoot over thorns.
He carried an iron spear,
charging on horseback,
striking quickly like flight.
Others were unable to lift it,
and in the army, he was known as Wáng Tiěqiāng (Iron Spear Wáng).
Liáng and Jìn contended for the realm and were fierce rivals.
Only Yànzhāng always inwardly slighted the King of Jìn,
saying to people:
"Yàcì is just a small child who fights chickens,
why should he be feared!"
Liáng divided the six prefectures of Wèi and Xiāng into two commands,
fearing that the Wèi army would not comply.
They dispatched Yànzhāng leading five hundred cavalry into Wèi,
garrisoning Jīnbō Tíng to guard against sudden change.
The Wèi army indeed mutinied,
attacking Yànzhāng at night.
Yànzhāng fled south,
and the Wèi people surrendered to Jìn.
The Jìn army attacked and captured Chánzhōu,
capturing Yànzhāng's wife and children and bringing them back to Tàiyuán.
They bestowed residences upon them,
providing supplies very generously.
Occasionally they sent envoys to invite Yànzhāng to defect,
Yànzhāng executed their envoys to sever relations.
However, the Jìn people feared Yànzhāng while he was in Liáng,
necessarily desiring to recruit him,
and they treated his wife and children even better.
Since Liáng lost Wèi and Bó,
and camped along the river facing Jìn,
Yànzhāng often served as the vanguard.
He was promoted to Defense Commissioner of Rǔ and Zhèng prefectures, Jiedushi of the Kuāngguó Army, and Deputy Commander of the Northern Expeditionary Camp.
Later, he was transferred to become Jiedushi of the Xuānyì Army.
At this time,
Jìn had already completely seized Héběi,
using iron chains to block the mouth of Déshèng,
and building two cities on the south and north banks of the river,
which they called
"Jiāzhài".
However, the Last Emperor of Liáng was foolish and chaotic,
and petty men like Zhào Yán and Zhāng Hànjié held power.
Many high officials and veteran generals were targets of slander and intrigue.
Although Yànzhāng was Deputy Commander,
his strategies were not adopted.
In the summer of Lóngdé 3,
Jìn took Yùnzhōu.
The Liáng people were greatly alarmed.
The Chancellor Jìng Xiáng, seeing the urgency of the situation,
put a rope inside his boot,
entered to see the Last Emperor,
and weeping said:
"When the former emperor seized the realm,
he did not consider your servant unworthy,
and none of my plans went unused.
Now the powerful enemy has not been eliminated,
yet Your Majesty neglects and ignores your servant's words.
If your servant is not employed,
it would be better to die!"
He then pulled out the rope intending to hang himself.
The Last Emperor sent someone to stop him,
and asked what he wanted to say.
Xiáng said:
"The situation is desperate!
Only Yànzhāng can handle this!"
The Last Emperor then summoned Yànzhāng to be the Commander,
appointing Duàn Níng as his deputy.
The Last Emperor asked for the date they would defeat the enemy.
Yànzhāng replied:
"Three days."
Everyone nearby burst out laughing.
Yànzhāng received the order and departed.
He rushed for two days until he reached Huázhōu.
He set up a great feast,
secretly sending men to prepare boats at Yángcūn.
He commanded six hundred armored soldiers, all carrying large axes,
taking smiths,
and preparing charcoal,
to sail downriver.
Yànzhāng attended the feast.
Halfway through the wine,
he pretended to rise to change clothes,
leading several thousand elite troops.
He followed the river to rush toward Déshèng.
The boat troops raised the chains and burned them apart.
Then, using giant axes, they chopped up the pontoon bridge,
while Yànzhāng led his troops to swiftly attack the Southern City.
The pontoon bridge was cut,
and the Southern City was consequently defeated.
This was exactly three days later.
At this time, Zhuāngzōng was in Wèi.
He had placed Zhū Shǒuyīn in charge of defending Jiāzhài.
When he heard Yànzhāng had been made Commander,
he was startled and said:
"Yànzhāng is valiant and fierce;
I have previously avoided his sharp attacks.
He is not Shǒuyīn's match.
However, Yànzhāng has few troops,
and prefers rapid combat.
He will certainly launch a swift attack on our Southern City."
He immediately rode rapidly to rescue it.
After traveling twenty *lǐ*,
he received a report from Jiāzhài saying:
"Yànzhāng's troops have already arrived."
By the time he arrived,
the Southern City had already fallen.
Zhuāngzōng evacuated the Northern City,
headed down to Yángliú.
He and Yànzhāng both floated on the river,
each traveling along one bank.
Whenever their boats encountered each other, they fought,
engaging in battle several dozen times a day.
Yànzhāng arrived at Yángliú,
and nearly captured it in his assault.
The Jìn forces built a rampart on the eastern bank of Bózhōu.
Yànzhāng led troops to attack it,
but failed to overcome it.
He returned to attack Yángliú,
but was defeated in battle.
At this time,
Duàn Níng already harbored treasonous intentions,
and was communicating with Zhào Yán and Zhāng Hànjié.
Yànzhāng was naturally outspoken and resolute.
He resented that Liáng was declining daily,
and hated the actions of Yán and his cohort.
He once said to people:
"Wait until I defeat the bandits and return,
then I shall execute the treacherous officials to apologize to the realm."
Yán and his cohort heard this and were afraid,
and joined forces with Níng to bring him down.
When they defeated the Southern City,
Yànzhāng and Níng each wrote a victory report to submit.
Níng sent men to inform Yán and his cohort to hide Yànzhāng’s report and submit his own.
The Last Emperor initially doubted the matter.
Later, when the envoy arrived at the army camp,
he only bestowed commendation upon Níng, ignoring Yànzhāng.
All the soldiers turned pale.
Upon the defeat at Yángliú,
Níng submitted a memorial stating:
"Yànzhāng was drunk and slighted the enemy, which led to defeat."
Zhào Yán and his cohort slandered him day and night from the court.
Consequently, Yànzhāng was dismissed,
and Níng was appointed Commander.
Yànzhāng rushed to the capital and went in for an audience.
Using his tablet, he drew lines on the ground,
personally explaining the details of the victory and defeat.
Yán and his cohort secretly instructed the relevant officials to impeach Yànzhāng for disrespect,
forcing him to return to his residence.
The Táng troops attacked Yǎnzhōu.
Mòdì summoned Yànzhāng and ordered him to guard the eastern route.
At this time,
all the victorious troops of Liáng belonged to Duàn Níng.
The capital only had five hundred Imperial Guard cavalry,
all newly conscripted soldiers,
who were unusable.
Therefore, they were assigned to Yànzhāng,
and Zhāng Hànjié was appointed supervisor over them.
Yànzhāng reached Dìfāng.
Due to the small number of troops, he was defeated in battle,
and retreated to defend Zhōngdū.
He was defeated again,
and fought desperately with his personal guard of more than a hundred cavalry.
The Táng general Xià Lǔqí was long acquainted with Yànzhāng
and recognized his voice.
He said,
"It is Wáng Tiěqiāng!"
He lifted his spear and stabbed him.
Yànzhāng was gravely wounded,
his horse stumbled,
and he was captured.
Zhuāngzōng saw him
and said,
"You always treated me as a mere child.
Are you convinced today?"
He also said,
"You are skilled in warfare.
Why did you not defend Yǎnzhōu but instead defended Zhōngdū?
Zhōngdū has no ramparts or fortifications.
How could you secure yourself?"
Yànzhāng replied,
"The great cause is already lost;
it is beyond what human effort can achieve!"
Zhuāngzōng felt compassion,
and bestowed medicine to treat his wounds.
Yànzhāng was a military man who was illiterate,
and often used a rustic saying to address people:
"A leopard dies leaving its skin;
a man dies leaving his name."
His fidelity and righteousness
were truly natural instincts.
Zhuāngzōng admired his bravery and valor
and wished to save his life.
He sent a messenger to comfort and persuade Yànzhāng.
Yànzhāng declined, saying,
"For over ten years, I fought bloody battles against Your Majesty.
Now my troops are defeated and my strength is exhausted.
What awaits me if not death?
Moreover, having received the grace of Liáng,
I cannot repay it without dying.
How could I serve Liáng in the morning and Jìn in the evening?
If I live, what face will I have to meet the people of the world?"
Zhuāngzōng again dispatched Míngzōng to go and persuade him.
Yànzhāng was ill and wounded,
lying down and unable to rise.
He looked up at Míngzōng,
calling his courtesy name, and said,
"Are you not Miàojíliè?
How could I be a man who seeks to cling to life?"
Consequently, he was executed,
at the age of sixty-one.
During the time of Jìn Gāozǔ,
Yànzhāng was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī.
Contemporaneous with Yànzhāng was a man named Péi Yuē,
who was a staff officer in Lùzhōu.
Zhuāngzōng appointed Lǐ Sìzhāo as the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhāoyì Army.
Yuē, as a deputy general, defended Zézhōu.
When Sìzhāo died,
his son Jìtāo rebelled using Zézhōu and Lùzhōu and surrendered to Liáng.
Yuē summoned the people of the prefecture, wept, and instructed them, saying:
"I served the former envoy for over twenty years.
I saw him distribute wealth to feed his soldiers,
desiring to avenge the feud with Liáng,
but unfortunately, he died young.
Now, the young master's father is unburied,
yet he turns against his sovereign and father.
I can die here,
but I cannot follow him to surrender to Liáng!"
All the populace were moved to tears.
Liáng sent Dǒng Zhāng to lead troops and besiege the city.
Yuē resisted the siege with the people of the prefecture
and requested aid from Zhuāngzōng.
At this time,
Zhuāngzōng was fighting the Liáng forces along the river.
He had already established his grand title (as Emperor).
When he heard that Jìtāo had rebelled and defected to Liáng,
he showed considerable worry.
But upon hearing that Yuē alone had not rebelled,
he rejoiced, saying,
"How have I been slighted by Jìtāo?
How have I favored Yuē?
Yet Yuē is able to distinguish between treachery and loyalty!"
He looked at Fú Cúnshěn and said,
"I would not begrudge Zézhōu being taken by Liáng.
One prefecture is easily obtained;
Yuē is difficult to obtain.
You recognize the opportune moment.
Go and retrieve Yuē for me."
Cúnshěn rode with five thousand cavalry quickly to Liáozhōu,
but the Liáng forces had already broken Zézhōu,
and Yuē was killed.
Moving to the time of Zhōu Shìzōng,
there was also a man named Liú Rénshàn.
Rénshàn, courtesy name Shǒuhuì,
was a native of Péngchéng.
His father, Jīn, served Yáng Xíngmì,
and served as Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Háozhōu and Chúzhōu,
and was famous for his valor and bravery.
Rénshàn, as a general,
valued scholars highly and treated wealth lightly.
His laws and commands were strict;
he was generally conversant with military texts.
He served Southern Táng (Nán Táng),
serving as General of the Left Gate Guard (Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèijiāngjūn) and Prefect of Huángzhōu and Yuánzhōu.
Wherever he went, his governance was praised.
Lǐ Jǐng placed him in charge of the Imperial Guard,
and appointed him Military Governor of the Wǔchāng Army.
When the Zhōu army campaigned against the Huái River region,
they first sent Lǐ Gǔ to attack Shòuchūn.
Jǐng sent the general Liú Yànzhēn to resist the Zhōu troops,
and appointed Rénshàn as Military Governor of the Qīnghuái Army,
stationing him at Shòuzhōu.
Lǐ Gǔ retreated to defend the pontoon bridge at Zhèngyáng.
Yànzhēn, seeing the Zhōu troops fall back,
believed they were afraid,
and urgently pursued them.
Rénshàn considered this inadvisable,
but Yànzhēn did not listen.
Rénshàn alone restrained his troops and defended the city.
Yànzhēn was indeed defeated at Zhèngyáng.
Shìzōng attacked Shòuzhōu,
surrounding it with several layers of forces.
Using square boats loaded with catapults (pào),
he attacked the city from the middle of the Féi River.
He also bundled hundreds of thousands of huge bamboo poles,
placed plank shelters on top,
and called them
"Zhúlóng" (Bamboo Dragons).
They carried armored soldiers to attack the city.
Furthermore, they broke the water fortress, causing the water to empty into the Féi River.
Attacking in a hundred ways,
from the first month until the fourth month, they could not take it.
The year grew extremely hot,
and the continuous rains lasted for a full ten days.
The water in the camps of the Zhōu troops was several feet deep.
The Huái and Féi Rivers swelled violently,
and the catapult boats and Zhúlóng were all swept away to the south bank,
and burned by Jǐng's troops.
Many Zhōu soldiers died.
Shìzōng moved east toward Háoliáng,
and appointed Lǐ Chóngjìn as the Commander-in-Chief (Dū Zhāotǎoshǐ) of Lúzhōu and Shòuzhōu.
Jǐng also sent his Grand Marshal, Qí Wáng Jǐngdá, and others to set up camps below Zǐjīn Shān,
creating an enclosed pathway leading into the city.
However, the armies of Chóngjìn and Zhāng Yǒngdé were suspicious of each other and did not cooperate.
Rénshàn repeatedly requested to lead a sally,
but Jǐngdá refused.
Because of this, he became resentful and sorrowful, and fell ill.
In the first month of the following year,
Shìzōng returned to the Huái River region.
He completely destroyed the camps at Zǐjīn Shān,
ruining the enclosed pathway.
Jǐng's troops were greatly defeated,
and many generals were captured.
Meanwhile, Jǐng's defending generals—Féng Yánlǔ of Guǎnglíng, Zhāng Shào of Guāngzhōu, Zhōu Zuò of Shūzhōu, Fāng Nà of Tàizhōu, and Fàn Zàiyù of Sìzhōu—
either fled or surrendered;
none of them could hold their positions.
Even Jǐng, his ruler, and his officials were all terrified,
presented memorials declaring themselves vassals,
and requested to surrender territory and offer tribute and taxes
to demonstrate their sincerity.
But Rénshàn alone held firm in defense,
and could not be taken.
Shìzōng ordered Sūn Shèng and the other envoys sent by Jǐng to approach the city walls and display themselves (to Rénshàn).
Rénshàn’s son, Chóngjiàn, taking advantage of his father's illness,
plotted with the generals to surrender.
Rénshàn immediately ordered him to be executed.
The Army Supervisor, Zhōu Tínggòu, wept at the central gate trying to save him,
but failed.
Thereupon, all the officers and soldiers were moved to tears,
and vowed to defend the city until death.
In the third month,
Liú Rénshàn's illness was severe,
and he no longer recognized people.
His deputy envoy, Sūn Yǔ, falsely wrote a letter in Rénshàn's name,
surrendering the city.
Shìzōng commanded that Rénshàn be carried to the front of the tent,
and he sighed deeply for a long time.
He bestowed upon him a jade belt and an imperial horse,
and then allowed him to return to the city to recuperate from his illness;
he died that day.
An imperial decree said
"Liú Rénshàn exerted his utmost loyalty to the one he served;
his integrity stood firm without blemish.
Among famous ministers of previous generations,
how many can be compared to him!
In My southern campaign,
having such a result is a great achievement."
He then appointed Rénshàn as Grand Commandant Supervising Affairs (Jiǎnxiào Tàuwèi), concurrent with Grand Secretary (Zhōngshū Lìng), and Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Tīnpíng Commandery.
Rénshàn died before he could accept the appointment,
aged fifty-eight.
Shìzōng sent an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices;
the funeral expenses were paid by the state,
and he was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Péngchéng Commandery.
He made his son, Chóngzàn, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Huáizhōu,
and bestowed upon them one manor and one dwelling, respectively.
Lǐ Jǐng, hearing of Rénshàn's death,
also posthumously granted him the title Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
Shòuzhōu's former administrative seat was Shòuchūn.
Shìzōng, because it was difficult to conquer,
subsequently moved the city to Xiàcài,
and restored its military commandery, calling it Zhōngzhèng Commandery,
saying:
"I do this to signal Rénshàn's integrity."
Alas!
The world had long despised Liáng!
However, for a scholar-official who unfortunately lived in that era,
not serving as a minister to it is acceptable;
but he who eats the ruler's salary
must surely die for the ruler's cause.
Someone like Yànzhāng
can be said to have met his proper end!
Rénshàn had already killed his own son to make his intentions clear;
how could anyone, while on the brink of death, change his allegiance?
Now, the Veritable Records (Shílù) of Zhōu Shìzōng record Rénshàn's letter of surrender,
which must have been the work of his deputy envoy, Sūn Yǔ, and others.
During Shìzōng's time,
Wáng Huán, serving Shǔ, defended Qínzhōu;
the siege lasted long without success.
When his strength was exhausted, he surrendered.
Shìzōng praised his loyalty somewhat,
but only went so far as to make him a Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn).
Examining Shìzōng's decrees and considering the difference in his treatment of the two men,
we know that Rénshàn was not the one who surrendered.
Since antiquity, loyal ministers and righteous gentlemen have been hard to find!
During the chaos of the Five Dynasties,
these three men
either emerged from the ranks of soldiers
or were ministers of illegitimate states—
how worthy of praise!
How worthy of praise!
Biographies of Those Who Died for Their Cause (Sǐshì Zhuàn), Chapter Twenty-One
Alas, how extreme!
From Kāipíng up to Xiǎndé,
spanning fifty-three years,
the realm saw five dynasties.
For a scholar-official unfortunate enough to be born during that time,
those who wished to preserve their integrity and serve only one ruler
were certainly rare.
In such a time,
if one demanded that officials either die or necessarily withdraw,
then the realm would have no officials left.
However, the established custom
subsequently regarded clinging to life and not withdrawing as a matter of course.
Even the Confucian scholars,
who studied benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
enjoyed the ruler's salary,
and held office in the ruler's state,
disregarded its survival or ruin.
They all remained composed, considering clinging to life a gain.
Not only did they feel no shame,
but they actually took pride in what they had gained—
how numerous they were!
Therefore, among those ministers who died for their cause,
I have made selections.
The gentleman, in judging others,
delights in bringing their good qualities to fruition, rather than demanding perfection;
how much more so when death is something people find difficult?
In regard to the Five Dynasties,
I found only three scholar-officials who preserved their integrity completely.
Those who initially lacked outstanding integrity
but ultimately died for their ruler's cause,
number fifteen men,
and those who died in battle are not included among them.
Yet, my selection of Wáng Qīng and Shǐ Yànchāo
had its purpose!
It had its purpose!
I composed the Biographies of Those Who Died for Their Cause.
Five men for whom biographies could not be compiled: Mǎ Yànchāo is appended to the biography of Zhū Shǒuyīn;
Sòng Lìngxún, Lǐ Xiá, Zhāng Yànqīng, and Zhèng Zhāoyè are only mentioned in the Imperial Annals (Běnjì).
Zhāng Yuándé
As for Zhāng Yuándé,
his hereditary background is unknown;
some say he was originally a Jìn man.
When young, he served Jìn,
but was not distinguished.
He followed Lǐ Hǎnzhī in rebelling against Jìn with Lùzhōu and surrendering to Liáng.
Hǎnzhī sent Yuándé to meet Liáng Tàizǔ.
During Tàizǔ's time,
Yuándé was promoted from General of the Metropolitan Guard (Jīnwú Wèi Jiāngjūn) to Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Càizhōu.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng of Liáng,
the Military Governor of Wèibó, Yáng Shīhòu, died.
The Last Emperor divided the six prefectures, including Wèi and Xiāng, into two military circuits (zhèn).
Fearing that the Wèi army would not comply,
he sent Liú Xún to command ten thousand troops
and garrison them at Wèi to guard against insurrection.
The Wèi army indeed rebelled,
forcing their Military Governor, Hè Délún, to surrender the two prefectures of Wèi and Bó to Jìn.
At this time,
Yuándé was defending Bèizhōu for Xún.
When the Prince of Jìn entered Wèi,
the various generals wanted to attack Bèizhōu first.
The Prince of Jìn said:
"Bèi City is small but strong;
it will be difficult to conquer quickly.
Moreover, although Yuándé relies on Liú Xún's troops,
it is connected head-to-tail with Cāngzhōu.
Now Dézhōu lies between them and is undefended.
It is better to capture it first;
then the power of Cāng and Bèi will be separated, making them easier to manage."
They then first surprised and defeated Dézhōu,
and afterward used five thousand troops to attack Yuándé.
Yuándé held fast and did not surrender,
so the Jìn army dug trenches and besieged him.
Later, Liú Xún was heavily defeated at the old Yuánchéng,
and fled south to Líyáng.
The Jìn army attacked and defeated Míngzhōu,
and Lái Zhāo, Prefect of Wèizhōu,
and Yán Bǎo, Military Governor of Xíngzhōu, both surrendered their cities to Jìn.
Jìn Zhāo, Prefect of Cízhōu, Zhāng Jūn of Xiāngzhōu, and Dài Sīyuǎn of Cāngzhōu all abandoned their cities and fled.
At this time,
Jìn had already captured all of Yān,
and Zhèn and Dìng were both attached to Jìn.
The land north of the Yellow River (Hé) and east of the mountains,
spanning a thousand *lǐ* in all directions,
comprising six military circuits and dozens of prefectures, all belonged to Jìn.
Only Bèi, one prefecture,
remained besieged for more than a year and could not be taken.
Yuándé's defense was already strong,
but the people of Bèi, hearing that Jìn had taken complete possession of Hébĕi,
and with food in the city almost exhausted,
urged Yuándé to surrender.
Yuándé refused to comply,
and was consequently killed.
After Yuándé had died,
the people of Bèi deliberated, saying:
"Jìn has besieged us for a long time.
If we surrender only after being desperate,
we fear none of us will be spared."
They then reported to Jìn, saying:
"We wish to surrender wearing armor and bearing arms.
After receiving amnesty, we will lay them down.
How about that?"
The Jìn army consented.
Three thousand people of Bèi came out to surrender.
When they had laid down their armor,
the Jìn troops surrounded them on all sides and killed them all.
Xià Lǔqí
Xià Lǔqí, courtesy name Bāngjié,
was a native of Qīngzhōu.
During the time of Táng Zhuāngzōng,
he was granted the name Lǐ Shàoqí.
Later, all those to whom Zhuāngzōng had granted a name
were allowed to revert to their original names.
Lǔqí first served Liáng as an officer (jūnxiào) in Xuānwǔ Commandery.
Afterwards, he defected to Jìn,
becoming Commander of the Imperial Guard (Wèihù Zhǐhuīshǐ).
He followed Zhōu Déwēi in attacking Liú Shǒuguāng at Yōuzhōu.
Shǒuguāng's generals, Shàn Tíngguī and Yuán Xíngqīn, prided themselves on their valor and courage.
Whenever Lǔqí fought with these two generals,
the fighting could not be halted,
and both armies would lay down their arms to watch.
Jìn had already subjugated Wèibó.
The Liáng general Liú Xún was stationed at the Huán Shuǐ (River).
Zhuāngzōng used one hundred cavalrymen to scout the enemy.
He encountered Xún's ambush troops.
They were surrounded several layers deep,
nearly unable to escape.
Lǔ Qí fought with all his might,
personally killing over one hundred men,
suffering more than twenty wounds on his body,
and broke through the siege with Zhuāngzōng and escaped.
Zhuāngzōng admired him even more,
and made him the Cízhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect).
He followed in the battle at Zhōngdū,
capturing Wáng Yànzhāng.
Zhuāngzōng praised his bravery,
awarded him a thousand bolts of silk,
and appointed him as Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner).
He was promoted to Héyáng Jiéduéshǐ (Military Governor).
His governance was beneficial and beloved.
He was transferred to govern Zhōngwǔ.
The people of Héyáng blocked his departure, wishing to keep him.
The elders went to the capital (Jīngshī) to beg for him to remain.
Míngzōng sent a court eunuch (Zhōngshǐ) to mollify them,
and only then was Lǔ Qí able to leave.
When the Táng army campaigned against Jīngnán,
Lǔ Qí was made the Zhāotǎo Fùshǐ (Deputy Pacification Commissioner).
He returned without achieving merit.
He was transferred to govern Wǔxìn.
Dǒng Zhāng of Dōngchuān rebelled
and attacked Suízhōu.
Lǔ Qí locked the city and resisted him.
For a month the relief troops did not arrive.
Food inside the city was exhausted.
Lǔ Qí slit his own throat and died,
aged forty-nine.
Wú Luán’s troops were still able to fight but did not fight;
Lǔ Qí died because his food was exhausted and his strength failed.
Therefore, their choices differed.
Yáo Hóng
Yáo Hóng
was originally a junior officer of Liáng.
Since Dǒng Zhāng was a Liáng general,
Hóng had once served Zhāng.
Later, serving the Táng, he became a Zhīhuīshǐ (Commander).
During the Chángxīng era,
Hóng was dispatched with a thousand men to guard Làngzhōu.
When Dǒng Zhāng rebelled,
he sent a man with a letter to entice Hóng.
Hóng received Zhāng’s letter,
and immediately tossed it into the latrine.
Later, Zhāng’s army attacked and breached Làngzhōu,
and captured Hóng.
Zhāng said:
"You are a brave soldier,
and I treated you generously.
Why have you betrayed me?"
Hóng cursed and said:
"Old rebel!
You were formerly a slave to Lǐ Qīláng,
sweeping horse manure.
When you received a chunk of leftover roast meat,
your gratitude was endless.
Now the Son of Heaven employs you as a Jiéduéshǐ,
why bother rebelling?
I am able to die for the state,
but I cannot live by following another man’s slave!"
Zhāng became angry.
He heated a cauldron in front of him,
and ordered ten strong men to carve off his flesh and eat it.
Hóng cursed loudly until death.
When Míngzōng heard of it, he wept,
promoted his two sons,
and provided generous aid to his family.
Wáng Sītóng
Wáng Sītóng
was a man from Yōuzhōu.
His father, Jìngróu,
married the daughter of Liú Rěngōng,
and begot Sītóng.
Sītóng served Rěngōng as the Yínhú [missing character] Zhīhuīshǐ (Commander).
When Rěngōng was imprisoned by his son Shǒuguāng,
Sītóng fled to Jìn,
and was made the Fēishèng Zhīhuīshǐ (Commander).
When Liáng and Jìn were facing off against each other at Shēn,
Sītóng was sent to build ramparts at Yángliú.
Due to his merit, he was promoted to Shénwǔ Shíjūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ (Supreme Commander of the Ten Armies of Shénwǔ).
He was repeatedly promoted until he became Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
Sītóng was a brave and courageous man.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
fond of learning,
quite enjoyed writing poetry,
valued righteousness over wealth,
and often showed respect to scholars.
However, he had never achieved military success in battle.
During Míngzōng's reign,
based on long service, he was made Kuāngguó Jūn Jiéduéshǐ.
He was transferred to govern Xióngwǔ.
At this time,
the Tǔfān frequently raided,
but Qínzhōu lacked protective fortifications.
Sītóng constructed over forty stockades to defend against them.
In the fifth year (of the reign era),
he came to court.
Míngzōng questioned him about border affairs.
Sītóng pointed out the mountains and rivers,
explaining their advantages and disadvantages.
After Sītóng left,
Míngzōng looked at his attendants and said:
"People say Sītóng is incompetent,
could he be like this?"
Thereupon, he first recognized Sītóng's talent,
and made him Yòu Wǔwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn, Jīngzhào Yǐn, and Xījīng Liúshǒu (Resident Commissioner of the Western Capital).
When Shí Jìngtáng campaigned against Dǒng Zhāng,
Sītóng served as the Xiānfēng Zhīhuīshǐ (Vanguard Commander).
The troops entered Jiànmén,
but the rear army did not follow up.
Sītóng fought Zhāng,
was defeated, and retreated.
When Jìngtáng's army withdrew,
Sītóng was transferred to govern Shānnán Xīdào.
Soon after, he again became Jīngzhào Yǐn and Xījīng Liúshǒu.
In the second month of the first year of Yìngshùn (934),
Prince of Lù, Cóngkē, rebelled at Fèngxiáng.
He quickly issued a manifesto to the four neighboring regions,
stating that wicked officials took advantage of the late emperor’s illness,
murdered the Prince of Qín, and installed a young heir;
that they suppressed and weakened the imperial clan,
and shook the feudal regions.
He explained his reasons for raising troops to quell the chaos.
Consequently, he sent the servant musician Ān Shíshí, bearing a five-stringed lute, to visit Sītóng,
intending to convey his intentions through entertainment.
At this time,
all the regional governors (Zhèn) were internally deliberating allegiance or defection.
Although they reported the letters and manifestos received from the Prince of Lù
upwards (to the court),
they did not stop receiving his envoys.
Only Sītóng seized Shíshí and Hǎo Xǔ, the Investigating Official sent by Cóngkē, and others, and sent them to the capital (Jīngshī).
Mǐndì praised his loyalty,
and immediately appointed Sītóng as Xīmiàn Xíngyíng Mǎbùjūn Dū Bùshǔ (Supreme Commander of the Mounted and Infantry Forces of the Western Campaign Headquarters).
In the third month,
he gathered the troops from various garrisons to besiege Fèngxiáng,
destroying the east and west gate cities.
Cóngkē’s army was weak, but his defense was extremely solid.
Many of the besieging soldiers were wounded or killed.
Cóngkē ascended the city wall, called out to the outside troops, and wept, saying:
"I followed the late emperor for twenty years.
In hundreds of battles, large and small,
my armor was never taken off my body,
and I am covered in scars.
Soldiers, you surely followed me before.
Now the late emperor has just abandoned the world,
yet the court trusts wicked men,
alienating flesh and blood (the imperial family).
What crime have I truly committed that I should be attacked?"
He then wept bitterly.
Those soldiers who heard him
all felt sorrow and pity for him.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo of Xīngyuán attacked the west side of the city.
He urged the battle very fiercely.
The soldiers resented him,
and the rebellious troops attacked Qiánzhāo.
Qiánzhāo fled.
Yáng Sīquán, the Yǔlín Zhīhuīshǐ (Feathered Forest Commander), shouted:
"The Prince of Lù
is our lord!"
He then led his army through the west gate and surrendered to Cóngkē.
Sītóng, however, was unaware of this,
and was still urging the fight.
Yǐn Huī, the Yánwèi Zhīhuīshǐ (Stern Guard Commander), waved his hand to his troops and said:
"The army on the west side of the city has entered and received rewards!
Why bother fighting!"
The soldiers cast off their armor and abandoned their weapons.
The sound could be heard for several *lǐ*,
and they all entered the city and surrendered.
The armies of the various garrisons all disintegrated.
Sītóng managed to escape alone.
When he reached Cháng'ān,
Liú Suìyōng, the Deputy Resident Commissioner of the Western Capital, shut the gates and refused him entry.
He then fled toward Tóngguān.
Cóngkē led his troops eastward.
Upon reaching Zhāoyìng,
his vanguard pursued and captured Sītóng.
Cóngkē rebuked him, saying:
"Can one escape punishment for their crime?"
Sītóng replied:
"It is not that I did not know that following the Prince would allow me to live,
but I feared that dying now, I could not face the late emperor in the afterlife."
Cóngkē was ashamed by his words,
but nevertheless killed him.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted him the title Shìzhōng (Chamberlain).
Sītóng fled eastward,
intending to submit himself to the Son of Heaven.
This differs from the flight of Yuán Xíngqīn,
thus he is granted a biography (for his virtuous death).
Zhāng Jìngdá
, courtesy name Zhìtōng, was a native of Dàizhōu
. His childhood name was Shēngtiě
. When young, relying on his skill in archery and horsemanship, he served Táng Zhuāngzōng
as a Tīngzhí Jūnshǐ. During Míngzōng's
reign, he became the Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry of Hédōng
, holding the title of Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Qīnzhōu
. He was successively promoted to Jìedùshǐ
of Zhāngguó and Dàtóng armies, and was transferred to govern Wǔxìn
and Jìnchāng. In the second year of Qīngtài
(935 CE), the Qìdān repeatedly violated the border
. Fèidì

(the Deposed Emperor) therefore made Shí Jìngtáng, the Jìedùshǐ of Hédōng, concurrently the Supreme Commander (Dū Zǒngguǎn) of the Barbarian and Han Cavalry and Infantry of the Dàtóng, Zhāngguó, Zhènwǔ, and Wēisài armies
. The troops stationed there gathered noisily, blocking Shí Jìngtáng
and shouting, "Ten thousand years (Wànsùi)!"
. Shí Jìngtáng
executed over thirty men to stop this. Fèidì
suspected that Shí Jìngtáng harbored rebellious intentions. He thus appointed Zhāng Jìngdá
as the Deputy Supreme Commander of the Northern Front, in order to divide Shí Jìngtáng's
forces. In the summer of the following year
, Shí Jìngtáng
was transferred to govern Tiānpíng. Subsequently, Zhāng Jìngdá
was made the Commissioner-in-Chief (Dū Bùshǔ) of the Barbarian and Han Cavalry and Infantry of the Dàtóng, Zhāngguó, Zhènwǔ, and Wēisài armies. Shí Jìngtáng
consequently rebelled because of this. Zhāng Jìngdá
was immediately appointed the Pacification Commissioner (Zhāotǎo Shǐ) for the Four Fronts of Tàiyuán. In the sixth month
, the army besieged Tàiyuán
. Zhāng Jìngdá
constructed a continuous wall and fence, using siege ladders (yúntī) and catapults (fēipào) to attack it
. But whenever the wall and fence he was building were about to be completed
, a great wind, rain, and flood would suddenly arrive and destroy them
. Shí Jìngtáng
requested aid from the Qìdān. In the ninth month
, Yēlǜ Déguāng
of the Qìdān entered from Yànmén, with flags and banners stretching over fifty *lǐ*
. Yēlǜ Déguāng
first sent a man to inform Shí Jìngtáng, saying: "I wish to defeat the enemy today; is this permissible?"
. Shí Jìngtáng
replied: "Your great army has come a long distance
, and the enemy's strength is currently flourishing
. The essential thing is to succeed
, speed is not necessary."
. Before the messenger had returned
to report, the armies had already engaged
. Zhāng Jìngdá
arrayed his troops at Xīshān. The Qìdān used three thousand light cavalry
, carrying leather whips and wooden clubs (bàng)
, neither the men nor the horses wore armor
, and rushed towards the Táng army
. The Táng army eagerly rushed out to meet them
. The Qìdān troops fled
. When the Táng troops chased them to Fénqǔ
, the ambush was sprung
. The Táng army was cut into two sections
. Those in the northern section all perished
. Over ten thousand men died
. Zhāng Jìngdá
gathered his troops and fortified Jìn'ān. The Qìdān besieged it
. Fèidì
dispatched Zhào Yánshòu, Fàn Yánguāng, and others to relieve the siege. Zhào Yánshòu
was stationed at Tuánbǎigǔ. Fàn Yánguāng
was stationed at Liáozhōu. Both were over a hundred *lǐ*
away from Jìn'ān. The Qìdān forces besieging Zhāng Jìngdá
, stretched south from Jìn'ān Zhai
, covering a length of over a hundred *lǐ*
, and a width of fifty *lǐ*
. When observed from Zhāng Jìngdá's
camp, they only saw yurts (qiónglú) continuously linked like hills and mounds
. They were surrounded on all four sides by hair ropes
, with bells attached for warnings
. Dogs were let loose to patrol
. If anyone from Zhāng Jìngdá's
army ventured out at night, they were immediately captured by the Qìdān
. Because of this, they remained behind their defenses and dared not go out again
. Zhào Yánshòu
and the others all had double intentions, and had no intention of rescuing Zhāng Jìngdá
. Zhāng Jìngdá
still had fifty thousand soldiers and ten thousand horses. After a long time, the provisions ran out
. They shaved wood and sifted dung to feed their horses
. When the horses died, they ate them
. Soon afterwards, all the horses were gone
. The Deputy Pacification Commissioner Yáng Guāngyuǎn
advised Zhāng Jìngdá to surrender to Jìn. Zhāng Jìngdá
felt that he could not bear to betray Táng, and that relief forces were about to arrive
. Yáng Guāngyuǎn
relentlessly urged him, so Zhāng Jìngdá
said: "Gentlemen, why do you pressure me so
? Why do you not kill me and then surrender?"
. Yáng Guāngyuǎn
immediately beheaded Zhāng Jìngdá and surrendered. Yēlǜ Déguāng
of the Qìdān heard that Zhāng Jìngdá was dead, mourned his loyalty
, and sent someone to collect his remains and bury him
. The Main Annals (Běnjì) criticized him for not executing Yáng Guāngyuǎn
, but rather encouraging Yáng Guāngyuǎn to kill him and surrender to the rebels. Therefore, the Annals did not record his death, but recorded that it was according to his will (zhì)
. However, the Biographies (Zhuàn) recorded his death
, ultimately commending him for not surrendering
. However, although he himself did not yield
, he encouraged others to surrender to the rebels
, and thus he cannot be considered to have died for his loyalty (Sǐ Jié)
. Zhái Jìnzōng
(with Zhāng Wàndí appended)
. Regarding Zhái Jìnzōng and Zhāng Wàndí, it is not known who they were
. Initially, they both served Táng
; later they served Jìn
. Zhái Jìnzōng
was the Prefect of Zīzhōu; Zhāng Wàndí
was the Prefect of Dēngzhōu. When Yáng Guāngyuǎn
rebelled, he used a hundred cavalrymen to coerce and seize the two prefects and brought them to Qīngzhōu
. Zhāng Wàndí
obeyed the order, but Zhái Jìnzōng
alone refused to yield. Yáng Guāngyuǎn
subsequently killed Zhái Jìnzōng. Chūdì
posthumously awarded Zhái Jìnzōng the title of Commander-in-Chief of the Left Martial Guard (Zuǒ Wǔwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn). When Yáng Guāngyuǎn's
rebellion was suppressed, a selective amnesty was granted to Qīngzhōu
. Although all of Yáng Guāngyuǎn's
sons and grandsons were pardoned and consoled, Zhāng Wàndí
alone was not pardoned. His crime was publicly announced and he was executed
. An imperial edict ordered the search for Zhái Jìnzōng's
body, to be returned and buried with heightened ceremony
. The funeral expenses were paid by the government
. His son, Rénqīn
, was made a Servant Official of the Eastern Section (Dōngtóu Gòngfèngguān). Shěn Bīn
. Shěn Bīn
, courtesy name Ānshí, was a native of Xiàpī
in Xúzhōu. When young, he served as a soldier
. Serving Liáng
, he became the Commander-in-Chief of Gǒngchén (Gǒngchén Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ). Later, he served Táng
. He followed the Prince of Wèi, Jìjí
, in conquering Shǔ, and suppressing Kāng Yánxiào
. For his accomplishments, he was made the Prefect of Guózhōu
, and subsequently served as Prefect of eight other prefectures, including Suí
and Zhào. In the first year of Kāiyùn
of Jìn (944 CE), he was the Prefect of Qízhōu
. The Qìdān violated the frontier and reached Yúlín
. As they passed Qízhōu
, Shěn Bīn
judged that the Qìdān had penetrated deep into Jìn territory and that their returning forces were exhausted and vulnerable to attack. He immediately used the prefectural troops to intercept them
. The Qìdān used elite cavalry to crush the gate
. Many of Shěn Bīn's
soldiers died. The city lacked defenses
. The barbarian general Zhào Yánshòu
left troops behind to launch a fierce attack. Zhào Yánshòu
summoned Shěn Bīn to surrender. From atop the city wall, Shěn Bīn
cursed Zhào Yánshòu, saying: "You and your father
made a flawed plan, trapped by the stink of mutton (xīngshān)
! How can you bear to use a pack of dogs and sheep (meaning the Qìdān)
to ravage the land of your fathers
? I, Bīn
, can only die for my country; I cannot imitate what you have done!"
. Soon afterwards, the city fell
. Shěn Bīn
killed himself. His family members were all captured by the barbarians
. Wáng Qīng
. Wáng Qīng
, courtesy name Qùxiá, was a native of Qǔzhōu
in Míngzhōu. Initially, he served Táng
as the Commander of Níngwèi (Níngwèi Zhǐhuīshǐ). Later, he served Jìn
as the Commander of the Imperial Guard of the Dedicated State (Fèngguó Dū Yúhòu). Ān Cóngjìn
rebelled at Xiāngzhōu. He followed Gāo Xíngzhōu
to attack him. After more than a year, they could not take the city
. Wáng Qīng
said to Gāo Xíngzhōu: "Ān Cóngjìn
relies on closing himself in an isolated city for self-defense. How can this situation last long?"
. He then requested permission to be the first to ascend the walls
. Consequently, they attacked and breached the city
. In the winter of the second year of Kāiyùn
(945 CE), he followed Dù Chóngwēi
to fight at Yángchéng. Wáng Qīng
, due to his achievements in fierce fighting, was considered the foremost among the infantry. He was promoted to Probationary Minister of Works (Jiǎnxiào Sītú)
. That winter
, Dù Chóngwēi's
army crossed the bridge to the south, while the barbarian army was positioned to the north to resist
. The barbarians used elite cavalry along Xīshān
to emerge behind the Jìn army, attacking Luánchéng
to the south, thereby cutting the Jìn supply route
. Wáng Qīng
said to Dù Chóngwēi: "The Jìn army is in danger
! We are now five *lǐ*
from Zhènzhōu, yet we are doomed to hold fast here
. Our camp is isolated and our food is running out
. What are we going to do
? I request to lead two thousand infantry as the vanguard
, seize the bridge and open the road
. If Your Excellency leads the other armies to follow and enter Zhènzhōu
, we will be able to defend ourselves."
. Dù Chóngwēi
consented, and sent him forward together with Sòng Yánjūn
. Wáng Qīng
fought the barbarians, defeated them
, and seized their bridge
. At this time
, Dù Chóngwēi
already harbored double intentions (of betrayal), hesitated, and refused to advance
. Sòng Yánjūn
also retreated and fled. Wáng Qīng
said: "I shall die here alone!"
. He then fought fiercely until his death
. He was fifty-three years old
. When Hàn Gāozǔ
ascended the throne, he posthumously granted Wáng Qīng
the title of Grand Tutor (Tàifù). Shǐ Yànchāo
Alas!
The chaos of the Wǔdài (Five Dynasties) reached its extreme,
was it not the time
of which the tradition speaks,
when “Heaven and Earth were closed,
and the worthy men concealed themselves”?
In this era,
ministers murdered their sovereigns,
and sons murdered their fathers,
yet the educated elite (jìnshēn zhī shì) secured their emoluments and stood in the court,
fully displaying a complete lack of shame or integrity—and this was universally true.
I had thought that throughout history, loyal ministers and righteous scholars often emerged in times of chaos,
and I am puzzled why there were so few mentionable figures at that time.
Could it truly be that there were none of them?
Although it is said that conflicts arose,
schools were abandoned,
and thus ritual and righteousness declined,
leading to the complete decay of customs,
reaching such a state,
yet since ancient times, the world has never been without people.
I believe there must have been scholars of integrity and self-regard
who loathed the world, went far away, and could not be seen.
Since ancient times, men of talent and virtue have had their qualities hidden within and not revealed externally;
some lived in poverty in mean alleys,
or consigned themselves to the wilderness.
Even the conduct of Yán Zǐ,
had he not met Zhòngní (Kǒngzǐ), his name would not have been known,
how much more so during a time when world changes were frequent
and the Way of the gentleman (jūnzǐ) was waning!
I further believe that there must have been those who possessed talent and ability,
cultivated integrity and righteousness,
yet were submerged among the lower classes,
perishing in obscurity without being heard of.
Seeking them in records and biographies,
due to the fragmentation and disunion of the chaotic age,
the texts are damaged and incomplete,
and they cannot be fully recovered.
However, I have managed to find only four or five people.
Those who lived in the mountains and forests amongst the elk and deer,
though not necessarily conforming to the Middle Way (zhōngdào),
yet compared to those who subsist on others’ stipends,
bow their heads, and endure shame,
which is better than having no shame in their hearts,
letting their bodies roam freely, and finding contentment?
I have found two such men:
named Zhèng Áo and Zhāng Jiànmíng.
Those whose minds were unbent by power or profit,
and whose decisions to leave or stay did not violate their sense of righteousness—
I have found one such man:
named Shí Áng.
Those who, if it benefited their sovereign,
incurred blame due to their loyalty,
and yet felt no need to justify themselves,
remaining silent until death—
these are the righteous scholars of antiquity—
I have found one such man:
named Chéng Fúyūn.
During the chaos of the Wǔdài,
the sovereign was not a sovereign,
the minister was not a minister,
the father was not a father,
the son was not a son;
even among brothers, husbands, and wives, the bounds of human relations (rénlún zhī jì)
were completely ruined,
and the Heavenly Principle (Tiānlǐ) was almost extinguished.
At such a time,
those who could cultivate themselves through filial piety and fraternal duty within one community,
and whose influence spread throughout the world,
perhaps still existed;
however, their deeds are not well documented,
and there is nothing that can be recorded sequentially.
Nevertheless, those whose names are occasionally seen in books,
I dare not let them be forgotten.
Among those whose brief accounts can be recorded,
I have found one man:
named Lǐ Zìlún.
I compose the account (zhuàn) of the first category (yī xíng).
Zhèng Áo (with Zhāng Jiànmíng appended)
Zhèng Áo, courtesy name Yúnsǒu,
was a native of Bǎimǎ in Huázhōu.
Because Táng Míngzōng’s ancestral temple name tabooed Áo,
the world circulated his courtesy name.
Áo was fond of learning in his youth
and quick with literary composition.
During the reign of Táng Zhāozōng,
he failed the civil service examination (jìnshì).
Seeing that the world was already in chaos,
he intended to shake off his robes and leave far away,
wishing to take his wife and children to live in seclusion with him.
His wife did not consent,
so Áo entered Shàoshì Shān to become a Daoist priest.
His wife frequently wrote letters urging Áo to return home;
he invariably threw them into the fire.
Later, when he heard that his wife and children had died,
he wept once and stopped.
Áo was previously good friends with Lǐ Zhèn.
Zhèn later served the Liáng dynasty and became prominent;
he wished to offer Áo an official salary.
Áo paid no attention to it.
Later, when Zhèn incurred guilt and was banished south,
Áo traveled a thousand lǐ on foot to visit him.
Because of this, those who heard of it held his conduct in even higher esteem.
Thereafter,
Áo heard that there was a five-needle pine (wǔ lì sōng) on Huàshān
whose resin melted into the ground,
transforming into medicine after a thousand years,
which could remove the three corpses (sān shī).
He therefore moved his residence to Huàyīn,
seeking it.
He was good friends with the Daoist priests Lǐ Dàoyīn and Luó Yǐnzhī;
the world dubbed them the Three High Scholars (sān gāoshì).
Áo farmed the land,
Yǐnzhī sold medicine to support himself,
and Dàoyīn possessed the art of fishing,
using a hook without bait.
He was also able to transmute stone into gold.
Áo once verified that this was true,
but did not seek it from him.
The military commissioner (jiédù shǐ) Liú Suínìng repeatedly sent him treasures and goods,
but Áo refused to accept any.
During the reign of Táng Míngzōng, he was summoned as Left Reminder (Zuǒ Shíyí); during the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ, he was summoned as Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū);
he did not rise to the summons in either case.
He was granted the title Master Xiāoyáo.
He died in the fourth year of Tiānfú
at the age of seventy-four.
Áo’s integrity was lofty.
He endured chaotic times without being bound by glory or profit;
he even abandoned his wife and children and left without looking back.
Was he not a man who severed himself from the world and deeply cherished his own person?
However, Áo was fond of drinking wine and playing board games (yì),
and occasionally left poems and writings among the populace.
People often copied these onto fine silk or plain cloth,
gifting them to each other as treasures,
even going so far as to draw pictures of him,
displaying them on the walls of their houses.
