Although his tracks were distant, his reputation became increasingly manifest,
differing from the likes of Shímén and Hézhù (the recluses mentioned in the Analects).
A contemporary of Áo was Zhāng Jiànmíng,
a native of Yān.
In his youth, he traveled in Héshuò through Confucian studies.
Later, he left to become a Daoist priest,
and was versed in the doctrines of Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzhōu.
Gāozǔ summoned him for an audience
and asked, "Can the Daoist school be used to govern the state?"
He replied:
“Dào (the Way)
is expressed by transcending the myriad things;
one who attains its ultimate limit
can govern Heaven and Earth while sitting calmly on his mat.”
Gāozǔ greatly admired his words
and invited him into the inner hall to lecture on the Dàodé Jīng,
and bowed to him as his teacher.
Jiànmíng heard the drums played in the palace at the proper hour,
and said:
“Does Your Majesty hear the drum?
Its sound is singular (yī), and nothing more.
Among the five notes (wǔ yīn) and twelve pitches (shí'èr lǜ),
the drum is none of them,
yet it is the drum that harmonizes them.
Now, the singular (yī)
is the foundation of all things;
one who can maintain singularity can govern the world.”
Gāozǔ praised him
and bestowed upon him the title Master Tōngxuán.
Later, the place of his end is unknown.
Shí Áng
Shí Áng
was a native of Línzī in Qīngzhōu.
His family owned several thousand scrolls of books.
He enjoyed inviting scholars from all directions;
regardless of how near or far the scholars were,
many came to Áng to study and seek knowledge.
Those who stayed and ate under his roof sometimes remained for years,
and Áng never showed any weariness.
Yet Áng did not seek official advancement.
The military commissioner Fú Xí esteemed his conduct
and summoned him to be the magistrate of Línzī (Línzī Lìng).
When Xí went to the capital for court audience,
the Surveillance Commissioner (jiānjūn) Yáng Yànlǎng managed the affairs of the Acting Commissioner (liúhòu).
Áng came to the government office to pay his respects on official business.
The attendant, knowing that Yànlǎng tabooed the character
"Shí" (stone),
changed his surname to
"Yòu" (right).
Áng hurried into the courtyard
and looked up to reprimand Yànlǎng, saying:
“Eunuch (Nèishì)! How dare you let private matters harm public affairs!
My surname is 'Shí',
not 'Yòu'.”
Yànlǎng was greatly angered,
flicked his robe, and rose to leave.
Áng immediately hurried out.
He resigned his office and returned home,
telling his son:
“I originally did not wish to serve in a chaotic age,
and indeed I was disgraced by a criminal official.
My sons and grandsons must take me as a warning!”
Shǐ Yànchāo,
was a man from Yúnzhōu.
He was brave, fierce, and swift.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ rose in Wèi,
Yànchāo was the Commander of the Hàn Lóngjié Army,
and followed with his troops.
When Tàizǔ entered the capital and ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Commander of the Hǔjié Army,
and garrisoned in Jìnzhōu.
Liú Mín attacked Jìnzhōu,
which had no main commander.
The Prefect, Wáng Wàngǎn, was unable to resist.
Yànchāo, with his garrison troops, held out for over a month.
Tàizǔ dispatched Wáng Jùn to relieve it,
and Mín's forces withdrew.
For his功 (gōng), he was promoted to Commander of the Right Flank of the Lóngjié Army,
and also served as Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu.
When Zhōu and Hàn battled at Gāopíng,
Yànchāo served as vanguard,
being the first to climb the ramparts and break the enemy formation.
For this功 (gōng), he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of the Gǎndé Army.
When Zhōu forces besieged Hàn Tàiyuán,
the Qìdān came to Hàn's aid,
emerging from Xīn and Dài.
Shìzōng dispatched Fú Yànqīng to resist them,
making Yànchāo the vanguard.
They fought at Xīnkǒu.
Yànchāo's courage and fury both erupted,
he rode and attacked left and right,
breaking apart and re-engaging several times,
and eventually died in battle.
At this time,
Shìzōng had defeated Hàn at Gāopíng,
and pressed on with his victory.
During the siege of the city,
the generals' opinions were not unified,
and thus no success was achieved for a long time.
Shìzōng wished to withdraw but had not yet decided.
Upon hearing that Yànchāo had died in battle,
he immediately ordered the army to return.
In the haste of the moment,
many lives were lost.
Shìzōng both regretted Yànchāo's death and was frustrated by the lack of success.
He worried and was so vexed that he did not eat for several days.
He posthumously bestowed the title of Tàishī upon Yànchāo,
and generously compensated his family.
Sūn Shèng
Sūn Shèng's original name was Fèng,
and also Jì.
He was a man from Mìzhōu.
He loved learning,
and was skilled in literature,
especially poetry.
When young, he became a Daoist priest,
residing in the Jiǎnjì Palace on Mount Lú.
He often painted the image of the Táng poet Jiǎ Dǎo and placed it on the wall of his room,
revering it morning and evening.
The Daoist priests of Jiǎnjì Palace disliked Shèng,
considering him a sorcerer,
and drove him out with a stick.
Thereupon, he dressed as a scholar and went north to Zhào and Wèi,
where he met Táng Zhuāngzōng in Zhènzhōu.
Zhuāngzōng appointed Shèng as Zuòzuò Zuǒláng.
During the Tiānchéng era,
Zhū Shǒuyīn was garrisoned in Biànzhōu,
and invited Shèng to be his Pànguān.
Shǒuyīn rebelled,
and was executed.
Shèng then abandoned his wife and children,
and fled between Chén and Sòng.
Ān Chónghuǐ disliked Shèng,
believing that Shèng was the one who instigated Shǒuyīn's rebellion.
He had Shèng's portrait painted and offered a reward for his capture,
but could not get him.
Consequently, he exterminated Shèng's family.
Shèng fled to Wú.
At this time,
Lǐ Jǐng was usurping the Yáng family,
and heavily recruited scholars from all directions.
He obtained Shèng,
was pleased with his literary talent,
and had him draft official decrees.
From this, Shèng became well-known.
Shèng was a stutterer,
and could not exchange greetings with people when he met them.
However, once he was seated,
his debates became sharp and eloquent,
and listeners forgot their weariness.
Jǐng especially loved him,
and brought him in for discussions.
Many of his suggestions were to Jǐng's liking,
so he appointed him Yòu Púyè,
and he and Féng Yánjǐ both served as Jǐng's prime ministers.
Shèng regarded Yánjǐ lightly as a person,
often saying:
"Is it acceptable to use a golden bowl and jade cup to hold dog feces?"
Shèng served Jǐng and his son for over twenty years,
reaching the official position of Sīkōng.
His family became increasingly wealthy and arrogant.
Whenever he ate, no tables were set.
He would have many singing girls each hold a dish,
standing in a circle to serve him.
This was called
"meat platters."
People at the time often imitated this.
When Zhōu Shìzōng attacked Huái,
Lǐ Jǐng was fearful.
He first sent Wáng Zhīlǎng, a commander from Sìzhōu, to Xúzhōu,
bearing a letter to seek peace,
but Shìzōng did not reply.
He then sent Hánlín Xuéshì Zhōng Mó and Wénlǐyuàn Xuéshì Lǐ Démíng with a memorial acknowledging himself as a subject,
but still received no reply.
Thereupon, he dispatched Lǐbù Shàngshū Wáng Chóngzhì as Shèng's deputy to present a memorial.
Mó and Shèng and others all stated that Jǐng was willing to cede the six prefectures of Shòu, Háo, Sì, Chǔ, Guāng, and Hǎi,
and pay an annual tribute of a million to aid the army.
However, Shìzōng had already seized Chú, Yáng, Háo, and Sì prefectures,
and wished to take all of Huáinán before stopping.
He therefore detained the envoys and did not send them back,
and attacked Shòuzhōu even more urgently.
Mó and the others saw that Shìzōng was heroic and martial, no match for Jǐng,
and that his army was very strong,
and that Shòuchūn was in danger.
So they said:
"We beg Your Majesty to grant us a five-day reprieve from execution,
and allow us to return to retrieve Jǐng's memorial,
offering all the prefectures north of the Huái River."
Shìzōng agreed,
and sent Gòngfèngguān Ān Hóngdào to escort Démíng and Chóngzhì back south,
while Mó and Shèng were both detained.
After Démíng and the others returned,
Jǐng regretted it,
and refused to cede the territory.
Shìzōng also returned to the capital due to the summer rains,
leaving Lǐ Chóngjìn and Zhāng Yǒngdé to separately attack Lú and Shòu.
All the prefectures of Yáng and Tài that Zhōu forces had gained
could not be held,
and Jǐng's forces revived.
Chóngjìn and Yǒngdé's two armies suspected each other,
and there was a rift.
Yǒngdé submitted a letter stating that Chóngjìn was rebelling,
but Shìzōng did not listen.
Jǐng, knowing the two generals' mutual suspicion,
sent a letter in a wax pellet to Chóngjìn,
urging him to rebel.
Initially,
when Shèng was dispatched as an envoy,
he told Chóngzhì:
"I will surely not escape this mission,
but I will never betray the one mound of earth at Yǒnglíng."
Yǒnglíng
was Jǐng's father's tomb.
When Chóngzhì returned,
Shèng and Zhōng Mó both arrived at the capital,
and were lodged at the Dūtíng Inn.
They were treated very generously;
whenever there was a court assembly, they would enter the cabinet,
and were made to stand after the officials of the Eastern Province.
When summoned for an audience, they were always served fine wine.
Later, Zhōu forces suffered several defeats,
losing all the prefectures they had gained.
Shìzōng was worried.
He summoned Shèng and asked about matters in Jiāngnán.
Shèng did not respond.
Shìzōng was angry,
but had no reason to express it.
Coincidentally, Chóngjìn came to present Jǐng's wax-pellet letter,
which contained many criticisms and accusations of Zhōu's faults.
From this, Shìzōng became enraged and said:
"Shèng came as my envoy,
saying that Jǐng feared my divine might,
and wished to face north as a subject,
guaranteeing no disloyalty.
How then can these accusatory words exist?"
He immediately summoned Hán Tōng, a Yúhòu of the Shìwèi Army, to arrest Shèng and imprison him.
His over two hundred followers were all killed.
As Shèng faced death,
Shìzōng still sent a close minister to question him,
but Shèng still did not respond.
His expression was calm and composed.
He straightened his clothes and cap, faced south, bowed, and said:
"This subject only wishes to repay the nation with his death!"
Then he went to his execution.
After Shèng's death,
Zhōng Mó was also demoted to Sīmǎ of Yàozhōu.
Later,
Shìzōng's anger subsided.
He pitied Shèng's loyalty
and regretted killing him.
He summoned and appointed Zhōng Mó as Wèiwèi Shàogīng.
Jǐng had already ceded the territory north of the Jiāng River,
so he sent Mó back.
When Jǐng heard of Shèng's death,
he also posthumously bestowed upon him the title of Lǔguó Gōng.
Collation Notes
Biography Volume 22
Āng's father (Fù) also loved learning;
throughout his life, he disliked Buddhist teachings (Fóshuō).
When the father died,
Āng recited the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents) before the coffin.
He said:
"This is what my late predecessor wished to hear."
He forbade his family from using Buddhist rites to mourn his predecessor.
During the time of Jìn Gāozǔ,
an imperial edict was issued throughout the realm seeking gentlemen of filiality and fraternity (xiàotì).

Wáng Quán, Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū); Shí Guāngzàn, Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Qīng); Tián Mǐn, Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ); Wáng Yán, Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng); and others collectively proceeded to the Eastern Upper Gate (Dōng Shàng Gémén).
They reported that Āng’s conduct and righteousness qualified him to answer the imperial edict.
Āng was summoned by edict to the capital (Jīngshī).
He was received in the private palace hall (Biàndiàn),
and appointed Assistant Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Chéng).
He was promoted to Vice Minister (Shǎoqīng).
When Chū Dì ascended the throne,
the Jìn administration deteriorated daily.
Āng repeatedly submitted memorials offering severe remonstrance.
(The emperor) did not listen.
Thereupon, he claimed illness and returned east,
ending his days at home in old age.
After Āng had departed,
the Jìn house fell into great turmoil.
Chéng Fúyūn
Chéng Fúyūn—
his hereditary background is unknown.
As a person, he was reserved and taciturn, yet courageous.
In his youth, he served as a soldier.
Due to military achievements, he was successively promoted to Commissioner of Militias (Tuánliàn Shǐ) of Míngzhōu.
During the reign of Jìn Chū Dì,
he was the Commander-in-Chief of the Right Flank of the Fèngguó Army (Fèngguó Yòuxiāng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ).
During the Kāiyùn era,
the Qìdān invaded.
Chū Dì campaigned north.
Soldiers of the Fèngguó Army seized the opportunity and set fire to the camp at night,
intending to use this as a pretext for rebellion.
Fúyūn personally fought the fire and was wounded.
The fire was extinguished, and the rebels could not proceed.
Fúyūn believed that the Qìdān would soon arrive in force,
and the Son of Heaven was currently with the army.
The capital (Jīngshī) was undefended and empty.
It was inappropriate to use a minor incident to disturb public confidence.
Therefore, he concealed the incident and did not report it.
The army general Lǐ Yīn, whose rank was subordinate to Fúyūn,
hoped for Fúyūn’s removal so he could replace him.
He therefore falsely accused Fúyūn of conspiring with the rebels,
arguing, "Otherwise, why did he not report it?"
Chū Dì imprisoned Fúyūn.
Everyone considered this an injustice.
Fúyūn ultimately refused to defend himself and was executed.
Lǐ Zìlún
Lǐ Zìlún
was a man from Shēnzhōu.
In the first month of Tiānfú 4,
the Ministry of Revenue (Shàngshū Hùbù) memorialized:
"Lǐ Zìlún, Staff Supervisor of Meritorious Service (Sīgōng Cānjūn) of Shēnzhōu, has lived with six generations of his family.
We have received an imperial order to follow the regulations."
According to the regulations,
for commendation of filiality and righteousness (xiàoyì jīngbiǎo),
an investigation and verification must first be conducted.
Those who are filial shall be exempted from service for life,
and the righteous family (Yìmén) shall still be honored with a commendation plaque.
We have received verification from the local prefecture (Běnzhōu) based on statements from village elders Chéng Yán and others, claiming that
Zìlún’s great-great-grandfather was Xùn.
Xùn fathered Càn,
Càn fathered Zé,
Zé fathered Zhōng,
Zhōng fathered Zìlún,
and Zìlún fathered Guānghòu.
The claim of six generations living together is true."
An edict designated the district (Xiāng) where they resided, Fēifú, as Xiàoyì Xiāng (Filiality and Righteousness District);
and Kuāngshèng Neighborhood (Lǐ) as Rénhé Lǐ (Benevolence and Harmony Neighborhood).
They were to be given a commendation plaque for their household gate according to the standards.
On the day Bǐngzǐ in the ninth month,
the Ministry of Revenue again memorialized:
"Previously, the Righteous Family (Yìmén) Wáng Zhòngzhāo of Dēngzhōu, who lived together for six generations,
had, for their commendation, a reception hall (tīngshì) and a walkway railing (bùlán),
a screen placed in front,
and a dark-capped main gate (wūtóu zhèngmén) erected.
The gate markers (fáyùe) were twelve *chǐ* high.
The tops of the two dark-capped pillars were covered with curved tiles (wǎtǒng).
A pair of ceremonial towers (què) were constructed, ten *zhàng* high,
located thirty-seven *chǐ* south of the dark-capped gate.
Locust and willow trees were planted on either side,
spaced fifteen *bù* apart.
We request to follow this precedent."
The edict stated:
"This is an old custom,
which is not included in the current regulations.
However, considering the appropriateness of the location,
raise the height of the outer gate.
Install large corner posts (chuòxiē) at the gate.
Build platforms (tái) on the left and right,
twelve *chǐ* high.
Their width, depth, and square shape shall be fitting.
Plaster them white and paint the four corners red.
So that those who are unfilial and unrighteous, upon seeing it,
may change their hearts and reform their conduct."
Biography of the Six Ministers of Táng, Chapter 23
How severe
was the Calamity of Bǎimǎ!
Alas,
it is enough to make one shed tears!
However, the life or death of a scholar
could hardly be a matter concerning only his own person!
Initially,
in the third year of Tiānyòu of Táng (906 CE),
the Prince of Liáng (Liáng Wáng) wished to appoint his favored retainer Zhāng Tíngfàn as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
The Táng Chancellor Péi Shū opined that the Tàicháng Qīng was traditionally held by members of the 'pure stream' (qīngliú) officials.
Tíngfàn was merely a retainer general (kèjiàng) of Liáng,
and was unsuitable.
The Prince of Liáng was greatly enraged by this,
saying:
"I always said that Péi Shū was sincere and upright, not prone to frivolity.
Is he now doing this too?"
In the fourth month of that year,
a comet appeared in the northwest,
sweeping across Wénchāng, Xuānyuán, and Tiānshì asterisms.
Chancellor Liǔ Càn sought to please the Prince of Liáng,
attributing the condemnation (the comet’s appearance) to the high ministers.

Consequently, Péi Shū, Left Minister (Zuǒ Púyè); Dúgū Sǔn, Right Minister (Yòu Púyè); Cuī Yuǎn; Zhào Chóng, retired Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo); Wáng Zàn, Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng); Wáng Pǔ, Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū); and Lù Yǐ, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū)—all were banished without cause.
On the same day, they were ordered to commit suicide at Bǎimǎ Station (Bǎimǎ Yì).
All officials (jìnshēn zhī shì) who sided with Táng and not with Liáng
were falsely accused of forming cliques (péngdǎng).
Several hundred people were implicated, banished, and died,
causing the imperial court to become empty.
In the third month of the following year,
Táng Āi Dì abdicated in favor of Liáng.

He dispatched Zhāng Wénwèi, Vice Minister of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Co-administrator of Affairs (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì), as the Envoy for the Investiture Ceremony (Cè Lǐ Shǐ).
Sū Xún, Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), served as the deputy.
Yáng Shè, Vice Minister of the Chancellery and Co-administrator of Affairs, was the Envoy in Charge of the Transmission of the Imperial Seal (Yā Chuánguó Bǎo Shǐ).
Zhāng Cè, Hanlin Academician and Chancellery Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén), served as the deputy.
Xuē Yíjǔ, Grand Censor (Yùshǐ Dàfū), was the Envoy in Charge of the Transmission of the Gold Seal (Yā Jīnbǎo Shǐ).
Zhào Guāngféng, Left Assistant Minister (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng), served as the deputy.
On the day Jiǎzǐ in the fourth month,
Wénwèi and the others, setting out from Shàngyuán Station, presented the Imperial Patent and Seals (Cè Bǎo).
They rode in a state carriage (lùchē),
escorted by the imperial guards (Jīnwú Zhàngwèi) and the ceremonial retinue of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Lǔbù).
They paid court to Liáng at Jīnxiáng Hall.
The Prince, wearing the ceremonial robe and crown (gǔnmiǎn), faced south.
Your Servitor Wénwèi and Your Servitor Xún presented the Imperial Patent and ascended the hall.
After they had read it,
Your Servitor Shè and Your Servitor Cè presented the Imperial Seal of the State (Chuánguó Xǐ).
Your Servitor Yíjǔ and Your Servitor Guāngféng presented the Gold Seal.
They ascended in sequence.
After they had read it,
they descended,
leading all the civil and military officials to face north, perform the ritual dance, and offer congratulations by bowing twice.
Now, between one Tàicháng Qīng and the state (Shèjì), which is heavier?
If Shū and the others had not died,
having cherished the position of one Minister,
would they have been willing to surrender the state to another?
Although the power of Shū and the others might not have been enough to preserve Táng,
they certainly would not have survived Táng’s demise alone.
Alas!
When Táng fell,
the worthy men and upright gentlemen had already perished with it.
Those remaining were all mediocre and cowardly incompetents, deceitful and cunning schemers, and scoundrels who chased profit and betrayed the country.
Otherwise,
how could they have endured such shame and humiliation in the court of Liáng!
This Biography of the Six Ministers of Táng is written.
Zhāng Wénwèi
Zhāng Wénwèi, courtesy name Yòuhuá,
was a native of Héjiān.
He first gained fame through his literary skills and conduct,
and passed the civil service examination (jìnshì).
During the time of Táng Zhāozōng,
he served as Academician-in-Waiting (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ).
At that time,
the Son of Heaven was weak,
and the imperial system had already collapsed.
Wénwèi, while residing in the Hànlín Academy
and drafting imperial edicts for the four quarters,
uniquely maintained the fundamental principles.
When Zhāozōng moved to Luò,
Wénwèi was appointed Vice Minister of the Chancellery and Co-administrator of Affairs.
When Liǔ Càn killed Péi Shū and seven others,
he indiscriminately implicated court officials
and constantly had them executed.
The officials (jìnshēn) looked at each other nervously,
none feeling safe.
Wénwèi exerted himself to defend and save them,
and many court officials relied on him to survive.
When Liáng Tàizǔ established his rule,
he retained Wénwèi as Chancellor.
The initial regulations and systems of Liáng were all finalized by Wénwèi.
Wénwèi was also filial and fraternal at home.
In the second year of Kāipíng,
Tàizǔ toured the north.
Wénwèi was left in the Western Capital (Xīdū).
He died suddenly from a violent illness.
He was posthumously granted the title Right Minister (Yòu Púyè).
Yáng Shè
Yáng Shè,
whose grandfather was Shōu,
was a chancellor during the reign of Emperor Yìzōng of Táng;
his father, Yán,
held the office of Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng).
Shè passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and during the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng, he served as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
When Emperor Āidì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Shè
came from a famous Táng family,
had traditionally maintained ritual standards and laws,
and his character was especially cautious and honest,
but unfortunately, he encountered the chaos of Táng's decline.
On the day he was appointed chancellor,
he wept facing his family,
and looking at his son Níngshì, he said:
“I cannot escape this net;
disaster is imminent
and will surely implicate you all.”
When Táng fell,
he served Liáng as Vice Minister of the Chancellery (Ménxià Shìláng) and Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
He held office for three years,
bowing his head and accomplishing nothing.
He was dismissed and made Executive Assistant of the Left (Zuǒ Púyè),
overseeing the examinations (*zhī gòngjǔ*).
He died several years later.
His son, Níngshì,
had literary talent
and was skilled in calligraphy.
He served successively Liáng, Táng, Jìn, Hàn, and Zhōu,
often retiring due to illness of the mind (*xīnjí*).
He resided in Luòyáng
and his highest office was Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
Zhāng Cè.
Zhāng Cè, courtesy name Shàoyì,
was a native of Dūnhuáng in Héxī.
His father, Tóng,
was the Commissioner of Military Affairs for Róngguǎn during Táng.
Cè was intelligent and fond of learning in his youth,
and mastered textual exegesis (*zhāngjù*).
His father, Tóng,
while residing in the Dūnhuà quarter of Luòyáng,
deepened a well and unearthed an ancient *dǐng* (tripod).
The inscription read:
“The first year of Huángchū of Wèi, second month of spring.
Artisan Jí Qiān.”
Tóng thought this unusual.
Cè, who was thirteen years old at the time,
was staying by Tóng’s side,
and submitted:
“In the twenty-fifth year of Jiàn'ān of Hàn,
Duke Cáo passed away,
and the reign era was changed to Yánkāng.
In the tenth month of that year,
Emperor Wén received the abdication
and changed the era name again to Huángchū.
Thus, there was no second month in the first year of Huángchū.
How can the inscription be mistaken?”
Tóng was greatly astonished by him.
In his youth, Cè was fond of Buddhist teachings (*fútú zhī shuō*),
so he shaved his head and became a monk,
residing at the Cí'ēn Temple in Cháng'ān.
When Huáng Cháo attacked Cháng'ān,
Cè returned to his original attire,
and escorted his parents to avoid the chaos,
living in the countryside for over ten years.
He was summoned and appointed Erudite of the Guǎngwén Academy (Guǎngwén Guǎn Bóshì).
Wáng Xíngyú of Bīnzhōu invited him to serve as Assistant Surveillance Commissioner (*guānchá zhīshǐ*).
When the Prince of Jìn, Lǐ Kèyòng, attacked Xíngyú,
Cè and a maid carried his mother on a shoulder litter while heading east,
traveling through deep snow.
Those who saw them pitied them.
When Grand Progenitor of Liáng (Liáng Tàizǔ) took control of the four garrisons,
he invited Cè to be Assistant Commissioner for Zhèng and Huá,
but Cè resigned due to his mother's mourning period.
When the mourning period ended,
he entered Táng service as Vice Director of the Bureau of Provisions (Shànbù Yuánwàiláng).
Hán Jiàn of Huàzhōu appointed him as judicial assistant (*pànguān*).
When Jiàn moved to Xǔzhōu,
he made Cè his chief secretary (*zhǎng shūjì*).
Jiàn sent Cè to Tàizǔ as an envoy.
Tàizǔ met him and happily remarked:
“Master Zhāng has arrived!”
He thus kept him and made him his chief secretary,
and recommended him to the court.
He was successively appointed Draftsman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén) and Academician of the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
Cè was promoted to Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng) and served as an Imperial Attendant (*fèngzhǐ*).
In the second year of Kāipíng,
he was appointed Vice Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng) and Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
and later transferred to Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
Due to a wind disease (*fēngyàng*), he was dismissed and made Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū),
retired,
and died in Luòyáng.
Zhào Guāngféng.
Zhào Guāngféng, courtesy name Yánjí,
whose father, Yǐn,
was Executive Assistant of the Left (Zuǒ Púyè) during Táng.
Guāngféng was famous in Táng for his literary conduct,
and people at the time praised him as upright, straightforward, gentle, and smooth,
calling him
“The Jade Ruler” (*yù jièchǐ*).
During the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng, he was Academician-in-Waiting (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ) and Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
Due to the chaos of the age, he abandoned office,
resided in Luòyáng,
and closed his door, severing ties with the world for five or six years.
When Liǔ Càn became chancellor,
he relied on an old kindness he owed Guāngféng,
and appointed Guāngféng as Vice Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shìláng) and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
When Táng fell,
he served Liáng as Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
He was successively promoted to Executive Assistant of the Left (Zuǒ Púyè),
and retired with the title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
When the Last Emperor (Mòdì) ascended the throne,
he was reinstated as Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
and later retired again with the title of Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
During the Tiānchéng era of Táng,
he was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo) at his residence,
ennobled as the Duke of Qí State (Qí Guó Gōng),
and died.
He was posthumously granted Grand Mentor (Tàifù).
Xuē Yíjǔ.
Xuē Yíjǔ, courtesy name Xīyòng,
was a native of Wénxǐ in Hédōng.
He served Táng as Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng) and Academician-in-Waiting (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ).
When Emperor Zhāozōng returned to Cháng'ān from Qí,
he heavily punished the eunuchs.
At that time, Yíjǔ composed eulogies for the portraits of Chief Commissioner Hán Quánhuì and others [eunuchs].
He was implicated and demoted.
Yíjǔ then personally attached himself to Grand Progenitor of Liáng (Liáng Tàizǔ).
Tàizǔ spoke on his behalf to the court,
and he was appointed Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
and later promoted to Grand Censor (Yùshǐ Dàfū).
In the third year of Tiānyòu,
when Tàizǔ returned to the army from Chánglú,
Emperor Āidì sent Yíjǔ to offer condolences.
Yíjǔ sought an audience using the ritual of a subject,
but Tàizǔ bowed and motioned for him to ascend the steps.
Yíjǔ said:
“Your Highness’s accomplishments and virtue benefit the people,
and the Three Spirits (Heaven, Earth, and Man) have changed the divination (mandate).
The Emperor is about to enact the matters of Shùn and Yǔ (abdication).
How dare your servant violate this?”
He then acknowledged himself as a subject, knelt, and performed the ceremonial dance.
Tàizǔ turned aside to avoid receiving his full obeisance.
When Yíjǔ returned,
he immediately urged Emperor Āidì to abdicate the throne.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Yíjǔ Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
He was successively appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Yíjǔ served as the Liáng chancellor for five years,
died,
and was posthumously granted Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng).
Sū Xún (with Dù Xiǎo appended).
Sū Xún,
it is unknown where he was from.
He was cunning and flattering by nature,
adulating others shamelessly,
and only pursued self-interest.
He served Táng as Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū).
At this time,
Tàizǔ had already assassinated Emperor Zhāozōng
and established Emperor Āidì.
All the former officials of Táng were resentful and grinding their teeth,
some bowing their heads fearing disaster,
others leaving and refusing to serve.
But Xún specifically attached himself to Liáng to seek advancement.
When the Liáng troops attacked Yáng Xíngmì,
they suffered a great defeat at the Bēihé River.
Tàizǔ was agitated and angry,
and impatient to receive the abdication.
He wanted to demand the Nine Distinctions (*jiǔ xī*) from Táng,
but none of the officials dared to address this suggestion.
Only Xún publicly advocated, saying:
“The achievements and virtue of the Prince of Liáng (Liáng Wáng)
show that the Mandate of Heaven belongs to him.
He should immediately accept the abdication.”
The following year,
Grand Progenitor of Liáng ascended the throne,
and Xún served as the Vice Envoy for the Inauguration Ceremony (*cèlǐ fùshǐ*).
Xún had a son, Kǎi
In the middle of the Qiánníng period, he passed the Imperial Examination and attained the rank of Jìnshì.
Emperor Zhāozōng had the academician Lù Yǐ review and fail him,
and Kǎi often felt ashamed and resentful.
When Emperor Zhāozōng was assassinated,
the Táng administration fell to the Liáng,
and Kǎi served as Qǐjū Láng (Diaries of Activity Recorder).
He associated closely with Liǔ Càn, Zhāng Tíngfàn, and others.
Consequently, he said to Tíngfàn:
“Indeed, a posthumous title (shì)
is used to change the name and value fidelity.
The former officials gave the late emperor the posthumous title ‘Zhāo’ (Brilliant),
but the name and the reality do not match.
You are the Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng),
and I am the Historian (Shǐguān).
We cannot remain silent.”
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial arguing against it.
Tíngfàn was originally a protégé general of the Liáng.
He had once sought the position of Tàicháng Qīng but failed to obtain it.
Tíngfàn also resented the Táng because of this.
Consequently, Kǎi's memorial was submitted to Tíngfàn.
Tíngfàn proposed:
“I have heard that firm adherence to duty is called Gōng (Reverent);
disruption that does not lead to loss is called Líng (Spiritual);
martial actions that do not succeed are called Zhuāng (Solemn);
encountering difficulties in the state is called Mǐn (Suffering);
achieving merit through circumstance is called Xiāng (Assisting).
I request that the posthumous title of Emperor Zhāozōng be changed to Emperor Gōnglíng Zhuāngmǐn,
and his temple name be Xiāngzōng.”
After Liáng Tàizǔ (Founding Emperor of Liáng) had ascended the throne,
he held a banquet in Xuándé Hall,
and looking upon his officials, he stated that his own virtue was meager and insufficient to bear the mandate of Heaven,
and that everything was due to the strength of the grandees who had supported him.
The former Táng officials, such as Yáng Shè and Zhāng Wénwèi, were all ashamed, prostrated themselves, and were unable to respond.
Only Xún, along with Zhāng Yī and Xuē Yíjǔ, lavishly praised the meritorious virtue of the King of Liáng,
and how he conformed to Heaven and responded to the people.
Both Xún and his son believed that by siding with the Liáng they had found their patron.
They looked forward day and night,
hoping to be promoted and employed.
However, Jìng Xiáng particularly disliked them.
He said to Tàizǔ:
“The House of Liáng has been newly established;
it ought to employ upright gentlemen to strengthen the moral customs.
Xún and his son are both without proper conduct
and should not be established in the new court.”
Consequently, both father and son were ordered to return to their fields and homes.
They then depended on Zhū Yǒuqiān in Hédōng.
Afterward,
Yǒuqiān rebelled against Liáng and surrendered to Jìn.
When the King of Jìn was about to ascend the throne,
he sought out surviving former Táng officials
to fill the vacancies in the government offices.
Yǒuqiān sent Xún to Wèizhōu.
At that time, Liáng had not yet been destroyed,
and many of the Jìn generals and ministers did not wish for the King of Jìn to assume the imperial title.
Although the King of Jìn's intention was keen,
none of the generals, ministers, or high officials had yet endorsed the proposal.
When Xún first arrived at Wèizhōu,
he immediately bowed facing the courtyard of the prefectural office where business was conducted,
and called it
“Bàidiàn” (bowing to the palace).
When he entered to pay respects,
he danced, cried out “Wànsuì” (Ten Thousand Years), and proclaimed himself a subject.
The King of Jìn was greatly pleased.
The next day, he presented
thirty brushes
named “Huàrì Bǐ” (Sun-Painting Brushes).
The King of Jìn was even more delighted,
and consequently appointed Xún as Deputy Commissioner of the Military Governor (Jiédù Fùshǐ).
Soon after, he died of illness.
When Emperor Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
Xún was posthumously granted the title of Zuǒ Púshè (Left Grandee Secretary).
As for Kǎi,
during the Tóngguāng period, he served as Shàngshū Yuánwàiláng (Supernumerary Director in the Department of State Affairs).
When Emperor Míngzōng ascended the throne,
ministers sought to punish him for the crime of arguing against the posthumous title,
and he died of worry.
When the Táng dynasty fell,
there was also Dù Xiǎo,
whose courtesy name was Míngyuǎn.
His grandfather, Shěnquán,
and his father, Ràngnéng,
both served as Táng Chancellors.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng,
when the armies of Wáng Xíngyú and Lǐ Màozhēn violated the capital,
Zhāozōng killed Ràngnéng at the Línjì to appease them.
Xiǎo, because his father died without fault,
was consumed by grief and deterioration during the mourning period.
After the mourning period ended,
he wore plain cloth and a simple scarf,
abandoning himself for more than ten years.
Cuī Yìn, when acting as Judge of the Salt and Iron Monopoly,
invited him to be a巡官 Xúnguān (Circuit Inspector),
and he was appointed County Commandant (Xiàn Wèi) of a metropolitan county
and Director of the Zhāowén Academy,
but he refused all positions.
Cuī Yuǎn, when acting as Judge of the Ministry of Revenue,
also invited him to be Xúnguān.
Someone said to Xiǎo:
“When Jī Kāng died,
his son, Shào, refused to serve, abandoning himself.
Shān Tāo rebuked him using the principle of the inherent nature of things,
and then he served.
Are you willing to tolerate the Dù family celebrating seasonal sacrifices for their ancestors on simple mats, just like the common people?”
Xiǎo then accepted the position.
He was successively promoted to Shànbù Lángzhōng (Director of the Bureau of Provisions) and Hànlín Xuéshì (Academician of the Hanlin Academy).
When Liáng Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng) and Fèngzhǐ (Receiver of Imperial Decrees).
In the second year of Kāipíng (908 CE),
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice-Director of the Chancellery) and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Executive of the Secretariat-Chancellery).
When Yǒu Guī established himself,
he was promoted to Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) and Grand Academician of the Jíxián Palace.
When Yuán Xiàngxiān and others were suppressing the bandits,
the army engaged in massive looting.
Xiǎo was killed by the mutinous soldiers.
He was posthumously granted the title of Yòu Púshè (Right Grandee Secretary).
Alas!
Who was it that first spoke of the theory of factions (Péngdǎng)?
This is worse than the 'starter of effigies' (zuòyǒngzhě)!
Truly, one can call them the 'inhumane persons'!
I once went to Fánchéng and read the Stele Commemorating Wèi's Acceptance of the Abdication (Wèi Shòu Chán Bēi).
I saw the officials of the Hàn praising the meritorious virtue of Wèi,
and engraving their names in large script,
listing themselves
to boast to the world.
I also read the Veritable Records of Liáng (Liáng Shílù)
and saw what Wénwèi and others did was like this.
I never fail to shed tears because of it.
To surrender the state to another person and then boast about it,
and subsequently become their ministers—
if these are not petty men (Xiǎorén),
who else could do it?
At the end of the Hàn and Táng dynasties,
their entire courts were composed of petty men.
But where were their gentlemen (Jūnzǐ)?
When the Hàn dynasty perished,
they first used the charge of factionalism to prohibit and imprison the worthy gentlemen of the realm.
And those who then established the court
were all petty men.
Afterward, the Hàn consequently perished.
When the Táng dynasty perished,
they again first used the charge of factionalism to kill all the officials in the court.
And the remaining survivors
were all mediocre, timid, unworthy, or insidious persons.
Afterward, the Táng consequently perished.
a man's state and remove its *jūnzǐ*,
must advance the theory of *péngdǎng*.
Those who wish to isolate the power of the sovereign and cover his ears and eyes,
must advance the theory of *péngdǎng*.
Those who wish to seize the state and give it to others,
must advance the theory of *péngdǎng*.
Now, as for those who are *jūnzǐ*,
they are usually seldom at fault.
When *xiǎorén* wish to impose blame upon them,
there are those who can be falsely accused,
and those who cannot be falsely accused;
it is impossible to reach them all.
But if one desires to take all the good men in the world,
seek out their kind, and completely eliminate them,
the only method is to point to them as *péngdǎng*.
Therefore, their relatives and old friends,
can be called *péngdǎng*;
their associates and close friends,
can be called *péngdǎng*;
those whose careers and studies are similar,
can be called *péngdǎng*;
their disciples and former subordinates,
can be called *péngdǎng*.
These several groups,
are all of their kind,
and they are all good men.
Therefore, it is said: those who wish to empty a man's state and remove its *jūnzǐ*,
need only use *péngdǎng* to condemn them,
and none will escape.
Now, the joy good men take in each other,
is because their nature is the same.
This is a natural principle.
Therefore, those who hear of goodness will surely praise and commend each other.
If they praise and commend, they are called *péngdǎng*.
Those who find good men will surely recommend and promote each other.
If they recommend and promote, they are called *péngdǎng*.
If people are made to hear of goodness but dare not praise it,
the sovereign's ears will not hear of good things happening below.
If people see good men but dare not recommend them,
the sovereign's eyes will be unable to see good men.
Good men daily drift away,
while *xiǎorén* daily advance.
In that case, the one who is the sovereign,
will be lost and confused, having no one with whom to plan measures for peace and security?
Therefore, it is said: those who wish to isolate the power of the sovereign and cover his ears and eyes,
must use the theory of *péngdǎng*.
If one *jūnzǐ* remains,
although the group of *xiǎorén* be many,
they will surely have something to fear,
and something they dare not do.
Only when the state is empty and without *jūnzǐ*,
can the *xiǎorén* indulge their ambitions and stop at nothing.
This was the case during the periods of Hàn and Wèi, and Táng and Liáng.
Therefore, it is said: that a state can be seized and given to others,
is because its state lacks *jūnzǐ*.
The state being empty and without *jūnzǐ*,
is due to their having been removed by means of *péngdǎng*.
Alas!
The theory of *péngdǎng*,
how can the sovereign fail to investigate it!
The tradition says
"One word can ruin a nation,"
does this not refer to this?
How can one fail to take warning!
How can one fail to be cautious!
Biography of the Adopted Sons (*Yì'ér Zhuàn*) Twenty-fourth
Alas!
The ways of the world declined,
human relations were ruined,
and the principle of closeness and distance reversed its constant order.
Weapons and war arose among blood relatives,
and disparate kinds combined to become father and son.
During the fifty years between Kāipíng and Xiǎndé,
the realm passed through Five Dynasties, but truly eight surnames held power.
Three of these arose from seeking adoption.
Generally, the most prominent among them seized the realm;
the next succeeded in establishing merit and fame, achieving positions as generals and prime ministers.
Was this not taking advantage of the gaps of the time,
combining through mutual interest and assisting one another?
Táng, which called itself Shātuó,
arose in Dàiběi.
Those who associated with them were all heroic, outstanding, and fierce warriors of the time.
They often adopted them as sons,
calling them
the "Army of Adopted Sons" (*Yì'ér Jūn*).
When they eventually possessed the realm,
they often used them to achieve great deeds and enterprises,
and when they perished, it was also due to them.
Tàizǔ had many adopted sons.
Nine of them are worthy of record.
One of them became Míngzōng.
The others are Sīzhāo, Sìběn, Sì'ēn, Cúnxìn, Cúnxiào, Cúnjìn, Cúnzhāng, and Cúnxián.
This Biography of the Adopted Sons is written.
Lǐ Cúnshěn,
later gained great prominence using the surname Fú,
so a separate biography is written for him.
Lǐ Sìzhāo
Lǐ Sìzhāo,
originally had the surname Hán.
He was the son of a commoner family in Tàigǔ County, Fénzhōu.
Tàizǔ went out hunting,
and arrived at his home.
Seeing a dense, vital energy in the woods there,
he found it very strange.
He summoned the father and questioned him.
The father said his family had just had a son.
Tàizǔ therefore gave gifts of gold and silk and took the child,
commanding his younger brother, Kèróu, to raise him as a son.
His initial name was Jìntōng;
later, his name was changed to Sìzhāo.
Sìzhāo was short in stature,
but his courage and bravery surpassed others.
Initially, he loved drinking alcohol;
Tàizǔ once mildly warned him about it,
and thereafter he never drank again throughout his life.
Tàizǔ loved his caution and sincerity,
and he frequently followed him on military campaigns,
serving as the Commander of the Inner Yamen.
In Shǎnzhōu, Wáng Gǒng fought with his older brother Kē for the position in Hézhōng.
[Tàizǔ] sent Sìzhāo to assist Kē,
defeating Gǒng at Yīshì,
and capturing three of his generals.
The Liáng army rescued Gǒng,
and Sìzhāo again defeated them at Húbìbǎo,
capturing one of their generals.
In the first year of Guānghuà,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī of Zézhōu attacked Lùzhōu and defected to Liáng.
Liáng sent Dīng Huì to support Hǎnzhī.
Sìzhāo fought Huì at Hánshān,
captured one of his generals,
and decapitated three thousand men.
He subsequently took Zézhōu.
In the second year,
Jìn sent Lǐ Jūnqìng to attack Liáng's Lùzhōu.
Jūnqìng was defeated by Liáng.
Tàizǔ poisoned Jūnqìng to death.
Sìzhāo then attacked and conquered it.
In the third year,
he went out to Shāndōng,
and took Liáng's Míngzhōu.
Liáng Tàizǔ personally led an army to attack him,
sending Gé Cóngzhōu to set an ambush at Qīngshānkǒu.
When Sìzhāo heard that Liáng Tàizǔ himself was approaching,
he abandoned the city and fled.
He encountered the ambush troops ahead,
and consequently suffered a great defeat.
In the first year of Tiānfù,
Liáng captured Hézhōng,
captured Wáng Kē,
and took Jìn, Jiàng, Cí, and Xí prefectures.
They then launched a major attack against Jìn,
besieging Tàiyuán.
Sìzhāo daily led elite cavalry to sally forth and strike the Liáng forces.
As heavy rain occurred,
the Liáng army withdrew.
Lǐ Táng, the Prefect of Fénzhōu for Jìn, rebelled and surrendered to the Liáng army.
After the Liáng army had left,
Sìzhāo recaptured Fénzhōu,
and executed Táng.
He then sallied out to Yīndì,
took Cízhōu,
and secured the surrender of its Prefect, Táng Lǐ.
He also took Xízhōu,
and secured the surrender of its Prefect, Zhāng Guī.
That year,
the Liáng army marched west and invaded the capital,
besieging Fèngxiáng.
Sìzhāo seized the opportunity to attack Liáng's Jìn and Jiàng prefectures.
He fought at Píngyáng,
capturing one Liáng general.
He advanced to attack Pú County.
Zhū Yǒuníng and Shì Shūcóng of Liáng brought ten thousand troops to meet and attack him.
Sìzhāo and his forces were defeated and fled.
Yǒuníng pursued them.
Jìn sent Lǐ Cúnxìn to lead troops to meet Sìzhāo,
but Cúnxìn was also defeated.
The Liáng army then besieged Tàiyuán,
and Cí, Xí, and Fén prefectures fell again to Liáng.
Tàizǔ was greatly frightened,
and plotted to flee to Yúnzhōu.
Lǐ Cúnxìn and others urged Tàizǔ to escape to the Qìdān.
Sìzhāo strongly argued that this was unacceptable.
Relying on the fact that Grand Consort Liú also spoke in agreement,
the plan was stopped.
Sìzhāo launched surprise attacks against the Liáng army day and night.
The Liáng army withdrew,
and Sìzhāo recaptured Fén, Cí, and Xí.
At this time,
Zhèn and Dìng had both severed ties with Jìn and sided with Liáng.
Jìn had lost the support of great states externally,
and had lost various prefectures internally.
Within successive years,
the isolated city was besieged twice.
During this period,
Sìzhāo's merits from fighting vigorously were the greatest.
In the third year of Tiānyòu (906),
(Lǐ Sìzhāo), together with Zhōu Déwēi, attacked the Liáng’s Lùzhōu.
Dīng Huì surrendered,
and Sìzhāo was made Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Zhāoyì Commandery.
Liáng sent Lǐ Sī'ān commanding 100,000 troops to attack Lù(zhōu),
constructing adjacent fortifications (jiāchéng) to surround it.
Liáng Tàizǔ once sent men to persuade Sìzhāo to surrender;
Sìzhāo beheaded the messenger,
closed the city gates, and resisted the siege.
After more than a year,
Zhuāngzōng finally attacked and broke through the adjacent fortifications.
Sìzhāo repaired and organized the soldiers and populace,
treating and nurturing them with great kindness.
Liáng and Jìn fought at Húliǔ.
The Jìn army was defeated,
and Zhōu Déwēi died in battle.
Zhuāngzōng was frightened,
and wished to withdraw the troops and return to Línpǔ.
Sìzhāo said:
“The Liáng army has already won,
and morning and evening they will be thinking of returning home.
If we withdraw our forces,
allowing them to rest,
reorganize and reappear,
how shall we withstand them?
We ought to use elite cavalry to harass them,
taking advantage of their weariness and exhaustion;
we can then achieve victory.”
Zhuāngzōng agreed with this.
At this time,
the Liáng army had already ascended Wúshíshān.
Zhuāngzōng sent Sìzhāo to turn and strike the north of the mountain,
while he himself led the Yínqiāng Jūn (Silver Spear Army), rushing forward and shouting:
“In today's battle,
those who capture the mountain will win!”
The Jìn troops all rushed to climb the mountain.
The Liáng army quickly descended
and formed ranks on the west side of the mountain.
The Jìn army attacked fiercely from above,
utterly defeating them.
Thereupon, the Jìn city of Déshèng was secured.
After Zhōu Déwēi died,
Sìzhāo temporarily supervised Yōuzhōu.
After several months,
Lǐ Shàohóng replaced him.
When Sìzhāo was about to leave,
the people of Yōuzhōu all wept and cried out, closing the pass and blocking him to make him stay.
Sìzhāo escaped by night
and was then able to depart.
In the nineteenth year,
he followed Zhuāngzōng to attack the Qìdān at Wàngdū.
Zhuāngzōng was surrounded by the Qìdān in dozens of layers.
Sìzhāo, with 300 cavalry, broke through the encirclement,
rescued Zhuāngzōng, and brought him out.
At this time,
Jìn sent Yán Bǎo to attack Zhāng Wénlǐ at Zhènzhōu.
Bǎo was defeated by the people of Zhèn(zhōu),
so Sìzhāo was appointed to replace him.
The Zhèn troops came out to plunder Jiǔmén;
Sìzhāo attacked them with surprise troops.
The Zhèn army was nearly wiped out.
The remaining three men hid within broken walls.
Sìzhāo rode his horse swiftly and shot at them,
but was instead shot by the bandits in the head.
Sìzhāo looked and saw the arrows in his quiver were gone.
He pulled the arrow out of his head,
shot and killed one man,
returned to camp, and died.
Among Sìzhāo's several sons,
Jìchóu was the eldest but timid.
His younger brother Jìtāo imprisoned him and established himself.
Zhuāngzōng was then locked in a stalemate with the Liáng forces along the river.
He did not have time to investigate the matter,
and therefore immediately appointed him Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu) of Zhāoyì Commandery.
Jìtāo entrusted his governance to Wèi Zhuó and Shēn Méng.
Zhuó and the others constantly urged Jìtāo to rebel,
but Jìtāo had not yet made a decision.
When Zhuāngzōng was at Wèi,
he summoned Surveillance Commissioner Zhāng Jūhàn and Judicial Aide (Pànguān) Rèn Huán regarding an affair.
Zhuó and the others assumed that Zhuāngzōng had summoned Jūhàn and the others to inquire about Jìtāo's actions,
and that Jìtāo was about to be executed.
Consequently, they used this argument to hasten him.
Jìtāo then sent his younger brother Jìyuǎn to defect to Liáng.
The Last Emperor of Liáng immediately appointed Jìtāo Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
After several months,
Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng.
Jìtāo was about to flee to Qìdān.
It happened that an amnesty arrived,
so he stopped.
He then followed his mother to pay respects at the capital (Jīngshī).
Jìyuǎn remonstrated, saying:
“Brother, as a subject and son,
you have gained the reputation of rebellion.
What face do you have left to see the Son of Heaven?
Moreover, Lùchéng is strong and the granaries are full.
It is better to close the city and consume the stored grain,
thus prolonging your years,
which is preferable to going and meeting execution.”
Jìtāo did not listen.
Jìtāo's mother, Lady Yáng Shì,
was skilled at accumulating wealth.
Throughout her life, she stored goods and traded,
until her assets reached a million (units of currency/value).
When Sìzhāo was surrounded by the Liáng forces in the adjacent fortifications for a full year,
military supplies ran out.
The accumulated wealth of Lady Yáng Shì
likely provided assistance.
When it came to this point,
she brought several hundred thousand liǎng of silver to the capital,
and heavily bribed the eunuchs and performers.
The eunuchs and performers all said:
“Jìtāo originally had no wicked intentions,
but was merely misled by wicked men.”
Lady Yáng fūrén also used bribes to see Empress Liú Huánghòu.
Empress Liú Huánghòu spoke on his behalf, saying:
“Sìzhāo was a meritorious subject;
he ought to receive pardon and clemency.”
Because of this, Zhuāngzōng released Jìtāo.
(Jìtāo) sometimes accompanied hunting expeditions,
and was favored without distinction.
Lǐ Cúnwò especially gritted his teeth,
and repeatedly disparaged and criticized him.
Jìtāo felt uneasy in his heart.
He again bribed eunuchs and performers to request a return to his commandery,
but Zhuāngzōng did not permit it.
Jìtāo secretly sent someone to inform Jìyuǎn,
ordering him to start a mutiny among the troops,
hoping the Son of Heaven would send him to quell and stabilize it.
The matter was exposed,
and he was beheaded at Tiānjīn Qiáo.
His two sons had previously been held as hostages by Liáng.
When Zhuāngzōng defeated Liáng, he recovered them.
He patted their backs and said:
“You are young,
yet you could still assist your father in rebellion.
What will you do when you grow older?”
When it came to this point, they were executed together.
Immediately, he sent men to execute Jìyuǎn,
and appointed Jìchóu to manage the affairs of Lùzhōu.
After a while,
Jìchóu was summoned back to the capital.
Jìchóu took all of Jìtāo's courtesans, concubines, and treasures,
but did not immediately set out on the journey.
His younger brother Jìdá angrily said:
“My brother (Jìtāo), father, and son were executed,
yet the eldest brother is unkind,
profiting from his assets
and committing adultery with his wives and concubines.
This is something I cannot tolerate!”
He then wore mourning attire,
led several hundred cavalrymen to sit by the jǐmén (halberd gate),
and ordered men to go in and kill Jìchóu.
Deputy Military Governor Lǐ Jìkē recruited over a thousand market people to attack Jìdá.
Jìdá fled outside the city
and cut his own throat, dying.
Sìzhāo had seven sons.
When it came to the reign of Míngzōng,
his son Jìnéng was implicated for having flogged and killed his mother's slave girl who managed the stores.
The slave girl's family reported the incident, claiming treason.
They claimed Jìnéng was rebelling.
He and his younger brother Jìxí were both killed.
Only one son, Jìzhōng, narrowly escaped.
Jìzhōng lived at Jìnyáng.
The remaining assets accumulated by Lady Yáng Shì were still considerable—tens of thousands (of units).
When Jìn Gāozǔ raised troops from Tàiyuán,
he summoned the Qìdān for assistance.
The Qìdān demanded bribes.
Gāozǔ borrowed from Jìzhōng to meet the amount needed.
When Gāozǔ entered and took the throne,
he greatly appreciated this deed,
and made Jìzhōng the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of the three prefectures of Yí, Dì, and Shàn.
He died during the Kāiyùn era.
The wealth accumulated by Lady Yáng Shì throughout her life
supported Sìzhāo and three of his sons.
Sìběn
Lǐ Sìběn,
whose original surname was Zhāng,
was a man from Yànmén.
Generations of his family served as garrison commanders of Tóngyě.
Sìběn served Tàizǔ when young.
Tàizǔ loved him,
granted him the surname and personal name,
and adopted him as a son.
He followed in the attack on Jūyōng Guān,
and due to his merits was promoted to Yì'ér Jūnshǐ.
He followed in defeating Wáng Xíngyú,
and was promoted to Wēiyuǎn Jūnshǐ.
He followed in attacking Luó Hóngxìn,
using vanguard troops to defeat Tāngyīn.
He followed Zhuāngzōng in defeating the fortified double wall (Jiāchéng) at Lùzhōu.
Due to accumulated military merits, he was promoted to Dàizhōu Cìshǐ, Yúnzhōu Fángyùshǐ, and Zhènwǔ Jiédùshǐ,
and was titled Wēixìn Kèhán.
In the 13th year of Tiānyòu [916 CE],
he followed Zhuāngzōng to attack Liú Xún at the former Yuánchéng,
conquering Míng and Cí Prefectures.
In the sixth month,
the army returned to Zhènwǔ.
The Qìdān entered Dàiběi,
and attacked Yùzhōu.
Sìběn died in battle.
Lǐ Sì'ēn
Sì'ēn,
whose original surname was Luò,
was a man of the Tǔyùhún tribe.
He served Tàizǔ when young,
was skilled at horsemanship and archery,
and became a general of the Tiělín Army.
Gradually, due to military merits, he was promoted to Tūzhèn Zhǐhuīshǐ,
was granted a surname and personal name,
and adopted as a son.
He followed in defeating Kāng Huáiyīng at Héxī,
and was promoted to Zuǒxiāng Mǎjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
He followed Lǐ Sìzhāo to aid Zhū Yǒuqiān at Hézhōng,
fiercely fighting the Liáng troops.
A spear struck him in the mouth,
but he continued fighting.
He was promoted to Liáozhōu Cìshǐ.
He followed Zhuāngzōng into Wèi,
and was promoted to Tiānxióng Jūn Mǎbù Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
When Liú Xún attacked Tàiyuán,
and his troops rushed toward Lèpíng,
Sì'ēn pursued them from the rear,
taking an alternative route and entering Tàiyuán first to defend it.
When Xún's troops departed,
Sì'ēn also led his troops to join Zhuāngzōng at Wèi,
and followed in the battle at Shēn.
He was promoted to Dàizhōu Cìshǐ, Shílǐng Guān Yǐběi Dū Zhī Bīngmǎshǐ, and Zhènwǔ Jiédùshǐ.
In the 15th year of Tiānyòu [918 CE],
he died in Tàiyuán.
He was posthumously granted the title Tàiwèi.
Lǐ Cúnxìn
Cúnxìn,
whose original surname was Zhāng,
and whose father was Jūnzhèng,
was a man of the tribe of the Huíhú, Lǐ Sīzhōng.
When Cúnxìn was young, he was skilled at horsemanship and archery,
could speak the languages of the Four Barbarians (Sì Yí),
and understood the scripts of the Six Barbarian States (Liù Fān Shū).
He followed Tàizǔ when Tàizǔ rose up in Dàiběi,
entered the pass and defeated Huáng Cháo,
and due to accumulated merits became Mǎbùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Thereupon he was granted a surname and personal name,
and adopted as a son.
Cúnxìn and Cúnxiào were both adopted sons.
In talent and bravery he was inferior to Cúnxiào,
but Cúnxìn refused to humble himself before him.
Because of this, their relations soured.
Whatever Cúnxiào did,
Cúnxìn constantly tried to undermine or provoke him,
and Cúnxiào eventually incurred guilt and died.
Cúnxìn repeatedly followed Tàizǔ in campaigns,
and due to his merits was appointed Chénzhōu Cìshǐ.
Tàizǔ sent generals with troops to rescue Zhū Xuān.
Cúnxìn was stationed at Shēnxian,
where he was attacked by Luó Hóngxìn.
Cúnxìn was defeated,
and Tàizǔ's son Luòluò was lost (killed).
Later, he followed Tàizǔ in attacking Liú Réngōng,
and suffered a great defeat at Ānsài.
Tàizǔ was furious,
and looked at Cúnxìn, saying:
"Yesterday I was drunk.
Could you not fight for me?
The ancients allowed three defeats,
you have already had two."
He intended to kill him,
but Cúnxìn kowtowed and apologized for his offense, thus escaping death.
Because of this, he lived in great fear and constantly claimed illness.
He died in the second year of Tiānfù [902 CE],
at the age of forty-one.
Lǐ Cúnxiào
Cúnxiào,
was a man from Fēihú, Dàizhōu.
His original surname was Ān,
and his personal name was Jìngsī.
Tàizǔ captured him while raiding Dàiběi,
employed him within his tent,
granted him a surname and personal name,
adopted him as a son,
and he frequently followed Tàizǔ as a cavalry general.
In the first year of Wéndé [888 CE],
Zhāng Yán of Hénán attacked and captured Héyáng.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī came and submitted to Jìn.
Jìn settled Hǎnzhī in Zézhōu,
and sent Cúnxiào, along with Xuē Ātán and Ān Xiūxiū, leading seven thousand troops to assist Hǎnzhī in counterattacking Héyáng.
Liáng also sent Dīng Huì and Niú Cúnjié to assist Yán.
They fought at Wēnxiàn.
The Liáng army first blocked the Tàiháng Mountains route.
Cúnxiào suffered a major defeat,
and Ān Xiūxiū was captured.
At this time,
Jìn had already acquired Zé and Lù (Prefectures),
and year after year marched out to Shāndōng,
competing with Mèng Fānglì for Xíng, Míng, and Cí (Prefectures).
Cúnxiào was never absent from the fighting.
When Fānglì died,
Jìn took the three prefectures,
and Cúnxiào's contribution was the greatest.
The next year,
the troops in Lùzhōu mutinied,
killed Lǐ Kègōng, and submitted to Táng.
Liáng sent Lǐ Dǎng to attack Lǐ Hǎnzhī at Zézhōu.
Cúnxiào brought five thousand cavalry to rescue him.
The Liáng army shouted to Hǎnzhī:
"You always rely on Tàiyuán for your life.
Now Shàngdǎng has submitted to Táng,
Táng forces are gathering in large numbers
and besieging Tàiyuán.
The Shatuo generals have no hole (refuge) in which to place themselves.
Upon whom else will you rely and not surrender?"
Cúnxiào took five hundred elite cavalry,
rode around the Liáng barricade, and shouted:
"I am a Shatuo who is seeking a hole (refuge)!
I am waiting for your flesh to feed my army!
Let the fat ones come out and fight!"
The brave Liáng general Dèng Jìyún led his troops out to fight.
Cúnxiào brandished his spear and captured him.
Lǐ Dǎng fled in defeat,
pursued all the way to Mǎláo Guān.
Cúnxiào then returned and attacked Lùzhōu.
Táng appointed Sūn Kuí as Lùzhōu Jiédùshǐ.
Kuí was a scholar,
who took three thousand Liáng soldiers as his guards,
wearing splendid robes and traveling beneath a large carriage canopy,
bearing the credentials of the governor and acting as the vanguard.
Cúnxiào ambushed them with three hundred cavalry in the valley west of Chángzǐ,
waited for Kuí's army to pass,
attacked transversely and cut them off,
capturing Kuí and returning (to Jìn).
Previously,
Liáng had sent Gé Cóngzhōu and Zhū Chóngjié to guard Lùzhōu while waiting for Kuí.
Hearing that Kuí had been captured,
they all abandoned the city and left.
Jìn thus recovered Lùzhōu.
At this time,
Zhāng Jùn and Hán Jiàn attacked Jìn,
striking Yīndì Guān.
Jìn used Lǐ Cúnxìn, Xuē Ātán, and others to resist Jùn,
and separately sent Cúnxiào's army to Zhàochéng.
The Táng army was defeated at Yīndì Guān.
Jùn retreated and secured Jìnzhōu,
and Hán Jiàn fled to Jiàngzhōu.
Cúnxiào attacked Jìnzhōu.
When Jùn's troops marched out to fight,
they were defeated again,
and consequently sealed their fortifications, daring not to leave.
Cúnxiào departed,
and attacked Jiàngzhōu.
Jùn and Jiàn both fled.
Li Cúnxiào had arms like an ape and was skilled in archery.
He wore heavy armor,
carried his bow in a case, placed his spear,
wielded an iron mace in his hand,
and went in and out of the ranks.
He was accompanied by only two cavalrymen.
When the battle was fierce, they exchanged horses,
moving up and down as if flying.
Initially,
Cúnxiào’s achievements in capturing Lùzhōu were the greatest,
but Tàizǔ instead appointed the great general Kāng Jūnlì as the Garrison Commander (Liúhòu) of Lùzhōu,
and Cúnxiào was made Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Fénzhōu.
Cúnxiào felt slighted by his merit
and did not eat for several days.
When he routed Zhāng Jùn,
he was promoted to Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Bīnzhōu.
In the second year of Dàshùn (891),
he was transferred to Garrison Commander (Liúhòu) of Xíngzhōu.
At that time,
the Jìn army attacked Zhào Chángshān for successive years.
Cúnxiào always served as the vanguard
and captured Línchéng and Yuánshì of Zhào.
The King of Zhào sought aid from Lǐ Kuāngwēi of Yōuzhōu.
When Kuāngwēi’s troops arrived,
the Jìn army consistently withdrew.
Cúnxiào had long held a grievance against Cúnxìn.
Cúnxìn slandered him, saying:
"Cúnxiào harbors disloyalty;
he always avoids attacking Zhào."
Cúnxiào felt uneasy,
so he joined Liáng and communicated with Zhào,
and submitted himself to Táng.
He then requested to muster troops to attack Jìn.
Táng ordered Wáng Róng, the King of Zhào, to assist him.
The next year,
Zhào had a falling out with Yōuzhōu.
Fearing the consequence, Zhào made peace with Jìn,
and instead used thirty thousand troops to help Jìn attack Cúnxiào.
Cúnxiào garrisoned the city and defended himself.
Tàizǔ personally led troops to approach his city,
digging trenches to surround it.
Cúnxiào sent troops out to strike and attack,
preventing the trenches from being completed.
The Deputy General Yuán Fèngtāo sent a messenger to persuade Cúnxiào, saying:
"The one you fear is merely the King of Jìn!
When the King waits for the trenches to be completed,
he will leave the remaining troops and depart.
The other generals are no match for you,
so what does a trench matter?"
Cúnxiào thought this was correct,
and allowed the troops to complete the trenches.
When the trenches were completed,
with deep moats and high ramparts,
the city could not be approached,
and Cúnxiào was then in distress.
Supplies within the city were exhausted.
He climbed the city wall and shouted, saying:
"Your son received the King's favor
and attained the rank of General and Minister.
How could I wish to abandon the relationship of father and son to side with enemies?
It was Cúnxìn who framed and trapped me!
I wish to see the King alive, say one word, and then die."
Tàizǔ pitied him,
and sent Lady Liú into the city to comfort and counsel him.
Lady Liú led him out together.
Cúnxiào kowtowed and begged for punishment, saying:
"Your son has rendered service to Jìn but committed no fault.
The reason I have come to this point
is entirely due to Cúnxìn's actions!"
Tàizǔ shouted at him, saying:
"You wrote proclamations
accusing me of a hundred faults—
were those also done by Cúnxìn?"
He was bound and loaded onto the rear carriage.
Upon reaching Tàiyuán,
he was executed by the tearing of his body by chariots (chēliè) as a public display.
However, Tàizǔ regretted his talent,
and mournfully lamented that his generals could not tolerate him.
Because of this, he did not attend to affairs for more than ten days.
Kāng Jūnlì had always been close friends with Cúnxìn.
While the two (Cúnxiào and Cúnxìn) were on bad terms,
Jūnlì constantly sided with Cúnxìn to undermine Cúnxiào.
After Cúnxiào died,
Tàizǔ played a board game with his generals.
When the conversation turned to Cúnxiào,
Tàizǔ wept profusely.
Jūnlì suggested this grief was insincere.
Tàizǔ grew angry
and poisoned Jūnlì to death.
Jūnlì had initially been a staff officer (Yájiàng) in Yúnzhōu.
During the reign of Táng Xīzōng,
he drove out Duàn Wénchǔ,
and rose up in Yúnzhōng together with Tàizǔ.
Jūnlì was actually the initiator of the event.
Afterward, he repeatedly established military merits,
and was nominated for Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Zhāoyì,
but was killed on account of Cúnxiào.
Cúnjìn
Lǐ Cúnjìn
was a native of Zhènwǔ.
His original surname was Sūn,
and his personal name was Chóngjìn.
Tàizǔ acquired him when he attacked and defeated Shuòzhōu,
bestowed upon him his (foster) surname and given name,
and raised him as a son.
He followed Tàizǔ into the Pass and defeated Huáng Cháo,
and was made Commander of the Adopted Sons Army (Yì'ér Jūnshǐ).
He followed Zhuāngzōng in battle at Bóxiāng.
He was promoted to Grand Marshal over the Cavalry and Infantry of the Traveling Camp (Xíngyíng Mǎbùjūn Dūyúhòu),
and subsequently served as Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Cízhōu and Qìnzhōu.
When Zhuāngzōng first gained Wèibó,
he appointed him Grand Commander of the Tiānxióng Army (Tiānxióng Jūn Dūbùshǔ).
He governed the rebellious Liáng troops
entirely according to the law.
If anyone committed an offense,
their head was immediately cut off and their body displayed in the marketplace.
The people of Wèi held their breath and feared him.
He followed in battle at Héshàng,
and based on his merit, he was promoted to Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhènwǔ Army.
At this time,
the Jìn army, having won at Déshèng,
established northern and southern camps (Zhài).
They constantly relied on boat troops to travel back and forth,
which was considered quite laborious.
Since there was no bamboo or stone north of the river (Héběi),
Cúnjìn then used reeds and grass ropes to connect large warships, forming a pontoon bridge (fúliáng).
Zhuāngzōng was greatly pleased
and took off his own robe to bestow upon him.
Jìn was suppressing Zhāng Wénlǐ in Zhènzhōu,
but for a long time failed to overcome him.
Furthermore, Shǐ Jiàntáng, Yán Bǎo, and Lǐ Sìzhāo successively died in battle.
Therefore, Cúnjìn was appointed to replace Sìzhāo as Commissioner of Pacification (Zhāotǎoshǐ),
and was stationed at Dōngyuán Crossing.
The soil at Dōngyuán was poor,
and constructing ramparts could not be accomplished.
Cúnjìn cut down timber to build a stockade.
When the Jìn army went out in the morning to forage,
Wénlǐ’s son, Chǔqiú, led more than a thousand troops to press Cúnjìn's stockade.
Cúnjìn went out to fight on the bridge,
killing almost all of Chǔqiú's soldiers,
but Cúnjìn also died in the ranks.
He was posthumously granted the title Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
His son, Hànsháo,
reverted to his original surname during the reign of Míngzōng,
and became the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Yángzhōu.
Lùwáng Cóngkē rebelled at Fèngxiáng.
Hànsháo and Zhāng Qiánzhāo gathered the Táng army to suppress him.
The Táng armies all surrendered to Cóngkē,
but only the armies of Hànsháo and Qiánzhāo refused to surrender,
and both fled to Shǔ.
Serving Shǔ,
he successively held the positions of Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Yǒngpíng, Xīngyuán, and Wǔxìn.
When he was seventy years old or more,
he died in Shǔ.
Cúnzhāng
Lǐ Cúnzhāng, courtesy name Déhuáng,
initially followed Tàizǔ into the Pass with Kāng Jūnlì and Xuē Zhìqín, etc.,
defeated Huáng Cháo,

Zhuāngzōng 好畋獵 (hǎo tiánliè) was fond of hunting.
He hunted in Zhōngmóu,
and trampled the people's fields.
The magistrate of Zhōngmóu county, Dāng Mǎ, immediately admonished him,
pleading for the people.
Zhuāngzōng was enraged,
and shouted at the magistrate to leave,
intending to kill him.
The actor Jìng Xīnmó (Jìng Xīnmó) knew this was unacceptable,
so he led the other actors to chase after the magistrate,
seized him, and brought him before the emperor's horse, scolding him:
"You are a county magistrate,
do you not know that our Son of Heaven is fond of hunting?
How dare you let the people cultivate their land to pay taxes!
Why don't you starve your county's people and clear this land
to prepare for our Son of Heaven's galloping?
Your crime deserves death!"
Then he stepped forward and asked for the immediate execution,
and the other actors all joined in harmony.
Zhuāngzōng laughed heartily,
and the magistrate was thus spared.
Zhuāngzōng once played with a group of actors in the courtyard,
looking around and shouting:
"Lǐ Tiānxià (Lǐ Tiānxià),
where is Lǐ Tiānxià?"
Xīnmó (Xīnmó) immediately stepped forward and slapped his cheek.
Zhuāngzōng's face changed color,
his attendants were all terrified,
and the group of actors were also greatly alarmed.
They all seized Xīnmó and questioned him:
"How dare you slap the Son of Heaven's cheek?"
Xīnmó replied:
"Lǐ Tiānxià (Lǐ Tiānxià)
is one person only;
who else would you call?"
Thereupon, all the attendants laughed,
Zhuāngzōng was greatly pleased,
and bestowed generous gifts upon Xīnmó.
Xīnmó once reported on matters in the palace hall.
There were many vicious dogs in the hall.
As Xīnmó left,
a dog rose and chased him.
Xīnmó leaned against a pillar and shouted:
"Your Majesty, do not let your children bite people!"
Zhuāngzōng's family lineage was of nomadic origin;
people of nomadic origin taboo dogs,
so Xīnmó used this to satirize him.
Zhuāngzōng was greatly enraged,
bent his bow and notched an arrow, intending to shoot him.
Xīnmó urgently cried out:
"Your Majesty, do not kill your subject!
Your subject and Your Majesty are one body;
killing me would be inauspicious!"
Zhuāngzōng was greatly surprised,
and asked him the reason.
He replied:
"Your Majesty founded the dynasty
and changed the era name to Tóngguāng (Tóngguāng).
Everyone in the world calls Your Majesty Emperor Tóngguāng (Tóngguāng Dì).
Moreover, Tóng (Tóng)
is 'copper'.
If you kill Jìng Xīnmó (Jìng Xīnmó),
then Tóng (Tóng) will have no guāng (guāng) (light/glory)!"
Zhuāngzōng laughed heartily,
and thus released him.
However, among the actors of that time,
only Xīnmó was particularly good at jesting,
his words were most notable,
and no other faults or evils of his were heard.
Those who ruined governance and disordered the state
were Jǐng Jìn (Jǐng Jìn), Shǐ Yànqióng (Shǐ Yànqióng), and Guō Méngāo (Guō Méngāo) three individuals, who were the worst.
At that time,
the actors entered and exited the palace chambers,
insulting and toying with officials;
the ministers were indignant and resentful,
but dared not voice their displeasure.
Some even attached themselves to them,
hoping for favor and fortune.
From the four directions, the regional governors
exchanged bribes,
and Jǐng Jìn (Jǐng Jìn) was the most central and influential in affairs.
Zhuāngzōng sent Jìn (Jìn) and others out to investigate among the people,
reporting everything, whether small or large.
Whenever Jìn (Jìn) reported on matters in the palace hall,
all attendants were dismissed,
and he participated in decisions regarding military and state affairs.
The Three Commissioners' Envoy, Kǒng Qiān (Kǒng Qiān), treated him as an elder brother,
calling him
"Bā Gē" (Bā Gē) (Eighth Brother).
When Zhuāngzōng first entered Luò (Luò),
he resided in the former palace of the Táng (Táng) dynasty,
but his consorts were not yet fully prepared.
The eunuchs, hoping to please him,
often spoke of seeing ghosts and spirits in the palace at night,
frightening each other.
Zhuāngzōng asked about ways to ward them off,
and they said:
"In the former Táng (Táng) era,
there were tens of thousands of people in the imperial harem.
Now that the palace is empty, there are many strange occurrences.
It should be filled with people for them to cease."
Zhuāngzōng was delighted.
Later, when Xìngzōng (Xìngzōng) returned to Luò (Luò),
Jìn (Jìn) brought a thousand women from Yè (Yè) to accompany him,
lining the roads,
without distinction between men and women.
Wèi Wáng Jìjí (Wèi Wáng Jìjí) had already conquered Shǔ (Shǔ).
Empress Liú (Liú) listened to the slander of the eunuchs
and sent Jìjí (Jìjí) to kill Guō Chóngtāo (Guō Chóngtāo) as a bandit.
Chóngtāo (Chóngtāo) had always envied actors,
and often restricted them,
so the actors were all pleased by his death.
The emperor's brother, Cúnyì (Cúnyì),
was Chóngtāo's (Chóngtāo's) son-in-law.
Jìn (Jìn) slandered him to Zhuāngzōng, saying:
"Cúnyì (Cúnyì) is about to rebel
to avenge his father-in-law."
Thereupon, he was imprisoned and killed.
Zhū Yǒuqīan (Zhū Yǒuqīan),
who had surrendered to Jìn (Jìn) from Liáng (Liáng) at Hébzhōng (Hébzhōng),
and when Zhuāngzōng entered Luò (Luò),
all the actors sought bribes from Yǒuqīan (Yǒuqīan).
Yǒuqīan (Yǒuqīan) could not provide them and declined.
Jìn (Jìn) then slandered Yǒuqīan (Yǒuqīan), saying:
"Chóngtāo (Chóngtāo) is about to be executed,
Yǒuqīan (Yǒuqīan) is not at ease,
he will certainly rebel;
he should be executed along with his family."
Thereupon, he and his five or six generals were all exterminated,
and the world could not bear their injustice.
Jìn (Jìn)'s
highest official rank reached Silver-Green Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū), Acting Left Vice Censor-in-Chief (Jiǎnjiào Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì jiān Yùshǐ Dàfū),
and Pillar of the State (Shàng Zhùguó).
As for Shǐ Yànqióng (Shǐ Yànqióng),
he served as the Director of Martial Virtues (Wǔdé Shǐ)
and resided in the capital Yè (Yè).
The governance of the six prefectures of Wèibó (Wèibó) was all decided by Yànqióng (Yànqióng).
From the Acting Grand Protector Wáng Zhèngyán (Wáng Zhèngyán) downwards,
all bowed their heads and served him.
At this time,
Guō Chóngtāo (Guō Chóngtāo) had been killed in Shǔ (Shǔ) without cause,
but the world did not yet know of his death.
They only saw his sons being killed in the capital,
and so the rumor spread, saying:
"Chóngtāo (Chóngtāo) killed Wèi Wáng Jìjí (Wèi Wáng Jìjí) and made himself king in Shǔ (Shǔ),
which is why his family was exterminated."
The people of Yè (Yè) heard this and
were in doubt.
Soon after,
Zhū Yǒuqīan (Zhū Yǒuqīan) was also killed.
Yǒuqīan's (Yǒuqīan's) son, Tínghuī (Tínghuī), was the Prefect of Chánzhōu (Chánzhōu).
An imperial edict ordered Yànqióng (Yànqióng) to kill him.
Yànqióng (Yànqióng) kept the matter secret
and galloped out of the city in the middle of the night.
The people of Yè (Yè) saw Yànqióng (Yànqióng) gallop out at night without cause,
and thus spread the alarming rumor, saying:
"Empress Liú (Liú) is angry that Chóngtāo (Chóngtāo) killed Jìjí (Jìjí),
and has already murdered the emperor and enthroned herself.
She urgently summoned Yànqióng (Yànqióng) to discuss matters."
The capital Yè (Yè) was greatly alarmed.
A person from Bèizhōu (Bèizhōu) who came to Yè (Yè)
returned with this story.
The garrison soldier Huángfǔ Huī (Huángfǔ Huī) heard it
and consequently coerced Zhào Zàilǐ (Zhào Zàilǐ) into rebellion.
When Zàilǐ (Zàilǐ) had already reached Guǎntáo (Guǎntáo),
Sūn Duó (Sūn Duó), the inspector of Yè (Yè) capital,
saw Yànqióng (Yànqióng) and requested troops to resist the bandits.
Yànqióng (Yànqióng) refused to provide them,
saying:
"The bandits haven't arrived yet.
Will it be too late to give troops when they arrive?"
Soon after, the bandits arrived.
Yànqióng (Yànqióng) went to the North Gate with troops,
but hearing the shouts of the bandits,
he was greatly terrified,
abandoned his troops, and fled,
returning alone to the capital.
That Zàilǐ (Zàilǐ) was able to enter Yè (Yè) and complete his rebellion
was due to Yànqióng (Yànqióng) enabling and releasing him.
Guō Mén Gāo's
name was Cóngqiān.
Mén Gāo was his stage name as an entertainer.
Although he had entered service as an entertainer,
he had also accumulated military merits,
and so he was appointed as the Commander of the Cóngmǎzhí.
The Cóngmǎzhí
were, in fact, the imperial guard.
Because Cóngqiān's surname was Guō,
he recognized Chóngtāo as his uncle,
and the imperial younger brother Cún'yì also took Cóngqiān as his adopted son.
When Chóngtāo died
and Cún'yì was imprisoned,
Cóngqiān hosted a banquet in the army,
and indignantly shed tears,
lamenting the injustice suffered by these two men.
At this time,
Wáng Wēn, a soldier of the Cóngmǎzhí, was guarding the forbidden palace.
He plotted a rebellion at night,
but the plot was discovered and he was executed.
Zhuāngzōng jokingly said to Cóngqiān:
"You sided with Cún'yì and Chóngtāo against me,
and then instigated Wáng Wēn to rebel.
What more do you intend to do?"
Cóngqiān was frightened,
and withdrawing, he incited his soldiers, saying:
"Spend all your wealth,
eat meat and drink wine;
don't plan for tomorrow."
When the soldiers asked the reason,
Cóngqiān then said:
"The Emperor, because of Wáng Wēn,
will, after Yè is conquered,
bury all of you alive."
The soldiers believed him,
and all desired to rebel.
Lǐ Sìyuán's forces rebelled
and advanced towards the capital.
Zhuāngzōng fled east to Biànzhōu,
but Sìyuán entered first.
Zhuāngzōng reached Wànshèng
but could not advance and returned.
His soldiers dispersed,
but there were still over twenty thousand remaining.
After a few days,
Zhuāngzōng again fled east to Sìshuǐ,
planning to secure the pass to resist.
On the first day of the fourth month, on a Dīnghài day,
he held court with his officials in the Zhōngxīng Diàn.
The prime ministers were dismissed after three *kè*.
The imperial guard cavalry in yellow armor were arrayed at the Xuānrén Mén, and the infantry at the Wǔfèng Mén, awaiting orders.
Zhuāngzōng entered the inner palace to eat.
Cóngqiān, from his camp, openly drew his sword and readied arrows,
then galloped to attack the Xìngjiào Mén,
engaging in archery with the yellow-armored cavalry.
Zhuāngzōng heard the commotion,
and led the princes and guards to strike the rebellious soldiers and exit the gate.
The rebellious soldiers set fire to the gate,
and scaled the city wall to enter.
Zhuāngzōng struck and killed several tens or hundreds of people.
The rebellious soldiers shot the Emperor from the upper story of a building.
The Emperor was gravely wounded
and fell beneath the corridor of the Jiàngxiāo Diàn.
From the Empress to the princes and attendants, all fled.
Around noon,
the Emperor died.
Shànyǒu, a man of the Wǔfāng,
gathered musical instruments and burned them.
Sìyuán entered Luò,
found his bones,
and buried them in the Yōng Líng in Xīn'ān.
Cóngqiān was appointed Governor of Jǐngzhōu,
but was killed shortly thereafter.
The tradition says:
"A ruler who begins with this
will surely end with this."
Zhuāngzōng was fond of entertainers,
and was assassinated by Mén Gāo,
and burned with musical instruments.
How could one not believe this!
How could one not take warning!

Zhāng Chéngyè
Zhāng Chéngyè, courtesy name Jìyuán,
was a eunuch during the reign of Emperor Xīzōng of Táng.
His original surname was Kāng.
Emasculated in childhood,
he became the adopted son of Zhāng Tài, a Court Attendant.
When the King of Jìn's forces attacked Wáng Xíngyú,
Chéngyè frequently traveled between the armies,
and the King of Jìn was pleased with his character.
When Zhāozōng was later pressured by Lǐ Màozhēn
and was about to flee to Tàiyuán,
he first sent Chéngyè on a mission to Jìn to convey his intentions,
