and subsequently appointed him as Supervisor of the Army for Hédōng.
Later, when Cuī Yìn executed eunuchs,
an imperial edict was issued to all localities to kill
all eunuchs who were outside the capital.
The King of Jìn pitied Chéngyè,
could not bear to kill him,
and hid him in Húlǜ Sì.
When Zhāozōng died,
Chéngyè was brought out
and reinstated as Supervisor of the Army.
When the King of Jìn was critically ill,
he entrusted Zhuāngzōng to Chéngyè, saying:
"I burden you all with my second son!"
Zhuāngzōng always treated Chéngyè like an elder brother.
Annually, he would ascend to the hall to pay respects to Chéngyè's mother,
showing him great affection and respect.
When Zhuāngzōng was in Wèi,
fighting against Liáng on the river for over ten years,
he entrusted all military and state affairs to Chéngyè,
and Chéngyè also devoted himself tirelessly.
Therefore, it was largely due to Chéngyè's efforts
that gold and grain were accumulated,
soldiers and horses were procured,
and agriculture and sericulture were encouraged,
thereby helping Zhuāngzōng achieve his great enterprise.
Chéngyè's contribution was significant.
From Empress Zhēnjiǎn, Consort Hán Défēi, Consort Yī Shúfēi, and all the princes who were in Jìnyáng,
Chéngyè disciplined them all according to the law,
and the powerful and noble all held back their hands and feared Chéngyè.
Annually, when Zhuāngzōng returned from Wèi to visit his parents,
he needed money for gambling and rewarding entertainers.
But Chéngyè was in charge of the treasury,
and no money could be obtained.
Zhuāngzōng then set up a banquet in the treasury.
When the wine flowed freely,
he had his son Jìjí dance for Chéngyè.
After the dance,
Chéngyè presented a precious belt, silk, and a horse as gifts.
Zhuāngzōng pointed to the pile of money and called Jìjí's pet name to Chéngyè, saying:
"Hégē is short of money,
you should give him a pile of money,
what use are the belt and horse?"
Chéngyè bowed and said:
"The state's money
is not for your servant to privately dispense."
Zhuāngzōng's words provoked him,
and Chéngyè angrily said:
"Your servant,
an old imperial envoy,
does not save this treasury money for his descendants,
but to assist the King in achieving his hegemonic enterprise!
If you wish to use it,
why must you ask your servant?
When wealth is exhausted and soldiers disperse,
will your servant alone suffer calamity?"
Zhuāngzōng looked at Yuán Xíngqīn and said:
"Bring the sword!"
Chéngyè rose,
grabbed Zhuāngzōng's clothes and wept,
saying:
"Your servant received the late King's dying entrustment
and swore to avenge the family's and state's enmity.
Today, if I die for the King's sake, protecting the treasury,
I will not be ashamed before the late King!"
Yán Bǎo from the side tried to release Chéngyè's hand and told him to leave.
Chéngyè clenched his fist, punched Bǎo and knocked him down,
cursing:
"Yán Bǎo,
you scoundrel of Zhū Wēn,
having received generous favors from Jìn,
cannot offer a single loyal word,
but instead resort to flattery to save yourself!"
The Empress Dowager heard of this
and sent for Zhuāngzōng.
Zhuāngzōng was extremely filial by nature.
Upon hearing the Empress Dowager's summons,
he was very afraid,
and then poured two cups of wine, apologizing to Chéngyè, saying:
"My mistake with the wine
has offended the Empress Dowager.
I wish you to drink this
to share my fault!"
Chéngyè refused to drink.
Zhuāngzōng went inside,
and the Empress Dowager sent someone to apologize to Chéngyè, saying:
"My child offended you,
and has already been whipped."
The next day,
the Empress Dowager and Zhuāngzōng both visited Chéngyè's residence
to comfort and console him.
Lú Zhì was addicted to wine, arrogant, and negligent.
He frequently insulted and slighted both Zhuāngzōng and the various princes.
Zhuāngzōng deeply resented this.
Chéngyè seized an opportunity and requested, saying:
“Lú Zhì is addicted to wine and rude.
I request permission from Your Highness to execute him.”
Zhuāngzōng said:
“I am currently recruiting and welcoming capable men in order to complete my great enterprise.
How excessively wrong your words are!”
Chéngyè stood up and offered congratulations, saying:
“If Your Highness can act like this,
then pacifying the world will be no difficulty!”
Zhì was consequently spared.
In Tiānyòu eighteenth year (921 CE),
Zhuāngzōng had already promised his generals that he would ascend the imperial throne.
Chéngyè was currently confined by illness.
When he heard this,
he traveled by sedan chair from Tàiyuán to Wèi,
and remonstrated, saying:
“Your Royal Highness and your father fought bloody battles against Liáng for thirty years.
The original intention was to avenge the grievances of the family and the state,
and to restore the altars of the Shè and Jì (the state) of Táng.
Now the chief villain (Zhū Wén) is not yet destroyed,
yet you hastily assume the respected title yourself.
This is not the original intention of Your Highness and your father,
and moreover, it will disappoint the expectations of the world.
This is impermissible!”
Zhuāngzōng apologized, saying:
“This is what the generals desire.”
Chéngyè said:
“That is not so.
Liáng
is the hated enemy of Táng and Jìn,
and is universally loathed by the world.
If Your Highness can truly eliminate this great evil for the world,
and avenge the profound enmity of the former sagely rulers,
and only then seek out a descendant of Táng and establish him,
if a descendant of Táng exists,
who would dare oppose you?
If Táng has no descendants,
then among the scholars of the world,
who could possibly contend with Your Highness?
I, your subject,
am merely an old slave of the Táng house!
I sincerely wish to witness the successful accomplishment of Your Royal Highness,
and then retire to the countryside,
having the officials escort me out of the Eastern Gate of Luòyáng,
and letting passersby point and sigh, saying, ‘This is an Imperial Envoy of the previous dynasty,
the Supervisor of Armies during the time of the former king.’
Would not both the subject and the ruler be glorified?”
Zhuāngzōng did not listen.
Chéngyè knew he could not remonstrate further,
and so he looked up to heaven and cried loudly, saying:
“My King brings this upon himself!
He has misled this old slave.”
He returned by sedan chair to Tàiyuán,
refused food, and died,
at the age of seventy-seven.
In Tóngguāng first year (923 CE),
he was posthumously granted the title of Superior General of the Left Wǔwèi Guard,
with the posthumous name Zhèngxiàn.
Zhāng Jūhàn
Zhāng Jūhàn, courtesy name Déqīng,
was the adopted son of Zhāng Cóngméi, the former Supervisor of the Palace Ward of Táng.
During the reign of Zhāozōng,
he served as the Supervisor of Armies for the Fànyáng Army,
and maintained good relations with the Jìedùshǐ Liú Rěngōng.
In the middle of the Tiānfù era (901-904 CE),
when a great purge of eunuchs occurred,
Rěngōng hid Jūhàn in a northern ravine of Dà'ānshān, allowing him to escape.
After that,
when the Liáng forces attacked Rěngōng,
Rěngōng sent Jūhàn to follow the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng) in attacking the Liáng-held prefecture of Lùzhōu in order to divert their troops.
Jìn subsequently captured Lùzhōu,
and appointed Jūhàn as the Supervisor of Armies for Zhāoyì.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he served alongside Guō Chóngtāo as a Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs).
After Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng, he became arrogant,
and the eunuchs consequently gained influence.
Furthermore, Guō Chóngtāo monopolized political power.
Jūhàn remained silent,
content merely to escape danger.
When the Prince of Wèi (Wèi Wáng) conquered Shǔ (Former Shǔ),
Wáng Yăn came to pay court in the capital.
He had traveled as far as Qínchuān,
when Míngzōng’s army mutinied at Wèi.
Zhuāngzōng was campaigning eastward,
fearing that Yăn might cause trouble.
He dispatched a messenger to rush an imperial decree to the Prince of Wèi ordering him to execute Yăn.
The imperial decree had already been sealed and signed,
but Jūhàn opened it and examined it.
The decree said
“Execute Yăn and his *yī xíng* (entire party/retinue).”
Jūhàn considered the killing of surrendered people inauspicious.
He thus plastered the decree onto a pillar,
rubbed away
the character *xíng*,
and changed it to the character
*jiā* (family/household).
At that time, over a thousand surrendered Shǔ people were traveling eastward with Yăn;
all of them were spared.
When Zhuāngzōng was assassinated,
Jūhàn met Míngzōng at the Zhìdé Palace,
and requested permission to retire to the countryside.
In Tiānchéng third year (928 CE),
he died in Cháng'ān,
at the age of seventy-one.
The literature of the Five Dynasties was crude,
and the duties of the official historians were abandoned amid the chaos of loss and disorder.
Many biographies and anecdotal writings were lost.
Therefore, the accounts of events,
are incomplete from start to finish,
and mixed with errors and falsehoods.
Regarding the rise of heroes and outstanding figures,
the victories and defeats in war,
and the periods of prosperity and collapse of states,
how could there not have been strategies from counselors,
and arguments from eloquent men?
Yet the written records are insufficient to reveal them,
thus causing them to vanish and leave nothing transmitted to later generations.
However, the deeds of Zhāng Chéngyè alone are prominent in people’s eyes and ears.
Even now, old veterans can still speak of them.
His discussions and counsel can be called truly outstanding!
They are truly not the words of a typical eunuch.
Since ancient times, eunuchs who have brought chaos to a state,
their source of disaster is deeper than that of women.
Women
are merely about sexual appeal;
the harm caused by eunuchs
is not limited to a single aspect.
This is because when they exercise power, they are close and familiar to the ruler.
Their methods are focused and ruthless.
They are able to hit the mark of the ruler’s desires with minor kindnesses,
and cement the ruler's heart with small demonstrations of trustworthiness,
thus ensuring the ruler trusts and favors them.
Once they are trusted,
they then hold sway over the ruler by inducing fear of misfortune or hope of good fortune.
Even if loyal ministers and great scholars stand arrayed in the court,
the ruler considers them distant and remote,
not comparable to the familiarity of those who attend to him in his rising and resting, eating and drinking, and stand before and behind him, and to his left and right—these are deemed more reliable.
Therefore, those before and behind, left and right, grow increasingly intimate,
while loyal ministers and great scholars become increasingly distant,
and the power of the ruler becomes increasingly isolated.
If his power is isolated,
then the fear of disaster grows increasingly urgent,
and those who hold sway become increasingly secure in their grip.
Safety or danger depends upon their pleasure or displeasure;
misfortune and calamity lurk behind the palace gates.
Then those who were previously deemed reliable
are precisely the source of the trouble.
When the trouble is already deep and the ruler realizes it,
and wishes to conspire with distant officials against the intimate attendants,
if he proceeds slowly, he nourishes the disaster and it deepens;
if he proceeds quickly, they hold the ruler hostage.
Even with sagely wisdom, one cannot plan against them.
If one plans, it cannot be achieved;
if one acts, it cannot be brought to success.
In the worst cases,
both sides suffer injury and both are defeated.
Therefore, the greater consequences lead to the collapse of the state;
the lesser consequences lead to the destruction of the ruler himself.
They allow cunning and powerful figures to use this weakness as a basis to rise up,
until they eliminate the entire lineage [of the eunuchs],
and kill them all to satisfy the hearts of the people of the world before stopping.
The disasters caused by eunuchs recorded in previous histories have always been like this,
and not just in one era.
Rulers
do not intentionally wish to nurture disaster within and alienate loyal ministers and great scholars without.
It is merely a consequence of gradual accumulation and the momentum of circumstances.
If misled by feminine charm,
if one fails to realize the mistake,
disaster will then strike.
But if the ruler once awakens to the danger,
he can seize and dismiss them.
When eunuchs create disaster,
even if the ruler wishes to repent and awaken,
the circumstances may prevent him from removing them.
The affairs of Táng Zhāozōng serve as an example of this.
Therefore, saying
“deeper than the harm caused by women”
refers to this situation.
How can one not be warned!
Zhāozōng trusted and was familiar with the eunuchs,
which led to his confinement in the Eastern Palace.
After he was released, he planned with Cuī Yìn,
and Yìn became Chancellor.
However, realizing he lacked the strength to act,
he summoned troops from Liáng.
As the Liáng troops were about to arrive,
the eunuchs took the Son of Heaven (the Emperor) hostage and fled to Qí.
The Liáng army besieged Qí for three years.
Although Zhāozōng was eventually released,
Táng perished.
Initially,
when Zhāozōng (昭宗) left (the capital),
the King of Liáng (Liáng Wáng 梁王) executed all of Táng’s (唐) eunuchs, including Dìwǔ Kěfàn (第五可範) and over seven hundred others.
As for those who were outside (the capital),
he ordered the entire realm to capture and kill them all.
However, many eunuchs were hidden and not killed by the various regional commanders (zhèn 鎮).
At that time,
the regional commanders (fāngzhèn 方鎮) usurped imperial prerogatives,
and all employed eunuchs to attend to their affairs,
with Wúyuè (吳越) having the most.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) was established,
he ordered the realm to search for the eunuchs from the former Táng era and send them all to the capital.
Several hundred people were found,
and the eunuchs consequently resumed holding power,
leading ultimately to ruin.
How is this different from seeking out a cart that has already overturned,
and personally driving upon its tracks?
It is truly lamentable!
Before Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
Chéngyè (承業) had already died.
Afterward, although Jūhàn (居翰) served as the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ 樞密使),
he did not wield power.
There was the Palace Affairs Commissioner (Xuānhuī Shǐ 宣徽使) Mǎ Shàohóng (馬紹宏),
who had previously been granted the surname Lǐ (李),
and was considerably trusted.
However, those who falsely accused and killed high ministers,
defiled themselves with bribes,
monopolized authority and benefits,
and incurred the resentment of the entire realm,
were the attendants and intimates,
the ranks of the inner palace officials and servants (huángmén nèiyǎng 黃門內養).
At that time,
Míngzōng (明宗) entered the capital from Zhènzhōu (鎮州) to pay court,
attending the imperial summons in the capital city.
Zhuāngzōng rather suspected that he harbored rebellious intentions,
and secretly sent Shàohóng to observe his movements.
Shàohóng, conversely, informed Míngzōng of the situation.
Míngzōng rebelled from Wèi (魏),
and everyone in the realm knew that the calamity arose in Wèi.
But who knew that the one who incited Míngzōng's disloyalty
was Shàohóng himself?
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜) had already conquered Shǔ (蜀),
but Zhuāngzōng believed the words of the eunuchs and grew suspicious of him.
However, Zhuāngzōng did not know of
Chóngtāo’s death;
it was all done by the eunuchs.
At this juncture,
all the elite troops of Táng were in Shǔ.
Had Chóngtāo not died,
when Míngzōng entered Luò (洛),
would there not have been the peril of him looking west?
Could he have smoothly taken over Táng and replaced it?
When Míngzōng subsequently entered (the capital) and was established (as emperor),
he again ordered the realm to capture and execute all the eunuchs.
The eunuchs fled and hid in the mountains and valleys,
many shaving their heads to become Buddhist monks (fútú 浮圖).
Over seventy who fled to Tàiyuán (太原)
were all captured and killed at the Dūtíng Relay Station (Dūtíng Yì 都亭驛),
their blood filling the courtyard.
In his later years, Míngzōng suffered frequent illnesses,
and Consort Wáng Shūfēi (王淑妃) monopolized the inner palace and interfered in government.
The eunuch Mèng Hànqióng (孟漢瓊) consequently gained power.
The King of Qín (Qín Wáng 秦王) entered to see Míngzōng, whose illness was already critical.
After leaving, he heard sounds of wailing,
and believed the Emperor had died.
He then plotted to enter the palace with soldiers,
fearing he would not be established (as successor).
The high minister Zhū Hóngzhāo (朱弘昭) and others were planning the affair,
but the discussion had not been resolved,
when Hànqióng abruptly entered to see Míngzōng,
and stated that the King of Qín was rebelling.
He immediately used soldiers to execute him,
thereby causing the King of Qín to incur a great crime,
and Míngzōng died with this unresolved resentment.
Later, Mǐndì (愍帝) fled to Wèizhōu (衞州).
Hànqióng went west to welcome the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì 廢帝) on the road.
The Deposed Emperor disliked him and had him executed.
Alas!
Human nature, when situated in peace and comfort,
unless it belongs to a sage or philosopher,
cannot endure long without arrogance and negligence.
The calamities caused by eunuchs and women do not arise in a single day;
they must wait for people to become arrogant and negligent before gradually infiltrating.
Míngzōng was not an indolent ruler,
yet he still suffered this fate;
it was probably because he had been on the throne for a relatively long time.
The rest (of the rulers) were mostly martial men who rose to power,
and their successors
reigned for a short period and did not live long,
thus the eunuchs did not have the opportunity to act.
The major harm caused by them
can generally be seen.
Only the proposal of Chéngyè
was remarkably admirable,
and Jūhàn changed a single character, thereby saving a thousand people.
When a superior man (jūnzǐ 君子) deals with others,
if there is any goodness in them,
he accepts it without fail.
I accept something from these two men.
I accept their goodness and warn against their evil,
which is what is meant by
“loving someone while knowing their faults,
and hating someone while knowing their virtues.”
Therefore, I have documented the reasons for their calamities and failures in this section.
Miscellaneous Biographies 27: Wáng Róng (王鎔).
Wáng Róng’s
ancestor was a surviving descendant of the Uighur Ābùsī (阿布思),
named Mònuògān (沒諾干).
He served as a cavalry general under Wáng Wǔjùn (王武俊) of Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
Wǔjùn adopted him as a son,
and he subsequently took the surname Wáng.
Mònuògān’s son was Mòtǎnhuó (末坦活).
Mòtǎnhuó’s son was Shēng (昇).
Shēng’s son was Tíngcòu (廷湊).
Tíngcòu’s son was Yuánkuí (元逵).
Yuánkuí’s sons were Shàodǐng (紹鼎) and Shàoyì (紹懿).
Shàodǐng’s son was Jǐngchóng (景崇).
The three generations starting from Shēng and earlier
were consistently cavalry generals of Zhènzhōu.
The four generations and five men starting from Jǐngchóng and earlier
all served as Military Commissioners (Jiédù Shǐ 節度使) of the Chéngdé Army (Chéngdé Jūn 成德軍).
Jǐngchóng’s office reached the rank of Acting Grand Commandant (Shǒu Tàilìwèi 守太尉),
and he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chángshān Commandery (Chángshān Jùn Wáng 常山郡王).
He died in the second year of Zhōnghé (中和) of Táng (882 CE).
His son Róng was established
at the age of ten.
At that time,
Jìn (晉) had recently acquired Tàiyuán (太原).
Lǐ Kuāngwēi (李匡威) occupied Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Wáng Chǔcún (王處存) occupied Zhōngshān (中山).
Hèlián Duó (赫連鐸) occupied Dàtóng (大同).
Mèng Fānglì (孟方立) occupied Xíngtái (邢臺).
Heroes arose on all four sides and fought amongst themselves.
Róng was situated in the middle of them,
and inherited the century-long enterprise of his ancestors and father.
His soldiers and horses were strong, and his accumulated wealth was great.
He served as a vassal of Táng for generations.
Therefore, although Róng was young,
he gained prestige relying on his inherited lineage.
When the regional commanders on all four sides deposed, established, or succeeded rulers,
those who had requests for Táng
all used Róng as an intermediary to report them.
When the Jìn troops emerged eastward from the mountains (Shāndōng 山東),
they had already defeated Mèng Qiān (孟遷),
and taken the three prefectures of Xíng (邢), Míng (洺), and Cí (磁).
In the first year of Jǐngfú (景福, 892 CE),
they launched a major attack on Zhào (趙),
and captured Línchéng (臨城).
Róng sought aid from Lǐ Kuāngwēi.
Kuāngwēi came to the rescue,
and the Jìn army withdrew.
The following year,
Jìn allied with Wáng Chǔcún to attack Róng at Jiāngù (堅固) and Xīnshì (新市).
The King of Jìn (Jìn Wáng 晉王) and Chǔcún both personally led their forces,
but Róng never personally oversaw the troops.

He dispatched Duàn Liàng (段亮), Commander of the Chuīfēng Training Regiment (Chuīfēng Dū Tuánliàn Shǐ 追風都團練使), Mǎ Kē (馬珂), Commander of the Jiǎnkòu Training Regiment (Jiǎnkòu Dū Tuánliàn Shǐ 翦寇都團練使), and others,
to place their troops under Kuāngwēi’s command, and nothing more.
Kuāngwēi fought at the Cí River (Cí Hé 磁河),
and the Jìn army was utterly defeated.
In the spring of the following year,
Jìn attacked Tiāncháng Garrison (Tiāncháng Jūn 天長軍).
Róng dispatched troops to rescue it,
but was defeated at Chìrì Ridge (Chìrì Lǐng 叱日嶺).
The Jìn army subsequently advanced out of Jǐngxíng (井陘).
Róng again sought aid from Kuāngwēi,
and the Jìn army withdrew.
Initially,
Kuāngwēi was attracted to the beauty of his younger brother Kuāngchóu’s (匡儔) wife and seduced her.
Kuāngchóu was enraged,
and while Kuāngwēi was rescuing Róng,
Kuāngchóu incited his army to mutiny and established himself (as commander).
Kuāngwēi was internally ashamed and dared not return,
so he surrendered his official seals and tallies to his younger brother,
and planned to flee to the capital.
When he traveled as far as Shēnzhōu (深州),
Róng, grateful for Kuāngwēi’s rescue,
sent men to welcome him,
housed him at Méiziyuán (梅子園),
and treated him as a father.
Kuāng Wēi’s guest, Lǐ Zhèngbào,
had travelled around Yān and Zhào in his youth.
He often lingered in Chángshān,
loving it so much he could not leave.
Zhèngbào and Kuāng Wēi were both demoralized, having lost their state.
They ascended the high tower west of the city together.
Looking out over the mountains and rivers,
they wept profusely.
Thereupon, they plotted with Kuāng Wēi to seize Wáng Róng and replace him.
They falsely claimed it was a death anniversary (jìrì),
causing Wáng Róng to dismiss his personal guards.
In the morning, they went to the residence to offer condolences.
Once they were seated firmly,
armored soldiers emerged from behind the screen,
holding Wáng Róng by both sleeves.
Wáng Róng said:
"My state survives relying on you, sirs.
I truly have no way to repay your great kindness.
The matter today
is what I am willing to accept."
Then he kowtowed and yielded his position to Kuāng Wēi.
Kuāng Wēi had always held Wáng Róng in contempt,
thinking he was incompetent.
Therefore, he rode side-by-side with Wáng Róng to the headquarters,
intending to take his place.
As they passed the Qīnshì Camp,
the soldiers closed the gates and raised a great uproar.
The sky rained with thunder and lightning;
fierce winds uprooted trees,
and roof tiles were all blown away.
Mò Jūnhé, a butcher, looked up and saw Wáng Róng,
recognizing him.
He leapt out from a gap in the wall,
pulled Wáng Róng onto his horse,
and carried him away, fleeing.
The chaotic army struck and killed Kuāng Wēi and Zhèngbào.
The Yān men all fled.
Although Kuāng Chóu regretted his brother’s actions,
he publicly denounced Wáng Róng fiercely in the name of righteousness.
Since Wáng Róng had lost the support of Yān,
and the Jìn army was urgently attacking Píngshān,
they coerced Wáng Róng into an alliance.
Wáng Róng subsequently made peace with Jìn.
Afterwards, Liáng Tàizǔ captured Jìn’s three prefectures, Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
He then wrote a letter summoning Wáng Róng,
instructing him to break ties with Jìn and defect to Liáng.
Wáng Róng hesitated and could not decide.
The Jìn general Lǐ Sìzhāo recaptured Míngzhōu.
Liáng Tàizǔ defeated Sìzhāo,
and Sìzhāo abandoned Míngzhōu and fled.
Liáng captured his baggage train.
They obtained a letter from Wáng Róng to Sìzhāo,
which mentioned many matters concerning Liáng.
Tàizǔ was enraged.
Consequently, he moved his troops to Chángshān.
He looked at Gě Cóngzhōu and said:
"If I capture Zhènzhōu, I will give it to you.
You shall be my vanguard."
Cóngzhōu reached Línchéng,
was struck by a stray arrow,
and lay in his litter.
The Liáng army was greatly disheartened.
Liáng Tàizǔ personally led his forces to the foot of the city wall
and burned its Southern Gate (Nánguān).
Wáng Róng was frightened.
He looked at his subordinates and said:
"The situation is desperate!
What shall we do?"
The Assistant Administrator, Zhōu Shì,
was a skilled debater.
He replied:
"This is difficult to contest by force,
but it can be won by reason."
Shì had a previous acquaintance with Liáng Tàizǔ.
Consequently, he requested permission to enter the Liáng camp.
Tàizǔ saw Shì approaching
and cursed, saying:
"I have often invited Wáng Róng by letter, but he did not come.
Now that I have arrived here,
and you come as an advocate,
it is too late!
Moreover, Jìn is my enemy,
yet Wáng Róng adheres to them.
I know Lǐ Sìzhāo is inside the city,
you can ask him to come out first."
Then he showed Shì the letter he had obtained from Wáng Róng to Sìzhāo.
Shì stepped forward and said:
"Does Liáng intend merely to seize one Zhènzhōu and stop there,
or does it desire to achieve hegemony over All Under Heaven (Tiānxià)?
Furthermore, a hegemon holds others accountable by righteousness and is not selfish.
Currently, the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) is above;
the regional lords (zhūhóu) maintain their fiefdoms and live in harmony with their neighbors.
This is how conflict is quelled
and the people are rested.
Formerly, when Cáo Gōng defeated Yuán Shào,
he obtained letters from Wèi generals and officials to Yuán Shào
and burned them all.
Is this not the act of a hero (yīngxióng)?
Now, Liáng knows that its military action lacks justification (wúmíng),
yet it uses Sìzhāo as an excuse.
Moreover, the Wáng clan, through five generations and six lords (gōng), has governed this territory.
Could they possibly lack dedicated warriors
such that they would rely on Sìzhāo?"
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased.
He rose, pulled Shì's sleeve, patted him, and said:
"I was just speaking in jest."
He then invited Shì to the seat of honor
and discussed making peace with Wáng Róng.
Wáng Róng sent his son, Wáng Zhàozuò, as a hostage.
Liáng Tàizǔ gave a daughter to him in marriage.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Wáng Róng as King of Zhào (Zhàowáng).
(Ancient texts read zhāo.)
(One version reads jué.)
When Wáng Róng’s paternal grandmother died,
all the regional governors (zhèn) offered condolences.
The Liáng envoy saw the Jìn envoy at the residence,
returned, and reported that the King of Zhào had divided loyalties (èr zhì).
At this time,
Luó Shàowēi of Wèibó died.
Liáng therefore intended to seize all of Héběi.
In the winter of the fourth year of Kāipíng,
they dispatched the Palace Attendant Dù Tíngyǐn to oversee Xià Yīn, a Wèibó general,
with three thousand troops, to attack Shēn and Jì prefectures.
Wáng Jǐngrén was appointed Commissioner for Northern Field Operations (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎo Shǐ).
Wáng Róng was afraid
and begged for troops from Jìn.
The Jìn forces defeated Jǐngrén at Bǎixiāng.
Liáng consequently lost Zhèn and Dìng prefectures.
Zhuāngzōng thereby grew stronger.
To the north, he conquered Yōu and Yān;
to the south, he annexed Wèibó.
Wáng Róng always followed him with troops.
Wáng Róng was extremely grateful to Jìn.
The following year,
he met Zhuāngzōng at Chéngtiān Commandery.
He presented a cup of wine to wish him longevity.
Zhuāngzōng, regarding Wáng Róng as his father's friend,
treated him with great respect.
When the wine was flowing freely, Zhuāngzōng sang for Wáng Róng,
drew his waist knife, cut his robe, and swore an oath,
promising to give a daughter in marriage to Wáng Róng’s son, Wáng Zhāohuì.
Róng was benevolent but not martial;
he never dared to lead troops in battle,
and when other armies attacked Zhào,
he often relied on neighboring troops for aid.
At that time,
while the various regional governors were being exhausted by warfare,
Zhào alone was at peace.
People enjoyed the Wang clan's lack of military engagement.
The residents and women of the capital wore voluminous robes and wide belts,
focusing on extravagance for amusement and pleasure.
Róng was especially arrogant due to his wealth and status,
and he also favored unorthodox paths,
refining elixirs,
seeking longevity.
He stayed and traveled with the Daoist Wáng Ruònè in Xīshān,
ascending the Shrine of the Queen Mother (Wángmǔ Cí).
He had women in embroidered brocade robes lead him up by pulling on them.
Whenever he went out,
he would forget to return for over a month,
leaving the governance to his eunuchs.
The eunuch Shí Xīméng slept and rose with Róng.
In the winter of Tiānyòu 18 (921 CE),
Róng left Xīshān and lodged at Gǔyíng Zhuāng.
When he was about to return to the prefectural seat,
Xīméng stopped him.
The eunuch Lǐ Hóngguī remonstrated, saying:
“The Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng) now exposes himself to arrows and stones personally,
yet Your Highness exhausts the military and state resources for hunting and traveling expenses,
leaving the city gates open and the palace empty,
failing to return for over a month.
You let a single man close the gates and refuse entry to your attendants.
Where does Your Highness plan to return?”
Róng was afraid
and hurried his carriage.
Xīméng firmly stopped him.
Hóngguī grew angry
and sent his personal guard commander Sū Hànghéng to lead troops, donning armor and exposing their blades before the tent, saying:
“The soldiers are tired!
We wish to follow the Prince back.”
Hóngguī then advanced and said:
“It is Xīméng who confuses the Prince!
Please kill him to apologize to the soldiers!”
Róng did not reply.
Hóngguī called upon Róng's armored guards to behead Xīméng,
and threw the head before Róng.
Róng, terrified,
hastily returned.
He ordered his son Zhāo Zuò and the great general Zhāng Wénlǐ to exterminate the families of Hóngguī and Hànghéng,
and arrested their deputy commanders, throwing them into prison
to thoroughly investigate their alleged rebellion.
All of the personal guards were frightened.
Wénlǐ incited them to cause trouble.
At midnight,
over a thousand personal guards climbed over the wall and entered.
Róng was at the time burning incense and receiving Daoist talismans with a Daoist priest.
The soldiers chopped off Róng's head,
hid it in a sleeve, and departed.
They then set fire to his palace and residences,
thereby wiping out the Wáng clan.
Róng's young son, Zhāo Huì,
was ten years old.
A soldier among the guards who was grateful to Róng
hid him in a pit.
When the chaos subsided,
he shaved his head
and dressed him in monk's robes.
He met Lǐ Zhèn, a man from Húnán,
who concealed Zhāo Huì in a tea basket
and carried him to Húnán.
He relied on Nányuè to become a Buddhist monk,
changing his name to Chóngyǐn.
During the reign of Míngzōng,
Zhāo Huì had grown up
and wished to return home.
Róng's former general Fú Xí was then the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Xuānwǔ Commandery.
Zhèn brought him to Xí,
and Xí submitted a memorial to the court.
Zhāo Huì presented himself, claiming to be the former Commander of the Central Army of Chéngdé Commandery,
and was appointed Kǎogōng Lángzhōng and Sīnóng Shàoqīng.
During the Xiǎndé reign of the Zhōu dynasty,
he was still serving as Shàofǔ Jiān.
Zhāng Wénlǐ
was a cunning and wicked man.
Róng was infatuated with him
and adopted him as a son,
calling him Wáng Démíng.
After Róng died,
Wénlǐ appointed himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
Zhuāngzōng initially accepted him,
but later learned he was communicating with Liáng,
and sent Fú Xí, a former Zhào general, and Yán Bǎo to attack him.
Ghosts cried at night in Wénlǐ's house,
the water in the wild river turned to blood,
and all the swimming fish died.
Wénlǐ was afraid
and died of carbuncles.
His son Chǔ Jǐn kept the death secret and continued to hold the defense,
defeating Xí and the others.
Lǐ Sìzhāo was appointed to replace them,
but Sìzhāo died from a stray arrow.
Lǐ Cúnjìn was appointed to replace him,
but Cúnjìn immediately died in battle again.
Then Fú Cúnshěn was appointed Commissioner for Expedition (Zhāotǎoshǐ),
and he subsequently defeated them.
They captured Wénlǐ's wife and sons Chǔ Jǐn, Chǔ Qiú, and Chǔ Qí, etc.,
breaking their legs and sending them back to Jìn.
The people of Zhào requested that they be pickled (in brine)
and Wénlǐ's corpse was displayed in pieces in the marketplace.
Luó Shàowēi
Luó Shàowēi, courtesy name Duānjǐ,
was originally from Chángshā.
His grandfather, Ràng,
moved north and became a resident of Guìxiāng in Wèizhōu.
His father, Hóngxìn,
served as a stable supervisor and died.
In the first year of Wéndé (888 CE),
the Ya Army (Yájūn) of Wèibó mutinied,
subsequently killing their commander, Lè Yànzhēn,
and setting up his general Zhào Wénjiàn as Acting Military Governor.
Soon after, they killed him too.
The Ya Army generals did not know whom to appoint,
so they gathered and shouted, saying:
“Who can be our commander?”
Hóngxìn stepped out from the crowd and responded, saying:
“I can be your commander.”
Hóngxìn's appearance was unusual;
his face was dark blue and black.
The army was impressed by him
and jointly appointed him Acting Military Governor.
When Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng ascended the throne,
he appointed Hóngxìn Military Governor.
[The ancient text uses 'zhú'.]
When Grand Progenitor of Liáng (Liáng Tàizǔ) was about to attack Jìn,
he begged Hóngxìn for grain.
Hóngxìn did not give it,
which created a rift.
The Liáng army attacked Wèi,
taking Líyáng, Qímén, and Wèixiàn.
They fought at Nèihuáng.
The Wèi army lost five battles out of five.
Hóngxìn was afraid
and requested an alliance,
and only then did the attack stop.
At this time,
Liáng was attacking Yǎn and Yùn to the east
and battling Jìn to the north.
Jìn sent Lǐ Cúnxìn to aid Zhū Xuān,
borrowing a route through Wèi.
When the Grand Progenitor heard this,
he sent an envoy to speak to Hóngxìn, saying:
“The Jìn people aim for Héshuò,
and when their army returns, they will destroy Wèi.”
Hóngxìn believed this to be true,
and thus dispatched troops to attack Cúnxìn at Xīnxiàn.
The Grand Progenitor sent Gě Cóngzhōu to assist him.
The Liáng army captured Luòluò, a prince of Jìn,
and sent him to Wèi.
Hóngxìn killed him,
thereby severing ties with Jìn.
The Grand Progenitor still suspected Hóngxìn of having divided loyalties,
so he treated Hóngxìn as an elder brother,
always using humble language and sending generous gifts to Wèi.
When Wèi envoys arrived at Liáng,
the Grand Progenitor would bow facing north to receive the gifts
and tell the envoys:
“My sixth elder brother is more than ten years my senior;
how dare I treat him lightly?”
Hóngxìn was greatly pleased,
believing that he was highly esteemed.
Therefore, when the Grand Progenitor traveled between Yān and Zhào,
and eventually seized Héběi,
Wèi did not cause him trouble.
When Hóngxìn died,
Shàowēi succeeded him.
Shàowēi loved learning, was skilled in calligraphy,
and was quite knowledgeable in literary composition.
He collected tens of thousands of volumes of books
and opened a hall to welcome scholars from all directions.
Hóngxìn, when serving the Táng,
because his ancestors were from Chángshā,
was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chángshā Commandery.
Shàowēi inherited his father's title, Prince of Chángshā.
Soon after Shàowēi took office,
Liú Rénngōng of Yōuzhōu attacked Wèi with 100,000 troops,
massacring Bèizhōu.
Shàowēi sought help from Liáng,
which greatly defeated the Yān army at Nèihuáng.
The following year,
the Grand Progenitor of Liáng sent Gě Cóngzhōu to join the Wèi army to attack Cāngzhōu,
taking Dézhōu.
They then defeated the Yān army at Lǎoyā Dī.
For this reason, Shàowēi was grateful for Liáng's assistance.
The Wèibó circuit first established the Yájūn (Elite Army) starting with Tián Chéngsì.
As the years passed, the Yájūn grew increasingly arrogant.
By the time of Shàowēi, two hundred years had passed,
and fathers and sons secured their unity through marriage across generations.
Former military governors such as Shǐ Xiànchéng, Hé Quán●, Hán Jūnxíong, and Lè Yànzhēn,
were all installed by the Yájūn,
who would immediately kill them whenever angered.
Shàowēi was vigorous, fierce, astute, and perceptive.
He was thoroughly versed in official administration.
His governance possessed authority and dignity,
yet his family had historically been installed by the Yájūn.
In the second year of Tiānyòu [905 CE],
the ground collapsed inside Wèizhōu city.
Shàowēi feared a rebellion.
Soon after, the elite commander Lǐ Gōngquán rebelled.
Shàowēi executed him,
and then secretly dispatched envoys to Liáng requesting troops,
intending to execute all of the Yájūn.
Liáng Tàizǔ agreed to this,
and sent Lǐ Sī'ān and others to attack Cāngzhōu,
summoning troops from Wèi.
Shàowēi therefore mobilized all the Wèi troops to follow them,
leaving only the Yájūn remaining.
(The next word in the ancient text is 'drove out/expelled'.)
Shàowēi's son, Tíngguī, was married to a Liáng woman.
Coincidentally, the Liáng woman died.
Tàizǔ secretly sent his guest commander Mǎ Sìxūn, who selected elite soldiers and concealed them inside the funeral carriages (or biers).
He had a thousand soldiers of the Chángzhí Army disguise themselves among the bearers and enter Wèi,
ostensibly to assist with the funeral.
Tàizǔ followed them closely with his main army.
That night, Shàowēi used several hundred of his own servant-soldiers,
joining Mǎ Sìxūn's troops to attack the Yájūn,
slaughtering them completely, including their family members.
Tàizǔ raced from Nèihuáng to Wèi.
The Wèi troops who were following the attack on Cāngzhōu had marched as far as Lìtíng;
upon hearing this, they all revolted,
entering the various prefectures of Chán and Bó.
The Wèi region fell into great chaos.
After several months,
Tàizǔ entirely pacified the region for him.
With the Yájūn dead,
and the Wèi troops all having rebelled,
Shàowēi's position became increasingly isolated.
Tàizǔ then sought to seize his territory.
Shàowēi began greatly to regret his actions.
That same year,
Tàizǔ again attacked Cāngzhōu,
stationing his troops at Chánglú.
Shàowēi supplied the Liáng troops.
From Cāng[zhōu] to Wèi, a distance of five hundred *lǐ*,
he erected courier stations and watchtowers.
He personally provided tents and various supplies.
The several hundred thousand Liáng soldiers were all fully provided for.
Shàowēi was severely strained by this effort.
When Emperor Zhāozōng moved east to Luòyáng,
an edict ordered all military governors to repair and manage the capital.
Shàowēi completed the construction of the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
He was additionally appointed Shǒu Shìzhōng (Acting Grand Councilor).
He was promoted and enfeoffed as the Prince of Yè (Yè Wáng).
Tàizǔ besieged Cāngzhōu but had not yet taken it,
when Liú Shǒuguāng joined the Jìn army to defeat the Liáng forces at Lùzhōu.
Tàizǔ returned from Chánglú.
Passing through Wèi,
he fell ill
and lay sick in the headquarters.
None of the generals were allowed to see him.
Shàowēi feared that Tàizǔ would eventually attack him,
so he seized the opportunity to enter and see him, saying:
"Now, all four quarters are raising arms.
Those who pose a threat to Liáng
do so because the Táng dynasty still exists.
The Mandate of Heaven has already departed from the Táng house.
It would be better to take the throne yourself soon."
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased,
and immediately hastened back home.
After Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
and planned to make Luòyáng his capital,
Shàowēi took fine timber from Wèi to build the Five Phoenix Tower (Wǔfèng Lóu) and the Front Hall of the Chaoyuan Palace.
He floated the materials up the river
and erected them in the capital.
Tàizǔ sighed and said:
"I heard that Xiāo Hé, when guarding Guānzhōng,
built the Wèiyāng Gōng for the Hàn dynasty.
How could that compare to Shàowēi crossing a thousand *lǐ* to accomplish this?
It is like divine transformation.
His merit far surpasses Xiāo Hé!"
He bestowed upon him precious belts and famous horses.
Liú Shǒuguāng, the Prince of Yān (Yān Wáng), imprisoned his father Rén'gōng,
and had a feud with his elder brother Shǒuwén.
Shàowēi speedily sent a letter advising Shǒuguāng and the others to surrender to Liáng.
Tàizǔ heard of this and laughed, saying:
"I have often attacked Yān but could not defeat it.
Now, Shàowēi's short note
is better than using one hundred thousand troops."
Whenever Tàizǔ had important matters,
he often sent envoys to consult him.
Shàowēi sometimes also sent hurried notes reporting his opinions.
The envoys would meet on the road,
and their messages often coincided.
Shàowēi, believing that Wèi had long been free of war,
wished to cut timber at Ānyáng Qímén to build ships.
From the Hé (Yellow River) he would enter Luò[yáng],
annually transporting one million *shí* of grain
to supply the capital.
Tàizǔ increasingly believed Shàowēi was entirely loyal,
and sent generals Chéng Hòu and Lú Níng to supervise the work.
Before the ships were completed, Shàowēi fell ill.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"Wèi is an old, large military command,
and has many external troops.
I request that a capable and highly esteemed minister of Liáng oversee it,
and I ask permission to retire to my residence to await death."
Tàizǔ immediately ordered his son Zhōu Hàn to oversee the affairs of the headquarters,
and instructed the envoy, saying:
"Go quickly.
Tell your master,
that for my sake, he must force himself to eat.
If, tragically, he does not recover,
I shall ensure his descendants are honored for generations.
By having Zhōu Hàn oversee the affairs of the headquarters now,
I still hope that you, Minister, will recover."
Shàowēi served Liáng.
He was repeatedly appointed Grand Preceptor (Tàishī) and concurrently Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
He died at the age of thirty-four.
He was posthumously granted Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
and given the posthumous name Zhēnzhuàng.
He had three sons:
Tíngguī,
whose official title reached Minister of the Court of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng) before he died.
Zhōu Hàn succeeded his father's position.
In the eighth month of the second year of Qiánhuà [912 CE], he was driven out by Yáng Shīhòu.
He was transferred to become the Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of the Xuānyì Army.
He died in office,
at the age of fourteen.
Zhōu Jìng replaced him as the Military Governor of the Xuānyì Army.
At the age of ten,
he was transferred to command the Zhōngwǔ circuit.
The following year,
he became Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān), Commandant of the Imperial Equerries (Fùmǎ Dūwèi), and Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Qīng).
During the reign of Táng Zhuāngzōng, he served as Grand General of the Metropolitan Guard (Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn).
Míngzōng appointed him Military Governor of the Kuāngguó Army.
He was later dismissed and served as Supreme General (Shàng Jiāngjūn).
He died in the second year of Jìn Tiānfú [937 CE],
aged thirty-two.
Tíngguī married two daughters of Liáng Tàizǔ:
one was Ānyáng Gōngzhǔ (Princess Ānyáng),
and the other was Jīnhuá Gōngzhǔ (Princess Jīnhuá).
Zhōu Hàn married the daughter of Mòdì (the Last Emperor),
named Shòuchūn Gōngzhǔ (Princess Shòuchūn).
Zhōu Jìng also married a daughter of Mòdì,
named Jìn'ān Gōngzhǔ.
Wáng Chǔzhí
Wáng Chǔzhí, whose courtesy name (zì) was Yǔnmíng,
was a native of Jīngzhào Wànnián.
His father, Zōng,
was skilled at accumulating wealth and goods;
his riches rivaled those of princes and marquises.
He served as an official in the Shéncè Army of Táng,
and his highest office reached Grand General of the Metropolitan Guard (Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn),
concurrently holding the title of Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of Xīngyuán.
His sons were Chǔcún and Chǔzhí.

Chǔcún, relying on his father's position, became General of the Valiant Guard (Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn) and Commissioner for the Management of Inner Palatial Affairs and Gardens, etc., in Dìngzhōu and adjacent areas.
In the sixth year of Qiánfú [879 CE],
he was immediately appointed Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of the Yìwǔ Army.
When Huáng Cháo captured Cháng'ān,
Chǔcún was moved by righteous indignation and wept,
leading his circuit troops to enter the pass and suppress the rebels.
When Huáng Cháo was defeated and merits were assessed,
for retaking cities and striking the rebels,
Lǐ Kèyòng was ranked first;
but for diligence in supporting the emperor and initiating the righteous cause,
Chǔcún was ranked first.
In the second year of Qiánníng [895 CE],
Chǔcún died while at his post.
Following the precedents of Hèshuò, the three armies
nominated Chǔcún's son, Gào, to be the Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
He was then appointed Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ),
and given the additional titles of Inspecting Minister of Works (Jiǎnxiào Sīkōng) and Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Chǔzhí served as Commander-in-Chief of the Central Army of the Rear Command (Hòuyuàn Zhōngjūn Dūzhī Bīngmǎ Shǐ).
In the third year of Guānghuà [900 CE],
Liáng troops attacked Dìngzhōu.
Gào sent Chǔzhí to lead troops to resist them.
They fought at Shā Hé,
but were defeated by the Liáng troops.
The returning troops entered the city and drove out Gào.
Gào fled and defected to Jìn.
The rebel troops nominated Chǔzhí as Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
Liáng troops besieged him.
Chǔzhí sent a person to inform Liáng,
requesting permission to cut ties with Jìn and serve Liáng,
and offered one hundred thousand bolts of silk to reward the army.
He then made an alliance with Liáng.
Liáng Tàizǔ memorialized Chǔzhí as Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of the Yìwǔ Army,
and he was repeatedly enfeoffed, eventually as Prince of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán Wáng).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Chǔzhí as Prince of Běipíng (Běipíng Wáng).
troops attacked Wáng Róng.
Róng sought aid from Jìn.
Chǔzhí also dispatched men to Jìn,
wishing to break with Liáng and pledge his service.
The Jìn troops rescued Róng.
Chǔzhí followed with five thousand troops,
and defeated the Liáng army at Bóxiāng.
Afterward, Jìn defeated Yān in the north,
seized Wèibó in the south,
and fought Liáng along the river.
For more than ten years,
Chǔzhí never failed to follow with troops.
Chǔzhí was fond of shamans (wū),
and a retainer named Lǐ Yīngzhī
was a deceptive sorcerer.
When Chǔzhí fell ill,
Yīngzhī cured him using unorthodox (zuǒdào) methods,
and Chǔzhí increasingly regarded him as divine.
He made him wear the robes of a Daoist priest
and appointed him Xíngyíng Sīmǎ (Field Army Marshal).
In military and governmental affairs, whether great or small,
everything was decided by him.
Originally,
Yīngzhī had obtained a young boy, Liú Yúnláng, at Xíngyì Lán,
and raised him as his son.
As Chǔzhí had no son,
Yīngzhī gave Yúnláng to Chǔzhí
and falsely claimed:
"This boy was born with extraordinary signs."
Chǔzhí raised him as his son,
renamed him Dū,
and loved him deeply.
Yīngzhī thus became increasingly arrogant.
He registered the able-bodied men within the commandery
and established a separate new army,
leading it himself.
He built a residence in Bólíng Fāng,
opening gates on all four sides,
and everything was done according to unorthodox methods.
Chǔzhí’s generals and officials knew that he would certainly cause trouble,
but none dared to remonstrate.
At this time,
Lǐ Kuāngchóu of Yōu Zhōu passed through Zhōngshān on his way to the capital (Jīngshī).
Chǔzhí concealed armored soldiers outside the city
to guard against the unexpected.
Once Kuāngchóu had departed,
the armored soldiers entered the city and surrounded Yīngzhī’s residence,
seized him, and killed him.
They then went to Chǔzhí and requested permission to kill Dū.
Chǔzhí refused.
The next day,
when merit was reviewed and rewards distributed,
he secretly recorded the names of the armored soldiers,
from the platoon commanders upward, and kept them in a separate register.
Afterward, he used various pretexts to execute them.
Over twenty years,
not one person escaped,
and Chǔzhí was ultimately killed by Dū.
Dū was cunning, obsequious, and resourceful.
Chǔzhí appointed him Jiédù Fùshǐ (Deputy Military Governor).
Zhāng Wénlǐ assassinated Wáng Róng.
Zhuāngzōng dispatched troops to punish Wénlǐ.
Chǔzhí conferred with his attendants, saying:
"Zhèn
is Dìng's shield.
Although Wénlǐ is guilty,
if Zhèn falls, Dìng cannot survive alone."
He then sent someone to request that Zhuāngzōng not mobilize his troops.
Zhuāngzōng took the wax letter Wénlǐ had sent to Liáng (which he had captured) and showed it to Chǔzhí, saying:
"Wénlǐ has betrayed me.
The campaign cannot be halted."
Chǔzhí had an illegitimate son named Yù.
When Gào fled to Jìn,
Yù also fled there.
The King of Jìn married his daughter to him
and made him the Xīnzhōu Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner of Xīn Prefecture).
When Chǔzhí saw that Zhuāngzōng was determined to punish Wénlǐ,
he grew more suspicious of his own position.
He secretly entered into communication with Yù,
making Yù go north to entice the Qìdān to enter the passes and divert the Jìn army.
Furthermore, he promised to summon Yù to be his heir.
Dū heard of this and was displeased.
Moreover, the people of Dìng all said that the Qìdān should not be summoned,
fearing they would bring disaster upon themselves.
Chǔzhí did not listen.
Since Yù had fled to Jìn,
he had always feared Chǔzhí would not tolerate him.
He was therefore greatly pleased
and thought he could take advantage of this opportunity to seize the position.
He immediately used generous bribes to entice Ābǎojī of Qìdān.
Ābǎojī mobilized his entire nation to invade.
The people of Dìng were all opposed to the Qìdān campaign.
The petty official Hé Zhāoxùn advised Dū to take action.
Dū then seized Chǔzhí,
imprisoned him in the Western Residence,
and declared himself Liúhòu (Acting Military Governor).
Virtually all of the Wáng clan descendants and Chǔzhí’s generals and officers were executed.
On the morning of the first day of the first month of the following year,
Dū paid homage to Chǔzhí at the Western Residence.
Chǔzhí sprang up, struck him in the chest, and shouted:
"Rebel!
How have I wronged you?"
However, his attendants were unarmed.
He then tried to bite Dū’s nose.
Dū tore away his sleeve and fled.
Chǔzhí was then killed.
Earlier,
a yellow snake had appeared in the memorial tower (bēilóu).
Chǔzhí regarded it as a dragon
and kept it hidden and sacrificed to it.
Furthermore, several hundred wild magpies
nested in the wheat fields.
Chǔzhí believed this was due to his virtue,
but the people of Dìng all knew these were ill omens,
saying:
"Snakes burrow in mountains and marshes,
but now inhabit human dwellings.
Magpies nest in trees,
but now descend to dwell in the fields.
This is the symbol of a commoner stealing a position
and the person in authority losing his proper place."
Soon after, Chǔzhí was indeed deposed and died.
After Zhuāngzōng defeated the Qìdān at Shā Hé,
he pursued the fleeing forces past Dìngzhōu.
He got along extremely well with Dū,
arranging for his son, Jìjí, to marry Dū’s daughter,
and appointed Dū as the Yìwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Yìwǔ Circuit).
In the second year of Tóngguāng (924 CE),
when Zhuāngzōng visited Yè,
Dū came to pay court.
He was granted immense wealth.
Because of Jìjí,
Zhuāngzōng treated Dū very favorably,
and granted everything he requested.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he rather disliked Dū’s character,
and Ān Chónghuǐ constantly restrained him according to the law.
Dū then began to harbor rebellious intentions.
At this time,
the Táng troops were attacking the Qìdān
and frequently passed through Dìngzhōu.
Dū was often deficient in providing supplies and provisions,
growing increasingly uneasy.
Hé Zhāoxùn plotted for Dū, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has just ascended,
and the four quarters have not yet submitted.
His authority is easily broken;
this is the time to plan for your own security."
Soon after, Zhū Shǒuyīn rebelled at Biànzhōu,
and Dū immediately rebelled as well.
He sent men with wax letters to recruit the five circuits of Qīng, Xú, Qí, Lù, and Zǐ,
arranging for them all to raise troops.
However, the five circuits did not respond.
Míngzōng dispatched Wáng Yànqiú to suppress him.
Dū again allied with Wáng Yù to recruit the Qìdān for assistance.
The Qìdān sent Tūněi leading ten thousand cavalry to rescue Dū.
Dū dispatched Commandant Zhèng Jìlín and Dù Hóngshòu, the commanding officer of Lóngquán Garrison, with two thousand men to meet the Qìdān.
They were defeated by Yànqiú.
Jìlín and Hóngshòu were captured.
Yànqiú challenged them, saying:
"I previously sent someone to persuade you to surrender,
why did you not submit?"
Hóngshòu replied:
"We have received favor in Zhōngshān for two generations;
we dare not harbor disloyalty."
He was then executed.
When Hóngshòu faced execution,
his demeanor was completely composed.
Yànqiú encamped his troops at Wàngdū,
and fought against Dū and the Qìdān.
He heavily defeated them at Qǔyáng.
Dū and Tūněi escaped with a few horsemen,
closed the city gates, and did not venture out again.
Initially,
an idle search in Zhuāngzōng's (莊宗) army yielded a young man.
Zhuāngzōng favored him,
ordered him to falsely assume the surname Lǐ (李),
named him Jìtáo (繼陶),
and raised him in the palace as his son.
When Míngzōng (明宗) ascended the throne,
Ān Zhònghuǐ (安重誨) sent him out to be given to Duàn Huái (段徊),
but Huái also disliked him and drove him away.
Dū (都) sent men to find him.
Upon this occasion,
he deceived his followers, saying:
"This is the Crown Prince of Zhuāngzōng."
Dū dressed him in the robes of the Son of Heaven,
made him patrol the top of the city walls,
to show him to Yàn Qiú (晏球)'s army.
Those soldiers who recognized him said:
"It is Jìtáo."
They all reviled him.
Dū remained inside the city.
Having few troops,
he only used two thousand Qìdān (契丹) men to guard the walls,
calling Hūtū Něi (呼禿餒) the King Něi (餒王),
and humbling himself to serve him.
If any of the generals wished to surrender,
Dū observed and scrutinized them strictly,
and there was no day without killings,
due to which he held the defense firmly for over a year.
In the second month of the fourth year of Tiānchéng (天成, 929 CE),
the city was breached.
Dū and his family all immolated themselves and died.
Consequently, the Wáng (王) family lineage was extinguished in Zhōngshān (中山).
Now, Chǔcún (處存) had a son named Yè (鄴),
Yè’s son was Tíngyìn (廷胤).
He was related to Zhuāngzōng through marriage,
was known for his bravery and vigor,
became a military officer (jūnxiào),
and was able to share hardships with his soldiers.
During Míngzōng's reign,
he successively served as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Bèi (貝), Xīn (忻), Mì (密), Chán (澶), and Xí (隰) prefectures.
When Fàn Yánguāng (范延光) rebelled in Yè (鄴),
Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) appointed Tíngyìn as the Central Army Commander (Zhōngjūn Shǐ) of Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠)’s Traveling Headquarters.
For his merit in defeating Yánguāng,
he was appointed Military Commissioner (Jié dù shǐ) of Zhāngdé (彰德) Command.
Earlier,
Chǔzhí (處直) had been imprisoned by Dū.
His youngest son, Wēi (威), fled north to Qìdān.
The Qìdān said to Jìn Gāozǔ:
"We wish to let Wēi inherit the rank and territory of his ancestors.
What do you think?"
Gāozǔ replied:
"By the law of the Central Plain (Zhōngguó),
one progresses from military officer to Governor,
then rises through the ranks of Regional Commissioner (Tuánliàn Fángyù) until reaching Military Commissioner.
I request that Wēi be sent back to the Central Plain
so that he may be promoted gradually."
The Qìdān angrily said:
"You yourself went from a feudal lord to the Son of Heaven.
Was there any gradual process for that?"
When Gāozǔ heard this,
he hastily moved Tíngyìn to garrison Yìwǔ (義武),
saying:
"He is also a descendant of the Wáng family."
Later, he was moved to Zhènhǎi (鎮海) and died there.
Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光).
Liú Shǒuguāng
was a man from Lèshòu (樂壽) county in Shēnzhōu (深州).
His father, Rén Gōng (仁恭),
served Lǐ Kějǔ (李可舉) of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
He was able to tunnel underground to form paths for attacking cities,
and in the army, he was nicknamed
"Liú Kūtóu" (劉窟頭, Liu the Cave Head).
He was gradually promoted to military officer based on merit.
Rén Gōng was a brave man,
fond of boasting.
When Kějǔ died,
his son Kuāngwēi (匡威) disliked Rén Gōng's character,
did not want him to remain in the army,
and transferred him to be the Magistrate (Xiàn Lìng) of Jǐngchéng (景城) county in Yíngzhōu (瀛州).
When the Yíngzhōu army rioted
and killed the Governor,
Rén Gōng recruited a thousand men from the county
and suppressed the riot.
Kuāngwēi was pleased,
reinstated him as a general,
and sent him to garrison Yùzhōu (蔚州).
The garrison troops, having exceeded their term of duty without being replaced,
all longed to return home
and expressed complaints.
Kuāngwēi was then expelled by his younger brother, Kuāngchóu (匡儔).
Rén Gōng, hearing of the chaos,
consequently led the garrison troops to attack Yōuzhōu.
When he reached Jūyōng Guān (居庸關),
he was defeated in battle,
and fled to Jìn (晉).
Jìn appointed him as Commandant (Zhèn Jiàng) of Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Rén Gōng was cunning and deceitful,
and skillful at serving people.
He was especially respectful in serving Gài Yù (蓋寓), the favored general of the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng).
Whenever he faced Yù, he would weep and shed tears,
claiming:
"I resided in Yān (燕) without offense,
yet was expelled due to slander."
He then spoke of the strengths and weaknesses of Yān,
and presented strategies for taking it.
The Prince of Jìn increasingly trusted and favored him.
In the first year of Qiánníng (乾寧, 894 CE),
Jìn attacked and defeated Kuāngchóu,
and then appointed Rén Gōng as acting Military Commissioner (Liúhòu) of Yōuzhōu.
Jìn left more than ten of its trusted aides, including Yān Liúdé (燕留得), to supervise Rén Gōng's army,
and requested an imperial commission for him from Táng (唐).
He was appointed Acting Minister of Works (Jiǎnxiào Sīkōng) and Military Commissioner of Lúlóng (盧龍) Command.
Later, when Jìn attacked Luó Hóngxìn (羅弘信),
it requested troops from Rén Gōng.
Rén Gōng refused to provide them.
The Prince of Jìn subtly blamed and reprimanded him in a letter.
Rén Gōng became furious,
seized the Jìn envoy,
and killed Yān Liúdé and the others, thereby rebelling.
The Prince of Jìn personally led an expedition against him.
They fought at Ānsài (安塞),
and the Prince of Jìn was severely defeated.
In the first year of Guānghuà (光化, 898 CE),
Rén Gōng sent his son, Shǒuwén (守文), to attack Cāngzhōu (滄州),
driving out the Military Commissioner Lú Yànwēi (盧彥威),
and subsequently taking Cāng (滄), Jǐng (景), and Dé (德) three prefectures.
He requested an imperial commission for his son from Táng.
Zhāozōng (昭宗) delayed this
and did not immediately comply.
Rén Gōng was enraged
and said to the Táng envoy:
"Tell the Son of Heaven for me:
I already possess the banner and tally (jīngjié),
I only want the genuine article from Cháng'ān (長安)!
Why is it that I repeatedly ask and do not receive it?"
Zhāozōng finally appointed Shǒuwén as the Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi (橫海) Command.
Rén Gōng and his son led the 100,000 troops of their two commands,
falsely claiming 300,000, to attack Wèi (魏),
and massacred Bèizhōu (貝州).
Luó Shàowēi (羅紹威) sought aid from Liáng (梁).
Liáng sent Lǐ Sī'ān (李思安) to relieve Wèi,
who utterly defeated Shǒuwén at Nèihuáng (內黃),
beheading fifty thousand men.
Rén Gōng fled,
and the Liáng army pursued and attacked him.
From Wèi to Chánghé (長河),
corpses lay across the ground for hundreds of *lǐ*.
From then on, the Liáng army attacked him year after year,
capturing his two prefectures, Yíng (瀛) and Mò (漠).
Rén Gōng became afraid
and reattached himself to Jìn.
In the third year of Tiānyòu (天祐, 906 CE),
Liáng attacked Cāngzhōu.
Rén Gōng mobilized every male within his territory, aged fifteen and above, and seventy and below.
He tattooed all their faces,
the inscription reading:
"Ding Bà Dū" (定霸都, Establishing the Hegemon's Capital).
He obtained 200,000 men.
They provided their own military provisions
and encamped at Wǎqiáo (瓦橋).
The Liáng army pitched camp at Chánglú (長蘆),
with deep moats and high ramparts.
Rén Gōng was unable to approach them.
Cāngzhōu was besieged for over a hundred days.
Food inside the city was exhausted.
People resorted to cannibalism,
breaking up bones to cook,
or eating balls made of mud plaster.
Sixteen or seventeen out of every twenty inhabitants died.
Rén Gōng sought aid from Jìn.
The Prince of Jìn attacked Lùzhōu (潞州) on his behalf to divert the Liáng siege.
Jìn captured Lùzhōu,
and the Liáng army subsequently withdrew.
However, Rén Gōng took advantage of the world being full of troubles,
grew arrogant due to his wealth and rank,
built a palace on Dà'ān Shān (大安山),
indulging in extreme extravagance.
He selected beautiful women from Yān to fill it.
Furthermore, he practiced alchemy with Daoist priests
hoping to achieve immortality.
He ordered the people of Yān to use mud plaster as currency,
collected all the bronze coins,
carved into a mountain and buried them there.
After this, he killed the workmen to silence them,
and later generations all remained ignorant of the location.
Rén Gōng had a favorite concubine, Luó Shì.
His son, Shǒu Guāng, had illicit relations with her.
Rén Gōng was enraged,
flogged Shǒu Guāng,
and banished him.
In the first year of Liáng Kāipíng [907 CE],
[The Liáng court] dispatched Lǐ Sī'ān to attack Rén Gōng.
Rén Gōng was at Dà'ān.
Shǒu Guāng brought troops in from outside,
defeated and repulsed Sī'ān,
then proclaimed himself Lú Lóng Jiédùshǐ.
He sent Lǐ Xiǎoxǐ and Yuán Xíngqīn with troops to attack Dà'ān Shān,
where they captured Rén Gōng and imprisoned him.
His elder brother, Shǒu Wén, hearing that their father was about to be imprisoned,
immediately led troops to attack Shǒu Guāng.
When he reached Lú Tái,
he was defeated by Shǒu Guāng.
He advanced to fight at Yù Tián,
and was defeated again,
so he requested troops from the Qìdān.
The following year,
Shǒu Wén led 40,000 Qìdān and Tǔhún troops to fight at Jīsū.
Shǒu Guāng’s army was defeated.
Shǒu Wén pretended he could not bear [to harm his brother],
stepped out of the formation, and called out to his men:
“Do not kill my younger brother!”
Shǒu Guāng’s general, Yuán Xíngqīn, recognized Shǒu Wén,
leapt from his horse and captured him,
and imprisoned him in a separate room.
Later, he killed him.
Shǒu Wén’s officers, Sūn Hè, Lǚ Yǎn, and others,
established Shǒu Wén’s son, Yán Zuò, to resist Shǒu Guāng.
Shǒu Guāng besieged them for over a hundred days.
Food within the city was exhausted.
Rice cost 30,000 cash [per measure].
People killed each other and ate [the bodies],
or ate packed earth.
Horses ate each other's manes and tails.
Yǎn and the others led the starving citizens in the city to feed on fermented grains (qu),
calling
this practice “Slaughter Duty” (Zǎiwù).
They killed [these citizens] daily to supply the army.
After a long time,
Yán Zuò’s resources were exhausted,
and he surrendered.
Shǒu Guāng was fundamentally mediocre and foolish.
Because of this [victory], he became even more arrogant.
He manufactured iron cages and iron brushes.
When people committed offenses,
they were seated inside the cage
and fire was lit outside,
or their skin was scrubbed and scraped off until they died.
The scholars and officials of Yān fled the disaster to other regions.
Shǒu Guāng himself wore reddish-yellow clothing [imperial color],
and said to his generals and officials:
“If I wear this and face south [rule],
can I become emperor of the world?”
Sūn Hè strongly remonstrated, saying it was impossible.
When Liáng attacked Zhào,
King of Zhào, Wáng Róng, requested aid from Shǒu Guāng.
Sūn Hè said:
“Now Zhào is innocent,
yet Liáng is attacking it.
Among the feudal lords sending troops to save Zhào,
whoever arrives first will dominate.
I fear that before the Yān army has even set out,
Jìn will have already defeated Liáng first.
This is an opportunity that cannot be missed.”
Shǒu Guāng said:
“The King of Zhào once made an alliance with me and then broke it.
Now, in his emergency, he comes back to rely on me.
Moreover, when two tigers are fighting,
it is worthwhile to wait for them.
I intend to be Biàn Zhuāngzǐ.”
Consequently, he did not dispatch troops.
The King of Jìn indeed rescued Zhào,
greatly defeating the Liáng forces at Bǎixiāng,
and advanced to plunder Xíng and Míng,
reaching Líyáng.
Shǒu Guāng heard that Jìn had emptied its territory to invade Liáng deeply.
He therefore mustered his troops and ordered strict preparedness,
sending people to provoke Zhèn and Dìng by saying:
“Yān has 300,000 elite troops.
If we lead the two territories to follow Jìn,
then who should lead this alliance?”
The Jìn people were troubled by this,
and discussed it, saying:
“Formerly, when Fū Chāi contended at the Huángchí conference,
Yuè invaded Wú.
Xiàng Yǔ was greedy for the benefit of attacking Qí,
and Hàn defeated Chǔ.
Now we have crossed a thousand *li* to attack others,
and powerful Yān is behind us.
This is a deep-seated threat.”
They therefore ordered the army to return.
Shǒu Guāng believed that the various territories feared his power,
so he subtly urged the territories to jointly promote and honor him.
Thereupon, the King of Jìn, along with Tiāndé Sòng Yáo, Zhènwǔ Zhōu Déwēi, Zhāoyì Lǐ Sìzhāo, Yìwǔ Wáng Chǔzhí, Chéngdé Wáng Róng, and others,
issued an imperial edict written in ink, honoring Shǒu Guāng as Shàngshū Lìng and Shàng Fù.
Shǒu Guāng also sent an envoy to inform Liáng,
requesting that he be granted the title of Commander-in-Chief of the Héběi Forces,
to attack Zhèn, Dìng, and Hédōng.
Liáng dispatched Wáng Tóng, the Gate Keeper, to appoint Shǒu Guāng as Héběi Inspector (Cǎifǎngshǐ).
The officials concerned reported to Shǒu Guāng that
when the Shàng Fù received the patent of appointment,
they followed the ceremonies used by the Táng Dynasty for investing a Tàiwèi.
Shǒu Guāng asked:
“Why do the regulations for this ceremony not include performing the suburban sacrifice to Heaven
and changing the era name?”
The officials replied:
“These are the rites belonging to the Son of Heaven.
Although the Shàng Fù is honored,
he is merely a subject.”
Shǒu Guāng angrily said:
“If I am the Shàng Fù,
then who should be the Emperor?
Moreover, today the world is fractured and split apart.
The great ones proclaim themselves Emperor,
and the small ones proclaim themselves King.
With Yān, which spans two thousand *li*,
can I alone not rule one region as Emperor?”
He immediately shackled the envoys from Liáng and Jìn and threw them into prison.
He placed an axe and a chopping block in his courtyard,
and issued an order saying:
“Whoever dares to remonstrate shall die!”
Sūn Hè stepped forward and said:
“At the defeat of Cāngzhōu,
Your Majesty granted your subject the grace of not killing him.
Regarding the affair of this day,
I dare not refrain from remonstrating.”
Shǒu Guāng became furious,
pushed him down onto the chopping block,
and ordered the soldiers to cut him up and devour him.
Hè shouted:
“In less than a hundred days,
a massive army will arrive!”
Shǒu Guāng ordered his mouth to be stopped and then pickled his body.
Consequently, in the eighth month of the first year of Liáng Qiānhuà [911 CE], Shǒu Guāng
proclaimed himself Emperor of Dà Yān,
changed the era name to Yìngtiān,
and appointed Wáng Tóng and Qí Shè as Left and Right Chancellors.
Jìn sent Lǐ Chéngxūn, the Tàiyuán Shǎoyǐn, to congratulate [Shǒu Guāng] on his investiture as Shàng Fù.
When he arrived in Yān,
Shǒu Guāng had already usurped the title of emperor.
The officials tried to force Chéngxūn to acknowledge Shǒu Guāng as his sovereign,
but Chéngxūn refused to yield,
and entered for an audience using the diplomatic rites between equal states.
Shǒu Guāng was enraged
and killed him.
The following year,
Jìn dispatched Zhōu Déwēi leading 30,000 men,
who joined the forces of Zhèn and Dìng to attack Yān.
They entered through Qígōu Guān.
The various prefectures of Chán, Zhuō, Wǔ, and Shùn all welcomed them and surrendered.
Shǒu Guāng was besieged for a full year,
and consistently lost every battle.
He then dispatched his military guest Wáng Zūnhuà to deliver a letter to Déwēi, saying:
“I have committed offenses against Jìn,
and have been misguided without reforming.
Now I am afflicted by distress.
May you, sir, skillfully plead on my behalf.”
Déwēi said to Zūnhuà:
“The Emperor of Dà Yān has not yet performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven.
How could he have reached such a state?
I have received orders to suppress the usurping rebellion;
I know nothing else.”
Shǒu Guāng became increasingly desperate.
He then presented a thousand bolts of silk, a thousand *liang* of silver, and a hundred rolls of brocade,
and sent his general Zhōu Zūnyè to tell Déwēi:
“My King appeals to you emotionally:
Wealth, honor, success, and failure
are the usual principles of human affairs.
Acknowledging merits and pardoning faults
is the work of a Hegemon.
Last year, Shǒu Guāng recklessly exalted himself,
fundamentally because he could not bear to be beneath Zhū Wēn.
How could he have expected the great state [Jìn] to expose its troops to harsh conditions for a full year?
We beg you to show a little forbearance.”
Déwēi refused.
Shǒu Guāng climbed the city wall and called out to Déwēi:
“You, sir, are a worthy man of the Three Jìn region.
Will you alone not relieve a man in danger?”
He sent someone to exchange the horse he was riding for Déwēi’s horse and departed,
and then announced:
“I will surrender when the King of Jìn arrives.”
The King of Jìn then personally came to the army camp.
Shǒu Guāng climbed the wall to see the King of Jìn.
The King of Jìn asked what he intended to do.
Shǒu Guāng replied:
“Today, I am merely meat on the cutting board.
The King may do as he wishes!”
Shǒu Guāng had a favorite, Lǐ Xiǎoxǐ,
who advised him not to surrender.
Shǒu Guāng therefore requested to wait until another day.
That evening,
Xiǎoxǐ defected and surrendered to the Jìn army.
The next morning,
the Jìn army attacked and breached the city,
capturing Rén Gōng and three hundred members of his family.
Shǒu Guāng and his wives, Lǐ Shì and Zhù Shì,
his sons Jì Xún, Jì Fāng, Jì Zuò, etc.,
fled south towards Cāng Zhōu.
They lost their way
and reached the border of Yànlè.
For several days, they had no food.
He sent his wife Zhù Shì to beg for food from a farm family.
The farm family found it strange and questioned her.
Zhù Shì told the truth,
and thus they were captured and sent to Yōu Zhōu.
At that time, King Jìn was holding a grand feast for his army.
A guest general brought Shǒu Guāng to him.
King Jìn jested with him, saying:
“Why is the host so eager to avoid his guests?”
Shǒu Guāng kowtowed and begged for death.
He ordered Shǒu Guāng and his father Rén Gōng to be shackled and brought along with the army.
As the army returned and passed through Zhào,
King Zhào, Wáng Róng, met with King Jìn.
They set out wine,
and when the wine was flowing, Wáng Róng requested:
“I wish to see Rén Gōng and his son.”
King Jìn ordered their shackles to be broken and them to be released,
and seated them at a lower position.
They ate and drank as usual,
showing no trace of shame.
When King Jìn arrived in Tài Yuán,
Rén Gōng and his son were dragged with ropes of braided silk and hemp,
and offered at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
When Shǒu Guāng was about to die,
he wept and said:
“I have no regrets about my death,
but the one who taught me not to surrender
was Lǐ Xiǎo Xǐ.
If the culprit does not die,
I shall complain about it in the underworld.”
King Jìn sent for Xiǎo Xǐ.
Xiǎo Xǐ glared and said:
“Imprisoning your father, murdering your brother,
and marrying your own flesh and blood –
was that also what Xiǎo Xǐ taught you?”
King Jìn was enraged,
and ordered Xiǎo Xǐ to be beheaded first.
Shǒu Guāng knew he could not escape,
and shouted:
“Your Majesty is restoring the Táng dynasty to achieve hegemony;
why not pardon me and let me offer my services?”
His two wives cursed from the side, saying:
“Things have come to this;
what is the point of living any longer?
We wish to die first!”
Then they both died.
King Jìn ordered Lǐ Cún Bà to take Rén Gōng to Yàn Mén,
pierce his heart to draw blood for sacrifice at the tomb of the former king,
and then execute him.
Collation Notes
Miscellaneous Biographies, Twenty-Eighth: Lǐ Mào Zhēn
Lǐ Mào Zhēn
was a native of Bó Yě, Shēn Zhōu.
His original surname was Sòng,
and his name was Wén Tōng.
He was a soldier in the Bó Yě army,
garrisoned at Fèng Xiáng.
When Huáng Cháo attacked the capital,
Zhèng Tián used the Bó Yě army to strike the rebels.
Mào Zhēn was promoted from squad leader to military officer for his merits.
In the first year of Guāng Qǐ,
Zhū Méi rebelled,
and Emperor Xī Zōng moved to Xīng Yuán.
Zhū Méi sent Wáng Xíng Yú to attack Dà Sàn Guān.
Mào Zhēn, along with the Imperial Guard Commander Lǐ Tín, defeated Xíng Yú at Dà Táng Fēng.
The following year,
Zhū Méi was defeated and killed.
For his merits, Mào Zhēn was promoted from commander of the Imperial Guards to Jìedùshǐ of Wǔ Dìng Command,
and was granted the imperial surname and name.
While escorting the emperor back east,
upon reaching Fèng Xiáng,
the Fèng Xiáng Jìedùshǐ Lǐ Chāng Fú and the Tiān Wēi Commander Yáng Shǒu Lì quarreled over the road
and attacked each other with troops.
Chāng Fú was defeated
and fled to Lǒng Zhōu.
Emperor Xī Zōng sent Mào Zhēn to attack and kill Chāng Fú,
and for this merit, he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Fèng Xiáng and Lǒng Yòu.
In the first year of Dà Shùn,
he was enfeoffed as King of Lǒng Xī Commandery.
In the second year,
the Chief Military Commissioner Yáng Fù Gōng fell into disgrace
and fled to Xīng Yuán.
The Xīng Yuán Jìedùshǐ Yáng Shǒu Liàng
was Fù Gōng’s adopted son,
and he took him in.
Mào Zhēn then submitted a memorial stating that Fù Gōng and his son were both guilty and deserved execution,
and thus requested to be appointed Southern Mountain Pacification Commissioner.
Emperor Zhāo Zōng, due to the eunuch connection,
found it difficult
and did not grant it.
Mào Zhēn, without authorization, mobilized troops and attacked and captured Xīng Yuán.
Fù Gōng and his son were killed.
Mào Zhēn submitted a memorial requesting that his adopted son, Jì Mì, provisionally manage the affairs of the Xīng Yuán military government.
Emperor Zhāo Zōng then transferred Mào Zhēn to be Jìedùshǐ of Shān Nán Xī Dào,
and appointed Chancellor Xú Yàn Ruò to govern Fèng Xiáng.
Mào Zhēn did not obey the imperial edict
and submitted a memorial arguing for himself, saying:
“I only fear that the military sentiment might suddenly change,
and the warhorses become difficult to restrain.
This would only cause the people of the imperial domain
to suffer due to this exchange;
I wonder where the imperial carriage, once forced to flee,
would go from here?”
Emperor Zhāo Zōng, finding Mào Zhēn’s memorial disrespectful,
could not tolerate it
and asked Chancellor Dù Ràng Néng about it.
Ràng Néng said:
“Mào Zhēn has a large territory and a strong army,
and the Táng forces are not yet capable of launching an expedition against him;
Fèng Xiáng is also close to the capital,
making it easy to be endangered and difficult to regret later.
Even if one wished to execute Cháo Cuò to appease the feudal lords at a later date,
I fear it would be impossible.”
Emperor Zhāo Zōng angrily said:
“I cannot sit idly and suffer humiliation!”
He then ordered Ràng Néng to mobilize troops,
and appointed Qín Wáng Sì Zhōu as Western Capital Pacification Commissioner.
When the order was issued,
the people in the capital markets all knew it was unwise
and gathered at Chéng Tiān Mén,
blocking the Chancellor to request not to raise an army.
They threw tiles and stones at the Chancellor.
The Chancellor got out of his carriage and ran,
losing his official seal.
People were greatly alarmed,
but Emperor Zhāo Zōng’s resolve grew stronger.
Qín Wáng led fifty-four divisions of the Imperial Guards to battle at Zhōu Zhì.
The Táng army was defeated and routed,
and Mào Zhēn then invaded the capital,
stationing his troops at Sān Qiáo.
Emperor Zhāo Zōng, from Ān Fú Mén,
killed two Chief Military Commissioners to appease Mào Zhēn
and ordered him to withdraw his troops.
Mào Zhēn had a long-standing grudge against Ràng Néng,
so he said:
“The ones who plotted to raise the army were not the two Chief Military Commissioners,
but Ràng Néng.”
He arrayed his troops at Lín Gāo Yì,
requesting Ràng Néng’s execution.
Ràng Néng said:
“I said it earlier,
only by killing me can the national crisis be relieved.”
Emperor Zhāo Zōng wept, his tears drenching his lapels.
He demoted Ràng Néng to Sī Hù Cānjūn of Léi Zhōu
and granted him death.
Mào Zhēn then withdrew his troops.
The ancient text has "生" (shēng).
The following year,
the Hé Zhōng Jìedùshǐ Wáng Chóng Yíng died,
and his sons Kē and Gǒng contended for the succession.
King Jìn Lǐ Kè Yòng requested Kē be installed,
while Mào Zhēn, along with Hán Jiàn and Wáng Xíng Yú, requested Gǒng be installed.
Emperor Zhāo Zōng did not agree.
Mào Zhēn and others were enraged.
They led the troops of the three commands to invade the capital,
plotting to depose Emperor Zhāo Zōng
and enthrone King Jí, Bǎo.
Before this could be achieved,
King Jìn also raised an army.
Mào Zhēn, in fear,
then killed Chancellors Wéi Zhāo Dù and Lǐ Xī,
leaving his adopted son Jì Péng with two thousand soldiers for imperial guard duties, and departed.
When the Jìn army arrived at Hé Zhōng,
Jì Péng and Xíng Yú’s brother Xíng Shí, among others, vied to abduct Emperor Zhāo Zōng to flee.
The capital fell into great chaos,
and Emperor Zhāo Zōng relocated to Shí Mén.
Mào Zhēn arrived at Hù Xiàn with his troops
and killed Jì Péng to redeem himself.
The Jìn army had already defeated Wáng Xíng Yú
and returned to Wèi Běi,
requesting to attack Mào Zhēn.
Emperor Zhāo Zōng believed that Jìn was distant while Mào Zhēn was near,
and thus wished to protect him as a favor,
hoping that he could be relied upon in times of urgency;
moreover, Mào Zhēn had already killed his son to redeem himself.
Thus, an edict was issued to recall the Jìn army.
Kè Yòng sighed, saying:
“If Táng does not execute Mào Zhēn,
its troubles will never end!”
As Emperor Zhāozōng returned from Shímén,
he increasingly recruited more than ten thousand troops, including the Ānshèng and Pěngchén armies,
and put the various princes in command of them.
Mào Zhēn, believing that the Táng court intended to punish him,
also prepared his troops and requested an audience.
The capital was greatly alarmed,
and the residents fled into the mountains and valleys.
Mào Zhēn then attacked the capital.
Emperor Zhāozōng sent Prince Tán to oppose him.
When Prince Tán reached Sānqiáo,
his army disintegrated,
and Emperor Zhāozōng moved to Huázhōu.
He sent the Chancellor Sūn Wò with troops to attack Mào Zhēn.
Hán Jiàn pleaded on Mào Zhēn’s behalf,
and the campaign was halted.
After a long time,
Mào Zhēn was promoted and appointed Shàngshū Lìng (Minister of the Department of State Affairs)
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí.
Subsequently,
Emperor Zhāozōng was deposed by the eunuchs.
After he was restored,
Chancellor Cuī Yìn wished to borrow the Liáng troops to execute the eunuchs,
and secretly plotted this with Grand Progenitor of Liáng (Liáng Tàizǔ).
The Chief Eunuch Hán Quánhuì and others
also relied on Mào Zhēn’s strength
as an external shield.
Mào Zhēn sent his son Jìyún with several thousand troops to guard the capital.
The eunuchs, relying on the Qí troops,
became increasingly arrogant and uncontrollable.
