In the first year of Tiānfù (901 CE),
Yìn summoned the Grand Progenitor of Liáng to the west.
When the Liáng army reached Tóngzhōu,
Quánhuì and the others became frightened,
and together with Jìyún, coerced Emperor Zhāozōng to flee to Fèngxiáng.
The Liáng army besieged it for over a year.
Mào Zhēn was defeated in every battle
and closed his defenses, not daring to leave the walls.
Firewood and food in the city were completely exhausted.
From winter to spring,
rain and snow fell relentlessly,
and those who froze or starved to death numbered thousands daily.
A *dǒu* of rice cost seven thousand cash.
People even burned human excrement and corpses to eat.
Fathers ate their own children.
When people fought over the flesh,
one would say:
"This is my child!
How dare you eat him!"
Human flesh cost one hundred cash per *jīn*,
while dog meat cost five hundred cash per *jīn*.
A father was willing to eat his own son,
yet human flesh was cheaper than dog meat.
The Son of Heaven (Emperor Zhāozōng) set up a small mill in the palace,
and ordered palace women to personally grind beans and wheat for the imperial meal.
In the rear palace and the residences of the sixteen princes,
three or four people died of cold and starvation daily.
The people in the city gathered and intercepted Mào Zhēn,
begging for a way to survive.
Mào Zhēn, desperate and cornered,
planned to surrender the Son of Heaven to Liáng in exchange for a truce.
Emperor Zhāozōng said to Mào Zhēn:
"The Six Palaces and I consume gruel one day
and unleavened bread the next.
How can we not make peace with Liáng?"
In the first month of the third year (903 CE),
Mào Zhēn agreed to peace with Liáng,
executed Hán Quánhuì and more than twenty others,
and sent their heads to the Liáng army.
The siege by Liáng was lifted.
Although the Son of Heaven was able to leave,
Liáng then coerced his migration eastward, and Táng subsequently perished.
Mào Zhēn not only caused the downfall of Táng,
but also brought hardship upon himself.
When the Grand Progenitor of Liáng ascended the throne,
the powerful regional warlords all successively declared themselves emperor.
Only Mào Zhēn was unable to do so;
he merely called himself the Prince of Qí,
established a government and appointed officials,
named his wife Empress,
and held court with signal whips and feathered fans,
imitating the movements and ceremonies of the Son of Heaven.
Mào Zhēn resided in Qí.
Due to his generosity, kindness, and love for the people,
the populace was quite content.
Once, due to the small territory and meager taxation,
he issued an order to monopolize oil sales.
He also prohibited the entry of pine firewood through the city gates,
because it could be used for torches.
A court jester mocked him, saying:
"Your servant requests that moonlight also be prohibited."
Mào Zhēn laughed and was not angry.
Initially,
Mào Zhēn defeated Yáng Shǒuliàng and seized Xīngyuán,
and Bīn, Níng, Fū, and Fāng Prefectures all submitted to him.
He held twenty prefectures.
When he was besieged by Liáng,
Xīngyuán fell to Shǔ.
After Kāipíng (907 CE),
Bīn, Níng, Fū, and Fāng fell to Liáng,
and Qín, Fèng, Jiē, and Chéng Prefectures then fell to Shǔ.
By the late years of Liáng,
he possessed only seven prefectures.
The twenty prefectures were: Qí, Lǒng, Jīng, Yuán, Wèi, Wǔ, Qín, Chéng, Jiē, Fèng, Bīn, Níng, Qìng, Yǎn, Fū, Fāng, Dān, Yán, Liáng, and Yáng.
After Emperor Zhuāngzōng had defeated Liáng,
Mào Zhēn, calling himself the Prince of Qí,
submitted a memorial positioning himself as an elder relative (Maternal Uncle).
When he heard that the emperor had entered Luò (Luòyáng),
he then submitted a petition acknowledging himself as a subject,
and sent his son Cóngyǎn to court.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng, regarding him as an elder,
treated him with great respect,
re-enfeoffed him as the Prince of Qín,
and did not refer to him by name in imperial edicts.
In the second year of Tóngguāng (924 CE),
he died of illness,
at the age of sixty-nine,
and was given the posthumous title Zhōngjìng.
Cóngyǎn was gentle and skilled in calligraphy and painting.
Mào Zhēn, acting under imperial authority, appointed Cóngyǎn as the Military Governor of the Zhāngyì Army.
When Mào Zhēn died,
he was appointed Military Governor of Fèngxiáng.
When Prince Wèi (Jìjí) campaigned against Shǔ,
Cóngyǎn served as the Commissioner for Army Provisioning, Transport, and Reception.
After Shǔ was pacified,
Jìjí ordered Cóngyǎn to escort Wáng Yǎn.
When they reached Fèngxiáng,
the Surveillance Commissioner Chái Chónghòu refused to admit them.
Cóngyǎn then traveled eastward to Huázhōu.
When he heard about the disaster involving Emperor Zhuāngzōng, he returned west.
When Emperor Míngzōng ascended the throne,
hearing that Chónghòu had once refused Cóngyǎn,
he sent someone to execute him.
Cóngyǎn submitted a letter,
stating that Chónghòu, while defending Fèngxiáng,
had not disturbed the troops or the populace,
and requested that his offense be pardoned.
Although the request was not granted,
scholars highly praised him for this action.
He subsequently held command successively at Xuānwǔ and Tiānpíng.
Cóngyǎn owned a thousand *qǐng* of land and a thousand *mǔ* of bamboo groves in Fèngxiáng.
Fearing that this would infringe upon the people’s livelihoods,
he never personally managed them.
The people of Fèngxiáng loved him.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì) rose up in Fèngxiáng
and was about to set out,
the people of Fèngxiáng knocked on his horse, begging to follow Cóngyǎn.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he once again appointed Cóngyǎn as the Military Governor of Fèngxiáng.
He died at the age of forty-nine.
Hán Jiàn
Hán Jiàn, courtesy name Zuǒshí,
was a native of Chángshè, Xǔzhōu.
In his youth, he was a military officer in Càizhōu,
serving under Lù Yànhóng, a general of the Zhōngwǔ Army.
He followed Yáng Fùguāng in attacking Huáng Cháo in Cháng'ān.
After Cháo was defeated,
Fùguāng also died.
Yànhóng and Jiàn, having no superior,
led their troops westward to welcome Emperor Xīzōng in Shǔ,
engaging in attack and plunder wherever they went.
When they reached Xīngyuán,
they drove out Niú Cóng
and occupied Shānnán.
Afterwards, they could not hold it.
Yànhóng fled eastward to Xǔzhōu,
and Jiàn then defected to Shǔ,
where he was appointed General of the Jīnwǔ Guard.
When Emperor Xīzōng returned to Cháng'ān,
Jiàn was made the Defense Commissioner of Tóngguān and the Prefect of Huázhōu.
Huázhōu had repeatedly suffered through major military campaigns,
and its households and population were scattered.
Jiàn, having been of humble origin in his youth,
was familiar with farming.
He cleared away the brambles
and supervised the people in cultivation and planting.
He went in and out of the villages
to inquire about their hardships.
Jiàn was initially illiterate.
He ordered people to label the utensils, crockery, beds, and couches he used,
writing down their names so he could see them.
Over time, he gradually mastered written characters.
When he saw the *Yùpiān* (a dictionary),
he rejoiced, saying:
"If I seek by category,
what will I fail to obtain?"
He subsequently mastered phonetics, rhymes, and metrical parallelism.
In his leisure time, he studied books and histories.
At that time,
the realm was already in chaos,
and all the regional governors were military men.
Only Jiàn managed and settled his soldiers and populace
and was fond of learning.
Chéng Ruì of Jīngnán, who at the time used the assumed surname Guō,
was also good at organizing the people of Jīngchǔ.
They were known at the time as
"Hán of the North and Guō of the South."
In the first year of Dàshùn (890 CE),
Jiàn took his troops and attached himself to Zhāng Jùn to attack Jìn.
Zhāng Jùn was defeated,
and Jiàn fled back from Hán Shān.
When Wáng Chóngyíng of Hézhōng died,
his sons Kē and Gǒng fought for the succession.
The Jìn people aided Kē,
and Jiàn, along with Wáng Xíngyú and Lǐ Mào-zhēn, aided Gǒng.
Zhāozōng did not allow this,
and Jiàn and the others were furious,
using the troops of their three commanderies to assault the Jīngshī.
Zhāozōng met Jiàn and the others and reproached them.
Wáng Xíngyú and Lǐ Mào-zhēn were terrified, shaking, sweating, and unable to speak,
only Jiàn stepped forward to present his case.
They then killed Chancellor Wéi Zhāodù, Lǐ Xī, and others,
and plotted to depose Zhāozōng.
However, the Jìn forces raised troops and were approaching,
Jiàn and the others were afraid,
and consequently returned.
The Jìn army demanded retribution from the three commanderies,
and their forces reached Huá Zhōu.
Jiàn ascended the city wall and shouted:
「Our humble region has never been disrespectful to the great state,
Why are we being attacked? 」
The Jìn people replied:
「You used troops to violate the Son of Heaven,
and murdered high officials,
This is why we are conducting a punitive campaign. 」
Afterward, they made peace with Jìn.
In the third year of Qiánníng (896 CE),
Lǐ Mào-zhēn again assaulted the Jīngshī.
Zhāozōng planned to flee to Tàiyuán,
and stopped temporarily north of the Wèi River.
Jiàn sent his son Yǔn to request the Emperor to seek refuge in Huá Zhōu.
Zhāozōng again wished to go to Fū Zhōu.
Jiàn pursued and overtook Zhāozōng at Fùpíng,
and weeping, said:
「The vassal officials are obstinate and difficult,
and it is not just Lǐ Mào-zhēn.
If you abandon the nearby capital region and tour the remote frontiers,
and the imperial carriage crosses the Yellow River,
it will be impossible to return! 」
Zhāozōng also wept,
and consequently sought refuge in Huá Zhōu.
At this time,
the Son of Heaven was isolated and weak,
only having the rear guard army and the troops of Lǐ Jūn, commander of the three battalions of Dìng Zhōu, totaling over a thousand men, as his escort,
and the various princes commanded them.
Since Jiàn had successfully acquired Zhāozōng's presence in his commandery,
he intended to control him.
Consequently, he requested the dismissal of the princes commanding the troops,
and the disbanding of the various rear guard armies.
He submitted repeated memorials, but received no reply.
Zhāozōng ascended the Qíyún Lóu,
looked northwest toward the Jīngshī,
and composed three stanzas of the *Púsàmán* lyric pattern, expressing his desire to return.
Its final stanza read:
「Wild smoke rises among the jade-green trees,
Travelers on the roads depart.
How can I find a hero,
To escort me back to the Grand Palace? 」
When the wine flowed freely,
he and his attending officials sang sadly until tears fell.
Jiàn and the princes all composed matching responses.
Jiàn was especially displeased in his heart,
so he sent someone to inform against the princes, claiming they plotted to kill Jiàn and kidnap the Son of Heaven to another commandery.
Zhāozōng summoned Jiàn,
intending to clarify the situation,
but Jiàn claimed illness and did not appear.
Zhāozōng then sent the princes themselves to visit him,
but Jiàn refused to see them,
and requested that the princes be confined to the Shíliù Zhái.
Zhāozōng found this difficult.
Jiàn then led several thousand elite soldiers to surround the temporary palace,
and demanded the execution of Lǐ Jūn.
Zhāozōng was extremely terrified,
and immediately issued an edict ordering Lǐ Jūn's execution,
completely disbanded the rear guard and the three battalion guards,
and imprisoned the princes in the Shíliù Zhái.
Zhāozōng increasingly regretted having gone to Huá Zhōu,
and dispatched Yán Wáng Jiè Pī as an envoy to Jìn,
to plot a restoration.
When Jiè Pī returned,
Jiàn, along with the Palace Commander Liú Jìshù, falsely accused the princes of treason,
and surrounded the Shíliù Zhái with troops.
The princes all climbed onto the roofs and shouted,
but they were subsequently killed.
Zhāozōng could do nothing about it,
and erected a Dézhèng Bēi for Jiàn to appease him.
After Jiàn had killed the princes,
he constructed Nánzhuāng,
erecting towers and pavilions,
intending to invite Zhāozōng to visit,
and thereby depose him and install Dé Wáng Yù.
His father, Shū Fēng, told Jiàn:
「You were merely a peasant between Chén and Xǔ,
who encountered the chaos of the time,
and received the great kindness of the Son of Heaven to reach this position.
To attempt a great deed with the mere hundred *lǐ* of land across two prefectures,
the calamity of having the entire clan destroyed,
I cannot bear to see it,
I would rather die first! 」
He then wept, sighing deeply.
Lǐ Mào-zhēn and Liáng Tàizǔ both wished to dispatch troops to welcome the Son of Heaven.
Jiàn became somewhat fearful,
and therefore stopped his plan.
In the first year of Guānghuà (898 CE),
Zhāozōng returned to Cháng'ān.
The Emperor personally painted a portrait of Jiàn,
enfeoffed Jiàn as Yǐngchuān Jùn Wáng,
and granted him a Tiě Quàn (Iron Certificate of Pardon).
Jiàn declined the princely title,
so he was subsequently enfeoffed as Xǔ Guó Gōng.
Liáng Tàizǔ led troops toward Cháng'ān,
and sent Zhāng Cúnjìng to attack Tóng Zhōu.
Jiàn's staff supervisor Sīmǎ Yè surrendered the city.
Tàizǔ ordered Yè to summon Jiàn,
and Jiàn subsequently came out and surrendered.
Tàizǔ reproached Jiàn for having betrayed him.
Jiàn replied:
「It was the scheme of Staff Supervisor Lǐ Jùchuān. 」
Tàizǔ grew angry,
and immediately killed Lǐ Jùchuān,
and took Jiàn along with him.
When Zhāozōng moved east,
Jiàn followed him to Luò.
Zhāozōng raised his cup and offered a toast to Tàizǔ and Jiàn, saying:
「Since moving the capital,
the state's situation has stabilized slightly.
The safety and danger of the state,
rest upon you two gentlemen. 」
Next, Empress Hé raised her cup.
Jiàn stepped on Tàizǔ's foot.
Tàizǔ then feigned drunkenness and departed.
Jiàn then went out,
and said to Tàizǔ:
「The Son of Heaven exchanged glances with a palace attendant,
and I heard the sound of weapons behind the curtain,
I fear you might not escape! 」
Because of this incident, Tàizǔ esteemed him highly,
and memorialized Jiàn as the Pínglú Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
Jiàn was appointed Sītú Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Tàizǔ was fierce and violent by nature,
and none of his subordinates dared to remonstrate with him,
only Jiàn occasionally offered remarks,
and Tàizǔ treated him with great tolerance.
Tàizǔ performed the suburban sacrifice at Luò,
and Jiàn served as the Grand Ceremony Commissioner.
He was later dismissed as Chancellor,
and sent out to govern Xǔ Zhōu.
When Tàizǔ died,
the Xǔ Zhōu army mutinied,
and he was killed,
at the age of fifty-eight.
Lǐ Rénfú
Lǐ Rénfú:
His ancestral background is unknown.
During the time of Táng Xīzōng,
there was a man named Tuòbá Sījìng,
who served as a deputy general in Xià Zhōu.
Later, because of his merit in helping defeat Huáng Cháo,
he was granted the surname Lǐ,
and appointed Xià Zhōu Jiédùshǐ.
Sījìng died.
In the second year of Qiánníng (895 CE),
his younger brother Sījiàn was made Jiédùshǐ.
Since the end of the Táng dynasty, the world had been in great chaos,
and many records compiled by the historians were incomplete.
The various commanderies seized the opportunity to rise up fiercely.
Unless someone achieved great good or evil conspicuously known throughout the world,
it is impossible to record their beginning and end.
At this time,
the armies of the commanderies of Xīngyuán, Fèngxiáng, Bīnníng, Fūfāng, Hézhōng, and Tóng Huá,
all rose up on four sides and fought amongst themselves.
Only Líng Xià never caused trouble for the Táng court,
nor did it achieve great merit.
During Zhū Méi's rebellion,
Sījìng and Lǐ Sīxiào of Fū Zhōu both stationed troops at Wèiqiáo.
Afterward,
when Huáng Cháo captured the Jīngshī,
Wáng Chóngróng, Lǐ Kèyòng, and others gathered the armies of various commanderies to defeat the rebels.
Sījìng participated in defeating Huáng Cháo and recovering the Jīngshī,
but none of his actions were ever particularly noteworthy,
therefore, Sījìng's lineage, merits, and faults are neither prominent nor recorded.
In the second year of Liáng Kāipíng,
Sījiàn died.
The army established his son Yíchāng as Liúhòu,
and he was immediately appointed Yíchāng as Jiédùshǐ.
The next year,
his general Gāo Zōngyì raised a rebellion,
killing Yíchāng.
At this time,
Rénfú was the Fānbù Zhǐhuīshǐ,
stationed outside with troops.
The army then welcomed Rénfú and installed him,
not knowing whether he was a close or distant relative of Sījiàn.
In the fourth month of that year,
Rénfú was appointed Jiǎnxiào Sīkōng and Dìngnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Throughout the era of Liáng,
he merely honored the legitimate court calendar.
At this time,
Qí Wáng Lǐ Màozhēn,
and Jìn Wáng Lǐ Kèyòng
often gathered troops to attack Rénfú,
and Liáng regularly sent out armies to save him.
Rénfú accumulated offices, reaching Jiǎnxiào Tàishī concurrent with Zhōngshū Lìng,
and was enfeoffed as Shuòfāng Wáng.
He died in the third month of the fourth year of Chángxīng,
and his son Yíchāo installed himself as Liúhòu.
Since Rénfú’s time,
many border generals claimed that Rénfú was secretly communicating with the Qìdān,
fearing he would become a border threat.
Míngzōng, capitalizing on his death,
appointed Yíchāo as Yánzhōu Cìshǐ and Zhāngwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and transferred Ān Cóngjìn, the Zhāngwǔ Jiédùshǐ, to replace him.
Fearing Yíchāo would not accept the transfer,
he dispatched Yào Yànchóu of Bīnzhōu with fifty thousand soldiers to escort Cóngjìn to his garrison.
Yíchāo indeed refused the replacement.
Cóngjìn and Yànchóu besieged him with their armies,
but failed to conquer the city after more than a hundred days.
The walls of Xiàzhōu had always been strong;
old locals transmitted the saying that Hèlián Bóbó had built them by steaming the earth.
Cóngjìn and his men dug tunnels,
but when they reached the foundation beneath the city, it was as hard as iron and stone,
and they could not chisel their way in.
Yíchāo recruited the Dǎngxiàng externally,
plundering the supply routes of Cóngjìn and his forces.
West of Shǎn,
for the common people to transport one *dǒu* of grain or one bundle of hay,
the expense was several thousands,
the people could not bear the burden,
and the roads were filled with distress.
Míngzōng consequently abandoned the siege,
appointing Yíchāo as Dìngnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
He died in the second year of Qīngtài.
His younger brother, Yīxīng,
accumulated offices, reaching Jiǎnxiào Tàishī concurrent with Shìzhōng,
and during the Zhōu Xiǎndé era,
was enfeoffed as Xīpíng Wáng.
His subsequent affairs are fully detailed in the National History.
Hán Xùn
Hán Xùn,
his ancestry is unknown.
He was initially an officer in the Lǐngwǔ army.
During the turmoil at the end of the Táng dynasty,
he occupied Lǐngyán,
and Táng immediately appointed him as Jiédùshǐ,
but the historical accounts fail to record this,
and his actions are not known.
In the third year of Liáng Kāipíng,
the Shuòfāng Jiédùshǐ Hán Xùn was enfeoffed as Yǐngchuān Wáng,
and this is the first time he appears in the historical record.
At this time,
Yáng Chóngběn of Bīnníng, Lǐ Zhōuyí of Fūyán, and Lǐ Màozhēn of Fèngxiáng
were all contending with Liáng,
but only Xùn and Lǐ Sījiàn of Xiàzhōu submitted to Liáng as vassals,
and never engaged in conflict using troops.
Lǐ Màozhēn once dispatched Liú Zhījùn to attack Xùn,
but could not overcome him.
Xùn also handled his subordinates well,
and everyone loved him,
building a living shrine for Xùn.
During the Zhēnmíng era,
Xùn died.
The army established his son Zhū as Liúhòu,
and Liáng immediately appointed him as Jiédùshǐ.
By the time of Zhuāngzōng,
Zhū was also concurrently appointed Héxī Jiédùshǐ.
In the fourth year of Tiānchéng,
Zhū died,
and Zhū’s son Chéng was immediately made Shuòfāng Jūn Liúhòu.
His general Lǐ Bīn rebelled.
Chéng then submitted a memorial requesting a commander from the court.
Míngzōng appointed Kāng Fú as Shuòfāng Héxī Jiédùshǐ to replace Chéng,
and thus, officials began to be appointed and replaced by the court.
The Hán clan, since Xùn took Lǐngwǔ,
had nothing noteworthy recorded throughout the succeeding generations,
and the fate of Chéng is unknown.
Yáng Chóngběn
Yáng Chóngběn
served Lǐ Màozhēn since childhood.
He adopted him as a son,
and he assumed the surname Lǐ,
with the personal name Jìhuī.
Màozhēn recommended Chóngběn as Jìngnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Liáng Tàizǔ attacked Qí but did not subdue it,
so he transferred his forces to attack Bīnzhōu.
Chóngběn welcomed him and surrendered.
Tàizǔ ordered him to revert to his original surname,
bestowed upon him the name Chóngběn,
and moved his family to Hézhōng to serve as hostages.
Chóngběn’s wife was beautiful.
When Tàizǔ deployed his armies,
he traveled frequently through Hézhōng,
and often slept with her.
Chóngběn’s wife was deeply mortified,
and privately sent someone to reproach Chóngběn, saying:
"A great man who cannot protect his spouse—
I have already become the wife of Zhū Gōng!
I have no face to look upon you;
there is only a sword and rope for me!"
Chóngběn wept bitterly and was enraged.
Afterward, the Liáng army lifted the siege of Qí,
Chóngběn’s wife was able to return,
and Chóngběn subsequently turned against Liáng and rejoined Màozhēn.
Màozhēn connected with the Shǔ forces in the west to join Chóngběn in attacking Yōng and Huà,
causing a great shock in Guānxī.
Tàizǔ led his army west to Hézhōng,
and dispatched Chēn Wáng Yǒu Yù to attack them.
Yǒu Yù died upon reaching Yǒngshòu,
and the Liáng army consequently retreated.
Chóngběn garrisoned at Měiyuán.
Tàizǔ again dispatched Liú Zhījùn, Kāng Huáiyīng, and others to attack him.
Chóngběn was utterly defeated,
and from then on, he never again marched east.
In the fourth year of Gānhuà,
he was assassinated by his son Yànlǔ.
Chóngběn’s adopted son, Lǐ Bǎohéng,
killed Yànlǔ and surrendered to Liáng.
Gāo Wànxīng
Gāo Wànxīng
was a native of Héxī.
At the end of Táng,
Héxī belonged to Lǐ Màozhēn.
Màozhēn’s general Hú Jìngzhāng was Yánzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wànxīng and his younger brother Wànjīn both served Jìngzhāng as cavalry generals.
Jìngzhāng died,
and his general Liú Wànzǐ replaced him as Cìshǐ.
In the second year of Liáng Kāipíng,
(Jìngzhāng) was buried south of the prefecture.
Wànzǐ was present at the gathering.
His general Xǔ Cóngshí killed Wànzǐ
and installed himself as Yánzhōu Cìshǐ.
At this time,
Wànxīng and his brother were both leading troops guarding the border.
Hearing that Wànzǐ was dead,
they surrendered to Liáng with several thousand of their subordinates.
Liáng Tàizǔ’s army was garrisoned at Hézhōng.
He dispatched Liú Zhījùn of Tóngzhōu with troops to reinforce Wànxīng,
attacking Dānzhōu,
and capturing its Cìshǐ, Cuī Gōngshí.
They advanced to attack Yánzhōu,
capturing Xǔ Cóngshí.
Lǐ Yánróng of Fūzhōu and Lǐ Yànyù of Fāngzhōu both abandoned their cities and fled.
Liáng Tàizǔ then appointed Wànxīng as Yánzhōu Cìshǐ and Zhōngyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and appointed Niú Cúnjié as Bǎodà Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Soon after, Liú Zhījùn rebelled,
so Cúnjié was transferred to govern Tóngzhōu,
and Wànjīn was appointed Bǎodà Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Wànxīng was repeatedly promoted, reaching Jiǎnxiào Tàishī concurrent with Zhōngshū Lìng,
and Bóhǎi Jùnwáng.
In the fourth year of Zhēnmíng,
Wànjīn died.
Wànxīng was then appointed Fūyán Jiédùshǐ,
promoted and enfeoffed as Yán'ān Jùnwáng,
and later transferred and enfeoffed as Běipíng Wáng.
When Liáng fell,
and Zhuāngzōng entered Luò,
Wànxīng once came to court.
In the third year of Tóngguāng,
he died at his post.
Wànxīng and his brother were both valiant and brave,
yet they never established great military achievements in battle.
However, because they surrendered to Liáng with their garrison troops,
Liáng's control over Fū, Fāng, Dān, and Yán began with Wànxīng.
Thus, the brothers guarded their territory for generations.
Wànxīng’s son Yǔntāo succeeded him.
In the first year of Chángxīng, he was transferred to garrison Ānguó,
and later transferred to Yìchéng,
dying during the Qīngtài era.
during the Kāiyùn period,
served as the Magistrate (Lìng) of Fūshī.
He was dismissed and lived at home.
At this time,
Zhōu Mì was the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngxìn Jūn.
The Qìdān destroyed the Jìn (Later Jìn),
and the army in Yánzhōu mutinied.
They expelled Zhōu Mì.
Zhōu Mì defended the Eastern City,
while the troops in the Western City appointed Yǔnquán as Liúhòu (Acting Governor).
Hearing that Hàn Gāozǔ had risen up in Tàiyuán,
he subsequently submitted to the Hàn (Later Hàn).
He was immediately appointed Jìedùshǐ.
He died in the third year of Guǎngshùn (953 CE).
Wēn Tāo
Wēn Tāo,
was a native of Huàyuán in Jīngzhào.
When young, he was a bandit.
Later, he served Lǐ Màozhēn,
and became the Garrison Commander of Huàyuán.
He falsely took the surname Lǐ,
with the given name Yàntāo.
Lǐ Màozhēn made Huàyuán County into Yàozhōu,
and appointed Tāo as the Cìshǐ (Prefect).
When Liáng Tàizǔ besieged Màozhēn at Fèngxiáng,
Tāo surrendered Yàozhōu to the Liáng (Later Liáng).
Soon after, he rebelled again and returned to Màozhēn.
Màozhēn again made Měiyuán County into Dǐngzhōu,
established the Yìshèng Jūn (Army),
and appointed Tāo as Jìedùshǐ.
During the time of the Last Emperor (Mòdì),
Tāo again rebelled against Màozhēn and surrendered to the Liáng.
The Liáng renamed Yàozhōu to Chóngzhōu,
Dǐngzhōu to Yùzhōu,
and Yìshèng to Jìngshèng Jūn (Army).
They then appointed Tāo as Jìedùshǐ,
restored his surname Wēn,
and changed his given name to Zhāotú.
Tāo spent seven years in the commandery.
All the imperial tombs of the Táng dynasty located within his jurisdiction,
he completely excavated,
taking the gold and treasures hidden within.
However, Zhāolíng was the most solid.
Tāo went down the burial passage.
He saw that the palace architecture and structure were grand and magnificent,
no different from the world of men.
In the center was the main sleeping chamber.
Stone couches were arranged in the east and west wings.
Inside the stone chests on the couches were iron caskets,
all containing the maps and documents of previous ages,
and the calligraphy of Zhōng [Yáo] and Wáng [Xīzhī].
The paper and ink were as new.
Tāo took all of them.
They were subsequently circulated among men.
Only Qiánlíng could not be opened due to wind and rain.
Afterward, Zhū Yǒuqīan rebelled against the Liáng,
and captured Tóngzhōu.
The Prince of Jìn brought troops to assist Yǒuqīan and advanced toward Huàyuán.
Tāo was afraid,
and requested to be moved to another commandery.
He was consequently moved to Zhōngwǔ.
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed the Liáng,
Tāo came from Xǔ to court.
Through the actor Jǐng Jìn, he offered a bribe to Empress Líu.
The Empress spoke on his behalf.
Zhuāngzōng treated Tāo very kindly,
and bestowed upon him the name Lǐ Shàochōng.
Guō Chóngtāo said:
"This is merely a tomb-robbing bandit!
His crime is unforgivable!"
Zhuāngzōng said:
"I have already pardoned him.
I must not break my word."
He quickly sent him back to his commandery.
When Míngzōng entered Luò,
[Tāo] and Duàn Níng were both arrested and imprisoned.
After a while, he was pardoned,
and ordered to return to private life in the countryside.
The following year,
he was exiled to Dézhōu,
and granted death.
Alas,
the pitfalls of lavish burials,
from the Qín and Hàn dynasties onward,
have mostly been adopted by intelligent and heroic rulers.
Even if there were scholars with lofty discourse and persuasive speech,
who fully explained the attendant misfortunes and blessings,
they were unable to enlighten those who were confused!
Is it not because the desire for wealth and high status
deeply indulges one’s selfish desires,
and the calamity that has not yet occurred,
is hard to describe when it is still formless,
and thus insufficient to move their hearts?
Nevertheless, those who hear the story of Wēn Tāo
can take a slight warning!
The rulers of the Five Dynasties,
often did not die a natural death.
How could they have time to worry about what came after?
Only Zhōu Tàizǔ was able to learn from the calamity caused by Tāo.
When he was nearing his end,
he wrote a letter to give to Shìzōng,
instructing him to use a clay coffin and paper garments for the shrouding.
Before the burial,
the coffin was opened to show the people.
After the burial,
a stone inscription was carved to inform later generations,
not to construct an underground palace (tomb),
and not to place concubines to guard the tomb.
His intention was earnest and heartfelt.
However, the verifiable records (shílù) do not mention whether the funeral arrangements were simple or lavish.
He also ordered that two sets of the formal robes (gǔnmiǎn), celestial cap (tōngtiānguān), and purple gauze robe (jiàngshāpáo) he wore during his life be buried—
one set in the capital (Jīngshī),
and one set in Chánzhōu;
furthermore, two swords and two suits of armor were buried—
one set in Hézhōng,
and one set in Dàmíng.
No one can fully explain the meaning of this instruction.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter 29: Lú Guāngchóu, Tán Quánbō
Lú Guāngchóu and Tán Quánbō
were both natives of Nánkāng.
Guāngchóu was magnificent in appearance,
but lacked other talents.
However, Quánbō was brave and possessed strategic insight.
Nevertheless, Quánbō always admired Guāngchóu as a man.
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
bandits rose up in the south.
Quánbō said to Guāngchóu:
"The world is in chaos.
This is truly the time for us.
We must not simply remain here in poverty and low status!"
Thereupon, they gathered troops together and became bandits.
The populace nominated Quánbō as their leader.
Quánbō said:
"Do you gentlemen merely want to be thieves?
Or do you wish to achieve great things?
If you wish to achieve great things,
you must obtain a good commander.
Sir Lú is magnificent and dignified;
he is truly your lord."
The populace feigned agreement.
Quánbō became angry.
He drew his sword and struck a piece of wood three times,
cutting it down.
He said:
"He who does not follow orders will be like this wood!"
The populace was frightened,
and subsequently established Guāngchóu as their commander.
At this time,
Wáng Cháo attacked and captured Lǐngnán.
Quánbō attacked Wáng Cháo,
taking Qiánzhōu and Sháozhōu from him.
He also sent Guāngchóu’s younger brother, Guāngmù, to attack Cháozhōu.
Guāngmù was fond of bravery but advanced recklessly.
Quánbō warned him to be cautious and measured,
but he did not listen.
[Quánbō] calculated that he would surely be defeated,
and thus set up surprise troops along his route of retreat.
Guāngmù was indeed defeated and fled.
The Cháo forces pursued him.
Quánbō used the ambush troops to intercept and strike them,
greatly defeating them.
He then captured Cháozhōu.
At this time,
Líu Yán rose up in Nánhǎi.
He attacked and drove away Guāngmù,
and attacked Qiánzhōu with tens of thousands of troops.
Guāngchóu was terrified.
He said to Quánbō:
"Qiánzhōu and Cháozhōu were both captured by you, Sir.
Today, none but you, Sir, can defend them."
Quánbō said:
"I know Líu Yán is easy to deal with!"
He then selected ten thousand elite soldiers,
and placed them in ambush in the mountain valleys.
He feigned preparation of a battleground south of the city,
and informed Yán of the date of the battle.
He sent out five thousand old and weak soldiers to fight.
When the battle was intense,
they feigned defeat and retreated.
Yán hastily pursued them.
The ambush troops were released,
and Yán was consequently severely defeated.
When Guāngchóu ranked the achievements of the battle,
Quánbō attributed all of them to the other generals.
Guāngchóu respected him even more deeply in his heart.
In the early Liáng (Later Liáng) period,
Jiāngnán and the areas south of the ridges (Lǐngbiǎo) were entirely held separately by the Wú and the Nán Hàn.
But Guāngchóu alone, with Qiánzhōu and Sháozhōu, requested mandate from the capital (Jīngshī),
wishing to open up roads,
and submit tribute and taxes.
Tàizǔ established the Bǎishèng Jūn (Army) for him,
and appointed Guāngchóu as Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner), concurrently serving as the Commissioner for Opening the Five Ridges (Wǔ Lǐng Kāitōngshǐ).
He also established the Zhènnán Jūn (Army),
and appointed him as Liúhòu.
, Guāngchóu
became ill.
He entrusted the credentials (tally and seal) to Quán Bō,
but Quán Bō refused to accept.
Guāngchóu died,
and Quán Bō established his son Yánchāng and served him.
Yánchāng enjoyed hunting,
so his general Lí Qiú closed the gates and resisted Yánchāng.
Yánchāng was killed.
Qiú then plotted to kill Quán Bō.
Quán Bō was afraid,
claiming illness and not appearing.
Qiú thereupon established himself
and requested an appointment from Liáng.
In the first year of Qiānhuà,
Qiú was appointed Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner).
Qiú suddenly died of a severe illness.
His general Lǐ Yàntú established himself.
Quán Bō became even more fearful,
and thus claimed his illness was critical,
closing his door and isolating himself.
Yàntú suspected him
and sent men to observe his movements.
Quán Bō responded to the observation by feigning his condition in order to avoid harm.
Yàntú died,
and the people of the prefecture mutually led each other to Quán Bō's residence,
knocking on the door and requesting him to come out.
Quán Bō then arose,
sent an envoy to request an appointment from Liáng,
and was appointed Fángyùshǐ.
Quán Bō governed Qiánzhōu for seven years
and had benevolent governance.
Yáng Lóngyǎn sent Liú Xìn to attack and capture Qiánzhōu,
bringing Quán Bō back to Guǎnglíng.
He died at the age of eighty-five.
During the time of Lú Shì,
Liú Yǎn had already taken Sháozhōu.
When Quán Bō was captured,
Qiánzhōu subsequently entered the domain of Wú.
Léi Mǎn.
Léi Mǎn
was a native of Wǔlíng.
He was fierce, valiant, and aggressive,
with tattooed skin and cropped hair.
During the Guǎngmíng era of the Táng dynasty,
Húnán suffered famine,
and bandits arose.
Mǎn, along with his fellow villagers Ōu Jǐngsī and Zhōu Yuè, gathered several thousand various Man tribesmen.
They hunted in the great marsh,
slaughtered game, and strained wine.
They selected the most heroic men from the assembly
and appointed them as corporals (wǔzhǎng).
They were called the Tǔtuán Army (Earth Corps Army).
The various Man tribesmen followed them,
pushing Mǎn to be their commander.
At this time,
Gāo Pián was garrisoned at Jīngnán.
He summoned Mǎn to serve under his banner
and used the Man army to attack the bandits.
When Pián was relocated to Huáinán,
Mǎn followed him to Guǎnglíng,
but then fled back,
killed the Regional Inspector Cuī Zhù,
and consequently occupied Lǎngzhōu,
requesting an appointment from Táng.
Emperor Zhāozōng designated Lǐ and Lǎng as the Wǔzhēn Circuit
and appointed Mǎn as Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor).
At this time,
Xiàng Guī, a native of Lǐyáng, killed the Regional Inspector Lǚ Zìmù and occupied Lǐzhōu.
Meanwhile, Sòng Yèchāng, Shī Yì, and other various Man tribesmen from the ravines and caves,
all raised troops and plundered areas outside the lake.
Mǎn also used light boats to travel up and down the Jīngjiāng River,
attacking and raiding prefectures and counties.
Yáng Xíngmì attacked Dù Hóng at Èzhōu.
Chéng Ruì of Jīngnán sent out troops to rescue Hóng.
Ruì was defeated in battle
and drowned near Jūnshān.
Mǎn suddenly attacked and broke Jīngnán,
but was unable to hold it,
so he burned and plundered almost everything before leaving.
Mǎn once dug a deep pond within the government compound.
Whenever a guest visited,
he would summon them to a banquet by the pond,
pointing to the water and saying:
"Flood dragons and water monsters all make their lairs here;
truly, it is the Water Palace."
When the wine flowed freely,
he would take a vessel from the table and toss it into the pond,
then strip naked and jump in,
retrieving the vessel and playing in the water.
After a long time, he would emerge,
adjust his clothes, and resume his seat,
completely composed in manner.
While Mǎn resided in Lǎngzhōu,
he diverted the Yuán River to moat the city,
built a long bridge over it,
making a strategy so it could not be attacked.
During the Tiānyòu era,
Mǎn died.
His son Yàngōng established himself.
Yàngōng attached himself to Yáng Xíngmì,
and also frequently attacked and plundered, causing trouble for Jīng and Hú.
In the first year of Kāipíng,
Mǎ Yīn dispatched troops to attack Yàngōng.
Relying on the moat for defense,
they could not breach it for more than a year.
In the third year,
Yàngōng fled to Yáng Xíngmì.
Mǎ Yīn captured his brother Yànxióng and seven others and sent them to Liáng,
where they were executed in the market of Biàn.
Yàngōng died in Huáinán,
and Lǐ and Lǎng subsequently fell under the control of Chǔ.
Zhōng Chuán.
Zhōng Chuán
was a native of Gāo'ān, Hóngzhōu.
He served the prefecture as a junior officer.
When Huáng Cháo attacked and plundered Jiānghuái,
bandits arose everywhere,
frequently occupying prefectures and counties.
Chuán used the prefectural troops to attack the bandits
and won repeatedly.
He then drove out the Guānchásǐ (Surveillance Commissioner)
and declared himself Liúhòu (Acting Military Governor).
The Táng dynasty designated Hóngzhōu as the Zhènnán Circuit
and appointed Chuán as Jiédùshǐ.
Dù Hóng, an actor from Jiāngxià,
also occupied Èzhōu.
Yáng Xíngmì repeatedly attacked him.
Hóng largely relied on Chuán for mutual support.
After a long time,
Hóng was defeated and died.
At this time,
Wēi Quánfěng, Hán Shīdé, and others separately occupied Fǔ and Jí prefectures.
Chuán was unable to control them all.
He attacked them with troops,
and they gradually obeyed his orders.
Only Quánfěng could not be subdued,
so Chuán personally led troops to besiege him.
A fire broke out in the city at night.
His generals requested an immediate attack.
Chuán said:
"I have heard that a gentleman does not press a man when he is in peril."
He then swept the ground and made a sacrifice to Heaven,
bowed twice towards the city,
and prayed, saying:
"If Quánfěng does not surrender,
it is not the fault of the people.
I pray to Heaven to stop the fire."
Quánfěng heard of this,
and the next day he also submitted to his authority,
requesting to marry his daughter to Chuán's son, Kuāngshí.
Chuán resided in Jiāngxī for over thirty years,
repeatedly receiving appointments as Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian) and Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat),
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánpíng.
In the third year of Tiānyòu,
Chuán died.
His son Kuāngshí declared himself Liúhòu
and requested an appointment from Táng.
Quánfěng said:
"I have allowed gentleman Zhōng to be Jiédùshǐ for three years;
I am now going to be it myself."
Soon after, Chuán's adopted son Yánguī competed with Kuāngshí for control
and requested troops from Yáng Wò.
Wò sent Qín Péi and others to attack Kuāngshí.
Kuāngshí was defeated
and captured and taken back to Guǎnglíng.
In the third year of Kāipíng,
Quánfěng and others raised troops in Jiāngxī
planning to recover the former territory of the Zhōng family.
Quánfěng was defeated by Zhōu Běn, a general of Yáng Lóngyǎn,
and Jiāngxī subsequently entered the domain of Wú.
Zhào Kuāngníng.
Zhào Kuāngníng, courtesy name Guāngyí,
was a native of Càizhōu.
His father, Déyīn, served Qín Zōngquán
and was the Regional Inspector of Shēnzhōu.
When Zōngquán rebelled,
Déyīn attacked and captured Xiāngyáng.
When the Grand Ancestor of Liáng attacked Càizhōu,
and Zōngquán was repeatedly defeated,
Déyīn thereupon surrendered with the seven prefectures of the Shānnán Dōngdào.
The Grand Ancestor of Liáng, when he first garrisoned Xuānwǔ,
had once been besieged by Zōngquán.
Hearing of Déyīn's surrender,
he was greatly pleased,
and memorialized to appoint him Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Mobile Camp (Xíngyíng Fù Dūtǒng)
and Commander of the Moving Army (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ) for the three circuits of Héyáng, Bǎoyì, and Yìchāng.
When he joined forces to attack Càizhōu
and defeated it,
Déyīn contributed greatly.
Déyīn died,
and his son Kuāngníng established himself.
At this time,
Chéng Ruì died,
and Léi Yàngōng launched a surprise attack, seizing Jīngnán.
Kuāng Níng sent his younger brother, Kuāng Míng, to drive out Yàngōng.
Tàizǔ nominated Kuāng Níng as Jīngxiāng Jiédùshǐ (Regional Governor),
making Kuāng Míng the Jīngnán Liúhòu (Acting Military Commissioner).
At this time,
the Táng dynasty was in decline,
and the regional governors no longer obeyed the Imperial Court.
Only the Kuāng Níng brothers maintained their tribute and taxes continuously.
Kuāng Níng was a person of very imposing demeanor,
his nature was straightforward and strict,
he enjoyed self-cultivation,
and rather fond of scholarship.
He accumulated several thousand volumes of books,
and his governance combined authority and benevolence.
Tàizǔ attacked Yǎnzhōu.
Zhū Jǐn sought aid from Jìn.
Jìn sent Shǐ Yǎn and others leading several thousand troops to rescue Jǐn.
Jǐn was defeated
and fled with Yǎn and the others to Huáinán.
Jìn Wáng Lǐ Kèyòng sent a person carrying documents and gifts, requesting transit through Kuāng Níng’s territory,
in order to visit Yáng Xíngmì
and request the return of Yǎn and the others.
The Jìn Wáng’s envoy was captured by the Liáng.
Tàizǔ was greatly enraged.
At this time,
Liáng had already defeated Yǎn and Yùn.
They sent Shì Shūcóng, Kāng Huái'yīng, and others to attack Kuāng Níng.
Shūcóng captured Bì and Suí prefectures,
and Huái'yīng captured Dèngzhōu.
Kuāng Níng, fearful,
requested an alliance,
and then the attacks ceased.
Tàizǔ assassinated Emperor Zhāozōng,
planning to usurp the Táng dynasty.
Fearing that the Kuāng Níng brothers would not submit,
he sent an envoy to inform them.
Kuāng Níng, weeping, replied to the envoy:
"We have received profound grace from the Táng;
we dare not harbor any other ambitions."
Tàizǔ sent Yáng Shīhòu to attack him.
Tàizǔ personally followed up with forces in Hànběi.
Kuāng Níng was defeated in battle
and fled by light boat to Yáng Xíngmì.
Shīhòu advanced and attacked Jīngnán.
Kuāng Míng fled to Shǔ.
When Kuāng Níng reached Guǎnglíng,
Xíngmì met him
and joked,
"When you were in command of your territory,
you used swift carriages and heavy horses
to send tribute yearly to the Liáng.
Now that you are defeated, do you finally come to me?"
Kuāng Níng said:
"My family has served the Táng as ministers for generations.
The annual required tribute
was not paid to the thief (Zhū Wén).
Now, because I refused to follow the thief,
my power is exhausted, and I take refuge with you, Sire.
My life or death rests entirely upon you!"
Xíngmì treated him generously.
Later, after Xíngmì died,
Yáng Wò gradually treated him disrespectfully.
Wò was holding a banquet
and eating green plums.
Kuāng Níng looked at Wò and said,
"Do not eat too many;
they bring on children's fevers."
The generals considered this disrespectful.
Wò banished Kuāng Níng to Hǎilíng,
where he was later killed by Xú Wēn.
Kuāng Míng died in Shǔ.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Thirtieth: Zhū Xuān (Younger Brother Jǐn)
Zhū Xuān
was a native of Xiàyì, Sòngzhōu.
When young, he followed his father in salt trafficking and became a bandit.
When his father was executed by law,
Xuān left and served Wáng Jìngwǔ, the Qīngzhōu Jiédùshǐ, as a military officer.
Jìngwǔ assigned him to his general Cáo Quánshèng.
In the second year of Zhōnghé (882 CE),
Jìngwǔ sent Quánshèng to enter the pass and participate in defeating Huáng Cháo.
On the return, they passed Yùnzhōu.
Xuē Chóng, the Yùnzhōu Jiédùshǐ, had died,
and his general Cuī Jūnyù had proclaimed himself Liúhòu (Acting Military Commissioner).
Quánshèng attacked and killed Jūnyù,
and consequently occupied Yùnzhōu.
Xuān, based on his military achievements,
became the Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry for Yùnzhōu.
Soon after, Quánshèng died.
The army nominated Xuān to be Liúhòu.
Emperor Xīzōng of Táng immediately appointed Xuān as Tiānpíng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Liáng Tàizǔ was stationed at Xuānwǔ
and treated Xuān as an elder brother.
When Tàizǔ first took up his post,
his military strength was still small,
and he was repeatedly besieged by Qín Zōngquán.
Tàizǔ begged Xuān for troops.
Xuān and his younger brother, Jǐn, led the troops of Yǎn and Yùn to relieve Biàn,
heavily defeating the Cài forces
and driving out Zōngquán.
At this time,
Tàizǔ had already launched a surprise attack and seized Huázhōu,
gradually intending to annex all the regional commands.
After Xuān and Jǐn returned,
Tàizǔ quickly issued a proclamation to Yǎn and Yùn,
stating that Xuān and Jǐn had heavily induced Xuānwǔ soldiers to defect eastward.
He then mobilized troops to retrieve the deserters
and consequently attacked them.
They thus became enemy states,
fighting fiercely between Cáo and Pú.
At this time,
Liáng was also attacking Xúzhōu to the east,
had the Cài bandits to the west,
and faced the powerful Jìn state to the north.
The Xuān and Jǐn brothers supported each other mutually,
but ultimately they were destroyed by Liáng.
In the fourth year of Qiánníng (897 CE),
Xuān was defeated
and fled to Zhōngdū,
where he was captured by Gě Cóngzhōu
and executed beneath the Biàn Qiáo bridge.
Today, common tradition refers to Xuān as the elder brother of Jǐn,
and adds the character
"Wáng"
to his name.
This is incorrect.
Jǐn
was Xuān's younger cousin (paternal uncle's son).
He followed Xuān and resided in Yùnzhōu,
where he was appointed a military officer.
When young, he was unrestrained and unconventional,
possessing great ambition.
Qí Kèràng, the Yǎnzhōu Jiédùshǐ, admired his character
and gave him his daughter as a wife.
When Jǐn went to personally fetch his bride,
he selected strong men to serve as sedan bearers,
and hid weapons inside the sedan chair.
Arriving at Yǎnzhōu that night,
the troops were unleashed,
and he consequently captured Kèràng
and proclaimed himself Liúhòu.
Emperor Xīzōng immediately appointed Jǐn as Tàiníng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
After Jǐn and Xuān had defeated Qín Zōngquán at Biànzhōu,
Liáng Tàizǔ accused Jǐn of enticing Xuānwǔ soldiers to defect and return (to him).
He sent Zhū Zhēn to attack Jǐn,
seizing Cáozhōu,
and also attacking Púzhōu,
while Tàizǔ personally attacked Yùn.
The Jǐn brothers traveled back and forth, supporting each other,
for over ten years,
fighting dozens of battles, large and small,
and repeatedly experiencing victories and defeats against Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ captured Xuān's generals Hè Guī and Hé Huáibǎo, along with Jǐn's elder relative, Qióng.
He then brought Qióng and the others beneath the walls of Yǎnchéng
and announced to Jǐn:
"Your elder relative is defeated!
Now Qióng and the others have surrendered;
you had better surrender yourself quickly."
Jǐn falsely replied,
"Understood."
He then sent his staff officer Hú Guī, carrying documents and gifts, to the army gate to request surrender.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased,
and came to Yánshòu Mén to speak with Jǐn.
Jǐn said,
"I wish to have Qióng come to deliver the seal and tally."
Tàizǔ trusted him
and sent the guest general Liú Hàn to escort Qióng there.
Jǐn hid strong men beneath the bridge.
He rode out alone to meet Qióng
and waved his hand, saying to Hàn,
"I request that Qióng come alone!"
When Qióng advanced,
the strong men seized him.
Jǐn immediately closed the gates,
rebuked Qióng for having surrendered first,
executed him,
and tossed his head outside the city walls.
Tàizǔ judged that the city could not be taken
and so left troops to besiege it before departing.
Jǐn defended himself by holding the city,
and fought against Gě Cóngzhōu and others below the city walls.
Jǐn's troops were repeatedly defeated.
Xuān was also defeated at Yùnzhōu,
so he begged Jìn for troops.
Jìn dispatched Lǐ Chéngsì, Shǐ Yǎn, and others with five thousand cavalry to rescue them.
Tàizǔ had already defeated Xuān,
and immediately hurried toward Yǎn.
Food was exhausted within Jǐn's city.
[Jǐn] and Chéngsì plundered for food between Fēng and Pèi.
The Liáng forces arrived unexpectedly.
Kāng Huáiyīng, a general under Jǐn, surrendered the city to Liáng.
Jǐn and his subordinates led their troops and fled to Yízhōu.
Yǐn Chǔbīn, the Administrator of Yízhōu, did not accept them.
They then fled to Hǎizhōu.
The Liáng forces chased them urgently.
So they defected to Huáinán.
Yáng Xíngmì, hearing of Jǐn's arrival,
was greatly pleased.
He unbuckled his jade belt and presented it to him.
He memorialized to appoint Jǐn as acting Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Wǔníng Army,
and made him Deputy Commissioner of Campaigns (Xíngjūn Fùshǐ).
Afterward,
Liáng dispatched Páng Shīgǔ, Gě Cóngzhōu, and others to attack Huáinán.
Xíngmì employed Jǐn,
who greatly defeated the Liáng forces at Qīngkǒu,
and beheaded Shīgǔ.

Xíngmì repeatedly memorialized for Jǐn to be appointed Deputy Supreme Commander of Campaigns for the Southeastern Circuits (Dōngnán Zhū Dào Xíngyíng Fù Dūtǒng), acting Military Governor of the Pínglú Army (Pínglú Jūn Jiédùshǐ), and Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Xíngmì died.
Wò and subsequently Lóngyǎn were enthroned.
Both were young.
Xú Wēn and his son Zhīxùn monopolized power.
Fearing Jǐn,
they wished to eliminate him.
Jǐn consequently planned to assassinate Zhīxùn.
[Jǐn] once, on the first day of the lunar month, sent his favorite concubine to visit Zhīxùn's residence.
Zhīxùn forced intercourse with her.
When the concubine returned, she accused him.
Jǐn became even more disgruntled.
He repeatedly urged Lóngyǎn to execute the Xú family
to remove a national threat,
but Lóngyǎn was unable to do so.
Later, Zhīxùn established the Jìnghuái Army at Sìzhōu
and sent Jǐn out as its Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ).
Just before [Jǐn] was due to depart,
Zhīxùn invited him for a night drinking session.
The next day,
Zhīxùn visited Jǐn to apologize.
Jǐn invited him up into the hall,
and presented his wife, Táo Shì.
As Zhīxùn was bowing,
Jǐn struck him down with his ceremonial tablet (hù).
Hidden soldiers burst out from the door
and killed him.
Previously,
Jǐn had tethered two fierce horses in the courtyard.
When Zhīxùn entered, [Jǐn] released the horses,
allowing them to kick and whinny at each other,
so outsiders did not hear the disturbance.
Jǐn carried Zhīxùn's head and rushed to show it to Lóngyǎn, saying:
"Today, I have eliminated a threat for Wú!"
Lóngyǎn said:
"This matter is not one I dare to know about!"
He immediately rose and entered the inner quarters.
Jǐn furiously struck the pillar with the head,
took up his sword, and went out.
The gate of the headquarters was already shut.
He consequently climbed over the wall
and broke his foot.
Jǐn realized his path was blocked,
and cried out loudly:
"I have removed a harm for ten thousand people,
but now I must die for it by myself!"
He then committed suicide by cutting his throat.
Xú Zhīgào of Rùnzhōu heard of the chaos,
and hurried with troops to Guǎnglǐng.
He executed Jǐn's entire family.
Jǐn's wife, Táo Shì, wept at the execution site.
His concubine said:
"Why are you weeping?
Now we will soon see our lord!"
Táo Shì wiped away her tears,
and cheerfully went to her death.
Those who heard of it mourned them.
Jǐn's reputation was high in Jiānghuái.
People feared him.
When he died,
his corpse was displayed at the North Gate of Guǎnglǐng,
but passersby secretly buried him together.
At this time,
many common people suffered from malaria.
They all took soil from his grave,
mixed it with water, and ingested it.
It was said that the sickness immediately healed.
They constantly added new soil,
and gradually a high mound was formed.
Xú Wēn and others detested this
and exhumed his corpse,
throwing it into the Léigōng Táng pond.
Later, Wēn fell ill,
and dreamt that Jǐn drew a bow and shot him.
Wēn was frightened.
He retrieved the bones with a net,
buried them beside the pond,
and erected a shrine above the grave.
Earlier,
Jǐn had suffered from a carbuncle.
When the doctor examined it,
he looked afraid.
Jǐn said:
"Just treat it.
I am not destined to die from this illness."
And so it happened.
He died at the age of fifty-two.
Wáng Shīfàn
Wáng Shīfàn
was a native of Qīngzhōu.
His father, Jìngwǔ,
served as a staff officer (Yájiàng) of the Pínglú Army.
In the first year of Guǎngmíng of Táng (880),
Hóng Bàláng of Wúdì became a bandit between Qí and Dì.
Ān Shīrú, the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Pínglú, dispatched Jìngwǔ to lead troops to attack and defeat him.
Jìngwǔ turned his forces against Shīrú and expelled him.
He declared himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
Commander-in-Chief Wáng Duó, acting under imperial authority, appointed Jìngwǔ as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ).
When Jìngwǔ died,
Shīfàn was still young.
Zhāng Chán, the Administrator of Dìzhōu, rebelled.
Zhāozōng believed Shīfàn was too young
and his subordinates would not obey him,
so he appointed Cuī Ānqián, Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàoshī), as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Pínglú.
Shīfàn refused to be replaced.
Chán welcomed Ānqián into Dìzhōu.
Shīfàn dispatched his general Lú Hóng to attack Chán.
Hóng turned his troops back and unexpectedly attacked Qīngzhōu.
Shīfàn pretended to reply courteously,
sending someone to meet Hóng and tell him:
"I am young and incapable of handling affairs;
I rely only on the mutual support of my generals.
Otherwise,
I will listen to whatever you decide to do."
Hóng, believing Shīfàn incapable of action,
hurried back
without making precautions.
Shīfàn laid an ambush on the road,
and instructed his retainer Liú Xún:
"When Hóng arrives,
behead him for me!
I will make you a staff officer (Yájiàng)."
The next day,
Hóng arrived.
Shīfàn went out to meet him.
Xún beheaded him at the table.
The hidden troops were dispatched
and killed all the remaining soldiers.
[Shīfàn] then immediately attacked Dìzhōu,
defeated Zhāng Chán,
and Ānqián fled back to the Capital (Jīngshī).
Zhāozōng then appointed Shīfàn as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ).
Shīfàn was quite fond of Confucian studies,
accumulating up to ten thousand scrolls of books.
His governance was both authoritative and benevolent.
Tàizǔ of Liáng besieged Zhāozōng at Fèngxiáng.
The eunuchs, Hán Quánhuì and others, forged an imperial edict summoning troops from all circuits to attack Liáng.
When the edict reached Qīngzhōu,
Shīfàn wept and said:
"The various circuits possess troops
precisely to guard the Son of Heaven.
Now the Son of Heaven is in danger and humiliated,
yet the various circuits instead use their troops merely for self-defense.
Although my strength is insufficient,
I must commit myself, win or lose."
He then dispatched an envoy to beg Yáng Xíngmì for troops.
At this time,
Liáng had already moved east and subjugated Yǎn and Yùn.
Shīfàn then dispatched Liú Xún and his younger brother Shīlǔ to separately attack Yǎn and Mìzhōu.
He dispatched Zhāng Jūhòu with two hundred brave men serving as sedan bearers,
hiding soldiers inside the sedan chairs.
They raced west toward the Liáng army,
claiming to be Shīfàn's envoys paying a courtesy visit to Liáng,
intending to seize and assassinate Tàizǔ.
Jūhòu reached the East Wall of Huàzhōu.
Lóu Jìngsī, the general commanding Huàzhōu, suspected something unusual,
cut open the sedan chairs to inspect them,
and discovered the soldiers.
Jūhòu immediately attacked and killed Jìngsī.
He used his troops to attack the West Wall,
but failed to overcome it and returned.
Liú Xún drove out Gě Cóngzhōu and took Yǎnzhōu,
and all the circuits of Pínglú rose up in arms to attack Liáng.
Afterward,
Great Ancestor of Liáng (Liáng Tàizǔ) returned eastward from Fèngxiáng.
He dispatched Zhū Yǒuníng to attack Shī Fàn,
but Yǒuníng died in battle.
He again dispatched Yáng Shīhòu to attack him,
garrisoning at Línqú.
Shī Fàn pressured him with troops,
but Shīhòu pretended to be timid and dared not emerge.
He secretly sent someone to pretend to say:
"The Liáng troops are few,
and are currently begging for reinforcements from Fèngxiáng.
Now the grain supply is about to run out,
so we must withdraw the army."
Shī Fàn thought this was true,
and so dispatched Shī Lǔ with all his troops to attack him.
Shīhòu resisted but did not engage.
When Shī Lǔ's troops retreated,
Shīhòu pursued and attacked them until Shèngwáng Shān.
Shī Lǔ was greatly defeated.
He then advanced upon his city,
and the separate Liáng general Liú Chóngbà captured his Dìzhōu.
Shī Fàn then requested surrender,
and the Great Ancestor (Tàizǔ) granted it.
Shī Fàn, wearing plain clothes and riding a donkey, went to Tàizǔ to beg for punishment.
Tàizǔ treated him with the rites due a guest.
After a long time,
he proposed Shī Fàn as the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Héyáng.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he summoned him to serve as General-in-Chief of the Right Metropolitan Guard (Yòu Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn),
residing in Luòyáng.
Tàizǔ inwardly wished to execute him,
but had not found a pretext to start.
Tàizǔ’s sons had already been enfeoffed as princes,
and were feasting in the palace.
The wife of Yǒuníng tearfully said to Tàizǔ:
"Your Majesty has transformed his household into a state,
and all your sons have received enfeoffment.
Yet my husband alone died in battle.
How can it be that his enemy is still at court!"
Tàizǔ flared up, pointed his hand like a halberd (in anger),
and said: "I had almost forgotten this scoundrel!"
He then dispatched men to Luòyáng to exterminate his entire clan.
When the messenger arrived,
he first dug a pit outside,
and then entered to inform him.
Shī Fàn prepared a feast and furnishings,
and drank wine with all his relatives.
He said to the messenger:
"Death
is something no man can escape,
let alone one who is guilty.
However, I fear that the young and old might lose proper order,
thereby shaming our ancestors below."
When the drinking was halfway through,
he ordered the young and old to rise sequentially
and go to the pit where they were executed.
All who heard of it grieved for him.
In the third year of Tóngguāng (Tóngguāng sānnían),
Shī Fàn was posthumously granted the title Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi).
Lǐ Hǎnzhi
Lǐ Hǎnzhi
was a native of Xiàngchéng, Chénzhōu.
His personality was fierce and brave,
and his strength equaled that of several men.
As a youth, he studied,
but failed to finish his schooling.
He left to become a monk,
but because of his shiftless nature,
he was not tolerated wherever he went.
He then begged for food in the market of Suānzǎo.
The market people all refused to give him anything.
Hǎnzhi threw his begging bowl to the ground,
tore his robes,
and then left to become a bandit.
At this time,
Huáng Cháo arose in Cáo and Pú,
and Hǎnzhi went to rely on him.
When Cháo crossed the Yangtze River northward,
Hǎnzhi and his subordinates fled to Huáinán,
and submitted themselves to Gāo Pián.
Pián proposed him as the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Guāngzhōu.
After about a year,
Qín Zōngquán urgently attacked Guāngzhōu.
Hǎnzhi could not defend it,
and returned to flee to Xiàngchéng,
where he gathered his remaining followers.
He relied on Zhūgě Shuǎng at Héyáng.
Shuǎng appointed Hǎnzhi as Prefect of Huáizhōu.
When Cháo had already been defeated and fled,
Shuǎng surrendered to Táng.
Emperor Xīzōng appointed Shuǎng as Commander of the Southeastern Campaigns (Dōngnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ),
in order to attack Zōngquán.
Shuǎng proposed Hǎnzhi as Deputy Commander,
giving him troops to garrison Sòngzhōu,
and also proposed him as Magistrate of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn) and Resident Retainer of the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū Liúshǒu).
Qín Zōngquán dispatched Sūn Rú to attack Hénán.
Hǎnzhi had few troops,
and fled west to Miǎnchí.
Rú burned the palaces and gates,
looted, and departed.
Hǎnzhi established a camp at Miǎnchí.
After more than a year,
Zhūgě Shuǎng died.
His general Liú Jīng installed Shuǎng's son Zhòngfāng.
Zhòngfāng was young,
and entrusted all matters to Jīng.
Jīng worried that Hǎnzhi was fierce and brave, and hard to control,
so he used troops to attack him.
Hǎnzhi counterattacked and drove Jīng away.
Hǎnzhi pursued him to Gǒngxiàn,
lined up boats at the Sìshǔi River,
preparing to cross the Yellow River (Hé).
Jīng dispatched Zhāng Yán to resist him on the riverbank.
Yán, however, betrayed Jīng
and joined Hǎnzhi to attack Héyáng together.
They were defeated by Jīng,
and retreated to defend Huáizhōu.
Soon afterward, Sūn Rú captured Héyáng,
and Zhòngfāng fled to Liáng.
The Liáng army attacked and drove Rú away.
Hǎnzhi suddenly took Héyáng,
and Yán took Hénán.
Both submitted to Liáng.
Hǎnzhi and Yán were both rebellious generals of Shuǎng.
When their affairs were established,
they clasped arms and made an oath,
swearing to share happiness and sorrow and never forget each other.
Hǎnzhi managed his troops without proper method;
his nature was harsh and cruel,
and he largely lost the hearts of his men.
But Yán was skilled at managing military affairs,
taught the people to sow and cultivate,
and aimed at accumulation [of supplies].
When Hǎnzhi used his troops,
Yán often supplied his needs.
Hǎnzhi's demands were endless,
and Yán suffered greatly from this.
Unable to provide everything,
Hǎnzhi summoned Yán's army officials and whipped them.
Yán became increasingly resentful.
Hǎnzhi deployed all his troops to attack Jìn and Jiàng.
Yán launched a night attack on Héyáng,
and Hǎnzhi fled to Jìn.
Jìn proposed Hǎnzhi as Prefect of Zézhōu,
and sent Lǐ Cúnxiào with thirty thousand troops to help Hǎnzhi attack Yán.
Yán sought aid from Liáng.
Hǎnzhi was defeated at the Yǎnhé,
and then returned to Tàiyuán.
Lǐ Kèyòng received him into his tent.
Hǎnzhi left his son Qí to serve Jìn,
and then went to Zézhōu.
Daily he used troops to raid and plunder the area between Huái and Mèng,
eating people as food.
The residents gathered and fortified on Móyún Shān.
Hǎnzhi attacked and killed them all,
establishing a stockade on top of it.
People at the time called him Lǐ Móyún (Li the Cloud-Climber).
At this time,
Jìn was actively seeking territory in Shāndōng,
and heavily relied on Hǎnzhi as a shield and defense.
When Lǐ Màozhēn and others encroached upon the Capital,
Kèyòng brought his troops north of the Wèi River (Wèiběi).
Emperor Xīzōng appointed Kèyòng as the Supreme Commander of the Four-Sided Campaign Camps of Bīnzhōu (Bīnzhōu Sìmiàn Xíngyíng Dūtǒng),
and proposed Hǎnzhi as his Deputy.
After defeating Wáng Xíngyú,
he was additionally granted the title of Acting Grand Marshal (Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi),
and a fief of one thousand households.
Hǎnzhi, believing his merit surpassed others in Jìn,
privately said to Gài Yù:
"Since I escaped from Héyáng,
I have relied on Jìn to tolerate me,
but I have not yet been able to repay this.
Now I am growing old
and unable to achieve anything.
If my prince would take pity on me,
and grant me a small prefecture (zhèn),
allowing me to rest my troops and nurture my health before retiring,
that would be fortunate!"
Yù relayed this to him,
but Kèyòng gave no reply.
On another day,
when generals were being selected to defend various prefectures,
Hǎnzhi was never mentioned,
and his heart grew increasingly discontent.
Yù informed Kèyòng,
fearing Hǎnzhi harbored different intentions.
Kèyòng said:
"Why would I grudge Hǎnzhi a single prefecture?
But the nature of an eagle
is that once it is full, it will fly away!"
In the first year of Guānghuà,
Xuē Zhìqín of Lùzhōu died.
Hǎnzhī immediately entered Lùzhōu,
and sent someone to report to Jìn Wáng, saying:
"Zhìqín was about to die,
and the new commander had not yet arrived.
The reason for this
was to guard against other bandits!"
Kèyòng was furious
and dispatched Lǐ Sìzhāo to attack him.
Hǎnzhī seized the Jìn defending generals Mǎ Gài, Yī Tán, and others,
and sent his son Hào to Liáng to beg for troops.
Liáng Tàizǔ sent Dīng Huì to guard Lùzhōu,
and appointed Hǎnzhī as the Jìedùshǐ of Héyáng.
He died of illness
when he reached Huáizhōu,
aged fifty-eight.
Hǎnzhī had initially betrayed Liáng and returned to Jìn.
Jìn Wáng appointed Hǎnzhī to guard Zézhōu,
and Hǎnzhī left his son Qí to associate with Zhuāngzōng,
with whom he was very familiar.
Later, Hǎnzhī betrayed Jìn and returned to Liáng.
Jìn Wáng was angry
and wanted to kill Qí.
Zhuāngzōng gave him a fast horse
and allowed him to flee to Liáng.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased to obtain Qí and his father,
and had him and Yǒulún lead troops to guard Zhāozōng.
Therefore, during Tàizǔ's time, Qí
always commanded the imperial guard.
When Mòdì executed Yǒuguī,
Qí was involved in the plot.
He was appointed Right Yǔlín Tǒngjūn and Cìshǐ of Chénzhōu.
He served Táng,
successively holding the posts of Cìshǐ of Wèi and Yǎn Prefectures,
and was promoted to Right Lǐngjūn Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
He died in the Tiānfú period,
aged seventy,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi.
Mèng Fānglì
Mèng Fānglì was
a native of Píngxiāng, Xíngzhōu.
In his youth, he was a soldier,
and was selected as a company commander for his bravery and strength.
In the Guǎngmíng period of Táng,
Gāo Xún, the Jìedùshǐ of Lùzhōu, attacked Zhūgě Shuǎng at Héyáng.
He sent Fānglì to lead troops through Tiānjǐng Pass as the vanguard.
Xún was driven away by his general Liú Guǎng,
and Guǎng was killed by rebellious soldiers.
Upon hearing of the chaos, Fānglì
led his troops from Tiānjǐng and occupied Lùzhōu.
Táng then made him the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì Army.
Zhāoyì controlled five prefectures: Zé, Lù, Xíng, Míng, and Cí,
with its seat in Lùzhōu.
Fānglì believed that Lùzhōu's mountains and rivers were high and perilous,
and its people were strong and fierce.
Since Liú Zhěn, they had often driven away their commanders.
Moreover, he was a native of Xíng,
so he moved his army to Xíngzhōu.
The people of Lù resented Fānglì's relocation,
and consequently submitted Zé and Lù Prefectures to Jìn.
Jìn sent Lǐ Kèxiū to be the Jìedùshǐ of Zéluò.
Fānglì then made Xíng, Míng, and Cí Prefectures his own Zhāoyì Army.
Jìn repeatedly dispatched Lǐ Cúnxiào and others to lead troops to scout Shāndōng.
The people of the three prefectures were almost entirely captured and plundered,
leaving thousands of miles of barren land,
with no one to cultivate or raise silkworms for several years.
Fānglì defended himself with isolated cities,
and sought aid from Liáng.
Liáng was then occupied with affairs in Yǎn and Yùn to the east,
and could not provide help.
In the first year of Wéndé,
Fānglì requested troops from Wáng Róng to attack Jìn,
and Róng agreed.
Fānglì then sent his general Xī Zhōngxìn to attack Jìn's Liáozhōu,
but Róng, due to other reasons, could not send troops.
As the troops failed to keep their appointment,
Zhōngxìn was greatly defeated,
and the Jìn army took advantage of the victory to attack him.
Fānglì's general Shí Yuánzuǒ was
skilled in military matters and very resourceful.
Fānglì had always trusted him.
When Zhōngxìn was defeated,
Yuánzuǒ was captured by the Jìn general Ān Jīnjùn.
Jīnjùn treated him generously
and asked for strategies to attack Xíng.
Yuánzuǒ said:
"Fānglì is good at defense, and Xíng city is strong.
If we attack it,
we will certainly not succeed.
We should quickly attack his Cízhōu.
When Fānglì comes to rescue,
we can defeat him."
Jīnjùn thought this was a good idea.
When they camped west of Fúshuǐ,
Fānglì indeed led troops to rescue,
but was defeated by Jīnjùn.
He galloped back into Xíngzhōu
and closed the city gates, no longer sallying forth.
There were no relief troops from outside,
and food in the city was almost exhausted.
Fānglì went out at night to inspect the city
and shouted orders to the guards,
but the guards did not respond.
Fānglì knew it was hopeless,
so he returned and drank poison, and died.
The army made his younger brother, Míngzhōu Cìshǐ, Qiān, the Liúhòu,
and sought aid from Liáng.
Liáng Tàizǔ sent Wáng Qiányù to lead three hundred cavalry to assist Qiān in defense.
Qiān seized Qiányù and surrendered to Jìn.
Jìn moved Qiān's clan to Tàiyuán,
and appointed him Cìshǐ of Fénzhōu.
Later, he was made Jìedùshǐ of Zéluò.
In the first year of Tiānfù,
Liáng sent Shì Shūcóng to attack Jìn.
He came out of Tiānjǐng Pass,
and Qiān opened the gates and surrendered,
serving as a guide for the Liáng army to attack Tàiyuán,
but they did not succeed.
When Shūcóng's army returned through Lù,
he took Qiān back to Liáng.
Liáng Tàizǔ detested his treachery
and killed him.
Wáng Kē
Wáng Kē was
a native of Hézhōng.
His paternal uncle, Chóngróng,
defeated Huáng Cháo with the Hézhōng army
and rendered meritorious service to Táng.
He was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng.
Chóngróng had no sons,
so he adopted his elder brother Chóngjiǎn's son, Kē, as his heir.
When Chóngróng died,
his younger brother Chóngyíng succeeded him.
When Chóngyíng died,
the army then, considering Kē to be Chóngróng's son,
appointed him.
Chóngyíng's sons, Gǒng, the Jìedùshǐ of Shǎnzhōu, and Yáo, the Cìshǐ of Jiàngzhōu,
contested the succession with Kē.
Gǒng and Yáo wrote to Liáng Tàizǔ,
stating that Kē was formerly a servant of the Wáng family,
with the pet name Zhōng'ér,
and should not be allowed to succeed.
Kē also sought aid from Jìn.
The Jìn people reported this to the court,
and Zhāozōng, for Jìn's sake,
agreed.
However, Gǒng and Yáo also allied with Wáng Xíngyú, Hán Jiàn, and Lǐ Màozhēn in the west for support.
Xíngyú and the others submitted joint memorials,
but Zhāozōng replied that Chóngróng and Jìn had rendered great service to Táng,
and since he had already agreed,
it could not be changed.
Xíngyú and the others were enraged,
and used troops to violate the capital,
killing Chancellor Lǐ Xī and others before leaving.
Gǒng and Yáo joined forces to attack Kē in Hézhōng.
Kē sought aid from Jìn,
and the Jìn army marched west to attack the three garrisons.
They proceeded to Jiàngzhōu,
beheaded Yáo, and passed through.
Upon reaching Wèiběi,
they defeated Xíngyú.
Zhāozōng finally appointed Kē as Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng.
Jìn married a daughter to him,
and sent Lǐ Sìzhāo to lead troops to assist Kē in attacking Gǒng's Shǎnzhōu.
Gǒng was cruel and severe.
He often beheaded people and threw their heads before him,
speaking and laughing as if nothing had happened,
which caused his subordinates great suffering.
The partial general Lǐ Fán, taking advantage of Gǒng's defeat in battle,
killed Gǒng
and declared himself Liúhòu.
At this time,
Liáng had already subjugated Zhèn and Dìng,
and was about to move his troops west.
However, Zhāozōng was deposed by Liú Jìshù,
and the capital was in great chaos.
Cuī Yìn secretly summoned Liáng to bring troops west.
Liáng Tàizǔ, seeing Kē in Héchōng,
feared he would become a problem,
so he turned to Zhāng Cúnjìng and Hóu Yán,
and gave them a large rope,
saying:
"Bind Kē and bring him to me!"
Cúnjìng and his troops marched out of Hánshān,
defeated the two prefectures of Jìn and Jiàng,
and sent Hé Yīn with troops to guard them,
cutting off Jìn's aid.
Cúnjìng besieged Héchōng.
Kē sent an urgent appeal to Jìn,
but Jìn could not advance because of Yīn.
Kē then sent his wife with a letter to Jìn Wáng, saying:
"The bandit's power is such
that we will be begging for food from Liáng morning and evening!
How can Your Excellency bear not to rescue us?"
Jìn Wáng replied:
"Liáng's troops are blocking the way,
and our numbers are unequal.
If we rescue you, Jìn will perish along with you.
It is better for you and Wáng Láng to surrender to the imperial court."
Kē then wrote a letter to Lǐ Màozhēn, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has just returned to power,
and has issued an edict to the vassal towns not to invade each other, in order to pacify the royal house.
Now Duke Zhū has abandoned the agreement and is attacking me;
his ambition will not stop at my humble city.
If my humble city perishes in the morning,
then the northwestern towns will not be able to be held by you gentlemen!
I wish to join Huázhōu in sending troops to Tóngguān to provide support."
Màozhēn did not reply.
Kē, at his wit's end,
then prepared boats on the river,
intending to return to the capital.
Kē ascended the city wall at night to address the defenders,
but the defenders all remained silent.
His adjutant Liú Xùn entered Kē's bedchamber at night to report,
and Kē shouted at him:
"Are the soldiers rebelling?!"
Xùn then removed his outer garment and searched himself before entering, saying:
"If Your Excellency has doubts,
please first cut off my arm!"
Kē said:
"The situation is critical!
What is the plan?"
Xùn said:
"If Your Excellency takes your family and crosses the river at night,
people will certainly fight for boats.
If one man makes trouble,
the great matter will be lost.
It is better to wait until dawn to explain the situation to the army;
those who are willing to follow will still be half.
Otherwise,
we should prepare a surrender document to delay Liáng's troops,
and then slowly plan our allegiance."
Kē thought this was a good idea.
Liáng Tàizǔ, upon submitting to Táng from Tóngzhōu,
immediately relied on Chóngróng.
Because Chóngróng's mother was Lady Wáng,
Liáng Tàizǔ traditionally regarded Chóngróng as his maternal uncle.
Kē then ascended the city wall and called out to Cúnjìng, saying:
"I have a generational friendship with Liáng Wáng.
Your troops should withdraw
and await Liáng Wáng's arrival;
I will then obey his command."
Cúnjìng then withdrew,
and sent a swift messenger to Tàizǔ in Luòyáng.
When Tàizǔ arrived at Héchōng,
he first went east of the city,
wept at Chóngróng's tomb, and then entered.
Kē wanted to appear before Tàizǔ with his hands bound and leading a sheep,
but Tàizǔ said to him:
"How can the kindness of Taishī Ājiù ever be forgotten?
If you, young master, appear in the ceremony of a vanquished state,
what would Taishī think of me?"
Kē met him on the road,
and they clasped hands and sighed.
Then Kē was moved to Biàn.
Tàizǔ, knowing Kē was Jìn's son-in-law,
suspected his disloyalty,
and ordered Kē to go west to pay respects.
When he reached Huázhōu,
he had someone kill him in the relay station.
Zàn
was a son of Chóngyíng.
After Liáng Tàizǔ captured Kē,
he personally took command of Héchōng Jìedùshǐ,
and appointed Zàn as an official.
Zàn served Liáng,
becoming a general of the imperial guards
and the Jìedùshǐ of Tàiníng and Zhènguó Armies.
During Mòdì's reign,
he became the Yin of Kāifēng.
In the fifth year of Zhēnmíng (919 CE),
he replaced Hè Guī as the Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Expeditionary Army.
At this time,
Jìn had already fortified Déshèng.
Zàn crossed the river from Líyáng to attack Chánzhōu,
but failed,
and retreated to Yángcūn,
blocking the upper reaches of the river,
where he was locked in a stalemate with the Jìn people for a year,
engaging in more than a hundred battles, large and small.
Zàn ultimately achieved nothing.
Mòdì sent Dài Sīyuǎn to replace him,
and Zàn returned to being the Yin of Kāifēng.
When Zhuāngzōng entered the capital from Yùn,
Mòdì heard that the Táng troops were approaching,
and wept day and night,
not knowing what to do.
He held the imperial seal himself,
pointed to his palace, and said to Zàn:
"Whether I can keep this
depends on your strategy!"
The Táng troops had already passed Wǎnqú.
Zàn led the city's inhabitants to ascend the walls and resist the defense.
The Táng troops attacked Fēngqiūmén.
Zàn opened the gate and surrendered,
prostrating himself and begging for death.
Zhuāngzōng comforted him and helped him up, saying:
"Our two families have been joined in marriage for generations,
but each subject serves his own lord.
What crime is there?"
He then appointed him Yin of Kāifēng,
and later promoted him to Jìedùshǐ of Xuānwǔ Army.
Soon after, former Liáng officials like Zhào Yán and Zhāng Hànjié were successively executed.
Zàn died of sorrow,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàishī.
Zhào Chōu
Zhào Chōu,
his ancestors were from Qīngzhōu.
For generations, they were adjutants in Chénzhōu.
When Chōu was young, he played in the street with other children,
arranging them into ranks,
and giving commands like a general.
Even the older children all obeyed his orders.
His father, Shúwén, saw this
and exclaimed:
"This child will make our family great!"
When he grew up,
he was skilled in archery,
courageous and resolute,
and valued loyalty and righteousness.
The刺shǐ (Prefect) heard of his talent
and summoned him to his command.
He was successively promoted to Dōuyúhòu of the cavalry and infantry of Zhōngwǔ Army.
When Wáng Xiānzhī raided Hénán,
he captured Rǔzhōu
and was about to invade Dōngdū.
Chōu led troops to defeat him,
and Xiānzhī then went south.
Soon after, Huáng Cháo rose up,
and the prefectures and counties everywhere
were often captured by the bandits.
Hundreds of heroes from Chénzhōu
went together to Zhōngwǔ Army,
requesting Chōu to be appointed Cìshǐ (Prefect) to protect themselves.
Zhōngwǔ Army then submitted a memorial recommending Chōu as Chénzhōu Cìshǐ.
Soon after, Cháo captured Cháng'ān.
Chōu told his generals and officials:
"In my estimation,
if Cháo is not executed by the people of Cháng'ān,
he will certainly lead his forces east.
My prefecture will be directly in his path!"
So, he built fortifications for defense,
moved residents within sixty li into the city,
selected their young men,
equipped them with weapons and armor,
and appointed his younger brothers Chǎng and Xǔ as generals.
When Cháo was defeated,
he indeed headed east.
He first sent Mèng Kǎi to occupy Xiàngchéng,
but Chǎng attacked and defeated him,
capturing Kǎi and returning with him.
Cháo arrived later
and was furious when he heard Kǎi had been captured.
When Zhuāngzōng's troops reached Biàn,
Mòdì was terrified and did not know what to do.
He ascended the Jiànguó Lóu (Building of Established State) to ask his ministers.
Some said:
“Jìn has come a great distance with an isolated army;
its strength is hard to maintain for long.
Even if they are allowed to enter Biàn,
they cannot hold it.
It is advisable to proceed to Luòyáng,
hold the dangerous passes, summon forces from all under Heaven,
and plan slowly.
The outcome of victory or defeat is not yet known.”
Mòdì hesitated.
Yán said:
“The situation is already like this.
If you descend this building,
who can protect you!”
Mòdì eventually died atop the building.
When Yán was in power,
Wēn Tāo of Xǔzhōu especially courted Yán.
Yán therefore looked to his attendants and said:
“I have always treated Tāo generously.
If I now flee to him in distress,
he will surely not be fortunate enough to take advantage of me for profit.”
So he fled to Tāo,
but Tāo cut off his head and presented it.
After Zhuāngzōng had destroyed Liáng,
Duàn Níng, whom Yán had always treated well, submitted a memorial requesting the execution of Yán's family.
They were then exterminated as a clan.
Alas,
the principle of fortune and misfortune,
how can it be uniform!
The fortune and misfortune of the noble person (jūnzǐ) and the base person (xiǎorén) are different.
Lǎozǐ said:
“Misfortune, alas, is what fortune leans upon;
fortune, alas, is what misfortune lies hidden beneath.”
Later generations, when discussing fortune and misfortune,
all take his words as the ultimate theory.
If one acts kindly and receives fortune,
how can one receive misfortune?
If one acts wickedly and receives misfortune,
how can one receive fortune?
Only when a jūnzǐ encounters what is not misfortune,
it may not necessarily fail to become fortune;
when a xiǎorén seeks what is not fortune,
it never fails to reach misfortune.
This is a natural principle.
In the beginning,
Chǒu relied on his foresight,
and deeply allied himself with Liáng Tàizǔ.
He and his descendants all enjoyed their emoluments and benefits.
He considered that he knew whom to entrust himself to.
How could he know that his clan would eventually be destroyed along with Liáng?
Chǒu’s pursuit of fortune with Liáng,
is perhaps what Lǎoshì referred to as fortune,
but it is not what a jūnzǐ seeks.
Should one not be cautious!
Féng Xíngxí
Féng Xíngxí, courtesy name Zhèngchén,
was a native of Jūnzhōu.
In the late Táng period,
Sūn Xǐ, a bandit from Shānnán, attacked the Prefect of Jūnzhōu, Lǚ Yè, with a thousand followers.
Yè could not defend against him.
Xíngxí, being a commander in the prefecture,
secretly selected brave soldiers and concealed them south of the river.
He alone took a small boat and went against Xǐ,
announcing:
“The people of the prefecture, hearing of your arrival,
all wish to submit!
However, knowing your troops are numerous,
the people fear being plundered and robbed.
Fearing they might be alarmed and disturbed,
please leave your troops north of the river,
and proceed only with a few trusted confidants.
