I am willing to act as your guide,
to comfort and pacify the prefectural people.
The matter can be settled immediately.”
Xǐ thought this was correct,
so he left his troops north of the river
and crossed the river only with Xíngxí.
When the military clerk came forward to pay respects,
Xíngxí struck Xǐ down,
and beheaded him.
The concealed troops launched their attack,
killing all of Xǐ’s followers.
The remaining troops north of the river,
hearing of Xǐ's death,
all scattered.
The Regional Commander (Jiédùshǐ) of Shānnán, Liú Jùróng, memorialized to appoint Xíngxí as Prefect of Jūnzhōu.
At that time,
Xīzōng was in Shǔ,
and tributes from various garrisons heading to the traveling court all passed through Shānnán.
Many bandits occupied the Chángshān mountains west of the prefecture to intercept and rob them.
Xíngxí completely defeated all these bandits.
Gě Zuǒ of Yángzhōu appointed Xíngxí as Chief Commandant (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ),
and ordered him to garrison Gǔkǒu with troops,
opening the road between Qín and Shǔ.
Xíngxí became known for this.
When Lǐ Màozhēn concurrently held Shānnán,
he sent his son Jìzhēn to guard Jīnzhōu.
Xíngxí drove him out,
and consequently occupied Jīnzhōu.
Zhāozōng then established Jīnzhōu as the Róngzhāo Army
and appointed Xíngxí as Regional Commander.
When Zhāozōng was in Qí,
Liáng Tàizǔ led his troops westward.
The Court Commissioner (Zhōngwèi), Hán Quánhuì, sent the palace eunuch Xī Wényàn and more than twenty others to summon troops from Jiānghuái
to resist Tàizǔ.
Xíngxí had already submitted to Liáng,
so he killed Wényàn and all the others.
When Tàizǔ attacked Zhào Kuāngníng in Xiāngyáng,
Xíngxí sent his son Xù with naval forces to rendezvous at Jūn and Fáng.
For his merit, he was promoted to Regional Commander of the Kuāngguó Army.
Xíngxí was strict and harsh, and lacked kindness,
but wherever he went, he always enjoyed heaven’s favor.
If there was drought and locusts in his territory,
flying birds would eat them.
In years of famine,
salt-tolerant grain (lǔgǔ) would spontaneously grow in the fields.
As the Táng dynasty declined,
he knew that Liáng would surely rise,
and he devoted himself fully and sincerely to serving Liáng.
He reached the official post of Sīkōng (Minister of Works),
was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chánglè Commandery,
and after his death was posthumously granted the title of Tàifù (Grand Tutor),
with the posthumous name Zhōngjìng.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter 31: Shì Shūcóng
Shì Shūcóng
was a native of Wèishì, Kāifēng.
He served as a corporal of the Liáng cavalry.
When the Liáng army attacked Huáng Cháo between Chén and Xǔ,
Shūcóng fought and repeatedly achieved merit.
Tàizǔ admired him
and appointed him commander of the rear guard cavalry.
He followed in the attacks on Xú and Yǎn,
and was memorialized for the post of Prefect of Sùzhōu.
When he was ordered to attack Xiāngyáng,
he was repeatedly defeated in battle.
He was demoted to Garrison Commander (Zhènè Shǐ) of Yángzháizhen.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Prefect of Cáozhōu.
When Tàizǔ subdued Hézhōng
and captured Jìn and Jiàng,
the Prince of Jìn sent an envoy to write to Tàizǔ seeking peace.
Tàizǔ considered the language in the Jìn letter disrespectful,
so he dispatched Shūcóng along with Hè Délún and others to attack them.
Shūcóng entered via Tàiháng,
captured Zé and Lù,
came out at Shíhuì,
and set up camp at Dòngwō.
After a long time, their supplies ran out,
and they returned.
He was memorialized for the post of Prefect of Jìnzhōu.
The Jìn forces recaptured Jiàngzhōu
and attacked Línfén.
Shūcóng selected two strong men who were deep-eyed and bearded,
and had them graze horses along the Xiānglíng road.
The Jìn forces thought they were Jìn soldiers,
and mingled along the road.
Waiting for them to become careless,
Shūcóng captured the two Jìn men and returned.
The Jìn forces were greatly alarmed,
thinking there were hidden troops,
and retreated to garrison Púxiàn.
Tàizǔ sent Yǒu Níng with ten thousand troops to meet Shūcóng to resist Jìn.
Yǒu Níng wished to rest the troops and wait.
Shūcóng said:
“If the enemy hears that reinforcements have arrived, they will surely flee.
If they flee, what merit will there be?”
He then attacked them by night.
The Jìn forces suffered a great defeat,
and they pursued them as far as Tàiyuán.
Tàizǔ was overjoyed and said:
“To break Tàiyuán, only Elder Shì can do it.”
Soon after, a great plague broke out among the troops.
Shūcóng ordered the troops to return,
issuing the command:
“Those who are too sick to walk must be burned.”
The sick soldiers were afraid
and all declared they were fine.
He then used elite soldiers as the rear guard and returned to Shíhuì.
He left a few cavalrymen,
and set up the great general's banners atop a high hill.
The Jìn troops suspected that he had an ambush,
and therefore dared not pursue.
After a long time,
he was transferred to be Regional Commander of the Bǎodà Army.
When Zhāozōng was moved to Luò,
he was appointed Right Leader of the Dragon Martial Army (Yòu Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn).
Tàizǔ sent Shūcóng and Lǐ Yānwēi and others to assassinate Zhāozōng,
and subsequently killed them.
Lǐ Yānwēi
Soon after, Qín Zōngquán 宗權 of Cài Zhōu 蔡州 defected to Huáng Cháo 黃巢.
Cháo's 巢's power grew formidable.
He then gathered all his forces to besiege Chén Zhōu 陳州,
setting up grindstones
to grind human flesh for food.
The people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 were afraid.
Chén Zhōu 陳州 said to his subordinates:
"Our family has been generals of Chén Zhōu 陳州 for three generations.
We will surely be able to defend this city.
You men,
you should seek life in death,
achieve great deeds and establish your careers.
It might well be because of this very moment."
All the people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 were encouraged and leaped with joy.
Cháo 巢 built a camp called Bā Xiān Yíng 八仙營 three li north of the city,
erecting palaces,
appointing officials,
and stockpiling provisions,
intending to wear down the city over a long period.
His army numbered two hundred thousand.
The people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 had several hundred giant crossbows,
but they were all broken and in disrepair.
Later-generation crossbow artisans did not even recognize their design.
Chén Zhōu 珍 created an innovative way to repair them.
Crossbow bolts could pierce five hundred paces,
penetrating both men and horses.
For this reason, Cháo 巢 dared not approach.
The siege lasted for three hundred days in total.
When Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu's supplies were almost exhausted,
he requested troops from Liáng 梁.
Liáng Tàizǔ 梁太祖 and Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 both personally led their forces to Chén Zhōu 陳州,
defeating Cháo's 巢's general Huáng Yè 黃鄴 at Xīhuá 西華.
Xīhuá 西華 had accumulated grain,
which Cháo 巢 relied on for provisions.
When Yè 鄴 was defeated,
Cháo 巢 then lifted the siege and departed.
When Liáng Tàizǔ 梁太祖 entered Chén Zhōu 陳州,
Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu and his brothers welcomed and paid respects to him at the head of his horse with utmost deference.
However, Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu secretly recognized that Tàizǔ 太祖 would surely accomplish great things.
So he humbled himself and yielded,
making plans for self-preservation.
Out of gratitude for Liáng's 梁's aid,
he erected a "living shrine" for Tàizǔ 太祖,
bowing and paying respects morning and evening.
He had his son, Yán 巖, marry Tàizǔ's 太祖's daughter,
who was known as Chánglè Gōngzhǔ 長樂公主.
After Huáng Cháo 黃巢 had departed,
Qín Zōngquán 秦宗權 again caused disturbance in Huaíxī 淮西,
capturing over twenty surrounding prefectures.
Chén Zhōu 陳州 was closest to Cài Zhōu 蔡州,
and Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu and his brothers vigorously resisted him,
ultimately preventing him from taking it.
Later, both Cháo 巢 and Zōngquán 宗權 were defeated and died.
Táng Zhāozōng 唐昭宗 then made Chén Zhōu 陳州 the Zhōngwǔ Jūn 忠武軍,
and appointed Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu as Jìdùshǐ 節度使.
Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu was already ill,
so he ceded his position to his younger brother, Chǎng 昶.
He died a few months later.
Chǎng 昶, taking advantage of the recent suppression of the great bandits,
rested his troops and promoted agriculture,
serving Liáng 梁 with particular diligence.
When Liáng's 梁's troops campaigned in all directions,
Chǎng 昶 supplied provisions and transport,
never slackening.
After Chǎng 昶 died,
Xǔ 珝 succeeded him.
Xǔ 珝 was quite learned.
He sought out the old irrigation works of Dèng Ài 鄧艾,
and breached Zhaíwáng Pí 翟王陂 to irrigate the commoners' fields.
The brothers resided in Chén Zhōu 陳州 for over twenty years,
and the people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 benefited greatly from them.
Liáng Tàizǔ 梁太祖 had already brought Hán Jiàn 韓建 to surrender,
taken Tóng 同 and Huá 華,
and transferred Xǔ 珝 to be Liúhòu 留後 of Tóng Zhōu 同州.
Upon entering Táng 唐,
he became Yòu Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn 右金吾衞上將軍.
After a year or so,
he was dismissed from office due to illness and returned home,
dying at his residence.
The people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 closed their markets in his honor.
Chén Zhōu's 陳 Zhōu's second son, Yán 巖,
served as Hùbù Shàngshū 戶部尚書 and Zūyōng Shǐ 租庸使 during the time of Liáng Mòdì 梁末帝.
He, along with Zhāng Hànjié 張漢傑, Hànlún 漢倫, and others, held power within the court.
Liáng 梁, ever since Tàizǔ 太祖, had been characterized by tyranny and slaughter.
However, Mòdì 末帝 was particularly gentle, soft, respectful, and cautious,
though his nature was mediocre and foolish.
Because Hànjié 漢傑 was his wife's relative,
and Yán 巖 was his son-in-law,
he trusted them implicitly.
The grand ministers and veteran generals all gnashed their teeth,
but Mòdì 末帝 alone did not realize this,
leading to his downfall.
Initially,
Yǒuguī 友珪 killed Tàizǔ 太祖 and established himself,
making Mòdì 末帝 the Dōngdū Liúshǒu 東都留守.
When Yán 巖 went to Dōngdū 東都,
Mòdì 末帝 drank with him,
and calmly revealed his true intentions to him.
Yán 巖 plotted for Mòdì 末帝,
sending someone to summon Yáng Shīhòu's 楊師厚's troops to start an uprising.
Yán 巖 returned to Xīdū 西都,
and ultimately, along with Yuán Xiàngxiān 袁象先, used the imperial guard to execute Yǒuguī 友珪,
taking the imperial seal to present to Mòdì 末帝.
After Mòdì 末帝 ascended the throne,
Yán 巖, considering his meritorious service to Liáng 梁
and his marriage to the princess,
and having heard that the Táng 唐驸马 Dù Cōng 杜悰 had reached the position of general and chancellor,
and lived very lavishly,
felt ashamed that he was not his equal.
So he seized good farmland and large residences throughout the empire,
and harshly extorted merchants and travelers.
His gate was like a marketplace.
Half of the tax and labor revenue
went into his private coffers.
Yán's 巖's meals invariably cost ten thousand coins.
At that time,
the Yábīng 牙兵 of Wèi Zhōu 魏州 were arrogant
and frequently caused disturbances.
Luó Shàowēi 羅紹威 executed all of them.
After Tàizǔ 太祖 died,
Yáng Shīhòu 楊師厚 expelled the Luó 羅 clan
and occupied Wèi Zhōu 魏州,
reinstating two thousand Yábīng 牙兵.
Mòdì 末帝 was troubled by this.
After Shīhòu 師厚 died,
Yán 巖 and Zūyōng Pànguān 租庸判官 Shào Zàn 邵贊 discussed, saying:
"Wèi 魏 has been a source of trouble for Táng 唐
for over a hundred years.
Since the time of the late emperor,
he always gnashed his teeth at Shàowēi 紹威,
because he was initially respectful but later arrogant.
Now the late emperor has just departed this world,
and Shīhòu 師厚 again causes Your Majesty worry.
The reason for this
is that Wèi 魏 has a large territory and many soldiers.
If Your Majesty does not control it at this time,
how can you be sure that future generations will not be like Shīhòu 師厚?
It would be better to divide Xiàng 相 and Wèi 魏 into two circuits,
then there will be no worries from the north."
Mòdì 末帝 agreed,
and so divided Xiàng 相, Chán 澶, and Wèi 衛 into the Zhāodé Jūn 昭德軍.
The Yábīng 牙兵 rebelled,
and surrendered Wèibó 魏博 to Jìn 晉,
whereby Liáng 梁 lost all of Héběi 河北.
At this time,
Liáng 梁 generals Liú Xún 劉鄩 and others were fighting against Zhuāngzōng 莊宗 between Chán 澶 and Wèi 魏,
and their forces suffered several defeats.
Yán 巖 said:
"Ancient kings would always perform suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
Your Majesty has not yet performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven since your enthronement.
Those who discuss this believe that the court is no different from a regional military command.
How can this command respect across the empire?
Although Héběi 河北 is lost now,
the empire is fortunately peaceful.
I wish Your Majesty would diligently perform this."
Jìng Xiáng 敬翔 thought it was not advisable,
saying:
"Now the national treasury is empty,
and taxes are extorted to supply the army.
If suburban sacrifices are held,
there will inevitably be rewards and gifts;
this is to gain an empty name and suffer real disadvantages."
Mòdì 末帝 did not listen,
and prepared the imperial carriage to visit Xījīng 西京.
Meanwhile, Zhuāngzōng 莊宗 seized Yángliú 楊劉.
Someone reported:
"Jìn 晉 troops have entered Dōngdū 東都!"
Another said:
"They have seized Sǐshuǐ 汜水!"
Another said:
"They have taken Yùn 鄆 and Pú 濮!"
A great wind uprooted trees in the capital.
Mòdì 末帝 was greatly alarmed.
His attendants looked at each other and wept.
Mòdì 末帝 then returned to Dōngdū 東都,
and thus the suburban sacrifice was not carried out.
Zhāng Wénlǐ 張文禮 of Zhèn Zhōu 鎮州 killed Wáng Róng 王鎔,
and sent someone to report to Liáng 梁, saying:
"Your servant has already summoned Khitans from the north.
If Liáng 梁 sends ten thousand troops out from Dé 德 and Dì Zhōu 棣州,
then the Jìn 晉 troops will be exhausted."
Jìng Xiáng 敬翔 thought it was advisable.
Yán 巖 and Hànjié 漢傑 both thought it was not,
so it was stopped.
Later, the dismissal of Wáng Yànzhāng 王彥章 and the appointment of Duàn Níng 段凝 were all due to Yán's 巖's influence.
Lǐ Yànwēi
was a man from Shòuzhōu.
While young, he served Liáng Tàizǔ (Zhu Wēn).
He was sharp and quick-witted,
skilled at gauging people's intentions.
Tàizǔ favored him,
raising him as a son,
and he falsely adopted the surname Zhū,
and the given name Yǒugōng.
He successively held the post of Cìshǐ (Prefect) of the two prefectures of Rǔzhōu and Yǐngzhōu.
When Zhāozōng moved down to Luòyáng,
he was appointed Yòu Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn (Commander of the Right Dragon Martial Guard).
Previously,
Liú Jìshù had deposed Zhāozōng,
establishing the Crown Prince Yù as the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
When Zhāozōng was restored,
believing the Crown Prince was young
and had been established by the rebels,
he pardoned him,
restoring his original title as Dé Wáng (Prince Dé).
When Zhāozōng returned from Qízhōu,
Tàizǔ saw that Yù's features were elegant and handsome,
and disliked him.
He said to the Chancellor, Cuī Yìn:
"Dé Wáng was once established by Jìshù.
How can he still be around?
Sir, report this to the Son of Heaven and have him executed."
Yìn memorialized this,
but Zhāozōng did not permit it.
On another day, he asked Tàizǔ about it.
Tàizǔ said:
"How would your servant dare speak of this?
Yìn merely wants to sell me out."
When Zhāozōng moved to Luòyáng,
he said to Jiǎng Xuánhuī:
"Dé Wáng
is my beloved son.
Why does Quánzhōng (Zhu Wēn) want to kill him?"
Thereupon, tears streamed down,
and he bit his finger until blood flowed.
Xuánhuī reported all this fully to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ disliked him even more.
At this time,
Zhāozōng changed the reign title to Tiānyòu,
and moved to the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū).
Being oppressed by Liáng,
the people of Jìn and Shǔ believed the name Tiānyòu was not established by Táng,
and no longer used it,
calling the era only Tiānfù.
Wáng Jiàn also sent manifestos throughout the realm,
raising troops to execute Liáng.
Tàizǔ became greatly afraid,
fearing Zhāozōng would flee to another stronghold.
He took 70,000 troops to Hézhōng,
secretly sending Jìng Xiáng to Luòyáng
to inform Yànwēi and Shì Shūcóng, etc.,
instructing them to carry out the regicide.
On the *Rénchén* day of the eighth month,
Yànwēi and Shūcóng, using Lóngwǔ troops, camped within the forbidden palace.
At the second watch of the night,
they used a hundred soldiers to knock on the palace gate, claiming to report on official business.
Concubine Péi Zhèngyī opened the gate and asked:
"How can reporting on official business require soldiers to enter?"
Shǐ Tài, a staff officer of the Lóngwǔ Guard, killed her,
and hurried to the Jiāolán Hall,
asking where Zhāozōng was.
Zhāozōng was currently drunk.
He stood up and ran.
Tài pursued him holding a sword.
Zhāozōng, in only his undergarments, circled a pillar while running.
Tài's sword reached him,
and Zhāozōng died.
When the news of the death reached Hézhōng,
Tàizǔ feigned shock,
throwing himself on the ground and wailing loudly,
cursing, saying:
"These wretches have failed me!
They have caused me to bear an evil name for later generations!"
When Tàizǔ arrived at Luòyáng,
he banished Yànwēi and Shūcóng to Lǐngnán,
and ordered Zhāng Tíngfàn to kill them.
As Yànwēi faced execution, he shouted loudly:
"You sell me out to silence me,
but what about divine justice?"
He looked at Tíngfàn and said:
"Keep up your efforts.
Sir, you will soon meet the same fate."
Thereupon, he was executed.
Afterward, his original name was restored.
During Zhuāngzōng's time,
a former Táng palace attendant named Jǐng Chà was found.
She reported that when Yànwēi and the others killed Zhāozōng,
several hundred imperial princes and relatives were also murdered,
and were placed together in one pit,
buried north of the Lóngxīng Temple.
She requested that they be combined into a single mound and reburied.
An imperial edict commanded that the former Pú Wáng be considered the head (of the burial),
and they be interred with the rites appropriate for the first rank.
Lǐ Zhèn
Lǐ Zhèn, courtesy name Xīngxù.
His grandfather, Bàozhēn,
was the Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor) of Lùzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Zhèn served Táng as Jīnwǔ Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Metropolitan Guards),
and was appointed Cìshǐ of Táizhōu.
As bandits arose in Zhèdōng,
he could not proceed,
and so he returned west.
Passing through Liáng territory,
he presented Tàizǔ with a strategy.
Tàizǔ kept him.
Tàizǔ concurrently held Yùnzhōu,
and appointed Zhèn as the Deputy Jiédùshǐ.
Zhèn reported on business in Cháng'ān,
staying at the Liáng residence.
The eunuch Liú Jìshù planned to depose Zhāozōng.
He sent his nephew Xīzhèng, through Chéng Yán, an official at the Liáng residence, to meet Zhèn, saying:
"Currently, the Sovereign is severe and harsh,
executing the innocent.
The Zhōngwèi fears disaster will reach him,
and plans to carry out a deposition and installation.
We ask you to cooperate with the officials of the various residences to stabilize the court and the provinces.
What do you say?"
Zhèn was greatly alarmed and said:
"A hundred-year-old slave serving a three-year-old master—
how dare you act like this!
Now Liáng Wáng, with an army of a million,
is relying on great righteousness to honor the Son of Heaven.
Gentlemen, do not commit this inauspicious act!"
Zhèn returned.
Jìshù eventually joined Yán and the others in deposing Zhāozōng,
confining him in the Eastern Palace,
calling him Tàishàng Huáng (Retired Emperor),
and establishing the Crown Prince Yù as the Son of Heaven.
At this time,
Tàizǔ was campaigning between Xíngzhōu and Míngzhōu.
Jìshù fraudulently issued an edict in the name of the Tàishàng Huáng to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ hesitated,
unsure what to do.
Zhèn said:
"The chaos caused by Shù Diāo and Yī Lì
provided the capital needed for the Hegemons to rise.
Now that the eunuchs are causing rebellion,
and the Son of Heaven is in danger and humiliation,
this is the moment for Your Highness to uphold righteousness and establish merit."
Tàizǔ had a great realization.
He imprisoned Jìshù's messenger
and sent Zhèn to the capital to meet Cuī Yìn,
plotting to restore Zhāozōng.
When Zhāozōng was restored to power,
Tàizǔ was overjoyed,
gripping Zhèn's hand and saying:
"Your counsel hit the mark!"
Wáng Shīfàn surrendered Qīngzhōu to Liáng.
Zhèn was sent to replace Shīfàn.
Shīfàn was suspicious and afraid,
not knowing what to do.
Zhèn said:
"Have you alone not heard of Zhāng Xiù of Hàn?
Xiù was an enemy of Cáo Gōng,
yet he submitted to Cáo Gōng rather than Yuán Shào,
because he knew Cáo Gōng had great ambition
and would not kill a person over a private feud.
Now Liáng Wáng is currently seeking to achieve great things.
Would he kill a loyal minister because of former grudges?"
Shīfàn immediately felt relieved
and went west to submit to Liáng.
When Zhāozōng moved to Luòyáng,
Zhèn traveled back and forth to the capital.
The court officials all viewed him askance,
but Zhèn regarded them as if they were nothing.
If he became slightly angered,
he would certainly condemn and punish them.
Therefore, whenever Zhèn arrived in the capital,
the court would certainly see demotions or dismissals.
People at the time referred to Zhèn as a Screech-Owl (*chīxiāo*).
When Tàizǔ committed regicide against Zhāozōng,
he sent Zhèn to the capital to plot it with Zhū Yǒugōng and Shì Shūcóng.
After Zhāozōng died,
Tàizǔ asked Zhèn how he should treat Yǒugōng and the others.
Zhèn said:
"In the past, Sīmǎ Shì of Jìn killed the ruler of Wèi but executed Chéng Jì.
If not,
how could they silence the mouths of the world?"
Tàizǔ thereupon placed the blame on Yǒugōng and the others and killed them.
Zhèn had previously attempted the *jìnshì* examination during the Xiántōng and Qiánfú periods,
repeatedly failing.
He especially resented the Táng high officials and nobles.
When Péi Shū and seven others were granted death at the Bái Mǎ Yì (White Horse Post Station),
Zhèn said to Tàizǔ:
"These individuals always referred to themselves as the Pure Stream (*qīngliú*).
They should be thrown into the river
to make them the Turbid Stream (*zhuóliú*)."
Tàizǔ laughed and followed his advice.
Tàizǔ (太祖) ascended the throne,
and he was successively promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書).
During Yǒuguī's (友珪) time,
Zhèn (振) replaced Jìng Xiáng (敬翔) as Chóngzhèng Yuànshǐ (崇政院使).
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) destroyed Liáng (梁) and entered Biàn (汴),
Zhèn (振) sought an audience with Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜).
Chóngtāo (崇韜) said:
"People say Lǐ Zhèn (李振) is an unparalleled genius of his generation,
but now that I see him,
he is merely an ordinary man!"
Soon after, he was executed.
Péi Dí.
Péi Dí (裴迪), courtesy name Shēngzhī (昇之),
was a man from Hédōng Wénxǐ (河東聞喜).
His personality was perceptive and quick-witted,
he was skilled at managing finances and taxation,
and expert in accounting records.
When Táng (唐) Sīkōng (司空) Péi Qú (裴璩) was Pàndùzhī (判度支),
he appointed him as Chūshǐ Xúnguān (出使巡官).
When Dūtǒng (都統) Wáng Duó (王鐸) garrisoned Huázhōu (滑州),
he recommended Dí (迪) as Gōngjūn Yuànshǐ (供軍院使) for Biàn (汴), Sòng (宋), Yùn (鄆) and other prefectures.
When Duó (鐸) became Zūyōngshǐ (租庸使),
he appointed him as Zūyōng Zhāonàshǐ (租庸招納使).
When Liáng Tàizǔ (梁太祖) garrisoned Xuānwǔ (宣武),
he appointed him Jiédù Pànguān (節度判官).
Tàizǔ (太祖) waged war in all directions,
and always kept Dí (迪) behind to manage military affairs and taxation.
Tàizǔ (太祖) then posted a notice on his gate,
claiming responsibility for military matters himself,
but entrusting all matters of commerce, finance, and lawsuits entirely to Dí (迪).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) attacked Qí (岐) in the west,
Wáng Shīfàn (王師範) plotted to attack Biàn (汴).
He sent the strong soldier Miáo Gōnglì (苗公立) carrying a letter to Biàn,
secretly watching for vulnerabilities.
Dí (迪) summoned Gōnglì (公立) and questioned him about the affairs in the east.
Gōnglì's (公立) face changed,
so Dí (迪) dismissed the attendants and secretly interrogated him,
obtaining all the details of the plot.
Dí (迪) did not have time to report the matter,
and sent Zhū Yǒuníng (朱友寧) with troops to patrol Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆).
Because of this, although Shīfàn (師範) launched his surprise attack, the matter ultimately failed.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) returned from Qí (岐),
all the generals and officials were bestowed the title
"Yíngluán Yèzàn Gōngchén" (迎鑾叶贊功臣).
When the generals and officials came in for an audience,
Tàizǔ (太祖) looked at Dí (迪) and said:
"The merit of aiding and assisting,
only Lord Péi (裴公) possesses it;
others are not fit to claim it."
Dí (迪) entered Táng (唐) service,
and was successively promoted to Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿).
Tàizǔ (太祖) ascended the throne,
summoned him and appointed him Yòu Púshè (右僕射),
but after staying for one year, he requested retirement due to age.
He retired with the title Sīkōng (司空),
and died at home.
Wéi Zhèn.
Wéi Zhèn (韋震), courtesy name Dōngqīng (東卿),
was a man from Wànnián (萬年) in Yōngzhōu (雍州).
His initial name was Zhào (肇).
His personality was forceful and quick,
and he possessed verbal eloquence.
He served Liáng Tàizǔ (梁太祖) as Dūtǒng Pànguān (都統判官).
Shēn Cóng (申叢) captured Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權).
He wanted to send him to Tàizǔ (太祖),
but also wanted to present himself to the capital,
and also wanted to use Zōngquán (宗權) as leverage to seize his troops.
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Zhèn (震) into Càizhōu (蔡州) to observe the situation.
Cóng (叢) sent three hundred cavalry soldiers to meet Zhèn (震),
intending to kill him,
but Zhèn (震) managed to escape through a stratagem.
He returned and reported to Tàizǔ (太祖), saying:
"Cóng (叢) is not worth worrying about.
The one plotting for him is the commander Péi Shè (裴涉),
who is an arrogant and mediocre man."
Cóng (叢) was later indeed killed by Guō Fán (郭璠).
Fán (璠) returned Zōngquán (宗權) to Tàizǔ (太祖).
Tàizǔ (太祖) wanted to magnify the importance of this event,
and requested to present the captive to Táng (唐).
Táng (唐) argued that when Shí Pǔ (時溥) defeated Huáng Cháo (黃巢),
only the severed heads were offered,
and that Zōngquán (宗權) was not worthy of being presented as a captive.
Zuǒ Shíyí (左拾遺) Xú Yànshū (徐彥樞) also submitted a memorial requesting that Zōngquán (宗權) be executed immediately wherever he was held.
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Zhèn (震) to the capital (Jīngshī) to report the matter.
After repeated discussions and arguments,
they finally took Zōngquán (宗權) captive.
Tàizǔ (太祖) was grateful to him,
and recommended him as Jiédù Fùshǐ (節度副使).
When Zhāozōng (昭宗) took refuge at Shímén (石門),
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Zhèn (震) through the secret paths between Guó (虢) and Lüè (略) to present a memorial to the Emperor's temporary residence (Xíngzài).
Zhāozōng (昭宗) bestowed upon him the name Zhèn (震).
Tàizǔ (太祖) had already defeated Yǎn (兗) and Yùn (鄆),
and subsequently attacked Wú (吳),
suffering a great defeat at Qīngkǒu (清口).
Tàizǔ (太祖) feared that the various garrisons would take advantage of the situation to plot against him.
Thus, he secretly prompted Dù Hóng (杜洪), Zhōng Chuán (鍾傳), Wáng Shīfàn (王師範), Qián Liú (錢鏐), and others to recommend him as Yuánshuài (元帥),
and also requested to concurrently govern Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
Zhāozōng (昭宗) initially refused.
Zhèn (震) argued strongly,
dared to speak arrogantly,
and his language was often disrespectful.
Zhāozōng (昭宗) finally granted Liáng (梁) Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
Tàizǔ (太祖) subsequently concurrently controlled four garrisons,
and recommended Zhèn (震) as Yùnzhōu Liúhòu (鄆州留後).
When Zhāozōng (昭宗) moved to Luò (洛),
Zhèn (震) entered service as Hénán Yǐn (河南尹) and Fùshǐ (副使) of the Liùjūn Zhūwèi (六軍諸衞).
Due to illness causing muteness,
he retired with the honorary post of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (太子太保).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) received the abdication,
his title was changed to Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅).
Mòdì (末帝) ascended the throne,
promoted him to Tàishī (太師),
and he died.
Kǒng Xún.
Kǒng Xún (孔循),
it is not known what his family background was.
Orphaned young,
he drifted to Biànzhōu (汴州).
The rich man Lǐ Rànglán (李讓闌) took him in,
and raised him as a son.
When Liáng Tàizǔ (梁太祖) garrisoned Xuānwǔ (宣武),
he adopted Lǐ Ràng (李讓) as his son,
so Xún (循) falsely claimed the surname Zhū (朱).
When he was slightly older,
he served in Tàizǔ's (太祖) headquarters.
The wet nurse of Tàizǔ's (太祖) sons was fond of him,
and adopted Xún (循) as her son.
The wet nurse's husband was surnamed Zhào (趙),
so Xún (循) again falsely claimed the surname Zhào (趙),
and his given name was Yīnhéng (殷衡).
When Zhāozōng (昭宗) moved east to Luòyáng (洛陽),
Tàizǔ (太祖) removed all of the Son of Heaven's attendants,
and replaced them entirely with Liáng (梁) men.
Wáng Yīn (王殷) was made Xuānhuī Shǐ (宣徽使),
and Xún (循) was made Deputy Commissioner.
Xún (循), along with Jiǎng Xuánhuī (蔣玄暉), Zhāng Tíngfàn (張廷範), and others, participated in the plot to assassinate Zhāozōng (昭宗).
Afterwards, Xún (循) and Xuánhuī (玄暉) fell out.
When Āidì (哀帝) ascended the throne,
he was preparing to perform the sacrifice in the Southern Suburb.
Xún (循) consequently conspired with Wáng Yīn (王殷) to slander Tàizǔ (太祖), saying:
"Xuánhuī (玄暉) privately serves Empress Dowager Hé (何太后),
and with Tíngfàn (廷範) and others, leads the Son of Heaven in the suburban sacrifice,
hoping to prolong the Táng (唐) dynasty."
Tàizǔ (太祖) was furious.
At this time,
Liáng (梁) troops attacked Shòuchūn (壽春),
were greatly defeated and returned.
Āidì (哀帝) sent Péi Dí (裴迪) to comfort the troops.
Tàizǔ (太祖) saw Dí (迪),
and his anger was extreme.
When Dí (迪) returned,
Āidì (哀帝) dared not perform the sacrifice.
Tàizǔ (太祖) was enfeoffed as Wèiwáng (魏王),
and granted the Nine Distinctions,
but Tàizǔ (太祖) refused to accept them.
Xuánhuī (玄暉) and Prime Minister Liǔ Càn (柳璨) successively rushed to Liáng (梁) to defend themselves.
Càn (璨) said:
"Since antiquity, when a true king rises,
there must first be an enfeoffed state.
The reason Táng (唐) has not immediately yielded the throne
is that you must first establish your state and be granted the Nine Distinctions,
and only then will the abdication occur."
Tàizǔ (太祖) said:
"Is it possible for me to become the Son of Heaven without going through the Nine Distinctions?"
Càn (璨) was terrified
and raced away.
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Xún (循) and Wáng Yīn (王殷) to assassinate Empress Hé (何皇后).
Consequently, Càn (璨), Xuánhuī (玄暉), Tíngfàn (廷範), and others were killed,
and Xún (循) was made Shūmì Fùshǐ (樞密副使).
When Táng (唐) perished,
he served Liáng (梁) as Rǔzhōu Fángyùshǐ (汝州防禦使), Zuǒwèi Dàjiāngjūn (左衞大將軍), and Zūyōngshǐ (租庸使).
He then finally changed his surname to Kǒng (孔),
and his given name to Xún (循).
During Zhuāngzōng's (莊宗) reign,
he served temporarily as Prefect of Biànzhōu (汴州).
Míngzōng (明宗) rebelled with the troops from Wèi (魏) and marched south.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) advanced east out of Sìshuǐ (汜水).
Xún (循) straddled both sides:
he sent people to welcome Míngzōng (明宗) at the North Gate,
and to welcome Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) at the West Gate.
The tents, provisions, and sacrificial animals provided
were identical in ceremony.
He warned his men, saying:
"Admit the one who arrives first."
Míngzōng (明宗) arrived first,
and consequently Xún (循) admitted him.
Míngzōng (明宗) ascended the throne,
and made him Shūmì Shǐ (樞密使).
When Míngzōng (明宗) visited Biànzhōu (汴州),
Xún (循) remained to guard the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū).
When a civilian violated the laws against yeast,
Xún (循) executed the entire family.
Míngzōng (明宗), knowing the injustice of it,
issued an imperial edict throughout the realm to abolish the yeast prohibition,
allowing the people to make yeast.
Xún was a man who was outwardly yielding and flattering but inwardly treacherous and cunning.
Ān Zhònghuǐ particularly trusted and relied upon him.
Everything Xún said,
was adopted and used.
Míngzōng once desired to have his imperial son marry Zhònghuǐ’s daughter.
Zhònghuǐ consulted Xún about this.
Xún said:
"As a minister holding confidential secrets,
it is not suitable for you to marry into the imperial family."
Zhònghuǐ believed him
and stopped the plan.
However, Xún secretly sent someone to inform Míngzōng,
asking that his own daughter be married to the imperial son.
Míngzōng immediately had the Prince of Sòng, Cónghòu, marry Xún’s daughter.
Zhònghuǐ then began to despise Xún’s character
and had him sent out as the Military Governor of the Zhōngwǔ Army.
He was then transferred to govern Hénghǎi,
and died while at the post
at the age of forty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Sūn Dézhāo
Sūn Dézhāo
was a native of Wǔyuán, Yán Zhōu.
His father, Wéi Zuì,
possessed talent and strategy.
When Huáng Cháo captured Cháng'ān,
Wéi Zuì led the youths from his home region.
He raised a thousand loyal troops
and attacked Cháo to the south at Xiányáng.
The general of Xīngpíng Prefecture admired his actions
and augmented his forces with two thousand prefectural troops.
For his merit in defeating the rebels,
he was appointed Grand General of the Right Metropolitan Prefecture Command (Yòu Jīnwú Wèi Dàjiāngjūn).
When Zhū Méi caused chaos in the capital (Jīngshī),
Emperor Xīzōng fled to Xīngyuán.
Wéi Zuì led troops to attack the rebels.
He was repeatedly promoted, eventually becoming the Military Governor of Fū Zhōu.
He was kept in the capital for imperial defense.
The officers and officials of Fū Zhōu went to the court gates to request Wéi Zuì be sent back to his post.
Tens of thousands of the capital's common people and the Shéncè Army again blocked his departure, urging him to stay.
He was transferred to be Military Governor of Jīngnán,
but remained in the capital overseeing arrangements,
and jointly managed the Shéncè Army,
being titled
"Commander of the Imperial Escort" (Hùjià Dū).
At this time,
the capital was in turmoil,
and the people all relied on him for security.
Dézhāo, benefiting from his father's position, became a Commander of the Shéncè Army.
In the third year of Guānghuà (900 AD),
Liú Jìshù deposed Emperor Zhāozōng
and imprisoned him in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
Chancellor Cuī Yìn planned a restoration
and secretly sent people to search for righteous men who could help accomplish the task.
Dézhāo, along with Sūn Chénghuǐ
and Dǒng Cóngshí, responded to Yìn.
Yìn tore his robe cuff to make a document and swore an oath.
On the first day of the first month of the first year of Tiānfù (901 AD),
before dawn,
Jìshù was about to attend court.
Dézhāo hid armed men by the side of the road,
intercepted his carriage, and beheaded him.
Chénghuǐ and the others separately sought out the remaining partisans and exterminated them all.
Zhāozōng heard the clamor outside
and was greatly alarmed.
Dézhāo rushed forward,
knocked on the gate and said:
"Jìshù has been executed!
The Emperor should be restored!"
Empress Hé called out:
"You must present the head of the traitor!"
Dézhāo threw the head inside.
Afterwards, Chénghuǐ and the others brought all the heads of the remaining partisans and presented them,
and Zhāozōng believed them.
Dézhāo broke the locks and brought Zhāozōng out.
The Emperor ascended the Dānfèng Tower and was restored.
For his merit, he was appointed Military Governor of Jìnghǎi Army,
granted the imperial surname Lǐ,
and titled
"Meritorious Minister, Loyal and Ardent, Who Supported the Fallen and Aided the Distressed" (Fúqīng Jìnàn Zhōngliè Gōngchén).
He and Chénghuǐ and the others were all appointed Military Governors and Grand Counselors (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
their portraits were painted in Língyān Pavilion,
and they were all retained in the capital.
They were titled
"The Three Envoys/Chancellors" (Sān Shǐ Xiāng);
their favor and trust were unparalleled.
At this time,
Cuī Yìn wanted to execute the Táng court eunuchs
and allied externally with Liáng for support.
The eunuchs, in turn, relied on Lǐ Màozhēn for protection,
leading to conflict between Liáng and Qí.
In the tenth month of winter,
the eunuch Hán Quánhuǐ coerced Zhāozōng to flee to Fèngxiáng.
Chénghuǐ and Cóngshí both followed,
but Dézhāo alone sided with Liáng.
He consequently led his troops to protect Yìn and the officials, safeguarding the Eastern Street,
and urged the Liáng troops to advance westward.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng greatly appreciated his allegiance
and presented him with a Dragon-Phoenix Sword and patterned fighting-cock gauze.
When Tàizǔ arrived at Huà Zhōu,
Dézhāo welcomed and received him by the roadside with military ceremony.
When Tàizǔ arrived at the capital,
he nominated Dézhāo as Acting Governor of Tóng Zhōu.
When Dézhāo was about to depart,
the capital's citizens again petitioned for him to stay,
so he was made Commissioner of Arrangements for the Two Streets.
When the Liáng forces besieged Fèngxiáng,
Dézhāo assigned his eight thousand troops to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ esteemed him even more
and sent him ahead to Luòyáng,
granting him a grand mansion.
When Zhāozōng moved east,
Dézhāo was appointed Grand General of the Left Majestic Guard (Zuǒ Wēiwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn),
but retired due to illness.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he bestowed upon Dézhāo a black silver belt, robes, a tablet, and a famous horse.
When his illness slightly subsided,
he was appointed Grand General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Dàjiāngjūn).
When Emperor Mò Dì succeeded to the throne,
Dézhāo was appointed Grand General of the Left Metropolitan Prefecture (Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn) and subsequently died.
Chénghuǐ and Cóngshí, having arrived at Fèngxiáng,
were killed along with the eunuchs.
Wáng Jìngráo
Wáng Jìngráo
was a native of Rǔyīn, Yǐng Zhōu.
He served the prefecture as a guard commander.
In the late Táng period,
when Wáng Xiānzhī and others attacked and plundered the area between Rǔ and Yǐng,
the prefectural governor was unable to resist.
Jìngráo subsequently took his place
and was immediately appointed Prefectural Governor (Cìshǐ).
Jìngráo was physically imposing and outstanding in appearance,
deeply courageous and powerful,
and skilled in using an iron spear
weighing thirty *jīn*.
Yǐng Zhōu bordered Huáixī
and was repeatedly attacked by Qín Zōngquán.
Jìngráo fought hard to repel him.
Although Zōngquán captured all the prefectures in Hénán,
Jìngráo alone could not be defeated.
Because of this, the people of the prefectures surrounding Yǐng
all relied on Jìngráo to avoid the bandits.
At this time,
everywhere else was ruined and devastated,
but Yǐng Zhōu alone retained twenty thousand households.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng attacked Huáinán
and passed through Yǐng Zhōu,
Jìngráo provided supplies to the Liáng troops very generously.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased
and nominated Jìngráo as Commander along the Huái River (Yánhuái Zhǐhuīshǐ).
Afterwards, when the Liáng troops attacked Wú,
Páng Shīgǔ died at Qīng Kǒu,
and the defeated soldiers fled home.
When they passed Yǐng,
there was heavy snow,
and the officers and soldiers were hungry and freezing.
Jìngráo stacked firewood all along the Huái River to cook congee and gruel to feed them.
Many of the fleeing soldiers relied on this to survive.
Tàizǔ nominated Jìngráo as Acting Governor of the Wǔníng Army,
and he was subsequently appointed Military Governor.
In the third year of Tiānyòu (906 AD),
he became Grand General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
Jìngráo retired due to illness
and later died at home.
Jiǎng Yīn
Jiǎng Yīn,
as a youth, was adopted by Wáng Chóngyíng
and falsely assumed the surname Wáng.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng took Hézhōng,
he favored Wáng Chóngyíng's descendants based on old friendship.
He nominated Yīn as a guard commander,
and Tàizǔ especially favored him.
When the Táng court moved to Luòyáng,
Yīn became Director of the Northern Bureau of the Court of the Imperial Insignia (Xuānhuī Běiyuàn Shǐ).
Tàizǔ had already subdued Xiāngyáng,
turned to attack Huáinán,
and returned to garrison Zhèngyáng.
Emperor Āidì sent Yīn to comfort the troops.
At this time,
Emperor Āidì was planning the suburban sacrifice.
Yīn had a rift with the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ), Jiǎng Xuánhuī, and others.
Consequently, he slandered them to Tàizǔ,
saying that Xuánhuī and the others were teaching the Son of Heaven to plan the suburban sacrifice to pray to Heaven,
and were waiting for the regional rulers who came to assist in the ceremony to plot a restoration.
Tàizǔ was greatly angered,
and Emperor Āidì had to choose a different date for the sacrifice.
At this time,
Tàizǔ was planning usurpation and regicide.
Empress Dowager Hé once wept and kowtowed, speaking on behalf of Xuánhuī and others:
"After the Prince of Liáng accepts the abdication,
I only wish that the children and mother of the Táng house may be spared."
Yīn then falsely accused Xuánhuī of having secretly slept with the Empress Dowager.
Tàizǔ executed Xuánhuī, along with Zhāng Tíngfàn and Liǔ Càn, and others,
and sent Yīn to murder the Empress Dowager in Jīshàn Palace.
Emperor Āidì issued an edict expressing shame and remorse,
stating that due to the matter concerning his Mother/Empress Dowager, he could not honor Heaven,
and thus ultimately canceled the suburban sacrifice.
Shùrén Yǒuguī was friendly with Yīn.
Yǒuguī assassinated Tàizǔ and established himself.
He appointed Yīn as Military Governor of the Wǔníng Army.
Mòdì ascended the throne
and replaced Yīn with the Prince of Fú, Yǒuzhāng.
Yīn refused the replacement.
Wáng Zàn was also a son of the Wáng clan.
Fearing that he would be implicated by Yīn,
he then stated that Yīn was not a son of the Wáng clan
but that his original surname was Jiǎng.
Mòdì issued an edict stripping him of his official ranks
and restoring his original surname,
dispatching Niú Cúnjié to suppress him.
Yīn and his entire family immolated themselves.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter Thirty-two: Liú Zhījùn
Liú Zhījùn, courtesy name Xīxián,
was a native of Pèi, Xúzhōu.
In his youth, he served Shí Pǔ.
When Pǔ and Liáng attacked each other,
Zhījùn surrendered to Liáng with two thousand men under his command.
Tàizǔ appointed him Commander of the Left Vanguard.
Zhījùn had a heroic and outstanding appearance.
He was capable of donning armor and mounting his horse,
wielding his sword and charging the enemy,
his bravery surpassing all the generals.
At this time,
Liú Kāidào’s reputation was prominent in the army.
He successively served as Prefect of the three prefectures Hǎi, Huái, and Zhèng.
He participated in conquering Qīngzhōu,
and for his merit was appointed Military Governor of the Kuāngguó Army.
Yáng Chóngběn of Bīnzhōu led sixty thousand troops to attack Yōngzhōu
and encamped at Měiyuán.
At this time,
Tàizǔ was leading his generals to attack Cāngzhōu.
Zhījùn, without waiting for orders,
together with Kāng Huáiyīng and others, defeated Chóngběn,
killing and capturing twenty thousand,
seizing three thousand horses,
and capturing one hundred of his subordinate officers.
Lǐ Sī'ān used fortified trenches to attack Lùzhōu.
After a long time, it did not fall.
Tàizǔ dismissed Sī'ān,
appointing Zhījùn as Campaign Commander of the Expeditionary Forces.
Before he reached Lù,
the fortified trenches were already broken.
He was transferred to Campaign Commander of the Western Route Expeditionary Forces,
defeating the Bīn and Qí troops at Mùgǔ.
At this time,
Gāo Wànxìng of Yánzhōu defected from Yáng Chóngběn and surrendered to Liáng.
Tàizǔ dispatched Zhījùn to meet Wànxìng
and attack and capture the four prefectures Dān, Yán, Fū, and Fāng.
He was additionally appointed Acting Grand Commandant and Attendant Counselor,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Dàpéng Commandery.
As Zhījùn's merits grew higher,
Tàizǔ's nature was highly suspicious
and he repeatedly executed his generals.
Wáng Chóngshī was killed despite being innocent,
causing Zhījùn to become increasingly afraid
and feel insecure.
Tàizǔ had already captured Fū and Fāng,
and sent Zhījùn to attack Bīnzhōu again.
Zhījùn had not yet departed, citing insufficient military provisions.
Tàizǔ visited Hézhōng,
and ordered the Commissioner of Palace Affairs, Wáng Yīn, to summon Zhījùn.
His younger brother, Zhīhuàn, who was Commander of the Imperial Army,
secretly sent someone to inform Zhījùn that it was unwise to come.
Zhījùn then rebelled
and submitted to Lǐ Màozhēn.
He used his troops to attack Yōng and Huà,
capturing Liú Hàn and sending him to Fèngxiáng.
Tàizǔ sent someone to say to Zhījùn:
"I treated you with the utmost sincerity.
Why have you betrayed me?"
Zhījùn replied:
"Wáng Chóngshī did not betray Your Majesty, yet his clan was exterminated.
I am not disloyal,
I merely fear death!"
Tàizǔ sent another message saying:
"I certainly knew this was your reason.
When I executed Chóngshī,
it was Liú Hàn who misled me,
causing you to reach this point.
How could I not regret this?
Now Hàn is dead,
but this is not enough to satisfy the blame."
Zhījùn did not reply.
He used his troops to cut off Tóngguān.
Tàizǔ dispatched Liú Xún and Niú Cúnjié to attack Zhījùn.
Zhījùn then fled to Màozhēn.
Màozhēn's territory was small
and he had nowhere to settle him.
He ordered him to attack Língwǔ to the west.
Hán Xùn reported the emergency.
Tàizǔ sent Kāng Huáiyīng, Kòu Yànqīng, and others to attack Bīnníng to pin him down.
Zhījùn heavily defeated Huáiyīng at Shēngpíng
and killed the Liáng general Xǔ Cóngshí.
Màozhēn was greatly pleased
and appointed Zhījùn as Military Governor of Jīngzhōu,
ordering him to attack Xīngyuán,
capture Xīng and Fèng,
and besiege Xīxiàn.
However, Màozhēn's attendants envied Zhījùn’s achievements
and used an affair to sow discord.
Màozhēn seized his army.
Zhījùn then fled to Shǔ.
Wáng Jiàn appointed him Military Governor of the Wǔxìn Army,
ordering him to attack Màozhēn in return
and capture the four prefectures Qín, Fèng, Jiē, and Chéng.
Although Jiàn treated Zhījùn very generously,
he secretly guarded against his talent.
He once said to his attendants:
"I am old now,
and I am about to die.
Zhījùn is not someone you can control;
it is better to deal with him early!"
Moreover, the people of Shǔ collectively envied him.
Zhījùn was dark-complexioned,
and his birth year was in the year of Chǒu (the Ox).
All of Jiàn’s sons
had the characters
"Zōng"
or
"Chéng"
in their names.
Thus, a rumor was fabricated in the streets and alleys, saying:
"When the black ox leaves the pen, the rope will break."
Jiàn hated him even more
and consequently had him executed.
Dīng Huì
Dīng Huì, courtesy name Dàoyǐn,
was a native of Shòuchūn, Shòuzhōu.
In his youth, he was skilled at singing funeral laments,
and was particularly adept at making the sound mournful, which pleased himself.
Later, he left and became a bandit.
He followed Huáng Cháo along with Tàizǔ of Liáng.
When Tàizǔ of Liáng garrisoned Xuānwǔ,
he made him the Grand Commander of Xuānwǔ.
In the fourth year of Guāngqǐ,
Zhāng Quányì of the Eastern Capital attacked and captured Héyáng,
driving out Lǐ Hǎnzhī.
Hǎnzhī summoned Jìn troops to besiege Héyáng.
Quányì reported the emergency.
At this time,
the Liáng army was in Wèi.
They dispatched Huì, along with Gé Cóngzhōu and others, leading ten thousand men to rescue him.
When Huì and the others reached Héyīn,
they consulted, saying:
"Hǎnzhī predicts that we will not dare to cross Jiǔdǐng,
believing our forces are few and have traveled a long distance,
and he does not anticipate our rapid arrival.
To strike where he does not expect
and attack when he is unprepared
is the winning strategy of military experts."
They then crossed Jiǔdǐng
and marched directly toward Héyáng.
They fought at Yǎnshuǐ.
Hǎnzhī was utterly defeated,
and the siege of Héyáng was lifted.
In the first year of Dàshùn,
the Liáng army attacked Wèi.
Huì and Gé Cóngzhōu conquered Líyáng and Línhé,
and then defeated Luó Hóngxìn at Nèihuáng.
The Liáng army attacked Shí Pǔ at Xúzhōu.
They sent Huì to separately attack Sùzhōu.
The Prefect Zhāng Jūn closed the gates and defended the city.
Huì built a dam on the Biàn River to flood its eastern side.
The city wall was destroyed,
and Jūn surrendered.
Zhū Jǐn of Yǎnzhōu led over ten thousand troops to attack Shànfù.
Huì fought Jǐn at Jīnxiāng
and utterly defeated them.
In the second year of Guānghuà,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī rebelled against Jìn
and surrendered Lùzhōu to Liáng.
Huì, starting from Héyáng, attacked Jìn’s Zézhōu
and captured it.
He was then made Provisional Administrator of the Zhāoyì Army.
Huì, fearing the mighty suspicion of Tàizǔ of Liáng,
often feigned illness for several years.
In the first year of Tiānfù,
Tàizǔ reinstated Huì as Military Governor of the Zhāoyì Army.
When Zhāozōng was assassinated,
Huì and the three armies wore white mourning clothes and expressed grief.
The Liáng army attacked Cāngzhōu of Yān.
The Prince of Yān, Shǒuguāng, begged Jìn for troops.
The Jìn people then attacked Lùzhōu for him.
Huì then surrendered to Jìn.
The Prince of Jìn brought Huì back to Tàiyuán
and granted him a grand residence;
his position ranked above the other generals.
When Zhuāngzōng was established,
he made Huì the Grand Campaign Commander.
In the seventh year of Tiānyòu,
he died of illness in Tàiyuán.
When Táng arose,
he was posthumously granted the title Grand Mentor.
Hè Délún.
was a man from Héxī.
In his youth, he was a military commander (yájiàng) of Huázhōu.
When Liáng Tàizǔ concurrently led Xuānyì,
Délún followed Tàizǔ on campaigns.
Due to his achievements, he was repeatedly promoted to Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú Army.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng (915 CE),
Yáng Shīhòu of Wèizhōu died.
Mòdì, believing that the Wèi troops were habitually arrogant and difficult to control,
divided Xiāng, Chán, and Wèi three prefectures to establish the Zhāodé Army,
appointing Zhāng Jūn as Jìedùshǐ.
The three prefectures of Wèi, Bó, and Bèi remained the Tiānxíong Army,
and Délún was appointed Jìedùshǐ.
(Mòdì) dispatched Liú Xún with sixty thousand troops to cross the river,
ostensibly to attack Zhèndìng.
Wáng Yànzhāng entered Wèizhōu with five hundred cavalry,
garrisoning Jīnbō Tíng (Gold Wave Pavilion) to guard against upheaval.
Half of the Wèi Yábīng (prefectural guards) were transferred into Zhāodé.
The Director of Taxes and Levies (Zūyōng Shǐ) sent a clerk (kǒngmù lì) to review the Wèi soldiers' registers
and inspect the government treasuries and armories.
Délún urged the Yábīng to start their journey.
The Yábīng and their relatives bid farewell to each other,
and cries filled the roads.
Zhāng Yàn, a commander of the Xiàojié Army, plotted with his men, saying:
"The Imperial Court believes our military commandery is too powerful
and has set up measures to destroy us.
Moreover, our six prefectures were formerly a feudal domain (fānfǔ),
and we have never been ordered far outside the Hémén region.
To suddenly leave our relatives
and abandon our homeland,
it is better to die than to live."
They then attacked Jīnbō Tíng together at night,
and Yànzhāng fled.
At dawn,
the Wèi troops attacked the headquarters city (Yáchéng),
killing over five hundred people.
They seized Délún and placed him high up in a tower,
allowing the soldiers to engage in mass looting.
Mòdì dispatched the Palace Attendant (Gòngfèng Guān) Hù Yì to rush to Wèi and issue an imperial decree to Yàn,
promising him the position of Prefect (Cìshǐ).
Yàn said to Yì:
"Report this to the Emperor for me:
The three armies have not failed the Imperial Court;
the Imperial Court has failed the three armies.
The anonymous carving up of territory and assignment of troops
is the reason for this chaos.
Just restore the six prefectures to Wèi
and order Liú Xún to return his troops,
and the Emperor can rest easy."
Yì returned
and reported that Yàn was raving and volatile (kuángjué) and nothing to fear,
and that it would be best to quickly urge Xún's troops to attack him.
Mòdì sent a messenger to inform Yàn
that the arrangements were already finalized
and could not be changed again.
The messenger returned three times.
Yàn angrily said:
"How dare this servant boy (yōngbǎo ér) act like this!"
He then summoned Sīkōng Tǐng, a former official of Luó Shàowēi, saying:
"Draft a memorial for me.
If they equivocate again,
I will cross the river and capture the Emperor!"
Mòdì replied with a soothing edict,
stating:
"Wáng Róng died,
and the people of Zhèn requested surrender.
I sent Xún with troops to pacify Zhènzhōu;
it was not for any other reason.
If Wèi is inconvenienced by this,
I will immediately recall Xún."
He warned Yàn not to cause trouble for the Imperial Court.
Yàn then brought up that Yáng Shīhòu, while garrisoned at Wèizhōu, had previously held the title of Commander of Pacification (Zhāotǎo Shǐ).
He forced Délún to memorialize this request.
Mòdì did not permit it.
When the Imperial Decree was announced to him,
Yàn tore the decree and threw it onto the ground,
saying:
"This foolish ruler lets others lead him by the nose.
It is difficult to serve him anymore!"
He then forced Délún to surrender to Jìn.
Délún, terrified, said:
"I shall only follow the General's command."
Thereupon, he dispatched his Yájiàng Cáo Tíngyǐn to present a letter to Zhuāngzōng.
When Zhuāngzōng entered Wèi,
Délún, claiming Yàn had coerced him,
secretly sent someone to complain to Zhuāngzōng.
Zhuāngzōng executed Yàn at Línqīng before entering Wèi.
Délún was transferred to become Jìedùshǐ of Dàtóng Army.
When he traveled to Tàiyuán,
the Army Supervisor (Jiānjūn) Zhāng Chéngyè detained him.
When Wáng Tán attacked Tàiyuán,
many of Délún's subordinates defected to Tán.
Chéngyè feared Délún would cause a revolt
and killed him.
Yán Bǎo.
Yán Bǎo, courtesy name Qióngměi,
was a man from Yùnzhōu.
In his youth, he was a Yájiàng under Zhū Jǐn.
When Jǐn fled to Huáinán,
Bǎo surrendered to Liáng.
During the time of Liáng Tàizǔ,
he served as Chief Commandant of All Armies (Zhūjūn Dū Yúhòu).
He often followed various generals on campaigns,
but never established independent military merit.
By the time of Mòdì,
Bǎo was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Bǎoyì Army.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng,
after Hè Délún surrendered Wèibó to Jìn,
the Jìn army captured Míng, Cí, Xiāng, and Wèi (prefectures).
They then moved their troops to besiege Xíngzhōu.
Mòdì dispatched Zhāng Wēn, the Commander-in-Chief of Capturing the Living (Zhuōshēng Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ), leading five hundred cavalry to rescue Bǎo.
When Wēn reached Nèihuáng,
he encountered the Jìn army
and surrendered to Jìn.
Jìn then sent Wēn, leading the surrendered Liáng troops, to the foot of the city to persuade Bǎo.
Bǎo consequently surrendered to Jìn.
The King of Jìn (Jìn Wáng) appointed Bǎo Grand Marshal Surveillance (Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi) and Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì),
concurrently leading the Tiānpíng Army as Jìedùshǐ and Commander of Pacification for the Southeastern Front (Dōngnán Miàn Zhāotǎo Shǐ).
His rank was placed above the other generals.
When Liáng and Jìn fought at Húliǔ,
the Jìn army was defeated.
Zhuāngzōng intended to lead his troops to retreat and secure Línpú.
Bǎo said:
"In determining victory, one must assess the situation (shì);
in engaging in decisive battle, one must assess the state of mind (qíng).
Once the state of mind and the situation are understood,
the decision must be made without hesitation.
Now the Liáng troops are distressed and exhausted;
their situation allows them to be defeated.
Yet, having won, they will be arrogant and negligent;
their state of mind is predictable.
This is a moment that must not be lost."
Zhuāngzōng bowed and thanked him, saying:
"Had it not been for you, Sire,
my endeavor would have almost failed."
He then reorganized the army and fought again,
subsequently defeating the Liáng troops.
In the eighteenth year (of Tiānyòu, 921 CE),
the Jìn army campaigned against Zhāng Wénlǐ at Zhènzhōu,
and Bǎo was appointed Commander of Pacification.
In the third month of the following year,
Bǎo was defeated in battle
and retreated to secure Zhàozhōu.
Mortified and angry, he developed a carbuncle and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
During the Tiānfú era of Jìn,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán Wáng).
Kāng Yánxiào.
Kāng Yánxiào
was a man from Northern Dài.
He was a soldier of the Tàiyuán army.
Having committed a crime, he fled to Liáng.
Mòdì sent Duàn Níng to command troops along the river
and appointed Yánxiào as Commander of the Left and Right Vanguards (Zuǒyòu Xiānfēng Zhǐhuīshǐ).
Yánxiào observed that Liáng Mòdì employed base individuals (qún xiǎo)
and knew he would surely perish.
He therefore defected to Táng with a hundred cavalry.
He was granted an audience with Zhuāngzōng at Cháochéng.
Zhuāngzōng removed his own imperial robe (yù yī) and golden belt (jīndài) and bestowed them upon him.
(Zhuāngzōng) appointed Yánxiào Prefect of Bózhōu, Commandant of the Běngrì Army, and concurrently Commander of Pacification for the Southern Front (Nánmiàn Zhāotǎo Zhǐhuīshǐ).
Zhuāngzōng dismissed the attendants and asked Yánxiào about matters concerning Liáng.
Yánxiào explained in full:
"Mòdì is weak and timid.
Zhào Yán is his son-in-law,
and Zhāng Hànjié's wife's family
all hold power.
Duàn Níng is wicked and dishonest,
and because he accepts many bribes he is made a great general.
Veteran generals from his father's time are all subordinate to him.
Wáng Yànzhāng,
a valiant general,
was sent with Hànjié to supervise and control his army.
Base men are promoted and appointed,
while loyal ministers and brave warriors are all estranged and ostracized.
This is the situation that guarantees its destruction."
Zhuāngzōng again asked about Liáng's plans.
He replied:
"When your servant was in Liáng,
I secretly heard their discussion: they plan a major campaign in the middle of winter.
They will send Dǒng Zhāng with the troops from Shǎn-Guó and Zé-Lù to exit at Shíhuì to attack Tàiyuán;
Huò Yànwēi with the troops from Guānxī, Rǔ, and Luò will raid Xíng-Míng and advance rapidly toward Zhèn-Dìng;
Wáng Yànzhāng with the Imperial Guards from the capital will attack Yùnzhōu;
and Duàn Níng with the armies along the river will confront Your Majesty."
When Zhuāngzōng first heard Yánxiào say that Liáng was certain to perish,
he was pleased.
But when he heard about their major campaign,
he was afraid.
He asked:
"How shall my generals defend against them?"
Yánxiào replied:
"Although the Liáng forces are numerous,
once divided they will have nothing left.
I request to wait until they are divided,
and take five thousand armored cavalry from Yùn and rush toward Biàn,
catching them by surprise,
and striking their empty heartland.
In less than ten days,
the realm will be settled."
Zhuāngzōng greatly praised his words.
Afterward, although Dǒng Zhāng and others did not deploy troops,
the Liáng troops were all assigned to Duàn Níng along the river,
and the capital was undefended.
Zhuāngzōng finally adopted Yánxiào's plan,
entering Biàn from Yùn,
and in only eight days destroyed Liáng.
For this merit, he was appointed Governor of Zhèngzhōu,
and granted the surname and personal name Lǐ Shàochēn.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Military Commissioner of the Bǎoyì Army.
In the third year,
during the campaign against Shǔ,
Yánxiào was made Commander of the Vanguard, Formation-Breakers, and Decapitators.
He conquered Fèngzhōu,
captured Gùzhèn,
and received the surrender of Xīngzhōu.
He fought Wáng Yǎn at Sānquán.
Yǎn was defeated and fled,
cutting the floating bridge across the Jíbó River.
Yánxiào built boats to cross,
and advanced to capture Miánzhōu.
Yǎn again cut the floating bridge across the Mián River.
Yánxiào said to Lǐ Yán, the Commander of Pacification and Recruitment:
"Our army has traveled a thousand *lǐ*,
entering another man's territory.
Our advantage lies in swift battle.
Taking advantage of Yǎn's disheartened state,
if we can just get a hundred horsemen across Lùtóuguān,
they will be too busy welcoming our surrender to resist.
If we repair the bridge,
we must stay here for several days,
which will allow Yǎn to close the passes and prepare his defenses.
Then the outcome of victory or defeat will be uncertain."
Thereupon, he and Yán mounted horses and floated across the river.
More than a thousand soldiers followed them across.
They then entered Lùtóuguān,
captured Hànzhōu.
After staying for three days,
the main army finally arrived.
Yǎn’s younger brother, Zōngbì, indeed surrendered Shǔ.
Yánxiào garrisoned Hànzhōu,
waiting for Wèi Wáng Jìjí.
When Shǔ was pacified,
Yánxiào’s achievements were the greatest.
Dǒng Zhāng, Commander-in-Chief of the Left Wing Cavalry and Infantry, ranked below Yánxiào,
but he was especially favored by Guō Chóngtāo.
Whenever Chóngtāo had military matters,
he only summoned Zhāng to discuss plans,
and did not consult Yánxiào.
Yánxiào was furious,
and reprimanded Zhāng, saying:
"I possess the merit of pacifying Shǔ.
You followed me as a servant,
yet you instead bow your head at Lord Guō's gate.
Since I am the supreme commander,
can I not execute you according to military law?"
Zhāng complained to Chóngtāo.
Chóngtāo relieved Zhāng of his military post
and proposed him as Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān.
Yánxiào grew even angrier and said:
"I faced bare blades
and endured dangers
to pacify the Two Chuān.
What merit does Zhāng have to receive the symbolic banners and seals!"
Thereupon, he went to see Chóngtāo and expressed that this was unacceptable.
Chóngtāo said:
"Is Shàochēn rebelling?
How dare you defy my command!"
Yánxiào was frightened and withdrew.
The next year, Chóngtāo died.
Yánxiào said to Zhāng:
"At whose gate will you bow your head now?"
Zhāng begged for mercy to escape harm.
When Jìjí returned the army,
he ordered Yánxiào to command the rear guard with twelve thousand men.
When they marched to Wǔlián,
they heard that Zhū Yǒuqīan had been executed without cause.
Yǒuqīan had a son, Lìngdé, in Suìzhōu.
Zhuāngzōng sent an envoy to command Jìjí to immediately execute him.
Jìjí did not send Yánxiào,
but instead sent Dǒng Zhāng.
Yánxiào was already suspicious,
and when Zhāng passed by Yánxiào's army,
he did not pay respects.
Yánxiào was greatly angered,
and said to his subordinates:
"We pacified Liáng in the south
and conquered Shǔ in the west.
The plans for this all came from Lord Guō;
but the hard labor of the galloping horses,
capturing cities and defeating the enemy, was done by me.
Now that Lord Guō is dead,
how can I survive?
Both Yǒuqīan and I deserted Liáng and pledged allegiance to Táng.
Yǒuqīan's disaster will soon reach me!"
Yánxiào's subordinates were all former generals of Yǒuqīan.
Knowing that Yǒuqīan had been executed along with his family,
they all cried loudly at the camp entrance, saying:
"Lord Zhū was innocent,
yet two hundred members of his family were executed.
Former generals often die with him.
Our death is certain!"
Yánxiào then led his forces from Jiànzhōu back into Shǔ,
proclaiming himself Military Commissioner of Xīchuān and Commander of the Three Chuān, etc.
He quickly issued a manifesto to the people of Shǔ.
Within a few days,
his forces numbered fifty thousand.
Jìjí sent Rèn Huán with seven thousand cavalry to pursue him.
They caught up with him at Hànzhōu.
Coinciding with this, Mèng Zhīxiáng attacked him from two sides.
Yánxiào was defeated in battle,
captured,
and transported in a cage-cart.
Huán set out wine in the military camp
and brought the cage-cart near his seat.
Zhīxiáng poured a large goblet of wine, offered it to him in the cart, and said:
"You escaped from the Liáng court and pledged allegiance.
You subsequently commanded banners and seals.
Now with the merit of having pacified Shǔ,
why worry about wealth and high rank,
yet end up in this cage-cart?"
Yánxiào replied:
"Guō Chóngtāo, a minister who supported the mandate,
whose merit was foremost,
captured the Two Chuān without bloodying his blade.
Suddenly, though innocent,
his entire household was executed.
Considering someone like Yánxiào,
how can I preserve my head?
It is for this reason I dared not return to court!"
Rèn Huán returned eastward.
When Yánxiào in the cage-cart reached Fèngxiáng,
Zhuāngzōng sent a eunuch to execute him.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Number 33: Zhāng Quányì
Zhāng Quányì, courtesy name Guówéi,
was a native of Línpú in Púzhōu.
When young, he worked for the county as a farmer's son.
The county magistrate frequently distressed and humiliated him.
Quányì consequently fled and joined Huáng Cháo’s rebels.
When Cháo captured Cháng'ān,
he made Quányì Minister of Personnel and Commissioner of Water Transport.
When Cháo’s rebels were defeated,
he left and served Zhūgě Shuǎng at Héyáng.
After Shuǎng died,
he served his son Zhòngfāng.
When Zhòngfāng was expelled by Sūn Rú,
Quányì and Lǐ Hǎnzhī divided the territory, occupying Héyáng and Luòyáng, and attached themselves to Liáng.
The two men were extremely friendly with each other.
However, Hǎnzhī was greedy and brutal by nature,
spending his days engaging in banditry and plundering.
Quányì was diligent and frugal,
managed his army systematically,
and encouraged the people to farm and cultivate.
Because of this,
Hǎnzhī was always short of food,
while Quányì always had surplus.
Hǎnzhī relied on Quányì for supplies,
but Quányì could not provide enough,
so a rift developed between the two men.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī mobilized troops to attack Jìn and Jiàng.
Zhū Quányì suddenly captured Héyáng.
Hǎnzhī fled to Jìn.
Jìn dispatched troops to assist Hǎnzhī,
and the siege of Quányì became extremely urgent.
Quányì sought military aid from Liáng.
Liáng dispatched Niú Cúnjié, Dīng Huì, and others with ten thousand soldiers to cross the river from Jiǔdǐng.
They defeated Hǎnzhī at the Yǎnshǔi River.
The Jìn army withdrew.
Liáng assigned Dīng Huì to guard Héyáng,
and Quányì returned to serve as the Prefect (Yǐn) of Hénán.
Quányì was grateful to Liáng for having rescued him,
and from then on, he served them wholeheartedly.
At that time,
Hénán had suffered from the warfare and destruction caused by Huáng Cháo and Qín Rú,
its cities and towns ruined,
with fewer than one hundred households remaining.
Quányì cleared the thorns and thickets,
encouraged farming and cultivation,
personally carried wine and food,
and comforted the populace working in the fields.
He built two cities, South and North, to settle them.
After several years,
the population and resources were fully restored and flourishing,
and the people depended greatly upon him.
When Liáng Tàizǔ forced Táng Zhāozōng to move eastward,
the restoration and maintenance of the palace complexes, government offices, and storehouses
were all due to Quányì's efforts.
Quányì's original given name was Yán.
Táng Zhāozōng bestowed upon him the name Quányì.
When Táng fell,
Quányì served Liáng
and requested to change his name again.
Tàizǔ bestowed upon him the name Zōngshì.
Tàizǔ was suspicious and jealous,
especially in his later years.
Quányì served him with increasing caution,
and ultimately managed to protect himself.
Whenever Liáng fought Jìn north of the Yellow River (Héběi),
and the Liáng forces frequently suffered defeats and losses,
Quányì would immediately gather soldiers, weapons, armor, and horses
and present them monthly to fill the gaps.
When Tàizǔ's army was defeated at Tiáoxiàn,
he became ill on the road.
Returning to Luò,
he visited Quányì’s Huìjié Garden to escape the summer heat,
staying for ten days.
Quányì’s wife and daughters were all forced to submit to his lust.
His son, Jìzuò, was overcome by indignation and shame,
and wanted to stab Tàizǔ.
Quányì stopped him, saying:
“When I was besieged at Héyáng by Lǐ Hǎnzhī’s army,
I ate sawdust for food.
I only had one horse,
which I planned to kill to feed the soldiers.
Death was imminent,
but the Liáng army rescued me,
allowing me to survive until today.
This great favor must not be forgotten.”
Jìzuò then stopped.
Once, someone spoke ill of Quányì to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ summoned Quányì,
his intentions unclear.
Quányì’s wife, Lady Chǔ, was intelligent, sharp-witted, and eloquent.
She quickly went in to see Tàizǔ,
and said in a stern voice:
“Zōngshì
is nothing but an old field-tiller!
He has guarded Hénán for thirty years,
opening up wilderness and tilling the soil,
gathering wealth and taxes,
to assist Your Majesty in establishing your enterprise.
Now he is old and frail,
and can do nothing more,
yet Your Majesty suspects him?
Why is this?”
Tàizǔ laughed and said:
“I have no malicious intent.
Old woman, do not speak so much.”
While Quányì served Liáng,
he was repeatedly appointed as the Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and his allotted stipend household reached thirteen thousand.

He concurrently held the positions of Jìedùshǐ (Military Governor) of Zhōngwǔ, Shǎn, Guó, Zhèng, Huá, and Héyáng circuits; Director of Affairs for the Six Armies and Various Guards; and Deputy Commander-in-Chief of All Military Forces in the Realm.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wèi.
Initially,
when Quányì was defeated by Lǐ Hǎnzhī,
his younger brother, Zhū Quánwǔ, and his family members were captured by the Jìn army.
The Prince of Jìn provided them with land and residences,
and treated them extremely well.
Quányì often secretly sent people to convey messages to Tàiyuán.
When Liáng fell,
Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn.
Quányì came from Luò to attend court,
bowing his head to the ground awaiting punishment.
Zhuāngzōng consoled him, saying:
“Your younger brother and nephews
are fortunate to be able to see you again.”
Quányì bowed low in submission, moved to tears.
Due to his advanced age, he could not easily move forward or rush about.
Zhuāngzōng sent someone to assist and support him up the steps.
A banquet and rewards were given with great cheer.
He ordered his imperial son, Jìjí, and imperial younger brother, Cúnjì, among others, to treat him as an elder brother.
Quányì then discarded the name bestowed by Liáng,
and requested to revert to his former name.
However, Quányì still did not feel secure.
He thus heavily bribed Empress Liú to seek her protection.
Previously,
the Last Emperor of Liáng (Liáng Mòdì) traveled to Luòyáng,
intending to perform the suburban sacrifice in the Southern Suburbs, but he did not succeed.
The ceremonial carriage and ritual instruments were still there.
Quányì therefore requested that Zhuāngzōng visit Luòyáng,
reporting that the ritual objects for the Southern Suburbs were ready.
Zhuāngzōng was greatly pleased,
and promoted Quányì to Grand Tutor (Tàishī) and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
In the eleventh month of the following year,
Zhuāngzōng visited Luòyáng
for the suburban sacrifice, but the ritual items were incomplete.
The ceremony was therefore postponed to the second month of the next year,
but Zhuāngzōng did not blame Quányì for his previous statement.
Due to the Empress,
he treated Quányì even more generously.
He frequently visited Quányì’s residence,
ordered the Empress to recognize Quányì as her father,
and changed his title to the Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng).
Initially,
when Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
he wanted to excavate Liáng Tàizǔ’s tomb,
open the coffin, and mutilate the corpse.
Quányì argued that although Liáng was an enemy,
its family had already been utterly destroyed,
which was sufficient revenge.
The humiliation of violating the coffin
was not suitable for a king demonstrating great magnanimity to the world.
Zhuāngzōng agreed,
and merely ordered the tomb gate to be leveled.
Quányì’s supervising general (Jiānjūn) once acquired Lǐ Déyù’s Píngquán Stone of Sobriety.
Déyù’s grandson, Yángǔ,
used Quányì's influence to request its return.
The supervising general said angrily:
“Since the chaos caused by Huáng Cháo,
none of the gardens and residences in Luòyáng could be guarded successfully.
Why should this one Píngquán stone be the exception!”
Quányì had once been a member of the Cháo bandits.
He took this as a veiled insult aimed at himself,
and became furious.
He submitted a memorial requesting the supervising general be executed by flogging.
The entire realm considered this a miscarriage of justice.
When hearing legal disputes,
he deemed the first person to file the complaint to be in the right.
The people found this rather vexing.
In the fourth year of Tóngguāng (926 CE),
Zhào Zàilǐ rebelled in Wèi.
Yuán Xíngqīn failed to achieve success in suppressing the rebels.
Zhuāngzōng wanted to lead the expedition himself.
All the high officials advised against this,
and suggested that Míngzōng should lead the forces.
At that time,
Guō Chóngtāo and Zhū Yǒuqiān had both already been killed.
Míngzōng came from Zhènzhōu to attend court.
Zhuāngzōng housed him in a private residence.
Zhuāngzōng was suspicious of him,
and did not want to dispatch him.
The officials pleaded insistently,
but Zhuāngzōng refused to follow their advice.
Finally, Quányì strongly advocated for it,
and Zhuāngzōng consented.
Shortly thereafter, Míngzōng reached Wèi and indeed rebelled.
Quányì died of worry,
at the age of seventy-five.
His posthumous title was Zhōngsù.
His son, Jìzuò,
held office up to Supreme General.
During the time of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he rebelled with Zhāng Cóngbīn at Héyáng.
He was sentenced to execution of his entire clan.
However, the Chancellor Sāng Wéihàn, citing the kindness Quányì had shown to his father, Gǒng, when Gǒng served him,
begged for Jìzuò’s life to be spared entirely.
This was not permitted.
Only Jìzuò and his wife and children were executed.
Zhū Yǒuqiān
Zhū Yǒuqiān, courtesy name Déguāng,
was a native of Xǔzhōu.
His original given name was Jiǎn.
He served as a soldier in the garrison of Miǎnchí.
He committed a crime and fled,
becoming a bandit between Shíháo and Sānxiāng.
Merchants and travelers all suffered greatly because of him.
After a long time,
he left and became a military officer in Shǎnzhōu.
Xiàng Xiān was a general of the Liáng,
never having had military accomplishments,
but solely because he was the maternal nephew, he commanded the imperial guard.
When Zhu Yǒu'guī was executed,
he had merit toward the Last Emperor (Mòdì).
He stayed in Sòngzhōu for more than ten years,
executing and heavily taxing its people,
and amassed wealth amounting to millions.
When Zhuānzōng destroyed the Liáng,
Xiàng Xiān came to the court at Luòyáng,
transporting his assets worth hundreds of thousands (of cash units),
and bribed the Táng generals, chancellors, court musicians, eunuchs, and Empress Liú, among others.
Because of this, everyone inside and outside (the court) unanimously praised his character.
Zhuānzōng treated him very generously,
bestowed upon him the name Lǐ Shào'ān,
changed the Xuānwǔ Army (Jūn) to the Guīdé Army (Jūn),
saying:
“The name Guīdé
was established for you.”
He was then sent back to his post.
He died that year,
at the age of sixty,
and was posthumously granted the title Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
Xiàng Xiān had two sons.
Zhèngcí served as far as Prefect (Cìshǐ),
and later served as the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Hénghǎi Army during the time of Zhōu Shìzōng.
The property Xiàng Xiān accumulated throughout his life amounted to tens of millions,
with four thousand residences (Dǐshě).
When he died,
he did not divide it among his sons,
but gave it all to Zhèngcí.
Zhèngcí initially became Vice Commissioner of the Flying Dragon (Fēilóng Fùshǐ) due to his father’s influence.
During the time of the Deposed Emperor of Táng,
he offered fifty thousand strings of cash (mín),
and was appointed Prefect of Qúzhōu.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he again offered fifty thousand strings of cash,
seeking to become a true Prefect.
He was appointed Prefect of Yóngzhōu.
This prefecture was west of Língwǔ,
within the territory of the Tǔfān.
Zhèngcí was apprehensive
and did not want to go.
He again offered tens of thousands of cash,
and was thus exempted.
Zhèngcí could not bear his indignation
and tried to hang himself with his belt.
His family members rescued him and stopped him.
During the time of the Emperor Chūdì,
he again offered thirty thousand strings of cash and ten thousand taels of silver.
Emperor Chūdì took pity on him
and intended to give him an interior prefecture,
but he died before this happened.
Zhèngcí accumulated money until it filled his rooms.
There was once a sound like an ox in the room,
and people thought it was a haunting sign (yāo).
They urged him to disperse the wealth he had accumulated to ward it off.
Zhèngcí said:
“I have heard that when things make a sound,
it is only seeking its own kind.
I should add more money,
and the sound will surely cease.”
Those who heard this repeated it as a joke.
Zhū Hànbīn
Zhū Hànbīn, courtesy name Jìchén,
was a man from Qiáo in Bózhōu.
His father, Yuǎnlǐ, was a military officer.
He fought with the Liáng army
and died at Qīngkǒu.
Hànbīn was a man of courage and strength.
Because his father had died fighting, Liáng Tàizǔ
took pity on him
and adopted him as a son.
At that time,
the Liáng was just attacking Yǎn and Yùn to the east.
Zhū Jǐn of Yùnzhōu recruited the swift and brave men in his army,
tattooing twin geese (yàn) on their cheeks,
and called them
the "Geese Sons Battalion" (Yànzǐ Dū).
When Tàizǔ heard of this,
he selected several hundred brave warriors,
named them
the "Fallen Geese Battalion" (Luòyàn Dū),
and made Hànbīn the Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ).
Even when Hànbīn became prominent,
people still referred to him as
“Zhū Luòyàn.”
Hànbīn served the Liáng as Commissioner of the Heavenly Might Army (Tiānwēi Jūnshǐ),
and successively served as Prefect of the five prefectures of Cí, Huá, Sòng, Bó, and Cáo, and as Military Governor of the Ānyuǎn Army (Ānyuǎn Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
When Zhuānzōng destroyed the Liáng,
Hànbīn was dismissed and made Commander of the Right Dragon Martial Guard (Yòulóngwǔ Tǒngjūn);
he was treated quite coldly.
Later, Zhuānzōng happened to visit his residence during an outing.
Hànbīn’s wife was beautiful and intelligent,
and served at the Emperor's side,
offering wine and food,
and presenting songs and dances.
Zhuānzōng was extremely pleased,
staying until the second night watch (gēng) before leaving.
Hànbīn gained favor from then on.
Previously,
when Hànbīn was in the Liáng,
he and Zhū Yǒuqiān were both adopted sons of Tàizǔ.
Since Yǒuqiān was older,
Hànbīn treated him as an elder brother.
After the fall of the Liáng,
Hànbīn repeatedly sent letters to Yǒuqiān,
but Yǒuqiān did not reply.
Hànbīn resented this.
Later, when Yǒuqiān was executed along with his clan,
everyone believed Hànbīn had a hand in it.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
because Hànbīn had been favored by Zhuānzōng,
Míngzōng disliked him,
and made him General-in-Chief of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn).
When Ān Chónghuǐ gained power,
Hànbīn attached himself to him,
and they intermarried.
Because of this, he was again able to become Military Governor of the Zhāoyì Army (Zhāoyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
When Chónghuǐ died,
Hànbīn was dismissed and made General-in-Chief (Shàngjiāngjūn),
and subsequently retired with the title Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo).
As a general, Hànbīn
never had military accomplishments,
but when governing, he was able to uphold the law,
and enjoyed granting favors.
People generally loved him.
He died in the second year of Qīngtài (935 CE),
at the age of sixty-four.
During the time of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he was posthumously granted Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàofù),
with the posthumous name Zhēnghuì.
Duàn Níng
Duàn Níng
was a native of Kāifēng.
His initial name was Míngyuǎn,
later changed to Níng.
He served as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) of Mǐnchí.
His father served Liáng Tàizǔ,
but was implicated in an affair and banished.
Later, Níng abandoned his post
and also served Tàizǔ,
becoming Military Inspector (Jūnxúnshǐ).
He also presented his younger sister to Tàizǔ (as a concubine).
The sister was beautiful,
and later became a Beauty (Měirén).
Níng was a treacherous and cunning person,
skilled at observing and anticipating others' wishes.
Also because of his sister,
Tàizǔ gradually trusted and favored him,
often instructing him to supervise the various armies.
He served as Prefect of Huáizhōu.
When Liáng Tàizǔ campaigned in the north,
he passed through Huáizhōu.
Níng offered extremely lavish gifts.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased.
When he passed through Xiāngzhōu,
Lǐ Sī'ān, the Prefect of Xiāngzhōu, offered gifts according to usual courtesy;
compared to Níng’s offering, it was meager.
Tàizǔ became angry,
and Sī'ān was consequently convicted and executed.
Níng was promoted to Prefect of Zhèngzhōu,
and put in charge of supervising troops along the river.
Lǐ Zhèn repeatedly requested his dismissal.
Tàizǔ said:
“Níng has not yet committed a crime.”
Zhèn replied:
“If we wait until he has committed a crime,
then the state (shèjì) will be ruined!”
However, Tàizǔ ultimately did not dismiss him.
When Zhuānzōng had taken Wèi Bó,
he faced the Liáng along the river.
The Liáng appointed Wáng Yànzhāng as the Commissioner of Pacification (Zhāotǎoshǐ),
with Níng as his deputy.
At this time,
