the Last Emperor (Mòdì) was confused and reckless,
and petty men like Zhào Yán and Zhāng Hànjié were in power.
Níng attached himself to Yán and the others and engaged in wicked acts.
As Commissioner of Pacification, Yànzhāng
in three days,
used a brilliant strategy to break the Southern Wall of Táng Désheng.
However, Níng and Yànzhāng each reported their accomplishments separately.
Yán and the others secretly concealed Yànzhāng’s report of merits
and attributed all the credit to Níng.
Níng then offered gold to Yán and the others,
and sought to replace Yànzhāng.
The Last Emperor was misled by the words of Yán and the others,
and finally appointed Níng as the Commissioner of Pacification,
stationing him at Wáng Cūn.
Shǎnzhōu Jìedùshǐ Wáng Gǒng
was severe and cruel.
He contended with his younger brother Kē for Hézhōng.
He was defeated in battle.
His general, Lǐ Fán, conspired with Yǒuqīan,
and together they killed Gǒng
and pledged allegiance to Liáng.
Tàizǔ appointed Fán to replace Gǒng.
Once Fán was established,
Yǒuqīan again attacked him with troops.
Fán managed to escape.
Liáng Tàizǔ again appointed Yǒuqīan to replace Fán.
When the Liáng troops attacked Lǐ Màozhēn in the west,
Tàizǔ passed through Shǎn on his way back and forth.
Yǒuqīan served him with exceptional diligence,
and thus requested:
"I originally had no merit,
but wealth and honor have come to this,
which is due to the Marshal's power!
Moreover, fortunately, we share the same surname.
I wish to change my name to be ranked among your sons."
Tàizǔ became even more fond of him,
and so changed his name Yǒuqīan,
and adopted him as a son.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he moved his garrison to Hézhōng,
and was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng,
and enfeoffed as Jì Wáng.
When Tàizǔ was assassinated,
Yǒuguī ascended the throne
and bestowed the title of Shìzhōng upon Yǒuqīan.
Although Yǒuqīan accepted the appointment,
his heart was often uneasy.
Soon after, Yǒuguī sent for Yǒuqīan to enter court for an audience.
Yǒuqīan did not go,
but instead pledged allegiance to Jìn.
Yǒuguī dispatched the Zhāotǎoshǐ Hán Qíng to lead Kāng Huáiyīng and other troops, numbering fifty thousand, to attack Yǒuqīan.
The Jìn Wáng marched out of Zé and Lù to rescue him.
He encountered Huáiyīng at Xièxiàn
and utterly defeated him.
Pursuing them to Báijìnglǐng,
they attacked by night with torches.
Huáiyīng was again defeated,
and the Liáng troops then retreated.
Yǒuqīan got drunk and slept in the Jìn Wáng's tent.
The Jìn Wáng looked at him
and said to his attendants,
"Although the Jì Wáng is very noble,
I regret that his arms are short!"
When Mòdì ascended the throne,
Yǒuqīan again became a subject of Liáng but did not sever ties with Jìn.
In the sixth year of Zhēnmíng (920 CE),
Yǒuqīan sent his son Lìngdé to attack Tóngzhōu,
expelling the Jìedùshǐ Chéng Quánhuī,
and then sought to concurrently govern the garrison.
Mòdì initially did not permit it,
but later agreed.
Before the imperial edict arrived,
Yǒuqīan rebelled again,
finally severing ties with Liáng and aligning with Jìn.
Mòdì sent Liú Xún and others to suppress him.
Xún was defeated by Lǐ Cúnshěn.
Jìn enfeoffed Yǒuqīan as Xīpíng Wáng,
and added the title Shǒu Tàiwèi.
His son Lìngdé was made Tóngzhōu Jìedùshǐ.
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng and entered Luò,
Yǒuqīan came to court,
was granted the name Lǐ Jìlín,
and received immense gifts.
The following year,
he was promoted to Shǒu Tàishī and Shàngshū Lìng,
and was granted an iron certificate (tiěquàn) exempting him from capital punishment.
His son Lìngdé was made Suízhōu Jìedùshǐ,
and Lìng Xī was made Zhōngwǔ Jūn Jìedùshǐ.
Over ten of his sons and generals became Cìshǐ.
The abundance of imperial favor
was unmatched at the time.
At this time,
eunuchs and actors held power,
and many sought bribes from Yǒuqīan.
Yǒuqīan could not provide them and declined,
which angered all the eunuchs and actors.
When the Táng army attacked Shǔ,
Yǒuqīan reviewed his elite troops
and ordered his son Lìngdé to lead them to join the army.
When Guō Chóngtāo was killed,
the actor Jǐng Jìn said:
"When the Táng army first set out,
Yǒuqīan thought they were going to attack him,
so he reviewed his troops in preparation."
He also said:
"He conspired with Chóngtāo to rebel."
Furthermore, he said:
"The reason Chóngtāo rebelled in Shǔ
was because Yǒuqīan was his internal support.
When Yǒuqīan saw Chóngtāo die,
he conspired with Cún Yì to avenge the Guō family."
Zhuāngzōng initially doubted the matter,
but the various actors and eunuchs spoke of it day and night.
Yǒuqīan heard this and was greatly afraid.
He planned to go to court to clear his name,
but his generals and officials all urged him not to go.
Yǒuqīan said:
"Duke Guō rendered great service to the state,
yet died from slander.
If I do not clear my name,
who will speak for me?"
So he went to court in a single carriage.
Jǐng Jìn had someone forge a letter of rebellion,
accusing Yǒuqīan of rebellion.
Zhuāngzōng was misled,
and so moved Yǒuqīan to be Yìchéng Jūn Jìedùshǐ.
He sent Zhū Shǒuyīn to surround his residence with troops at night,
drove Yǒuqīan out beyond the Huī'ān Gate,
killed him,
and restored his original name.
An edict ordered Wèi Wáng Jìjí to kill Lìngdé in Suízhōu,
Wáng Sītóng to kill Lìng Xī in Xǔzhōu,
and Xià Lǔqí to exterminate his family in Hézhōng.
When Lǔqí arrived at his home,
Yǒuqīan's wife, Lady Zhāng, led over two hundred members of her clan to see Lǔqí and said:
"The Zhū clan should die,
but please do not implicate innocent people."
She then separated about a hundred of her maids and servants
and took a hundred members of her clan to their execution.
Lady Zhāng went into her room, took out her iron certificate, and showed it to Lǔqí, saying:
"This was bestowed by the Emperor,
I don't know what it means!"
Lǔqí also felt ashamed because of it.
After Yǒuqīan's death,
his generals Shǐ Wǔ and seven others were all implicated with Yǒuqīan and exterminated,
which the world considered unjust.
Yuán Xiàngxīan
Yuán Xiàngxīan
was a native of Xiàyì, Sòngzhōu.
He was a descendant of Nányáng Wáng Shùjǐ of Táng.
His father, Jìngchū,
was Liáng Tàifǔ Qīng and Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and married Tàizǔ's sister,
who was Wàn'ān Dàcháng Gōngzhǔ.
As a nephew of Liáng, Xiàngxīan served as Xuānwǔ Jūn Nèiwài Mǎbù Jūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ,
and successively held the positions of Cìshǐ of Sù, Míng, and Chén three prefectures.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was successively promoted to Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn and Zài Jīng Mǎbù Jūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ.
When Tàizǔ was assassinated,
Yǒuguī ascended the throne.
Mòdì remained to guard Dōngdū,
and consulted Zhào Yán about important matters.
Yán said:
"This matter is as easy as turning over one's hand.
If we can just get the Zhāotǎoshǐ Yáng Lìnggōng to say a word to the imperial guards,
then the matter can be accomplished."
Mòdì immediately sent someone to Wèizhōu
to inform Yáng Shīhòu of the plan.
Shīhòu sent his副general Wáng Shùnxián to Luòyáng to conspire with Xiàngxīan,
and Xiàngxīan agreed.
At this time,
Liú Chóngyù, a general of the Lóngxiáng Army, was garrisoned in Huáizhōu.
He caused a disturbance with his army.
Yǒuguī sent Huò Yànwēi to defeat him at Yānlíng.
The remaining troops scattered and fled,
and the pursuit was very urgent.
Mòdì immediately summoned the Lóngxiáng Army in Dōngjīng and told them:
"The Emperor, because of Chóngyù,
wants to summon all the Lóngxiáng Army to Luò and execute them."
He then forged an imperial edict from Yǒuguī and showed it to them.
The Lóngxiáng Army was terrified
and did not know what to do.
So he told them:
"Yǒuguī assassinated his father and his lord;
he is a villain of the world!
If you can rush to Luòyáng and capture him,
and offer his head in sacrifice to the former emperor,
then you will turn misfortune into fortune."
The soldiers enthusiastically said:
"The King's words are right!"
Mòdì immediately sent a urgent report,
stating:
"The Lóngxiáng Army has rebelled."
When Xiàngxīan heard this,
he immediately led a thousand imperial guards into the palace to attack Yǒuguī.
Yǒuguī died.
When Mòdì ascended the throne,
he appointed Xiàngxīan as Zhènnán Jūn Jìedùshǐ, Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì, Kāifēng Yǐn, and Pàn Zài Jīng Mǎbù Jūn Zhū Jūnshì.
In the fourth year of Zhēnmíng (918 CE),
he became Pínglú Jūn Jìedùshǐ,
and was moved to govern Xuānwǔ.
At this time,
Táng had already conquered Yùnzhōu.
Níng then diverted the river from Suānzǎo eastward toward Yùn,
to cut off the Táng army.
It was named
the "Hùjià Shuǐ" (Imperial Guarding Water).
Zhuāngzōng traveled from Yùn toward Biàn.
The Biàn troops had all joined Níng.
The capital (Jīngshī) was undefended,
so he sent Zhāng Hànlún on an express ride to summon Níng from the riverside (Héshàng).
Hànlún fell from his horse mid-route,
injured and unable to proceed.
Shortly after, Liáng perished.
Níng led 50,000 elite troops to surrender to Táng.
Zhuāngzōng bestowed upon him a brocade robe and an imperial horse.
The next day,
Níng memorialized:
"The treacherous individuals of the former Liáng, such as Zhào Yán, Zhāng Hànjié, and more than ten others, abused their authority,
harming the common people.
I request that they all be executed along with their clans."
Níng came and went in the Táng court without shame.
He viewed the Táng generals and chancellors like entertainers.
Through the actor Jǐng Jìn, he offered bribes to Empress Liú,
seeking favor and patronage.
Zhuāngzōng cherished and loved him greatly,
bestowed upon him the name Lǐ Shàoqīn,
and made him the Jìedùshǐ of Tàiníng Commandery.
After staying for more than a month,
he spent several hundred thousand (coins) from the treasury.
The relevant officials requested that he be forced to repay it.
Zhuāngzōng released him (from the debt).
Guō Chóngtāo insisted firmly,
believing this was unacceptable.
Zhuāngzōng angrily said:
"I am controlled by you, my lord,
and have no freedom at all!"
He ultimately released him (from the debt).
Zhuāngzōng sent Lǐ Shàohóng to supervise the various generals in preparing against the Qìdān.
Níng was stationed at Wǎqiáo Pass.
Because he fawned upon Shàohóng,
Shàohóng repeatedly recommended Níng as suitable for great use.
Guō Chóngtāo consistently thought this unacceptable.
(Níng) was promoted to Jìedùshǐ of Wǔshèng Commandery.
When Zhào Zàilǐ rebelled,
Shàohóng requested Níng be made the Commander of Pacification and Inquiry.
Zhuāngzōng ordered Níng to memorialize his plans and strategies.
The auxiliary generals Níng requested
were all his former associates.
Zhuāngzōng grew suspicious,
and stopped the appointment.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
(Níng) was forced to retire to his homeland.
The following year,
he was exiled permanently to Liáozhōu,
and granted death.
Liú
Liú,
was a man from Yōngqiū in Biànzhōu.
His family served as staff officers of the Xuānwǔ Army for generations.
When the Grand Progenitor of Liáng governed Xuānwǔ,
(Liú) was appointed as a Squad Leader from the ranks of the soldiers.
He gradually moved up to Staff Officer through military achievements,
and became the Area Commander of Xiāngzhōu.
Wáng Bān, the Jìedùshǐ of Shānnán, was killed by rebel troops.
The rebels promoted (Liú) to Acting Military Governor.
He falsely agreed to the position.
The next day, he feasted the troops in the courtyard.
He concealed armored soldiers behind the screens.
When the drinking was halfway through,
he captured and killed those who had initiated the rebellion.
Just then, troops sent by Liáng under Chén Huī also arrived.
Xiāngzhōu was pacified.
For his merit, he was appointed Prefect of Fùzhōu,
and later transferred to Bózhōu and Ānzhōu.
During the reign of the Last Emperor,
he served as the Acting Military Commissioner of Jìnzhōu.
For a total of eight years,
he fought daily battles with the Jìn people.
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
(Liú) came to court.
Zhuāngzōng comforted him, saying:
"Marquis Liú is well, I trust?
You have resided on the southern border of Jìnyáng for a long time.
I have not heard from you sooner.
To visit me today,
is this not rather late?"
(Liú) kowtowed and apologized for his fault.
He was sent back to his garrison,
and subsequently made Jìedùshǐ.
He was transferred to govern Ānyuǎn.
In the first year of Tiānchéng,
Shǐ Jìngróng replaced him.
(Liú) returned to the capital.
Before arriving,
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Wǔshèng Commandery.
He died from illness on the way,
and was posthumously granted Shìzhōng.
Zhōu Zhīyù
Zhōu Zhīyù, courtesy name Hǎowèn,
was a man from Yōuzhōu.
He served as a cavalry general under Liú Rén'gōng.
When Rén'gōng was imprisoned by his son Shǒuguāng,
Zhīyù left and served Shǒuguāng's elder brother, Shǒuwén.
Shǒuguāng subsequently attacked and killed Shǒuwén.
(Zhīyù) then joined Zhāng Wànjìn in installing Shǒuwén's son Yánzuò and served him.
Shǒuguāng again killed Yánzuò,
replacing him with his own son, Jìwēi.
Wànjìn killed Jìwēi,
and fled together with Zhīyù to Liáng.
The Grand Progenitor of Liáng was extremely pleased upon acquiring Zhīyù.
He established the Guīhuà Army for him,
making Zhīyù the Commander.
All who were captured in battles against Jìn,
as well as soldiers who turned against Jìn and returned to Liáng,
were placed under Zhīyù's command.
Liáng and Jìn confronted each other along the river for more than ten years.
In breaking the strong and penetrating enemy lines,
the Guīhuà Army was the foremost.
However, Zhīyù's rank did not exceed that of a Prefect.
When Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
Zhīyù and Duàn Níng were stationed along the river.
Hearing that Liáng had perished,
(Zhīyù) wanted to commit suicide.
He was stopped by his retainers and old friends,
and subsequently surrendered to Táng.
Zhuāngzōng particularly favored and treated him well.
The generals, jealous of his favor,
shot at him during a hunt.
Zhīyù fled and escaped death.
Zhuāngzōng had the shooters executed,
and made Zhīyù the Prefect of Fángzhōu.
During the reign of Míngzōng,
he successively served as Prefect of Jiàngzhōu and Zīzhōu,
and was promoted to Commissioner of Regimental Training of Sùzhōu and Acting Military Governor of Ānzhōu.
Wherever he served, he implemented good governance.
Ānzhōu was near the Huái River.
The local custom frowned upon the sick.
When parents fell ill,
they were placed in another room.
Food and drink were tied to a bamboo pole and handed to them;
they were not approached until death.
Zhīyù was deeply distressed by this,
and provided moral instruction.
Because of this, the custom was gradually reformed.
He was dismissed and made Commander of the Right Divine Martial Army.
He died during the Yìngshùn era,
and was posthumously granted Grand Tutor.
Lù Sīduó
Lù Sīduó,
was a man from Línhuáng in Chánzhōu.
In his youth, he served Liáng as a soldier in the Xuānwǔ Army.
He became famous for his archery skills.
He was repeatedly promoted to Area Commander of the Left Wing of Gǒngchén,
concurrently holding the position of Prefect of Ēnzhōu.
When Liáng and Jìn were locked in confrontation along the river,
Sīduó carved his name onto his arrow shafts before shooting them at the Jìn army.
One arrow struck Zhuāngzōng’s saddle.
Zhuāngzōng retrieved the arrow,
saw Sīduó’s name,
and was impressed by him.
Afterward, when Liáng was destroyed,
Sīduó went to audience.
Zhuāngzōng brought out that arrow and showed it to him.
Sīduó prostrated himself and requested death.
Zhuāngzōng comforted him and helped him rise,
appointing him Area Commander of the Right Wing of Lóngwǔ.
During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he served as Prefect of Chénzhōu and Càizhōu.
He died at the age of fifty-four.
While Sīduó was in Chénzhōu,
he implemented good governance.
Just before his death, he instructed his son, saying:
"The people of Chénzhōu love me;
when I die, bury me there."
He was subsequently buried in Chénzhōu.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter 34: Zhào Zàilǐ.
Zhào Zàilǐ, courtesy name Gànchén,
was a native of Zhuōzhōu.
In his youth, he served Liú Rén'gōng as a military officer.
Rén'gōng sent him to assist his son, Shǒuwén, in capturing Cānɡzhōu by surprise.
Later, Shǒuwén was killed by his younger brother, Shǒuguāng.
Zàilǐ then fled to Jìn.
During the time of Zhuānɡzōnɡ,
he served as the Commander (Zhīhuīshǐ) of the Xiàojié corps,
leading Wèi troops to garrison Wǎqiáo Guān.
Returning to Bèizhōu,
the soldier Huánɡpǔ Huī caused a rebellion.
They nominated their general Yánɡ Rénshènɡ as the leader,
but Rénshènɡ refused to follow,
so they killed him.
They nominated another junior officer,
the junior officer refused to follow,
so they killed him again.
They then carried the two heads and went to Zàilǐ.
Zàilǐ heard of the chaos.
His clothes were not properly belted,
and he was climbing over a wall to flee,
when Huī dragged him down by his feet.
They surrounded him with naked blades,
showed him the two heads,
and said:
“Those who do not follow us will end up like these heads!”
Zàilǐ followed them,
and thus rebelled.
Zàilǐ returned from Bèizhōu to attack Wèi,
and allowed his army to plunder greatly.
At this time,
Wánɡ Zhènɡyán, the Administrator (Yǐn) of Xīnɡtánɡ, was old, sick, and confused.
Hearing that Zàilǐ had arrived,
he called for clerks to draft a memorial.
The clerks had already fled and dispersed,
but Zhènɡyán still did not know.
He was leaning on his desk, greatly angered,
when his attendants reported, saying:
“The bandits are already killing people in the marketplace.
Officials and citizens have all fled.
Who is it you wish to summon?”
Zhènɡyán was greatly astonished and said:
“I was completely unaware of this.”
He immediately sought a horse intending to leave.
An officer said:
“Your wife and children have been captured by the bandits.
How can you get a horse?”
Zhènɡyán was terrified.
He walked out of the yamen gate,
saw Zàilǐ,
looked toward him and bowed low.
Zàilǐ called out to Zhènɡyán, saying:
“Why do you humble yourself so deeply, Duke!
This is the sentiment of the soldiers,
it is not my personal intention.”
Zàilǐ immediately proclaimed himself Commander (Liúhòu) of the Military Forces.
Zhuānɡzōnɡ sent Yuán Xínɡqīn to suppress him.
Xínɡqīn attacked Wèi but could not overcome it.
Then, Mínɡzōnɡ was sent to replace Xínɡqīn.
When Mínɡzōnɡ arrived at Yè,
his army mutinied.
Consequently, he entered the city and joined Zàilǐ.
Mínɡzōnɡ's army turned back toward the capital,
and Zàilǐ remained in Wèi.
When Mínɡzōnɡ ascended the throne,
he appointed Zàilǐ as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Yìchénɡ Command.
Zàilǐ did not accept the mandate.
Consequently, he was appointed Garrison Commander (Liúshǒu) of Yè Dū and Administrator (Yǐn) of Xīnɡtánɡ.
After a long time,
Huánɡpǔ Huī and the others all departed.
Zàilǐ was alone in Wèi.
He worried about the arrogance of the Wèi army,
and feared disaster would follow.
So he requested to be transferred to Hénɡhǎi Command.
He subsequently governed Tài'níng, Kuānɡguó, Tiānpínɡ, Zhōnɡwǔ, Wǔníng, Guīdē, and Jìnchānɡ commands.
Wherever he went, his mansions and shops were lined up,
accumulating wealth amounting to tens of millions.
During the time of Jìn Chūdì,
Zàilǐ was made the Supreme Marshal (Dōuyúhòu) of the Cavalry and Infantry of the Northern Campaign Headquarters,
for the purpose of attacking the Qìdān.
He never achieved military merit in battle.
When Zàilǐ was in Sònɡzhōu,
the people suffered especially under him.
When he was later dismissed and left,
the people of Sònɡ happily said to each other:
“Pulling a nail from the eye,
how joyous is that!”
Soon after, he again received an imperial edict assigning him to office.
He then registered all households within his jurisdiction,
levying one thousand coins per person.
He named this tax
the “Nail-Pulling Tax” (Bádīnɡ Qián).
When Jìn perished,
and the Qìdān entered Biàn,
Zàilǐ rushed from Sònɡ to Luòyánɡ,
where he encountered Qìdān officials such as Zhuāilá.
He bowed at the head of their horses.
Zhuāilá and his soldiers jointly humiliated him,
demanding and seizing his wealth.
Zàilǐ could not bear the humiliation and anger.
Traveling until he reached Zhènɡzhōu,
he heard that many Jìn officials had been chained by the Qìdān.
In the middle of the night, terrified and confused,
he untied his sash, went to the horse stable, hanged himself, and died.
He was sixty-two years old.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted him the title of Director of the Secretariat (Zhōnɡshū Lìnɡ).
Huò Yànwēi
Huò Yànwēi, courtesy name Zǐzhònɡ,
was a native of Qǔzhōu, Mínɡzhōu.
In his youth, he suffered through military turmoil.
Huò Cún, a general of Liánɡ, captured him.
He admired his outstanding vigor,
and raised him as his adopted son.
He once followed Cún into battle,
and was hit by an arrow,
losing sight in one eye.
Later, he served Liánɡ Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ also favored him.
He was gradually promoted to Army Commander (Jūnshǐ) of the Left Lónɡxiánɡ Corps and General-in-Chief (Shànɡ Jiānɡjūn) of the Right Jiānmén Guard.
He participated in the execution of Yǒuɡuī.
For this merit, he was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Mínɡzhōu.
He was transferred to be Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Bīnnìnɡ Command.
Lǐ Màozhēn sent Liánɡ traitorous general Liú Zhījùn to attack Bīnzhōu.
Yànwēi held fast in defense for over a year.
Whenever he captured soldiers belonging to Zhījùn,
he always released them back.
Zhījùn was grateful for this virtue,
and thereafter ceased attacking.
He was transferred to govern Yìchénɡ Command,
and then transferred to Tiānpínɡ Command.
He also held the concurrent post of Commissioner of Pacification and Mobilization (Zhāotǎoshǐ) of the Northern Campaign Headquarters.
He maintained a standoff with the Jìn army along the river.
Yànwēi suffered repeated defeats,
and was demoted to Garrison Commander (Liúhòu) of Shǎnzhōu.
When Zhuānɡzōnɡ destroyed Liánɡ,
Yànwēi came from Shǎn to the capital to pay homage.
Zhuānɡzōnɡ held a banquet in the former Chónɡyuán Hall of Liánɡ.
Yànwēi, along with Liánɡ generals Duàn Nínɡ and Yuán Xiànɡxiān, were all present.
When Zhuānɡzōnɡ was tipsy from wine,
he pointed to Yànwēi and the others, raised his cup, and offered a toast to Mínɡzōnɡ, saying:
“These were all formidable enemies just the other day,
now they attend us while we drink.
This is your merit, Minister.”
Yànwēi and the others were terrified and prostrated themselves, begging for death.
Zhuānɡzōnɡ comforted them, saying:
“I was just jesting with you, Commanders.
Gentlemen, do not be afraid.”
He bestowed upon him the new name Lǐ Shàozhēn.
The following year,
he was transferred to govern Wǔníng Command.
He followed Mínɡzōnɡ to attack the Qìdān.
Mínɡzōnɡ admired his character,
and treated him with great intimacy and favor.
Afterward,
Zhào Zàilǐ rebelled.
Yànwēi separately attacked Zhào Tài in Xīngzhōu,
and defeated him.
He returned and assigned his troops to Míngzōng to attack Zàilǐ.
Míngzōng’s army mutinied.
Zhāng Pòbài, a military clerk of the Cóngmăzhí corps, led the masses to kill the generals and officers.
They set fire to the camp, burning it and shouting loudly.
Míngzōng scolded them, saying:
“Since I became a commander more than ten years ago,
how have I wronged you fellows?
Now the rebel city is about to be captured,
this is the time for you fellows to establish merit and fame and acquire wealth and honors.
Moreover, you are the Emperor’s personal army,
why turn and follow the rebels?”
The soldiers replied:
“What crime have the people in the city committed?
The garrison troops merely wish to return home but cannot!
The Emperor does not grant clemency and pardon;
his intent is set on total extermination.
Furthermore, we heard that after Wèi is defeated,
he intends to bury all the Wèibó armies alive.
We originally had no rebellious intent;
we just fear death!
Now we should join forces with those in the city,
repel the troops from the various circuits,
ask the Emperor to rule the south of the Yellow River (Hénán),
and let Your Grace (Lìnggōng) command the north of the Yellow River (Héběi).”
Míngzōng wept and tried to persuade them,
but the mutinous soldiers formed a circle and shouted:
“If Your Grace does not wish to rule Héběi,
then others will take it.
We are wolves and tigers;
how would we recognize hierarchy?”
Yànwēi and Ān Chónghuǐ advised Míngzōng to agree to it.
So, he led his troops into the city,
and joined Zàilǐ.
Yànwēi alone did not enter.
When Míngzōng entered the city,
he held a great feast with wine for Zàilǐ.
But the troops who remained outside, hearing that Míngzōng had rebelled,
all dispersed and fled.
Only the five thousand men led by Yànwēi camped in the northwest corner of the city and remained motionless.
After two days,
Míngzōng came out again,
secured Yànwēi’s troops,
and went to Wèixiàn.
He planned to return to Zhènzhōu,
but Yànwēi and Chónghuǐ advised Míngzōng to lead the troops southward.
When Zhuāngzōng died,
Yànwēi followed Míngzōng into Luòyáng.
He was the first to lead the officials in urging Míngzōng to ascend the throne.
All critical matters, both internal and external,
were decided by Yànwēi.
Yànwēi had always held grudges against Duàn Níng and Wēn Tāo.
Therefore, he arbitrarily arrested Níng and Tāo and threw them into prison,
intending to kill them.
Ān Chónghuǐ said:
“The wickedness of Níng and Tāo
is known throughout the realm.
However, the Sovereign is currently suppressing internal disorder
and must demonstrate grace and trustworthiness to the people.
How can this be the time for you to take private revenge?”
Yànwēi then stopped.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he pardoned Níng and Tāo,
and released them to return to their fields and villages.
Subsequently, they were ultimately granted death (forced suicide).
Yànwēi was transferred to command Pínglú.
When Zhū Shǒuyīn rebelled,
and was executed,
Yànwēi dispatched an envoy on horseback to present two arrows as congratulations.
Míngzōng bestowed two arrows upon him in return.
In the custom of the barbarians (Yídí),
when raising an army and commanding the masses,
the transmission of arrows serves as the signal or order.
However, it is not permissible for subordinates to employ this against superiors.
Míngzōng originally came from the barbarians,
and Yànwēi was a military man.
Neither sovereign nor minister understood ritual propriety,
and many of their actions were of this kind.
However, Yànwēi had a retainer named Chúnyú Yàn.
He was a man from Dēngzhōu.
When young, he passed the examination for the Classicist (Míngjīng) degree.
Encountering a turbulent age,
he sought refuge with Yànwēi.
He had followed him since Yànwēi was an assistant general (piānpí).
Yànwēi once lost a battle and escaped alone.
None of the troops under his command followed him.
Only Yàn followed him on foot through the thorny thickets with a single sword, thus helping him escape.
Yànwēi respected his righteousness highly.
In all the circuits he subsequently governed,
he consistently invited Yàn to follow him.
Regarding his family affairs, regardless of size,
all were decided by Yàn.
Because of this, Yànwēi managed to commit few mistakes.
At that time, when various circuit commanders invited and appointed officials,
they all regarded Yàn as the model.
In the winter of Tiānchéng 3 (928 CE),
Yànwēi died in his post.
At this time,
Míngzōng was hunting in the nearby suburbs.
A horseman from Qīngzhōu galloped in to report Yànwēi’s death.
Míngzōng returned to the palace weeping,
suspended court sessions,
and furthermore, throughout that month, no music was performed.
He posthumously conferred upon Yànwēi the title of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī)
and granted him the posthumous name Zhōngwǔ.
Fáng Zhīwēn
Fáng Zhīwēn, courtesy name Bóyù,
was a man from Xiáqiū, Yănzhōu.
In his youth, due to his bravery and strength, he became a soldier (guānjiàn) in the Chìjiăndū corps.
Later, he was attached to the Mădòu Army in Wèizhōu.
He gradually rose to become Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ) of the Qīnsuí Army.
When Zhuāngzōng took Wèibó,
he acquired Zhīwēn,
bestowed upon him the surname Lǐ,
and gave him the name Shàoyīng.
He made him Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Chánzhōu,
and he subsequently held the post of Prefect of the two prefectures of Cáo and Bèi,
and guarded Wăqiáo Pass.
When Míngzōng rebelled from Wèi and led his troops southward,
Zhīwēn was the first to rush and join him.
In Tiānchéng 1 (926 CE),
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Tàiníng Command.
The following year,
he served as Commander of Pacification (Zhāotăoshǐ) for the Northern Front,
stationed at Lútái.
Míngzōng sent Wū Zhèn to replace Zhīwēn and have him return to his circuit.
The garrison troops, led by the Xiàojié Army general Lóng Ăng and others, attacked and killed Zhèn.
The Xiàojié
was the army of Wèizhōu.
In Wèizhōu, ever since Luó Shàowēi executed the Headquarters Army (Yájūn),
and Yáng Shīhòu became Jìedùshǐ,
the Silver Spear Xiàojié Army was reestablished.
During the reign of the Last Emperor of Liáng (Liáng Mòdì),
Shīhòu nearly became a threat to Liáng.
When Shīhòu died,
Hè Délún replaced him.
The Last Emperor worried that the Wèi army was too powerful to control,
and plotted with Zhào Yán and others to divide Xiāng and Wèi into two circuits.
Because of this, the Wèi army mutinied,
coerced Délún to rebel against Liáng and surrender to Jìn.
Liáng consequently lost Héběi.
After Zhuāngzōng acquired the Wèi troops,
he fought against Liáng on the Yellow River,
gaining merit repeatedly.
He promised the army a huge reward upon the destruction of Liáng.
When Liáng perished,
although the Wèi army was given gifts repeatedly,
they were arrogant, unrestrained, and never satisfied,
always harboring resentment and discontent.
The revolt of Huángpǔ Huī
and the coercion of Zhào Zàilǐ to enter Wèi,
were all done by this army.
When Míngzōng came to the throne,
Zàilǐ commanded Tiānxióng Command.
Since the Wèi army was notoriously arrogant,
he constantly feared disaster
and did not feel secure remaining there.
He secretly sent someone to complain to Míngzōng,
requesting permission to leave the post.
Míngzōng then used the Imperial Prince Cóngróng to replace Zàilǐ,
and dispatched nine divisions (zhǐhuī) of the Wèi Xiàojié Army to garrison Lútái in the north.
On the day the army departed,
they were not given weapons or armor;
they only used long poles tied with banners to mark the units.
The soldiers were rather doubtful and suspicious.
The following year,
Míngzōng sent Wū Zhèn to replace Zhīwēn in the garrison duty,
but Zhīwēn was especially unhappy about it.
The garrison army at Lútái was divided into two camps, east and west of the water.
When Zhèn first arrived,
he met with Zhīwēn at the East Camp.
While they were playing dice,
the Xiàojié Army mutinied,
shouting outside the gate.
Zhīwēn immediately mounted his horse and went out.
The mutineers attacked and killed Zhèn,
and held the reins to restrain Zhīwēn.
Zhīwēn lied, saying:
“The cavalry are all in the West Camp.
Now that we only have infantry here,
I fear we can accomplish nothing.”
Zhīwēn then leaped onto his horse, boarded a boat, crossed the river, and entered the West Camp.
He used the cavalry to kill all the mutineers.
Míngzōng issued an edict
to execute all their family members in Wèizhōu.
In total, the families of the nine divisions, more than three thousand households and tens of thousands of lives,
were driven to the banks of the Zhāngshuǐ River and killed.
The Zhāngshuǐ River changed color because of it.
The arrogant soldiers of Wèi
were thus wiped out.
Míngzōng knew that the mutiny had originated with Zhīwēn,
but pardoned him and did not question it.
He transferred him to command Wǔníng,
added the concurrent title of Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng),
and subsequently commanded Tiānpíng and Pínglú.
Initially,
Míngzōng (明宗) served as the Commander for the Northern Frontier Pacification (Běimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ),
and Zhīwēn (知溫) was the Deputy Commander.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) was a subordinate general, he served Zhīwēn with great deference,
but later, he became displeased over an incident during a drinking session.
When the Deposed Emperor raised troops at Fèngxiáng (鳳翔),
and Emperor Mǐn (Mǐndì 愍帝) fled,
Zhīwēn seized the opportunity and harbored intentions of usurpation.
He said to his administrator, Lǐ Chōng (李沖):
“I have several storerooms full of cash
and several thousand trained soldiers.
If I use this moment to raise the banner of righteousness (jiànyì),
success is certain.”
Chōng replied:
“The current Son of Heaven is weak (cánruò),
and the people, high and low, are disaffected.
However, the military might of the Prince of Lù (Lù Wáng) is immense.
The outcome is uncertain.
I request to travel west with a memorial to observe the situation.”
When Chōng arrived at the capital (Jīngshī),
the Deposed Emperor had already entered and been enthroned.
Chōng immediately presented a memorial offering congratulations,
and upon returning, persuaded Zhīwēn to come to court.
The Deposed Emperor greatly comforted and rewarded him.
Zhīwēn returned to his post
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōngpíng (Dōngpíng Wáng).
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng) reported:
“When conferring titles upon princes and dukes by mandate (cèbài),
the Emperor personally attends the pavilion (línxuán) and dispatches the mandate.
For those who are outside the capital,
the mandate is commissioned by an envoy in the main court (zhèngyá).
However, there is no explicit regulation in the existing records (gùshì) stating that
the imperial equipage (lǔbù), military band (gǔchuī), imperial carriages (lùchē), and ritual implements (fǎwù) should not leave the capital city.
Now, the Prince of Běipíng (Běipíng Wáng) Dékūn (德鈞) and the Prince of Dōngpíng Zhīwēn are receiving their seals and commissioned mandates.
We request that the Ministry of War (Bīngbù), the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng), and the Court of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú) be instructed
to provide the lǔbù, gǔchuī, lùchē, and fǎwù to proceed to their respective circuits (běndào).
After the ceremonies are complete, they shall be returned to the relevant offices.”
While Zhīwēn was at his post,
he constantly levied heavy taxes on his people,
amassed huge wealth (jùwàn),
built a residence in the southern city of Qīngzhōu (青州),
traveled with singers and courtesans,
and indulged in pleasure, neglecting political affairs.
In the first year of Tiānfú (天福) (936 CE), he died in office
and was posthumously granted the title Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
After Zhīwēn died,
his son Yànrú (彥儒) offered 30,000 *mín* of his father’s cash, 30,000 bolts of silk and cloth, 100 ounces of gold, 1,000 ounces of silver, 1,500 *jin* of tea, and 100,000 ounces of silk thread.
He was appointed Prefect of Yízhōu (Yízhōu Cìshǐ).
It is said that
those among his generals and officials who shared the rest of his wealth (yúzī) all became wealthy families.
Wáng Yànqiú (王晏球)
Wáng Yànqiú, courtesy name Yíngzhī (瑩之),
was a native of Luòyáng (洛陽).
He met with turmoil in his youth
and was abducted by bandits.
A rich man from Biànzhōu (汴州) named Dù (杜氏) obtained him,
raised him as his son,
and he assumed the surname Dù.
When Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) of Liáng (Liáng Tàizǔ) was stationed at Xuānwǔ (宣武),
he selected talented and martial sons of wealthy families to serve under his banner,
naming them
the “Hall Guard Army” (Tīngzǐ Dū).
Yànqiú was unrestrained and possessed great integrity (dàjié).
He served as the Commander-in-Chief of the Hall Guard Army.
After the Grand Ancestor ascended the throne,
Yànqiú became General of the Right Qianniu Guard (Yòu Qiānniú Wèi Jiāngjūn).
When Yǒuguī (友珪) established himself,
the garrison troops of Lóngxiáng (龍驤) revolted
and marched from Huáizhōu (懷州) toward the capital.
Yǒuguī sent Yànqiú to attack and defeat them at Héyáng (河陽).
For this achievement, he was promoted to Commander of the First Lóngxiáng Division.
When the Last Emperor (Mòdì) ascended the throne,
Yànqiú was promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Four Lóngxiáng Divisions.
Liáng sent Lǐ Bà (李霸), a general of the Captured-Alive Army (Zhuōsheng Jūn), with 1,000 men to garrison Yángliú (楊劉).
Bà started a revolt at night,
entering through the water gate.
He set fires and shouted loudly,
tying cloths soaked in oil to long poles
to set fire to Jiànguó Gate from below.
Yànqiú, hearing the disturbance,
did not wait for orders.
He led 500 cavalry of the Lóngxiáng Army to attack them.
The momentum of the rebels was slightly repelled.
The Last Emperor ascended a tower and saw this,
crying out:
“Is that not my Lóngxiáng Army!”
Yànqiú reported:
“The rioters
are merely one division (yīdū) led by Lǐ Bà.
Your Majesty should strictly guard the palace city,
and entrust me with defeating the rebels.”
At dawn, he killed them all.
For this achievement, he was appointed Prefect of Chánzhōu (Chánzhōu Cìshǐ).
The ancient text reads Dān (單).
When the Liáng and Jìn (晉) armies were stationed along the Yellow River,
Yànqiú was made Commander-in-Chief of the Mobile Camp Infantry and Cavalry.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) entered Biàn (汴),
Yànqiú pursued him with his troops.
When he reached Fēngqiū (封丘),
he heard that the Last Emperor had died.
He immediately laid down his armor and surrendered to Táng (唐).
Zhuāngzōng bestowed upon him the name Lǐ Shàoqián (李紹虔),
appointed him Defense Commissioner of Qízhōu (Qízhōu Fángyùshǐ),
and stationed him at Wǎqiáo Pass (Wǎqiáo Guān).
When Míngzōng (明宗) launched his military revolt,
marching south from Yè (鄴),
he sent someone to recruit Yànqiú.
Yànqiú followed him to Luòyáng,
and was appointed Military Commissioner of Guīdé Circuit (Guīdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
When Wáng Dū (王都) of Dìngzhōu (定州) rebelled,
Yànqiú was made the Pacification Commissioner
to attack him, along with Zhāng Yánlǎng (張延朗), the Southern Court Commissioner of the Palace Secretariat (Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ), and others.
Dū sent people north to solicit the Qìdān (契丹).
The Qìdān dispatched Tūněi (禿餒) leading 10,000 cavalry to aid Dū.
Yànqiú, hearing that Tūněi’s troops were about to arrive,
left Zhāng Yánlǎng to garrison Xīnlè (新樂)
and personally went to intercept them at Wàngdū (望都).
The Qìdān, however, entered Dìngzhōu via another route
and, together with Dū, launched a surprise attack on Yánlǎng’s army.
Yánlǎng was utterly defeated.
He gathered the remaining troops and joined Yànqiú, retreating toward Qǔyáng (曲陽).
Dū pursued them, taking advantage of his victory.
Yànqiú arrived first at a waterside,
and was sitting down, giving commands to a Hu (胡) officer,
when Dū’s troops suddenly arrived.
Yànqiú and a dozen or so men around him continuously shot arrows at them.
Dū’s troops gradually retreated,
and Yànqiú’s rear forces also arrived.
Yànqiú stood on a high ridge,
ordering all his generals to sheath their bows and arrows and use short weapons (duǎnbīng);
anyone who looked back would be executed.
Fú Yànqīng (符彥卿) attacked the enemy’s left flank with the left army,
and Gāo Xíngguī (高行珪) attacked the enemy’s right flank with the right army.
The cavalry in the central army rode headlong into Dū’s army while holding their horses’ necks.
Dū was then totally routed.
From Qǔyáng to Dìngzhōu,
dead bodies and discarded armor littered the ground for more than sixty *lǐ*.
Dū and Tūněi entered the city
and dared not venture out again.
The Qìdān again sent Tìyǐn (惕隱) with 7,000 cavalry to reinforce Dū.
Yànqiú met them at the Táng River (Táng Hé)
and pursued them, attacking them all the way to Mǎnchéng (滿城).
He beheaded 2,000 men
and captured 1,000 horses.
Since China (Zhōngguó) had experienced much turmoil,
the Qìdān had grown strong in the north.
All the northern barbarians, regardless of size, feared and submitted to them.
Chinese troops who encountered the Qìdān
had never once achieved even a small victory.
Since Yànqiú defeated Tūněi
and also drove away Tìyǐn,
their remaining troops fled and dispersed into villages.
The villagers struck and killed them everywhere with hoes, rakes, and wooden staffs,
leaving no survivors.
Tìyǐn fled with a few dozen cavalrymen to the west of Yōuzhōu (幽州),
where he was captured by Zhào Dékūn (趙德鈞) and sent to the capital.
Míngzōng issued an edict reproaching and criticizing the Qìdān.
Later, the Qìdān repeatedly sent envoys to China
requesting the return of Tìyǐn and others.
Their language was very humble and submissive,
but Míngzōng immediately had the envoys executed to cut off contact.
At this time,
the might of China was greatly revered,
and the Qìdān became slightly weakened and subdued.
This began with Yànqiú.
Yànqiú attacked Dìngzhōu,
but could not capture it for a long time.
Míngzōng repeatedly sent people to urge him to defeat the rebels quickly.
Yànqiú believed that a hurried attack was ill-advised.
His subordinate generals, Zhū Hóngzhāo (朱弘昭) and Zhāng Qiánzhāo (張虔釗), publicly declared:
“Yànqiú is merely timid!”
They then led troops forward.
The troops were indeed defeated,
suffering more than 3,000 casualties.
Consequently, the generals dared not speak of attacking again.
Yànqiú then rested and recuperated his soldiers,
using the taxes levied from his three prefectures (sānzhōu) for their upkeep.
He used all his salary income to provide beef and wine
and held banquets with his generals every day.
After a long time,
food ran out within Dū’s city.
Dū first expelled over ten thousand of his own citizens
and frequently conspired with Tūněi to break the siege and escape,
but they failed.
Dū’s general Mǎ Ràngnéng (馬讓能) surrendered the city,
and Dū burned himself to death.
Yàn Qiú, as a general, possessed strategic acumen,
and excelled at caring for his soldiers.
When he attacked Tūněi,
he had already transformed defeat into merit,
and although all the generals wished to pursue the victory and capture Dū,
Yàn Qiú returned;
he alone did not move forward,
and ultimately wore them out by prolonged resistance.
Since the third year of Tiānchéng (928), the fourth month, when Dū rebelled,
it was not until the second month of the following year that he finally subdued them.
In the army, he had never executed a single person.
For the merit of defeating Dū,
he was appointed Tiānpíngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
He was then transferred to Pínglú,
and progressively promoted until he concurrently held the position of Zhōngshū Lìng.
He died that year,
at the age of sixty-two,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi.
Ān Chóngbà
Ān Chóngbà,
was a man from Yúnzhōu.
Initially, he served Jìn Wáng (*Zhuāngzōng*) together with Míngzōng.
Chóngbà incurred an offense and fled to Liáng,
and later fled to Shǔ.
Chóngbà was cunning, deceitful, and highly resourceful,
and adept at serving others.
Shǔ Wáng Jiàn appointed him as a trusted general.
When Wáng Yăn succeeded (to the throne),
being young,
the eunuch Wáng Chéngxiū held power.
Chóngbà deeply befriended Chéngxiū to secure his own position.
At the end of the Liáng dynasty,
Shǔ captured the three prefectures of Qín, Chéng, and Jiē from Lǐ Màozhēn.
Chóngbà advised Chéngxiū to request to govern Qínzhōu.
Yăn made Chéngxiū the Jiédùshǐ,
and Chóngbà served as his deputy.
Chóngbà and Chéngxiū collected many flowers and trees from Qínzhōu and presented them to Yăn,
and invited Yăn to tour the east.
When the troops of Táng Wèi Wáng attacked Shǔ,
Chéngxiū was terrified,
and asked Chóngbà about it.
Chóngbà said:
“Jiànmén is the most dangerous natural pass in the world.
Even if they have elite troops,
they cannot pass through.
However, since you have received the state’s favor,
when you hear of danger, you cannot fail to respond.
I request to travel west with you.”
Chéngxiū had always deeply trusted him,
and thought this was correct.
Chéngxiū organized his troops and was about to depart.
The people of Qín came to see him off,
and drank farewell wine outside the city.
When the drinking ceased,
Chéngxiū started on the road.
Chóngbà stood before Chéngxiū's horse,
and took his leave, saying:
“Qín and Lǒng cannot be lost.
I wish to remain and guard them for you.”
Chéngxiū had already started on his way,
and could do nothing about it.
After the Táng army defeated Shǔ,
Chóngbà also surrendered the three prefectures of Qín, Chéng, and Jiē to Táng.
Míngzōng appointed him as Làngzhōu Tuánliànshǐ.
He was later dismissed and made Zuǒ Wèi Dàjiāngjūn.
After a long time,
he was appointed Kuāngguójūn Jiédùshǐ.
During the time of Fèi Dì,
he served as Jīngzhào Yǐn and Xījīng Liúshǒu,
was transferred to govern Dàtóng,
then relieved due to illness and returned,
and died in Lùzhōu.
Wáng Jiànlì
Wáng Jiànlì,
was a man from Yúshè in Liáozhōu.
When Táng Míngzōng was Dàizhōu Cìshǐ,
he appointed Jiànlì as a Yúhòujiāng.
Zhuāngzōng once sent a female attendant to Dàizhōu to sacrifice at a tomb.
The female attendant harassed the people of Dài.
Jiànlì arrested and flogged her.
Zhuāngzōng was furious,
and wanted to kill Jiànlì.
Míngzōng sheltered him so that he escaped death.
When Míngzōng rebelled starting from Wèi,
and approached the capital,
Empress Cáo and Consort Wáng Shūfēi were both in Chángshān.
Jiànlì killed the Chángshān Surveillance Commissioner and the defending troops,
and Míngzōng's family members were thus unharmed.
Because of this, Míngzōng loved him even more.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he appointed him Chéngdéjūn Jiédù Fùshǐ.
Later, he was appointed Jiédùshǐ, Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi, and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Jiànlì had always been in disagreement with Ān Chónghuǐ.
Wáng Dū of Dìngzhōu had dual loyalties,
and frequently sent letters to Jiànlì,
proposing they become sworn brothers.
Chónghuǐ learned of this and reported it.
Míngzōng did not wish to harm Jiànlì,
and urgently recalled him to the capital.
When Jiànlì came in for an audience,
he also spoke extensively about Chónghuǐ's faults.
Míngzōng became very angry,
and wanted to immediately dismiss Chónghuǐ.
The officials and attendants around him subtly persuaded Míngzōng to desist,
and he stopped.
Nevertheless, he ultimately made Jiànlì Yòu Púshè, Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì, and Controller of the Three Bureaus (*Pàn Sānsī Shì*).
After serving for more than a year,
he claimed that he was illiterate,
and requested to be relieved of the Controller of the Three Bureaus position.
Míngzōng did not grant permission.
After a long while,
Jiànlì claimed to be ill.
Míngzōng laughed and said:
“It is common for people who feign illness to truly contract one.”
He was then sent out as Pínglú Jiédùshǐ,
and later transferred to Shàngdǎng.
Jiànlì was depressed and dissatisfied,
and eventually requested to resign his post.
He was then permitted to retire with the title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
Jiànlì repeatedly requested an imperial audience,
but it was not granted.
He then went personally to the capital,
and forced his way to the rear building to see Míngzōng.
He wept and said that he was innocent,
but had been rejected by Chónghuǐ.
Míngzōng said:
“You served as a Jiédùshǐ,
but did not conduct good deeds.
Was it only Chónghuǐ who slandered you!”
He bestowed upon him tea and medicine, and sent him away.
When Fèi Dì ascended the throne,
he was again appointed Tiānpíngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
During the time of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he was transferred to govern Pínglú.
In the fifth year of Tiānfú (940), he came to the court for an audience.
Gāozǔ comforted him, saying:
“Elder brother of thirty years ago,
you need not perform the full ritual bow!”
He was granted a sedan chair to enter the court,
was provided two eunuchs to support him up to the palace hall,
and the audience and banquet were extremely gracious.
He was then transferred to Zhāoyì,
and bestowed with a jade axe and Shǔ horses.
He was successively enfeoffed as Hán Wáng.
Jiànlì loved to kill people.
In his later years, he finally became devoted to the Buddhist Law,
and forbade the killing of living beings.
Wherever he went, the people became slightly more settled.
He died at the age of seventy,
and was posthumously granted Shàngshū Lìng.
His son, Shǒu'ēn,
entered service through hereditary privilege,
and gradually rose to various positions as Wèi Jiāngjūn.
After Jiànlì died,
his family lived in Lù.
Shǒu'ēn received leave from the capital to return home,
just as the Qìdān destroyed Jìn.
Zhāng Cóng'ēn, the Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ, was related to Shǒu'ēn by marriage.
He therefore appointed Shǒu'ēn as acting Xúnjiǎnshǐ,
to guard Lùzhōu,
while Cóng'ēn went to seek an audience with the Qìdān.
After Cóng'ēn departed,
Shǒu'ēn immediately plundered Cóng'ēn's family wealth,
and surrendered Lùzhōu to Hàn.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Shǒu'ēn as Zhāoyìjūn Jiédùshǐ,
transferred him to govern Jìngnán and serve as Xījīng Liúshǒu,
and added the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Shǒu'ēn’s nature was greedy and vulgar;
the people suffered greatly because of him.
At that time, Zhōu Tàizǔ, serving as Shūmìshǐ, led the armies of Bái Wénkē and others to the west to suppress the Three Rebellions.
When he returned and passed through Luòyáng,
Shǒu'ēn, viewing himself as a powerful minister,
rode out in a sedan chair to welcome him.
Tàizǔ was enraged.
On that very day, using the practice of drawing lots (*Tóuzi*), he commanded Wénkē to replace Shǒu'ēn as Liúshǒu.
Meanwhile, Shǒu'ēn was just arriving at the residence for the audience,
sitting in the guest room awaiting the meeting.
Then an official rode quickly to report that the new Liúshǒu had already started handling affairs at the headquarters.
Shǒu'ēn was greatly shocked,
not knowing what to do.
He was subsequently dismissed and left,
serving as an honorary official in the capital.
Later, when Yǐn Dì killed Shǐ Hóngzhào and others,
he summoned the officials to the hall to console and instruct them.
The officials were terrified,
and none dared to speak.
Only Shǒu'ēn stepped forward and replied:
“Your Majesty has only just woken up from sleep.”
All who heard this drew back their necks (in fear).
During the Xiǎndé period,
he served as Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn until his death.
Alas!
Dàodé Rén Yì (Virtue, Morality, Benevolence, and Righteousness)
are the means by which governance is established,
and laws, institutions, and disciplinary codes (făzhì gāngjì)
are also the means by which they are maintained.
In kingdoms that have been in turmoil or fallen since antiquity,
they must first destroy their laws and institutions before chaos follows.
Chaos and destruction multiply each other,
until all disciplinary codes (gāngjì) are utterly lost,
then they must reach the extreme of great chaos before they can turn back.
This is the natural course of events,
and the era of the Wǔdài (Five Dynasties) exemplified this.
If Wén Kē and Shǒu Ēn were both officials holding positions as both generals and chancellors,
they were great ministers of Hàn,
yet Zhōu Tàizǔ easily replaced them with a mere junior official (or deputy head) of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ tóuzi),
like rotating garrison soldiers.
At that time,
Tàizǔ and Hàn had not yet had any initial discord,
and his ambition to disregard the sovereign and rebel against his superior
should not yet have germinated in his heart.
Yet, why were his actions
like this?
It is likely because such acts had become customary,
so they were executed simply amidst his momentary pleasure, anger, or commands,
and Wén Kē dared not disobey,
nor could Shǒu Ēn refuse.
Since Tàizǔ handled it without hesitation,
and the ruler and ministers of the Hàn court also ignored it and did not question it,
the fact that high and low were peacefully unconcerned
— was this not because the laws, institutions, and disciplinary codes (făzhì gāngjì) of the court had been destroyed and chaos had multiplied for
a long time,
culminating and reaching this extreme point?
Therefore, those who plan well for the realm
dare not ignore the minute details,
but constantly prevent gradual decline.
Should one not be cautious!
Kāng Fú
Kāng Fú,
was a man from Yùzhōu,
whose family served as military officers for generations.
Fú served the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng) as a deputy general (piānjiàng) based on his skill in archery and horsemanship.
Zhuāngzōng once said:
"My family makes a living from sheep and horses,
and Fú's appearance resembles a Hú person (barbarian) and he is robust;
the Hú are suited for sheep and horses."
So, he ordered Fú to manage the horses in Xiāngzhōu,
serving as the director of the minor stud farm (xiǎo mǎfāng shǐ).
After a year, the horses greatly multiplied and thrived.
When Míngzōng rebelled from Wèi
and his troops passed through Xiāngzhōu,
Fú surrendered with two thousand horses from the minor stud farm.
Míngzōng's military strength thus grew greater.
When Míngzōng entered the capital and ascended the throne,
he appointed him Director of Fēilóng (Fēilóng Shǐ),
and concurrently Governor (Cìshǐ) of Cízhōu and Surveillance Commissioner (Bīngmǎ Dūjiān) of Xiāngzhōu.
He followed Liú Xùn to suppress Jīngnán,
but returned without merit.
Fú had no other special talents as a general,
but he was skilled in various Róng (barbarian) languages.
Míngzōng often summoned him into the private palace chambers (biàndiàn)
to consult him on foreign affairs.
Fú would always reply using Fān (barbarian) language.
The Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ), Ān Zhònghuǐ, disliked him,
and often warned Fú, saying:
"Do not carelessly submit memorials,
or you shall be executed!"
Fú was afraid,
and requested an outside post.
When Hán Zhū of Língwǔ died,
his younger brother Chéng was installed,
but the deputy general Lǐ Cóngbīn raised a rebellion.
Chéng submitted a memorial requesting the court appoint a commander.
Zhònghuǐ believed that Língwǔ was deep within barbarian territory,
and those appointed as commanders often met with disaster,
so he appointed Fú as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Liángzhōu,
and Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Shuòfāng and Héxī Command.
Fú entered to see Míngzōng,
and weeping, said he had been forced out by Zhònghuǐ.
Míngzōng summoned Zhònghuǐ to change Fú's assignment to another command.
Zhònghuǐ said:
"Fú had no achievements when he was a Governor (Cìshǐ), yet he was given the insignia of a Military Governor (jiémáo).
How dare he be selective!"
Míngzōng was angry,
and said to Fú:
"Zhònghuǐ sending you
was not my intention.
I shall dispatch troops to guard you;
you need not worry."
He then ordered General Niú Zhìróu to escort Fú with troops.
When they reached Fāngqú,
the Qiāng barbarians indeed came out to ambush Fú.
Fú used his troops to attack and drive them off.
When they reached Qīnggāng Xiá,
they encountered snow.
Fú climbed a mountain and saw smoke and fire in the valleys,
where there were several thousand tents of the Tǔfān (Tibetans),
who were unaware of Fú's arrival.
Fú divided his troops into three columns,
and attacked them by surprise.
The Tǔfān were greatly terrified,
abandoned their wagons and tents, and fled.
Fú slaughtered almost all of them,
and captured a great amount of raw jade (yùpǔ), patterned silk (língjǐn), sheep, and horses.
From this, his prestige greatly increased.
Fú stayed in Língwǔ for three years.
Every year was prosperous and bountiful.
He possessed a thousand teams of horses,
and the Fānyí (barbarians) feared and submitted to him.
Those who reported on affairs suspected Fú had treacherous intentions,
and Zhònghuǐ also said that Fú would surely betray the court.
Míngzōng sent someone to tell Fú:
"What have I failed to give you that you wish to betray me!"
Fú replied:
"I have received profound national grace,
and would rather die than harbor disloyalty."
He then begged to return to the capital,
but was not permitted.
Fú submitted his memorial a second time,
and immediately followed it by arriving himself.
Míngzōng did not punish him,
but transferred his command to Zhāngyì.
He successively commanded Jìngnàn and Xióngwǔ,
and served as the Commissioner of the Western Front (Xīmiàn Dūbùshǔ).
During the time of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he was transferred to command Hézhōng.
After his term, he returned
and died in the capital (Jīngshī).
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī),
and given the posthumous name Wǔ'ān.
Fú’s family origins were of the Yídí (Eastern and Northern Barbarians).
The Yídí valued the Shātuó,
so he always claimed to be of the Shātuó tribe.
Fú once fell ill and lay in his inner chamber.
His subordinates entered to ask about his health
and saw his brocade quilt (jǐnqīn).
They looked at each other and secretly joked, saying:
"The brocade quilt is spoiled (làn xī)!"
Fú heard this
and angrily said:
"I am of the Shātuó tribe!
How dare you call me Xī (Xi people)?
Those who heard this laughed at him.
Guō Yánlǔ
Guō Yánlǔ,
was a man from Miánshàng, Qìnzhōu.
His father, Ráo,
served Jìn with valor and bravery,
established military merits numerous times,
and served as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Qìnzhōu for nine years.
His governance was benevolent and beloved,
and the people of the prefecture missed him.
Yánlǔ became a general by excelling with the spear (shuò),
and was successively promoted to Grand Military Commissioner of Shénwǔ (Shénwǔ Dū Zhī Bīngmǎ Shǐ).
When Zhū Shǒuyīn rebelled,
he participated in the attack on Biànzhōu.
For the merit of being the first to ascend the walls, he was made Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry of Biànzhōu (Biànzhōu Mǎbùjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ),
and was successively promoted to Governor (Cìshǐ) of Fùzhōu.
Yánlǔ sighed and said:
"My late father governed Qìnzhōu for nine years,
and the people miss him even now.
Since I am now fortunate enough to become a Governor (Cìshǐ),
how dare I forget the aspiration of my late father!"
Because of this, he further encouraged himself through integrity and fairness,
and the people greatly depended on him.
When his term was completed,
the people of the prefecture requested him to stay,
but this was not granted.
They all blocked the road, grasping at him and crying out.
During the Tiānfú era,
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dānzhōu,
and died in office.
At that time,
Governors (Cìshǐ) were all appointed based on military merit.
Those who reported on affairs frequently criticized this,
saying that when the realm was tumultuous
and the people's strength was exhausted,
it was inappropriate to assign Governors (Cìshǐ) positions to military men (wǔfū),
who would rely on their achievements to indulge their subordinates,
and cause considerable harm.
Yet Yánlǔ and his father
were notably famous specifically for their good governance.
Alas!
How could the people of the Five Dynasties endure such a plight?
Above, they were pressed by urgent military levies and taxes;
below, they were distressed by harsh exactions and oppression.
Since Zhuāngzōng's reign,
the practice of regional commanders offering tribute slightly increased,
and by the time of Jìn, it became countless.
The
"Tiān Dū" (Adding to the Capital)
and
"Zhù Guó" (Assisting the State)
items
were often counted in thousands.
As for coming to court, being sent on missions, buying feasts, or atoning for sins,
none did not involve offering tribute.
And if meritorious officials and great generals
unluckily died,
their descendants would often use their family wealth to seek the position of Cìshǐ (Prefect),
with those offering more receiving large, desirable prefectures.
Indeed, since even the Son of Heaven conducted affairs through bribery,
how could their people possibly endure it?
At such a time,
honest and incorruptible officials like Yánlǔ
were truly rare and precious!
Collation Notes
Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter 35: Huá Wēnqí
Huá Wēnqí, courtesy name Dérùn,
was a native of Xiàyì in Sòngzhōu.
His family was originally farmers.
Wēnqí was seven chì tall.
In his youth, he followed Huáng Cháo as a bandit.
When Cháo captured Cháng'ān,
he appointed Wēnqí as Gòngfèngguān Dūzhī (Director of the Court Attendants).
When Cháo was defeated,
Wēnqí fled to Huázhōu.
Considering his imposing appearance,
and fearing he would not be tolerated,
he threw himself into the Báimǎ Hé (White Horse River).
He drifted for dozens of lǐ,
but did not die,
and people by the river pulled him out.
He then tried to hang himself in a mulberry grove,
but the mulberry branches always broke.
So he went to Zuòxiàn.
There, a farmer saw him and said,
"Your appearance is dignified and imposing;
you are no ordinary man!"
And so, he hid him in his home.
More than a year later,
he heard that Zhū Yù, the Cìshǐ of Púzhōu, was recruiting soldiers,
so he went to join him.
Later, he served Liáng,
and became the Kāidào Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander for Opening Roads).
Through repeated military achievements, he became the Cìshǐ of Jiàng and Dì two prefectures.
Dìzhōu suffered from river floods.
Wēnqí moved the prefecture to Xīnzhōu to avoid them,
and the people benefited from this.
He successively served in Qí and Jìn two prefectures.
When Zhuāngzōng attacked Jìnzhōu,
he could not conquer it for over a month.
Liáng Mòdì praised Wēnqí for his good defense,
and elevated Jìnzhōu to Dìngchāng Jūn (Dingchang Military Prefecture),
appointing Wēnqí as Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor).
He was impeached for kidnapping a woman from his prefecture,
sued by her husband,
and dismissed as Jīnwǔwèi Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards) and Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn (Commander of the Left Dragon Martial Guard).
When Zhū Yǒuqīan rebelled in Hézhōng and submitted to Jìn,
Mòdì appointed Wēnqí as Rúzhōu Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner of Ruzhou) and Hézhōng Xíngyíng Páizhènshǐ (Field Commander of the Battle Formations in Hezhong).
He was later promoted to Yàozhōu Guānchá Liúhòu (Acting Military Commissioner of Yaozhou).
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
he met Wēnqí
and said,
"This is the one who defended Píngyáng for Liáng!"
He praised him,
and then converted Yàozhōu into Shùnyì Jūn (Shunyi Military Prefecture),
appointing Wēnqí as Jiédùshǐ,
and later transferring him to govern Xióngwǔ.
During Míngzōng's reign, he came to court
and wished to remain at the palace,
so he was appointed Zuǒ Xiāowèi Shàngjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Left Swift Guard).
More than a year later,
Míngzōng said to the Pí Mìshǐ (Privy Councilor) Ān Chónghuǐ,
"Wēnqí is an old veteran;
he should be given an important command."
Chónghuǐ, not wanting to grant it,
replied that there were no vacancies.
Another day,
Míngzōng brought up the topic again,
and Chónghuǐ said,
"The only one who can be replaced is the Pí Mìshǐ."
Míngzōng said,
"That can be done."
Chónghuǐ could not answer.
Wēnqí, hearing this, was afraid,
and feigned illness, not appearing for several months.
Eventually, he was appointed Zhènguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Zhenguo).
During Fèidì's reign,
he retired as Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince).
He died in Tiānfú first year (936 AD),
and was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Tàifù (Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince).
Cháng Cóngjiǎn
Cháng Cóngjiǎn
was a native of Chénzhōu.
His family was originally butchers of sheep.
Cóngjiǎn left to serve Jìn as a military officer.
He could single-handedly fight several men
and was skilled with a spear.
When Zhuāngzōng campaigned to besiege cities,
Cóngjiǎn often led the assault with ladders.
Zhuāngzōng admired his bravery
and promoted him repeatedly based on his merits to Bùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Infantry).
When Zhuāngzōng's army was arrayed against the Liáng army,
a Liáng soldier carrying a large banner moved in and out of the ranks.
Zhuāngzōng climbed a high mound and saw him,
sighing,
"That fierce warrior,
who can capture him for me?"
Cóngjiǎn immediately stepped forward and requested to go.
Zhuāngzōng cherished him
and did not permit it.
Cóngjiǎn secretly led a few horsemen,
galloped into the Liáng army,
seized their banner, and returned.
The whole army cheered.
Zhuāngzōng lauded his bravery
and bestowed generous rewards upon him.
Cóngjiǎn once suffered a wound from a stray arrow;
the arrowhead lodged in his thigh bone.
He ordered a craftsman to remove it.
The craftsman had no suitable medicine
and intended to chisel the bone,
which everyone thought was impossible.
Cóngjiǎn immediately urged him to chisel.
The craftsman hesitated and could not bring himself to do it.
Cóngjiǎn scolded him to chisel quickly.
Those watching around him
all seemed unable to bear the pain,
but Cóngjiǎn remained composed, speaking and laughing as usual.
However, his personality was violent and difficult to control,
and Zhuāngzōng often bent the law to accommodate him.
He was successively promoted to Càizhōu Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner of Caizhou).
During Míngzōng's reign,
he successively served as Fángyùshǐ for Lín, Rǔ, Fén, and Jīn four prefectures.
Míngzōng once warned him,
"Wealth and status are precious,
but you cannot preserve them.
The late emperor could pardon you;
I fear I cannot."
Cóngjiǎn's nature was incorrigible,
and Míngzōng did not blame him further.
When Fèidì raised an army in Fèngxiáng,
Cóngjiǎn and the forces from various garrisons besieged him.
Eventually, the besieging army collapsed,
and Cóngjiǎn fled east,
where he was captured.
Fèidì reproached him for not surrendering.
Cóngjiǎn said,
"One who serves a lord dares not have two hearts."
Fèidì released him
and appointed him Yǐngzhōu Tuánliànshǐ (Militia Commissioner of Yingzhou).
When Jìn Gāozǔ raised an army in Tàiyuán,
Fèidì prepared to personally lead an expedition
and summoned Cóngjiǎn as Zhāotǎo Fùshǐ (Deputy Commander of the Expeditionary Force).
He followed him to Héyáng
and was appointed Héyáng Sānchéng Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the Three Cities of Heyang).
When Fèidì returned to Luòyáng,
Cóngjiǎn immediately surrendered to Jìn.
He successively governed Zhōngwǔ and Wǔníng,
and then entered court as Zuǒ Jīnwúwèi Shàngjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Left Imperial Guards).
He died at the age of sixty-five
and was posthumously granted Tàishī (Grand Preceptor).
Cóngjiǎn was fond of eating human flesh,
and wherever he went, he would secretly capture children from the common people to eat.
A rich man in Xǔzhōu had a jade belt that Cóngjiǎn coveted but could not obtain.
He sent two soldiers to break into his house at night, kill him, and take it.
The soldiers scaled the wall at night
and hid among the trees.
They saw the couple treating each other with great respect.
The two soldiers sighed,
"Our lord wishes to seize their treasure
and harm these people.
We will surely not escape retribution."
Thereupon, they leapt out and informed the couple,
telling them to quickly present the belt.
Then they scaled the wall and left,
and their whereabouts were unknown.
Zhāng Jūn (younger brother Jiān)
Zhāng Yún,
was a native of Hǎizhōu.
Generations of his family had engaged in trade, relying on wealth.
*Yún* served *Shī Pǔ* (a *Jiédùshǐ*) as the Prefect (*Cìshǐ*) of Sùzhōu.
When the Liáng forces attacked *Pǔ* and took Sùzhōu,
they captured *Yún*.
Liking his eloquence and wisdom,
they appointed him as a Visiting General (*Kèjiàng*) of the Four Garrisons and Commander (*Jūnshǐ*) of the Permanent Directorate,
and he was successively promoted to Commissioner of Palace Affairs (*Xuānhuīshǐ*).
*Mòdì* (the Last Emperor) divided Xiāngzhōu, Chánzhōu, and Wèizhōu into the Zhāodé Army,
and appointed *Yún* as the *Jiédùshǐ*.
Because of this, the Wèibó Army revolted and defected to Jìn.
When the King of Jìn attacked Xiāngzhōu,
*Yún* abandoned the city and fled.
Later, he was appointed *Jiédùshǐ* of the Yǒngpíng Army.
When Liáng fell, he served Táng,
retaining the position of Prefect of Jīngzhào (*Jīngzhàoyǐn*).
Following *Guō Chóngtāo* in the campaign against Shǔ,
he served as the Pacification Commissioner (*Ānfǔshǐ*) for the Two Rivers of Jiànnán.
After Shǔ was pacified,
he was appointed Prefect of Hénán (*Hénányǐn*),
and later transferred to govern Xīngyuán.
*Yún* once fell ill
and refused to see his generals and officials.
The Deputy Commissioner (*Fùshǐ*), *Fú Yànlín*, entered to inquire about his health,
but *Yún* again refused to see him.
*Yànlín* suspected *Yún* had already died,
and immediately requested the release of the tally and seal.
*Yún* became enraged,
ordered his attendants to arrest *Yànlín* and imprison him,
reporting that he was rebelling.
*Míngzōng* knew that *Yànlín* had no intent to rebel,
summoned *Yànlín*, and released him.
He feigned transferring *Yún* to be the Resident General (*Liúshǒu*) of the Western Capital,
but secretly instructed the gatekeepers not to let him in.
When *Yún* arrived at Cháng’ān, he was unable to enter,
so he went to the capital court,
where he was appointed General-in-Chief of the Left Cavalry Guard (*Zuǒ Xiāowèi Shàng Jiāngjūn*).
*Yún*'s younger brother, *Jiān*,
when *Yún* was Prefect of Jīngzhào (*Jīngzhàoyǐn*),
was appointed Commander of the Internal Guard (*Yánèi Zhǐhuīshǐ*) and Commissioner for the Establishment of Agricultural Colonies at the Sānbái Canal (*Sānbáiqú Yíngtián Zhìzhìshǐ*).
When *Yún* campaigned west against Shǔ,
he left *Jiān* to guard Jīngzhào.
After Shǔ was pacified,
Wèi Wáng (*Wáng Jìjí*) led his army back,
reaching Xīngpíng.
Meanwhile, *Míngzōng* had risen up in Wèi,
and the capital was in great chaos.
*Jiān* then cut the floating bridge at Xiányáng to obstruct *Jìjí*.
*Jìjí* consequently committed suicide.
Earlier,
*Yún* had replaced *Kāng Huái'yīng* as *Jiédùshǐ* of the Yǒngpíng Army.
When *Huái'yīng* died,
*Yún* immediately plundered his family's wealth.
He also dug up the grounds of the former Táng palace
and found a large amount of gold and jade.
There was a brigade general named *Hóumòchén Wēi*,
who had previously participated with *Wēn Tāo* in excavating the various Táng mausoleums
and had divided the treasures.
*Yún* used a pretext to kill *Wēi* and seize the wealth.
When Wèi Wáng (*Wáng Jìjí*) died south of the Wèi River,
*Jiān* took all of his travel baggage.
When *Wáng Yǎn* traveled from Shǔ to Qínchuān,
*Zhuāngzōng* sent the eunuch *Xiàng Yánsì* to kill him.
*Yánsì* consequently took all of *Yǎn*'s treasures from Shǔ.
When *Míngzōng* ascended the throne,
he immediately sent men to arrest and execute the eunuch.
*Yánsì* fled,
and the Shǔ treasures were subsequently seized by *Jiān*.
Because of this, the wealth of both brothers reached enormous sums.
However, *Yún* was personally fond of giving charity,
and relying on his own wealth,
he did not engage in extortion wherever he was stationed.
The people benefited from this and lived in peace.
*Jiān*, however, was addicted to wine, greedy, and vulgar,
serving successively as Prefect (*Cìshǐ*) of Yízhōu and Mìzhōu.
During the reign of Jìn Chūdì,
he was sent as a general to buy horses from the Huíhú (Uighurs).
He was implicated because the horses were not up to standard,
and the relevant officials investigated the valuation.
*Jiān*, due to his vulgar nature,
died of vexation.
*Yún* resided in Luòyáng,
hoarding his wealth,
satisfying himself with wine, women, music, and courtesans for more than ten years.
People called him
"Earthly Immortal."
In the second year of Tiānfú (937 CE),
he moved his residence to Cháng’ān.
That year,
*Zhāng Cóngbīn* raised a rebellion
and entered Luòyáng,
which *Yún* thus escaped.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Shàoshī*).
Alas,
many revolts occurred during the Five Dynasties,
but I find the case involving *Míngzōng* particularly difficult to state!
It only concluded after Wèi Wáng (*Wáng Jìjí*) perished.
*Zhuāngzōng* was assassinated.
*Jìjí*, as the emperor's eldest son, held massive military power
but died outside the capital and failed to be established as emperor.
This was a major event,
yet previous historians did not record the reason why this happened.
The life or death of *Jìjí*
did not directly benefit or harm *Zhāng Jiān*.
Why did *Jiān* obstruct him and prevent him from moving east?
Was he perhaps ordered by someone to do this?
However, *Míngzōng* felt deeply indebted to *Fú Yànchāo*
but did not treat *Jiān* generously.
This is another point of suspicion.
Otherwise,
did ministers who favored disorder
merely respond immediately upon hearing the news?
If *Jiān* had not cut the floating bridge,
and *Jìjí* had been able to proceed east with his army,
*Míngzōng* might not have been able to establish himself.
Thus, the death of *Jìjí*,
due to *Jiān*'s obstruction,
was certainly not a minor consequence!
Yáng Yànxún
*Yáng Yànxún*, courtesy name Chéngzhāng,
was a native of Báodǐng in Hézhōng.
In his youth, he served *Wáng Shīfàn* of Qīngzhōu.
*Shīfàn* loved learning
and amassed ten thousand scrolls of books,
placing *Yànxún* in charge of them.
*Yànxún* was clever and perceptive,
and thus gained trust and favor.
*Shīfàn* surrendered to Liáng,
but was later killed.
Having nowhere to go,
*Yànxún* went to Wèi
and served *Yáng Shīhòu* as a Visiting General (*Kèjiàng*).
Wèibó revolted against Liáng and joined Jìn.
*Yànxún* consequently stayed and served Jìn.
When *Zhuāngzōng* destroyed Liáng,
he appointed *Yànxún* as Deputy Commissioner of Introductions (*Yǐnjìn Fùshǐ*),
sending him on missions to Wú and Shǔ,
where he always executed imperial directives successfully.
He successively held the posts of Prefect (*Cìshǐ*) of Dézhōu and General of the Feathered Forest (*Yǔlín Jiāngjūn*).
When Jìn Gāozǔ governed Tàiyuán,
Fèidì (the Deposed Emperor) suspected he had disloyal intentions,
and selected the most prudent and sincere generals to assist him.
Thus, *Yànxún* was appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Tàiyuán (*Tàiyuán Jiédù Fùshǐ*).
Afterwards, Jìn Gāozǔ was transferred due to suspicion.
Wishing to defy the order and not move,
he asked *Yànxún*.
*Yànxún* dared not speak plainly,
so he said:
"Can the strength of Tàiyuán
resist Táng?
Your Grace must consider this carefully!"
Since *Gāozǔ*'s intention to rebel was already decided,
*Yànxún* dared not speak further.
*Gāozǔ*'s attendants, believing *Yànxún* held differing views,
wanted to kill him.
*Gāozǔ* hastily stopped them,
saying:
"This one Deputy Commissioner
I shall personally protect."
Thus, *Yànxún* was spared.
At this time,
*Gāozǔ* sought aid from the Qìdān.
Yēlǜ Déguāng of Qìdān established *Gāozǔ* in Tàiyuán
and sent troops to escort him to the river.
*Yànxún* served as Commissioner of Palace Affairs (*Xuānhuīshǐ*),
frequently traveling back and forth to the barbarian encampment.
*Déguāng* also admired his character.
The following year,
he was appointed *Jiédùshǐ* of the Gǎndé Army,
then returned to the court as Commissioner of Palace Affairs (*Xuānhuīshǐ*),
and was later appointed *Jiédùshǐ* of the Ānguó Army.
In the seventh year of Tiānfú (942 CE),
he was transferred to govern Zhènguó.
He encountered a year of great famine,
but his administration showed compassion and favor.
Due to suffering from wind-stroke (*bìng fēng*), he was dismissed and made General-in-Chief of the Right Metropolitan Guard (*Yòu Jīnwúwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn*).
He died at the age of seventy-four,
and was posthumously granted the title Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Tàishī*).
Lǐ Zhōu
*Lǐ Zhōu*, courtesy name Tōnglǐ,
was a native of Nèiqiū in Xíngzhōu,
and a descendant of *Lǐ Bǎozhēn*, the Táng *Jiédùshǐ* of the Zhāoyì Army.
His father, *Jǔ*,
did not serve as an official during the times of worldly turmoil,
and once said to *Zhōu*:
"Hándān is a place of military action.
Since the world is currently unstable,
you should join the military to restore our family."
at age sixteen became the commander for capturing bandits in Nèiqiū.
He was renowned for his bravery.
At that time,
the armies of Liáng and Jìn contended for Shāndōng.
Bandits swarmed the roads,
and travelers had to be protected by soldiers.
Lú Yuè, a man from Nèiqiū, was about to move his family to Tàiyuán.
He stayed at an inn,
hesitating and daring not to proceed.
Zhōu pitied him,
and escorted him to Xīshān (Western Mountains).
A bandit shot at Yuè from the woods,
hitting his horse.
Zhōu shouted loudly, saying:
"I am here!
Who dares to do such a thing?"
The bandits heard his voice,
and said:
"This is Lǐ Zhōu!"
They consequently scattered and fled.
Zhōu escorted Yuè all the way to Tàiyuán.
Yuè said to him:
"When I was young, I studied astronomy and calendrics,
and I am skilled at physiognomy.
Your face is square, your nose bridge high,
your eyebrows and eyes clear and penetrating,
and you are seven *chǐ* tall.
You are truly destined to be a general or a chancellor.
I have observed the celestial phenomena,
and Jìn is certainly destined to possess the realm.
You ought to stay and serve Jìn,
in order to achieve wealth and honor."
Zhōu declined, citing his mother's age, and returned home.
At that time,
Liáng sent Gě Cóngzhōu to attack and take Xíng and Míng [Prefectures].
The Prince of Jìn fortified his troops at Qīngshān Kǒu (Qīngshān Pass).
Zhōu did not know where to go,
so he recalled Yuè's words.
He went to Qīngshān and pledged allegiance to Jìn.
The Prince of Jìn appointed Zhōu as the Commander of the Wànshèng Huángtóu Army.
Afterwards, he frequently achieved merit while following campaigns and expeditions.
During the battle of Bǎixiāng,
he was the first to scale the walls,
and was promoted to Kuāngbà Commander,
defending Yángliú.
As a general, Zhōu was extremely brave.
Regarding his deployment of troops,
he was skilled at defense,
and capable of sharing hardship and ease with his soldiers.
The Liáng army attacked Zhōu.
Zhōu held the defense firmly.
After a long time,
Zhōu heard of his mother’s death and rushed home.
Zhuāngzōng sent another general to replace Zhōu in defense.
The position was almost broken by the Liáng army.
Zhuāngzōng immediately recalled Zhōu to return and defend it,
and thus it was saved from defeat.
Later, the Liáng people, having already defeated Déshèng,
proceeded eastward to attack Yángliú.
They used huge battleships to block the river,
cutting off Jìn's supply routes and reinforcements.
Zhōu sent a messenger to rush to Zhuāngzōng requesting aid,
requesting him to march a hundred *lǐ* a day to relieve the emergency.
Zhuāngzōng laughed and said:
"Zhōu is defending for me,
why worry!"
He marched sixty *lǐ* a day,
traveling and hunting simultaneously,
saying:
"Zhōu is not an opponent that the Liáng generals can match."
By the time he arrived,
Zhōu had already been without provisions for three days.
Zhuāngzōng gathered huge piles of firewood, poured oil on them,
and followed the current to launch fire, burning the Liáng ships.
The Liáng army withdrew.
Zhuāngzōng saw Zhōu and comforted him, saying:
"If not for you, sir,
the generals would have been captured by Liáng!"
He successively served as the Prefect of Xiāng and Cài Prefectures.
During Míngzōng's reign,
he was appointed Jìedùshǐ (Military Governor) of the Wǔxìn Army,
and transferred to govern Jìngnán,
successively governing the four circuits of Wǔníng, Ānyuǎn, Yǒngxīng, and Xuānwǔ.
Wherever he went, he implemented many benevolent policies.
During Jìn Gāozǔ's reign,
he again governed Jìngnán,
and was later relieved and returned.
When Emperor Chū visited Chányuān,
he appointed Zhōu to remain and guard Dōngjīng (Eastern Capital).
Upon returning,
he was appointed Kāifēng Yǐn (Magistrate of Kāifēng).
He died at the age of seventy-four,
and was posthumously granted the title Tàishī (Grand Tutor).
Liú Chǔràng
Liú Chǔràng, courtesy name Déqiān,
was a man from Cāngzhōu.
In his youth, he was a close subordinate of Zhāng Wànjìn.
When Wànjìn entered Liáng service,
and became the Jìedùshǐ of the Tàiníng Army,
he appointed Chǔràng as a Staff General (*Yájiàng*).
Wànjìn rebelled against Liáng and submitted to Jìn.
Liáng sent Liú Xún to attack him.
Wànjìn sent Chǔràng to request aid from Jìn.
The Prince of Jìn was currently engaged in a stalemate with Liáng,
and could not dispatch troops.
Chǔràng then cut off his ear at the military gate and pleaded, saying:
"The reason Wànjìn is being besieged
is because he defected to Jìn.
How can you disregard his distress?
If troops are not dispatched,
I request permission to die!"
The Prince of Jìn admired his spirit,
and said:
"A righteous scholar!"
And for his sake, he dispatched troops.
Before they crossed the river,
Wànjìn was defeated by the Liáng army.
Chǔràng consequently remained and served Jìn.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Minister of the Guest Hall (*Kèshěng Shǐ*).
He frequently traveled on missions to the four quarters,
