and his reports were often pleasing to the emperor.
During the Tiānchéng era,
he was promoted to Ushering Commissioner (*Yǐnjìn Shǐ*).
He was repeatedly promoted to Grand General of the Left Xiāowèi Guard.
During the reign of Emperor Fèi,
the troops in Wèizhōu mutinied,
driving out their commander Liú Yánhào.
Fàn Yánguāng was sent to suppress the revolt,
and Chǔràng was appointed Chief Transport Commissioner for Héběi.
When Jìn Gāozǔ was established,
he successively served as Commissioner of the South Court of the Privy Council (*Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ*).
When Fàn Yánguāng rebelled,
Gāozǔ appointed Yáng Guāngyuǎn as the Chief Suppression Commissioner,
and Chǔràng participated in his military affairs.
Soon after, the Deputy Suppression Commissioner Zhāng Cóngbīn rebelled in Héyáng.
Chǔràng detached troops and defeated Cóngbīn.
Upon returning,
he attacked Yè with Guāngyuǎn.
They were unable to take it for over a year.
Subsequently, Yánguāng intended to surrender but hesitated.
Chǔràng entered the city,
reasoned with him regarding misfortune and fortune,
and Yánguāng then came out and surrendered.
According to Táng statutes,
the Privy Council Commissioner (*Shūmì Shǐ*) was usually held by eunuchs.
Since Liáng employed Jìng Xiáng and Lǐ Zhèn,
and until Zhuāngzōng began employing military officials,
their power greatly outweighed that of the generals and chancellors.
During Gāozǔ's reign,
the chancellors Sāng Wéihàn and Lǐ Sōng concurrently held the position of Shūmì Shǐ.
Chǔràng and the other eunuchs were inwardly displeased by this.
When Guāngyuǎn was suppressing Yánguāng,
since the heavy forces of Jìn were under his command,
his actions were often arrogant and willful.
The requests he made,
Gāozǔ frequently restrained and suppressed.
Chǔràng spoke to Guāngyuǎn, saying:
"This is not the Emperor's intention;
it is all Wéihàn, Sōng, and others who are jealous of you, sir!"
Guāngyuǎn became greatly enraged.
When the campaign ceased,
Guāngyuǎn met Gāozǔ,
and complained that Wéihàn and the others had thwarted him.
Gāozǔ had no choice,
but to dismiss Wéihàn and the others,
appointing Chǔràng as Shūmì Shǐ.
While Chǔràng was in office,
everything he presented
was often not satisfactory to the emperor.
Chǔràng then went into mourning for his mother's death.
Gāozǔ subsequently did not appoint a Shūmì Shǐ again,
handing the commissioner's seal to the Secretariat and abolishing the post.
Chǔràng observed the mourning period for a full year.
He was restored to office as Jìedùshǐ of the Zhāngdé Army and Grand General of the Right Jīnwǔ Guard.
He died of illness,
at the age of sixty-three,
and was repeatedly granted the posthumous title Tàishī.
Lǐ Chéngyuē
Lǐ Chéngyuē, courtesy name Déjiǎn,
was a man from Jìmén.
In his youth, he served Liú Rěngōng,
becoming the Circuit Inspector of the Eight Armies North of the Mountains (*Shānhòu Bājūn Xúnjiǎn Shǐ*),
commanding two thousand cavalry soldiers.
When Rěngōng was imprisoned by his son Shǒuguāng,
Chéngyuē fled to Jìn with his cavalry.
The Prince of Jìn appointed him Kuāngbà Commander.
He followed in the destruction of Jiázhài (Enclosed Stockade),
and fought at Línqīng.
For his merits, he was successively promoted to Prefect of Míng and Fén Prefectures, and Training Commissioner of Yǐng Prefecture.
era,
Máo Zhāng, the Jiédùshǐ of Bīnzhōu, harbored rebellious intentions.
Míngzōng appointed Chéngyuē as the Deputy Jiédùshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
sending him there to monitor Zhāng’s movements.
Chéngyuē met Zhāng
and advised him regarding the consequences (of fortune and misfortune).
Later, Míngzōng dispatched someone to replace Zhāng,
and Zhāng immediately accepted the replacement.
Míngzōng was greatly pleased
and immediately appointed Chéngyuē as the Jiédùshǐ of Qiánnán.
Chéngyuē governed the various barbarian tribes with kindness and trust,
encouraged the people in farming and sericulture,
and established schools.
After residing there for several years,
when it was time for his replacement,
the people of Qiánnán went to the capital requesting that he remain,
and he was permitted to stay for one more year.
He was summoned and made the Zuǒ Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn,
then changed to Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn,
appointed as the Jiédùshǐ of the Zhāoyì Army,
and later returned to being Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn.
In the Tiānfú second year (937),
he was promoted to Zuǒ Xiāowèi Shàng Jiāngjūn.
He repeatedly requested retirement,
but it was not granted.
He died at the age of seventy-five,
and was posthumously granted the rank of Tàizǐ Tàishī.
Zhāng Xīchóng
Zhāng Xīchóng, courtesy name Défēng,
was a man from Jì in Yōuzhōu.
When young, he loved learning
and was well-versed in the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū.
Since Liú Shǒuguāng disliked scholars,
Xīchóng therefore served in the military as a General of the Vanguard,
leading troops to guard Píngzhōu.
After that, the Qìdān attacked and captured Píngzhōu,
seized Xīchóng,
and, knowing he was a scholar,
made him the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ of the Lúlóng Army.
During Míngzōng's time,
Lú Wénjìn defected and returned from Píngzhōu,
so the Qìdān subsequently appointed Xīchóng to replace Wénjìn as the Jiédùshǐ of Píngzhōu,
dispatching their own trusted general with three hundred cavalrymen to supervise him.
After dwelling there for more than a year,
the barbarian general liked his personality,
and the supervisory troops gradually became lax.
Xīchóng then plotted with his subordinates to flee south.
His subordinates all said that the troops were numerous,
and they could not all flee together,
fearing they would not escape;
thus, they advised Xīchóng to leave alone.
Xīchóng said:
"The barbarian troops guarding us are merely three hundred cavalrymen.
If we kill their general,
their soldiers will certainly scatter and flee.
Furthermore, Píngzhōu is over a thousand *lǐ* from the barbarian encampment.
Should they hear of the disorder and call for troops,
we will already be within the Hàn borders!"
Everyone agreed this was good.
They first dug a pit,
lining it with quicklime.
The next day,
the barbarian general came to pay respects to Xīchóng.
Xīchóng gave him wine to drink,
killed him in the pit,
and the soldiers all dispersed and fled.
Xīchóng led his subordinates
and returned south with twenty thousand people.
Míngzōng praised him
and appointed him Fángyùshǐ of Rǔzhōu.
He was promoted to Jiédùshǐ of Língwǔ.
Língzhōu bordered the Róngdí tribes;
the soldiers guarding the routes for military supplies
constantly suffered from plundering raids.
Xīchóng therefore established military colonies,
taught the troops to farm,
so the army had sufficient provisions,
thereby saving on transport and supply costs.
Míngzōng issued an imperial decree praising him.
Xīchóng managed and provided for his officers and troops
and gathered in the Yi tribes.
From the Huíhú to Guā and Shā, all dispatched envoys to submit tribute.
After residing there for four years,
he submitted a memorial requesting return to the interior,
and was transferred to govern Bīnníng.
When Jìn Gāozǔ entered the capital and ascended the throne,
Xīchóng was again appointed Jiédùshǐ of Língwǔ.
Xīchóng sighed and said:
"I am destined to grow old and die on the frontier;
is this not fate?"
Xīchóng served his mother with extreme filial piety;
morning and evening when his mother ate,
he would always attend and stand beside her,
daring to withdraw only after the meal was cleared.
As a general, he had no fondness for music or women.
He enjoyed reading
and was somewhat knowledgeable about astronomy and the calendar.
In the Tiānfú third year (938),
the Moon occulted the large star in the Hyades.
Xīchóng sighed and said:
"The large star in the Hyades
represents a frontier general.
Perhaps I am the one meant by this!"
He died in the first month of the following year,
and was posthumously granted the rank of Tàishī.
He had a son named Rénqiān.
Xiānglǐ Jīn
Xiānglǐ Jīn, courtesy name Fèngjīn,
was a man from Bīngzhōu.
He was courageous and fierce,
yet was able to humble himself and respect scholars/officers.
He served the King of Jìn as a Commander in the Five Camps Army.
In the battles between Liáng and Jìn at Bǎixiāng and Húliǔ,
he achieved merit in all,
and was promoted to Huángjiǎ Zhǐhuīshǐ.
During the Tóngguāng
era, he was appointed Cìshǐ of Xīnzhōu.
At that time,
all the prefectures employed military men,
many of whom used their personal followers to manage the fields and government business,
exploiting public and private resources
for their own personal profit.
Jīn alone forbade his followers from interfering in affairs,
generously providing for their maintenance,
allowing them only to manage household matters.
He was promoted to Fángyùshǐ of Lǒngzhōu.
When the Deposed Emperor raised troops in Fèngxiáng,
he hastily sent proclamations to the neighboring regions,
but none of the neighbors had yet responded.
Only Jīn first dispatched his Judicial Assistant, Xuē Wényù, to meet the Deposed Emperor,
traveling back and forth to strategize.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he rewarded him for his service,
appointing him Jiédùshǐ of the Bǎoyì Army.
When Jìn Gāozǔ rebelled in Tàiyuán,
the Deposed Emperor made Jīn the Commander-in-Chief of the Infantry on All Four Sides of Tàiyuán.
When Gāozǔ entered and took the throne,
Jīn was transferred to govern Jiànxióng,
and was later dismissed to the rank of Shàng Jiāngjūn.
He died in the Tiānfú fifth year (940),
and was posthumously granted the rank of Tàishī.
Zhāng Tíngyùn
Zhāng Tíngyùn,
was a man from Xiāngyì in Kāifēng.
When young, he was a soldier in the Xuānwǔ Army;
he left to serve Jìn,
gradually advancing through the military ranks.
He often followed Zhuāngzōng on campaigns,
being the first to climb the ramparts and fighting bravely.
His body was covered in battle wounds.
Zhuāngzōng admired his bravery
and made him the Commander-in-Chief of the Infantry for the Twenty Huángjiǎ Divisions of the Imperial Guard, and Inspector of the Three Cities of Wèibó.
At that time,
Zhuāngzōng was in Wèi,
accompanied by Empress Liú.
Clan Liú often allowed her subordinates to harass people and commit illegal acts,
and no one dared to speak out.
Tíngyùn consistently arrested and executed them.
When Lǐ Jìtāo rebelled in Lùzhōu,
Zhuāngzōng sent Míngzōng as the Commander of Pacification,
Yuán Xíngqīn as the Commander-in-Chief of Deployment,
and Tíngyùn as the Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry,
leading the troops as the vanguard.
When Tíngyùn arrived at Lù
(it was already dusk),
he immediately led over a hundred soldiers to cross the moat and scale the wall.
The city defenders could not resist,
and Lùzhōu was subsequently defeated.
The next morning,
Míngzōng and Xíngqīn arrived later.
Míngzōng was quite displeased in his heart concerning this.

Due to his merit, Tíngyùn was promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Yǔlín Guard, Cìshǐ of the three prefectures of Shēn, Huái, and Yí, Fángyù Tuánliànshǐ of the four prefectures of Jīn, Yǐng, Lǒng, and Jiàng, and Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn.
During the Kāiyùn
era, he died of illness.
Tíngyùn was a military man;
he recognized no more than a few characters,
yet throughout his life he respected literati.
He once followed Míngzōng in defeating Liáng’s Yùnzhōu,
capturing the Judicial Assistant Zhào Fèng.
Tíngyùn said to him:
"Looking at your appearance, you must be a scholar;
you may hold nothing back."
Fèng answered truthfully,
and Tíngyùn promptly recommended him to Míngzōng.
Later, Fèng achieved the high position of Chancellor.
He repeatedly recommended Tíngyùn to Ān Chónghuǐ,
and Chónghuǐ mentioned it frequently.
Míngzōng, however, still resented Tíngyùn for the gap created when Lù was defeated
and ultimately held a grudge against him.
Thus, Tíngyùn was never granted a high administrative post.
Tíngyùn was habitually upright and frugal;
having governed seven prefectures,
on the day of his death,
his family had no savings left.
Mǎ Quánjié
, courtesy name Dàyǎ,
was a man from Yuánchéng, Dàmíng.
During the Tóngguāng reign period of the Táng
Dynasty, Quánjié served as the Commander for Taking Captives (Zhuōshēng Zhīhuīshǐ).
When Zhào Zàilǐ rebelled at Yèdū,
he appointed Quánjié as the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry (Mǎbùjūn Zhīhuīshǐ).
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he successively held the positions of Prefect (Cìshǐ) of the four prefectures of Bó, Dān, Yǐng, and Yí, and Defender (Fángyùshǐ) of Jīn Prefecture.
During the reign of Fèidì,
the Shǔ people attacked Jīn Prefecture.
The prefectural troops numbered only a few hundred.
Quánjié dispersed his family wealth
and, with the soldiers, held the position firmly.
When the Shǔ people withdrew,
Fèidì summoned Quánjié
and appointed him Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu) of Cāng Prefecture.
When Jìn Gāozǔ entered and established the dynasty,
he immediately appointed Quánjié as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Hénghǎi Army,
transferred him to garrison Ānyuǎn,
replacing Lǐ Jīnquán.
Jīnquán rebelled and submitted to Lǐ Yán.
Gāozǔ dispatched thirty thousand troops
and ordered Quánjié and Ān Shěnhuī to suppress him.
Jīnquán fled south.
Lǐ Yán's general Lǐ Chéngyù defended Ān Prefecture.
Quánjié fought Chéngyù south of the prefecture,
severely defeating Chéngyù,
beheading three thousand men,
and capturing over a thousand alive.
Chéngyù abandoned the city and departed.
Shěnhuī pursued him to Yúnmèng,
where he captured Chéngyù and two thousand of his soldiers.
Quánjié executed fifteen hundred men
and sent the remaining soldiers, along with Chéngyù, to the capital (Jīngshī).
Chéngyù said to Quánjié
: "The wealth I plundered in the city
, measured in millions,
has all been taken by the General.
When I see the Son of Heaven,
I must report this before accepting execution."
Quánjié was frightened.
Consequently, he killed Chéngyù.
Gāozǔ ignored the matter and did not question him,
transferring Quánjié to govern Zhāoyì.
He was then transferred to Ānguó.
He followed Dù Chóngwēi in suppressing Ān Chóngróng,
and due to his merits, was transferred to govern Yìwǔ.
Since Chūdì fell out with the Qìdān,
Quánjié was never absent from military service.
In the first year of Kāiyùn,
he served as the Overall Supervisor of Mobilized Camps (Xíngyíng Dū Yúhòu).
The Qìdān and the main Jìn army faced each other between Chán and Wèi.
Quánjié separately attacked Báituán City,
captured it,
and took seven hundred captives.
He conquered Tài Prefecture,
captured two thousand people,
and received the surrender of its defending general, Jìn Tíngqiān.
In the fourth month,
the Qìdān were defeated at Qīchéng
and withdrew their troops, heading north along separate routes.
Quánjié defeated them at Dìngfēng
and captured their general, Ān Huī.
In the seventh month,
he was transferred to become the Governor (Yǐn) of Guǎngjìn,
serving as the Acting Administrator (Liúshǒu) of Yèdū.
In the tenth month,
Dù Chóngwēi was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Pacification (Zhāotǎoshǐ),
with Quánjié as his deputy.
They heavily defeated the Qìdān at Wèicūn.
Quánjié was humble and careful in character,
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
Whenever he handled administrative or judicial decisions,
he invariably asked what the law prescribed.
Initially,
when transferred to Guǎngjìn,
he passed through Yuánchéng,
wore a white scholar's robe (báilán), and paid respects to his county magistrate.
The people of the region considered this an honor.
In the second year of Kāiyùn,
he was transferred to garrison Shùnguó,
but died before arriving,
at the age of fifty-five.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Counselor (Zhōngshū Lìng).
Huángfǔ Yù
Huángfǔ Yù
was a man from Zhēndìng, Chángshān.
He was known for his bravery and strength,
and had a curly beard and was skilled in archery.
In his youth, he followed Táng Míngzōng on campaigns.
He served the Táng and became Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Wǔshèng Army.
Wherever he went, he was harsh and tyrannical,
focusing on executions and levies.
Many of his guests and subordinates resigned their posts and fled
to avoid his harm.
During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he successively governed the four garrisons: Yìwǔ, Zhāoyì, Jiànxióng, and Héyáng.
He was then relieved of duty and appointed Commander of the Shénwǔ Army (Tǒngjūn).
When the Qìdān invaded
and captured Bèi Prefecture,
Chūdì appointed Gāo Xíngzhōu as the Overall Commander of Mobilized Camps on the Northern Front (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Dū Bùshǔ),
and appointed Yù as the Commander of the Right Wing Cavalry Formation (Mǎjūn Yòuxiāng Páizhènshǐ).
At that time,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn in Qīng Prefecture occupied the city and rebelled.
Chūdì then sent Lǐ Shǒuzhēn and Yù to divide their forces and guard Yùn Prefecture.
Yù and the others reached Mǎjiādù,
just as the Qìdān were about to cross the river to assist Guāngyuǎn.
Yù and the others attacked and defeated them.
For his merit, he was appointed Military Commissioner of the Yìchéng Army (Yìchéngjūn Jiédùshǐ) and Overall Commander of Cavalry (Mǎjūn Dū Zhīhuīshǐ).
In the second year of Kāiyùn,
the Qìdān raided Xīshān,
sending their vanguard Zhào Yánshòu to besiege Zhèn Prefecture.
Dù Chóngwēi dared not sortie to fight.
Yánshòu divided his troops and plundered widely,
attacking and capturing nine counties including Luánchéng and Báixiāng,
reaching Xíng Prefecture in the south.
It was New Year's Eve (Suìchú) at that time.
Chūdì drank excessively with his close officials,
fell ill,
and could not lead the expedition.

He therefore sent Zhāng Cóng'ēn, the Supervising Commissioner of Mobilized Camps on the Northern Front (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Dūjiān), to join Mǎ Quánjié, Ān Shěnqí, and Yù, among others, to resist the enemy.
Cóng'ēn and his colleagues arrived at Xiāng Prefecture
and deployed their army south of the Ānyáng River.
They sent Yù and Mùróng Yànchāo to lead several thousand cavalry forward to observe the barbarians.
Yù crossed the Zhāng River
and encountered tens of thousands of barbarians.
They fought continuously for over ten *lǐ*
until reaching Yúlín.
They were surrounded by the barbarians.
Yù's horse was hit by an arrow and fell.
He obtained the horse of his servant, Dù Zhīmǐn,
and mounted it to continue fighting.
Zhīmǐn was captured by the barbarians.
Yù said to Yànchāo
: "Zhīmǐn
is a man of righteousness;
how can we allow him to be lost!"
Immediately, he and Yànchāo spurred their horses into the enemy lines,
rescued him, and returned.
The barbarian troops fought Yù
from noon (wǔ) until the middle of the afternoon (wèi),
dispersing and re-forming,
sending out more troops,
and their momentum was extremely strong.
Yù cautioned Yànchāo, saying
: "Given the situation today,
it is either fight or flee.
Fighting still offers a chance of survival,
but fleeing means death.
Since death is certain,
to fight to the death
would still be sufficient to repay the nation."
Zhāng Cóng'ēn and the various generals were concerned that Yù had not sent back a report after observing the barbarians,
and all believed that Yù had already fallen captive.
Soon after, a galloping rider reported that Yù was surrounded.
Ān Shěnqí prepared to lead troops to reinforce him.
Cóng'ēn suspected the messenger was deceiving them
and did not want to go.
Shěnqí said
: "Success or failure depends on Heaven.
We should share the danger together.
Even if the barbarians do not come south,
if we lose Huángfǔ Yù,
what face will we have left to see the Son of Heaven!"
He immediately led his cavalry across the river.
All the armies followed him north,
engaging the barbarians for over ten *lǐ*.
When the barbarians saw the relief forces arriving,
they immediately dispersed and departed.
Yù, Shěnqí, and the others collected their troops and moved south.
The Qìdān also all withdrew north.
At this time,
the Qìdān troops had penetrated deeply,
and both men and horses were exhausted.
When they returned,
the various Jìn generals failed to pursue them.
Instead, Cóng'ēn led Yù and the others to retreat and hold Líyáng,
allowing the barbarians to escape.
In the winter of the third year,
Dù Chóngwēi was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Pacification (Dū Zhāotǎoshǐ),
and Yù was appointed Overall Commander of the Right Wing Cavalry (Mǎjūn Yòuxiāng Dū Zhīhuīshǐ),
garrisoned at Zhōngdù.
Chóngwēi had already secretly sent overtures of submission to the Qìdān
and concealed soldiers within his tent.
He summoned all the generals to sit in ranks
and announced his surrender to the barbarians.
Yù and the other generals were astonished and unable to respond.
Chóngwēi presented the memorial of surrender.
Yù and the others bowed their heads and signed their names in sequence.
He immediately ordered the troops to remove their armor and surrender.
The Qìdān sent Yù and Zhāng Yànzé to enter the capital first.
When Yù traveled to Píngjí,
he cut his own throat and died.
Alas!
When the Liáng fell and Jìng Xiáng died,
he could not be considered one who died for his integrity;
when the Jìn fell and Huángfǔ Yù died,
he could not be considered one who died for his mission.
How could I have no opinion on this?
In the usurpation of the Táng by the Liáng,
Xiáng's schemes accounted for the majority of the actions.
Is it acceptable
for a son to assist his father in murdering his grandfather?
That he was not executed by axe and sword
was a fortunate escape.
When the Jìn army surrendered to the Khitans,
the officers and soldiers initially did not know;
when they were ordered to lay down their armor,
the sound of weeping shook the heavens.
Therefore, was surrendering truly their desire?
Had Yù bravely rolled up his sleeves and stood up,
killing Zhòngwēi right there,
even if he unfortunately could not have avoided being harmed,
he would still have attained a worthy death.
Would his righteousness and valor not have been outstanding (liè liè) then?
Since he bowed his head and submitted to the command,
and together with others caused the ruin of his own nation,
even his death cannot redeem it.
How could he be worthy of esteem?
The gentleman, when judging others,
sometimes extends leniency (shù)
and sometimes demands perfection (bèi).
Leniency
thus broadens the path for correcting faults and making a fresh start;
perfection is difficult to attain;
because it is difficult to attain,
it is therefore highly valuable.
However, knowing what can be forgiven
and what is truly estimable,
is that not yet more difficult?
Ān Yànwēi
Ān Yànwēi, courtesy name Guójùn,
was a man from Guō County in Dài Prefecture.
In his youth, he served as a soldier under the banner of Táng Míngzōng.
Yànwēi was skilled in archery
and quite knowledgeable about military strategy.
When Míngzōng was stationed in Tiānpíng, Xuānwǔ, and Chéngdé,
Yànwēi often served as a staff general,
and was trusted for his prudence and integrity.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
Prince Cóngróng was stationed in Yè,
and Yànwēi was made Commander of the Hùshèng forces.
When Cóngróng was appointed to manage the Six Armies,
Yànwēi was promoted to Commander of the Pěngshèng forces
and concurrently held the title of Military Governor (jiédùshǐ) of Níngguó Command.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Yànwēi was appointed Commissioner of the Northern Capital (Běijīng liúshǒu),
and later transferred to govern Guīdé.
At this time,
the Yellow River breached its banks at Huá Prefecture,
and Yànwēi was ordered to repair the breach.
Yànwēi used his private money to recruit people to repair the dike.
He was promoted to Commissioner of the Western Capital (Xījīng liúshǒu).
He encountered a great famine that year.
Yànwēi distributed aid and pacified the starving populace.
When people violated the law,
he generally treated them with leniency,
and the starving people loved him
and could not bear to leave.
Upon mourning the death of his mother,
his grief and debilitation exceeded the prescribed limits.
When the Last Emperor (Chū Dì) broke the alliance with the Qìdān,
Yànwēi was appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Expeditionary Army (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Fù Dūtǒng).
Yànwēi dedicated all his family assets to support the military expenditure.
He died of illness in the capital.
Yànwēi belonged to the same clan as Consort Dowager Ān.
The Last Emperor served him, treating him as an uncle (jiù),
but Yànwēi never spoke of this relationship.
When he died,
the Consort Dowager personally mourned him,
and only then did people realize they were of the same clan.
At that time, his cautiousness and gravity were praised even more.
Lǐ Qióng
Lǐ Qióng
was a man from Rá’ān, Cāng Prefecture.
In his youth, he was a cavalry general,
serving with Jìn Gāozǔ under the banner of Táng Míngzōng.
In the second year of Tóngguāng (924),
the Qìdān invaded the frontier.
Míngzōng went out to Zhuō Prefecture
and met the Qìdān.
He fought but did not win.
The various generals gradually withdrew,
but Jìn Gāozǔ alone continued fighting.
The Qìdān increasingly gathered and encircled him.
Qióng grabbed Gāozǔ’s clothes and fled with him.
When they reached the Liú-Lǐ River, the pursuing troops were about to catch up.
Qióng swam across the water and reached the south bank first.
When Gāozǔ reached the middle of the river,
his horse stumbled.
Qióng used a long spear to pull him out
and then gave Gāozǔ the horse he was riding.
He walked alongside, protecting him,
and after running for more than ten *lǐ*,
they managed to escape.
When Míngzōng carried out his military coup in Wèi and marched south,
Qióng followed Gāozǔ with three hundred horsemen, rushing ahead to Biàn Prefecture.
When Gāozǔ became Military Governor of Bǎoyì Command,
he made Qióng Commander of his personal guard unit.
When Gāozǔ established his dynasty,
he appointed Qióng Superintendent of the Imperial Guard (Hùshèng Dōu Yúhòu),
and bestowed upon him much gold and silk,
but did not grant him high office or rank.
Qióng also felt frustrated.
After a long time,
he was appointed Prefect of Xiāng and Shēn Prefectures.
During the reign of the Last Emperor,
he served as Prefect of Dì Prefecture.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn rebelled
and sent a letter inviting Qióng to join him.
Qióng refused and did not accept.
He was promoted to Commissioner of Militias (Tuánliànshǐ) of Míng Prefecture,
and later became Commander of the Right Wing of the Imperial Guard (Hùshèng Yòuxiāng Dōu Zhǐhuīshǐ).
When the Jìn fell,
and the Qìdān entered the capital,
Qióng was made Prefect of Wēi Prefecture.
Traveling to his post, when he reached Zhèng Prefecture,
he encountered bandits and was killed.
Liú Jǐngyán
Liú Jǐngyán
was a man from Yán Prefecture.
His family was habitually wealthy,
and he was able to use his resources to associate with heroes and talented men.
He served Gāo Wànjīn as a personal subordinate (bùqǔ),
and later became Prefect of Dān Prefecture.
When Jìn Gāozǔ raised an army in Tàiyuán,
the deposed Táng emperor mobilized one soldier out of every seven households as a volunteer force (yìbīng).
Yáng Hànzhāng, the Military Governor of Yán Prefecture, mobilized local people to proceed to the capital.
Before they set off,
Jǐngyán sent someone to incite their anger.
The volunteers rioted,
killed Hànzhāng,
and welcomed Jǐngyán to take charge as Acting Governor (liúhòu).
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he immediately appointed Jǐngyán Military Governor.
Jǐngyán's subordinate, Xióng Jiǎo,
was a man of great intelligence.
He secretly perceived that Jǐngyán was arrogant and difficult to control,
and feared that he harbored disloyal intentions.
He wished to fool him with profit,
so he spoke to Jǐngyán,
saying that border regions could not be safe for long,
and set forth a strategy for protecting his reputation and enjoying profits.
He said that Bīn and Jīng had much good farmland,
and the profit was a hundredfold;
it would be advisable to purchase much land there to profit and enrich himself.
Jǐngyán believed him.
After a year,
his gains were substantial.
Jǐngyán sent Jiǎo to the capital for an audience.
Jiǎo then said:
"Jǐngyán should not remain on the frontier;
he should be relocated to the interior."
Thus, Jǐngyán was transferred to Bīn Prefecture.
Jiǎo entered the court and was appointed Supervising Censor (bǔquē).
Jǐngyán was then transferred again to govern Bǎoyì.
He had not resided there long
when he was again transferred to Wǔshèng.
Jǐngyán then realized that Jiǎo had betrayed him.
Consequently, he falsely reported that Jiǎo had concealed his jade belt.
Jiǎo was consequently demoted to Magistrate of Shàngjīn, Shāng Prefecture.
Fearing that Jǐngyán would have him harmed on the road,
Jiǎo fled
and hid in the mountains.
In the third year of Kāiyùn (946),
Jǐngyán was dismissed from Wǔshèng
and retired with the title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàishī),
residing in Huà Prefecture.
When the Qìdān invaded the capital,
Zhōu Mì was appointed to govern Yán Prefecture.
Jǐngyán then returned to his ancestral home.
However, the people of the prefecture drove Mì away
and installed Gāo Yǔnquán.
Yǔnquán's wife, née Liú,
was Jǐngyán's granddaughter.
Jǐngyán possessed abundant good fields, grand mansions, and many servants.
The Dǎngxiàng Sī family kept livestock near the suburbs
and were particularly wealthy and powerful.
Jǐngyán associated with them,
which made Yǔnquán quite uneasy.
When Yǔnquán's wife returned home to visit her family during festivals,
Jǐngyán said to her:
"Gāo Lang is merely a county magistrate,
yet he holds this prefecture.
Can this be maintained?"
Yǔnquán disliked him even more,
and also coveted his fields and residence.
Thus, he falsely accused him of rebellion and killed him.
He was over eighty years old.
In the summer of the fifth year of Tiānfú (940 CE),
Gāozǔ used Mǎ Quánjié to replace Jīn Quán.
Since Rénzhǎo's two sons desired to travel to the capital to appeal their father's wrongful death,
Hàn Róng became greatly fearful.
He deceived Jīn Quán, saying:
"The Son of Heaven previously summoned Hàn Róng,
but you violated the edict by not sending him.
Regarding Rénzhǎo's death,
his two sons are about to appeal to the court.
Now, using Quánjié to replace you,
this means summoning you to face trial."
Jīn Quán believed this,
and consequently rebelled,
sending his submission to Lǐ Jǐng.
Gāozǔ dispatched thirty thousand troops, entrusting them to Quánjié to suppress the rebellion.
Lǐ Jǐng sent his general Lǐ Chéngyù into Ānzhōu.
Jīn Quán then fled south.
Traveling until he reached Wèi Chuān,
he stretched his neck, looked north,
wept, and departed.
Lǐ Jǐng appointed Jīn Quán as Tiānwēi Commander.
During the time of Hàn Yǐndì,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn rebelled at Hézhōng
and begged Lǐ Jǐng for troops.
Jīn Quán, who was Lǐ Jǐng's Rùnzhōu Jiédùshǐ,
went out to Shùyáng with Zhā Wénhuī and others.
All of Lǐ Jǐng's generals were eager to attack and seize territory,
but Jīn Quán alone believed that the distance was too great to reach the objective,
and that it was impossible to proceed.
Thus, they stopped.
Afterwards, he was never employed again,
and his end is unknown.
Yáng Sīquán.
Yáng Sīquán
was a native of Xīnpíng, Bīnzhōu.
He served the Liáng dynasty as Controller of the Cranes, Right First Army Commissioner.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed the Liáng,
he was made Jiāmǎ Area Commander.
During the reign of Míngzōng,
Qín Wáng Cóngróng was made Hédōng Jiédùshǐ.
Féng Yūn was appointed as his deputy,
and Sīquán was appointed Běijīng Infantry Area Commander to assist and protect him.
Cóngróng was habitually arrogant,
and many of his actions were unlawful.
At this time,
Sòng Wáng Cónghòu was the Prefect of Hénán.
Cónghòu was young,
modest, respectful, and fond of rites.
Míngzōng secretly sent people to casually speak of Cónghòu's virtues,
in order to admonish and encourage Cóngróng.
Cóngróng was displeased
and told Sīquán:
"The whole empire esteems Hénán (Cónghòu) but not me.
I am about to be deposed.
What should be done?"
Sīquán replied:
"You have armed soldiers,
and Sīquán is here,
why worry!"
He then advised Cóngróng to recruit fearless warriors and increase the amount of sharp weaponry as preparation.
Féng Yūn worried about this
and reported the matter.
Míngzōng summoned Sīquán back to the capital.
Due to Cóngróng's relationship,
he did not hold him accountable.
Later, he became Right Yǔlín Area Commander,
leading troops to garrison Xīngyuán.
Lù Wáng Cóngkē rebelled at Fèngxiáng.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo of Xīngyuán gathered the forces of the various circuits to suppress the rebels.
The troops of the various circuits surrounded Fèngxiáng.
Sīquán attacked the west side of the city,
and Yánwèi Commander Yǐn Huī attacked the east side,
breaking both outer fortress walls.
Cóngkē ascended the city wall and called out to the outside troops,
declaring that he was not a rebel.
His words were extremely sorrowful,
and all the outside soldiers who heard him felt pity.
However, Qiánzhāo urged the battle very aggressively,
and the soldiers turned their weapons and chased Qiánzhāo away.
Sīquán then called out to his men, saying:
"Lù Wáng is truly our lord!"
He immediately led his soldiers into the city and surrendered.
Huī, hearing that Sīquán had already surrendered,
also waved his command flag, ordering his army to remove their armor.
Due to this, the troops of all the circuits scattered.
Sīquán and Huī entered to see Cóngkē.
Sīquán stepped forward and said:
"Your servant loyally supports Your Highness.
If Your Highness succeeds,
I request that you do not appoint me as a Fángyù (Defense) or Tuánliàn (Militia) Commissioner."
He then took a piece of paper from his bosom and said:
"I wish you would record my name as proof."
Cóngkē immediately wrote:
"Appointable as Bīnníng Jiédùshǐ."
When Fèidì entered and took the throne,
Sīquán was appointed Jìngnán Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Later, he became Right Lóngwǔ Commander and Left Guard Supreme General.
In the eighth year of Tiānfú (943 CE),
he died in the capital,
and was posthumously granted the title Tàifù.
Yǐn Huī.
Yǐn Huī
was a native of Dàmíng, Wèizhōu.
He followed Fèidì when he entered Luòyáng.
Jìn Gāozǔ came to pay court,
and met Huī on the road.
Huī was still the Yánwèi Commander at that time.
Relying on his merit from surrendering first,
he would not yield to Gāozǔ;
he remained mounted, held his whip across his body, and saluted him.
Gāozǔ was enraged
and told Fèidì that Huī should not be given a major circuit.
Consequently, he was appointed Yìngzhōu Jiédùshǐ.
When Jìn Gāozǔ entered and took the throne,
Huī was dismissed and made Right Guard Grand General.
Fàn Yánguāng rebelled
and sent a letter inviting Huī to join.
Huī became afraid
and fled to Huáinán,
where he was killed by others.
He had a son named Xūn.
Wáng Hóngzhì.
Wáng Hóngzhì—
it is unknown what family he was originally from.
During the reign of Táng Míngzōng,
he served as the Prefect of Hé and Jiē prefectures, Right Qiānniú Guard General, and Wèizhōu Prefect.
Lù Wáng Cóngkē rebelled at Fèngxiáng
and led his troops east to Shǎn.
Mǐndì was afraid
and fled during the night with over a hundred riders.
When he reached seven or eight *lǐ* east of Wèizhōu,
he encountered Jìn Gāozǔ, who was coming to pay court in the capital.
The attendants shouting warnings in the vanguard did not step aside.
Mǐndì sent his staff to reprimand them.
They replied:
"This is Shí Jìngtáng, the Chéngdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ."
Mǐndì immediately dismounted and wept loudly,
saying to Jìngtáng:
"Lù Wáng has rebelled,
Kāng Yìchéng and others have all betrayed me.
I have nowhere to rely upon.
The Eldest Princess advised me to meet you on the road."
Gāozǔ said:
"Wáng Hóngzhì, the Prefect of Wèizhōu,
is a veteran general
and is moreover well-informed about current affairs.
Please rely on him for planning."
He immediately rode ahead quickly to see Hóngzhì and said:
"The Sovereign is in great danger.
I am a relative by marriage.
How can we ensure his safety?"
Hóngzhì said:
"The Son of Heaven fleeing from rebels
has happened since ancient times.
However, are the generals and high ministers following him?"
He replied:
"No."
"Are the state treasures, the imperial chariot, and the ritual objects following him?"
He replied:
"No."
Hóngzhì sighed and said:
"As the saying goes, when a great tree is about to topple,
it cannot be held up by a single rope.
Now, the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots
flees with a hundred riders,
yet not a single general or high minister follows him.
Thus, the allegiance of the people is known.
Even if you wish to restore him,
how can it be achieved!"
He then followed Gāozǔ and went up to pay respects at the relay station.
Gāozǔ then reported Hóngzhì's words to Mǐndì.
The Commanders of the Bow and Arrow Depot, Shā Shǒuróng and Bēn Hóng, advanced and said to Gāozǔ:
"The Sovereign
is Míngzōng's beloved son,
and you
are his beloved son-in-law.
You cannot repay the state at this time,
but instead ask where the ministers and state treasures are.
Are you also helping the rebels?"
They then drew their waist knives and stabbed Gāozǔ.
Chén Huī, Gāozǔ's personal general, defended him.
Shǒuróng and Huī died fighting,
and Hóng Jìn also slit his own throat.
Gāozǔ then killed all the troops following the Emperor,
leaving the Emperor alone at the relay station, and departed.
His eldest son, Xíngcóng,
was the Cìshǐ of Dézhōu.
After being dismissed,
he remained in the capital,
and was also executed.
His second son, Xíngqiān,
was Yǔnquán's father-in-law.
He made a memorial claiming he was not a son of the Liú clan,
and thus was spared execution.
Collators' Notes
Miscellaneous Biographies 36: Lú Wénjìn
Lú Wénjìn, courtesy name Dàyòng,
was from Fànyáng.
He served as a cavalry general under Liú Shǒuguāng.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng attacked Fànyáng,
Wénjìn surrendered early and was appointed Cìshǐ of Shòuzhōu.
Zhuāngzōng assigned him to his younger brother, Cúnjǔ.
Cúnjǔ was the Tuánliànshǐ of Xīnzhōu,
commanding the Eight Armies from Shānhòu.
When Zhuāngzōng and Liú Xún were stalemated at Shēn,
he summoned Cúnjǔ to lead his troops to attack Xún.
Cúnjǔ recruited several thousand elite soldiers from Shānhòu
and levied horses from the people.
The people exchanged ten oxen for one horse.
Everyone in Shānhòu resented this,
and the soldiers were also unwilling to march south.
When they reached Qígōu Pass,
they gathered and plotted a rebellion.
Wénjìn had a daughter who was young and beautiful.
Cúnjǔ sought her as a concubine.
Wénjìn, being a subordinate general, dared not refuse,
and although he agreed,
he always felt resentful.
Consequently, he joined the rebellious army, killed Cúnjǔ, and revolted.
He attacked Xīnzhōu,
but failed.
He attacked Wǔzhōu,
but also failed.
He then fled to the Qìdān,
who made him guard Píngzhōu.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
Wénjìn led tens of thousands of people from Píngzhōu to return to the Táng.
Míngzōng was extremely pleased to receive him
and appointed him Jiéduànshǐ of Yìchéng Jūn.
After more than a year,
he was transferred to govern Wēishèng,
given the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
entered court as Shàngjiàngjūn,
then went out to govern Zhāoyì,
and was later transferred to Ānyuǎn.
When Jìn Gāozǔ was established,
he made a father-son pact with the Qìdān.
Wénjìn feared for his safety.
In the winter of Tiānfú 1 (936 CE),
he killed his Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Féng Zhīzhào and Fùshǐ Dù Zhòngguì,
and sent an offer of submission to Lǐ Cóngkē.
Cóngkē sent troops to welcome him.
Wénjìn had governed several prefectures
and often implemented good policies.
The soldiers and people loved him.
When he was about to depart,
he took a few horsemen
and went to the camp himself to bid farewell to his generals and soldiers.
He explained his intention to avoid the Qìdān.
The generals and soldiers all prostrated themselves twice in farewell,
and then he fled south.
Cóngkē appointed Wénjìn as Tiānxíong Tǒngjūn and Xuánrùn Jiéduànshǐ.
Wénjìn was seven feet tall
and had a magnificent appearance.
Since his flight to the Qìdān,
he frequently led the Qìdān to raid and plunder the area between Yōu and Jì,
capturing its people.
He taught the Qìdān Chinese weaving and craftsmanship, making them fully equipped.
The Qìdān became stronger because of this.
During the Tóngguāng reign,
the Qìdān frequently sent Xī cavalry in and out of the passes,
raiding Yān and Zhào.
People had no peaceful years.
Táng troops were stationed in Zhuōzhōu,
and yearly provisions were transported.
From Wǎqiáo Pass to Yōuzhōu,
soldiers were heavily guarded and scouts were deployed,
but they constantly suffered from robbery and plunder.
He was a menace to the Táng for over ten years;
all of this was Wénjìn's doing.
When he fled south,
he began to humble himself and conceal his true nature,
striving to be respectful and cautious.
He courteously received literati,
modest as if he lacked something.
His discussions
were only about recent court ceremonies and stories of the imperial offices,
never mentioning military matters.
Later, he died in Jīnlíng as Zuǒwèi Shàngjiàngjūn.
Lǐ Jīnquán
Lǐ Jīnquán's
ancestors came from Tǔyùhún.
As a youth, Jīnquán was a servant of Táng Míngzōng.
Being brave and skilled in horsemanship and archery,
he often followed Míngzōng in battles.
For his merits, he became a Cìshǐ.
During the Tiānchéng reign,
he served as Jiéduànshǐ of Zhāngyì Jūn.
While in office, he was notoriously greedy and tyrannical.
After his dismissal and return,
he presented several dozen horses.
A few days later,
he presented more.
Míngzōng said to him:
"Are you troubled by too many horses?
Why do you keep presenting them?
And how was your governance in Jīngzhōu?
Surely you were not just preoccupied with horses?"
Jīnquán was ashamed and could not reply.
He was transferred to govern Hénghǎi.
After a long time,
he was dismissed and made Yòuwèi Shàngjiàngjūn.
During Jìn Gāozǔ's time,
Wáng Huī, the Túnfáng Zhǐhuīshǐ of Ānzhōu, killed the Jiéduànshǐ Zhōu Guī.
Gāozǔ sent Jīnquán with a thousand cavalrymen to go there,
and issued an imperial edict inviting Huī to surrender, saying:
"If Huī surrenders,
he shall be made Cìshǐ of Tángzhōu."
He also sent a trusted arrow (a symbol of authority) to Ānzhōu,
declaring that not a single person would be harmed,
and warned Jīnquán, saying:
"Do not break my promise."
Before Jīnquán arrived,
Ān Cóngjìn of Xiāngzhōu, believing Huī would surely flee south of the Yángzi River,
sent elite troops to block his main escape route.
When Huī heard Jīnquán was coming,
he indeed fled south,
and was killed by Cóngjìn's troops.
Jīnquán arrived later
and captured several hundred remnants of Huī's faction,
all of whom he sent to the capital.
During Huī's rebellion,
the city was plundered for three days.
Jīnquán coveted the plundered wealth.
He then arrested and killed more than ten of Huī's generals, including Wǔ Kèhé.
Kèhé shouted:
"Wáng Huī, who started the rebellion,
was still granted an oath of trust
and made a Cìshǐ.
What crime have we committed
that we are to be killed instead?
If this is the court's command,
how can trust be shown?
If the general violates the edict and kills those who surrender,
he too will not escape punishment!"
Gāozǔ could not refute this.
He immediately appointed Jīnquán as Jiéduànshǐ of Ānyuǎn Jūn.
Jīnquán's Zuǒdū Yāyá Míng Hànróng abused his power.
His actions were unlawful.
Gāozǔ was troubled by this
and did not wish to implicate a meritorious official because of Hànróng.
He selected an honest official, Jiǎ Rénzhǎo, to replace him,
and also summoned Hànróng.
Hànróng advised Jīnquán to keep him and not send him away.
Jīnquán's guest, Páng Lìngtú, advised him, saying:
"Rénzhǎo once served Wáng Yànqiú.
When Yànqiú attacked Wáng Dū at Zhōngshān,
Dū sent a skilled archer to ascend the wall and shoot at Yànqiú.
He hit Yànqiú's helmet.
Rénzhǎo drew his bow from behind
and shot the skilled archer.
With one shot, he killed him.
Yànqiú sought the person,
wishing to reward him handsomely,
but Rénzhǎo retreated and said nothing.
This is a loyal minister of the realm.
When Dū was defeated,
Yànqiú sent Rénzhǎo to present the victory report to the capital.
All the rewards he received were very generous,
but he distributed them all among his poor old friends and relatives.
This is an incorruptible scholar of the realm.
A person like this,
how could he plan for others without good intentions?
You should accept Rénzhǎo and send Hànróng away."
When Hànróng heard this,
he sent someone by night to kill Lìngtú and poison Rénzhǎo.
Rénzhǎo's tongue rotted, and he died.
Hóng Zhì, following the command of the deposed emperor, resided in the prefectural office.
Hóng Zhì had a son, Luán.
He was a Diànzhí.
When the deposed emperor was installed,
Luán was dispatched to bring a cup of poisoned wine (zhèn) to Hóng Zhì.
Initially,
Mǐn Dì was in Wèizhōu.
Hóng Zhì ordered a wine merchant from the market to offer wine.
When Mǐn Dì saw it,
he was greatly startled
and immediately collapsed to the ground.
After a long while, he revived.
Hóng Zhì said,
"This is a wine merchant.
He wishes to offer wine to comfort your boredom."
Mǐn Dì accepted it,
and from then on, a cup was offered daily.
When Luán arrived with the poisoned wine,
he had the wine merchant offer it.
Mǐn Dì drank it without suspicion,
and subsequently collapsed and died.
Hóng Zhì later served the Jìn as the Fèngxiáng Xíngjūn Sīmǎ,
and retired as Guānglù Qīng.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàifù.
Liú Shěnjiāo
Liú Shěnjiāo, courtesy name Qiúyì,
was a native of Wén'ān, Yōuzhōu.
In his youth, he had some knowledge of books
and was skilled in official affairs.
He served as the Tángxīng Lìng
and was later appointed to Fànyáng Yákào.
When Liú Shǒuguāng usurped the throne,
he appointed Shěnjiāo as Bīngbù Shàngshū.
After Shǒuguāng's defeat,
he returned to Tàiyuán.
Táng Zhuāngzōng appointed him as a Cóngshì.
Later, Zhào Déjūn took charge of Fànyáng,
and Běimiàn Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Mǎ Shàohóng invited Shěnjiāo to be his Pànguān.
When Wáng Yànqiú campaigned against Wáng Dū,
he was appointed Zhuǎnyùn Gōngjūnshǐ.
After Dìngzhōu was pacified,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Liáozhōu.
He again served as Běimiàn Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
then was transferred to Cízhōu Cìshǐ.
He resigned from office due to his mother's old age.
After his mother's death,
his grief and emaciation exceeded proper decorum,
and he remained out of office for several years.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn attacked Fàn Yánguāng in Wèizhōu,
and Shěnjiāo again served as Gōngjūnshǐ.
At this time,
Jìn Gāozǔ divided the Hùbù, Dùzhī, and Yántiě into three separate commissioners.
After more than a year,
the three agencies became increasingly troublesome and inefficient,
so they were combined again into one.
Shěnjiāo was appointed Sānsī Shǐ.
Some counselors proposed inspecting all the cultivated land in the empire
to increase rental income.
Shěnjiāo said,
"There is a fixed quota for rent,
and for many years, there has been no uncultivated land in the empire.
The suffering and happiness of the people
are not equal."
So, the inspection was stopped,
and the people benefited by not being disturbed.
He was promoted to Yòuwèi Shàngjiāngjūn and Chénzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He went out to inspect the people's fields
and found their farming tools to be crude and inferior.
So, he took farming tools from Hébĕi as models
and had new ones cast for the people.
After Ān Cóngjìn was pacified,
Shěnjiāo was transferred to Xiāngzhōu,
then to Qīngzhōu,
and in both places, he governed well.
He was dismissed and returned.
When the Qìdān invaded the capital,
they left Xiāo Hàn behind and departed.
Hàn again appointed Shěnjiāo as Sānsī Shǐ.
Shortly after, Hàn summoned Xǔ Wáng Cóngyì to guard the capital.
Hàn Gāozǔ raised an army in Tàiyuán.
Cóngyì summoned Gāo Xíngzhōu to resist Gāozǔ,
but Xíngzhōu did not arrive.
Cóngyì's mother, Wáng Shúfēi, consulted with her officials about welcoming Gāozǔ.
Some suggested that since there were still several thousand Yàn soldiers in the capital,
they could defend the city and wait for Xíngzhōu.
Shúfēi disagreed,
and the discussion remained undecided.
Shěnjiāo stepped forward and said,
"I am a native of Yàn.
Now, I am defending the city for Yàn,
and I should plan for Yàn.
However, the circumstances make it impossible to succeed.
Her Highness the Grand Consort's words are correct."
Cóngyì then ceased making preparations
and sent someone west to welcome Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ arrived,
he dismissed Shěnjiāo and did not employ him.
During Yǐn Dì's reign,
he served as Rǔzhōu Fángyùshǐ
and gained a reputation for competence.
He died in the third year of Qiányòu (950 CE)
at the age of seventy-four.
The people of Chuān gathered and wept before his coffin,
submitting memorials requesting that he be buried in the nearby suburbs
so that the people could offer sacrifices at the appropriate times each year.
An imperial edict specially posthumously granted him the title of Tàiwèi,
and ordered the erection of a shrine and a stele.
Wáng Zhōu
Wáng Zhōu
was a native of Wèizhōu.
In his youth, he joined the army due to his bravery and strength.
He served Táng Zhuāngzōng and Míngzōng
as a Bìxiào.
For his meritorious service in fierce battles, he was appointed Cìshǐ.
During the Tiānfú reign of Jìn,
he followed Yáng Guāngyuǎn in campaigning against Fàn Yánguāng in Wèizhōu,
and also followed Dù Chóngwēi in campaigning against Ān Chóngróng in Zhènzhōu.
In both instances, he performed meritoriously.
He successively served as Jiédùshǐ of Bèizhōu and Jìngzhōu.
In Jìngzhōu, Zhāng Yànzé had governed harshly and cruelly,
causing many people to flee.
Zhōu then adopted a more lenient approach,
inquired about the people's suffering,
and abolished more than twenty oppressive practices.
All the people returned.
He was successively transferred to the four prefectures of Wǔshèng, Bǎoyì, Yìwǔ, and Chéngdé,
and in all of them, he governed well.
When a bridge in Dìngzhōu collapsed,
overturning the people's grain carts,
Zhōu said,
"The bridge was not repaired;
it is the fault of the Cìshǐ."
So, he compensated the people with grain
and had the bridge repaired for them.
When Dù Chóngwēi surrendered to the Qìdān,
the Qìdān army passed through Zhènzhōu.
They approached the city and called out to Zhōu, urging him to surrender.
Zhōu wept and said,
"Having received profound kindness from the Jìn,
if I cannot die fighting but surrender the city instead,
how can I face the sovereign and the scholar-officials when I go south!"
He then drank heavily,
sought a knife, and wanted to commit suicide.
His family stopped him,
and he was forced to surrender.
The Qìdān appointed Zhōu as the Wǔshèngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to govern Wǔníng.
He died in office
and was posthumously granted the title of Zhōngshū Lìng.
Gāo Xíngzhōu (Xíngguī's biography attached)
Gāo Xíngzhōu, courtesy name Shàngzhì,
was a native of Guīzhōu.
His family had for generations been garrison commanders of Huáiróng.
His father was Sījì.
Sījì and his brothers were all renowned in the northern border region for their martial prowess,
serving as garrison commanders under Yōuzhōu Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Kuāngwēi.
When Kuāngwēi was usurped by his brother Kuāngchóu,
the Jìn Wáng was about to suppress the rebellion
and deliberated, saying,
"Gāo Sījì and his brothers are at Kǒnglǐngguān,
with three thousand soldiers.
These will be a future problem.
It would be better to send someone to recruit them.
If Sījì serves us,
then nothing will be impossible."
Kèyòng sent someone to recruit Sījì and his brothers.
The people of Yàn valued loyalty and righteousness.
Sījì and others, hearing that the Jìn army was avenging Kuāngwēi,
joyfully followed them
and became the vanguard of the Jìn army.
Kuāngchóu, hearing that Sījì and his brothers had all defected,
abandoned the city and fled.
Kèyòng appointed Liú Rén'gōng to guard Yōuzhōu,
appointed his eldest brother as Xiānfēng Dūzhǐhuīshǐ,
Sījì as Zhōngjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ,
and his younger brother as Hòujūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ.
The Gāo brothers shared command of the Yàn army.
Kèyòng, upon parting, told Rén'gōng,
"The Sījì brothers
wield influence over an entire region.
Those who will cause trouble for Yàn
will definitely be the Gāo family.
You should guard against them well."
Kèyòng left a thousand Jìn soldiers to guard Rén'gōng.
However, many Jìn soldiers violated the law,
and Sījì and others frequently executed them.
Kèyòng blamed Rén'gōng for this,
and Rén'gōng complained about the Gāo family.
Consequently, Jìn executed all the Sījì brothers.
Rén-gōng appointed the son of his brother Mǒu, Xíng-guī, as a Yá-jiàng,
and Sī-jì's son Xíng-zhōu was about ten years old,
and also took him under his command,
when he grew a little older,
he was appointed a military post.
When Rén-gōng was imprisoned,
and Shǒu-guāng ascended (the throne),
he made Xíng-guī the Cì-shǐ of Wǔzhōu.
After that, Shǒu-guāng betrayed Jìn,
and the Jìn army attacked him.
Shǒu-guāng's general Yuán Xíng-qīn was pasturing horses behind the mountains,
when he heard that Shǒu-guāng was about to be besieged.
He immediately led the horses he was pasturing to go assist,
but the soldiers under his command mutinied on the way,
and nominated Xíng-qīn as the Yōuzhōu Liú-hòu.
Xíng-qīn said:
"The one I fear is Xíng-guī."
He then sent men to Huáiróng,
captured Xíng-guī's son and restrained him.
When the army passed Wǔzhōu,
he summoned Xíng-guī and said:
"Shǒu-guāng can be captured and replaced.
You should follow me;
otherwise,
we will kill your son."
Xíng-guī replied:
"Both you and I are generals of Duke Liú,
yet you tolerate betraying him?
I must remain loyal to the Liú clan;
why should I still care about my son!"
Xíng-qīn immediately used his troops to besiege Xíng-guī.
After more than a month,
the food inside Xíng-guī's city ran out.
He summoned the people of his prefecture and announced:
"It is not that I failed to defend for you elders,
but now Duke Liú's relief troops have not arrived.
What is to be done?
You may kill me and surrender to Jìn."
The elders all wept,
and wished to defend until death.
At this time,
Xíng-zhōu happened to be accompanying Xíng-guī in Wǔzhōu.
That very night, they lowered Xíng-zhōu down (by rope) to gallop into Jìn and meet Zhuāng-zōng.
Zhuāng-zōng then sent Míng-zōng to rescue Wǔzhōu.
By the time (Míng-zōng) arrived,
Xíng-qīn had already lifted the siege and left,
and Xíng-guī then surrendered to Jìn.
During Zhuāng-zōng's time,
he successively served as the Cì-shǐ of the three prefectures Shuò, Xīn, and Lán, and as the Jié-dù-shǐ of Dàtóng Army.
When Míng-zōng entered and ascended (the throne),
he was transferred to govern Wēishèng and Ānyuǎn.
Xíng-guī was greedy and base by nature,
and much of what he did was illegal.
The Deputy Commissioner Fàn Yán-cè,
was a rigid and upright man.
He repeatedly admonished him,
but Xíng-guī did not listen,
and harbored resentment against him.
Soon after, some garrison soldiers planned a rebellion.
Xíng-guī discovered it first,
and secretly moved the weapons from the armory to another location.
When the garrison soldiers rebelled,
they rushed to the armory to seize weapons but found nothing,
so they scattered and fled.
Xíng-guī pursued and killed them.
He then falsely reported that Yán-cè had participated in the rebellion,
and both he and his son were killed.
The whole realm considered this an injustice.
Xíng-guī died while serving in his commandery,
and was posthumously granted the title Tài-wèi.
At the time Xíng-guī surrendered to Jìn,
Xíng-zhōu was serving under Míng-zōng's command.
He was initially a Pí-jiàng.
Zhào Dé-jūn recognized him,
and said to Míng-zōng:
"This young man has a robust appearance but is cautious,
he will certainly become very noble later;
you should treat him well."
When the Liáng and Jìn armies were stationed along the river,
Zhuāng-zōng sent Míng-zōng eastward to attack Yùnzhōu by surprise.
Xíng-zhōu commanded the vanguard.
They encountered rain during the night.
Everyone in the army wanted to stop and not advance,
but Xíng-zhōu said:
"This is Heaven assisting us!
The people of Yùn rely on the rain,
and will not be prepared for our arrival.
We should take them by surprise."
That night, he immediately galloped across and crossed the Jì River,
and entered their city.
The people of Yùn were only then becoming aware,
and consequently captured it.
When Zhuāng-zōng destroyed Liáng,
due to his achievements, he was given the title of Cì-shǐ of Duānzhōu.
He was promoted to Jiàngzhōu.
During Míng-zōng's time,
he followed (the emperor) to pacify Zhū Shǒu-yīn,
and captured Wáng Dū.
He was promoted to Tuán-liàn-shǐ of Yǐngzhōu, and Jié-dù-shǐ of Zhènwǔ Army.
He successively governed Zhāngwǔ and Zhāoyì.
During Jìn Gāo-zǔ's time,
he served as the Xījīng Liú-shǒu,
and was transferred to govern Tiānxíong.
When Ān Cóng-jìn rebelled,
Xíng-zhōu was made Xiāngzhōu Xíngyíng Dū Bùshǔ,
he attacked and pacified the rebellion,
and was transferred to govern Guīdé.
During Chū-dì's time,
he replaced Jǐng Yán-guǎng as Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
At this time,
Lǐ Yàn-tāo, Féng Yù, and others were influential in government,
so he requested to return to his regional post.
When the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
they left Xiāo Hàn to guard Biàn,
Hàn soon abandoned it and left.
They summoned the former Táng Prince of Xǔ, Cóng-yì, to enter Biàn.
Meanwhile, Hàn Gāo-zǔ rose up in Tàiyuán.
Cóng-yì sent someone to summon Xíng-zhōu,
intending to use him to resist Hàn.
Xíng-zhōu sighed and said:
"It is difficult to assist a declining age,
let alone a child's game!"
So he did not comply.
When Hàn Gāo-zǔ entered the capital,
he conferred upon Xíng-zhōu the title Shǒu Zhōng-shū-lìng,
transferred him to govern Tiānpíng Army,
and enfeoffed him as the Prince of Línqīng.
When Zhōu Tài-zǔ entered and ascended (the throne),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title Shàng-shū-lìng,
and was further enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín.
He had a son, Huái-dé.
Bái Zài-róng
It is unknown what lineage Bái Zài-róng came from.
In his youth, he was a soldier.
Between the Táng and Jìn dynasties,
he served as the Hùshèng Zhǐhuīshǐ.
When the Qìdān invaded the capital,
Zài-róng followed the Qìdān back north.
When they reached Zhènzhōu,
the Qìdān left Má Dá to guard Zhènzhōu and departed.
Many Jìn people who had followed them stayed there.
Not long after,
Lǐ Jūn, Hé Fú-jìn,
and others planned to drive out Má Dá.
They sent someone to summon Zài-róng.
Zài-róng hesitated and did not want to go,
but the soldiers pressured him,
so he went.
They jointly attacked him.
Má Dá fled.
The various generals, believing Zài-róng had the highest rank,
then nominated him as Liú-hòu.
Zài-róng came from the ranks,
was greedy and lacked strategy.
At this time,
Lǐ Sōng, Hé Níng, and others had followed the Qìdān and remained in Zhènzhōu.
Zài-róng surrounded their residences with troops,
and extorted goods from them.
He also wanted to harm Sōng and seize his property.
Lǐ Gǔ spoke to him, saying:
"You gentlemen personally suffered under the Qìdān,
and worried about death constantly.
However, the expulsion of Má Dá
was the work of everyone,
not solely due to your power.
Now that you have just found a path to survival,
and you immediately kill a Prime Minister,
the Qìdān might not even have done this.
Moreover, when you return to the capital someday,
and the Son of Heaven asks where the Prime Minister is,
how will you answer him?"
Zài-róng remained silent,
and then stopped.
However, he detained everyone who had previously served Má Dá and seized their wealth.
The people of the commandery called him
"Bái Má Dá."
When Hàn Gāo-zǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Zài-róng as Liú-hòu,
and promoted him to Jié-dù-shǐ of Yìchéng Army.
He was dismissed and returned to the capital.
When Zhōu Tài-zǔ entered the capital with his army,
the soldiers attacked Zài-róng at his residence,
and took all his wealth.
Later, (Zhōu Tài-zǔ) came forward and announced:
"The officers and soldiers previously served the Duke under his command.
To be so disrespectful all of a sudden,
how can they still have the face to see the Duke again!"
He then executed him,
carried his head away and left.
His family ransomed his head with silk and buried him.
Ān Shū-qiān
was a man of the Three Tribes of the Shātuó.
When young, he excelled at horsemanship and archery.
He served Táng Zhuāngzōng,
who appointed him Fèng'ān Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commissioner of the Fèng'ān Command).
During Míngzōng's time, he participated in the campaign against Wáng Dū,
and was appointed Cìshǐ (Prefect) of Qínzhōu.
Following the attack on the Qìdān,
he became Xiānfēng Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Vanguard),
and due to his merit, was appointed Zhāowǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the Zhāowǔ Army).
He successively held the four garrisons of Jìngnán, Hénghǎi, Ānguó, and Jiànxióng.
Shūqiān was imposing in appearance,
but illiterate (did not understand characters).
His actions were often coarse and vulgar,
so people called him
"The Stele Without Characters" (Mòzì Bēi).
During the time of Jìn Chūdì,
he served as Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Left Guards of Jīnwú).
When the Qìdān invaded the capital (Jīngshī),
the officials of Jìn welcomed Yēlǜ Déguāng at Chìgāng.
Shūqiān stepped out of the ranks and spoke in a foreign dialect (Yíyán).
Déguāng praised him, saying:
"Is this not Ān Mòzì?
When you were in Xíngzhōu,
you had already pledged your sincerity.
Now that I have arrived here,
I shall give you a place to eat."
Shūqiān bowed again.
He was then appointed Zhènguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the Zhènguó Army).
When Hàn Gāozǔ assumed the throne,
he was dismissed and returned to the capital (Jīngshī).
Since he had often secretly attached himself to the Qìdān,
he was deeply ashamed and fearful.
He retired with the title of Tàizǐ Tàishī (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince).
When Zhōu Tàizǔ's troops entered the capital (Jīngshī),
the soldiers heavily looted the area.
Shūqiān's family wealth was already exhausted,
but the soldiers suspected he had things hidden,
and whipped and plundered him incessantly.
Severely injured,
he returned to Luòyáng,
where he died,
aged seventy-two.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter 37: Zhái Guāngyè.
Zhái Guāngyè, courtesy name Huàjī,
was a native of Juànchéng, Púzhōu.
His father, Jǐngkē,
was unconventional and courageous.
When Liáng and Jìn confronted each other along the river,
Jǐngkē gathered the villagers and defended the Yǒngdìng Post Station.
The Jìn forces attacked it,
and for over a year could not take it.
Jǐngkē eventually died in battle.
Guāngyè was ten years old at the time,
and was captured by the Jìn army.
Míngzōng admired his brilliance and intelligence,
and constantly kept him nearby.
Guāngyè served Táng,
and his highest office reached Yàozhōu Tuánliànshǐ (Head of Militia Training of Yàozhōu).
During the time of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he successively served as Cìshǐ (Prefect) of the two prefectures of Dìzhōu and Yízhōu, and Fù Liúshǒu (Deputy Resident General) of Xījīng (Western Capital).
After Chūdì defeated Yáng Guāngyuǎn,
he appointed Guāngyè as Qīngzhōu Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner of Qīngzhōu).
Guāngyè recruited and managed soldiers and civilians,
showing great kindness and benevolence.
When the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
they sent Guāngyè to govern Cáozhōu.
Xǔ Wáng Cóngyì entered the court,
and appointed him Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs).
When Hàn Gāozǔ entered the capital (Jīngshī),
he was transferred to Yòu Lǐngjūn Wèi Dàjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Right Leader of the Army Guard) and Zuǒ Jīnwú Dàjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Left Jīnwú),
serving concurrently as Jiēshǐ (Street Commissioner).
When Zhōu Tàizǔ assumed the throne,
he was appointed Xuānhuīshǐ (Commissioner of the Palace) and Shūmì Fùshǐ (Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs).
He was later sent out to govern Yǒngxīng Jūn,
and died in office.
Guāngyè was silent, reflective, and resourceful.
He was known for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
Although he was high in rank,
he did not accumulate wealth.
He always resided in borrowed official quarters,
which were sparse and barely kept out the wind and rain.
He lived harmoniously with his relatives,
wearing rough clothes and eating coarse food.
He shared his resources equally with them,
and Guāngyè remained completely content with this state of affairs.
Daily, he took pleasure in drinking with guests and collecting books.
In his governance,
he aimed primarily for leniency, tranquility, and recuperation for the people.
When his illness became critical,
he instructed his attendants:
"Upon my death, take my corpse back to Luòyáng.
Do not delay here long, causing trouble for the military administration."
After he died,
the people of the prefecture submitted a memorial requesting permission to bury him there and establish a shrine,
but this was not granted.
Féng Huī
Féng Huī
was a native of Wèizhōu.
He served as a soldier in the Xiàojié Army,
and was promoted to Duìzhǎng (Squad Leader) due to his merit.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng entered Wèi,
and contended with Liáng along the river,
Huī, as a Squad Leader, defected to the Liáng army.
Wáng Yànzhāng, recognizing Huī's bravery and strength,
assigned him to his command.
When Liáng fell,
Zhuāngzōng pardoned Huī without punishment.
He followed Míngzōng in campaigning against Yáng Lì.
When Wèi Wáng Jìjí pacified Shǔ,
Huī was successively promoted to Cìshǐ (Prefect) of the two prefectures of Kuízhōu and Xīngzhōu.
When Dǒng Zhāng rebelled in Dōngchuān,
Huī followed Jìn Gāozǔ to campaign against Zhāng.
The army reached Jiànmén.
Since Jiànmén was defended by troops,
they could not enter.
Huī took an alternate route and emerged on their left flank,
defeating almost all the defending Shǔ soldiers.
At that time, Jìn Gāozǔ recalled the army,
and appointed Huī as Cìshǐ (Prefect) of Chánzhōu.
During the Tiānfú reign,
Fàn Yánguāng rebelled in Wèizhōu
and sent Huī to raid Huázhōu.
He was unsuccessful,
and subsequently entered Wèi,
defending it for Yánguāng.
Later, he surrendered
and was appointed Yìchéng Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the Yìchéng Army).
He was transferred to govern Língwǔ.
Since the time of Táng Míngzōng, Língwǔ
had purchased horses, acquired grain,
invited various tribes to submit,
and granted stipends to the soldiers.
Annually, the expenditure cost sixty million *duzhī* cash.
West of the passes (Guān),
transport and supply operations
were unbearable for the populace,
leading to massive displacement and flight.
Between Qīnggāng and Tǔqiáo,
the Dī and Qiāng tribes plundered the roads.
Merchants and travelers had to move with military escorts.
When Huī first arrived,
he extended kindness and trust.
The tribes cherished his benevolence
and ceased their plundering and encroachment.
Then, he greatly expanded the military farms (túntián) to reduce the need for supply transport.
He constructed over a thousand storage facilities, warehouses, and post-houses.
He often used his own salary money,
and the people were not subjected to increased taxes.
The territory under his jurisdiction was greatly stabilized.
Jìn Gāozǔ issued an imperial edict commending and praising him.
Tuòbá Yànchāo of the Dǎngxiàng was the largest tribe.
The alignment or defection of the other tribes was always determined by Yànchāo's actions.
When Huī arrived,
Yànchāo came to pay his respects.
Huī detained him
and built a mansion for him within the city.
He gave him rich gifts
and strove to satisfy his wishes.
Once Yànchāo was retained,
the various tribes competed to trade sheep and horses.
Within a year, five thousand horses were acquired.
Jìn saw that Huī had many horses and had won the hearts of the barbarians (Yí),
and conversely regarded this as a threat.
He was transferred to govern Jìngnán,
and then transferred again to Bǎoyì.
In the middle of the year,
he was summoned back to serve as Shìwèi Bùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (Commander-in-Chief of the Metropolitan Infantry Guard),
concurrently holding the position of Héyáng Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Héyáng).
Huī then finally realized that Jìn intended to harm him.
At this time,
Chū Dì was confused and erratic.
Féng Yù, Lǐ Yàntāo, and others held power.
Huī catered to them deliberately,
and consequently was able to return to govern Língwǔ.
At the time, Wáng Lìngwēn was governing Língwǔ,
but he had lost the trust of the non-Han tribes (Yíluò),
causing great trouble along the border.
Huī immediately requested, saying:
"Now the court is busy with many affairs,
and certainly cannot send troops to reinforce your servant.
I wish to recruit my own soldiers for protection."
He then managed to recruit over a thousand soldiers.
When he traveled to Méishù,
the barbarians (Fānyí) gradually came to pay their respects.
Huī looked at one of the leaders
and pointed at the sword he wore, saying:
"Is this the sword of the Wáng clan of Bǎnqiáo?
I have heard that the Wáng clan’s sword is the sharpest weapon under Heaven."
He bent down and took it from the man's waist,
acting as if he intended to examine it;
then, he struck and killed the leader.
The dozen or so horsemen who followed him were all killed as well.
The Deputy General Yào Yuánfú said:
"We are still five or six hundred *lǐ* away from Língwǔ.
What should we do?"
Huī laughed and said:
"This man was a prominent figure among the Yíluò,
relied upon by his tribe.
Since I was able to kill him,
how would the rest dare to make trouble!"
Soon after, all the tribes used their soldiers to block the roads.
Huī used words to placate and instruct them.
Only the tribe of the executed leader sought battle,
so Huī fought them, defeated them, and put them to flight.
Thereafter, the various tribes dared not make a move.
When Huī arrived at Língwǔ,
he comforted and pacified the border regions.
For more than ten years,
his kindness and trust became widely recognized.
His highest official post reached Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chénliú.
He died in Guǎngshùn 3 (953),
and was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Wèi.
His son was Jìyè.
Huángfǔ Huī
Huángfǔ Huī
was a man from Wèizhōu.
He served as a soldier in the Wèi army,
garrisoning Wǎqiáo Pass.
When his year of service was up and he was supposed to return home to be replaced,
he was instead detained to garrison Bèizhōu.
At this time,
Táng Zhuāngzōng had already lost governance,
and the people throughout the land were estranged.
Huī was fierce, brave, and reckless.
One night, he gambled among the troops.
When he lost,
he plotted rebellion with his followers.
He kidnapped their Area Commander Yáng Rénshèng and said:
"The reason Táng was able to defeat Liáng and gain the empire
was by first gaining Wèi and taking complete control of the Hébĕi troops.
The Wèi army has not taken off its armor or unbridled its horses for more than ten years.
Now the world is settled,
but the Son of Heaven does not remember the long years of hardship endured by the Wèi army in garrison.
We are close to home,
yet we cannot see our families.
The officers and soldiers now long to return home irresistibly;
you must travel with us.
Should the Son of Heaven unfortunately become angry at our army,
then sitting firmly in control of one prefecture
would be sufficient to start a major undertaking."
Rénshèng said:
"How foolish your plan is!
Now we have an enlightened ruler above us,
the world is united,
and there are no less than several hundred thousand
elite armored and sharp-witted soldiers.
Each of you has family members.
Why do you utter such inauspicious words?"
The soldiers knew they could not force him,
so they executed him.
They then acclaimed a junior officer as their leader.
When he refused,
they executed him as well.
They then carried the two heads to the Deputy General Zhào Zàilǐ.
Zàilǐ agreed to follow them.
That night, they burned Bèizhōu and entered Wèi.
Zàilǐ appointed Huī as Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry.
Huī led several hundred armored cavalry,
heavily looting the city.
When he arrived at a commoner's house,
he asked their surname.
They said:
"The surname is Guó (meaning 'state' or 'nation')."
Huī said:
"I should destroy the Guó!"
Then he killed everyone there.
He then arrived at another house,
asked their surname,
and they said:
"The surname is Wàn (meaning 'ten thousand')."
Huī said:
"It is enough for me to kill ten thousand households!"
Then he killed everyone there too.
When Míngzōng entered Wèi,
he immediately plotted with Zàilǐ.
The calamity involving Zhuāngzōng began with Huī.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
Huī was promoted from a common soldier to Prefect of Chénzhōu.
Throughout the rest of the Táng dynasty, he remained a prefect.
During the Tiānfú era of Jìn,
he resided in the capital as a Commandant of the Guard (Wèi Jiāngjūn).
Zàilǐ had already held a military governorship (Máo Jié).
When he was dismissed from his post and came to the court,
Huī went to visit him and said:
"We rose together at Gānlíng,
and ultimately achieved great deeds,
but it was initiated by me.
You are now rich and honored;
can you help me?
If not,
disaster will arise right here in this seat!"
Zàilǐ was afraid,
and quickly gave him several thousand units of valuables and silk.
He then offered him wine.
Huī drank normally,
did not offer thanks, and left.
After a long time,
he became Prefect of Mìzhōu.
When the Khitans violated the palace,
Huī led the people of his prefecture to flee to Jiāngnán.
Lǐ Jǐng appointed him Prefect of Shèzhōu and Regional Governor of Fènghuà Army (Fènghuà Jūn Jiédù Shǐ),
garrisoning Jiāngzhōu.
When the Zhōu army campaigned against the Huái River region,
Jǐng appointed Huī as the Commissioner for Relief and Support for the Northern Expeditionary Camp (Bĕimiàn Xíngyíng Yīngyuán Shǐ).
He was stationed at Qīngliú Pass.
He was defeated by the Zhōu army,
and both he and his Supervising Commander Yáo Fèng were captured.
Shìzōng summoned him for an audience.
Huī had fresh wounds covering his body.
Shìzōng pitied him,
and bestowed upon him a golden belt, a saddle, and a horse.
He died a few days later.
Fèng was appointed General-in-Chief of the Left Guard of the Reserves (Zuǒ Túnwèi Shàng Jiāngjūn).
Táng Jǐngsī
Táng Jǐngsī
was a native of Qínzhōu.
As a youth, he was skilled at wrestling (jué dǐ)
and made a living by butchering dogs.
Later, he left to become a soldier,
and was successively promoted to Commander (Zhīhuī Shǐ).
When Táng Prince of Wèi Jìjí campaigned against Shǔ,
Jǐngsī defended Gùzhèn for Shǔ.
When Jìjí's troops arrived,
Jǐngsī surrendered the city,
and was appointed Prefect of Xīngzhōu.
During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he served as Adjutant in the Campaigning Army of Bèizhōu.
During the reign of Chū Dì,
the Khitans attacked and captured Bèizhōu.
Jǐngsī was captured by Zhào Yánshòu,
who appointed him Commissioner of Trenches and Fortifications (Háozhài Shǐ).
When the Khitans destroyed Jìn,
they appointed Jǐngsī as Defense Commissioner of Bózhōu.
During the reign of Hàn Gāozǔ,
he served as Adjutant in the Campaigning Army of Dèngzhōu.
Later, he became the Inspection Commissioner along the Huái River.
The Hàn laws were cruel,
and when Shǐ Hóngzhào was in power,
he enjoyed using accusations to kill people.
Jǐngsī had a slave
who once asked for something that was not granted to his satisfaction.
He then rushed to see Hóngzhào,
saying that Jǐngsī was communicating with Lǐ Jǐng
and privately hoarding weapons and armor.
Hóngzhào dispatched an official with thirty cavalrymen to arrest Jǐngsī.
The slave said to the official:
"Jǐngsī is a brave man.
If you get him, kill him;
otherwise, you will lose him."
When the official arrived,
Jǐngsī stepped forward,
embraced the official with both hands, cried out his grievances,
and requested to be sent to prison to explain himself.
The official brought the slave and Jǐngsī together for verification.
Jǐngsī said:
"My house is here;
please search it.
If there are ten thousand cash,
that would be for receiving foreign bribes.
If there is one set of armor,
that would be for privately hoarding weapons."
The official searched it,
and found only a single clothes chest,
military records, and grain registers, nothing more.
The official pitied him and leniently released him.
Jǐngsī requested to be shackled and sent to the capital to clear his name.
Jǐngsī had a servant, Wáng Zhīquán, in the capital.
When Zhīquán heard that Jǐngsī had been accused,
he went to see Hóngzhào,
and volunteered to be imprisoned first to prove Jǐngsī was not rebellious.
Hóngzhào took pity on him,
sent Zhīquán to prison,
and daily provided him with wine and food.
Jǐngsī, already shackled, set off on the road.
The people of Yǐng and Bó followed him to the capital to jointly clear his name.
Hóngzhào then interrogated the slave,
who confessed fully.
He then memorialized for the slave to be executed and Jǐngsī to be released.
Later, he followed Shìzōng in the battle of Gāopíng.
Shìzōng took several thousand surrendered Hàn soldiers and formed the Xiàoshùn Command,
appointing Jǐngsī as its commander.
He was again garrisoned on the Huái River.
When the Zhōu army attacked Huáinán,
he was awarded the title of Ráo Zhōu Cìshǐ for his merits,
and then promoted to Háo Zhōu Cìshǐ.
When the enemy attacked Háo Zhōu,
he died from severe battle wounds,
and was posthumously granted the title of Wǔqīng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Wáng Jìn
Wáng Jìn was
a native of Liángxiāng, Yōuzhōu.
He was brave and fierce,
able to run as fast as a galloping horse.
When he was young, he gathered followers and became a bandit,
which troubled the local community.
Fú Yànchāo sent someone to bribe him and recruit him into his command.
When Yànchāo was garrisoned at Ānyuǎn Jūn,
there was a disturbance in the army.
He sent Jìn to quickly report to the capital.
Míngzōng was surprised by his swift arrival,
praised his physical strength,
and assigned him to the Níngwèi Command.
Hàn Gāozǔ was the Shìwèi Qīnjūn Zhīhuīshǐ
and appointed Jìn as a military officer.
When Gāozǔ was garrisoned at Hédōng,
he took Jìn with him.
Whenever there was an emergency,
he would send Jìn to gallop to the capital,
completing the round trip in no more than five or six days.
Because of this, he grew to love and trust him even more,
and he was repeatedly promoted to Fèngguó Jūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
He followed Zhōu Tàizǔ when he rose up in Wèi,
and was promoted to Hǔjié Yòuxiāng Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
He successively served as Rǔ and Zhèng Zhōu Fángyùshǐ, and Zhāngdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the autumn of Xiǎndé 1st year,
he died of illness,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī.
One version reads "初" (chū, initially).
Alas!
When I narrate old histories,
upon reaching the affairs of Wáng Jìn,
I never fail to close the book and sigh, saying: How extreme!
The rulers of the Five Dynasties
all rose from military backgrounds,
and those with whom they associated were brave men and fierce soldiers,
each carving up territory to be enfeoffed as marquises and kings.
How is this different from wolves herding these people?
Although their patronage and opportunities
arose from a temporary stroke of luck,
they still invariably had to expose themselves on the battlefield,
possessing either the bravery of a hundred men
or the merit of a single day's labor.
But for someone like Jìn,
who merely by his swift feet and good running ability came to hold the banner and staff of office,
how exceedingly strange it is!
Is it not that the use of official positions
changes in importance with the times?
When the world is well-governed, gentlemen occupy them and they are valued;
when the world is in chaos, lesser men easily obtain them and they are trivialized?
Or is it that obtaining advantage through chance and good fortune,
though not unheard of,
is especially prevalent in times of chaos,
and when it reaches its extreme,
it results in such cases?
Or could there be even more extreme examples than this?
At this time,
those who ruled a state for a long period governed for no more than ten-plus years;
for a short period, three or four years, or even one or two years.
The people of the world
saw their superiors easily changing rulers and replacing states,
as if merely changing garrisons, no different.
Since it was so trivial,
how much more so for those below them!
As for people like Jìn,
