are they even worth mentioning?
As the Yì Jīng says of "Fǒu" (Obstruction) and "Tài" (Peace), flourishing and declining,
gentlemen and lesser men constantly alternate between high and low positions.
Seeing those in high positions like Jìn and his ilk,
one can imagine those below them.
I record Jìn's story
to lament the disorder among these people,
and to show how many worthy and noble men of that time were in low positions!
How many could one possibly count!
How many could one possibly count!
Cháng Sī
Cháng Sī, courtesy name Kègōng,
was a native of Tàiyuán.
Initially, he followed Táng Zhuāngzōng as a soldier,
and later became the Chángjiàn Zhīhuīshǐ.
Through the Táng and Jìn dynasties, he served as Liùjūn Dūyúhòu.
When Hàn Gāozǔ was the Hédōng Jiédùshǐ,
he appointed Sī as the Láochéng Zhīhuīshǐ.
When Gāozǔ entered the capital and ascended the throne,
Sī was made the Wǔshèng Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and then transferred to govern Zhāoyì.
Sī rose from a military soldier,
never having achieved battle merits.
He merely happened to encounter the rise of the Hàn dynasty
and thus came to hold the banner and staff of office.
He stayed in Lùzhōu for five years,
making wealth accumulation his business,
yet his nature was base and frugal.
Initially,
when Sī was obscure,
Zhōu Tàizǔ was young, an orphan without support,
and ate at Sī's house.
He regarded Sī as his uncle.
Later, Sī and Zhōu Tàizǔ both encountered the Hàn dynasty and attained wealth and status.
After Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he always addressed Sī as Uncle Cháng,
and bowed to his wife
with the rites due to family members.
In Guǎngshùn 3rd year,
he was transferred to govern Guīdé.
After residing there for three years, he came to court.
He was then transferred to Pínglú.
Sī then addressed the emperor, saying:
"Your servant resides in Sòng,
and the people of Sòng owe your servant one hundred thousand taels of silk interest.
I wish to present the bonds to Your Majesty."
Tàizǔ nodded,
then immediately burned the bonds,
and issued an edict to Sòngzhōu to cancel all of them.
Sī resided in Qīngzhōu.
More than a year later, he fell ill,
returned to Luòyáng,
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhōngshūlìng.
Sūn Fāngjiàn
Sūn Fāngjiàn
was a native of Qīngyuàn, Zhèngzhōu.
Initially,
to the northwest of Dìngzhōu, there was Lángshān Fort.
The people of Dìng often took refuge there to avoid the Qìdān.
A nun named Shēnyì resided within it
and attracted people with Buddhist teachings,
many of whom returned to her.
After the nun died,
the fort residents said her body did not decay,
so they revered and served her.
The nun's surname was Sūn.
Fāngjiàn considered himself a relative of the nun
and immediately continued her practices.
The fort residents elected him as their leader.
During the time of Jìn Chūdì,
the Yìwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ disliked Fāngjiàn's gathering of followers in the mountains,
fearing he would become a border threat.
Therefore, he memorialized to have him appointed as a Yóuyìshǐ.
Fāngjiàn then sought something which he did not get,
so he allied with the Qìdān to the north.
Later, the Qìdān destroyed the Jìn dynasty
and appointed Fāngjiàn as the Yìwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Afterward, they transferred Fāngjiàn to Yúnzhōng.
Fāngjiàn refused the order
and led his followers back into Lángshān.
When Hàn Gāozǔ rose,
the Qìdān set fire to Dìngzhōu,
and carried its people north.
Fāng Jiàn heard of this,
entered from Wángshān,
occupied it, and returned to the Hàn.
Gāozǔ praised him,
and immediately appointed Fāng Jiàn as Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ Army.
During Zhōu Tàizǔ's time,
he was transferred to govern Zhènguó,
and his younger brother Xíngyǒu was made Liúhòu of Dìngzhōu.
When Shìzōng attacked Tàiyuán,
Fāng Jiàn paid court at the Emperor's temporary residence,
and followed him back to the capital.
Upon reaching Luò, he fell ill,
and was transferred to govern Kuāngguó.
He died in Luòyáng
at the age of sixty-two,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī.
Collation Notes
Miscellaneous Biographies, No. 38: Wáng Jùn
Wáng Jùn, courtesy name Xiùfēng,
was a native of Ānyáng, Xiàngzhōu.
His father, Fēng,
was a commanding officer of the Le Camp.
When young, Jùn served Liáng Jìedùshǐ Zhāng Jūn by virtue of his good singing.
After Táng Zhuāngzōng had taken Wèibó,
Jūn abandoned Xiàngzhōu
and fled back to the capital.
When Zūyōngshǐ Zhào Yán passed by Jūn's house,
Jūn ordered Jùn to sing to accompany the wine,
and Yán saw him and was pleased.
At this time, Yán was influential,
so Jūn gave Jùn to Yán.
When Liáng fell,
Yán's clan was executed,
and Jùn became a wanderer among the people.
After a long time,
he served Sānsīshǐ Zhāng Yánlǎng,
but Yánlǎng did not favor him much.
When Jìn Gāozǔ destroyed Táng
and killed Yánlǎng,
Hàn Gāozǔ at that time rose in rebellion with Jìn,
and consequently all of Yánlǎng's property was bestowed upon him.
Thus, Jùn came to serve Hàn Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ was stationed in Hédōng,
Jùn was a guest general.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Jùn as Kèshěngshǐ.
The Hàn sent Guō Cóngyì to suppress Zhào Sīwǎn,
and appointed Jùn to supervise his army.
He was successively promoted to Xuānhuī Běiyuànshǐ.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ was stationed in Tiānxíong Army,
Jùn served as監軍 (Jiānjūn).
After Hàn Yǐndì had killed Grand Minister Shǐ Hóngzhào and others,
he also sent people to kill Zhōu Tàizǔ and Jùn and others.
Jùn and the others then, with Tàizǔ, raised an army to attack the capital.
When Tàizǔ supervised the state,
by order of the Hàn Empress Dowager, Jùn was appointed Shūmìshǐ.
When Tàizǔ led his troops north,
upon reaching Chánzhōu,
the army turned back towards the capital.
At this time,
Tàizǔ had already sent Féng Dào to welcome Xiāngyīn Gōng Yūn from Xúzhōu,
and the Hàn imperial clan's Càiwáng Xìn was in Xǔzhōu.
Jùn conspired with Wáng Yīn
to send the Shìwèi Mǎjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ Guō Chóng with troops to Sòngzhōu, and former Shēnzhōu Cìshǐ Mǎ Duó to Xǔzhōu to await developments.
Chóng and Duó then killed Yūn and Xìn.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Jùn as Yòupúyè, Ménxiàshìláng, and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì,
and Supervisor of National History.
When Liú Mín attacked Jìnzhōu,
Jùn served as Xíngyíng Dūbùshǔ,
empowered to act as he saw fit.
He separately dispatched Chén Sīràng and Kāng Yánzhǎo to exit from Wūlǐng to Jiàngzhōu to meet Jùn.
When Jùn arrived at Shǎnxzhōu,
he lingered and did not advance.
Tàizǔ sent an envoy, Zhái Shǒusù, to hasten to Shǎnxzhōu
and inform Jùn of his intention to personally lead the campaign.
Jùn dismissed his attendants and said to Shǒusù:
"Jìnzhōu city is strong and cannot be approached,
and Liú Mín's troops are sharp and not yet to be resisted.
The reason I remain here
is not cowardice;
it is because I am waiting for something.
Furthermore, Your Majesty has just ascended the throne,
and the various regional governors
have not yet been brought under your awe and virtue;
how can you act rashly!
Moreover, Mùróng Yànchāo of Yǎnzhōu has already revealed signs of rebellion.
If Your Majesty goes out to Sìshuǐ,
then Yànchāo will enter the capital.
How will Your Majesty deal with him?"
Shǒusù hastened back
and fully recounted Jùn's words.
At this time,
Tàizǔ had already issued an edict to travel west.
Hearing Jùn's words,
he immediately pulled his own ear and said:
"He almost ruined my plan!"
Thereupon, he stopped and did not go.
Jùn's army set out from Jiàngzhōu.
The vanguard reported passing Mēngkēng,
and Jùn was pleased.
He said to his subordinates:
"Mēngkēng
is the strategic pass between Jìn and Jiàng.
Mín did not divide his troops to guard it,
allowing us to pass here.
It is clear that he is bound to be defeated."
When Jùn's army was one shě from Jìnzhōu,
Mín heard that the Zhōu army had arrived in great numbers,
and immediately retreated.
All the generals wanted to pursue him,
but Jùn hesitated, unable to decide.
The next day,
he sent cavalry to pursue Mín,
but they did not catch him and returned.
He participated in the campaign against Mùróng Yànchāo,
serving as Suíjià Dūbùshǔ,
leading the troops to be the first to ascend.
Jùn and Tàizǔ both rose from Wèi,
and he considered his功 as assisting the founding of the dynasty,
taking the responsibility for the empire upon himself.
Whatever he discussed or requested,
regardless of the size of the matter,
he expected to get it.
If it was even slightly not to his liking,
his words and expression were often disrespectful.
Tàizǔ always tolerated him.
Jùn was two years older than Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ often called Jùn "elder brother"
or by his courtesy name.
Jùn consequently became even more arrogant.
Zhèng Rénhuì, Lǐ Chóngjìn, Xiàng Xùn, etc.,
were all Tàizǔ's former subordinate generals.
When Tàizǔ first ascended the throne,
he was modest and not yet willing to promote them,
but Jùn was secretly jealous of them.
After returning from defeating Mùróng Yànchāo,
he immediately offered to resign from the Shūmì post to probe the Emperor's intentions.
Tàizǔ comforted and appeased him.
Jùn sent out many letters to the various regional governors,
seeking their endorsement.
After several days,
all the regional governors sent fast riders to present letters to Jùn,
which greatly alarmed Tàizǔ.
Jùn repeatedly submitted memorials requesting resignation
and consequently stopped attending to affairs.
Tàizǔ sent a close minister to summon him, saying:
"If you do not come out,
I will personally go to visit you."
Jùn said:
"If the imperial carriage were to come,
it would bring unforeseen misfortune upon your servant."
However, he showed no intention of coming out.
Shūmì Zhíxuèshì Chén Tóng was on good terms with Jùn.
Tàizǔ immediately sent Tóng to summon Jùn.
Tóng returned and reported:
"Jùn's attitude has somewhat softened,
but he requests Your Majesty to loudly declare that the imperial carriage is being prepared
as if you are about to visit him,
then Jùn will surely come out."
Tàizǔ reluctantly agreed.
When Jùn heard that Tàizǔ was about to come,
he immediately hastened in to pay his respects.
Jùn had built a main hall in the Privy Council office,
which was extremely lavish.
He invited Tàizǔ to visit,
and was greatly rewarded.
Tàizǔ built a small hall in the imperial garden,
and Jùn immediately reported:
"There are already many palaces and houses;
what is the use of this?"
Tàizǔ said:
"There are not a few rooms in the Privy Council office;
why did you also need to build something?"
Jùn was ashamed and unable to reply.
Wáng Jùn was made Píshūshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs) and concurrently Zǎixiàng (Chancellor).
He also requested to concurrently command Pínglú.
Having already received the mandate,
he temporarily proceeded to the commandery,
and further requested to borrow ten thousand rolls of silk damask from the Zuǒcáng Treasury.
Tàizǔ (Emperor Tàizǔ) reluctantly agreed to all requests.
He then requested to use Pín Kàn and Chén Tóng to replace Lǐ Gǔ and Fàn Zhì as Chancellors.
Tàizǔ said:
"The dismissal or appointment of a Chancellor,
how can it be done hastily?
We must deliberate upon this slowly."
Jùn argued and requested incessantly,
his language gradually becoming disrespectful.
It was high noon,
and Tàizǔ had not yet eaten.
Jùn continued to argue relentlessly.
At this time, it was the Hánshí (Cold Food Festival) holiday.
Tàizǔ said:
"Wait until the holiday is over,
and I will act on your behalf."
Only then did Jùn withdraw.
Tàizǔ was finally unable to tolerate him.
The next day, he held court in the Biàndiàn (Informal Hall),
summoned all officials to enter,
and immediately confined Jùn to a separate dwelling.
Tàizǔ saw Féng Dào,
and wept, saying:
"Jùn insulted me;
I could not endure it!"
Jùn was immediately demoted to Shāngzhōu Sīmǎ (Administrator of Shāng Prefecture),
and died at the place of banishment.
After Jùn had been dismissed,
Tàizǔ, recalling that Jùn had supervised the compilation of the Guóshǐ (History of the Dynasty),
suspected that the records he had written were inaccurate.
Consequently, he summoned the historiographers to retrieve and read the Rìlì (Daily Records).
The historiographers, believing that matters within the imperial palace were not meant to be known outside,
feared being punished for revealing secrets.
After Jùn was banished,
Lǐ Gǔ supervised the compilation.
He therefore requested that trusted retainers be ordered to record palace affairs and submit them to the Shǐguǎn (Historiography Office).

Thereupon, he ordered the Píshū Zhí Xuéshì (Scholar Directly Attached to the Bureau of Military Affairs) to record [these affairs] at the Píshūyuàn (Bureau of Military Affairs) and send them to the Shǐguǎn.
This practice began from this point.
Wáng Yīn
Wáng Yīn,
was a native of Dàmíng.
In his youth, he was a common soldier.
Due to his military merits, he was successively promoted to Língwǔ Mǎbùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (Supreme Commander of the Cavalry and Infantry of Língwǔ).
During the reign of the Deposed Emperor of Táng (Later Táng),
he followed Fàn Yánguāng to suppress Zhāng Lìngzhāo in Wèi.
For his merit, he was appointed Qízhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Qí Prefecture).
During the Tiānfú era of Jìn (Later Jìn),
he was transferred to be Yuánzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yīn was renowned for his filial piety in serving his mother.
If he wished to associate with someone,
he always informed his mother first.
If his mother disapproved,
he never dared to go.
When he became Cìshǐ,
and made a minor mistake in governance,
his mother reprimanded him.
Yīn immediately took a staff and handed it to a maidservant or attendant,
and had himself beaten in front of his mother.
When his mother died and he was observing mourning rites,
Jìn Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn) ordered Yīn to resume office,
making him Xiànzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yīn requested to complete the mourning period.
When the mourning period was over,
the Deposed Emperor (Chū Dì) appointed him Fèngguó Yòuxiāng Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (Supreme Commander of the Right Wing of the Fèngguó Army).
Later, he followed Hàn Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn) to suppress Dù Chóngwēi.
He was the first to ascend the wall and fought fiercely.
An arrow struck his head;
the arrowhead emerged from his mouth, yet he did not die.
Gāozǔ praised him,
making him Shìwèi Bùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (Supreme Commander of the Palace Guard Infantry),
concurrently serving as Níngjiāngjūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the Níngjiāng Army).
When the Qìdān violated the border,
Hàn (Later Hàn) sent Yīn with troops to garrison Chánzhōu.
After Yǐndì (Emperor Yǐn) had already killed Yáng Bīn and others,
he ordered Lǐ Hóngyì, the Zhènníngjūn Jiédùshǐ, to kill Yīn at Chánzhōu.
He also ordered Guō Chóng to kill Zhōu Tàizǔ (Emperor Tàizǔ of Zhōu) at Wèi.
When the imperial decree reached Chánzhōu,
Hóngyì, fearing that the matter would fail,
instead informed Yīn.
Yīn sent a messenger galloping to Wèi to inform Zhōu Tàizǔ,
and consequently raised an army in revolt.
When Tàizǔ entered the capital and ascended the throne,
Yīn was appointed Shìwèi Qīnjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (Supreme Commander of the Palace Guard and Imperial Army).
He was sent out to serve as Tiānxíongjūn Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Chancellor).
He still commanded the Imperial Army,
and all areas north of the Yellow River (Hé) were under Yīn's command.
Yīn was rather dedicated to accumulating wealth.
Tàizǔ heard of this and disliked it.
He sent someone to say to him:
"When I rose up in Wèi,
were the treasuries and granaries lacking in stores?
You serve the state;
that is enough."
Yīn did not listen.
Yīn and Wáng Jùn had both followed Tàizǔ when he rose up in Wèi.
After Jùn incurred guilt,
Yīn felt uneasy.
In the ninth month of autumn in the third year of Guǎngshùn (953), on the Yǒngshòu Festival,
Yīn requested to enter the capital to offer birthday congratulations.
Tàizǔ granted his request,
but fearing Yīn might be suspicious,
he subsequently sent an envoy to stop him.
The following year,
Tàizǔ performed rites at the Southern Suburb (Nánjiāo).
That winter,
Yīn came to the court.
Yīn held military power;
his duty was security and protection.
Whenever he went out or came in, he was often accompanied by troops.
He also requested arms and armor,
in preparation for unforeseen events.
At this time,
Tàizǔ was confined to bed by illness.
He suspected Yīn had ulterior motives.
He therefore forced himself, despite his illness, to hold court in the Zīdé Diàn (Zīdé Palace).
When Yīn entered to pay respects,
Tàizǔ immediately ordered his arrest,
stripped him of all his current offices and titles,
and banished him permanently to Dēngzhōu.
Soon after, he had him executed,
and relocated his family members to Dēngzhōu.
Líu Cí
Líu Cí, courtesy name Hǎoqiān,
was a native of Yuánchéng, Dàmíng.
In his youth, he served Yáng Shīhòu.
He was famous for his bravery and ferocity.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng (Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng) besieged Wèibó,
and fought Lǐang (Later Liáng) along the river (Jiā Hé),
Cí was made Xiàojié Jūnshǐ (Commander of the Demonstrated Loyalty Army) for his military merits.
He was promoted to Chángjiàn Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander of the Long Swords).
Due to an offense, he was demoted to Rǔzhōu for more than ten years.
During the reign of the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì),
an imperial decree ordered all prefectures and commanderies to select the valiant and brave to serve in the Imperial Guards (Jìnjūn).
Cí was selected to be an officer in the Jìnjūn.
He followed campaigns that defeated Zhāng Cóngbīn and Yáng Guāngyuǎn.
For his merit, he was promoted to Fèngguó Dìyī Jūn Dōuyúhòu (Supreme Marshal of the First Fèngguó Army).
He followed Mǎ Quánjié in defeating Ānzhōu.
For his merit, he was promoted to Zhǐhuīshǐ (Commander).
He followed Dù Chóngwēi in defeating Zhènzhōu.
For being the first to ascend the wall, he was appointed Bìzhōu Cìshǐ.
When the Jìn army suppressed Ān Cóngjìn,
he served as Xiāngzhōu Xíngyíng Dūyúhòu (Supreme Marshal of the Xiāng Prefecture Field Command).
For his merit, he was promoted to Bìzhōu Tuánliànshǐ (Militia Commissioner of Bì Prefecture).
He was transferred to Fángzhōu.
For over a year,
his administration was not harsh or oppressive,
and the people found it quite convenient.
On days of leisure, Cí
habitually wore armor, using a spear as a pillow while sleeping.
He said to others:
"I achieved wealth and honor through this;
how can I forget it for even a single day?
Moreover, human nature is easily accustomed [to ease].
If I once slacken my physical strength,
how shall I repay the state if trouble arises!"
During the reign of Hàn Gāozǔ,
he was again made Fèngguó Yòuxiāng Dūzhǐhuīshǐ.
When the Hàn army suppressed Lǐ Shǒuzhēn at Hézhōng,
Cí, as Shìwèi Bùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ concurrently serving as Níngjiāngjūn Jiédùshǐ,
was appointed Xíngyíng Dūyúhòu (Supreme Marshal of the Field Command).
For his merit, he was appointed Zhènguójūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ entered the capital and ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
He successively governed Ānguó and Héyáng Sānchéng (three prefectures).
When Shìzōng (Emperor Shìzōng) fought at Gāopíng,
the armies of Fán Àinéng and others were defeated and fled south.
They met Cí and stopped him, saying:
"The army is defeated!
You should not advance further."
Cí did not listen.
He immediately urged his troops forward to advance.
Shìzōng praised him,
and made him Suíjià Dūbùshǔ (Supreme Commander Accompanying the Emperor).
When the army returned,
he was appointed Hédōng Xíngyíng Fù Dūbùshǔ (Deputy Supreme Commander of the Hédōng Field Command),
and transferred to govern Yǒngxīng.
The following year, he died at his post,
aged sixty-five.
He was posthumously granted the title Shìzhōng (Chamberlain),
with the posthumous name Zhōnghuì.
Wáng Huán
Wáng Huán,
was a native of Zhèndìng, Zhènzhōu.
Because of his courage and strength, he served Mèng Zhīxiáng as a charioteer (Yùzhě).
When Zhīxiáng usurped the imperial title in Shǔ (Former Shǔ),
he made [Huán] command the imperial guards (Wèibīng).
During the chaos of the Kāiyùn era of Jìn (Later Jìn),
Qín, Fèng, Jiē, and Chéng Prefectures fell into the control of Shǔ.
Mèng Chǎng appointed Huán as Fèngzhōu Jiédùshǐ.
ascended the throne.
The following year,
he sent Wáng Jǐng and Xiàng Xùn to attack Qín and Fèng Zhōu.
They were repeatedly defeated by Huán.
All the high officials requested the troops be withdrawn.
Shìzōng said:
"I wish to unite all under Heaven and make it my home,
but my civilizing influence has not reached Qín and Fèng.
Now that the troops have already been dispatched,
to return without achieving merit,
I would feel ashamed."
So, he resolved to attack them.
The supply route for the Zhōu troops was quite difficult.
Chǎng sent five thousand troops out of Tángcāng, reaching Huánghuā Gǔ to contest the supply route.
Jǐng and Xùn knew of their approach beforehand.
They ordered the formation commander, Zhāng Jiànxióng, to position two thousand troops at the mouth of the valley.
Separately, they sent a vice-general with a thousand elite soldiers to emerge behind them,
ambushing them at Tángcāng to await their return.
The Shǔ troops met Jiànxióng in the front.
They were defeated in battle.
They retreated, fleeing toward Tángcāng.
The ambush was sprung,
and they were completely slaughtered.
Because of this, all the Shǔ soldiers guarding the various forts and castles dispersed.
Initially,
Chǎng had sent his Jiedushi of Qín Zhōu, Gāo Chǔchóu, with troops to reinforce Huán.
Before they arrived,
they heard that the Tángcāng troops had been defeated,
and they too dispersed and returned.
Chǔchóu’s Administrator (Pànguān), Zhào Pín, closed the city gates and refused to let him enter.
Chǔchóu then fled to Chéngdū.
Pín then surrendered the city.
Chéng and Jiē Zhōu subsequently also surrendered.
Only Huán held out staunchly for more than a hundred days,
before they were finally overcome.
Shìzōng summoned Huán for an audience,
and sighed, saying:
"The three prefectures have already surrendered,
but Huán alone held fast to his defense.
I repeatedly sent letters inviting his surrender,
but Huán did not reply.
Even when his strength was exhausted and he was captured,
although he was unable to die,
he was faithful to those whom he served.
Employing him can encourage those who serve their lords."
Thereupon, he appointed Huán as General of the Right Valiant Guard (Yòu Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn).
At this time,
the Zhōu army was already campaigning against Huái (Huáinán).
He immediately appointed Huán to assist Hóu Zhāng as Vice Commander (Fù Bùshǔ) for the assault and capture of the enemy city water defenses.
Originally,
when the Zhōu army campaigned southward,
Lǐ Jǐng arrayed troops along the Huái River.
Their naval vessels were very numerous.
The Zhōu army lacked the equipment for naval warfare.
Shìzōng was concerned about this.
Therefore, he established a ship construction bureau west of the capital city (Jīngchéng).
They built several hundred warships.
He recruited captured soldiers who had surrendered from Jǐng,
and taught them naval warfare.
The following year,
Shìzōng campaigned against Huái again.
He ordered Huán to command several thousand naval troops,
entering the Huái River via the Cài Hé.
Huán resided among the troops,
but had not achieved any battle merits.
Shǔ soldiers captured along with Huán,
Shìzōng did not execute.
He incorporated all of them into the army.
Later, many fled south to Jǐng.
Shìzōng treated Huán even more trustingly.
Soon after, Jǐng's generals Xǔ Wénzhěn, Biān Hào, and others were all captured.
Shìzōng appointed all of them as generals,
giving them residences in the capital (Jīngshī) alongside Huán and others.
Yearly gifts and provisions were very generous.
The following year, he again journeyed to Huáinán,
and again brought Huán along.
Huán fell ill,
and died in Sì Zhōu.
Zhé Cóngruǎn
Zhé Cóngruǎn’s courtesy name was Kějiǔ.
His original name was Cóngyuǎn.
To avoid the personal name of Hàn Gāozǔ,
he changed it to Ruǎn.
He was a man from Yúnzhōng.
His father, Sìlún,
was the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Lín Zhōu.
Cóngruǎn’s character was
gentle, respectful, and elder-like.
While observing mourning for his father,
he became known for his filial piety.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng was stationed in Tàiyuán,
he made him a Yajiang (Camp General).
Later, he made him the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Fǔ Zhōu.
When Jìn Chūdì broke the alliance with the Qìdān,
Cóngruǎn used troops to attack the Qìdān,
capturing more than ten of their forts and castles.
He was promoted to Training Commissioner (Tuánliànshǐ) of his prefecture,

and concurrently held the posts of Cìshǐ of Shuò Zhōu, Protector-General of Anbei (Ānběi Dūhù), Jiedushi of Zhènwǔ Army (Zhènwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ), and Supreme Commander of the Infantry and Cavalry (Mǎbù Jūn Dū Yúhòu) for the Campaign Headquarters on the Southwestern Front against the Qìdān.
When Hàn Gāozǔ entered and established the dynasty,
he established the Yǒng'ān Army in Fǔ Zhōu,
and appointed Cóngruǎn as Jiedushi.
The following year,
he ordered his clan to pay court in the capital (Jīngshī).
He transferred the administration to Wǔshèng.
Immediately, he appointed Cóngruǎn's son, Déyǐ, as Training Commissioner of Fǔ Zhōu.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ entered and established the dynasty,
Cóngruǎn was successively transferred to the three commands of Xuānyì, Bǎoyì, and Jìngnán.
In Xiǎndé second year (955 CE),
he was dismissed and returned to the capital (Jīngshī).
He died when he reached Luòyáng.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor (Zhōngshū Lìng).
Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter 39: Zhū Shǒuyīn
Zhū Shǒuyīn,
served Táng Zhuāngzōng as a slave when young.
His name was Huì’ér.
When Zhuāngzōng studied,
Huì’ér always waited upon him.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he made his personal attendants into the Army of the Perpetual Guard (Chángzhí Jūn).
He appointed Shǒuyīn as the commander of that army.
Therefore, he had never been employed in battle.
However, he liked to speak of people's private secrets and faults to ingratiate himself.
Zhuāngzōng considered him loyal,
and promoted him to Supreme Commander (Dū Yúhòu) of the Barbarian and Chinese Infantry and Cavalry,
sending him to defend Déshèng.
When Wáng Yànzhāng attacked Déshèng,
Shǒuyīn was unprepared.
The south city was thus breached.
Zhuāngzōng said:
"A talentless donkey,
indeed ruined my affairs!"
Míngzōng requested that Shǒuyīn be punished according to military law,
but Zhuāngzōng refused to listen.
In Tóngguāng second year (924 CE),
he was appointed Jiedushi of the Zhènwǔ Army.
At this time,
Zhuāngzōng had just entered Luò.
Shǒuyīn served as Inspector and Supervisor of the capital (Jīngshī).
Relying on the emperor’s favor, he was arrogant and reckless,
insulting and slighting meritorious veterans.
He formed a close alliance with the actor Jǐng Jìn.
After Prince of Wèi, Jìjí, had already killed Guō Chóngtāo,
Jǐn falsely accused Zhū Yǒuqiān of plotting rebellion with Chóngtāo.
Zhuāngzōng sent Shǒuyīn to surround his residence and kill him.
At this time,
Míngzōng came to court from Zhèn Zhōu,
and stayed in his private residence.
Zhuāngzōng, being then misled by petty men,
was suspicious of high officials.
He sent Shǒuyīn to spy on Míngzōng's movements.
Shǒuyīn secretly sent someone to tell Míngzōng:
"He whose rank surpasses all officials faces personal danger.
He whose merit covers the world goes unrewarded.
You, Lord, can be said to have high rank and manifest merit.
You should plan for your return to your own territory.
Do not meet disaster!"
Míngzōng replied:
"I am merely a common man in Luòyáng.
What can I possibly do!"
Soon after, Míngzōng finally rebelled at Wèi.
Zhuāngzōng campaigned eastward.
Shǒuyīn commanded the cavalry, forming ranks outside Xuānrén Mén to await the emperor’s carriage.
Guō Cóngqiān started the uprising,
breaching the Xīngjiào Mén to enter.
Zhuāngzōng urgently summoned Shǒuyīn's forces,
but Shǒuyīn held his troops still.
Zhuāngzōng, accompanied only by the princes and more than a hundred eunuchs, shot at the rebels.
Shǒuyīn and his troops never arrived.
They were relocating their troops to rest at the foot of Běimáng Shān.
When they heard that Zhuāngzōng had died,
Shǒuyīn immediately rode into the palace,
selecting and loading imperial consorts and treasures to take back.
He allowed his soldiers to loot and plunder.
He sent men to urge Míngzōng to enter Luò.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Shǒuyīn as Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì), Prefect of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn), and Commissioner overseeing the Six Armies and all Guards (Pàn Liùjūn Zhūwèi Shì).
The following year,
he was transferred to Jiedushi of the Xuānwǔ Army.
In the ninth month,
Míngzōng decreed that he would visit Biàn Zhōu.
Discussions among officials were noisy.
Some believed he was campaigning against Wú,
others thought that a powerful vassal in the east had become defiant,
and he was going to deal with him.
Shǒuyīn felt particularly uneasy.
Therefore, he killed the Commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ), Mǎ Yànchāo,
closed the gates, and rebelled.
Míngzōng traveled until he reached Jīng Shuǐ.
When he heard that Shǒuyīn had rebelled,
he sent Fàn Yánguāng to rush troops to the city walls.
The people of Biàn opened the gates and admitted Yánguāng.
Shǒuyīn killed his own clan,
and then stretched out his neck, ordering his attendants to execute him.
When Míngzōng arrived at Biàn Zhōu,
he ordered that his corpse be whipped,
his head exposed in the marketplace for seven days,
and then sent to be displayed in Luòyáng.
was about to rebel,
he summoned the Commander-in-Chief Mǎ Yànchāo to scheme with him.
Yànchāo refused to comply,
so Shǒuyīn killed him.
Míngzōng pitied Yànchāo's death,
and made his son Chéngzuò the Magistrate (Zhǎngshǐ) of Míngzhōu.
Dǒng Zhāng.
Dǒng Zhāng's
family background is unknown.
In his youth, along with Gāo Jìxīng and Kǒng Xún, he was a household servant (jiātóng) for the rich Bìanzhōu man Lǐ Ràng.
When Liáng Tàizǔ was garrisoned at Xuānwǔ,
he adopted Ràng as his son,
who became Zhū Yǒuràng.
Because of Yǒuràng,
all his servants and slaves were able to serve Liáng Tàizǔ.
Zhāng became a commander (Zhǐhuīshǐ) through military merit.
When Jìn's Lǐ Jìtāo rebelled with Lùzhōu and surrendered to Liáng,
Mòdì sent Zhāng to attack and conquer Zézhōu,
immediately appointing Zhāng as its Prefect (Cìshǐ).
After Liáng perished,
Zhāng served Táng as the Jìedùshǐ of Bīnnìng,
and was friendly with Guō Chóngtāo.
When Chóngtāo campaigned against Shǔ,
he made Zhāng the Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry of the Right Flank (Xíngyíng Yòuxiāng Mǎbùjūn Dōu Yúhòu) for the field army.
All military matters, whether major or minor,
he participated in deciding.
After Shǔ was pacified,
Zhāng was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Jiànnán Dōngchuān,
while Mèng Zhīxiáng was stationed at Xīchuān.
Thereafter,
the two men developed rebellious intentions.
Ān Chónghuǐ wielded power from the court.
Many advisors said that Zhīxiáng certainly would not serve Táng,
but that Zhāng was the one who could control Zhīxiáng.
They often praised Zhāng for his loyalty and righteousness.
Chónghuǐ believed this to be true,
and greatly favored and promoted him,
thus Zhāng became increasingly arrogant.
In the fourth year of Tiānchéng
(929 CE), Míngzōng performed the Heaven Worship ceremony in the Southern Suburbs.
An edict ordered the Two Chuān (Liǎngchuān) regions to contribute 500,000 items to aid the Southern Suburbs ceremony.
He sent Lǐ Rénjǔ carrying a letter from Ān Chónghuǐ to admonish Zhāng.
Zhāng complained and was unwilling to produce the full amount,
only providing 100,000.
Moreover, due to a certain matter, he intended to kill Rénjǔ.
Rénjǔ was spared by weeping profusely,
and upon returning, he reported that Zhāng would surely rebel.
Subsequently, when envoys reached Dōngchuān,
Zhāng became even more haughty and disrespectful.
When the envoys returned,
many reported that Zhāng intended to rebel.
Chónghuǐ was concerned about this,
and gradually selected generals and officials to serve as Prefects (Cìshǐ) in the Two Chuān regions,
assigning elite troops as their personal guards,
distributing them among the various prefectures.
Furthermore, he divided Làngzhōu to establish the Bǎoníng Army,
appointing Rénjǔ as its Jìedùshǐ.
He sent Yáo Hóng with a thousand soldiers to accompany Rénjǔ and garrison Làngzhōu.
Zhāng and Zhīxiáng sensed that Táng suspected them
and was restricting their territory.
Consequently, they plotted together to rebel.
Zhāng immediately arranged for his son to marry Zhīxiáng's daughter to solidify their alliance.
He also sent his general Lǐ Yànzhāo to block Jiànménguān (Sword Gate Pass), building seven stockades there,
and established an additional pass north of Jiànménguān,
named Yǒngdìng.
Any Táng garrison soldiers
attempting to return east were intercepted and detained.
Those who were captured while attempting to escape
were covered with iron cages
and roasted over fire,
or they had flesh cut from them and their faces nailed,
or their hearts cut out and eaten.
In the ninth month of the first year of Chángxīng (930 CE),
Zhīxiáng attacked and captured Suìzhōu,
and Zhāng attacked and captured Làngzhōu,
seizing Lǐ Rénjǔ and Yáo Hóng,
and killing them both.
Initially,
when Zhāng and others rebelled,
Táng only executed Zhāng's family members.
Zhīxiáng's wife and children were all in Chéngdū,
and his distant relatives remaining in the capital were not executed.
Shí Jìngtáng campaigned against Zhāng and the others,
but after a long time, the troops achieved no success.
Furthermore, supplies west of the passes were insufficient,
exhausting the people near and far.
Míngzōng worried about this.
Ān Chónghuǐ personally went to supervise the army,
but Jìngtáng did not accept him.
Chónghuǐ was subsequently disgraced and died,
and Jìngtáng also returned.
Míngzōng then sent Sū Yuàn, the Xīchuān memorial officer, and Liú Chéng, the Dōngchuān military commander, west to return,
to admonish Zhāng and the others to reform their ways.
Zhīxiáng sent someone to inform Zhāng
that he wished to apologize and surrender together.
Zhāng said:
"Táng did not kill Lord Mèng's family.
Their favor toward Xīchuān is generous.
Where are my descendants?
What is there to apologize for!"
Because of this, Zhāng suspected Zhīxiáng of betraying him.
In the fourth month of the third year [of Chángxīng, 932 CE],
he attacked Zhīxiáng with ten thousand troops.
They fought at Mímóu,
where Zhāng was routed,
and fled back to Zǐzhōu.
Previously,
Wáng Huī, the Táng Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Língzhōu, was returning upon being replaced, and passed by Zhāng.
Zhāng invited him to stay.
When this occurred,
Huī seized Zhāng and killed him,
sending his head to Zhīxiáng.
Fàn Yánguāng.
Fàn Yánguāng, courtesy name Zǐguī,
was a native of Línzhāng, Xiāngzhōu.
When Táng Míngzōng was a Jìedùshǐ,
he placed Yánguāng under his command,
but did not yet regard him highly.
Míngzōng captured Yùnzhōu,
and the Liáng forces were blocking Yángliǔ.
Their vanguard general, Kāng Yánxiào, secretly sent overtures of surrender to Míngzōng.
Míngzōng sought someone who could convey Yánxiào’s message to Zhuāngzōng.
Yánguāng immediately volunteered to go.
He carried Yánxiào's message, written in a wax pellet,
went west to meet Zhuāngzōng and delivered it.
He also said:
"Although Yánxiào now has the intention to surrender,
the Liáng troops blocking Yángliǔ are very numerous,
and they cannot yet be challenged.
It would be better to build a fortification at Mǎjiākǒu to secure Wènyáng."
Zhuāngzōng agreed.
When the fort was completed,
Liáng sent Wáng Yànzhāng to urgently attack the new fort.
Míngzōng sent Yánguāng on a secret mission to request troops.
He reached the riverbank at night
and was captured by the Liáng troops.
He was sent to the capital (Jīngshī),
and Yánguāng was imprisoned.
He was beaten hundreds of times
and threatened with bare blades,
but Yánguāng ultimately refused to disclose matters concerning Jìn.
He was imprisoned for several months,
gradually gaining the protection of the jailers.
When Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
the jailers removed his fetters
and released him after bowing.
Zhuāngzōng saw Yánguāng,
was delighted,
and appointed him Director of the Ministry of Works (Jiǎnxiào Gōngbù Shàngshū).
During Míngzōng's reign,
he served as the Commissioner of the Southern Court of the Privy Council (Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ).
When Míngzōng traveled to Bìanzhōu,
reaching Xíngyáng,
Zhū Shǒuyīn rebelled.
Yánguāng said:
"Shǒuyīn's signs of rebellion have just appeared.
If we delay and allow him to make preparations,
the city will become fortified and hard to approach.
Therefore,
nothing is better than taking advantage of his unpreparedness and attacking immediately.
I request five hundred cavalry
to ride rapidly to the base of the city
and shock them with divine speed."
accordingly, he took five hundred cavalry
and galloped rapidly from dusk until midnight,
traveling two hundred *lǐ*,
and fought below the city walls.
At dawn,
Míngzōng also rode up rapidly.
When the Bìan troops saw the Son of Heaven's carriage,
they opened the gate.
Yánguāng entered first,
and there was still fighting in the alleys,
resulting in many deaths and injuries.
Shǒuyīn died,
and Bìanzhōu was pacified.
The next year,
he was transferred to be the Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs),
and then went out to serve as the Jiéduūshǐ of Chéngdé Army.
After Ān Chónghuǐ died,
Yán'guāng was again recalled to serve as Shūmìshǐ, alongside Zhào Yánshòu.
Míngzōng asked Yán'guāng how many horses he had.
He replied:
"Thirty-five thousand cavalry."
Míngzōng patted his thigh and sighed, saying:
"I have been amidst war for forty years.
Since the time Tàizǔ was in Tàiyuán,
the number of horses did not exceed seven thousand.
When Zhuāngzōng took Héběi
and fought the Liáng family by the river,
there were only ten thousand horses.
Now we have thirty-five thousand horses and yet cannot unite All Under Heaven.
I am old,
what good is having so many horses!"
Yán'guāng then said:
"Your servant once calculated
that the expense of one horse
could support five foot soldiers.
Thirty-five thousand horses
is the provision for one hundred and seventy-five thousand soldiers."
Míngzōng said:
"We fatten our warhorses while our people are thin—
this is what shames me!"
Lǐ Rénfú of Xiàzhōu died,
and his son Yíchāo established himself and demanded the official banners and staffs (máojié).
Míngzōng sent Ān Cóngjìn to replace him,
but Yíchāo refused the replacement.
An army was sent to attack him,
but for a long time, it could not overcome him.
Liú Suìnìng, the Prefect of Xízhōu, rode in post haste to have an audience and present a strategy,
saying that the people of Suī and Yín prefectures
all had intentions of turning inwards (submitting),
and he requested that the two prefects be dismissed to encourage their surrender.
Yán'guāng said:
"The imperial army’s mission to punish the crime
is primarily aimed at Yíchāo.
Once Xiàzhōu is defeated,
how can Suī and Yín be worth considering!
If Xiàzhōu is not defeated,
even if we obtain Suī and Yín,
we will not be able to hold them."
Suìnìng then requested to personally ride in and persuade Yíchāo to come out and surrender.
Yán'guāng said:
"If we lose one Suìnìng,
it is not regrettable should the worst happen,
but what is regrettable is the integrity of the imperial court."
At this time,
Consort Wáng Shūfēi was powerful;
Suìnìng and his brothers had a prior connection with the Consort,
and they relied on her to receive imperial favor and honor.
Whatever they said was always listened to,
and because of the Consort, many high officials
did not dare to argue.
Only Yán'guāng calmly dissuaded and stopped him.
Míngzōng became ill
and could not hold court.
The people in the capital, Jīngshī,
were agitated and had divergent opinions,
hiding and fleeing into mountains and valleys,
or seeking refuge in military camps.
The officials concerned could not prevent this.
Some advised Yán'guāng to control them with strict laws.
Yán'guāng said:
"To control movement, one must use stillness.
We should wait a little."
After a while, Míngzōng's illness slightly improved,
and the capital finally settled down.
At this time,
the Prince of Qín held military power and was extremely arrogant,
while the Prince of Sòng was weak and moreover stationed outside.
Many commentators favored the Prince of Lù.
Yán'guāng feared that disaster might befall him,
so he requested to be relieved and retire.
Yánshòu secretly perceived that Yán'guāng intended to avoid disaster,
and also hurriedly requested to be relieved.
Míngzōng pleaded with them repeatedly to stay,
but the two men's pleas for resignation became increasingly earnest,
followed by tears.
Míngzōng had no choice
but to relieve both of them.
Yán'guāng returned to govern Chéngdé,
and Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yūn were appointed as Shūmìshǐ.
Afterwards, the Prince of Qín raised troops and was executed;
Míngzōng died,
the Prince of Lù rebelled,
killed Emperor Mǐn,
and the Táng court fell into great chaos.
Hóngzhāo and Yūn were both caught in the disaster and died.
The Last Emperor (Mòdì) again issued an edict appointing Yán'guāng as Shūmìshǐ
and granted him the title of Jiéduūshǐ of Xuānwǔ Army.
When Tiānxióng Army mutinied
and drove out the Jiéduūshǐ Liú Yánhào,
Yán'guāng was sent to suppress and pacify it,
and was immediately made the Jiéduūshǐ of Tiānxióng Army.
Yán'guāng often dreamed of a large snake entering his belly through his navel,
which was half-in when it was pulled out.
He asked the diviner Zhāng Shēng, who was amongst his retainers,
about it.
Zhāng Shēng praised him, saying:
"A snake
is a type of dragon. Entering the belly
is a sign of kingship."
Since the time Yán'guāng was obscure,
Zhāng Shēng had predicted that he would certainly become noble.
Yán'guāng had always regarded him as divinely inspired
and kept him among his retainers;
his predictions often came true.
Yán'guāng therefore took his words as truth
and consequently harbored unconventional ambitions.
When Jìn Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán,
the Last Emperor sent Yán'guāng with twenty thousand troops to garrison Liáozhōu,
to form a pincer movement with Zhào Yánshòu.
However, Yánshòu defected first,
and Yán'guāng alone did not surrender.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Yán'guāng's congratulatory memorial arrived significantly later than those of the other feudal lords,
and furthermore, his daughter was the consort of the Last Emperor's son, Chóngměi.
Because of this, he harbored rebellious sentiments.
Gāozǔ enfeoffed Yán'guāng as the Prince of Línqīng to reassure him.
There was a man from Píngshān named Bì Qióng,
who served as the commander of the Inner Prefecture (Yánèi Zhǐhuīshǐ) under Dǒng Wēnqí, the Jiéduūshǐ of Chéngdé Army.
Later, when Wēnqí was captured by the Qìdān,
Qióng killed Wēnqí's entire family,
buried them in one pit,
and took possession of their family wealth, amounting to tens of millions.
When Jìn Gāozǔ came to power,
he appointed Qióng as the Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Qízhōu.
Qióng carried his vast wealth
and passed through Wèi territory on the road.
Yán'guāng secretly sent someone with a letter to lure him,
but Qióng did not comply.
Yán'guāng became angry
and selected soldiers to lie in ambush on the border.
They watched for Qióng's passing,
killed him at Xiàjīn,
took all his wealth,
and reported it as a mistaken killing by the patrolling soldiers.
Because of this, Gāozǔ suspected that he would certainly cause rebellion,
and therefore went to Biànzhōu.
In the sixth month of Tiānfú 2 (937 CE),
Yán'guāng finally rebelled.
He sent his staff general Sūn Ruì and Chénzhōu Prefect Féng Huī
with twenty thousand troops to resist at Líyáng,
and plunder Huá and Wèi.
Gāozǔ appointed Yáng Guāngyuǎn as the Commander-in-Chief (Zhāotǎoshǐ),
who led the army and crossed Húliáng from Huázhōu to attack him.
Ruì was reckless, frivolous, and without strategy;
when the army marched, he had over ten singing girls accompanying him.
He held up a parasol and waved a fan,
singing heartily, eating, and drinking as usual.
The soldiers suffered greatly from the intense heat
and were all unwilling to fight for him.
Guāngyuǎn captured a spy
and learned their plan.
He lured Ruì and others across the river,
and attacked them when they were half-way across.
Many soldiers drowned.
Ruì and Huī retreated into Wèi
and barricaded themselves, refusing to come out.
Initially,
Yán'guāng was undecided about rebelling
but fell seriously ill and could not get up.
Ruì then secretly summoned Huī into the city
and forced Yán'guāng to rebel.
Yán'guāng was confused and frightened,
and subsequently followed them.
When Gāozǔ heard that Yán'guāng was using Ruì and the others to rebel,
he laughed and said:
"Although I am not mighty in war,
I once followed Míngzōng to conquer All Under Heaven,
attacking strongholds and defeating powerful foes many times.
Someone like Yán'guāng is already no match for me,
let alone the child's play of Ruì and the others?
We will take this child soon!"
Thus, he resolved to suppress him.
Fàn Yán'guāng initially had no intention of rebelling.
After Ruì and the others were defeated,
Yán'guāng sent his staff commander, Wáng Zhīxīn, bearing a memorial to surrender.
Gāozǔ refused to see him
and sent Zhīxīn to the Wǔdé Office.
Yán'guāng then attached a memorial requesting surrender to Yáng Guāngyuǎn.
He received no reply,
and Yán'guāng consequently held firm in his defense.
The Jìn shot two hundred messages attached to arrows into the city,
pardoning all the Wèi people,
and offering rewards to anyone who could kill Yán'guāng.
However, the city of Wèi was strong and difficult to capture;
the attack lasted over a year without success.
The army was exhausted and food supplies were running out.
Shí Áng, Assistant Secretary of the Imperial Clan Court, submitted a memorial offering the strongest remonstrance,
requesting Yán'guāng be pardoned,
and volunteering to enter the city alone in a plain carriage to persuade him to surrender.
Gāozǔ also felt regret and became enlightened.
In the ninth month of the third year [of Tiānfú],
he sent an usher into Wèi to pardon Yán'guāng.
Yán'guāng then surrendered.
He was officially titled Prince of Dōngpíng Commandery and Military Governor of Tiānpíng Circuit,
and was granted an iron certificate (tiějuàn).
A few months later, he came to court.
Feeling ashamed, he requested retirement,
and was made Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàishī) and allowed to retire.
Initially,
when Gāozǔ pardoned the surrendering Yán'guāng,
he spoke to the envoy, telling him:
“I promise you will not be executed.
If I kill him after he surrenders,
how can I rule the country?”
Yán'guāng consulted with his Deputy, Lǐ Shì.
Shì said:
“The Sovereign is sincere in his trustworthiness and clear in his righteousness.
If he promises you will not die,
then you will not die.”
Thereupon, he surrendered.
When he retired and resided in the capital,
he was invited to feasts and granted audiences seasonally.
Gāozǔ treated him equally with the other ministers,
but secretly did not want him to remain in the capital.
After more than a year,
Gāozǔ sent Liú Chùràng, the Commissioner of the Palace Gate and Arms, carrying wine, to visit Yán'guāng at night.
He said:
“When His Majesty sent Chùràng here,
it happened that a Qìdān envoy had just arrived.
The emperor of the Northern Court asked where Jìn’s rebel minister in Wèibó was.
He fears that Jìn cannot control him
and says that we should chain him up and bring him here
to prevent him from becoming a future trouble for the Central States.”
Yán'guāng wept upon hearing this,
not knowing what to do.
Chùràng said:
“You should go to Luòyáng for now
to avoid the Qìdān envoy.”
Yán'guāng said:
“Yáng Guāngyuǎn is serving as the Resident-General of Hénán.
He is my enemy.
I have property and residences in Héyáng.
Can I go there?”
Chùràng said:
“You may.”
Thereupon, Yán'guāng gathered his treasury and returned to Héyáng.
His traveling baggage filled the roads.
Guāngyuǎn, coveting his wealth,
indeed planned against him.
He then presented a memorial, saying:
“Yán'guāng is a fickle and treacherous minister.
If you do not deal with him,
he will either flee north to the Hú or south to Wúyuè.
I request that he be confined in Luòyáng.”
Gāozǔ hesitated and could not decide.
Guāngyuǎn concurrently governed Héyáng,
and his son, Chéngxūn, managed the prefectural affairs there.
Guāngyuǎn then sent Chéngxūn with troops to coerce Yán'guāng into committing suicide.
Yán'guāng said:
“The Son of Heaven granted me an iron certificate
and promised I would not die.
How can this happen?”
Chéngxūn then had brave soldiers drive him onto a horse.
When they reached the pontoon bridge,
they pushed him into the water, where he drowned.
They reported that Yán'guāng had thrown himself into the water and died,
and subsequently seized all his wealth.
Gāozǔ, deeming this consistent with his own wishes,
did not inquire further.
He suspended court sessions in mourning for him
and granted him the posthumous title of Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
Cáo Qiān, the Military Commissioner for Water Transport, found his floating corpse at Miùjiātān.
An edict permitted his return and burial in Xiāngzhōu.
After the burial,
the tomb frequently collapsed,
breaking his coffin and casket,
and his skull fragments were scattered.
Previously,
Mì Qióng killed Dǒng Wēnqí and seized his wealth.
Then Yán'guāng killed Qióng and seized his wealth.
And ultimately, Yán'guāng was killed by Guāngyuǎn because of his wealth.
Yet Guāngyuǎn himself could not escape misfortune either.
When Yán'guāng rebelled,
there was a man named Lǐ Yànxún,
who served as the Military Commandant of Héyáng.
When Zhāng Cóngbīn rebelled in Héyáng,
Yànxún joined him.
When Cóngbīn was defeated,
Yànxún fled to Wèi.
Yán'guāng made him Superintendent of the Infantry,
and assigned him to defend the city.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn, the Commissioner of Recruitment and Pacification, knew that Yànxún was from Xíngzhōu,
and that his mother was still alive.
He therefore sent men to Xíngzhōu,
brought the mother to the base of the city wall,
and showed her to Yànxún to induce him to surrender.
Yànxún looked down and saw her,
then shot and killed her himself.
When Yán'guāng surrendered,
Jìn Gāozǔ appointed Yànxún as Prefect of Fángzhōu.
The high ministers argued that Yànxún should be executed for killing his mother.
Gāozǔ held that the amnesty order had already been issued,
and trustworthiness could not be breached.
Later, he was executed for corruption.
Alas,
how profound
is the human tendency toward habituation!
Therefore, the methods used by the sages regarding benevolence and righteousness are deeply intricate.
In their teaching,
they labor without being weary,
proceed slowly without forcing haste,
wishing the people to gradually become accustomed and spontaneously follow them,
until they are comfortable with them and they become established customs.
Yet, when the people are ignorant,
if they habitually see good, they are content to do good;
if they habitually see evil, they are content to do evil.
The chaos of the Five Dynasties
had roots that went far back.
Since the decline of the Táng,
with wars and famines,
fathers could not raise their children,
and children could not support their parents.
Initially,
inability for kin to protect each other
came from misfortune.
Because of this, ritual and righteousness were daily abandoned,
and affection and love became daily thinner.
The habituation lasted long and ultimately led to great decay,
to the point where father and son
mutually harmed each other.
During the time of the Five Dynasties,
the calamities cannot be fully recounted.
By human nature, there is no one who does not know to love their parents,
and no one who does not know to despise lack of filial piety.
Yet Yànxún bent his bow and shot his mother,
and Gāozǔ proceeded to pardon him.
Not only did Yànxún himself not recognize this as a great evil,
but Gāozǔ also felt comfortable with it and did not consider it strange.
Is this not the result of prolonged accumulated habituation?
The saying goes:
“Natures are close;
habits make them far apart.”
Carried to the extreme,
it makes human hearts worse than birds and beasts.
Is this not lamentable!
If an evil like Yànxún’s
was accepted calmly and not regarded as strange,
then Jìn Chūdì’s abandonment of his father
was naturally viewed by the entire world as not being wrong.
Lóu Jìyīng
Lóu Jìyīng
was of unknown origin.
He served through the Liáng and Táng dynasties,
as Prefect of Jiàng and Jì Prefectures, Commissioner of Water and Land Transport for the Northern Front, and Regimental Commander of Yàozhōu.
During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ,
he was General-in-chief of the Left Gānmén Guard.
Jìyīng’s son’s wife
was Wēn Yánzhǎo’s daughter.
Since Míngzōng’s time, when her father, Tāo, was executed,
Yánzhǎo and his brothers had been banished to reside in Xǔzhōu,
and their hearts constantly harbored resentment.
When Fàn Yán'guāng rebelled,
Jìyīng had a younger brother who was the City Commander of the inner walled city of Wèizhōu.
Yán'guāng sent a messenger with a wax-sealed letter to recruit Jìyīng.
Jìyīng then sent Yánzhǎo to enter Wèi to see Yán'guāng.
Yán'guāng was greatly pleased,
and gave him an authorization arrow,
ordering him to secretly plan for Xǔzhōu.
Yánzhǎo, with his younger brothers Yánjùn and Yángǔn, recruited a thousand desperate men,
and set a date to attack Xǔzhōu.
However, Cháng Cóngjiǎn, the Military Governor of Xǔzhōu, because of Yán'guāng’s rebellion,
suspected that there might be sympathizers,
and maintained very strict preparations.
Before Yánzhǎo could launch the attack,
Yán'guāng’s wax letter matter was revealed in the capital.
Jìyīng was greatly frightened and felt insecure,
and fled to Xǔzhōu.
Gāozǔ issued an edict to invite and comfort him,
and restore him to his position.
Jìyīng was too afraid to come out.
but Yánzhǎo, due to his daughter's relationship, could not bear to do it.
Zhāng Cóngbīn rebelled in Luòyáng.
Yánzhǎo and his brothers then fled with Jìyīng to join Cóngbīn at Sìshuǐ.
Jìyīng knew that the Wēn shì had initially wanted to kill him;
conversely, he slandered Yánzhǎo and his brothers to Cóngbīn,
and Cóngbīn killed them.
When Cóngbīn was defeated,
Jìyīng was killed by Dù Chóngwēi.
Ān Chóngróng
Ān Chóngróng,
whose childhood name (xiǎo zì) was Tiěhú,
was a man from Shuòzhōu.
His grandfather, Cóngyì,
was the Cìshǐ of Lìzhōu.
His father, Quán,
was the Cìshǐ of Shèngzhōu and the Commander of the Infantry and Cavalry of Zhènwǔ.
Chóngróng was strong,
skilled in riding and archery,
and served as the Border Patrol Commander of Zhènwǔ.
When Jìn Gāozǔ raised troops in Tàiyuán,
he sent Zhāng Yǐngyīn to recruit Chóngróng.
His mother and elder brother both thought this was inadvisable,
but Chóngróng had already agreed to Yǐngyīn's request.
His mother and brother planned to kill Yǐngyīn together to stop him,
Chóngróng said:
"Not yet.
I must divine for Mother."
He then set up an arrow [target],
shot at it from a hundred paces,
and said:
"If Shígōng becomes the Son of Heaven, it will hit."
With one shot, it hit.
He set up another arrow [target] and shot at it,
saying:
"If I become a Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ), it will hit."
With one shot, it hit again.
His mother and brother then consented,
and Chóngróng, with a thousand border patrol cavalry, defected and entered Tàiyuán.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Chóngróng as the Military Governor of Chéngdé Jūn.
Although Chóngróng was a military man,
he was knowledgeable about clerical affairs,
and his subordinates could not deceive him.
There was a couple who sued their son for being unfilial.
Chóngróng drew his sword and handed it to the father,
ordering him to kill the son himself.
The father wept and said:
"I cannot bear to!"
The mother, standing nearby, shouted abuse,
seized the sword from the father, and chased the son away.
When questioned,
she turned out to be the stepmother.
Chóngróng shouted at the stepmother to leave,
and later shot and killed her.
Chóngróng had risen from a common soldier,
and violently attained wealth and nobility.
Observing that the Deposed Emperor of Táng and Jìn Gāozǔ had both attained the realm starting from regional lords,
he often said to people:
"Does the Son of Heaven really come from a special lineage?
He is merely the one who has strong troops and sturdy horses!"
Although he harbored rebellious intentions,
he had not yet shown any outward sign.
At that time,
Gāozǔ had pledged to the Qìdān to be their 'son'.
The Qìdān became extremely arrogant,
and Gāozǔ served them ever more respectfully.
Chóngróng was furious,
holding that
"To humble the Central Plain (Zhōngguó) to elevate barbarians,
exhaust an already worn-out populace,
and satisfy an insatiable appetite [of the Qìdān]—
this is the eternal shame of Jìn!"
He repeatedly used this issue to criticize Gāozǔ.
When Qìdān envoys passed through Zhènzhōu,
Chóngróng sat cross-legged rudely,
showed them no respect,
and sometimes seized and executed them.
At this time,
the Tǔhún Bái shì were enslaved by the Qìdān
and suffered from their tyranny.
Chóngróng lured them into the passes (the interior).
The Qìdān repeatedly sent envoys to reprimand Gāozǔ
and demand the return of their [previous] envoys.
Gāozǔ bowed and lowered his head before the envoys,
accepting the criticism ever more carefully,
and offered many fine words to excuse himself,
but he tolerated Chóngróng and could not restrain him.
Subsequently, he sent the Palace Attendant Zhāng Chéng with two thousand soldiers to search for the Tǔhún in the valleys of Bīng, Zhèn, Xīn, and Dài,
and drove them all out beyond the passes.
The Tǔhún left but returned,
and Chóngróng eventually took them in.
Consequently, he gathered fugitives,
instructed the people to sow millet,
fed ten thousand horses,
and his actions became increasingly arrogant.
Due to a fit of anger, he killed Commander Jiǎ Zhāng
and falsely accused him of rebellion.
Zhāng's daughter was still young,
and Chóngróng intended to spare her.
The daughter said:
"Thirty members of my family all died by the sword;
only my father and I remained alive.
Now that my father is dead,
how can I bear to live alone?
I request to meet my death!"
Thereupon, he killed her.
The people of Zhènzhōu consequently admired the steadfastness of Jiǎ's daughter
and knew that Chóngróng was bound to fail.
As Chóngróng became increasingly ostentatious,
he thought the standard Gold Fish Pouch (Jīnyúdài) was not noble enough,
so he carved fish ornaments out of jade and wore them.
He married two wives,
and Gāozǔ, on account of this, elevated the titles and ranks of both.
In the summer of the sixth year of Tiānfú [941 CE],
the Qìdān envoy Yèlá passed through Zhènzhōu.
Chóngróng harassed and insulted him.
Yèlá spoke disrespectfully,
Chóngróng became angry,
detained Yèlá,
and used light cavalry to raid the people in the southern border of Yōuzhōu,
relocating them to Bóyě.
He submitted a memorial which read:
"Your subject recently received the news that the Pacified Tǔhún, Bái Chéngfú, Hèlián Gōngdé, and others, leading over thirty thousand households of their own clans, came fleeing from Yīngzhōu.

Furthermore, news was received that the Unpacified Tǔhún, Hún, Qìbì, and the Three Tribes of the Two Tūjué, including the leaders of the North and South, Shātuó, Ānqìng, and Jiǔfǔ, have each led their clans, cattle, sheep, wagons, tents, and armored horses, fleeing via seven or eight routes.
They fully reported the atrocities committed by the Qìdān,
who have been plundering people, sheep, and horses.
Since the second month of this year,
[the Qìdān] have issued orders to the various barbarian groups,
reviewed the strong and vigorous,
prepared military equipment,
and scheduled a southbound invasion before autumn.
The various foreign tribes sincerely feared that Heaven would not protect them
and that their clans would be destroyed,
so they wished to surrender themselves first.
The effective fighting force among these tribes totals about a hundred thousand.

Moreover, leaders of the Dǎngxiàng along the river and the various Yìyuèlì tribes both in front of and behind the mountains all sent emissaries bringing the official commissions, imperial rescripts, and banners granted by the Qìdān to offer submission.
They all wailed, declaring their grievances,
and wished to prepare their weapons and armor to avenge themselves.
Furthermore, news was received that Zhào Chóng, the Deputy Military Governor of Shuòzhōu, killed Military Governor Liú Shān
and returned with the city [to allegiance].
I humbly submit that the various foreign tribes arrived without being summoned,
and Shuòzhōu returned without being attacked—
although this relates to human sentiment,
it is entirely due to the will of Heaven.
I also recall the generals who fell into the control of the barbarians;
they were originally men of merit,
who long enjoyed wealth and rank.
Now they are trapped deep within the barbarian borders
and cannot endure the cruelty.
They look eagerly toward the Imperial Court,
and their desire to return is understandable.
If they merely hear the broadcast declaration,
they will surely turn their weapons against the enemy."
His memorial contained several thousand characters.
He also wrote letters and sent them to the high officials of the court and the regional governors (fānzhèn) in the four directions,
all arguing that the Qìdān could be conquered.
Gāozǔ was troubled by this,
and therefore went on an inspection tour to Yè.
He replied to Chóngróng, saying:
"Previous generations maintained peaceful relations with the captives [barbarians];
this was all done for the sake of the entire realm.
Now I serve them with the whole realm as their vassal,
while you resist them with just one circuit.
The disparity in strength is immense;
do not bring disgrace upon yourself!"
Chóngróng believed that Jìn could do nothing against him,
and his intention to rebel was thus finalized.
Although Chóngróng used the Qìdān issue as his rallying cry,
he secretly sent men to form an alliance with Liú Xī, the Military Governor of Yōuzhōu.
The Qìdān also welcomed the complications within Jìn,
rejoicing in Chóngróng's rebellion,
hoping to exhaust both sides.
They wished to use this opportunity to spy on the Central Plain,
and therefore did not vent their anger upon Chóngróng.
When Ān Chóngróng was about to rebel,
his mother again thought it was inadvisable.
Chóngróng said:
"I shall divine for mother."
He pointed toward the dragon's mouth on the flagpole beneath his hall and shot upward at it,
saying:
"If I am to possess the realm, then I shall hit it."
With one shot he struck it,
and his mother then permitted it.
Liú Yán, the Magistrate of Ráoyáng, presented five-colored water birds.
Chóngróng said:
"These are the Fèng."
He kept them in the rear pond.
He also had someone make and present a large iron whip.
He deceived his people, saying:
"The whip has divine power;
if pointed at a person,
that person will immediately die."
He styled
himself "Tiěbiān Lángjūn,"
and whenever he went out, he used it as his vanguard.
The iron Hú barbarian figure holding the gate in Zhènzhōu's city wall,
without cause, had its head fall off.
Tiě Hú
was Chóngróng's childhood name.
Although he greatly disliked this,
he did not realize the implication.
That winter,
Ān Cóngjìn rebelled at Xiāngyáng.
When Chóngróng heard of it,
he also raised troops.
That year,
Zhènzhōu suffered a great drought and locusts.
Chóngróng gathered several tens of thousands of famine victims,
drove them toward Yè,
and publicly announced he was entering for an audience.
When they traveled to Pòjiādī in Zōngchéng,
Gāozǔ sent Dù Chóngwēi to oppose him.
When the armies had already joined battle,
his general Zhào Yànzhī had a grudge against Chóngróng.
Facing the array, he furled his banner and fled to the Jìn army.
His armor, saddles, and reins were all decorated with silver.
The Jìn army did not know he had come to surrender,
and they fought among themselves to kill him and divide his possessions.
When Chóngróng heard that Yànzhī had surrendered to Jìn,
he became greatly fearful,
and retreated into the baggage train.
His twenty thousand troops all scattered and fled.
That winter was bitterly cold.
The fleeing soldiers, starving, frozen, and massacred, were utterly annihilated.
Chóngróng alone fled back with just over ten horsemen,
making armor out of ox and horse hides,
and driving the provincial inhabitants to defend the city and await the attack.
When Chóngwēi's army reached the city wall,
a subordinate general of Chóngróng's led the imperial army in through the Shuǐniǎn Gate on the west side of the city,
killing more than twenty thousand defenders.
Chóngróng used several hundred Tǔhún cavalry to guard the inner citadel (yáchéng).
Chóngwēi sent men to capture him,
cut off his head, and present it.
Gāozǔ received the trophy head on the imperial tower,
and ordered the head to be lacquered and sent to Qìdān.
Chéngdé Commandery was changed to Shùndé,
Zhènzhōu was named Héngzhōu,
and Chángshān was named Héngshān.
Ān Cóngjìn.
Ān Cóngjìn
was a man of the Suǒgé tribe from Zhènwǔ.
His grandfather and father both served the Táng as cavalry commanders.
Cóngjìn first followed Zhuāngzōng during the military campaigns,
serving as the Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guard Cavalry (Hùjià Mǎjūn Dūzhǐhuǐshǐ),
and concurrently holding the post of Prefect of Guìzhōu.
During Míngzōng's time,
he served as Military Commissioner (Jiéduéshǐ) of Bǎoyì and Zhāngwǔ commanderies.
He had never commanded troops on punitive expeditions.
When Lǐ Yíchāo established himself independently at Xiàzhōu,
Cóngjìn once went there with troops,
but ultimately achieved nothing.
When Mǐndì ascended the throne,
he was transferred to govern Shùnhuà,
and served as Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Cavalry Guards (Shìwèi Mǎjūn Dūzhǐhuǐshǐ).
When Prince Lù rebelled at Fèngxiáng,
Cóngjìn patrolled and inspected the capital city.
He killed the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ), Féng Yūn,
and sent a pledge of loyalty to Cóngkē.
When Emperor Mǐn fled,
and Cóngkē was about to arrive at the capital,
Cóngjìn led the officials to line up and welcome him in the suburbs.
During the Qīngtài era,
he was transferred to command Shānnán Dōngdào.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
Gāozǔ's seizure of the realm was not legitimate,
and he was often ashamed of this.
The various border garrisons were often problematic,
and he was excessively lenient with them.
Consequently, the officials in the border garrisons
were either uneasy themselves,
or admired what Gāozǔ had done,
believing that a revolt could succeed.
Therefore, during his seven years on the throne,
six rebellions arose,
with Cóngjìn being the last to revolt,
but none of them escaped punishment.
Ever since Fàn Yánguāng rebelled at Yè,
Cóngjìn had harbored rebellious intentions.
Relying on the river for defense,
he recruited and gathered fugitives
and increased his military forces.
He often arbitrarily detained
the tribute shipments from the south that passed through Xiāngyáng.
He intercepted traveling merchants
and tattooed (qíng) them all to fill his army ranks.
He secretly allied and colluded with Ān Chóngróng,
planning to support each other as horns (biǎo è).
Gāozǔ worried about this
and planned to transfer Cóngjìn.
He sent a messenger to say:
"Jiànlì, Prince of Dōngpíng, has come to court,
and wishes to return to his hometown,
so he has been transferred to Shàngdǎng.
I have emptied Qīngzhōu to await you, my Lord.
If you sincerely wish to go,
I will immediately issue the decree."
Cóngjìn replied:
"If Qīngzhōu is moved south of the Hàn River,
your subject will immediately proceed to the post."
Gāozǔ tolerated him with generosity.
His son, Ān Hóngchāo, was Vice Commissioner of Palace Parks (Gōngyuàn Fùshǐ),
residing in the capital.
Cóngjìn requested that he be granted leave to return home,
but the emperor ultimately did not send him.
Wáng Lìngqiān and Pān Zhīlín
were both garrison generals (yájiàng) under Cóngjìn.
They had served Cóngjìn for the longest time
and knew he was bound to fail,
so they offered strong remonstrance.
Cóngjìn sent his son Hóngchāo to tour Nánshān with Lìngqiān.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he ordered men to push Lìngqiān off a cliff to his death.
In the sixth year of Tiānfú (941 CE),
Ān Chóngróng seized and killed the Qìdān envoy,
revealing his intent to rebel.
Gāozǔ went to Yè because of this,
leaving Zhèng Wáng Chóngguì to guard the capital.
The Chancellor, Hé Níng, said:
"Your Majesty is heading north;
Cóngjìn will surely rebel.
How will you control him?"
Gāozǔ said:
"What are your thoughts, my Lord?"
Níng said:
"Your subject has heard in military strategy,
'He who preempts others seizes the advantage.'
I request that a dozen blank imperial decrees be handed to Prince Zhèng,
so that in an emergency he can order a general to go forth."
Cóngjìn heard that Gāozǔ was north,
and consequently killed Zhīlín and rebelled.
Prince Zhèng used the blank imperial decrees to authorize Lǐ Jiànchóng, Guō Jīnhǎi, and others to suppress the rebellion.
Cóngjìn led his troops to attack Dèngzhōu,
but failed to conquer it.
He advanced to Húyáng,
where he met Jiànchóng and the others.
He was greatly alarmed,
thinking their speed was miraculous,
and was again afflicted by wildfire,
leading to a great defeat.
Cóngjìn fled back to Xiāngyáng with several tens of horsemen.
Gāozǔ sent Gāo Xíngzhōu to surround him.
After more than a year, supplies ran out,
and Cóngjìn burned himself to death.
His son, Ān Hóngshòu, and forty-three of his general staff were captured and sent to the capital.
Gāozǔ received the captives on the imperial tower,
displayed them in the marketplace, and executed them.
Xiāngyáng was demoted to a Defensive Prefecture (fángyù).
Lìngqiān was posthumously granted the title of Prefect of Zhōngzhōu,
and Zhīlín, Prefect of Shùnzhōu.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn, courtesy name Démíng,
had a father named Ā Chuò,
and was probably a man of the Shātuó tribe.
Guāngyuǎn's initial name was Ā Tán.
He served as a cavalry commander under Táng Zhuāngzōng,
and followed Zhōu Déwēi to fight the Qìdān at Xīnzhōu,
where he broke one of his arms,
and was subsequently retired from service.
After a long time,
he was made Commander-in-Chief of the Yōuzhōu Cavalry and Infantry (Yōuzhōu Mǎbùjūn Dūzhǐhuǐshǐ),
garrisoning Wǎqiáo Pass.
Guāngyuǎn was a man afflicted by baldness and a broken arm.
He was illiterate,
but he possessed shrewd intelligence
and excelled in administrative affairs.
During Míngzōng's time,
he served as Prefect (Cìshǐ) of the four prefectures Guī, Yíng, Jì, and Yì,
and was known for his effective governance.
Initially,
the Táng army defeated Wáng Dū at Zhōngshān,
and captured Qìdān General Cèlà and more than ten others.
Afterward, Qìdān established peaceful relations with Zhōngguó,
and sent envoys to request Cèlà and the others.
Míngzōng discussed this with his ministers,
who all wished to return them,
but Guāngyuǎn alone disagreed,
saying:
"Cèlà and the others are Běi Dí skilled in warfare.
If they lose them, it is like losing limbs.
Moreover, having stayed here for a long time,
they are intimately familiar with the affairs of Zhōngguó.
How could returning them be advantageous to us!"
Míngzōng said:
"The Fānrén value oaths and covenants.
Since they are already on good terms with us,
how could they betray us?"
Guāngyuǎn said:
"I fear that later regret will be too late!"
Míngzōng praised his argument,
and ultimately did not send Cèlà and the others back.
Guāngyuǎn was promoted from Prefect of Yì Zhōu to Military Commissioner of the Zhènwǔ Army.
In Qīngtài second year (935),
he was transferred to command at Zhōngshān,
concurrently serving as Chief Marshal of the Northern Campaign Army,
defending against Qìdān between Yún and Yīng.
When Jìn Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán,
Mòdì appointed Guāngyuǎn to assist Zhāng Jìngdá as Deputy Commissioner of Four-Front Pacification of Tàiyuán.
He was defeated by Qìdān
and retreated to defend Jìn'ān Zhài.
Qìdān besieged them for several months.
When the provisions for men and horses were exhausted,
they killed the horses and ate them.
When the horses were finished,
Guāngyuǎn then killed Jìngdá and surrendered.
Yēlǜ Déguāng saw him
and jested, saying:
"You fellows are truly 'wicked Han boys' (È Hàn'ér)."
Guāngyuǎn and the other generals initially did not realize he was mocking them,
and replied with modest words.
Déguāng said:
"To eat ten thousand warhorses
without using salt or cheese—
are you not 'wicked Han boys'!"
Guāngyuǎn and the others were greatly ashamed and submitted.
Déguāng asked:
"Are you afraid?"
They all replied:
"Extremely afraid."
He asked:
"What do you fear?"
They replied:
"We fear that His Majesty will be taken to Fān (Khitan territory)."
Déguāng said:
"My country has no lands or official titles to accommodate you.
You all should endeavor to serve Jìn."
Jìn Gāozǔ appointed Guāngyuǎn as Military Commissioner of the Xuānwǔ Army and Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards Cavalry and Infantry.
When Guāngyuǎn presented himself at court,
he feigned a melancholy demeanor,
constantly appearing as if he held some grievance.
Gāozǔ suspected that he was dissatisfied with something,
and sent someone to ask him.
He replied:
"I am not dissatisfied regarding wealth and honors;
I am only ashamed that I did not die in the right place, unlike Zhāng Shēngtiě.
This is my constant regret!"
Because of this, Gāozǔ considered him loyal
and trusted him greatly.
When Fàn Yánguāng rebelled,
Guāngyuǎn was appointed Chief Pacification Commissioner of Wèifǔ.
For a long time, he could not subdue him.
Gāozǔ eventually used other strategies to make Yánguāng surrender.
Guāngyuǎn, holding heavy troops in the field,
believed Gāozǔ feared him,
and began acting arbitrarily and aggressively.
Gāozǔ always treated him with extreme indulgence.
He selected Guāngyuǎn's son Chéngzuò to marry Princess Cháng'ān,
and his second son Chéngxìn and others were all given extraordinary promotions and titles;
the favors and honors were unparalleled.
The Commissioner of Military Affairs, Sāng Wéihàn, disliked him
and repeatedly spoke out against him.
When Guāngyuǎn came to court from Wèi,
he frequently pointed out that Wéihàn abused his power and was difficult to control.
Gāozǔ had no choice
but to dismiss Wéihàn and send him out to Xiāng Zhōu.
He also transferred Guāngyuǎn to be Defender of the Western Capital,
concurrently garrisoning Héyáng,
and stripped him of his military command.
Guāngyuǎn began to harbor great resentment,
secretly offering treasures and goods to Qìdān,
complaining that he had been alienated and rejected by Jìn.
The thousand personal retainers he kept
violated the law and broke prohibitions between the Hé and Luò Rivers,
acting worse than bandits.
In Tiānfú fifth year (940),
he was transferred to command at Pínglú,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōngpíng.
Guāngyuǎn requested that his sons travel with him.
Consequently, Chéngzuò was appointed Prefect of Shàn Zhōu,
Chéngxūn was appointed Defense Commissioner of Lái Zhōu.
Father and sons all traveled east,
their carriages and cavalry stretching for dozens of miles.
When Chūdì ascended the throne,
Guāngyuǎn was appointed Grand Preceptor
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Shòu.
At this time,
Jìn was short of horses,
so they requisitioned horses throughout the realm to supplement the army.
Jǐng Yánguǎng requested the return of 300 government horses that Guāngyuǎn had previously borrowed.
Guāngyuǎn angrily said:
"These horses were bestowed upon me by the former emperor.
How dare they try to take them back?
This is accusing me of rebellion!"
Thereupon, he plotted insurrection.
Then Chéngzuò fled home from Shàn Zhōu.
Chūdì immediately made Chéngzuò Prefect of Zī Zhōu
and sent an envoy to bestow upon him a jade belt and imperial horse to placate him.
Guāngyuǎn became even more arrogant,
and subsequently rebelled.
He summoned Qìdān to invade,
and they captured Bèi Zhōu.
Zhōu Rú, the Prefect of Bó Zhōu, also rebelled and surrendered to Qìdān.
At this time,
Chūdì and Yēlǜ Déguāng were facing each other between Chán and Wèi.
Dòu Yí, the Surveillance Deputy of Yùn Zhōu, planned military affairs in the camp,
advising:
"If we do not now use heavy troops and a great general to guard the Bó Zhōu crossing,
and Rú is allowed to lead Qìdān east across the river to link up with Guāngyuǎn,
then Hénán (the region south of the Yellow River) will be in danger!"
Chūdì then sent Lǐ Shǒuzhēn and Huángpǔ Yù with ten thousand soldiers downstream along the river.
Rú indeed led Qìdān to cross the river from Mǎ Jiā Dù.
Just as they were building fortifications,
Shǒuzhēn and the others quickly attacked them.
Qìdān was utterly defeated,
and contact with Guāngyuǎn was thus severed.
Déguāng heard that the army by the river had been heavily defeated,
and engaging Jìn in a decisive battle at Qī Chéng,
he was also defeated.
After Qìdān had gone north,
Chūdì again sent Shǒuzhēn and Fú Yànqīng to attack Guāngyuǎn in the east.
Guāngyuǎn fortified the city and held firm.
From summer to winter,
the people inside the city nearly resorted to cannibalism until they were almost all gone.
Guāngyuǎn looked north toward Qìdān,
kowtowing and calling out to Déguāng:
"Did Your Majesty mislead Guāngyuǎn!"
His son Chéngxūn and others urged Guāngyuǎn to surrender.
Guāngyuǎn said:
"When I was in Dàiběi,
I once offered paper money to the Heavenly Pond.
Whenever I tossed it in, it would sink.
People said that I was destined to become the Son of Heaven.
I should wait for the right moment;
do not discuss surrender lightly."
Chéngxūn knew the situation was hopeless,
so he killed Surveillance Deputy Qiū Tāo of the Military Commission and close generals Dù Yánshòu, Yáng Zhān, Bái Yánzuò, and others.
He kidnapped Guāngyuǎn and imprisoned him,
then sent men to submit a memorial confessing guilt and awaiting punishment.
Chéngxìn and Chéngzuò both went to the palace gates to surrender themselves,
and Guāngyuǎn also submitted a petition requesting death.
Chūdì made the two sons Imperial Guard Generals,
and granted Guāngyuǎn an imperial edict
promising to spare his life.
All the ministers, however, deemed this unacceptable,
so an imperial order commanded Lǐ Shǒuzhēn to handle the matter at his discretion.
Shǒuzhēn sent the Deputy Commissioner of the Reception Bureau, Hé Yánzuò, to kill him at his residence.
When Yánzuò arrived at his residence,
Guāngyuǎn was inspecting horses in the courtyard.
Yánzuò sent a garrison commander inside to address him, saying:
"The imperial envoy is at the gate.
He wishes to return and report to the Son of Heaven,
but lacks an object to rely on (as proof)."
Guāngyuǎn asked:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"We wish to obtain the Great King's head!"
Guāngyuǎn said:
"What crime have I committed?
Previously, I surrendered Jìn'ān Zhài to Qìdān,
allowing your family to be Son of Heaven for generations.
I also hoped to enjoy wealth and honor for the rest of my life.
Instead, you repay my heartlessness like this!"
He was then executed,
and reported officially as having died of illness.
Chéngxūn served Jìn as Defense Commissioner of Zhèng Zhōu.
When Déguāng destroyed Jìn,
he sent someone to summon Chéngxūn to the capital.
He chastised him for having kidnapped his father,
and had him cut into pieces and eaten.
He then appointed Chéngxìn as Military Commissioner of Pínglú.
Hàn Gāozǔ posthumously granted Guāngyuǎn the title Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and enfeoffed him as the Prince of Qí.
He commanded Zhāng Zhèng, Secretary of the Secretariat, to compose an epitaph inscription for Guāngyuǎn and give it to Chéngxìn,
ordering it to be carved onto a stone tablet in Qīng Zhōu.
After the tablet was erected,
there was a great clap of thunder and lightning from the sky,
which struck and broke it.
