Āchuài initially did not have this surname;
later he changed his name to Jiān and adopted the surname Yáng shì.
Guāngyuǎn's initial name was Tán.
In Qīngtài second year (935 CE),
the relevant officials stated that all characters containing radicals that conflicted with the personal names of Míngzōng should be changed.
Therefore, he was bestowed the name Guāngyuǎn.
Guāngyuǎn was afflicted by baldness,
and his wife was also lame in her foot.
People composed a saying about this:
“Since ancient times, how could there be a bald and sore-ridden Son of Heaven, and a lame-footed Empress?”
This story was passed around as a joke.
However, calling upon the barbarians (Yídí) caused the primary disaster in the realm,
eventually destroying the Jìn clan,
leaving the Central Plains (Zhōngguó) devastated for over thirty years.
All this was done by Guāngyuǎn.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Fortieth: Dù Chóngwēi
Dù Chóngwēi,
was a man from Shuòzhōu.
His wife, Shí shì,
was the younger sister of Jìn Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Shí shì as a Gōngzhǔ (Princess),
and appointed Chóngwēi as the Cìshǐ (Prefect) of Shūzhōu,
to command the Palace Guards (Jìnbīng).
He followed Hóu Yì in attacking and defeating Zhāng Cóngbīn at Sìshuǐ,
and for this merit, he was appointed Jìedùshǐ (Military Governor) of Lùzhōu.
When Fàn Yánguāng rebelled at Yè,
Chóngwēi followed Gāozǔ to attack and subdue Yánguāng,
was transferred to lead Zhōngwǔ Command,
and given the additional title Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
He was then transferred again to lead Tiānpíng Command,
and promoted to Commander-in-Chief (Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ) of the Imperial Guards (Shìwèi Qīnjūn).
When Ān Chóngróng rebelled,
Chóngwēi met him in battle at Zōngchéng.
Chóngróng formed a Crescent Moon formation,
and Chóngwēi attacked it, but it held firm.
Chóngwēi wanted to fall back slightly and observe the situation,
but his subordinate general, Wáng Chóngyìn, said:
“When two armies are engaged,
the one who retreats first loses.”
Thus, the troops were divided into three divisions.
Chóngwēi first used the left and right divisions to strike the enemy's two flanks.
When the battle was intense,
Chóngyìn used elite soldiers to strike their central army.
Chóngróng's general, Zhào Yànzhī, defected,
and Chóngróng consequently suffered a major defeat.
He fled back to Zhènzhōu,
barricaded his camp, and dared not venture out.
Chóngwēi attacked and overcame him,
and for this merit, Chóngwēi was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Chéngdé Army.
Chóngwēi originated from the military ranks,
lacked moral conduct, and knew nothing of military strategy.
After capturing Zhènzhōu,
he seized all the accumulated stores in the official treasury and all of Chóngróng's assets,
and confiscated them for his own family.
Gāozǔ knew about this but did not question him.
When Emperor Chū Dì broke off relations with the Qìdān,
the Qìdān repeatedly invaded year after year.
Chóngwēi merely closed his city gates and defended himself.
Many towns and cities in the surrounding prefectures were slaughtered.
The Hu cavalry drove tens of millions of the common people past his city wall,
Chóngwēi ascended the wall and watched them,
but never once went out to rescue them.
In Kāiyùn first year (944 CE),
Chóngwēi was given the additional title Northern Commander-in-Chief of Military Operations (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ).
The following year,
he led troops to attack Tàizhōu,
and captured Mǎnchéng and Suìchéng.
The Qìdān had already departed and reached Gǔběi.
They then turned their troops back to strike [Chóngwēi].
Chóngwēi and his forces fled south.
When they reached Yángchéng,
they were surrounded by the captives (Lǔ).
Fortunately, Fú Yànqīng and Zhāng Yànzé seized the opportunity of a great wind to launch a spirited attack,
and the Qìdān suffered a major rout.
The generals wanted to pursue them,
but Chóngwēi used a colloquial saying, stating:
“We met the bandit and kept our lives;
do we still expect to recover our possessions?”
He then gathered his horses and rode quickly back.
While Chóngwēi resided in Zhènzhōu,
he heavily taxed the common people,
and the households and populace became impoverished and exhausted.
Fearing the Qìdān's impending arrival,
he repeatedly submitted memorials begging to return to the capital (Jīngshī).
Before receiving a reply,
he hastily set off on the road.
The court could not stop him.
Consequently, Chóngwēi was immediately appointed Resident Governor (Liúshǒu) of Yè Dū.
However, he had left over a hundred thousand *hú* of private grain stored in Zhènzhōu.
Wáng Qīnzùo, the Director of the Palace Attendants (Diànzhōngjiān), purchased it for military provisions,
and reported the amount.
Several tens of thousands of bolts of silk were given to compensate him.
Chóngwēi became furious and said:
“I am not a rebel;
how can this property be registered and confiscated!”
In the autumn of the third year (946 CE),
when Gāo Móuhàn of the Qìdān falsely offered to surrender Yíngzhōu,
Chóngwēi was once again appointed Northern Commander-in-Chief of Military Operations.
That autumn,
the realm suffered a great flood,
with continuous rain for over sixty days.
Starving corpses filled the roads.
The residents tore down wood for cooking fuel,
and chopped up straw mats to feed their horses and oxen.
Chóngwēi's army marched through the muddy floodwaters.
The mobilization and supply demands (Gōngkuì)
caused distress and hardship both near and far.
When Chóngwēi arrived at Yíngzhōu,
Móuhàn had already abandoned the city and left.
Chóngwēi retreated and garrisoned Wǔqiáng.
The Qìdān then invaded Zhèn and Dìng.
Chóngwēi hurried west toward Zhōngdùqiáo (Middle Ford Bridge),
and established a camp opposite the barbarians across the Hūtuó River.
The subordinate generals Sòng Yànjūn and Wáng Qīng crossed the water and fought fiercely,
but Chóngwēi held his army back and did not move.
Yànjūn was subsequently defeated,
and Qīng died in battle.
The Commissioner of Transport (Zhuǎnyùnshǐ), Lǐ Gǔ, suggested to Chóngwēi that he use tripods made of wood to construct a bridge,
and recruit soldiers willing to fight to the death to cross the river and attack the bandits.
All the generals agreed with this,
but Chóngwēi alone refused permission.
The Qìdān dispatched cavalry at night, traveling along the western mountains to attack Luánchéng,
cutting off the rear of Chóngwēi's army.
At this time,
Chóngwēi already harbored treacherous intentions,
and his grain supply route was cut off.
He secretly sent men to the Qìdān to request surrender.
The Qìdān were greatly pleased,
and promised to give the Central Plains (Zhōngguó) to Chóngwēi so he could become Emperor.
Chóngwēi believed this to be true.
He then concealed armored soldiers,
and summoned the generals to inform them of his surrender to the barbarians (Lǔ).
The generals were stunned.
Since the supreme general had surrendered first,
they all obeyed his command.
Chóngwēi produced a surrender document and made the generals sign their names.
He then ordered the soldiers to form a battle array outside the stockade.
The soldiers were still leaping with joy, thinking they were going into a decisive battle.
Chóngwēi informed them that the grain was exhausted and they were surrendering.
The soldiers removed their armor and wept loudly,
their voices shaking the plains.
The Qìdān bestowed an ochre robe (Zhěpáo) upon Chóngwēi,
and made him wear it to show the armies.
They appointed Chóngwēi Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
When the Qìdān invaded the capital (Jīngshī),
Chóngwēi stationed the Jìn troops at Chénqiáo.
The officers and soldiers suffered freezing and starvation,
unable to bear the hardship.
When Chóngwēi traveled along the roads,
the market people followed and abused him.
Chóngwēi bowed his head, not daring to look up.
When the Qìdān occupied the capital,
they levied money and silk from the city to reward the army.
None of the generals and ministers were spared,
and Chóngwēi was required to pay ten thousand *mín* (strings of cash).
He then complained to the Qìdān, saying:
“I surrendered first with one hundred thousand Jìn troops;
am I alone not to be exempted from the levy?”
The Qìdān laughed and exempted him,
and sent him back to Yè Dū.
The following year,
when the Qìdān returned north,
Chóngwēi and his wife, Shí shì, went to the barbarian camp to bid farewell.
When Hàn Gāozǔ pacified the capital,
he appointed Chóngwēi Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Jìedùshǐ of Guīdé Army.
Chóngwēi was afraid,
and refused the mandate.
Hàn Gāozǔ dispatched Gāo Xíngzhōu to attack him,
but did not succeed.
Gāozǔ then personally led the attack against him.
He sent the Gěishìzhōng (Attendant Censor), Chén Tóng, with an imperial edict to summon him.
Chóngwēi did not obey the command,
and the Hàn forces were defeated several times.
They besieged him for over a hundred days.
Initially,
the Qìdān had left fifteen hundred Yān troops in the capital.
When Gāozǔ entered from Tàiyuán,
informants claimed they were about to rebel.
Gāozǔ executed them all at Fántái.
Those who escaped fled to Yè.
Zhāng Liǎn, a Yān general, already had two thousand troops stationed in Yè.
Hearing that the Yān troops had been killed,
he advised Chóngwēi to hold fast and defend.
Gāozǔ regretted having killed the Yān troops,
and
repeatedly sent people to entice Liǎn and the others.
Liǎn climbed the city wall and shouted:
“As for the execution at Fántái,
what crime did the Yān troops commit?
Since we have no chance to live,
we request to defend this place until death!”
Dù Zhòngwēi's food was entirely depleted;
they ground up yeast/leaven and ate it.
Many citizens climbed over the walls and surrendered,
all lacking a human complexion.
Zhòngwēi then sequentially dispatched the judge (Pànguān) Wáng Mǐn and his wife to request surrender.
Gāozǔ permitted it.
Zhòngwēi wore plain clothing and came out to see Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ pardoned Zhòngwēi,
and appointed him acting Grand Tutor (Jiǎnxiào Tàishī), Grand Mentor (Shǒu Tàifù), and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
He executed all of Liǎn and Zhòngwēi's generals and officials,
but seized their private treasuries,
and returned with Zhòngwēi to the capital (Jīngshī).
Gāozǔ became gravely ill.
He looked upon his high ministers and said:
“Guard carefully against Zhòngwēi!”
Gāozǔ died.
The news of death was kept secret and not announced.
The high ministers then collectively executed him,
and exposed the corpses of his sons Hóngzhāng, Hóngcàn, and Hóngsuì in the marketplace.
Market people kicked them and reviled them.
Officials could not stop them.
They were torn limb from limb and trodden upon.
In a moment, they were completely destroyed.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn
was a native of Héyáng.
When Jìn Gāozǔ was stationed at Héyáng,
he made him a guest general (Kèjiàng).
Afterward, he often followed Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Commissioner of the Guest Bureau (Kèsǐng Shǐ).
He oversaw the army of Mǎ Quánjié in defeating Lǐ Jīnquán at Ānzhōu.
Due to this merit, he was appointed Commissioner of the Court of the Imperial Insignia (Xuānhuī Shǐ).
When Chūdì ascended the throne,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn rebelled,
and invited the Qìdān to invade.
Shǒuzhēn held the position of Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of the Yìchéng Army,
and served as Commander of the Metropolitan Cavalry (Dōu Yúhòu) of the Palace Guard.
He followed Chūdì to Chánzhōu.
Mádá entered Yùnzhōu with crack troops,
crossed Mǎjiākǒu,
and established a stockade east of the river (Hédōng).
Shǒuzhēn quickly went and defeated them.
Many Qìdān soldiers drowned.
He captured several hundred horses
and more than seventy subordinate generals.
He was transferred to lead the Tàiníng Army Jiédù Shǐ,
and used twenty thousand troops to attack (Yáng Guāngyuǎn).
Guāngyuǎn surrendered.
His former subordinate Sòng Yán took all of Guāngyuǎn's treasures, famous concubines, and fine horses and presented them to Shǒuzhēn.
Shǒuzhēn appreciated this gesture,
and secretly kept Yán under his banner.
At this time,
whenever troops were deployed to defeat rebels,
there would certainly be a decree of amnesty for the remaining collaborators.
However, more than ten members of Guāngyuǎn's faction were fugitives.
The hunt for them was very intense.
The Privy Council Commissioner (Shūmì Shǐ) Sāng Wéihàn delayed the issuance of the pardon decree,
and it was not handed down for a long time.
An informant reported that Yán was hiding at Shǒuzhēn's location.
An imperial edict ordered Yán to be seized and killed.
Shǒuzhēn was furious,
and thus held a grudge against Wéihàn.
When rewarding the soldiers who had defeated the rebels,
Shǒuzhēn distributed pieces of wood dyed with faded tea (in lieu of valuables).
The army was greatly enraged.
They wrapped silk around (one of the wooden pieces) to form a human head,
and displayed it on a stake among the trees,
saying:
"This is Shǒuzhēn's head."
Shǒuzhēn, due to his merit, was appointed Concurrent Grand Councilor (Tóng Píngzhāng Shì).
He was granted Guāngyuǎn's former mansion.
Shǒuzhēn took neighboring official and civilian residences and greatly renovated the complex.
It became the finest in the capital (Jīngshī).
Chūdì personally visited,
and granted feasts and generous favors,
surpassing those given to the other generals.
When the Qìdān invaded,
Chūdì again proceeded to Chánzhōu.
Dù Zhòngwēi was made Commissioner for Pacifying the North (Běimiàn Zhāotǎo Shǐ),
and Shǒuzhēn was made Chief Supervisor (Dūjiān).
The Jìn troops were habitually arrogant,
and both Shǒuzhēn and Zhòngwēi, as generals, lacked discipline.
Wherever the mobile camp went,
the domestic animals and livestock of the residents were completely emptied out,
even the grass and trees were consumed entirely.
When the army was initially deployed,
there were grants and rewards,
called
"Putting on the Armor Money" (Guàjiǎ Qián).
And when they returned triumphantly,
additional rewards were given for their efforts,
called
"Removing the Armor Money" (Xièjiǎ Qián).
The expense of their departure and return
was usually no less than 300,000 (units of currency).
Because of this, the state and private resources of the Jìn suffered severe hardship.
Shǒuzhēn and Zhòngwēi jointly attacked and took Tàizhōu,
and broke Mǎnchéng,
killing more than two thousand people.
Returning,
he was made Grand Commander (Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ) of the Palace Guard,
and led the Tiānpíng Army Jiédù Shǐ.
He also led Guīdé.
At this time,
Chūdì sent someone with a letter to persuade Zhào Yánshòu to return to the state.
Yánshòu falsely claimed that he longed to return,
and wished to have Jìn troops as a supporting force.
The Qìdān officer Gāo Móuhàn also falsely claimed that Yíngzhōu would surrender.
Chūdì believed this to be true,
and ordered Dù Zhòngwēi and others to lead troops to support them.
Initially,
the Jìn high ministers all said that Zhòngwēi was disloyal,
and harbored resentment,
and should not be used.
Therefore, Shǒuzhēn was used (for the main command position).
At this time,
Zhòngwēi was stationed at Wèizhōu.
Shǒuzhēn often led troops and passed through Wèi.
Zhòngwēi treated him very generously,
often presenting him with weapons, armor, gold, and silk.
Chūdì once said to Shǒuzhēn:
"You constantly distribute your family wealth to the soldiers.
Can this be called loyalty to the state!"
Shǒuzhēn bowed and replied:
"This was all given to your subject by Zhòngwēi."
Consequently, he requested to go north together with Zhòngwēi.
Thus, Zhòngwēi was ultimately made Commissioner for Pacification (Zhāotǎo Shǐ),
Shǒuzhēn was made Chief Supervisor (Dūjiān),
and they were stationed at Wǔqiáng.
When the Qìdān raided Zhèn and Dìng,
Shǒuzhēn and his army were stationed at Zhōngdù.
Consequently, he and Zhòngwēi surrendered to the Qìdān.
The Qìdān appointed Shǒuzhēn Minister of the Masses (Sītú).
When the Qìdān violated the capital (Jīngshī),
they appointed Shǒuzhēn the Tiānpíng Army Jiédù Shǐ.
When Hàn Gāozǔ entered the capital,
Shǒuzhēn came to court,
and was appointed Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) and Hézhōng Jiédù Shǐ.
Gāozǔ died.
Dù Zhòngwēi died.
Shǒuzhēn was afraid,
and felt uneasy.
He thought that the Hàn dynasty was newly established,
Yǐndì had just ascended the throne,
and the empire was easy to scheme against.
Furthermore, the monk Zǒnglún, who was under his roof, secretly influenced Shǒuzhēn with arcane arts,
and told him that he possessed the appearance of extraordinary destiny.
Shǒuzhēn then decided decisively to rebel.
Moreover, Zhào Sīwǎn had already rebelled in Jīngzhào.
He sent someone to present Shǒuzhēn with an ochre-yellow robe.
Shǒuzhēn was overjoyed,
believing that Heaven and men were both responding (to his destiny).
He then mobilized troops and occupied Tóngguān in the west,
and recruited and lured bandit forces.
In various places, secret uprisings occurred.
The Hàn dispatched Bái Wénkē, Cháng Sī, and others to lead armies and attack them.
Soon after, Wáng Jǐngchóng also rebelled in Fèngxiáng.
Jǐngchóng and Sīwǎn sent people to endorse Shǒuzhēn as the Prince of Qín (Qín Wáng).
Shǒuzhēn conferred official titles and ranks upon Jǐngchóng and the others.
He also sent spies with secret wax-pellet letters to Wú, Shǔ, and the Qìdān,
asking them to mobilize troops to divert the Hàn forces.
Wénkē and the others attacked Jǐngchóng and Sīwǎn for a long time without success.
Yǐndì then sent the Privy Council Commissioner Guō Wēi, leading the Palace Guard, to oversee Wénkē and the others in the attack.
All the generals requested to attack Sīwǎn and Jǐngchóng first.
Wēi’s plan was uncertain as to where to strike.
When they traveled to Huàzhōu,
the Jiédù Shǐ Hù Yànkē said to Wēi:
"The three rebels are linked together.
They take Shǒuzhēn as their head.
If Shǒuzhēn is defeated first,
then Sīwǎn and Jǐngchóng can be broken merely by spreading the news.
If we abandon the near target to plot against the distant ones,
and allow Shǒuzhēn to launch troops from the rear,
while Sīwǎn and Jǐngchóng resist us in the front,
then the Hàn army will be defeated."
Wēi considered this correct,
and consequently attacked Shǒuzhēn first.
At this time,
Féng Dào had been dismissed from the chancellorship and was residing in Héyáng.
Wēi, having just mobilized his troops,
passed by Dào’s residence and asked for strategy.
Dào said:
“Do you know the game of bó (gambling/dice)? ”
Wēi, who was unruly in his youth
and fond of gambling with dice (pú bó),
thought Dào was mocking him,
and became visibly angry.
Dào said:
“In any game of bó, he who has more money will usually win more;
he who has less money will usually lose more.
It is not that he is bad at gambling;
the reason for his loss
is the circumstance (shì).
Now, when combining the troops of all generals to attack a single city,
if you compare the disparity in numbers,
the victory or defeat can be known. ”
Wēi gained great enlightenment
and planned to wear them down through delay and prolonged constraint.
He then divided his generals into three stockades (zhà),
fencing in three sides of the city,
but leaving the south side open.
He dispatched corvée laborers (dīng fū) from five counties to build a long wall connecting the three stockades.
Shǒu Zhēn sent his troops out to destroy the long wall;
Wēi immediately repaired the damage.
Shǒu Zhēn consistently marched out to contest this,
and Shǒu Zhēn’s troops usually lost thirty to forty percent (of their strength).
This continued for over a year.
Shǒu Zhēn’s forces within the city were negligible,
and their food supplies were also exhausted;
they resorted to cannibalism.
Wēi said:
“It is time. ”
He then set a date,
urged his troops, and attacked from four sides, breaking and taking the city.
Initially,
Shǒu Zhēn summoned Zǒng Lún and asked him whether he would succeed.
Zǒng Lún said:
“Your Highness is destined to possess the entire realm,
however, your corresponding astrological field (fēnyě) is currently afflicted by disaster.
Wait until the slaughter is nearly complete,
then Your Highness’s enterprise will succeed. ”
Shǒu Zhēn believed this to be true.
Once, he gathered his generals and officials for a great feast.
Shǒu Zhēn pointed at a painted tiger image and said:
“He who holds the Mandate of Heaven will shoot through its palm. ”
He drew his bow and fired one arrow, striking the palm.
The generals and officials all prostrated themselves to offer congratulations,
and Shǒu Zhēn became even more arrogant due to this self-assurance.
When the city fell,
Shǒu Zhēn and his wife and children immolated themselves.
The Hàn army entered the city,
beheaded him amidst the smoke and ashes,
and transported the head to the capital,
where it was displayed on a pole in the southern market.
All his remaining partisans were dismembered.
Zhāng Yànzé
Zhāng Yànzé’s
ancestors were originally from the Turkic (Tūjué) tribe.
Later, they migrated to Yīnshān,
and then moved again to Tàiyuán.
Yànzé was a man who was fierce, brave, cruel, and ruthless.
His eyeballs were yellow and glowed at night,
and his gaze was like that of a fierce beast.
He became a cavalry commander because of his skill in archery,
and frequently followed Zhuāngzōng and Míngzōng in battles and campaigns.
He was connected by marriage to the Jin Gāozǔ.
During the time of Gāozǔ,
he was already the Commander-in-Chief of the Right Wing of the Hùshèng Army and Prefect of Cáozhōu.
After participating in the suppression of Fàn Yán’guāng,
he was appointed Jìnguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Within the same year,
he was transferred to govern Zhāngyì.
His administration was tyrannical and cruel.
He often became angry with his son
and repeatedly flogged and humiliated him.
The son fled to Qízhōu.
The prefecture arrested him and sent him to the capital.
Gāozǔ returned him to Yànzé.
Yànzé submitted a memorial requesting permission to kill him.
His confidential secretary (zhǎng shūjì), Zhāng Shì, refused to draft the memorial for him
and repeatedly advised him to stop.
Yànzé grew angry,
drew his bow, and shot at Shì.
Shì ran away and escaped.
Shì had always been highly regarded by Yànzé
and entrusted with many affairs.
The petty individuals surrounding Yànzé had long been jealous of him,
so they jointly slandered Shì,
and also pressured him, saying:
“If you do not leave quickly,
disaster will overtake you. ”
Shì then fled.
Yànzé sent Commander Lǐ Xīng with twenty horsemen to pursue him,
and instructed them:
“If Shì refuses to come back,
you must bring back his head! ”
When Shì reached Yǎnzhōu,
the Prefect escorted him with soldiers to Bīnzhōu.
The Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Zhōu detained Shì
and quickly reported the matter.
An imperial edict exiled Shì to Shāngzhōu.
Yànzé sent the Army Supervisor (Sīmǎ) Zhèng Yuánzhāo to the palace court to argue and petition,
demanding that he must obtain Shì,
and further said:
“If Yànzé does not get Zhāng Shì,
there will be unpredictable trouble. ”
Gāozǔ had no choice
and granted his request.
When Yànzé captured Shì,
he cut out his heart, slit his mouth, severed his hands and feet, and then executed him.
Gāozǔ sent Wáng Zhōu to replace Yànzé,
and appointed Yànzé General-in-Chief of the Right Wǔwèi Army.
Zhōu reported twenty-six instances of Yànzé’s unlawful conduct,
and also described the state of wretched exhaustion among the people of Jīng (Jīngzhōu).
Shì’s father, Duó, went to the palace court to appeal his grievance.
The Remonstrance Grand Masters (Jiànyì Dàfū) Zhèng Yìshòu and Cáo Guózhēn,
together with the Presidents (Lángzhōng) of the Ministry of Punishments Lǐ Tāo and Zhāng Lín,
and the Extra-Numerary Secretaries (Yuánwàiláng) Má Tāo and Wáng Xǐ knelt at the palace gate and submitted memorials,
arguing the injustice of Yànzé’s killing of Shì.
None were heeded.
Tāo met Gāozǔ and remonstrated sharply.
Gāozǔ said:
“Yànzé is a meritorious minister;
I once promised him immunity from death. ”
Tāo said sternly:
“If Yànzé’s crime can be tolerated,
where is Yán’guāng’s Iron Scroll (Tiějuàn) now! ”
Gāozǔ became angry
and stood up to leave.
Tāo followed him, continuing his remonstrance tirelessly.
Gāozǔ, having no alternative,
summoned Shì’s father Duó, younger brother Shǒu Zhēn, and son Xī Fàn, among others,
and appointed them to office.
He waived taxes for the people of Jīngzhōu
and exempted them from miscellaneous labor services for one year.
He issued an edict acknowledging his own fault (zuì jǐ).
However, Yànzé was only stripped of his rank and degraded in title.

Thereupon, Guózhēn and others, along with the Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) Wáng Yìjiǎn, led the censors of the Three Bureaus to the Palace Gate and repeatedly submitted memorials arguing the case,
but received no response.
During the time of Emperor Chūdǐ,
Yànzé served as General-in-Chief of the Left Lóngwǔ Army,
was promoted to Supreme General of the Right Wǔwèi Army,
and further promoted to Commander of the Right Shénwǔ Army.
Since the Qìdān started warring with Jìn north of the Yellow River,
Yànzé was in the thick of the fighting
and repeatedly achieved military merit.
He was appointed Zhāngguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
When fighting the Qìdān at Yángchéng,
he was surrounded by the Qìdān,
and there was no water in the army.
Wells dug consistently collapsed.
Furthermore, there was a great wind.
The Qìdān, with the wind at their backs, raised dust and attacked with great ferocity.
The army was greatly fearful.
Yànzé asked his generals for advice.
The generals all said:
“Now the barbarians (lǔ) are favored by the wind,
and we are downwind from them.
We should wait for the wind to change before we can fight. ”
Yànzé agreed.
All the generals left.
The flank general (Piān Jiàng) Yào Yuánfú alone remained
and said to Yànzé:
“The army is already severely hungry and thirsty.
If we wait for the wind to change,
we will all be captured by the barbarians!
Moreover, fighting against the wind
will make the enemy think we certainly cannot do it,
which is what is called catching them by surprise. ”
Yànzé immediately removed the barricades (jù mǎ) and fought hard.
The Qìdān fled north for over twenty lǐ.
Yànzé pursued them to Wèicūn,
where he defeated them again soundly.
The Qìdān retreated and left.
In the autumn of the third year of Kāiyùn (946 CE),
Dù Chóngwēi was the Commander-in-Chief of the Mobilized Forces (Dū Zhāotǎo Shǐ),
Lǐ Shǒu Zhēn was the Cavalry and Infantry Supervisor (Bīngmǎ Dūjiān),
and Yànzé was the Commander of Cavalry Array (Mǎjūn Dū Páizhèn Shǐ).
Yànzé moved back and forth between Zhèn and Dìng.
He defeated the Qìdān at Tàizhōu,
beheading two thousand enemy soldiers.
Chóngwēi and Shǒu Zhēn attacked Yíngzhōu but failed to capture it.
They retreated to Wǔqiáng.
Hearing that the Qìdān had emptied their country to invade,
they were fearful and confused, not knowing where to go.
Just then, Yànzé arrived
and described how the barbarians could be defeated.
They then followed Chóngwēi and the others west toward Zhènzhōu.
Yànzé served as the vanguard.
Upon reaching Zhōngdù Qiáo,
it had already been occupied by the barbarians.
Yànzé still fought fiercely to contest the bridge,
burning half of it.
The barbarians suffered a minor defeat and retreated.
They then pitched camp along the river.
On the *bǐngyín* day of the twelfth month,
Zhòngwēi and Shǒuzhēn rebelled and surrendered to the Qìdān.
Yànzé also surrendered.
Yēlǜ Déguāng violated the imperial seat (the capital).
He dispatched Yànzé and Fù Zhù'ér with two thousand cavalry to enter the capital first.
Yànzé doubled his marching speed and pressed on quickly.
Upon reaching the river,
they held gags in their mouths and crossed at night.
On the night of the *rénshēn* day, at the fifth watch (dawn),
they cut down the gate bars and entered through the Fēngqiūmén.
A moment later,
a fire broke out inside the palace.
The Abdicated Emperor (Chū Dì) drew his sword, gathering more than ten concubines, intending to rush into the fire,
but he was restrained by the minor official Xuē Chāo.
Yànzé entered through the Kuānrénmén, carrying Déguāng’s letter to the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
The fire was then extinguished.
Kāng Fúquán, the Grand Palace Commander-in-Chief, was quartered and guarded the Kuānrénmén.
He ascended the tower to spy on the rebels.
Yànzé shouted to him and made him come down.
All the gates were then opened.
Yànzé stationed his troops in front of the Míngdélóu,
and sent Fù Zhù'ér in to convey the proclamation of the Martial King (Róng Wáng).
The Emperor (Dì) removed his yellow robe,
donned plain clothes, bowed twice, and accepted the mandate.
He sent someone to summon Yànzé.
Yànzé declined, saying:
“Your servant has no face to see Your Majesty.”
He sent another messenger to summon him,
but Yànzé only smiled and did not reply.
The next day,
the Emperor (Dì) was moved to the Kāifēng Fǔ.
The Emperor (Dì), the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu), and the Empress (Huánghòu) rode in shoulder palanquins.
More than ten palace women and eunuchs followed on foot.
Yànzé sent Lǐ Jūn, the Kònghè Commander, with troops to guard them.
Internal and external communication was cut off.
The memorials submitted by the Emperor (Dì) and the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) to Déguāng,
had to be shown to Yànzé first before they dared to be dispatched.
The Emperor (Dì) requested several lengths of silk from the inner treasury.
The custodian said:
“This does not belong to the Emperor (Dì).”
He did not give it.
He also sent someone to request wine from Lǐ Sōng.
Sōng said:
“It is not that your servant's household has wine and dares to be stingy;
I fear Your Majesty is anxious and distressed,
and drinking it might lead to unforeseen calamity.
Therefore, I dare not present it.”
The Emperor’s maternal aunt, Princess Wūshì (Dì Gū Wūshì Gōngzhǔ), secretly bribed the gate guard,
was allowed to enter and bid farewell to the Emperor (Dì).
She returned to her residence and hanged herself.
When Déguāng crossed the river,
the Emperor (Dì) wanted to greet him in the suburbs.
Yànzé refused to allow it,
and sent a message to Déguāng.
Déguāng replied:
“There cannot be two suns in the sky.
How can two Sons of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) meet on the road?”
The Emperor therefore stopped.
Previously,
when Yànzé arrived at the capital (Jīngshī),
Lǐ Tāo said to others:
“My disaster has arrived!
Rather than hiding in a ditch and not escaping death,
it is better to go and meet him.”
Tāo met Yànzé,
and used coarse language to mock himself (or provoke death).
Yànzé laughed and treated him generously.
Yànzé believed he had rendered service to the Qìdān.
He indulged in drinking day and night to amuse himself.
When going out or entering, his mounted escort was always several hundred men,
and he still inscribed on his banners:
“Loyal Heart for the Sovereign.”
After forcing the removal of the Abdicated Emperor (Chū Dì),
he proceeded to cart off the inner treasury,
transporting it to his private residence.
Consequently, he allowed his soldiers to heavily loot the capital (Jīngshī).
When soldiers captured criminals during patrols,
Yànzé was too drunk to interrogate them.
He would glare at them fiercely,
and raise three fingers.
The soldiers would then immediately drive them out and sever them at the waist and neck.
Dīng Shì, Lady of Chǔguó and mother of Imperial Prince Yánxù, was beautiful.
Yànzé sent someone to request her from the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) hesitated and had not yet complied,
so he immediately kidnapped her.
Yànzé had a grudge against the Gémén Envoy Gāo Xūn.
He took advantage of his drunkenness to enter Gāo Xūn's house,
killed several people, and left.
When Yēlǜ Déguāng arrived at the capital (Jīngshī),
he heard of Yànzé’s kidnapping and plundering,
and became furious.
He had him put in chains.
Gāo Xūn also filed a personal complaint with Déguāng.
Déguāng showed Gāo Xūn’s petition to the hundred officials and the capital populace,
and asked:
“Should Yànzé be executed or not?”
All the officials pleaded for no pardon,
and the capital populace vied to submit petitions detailing his evils.
Déguāng then ordered Gāo Xūn to oversee the execution.
The sons and grandsons of the officials and scholars previously killed by Yànzé,
all wore mourning clothes, carried staffs, and wailed.
They followed him, cursing and railing,
and struck him with their staffs.
Yànzé bowed his head and did not utter a single word.
When they reached the Northern Market,
his wrists were cut to free the chains,
and then the execution was carried out.
Xūn cut out his heart to sacrifice to the dead.
The market people scrambled to break open his skull,
extract his marrow,
cut his flesh into pieces, and eat it.
Alas!
The affair of the Jìn was ugly,
and the evil reached its extreme!
That it suffered catastrophe, chaos, overthrow, and ruin was inevitable,
a natural consequence.
Even if Zhòngwēi and the others had not rebelled and surrendered to the captives,
it would not necessarily have avoided ruin;
however, the opportunity provided to the captives,
began with Jǐng Yánguǎng,
but those who ultimately completed the Jìn disaster,
were these three men.
Seeing the death of Zhòngwēi and Yànzé,
and the satisfaction of the Jìn people (Jìn rén),
one can know that their fury, hatred, grievance, and anger toward these men,
was not just for a single day.
As for fighting over the already executed corpse,
slicing its flesh,
extracting and eating its marrow,
tearing it apart, and trampling on it,
finished in a brief moment—
how extreme this was!
This is unprecedented since ancient times.
However, at that time,
all of Jìn's military forces were stationed in the north.
The survival or ruin of the state,
depended on the success or failure of these three men.
Thus, their responsibility can be called weighty.
If the world hated them as such,
yet Jìn continued to rely on them this way,
and ultimately never realized the truth,
was this not what is meant by
“Rulers facing chaos
each deem their own ministers worthy”?
Miscellaneous Biographies, Forty-First: Wáng Jǐngchóng
Wáng Jǐngchóng
was a native of Xíngzhōu.
He was perceptive, quick-witted, and eloquent.
He was skilled at serving others.
When Emperor Míngzōng of Táng was stationed in Xíngzhōu,
he made him a *yájiàng* (head of staff).
Afterward, he often followed Míngzōng,
serving under his command.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Tōngshì Shèrén (Secretarial Court Gentleman).
He successively held the post of Yǐnjìn Gémén Shǐ (Envoy for Introducing Guests at the Palace Gate).
Whenever edicts were urgently dispatched to regional governors or army supervisors for campaigns,
Jǐngchóng was always employed.
Later, he served the Jìn.
He was successively appointed Grand General of the Left *Jīnwú Wèi*.
He often felt dissatisfied that the ruler was unable to utilize his talents.
When the Jìn fell,
Xiāo Hàn occupied the capital (Jīngshī).
Jǐngchóng heavily bribed Xiāo Hàn's general Gāo Móuhàn to seek employment.
Soon after, Hàn returned north.
He allowed Prince Cóngyì of Xǔ (Xǔ Wáng Cóngyì) to reside in the capital (Jīngshī).
Jǐngchóng was appointed Xuānhuī Envoy and Supervisor of the Left Treasury.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn (Hàn Gāozǔ) rose up in Tàiyuán,
Jǐngchóng took the treasury gold and rushed to meet Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ arrived at the capital (Jīngshī),
he appointed Jǐngchóng Grand General of the Right *Wèi*.
He did not yet consider him extraordinary.
When Gāozǔ attacked Yè,
Jǐngchóng was unable to follow.
He then requested the Residence Memorial (qǐjū biǎo) from the commander remaining behind in the capital,
went to the temporary imperial residence (xíngzài) to see Gāozǔ,
and asked to remain in the army to offer his services.
He outlined strategies for attack and warfare to Gāozǔ.
He was extremely eloquent.
Gāozǔ then considered his talent extraordinary.
One version uses the character *gōng*.
At that time,
the Hàn (Dynasty) had just been established.
Hóu Yì, the Marquis of Fèngxiáng, and Zhào Zàn of Yǒngxīng, had both previously received commissions from the Qìdān.
When Gāozǔ ascended (the throne),
Yì and the others looked inward and felt suspicion (of themselves).
Therefore, they secretly summoned Shǔ people for aid.
Gāozǔ worried about this.
When Yè had been captured,
Yì and the others became fearful,
and all requested to attend court.
It happened that the Huíhú came to offer tribute,
saying that they were blocked by the Dǎngxìng and could not pass through,
and requested Hàn troops for assistance.
Gāozǔ sent Jǐngchóng with soldiers to welcome the Huíhú.
When Jǐngchóng was about to depart,
Gāozǔ was already ill.
He summoned him into his bedchamber and warned him, saying:
"Yì and the others have already come,
which is good.
If they still hesitate,
then manage them expediently."
When Jǐngchóng traveled to Shǎn,
Zhào Zàn had already headed east to attend court,
but the Shǔ troops were currently raiding Nánshān.
Jǐngchóng attacked and defeated the Shǔ troops,
pursuing them to Dàsànguān before returning.
Gāozǔ then decreed that Jǐngchóng concurrently serve as Fèngxiáng Surveillance Commissioner.
When Jǐngchóng arrived at Fèngxiáng,
Hóu Yì had not yet shown intent to leave,
and then Gāozǔ passed away.
Some advised Jǐngchóng that he should quickly execute Yì.
Jǐngchóng considered that he had received the commission solely from the Former Emperor, and the young sovereign was unaware of it,
so he hesitated and could not decide.
Chéng Wò, Yì's aide,
was from the same village as Jǐngchóng,
and they were old friends.
He went and persuaded Jǐngchóng, saying:
"I am an old friend of yours.
My rank does not exceed that of a subordinate official,
but you are already noble.
Why do you wish to harm someone through treachery and cunning in order to gain (power)?
Marquis Hóu and his son have hundreds of loyal soldiers.
Do not recklessly strike,
or disaster will soon befall you!
If it were not for me,
who would tell you this?"
Thereupon, Jǐngchóng largely ceased wanting to kill Yì.
Yì then fled.
Jǐngchóng greatly regretted having missed the opportunity to kill him.
Yì arrived at the Capital.
Yǐndì had just been enthroned.
Shǐ Hóngzhào, Yáng Bīn, and others held power.
Yì then heavily bribed Bīn and the others,
and secretly used affairs to incriminate Jǐngchóng.
Soon after, Yì was appointed Magistrate of Kāifēng.
Jǐngchóng felt uneasy in his heart.
He hinted to the military and civil officers of Fèngxiáng to request that he take charge of the prefecture's affairs.
The court worried about this,
and appointed Jǐngchóng as Resident Commissioner of Bīnzhōu,
and made Zhào Huī the Military Governor of Fèngxiáng.
Jǐngchóng then rebelled,
killing all the family members of Hóu Yì.
He and Zhào Sīwǎn jointly acclaimed Lǐ Shǒuzhēn as the Prince of Qín.
Yǐndì immediately ordered Zhào Huī to suppress them.
Jǐngchóng went west to recruit Shǔ people for help.
The Shǔ troops reached Bǎojī,
but were defeated by Huī's generals, Yuè Yuánfú and Lǐ Yàncóng.
Huī attacked Fèngxiáng,
dug trenches and besieged it,
and repeatedly challenged them with elite troops.
Jǐngchóng did not go out.
Huī then ordered a thousand men to hide about thirty *lǐ* south of the city.
They falsely made Shǔ military banners
and descended along Nánshān,
proclaiming loudly that the Shǔ relief troops had arrived.
A moment later, dust rose.
Jǐngchóng believed it to be true,
and ordered several thousand men to break through the siege and exit in response.
Huī had set an ambush and waited for them.
Jǐngchóng's army was utterly defeated,
and thereafter dared not sortie again.
The following year,
Shǒuzhēn and Sīwǎn were successively defeated.
Zhōu Càn, a retainer of Jǐngchóng, said to Jǐngchóng:
"The reason you were able to hold this place
was because of Hézhōng and Jīngzhào.
Now they are all defeated.
What do you rely on?
It is better to surrender."
Jǐngchóng said:
"Indeed, I have burdened you gentlemen.
However, the situation is desperate.
I wish to attempt a plan that has one chance in ten thousand of succeeding, is that permissible?
I hear that Zhào Huī's elite troops are all north of the city.
Now I will send Gōngsūn Niǎn and others to burn the east gate and pretend to surrender.
I will use my personal guards to attack their troops north of the city.
Even if we fail and die,
it is better than being captured without resistance."
Càn and the others all agreed.
At dawn,
Niǎn burned the east gate and was about to surrender,
when a fire broke out inside the headquarters.
Jǐngchóng had set himself on fire.
Niǎn then surrendered to Huī.
Zhào Sīwǎn.
Zhào Sīwǎn
was a native of Wèizhōu.
He served as a personal guard commander for Zhào Zàn, the Military Governor of Hézhōng.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he transferred Zàn to govern Yǒngxīng.
Zàn went to the Capital to attend court,
leaving Sīwǎn and several hundred soldiers in Yǒngxīng.
Gāozǔ sent Wáng Jǐngchóng to Yǒngxīng,
to join Qí Zàngzhēn with troops to welcome the Huíhú.
He secretly entrusted the affairs in the west to him.
When Jǐngchóng arrived at Yǒngxīng,
although Zàn had gone to court,
the Shǔ troops he had summoned had already occupied Zǐwǔ Valley.
Jǐngchóng used Sīwǎn's troops to attack and drive them away.
He then traveled west together with Sīwǎn.
However, since they were not his own troops,
he feared Sīwǎn and the others might harbor disloyalty,
and intended to tattoo their faces so they would be bound to follow him.
But he found it difficult to state this directly,
so he slightly and subtly hinted at his meaning.
Sīwǎn loudly requested to be tattooed first to lead the masses.
Qí Zàngzhēn disliked this (Sīwǎn's eagerness),
and secretly urged Jǐngchóng to kill Sīwǎn.
Jǐngchóng did not listen,
and traveled west together with him.
Gāozǔ sent an envoy to summon Sīwǎn and the others.
At this time, Hóu Yì came to court.
Sīwǎn took his troops and followed Yì eastward back home.
Sīwǎn said to his subordinate Cháng Yànqīng:
"Lord Zhào (Zàn) has already fallen into others' hands.
If we arrive,
we will all die as well.
What shall we do?"
Yànqīng said:
"We will change our plans when the situation arises;
do not speak of it prematurely."
Yì traveled until he reached Yǒngxīng.
Ān Yǒuguī, the Vice Commissioner of Yǒngxīng, came out to welcome Yì.
They drank wine at the suburban pavilion.
Sīwǎn stepped forward and said:
"The soldiers are quartered east of the city,
but the families of the officers and men are all residing inside the city.
I request permission for the troops to enter the city to fetch their family members."
Yì trusted him and considered this reasonable.
Sīwǎn entered the city with his subordinates.
A prefectural officer was sitting at the city gate.
Sīwǎn struck him,
seized his waist-saber and killed him,
and simultaneously executed more than ten gatekeepers,
then closed the gate, raided the arsenal for weapons, and rebelled.
Gāozǔ sent Guō Cóngyì and Wáng Jùn to suppress him.
After a year, they could not overcome him.
Then Wáng Jǐngchóng also rebelled,
and together with Sīwǎn, they both offered their allegiance to Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
Shǒuzhēn made Sīwǎn the Military Governor of Jìnchāng Command.
Yǐndì sent Guō Wēi west to oversee the troops of the various generals,
and first besieged Shǒuzhēn at Hézhōng.
After a few months,
food ran out inside Sīwǎn’s city.
He killed people and ate them.
Whenever he gave a feast,
he killed several hundred people,
butchering them exactly like sheep and pigs.
Sīwǎn took their gallbladders and swallowed them with wine,
and said to his subordinates:
"If you eat a thousand gallbladders,
your courage will be unmatched!"
exhausted his strategies,
and recruited men to dig a secret tunnel,
intending to flee to Shǔ.
His Staff Supervisor, Chén Ràngnéng, said to Sī Wǎn
"Compared to the state, Lord, you have no great fault,
but you fear death, which is why you are doing this!
Now the state is employing troops on three fronts,
and is endlessly weary and worn out.
If you can sincerely and suddenly turn around and demonstrate obedience,
taking the lead to surrender,
using merit to compensate for your faults,
you might yet live;
if you merely sit and defend this destitute city,
you will only wait for death."
Sī Wǎn agreed with this.
Thereupon he dispatched the Commissioner of Training, Liú Guī, to Fèng Cóngyì to beg for surrender.
He also sent his general, Liú Jūn, to present a memorial to the imperial court.
[The court] appointed Sī Wǎn as Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu) of the Zhènguó Army,
urging him to proceed to his post.
Sī Wǎn delayed and did not go.
Shǔ secretly sent people to entice Sī Wǎn.
Sī Wǎn was about to flee to Shǔ.
Fèng Cóngyì also became suspicious of him.
He then sent someone to inform Guō Wēi,
and Wēi ordered Cóngyì to eliminate him.
Cóngyì therefore entered the city and summoned Sī Wǎn,
urging him to set out immediately.
When he arrived, he was captured.
Sī Wǎn asked:
"What means of execution will be used?"
The informant replied:
"Staking."
Sī Wǎn shouted sternly:
"Tell Duke Guō for me:
My death is not enough to atone for my guilt,
but the vile cruelty of staking
is a disgrace to a brave man.
I hope you will grant me a slight reprieve [from that method]."
Cóngyì permitted it.
Father and son were both executed by beheading in the marketplace.
Mùróng Yànchāo
Mùróng Yànchāo
was a man of the Tǔyùhún tribe,
and the younger paternal half-brother of Han Gāozǔ.
He once falsely adopted the family name Yán.
Yànchāo had a dark complexion and a foreign beard,
and was nicknamed Yán Kūnlún.
When young, he served Táng Míngzōng as a military officer,
and was repeatedly promoted to Prefect (Cìshǐ).
During the period between the Táng and Jìn dynasties,
he successively governed the four prefectures of Cí, Shàn, Pú, and Dì.
While stationed at Púzhōu, he was convicted of taking bribes related to brewing yeast;
the law decreed death,
but Han Gāozǔ submitted a memorial from Tàiyuán arguing in his defense,
so his sentence was reduced from death.
He was exiled to Fángzhōu.
When the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
and Han Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán,
Yànchāo fled from his place of exile and returned to Hàn.
He was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhènníng Army.
When Dù Chóngwēi rebelled in Wèi,
Gāozǔ made Gāo Xíngzhōu, Military Governor of the Tiānpíng Army, the Commander-in-Chief (Dū Bùshǔ) to suppress him,
and made Yànchāo the Deputy.
Yànchāo and Xíngzhōu often disagreed in their planning.
Xíngzhōu employed a cautious military strategy.
Though the troops reached the city wall,
they did not advance for a long time.
Yànchāo wanted to advance quickly and fight,
but Xíngzhōu did not permit it.
Xíngzhōu had a daughter married to Chóngwēi’s son.
Yànchāo publicly stated that Xíngzhōu, because of his daughter,
was sparing the rebel city and refusing to attack.
Xíngzhōu became furious.
Gāozǔ, hearing that the two men could not cooperate,
feared a different outcome,
and therefore hastily led a personal campaign.
Yànchāo repeatedly used matters to insult and humiliate Xíngzhōu.
Xíngzhōu could not tolerate it.
He met the Chancellor weeping and sobbing,
and stuffed his mouth with feces to protest.
Gāozǔ knew the fault lay with Yànchāo.
He sent someone to comfort and console Xíngzhōu,
summoned Yànchāo to reprimand him,
and further sent him to Xíngzhōu to apologize for his error.
Xíngzhōu's anger gradually subsided.
At this time,
the Hàn army had been camped beneath the city of Wèi for a long time.
Chóngwēi’s defense grew stronger.
All the generals knew it was not yet the time to attack,
and were waiting for an opening.
But Yànchāo alone insisted it could be attacked quickly.
Gāozǔ believed him.
Consequently, he personally supervised the soldiers and fiercely attacked,
resulting in over ten thousand dead and wounded.
After this, no one dared to speak of attacking again.
Later, Chóngwēi surrendered.
Gāozǔ appointed Xíngzhōu as Military Governor of the Tiānxióng Army.
Xíngzhōu declined, not daring to accept.
Gāozǔ sent Sū Féngjí to explain to him, saying:
"I will relocate Yànchāo for you."
Xíngzhōu then accepted.
Yànchāo was consequently moved to govern Tài'níng.
After Yǐndì had killed Shǐ Hóngzhào and others,
he again sent men to Wèi to kill Zhōu Tàizǔ and Wáng Jùn.
Fearing that the mission would fail,
he summoned various generals to enter and defend the capital.
When the envoy reached Yǎnzhōu,
Yànchāo was eating.
He put down his spoon and chopsticks and set off.
When the Zhōu forces assaulted the capital,
Hóu Yì, the Prefect of Kāifēng, said to Emperor Yǐn:
"As for the approaching Northern troops,
their families are all in the capital.
We should close the gates to blunt their edge,
and send their wives and children up to the battlements to call out to the Northern forces.
This might cause them to discard their armor."
Yànchāo mocked Yì, saying:
"Yì is old!
This is a coward's plan."
Emperor Yǐn then sent Yànchāo to assist Yì,
leading troops in the northern suburbs.
When the Zhōu troops arrived,
Yì defected and surrendered to Zhōu that night.
Yànchāo fought fiercely at Qīlǐ.
Emperor Yǐn came out to console the army.
The Empress Dowager sent someone to tell Yànchāo to guard the Emperor well.
Yànchāo replied with bluster, saying:
"What can the Northern troops accomplish?
I should just yell 'Sit down!' at them on the battlefield and make them return to their camps."
He also said to Emperor Yǐn:
"Your Majesty, there is nothing going on in the palace.
Tomorrow you can come out and watch your servant fight."
The next day, Emperor Yǐn again came out to console the army.
Yànchāo was defeated in battle and fled to Yǎnzhōu.
Emperor Yǐn was assassinated in the northern suburbs.
Zhōu Tàizǔ entered and ascended the throne.
Yànchāo felt uneasy.
He repeatedly sent gifts.
Tàizǔ responded by presenting him with a jade belt,
and also bestowed an imperial edict to comfort him,
addressing Yànchāo as "younger brother" and not by name.
He further sent the Hanlin Scholar Lǔ Chóngliàng to go and console him.
Yànchāo's heart grew even more suspicious and fearful.
Subsequently, Liú Mín established himself in Tàiyuán,
and sent troops to attack Jìn and Jiàng.
Tàizǔ dispatched Wáng Jùn to lead military operations in the west.
Yànchāo seized this opportunity to plan a rebellion as well.
He sent his Staff Head (Yāyá), Zhèng Lín, to the capital seeking permission to appear at court.
Tàizǔ knew this was a deceitful maneuver,
but granted permission via a handwritten edict.
Yànchāo then claimed that there were many bandits within his jurisdiction and stopped [his planned trip].
He also fabricated a letter supposedly written by Gāo Xíngzhōu and submitted it.
The words therein all pointed out the errors and faults of Zhōu [Tàizǔ],
as if seeking to rebel together.
Tàizǔ verified that the seal imprint was fake,
and showed the letter to Xíngzhōu.
Yànchāo also sent someone south to form an alliance with Lǐ Jǐng.
Jǐng sent troops to attack Shùyáng for him,
but was defeated by the Zhōu forces.
Meanwhile, Liú Mín failed to conquer Jìn and Jiàng
and retreated.
Tàizǔ then sent Cáo Yīng, Commander of the Palace Guard Infantry, and Xiàng Xùn, Commissioner of the Guest Department, to suppress him.
Yànchāo closed the city gates and defended himself.
Féng Dào was personally capable of practicing self-discipline and leading a frugal life.
When Jìn and Liáng were encamped across the river from each other,
Féng Dào stayed within the army camp,
built a single thatched hut,
did not set up a bed or mat,
and slept only on a bundle of hay.
The stipend he received,
he ate and drank from the same vessels as his servants and attendants,
and his disposition was calm and serene.
When generals who had plundered beautiful women gave them to Féng Dào,
Féng Dào could not decline,
so he placed them in a separate chamber,
sought out their masters, and returned them.
When (Féng) Dào, serving as the *Xuéshì*, was mourning his father in Jǐngchéng,
he encountered a year of famine,
and he took out everything he possessed to aid his fellow villagers.
He then retired to cultivate the fields,
and personally carried firewood.
For those whose fields lay fallow and uncultivated,
and for those unable to farm due to lack of strength,
Féng Dào would go at night
and secretly plow for them.
Those people later apologized shamefully,
but Féng Dào definitely did not regard it as an act of virtue.
When the mourning period ended,
he was again summoned to serve as the Hànlín Xuéshì.
Traveling until he reached Biànzhōu,
he encountered the unrest caused by Zhào Zàilǐ.
Míngzōng led troops returning from Wèi,
and invaded the capital city (*Jīngshī*).
Kǒng Xún advised Féng Dào to wait by staying a little while longer,
Féng Dào said:
“I have received an imperial decree to proceed to the palace;
how can I remain here arbitrarily!”
He then hastened quickly to the capital city (*Jīngshī*).
Zhuāngzōng was assassinated,
and Míngzōng ascended the throne.
He was well acquainted with Féng Dào’s character,
and asked Ān Chónghuǐ:
“Where was Féng Dào during the former Emperor’s reign?”
Ān Chónghuǐ replied:
“He was a *Xuéshì*.”
Míngzōng said:
“I have always known this;
this is truly my Zǎixiàng.”
He appointed Féng Dào as Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì,
and later transferred him to Bīngbù Shìláng.
After more than a year,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
During the years between Tiānchéng and Chángxīng,
the harvests were repeatedly abundant,
and the Central Plains (*Zhōngguó*) were peaceful.
Féng Dào once admonished Míngzōng, saying:
“When your servant was the Administrator of Records (*Zhǎngshūjì*) in Hédōng,
I was sent on a mission to Zhōngshān.
I traversed the peril of Jǐngxíng Pass,
fearing my horse might stumble and fall,
and I dared not relax my hold on the reins.
But when I reached flat ground,
I thought there was nothing to worry about,
and the horse immediately stumbled and was injured.
Generally, those who tread in danger worry deeply and thus achieve safety,
while those who live in peace find calamity arises from what they overlook.
This is the constant nature of human affairs.”
Míngzōng asked:
“Although the world is abundant,
are the common people truly relieved?”
Féng Dào replied:
“High grain prices starve the farmers;
low grain prices harm the farmers.”
He then recited the “Tían Jiā Shī” (Field Family Poem) by the literatus Niè Yízhōng,
whose words were accessible and easy to understand.
Míngzōng instructed his attendants to record the poem,
and often recited it to himself.
A commander of the water transport troops found a jade cup in Línhé Xiàn,
which bore the inscription
“Precious Treasure Transmitted by the State, Ten Thousand Years Cup.”
Míngzōng loved it greatly,
and showed it to Féng Dào.
Féng Dào said:
“This is merely a tangible treasure of a former age;
a true ruler possesses intangible treasures.”
Míngzōng asked what they were.
Féng Dào replied:
“Benevolence and righteousness (*Rényì*)
are the treasures of emperors and kings.
Thus it is said: ‘The great treasure is the position (the throne);
what is used to guard the position is benevolence (*rén*).’”
Míngzōng was a martial ruler,
and did not immediately understand his words.
After Féng Dào had departed,
he summoned his attending officials to lecture on the meaning,
and he accepted the advice with praise.
Féng Dào served as chief minister to Míngzōng for more than ten years.
When Míngzōng died,
he served as chief minister to Mǐndì.
The Prince of Lù rebelled in Fèngxiáng,
and Mǐndì fled to Wèizhōu.
Féng Dào led the civil officials to welcome the Prince of Lù into the capital,
who then became Fèidì,
and Féng Dào subsequently served as his chief minister.
After Fèidì ascended the throne,
Mǐndì was still in Wèizhōu.
Three days later,
Mǐndì was finally assassinated and died.
Later, Fèidì sent Féng Dào out of the capital to be the Jiédùshǐ of Tóngzhōu.
After a year,
he was appointed Sīkōng.
When Jìn destroyed Táng,
Féng Dào again served Jìn.
Jìn Gāozǔ appointed Féng Dào as Shǒu Sīkōng, Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì,
raised him to Sītú,
concurrently Shìzhōng,
and enfeoffed him as Lǔguó Gōng.
When Gāozǔ died,
Féng Dào served as chief minister to Chūdì.
He was raised to Tàiwèi,
enfeoffed as Yānguó Gōng,
then dismissed to become the Jiédùshǐ of Kuāngguó Jūn,
and subsequently transferred to govern Wēishèng.
Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
and Féng Dào again served Qìdān.
He paid court to Yēlǜ Déguāng in the capital city (*Jīngshī*).
Yēlǜ Déguāng reprimanded Féng Dào for his dishonorable service to Jìn,
and Féng Dào could not respond.
He then asked:
“Why have you come to pay court?”
He replied:
“Lacking city walls and lacking soldiers,
how dare I not come.”
Yēlǜ Déguāng mocked him, saying:
“What kind of old fellow are you?”
He replied:
“An old fellow who is stupid and stubborn, lacking talent and lacking virtue.”
Yēlǜ Déguāng was pleased,
and appointed Féng Dào as Tàifù.
When Yēlǜ Déguāng returned north,
Féng Dào followed him to Chángshān.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Féng Dào returned to Hàn,
and served as Tàishī by imperial summons.
When Zhōu destroyed Hàn,
Féng Dào again served Zhōu.
Zhōu Tàizǔ appointed Féng Dào as Tàishī,
concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng.
In his youth, Féng Dào was able to cultivate admirable behavior to gain renown in the world.
When he became a high minister,
he especially strove for gravity and composure to stabilize affairs.
Having served four dynasties (*xìng*) and ten rulers,
he increasingly regarded himself as a veteran of virtue.
Nevertheless, the scholars of that era, regardless of their wisdom or folly, all revered Féng Dào as a Grand Elder (*Yuánlǎo*),
and were happy to speak highly of him.
Yēlǜ Déguāng once asked Féng Dào, saying:
“How can the common people of the world be saved?”
Féng Dào replied in a lighthearted manner, saying:
“If the Buddha were to appear at this time, he could not save them;
only the Emperor can save them.”
Everyone believed that the Qìdān did not exterminate the people of the Central Plains (*Zhōngguó*)
due to Féng Dào’s single good word.
When Zhōu troops rebelled,
and invaded the capital city (*Jīngshī*),
Yǐndì had already died.
Tàizǔ assumed the Hàn ministers would certainly nominate him for the throne,
but when he met Féng Dào,
Féng Dào showed absolutely no such intention.
Tàizǔ usually showed great deference to Féng Dào,
but this time reluctantly paid obeisance to him (formally).
Féng Dào received it as if it were a normal occurrence.
Tàizǔ's enthusiasm was somewhat dampened.
Knowing that the Hàn dynasty could not yet be replaced,
he thus feigned establishing Xiāngyīn Gōng Yūn as the Hàn successor,
and dispatched Féng Dào to welcome Yūn from Xúzhōu.
Before Yūn arrived,
Tàizǔ led troops north to Chánzhōu,
then turned his army back,
and subsequently replaced the Hàn dynasty.
Commentators claimed that Féng Dào was able to frustrate Tàizǔ's scheme and delay him,
and ultimately did not hold Féng Dào responsible for the downfall of Jìn and Hàn.
Yet, Féng Dào also never took the demise of a ruler or the ruin of a state to heart.
At that time,
the world was in great chaos,
and barbarian tribes invaded repeatedly.
The fate of the common people
was more precarious than being hung upside down.
Féng Dào nevertheless proclaimed himself
“Chánglè Lǎo” (Old Man of Perpetual Joy),
and wrote a text of several hundred words,
listing the ranks, honors, official posts, and titles he had acquired serving four dynasties and Qìdān, regarding them as his glory.
He described himself:
“Filial at home,
loyal to the state,
having been a son, a younger brother, a servant, a teacher/elder, a husband, and a father,
having sons and grandsons.
Sometimes I open a scroll,
sometimes I drink a cup,
I savor tastes, distinguish sounds, and wear colored silks,
growing old peacefully in the present age,
old and happy by myself.
What joy is like this?”
This was his self-description.
Initially,
when Yànchāo rebelled,
his adjudicant, Cuī Zhōudù, remonstrated, saying:
“Lǔ
is a land of poetry and books.
Since Bóqín, none have been able to dominate as hegemon.
However, many have guarded it with rites and righteousness and maintained their lineage for a long time.
Now, you, Duke, are heroic and mighty,
a hero of your generation.
If you assess your strength and the times before acting,
you can preserve your wealth and status throughout your life.
Lǐ Hézhōng, Ān Xiāngyáng, and Zhènyáng Dù Lìnggōng
are recent examples for reflection.”
Yànchāo was greatly enraged,
but he had no means to harm him immediately.
Later, when he was besieged,
he massively extorted the city's civilian wealth to reward his army.
Yán Hónglǔ, the former Sīmǎ of Shǎnzhōu, feared his flogging
and offered all his family wealth.
Yànchāo believed it was not exhaustive,
and also wanted to punish Zhōudù.
So he ordered Zhōudù to supervise the seizure of Hónglǔ's family assets.
Zhōudù said to Hónglǔ:
“Your life or death
depends on the amount of wealth.
Please do not hide anything.”
Hónglǔ sent his household servants with Zhōudù to dig and search, but found nothing.
Yànchāo then sent Zhèng Lín to press him with a blade.
Hónglǔ, in terror, bowed to his wives and concubines.
His wives and concubines all said there was nothing hidden.
Zhōudù went in to report to Yànchāo,
but Yànchāo did not believe him
and imprisoned Hónglǔ and Zhōudù.
Hónglǔ’s wet nurse found a gold armlet in the mud and offered it to Yànchāo,
hoping to redeem Hónglǔ.
Yànchāo was furious
and sent military officers to flog Hónglǔ and his wife until their flesh was rotten and they died.
Then he executed Zhōudù in the marketplace.
That year, the planet Zhēnxīng violated the constellations Jué and Kàng.
The divination said:
“Jué and Kàng
are the division of Zhèng,
and Yǎnzhōu corresponds to it.”
Yànchāo immediately led his military officials and officers thirty *lǐ* out of the west gate on foot to offer sacrifices,
welcoming it to Kāiyuán Sì,
and sculpted its image to serve it.
He visited it once daily
and also made civilian households erect yellow banners to avert the evil.
Yànchāo was a man of much cunning and fond of accumulating wealth.
While stationed, he once set up a pawnshop.
Some unscrupulous people used fake silver to pawn,
which the chief clerk eventually discovered after a long time.
Yànchāo secretly instructed the chief clerk to bore a hole in the treasury wall at night,
move all the gold and silk to another place, and then report a theft.
Yànchāo immediately posted a notice in the market,
asking people to declare what they had pawned to be reimbursed.
Everyone scrambled to declare their pawned items.
Afterward, those who had pawned fake silver were found,
placed in a deep chamber,
and made to teach more than ten people to work day and night,
all making items with iron as the core wrapped in silver,
which was called
“iron-core silver” (tiě tāi yín).
When he was besieged,
he encouraged those defending the city, saying:
“I have several thousand *dìng* of silver;
I will give it all to you.”
The soldiers privately said to each other:
“This is iron-core stuff,
what good is it again?!”
None would serve him.
The next year, in the fifth month,
Tàizǔ personally led an expedition.
The city fell.
Yànchāo and his wife both threw themselves into a well and died.
His son, Jìxūn, led his five hundred followers and fled but was captured.
His clan was then exterminated.
When Yǎnzhōu was pacified,
Tàizǔ issued an edict posthumously granting Yán Hónglǔ the title of Zuǒ Xiāowèi Dàjiāngjūn, and Cuī Zhōudù that of Mìshūjiān.
Collation Notes
Miscellaneous Biographies, Forty-Second
The *zhuàn* says:
“Rites, righteousness, integrity, and shame
are the four pillars of the state.
If the four pillars are not extended,
the state will perish.”
How excellent
Guǎn Shēng’s words are!
Rites and righteousness
are the great laws for governing people;
integrity and shame
are the great principles for establishing oneself.
Indeed, if one lacks integrity,
there is nothing one will not take;
if one lacks shame,
there is nothing one will not do.
If a person is like this,
then calamity, chaos, ruin, and destruction
will also be all-encompassing.
How much more so if one is a high minister who takes and does everything,
then how can the world not be in chaos,
and how can the state not perish!
When I read FÉNG Dào’s *Chánglè Lǎo*,
I saw him describe himself as glorious,
which can be said to be utterly shameless.
From this, the state of the world can be understood.
Among the Five Dynasties, I found three individuals of complete integrity
and fifteen ministers who died for their cause.
Yet, I am surprised that many scholars, dressed as Confucians and claiming to study the ancients,
who enjoyed people’s salaries and held positions in their states,
allowed the virtues of loyalty and righteousness
to appear solely among military men and common soldiers.
Could it be that among scholars, there were truly no such people?
Or could it be that noble-minded individuals detested the chaos of the times,
scorned their era, and were unwilling to serve?
Or were the rulers of the world not worth considering,
and thus unable to attract them?
Confucius said:
“In a town of ten households,
there will surely be those who are loyal and trustworthy.”
How could this be an empty statement!
I once obtained a short story from the Five Dynasties period,
which recorded the deeds of WÁNG Níng’s wife, Lǐ Shì.
That even a woman could be like this
shows that such people indeed existed in the world but were not seen.
Níng’s family lived between Qīng and Qí.
He served as the Sīhù Cānjūn of Guózhōu
and died in office from illness.
Níng’s family was always poor.
His son was still young.
Lǐ Shì carried her son
and bore his remains back home.
Passing east through Kāifēng,
she stopped at an inn.
The innkeeper, seeing a woman traveling alone with a child, suspected her
and refused her lodging.
Lǐ Shì, seeing it was already dusk,
refused to leave.
The innkeeper pulled her arm to put her out.
Lǐ Shì looked up to heaven and wailed:
“I am a woman,
unable to preserve my chastity,
and yet this hand has been grabbed by a man?!
I cannot let one hand contaminate my whole body!”
She immediately took an axe and cut off her own arm.
Passersby who saw it gathered around, lamenting her,
some snapping their fingers in dismay,
others shedding tears for her.
The Yǐn of Kāifēng heard of it
and reported the matter to the court.
The officials granted medicine to seal her wound
and amply compensated Lǐ Shì,
while flogging the innkeeper.
Alas,
may those gentlemen who do not cherish themselves and endure shame to cling to life
feel a little shame upon hearing the story of Lǐ Shì!
FÉNG Dào
FÉNG Dào, courtesy name Kědào,
was a native of Jǐngchéng, Yíngzhōu.
He served Liú Shǒuguāng as a Cānjūn.
When Shǒuguāng was defeated,
he left to serve the eunuch Zhāng Chéngyè.
Chéngyè supervised the Hédōng army
and made him an巡官 (Xúnguān).
He recommended him to the King of Jìn for his literary talent,
where he became the Zhǎngshūjì of Hédōng Jiédù.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Hùbù Shìláng
and concurrently Hànlín Xuéshì.
Dào (Fèng Dào) had previously served nine rulers,
and never offered remonstrance.
When Shìzōng first ascended the throne,
Liú Mín attacked Shàngdǎng.
Shìzōng said:
"Liú Mín underestimates me,
believing that since I am newly established and the state is undergoing a great mourning,
I will surely be unable to deploy troops to fight.
Moreover, those skilled in using troops strike when the enemy is unprepared.
I ought to lead the troops myself and attack him."
Dào then earnestly remonstrated,
believing it was impossible (unwise).
Shìzōng said:
"I have seen how Táng Tàizōng pacified the empire;
whether the enemy was great or small, he always led the campaigns himself."
Dào said:
"Your Majesty cannot yet be compared to Táng Tàizōng."
Shìzōng said:
"Liú Mín's forces are a disorderly rabble;
if they meet my army,
it will be like a mountain crushing an egg."
Dào said:
"Can Your Majesty ensure that the mountain you create is stable?"
Shìzōng was angered,
stood up and left,
and ultimately led the troops himself to attack Mín.
He indeed defeated Mín at Gāopíng.
Shìzōng took Huáinán,
secured the Three Passes (Sānguān),
and the rise of his martial prestige began with Gāopíng.
When he attacked Mín,
he disdained Dào and did not allow him to accompany him,
instead making him the Official in Charge of the Mausoleum for Tàizǔ.
After the funeral was complete, Dào died,
aged seventy-three.
His posthumous title was Wényì,
and he was posthumously enfeoffed as Yíng Wáng.
After Dào died,
people of the time all praised and admired him,
saying that he shared the same longevity as Kǒngzǐ (Confucius).
Their eagerness to praise him was indeed like this.
Dào had a son, Jí.
Lǐ Qí (elder brother Tǐng)
Lǐ Qí, courtesy name Táixiù,
was a native of Héxī Dùnhuáng.
His elder brother, Tǐng,
during the end of the Táng dynasty, passed the *jìnshì* examination,
and served as Supervising Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
When he incurred the mourning for a parent,
he was too poor to afford a funeral,
and had to beg for food before he could bury them.
Tǐng lay hungry in his mourning hut;
those who heard of it pitied him.
When the mourning period was complete,
he returned to his post as Censor (Yùshǐ).
Chéng Ruì of Jīngnán appointed him Archivist (Zhǎng Shūjì).
The Wú army besieged Dù Hóng.
Liáng Tàizǔ sent Ruì, along with Mǎ Yīn and others, to rescue Hóng.
Ruì loaded tens of thousands of soldiers onto large ships.
Tǐng offered advice to Ruì, saying:
"Now one boat holds a thousand armed soldiers,
with twice that amount of dry rations.
In an emergency, they cannot be mobilized quickly.
If they are constrained by the enemy,
then Wǔlíng and Wǔ'ān will certainly become future troubles for you, Sir.
It would be better to station elite troops at Bālíng,
fortify them and avoid battle.
When the Wú army runs out of provisions,
the siege will be lifted."
Ruì did not listen,
and indeed suffered defeat
and drowned.
Zhào Kuāngníng, who governed Xiāngyáng,
again appointed him Archivist.
Tàizǔ defeated Kuāngníng
and captured Tǐng.
He rejoiced, saying:
"This is truly an Archivist!"
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Vice Director of the Bureau of Merits (Kǎogōng Yuánwàiláng) and Drafter of Imperial Edicts (Zhī Zhìgào).
Tǐng surmised that Tàizǔ did not wish to primarily employ former subordinates (of the deposed regime),
so he firmly declined the appointment
and was sent out to govern Cáo Zhōu.
Cáo Zhōu had always been notoriously difficult to govern.
More than ten former Prefects (Cìshǐ)
had all been dismissed due to failure.
When Tǐng arrived,
he became known for his administrative competence.
He was promoted to Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Bīngbù Lángzhōng) and Academician in Residence of the Palace of Elevated Administration (Chóngzhèng Yuàn Zhí Xuéshì).
Féng Xíngxí of Xǔ Zhōu fell ill.
Xíngxí had two thousand personal bodyguards (yábīng),
who were all former soldiers of Cài (Zhōu).
Tàizǔ feared they might revolt.
Xíngxí was severe and cruel by nature.
His subordinate Wèi Jùn offered earnest remonstrance.
Xíngxí became enraged,
falsely accused him of corruption and threw him in prison,
intending to execute him.
Tàizǔ then sent Tǐng to replace Xíngxí as Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
When Tǐng arrived at Xǔ Zhōu,
he stayed at the courier station
and comforted the generals and officials.
Xíngxí was critically ill
and wished to have someone receive the imperial decree on his behalf.
Tǐng said:
"Facing east, while wearing court robes,
is the proper etiquette (lǐ)."
Tǐng then immediately entered the bedchamber to see Xíngxí,
conveying Tàizǔ's message.
Xíngxí was moved to tears,
removed his official seal, and handed it to Tǐng.
Tǐng then investigated Jùn's injustice,
immediately released him,
and returned to report to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ happily remarked:
"Tǐng has indeed accomplished my task."
It happened to be a famine year,
and bandits ravaged the areas between Biàn and Sòng,
with Cáo Zhōu being especially afflicted.
Tàizǔ again sent Tǐng to govern the area.
When Tǐng arrived, he searched for the bandits,
apprehended the high-ranking officer Zhāng Yànkē, Tǐng's nephew Lǐ Jiāo, and others,
along with over a hundred of the personal bodyguards.
He executed them all.
He was summoned and appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left (Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū).
Tàizǔ traveled to Héběi,
and upon reaching Nèihuáng,
he looked at Tǐng and said:
"Why is this place called Nèihuáng (Inner Huáng)?"
Tǐng said:
"Hénán has Wàihuáng (Outer Huáng) and Xiàhuáng (Lower Huáng),
therefore this place is named Nèihuáng."
Tàizǔ asked:
"Where are Wàihuáng and Xiàhuáng?"
Tǐng replied:
"In the Qín dynasty, there was the Commandant of Wàihuáng (Wàihuáng Dūwèi),
which is now in Yōngqiū;
Xiàhuáng was abolished by the Běi Qí dynasty,
and is now in Chénliú."
Tàizǔ generally disliked scholars (Rúzhě),
but hearing Tǐng's words, he was greatly pleased.
When Yǒuguī ascended the throne,
he appointed him Regular Attendant (Chángshì) of the Right Palace (Yòu Sànqí Chángshì),
serving as Imperial Lecturer (Shìjiǎng).
When Yuán Xiàngxiān was suppressing bandits,
Tǐng was killed by mutinous soldiers.
Qí, in his youth, passed the *jìnshì* and *bóxué hóngcí* examinations.
He was progressively promoted to Palace Supervising Censor (Diànzhōng Shì Yùshǐ).
He and his elder brother, Tǐng, were both famous for their literary talent.
When the Táng dynasty fell,
he served Liáng Tàizǔ as Academician of the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì).
When the Liáng forces campaigned in all directions,
the imperial edicts issued
were all written by Qí.
Whenever he put pen to paper, he captured Tàizǔ's intentions perfectly.
During the reign of Mòdì,
he served as Vice President of the Censorate (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) and Left Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng).
He was appointed Commissioner of the Central Secretariat and Chancellery (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì),
serving as Chancellor (Zǎixiàng) along with Xiāo Qǐng.
Qǐng was naturally cautious, careful, and thorough,
whereas Qí was unconventional, proud, and defiant,
not constrained by minor conventions.
The two men often disagreed.
Internally, Qí allied himself with Zhào Yán, Zhāng Hànjié, and others for support,
thus Qǐng's suggestions were often obstructed.
Qǐng once seized upon Qí's misconduct.
A clerk privately favored by Qí was supposed to receive a probationary official position (*shì guān*).
Qí changed the *shì* (probationary) title to *shǒu* (acting/substantive).
This was exposed by Qǐng.
Mòdì was greatly enraged
and intended to banish him,
but Yán and the others intervened and pleaded for him.
Consequently, he was only dismissed and made Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo).
Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
obtained Qí (Lǐ Qí),
intending to make him Prime Minister,
but many of the former officials of Liáng were jealous of him,
so they made him Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel).
In the autumn of the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE),
the world suffered great floods,
and the capital suffered from a severe lack of food.
Zhuāngzōng issued an imperial edict written in cinnabar ink ordering all officials to submit confidential memorials.
Qí submitted a memorial several thousand words long,
but its arguments were rambling and worthless,
yet Zhuāngzōng alone praised and valued it highly,
and consequently made him Guójì Shǐ (Commissioner of National Finance).
Just as he was about to make him Prime Minister,
Zhuāngzōng died.
Míngzōng entered Luòyáng.
The assembled officials urged him to ascend the throne.
The relevant authorities prepared the ceremony,
following the precedent of immediate enthronement before the coffin.
Huò Yànwēi, Kǒng Xún, and others requested changing the state title,
and severing the connection to the Earth Virtue.
Míngzōng was a martial ruler,
who did not understand these theories.
He asked, "What is meant by changing the title?"
They replied:
"Zhuāngzōng received the bestowed surname from Táng and became part of the imperial lineage.
He succeeded Zhāozōng to establish his rule,
and titled the state Táng.
Now, the Mandate of Heaven for Táng is severed.
It is proper to change the title to renew yourself."
Míngzōng was skeptical of this,
and referred the matter to the assembled officials.
The officials remained noncommittal and undecided.
Qí argued:
"Your Highness is the most virtuous of the imperial clan,
having established merit through three generations.
Now you have raised troops and advanced upon the palace,
under the pretext of rushing to the rescue.
If you were to now change the dynastic title,
making the Late Emperor merely a common stranger,
then where would the solitary imperial coffin
find rest and reliance!"
Míngzōng considered this correct,
and therefore proclaimed the mourning rites, assumed the mourning attire,
and only then ascended the throne.
He made Qí Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Vice Censor-in-Chief).
Since the disturbances and chaos of the late Táng period,
the court rites had deteriorated.
The Son of Heaven never held general audiences,
and the system of "Entering the Inner Court" was also abolished.
Officials of the Cháng Cān rank who arrived at the Main Court
would, upon hearing that the Emperor was not present, immediately withdraw.
Only high ministers who had memorials to present
met the Emperor once daily in the Inner Hall.
Attendants and officials from the inner departments,
merely had an audience twice daily.
When Míngzōng first ascended the throne,
he issued an edict to the assembled officials
that they should, once every five days, follow the Prime Ministers into the Inner Hall for an audience.
This was called Qǐjū (Reporting on Daily Life).
Qí considered this not to be the old Táng precedent.
He requested abolishing the five-day Qǐjū,
and restoring the Rù Gé (Entering the Inner Court) on the first and fifteenth day of the lunar month.
Míngzōng said:
"The five-day Qǐjū
is my method for frequently seeing my officials,
and cannot be abolished.
However, the Shuò Wàng Rù Gé can be restored."
However, according to Táng precedent,
the Son of Heaven governed from the hall daily to see the officials;
this was called Cháng Cān (Regular Audience).
On the first and fifteenth day of the lunar month, sacrifices were offered at the imperial tombs.
Due to feelings of deep remembrance,
the Emperor could not proceed to the Front Hall.
Instead, he governed from the Inner Hall to see the officials.
This was called Rù Gé.
Xuānzhèng
was the Front Hall,
and was called the Yá (Court or Office).
The Yá had an imperial guard contingent.
Zǐchén
was the Inner Hall,
and was called the Gé (Inner Court).
When the Emperor did not govern from the Front Hall but instead governed from Zǐchén,
he would summon the imperial guard contingent from the Main Court,
and enter through the Inner Court Gate.
The various officials waiting for the audience at the Yá
would then follow him in for the audience.
Therefore, it was called Rù Gé (Entering the Inner Court).
The Yá
was for the formal audience,
and its rites were high.
The Gé
was for informal meetings,
and its affairs were less critical.
After Qiánfú,
due to the chaos, the rites were neglected.
The Son of Heaven could not see officials daily but saw them only on the first and fifteenth.
Consequently, the imperial guard contingent at the Main Court was abolished on regular days,
but the Rù Gé audience on the first and fifteenth retained the guard contingent.
Later, this became customary,
and Rù Gé came to be regarded as the more important event.
Even when the Emperor proceeded to the Front Hall,
it was still referred to as Rù Gé.
This practice was later also abolished,
but was now restored.
However, the relevant authorities were unable to properly rectify the procedures.
All officials entered to see the Emperor once every five days at the Zhōngxīng Diàn,
which was an Inner Hall.
This was a remnant of the Rù Gé system,
yet it was called Qǐjū.
The Emperor proceeded once on the first and fifteenth to the Wénmíng Diàn,
which was the Front Hall.
Conversely, this was called Rù Gé.
