Qí was unable to correct any of these irregularities.
Qí further proposed:
"During Rù Gé, there are officials waiting to be summoned and those waiting for sequential audience who discuss state affairs.
But during the Nèidiàn Qǐjū (Inner Hall Audience),
officials are seen once and then withdrawn.
Those who wish to speak
have no means to personally express themselves.
This does not fulfill the intention of frequently seeing the assembled officials."
Míngzōng then decreed that on the day of Qǐjū, those who had matters to discuss
were permitted to step forward and express themselves.
He further decreed that all officials should present themselves for sequential rotational audience.
At this time,
the Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Ān Chónghuǐ, held absolute power and managed state affairs.
The advance escort of Chónghuǐ passed the gate of the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái mén).
The Palace Attendant, Mǎ Yán, accidentally bumped into them.
Chónghuǐ immediately beheaded Yán at the gate of the Censorate before reporting the incident.
Qí, being the Zhōngchéng (Vice Censor-in-Chief),
feared Chónghuǐ and dared not impeach him.
Fearing that the remonstrance officials would list his failures,
he sought help from the Prime Minister Rèn Yuán to inform Chónghuǐ first before raising the impeachment.
Nevertheless, he remained evasive and dared not state the matter directly.
Dòulú Gé and others were dismissed as Prime Ministers.
Rèn Yuán discussed appointing Qí as Prime Minister,
but Kǒng Xún and Zhèng Jué thwarted this,
so it was stopped.
Qí was promoted to Shàngshū Yòu Púshè (Right Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs).
Qí submitted a document to the Central Secretariat
stating that the Kāiyuán Lǐ (Rites of the Kāiyuán Era) decreed:
"On the day the Púshè assumes office,
the Central Secretariat and the Chancellery shall lead all officials in escorting him to the post."
The Central Secretariat forwarded this to the Tàicháng.
The Department of Rites reported that there was no text authorizing the "escorting to the post" ceremony.
Furthermore, Qí had already received the new appointment,
and attempting to raise the ceremony again
was inappropriate in all cases.
Míngzōng campaigned against Wáng Dū.
Having already defeated Dìngzhōu,
he returned to Luò from Biàn.
Qí was supposed to lead the officials to the Shàngdōng Mén (Upper Eastern Gate),
but instead requested to proceed to Yǎnshī to respectfully welcome the Emperor.
His memorial stated:
"The fierce faction of the Qìdān was defeated,
and the rebellious city of Zhēndìng was broken."
He was punished for mistakenly referring to Dìngzhōu as Zhēndìng,
resulting in the forfeiture of one month's salary.
Huò Yànwēi died.
An edict ordered Qí to compose the inscription for his tomb spirit-way stele.
Yànwēi was a former general of Liáng,
and Qí was a former minister of Liáng.
Qí, regarding Yànwēi's service under Liáng, did not label it "false."
This was refuted by Féng Dào.
Qí was a person who valued keeping promises
and enjoyed praising the virtues of others.
In his youth, he was known for his literary skills,
and was quite proud of this.
After achieving high status,
he carved ivory tablets with gold characters stating:
"Former Xiānggòng Jìnshì Lǐ Qí,"
and always kept them beside his seat.
As a person, he lacked solemnity
and did not understand how to advance or retreat.
Therefore, he was frequently obstructed by his contemporaries.
He retired with the title of Tàizǐ Shàofù (Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent).
He died
at the age of sixty.
Zhèng Jué.
Zhèng Jué
was a great-grandson of the Táng Prime Minister Qǐ.
His father, Huī,
served as the Deputy to Zhāng Quányì, the Hénán Yǐn.
Jué lived in Hénán in his youth, relying on Quányì.
He repeatedly failed the official examination for the Jìnshì degree.
Quányì subsequently recommended Jué to the relevant authorities,
whereupon he passed the examination.
During the reign of Zhāozōng,
he served as Jiānchá Yùshǐ (Investigating Censor).
When Liáng Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
Jué was appointed Zuǒ Bǔquē (Remonstrance Official).
Because of Quányì, various ministers of Liáng frequently recommended him.
He was successively appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretary of the Central Secretariat) and Hànlín Xuéshì Fèngzhǐ (Academician of the Hànlín Academy by Imperial Edict).
During the reign of the Last Emperor,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice Director of the Central Secretariat) and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Concurrently Manager of Affairs for the Central Secretariat and the Chancellery).
from Yùnzhōu. Mòdì
heard that the Táng troops were about to arrive,
terrified and did not know what to do.
He embraced Lǐ Zhèn, Jìng Xiáng, and others, weeping bitterly.
Consequently, he summoned Wáng Yù and asked what course of action should be taken.
Wáng Yù said:
"Your subject has one plan,
I wonder if Your Majesty can execute it or not?"
Mòdì asked what the plan was.
Wáng Yù said:
"I request to receive Your Majesty's Chúanguó Bǎo (Imperial Seal) and rush into the Táng army,
in order to delay their advance,
while waiting for the reinforcement troops to arrive."
The Emperor said:
"The situation is urgent.
The Seal is indeed not worth cherishing,
but regarding your mission,
can you resolve the matter?"
Wáng Yù bowed his head, slowly pondered, and said:
"I just fear it will not be easily resolved."
Thereupon, everyone around them all burst into laughter.
Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn.
Wáng Yù led the numerous officials to welcome and pay respects on the side of the road.
He was demoted to Sīhù Cānjūn of Láizhōu.
Later, he was transferred (by assessment) to Cāozhōu Sīmǎ.
Zhāng Quányì spoke on his behalf to Guō Chóngtāo.
He was again summoned to be Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
Míngzōng ascended the throne.
He wanted to appoint Rèn Huán as Chancellor,
but Ān Chónghuǐ considered Huán to be a recent appointee,
and did not want him to be the sole Chancellor.
He asked the Privy Council Commissioner, Kǒng Xún.
Xún had previously served Liáng,
and was friendly with Wáng Yù.
Consequently, he mentioned that Wáng Yù, a former Liáng Chancellor,
was cautious by nature and a senior statesman.
Thus, Wáng Yù was appointed Píngzhāngshì.
Míngzōng visited Biànzhōu.
The families of the six armies moved from Luò to Biàn.
However, Míngzōng also wanted to visit Yèdū.
The soldiers were worried and resentful,
and many high officials spoke against it.
Míngzōng did not heed them.
High and low officials were in uproar,
increasingly creating agitation.
Only Wáng Yù praised the plan,
believing it should proceed.
Zhào Fèng strongly advised Ān Chónghuǐ.
Chónghuǐ was startled and fearful,
and entered to see Míngzōng and strongly remonstrate.
An edict was then issued to halt the journey.
Yet Wáng Yù again praised it,
believing it was appropriate to stop.
Wáng Yù, while serving as Chancellor, was inactive and achieved nothing.
Moreover, he was deaf.
When Kǒng Xún was dismissed as Privy Council Commissioner,
Wáng Yù felt uneasy,
and urgently requested to resign due to illness.
Míngzōng repeatedly asked him to stay,
but Wáng Yù's memorials were submitted four times.
He was then appointed Zuǒ Púshè (Left Executive Secretary) and retired.
He was granted an estate in Zhèngzhōu.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title Sīkōng.
Lǐ Yú
Lǐ Yú, courtesy name Zǐhuì,
was a native of Wúdì, Bóhǎi.
Yú was cautious, serious, and taciturn by nature,
fond of studying,
and wrote gǔwén (classical prose).
Lú Yànwēi, the Jiédùshǐ of Cāngzhōu, appointed Yú as the Chief Clerk
of Ānlíng. He resigned due to the mourning period for his mother.
Later, he traveled to Guānzhōng.
When Liú Jìshù imprisoned Zhāozōng
in the Eastern Palace, Yú used a letter to persuade Hán Jiàn,
urging him to plan for the restoration.
His words were very inspiring.
Jiàn was unable to follow the advice,
so he left for Luòyáng.
He passed the Jìnshì and Hóngcí examinations,
and became Cānjūn of Hénán Fǔ.
During the Disaster of Bǎimǎ,
Yú again left for Shāndōng.
He became friendly with Lǐ Yánguāng.
Yánguāng served Liáng Mòdì as Shìjiǎng based on his classical scholarship,
and repeatedly recommended Yú.
Yú was consequently summoned.
After a long time,
he was appointed Zuǒ Shíyí and Zhí Xuéshì of the Chóngzhèng Yuàn.
Prince Héng, Yǒuliàng,
was Mòdì's elder brother.
The high ministers of Liáng, including Lǐ Zhèn, all bowed to him,
but Yú alone performed the cháng yī (long bow).
Mòdì criticized Yú for this, saying:
"I, the Emperor, bow to Prince Héng,
yet you only perform the yī,
is this acceptable?"
Yú said:
"If Your Majesty receives him according to the rites appropriate for a family member,
then bowing is appropriate.
Your subject has no private relationship with the Prince,
how could I improperly humble myself?"
He was dismissed for speaking controversially and offending the Emperor's will,
and reduced to Guānchá Pànguān of Dèngzhōu.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
Yú attended court in the capital.
The various high officials of Táng had long heard that Yú studied the Classics,
and respected him.
He was appointed Zhǔkè Lángzhōng and Hànlín Xuéshì.
When Prince Wèi, Jìjí, attacked Shǔ,
Yú was appointed Dūtǒng Pànguān for the campaign.
The roads into Shǔ were rugged and dangerous.
Discussants suggested that the army should advance slowly, waiting for a change in circumstances,
The Zhāotǎoshǐ, Guō Chóngtāo, asked Yú for a decision.
Yú said:
"Wáng Yǎn is decadent and neglectful,
throwing the state's government into chaos.
His people are weary of him.
If we take advantage of their sudden confusion,
and strike where they are unprepared,
the advantage lies in speed.
We cannot delay."
Chóngtāo agreed with him,
and wherever they arrived, the populace came out to surrender,
thereby leading to the destruction of Shǔ.
Earlier,
when the army reached Bǎojī,
Chén Yì, the Zhāotǎo Pànguān, claimed illness and requested to remain behind.
Yú said sharply:
"Chén Yì advances when he sees profit,
and stops when he perceives difficulty.
Now the main army is crossing dangerous terrain,
and people's minds are easily shaken.
It is precisely fitting to execute him as a public warning."
Because of this, no one in the army dared to speak of staying behind.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he was successively promoted to Bīngbù Shìláng Chéngzhǐ.
Míngzōng performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven.
Yú drafted the edicts of grace for Chancellors Féng Dào and Zhào Fèng.
Dào disliked the wording,
and he was dismissed to become Tàicháng Qīng.
When Rèn Huán was dismissed as Chancellor,
Yú was then appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
When Yú served as Chancellor,
he did not build a mansion,
but borrowed the Yánbīnguǎn to live in.
Yú was ill.
Míngzōng sent a eunuch to visit him.
The eunuch saw his ruined blankets and worn mat,
with the four walls utterly bare.
Míngzōng sighed in admiration,
and ordered ceremonial tent furnishings to be bestowed upon him.
Prince Lù rebelled,
and attacked the capital.
Mǐndì fled during the night.
The next day, Yú and Féng Dào arrived at Duānmén.
They heard the Emperor had already left,
and that Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yūn had both died.
Yú wanted to go to the Chancellery to await the Empress Dowager's instructions.
Dào said:
"Prince Lù has already posted notices everywhere promising amnesty,
and will arrive immediately.
Why should we wait for the Empress Dowager's order?"
So they went out together to welcome him.
The Deposed Emperor entered and took the throne.
He dismissed Dào and sent him out to govern Tóngzhōu,
and appointed Liú Xù as Chancellor.
Xù was impatient and narrow-minded by nature,
while Yú was fundamentally upright and resolute.
Whenever they acted, they conflicted.
Xù was related to Féng Dào by marriage.
Yú frequently taunted Xù about this,
and the two men ended up shouting insults at each other.
Consequently, both were dismissed.
Yú retained the title of Zuǒ Púshè.
At this time,
warfare was flourishing,
and there were many affairs of state.
When Yú was Chancellor,
he wanted to establish governance based on ancient principles.
He requested the distribution of the Táng Liùdiǎn to all departments,
so that each could fulfill their specific duty,
that prefectures and counties select scholars,
and implement the Xiāngyǐn Jiǔ Lǐ.
The era considered him impractical and his ideas were not adopted.
When Mǐndì ascended the throne,
he was intent on good governance.
He frequently summoned the Academicians
to inquire about current affairs.
But because he considered Yú too formal,
he never consulted him.
The Deposed Emperor also said that Yú and his peers were useless.
He often pointed at the Chancellors and said:
"These are just 'porridge-and-rice monks'!"
meaning they ate their fill all day long,
but put their minds to no use.
He died of illness in the second year of Qīngtài.
Lú Dǎo
was a man from Fànyáng.
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
he passed the *jìnshì* examination
and served as Censor Investigating the Palace (*Jiānchá Yùshǐ*). When Táng fell, he served Liáng.
He was repeatedly promoted to Director of the Left Bureau (*Zuǒsī Lángzhōng*) and Investigating Censor-General with Judicial Responsibilities (*Shìyùshǐ Zhī Záshì*),
but resigned due to illness.
During the reign of Táng Míngzōng,
he was summoned and appointed
Grand Master Remonstrant of the Right (*Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū*),
and later promoted to Secretariat Drafter (*Zhōngshū Shèrén*). Lù Wáng Cóngkē used troops from Fèngxiáng
to invade the capital. Mǐn Dì
fled to Wèizhōu. Chancellors Féng Dào and Lǐ Yú
assembled the various officials at Tiāngōng Sì (Temple of the Heavenly Palace).
They planned to go out and welcome Lù Wáng in the suburbs.
The capital was greatly terrified,
and the inhabitants hid and scattered.
The officials were slow to gather,
only Dǎo and Drafter Zhāng Zhāo arrived first. Féng Dào
requested Dǎo to draft the memorial urging Cóngkē to ascend the throne.
Dǎo said:
"If Lù Wáng enters the court,
welcoming him in the suburbs is acceptable.
But matters concerning urging ascension,
how can they be lightly discussed!" Dào said:
"Can
the urging of ascension be stopped?"
Dǎo said:
"The Son of Heaven is currently suffering exile outside the city.
To suddenly urge someone to take the high position,
if Lù Wáng holds fast to his principles and refuses,
and blames us for disloyalty and lack of righteousness,
what words shall we use to answer?
Furthermore, the Sovereign and Lù Wáng
are both sons of the Empress Dowager.
It would be better to lead the officials to the palace gate
and seek the Empress Dowager's instruction." Before he finished speaking,
a report came, saying:
"Lù Wáng
has arrived." Ān Cóngjìn, the Inspector of the Capital City,
urged the officials to line up and welcome him,
and the officials scattered away hurriedly. Lù Wáng stopped
outside Zhèngyángmén. Dào
again urged Dǎo to draft the memorial,
but Dǎo replied as before. Lǐ Yú said:
"We are criminals,
and Drafter Lú's
words are correct."
Dǎo ultimately refused to draft the memorial. Later, Dǎo served Jìn
as Vice Minister of Personnel (*Lìbù Shìláng*).
He died in the sixth year of Tiānfú (941 CE),
aged seventy-six. Sīkōng Tǐng.
Sīkōng Tǐng
was a man from Qīngyáng,
Bèizhōu. During the time of Táng Xīzōng,
he failed the *jìnshì* examination.
Afterward,
he went to serve as Luó Shàowēi's private secretary. After Shàowēi died,
he entered Liáng
and became Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury (*Tàifǔ Shǎoqīng*). When Yáng Shīhòu was garrisoned at Tiānxióng,
Tǐng resigned his post
and went to rely on him. After Shīhòu died,
Hè Délún
replaced him. During the upheaval caused by Zhāng Yàn,
Yàn ordered the Judicial Administrator (*Pànguān*) Wáng Zhèngyán
to draft a memorial criticizing and denouncing the Liáng ruler and his ministers.
Zhèngyán normally lacked literary skill,
and being pressed by soldiers' weapons,
sweat streamed down his back;
he could not put his brush to paper. Yàn became angry,
pushed Zhèngyán off the couch,
and scolded him, saying:
"This dullard
insults me!" He looked around at the clerks and asked who could draft the memorial.
A clerk immediately said that Tǐng had been Luó Wáng's secretary.
Yàn then sent a swift rider to summon him.
Tǐng's clothes had been stolen by the rampaging soldiers;
he arrived covering his body with ragged clothing.
He saw Yàn and made a long bow,
his spirit and demeanor composed.
He quickly composed the document with his brush,
and the language was quite simple and coarse.
Yàn, because it was easy
to understand,
was very pleased,
and immediately provided him with clothes, servants, and horses,
then appointing him as Délún's Judicial Administrator. Délún surrendered Wèibó
to Jìn. The King of Jìn
concurrently took charge of Tiānxióng,
and kept Tǐng as the Judicial Administrator. When Liáng and Jìn were facing off along the Yellow River,
Tǐng was often made Acting Administrator of Military Affairs.
Tǐng was disliked by Guō Chóngtāo,
and Chóngtāo frequently reported
that he accepted bribes. The Commander of the Guards (*Dū Yúhòu*), Zhāng Yù, had many faults,
and Tǐng repeatedly disciplined him according to law.
Tǐng had a nephew in Liáng.
He sent a household servant
to summon him. Yù captured this servant,
claiming
he was corresponding with Liáng.
Zhuāngzōng then executed him. Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter 43: Liú Xù.
Liú Xù
was a man from Guīyì,
Zhuōzhōu. Xù was handsome and refined in manner.
He, along with his elder brother Xuān,
and his younger brother,
were all known for their love of learning
between Yān and Jì. Later,
he became Judicial Investigator (*Tuīguān*) for Wáng Chǔzhí, the Military Commissioner (*Guānchá*) of Dìngzhōu.
Chǔzhí was imprisoned by his son Dū. Xù's brother Xuān
was also killed by an enemy family,
so Xù fled to Cāngzhōu. When Táng Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
Xù was appointed
Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Bóshì*),
and made Academician of the Hanlin Academy (*Hànlín Xuéshì*).
During Míngzōng's time,
he was repeatedly promoted to Vice Minister of War (*Bīngbù Shìláng*) and held that office. Míngzōng deeply respected Xù
and admired his refined demeanor,
promoting him to Academician of the Duānmíng Palace.
In the third year of Chángxīng (932 CE),
he was appointed Vice Minister of the Secretariat, concurrently Minister of Justice, and Commissioner for the Affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery (*Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*).
Xù went to the gates of Zhōngxīng Hall to express thanks,
but as there was a major sacrifice that day, the Emperor was not holding court.
Xù entered the Duānmíng Palace to express his thanks. Xù's promotion from Academician of the Duānmíng Palace
to Chancellor
was considered a great honor at the time. When Fèi Dì (the Deposed Emperor) ascended,
Xù was promoted to Minister of Personnel (*Lìbù Shàngshū*), Vice Minister of the Chancellery (*Ménxià Shìláng*),
and Supervisor of the Compilation of National History (*Jiānxiū Guóshǐ*).
Initially,
when Fèi Dì took power,
he asked Wáng Méi,
the Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (*Sānsī Shǐ*):
"What is the amount in the treasuries and granaries?"
Méi replied:
"The amount is several million."
But when the emperor demanded funds to reward the army and not even one-tenth was available,
Fèi Dì became furious,
dismissed Méi,
and ordered Xù to concurrently administer the Three Bureaus. Xù was meticulous by nature,
and he especially hated the pervasive corruption
and decay in the Three Bureaus.
He therefore audited the documents and ledgers,
verified the genuine amounts,
and completely remitted the remaining taxes and accumulated debts. In the past, officials took advantage of the accumulated debts of many years,
covering them up without issuing clearances,
and thus used them to manipulate prefectures and counties to extort bribes.
When Xù cancelled all these debts,
the common people were joyful and regarded it as benevolent,
but all the clerks of the Three Bureaus were dejected and resentful. Previously,
Féng Dào and Xù were related by marriage
and served together as Chancellors.
When Dào was dismissed,
Lǐ Yú replaced him. Yú had always disliked Dào's character.
Whenever there was a policy that caused delay or failure,
he would point it out
and mock Xù, saying:
"This is the work of your relative, the Venerable Lord!" Xù was naturally intolerant of others,
while Yú was exceptionally upright and firm.
Consequently,
they often insulted and reviled each other. The clerks and scribes in the Chancellery
disliked the strictness and integrity of these two men,
so they started rumors together.
When the matter came to Fèi Dì's attention,
he dismissed both of them,
appointing Xù as Minister of the Right (*Yòu Púshè*). At this time,
the various clerks of the Three Bureaus, carrying their seals,
gathered outside Yuèhuámén.
Hearing the Imperial Edict dismissing Xù from the Chancellery,
they all cheered and congratulated each other, saying:
"From now on, we fellows shall live comfortably!"
Xǔ was in the position of Chancellor,
but was unfamiliar with historical precedents (diǎngù).
Initially,
when Míngzōng died,
the Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng), Cuī Jūjiǎn,
ought by precedent to have served as the Commissioner of Rites (Lǐyí Shǐ).
Jūjiǎn declined, citing the taboo name Lǐ of his ancestor.
Féng Dào changed Jūjiǎn to be Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān).
Jūjiǎn was resentful at losing the position.
Lǐ Xiáng, a Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén), drafted an imperial patent (gàocí) for Jūjiǎn,
which included
the phrase "hearing the name causes fear in the heart."
Xǔ immediately changed it to read
"having shame and maintaining integrity" (Yǒu Chǐ Qiě Gé).
Jūjiǎn protested, saying:
"There is a standard regulation (lìng shì) regarding taboo names.
What crime have I committed?"
Those who heard this at the time all repeated it as a joke.
When he became a Grand Master (Púshè),
he encountered rain while entering court.
The ranks were moved under the corridor.
An official from the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái Lì) directed the Grand Master to stand below the Censor-in-Chief (Zhōngchéng) and the Censors (Yùshǐ).
Xǔ questioned the official about the precedent (gù shì),
but from the Chancellors (Zǎixiàng) down to the officials of the Censorate (Tái Shěng), no one knew it.
At this time,
Féng Dào had been dismissed as Chancellor and made Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Since the Suí and Táng dynasties,
the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) held no substantive duties
and were not specially established.
When Dào became Sīkōng,
he asked the relevant officials about his court rank order,
but they were also unable to determine it.
Because of this, he did not enter the main court hall;
he waited until the officials of the Censorate and the Two Provinces (Liǎng Shěng) had entered before he entered,
and when the Chancellors left, he followed them out.
When Xǔ became Púshè,
he considered himself to be in the same situation as Dào, having been dismissed from the Chancellorship.
Consequently, he followed Dào in entering and leaving [the court].
The relevant authorities could not impeach or correct him,
but critics often laughed at him secretly.
During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ,
Zhāng Cóngbīn rebelled
and killed the Imperial Son Chóngyì in Luòyáng.
Consequently, Xǔ was made Resident Administrator of the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū Liúshǒu)
and concurrently administered the Salt and Iron Monopolies (Pàn Yántiě).
During the Kāiyùn era,
he was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Concurrently Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì),
and again administered the Three Bureaus (Sānsī).
When the Qìdān invaded the capital,
Xǔ was dismissed due to an eye ailment and made Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo).
He died that year,
at the age of sixty.
Lú Wénjì
Lú Wénjì, courtesy name Zǐchí.
His grandfather, Jiǎnqiú,
served as the Military Commissioner (Jiédù Shǐ) of Tàiyuán during the Táng dynasty.
His father, Sìyè,
reached the office of Right Remonstrator (Yòu Bǔquē).
Wénjì passed the *jìnshì* examination.
He served the Liáng dynasty as Vice Minister of Personnel (Xíngbù Shìláng) and Scholar of the Jíxián Hall (Jíxián Diàn Xuéshì).
During the reign of Táng Míngzōng,
he became Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
When he first took office
and all the officials were paying respects at the Censorate,
an attendant reported that the communications officers (Jìnzòu Guān) from the various circuits wished to offer congratulations.
Wénjì asked:
"What should be done?"
The attendant replied:
"When the imperial court was in Cháng'ān,
the communications officers treated the Grand Masters (Dàfū) and Censor-in-Chiefs (Zhōngchéng) as mere clerks (Xūshǐ).
Since the decline of Táng,
when the Son of Heaven became weak
and the feudal lords grew powerful,
tribute payments failed to arrive.
The court tolerated the regional garrisons (Fāng Zhèn)
and indulged the residence clerks (Dǐ Lì).
When the Dàfū and Zhōngchéng assume office,
the Jìnzòu Guān come to the guest area to present their names,
and are offered tea and wine but are not granted an audience.
This has been passed down and regarded as the precedent."
Wénjì said:
"Although my virtue is scant,
how dare I abandon the old system?"
He then dispatched an official to instruct them.
The Jìnzòu Guān angrily brandished their arms and clamored to leave.
Having no choice, they entered for the audience.
Wénjì sat on his couch, holding his ceremonial tablet (hù) upright.
The Censorate clerk announced their names and directed them in the ritual prostration.
After they left,
they were overwhelmed by indignation and anger.
They complained to the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ), Ān Chónghuǐ.
Chónghuǐ said:
"I am unfamiliar with the precedent.
You may appeal to the court."
They immediately led each other to the Palace Gate (Gémén), requesting an audience to present their complaint in writing.
Míngzōng asked the Chancellor, Zhào Fèng:
"What rank of external official do the communications clerks resemble?"
Fèng replied:
"They are the rank of those who deliver dispatches (fādì zhìhòu) in the prefectures and districts."
Míngzōng said angrily:
"They are just mere clerks and servants!
How dare they treat my legal officials with contempt!"
They were all punished with the rod and sent away.
Wénjì also requested the complete restoration of the system of periodic evaluations (jiàokǎo fǎ) for central and local officials.
The generals, chancellors, and the Son of Heaven himself would record the results.
Although the imperial decree was put into effect,
the officials were ultimately not evaluated.
After more than a year,
he was promoted to Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū).
Wénjì had a long-standing feud with the Chancellor Cuī Xié.
Xié appointed Yú Yè as Director in the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù Lángzhōng).
Wénjì was greatly angered
because Yè (邺) was homophonous with his father's name, Yè (業).
Yè went to the Ministry to report for duty and pay his respects,
but Wénjì refused to see him.
Consequently, Wénjì requested several consecutive days of leave.
Soon after, Yè, who was meant to travel on an imperial mission, had not yet departed.
Wénjì immediately returned to his duties.
Yè, driven by drunken indignation, hanged himself and died.
Wénjì was implicated and demoted to Judicial Administrator (Sīmǎ) of Shízhōu.
After a long time,
he became Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān) and Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
He was sent on an imperial mission to Shǔ.
Passing through Fèngxiáng,
at that time the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) was the Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng (Fèngxiáng Jiédù Shǐ).
Wénjì was impressive in appearance and his voice was clear and resonant.
The Deposed Emperor was struck by him.
Later, when the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he wanted to choose a Chancellor.
He inquired among his attendants.
The attendants all said:
"Wénjì and Yáo Yǐ possess popular esteem."
The Deposed Emperor then wrote the names of all the respected officials on slips and placed them inside a glass vase.
That night, he burned incense and prayed to Heaven.
He used chopsticks to pick one out,
and Wénjì’s name was the first one drawn.
Happily, he appointed him Chancellor.
He was subsequently appointed Vice Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Concurrently Grand Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
At this time,
there were many affairs in the realm.
The Deposed Emperor repeatedly held Wénjì accountable for them.
Wénjì then requested the abolition of the court audience held every five days (Wǔ Rì Qǐjū),
in order to revert to the Táng dynasty precedent.
He asked to open the Yányīng Hall,
hoping to discuss and memorialize state affairs in a relaxed manner.
The Deposed Emperor believed that the Wǔ Rì Qǐjū
was the means by which Míngzōng met his officials,
and should not be abolished.
Furthermore, discussing matters in the informal palace hall (Biàndiàn)
allowed for ease and comfort,
so why was the Yányīng Hall necessary?
Consequently, he decreed that if the Chancellors had matters to present,
they should simply proceed to the Gémén and request an audience without needing a specific schedule.
When Jìn Gāozǔ raised an army in Tàiyuán,
the Deposed Emperor campaigned north.
Passing by, he paid respects at Huī Líng.
Resting in a military hut (zhàng shè),
he looked at Wénjì and said:
"Since I first met you in Fèngxiáng,
I have not treated you as an ordinary person.
Since you became Chancellor,
I have inquired among public opinion,
and they all said you could bring about Great Peace (Tàipíng).
Now, I have been reduced to this state.
What should you do?"
Wénjì was greatly fearful and apologized for his failings.
When the Deposed Emperor reached Héyáng,
Wénjì advised the Emperor to secure the bridge and defend himself,
but the Emperor did not listen.
When Jìn Gāozǔ entered and established his reign,
Wénjì was dismissed and made Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
He was successively promoted to Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàishī)
and retired.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ entered and established his reign,
Wénjì was immediately appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng) at home.
He died
at the age of seventy-six,
and was posthumously granted the title Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
Mǎ Yìnsūn
, courtesy name Qìngxiān,
was a man of Shānghé, Dì Zhōu.
His character was timid and dull.
When young, he loved learning
and studied Hán Yù's style of composition.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination.
Under the Táng [Dynasty], he served Lù Wáng Cóngkē as Assistant Commissioner (Zhīshǐ) of the Hézhōng Commandery.
Cóngkē was expelled by Yáng Yànwēn
and was dismissed, residing in a manor in the capital.
Yǐnsūn followed him and did not leave.
When Cóngkē became the Magistrate of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào Yǐn)
and was transferred to govern Fèngxiáng,
Yǐnsūn constantly followed him
and was made Judging Official (Pànguān) of the Commandery.
When the Prince of Lù was about to raise troops in rebellion,
he completed the plans with his officers, including Hán Zhāoyìn.
He summoned Yǐnsūn and told him:
"I have received the mandate to move my garrison.
The road passes through the capital.
Which direction should I proceed for convenience?"
Yǐnsūn replied:
"When the ruler commands
a summons, one does not wait for the carriage.
Now, Your Highness is a royal relative of the state,
and the late emperor has only recently passed away.
Attending the mourning rites and proceeding to your garrison
is the loyalty of a subject and a son."
Everyone nearby laughed at his foolishness,
but Cóngkē cherished him in his heart.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì) assumed the throne,
he made Yǐnsūn Director in the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Lángzhōng) and Academician of the Hànlín Academy.
After a long time,
he was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
Yǐnsūn was unfamiliar with worldly affairs,
and thus many government matters became blocked.
At this time,
Féng Dào was dismissed as Military Governor of the Kuāngguó Army
and appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Since the Táng [Dynasty], the post of Sīkōng had never been awarded by special appointment.
The relevant officials were unaware of the precedents,
and debaters at court were agitated.
Some said that Sīkōng was one of the Three Dukes
and therefore a prime ministerial duty,
and should participate in major governance.
But Grand Councilor Lú Wénjì alone held that the duty of Sīkōng
was merely sacrifices and sweeping.
Yǐnsūn could not decide any of these issues.
At that time, Liú Xù was also dismissed as Grand Councilor and made Palace Gate Keeper (Púyè).
Kǒng Zhāoxù, Right Palace Assistant Consultant (Yòu Sànqí Chángshì), suggested:
"The rank of Chángshì should precede that of Púyè."
Yǐnsūn ordered the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) to check the precedents.
The Censorate reported:
"No precedent can be found,
but according to the current North/South ranking system
, the Chángshì is positioned in front."
Yǐnsūn immediately ruled on the Censorate's report and implemented it.
Liú Xù was greatly angered.
Cuī Jūjiǎn announced loudly at court
, saying: "If Kǒng Zhāoxù understands etiquette,
then there is no one at court who understands etiquette!
Moreover, the Púyè is the master and chief of all officials.
The Grand Censor (Zhōngchéng) and Grand Masters (Dàfū) take their places to show respect,
while the Chángshì ranks beneath the Six Ministers of the Southern Palace.
How much more so below the Púyè?
Zhāoxù is a foolish child,
how could he know the proper procedures?"
When court officials heard Jūjiǎn's words,
the circulating debate gradually subsided.
Yǐnsūn often failed to decide when facing matters.
At that time, he was called
"The Three No-Opens"
, meaning he did not open his mouth to debate,
he did not open the seal to execute affairs,
and he did not open his gate to receive officials and scholars.
When the Jìn army mobilized in Tàiyuán,
the Deposed Emperor fled to Héyáng.
At this time, the situation was already critical and urgent.
Yǐnsūn traveled from Luò [yáng] to the temporary imperial residence (Xíngzài) to pay homage.
Everyone hoped he would offer some suggestion,
but Yǐnsūn merely presented three hundred bolts of patterned silk.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn entered and took the throne,
Yǐnsūn was dismissed and returned to his home village.
Since Yǐnsūn had learned Hán Yù's style of writing,
he frequently denounced the teachings of the Buddhists (Fútú Shì).
However, when he was dismissed and returned home,
he instead turned to studying Buddhism.
He compiled the *Fǎxǐ Jí* (Collection of Dharma Joy) and the *Fóguó Jì* (Record of the Buddhist Country), which circulated in the world.
People at the time mocked him
, saying: "He wasn't fully flattering Qīngtài,
so now he comes to flatter the Buddha."
Qīngtài
was the reign title of the Deposed Emperor.
Someone joked to Yǐnsūn
: "You traditionally admired Hán Yù's character,
and always recited Fù Yì's treatise.
Now you turn around and flatter the Buddha.
Is the Buddha flattering you,
or are you flattering the Buddha?"
Yǐnsūn replied:
"How do you know it isn't the Buddha flattering me?"
People at the time spread this story as a joke.
Later, he served as Guest of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Bīnkè), holding duties remotely (Fēnsī) and residing in Luòyáng.
He died during the Guǎngshùn era of the Zhōu [Dynasty].
After Yǐnsūn died,
a maid in his household claimed to speak for Yǐnsūn.
Initially,
Cuī Xié served as Grand Councilor under Míngzōng.
While in office, he achieved nothing notable.
After he died,
someone claimed to speak for his ghost in the household.
Yǐnsūn's case was similar.
People at the time mocked them
, saying: "They could not speak when alive,
but speak only after death
." Yáo Yǐ
Yáo Yǐ
, courtesy name Bǎizhēn,
was a man of Cháng'ān, Jīngzhào.
He was slow-witted in his youth
and paid no attention to his appearance or demeanor.
People at the time did not recognize his talent.
Sīkōng Tú, the recluse of Mount Zhōngtiáo, met him once and found him remarkable,
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination.
Serving the Liáng [Dynasty], he was an Academician of the Hànlín Academy and Drafter in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
When Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng destroyed the Liáng [Dynasty],
Yǐ was demoted to Administrator (Sīmǎ) of Fù Zhōu.
Afterward, he was made Left Palace Assistant Consultant (Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì), concurrently Vice Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shìláng), and Vice Director of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng).
The Deposed Emperor wished to select a Grand Councilor
, and chose contemporary officials known for their integrity and reputation
. He chose Lú Wénjì and Yǐ.
Consequently, Yǐ was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Grand Councilor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
Yǐ's character was benevolent and forgiving.
He did not know the count of cash strings, coins, or ounces.
He managed his household without method.
While in the position of Grand Councilor, he was timid and accomplished nothing.
The Táng system divided the Ministry of Personnel into three sections (*quán*):
the Minister (Shàngshū) managed one section, called the Shàngshū Quán;
the two Vice Ministers (Shìláng) managed the other two, called the Zhōng Quán and Dōng Quán.
Every year, the selection process began in the last ten days of the first month of winter,
and concluded in the third month of spring.
During the Tiānchéng era,
when Féng Dào was Grand Councilor,
he suggested:
"The realm is not yet unified.
Only a few hundred individuals are selected annually.
Yet the Ministry of Personnel uses three sections for separate registration.
Although it is called an old precedent,
in reality, it is merely complicated and useless."
An edict was issued to merge the three sections into one,
so that the Minister and Vice Ministers jointly managed the selection affairs.
When Yǐ and Lú Wénjì became Grand Councilors,
they petitioned to revert the sections back to three.
However, the old standards regarding seniority (*xúnzī*) and longevity (*zhǎngdìng*),
having been in place for many years, were often flawed.
They subsequently added to and subtracted from them.
Many candidates found this inconvenient
, and often intercepted the Grand Councilors
, complaining loudly and disrespectfully.
Yǐ and the others could do nothing about it,
so the Deposed Emperor had to issue an edict to prohibit this behavior.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn was established,
Yǐ was dismissed and made Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū).
He died
at the age of seventy-five.
On the day he died, his household had no remaining wealth.
His body could not be entombed.
Only after the government provided funeral gifts and grants could the entombment take place.
Those who heard of this pitied him.
Liú Yuè
Liú Yuè, courtesy name Zhāofǔ,
was a man of Luòyáng.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Zhènghuì, Minister of Revenue (Mínbù Shàngshū) of the Táng [Dynasty].
Chóngguī and Chóngwàng were his paternal uncles.
Yuè was the son of a prominent family.
He loved learning,
was keen in literary composition,
and skilled in debate.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination.
Serving the Liáng [Dynasty], he was Left Reminder (Zuǒ Shíyí) and Supervising Censor (Shì Yùshǐ).
During the reign of the Last Emperor (Mò Dì),
he became an Academician of the Hànlín Academy.
He progressively rose through office to become Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng).
[he was] demoted to Jūnzhōu Sīmǎ,
and then subsequently re-appointed as Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
During the reign of Táng Míngzōng,
he served as Lìbù Shìláng.
According to standard practice,
for the official credentials (gàoshēn) of civil and military officials issued by the Ministry of Personnel,
one had to pay money for the red glue, paper, and rollers before they were issued.
Those of high rank were granted them freely,
but the poor, being unable to pay the money,
often only received the imperial decree (chìdié) but not the official credentials.
Due to the chaos of the Five Dynasties period,
this became the norm,
and those with low ranks were no longer issued official credentials.
The Secretariat (Zhōngshū) merely recorded the wording of the edicts (zhìcí)
and compiled them into official registers (chìjiǎ).
Yuè submitted a proposal,
arguing
that
"The wording of the edict either appoints someone based on their talent and ability,
or praises their meritorious deeds,
or reiterates instruction and warning.
However, since those who receive office are not issued official credentials,
they all remain ignorant of the reasons for their appointment.
This is not how the words of the sovereign should announce and proclaim orders.
I request that they all be granted the credentials."
and this practice began with Yuè.
The chancellor Féng Dào came originally from a farming family,
his appearance was crude and rustic,
and many court officials mocked his coarseness.
One morning, when Dào entered court,
Bīngbù Shìláng Rèn Zàn and Yuè were behind him.
Dào repeatedly looked back as he walked.
Zàn asked Yuè:
"Why does Dào keep looking back?"
Yuè replied:
"He left behind his Rabbit Garden Primer."
The Rabbit Garden Primer
was something recited by farmers and shepherds, taught by common scholars in local schools.
Thus, Yuè used this example to ridicule Dào.
Dào heard this and was greatly enraged,
and transferred Yuè to Mìshū Jiān.
Later, when Lǐ Yú became chancellor,
Yuè was promoted to Tàicháng Qīng.
Previously,
Zhèng Yúqìng had collected models of correspondence concerning auspicious and inauspicious matters among officials and commoners during the Táng dynasty,
mixed them with the family rites of the time,
and produced two scrolls of ritual documents (shūyí).
Míngzōng, seeing that it contained rules for resuming office during mourning (qǐfù) and for 'dark marriage' (mínghūn, marrying the deceased),
sighed and said:
"Scholars exist to elevate filial piety and fraternity and strengthen customs.
Moreover, unless there are military matters [requiring urgent service],
is resuming office during mourning permissible?
Marriage
is an auspicious rite;
is it permissible to apply it to the dead?"
He then ordered Yuè to select scholars learned in literature and knowledgeable about antiquity and the present,
to jointly revise and finalize the work.
Yuè, along with Tàicháng Academicians Duàn Yóng and Tián Mǐn and others, augmented and reduced the text.
However, the contents were derived from vulgar popular customs,
all things commonly seen and transmitted by ordinary families and women of the time,
and frequently distorted the original meanings.
Nevertheless, they still retained some vestiges of proper ritual.
Later, [the rites] were lost,
making it even more impossible to trace their origins,
and in their marriage rite of the bridegroom personally meeting the bride,
there was the notion of
the woman sitting on the husband’s saddle and joining her hair ornaments,
Households of dukes and ministers
largely followed and used these practices.
When a long time had passed,
they became even more erroneous and laughable,
and there were many such examples.
Yuè died while in office
at the age of fifty-six,
and was posthumously granted the title of Lìbù Shàngshū.
His son was
Wēnsǒu.
Alas,
how intense
is man’s penchant for creating rituals!
If those in power do not demonstrate proper rites,
causing people to lose sight of the origins
and instead transmit the errors of custom,
people will still earnestly cling to and practice them.
During the chaos and warfare of the Five Dynasties,
there had long been no time for rites!
Míngzōng was a martial sovereign,
originating from the northern barbarians (Yídí),
and unversed in written learning,
yet he was able to demonstrate an intent to have his people understand ritual.
However, Yuè and his colleagues were all contemporary Confucians,
yet ultimately failed to illuminate anything new,
merely augmenting and reducing the existing text.
Nonetheless, subsequent generations of officials and commoners, for matters both auspicious and inauspicious,
all took Yuè’s text as their standard,
and of that, three or four tenths have again been distorted and lost.
How greatly lamentable!
Mǎ Gǎo
Mǎ Gǎo.
His lineage is unknown.
In his youth, he passed the examination for the Confucian classics (Míng Jīng),
and also the extensive literature (Hóng Cí) examination.
and was renowned in the world for his knowledge of rites.
During the reign of Táng Zhuāngzōng,
he was repeatedly promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén, Xíngbù Shìláng, and acting Tàicháng Qīng.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he succeeded Táng Tàizǔ and Táng Zhuāngzōng but did not establish shrines for his own ancestors.
Gǎo stated:
"In the Hàn dynasty, when vassal kings entered the lineage of succession,
they invariably established separate ancestral shrines (qīnmiào).
Guāngwǔ Huángdì established four shrines in Nányáng.
I request that, following the precedent of the Hàn dynasty,
shrines be established to express filial offerings."
Míngzōng submitted this motion for deliberation,
and Lǐbù Shàngshū Xiāo Qǐng and others requested that Gǎo's motion be followed.
The chancellor Zhèng Yù and others discussed introducing the examples of Emperor Huán and Emperor Líng of Hàn for comparison,
arguing that Emperor Líng had honored his grandfather, Jiědú Tíng Hóu Shū, as Xiàoyuán Huáng,
and his father Cháng as Xiàorén Huáng.
They requested that the relevant officials be ordered to determine posthumous titles for the four generations of ancestors as *Huáng* (Sovereign),
and establish imperial gardens and tombs following Hàn precedent.
The matter was sent down to the Tàicháng,
and Academician Wáng Pī argued that Emperor Huán of Hàn honored his grandfather as Xiàomù Huángdì,
and his father as Xiàochóng Huángdì.
Gǎo held that Xiàomù and Xiàochóng included *Huáng* but lacked *Dì* (Supreme Emperor),
and that only Sūn Hào of Wú honored his father Hé as Wén Huángdì,
which could not be taken as a model.
Yòu Púshè Lǐ Qí and others agreed with Gǎo's deliberation.
Míngzōng issued an edict, saying:
"The Five Emperors did not inherit each other's rites,
nor did the Three Kings maintain the same music.
Yet, *Huáng* (Sovereign) and *Dì* (Emperor),
though terms used in different ages, are distinct titles.
Ever since Yíng Qín,
they have combined these titles.
I occupy the position of the Nine-Five,
and am revered by the multitudes.
Why should I combine the two names upon my humble self,
yet begrudge a single character (*Dì*) to my ancestors?"
He then commanded the chief ministers to gather all officials in the Secretariat,
so that each could present their views.
Lǐ Qí and others requested that the immediate ancestors be honored as *Huángdì*,
and the great-grandparents as *Huáng*.
Chancellor Zhèng Yù combined the collective deliberation and presented the memorial, saying:
"Rites are not handed down from Heaven but originate from human sentiment.
They can be stopped or carried out,
and have both detriments and benefits.
Currently, the deliberators cite antiquity,
taking the Hàn dynasty as their basis.
But upon what did the regulations made by Hàn themselves rely?
During the Kāiyuán period,
Gāotáo was honored as Démíng Huángdì,
and Liáng Wǔzhāo Wáng was honored as Xīngshèng Huángdì;
shrines were established for both in the Capital.
These are the precedents of the Táng house.
I request that the four generations of ancestors all be given the title *Dì* (Emperor), as stated in the imperial edict,
and that shrines be established in the Capital."
The edict approved the addition of *Dì* to the title,
but commanded that the shrines be established in Yìngzhōu.
Liú Yuè (劉岳) revised the protocols for mourning attire,
and his additions or deletions
were all decided by Gǎo (縞).
Gǎo also stated:
“The mourning ritual of coarse and hemp attire
is used to distinguish closeness and distance in kinship,
and to clarify what is doubtful or ambiguous.
According to the ritual codes (Lǐ),
a paternal uncle does not wear mourning clothes for his niece-in-law (or vice versa, i.e., relationships between men and women of the same generation),
pushing them towards distance.
During the reign of Táng Tàizōng (唐太宗),
the relevant department debated making the period of mourning for an elder brother’s wife ‘Minor Coarse Mourning (xiǎogōng, 小功)’ for five months.
Now, the relevant department grants leave for ‘Major Coarse Mourning (dàgōng, 大功)’ for nine months,
which is incorrect.”
The Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì, 廢帝) handed down the proposal,
and Duàn Yǒng (段顒), a Libationer of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Bóshì, 太常博士), argued
that “the granting of leave for mourning an elder brother’s wife under the ‘Major Coarse Mourning’ standard
is stipulated in the Statutes (Lìng).
That the Statutes differ from the Rituals (Lǐ) is not unique to this case,
and there are five points of difference regarding mourning attire.
In the Rituals,
maternal aunts (yí, 姨) and maternal uncles (jiù, 舅) both wear ‘Minor Coarse Mourning’;
in the Statutes, they all wear ‘Major Coarse Mourning.’
A wife’s parents, sons-in-law, and grandsons/nephews on the female side (wàishēng, 外甥) all wear ‘Fine Mourning (sī, 緦)’ in the Rituals;
in the Statutes, they all wear ‘Minor Coarse Mourning.’
The Rituals and the Statutes are thus fundamentally incompatible.”
Zhào Xián (趙咸), Right Grand Master of Remonstrance and Assistance (Yòu Zànshàn Dàfū, 右贊善大夫), further argued,
“When dealing with mourning,
rather than making it easy,
it is better to be sorrowful.
The Five Degrees of Mourning (wǔfú, 五服) in the Yílǐ (儀禮)
are sometimes determined by the designation (of the relationship),
and sometimes regulated based on the status of the honored party.
By extending benevolence and drawing upon righteousness,
each situation has its appropriate standard.
According to the Rituals, one wears ‘Major Coarse Mourning’ for the wife of one’s elder brother’s son.
Yet, now, one wears ‘Minor Coarse Mourning’ for the mother of one’s elder brother’s son (i.e., the elder brother’s wife).
This is an inversion of the proper order of severity.
By designation, the wife of an elder brother’s son is distant;
but by honoring status, the elder brother’s wife (sǎo, 嫂) is not lowly.
The practice of wearing ‘Major Coarse Mourning’ for the elder brother’s wife
has been established for a long time.
The Statutes
are the laws of the state
and cannot be abolished.”
Cáo Chēn (曹琛), Director of the Bureau of Seals (Sīfēng Lángzhōng, 司封郎中),
requested that the proposal be submitted,
and also that a definitive opinion be established regarding the points where the Rituals and the Statutes conflicted.
An imperial edict ordered the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng, 尚書省) to convene the hundred officials for deliberation.
Liú Xù (劉昫), Left Vice-Director (Zuǒ Púshè, 左僕射), and others argued:
“The Statutes contain no explicit text regarding mourning attire.
The granting of ‘Major Coarse Mourning’ leave for an elder brother’s wife
is merely an appendage to the Statutes concerning leave for repose (jiǎnìng, 假寧),
and the imperial orders do not specify the duration in months or years.
We request that all mourning attire be definitively standardized according to the Kāiyuán Lǐ (開元禮, Kāiyuán Ritual Code),
and that the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng, 太常) fully detail the system of the Five Degrees of Mourning
and attach it to the Statutes.”
The inclusion of the Five Degrees of Mourning in the Statutes
started with Gǎo.
Gǎo,
during the reign of Míngzōng (明宗), was once punished for mishandling an appeal case
and demoted to Surveillance Cavalry Administrator of Suízhōu (Suízhōu Sīmǎ, 綏州司馬).
He was later reinstated as Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Bīnkè, 太子賓客)
and promoted to Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng, 戶部侍郎) and Vice-Minister of the Ministry of War (Bīngbù Shìláng, 兵部侍郎).
When Lú Wénjì (盧文紀) became chancellor,
he disdained Gǎo for being an old-fashioned pedant
and transferred him to Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, 國子祭酒).
He died
at the age of eighty,
and was posthumously granted the title Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū, 兵部尚書).
Cuī Jūjiǎn (崔居儉)
Cuī Jūjiǎn
was a native of Qīnghé (清河).
Both his grandfather Lǐ (蠡) and his father Ráo (蕘) were famous officials during the Táng (唐) dynasty.
Jūjiǎn excelled in literary composition,
and his disposition was pure and elegant.
When young, he passed the presented scholar (jìnshì, 進士) examination.
During the Zhēnmíng (貞明) era of the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
he served as a Scholar of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén, 中書舍人), Academician of the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì, 翰lín學士), and Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, 御史中丞).
During the reign of Táng Zhuāngzōng (唐莊宗),
he served as Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Shìláng, 刑部侍郎) and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng, 太常卿).
The Cuī (崔) clan, along with the Lú (盧) and Zhèng (鄭) clans, had been classified as major families (jiǎzú, 甲族) since the Latter Wèi (後魏), Suí (隋), and Táng dynasties.
Regarding matters of fortune and misfortune (i.e., rituals),
each compiled its own family ritual codes (jiālǐ, 家禮).
In later generations, their descendants
relied solely on their prestigious family background to hold themselves high,
which incurred the jealousy of the world.
When Míngzōng died,
Jūjiǎn was, according to precedent, appointed Commissioner of Rituals (Lǐyí Shǐ, 禮儀使).
Jūjiǎn, citing the taboo on his grandfather’s personal name Lǐ (蠡),
declined the appointment.
The Chancellor, Féng Dào (馮道), immediately transferred Jūjiǎn to Supervisor of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān, 祕書監).

Jūjiǎn successively held the posts of Vice-Minister of the Ministry of War, Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Shìláng, 吏部侍郎), Vice-Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng, 尚書左丞), and Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū, 戶部尚書).
He died in the fourth year of Tiānfú (天福) of the Jìn (晉) dynasty
at the age of seventy,
and was posthumously granted the title Right Vice-Director (Yòu Púshè, 右僕射).
Jūjiǎn was poor at managing his livelihood;
even when holding high office,
he often lacked clothing.
On the day he died, he was too poor to afford a burial,
which saddened those who heard about it.
Cuī Zhuó (崔梲)
Cuī Zhuó, courtesy name Zǐwén (子文),
was a native of Ānpíng (安平) in Shēnzhōu (深州).
His father Zhuó (涿)
served as Director in the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Lángzhōng, 刑部郎中) late in the Táng dynasty.
The younger Zhuó was fond of learning from a young age,
read widely in the classics and histories,
and excelled in literary composition.
Caught in the chaos of the world,
he lived in seclusion in Huátái (滑臺).
He did not venture out into the neighborhoods for more than ten years,
and few people knew his face.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (貞明) of the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
he was ranked first (jiǎ kē, 甲科) in the presented scholar examination.
Wáng Zàn (王瓚), the Prefect of Kāifēng (Kāifēng Yǐn, 開封尹), appointed him to manage records and memorials.
Zhuó was extremely filial by nature.
When his father Zhuó fell ill,
he refused to take medicine,
saying:
“Life and death are decreed by fate;
why use medicine?”
The younger Zhuó repeatedly offered medical treatment,
but it was not accepted.
Whenever guests came to inquire about the illness,
Zhuó would greet and bow to them outside the gate,
weeping as he informed them.
The elder Zhuó ultimately died without taking medicine.
Zhuó was heartbroken and devastated during the mourning period.
When the mourning period was over,
Táng Míngzōng appointed him Investigating Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ, 監察御史).
He did not accept the post.
When he was appointed again a year later,
he finally accepted.
He was successively promoted to Director of the Ministry of Justice (Dūguān Lángzhōng, 都官郎中) and Academician of the Hanlin Academy.
During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖),
he served as Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Revenue and concurrently Chief Academician (Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ, 學士承旨),
and provisionally oversaw the metropolitan examination (gòngjǔ, 貢舉) of the second year of Tiānfú.
Previously,
when Zhuó served as an Academician,
he once drafted an imperial edict
that was revised by the Chancellor, Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰).
Zhuó, citing the Táng precedent that an Academician who had a drafted edict revised should be dismissed,
cited classics and relied on precedents to argue his case,
which made Wéihàn quite displeased.
Since Zhuó was solely dedicated to literature when young
and was unable to manage practical affairs,
Wéihàn ordered Zhuó to oversee the metropolitan examination.
Zhuó indeed failed to fulfill his duty.
At that time, there was a presented scholar named Kǒng Yīng (孔英),
who had a reputation for ugly conduct
and was generally disliked by the public.
After Zhuó received the appointment,
he went to see Wéihàn.
Wéihàn was habitually noble,
strict and venerable, and spoke concisely.
He said to Zhuó:
“Kǒng Yīng is coming (to take the exam).”
Zhuó did not grasp his intention.
He thought Wéihàn mentioned Kǒng Yīng as a recommendation,
so he passed Yīng in the examination.
Public opinion strongly condemned this action.
Zhuó was immediately dismissed from the Academicians,
appointed Vice-Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs,
and then transferred to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
In the fifth year,
Gāozǔ commanded the Tàicháng to restore the Civil and Military Dual Dances,
and to carefully finalize the Rites and Musical Chapters for the primary and winter imperial audiences.
Since the disturbances at the end of the Táng dynasty,
the system of rites and music had been lost for a long time.
Zhāng Zhuō, along with the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Dòu Zhēngù, Xíngbù Shìláng Lǚ Qí, and Lǐbù Shìláng Zhāng Yǔn, drafted and finalized these measures.
That year during the Winter Solstice,
Gāozǔ held the imperial audience in Chóngyuán Diàn.
The palace instruments were set up in the courtyard,
the Dual Dances were positioned to the north,
and the singers (Dēnggē) were placed above.
The performers of the Civil Dance (Wénwǔ Láng) formed eight ranks (bāyì),
numbering sixty-four men.
They wore the advanced scholar's cap (Jìnxián),
yellow gauze robes,
white inner garments (Zhōngdān),
white stitched silk/leather aprons (dāng),
white cloth large-mouthed trousers,
and leather belts and boots.
They held the flute (Yuè) in the left hand,
and the pheasant plume (Zhái) in the right.
There were two conductors (Yǐnzhě) holding yak-tail banners (Dú).
The performers of the Military Dance (Wǔwǔ Láng) formed eight ranks (bāyì),
numbering sixty-four men.
They wore flat turban-cloth (Píngjīn Cè),
crimson silk-cloth large sleeves, embroidered aprons (Dāngjiǎ) with gold ornamentation,
white stitched silk/leather,
brocade coiled-serpent (Téngshé) uplifted-ridge belts,
leopard-patterned large-mouthed trousers,
and black boots.
They held the shield (Gān) in the left hand,
and the axe (Qī) in the right.
There were two conductors holding banners (Jīng).
In addition, there were twelve drum-and-pipe sections,
carried by men draped in bear and leopard skins,
symbolizing the hundred beasts leading the dance.
Each section was set up with one feather-canopy drum (Yǔbǎo Gǔ),
one large drum,
and one bronze bell (Jīn Chún).
There were two performers each for singing (Gē), vertical flutes (Xiāo), and reed pipes (Jiā).
When the princes and dukes offered congratulations for long life,
the Son of Heaven raised his goblet,
and Xuántóng was performed.
At the third toast,
the singers (Dēnggē) performed Wéntóng.
When the food was raised,
the Civil Dance performed the music of Zhāodé,
and the Military Dance performed the music of Chénggōng.
When the ceremony was complete,
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased,
and bestowed gold and silk upon Zhāng Zhuō.
All the officials and attendants who witnessed it sighed in admiration.
However, the rites and music had been abandoned for so long,
and the compositions were simple and erroneous.
Moreover, they were followed by the Qiūcí Nícháng Fǎqǔ tradition,
which mixed and disordered the proper court music (Yǎyīn).
The musicians and dancers,
were mostly performers from the Jiao Fang (imperial music bureau), merchants, or people avoiding mandatory service in the prefectures and counties.
Furthermore, there were no elderly masters or skilled craftsmen to instruct them.
On the New Year's Day the following year,
they performed again in the court,
but the singers (Dēnggē) emitted mournful, despairing, and unsettling sounds,
like the tunes of Xièlù and Yúbìn.
The rows and movements of the dancers,
all failed to follow the rhythm,
and all who heard them were saddened and angered.
Gāozǔ passed away that year.
Zhāng Zhuō, due to paralysis (fēngbì), was reassigned as Tàizǐ Bīnkè with duties in Xījīng, where he eventually died.
In the second year of Kāiyùn,
Tàicháng Shàoqīng Táo Gǔ proposed the abolition of the Dual Dances.
The following year,
the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
and Yēlǜ Déguāng entered the capital.
The Tàicháng requested the preparation of the full imperial escort (Fǎjià) to welcome him.
When the musicians practiced the honor guard drums and pipes,
the residents of the capital who heard it shed tears.
Lǐ Yì
Lǐ Yì,
was a native of Jīngzhào.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was quite skilled in literary composition.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, he passed the Jinshi examination,
and served as Mìshūshěng Jiàoshūláng and Jíxián Jiàolǐ.
When Táng fell,
he served Liáng as Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
and was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén and Hànlín Xuéshì.
When Liáng fell,
he was demoted to serve as Sīmǎ of Huáizhōu.
Upon receiving amnesty, he was granted a minor transfer,
and gradually promoted to Wèiwèi Shàoqīng.
During the Tiānchéng era,
he was again appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén and Hànlín Xuéshì,
and successively promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng Chéngzhǐ.
At this time, Yòusànqí Chángshì Zhāng Wénbǎo was in charge of the official examinations (Gòngjǔ).
When the list of successful Jinshi candidates was released,
the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū) found some errors in the results.
Zhāng Wénbǎo then requested that the Hànlín Xuéshì Yuàn compose regulated poetry and prose (Shī Fù) to serve as the standard format for the Gòngjǔ.
The compositions made by scholars Dòu Mèngzhēng and Zhāng Lì were not skillfully done,
so Lǐ Yì was ordered to compose them.
Lǐ Yì laughed and said:
"A young person passing the Jinshi examination
is merely a matter of chance.
The younger generation is formidable,
and those yet to arrive cannot be estimated.
Even if I were to take the Ministry of Rites examination again,
I might not necessarily pass;
how can I set the standard format for these talents?"
Those who heard him praised his understanding of decorum.
Later he was transferred to Xíngbù Shàngshū with duties in Luòyáng,
where he died
at over seventy years old.
Miscellaneous Biographies, Chapter Forty-four. Hé Níng
Hé Níng, courtesy name Chéngjī,
was a native of Xūchāng, Yùnzhōu.
His ninth-generation ancestor, Féng Yáo, was a Táng Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
but his later descendants subsequently ceased to serve in office or study.
Níng's father, Jǔ,
was fond of wine
and disregarded minor rules of conduct,
but he uniquely favored men of refined culture.
He often spent his wealth to associate with them,
and because of this, Hé Níng was able to associate with them.
And Hé Níng, being intelligent in his youth,
had an outstanding appearance and spirit.
He passed the Jinshi examination,
and Hè Guī, the Liáng Yìchéng Jūn Jiédùshǐ, hired him as an aide (Cóngshì).
Hè Guī fought against Táng Zhuāngzōng at Húliǔ.
Hè Guī was defeated
and fled alone.
Only Hé Níng followed him.
Hè Guī looked back and saw Níng,
waving his hand to signal him to leave.
Hé Níng said:
"A true man should die for the person who truly knows him.
My only regret is not yet finding a place to die.
How can I leave?"
Soon after, a solitary cavalryman chased Hè Guī, nearly catching up.
Hé Níng shouted at him, but the man did not stop.
Hé Níng immediately drew his bow and shot him dead,
and Hè Guī thus managed to escape.
When Hè Guī returned,
he instructed his sons, saying:
"Hé Níng
is a man of commitment and integrity.
He will surely attain wealth and high rank later on;
you must serve him respectfully!"
Consequently, he married his daughter to him.
During the Tiānchéng era,
he was appointed Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
and was successively promoted to Zhǔkè Yuánwàiláng,
Zhī Zhìgào;
Hànlín Xuéshì,
and was put in charge of the Gòngjǔ.
At that time,
most Jinshi candidates were superficial and volatile,
enjoying creating clamor to sway the presiding officials.
Whenever the presiding official posted the list (Bǎng),
they would surround the area with thorn barriers,
and close the department gates,
prohibiting entry or exit as a regular practice.
Hé Níng removed the thorn barriers and opened the gates,
yet the scholars were all reverent and created no clamor.
Those he selected were the outstanding talents of the time,
and it was said that he had chosen the right people.
In the early Jìn dynasty,
he was appointed Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì,
concurrently serving as Pàn Dùzhī,
and as Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ.
Gāozǔ frequently summoned him
to ask about current affairs,
and all of Hé Níng's replies were agreeable to the Emperor.
In the fifth year of Tiānfú,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Gāozǔ was about to proceed to Yè,
but Ān Cóngjìn of Xiāngzhōu's intention to rebel was already evident.
Níng said:
“If Your Majesty proceeds to Yè,
Cóngjìn will certainly rebel at this time.
What should be done then? ”
Gāozǔ said:
“How do you intend to deal with it? ”
Níng said:
“To preempt others
is the means by which to seize control.
I request to write more than ten imperial edicts (Xuānchì),
and bestow them upon the Prince of Zhèng.
If there is an emergency, command a general to attack him.”
Gāozǔ considered this wise.
At this time,
the Prince of Zhèng was the Prefect of Kāifēng (Kāifēng Yǐn),
and remained behind, not following the emperor’s tour.
Thus, the imperial edicts (Xuānchì) were bestowed upon him.
When Gāozǔ arrived at Yè,
Cóngjìn indeed rebelled.
The Prince of Zhèng immediately used the edicts to command cavalry generals Lǐ Jiànchóng, Jiāo Jìxūn, and others to suppress him.
Cóngjìn believed that Gāozǔ was merely proceeding to Yè,
and did not expect the swiftness of the Jìn troops.
He traveled as far as Huāshān,
where he encountered the troops of Jiànchóng and the others.
He thought this miraculous,
and subsequently fled in defeat.
When Chū Dì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Minister of the Right (Yòu Púshè).
After more than a year,
he was dismissed from the concurrent title of Administrator (Píngzhāng Shì),
and transferred to Minister of the Left (Zuǒ Púshè).
During the time of Hàn Gāozǔ,
he was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù),
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Lǔguó.
He died in the second year of Xiǎndé [955 CE],
aged fifty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title of Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng).
Níng loved to embellish his carriages and clothes.
In writing essays, he considered quantity to be richness.
He had a collection of over a hundred scrolls (juǎn).
He once personally carved the printing blocks to circulate them in the world,
but those who knew better largely disapproved.
However, his nature was joyful and kind,
and he enjoyed praising and recommending junior scholars.
According to the traditions of the Táng dynasty,
the Examiner-in-Chief (Zhī Gòngjǔ) would highly value the rank of the *jìnshì* he passed,
based on the rank he himself achieved when he passed the exams.
When Níng passed the *jìnshì* exam, he ranked fifth.
Later, when he served as Examiner-in-Chief (Zhī Jǔ),
he selected Fàn Zhì as the fifth-ranked scholar.
Later, Zhì achieved the position of Chancellor (Zǎixiàng),
was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lǔguó,
and his official post reached Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
All these positions were the same as Níng’s,
which was considered an honor at the time.
Zhào Yíng
Zhào Yíng, courtesy name Xuánhuī,
was a native of Huáyīn in Huàzhōu.
He was pure and generous in character,
and possessed fine bearing and appearance.
He served the Liáng general Kāng Yánxiào as an aide (Cóngshì).
When Jìn Gāozǔ was the Military Governor of Bǎoyì Circuit (Bǎoyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ),
he employed Yíng as his chief secretary (Zhǎng Shūjì).
From then on, whenever Gāozǔ moved circuits, he always brought Yíng along.
When Gāozǔ was about to raise troops in Tàiyuán,
he consulted his various generals and officials.
Some generals and officials supported the plan,
but Yíng alone showed fear in his expression,
and advised Gāozǔ not to rebel.
Although Gāozǔ did not follow his advice,
he cherished him deeply in his heart.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,

Yíng was appointed Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Chief Compiler (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ), Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng), and Administrator of the Ministries (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
He was repeatedly promoted, eventually becoming Grand Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Lìng).
He was sent out to serve as the Military Governor of Jìnchāng Circuit (Jìnchāng Jūn Jiédùshǐ) and Prefect of Kāifēng (Kāifēng Yǐn).
At this time,
Chū Dì was young and confused,
and Féng Yù,
Lǐ Yàntāo, and others held power.
They contended for power with Sāng Wéihàn.
They consequently collaborated to slander and remove Wéihàn.
Believing Yíng to be pliable and easily controlled,
they subsequently brought him back to serve as Chancellor (Xiàng).
When the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
Yíng followed Chū Dì in the forced northward migration among the captives.
Yíng served Wùyù as Grand Guardian to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
During the time of Zhōu Tàizǔ,
when diplomatic relations were established with the Qìdān,
Tàizǔ dispatched Tián Mǐn, Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng), as an envoy to the Qìdān.
He encountered Yíng in Yōuzhōu.
When Yíng saw Mǐn, his grief was overwhelming.
Yíng's sons were Yìzé and Yìcóng.
When Yíng was moved northward,
Yìcóng was with him,
but Yìzé remained behind serving Hàn.
Yìzé's official post reached Director in the Ministry of Justice (Xíngbù Lángzhōng).
Later, Yíng became ill and was about to die.
He requested the Qìdān,
wishing for his corpse to be returned to the Central Plain (Zhōngguó).
The Qìdān granted the request.
When he died,
Yìcóng was sent to accompany his coffin on its return south.
Tàizǔ took pity on him,
posthumously granted Yíng the title of Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
and he was buried in Huáyīn.
Féng Yù
Féng Yù, courtesy name Jǐngchén,
was a native of Dìngzhōu.
As a youth, he stood for the *jìnshì* exams but did not pass.
Féng Yūn, who was Military Governor of Hédōng Circuit (Hédōng Jiédùshǐ),
invited him to serve as an Investigating Officer (Tuīguān).
Upon entering court, he was appointed Investigating Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ).
He was repeatedly promoted to Director in the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù Lángzhōng).
He served as a Judicial Aide in the Salt and Iron Commission (Yántiě Pànguān).
Jìn Chū Dì married Yù’s elder sister as Empress (Hòu).
Yù, as a relative of the Empress, was put in charge of drafting edicts (Zhī Zhìgào),
and appointed Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
Yù was illiterate,
but served alongside Yīn Péng as Secretariat Drafter (Shèrén).
The drafting of edicts was always handed to Péng to write on his behalf.
After a short time,
Yù was sent out to serve as Garrison Commissioner of Yǐngzhōu (Yǐngzhōu Tuánliànshǐ),
and appointed Academician of the Duānmíng Palace (Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì) and Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng).
He was transferred to Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ), Vice Minister of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng), and Administrator of the Ministries (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
At this time,
Chū Dì was young and confused,
and Empress Féng held power.
All major military and state affairs
were decided solely by Yù.
Yù once took leave due to illness.
From Inspectors (Cìshǐ) upwards,
the Chancellors dared not make any appointments or assignments,
waiting for Yù’s decision.
Yù appointed Secretariat Drafter Lú Jià as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng).
Sāng Wéihàn considered this unacceptable because Jià’s qualifications and reputation were shallow.
Because of this, a rift formed between Yù and Wéihàn.
Wéihàn was consequently dismissed as Chancellor.
When Yù was Chancellor,
bribes came from all directions,
and his accumulated wealth amounted to immense sums.
When the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
Zhāng Yànzé was the first to enter the capital (Jīngshī) with his troops.
His soldiers competed to be the first to enter Yù’s house,
and his wealth was completely exhausted in a single night.
The next day, when he saw Yànzé,
he still offered a flattering smile,
claiming he wished to obtain the Jìn imperial jade seal (Yùxǐ) to present to the Qìdān,
hoping for favor and reward.
Yànzé did not accept.
When Chū Dì went north,
Yù followed him into the Qìdān territory.
The Qìdān made him Grand Guardian to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
In the third year of Guǎngshùn of Zhōu [953 CE],
his son Jié fled from the Qìdān and returned.
Yù became fearful,
and died of worry.
Lú Zhì
Lú Zhì, courtesy name Zǐzhēng,
was a native of Hénán.
His father, Wàng,
was Director in the Ministry of Merits (Sīxūn Lángzhōng) during the Táng dynasty.
Zhì was intelligent and wise as a child,
and skilled in composition.
He served Táng as Secretariat Aide (Mìshū Láng).
Upon mourning his mother,
he resigned his post.
Later, he left to travel in Tàiyuán.
The Prince of Jìn appointed him Chief Secretary to the Military Governor of Hédōng (Hédōng Jiédù Zhǎng Shūjì).
Zhì, along with Zhāng Chéngyè and others, settled the plan to establish Zhuāngzōng as successor.
When Zhuāngzōng was about to ascend the throne,
he appointed Zhì as Commissioner for Grand Ceremonies (Dà Lǐ Shǐ),
and conferred upon him the title of Minister of Rites in the Provisional Government (Xíngtái Lǐbù Shàngshū).
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he wished to appoint Zhì as Chancellor (Xiàng).
Zhì's nature was casual and unconventional,
and he did not want to take on responsibility.
He therefore firmly declined the appointment.
He was appointed Prefect of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán Yǐn) and Resident Governor of the Northern Capital (Běijīng Liúshǒu).
He was transferred to Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū) and Academician of the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì).
He followed the campaign to pacify Liáng,
and provisionally oversaw the taxation of grain and labor (Zūyōng).
He was transferred to Minister of the Ministry of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū).
Later, he became Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Chief Compiler (Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ),
and was moreover granted
the title "Meritorious Minister for Discussion, Reflection, and Assistance" (Lùn Sī Kuāng Zuǒ Gōngchén).
In the first year of Tiānchéng [926 CE],
he was appointed Military Governor of Kuāngguó Circuit (Kuāngguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ).
In the third year,
he was appointed Minister of the Ministry of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū),
and concurrently managed the affairs of the Grand Courtier of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng Shì).
He successively governed the circuits of Héyáng and Hénghǎi.
Initially,
Liáng (梁) had usurped Táng (唐),
enfeoffed Āidì (哀帝) as Jìyīn Wáng (濟陰王),
and subsequently poisoned and killed him,
burying him in Cáozhōu (曹州).
In Tóngguāng (同光) third year (925 CE),
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) was about to discuss reburial,
but Cáo Tàihòu (曹太后) passed away,
and the plan was therefore halted.
Following his old mound,
they slightly broadened its perimeter,
and offered sacrifices to him seasonally.
Zhì (質) then proposed establishing a temple and conferring a posthumous title.
The posthumous title was Zhāoxuān Guāngliè Xiàohuángdì (昭宣光烈孝皇帝),
and the temple name was Jǐngzōng (景宗).
On the day Wùshēn (戊申) of the eighth month of Tiānchéng (天成) fourth year (929 CE),
Míngzōng (明宗) presided at the Wénmíng Diàn (文明殿),
sending Zhì (質) to bear the document of enfeoffment and establish the temple in Cáozhōu (曹州).
However, critics believed that Huī Wáng (輝王) had unfortunately been installed by a rebellious minister,
and that Zhāozōng (昭宗) and Hé Huánghòu (何皇后) had both been assassinated by Liáng (梁),
leading subsequently to the downfall of the state.
Therefore,
"Zhāoxuān Guāngliè" (昭宣光烈)
was not an appropriate appellation,
and moreover, establishing a temple and calling him a Zōng (宗) without admitting him to the Tàimiào (太廟)
was all improper.
Everyone criticized Zhì (質) for this,
and the high officials also knew it was unacceptable.
They then memorialized to remove the temple name.
Qín Wáng Cóngróng (秦王從榮) was executed for sedition,
and Zhì (質), as the Right Assistant Director (Yòu Púshè), temporarily managed the affairs of Hénán Fǔ (河南府).
Fèidì (廢帝) rebelled at Fèngxiáng (鳳翔),
and Mǐndì (愍帝) dispatched troops to execute him,
emptying the state treasury for generous rewards.
But when the troops reached Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), they all mutinied and defected.
Fèidì (廢帝) led all of them eastward,
promising enormous rewards if the endeavor succeeded,
which exceeded the expectations of the soldiers.
When Fèidì (廢帝) entered and was enthroned,
the responsible officials submitted lists showing a very low number (of troops/citizens),
and Fèidì (廢帝) became violently enraged.
From the various garrisons down to the Regional Inspectors (Cìshǐ),
all contributed money and silk to aid state expenditures,
but it was still insufficient.
Wáng Méi (王玫), the Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Sānsī Shǐ), requested to levy citizens' assets to supplement the use.
Zhì (質) was then ordered, along with Méi (玫) and others, to jointly deliberate on the tax quotas.
However, the distribution was unequal between the rich and the poor,
causing grievances and lawsuits to arise simultaneously,
filling the prisons with detainees.
Within six or seven days,
the amount collected did not reach one hundred thousand.
Fèidì (廢帝) worried about this,
and thus ordered Zhì (質) and others to levy a five-month house tax on the citizens.
Because of this, the people complained bitterly.
When Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) entered and was enthroned,
Zhì (質), due to illness, was transferred to an administrative position in the Western Capital (Xījīng),
and was appointed Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
He died
at the age of seventy-six,
and was posthumously granted the title Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàishī),
with the posthumous title Wénzhōng (文忠).
Lǚ Qí (呂琦)
Lǚ Qí (呂琦), courtesy name Huīshān (輝山),
was a man from Āncì (安次) in Yōuzhōu (幽州).
His father, Yǎn (兗),
served as the Deputy Administrator (Jiédu Pànguān) for the Hénghǎi Army Military Commissioner (Jiédu Shǐ).
The Military Commissioner Liú Shǒuwén (劉守文) and his younger brother Shǒuguāng (守光) attacked each other with troops.
Shǒuwén (守文) was defeated and died.
His officials and people installed his son Yánzuò (延祚) and served him,
taking Yǎn (兗) as their chief strategist.
Subsequently, Yánzuò (延祚) was again defeated by Shǒuguāng (守光),
and Yǎn (兗) was killed.
Shǒuguāng (守光) was angry at Yǎn (兗),
and executed his entire family.
Qí (琦), at the age of fifteen,
was captured
and was about to face execution.
Zhào Yù (趙玉), Yǎn's (兗) former retainer, deceived the jailer, saying:
"This is my younger brother."
The jailer believed him,
and allowed Qí (琦) to leave.
Yù (玉) and Qí (琦) managed to flee together,
but Qí’s (琦) feet were weak and he could not walk.
Yù (玉) carried him and traveled,
traversing several hundred *lǐ*.
They changed their names,
begging for food along the road,
thus escaping death.
Qí (琦) was a man of fine appearance and manner,
and highly valued integrity and determination.
