Having lost his family when young,
he traveled and studied between Fén (汾) and Jìn (晉).
When Táng Zhuāngzōng (唐莊宗) was garrisoned in Tàiyuán (太原),
he appointed him as the Judicial Investigator (Jūnshì Tuīguān) for Dàizhōu (代州).
Later, he served as the Judicial Investigator for Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞), the Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi (橫海),
and entered the court as Palace Attendant Censor (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ).
During Míngzōng’s (明宗) reign,
he served as a Supernumerary Director (Yuánwàiláng) of the Bureau of Carriages and Horses (Jiàbù),
concurrently holding the post of Attendant Censor (Shìyùshǐ) and managing miscellaneous affairs.
A storehouse official in Héyáng (河陽) stole the goods he supervised,
and was handed over to the Military Inspector's prison.
The jailer, Yǐn Xùn (尹訓), accepted bribes and manipulated the case,
so the wronged party petitioned the court.
The case was sent down to the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) for investigation and verification.
Evidence of Xùn’s (訓) bribery was obtained,
and a memorial was submitted to summon Xùn (訓) to the Censorate.
Xùn (訓) was protected by Ān Chónghuǐ (安重誨),
who refused to release him.
Qí (琦) pressed the demand relentlessly.
Xùn (訓), fearing the consequences, committed suicide,
and the case was resolved.
Many people were spared.
After more than a year,
he was promoted to Director of the Bureau of Rites (Lǐbù Lángzhōng) and Compiler in the Historiography Institute (Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn).
During the Chángxīng reign,
Emperor Fèi lost Hèzhōng,
and was dismissed to reside in Qīnghuà Fāng.
He was in the same alley as Qí,
and Qí often went to visit him.
Later, Emperor Fèi ascended the throne,
treating Qí very favorably.
He was appointed Zhī Zhìgào, Gěishì Zhōng, Shūmìyuàn Zhíxuèshì, and Duānmíngdiàn Xuéshì.
At this time,
Jìn Gāozǔ was stationed in Hédōng,
and harbored ulterior motives.
Emperor Fèi worried about this,
and Qí and Lǐ Sōng were both on call for consultation,
offering much beneficial planning.
Qí said:
“The trouble in Tàiyuán
will surely involve the Qìdān for assistance.
It is better to preemptively control it.”
Ever since Wáng Dū rebelled in Dìngzhōu during Míngzōng’s time,
the Qìdān had sent Tūněi, Cuòlà, and others to assist Dū.
However, they were defeated by Zhào Déjūn and Wáng Yànqiú.
Tūněi was killed,
and Cuòlà and others were all sent to the capital.
Thereafter, the Qìdān repeatedly sent envoys to request the return of Cuòlà and others,
their words being very humble and respectful.
Míngzōng invariably executed their envoys and did not reply.
Moreover, Dōngdān Wáng fled into China.
Because of this, the Qìdān frequently sought peace.
Qí then said:
“Given the current situation,
it is better to establish peace with the Qìdān.
Following the precedent of the Hàn dynasty,
we should annually provide gold and silk,
and marry off a daughter to them,
so that powerful vassal states and great garrisons will have no external allies to draw upon,
which can quell their rebellious intentions.”
Sōng conveyed Qí's words to Sānsī Shǐ Zhāng Yánlǎng.
Yánlǎng said joyfully:
“If it can alleviate the nation's troubles,
even if the state expends tens of thousands of strings of cash annually,
charging me to make up the difference would be acceptable!”
They then jointly proposed the matter.
Emperor Fèi was greatly pleased.
Another day, he asked Shūmì Zhíxuèshì Xuē Wènyù about Qí’s and others’ proposal.
Wènyù strongly deemed it wrong,
and then recited Róng Yù's
poem, “The altars of soil and grain rely on an enlightened ruler,
safety and danger are entrusted to a woman,”
to criticize Qí and the others.
Emperor Fèi became furious,
and urgently summoned Sōng, Qí, and others, asking how their plan for peace with the barbarians was.
Perceiving the emperor’s angry expression,
Qí and others quickly said:
“Your ministers’ plan for the nation
is not to seek profit for the Qìdān from China.”
The emperor immediately erupted in anger, saying:
“Do you, my lords, assist me wishing to achieve great peace in such a manner?
I have one daughter who is still young,
and you wish to abandon her to the barbarians?
Gold and silk are for supporting soldiers and defending the nation,
yet you would give them to aid the enemy?
Is that permissible?”
Sōng and the others, terrified, bowed in apology,
bowing countless times.
Qí, due to fatigue in his legs,
could not continue bowing and stopped first.
The emperor said:
“Lǚ Qí is stubborn;
does he consider me a mere person?”
Qí replied:
“Your minister has always been frail,
and is exhausted from too much bowing.
Please allow your minister a short rest.”
After a moment, his breathing settled,
and he reported:
“If Your Majesty deems your ministers' words incorrect,
you may punish them.
What good is bowing?”
The emperor's anger slightly subsided,
saying:
“No need to bow.”
He bestowed a cup of wine and dismissed them,
and the proposal was subsequently dropped.
Consequently, Qí was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
After residing there for several months,
he was again made Duānmíngdiàn Xuéshì.
Later, Jìn Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán,
and indeed brought in the Qìdān for assistance,
thus causing the fall of the Táng dynasty.
Qí served the Jìn dynasty as Mìshū Jiān,
and was successively promoted to Bīngbù Shìláng.
He died in Tiānfú eighth year.
Zhào Yù served as Zhífāng Yuánwàiláng.
Qí treated him like a father.
When Yù was ill,
Qí personally tasted his medicine and attended to him.
When Yù died,
Qí managed the funeral arrangements for his family.
Yù’s son, Wéndù, was orphaned young.
Qí taught him to study,
as if he were his own son.
Later, Wéndù passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*.
Qí had sons Yúqìng and Duān.
Xuē Róng
Xuē Róng
was a native of Píngyáo, Fénzhōu.
In his youth, he was renowned for his Confucian scholarship.
During the reign of Táng Míngzōng, he served as Yòubǔquē,
and was concurrently a scholar in the Hóngwén Guǎn.
When Jìn Gāozǔ was stationed in Tàiyuán,
Róng served as Guānchá Pànguān.
When Gāozǔ was transferred to Yùn,
he wished to hold Tàiyuán and defy the imperial command.
He met with his aides and subordinates,
asking them for their opinions.
Among those present, some supported him,
while others were too afraid to speak.
Róng alone calmly replied:
“Róng is merely a Confucian scholar;
I have never studied military affairs.
How can the principles of advance, retreat, survival, and destruction be easily spoken of?”
Gāozǔ did not reprimand him.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Róng was appointed Lìbù Lángzhōng,
concurrently Shìyùshǐ Zhī Záshì.
He was successively appointed Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū,
and then promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Róng said:
“Literary composition is not my forte.”
He then declined the appointment and did not accept it.
At that time, an imperial edict ordered the repair of the Luòyáng Dàinèi.
Róng submitted a memorial of strong remonstrance.
Gāozǔ praised and accepted his words,
and immediately issued an edict to cease the project.
He was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
then transferred to Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and assigned to Fēnsī Xī Jīng.
He died
at the age of sixty.
Hé Zé
Hé Zé
was a native of Guǎngzhōu.
His father, Dǐng,
served as Róngguǎn Jīnglüèshǐ at the end of the Táng dynasty.
Zé was fond of learning in his youth
and excelled in poetry.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*
and became Luòyáng Lìng.
Táng Zhuāngzōng was fond of hunting
and often trampled on people's fields.
Zé secretly hid in the weeds to wait for Zhuāngzōng.
He intercepted the emperor's horse and remonstrated, saying:
“Your Majesty has not yet unified the realm to cease warfare,
yet you oppress and exhaust the people with heavy taxes to supply the army.
Now the fields are nearing harvest.
How can you indulge in hunting and harm the abundant crops?
How will the people pay their taxes,
and how will officials urge them to farm?
If Your Majesty does not listen to your minister's words,
I beg to be granted death before your horse,
so that future generations may know of Your Majesty's transgressions.”
Zhuāngzōng laughed heartily
and ceased his hunting for his sake.
Zé was appointed Cāngbù Lángzhōng.
During Míngzōng’s reign,
he repeatedly submitted memorials on current affairs.
When Míngzōng visited Biànzhōu,
he also wished to visit Yè,
but public sentiment was against it.
High officials repeatedly advised against it, but he did not listen.
Zé prostrated himself before the palace gate and remonstrated strongly.
Míngzōng praised him
and appointed him Lìbù Lángzhōng and Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn.
Though Zé spoke frankly externally,
he was actually insidious and obsequious internally.
Once, during an inner court audience,
after the assembly retired,
he alone remained.
He tapped his forehead with his tablet,
looked north, and cried out:
“Enlightened ruler!
Enlightened ruler!”
All who heard him laughed at him.
During the Fìve Dynasties period,
the people suffered from warfare.
Often, claiming parental illness, they would cut off a piece of their flesh,
or after a parent's death, cut their breasts or reside in a hut by the tomb,
to seek exemption from prefectural and county taxes and labor service.
The Hùbù annually issued countless exemption certificates,
and ordered prefectures and counties to provide paper,
which was called
“exemption paper.”
Zé submitted a memorial detailing its abuses, and Míngzōng issued an edict to abolish all Hùbù exemption paper.
ZÉ had an old acquaintance with Prime Minister Zhào Fèng.
He frequently made private requests to Fèng,
asking to be a Supervising Remonstrator.
Fèng thought little of his character,
and appointed him Grand Court أقلل 少卿 (Tàicháng Shàocīng).
Before the imperial edict was issued, Zé knew about it in advance.
He immediately claimed his new office and submitted a memorial of self-recommendation.
The memorial was sent down to the Central Secretariat.
Fèng and others said:
"Zé claimed his new office before receiving the official appointment,
which is an insult to the court.
We request that he be punished according to the law."
He was then made Grand Coachman 少卿 (Tàipú Shàocīng) and retired,
residing in Héyáng.
Zé was already seventy years old at the time,
but still hoped for official advancement.
He sent his maid Yízǐ to the suggestion box to submit a memorial discussing affairs,
requesting the establishment of Qín Wáng as crown prince.
Qín Wáng was inherently arrogant
and often harbored rebellious intentions.
This eventually led to his downfall,
and it began with Zé.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Zé was summoned to be Grand Court 少卿 (Tàicháng Shàocīng),
but he died of illness at home.
WÁNG Quán
WÁNG Quán, courtesy name Xiùshān,
was a native of Tàiyuán.
He was the great-grandson of Táng Zǔ Púyè Qǐ.
His father, Ráo,
held the office of Yòusī Lángzhōng.
Quán passed the imperial examination for jinshi,
and became Yòu Bǔquē.
When the Táng dynasty fell,
he served Liáng as Zhífāng Yuánwàiláng, Zhī Zhìgào, and Hàlín Xuéshì,
and was successively promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
Quán was demoted to Suízhōu Sīmǎ.
He was later recalled to be Yòu Shùzǐ,
and successively promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū.
During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ, he was Bīngbù Shàngshū.
At this time,
Gāozǔ treated the Qìdān as a father.
Quán was to be dispatched as an envoy.
He sighed and said:
"Although I am untalented,
how can I bow before the yurts?"
He therefore declined to go,
and for this reason, he was suspended from his post.
A year later, he retired as Tàizǐ Shàofù.
He died
at the age of seventy-eight,
and was posthumously granted Zuǒ Púyè.
SHǏ Guī
SHǏ Guī
was a native of Shíyì, Chángshān.
He was intelligent, astute, and fond of learning.
As the magistrate of Níngjìn and Lèshòu counties,
he governed well,
and the county people erected steles to praise him.
When Guō Chóngtāo garrisoned Chéngdé,
he appointed Guī as his aide.
During Míngzōng's reign,
he served as Shàngshū Láng.
When Ān Chónghuì became Pímìshǐ,
he recommended Guī to be Zhí Xuéshì.
According to custom,
although the position of Zhí Xuéshì was esteemed,
he was responsible for receiving and handling documents,
and participating in various administrative affairs,
no different from a Pànguān.
Chónghuì was not well-read,
and relied on Guī for consultations.
He first obtained permission for Guī to ascend the hall and attend.
The custom of Pímì Zhí Xuéshì ascending the hall began with Guī.
He was later changed to Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and put in charge of the personnel selection of the Ministry of Personnel.
When Chónghuì was defeated and died,
Guī was sent out as Bèizhōu Cìshǐ.
After being dismissed, he returned to Chángshān,
cut off all social interaction,
and traveled in a covered carriage when going out in the neighborhoods.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was summoned and appointed Xíngbù Shìláng and Yántiě Fùshǐ,
then promoted to Lìbù Shìláng,
and again put in charge of personnel selection,
earning a reputation for competence.
He was dismissed due to illness
and died in Chángshān.
LÓNG Mǐn
LÓNG Mǐn, courtesy name Yùnà,
was a native of Yǒngqīng, Yōuzhōu.
In his youth, he served in the prefecture,
acting as Cānjūn.
When Liú Shǒuguāng rebelled,
Mǐn fled to Cāngzhōu,
and then became a sojourner in Liáng,
not receiving an appointment for a long time.
Mǐn had always been good friends with Féng Dào.
When Dào became Táng Zhuāngzōng's aide,
Mǐn secretly went to rely on him.
Inspector Zhāng Chéngyè said to Dào:
"I heard you have a guest,
you can bring him with you."
Dào presented Mǐn to Chéngyè.
Chéngyè appointed Mǐn as Jiānjūn Xúnquán,
and made him responsible for managing memorials.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
Mǐn was summoned and appointed Sīmén Yuánwàiláng.
Mǐn's father, Xiánshì,
was over seventy,
and his paternal grandfather was over ninety,
both residing in Yè.
Mǐn therefore requested to be Xīngtáng Yǐn,
and was known for his filial piety towards his grandparents and father.
Upon his mother's death,
he left his post.
When Zhào Zàilǐ rebelled,
he forced Mǐn to resume his duties.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
Zàilǐ was garrisoned in Cāngzhōu,
and Mǐn was then able to resume mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was successively appointed Bīngbù Shìláng.
When Féng Yūn was left in charge of Běijīng,
he appointed Mǐn as Fù Liúshǒu.
When Yūn was appointed Pímìshǐ,
Mǐn was appointed Lìbù Shìláng.
At this time,
Jìn Gāozǔ rose in Tàiyuán
and requested troops from the Qìdān.
The deposed emperor of Táng was in Huáizhōu.
Zhào Déjūn and his son had rebellious intentions,
and Zhāng Jìngdá was stationed in Jìn'ān,
making the situation extremely precarious.
The deposed emperor asked his ministers for advice.
Mǐn said:
"What Jìn relies on is the Qìdān.
Dōngdān Wáng, a dethroned ruler,
is now in the capital.
If we send troops to escort Dōngdān from Yōuzhōu into Xīlóu,
the Qìdān will have internal worries,
how will they have time to assist Jìn?
If Jìn loses the Qìdān,
the great cause will be lost."
He also said to Lǐ Yì:
"Mǐn
is a native of Yān,
and knows Déjūn well.
As a general, Déjūn defends cities by entrenching and encouraging brave soldiers,
that's all.
To face a great enemy and fight with disregard for his own life,
that is not his ability.
What's more, he harbors rebellious intentions.
Now I hear that there are still
five thousand horses before the imperial carriage.
I wish to obtain a thousand strong horses
and a thousand brave soldiers,
along with the valiant general Láng Wànjīn.
Starting from Píngyáo, along the mountains, braving through the barbarians,
and rushing to Guānzhài,
fighting and marching,
if half of them reach,
then the matter will be accomplished!"
Yì relayed this to the deposed emperor,
but the deposed emperor was unable to make use of it.
Nevertheless, everyone admired his bold words.
During the Jìn dynasty, he served as Tàicháng Qīng,
and was an envoy to Wúyuè.
At that time,
envoys to Wúyuè
all bowed before the King of Wúyuè,
but Mǐn alone saluted him with a bow.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Gōngbù Shìláng.
In the first year of Gānyòu,
he died of a carbuncle on his head,
and was posthumously granted Yòu Púyè.
Collation Notes
Miscellaneous Biographies, Forty-fifth, LǏ Sōng
LǏ Sōng
was a native of Ráoyáng, Shēnzhōu.
Sōng was intelligent and astute in his youth,
and skilled in writing.
He served as Zhènzhōu Cānjūn.
When Táng Wèi Wáng Jìjí was Xīngshènggōng Shǐ,
and also held the title of Zhènzhōu Jiédùshǐ,
he appointed Tuīguān Lǐ Ráo as Zhǎng Shūjì.
Sōng said to Zhǎng Shū Lǚ Róu:
"Wèi Wáng is an imperial prince,
the hope of the realm.
The duty of writing memorials
is not suitable for Ráo."
Róu secretly had Sōng substitute for him,
and showed it to Lú Zhì and Féng Dào.
Dào and others all considered it excellent.
Sōng was then appointed Xīngshènggōng Xúnquán,
and became Xiélǜ Láng.
Jìjí, along with Guō Chóngtāo, campaigned against Shǔ.
Sōng was appointed as Recorder (zhǎng shūjì).
After Jìjí had already defeated Shǔ,
Empress Liú listened to the words of slanderers,
secretly dispatched men to Shǔ,
instructing Jìjí to kill Chóngtāo.
Public morale was unsettled.
Sōng went in to see Jìjí and said:
"Why does Your Highness undertake such a perilous affair?
If you truly cannot tolerate Chóngtāo,
what harm is there in waiting until Luòyáng to execute him?
Now the army is five thousand *lǐ* distant,
killing a high minister without a clear, immediate decree,
shakes the popular sentiment;
this is inviting rebellion."
Jìjí said:
"I also regret it.
What can be done?"
Sōng then summoned three or four scribes,
ascended a tower and removed the ladder.
That night, he used yellow paper to forge an imperial edict,
reversed the seal of the Commander-in-Chief (dūtǒng) for use,
and the next morning announced it to all the armies.
Only then did morale stabilize.
When the army returned,
Jìjí died on the road.
When Sōng arrived at the capital (Jīngshī),
Rèn Yuán was overseeing the Three Judicial Offices (sān sī),
and employed Sōng as Judicial Officer of the Salt and Iron Monopoly (yántiě pànguān).
Due to a domestic mourning duty (nèi yōu), he resigned his post and returned to his home village.
After the mourning period was complete,
Fàn Yánguāng was residing in Zhènzhōu
and invited Sōng to serve as Recorder.
When Yánguāng became Commissioner of Military Affairs (shūmì shǐ),
Sōng was appointed as Reminder (shíyí),
and served directly in the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Yuàn).
He was successively promoted to Assistant Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng) and Academician of the Duānmíng Hall (Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì).
During the Chángxīng reign,
Míngzōng was advanced in years,
and Prince Cóngróng of Qín committed many illegal acts.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn (Shí Jìngtáng) served as Deputy Commander of the Six Armies (liù jūn fù shǐ).
Fearing that disaster would reach him,
he requested to be sent out to an external domain (wài fān).
At this time,
the Qìdān entered Yànmén,
and Míngzōng was selecting a general to defend Tàiyuán.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn desired this post.
The Commissioners of Military Affairs, Fàn Yánguāng and Zhào Yánshòu, etc., discussed the choice of general.
They failed to make a decision for a long time.
Míngzōng became extremely angry
and reproached Yánshòu and the others.
Yánshòu and the others were terrified
and wished to recommend Kāng Yìchéng for the selection.
Sōng alone said:
"Tàiyuán
is the northern gate of the state.
It must be entrusted to a high official;
no one but Shí Jìngtáng will suffice!"
Consequently, Sōng's recommendation was followed.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn was deeply grateful for this service,
and secretly sent someone to thank Sōng, saying:
"He who creates a Buddhist pagoda
must cap its spire."
This was intending for Sōng to see his (Gāozǔ's) affair through from beginning to end.
Later, Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn entered the capital with his troops.
Sōng hid in a civilian house in Yīquè.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn summoned him to be Assistant Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shìláng),
and appointed him Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Shìláng), concurrently Executive of the Secretariat-Chancellery (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì), and Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ).
He suffered domestic mourning (dīng nèi jiān),
but was recalled to office (qǐ fù).
When Gāozǔ died,
Emperor Chūdì ascended the throne.
He appointed Sōng to concurrently manage the Three Judicial Offices (pàn sān sī),
and Sōng managed the Bureau of Military Affairs alongside Féng Yù.
At this time,
the Jìn army defeated the Qìdān at Yángchéng.
Zhào Yánshòu, who was in Yōuzhōu,
falsely claimed he wished to defect back (sī guī) to lure the Jìn troops.
Sōng and the others believed him.
Initially,
when Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn (Liú Zhīyuǎn) was in Jìn,
he managed the Imperial Guards,
serving as Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Command (shìwèi dū zhǐhuī shǐ).
He was invested with the title Píngzhāngshì (Executive) simultaneously with Dù Chóngwēi.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn considered this an insult.
He was angry and refused to express gratitude.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn dispatched Hé Níng to enlighten him,
and only then did he express gratitude.
Subsequently, Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn was sent out to reside in Tàiyuán,
and Chóngwēi replaced him as Commander of the Palace Command (shìwèi shǐ).
Sōng also frequently praised Chóngwēi's talent.
Consequently, Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn viewed Sōng as someone who sought to displace him,
and deeply resented him.
Furthermore, Sōng believed Yánshòu's deception to be genuine,
and ultimately ordered Chóngwēi to lead a large army.
Subsequently, this army was defeated at Zhōngdù,
and the Jìn dynasty consequently fell.
Yēlǜ Déguāng of Qìdān invaded the capital.
Déguāng had long heard Yánshòu and others praise Sōng's character.
When he entered the capital,
he said to people:
"In conquering the Southern Court,
I have gained Sōng alone!"
He then appointed Sōng as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàishī).
When the Qìdān returned north,
they ordered Sōng and his clan to travel with them,
and left them in Zhènzhōu.
Subsequently, Mábā abandoned Zhènzhōu,
and Sōng, along with Féng Dào and others, were able to return.
Emperor Gāozǔ (of Hàn) had long been displeased with Sōng,
and Sōng was further slandered by those who bore him ill will.
They claimed Sōng had been treated generously by the Qìdān.
Therefore, when Sōng encountered the powerful officials of Hàn,
he was always watchful, extremely
humble and cautious, not daring to offend anyone.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn entered the capital,
he bestowed Sōng’s residence upon Sū Féngjí.
Sōng's family, having suffered during the chaos,
had buried much gold and treasure.
Féngjí acquired all of it.
Furthermore, Sōng's younger brother Yǔ and [●] were staying in the same quarters as Féngjí's sons and younger brothers.
When drunk,
they voiced resentment,
believing that their residence had been seized.
Sōng also presented the deed of the house to Féngjí,
making Féngjí especially unhappy.
The laws of Hàn were inherently strict,
and Yáng Bīn and Shǐ Hóngzhào often abused the penal codes.
Yǔ’s servant, Gě Yányù, who traded commercially for Yǔ,
had often embezzled his funds.
Yǔ had administered a lashing punishment to him.
Yányù stayed the night at the house of Lǐ Chéng, a subordinate of Féngjí,
and informed Chéng of the situation.
At this time,
Emperor Gāozǔ (of Hàn) was about to be interred in Ruìlíng,
and Lǐ Shǒuzhēn of Hézhōng had rebelled.
Chéng then instructed Yányù to report a conspiracy,
claiming Sōng and his nephew Wáng Níng planned to set fire to the capital during the imperial funeral,
and that they communicated with Shǒuzhēn via wax pellet letters.
Féngjí dispatched men to summon Sōng to his residence,
and calmly informed him.
Sōng knew he would not escape,
and thus entrusted his young daughter to Féngjí.
Féngjí sent Sōng to the prison of the Palace Command (shìwèi yù).
Sōng rode out on his horse.
His attendants had all left,
there was not a single person remaining.
Sōng said angrily:
"Since ancient times, how could there be a person who does not die?
But also, how could there be a state that does not perish?"
Thereupon, he falsely confessed,
and his clan was exterminated.
Sōng had long been on good terms with the Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Xú Táifú.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of Hòu Zhōu entered and established the dynasty,
Táifú reported to the Chancellor, Féng Dào,
requesting the execution of Gě Yányù.
Dào considered that Yányù had already been pardoned several times,
and found it difficult.
The Commissioner of Military Affairs, Wáng Jùn, heard of this,
praised Táifú's sense of righteousness,
and memorialized for Yányù's execution.
Lǐ Lín
Lǐ Lín
was a son of the imperial clan of Táng.
His paternal uncle Yáng served the Táng court,
and during the Xiántōng reign, served as Attendant Censor (Gěishì Zhōng).
In his youth, Lín sat for the *jìnshì* examination,
but repeatedly failed to pass.
He traveled between the various states of Héshuò,
calling himself the Recorder of the Qīnghǎi Army.
He sought an audience with Wáng Chǔzhí in Dìngzhōu,
but Chǔzhí treated him without respect.
He then changed his green robes
to scarlet robes,
and sought an audience with Lǐ Hóngguī of Chángshān.
Hóngguī recommended him to Wáng Róng, Prince of Zhào.
Róng kept him on as a staff administrator (cóngshì).
Subsequently, Zhāng Wénlǐ assassinated Róng and established himself (as ruler).
He sent Lín to confer with Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng in Tàiyuán.
Lín was eloquent and daring in speech.
He secretly devised for Zhuāngzōng strategies by which Wénlǐ could be defeated.
After Wénlǐ was defeated,
Zhuāngzōng appointed Lín as an aide (zhī shǐ).
He appointed Lín Zōngzhèng Qīng (Minister of the Court of the Imperial Clan).
He made Lǐ Qióng the Shǎo Qīng (Vice Minister).
The tombs of Xiànzǔ and Yìzǔ were in Zhàozhōu, Zhāoqìng Xiàn.
When the Táng state was first established,
Lín and Qióng submitted a memorial:
"Xiànzǔ Xuān Huángdì (Emperor Xuān, Xiànzǔ) has the Jiànchū Líng (Mausoleum),
and Yìzǔ Guāng Huángdì (Emperor Guāng, Yìzǔ) has the Qǐyùn Líng (Mausoleum).
We request setting up Táilìng (Mausoleum Superintendents)."
More than a hundred local ruffians claimed to be members of the Imperial Clan.
The Zōngzhèng (Court of the Imperial Clan) lacked genealogy records,
so they could not verify the claims.
There was a commoner who went to the office and claimed that his family had served for generations as Táilìng of Dānyáng Jìnglíng.
He heavily bribed the Zōngzhèng officials.
Lín and Qióng did not examine the details further,
and consequently appointed him as the Lìng (Superintendent).
The commoner immediately took up a crimson banner, recruited followers (bùqǔ),
and seized and appropriated more than a hundred qǐng of civilian land,
claiming it was land adjacent to the mausoleum grounds.
The commoners appealed to the authorities,
but the matter could not be resolved,
and was reported to the emperor.
Zhuāngzōng ordered the Gōng Qīng (Dukes and Ministers) and Bóshì (Scholars/Erudites)
to investigate the locations of the mausoleums of the former Táng emperors.
The Gōng Qīng and Bóshì reported:
"Dānyáng is in the present-day Rùnzhōu,
but Jìnglíng is not related to the affairs of [our] Táng state.
Lín is unlearned and ignorant,
and is unfit to serve among the Jiǔ Qīng (Nine Ministers)."
He was punished by demotion to Sīnóng Shǎo Qīng (Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries),
and sent out to serve as Hézhōng Jiédù Fùshǐ (Deputy Military Commissioner of Hézhōng).
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
because Lín was an old acquaintance,
he was recalled.
He was successively promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū (Minister of the Ministry of Revenue).
Lín harbored the intention of hoping for a great appointment.
He once said to Féng Dào and Zhào Fèng:
"According to the precedents of the Táng family,
members of the Imperial Clan are all Zǎixiàng (Chancellors).
Now Tiānzuò (the Divine Mandate) has restored our house.
It is proper to follow the old statutes.
Although Lín is not talented,
I previously served in Zhuāngzōng's headquarters (bàfǔ),
and I knew the present Son of Heaven when he was in his princely residence (fāndǐ).
When discussing ability and comparing achievements,
why should I fall behind everyone else?
To be kept long in the ranks of ordinary officials,
does this sit well with you gentlemen?"
Dào and the others disliked his words.
Later, an agent of Yáng Pǔ came to Lín to discuss matters.
Lín said to Ān Chónghuǐ:
"Yáng Pǔ has wished to submit to the court for a long time.
If the court sends an envoy to advise him,
he can be summoned."
Chónghuǐ believed him,
and gave a jade belt to the agent as a token of sincerity.
After a long time, there was no result.
Because of this, Lín was demoted to Yǎnzhōu Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (Mobilization Commandant of Yǎnzhōu).
Lín had an old relationship with the Fèi Dì (Deposed Emperor).
During Mǐndì's time,
he served as Bīngbù Shàngshū (Minister of the Ministry of War).
He was serving as an envoy to Húnán.
When he heard that the Deposed Emperor had been established,
he was delighted,
believing that he would surely be appointed as Chancellor.
Returning, he passed through Jīngnán.
He said to Gāo Cónghuǐ:
"A scholar certainly experiences times of decline and prosperity.
I have not been employed by the age for a long time.
Now the new Son of Heaven has ascended the throne,
I am about to be employed!"
He then approached Cónghuǐ, requesting treasures and goods to present as congratulations.
Cónghuǐ gave him two red horse-hair whisks,
and one guǒ (baboon/monkey) pelt,
and then prepared a feast for Lín.
He asked his deputy, Mǎ Chénghàn:
"Among the ministers of the current court,
who holds the promise of high ministerial office (Gōng Fǔ)?"
Chénghàn replied:
"Shàngshū (Minister) Cuī Jūjiǎn, Zuǒ Chéng (Left Administrator) Yáo Yǐ,
and next is Tàicháng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) Lú Wénjì."
Cónghuǐ smiled and looked at his attendants.
He fetched the report from the Jìnzòuguān (Reporting Official) and showed it to Lín.
Yǐ and Wénjì had both already been appointed Píngzhāngshì (Chancellors).
Lín was ashamed and lost color.
Returning,
he presented his pelt and whisks.
The Fèi Dì ultimately did not employ him.
Previously,
Lǐ Yú became Chancellor after serving as Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices),
and Lú Wénjì replaced him.
When Wénjì became Chancellor,
Lín then requested to be made Tàicháng Qīng.
When he received the appointment,
he offered his gratitude in the middle of the court and said:
"Your subject has undeservedly attained the qualifications for chancellorship."
The court officials passed this around as a joke.
Lín served the Jìn dynasty and was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince).
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Lín Sītú (Minister of Education).
He died a few months later,
at the age of eighty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title Tàifù (Grand Tutor).
Jiǎ Wěi
Jiǎ Wěi,
was a native of Huòlù, Zhènzhōu.
In his youth, he attempted the Jìnshì examination but failed.
The prefecture appointed him Cānjūn (Staff Officer).
During the Tiānchéng reign of the Táng dynasty,
when Fàn Yán'guāng governed Chéngdé,
he was appointed as Zhàozhōu Jūnshì Pànguān (Military Adjudicant of Zhàozhōu).
He was promoted to Shíyì Lìng (Magistrate of Shíyì).
Wěi excelled in historical studies.
Since the time after Wǔzōng of the Táng dynasty, there had been no Shílù (Veritable Records),
and the office of the historian was defunct.
Wěi collected and arranged reported accounts
to produce sixty-five volumes of the Táng Nián Bǔ Lù (Supplementary Records of the Táng Years).
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
the Imperial House was weak,
the various lords were powerful,
and military campaigns were launched without authorization.
The world was full of events.
Therefore, there were many omissions and errors in the accounts Wěi compiled.
However, during times of destruction and disorder,
the rough preservation of events
was still a supplement to historical accounts.
During the Tiānfú reign of the Jìn dynasty, he served as Tàicháng Bóshì (Scholar of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
This was not his preference,
and he repeatedly requested a historical post.

He was reassigned as Túntián Yuánwàiláng (Supernumerary Director of the Bureau of Military Lands), Qǐjū Láng (Diarist of Activity and Repose), and Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn (Compiler in the Historiography Institute),
and participated in compiling the History of Táng.
He observed mourning for his mother.
When the mourning period was over,
he became Zhī Zhìgào (Drafting Official).
He was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretariat Drafter), Jiànyì Dàfū (Grand Master Remonstrant), and Jìshì Zhōng (Attendant Censor),
and was again appointed Xiūzhuàn (Compiler).
During the time of Hàn Yǐndì,
he was ordered, along with Wáng Shēn and Dòu Yǎn, to compile the Veritable Records of Jìn Gāozǔ, Chū Dì, and Hàn Gāozǔ.
Initially,
when Sāng Wéihàn was Chancellor,
he always disliked Wěi's character
and treated him very poorly.
Wěi wrote the biography of Wéihàn,
stating
that "When Wéihàn died,
he possessed eight thousand tǐng of silver."
Hànlín Xuéshì (Academician of the Hanlin Academy) Xú Táifú thought this was unacceptable
and repeatedly criticized Wěi for it.
Wěi, having no choice,
changed the figure to several thousand tǐng.
In Guǎngshùn first year (951 CE), the Veritable Records were completed.
Wěi requested a promotion but did not receive it.
Because of this, he harbored resentment.
At that time,
Chancellor Wáng Jùn supervised the compilation of the National History.
Wěi, writing the Daily Records (Rìlì),
spoke frequently of the faults of the current high ministers.
Jùn saw this
and angrily said:
"The sons and younger brothers of Jǐshì (Attendant Censor) Jiǎ also require pedigree and status for their careers.
How can he repeatedly slander the gentlemen of the current court,
leaving their descendants with no means of advancement?"
He reported this to Tàizǔ.
Wěi was demoted to Pínglú Jūn Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (Mobilization Commandant of the Pínglú Army).
He died the following year in Qīngzhōu.
Duàn Xīyáo
Duàn Xīyáo,
was a native of Hèněi.
When Jìn Gāozǔ was Hédōng Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner of Hédōng),
he made Xīyáo his Pànguān (Adjudicant).
Gāozǔ's army was stationed at Xīnzhōu.
In the army, there were those who supported Gāozǔ and shouted "Ten Thousand Years!"
Gāozǔ was terrified and confused,
not knowing what to do.
Xīyáo advised Gāozǔ to execute the ringleaders of the disturbance,
and only then did it stop.
When Gāozǔ was about to raise troops in Tàiyuán,
he consulted with his advisors and subordinates.
Xīyáo believed it was inadvisable.
Although Gāozǔ did not heed him,
he still respected his character
and did not reprimand him.
When Gāozǔ entered and took the throne,
Xī Yáo, compared to the other generals and officials,
received the least favor.
After a long time,
he was gradually promoted to Jiànyì Dàfū,
and sent as an envoy to Wúyuè.
At that time,
the Jiāng and Huái Rivers were not navigable;
all who traveled as envoys to Wúyuè sailed across the sea,
and often suffered from wind and waves.
When Xī Yáo crossed the sea
and encountered a great storm,
everyone around him was frightened,
but Xī Yáo said:
“I have never deceived anyone in my life.
If you rely on me,
you can be without fear!”
Soon after, the wind also stopped.
He successively served as the Cìshǐ of the three prefectures of Lái, Huái, and Dì.
During the reign of Chūdì,
he served as Lìbù Shìláng,
and judged matters for the Eastern and Western Personnel Bureaus (Quán),
and was successively promoted to Lǐbù Shàngshū.
He died
at the age of seventy-nine,
and was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
Zhāng Yǔn
Zhāng Yǔn
was a native of Zhènzhōu.
In his youth, he served in the prefecture as Cānjūn for Zhāng Wénlǐ.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng attacked Zhāng Wénlǐ,
Yǔn escaped and surrendered.
Zhuāngzōng imprisoned him,
but when Wénlǐ was defeated,
he released him and made him Gōngcáo of Wèizhōu.
Zhào Zàilǐ appointed him as a Jiédù Tuīguān.
He successively served as Zhǎngshūjì in the two garrisons of Cāng and Yǎn.
He returned to court as Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
was successively promoted to Shuǐbù Yuánwàiláng,
and Zhī Zhìgào.
When Fèidì’s imperial son, Zhòngměi, became Hénán Yǐn
and was in charge of the Six Armies,
because Yǔn was firm and upright,
he appointed Yǔn as Jǐshìzhōng,
serving as Pànguān for the Six Armies.
When dismissed,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne
and repeatedly granted general amnesties across the realm,
Yǔn wrote a treatise arguing against the amnesty and presented it, saying:
“Guǎnzǐ said: ‘Amnesty generally brings minor benefits but major harms;
in the long run, its disaster cannot be overcome.
Absence of amnesty brings minor harms but major benefits;
in the long run, its blessings cannot be surpassed.’
Furthermore, when Wú Hàn of the Hàn dynasty was gravely ill,
the Emperor asked Hàn what he wished to say.
Hàn replied: ‘I only wish Your Majesty would grant no amnesties!’
Indeed, granting amnesty should not be considered kindness,
and failing to grant amnesty should not be considered unkindness,
because the purpose is to punish the guilty.
Since antiquity, it has been universally believed that in times of flood or drought, one should issue virtuous decrees to pardon faults,
open prisons and release inmates,
hoping to move Heaven’s heart and alleviate the disaster.
This is wrong.
Suppose there is a lawsuit involving two people,
one guilty and one innocent.
If the guilty one is pardoned,
then the innocent one harbors resentment.
This is the way to bring about disaster,
not the technique to remedy disaster.
Furthermore, when villains encounter a natural disaster,
they all rejoice and encourage each other to commit evil,
saying: ‘The state is about to grant amnesty;
it must pardon us to remedy the disaster.’
If this happens,
then it is teaching the people to do evil.
Now, the way of Heaven
is to bless the good and punish the wicked.
If one pardons evil people and turns disaster into fortune,
it would mean that Heaven rejoices in people committing evil.
Whenever Heaven sends down disaster,
it is merely to warn the ruler to restrain his desires,
to strive for diligence and thrift,
to show compassion to the desolate and the solitary,
and to correct punishments.”
At that time,
Jìn Gāozǔ was particularly fond of his subjects speaking out,
and upon reading it, he was greatly pleased.
Yǔn served Hàn (Hou Hàn) as Lìbù Shìláng.
When Yǐndì executed ministers,
everyone in the capital was terrified.
Yǔn often retired from court but dared not return home,
staying instead at the Xiàngguó Sì.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ entered the capital with his troops,
Yǔn hid in the ceiling rafters of the Buddhist hall,
fell down and died,
at the age of sixty-five.
Wáng Sōng
Wáng Sōng’s
father, Huī,
was the Zǎixiàng under Táng Xīzōng.
Sōng passed the Jìnshì examination.
During the Hòu Táng period,
he successively served as Xíngbù Lángzhōng.
At the end of Táng,
he served in regional military commands.
When Jìn Gāozǔ governed Tàiyuán,
he appointed Sōng as Jiédù Pànguān.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū,
and was successively promoted to Gōngbù Shàngshū.
When Chūdì was moved north,
Xiāo Hàn established Xǔ Wáng Cóngyì in the capital
and made Sōng the Zuǒ Chéngxiàng.
When Hàn Gāozǔ entered Luòyáng,
he first sent people with a hasty decree instructing all officials in the Eastern Capital who had received the false mandate to burn them,
so that they would not doubt themselves.
Therefore, the Yùshǐ Tái collected all the false imperial edicts from the officials and burned them.
Sōng pointed to his chest with his finger,
used Guō Zǐyí as a reference to satirize himself,
and said to others:
“This is indeed the Zhōngshū Lìng who served twenty-four imperial inspections.”
Those who heard this laughed at him.
Later, Sōng's son, Rénbǎo, served as the Hézhōng Zhīshǐ under Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
When Shǒuzhēn rebelled,
Sōng, on account of his son, submitted a memorial to explain himself.
Gāozǔ pitied him,
but simply ordered him to relinquish his post.
Sōng had land east of the city.
He traveled between there and the capital throughout the years.
He died of illness.
Péi Hào
Péi Hào, courtesy name Sīdōng,
was a native of Hédōng.
Since the Jìn and Wèi dynasties, the Péi clan
had been famous nobility for generations.
Those who resided in Yān were called
“Eastern Relatives” (Dōng Juàn),
those who resided in Liáng were called
“Western Relatives” (Xī Juàn),
and those who resided in Hédōng were called
“Central Relatives” (Zhōng Juàn).
Hào came from a famous family,
and his appearance and demeanor were refined and elegant.
His nature was firm and impetuous,
straightforward and holding nothing back.
In his youth, he loved learning.
During the Guānghuà era of the Táng dynasty, he passed the Jìnshì examination,
and was appointed Jiàoshū Láng, Shíyí, and Bǔquē.
He served the Liáng dynasty as Hànlín Xuéshì and Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He served the Hòu Táng dynasty as Lǐbù Shìláng.
Hào enjoyed discussion and critique.
Whenever he pointed out deficiencies in the court,
he often denounced powerful ministers.
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
Due to old age, he was appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū and retired.
Jìn Gāozǔ raised him up to be Gōngbù Shàngshū,
but he again requested retirement due to age,
and was appointed Yòu Púyè and retired.
He died
at the age of eighty-five,
and was posthumously granted Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
Hào had been at court for a long time due to his literary talent.
The Chancellors Mǎ Yìnsūn and Sāng Wéihàn
were both Jìnshì graduates selected by Hào while he served at the Ministry of Rites.
Later, when Yìnsūn managed the examinations,
and the results were posted,
he led the new Jìnshì to visit Hào.
Hào happily composed a poem, saying:
“A disciple under the gate sees a disciple under the gate.”
This was widely regarded as an honor.
After Wéihàn had become Chancellor,
he once visited Hào.
Hào neither welcomed him nor saw him off.
Someone asked him about this,
and Hào replied:
“When I see Lord Sāng in the Central Secretariat,
he is a high official.
When Lord Sāng sees me in my private residence,
he is my disciple.
What need is there for welcoming or seeing off?”
People also considered this proper.
Wáng Rényù
Wáng Rényù, courtesy name Déniǎn,
was a native of Tiānshuǐ.
In his youth, he did not study books,
and took pleasure in dogs, horses, shooting, and hunting.
He only began studying at the age of twenty-five.
However, he was a talented and remarkable person,
and became famous for his literary compositions between Qín and Lǒng.
The Commander of Qín appointed him as Jiédù Pànguān of Qínzhōu.
Qínzhōu was incorporated into Shǔ,
and Rényù subsequently served Shǔ as Zhōngshū Shèrén and Hànlín Xuéshì.
The Fǔběn text has these three characters.
Táng Zhuāngzōng pacified Shǔ
. Rén Yù served Táng
, and later again became Qínzhōu Military Governor’s Staff Supervisor (Jiédu Pànguān)
. Wáng Sītóng garrisoned Xīngyuán
and appointed him as a subordinate official (Cóngshì)
. When Sītóng served as Resident Overseer (Liúshǒu) in Xījīng
, he made him a Staff Supervisor (Pànguān)
. Fèidì (The Deposed Emperor) raised troops at Fèngxiáng
. Sītóng was defeated in battle
. Fèidì captured Rén Yù
, and hearing of his reputation, did not kill him
, but kept him within the army
. From the time Fèidì started his rebellion
until he ascended the throne
, the imperial edicts (zhàoshū) and proclamations (gàomìng) that were dispatched quickly to the various garrisons (zhèn)
were all written by Rén Yù
. After a long time
, he was made Clerk of the Director of Imperial Manufactories (Dūguān Lángzhōng) acting concurrently as a Hanlin Academician (Hànlín Xuéshì)
. When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne
, he was dismissed from his post and made a Director (Lángzhōng)
, subsequently serving as Director of the Ministry of Personnel Registration (Sīfēng Zuǒsī Lángzhōng) and Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū)
. During the time of Hàn Gāozǔ
, he was again made Hanlin Academician Compiler (Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ)
, and progressively promoted to Minister of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū)
, before being dismissed and made Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū) and Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo)
. He died in the third year of Xiǎndé
, at the age of seventy-seven
, and was posthumously granted the title of Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàoshī)
. Rén Yù was naturally knowledgeable about music theory (yīnlǜ)
. When Jìn Gāozǔ first standardized the court music (Yǎyuè)
and hosted a banquet for his ministers in the Yǒngfú Diàn
, the Huángzhōng (Yellow Bell mode) was played
. Rén Yù heard it and said
: "The sound is neither pure nor solemn, and lacks harmony
. There must be conflict arising within the forbidden palace
." Soon after
, two military officers fought outside the Shēnglóng Mén
. People considered him divine
. He enjoyed writing poetry
. When he was young
, he once dreamed that his intestines and stomach were split open
, and washed with water from the Xījiāng (West River)
. Looking down, he saw that the sand and stones in the river were all covered in Zhuàn (Seal Script) and Zhòuwén (Great Seal Script) characters
. Because of this, his literary talent significantly improved
. He compiled the more than ten thousand poems he had written in his lifetime into one hundred volumes
, titled the Xījiāng Jí (Collection from the West River)
. Rén Yù and Hé Níng were both famous for their literary works during the Five Dynasties period
. They also both served as Chief Examiners (Zhī Gòngjǔ)
. Wáng Pǔ, a disciple of Rén Yù
, and Fàn Zhì, a disciple of Níng
, both reached the position of Chancellor (Zǎixiàng)
. People at the time praised them for selecting talented individuals
. Péi Yǔ
. Péi Yǔ’s courtesy name was Yònghuà
. His father, Zhì
, served as Chancellor (Xiāng) to Táng Xīzōng
, and held the office of Minister of Works (Sīkōng)
. Yǔ, being the son of a Rank One official
, became the Commandant (Wèi) of Shòu'ān in Hénán
, later changed to Investigating Censor (Jiānchá Yùshǐ)
. During the reign of Táng Míngzōng
, he served as Director in the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Lángzhōng)
. He and Lù Chóng, the Right Grand Master of Remonstrance (Yòu Sǎnqí Chángshì)
, were sent on an embassy to Mǐn
. At that time
, Qián Liú, the King of Wúyuè
, had a rift with Ān Chónghuǐ
. Yǔ and his companions were detained for a year
, and Chóng died of illness
. Later, Liú sent Yǔ back
. Yǔ requested to carry Chóng’s body back with him
. Liú initially refused
, but Yǔ moved Liú with his words
. Liú compassionately granted the request
, and consequently attached a memorial (biǎo) of surrender to Yǔ
. Míngzōng was extremely pleased to receive Liú’s memorial
. Because of this, Wúyuè resumed communication with the central court (Zhōngguó)
. Yǔ escorted Chóng’s remains back to the capital (Jīngshī)
. When he returned Chóng’s luggage and possessions to his family
, all scholars praised Yǔ’s righteousness
. Yǔ
, during the reign of Zhōu Tàizǔ
, served as Left Grand Master of Remonstrance (Zuǒ Sǎnqí Chángshì)
. He died
. Wáng Yán
. Wáng Yán's courtesy name was Shìměi
. He was a native of Chángfēng in Màozhōu
. In his youth, he loved learning
. He once presented a fu (rhapsody) to Lǐ Qí
, the Chancellor of Liáng
. Qí praised him highly
and recommended him as Magistrate (Xiànlìng) of Jìmò
, he was an old acquaintance of Yán
, and summoned him to serve as Left Court Counselor (Zuǒ Bǔquē)
. He was promoted to Auxiliary Director of the Ministry of Waterways (Shuǐbù Yuánwàiláng)
, and Concurrent Drafter of Edicts (Zhī Zhìgào)
. He was appointed Secretary of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén)
, and temporarily oversaw the imperial examinations (Quán Zhī Gòngjǔ)
. Lú Wénjì
, the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū)
. At this time
, Xié’s son, Qí
. Wénjì said to Yán
: "I have previously praised you in court
. When selecting scholars through the examinations
, one must look for true effectiveness
, and should not choose people based on empty reputation
. In the past, there was a man from Yuè skilled in swimming
. When his son was exactly one year old (zuì)
, the mother placed him floating on the water
. People were surprised and asked about it
, and she replied: 'Since his father is skilled at swimming
, the son will certainly be able to do it'
. Is such a course of action acceptable
?" Yán withdrew and laughed, saying
: "The words of Lord Lú
are aimed at Cuī Xié
. He resents the father and thus extends his malice to the son
!" The following year
, he selected Qí for the highest grade (Jiǎkē)
. Everyone praised his fairness
. He was progressively promoted to Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū)
, and retired (zhìshì) as Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo)
. He died
at the age of seventy-three
. Yán was a person who valued his promises
and shared deep affection with his younger brother, Guī
. During the period of the Five Dynasties
, his family integrity (jiāfǎ) was highly praised
. Mǎ Chóngjī
. Mǎ Chóngjī's courtesy name was Dòngwēi
. His ancestors originated from the Northern Di (Northern Barbarians)
, and his family served in the military generation after generation
. Chóngjī studied divination and arithmetic techniques (shùshù) in his youth
. He was skilled in Tàiyī, Wǔjì, Bāxiàng, and the Sāntǒng Dàlì calendar systems
. He resided in Tàiyuán
. When Táng Zhuāngzōng governed Tàiyuán
, whenever he mobilized troops for campaigns
, he invariably consulted Chóngjī
. Chóngjī’s predictions were never inaccurate
, so he was appointed Judicial Reviewer (Dàlǐ Sīzhí)
. During the reign of Míngzōng
, he was dismissed and unused
. When Jìn Gāozǔ refused the imperial command at Tàiyuán
, Fèidì dispatched troops to besiege it
. The situation was extremely perilous and urgent
. Gāozǔ ordered Chóngjī to perform divination
. The hexagram Tóngrén (Fellowship) was encountered
. He said
: "This is the image of Heaven and Fire
. Qián (Heaven) is vigorous (jiàn), and Lí (Fire) is bright (míng)
. Vigor is the virtue of the ruler
, and brightness means facing south and leading
, which is the means by which the world is governed
. Tóngrén means unity among people
; there must be someone who will unite with us
. The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says: 'Fighting in Qián'
. Qián
is the northwest
. It also says: 'Meeting in Lí'
. Lí
is the south
. Will those who unite with us come from the north to the south
? Qián
is the northwest
. We will fight and win
. Will this happen around the transition between the ninth and tenth months
?" In the ninth month of that year
, the Qìdān assisted Jìn in defeating the Táng army
, and Jìn consequently obtained the empire
. Chóngjī was appointed Right Grand Master for Assisting Goodness of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Yòu Zànshàn Dàfū)
, and promoted to Director of the Astronomical Bureau (Sītiān Jiān)
. The following year
, Zhāng Cóngbīn rebelled
. Gāozǔ ordered Chóngjī to perform divination
. The hexagram Suí (Following/Attending) was encountered
. He said
: "Looking south toward Xīmù
, the wood (trees) cannot sustain itself
. Emptiness leads to movement
, and movement follows its defeat
. The year is approaching autumn
, he will be unable to succeed
!" In the seventh month, Cóngbīn was defeated
. Gāozǔ was greatly pleased
In Tiānfú Sān Nián (938 CE),
Mǎ Chóngjī submitted a memorial, stating:
“The calendar and celestial phenomena [lìxiàng]
are what the True King uses to rectify the origin of the singular primary force [yīqì zhī yuán]
and proclaim the mandate to all nations.
However, the records from antiquity and modern times,
when examined, show many discrepancies.
The Xuānmíng calendar [Xuānmíng Lì] correctly determines the beginning of months and periods [qìshuò], but the stellar positions do not match the observation;
the Chóngxuán calendar [Chóngxuán Lì] correctly determines the five planets [wǔxīng], but the annual discrepancy [suìchā] is one day.
By taking the periods and new moons from the Xuānmíng calendar
and combining them with the positions of the five planets from the Chóngxuán calendar,
referencing the two calendars against each other,
only then do they conform.
All calendars from previous generations
have begun the year with the eleventh month (ziyǐ month), representing the starting point of Heaven’s rectification [Tiānzhèng shíyī yuè],
and used the jiǎzǐ cycle of the remotest antiquity as the grand epoch [shàngyuán].
The greater the accumulation of years,
the greater the resulting discrepancy.
I have ventured to combine these two calendars
and create a new method
by taking the twelfth year of the Tiānbǎo era (Yǐwèi) of the Táng dynasty (755 CE) as the grand epoch,
and the central period [zhōngqì] of Rain Water [Yǔshuǐ] in the first month as the start of the periods [qìshǒu].”
An edict was issued instructing the Directorate of Astronomy [Sītiān Jiàn], Zhào Rénqí, Zhāng Wénhào, and others to examine the merits and flaws.
Rénqí and the others reported:
“We have used Mǎ Chóngjī’s calendar to calculate the new moon of the first month of next year, Gēngzǐ (940 CE),
and they all correspond without error.”
Thereupon, an edict was issued to promulgate it,
naming it the Tiáoyuán Lì.
After being implemented for several years, it quickly became inaccurate,
so it was abandoned.
Mǎ Chóngjī further submitted:
“The method of the water clock [lòukè zhī fǎ]
uses the culmination of stars [zhōngxīng] to determine day and night as one hundred units [kè].
Eight units and twenty-sixtieths of a unit [bā kè liùshí fèn kè zhī èrshí] constitute one hour [shí],
and the hour is defined as exactly four units and ten-sixtieths.
This is the method used since antiquity.
Now, this transmission has been lost;
noon [wǔzhèng] is taken as the beginning of the hour,
encroaching into the wèishí period by four units and ten-sixtieths to be designated as wǔ.
Because of this, the times for day, night, dusk, and dawn
have all lost their correctness.
I request that the ancient system be restored.”
This was accepted.
Mǎ Chóngjī died at the age of sixty-four.
Zhào Yányì
Zhào Yányì, courtesy name Zǐyīng,
was a native of Qínzhōu.
His great-grandfather, Shěnggōng, was skilled in numerology and divination techniques [shùshù],
and fled the chaos to Shǔ.
His father, Wēn Guī,
served Wáng Jiàn, the King of Shǔ, as the Director of Astronomy.
Whenever Wēn Guī calculated good or bad fortune for Wáng Jiàn,
if it was slightly inaccurate,
Jiàn would immediately subject him to questioning and reproach.
When Wēn Guī was about to die,
he admonished his sons and grandsons, saying:
“Numerology [shùshù]
is our hereditary profession.
However, I served in a chaotic kingdom,
and have several times committed offenses and narrowly escaped death!
If my descendants can enter officialdom through other paths,
they need not pursue this.”
Nevertheless, Yányì, in his youth, also used this skill to enter the service of Shǔ as Director of Astronomy.
When Shǔ fell,
he served the Táng dynasty as an Astrologer [Xīngguān].
Yányì was proficient in the Three Methods [Sān Shì]
and was quite skilled in physiognomy [xiàng rén].
When the Qìdān destroyed the Jìn dynasty,
Yányì followed the barbarians to Zhènzhōu.
Lǐ Jūn and Bái Zàiróng planned to expel Mádá [Mahad] and return to the Hàn regime,
but they were hesitant and undecided.
Yányì, under the guise of discussing numerology, endorsed and encouraged their plan.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of the Zhōu dynasty marched his troops from Wèi into the capital,
Tàizǔ summoned Yányì and asked:
“Is the short duration of the Hàn dynasty’s mandate [Hàn Zùo]
due to the calculation of Heaven [tiānshù]?”
Yányì replied:
“A king who governs the world
should rely on benevolence, grace, and virtue [rén ēn dé zé].
However, the laws of the Hàn dynasty were severe and cruel,
and punishments were arbitrary and excessive.
The whole world cried out injustice—
this is the reason for its downfall!”
At that time,
Tàizǔ was surrounding the residences of Sū Féngjí and Liú Zhū with soldiers,
intending to execute their entire families.
Upon hearing Yányì’s words, Tàizǔ was struck with awe,
and consequently spared their families,
allowing both households to survive.
Yányì served the Zhōu dynasty as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury [Tàifǔ Qīng] and concurrently supervised the Directorate of Astronomy [Pàn Sītiān Jiàn],
and died of illness.
Alas!
Regarding the rites, music, literature, and culture of the Five Dynasties [Wǔdài],
I have nothing to adopt.
But if later generations wish to know about them,
they cannot be abandoned.
Therefore, I compile the Records of the Directorate of Astronomy and the Geography Department [Sītiān Zhífāng Kǎo].
Record of the Directorate of Astronomy, Part One [Sītiān Kǎo Dì Yī]
The Directorate of Astronomy is in charge of the phenomena of the sun, moon, and stars.
The complete celestial circuit of one year,
the four seasons,
the twenty-four solar terms [èrshísì qì],
the seventy-two pentads [qīshí'èr hòu],
and the passage through the ten days and twelve terrestrial branches [shí rì shí'èr chén],
are used to establish the calendar.
Diligent observation of their changes
is used for divination [zhān].
Divination [zhān] refers to
an unusual portent [fēicháng zhī zhào],
used to verify good and bad fortune,
to seek Heaven’s will,
and to enlighten human affairs;
its techniques [shù] are preserved by the relevant officials.
The calendar [lì] refers to
regular and constant calculations,
used to forecast cold and heat,
to anticipate the Way of Heaven,
and to encourage human endeavor;
its methods [fǎ] are trusted by the world.
Techniques [shù] are used occasionally,
but the methods [fǎ] cannot be wrong for even a single day.
A difference of a hair’s breadth
will confuse the sequence of Heaven and man [tiānrén zhī xù]
and disrupt the timing of all affairs.
This is indeed what the possessor of a state regards as serious.
From the time Yáo commanded Xī and Hé, as seen in the documents,
the culmination of stars and the remaining days for intercalation [rùn yú]
roughly preserve the main principles.
However, in the more than a thousand years between the Three Dynasties [Sāndài],
the extant texts were lost and the practice fell into disuse,
with nothing recorded in the Six Classics.
And the followers of Kǒngzǐ [Confucius]
also never discussed it.
It was only in later generations
that this knowledge originated solely from the School of Yīn and Yáng [yīnyáng zhī jiā];
the matter itself is important,
but the scholarship is superficial.
The connection between Heaven and man [tiānrén zhī jì]—
how distant and subtle it is!
Yet, it entrusts a scholar of mere technique [yī yì zhī shì]
to perform calculations and integral arithmetic,
seeking upwards tens of millions of years into the past,
to find the moment when the jiǎzǐ cycle begins, the new moon, midnight, and the winter solstice all occur simultaneously,
and the sun, moon, and five planets all meet at the zǐ position.
This is called the grand epoch [shàngyuán],
and is used as the start of the calendar.
It seems that after the Hàn dynasty,
this theory first began to be clearly seen in the world,
and its origin and development stop here.
Was this truly the method of Yáo, Shùn, and the Three Dynasties?
It is impossible to verify.
Nevertheless, since then,
although the techniques of calendar experts [lìjiā zhī shù]
have varied greatly across generations,
they have never failed to be fundamentally rooted in this principle.
At the beginning of the Five Dynasties,
following the tradition of the Táng dynasty,
the Chóngxuán Lì was used.
Up until the reign of Gāozǔ of the Jìn dynasty,
the Director of Astronomy, Mǎ Chóngjī,
began to create a new calendar.
He no longer calculated back to the ancient grand epoch (jiǎzǐ, winter solstice, and the conjunction of the seven luminaries),
but started the grand epoch from the twelfth year of the Tiānbǎo era (Yǐwèi) of the Táng dynasty (755 CE),
and used Rain Water in the first month as the start of the periods.
Originally,
during the Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
the technician Cáo Shìwěi first altered the ancient method,
using the fifth year of the Xiǎnqìng era (660 CE) as the grand epoch,
and Rain Water as the start of the year.
It was named the Fútiān Lì.
However, it was popularly called the Minor Calendar [Xiǎo Lì]
and was only circulated among the common people.
But Mǎ Chóngjī adopted this method
and applied it in the imperial court,
and it was granted the name Tiáoyuán Lì.
However, after being implemented for five years,
it quickly became inaccurate and unusable,
and the Chóngxuán Lì was restored.
During the Guǎngshùn era of the Zhōu dynasty (951–953 CE),
Wáng Chǔnè, a Doctor in the Directorate of Education [Guózǐ Bóshì],
privately compiled the Míngxuán Lì at home.
Among the common people, there was also the Wànfēn Lì,
and in Shǔ, there were the Yǒngchāng Lì and the Zhèngxiàng Lì;
Nán Táng had the Qízhèng Lì.
Regarding calendar makers during the period of the Five Dynasties,
those that can be verified
stop here.
Since the methods of the Tiáoyuán Lì were not ancient,
the Míngxuán Lì remained privately stored in his home,
and the Wànfēn Lì was only used among the common people,
their methods are not worth recording.
Furthermore, the Yǒngchāng Lì, Zhèngxiàng Lì, and Qízhèng Lì
were only used within their respective states,
and are now also lost
and can no longer be seen.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he outwardly campaigned against usurpers and rebels,
and inwardly reformed laws and regulations.
The Academician of the Duānmíng Hall, Wáng Pò,
was skilled in calendrical calculations.
Therefore, an imperial edict commanded Pò to compile and finalize [a new calendar].
After more than a year,
Pò submitted a memorial, saying: "I have heard that the work of the Sages
lies in understanding the transformations between Heaven and humanity.
The movements of human emotions
can be known through words;
the movements
of the Way of Heaven
should be known through numbers.
As for the use of numbers,
the Sages used them to observe the Way of Heaven.
Years, months, days, and hours
are formed thereby;
yin and yang, cold
and heat,
are regulated thereby;
the governance of the four directions
is carried out thereby.
Indeed, for those who govern a state,
who establish the beginning and set the ultimate standard,
they must embody its origin;
who administer policies and evaluate achievements,
they must follow its years;
who initiate rites and perform music,
they must rectify its first day of the month;
the three types of farmers and the hundred artisans
must conform to its seasons;
the five punishments and nine campaigns
must follow its energies;
and all other affairs
must accord with its sun and moon.
It is for this reason that when Sages receive the mandate [of Heaven],
they must regulate calendrical calculations.
Thus, the Five Records have constant measures,
the various omens have constant responses,
and the correct calendar is implemented throughout the world.
Since the late Táng dynasty,
calendars have passed through many courts.
In times of disorder, Heaven's [principles] were lost,
for nearly a hundred years.
Heaven's calendrical calculations
have merely become muddled and outdated.
Your Majesty follows ancient practices,
reverently fearing Heaven above,
consulting various officials,
and reviving fallen institutions.
Although I am not capable,
how dare I not obey the imperial edict?
Therefore, I encompass all phenomena as a standard,
align the Seven Regulators to establish the epoch,
measure the gnomon and arrow to observe the qi,
examine the early and late moon to determine the new moon,
clarify the nine paths to calculate the moon's position,
correct for speed variations to predict the stars,
examine the obliquity of the ecliptic,
and discern the rising and falling of celestial forces,
whereby eclipses are precisely detailed.
Indeed, the Way of establishing Heaven
is said to be yin and yang.
Yin and yang each have their numbers,
and when combined, they transform and complete.
The number of strokes for yang is thirty-six;
the number of strokes for yin is twenty-four.
Odd and even mutually determine,
two yangs and three yins
equally yield seventy-two.
When equal, the numbers of yin and yang combine.
Seventy-two
is the number of transformation and completion.
Transformation and completion are called the numbers of the Five Phases.
Multiplied by five,
one obtains the number of a cycle.
Exceeding this [number]
is called "qi fullness";
falling short [of it]
is called "new moon emptiness."
As for adapting to changes and applying [these numbers] differently,
there is nothing that is not understood.
Therefore, seventy-two is taken as the constant method.
The constant method [jīngfǎ]
is the commonly used method.
One hundred
is the segment of numbers,
advancing and retreating according to the method [fǎ],
without losing its original position,
hence it is called the general method [tōngfǎ].
Using the general method to advance the constant method [jīngfǎ],
one obtains seven thousand two hundred,
which is called the comprehensive method [tǒngfǎ].
From the epoch to the constant [jīngfǎ],
this method is used first;
it is the comprehensive method of all calendrical methods.
Using the general method to advance the comprehensive method [tǒngfǎ],
one obtains seven hundred and twenty thousand.
Below the qi and new moon,
the fractions must be entirely collected,
which is called the complete rate [quánlǜ].
Using the general method to advance the complete rate [quánlǜ],
one obtains seventy-two million,
which is called the grand rate [dàlǜ],
and from which the epochal cycle [yuánjì] is born.
The epoch [yuán] is when
years, months, days, and hours are all jiǎzǐ;
the sun, moon, and five planets all align in zǐ;
and [they are] in the middle of expansion and contraction, earlier and later,
which is called the alignment of the Seven Regulators.
In ancient times,
a gnomon was erected in Yángchéng,
because of its proximity to Luò.
However, it was considered insufficient in its central position,
being in the eastern part of Luò.
In the twelfth year of Kāiyuán,
envoys were sent throughout the realm to observe shadows.
To the south, they reached Línyì;
to the north, they reached Héngyě.
In the middle, they found Yuètái in Jùnyí,
which corresponded to the north-south meridian [xián],
and was located in the center of the earth.
When the Great Zhōu established its state,
it set its capital in Biàn.
A gnomon was erected and an arrow placed,
to measure the sundial and clepsydra at Yuètái,
to serve as the central number.
When the sundial and clepsydra are accurate,
then the arrival of the sun [solstice],
and the corresponding qi [seasonal nodes],
are obtained.
Both the sun and moon have periods of expansion and contraction.
When the sun expands and the moon contracts,
then the [true] new moon occurs later than the mean.
When the moon expands and the sun contracts,
then the [true] new moon occurs earlier than the mean.
From ancient times, the method for early and late moon [tiǎonüè]
was mostly based on uniform motion calculations;
when incorporated into calendars, there were both prior discrepancies [errors]
and inconsistent gradual decreases [in accuracy].
The old techniques of Huángjí [calendar]
were circuitous and difficult to use.
Down to various later calendars,
they were crude and had many errors.
Now, the early and late moon of the lunar mansion [yuèlín tiǎonüè]
is corrected according to the calendar;
the early and late moon of the sun's position [rìchán tiǎonüè]
is adjusted when used.
What is obtained
is the exact day of the lunar mansion.
A single day
is divided into nine divisions.
For each division, gains and losses
gradually decrease in a consistent manner.
The method of early and late moon [tiǎonüè]
can be said to be precise.

Entry of the Solar Position (*Rìchán*) into the Calendar

If it is more,

Ecliptic Solar Degrees

Solar Position at Noon (*Wǔzhōng*)

Subtract half of the modulus (*bànfǎ*).
This yields the minutes/fractions after noon (*wǔhòu fēn*);
If insufficient,
Subtract the remainder (in the opposite direction),
This yields the minutes/fractions before noon (*wǔqián fēn*).

Entry of the Solar Position at Noon into the Calendar

If it is after noon,

Central Gnomon Shadow at *Yuètái*

Dawn and Dusk Minutes/Fractions
Set the minutes/fractions of the calendar entry for each.

If decreasing (*sǔn*), add this result to the lower dusk minutes/fractions; if increasing (*yì*), subtract it.

Sunrise and Sunset Time Periods (*Chén*) and Quarters (*Kè*)
Set the dawn and dusk minutes/fractions.
Add 180 to the dawn reading, and subtract it from the dusk reading,
This yields the sunrise and sunset minutes/fractions.

This yields the number of periods (*chén shù*);
If the remainder reaches the *jīngfǎ*,
This yields the quarters (*kè*);

This is the time period (*chén*) and quarters (*kè*) of sunrise and sunset.
Day and Night Quarters (*Kè*)
Set the sunset minutes/fractions.
Subtract the sunrise minutes/fractions from it.

The red道
is the celestial girdle.
Its form is circular and flat,
and it records the constant numbers of the lunar lodges and degrees.
The yellow道
is the sun's orbit.
Half of it is within the red道,
and half is outside the red道,
twenty-four degrees away from the pole.
When it is close to the red道,
its inclination is oblique;
when it is far from the red道,
its inclination is straight.
When oblique,
the sun's movement should be slower;
when straight,
the sun's movement should be faster.
Therefore, before and after the two equinoxes, its degrees are added;
before and after the two solstices, its degrees are subtracted.
The nine道
are the moon's orbit.
Half of it is within the yellow道,
and half is outside the yellow道,
six degrees further from the pole.
Emerging from the yellow道
is called zhèngjiāo;
entering the yellow道
is called zhōngjiāo.
If zhèngjiāo is in the lunar lodge of the autumn equinox,
and zhōngjiāo is in the lunar lodge of the spring equinox,
then it is even more oblique than the yellow道.
If zhèngjiāo is in the lunar lodge of the spring equinox,
and zhōngjiāo is in the lunar lodge of the autumn equinox,
then it is, on the contrary, straighter than the yellow道.
If zhèngjiāo and zhōngjiāo are in the lunar lodges of the two solstices,
then its inclination is slightly oblique.
Therefore, by comparing its distance from the two solstices and two equinoxes,
to ascertain its obliqueness or straightness,
the numbers for addition and subtraction are obtained.
Although the theory of the nine道 has existed since ancient times,
it was probably known but not in detail,
with only inherited texts,
but no practical use for calculation.
Now, the full circuit of the yellow道
is divided into eight sections;
within each section,
it is divided into nine道;
making a total of seventy-two道,
so that the sun and moon have no hidden inclinations or straightnesses.
The method of the nine道
can be said to be clear.
The movement of stars:
they are fast when near the sun,
and slow when far from the sun.
When extremely far from the sun,
their momentum ceases and they stop.
In all ancient calendars,
the segmentation was inaccurate,
and the increases and decreases had no standard;
today, if the daily movement is still large,
the next day it stops;
from stopping to receding,
only uniform motion is used,
and the degree of movement within a segment is still taken as the number for the calendar: all these are not based on fundamental principles,
thus leading to discrepancies.
Now, we calculate the accumulated daily movement
to create changing segments.
Then, from fast it gradually slows down,
and stops when its momentum ceases.
From stopping it moves again,
also accumulating subtly before increasing significantly.
Separate variable calendars for various segments are established
to calculate the variable differences,
so that the variable differences for various segments
meet and correspond.
The swiftness and slowness of the stars
can thus be known.
It has been handed down since ancient times
that if it is within fifteen degrees of the node,
then there will be a solar or lunar eclipse.
They did not know that the obscuration of the sun and moon
is different in principle
from the projection of a dark void.
Now, by considering the sizes of the sun's and moon's diameters,
comparing the distance from the node,
the obliqueness or straightness of the yellow道,
and the rising and falling of the celestial inclination,
and calculating the fractions for upward and sideways views,
the actual conditions of eclipses are obtained.
Your servant has examined previous generations,
and there are no texts concerning the beginning and end of the eclipse deity.
Recently, the minor arts of celestial observation and divination,
unable to grasp the overall picture,
resulted in the method of "equal connection."
This was probably adopted for convenience,
to seek shortcuts,
and thus there were numbers for retrograde motion of the nodes.
Later scholars could not understand this in detail,
and so they spoke of "nine luminaries" in the calendar,
taking them as a fixed pattern for calendar annotations.
Now, these are all abolished and removed.
I have respectfully compiled four chapters on calculating the sun, calculating the moon, calculating the stars, and calculating convergence and divergence,
combined into one volume of Lìjīng,
eleven volumes of Lì,
three volumes of Cǎo,
and one volume of Xiǎndé Sān Nián Qīzhèng Xìxíng Lì,
to be known as Qīntiān Lì.
In ancient times, Emperor Yáo
reverently complied with august heaven.
Your Majesty's examination of the celestial phenomena, the sun, moon, and stars,
is the way of Táng Yáo.
The way of Heaven is profound and distant,
not something your humble servant can fully comprehend.
Shìzōng praised it.
An imperial edict instructed the Sītiānjiān to use it,
starting from the first day of the first month of the following year.
The Xiǎndé Qīntiān Lì
recounts the beginning of the Upperspan Jiǎzǐ cycle,
up to the current Xiǎndé Sān Nián Bǐngchén,
accumulating 72,698,452 suàn and more.

Entering Lunar Distance into the Calendar.
Set the Shuò Jī (Accumulated New Moon).
Divide by the Lí Lǜ.
The remainder, modulo the Tǒng Fǎ, yields the days,
which is the normal celestial time-added New Moon entry into the calendar.
Successively add the Xiàng Cè (Image Modulus).
If exceeding the Lí Cè, divide by it.
This yields the entry into the calendar for the quarters, full moon, and next new moon.
Lunar Distance Tiǎo Nǜ (Acceleration/Deceleration).
Set the calendar entry fraction.
Using the fixed Tiǎo Nǜ numbers for the Rì Chán (Sun's path),
subtract for *tiǎo* (acceleration), and add for *nǜ* (deceleration).
Divide by the Chéng Jié.
This is the Xiàn Shù (limit number).
Multiply the remainder by the gain/loss rate associated with the entered limit.
Divide by the Chéng Jié,
and use this to adjust the limit's Tiǎo Nǜ into the fixed number (Dìng Shù).
Fixed Dates for Shuò, Xián, and Wàng.
Using the fixed Tiǎo Nǜ numbers for the Rì Chán and Yuè Lí,
subtract for *tiǎo* and add for *nǜ* to the standard fractions of Shuò (New Moon), Xián (Quarters), and Wàng (Full Moon).
This is the fixed day (Dìng Rì).
If the Dìng Shuò (Fixed New Moon) time is after sunset,
then advance one day;
but if there is a primary conjunction sight, do not advance.
If the Xián Wàng (Quarters/Full Moon) time is before sunrise,
then retreat one day;
if the sun has already risen but there is a primary conjunction sight, apply the same rule.
If the first day of the calendar has a conjunction,
determine it by adjusting the phases.
If the Heavenly Stem (*gān*) of the Fixed New Moon is the same as the subsequent New Moon,
it is a long month (*dà*);
if it is different,
it is a short month (*xiǎo*);
if there is no Zhōng Qì (principal solar term),
it is an intercalary month (*rùn*).
Degrees of the Sun/Moon at the Time-Added New/Full Moon.

Using the fixed Tiǎo Nǜ numbers for the Rì Chán and Yuè Lí,
subtract for *tiǎo*, and add for *nǜ*.
This is the Fixed New Moon time-added entry into the calendar.
Multiply the calendar fraction by its solar gain/loss rate.
Divide by the Tǒng Fǎ.
Adjust the resulting gain/loss amount below (the main value).
This is the Dìng Shù (fixed number).
Set the Fixed New Moon calendar fraction.
Simplify by the Tōng Fǎ (general modulus).
Add the Dìng Shù if gaining, subtract if losing.
Apply the respective Xiù Suàn (constellation calculation) relative to the Winter and Summer Solstices.
This is the required result.
Lunar Distance Crossing the Nodes.
Set the Shuò Jī.
Divide by the Jiāo Lǜ.

Successively add the Wàng Cè.

Using the fixed Rì Chán Tiǎo Nǜ numbers for each,

This results in the Cháng Rì (standard day) for node crossing.

Multiply by the Jīng Fǎ.
Divide by the Píng Lí.

This is the Dìng Rì (fixed day) for node crossing.
