Multiply by 254.
Divide by 19.
Then divide by the Tǒng Fǎ again,
resulting in the degree of node crossing.
Use this to subtract from the Solar degree at the time-added New Moon.
This is the Xiù Dù (constellation degree) of the Yuè Lí (Lunar distance) crossing the Huáng Dào (Ecliptic) just before the New Moon.
Constellation Sequence of the Nine Paths.
The Moon's deviation (Yuè lí) enters and exits the Huángdào (Ecliptic) by six degrees.
Its changes follow the eight seasonal nodes (Bājié),
where obliquity and straightness are unequal.
Therefore, the Moon has nine paths (Jiǔdào).
The Huángdào’s Bājié,
each has nine limits (Jiǔxiàn).
If calculating starting from the straight intersection (Zhèngjiāo),
the lunar mansion in the first limit after the Bājié,
is the Moon traveling its first path in that node.
Starting with the lunar mansion of the second limit,
is the Moon traveling its second path in that node.
The limit from which the calculation starts is taken as the first limit after the Zhèngjiāo.
The initial ratio (Chū lǜ) is eight;
subtract one for each limit;
by the end of the nine limits,
the final ratio (Mò lǜ) is zero.
Then, for the next nine limits,
the initial ratio is zero;
add one for each limit;
the final ratio is eight,
reaching the lunar mansion of the full semi-intersection (Yīnbàn jiāo).
After this, there are also nine limits;
the initial ratio is eight;
subtract one for each limit;
the final ratio is zero.
Then, for the next nine limits,
the initial ratio is zero;
add one for each limit;
the final ratio is eight,
returning to meet the Huángdào,
which is called the middle intersection (Zhōngjiāo).
From the Zhōngjiāo to the Zhèngjiāo,
proceed in the same manner.
Separately set the degree of the limit being entered;
multiply it by the limit ratio (Xiàn lǜ);
this is the general difference (Fànchā).
For the nine limits before and after the Zhèngjiāo and Zhōngjiāo,
multiply the result by the number of limits between the lunar mansion and the two solstices (Èr zhì).
For the nine limits before and after the semi-intersection (Bànjiāo),
multiply the result by the number of limits between the lunar mansion and the two equinoxes (Èr fēn). In all cases, divide by the established calculation method (Jīngfǎ),
this is the Huángdào difference (Huángdào chā).
If following the lunar mansion of the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì),
the nine limits before and after the Zhèngjiāo are subtracted,
and the nine limits before and after the Zhōngjiāo are added.
If following the lunar mansion of the Summer Solstice (Xiàzhì),
the nine limits before and after the Zhèngjiāo are added,
and the nine limits before and after the Zhōngjiāo are subtracted.
Generally, after the Moon's Zhèngjiāo, it moves outside the Huángdào;
after the Zhōngjiāo, it enters inside the Huángdào.
For the nine limits before and after the Bànjiāo,
if following the lunar mansion of the Spring Equinox (Chūnfēn),
moving outside the Huángdào,
or following the lunar mansion of the Autumn Equinox (Qiūfēn),
entering inside the Huángdào: in both cases, the difference is added;
if following the lunar mansion of the Chūnfēn,
entering inside the Huángdào,
or following the lunar mansion of the Qiūfēn,
moving outside the Huángdào: in both cases, the difference is subtracted.
Reduce the Fànchā by four;
subtract the Huángdào difference from it;
this is the Red Path difference (Chìdào chā).
For the nine limits before and after the Zhèngjiāo and Zhōngjiāo,
the difference is always added.
For the nine limits before and after the Bànjiāo,
the difference is always subtracted.
Apply the addition or subtraction of the two differences (Huáng and Chì) to the Huángdào;
this gives the order of the lunar mansions on the Jiǔdào;
categorize the resultant fractional part into the numbers of deficiency (shǎo), excess (tài), and half (bàn).
Each of the Bājié has nine paths,
completing seventy-two paths in total.
Lunar Degree at the Jiǔdào Zhèngjiāo
Set the lunar mansion degree of the Moon's deviation (Yuè lí) at the Zhèngjiāo of the Huángdào;
multiply by the ratio of the limit being entered;

Use this to find the two differences (Huáng and Chì),

To calculate the Shuò from the Wàng,

subtract for tiǎo, and add for nu;

Morning (Chén) and Evening (Hūn) Lunar Degree
Set the Chén and Hūn fraction for that day;
subtract the Dìng fēn from it;

subtract in reverse,

If *before*, add to the augmented time Moon; if *after*, subtract from the augmented time Moon;
this is the Chén Hūn lunar degree.
Chén Hūn Calculation Accumulation
Set the Jiā shí xiàng jī (augmented time calculation accumulation);
based on the *before* and *after* degrees of the preceding calculation (qián xiàng),
subtract for *before*, add for *after*;
then, based on the *before* and *after* degrees of the subsequent calculation (hòu xiàng),
add for *before*, subtract for *after*;
this is the required result.
Daily Chén Hūn Lunar Degree
Cumulatively calculate the degree of deviation (Lí dù) from the subsequent calculation (Hòu xiàng);
subtract this from the Chén Hūn xiàng jī;
this result is added;
if insufficient,
subtract in reverse,
this result is subtracted.
Divide this by the number of days to the Hòu xiàng;
use the result to add or subtract the daily deviation degree (Měi rì lí dù);
this is the defined degree (Dìng dù).
Cumulatively add the Chén Hūn lunar degree,
assign the Jiǔdào sù cì;
this is the required result.
Moon's Distance Degree from the Huángdào
Set the defined day (Dìng rì) of entrance into the intersection (Rù jiāo).
If below the center of the intersection (Jiāo zhōng),
the Moon travels the Yang Path (Yángdào);
if above,
remove it (subtract it from the full cycle),
the Moon travels the Yin Path (Yīndào). In all cases, apply the Jīngfǎ for conversion.
Use the result to subtract nine hundred and eighty;
multiply by the remainder;
divide by five hundred and fifty-six;
this is the fraction (fēn);
if the result reaches the Jīngfǎ, convert to degrees.
If traveling the Yángdào,
it is outside the Huángdào;
if traveling the Yīndào,
it is inside the Huángdào.
This is the required degree of the Moon's distance inside or outside the Huángdào.
Solar (Rì) and Lunar (Yuè) Eclipse Limits (Shí xiàn)
Set the defined day of intersection (Dìng jiāo) traveling the Yīn and Yáng paths.
If below the center of the semi-intersection (Bànjiāo zhōng),
this is *after intersection* (jiāo hòu);
if above,
use it to subtract from the Jiāo zhōng,
this is *before intersection* (jiāo qián). In all cases, apply the Tǒngfǎ for conversion,
this is the fraction distance from the intersection (Jù jiāo fēn).
The visually observed Jù jiāo fēn at Shuò,
if it is below 4,219 for the Yángdào, or below 10,383 for the Yīndào,
the Sun enters the eclipse limit.
The visually observed Jù jiāo fēn at Wàng, if it is below 6,995 for both the Yīn and Yáng paths,
the Moon enters the eclipse limit.
Defined Fraction (Dìng fēn) of Augmented Time (Jiā shí) at Maximum Eclipse (Shí shèn) for Sun and Moon
Set the Shuò Dìng fēn.
If above the Bàntǒng (semi-total),
subtract the Bàntǒng from it;
if below the Bàntǒng,
use it to subtract from the Bàntǒng: this is the fraction distance from noon (Jù wǔ fēn).
Multiply it by eleven;
divide by the Jīngfǎ.
If the original Shuò Dìng fēn was below the Bàntǒng,
subtract this result from the Bàntǒng;
if it was above,
add this result to the Shuò Dìng fēn: this is the Dìng fēn of the augmented time for a solar eclipse.
For Wàng, subtract the Chén fēn (morning fraction) of that day from 1,620;
multiply the remainder by 245;
divide by 313;
use the result to subtract from 245;
use the remainder to adjust (add or subtract) the Wàng Dìng fēn;
this is the Dìng fēn of the augmented time for a lunar eclipse.
Solar Eclipse Constant Standard (Cháng zhǔn)
Set the middle standard (Zhōng zhǔn);
multiply it by the numerical value of that day's position inside or outside the Chìdào (Equator);
divide by 2,513;
this is the Huángdào entry and exit eclipse difference (Shí chā).
Multiply the Jù wǔ fēn subtracted from the semi-day fraction (Bàn zhòu fēn) by the result;
divide by the Bàn zhòu fēn;
if inside the Chìdào, subtract from the Zhōng zhǔn; if outside the Chìdào, add to the Zhōng zhǔn;
this is the Rì shí Cháng zhǔn.
Solar Eclipse Defined Standard (Dìng zhǔn)
Set the solar longitude entry into the calendar,
use the standard method to calculate it.
If it is below 3,287,
use it to subtract 3,287,
this is the time after the two solstices (èrzhì hòu);
If it is above this,
subtract 3,287,
this is the time before the two equinoxes (èrfēn qián).
If it is above 6,574,
use it to subtract 9,861,
this is the time after the two equinoxes (èrfēn hòu);
If it is above this,
subtract 9,861,
this is the time before the two solstices (èrzhì qián).
Divide each result by three (sānyuē zhī).
For the periods around the two solstices (èrzhì), use subtraction; for the periods around the two equinoxes (èrfēn), use addition of 2,772,
to get the ecliptic obliquity eclipse correction (huángdào xiézhèng shí chā).
Multiply this by the distance from noon portion (jùwǔ fēn).
Divide by the half-day portion (bànzhòu fēn).
Add this to the constant standard (chángzhǔn),
to get the fixed standard (dìngzhǔn).
Solar Eclipse Magnitude (rì shí fēn)
Add the fixed standard (dìngzhǔn) to the central limit (zhōngxiàn),
to get the fixed standard for the Nodal Path (yīndào dìngzhǔn);
Subtract the central limit,
to get the fixed limit for the Nodal Path (yángdào dìngxiàn).
If it is insufficient to subtract,
reverse the subtraction,
to get the portion outside the limit (xiànwài fēn).
Observe the distance from the Node (jùjiāo fēn) in the Nodal Path (yīndào).
If the distance is above the fixed standard (dìngzhǔn),
and below the fixed limit (dìngxiàn),
this is an eclipse in the Nodal Path (yīndào shí);
Then, set the fixed limit (dìngxiàn),
subtract the distance from the Node (jùjiāo fēn),
to get the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn).
If the distance is below the fixed standard (dìngzhǔn),
although it is called the Nodal Path (yīndào),
it is also considered an eclipse in the Nodal Path (yángdào shí);
Then add the fixed limit for the Nodal Path (yángdào dìngxiàn),
to get the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn).
If there is a portion outside the limit (xiànwài fēn),
then subtract that portion outside the limit,
to get the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn).
If it is insufficient to subtract,
there is no eclipse.
For the distance from the Node (jùjiāo fēn) in the Nodal Path (yángdào),
If it is below the fixed limit (dìngxiàn),
it is within the fixed eclipse limit (rù dìng shí xiàn);
Then use it to subtract the fixed limit for the Nodal Path (yángdào dìngxiàn),
to get the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn).
Set each magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn),
and divide all by 478,
to get the major magnitude portion of the solar eclipse (rì shí zhī dàfēn);
The remainder is the minor magnitude portion (xiǎofēn).
The major magnitude portion (dàfēn) is designated using ten as the limit;
The minor magnitude portion (xiǎofēn) is designated using half, and strong/weak (jiāng ruò).
Lunar Eclipse Magnitude (yuè shí fēn)
Observe the distance from the Node (jùjiāo fēn).
If it is below the central standard (zhōngzhǔn),
it is total (jì);
If it is above this,
use it to subtract the eclipse limit (shíxiàn),
to get the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn).
Set this value,
divide by 526,
to get the major magnitude portion of the lunar eclipse (yuè shí zhī dàfēn);
The remainder is the minor magnitude portion (xiǎofēn).
The major magnitude portion (dàfēn) is designated using ten as the limit;
The minor magnitude portion (xiǎofēn) is designated using half, and strong/weak (jiāng ruò).
Solar Eclipse General Use Portion (rì shí fànyòng fēn)
Set the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn).
If it is above 1,912,
use it to subtract 4,780;
Square the remainder,
and divide by 63,272;
Subtract this from 647,
to get the General Use Portion (fànyòng fēn).
If it is below 956,
use it to subtract 1,912,
multiply the remainder by the general modulus (tōngfǎ),
and divide by 735;
Subtract this from 517,
to get the General Use Portion (fànyòng fēn).
If it is above 956,
square the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn),
and divide by 2,362;
Subtract this from 387,
to get the General Use Portion (fànyòng fēn).
Lunar Eclipse General Use Portion (yuè shí fànyòng fēn)
Set the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn).
If it is above 2,104,
use it to subtract 5,260;
Square the remainder,
and divide by 69,169;
Subtract this from 711,
to get the General Use Portion (fànyòng fēn).
If it is above 1,052,
use it to subtract 2,140;
Take the remainder,
and divide by seven;
Subtract this from 567,
to get the General Use Portion (fànyòng fēn).
If it is below 1,052,
subtract the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn) from 1,052;
Square the remainder,
and divide by 2,654;
Subtract this from 417,
to get the General Use Portion (fànyòng fēn).
Fixed Portion for Solar/Lunar Eclipse Beginning and End Time Additions
Set each General Use Portion (fànyòng fēn),
multiply it by the mean recession (pínglí),
and divide by the solar recession rate (rìlí chéng),
to get the Fixed Use Portion (dìngyòng fēn).
Subtract this from the New/Full Moon fixed portion (shuòwàng dìngfēn),
to get the beginning of obscuration (kuīchū).
Add it,
to get the end of restoration (fùmò).
Add the time constant portion (jiāshí chángfēn),
and calculate it according to the method for the moment of maximum eclipse (shíshèn shù),
to find the fixed portions for the beginning of obscuration (kuīchū) and the end of restoration (fùmò).
Set the fixed portions for the beginning (chū), maximum (shèn), and end (mò),
and divide each by the hour modulus (chénzé),
to get the hours (chén);
Divide by the standard modulus (jīngfǎ),
to get the quarters (kè): these are the hours and quarters of the beginning, maximum, and end.
Origin of Eclipse Obscuration (kuī shí suǒ qǐ)
The obscuration of a solar eclipse begins from the west,
the obscuration of a lunar eclipse begins from the east.
If the eclipse magnitude portion (shífēn) is small,
and the Moon travels the Nodal Path (yángdào),
then the solar eclipse is biased toward the south (piānnán),
and the lunar eclipse is biased toward the north (piānběi);
If it is the Nodal Path (yīndào),
then the solar eclipse is biased toward the north (piānběi),
and the lunar eclipse is biased toward the south (piānnán): these are the constant rules (chángshù).
After Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring),
and before Lìxià (Beginning of Summer),
if the eclipse magnitude portion is large,
then the solar eclipse is biased toward the south (piānnán),
and the lunar eclipse is biased toward the north (piānběi);
After Lìqiū (Beginning of Autumn),
and before Lìdōng (Beginning of Winter),
if the eclipse magnitude portion is large,
then the solar eclipse is biased toward the north (piānběi),
and the lunar eclipse is biased toward the south (piānnán): this is the ecliptic obliquity (huángdào xiézhèng).
Before the crossing of the Nodal Path (yángdào jiāo),
and after the crossing of the Nodal Path (yīndào jiāo),
if the eclipse magnitude portion is large,
then the solar eclipse is biased toward the south (piānnán),
and the lunar eclipse is biased toward the north (piānběi);
After the crossing of the Nodal Path (yángdào jiāo),
and before the crossing of the Nodal Path (yīndào jiāo),
if the eclipse magnitude portion is large,
then the solar eclipse is biased toward the north (piānběi),
and the lunar eclipse is biased toward the south (piānnán): this is the Nodal Obliquity (jiǔdào xiézhèng).
The deviation caused by the ecliptic (huángdào) relative to the constant rules (chángshù) is small,
and the deviation caused by the Nodes (jiǔdào) relative to the ecliptic (huángdào) is one-quarter more: all calculations are based on noon (jùwǔ).
Regarding whether it is before noon (wǔqián) or after noon (wǔhòu),
one principle biases toward the south (piānnán),
one principle biases toward the north (piānběi),
and calculate the varying increase or decrease (xiāoxī) in the eclipse magnitude portion,
to determine the direction (fāng) of the beginning (chū), maximum (shèn), and end (mò),
and then the desired result is obtained.
Portion of Emerging or Setting While Eclipsed (dài shí chūrù fēn)
Observe the portion of the body's rising or setting (rìchūrù fēn).
If it is above the fixed portion for the beginning of obscuration (kuīchū dìngfēn),
and below the fixed portion for the end of restoration (fùmò dìngfēn),
then it emerges or sets while eclipsed (dài shí chūrù).
If the moment of maximum eclipse (shíshèn) is below the rising/setting portion (chūrù fēn),
subtract the fixed portion for the end of restoration (fùmò dìngfēn) from the rising/setting portion (chūrù fēn),
to get the difference for emerging/setting while eclipsed (dài shí chā).
If the moment of maximum eclipse (shíshèn) is above the rising/setting portion (chūrù fēn),
subtract the rising/setting portion (chūrù fēn) from the fixed portion for the beginning of obscuration (kuīchū dìngfēn),
to get the difference for emerging/setting while eclipsed (dài shí chā).
Set each difference for emerging/setting while eclipsed (dài shí chā),
multiply it by the magnitude difference from totality (jù shí fēn),
and divide by the Fixed Use Portion (dìngyòng fēn).
For the Sun, divide by 478; for the Moon, divide by 526,
to get the major magnitude portion of emerging/setting while eclipsed (dài shí zhī dàfēn);
The remainder is the minor magnitude portion (xiǎofēn).
Eclipse Gēng (Watch) and Chóu (Score) Calculation (shí rù gēng chóu)
Set the fixed portions for the beginning (chū), maximum (shèn), and end (mò).
If it is below the dawn portion (chénfēn),
add the dusk portion (hūnfēn) to it;
If it is above the dusk portion (hūnfēn),
subtract the dusk portion from it: then divide all by the Gēng use portion (gēngyòng fēn),
to get the Gēng number.
The remainder,
is divided by the Chóu use portion (chóuyòng fēn),
to get the Chóu number.

Biànduàn | Biànrì | Biàndù | Biànlì Xījiàn: 17 | 34 (1) | 29 (54) Shùnjí: 11 | 18 (24) | 16 (4) Shùnchí: 16 | 11 (43) | 10 (10) Qiánliú: 2 (68) Xīfú: 11 | 6 | 2 Chénjiàn: 11 | 6 | 2 Hòuliú: 2 (68) Shùnchí: 16 | 11 (43) | 10 (10) Shùnjí: 11 | 18 (24) | 16 (4) Chénfú: 17 | 34 (1) | 29 (54) Zhōngrì Zhōngxīng (Mean Day and Mean Star Position)
Set the Qìjī (Temporal Accumulation).
Divide it by the star's Zhōulǜ (Orbital Rate),
to get the number of revolutions.
The remainder is the accumulation of Qì at the celestial mean before the conjunction (Tiānzhèng Zhōngqì Qiánhé).
Use this to subtract the Suìlǜ (Annual Rate),
yielding the accumulation of Qì at the celestial mean after the conjunction (Tiānzhèng Zhōngqì Hòuhé) of the previous year.
If it is insufficient for subtraction,
then add the Suìlǜ to subtract it,
yielding the Hòuhé of the year before the previous year's Tiānzhèng Zhōngqì.
Simplify each result using the Tǒngfǎ (General Modulus),
yielding days and degrees,
which are the required mean day and mean star position of the smooth conjunction (Pínghé Zhōngrì Zhōngxīng).
Set the Zhōngrì.
Accumulatively add the Biànrì of each segment,
which yields the Zhōngrì of each segment.
Set the Zhōngxīng (Mean Star Position).
Add the Biàndù sequentially for prograde motion and subtract it for retrograde motion,
thus obtaining the Zhōngxīng of each segment.
For Venus (Jīn) and Mercury (Shuǐ), Evening Setting (Xīfú) and Morning Appearance (Chénjiàn)
are both considered retrograde variations (Tuìbiàn). Rùlì (Entering the Calendar)
Set the Biànlǜ.
Multiply it by the number of revolutions.
Divide it by the Lìlǜ.
The remainder, if full to the Tǒngfǎ, yields degrees.
If the result is less than the Lìzhōng,
it is deemed "Before" (Xiān);
if it is greater than the Lìzhōng,
subtract the Lìzhōng,
and the remainder is deemed "After" (Hòu): this is the required calendar entry (Pínghé Rùlì) for the smooth conjunction.
Accumulatively add the Biànlì (Calendar Variation) for each segment,
yielding the Rùlì for each segment. Xiānhòu Dìngshù (Fixed Numbers for Before/After)
Set the Calendar Entry Fractions (Rùlì Fēn).
Multiply them by the correction rate for degrees.
Divide by the Jīngfǎ (Standard Modulus).
Use the result to adjust (gain or lose) the subsequent Before/After numbers (Xiānhòu Shù).
This is the required result. Chángrì Dìngxīng (Standard Day and Fixed Star Position)
Set the Zhōngrì and Zhōngxīng.
For each, use the Xiānhòu Dìngshù,
adding the "Before" result and subtracting the "After" result.
Retain and use the Xiānhòu Shù of the preceding segment.

For Venus (Tàibái), the prograde motion (Shùnfújiàn) and the segments following the first direct fast (Qián Shùnjí) and synodic fast (Cìjí), and the segment following the last synodic slow and synodic fast (Hòu Cìchí Cìjíjí), and for Mercury (Chénxīng), the prograde motion (Shùnfújiàn) and the segments following the first fast (Qiánjí) and the last slow (Hòuchí),
all use subtraction for "Before" and addition for "After."
These results are the Standard Day and Fixed Star Position (Chángrì Dìngxīng) for their respective segments.
Set the Dìngxīng.
Add the Ecliptic Lodge Sequence (Huángdào Xiùcì) corresponding to the celestial mean day (Tiānzhèng Zhōngqì) of that year, and name it thus.
This yields the degree of the lodge sequence at the time adjustment (Jiāshí) of the last day of each segment. Yíngsuō Dìngshù (Fixed Numbers for Advance/Retard)
Set the Chángrì.
If it is less than the middle of the year (Suìzhōng),
it is considered "In Advance" (Zài Yíng);
if it is greater than the Suìzhōng,
subtract the Suìzhōng,
and the remainder is considered "In Retard" (Zài Suō): this is the Chángrì entering the Yíngsuō Calendar (Rù Yíngsuō Lì).
Set the Calendar Fraction (Lìfēn).
Multiply it by the correction rate for days.
Divide by the Jīngfǎ.
Use the result to adjust (gain or lose) the subsequent Advance/Retard numbers (Yíngsuō Shù).
This yields the required result. Dìngrì (Fixed Day)
Set the Chángrì.
Subtract the Yíngsuō Dìngshù for Advance (Yíng) and add it for Retard (Suō),
yielding the Dìngrì.
Add the Tiānzhèng Zhōngqì of that year and name it thus.
This is the day and time designation (Rìchén) of the last day of each segment, plus time adjustment. Rù Zhōngjié (Entering the Middle Term)
Set the Dìngrì.
Divide it by the Qìcè (Solar Term Rate).
Count beginning from the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì).
This is the number of days entering the respective solar term (Qì). Píngxíng Fēn (Mean Motion Rate)
Set the Dìngrì.
Subtract the Dìngrì of the preceding segment,
yielding the Day Rate (Rìlǜ).
Subtract the Fixed Star Position (Dìngxīng) from the Dìngxīng of the preceding segment,
yielding the Degree Rate (Dùlǜ).
Convert the Dùlǜ to a common unit.
Multiply it by the Jīngfǎ.
Divide by the Rìlǜ converted to a common unit.
This is the Píngxíng Fēn. Chūmò Xíngfēn (Initial and Final Motion Rates)
The Píngxíng Fēn of the segment near setting/occultation (Jìnfú) and the setting segment (Fúduàn),
sum them and take half,
yielding the Near Setting Motion Rate (Jìnfú Xíngfēn) for that segment.
Subtract this from the Píngxíng Fēn.
Subtract the remainder from the Píngxíng Fēn,
yielding the Far Setting Motion Rate (Yuǎnfú Xíngfēn) for that segment.
The Near Station Motion Rate (Jìnliú Xíngfēn) for the segment near stationing (Jìnliú Duàn) is zero.
Double the Píngxíng Fēn yields the Far Station Motion Rate (Yuǎnliú Xíngfēn) for that segment.
For segments that are neither near setting nor near stationing,
use the Píngxíng Fēn of the two prograde segments,
sum them and take half,
yielding the motion rate of the last day of the preceding segment and the first day of the following segment.
Subtract this from the Píngxíng Fēn of the current segment.
If the Píngxíng Fēn is greater,
then add it to the Píngxíng Fēn.
If the Píngxíng Fēn is smaller,
then subtract it from the Píngxíng Fēn.
This yields the motion rate for the first day of the preceding segment and the last day of the following segment.
For segments that are neither near setting nor near stationing,
if the motion is retrograde, use the Near Fast Motion Rate (Jìnjí Xíngfēn) of the slow segment (Chíduàn),
as the Near Slow Motion Rate (Jìnchí Xíngfēn) of the fast segment (Jíduàn).
Subtract the result obtained from the Píngxíng Fēn.
If the Píngxíng Fēn is greater,
then add it;
if it is smaller, then subtract it: these all yield the Far Slow Motion Rate (Yuǎnchí Xíngfēn). Chūxíng Yèbàn Xiùcì (Lodge Sequence at Midnight of Initial Motion)
Set the Jīngfǎ.
Subtract the fraction of time adjustment (Jiāshí Fēn) for the last day of the preceding segment.
Multiply the remainder by the motion rate (Xíngfēn) of the last day of the preceding segment.
Divide by the Jīngfǎ.
Use the result to add (prograde) or subtract (retrograde) the lodge degree (Xiùdù) with time adjustment of the last day of the preceding segment.
This is the lodge degree at midnight after dusk (Hūnhòu Yèbàn Xiùdù) of the initial motion of this segment. Měirì Xíngfēn (Daily Motion Rate)
Subtract the Initial and Final Motion Rates (Chūmò Xíngfēn) from each other,
yielding the difference rate (Chālǜ).
Divide the accumulated number of days between midnight after dusk of the initial motion of this segment and midnight after dusk of the initial motion of the next segment by this difference rate.
This is the daily difference (Rìchā).
Take half of the Rìchā.
Subtract it if the final motion rate is greater (Duō), and add it if the final motion rate is smaller (Shǎo), to the Initial and Final Fixed Motion Rates (Chūmò Dìngxíngfēn) for that segment.
Set the Initial Fixed Motion Rate (Chū Dìngxíngfēn).
If the final motion rate is greater (Mò Duō), accumulatively add the Rìchā; if the final motion rate is smaller (Mò Shǎo), accumulatively subtract the Rìchā.
This is the Daily Motion Rate (Měirì Xíngfēn).
Add (prograde) or subtract (retrograde) the Xiùdù at midnight after dusk of the initial motion using the Měirì Xíngfēn.
This is the lodge degree reached at midnight after dusk each day. Xiān Dìngrì Hūnhòu Yèbàn Xiùcì (Pre-Fixed Day Lodge Sequence at Midnight After Dusk)
Accumulatively count the number of days from the initial day to the required day.
Multiply this by the daily difference (Rìchā) of the segment.
If the final motion rate is greater (Mò Duō), add the result to the initial daily motion rate; if the final motion rate is smaller (Mò Shǎo), subtract it.
This is the daily motion rate for that day.
Sum it with the initial day's rate and take half.
Multiply this by the accumulated number of days.
Use this to add (prograde) or subtract (retrograde) the lodge sequence at midnight after dusk of the initial motion of that segment.
This is the required result. Qīntiān Bù Fāliǎn Shù (Qīntiān Step Convergence/Divergence Algorithm)

Chart of Qì Hòu (Climatic Phases) Dōngzhì (Winter Solstice), middle of the eleventh month: Earthworms coil; Elks' horns shed; Water springs move. Xiǎohán (Lesser Cold), beginning of the twelfth month: Geese fly north; Magpies begin to nest; Pheasants begin to crow. Dàhán (Greater Cold), middle of the twelfth month: Chickens begin to brood; Fierce birds fly swiftly; The bottom of lakes and marshes becomes hard. Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring), beginning of the first month: East wind thaws the ice; Hibernating insects begin to stir; Fish ascend to the ice. Yǔshuǐ (Rain Water), middle of the first month: Otters offer fish; Swans and geese arrive; Grass and trees begin to sprout. Jīngzhé (Awakening of Insects), beginning of the second month: Peach trees begin to blossom; Orioles (Cānggēng) sing; Eagles transform into doves (Jiū). Chūnfēn (Spring Equinox), middle of the second month: Swallows (Xuánniǎo) arrive; Thunder gives voice; Lightning begins. Qīngmíng (Clear and Bright), beginning of the third month: Paulownia trees begin to blossom; Field mice transform into quails (rú); Rainbows first appear. Gǔyǔ (Grain Rain), middle of the third month: Duckweed begins to grow; Cooing doves smooth their feathers; Hoopoes (Dàishèng) descend upon the mulberry trees. Lìxià (Beginning of Summer), beginning of the fourth month: Mole crickets sing; Earthworms emerge; Chinese cucumber (Wángguā) grows. Xiǎomǎn (Grain Buds), middle of the fourth month: Bitter herbs flourish; Deciduous grasses die; Lesser heat arrives (Xiǎoshǔ zhì). Mángzhòng (Grain in Ear), beginning of the fifth month: Mantises hatch; Shrikes (Jú) begin to sing; Mockingbirds (Fǎnshé) become silent. Xiàzhì (Summer Solstice), middle of the fifth month: Deer shed their antlers; Cicadas (Tiáo) begin to sing; Pinellia ternata (Bànxià) grows. Xiǎoshǔ (Lesser Heat), beginning of the sixth month: Warm winds arrive; Crickets inhabit the walls; Eagles begin to practice flying. Dàshǔ (Greater Heat), middle of the sixth month: Rotten grass transforms into fireflies; The soil is moist and the heat is humid; Heavy rains fall seasonally. Lìqiū (Beginning of Autumn), beginning of the seventh month: Cool winds arrive; White dew descends (Báilù); Cold cicadas chirp. Chǔshǔ (End of Heat), middle of the seventh month: Eagles sacrifice birds; Heaven and Earth begin to become severe; Grains ripen. Báilù (White Dew), beginning of the eighth month: Swans and geese arrive; Swallows (Xuánniǎo) depart; All birds store provisions. Qiūfēn (Autumn Equinox), middle of the eighth month: Thunder ceases sound; Hibernating insects block their burrows; Waters begin to dry up. Hánlù (Cold Dew), beginning of the ninth month: Swans and geese arrive as guests; Sparrows enter the water and become clams (gé); Chrysanthemums display yellow flowers. Shuāngjiàng (Frost's Descent), middle of the ninth month: Jackals sacrifice beasts; Grasses and trees turn yellow and fall; Hibernating insects all shelter. Lìdōng (Beginning of Winter), beginning of the tenth month: Water begins to freeze; Earth begins to harden; Pheasants enter the water and become large clams (shèn). Xiǎoxuě (Lesser Snow), middle of the tenth month: Rainbows hide and are not seen; Heavenly Qì ascends and Earthly Qì descends; Blockage creates winter. Dàxuě (Greater Snow), beginning of the eleventh month: Kingfishers (Hé Niǎo) stop singing; Tigers begin to mate; Lì Tǐng grass emerges. are each assigned to a central Jí (Zhōngjié),
which is the initial Hòu.
By successively adding the Hòu Rate (Hòu Cè),
one obtains the subsequent Hòu.
The sixty-four hexagrams
are assigned to the central Qì (Zhōngqì),
which is the Duke Hexagram (Gōng Guà).
By successively adding the Hexagram Rate (Guà Cè),
one obtains the subsequent hexagrams.
Assign the Hòu Hexagram (Hòu Guà),
and add the Outer Rate (Wài Cè) to it,
which gives the Outer Hexagram (Wài Guà).
The Five Phases (Wǔ Xíng) governing
are determined by assigning them to the four Lì Jí (Sì Lì zhī Jié);
this marks the beginning of the governing periods for Wood in Spring, Fire in Summer, Metal in Autumn, and Water in Winter.
Assign the Jí of the Four Seasons (Sì Jì zhī Jié),
and add the Link Rate (Wéi Cè) to each,
which is the period when Earth governs.
For the Mo Rì (Disappearing Day),
if the minutes of the Zhōng Jié exceed 5626 65/100 seconds,
use the subtraction calculation method (Jiǎn Tǒng Fǎ).
This results in the Mo Fēn (Disappearing Minutes).
Use the comprehensive Qì Rate (Tōng Qì Cè) to multiply it.
Divide by the Qì Excess (Qì Yíng),
and a full Tǒng Fǎ (Calculation Unit) represents a day.
Use this to add the Qì and determine the period,
which is the sought-after Mo Rì.
For the Miè Rì (Extinguished Day),
if the minutes of the regular Shuò (Cháng Shuò) are less than the Shuò Xū (Shuò Deficiency),
this results in the Miè Fēn (Extinguished Minutes).
Multiply this by the Shuò Ratio (Shuò Lǜ).
Divide by the Shuò Deficiency (Shuò Xū),
and a full Tǒng Fǎ represents a day.
Use this to add the Shuò and determine the period,
which is the sought-after Miè Rì.
Above are the four chapters of the Qīntiān Lì Jīng (Classic of the Qīntiān Calendar) compiled by Pǔ.
The old historical records lack one chapter, the Bù Fāliǎn (Calculation of Emission and Convergence),
but the three remaining chapters
are simple, incomplete,
and insufficient to serve as a model.
Since Pǔ’s calendar had rarely been transmitted across generations,
I once inquired of the Assistant Editor Liú Xīsǒu.
Xīsǒu sought out and obtained the original classic text for me,
and only then was Pǔ's calendar fully prepared.
Xīsǒu loves learning and understands history and classics,
especially excelling in astronomy and calendrical calculation (Xīng Lì).
He once said to me:
“The methods of those in previous generations who created calendars
differed and contained many errors.
It was not until Yī Xíng of the Táng dynasty that the Dàyǎn Lì (Dàyǎn Calendar) was created, based on the median numbers of Heaven and Earth,
which was the most precise.
Later generations of skilled calendar masters
all used his methods,
merely copying the minutes and simulating the numbers.
As for Pǔ, he was also able to establish his own school.
Pǔ’s calendrical method
summarized the variations in the Sun’s movement (Rì Chán) into two calendars, the Yíng (Excess) and Suō (Deficiency).
It divided the Moon’s elongation (Yuè Lí) into two hundred forty-eight periods of Chí (Slow) and Jí (Fast),
in order to examine the gradual recession and waning,
and to verify the waxing and waning (tiǎo nú),
thus correcting the new and full moons (Shuò Wàng).
He corrected the nine limits of the celestial equator (Chì Dào),
changed the rate numbers (Lǜ Shù),
to calculate the ecliptic (Huáng Dào),
ensuring the Sun’s movement had a constant measure.
He divided the ecliptic into eight Jí,
distinguished between their interior and exterior (Nèi Wài),
to measure the nine orbits (Jiǔ Dào),
ensuring the Moon’s path was like a cycle,
and thus the two Luminaries (Èr Yào) harmonize.
He observed the ascent and descent of the celestial configuration (Tiān Shì),
examined the obliquity and rectitude of the orbits (Guǐ Dào),
to regulate the eclipse variation (Shí Chā),
ensuring the conjunctions (Jiāohuì) were precise.
He measured the central gnomon shadow (Zhōng Guǐ) on the terrace of Mount Yuè,
to distinguish between the length of day and night at the two solstices (Èr Zhì),
thus validating the orbit and clepsydra (Guǐ Lòu).
He calculated the retrograde, prograde, occultation, and station of the stars (Xīng Xíng zhī Nì Shùn, Fú Liú),
ensuring the slowness and urgency had gradients,
and thus the Five Planets (Wǔ Wěi) were aligned.
However, he was unable to make it vastly profound and simple (Hóng Shēn Jiǎnyì),
but rather adopted the direct and urgent path.
Regarding his strengths,
even if a sage were to emerge, they could not discard them.”
Xīsǒu’s words are generally like this;
readers may verify them. Examination of Celestial Administration (Sī Tiān Kǎo) II
Formerly, when Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) compiled the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals), both Heaven and man were covered.
When I compiled the Benjì (Basic Annals),
I recorded man but not Heaven;
how dare I differ from the sage!
Although the writing style differs,
the intent is the same.
Since the time of Yáo, Shùn, and the Three Dynasties (Sān Dài),
none failed to invoke Heaven when undertaking affairs,
and Kǒngzǐ, when editing the Shī (Odes) and Shū (Documents), did not omit this.
Generally, the sage does not sever Heaven from man,
nor does he equate Heaven with man.
Severing Heaven from man causes the Way of Heaven (Tiān Dào) to cease;
equating Heaven with man causes human affairs (Rén Shì) to become confused.
Therefore, it is always retained but not thoroughly investigated.
Although the Chūnqiū records solar eclipses, stellar abnormalities, and similar events,
Kǒngzǐ never explained the reasons for them,
thus his disciples and followers
were unable to transmit any such explanations to later generations.
If so, does Heaven really participate in the affairs of man?
Or does it not participate?
I say: Heaven,
I do not know.
One may appeal to the words of the sages.
The Yì (Classic of Changes) states:
“The Way of Heaven (Tiān Dào) diminishes the full and augments the humble;
the Way of Earth (Dì Dào) changes the full and flows towards the humble;
the spirits and ghosts (Guǐ Shén) harm the full and bless the humble;
the Way of Man (Rén Dào) detests the full and favors the humble.”
This is the most detailed and clear articulation by the sage
concerning the utmost relationship between Heaven and man.
Regarding Heaven, Earth, and the spirits and ghosts,
the description treats them as unknowable;
that which is knowable
is man alone.
Now, when the sun reaches noon, it begins to decline;
fullness and decay must eventually return.
Heaven,
I do not know,
but I see its diminution and augmentation in things.
Those grasses and trees that are complete
change and fall into decay;
things that are low
advance and circulate.
Earth,
I do not know,
but I see its transformation and flow in things.
Those among men who are greedy and boastful incur much misfortune;
those who maintain restraint gain much fortune.
Spirits and ghosts (Guǐ Shén),
I do not know,
but I see the fortune and misfortune of men.
Since the minds of Heaven, Earth, and the spirits and ghosts
cannot be known,
we gauge them based on what they manifest in things.
Therefore, we speak based on their observable traces,
saying "diminish and augment,"
saying "transform and flow,"
saying "harm and bless."
As for man,
he is knowable;
thus, his emotions are directly stated as "detest and favor."
Though the knowable and unknowable
are described with different words,
when compared and combined,
they are not different from man.
Whether they truly participate in the affairs of man
or do not participate in the affairs of man,
is what we do not know.
Because they are unknowable,
we always honor them and keep them distant;
because they are not different from man,
we merely cultivate our human affairs (Rén Shì).
Human affairs (Rén Shì)
are the will of Heaven (Tiān Yì).
The Shū (Classic of Documents) states:
“Heaven sees according to the sight of my people;
Heaven hears according to the hearing of my people.”
There has never been a case where the hearts of the people below were pleased,
yet the will of Heaven above was angry;
there has never been a case where the principles of man below were perverse,
yet the Way of Heaven above was compliant.
Therefore, when the sovereign rules the world (tiānxià),
treats the populace as children (zǐ shēngmín),
spreads virtue, and administers government
in order to comply with the human heart,
this is called serving Heaven (Fèng Tiān).
As for the celestial bodies (Sān Chén) and Five Planets (Wǔ Xīng) constantly moving without cease,
they cannot avoid the variations of excess, deficiency, error, and deviation (yíng suō chā tè),
and prognostications regarding them sometimes hit and sometimes miss,
such that they cannot be taken as constant principles—
that is the duty of the responsible officials (Yǒu Sī).
The conduct of the sovereigns described in the Běnjì (Basic Annals) is detailed,
and their rise, fall, order, and chaos can be seen there.
As for the retrograde, prograde, and altered appearance of the celestial bodies and Five Planets,
which are matters divined by the responsible officials (Yǒu Sī),
they are therefore recorded under their respective offices,
to be included in the Sī Tiān Kǎo (Examination of Celestial Administration).
Alas!
After the Sages passed away, heterodox doctrines arose.
Since the Qín and Hàn Dynasties,
scholars have been affected by calamitous anomalies,
and the theories of astronomy and the Five Phases
have become overwhelmingly complex.
What I have recorded
cannot but differ from the Chūnqiū;
those who examine it can understand.

During the turbulent era of the Five Dynasties,
records were incomplete,
and what the historical officials recorded also varied in detail;
such were the major transformations involving the sun, moon, and the five planets.
As for the manifestations of atmospheric phenomena and strange vapours,
they appeared, disappeared, and dissipated irregularly,
making them especially difficult to record accurately.
During the period of the Five Dynasties,
the sun frequently exhibited haloes, coronas, rings, loops, knots, embraces, supports, shoes, and backing vapours.
Out of ten days, seven or eight were common,
and their complexity cannot be fully written down,
with backing vapours being particularly numerous.

a white rainbow spanned the sky.
These are the most extraordinary among them.
As for things like the fire emerging from the Jiāngshǔi (river water) at Yánglín in Wú, or the heaven raining beans in Mǐn,
these were all beyond the sight and hearing of the central territories [Zhōngguó],
and it is impossible to record them all.
Chapter 3: Study of the Provinces (Zhífāng Kǎo)
Alas!
From the Sāndài (Three Dynasties) onwards, none failed to govern by dividing the territory.
Later generations, drawing lessons from antiquity and correcting shortcomings,
first instituted the commandery (jùn) and county (xiàn) system throughout the realm.
But since the time of Qín and Hàn,
how does the longevity of these states compare to that of the Sāndài?
When they perished,
they invariably dissolved,
sometimes reaching the point where they had no territory left to sustain themselves.
If one grasps the essential principle,
then even ten thousand states can be governed peacefully;
if one loses what should be upheld,
then even unifying the entire realm cannot maintain peace.
Is this not fundamentally rooted in virtue (dàodé)?
During the prosperous time of the Táng,
although the realm was nominally divided into ten Dào (circuits),
its political structure had not yet fragmented.
When it declined,
military Jiédù (Governors) were appointed,
known as Fāngzhèn (regional garrisons).
The largest Zhèn controlled over ten Zhōu (prefectures),
and the smallest still controlled three or four.
Therefore, when the troops became arrogant, they drove out their commanders;
when the commanders became strong, they rebelled against the superior authority.
The land was held hereditarily by them,
and weapons of war arose, leading to mutual encroachment.
The state of the realm,
from this point, became divided.
However, the Táng, since its middle period, had experienced many troubles.
Its revival from decline and rescue from calamity
were often reliant on the support of these garrison troops,
yet aggression, disorder, and eventual collapse
were also ultimately caused by them.
Is this not the very nature of benefits and harms?
Since the time of [Emperors] Xī and Zhāo,
fragmentation increased daily.
In the early Liáng period,
the realm was separately divided into eleven states:
In the south, there were Wú, Zhè, Jīng, Hú, Mǐn, and Hàn;
in the west, Qí and Shǔ;
in the north, Yān and Jìn.
And the Zhū clan held seventy-eight Zhōu, forming the [Hòu] Liáng.
Zhuāngzōng initially rose up in Bīng and Dài,
took Yōu and Cāng,
possessing thirty-five Zhōu.
Afterward, he further took sixteen Zhōu, including Liáng, Wèi, and Bó,
totaling fifty-one Zhōu, with which he destroyed the [Hòu] Liáng.
When the King of Qí acknowledged vassalage,
[Zhuāngzōng] gained seven more of his Zhōu.
During the Tóngguāng period, Shǔ was defeated,
but later lost again,
only retaining the four Zhōu of Qín, Fèng, Jiē, and Chéng.
Furthermore, the two Zhōu of Yíng and Píng fell to the Qìdān.
One Zhōu was newly established by them.
This totaled one hundred and twenty-three Zhōu, forming the [Hòu] Táng.
When the Shí clan was established [as rulers],
they ceded sixteen Zhōu to the Qìdān,
but gained Jīn Zhōu from Shǔ.
Furthermore, one Zhōu was newly established.
This totaled one hundred and nine Zhōu, forming the [Hòu] Jìn.
In the beginning of the Liú clan [rule],
Qín, Fèng, Jiē, and Chéng again returned to Shǔ.
During the time of [Emperor] Yǐndì, one Zhōu was newly established.
This totaled one hundred and six Zhōu, forming the [Hòu] Hàn.
When the Guō clan replaced the [Hòu] Hàn,
ten Zhōu went to Liú Mín.
Shìzōng took Qín, Fèng, Jiē, Chéng, Yíng, Mò, and fourteen Zhōu in Huáinán.
Furthermore, five Zhōu were newly established, and three were abolished.
This totaled one hundred and eighteen Zhōu, forming the [Hòu] Zhōu.
The rise of the Sòng followed this [territory].
This is the general outline of the Central Plains (Zhōngguó).
As for the other outlying dependencies,
the strong annexed the weak,
and gains and losses were not constant.
By the end of the [Hòu] Zhōu,
Mǐn had already perished,
and seven states remained:
Twenty-one Zhōu south of the Jiāng (Yangtze River) formed the Nán Táng;
forty-six Zhōu south of Jiàn and including the western part of Shānnán Dào formed Shǔ;
ten Zhōu in Húnán and Húběi formed Chǔ;
thirteen Zhōu east and west of Zhè formed Wúyuè;
forty-seven Zhōu north and south of the Lǐng formed Nán Hàn;
ten Zhōu north of Tàiyuán formed Dōng Hàn;
and the three Zhōu of Jīng, Guī, and Xiá formed Nán Píng.
Combining all the possessions of the Central Plains (Zhōngguó),
there were two hundred and sixty-eight Zhōu,
and the Jūn (military regions) are not included here.
The borders of the Táng were extensive,
fully recorded by earlier historians,
but nominal Zhōu under loose control (jīmí) or remote administration were included among them.
During the chaotic era of the Wǔdài (Five Dynasties),
records are incomplete,
and at times there were abolitions or mergers [of prefectures],
or they fell to the barbarians (Yídí);
therefore, the details cannot be fully investigated.

Liáng converted Biànzhōu to Kāifēng Fǔ,
and established it as Dōngdū.
After the Hòu Táng destroyed the Liáng,
it was restored as Xuānwǔ Jūn.
In the third year of Tiānfú (938) of the Jìn, it was promoted to Dōngjīng.
The Hàn and Zhōu dynasties followed this.
Luòyáng,
the Liáng, Táng, Jìn, Hàn, and Zhōu often considered it a capital.
The Táng formerly designated it Dōngdū.
The Liáng designated it Xīdū.
The Hòu Táng designated it Luòjīng.
The Jìn designated it Xījīng,
and the Hàn and Zhōu dynasties followed this.
Yōngzhōu,
was formerly the imperial capital (Shàngdū) during the Táng.
When Zhāozōng moved to Luòyáng,
it was abolished and made into Yòuguó Jūn.
Early in the Liáng dynasty, Jīngzhǎo Fǔ was renamed Dà'ān,
and Yòuguó Jūn was renamed Yǒngpíng.
When Táng destroyed Liáng,
it was restored as Xījīng.
Jìn abolished it and made it Jìnchāng Jūn.
The Hàn renamed it Yǒngxīng,
and the Zhōu followed this.
Cáozhōu,
formerly belonged to the Xuānwǔ Jūn Jiédù.
In the second year of Kāiyùn (945) of the Jìn, Wēixìn Jūn was established.
Early in the Hàn dynasty,
the command was abolished.
In the second year of Guǎngshùn (952) of the Zhōu, Zhāngxìn Jūn was re-established.
Sòngzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Xuānwǔ Jūn Jiédù.
Early in the Liáng dynasty, Xuānwǔ Jūn was relocated there.
When Táng destroyed Liáng,
it was renamed Guīdé.
Chénzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Zhōngwǔ Jūn Jiédù.
In the second year of Kāiyùn (945) of the Jìn, Zhèn'ān Jūn was established.
Early in the Hàn dynasty,
the command was abolished.
In the second year of Guǎngshùn (952) of the Zhōu, it was restored.
Xǔzhōu,
formerly called Zhōngwǔ during the Táng.
Liáng renamed it Kuāngguó.
When Táng destroyed Liáng,
it was restored to Zhōngwǔ.
Huázhōu,
formerly called Yìchéng during the Táng.
To avoid the taboo name of the Liáng King's father, it was renamed Xuānyì.
When Táng destroyed Liáng,
its former name was restored.
Xiāngzhōu,
formerly called Shānnán Dōngdào during the Táng.
Between the Táng and Liáng eras, it was renamed Zhōngyì Jūn.
Later, Yánzhōu became Zhōngyì,
and Xiāngzhōu was restored to Shānnán Dōngdào.
Dèngzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédù.
After Liáng defeated Zhào Kuāngníng,
Xuānhuà Jūn was established by splitting Dèngzhōu.
Táng renamed it Wēishèng.
Zhōu renamed it Wǔshèng.
Ānzhōu,
Liáng established Xuānwēi Jūn.
Táng renamed it Ānyuǎn,
Jìn abolished it.
Hàn restored it as Ānyuǎn,
and Zhōu abolished it again.
Jìnzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Hùguó Jūn Jiédù.
In the fourth year of Kāipíng (910) of the Liáng, Dìngchāng Jūn was established.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (917), it was renamed Jiànníng.
Táng renamed it Jiànxióng.
Jīnzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédù.
At the end of the Táng, Róngzhāo Jūn was established,
but was shortly abolished,
and subsequently fell to Shǔ.
During the time of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn,
Huáidé Jūn was established again,
but soon abolished.
Shǎnzhōu,
formerly called Bǎoyì during the Táng.
Liáng renamed it Zhènguó.
Hòu Táng restored it to Bǎoyì.
Huàzhōu,
formerly called Zhènguó during the Táng.
Liáng renamed it Gǎnhuà.
Hòu Táng restored it to Zhènguó.
Tóngzhōu,
formerly called Kuāngguó during the Táng.
Liáng renamed it Zhōngwǔ.
Hòu Táng restored it to Kuāngguó.
Yàozhōu,
originally Huàyuán Xiàn.
At the end of the Táng, it belonged to Lǐ Màozhēn,
who established it as Yàozhōu,
and established Yìshèng Jūn.
During the reign of the Last Emperor (Mòdì) of Liáng,
Mào Zhēn's adopted son Wēn Tāo surrendered the prefecture to Liáng.
Liáng renamed Yàozhōu to Chóngzhōu,
and Yìshèng to Jìngshèng.
Hòu Táng restored it as Yàozhōu,
and renamed the command Shùnyì.
Yánzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Bǎodà Jūn Jiédù.
Liáng established Zhōngyì Jūn.
Táng renamed it Zhāngwǔ.
Wèizhōu,
formerly called Dàmíng Fǔ during the Táng,
where Tiānxíong Jūn was established.
The Five Dynasties all followed this.
Hòu Táng established Yèdū,
the Jìn and Hàn followed this,
but Zhōu abolished it.
Dàmíng Fǔ,
Hòu Táng called it Xīngtáng,
Jìn called it Guǎng Jìn,
Hàn and Zhōu restored the name Dàmíng.
Chánzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Tiānxíong Jūn Jiédù.
In the ninth year of Tiānfú (944) of the Jìn, Zhènníng Jūn was established.
Xiāngzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Tiānxíong Jūn Jiédù.
The Last Emperor (Mòdì) of Liáng split it off and established Zhāodé Jūn.
When the Tiānxíong Jūn rebelled,
it subsequently fell to the Jìn.
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
it returned to Tiānxíong.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn established Zhāngdé Jūn.
Xíngzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Zhāoyì Jūn Jiédù.
The Zhāoyì circuit governed the five prefectures of Zézhōu, Lùzhōu, Xíngzhōu, Míngzhōu, and Cízhōu.
At the end of the Táng, Mèng Fānglì became the Zhāoyì Jūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner),
and relocated the military headquarters to Xíngzhōu,
while Zézhōu and Lùzhōu prefectures fell to the Jìn.
Fānglì only controlled Xíngzhōu, Míngzhōu, and Cízhōu, three prefectures.
Therefore, at the end of the Táng, there were two Zhāoyì Jūn.
During the conflict between Liáng and Jìn,
sometimes they belonged to Liáng,
and sometimes they belonged to Jìn.
Liáng designated the three prefectures of Xíngzhōu, Míngzhōu, and Cízhōu as Bǎoyì Jūn.
When Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
he renamed it Ānguó.
Zhènzhōu,
formerly called Chéngdé Jūn.
Early in the Liáng dynasty, because the sound *chéng* violated the imperial taboo,
it was renamed Wǔshùn.
Táng restored the name Chéngdé.
Jìn again renamed it Shùndé.
Hàn restored the name Chéngdé.
Píngliáng,
formerly belonged to Jīngzhōu.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, Wèizhōu fell to the Tǔbō,
and Wèizhōu was temporarily established in Píngliáng, causing the (original) county to be abolished.
In the third year of Qīngtài of the Later Táng,
the two garrisons (zhèn) of Ānguó and Yàowǔ, which belonged to the former Píngliáng, were used to establish Píngliáng County,
subordinate to Jīngzhōu.
Línjīng,
formerly belonged to Jīngzhōu.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, Yuánzhōu fell to the Tǔbō,
and Yuánzhōu was temporarily established in Línjīng, while Jīngzhōu concurrently governed its people.
In the third year of Qīngtài of the Later Táng, it was separated and attached to Yuánzhōu.
Xiánníng in Fūzhōu,
was abolished by the Zhōu.
Jìshān,
formerly belonged to Hézhōng,
Táng separated and attached it to Jiàngzhōu.
Wǔchéng and Lǚxiāng in Cízhōu,
were abolished by the Zhōu.
Dàmíng County in Dàmíng Fǔ,
was formerly called Guìxiāng.
The Later Táng changed its name to Guǎngjìn,
and the Hàn changed its name to Dàmíng.
Chánglú and Qiánfú in Cāngzhōu,
were abolished by the Zhōu and merged into Qīngchí;
Wúdì,
the Zhōu established Bǎoshùn Jūn there.
Ānlíng,
formerly belonged to Jǐngzhōu,
the Zhōu separated and attached it to Dézhōu.
Dùnqiū in Chánzhōu,
the Jìn established Déqīng Jūn there.
Wǔshuǐ in Bózhōu,
was abolished by the Zhōu and merged into Liáochéng.
Bóyě,
formerly belonged to Shēnzhōu,
the Zhōu separated and attached it to Dìngzhōu.
Wǔkāng,
formerly belonged to Húzhōu,
the Liáng separated and attached it to Hángzhōu.
Mǐnqīng in Fúzhōu,
in the first year of Qiānhuà of the Liáng,
Wáng Shěnzhī established it at Méixī Chǎng.
Wújiāng in Sūzhōu,
in the third year of Kāipíng of the Liáng,
Qián Liú established it.
Wànghǎi in Míngzhōu,
in the third year of Kāipíng of the Liáng,
Qián Liú established it.
Chángsōng in Chǔzhōu,
was formerly called Sōngyáng,
the Liáng changed its name to Chángsōng.
Lóngxǐ in Tánzhōu,
in the third year of Qiányòu of the Hàn,
Mǎ Xīfàn established it.
Tiāncháng and Liùhé,
formerly belonged to Yángzhōu.
The Southern Táng made Tiāncháng a Jūn (military prefecture),
and Liùhé an Xióngzhōu,
the Zhōu restored the former arrangement.
Hànyáng,
formerly belonged to Èzhōu,
the Zhōu established Hànyáng Jūn.
Yìchuān,
formerly belonged to Miǎnzhōu,
the Zhōu separated and attached it to Ānzhōu.
Lèxiāng in Xiāngzhōu,
was abolished by the Zhōu and merged into Yíchéng.
Líntuān in Dèngzhōu,
the Hàn changed its name to Línsè;
Jútán and Xiàngchéng,
were abolished by the Zhōu.
Jìnglín in Fùzhōu,
the Jìn changed its name to Jǐnglíng.
Jiānlì,
formerly belonged to Fùzhōu,
the Liáng separated and attached it to Jiānglíng.
Cíqiū in Tángzhōu,
was abolished by the Zhōu.
Qiányuán in Shāngzhōu,
the Hàn changed its name to Qiányòu,
and separated and attached it to Jīngzhào.
Luònán,
formerly belonged to Huàzhōu,
the Zhōu separated and attached it to Shāngzhōu.
Tángchéng in Suízhōu,
the Liáng changed its name to Hàndōng,
the Later Táng restored the old name,
the Jìn again changed it to Hàndōng,
and the Hàn restored the old name.
Xióngshèng Jūn,
originally Gùzhèn in Fèngzhōu,
the Zhōu established it as a Jūn.
Tiānshuǐ and Lǒngchéng in Qínzhōu,
were abolished at the end of the Táng dynasty,
the Later Táng restored them.
Lìtíng in Chéngzhōu,
was established by the Later Táng.
Since the Táng had Fāngzhèn (regional military governors),
historians did not record them in geographical texts,
believing that matters related to the military affairs of the Fāngzhèn
were not within the purview of the department of geography (Zhífāng).
However, later generations followed this practice,
using Jūn (military prefecture) to name places,
and thus obscuring the name of the Zhōu (prefecture).
Moreover, those Jūn established today
are merely elevated to the importance of a Zhōu or Fǔ based on a nominal title,
this cannot be left unrecorded.
All Zhōu and Xiàn (counties)
that were abolished during the Five Dynasties having existed in the Táng dynasty,
or those established during the Five Dynasties that exist today,
as well as counties that were separated and attached (to other prefectures) and are still governed as such today,
should all be listed to complete the records of the department of geography.
The rest, which were once established and then abolished,
or once renamed or separated and then restored to their former state,
are not worth recording.
Mountains, rivers, produce, and customs
are the responsibility of the department of geography,
but the Five Dynasties was a short era,
and there were no geographical changes,
thus they are also not recorded again;
instead, the names of the Fāngzhèn and Jūn are recorded,
so that they may be cross-referenced with previous histories.
For instance, the current Yǒngxīng,
was originally the name of a Jiédù Jūn (military command),
and now the appointed governor is called Zhī Yǒngxīng Jūn Fǔ Shì (Manager of the Affairs of the Yǒngxīng Military Prefecture),
without mentioning Yōngzhōu Jīngzhào (the traditional regional name),
this is the case.
Alas!
Since the Táng lost its governance,
the world seized the opportunity;
tattoed convicts, robbers, and traders
wore imperial robes (gǔn miǎn) and stood high and magnificent.
Wú and the Southern Táng,
were seized by treacherous strongmen.
Shǔ was dangerous but wealthy,
Hàn was dangerous but poor;
the poor could strengthen themselves,
the wealthy perished first.
Mǐn was crude, Jīng was cramped,
Chǔ opened up the lands of the barbarians (Mán).
Oppression and pillage were unbearable,
Wú and Yuè were the worst offenders.
Humans were treated as sacrificial animals (láoshēng),
the Dàn people of the ridge suffered under Liú.
Within a hundred years,
they rose together to vie for supremacy;
mountains and rivers were cut off,
and communication (fēngqì) ceased.
The saying goes: When the clear wind rises,
all darkness submits;
when the sun and moon appear,
the faint fire ceases.
Therefore, when the True Man (zhēnrén) arises, the world becomes unified.
Composed the Hereditary Houses of the Ten Kingdoms.
Hereditary House of Wú, First: Yáng Xíngmì (Son Wò, Lóngyǎn, Pǔ)
Yáng Xíngmì, courtesy name Huàyuán,
was a native of Héféi, Lúzhōu.
He was tall and strong,
able to lift a hundred jin (catties) by hand.
During the Qiánfú era of the Táng,
when numerous bandits arose in Jiāng and Huái,
Xíngmì was captured as a bandit,
but Prefect Zhèng Qǐ found his appearance remarkable,
released him from his bonds, and let him go.
Later he responded to the recruitment call to become a prefectural soldier,
served garrison duty in Shuòfāng,
and was promoted to squadron leader (Duìzhǎng).
When his term of service was over and he returned from garrison duty,
the military officials disliked him,
and again ordered him out for garrison duty.
As Xíngmì was about to leave,
he passed the military official's residence;
the official pretended to speak kindly,
asking Xíngmì what he desired before departing.
Xíngmì forcefully replied:
"I only lack your head!"
He immediately cut off his head,
carried it out,
and consequently raised an army to revolt,
styling himself Commander of the Eight Camps (Bāyíng Dū Zhī Bīngmǎ Shǐ).
Prefect Láng Yòufù abandoned the city and fled,
and Xíngmì consequently occupied Lúzhōu.
Yìngzhōu,
formerly belonged to the Dàtóng Jūnjiédù.
When Táng Míngzōng ascended the throne,
because he was a native of Yìngzhōu,
he established Zhāngguó Jūn.
Xīnzhōu,
Wēisài Jūn was established in the first year of Táng Tóngguāng.
Fǔzhōu,
Yǒng'ān Jūn was established by Jìn,
Hàn abolished it,
and Zhōu restored it.
Bìngzhōu,
Later Táng established the Northern Capital,
and its army was still called Hédōng.
Lùzhōu,
formerly called Zhāoyì during Táng.
During the time of Liáng Mòdì, it belonged to Liáng,
and was renamed Kuāngyì.
After a year or so,
Táng destroyed Liáng,
and it was renamed Ānyì.
Jìn restored it to Zhāoyì.
Lúzhōu,
when Zhōu Shìzōng conquered Huáinán,
he established Bǎoxìn Jūn.
Shòuzhōu,
formerly called Zhōngzhèng during Táng,
Southern Táng renamed it Qīnghuái.
When Zhōu Shìzōng pacified Huáinán,
it was restored to Zhōngzhèng.
During the Five Dynasties period,
the outer dependent prefectures,
Yángzhōu was called Huáinán,
Xuānzhōu was called Níngguó,
Èzhōu was called Wǔchāng,
Hóngzhōu was called Zhènnán,
Fúzhōu was called Wǔwēi,
Hángzhōu was called Zhènhǎi,
Yuèzhōu was called Zhèndōng,
Jiānglíng Fǔ was called Jīngnán,
Yìzhōu and Zǐzhōu were called Jiànnán Dōng and Xīzhōu,
Suízhōu was called Wǔxìn,
Xīngyuán Fǔ was called Shānnán Xīdào,
Yángzhōu was called Wǔdìng,
Qiánzhōu was called Qiánnán,
Tánzhōu was called Wǔ'ān,
Guìzhōu was called Jìngjiāng,
Róngzhōu was called Níngyuǎn,
Yōngzhōu was called Jiànwǔ,
Guǎngzhōu was called Qīnghǎi,
all were former names from Táng,
unchanged throughout the Five Dynasties,
and remain so to this day.
As for other names changed or established by usurping regimes,
they cannot all be verified,
and are not worth mentioning.
Those that are still in use today
are briefly noted in the record.
Jìzhōu,
established in the second year of Zhōu Guǎngshùn,
had Jùyě and Yùnchéng from Yùnzhōu,
Rènchéng from Yǎnzhōu,
and Jīnxiāng from Shànzhōu assigned as its subordinate counties, and its seat was in Jùyě.
Shànzhōu,
at the end of Táng, Dàngshān from Sòngzhōu,
which was the hometown of Liáng Tàizǔ,
was used to establish Huīzhōu,
and later its seat was moved to Shànfù.
After Later Táng destroyed Liáng,
Huīzhōu was renamed Shànzhōu.
The establishment and relocation of its subordinate counties
differ in records,
but now it governs Shànfù, Dàngshān, Chéngwǔ, and Yútái four counties.
Yàozhōu,
established by Lǐ Màozhēn,
its seat was in Huàyuán county.
In the early Liáng, it was renamed Chóngzhōu,
and in the first year of Táng Tóngguāng, it was restored to Yàozhōu.
Jiězhōu,
established in the ninth month of the first year of Hàn Qiányòu,
had Wénxǐ, Ānyì, and Jiěxiàn from Hézhōng assigned as its subordinates, and its seat was in Jiě.
Wēizhōu,
established in the fourth year of Jìn Tiānfú,
had Fāngqú from Língzhōu,
and Mùbō and Mǎlíng three towns from Níngzhōu assigned as its subordinates, and its seat was in Fāngqú.
In the second year of Zhōu Guǎngshùn, it was renamed Huánzhōu,
and in the fourth year of Xiǎndé, it was abolished and became Tōngyuǎn Jūn.
Six Jūn were established during the Five Dynasties,
all had their seats in counties
and were subordinate to prefectures,
hence they are not listed separately.
Jiān refers to
names of offices for specific affairs,
hence they are not recorded in geography.
The Imperial Dynasty's Jūn and Jiān began to establish subordinate counties,
and were ranked alongside prefectures.
Qiánzhōu,
established by Lǐ Màozhēn,
its seat was in Fèngtian county.
Cízhōu,
Liáng renamed it Huìzhōu,
Táng restored it to Cízhōu.
Jǐngzhōu,
formerly had its seat in Gōnggāo during Táng.
In the third year of Zhōu Xiǎndé, it was abolished and became Dìngyuǎn Jūn,
its subordinate Ānlíng county was assigned to Dézhōu,
Gōnggāo county was abolished and merged into Dōngguāng county,
which became the seat of Dìngyuǎn Jūn.
Bīnzhōu,
established in the third year of Zhōu Xiǎndé,
named after its coastal location.
Initially,
during the Five Dynasties period,
a salt taxation office was established by the sea,
later becoming Shànguó Jūn.
Zhōu then established the prefecture,
assigning Bóhǎi and Pútái from Dìzhōu as its subordinate counties, and its seat was in Bóhǎi.
Xióngzhōu,
established in the sixth year of Zhōu Xiǎndé after conquering Wǎqiáo Guān,
its seat was in Guīyì;
Róngchéng from Yìzhōu was assigned as its subordinate,
but it was soon abolished.
Bàzhōu,
established in the sixth year of Zhōu Xiǎndé after conquering Yìjīn Guān,
its seat was in Yǒngqīng,
Wén'ān from Mòzhōu,
and Dàchéng from Yíngzhōu were assigned as its subordinates.
Tōngzhōu,
originally the eastern border of Hǎilíng.
Southern Táng established Jìnghǎi Zhìzhìyuàn.
When Zhōu Shìzōng conquered Huáinán,
it was promoted to Jìnghǎi Jūn.
Later, Tōngzhōu was established,
and its territory was divided to establish Jìnghǎi and Hǎimén two counties as its subordinates, and its seat was in Jìnghǎi.
Jūnzhōu,
established by Southern Táng Lǐ Jǐng.
Gāo'ān, Shànggāo, Wànzǎi, and Qīngjiāng four counties from Hóngzhōu were assigned as its subordinates, and its seat was in Gāo'ān.
Jiànzhōu,
established by Southern Táng Lǐ Jǐng,
Yánpíng, Jiànpǔ, and Fùshā three counties from Jiànzhōu were assigned as its subordinates, and its seat was in Yánpíng.
Quánzhōu,
established by Chǔ Wáng Mǎ Xīfàn.
Xiāngchuān county from Tánzhōu was renamed Qīngxiāng county,
and Guànyáng county was also assigned as its subordinate, and its seat was in Qīngxiāng.
Xiùzhōu,
established by Wúyuè Wáng Qián Yuánguàn.
Jiāxīng county from Hángzhōu was assigned as its subordinate, and its seat was there.
Xióngzhōu,
established by Southern Hàn Liú Yǎn, assigning Bǎochāng from Sháozhōu,
its seat was in Bǎochāng.
Yīngzhōu,
established by Southern Hàn Liú Yǎn, assigning Zhēnyáng from Guǎngzhōu,
its seat was in Zhēnyáng.
Kāifēng Fǔ formerly governed six counties.
In the first year of Liáng Kāipíng,
Suānzǎo and Chángyuán from Huázhōu,
Zhōngmóu and Yángwǔ from Zhèngzhōu,
Xiāngyì from Sòngzhōu,
Kǎochéng from Cáozhōu (renamed Dàiyì),
Fúgōu and Líng from Xǔzhōu,
and Tàikāng from Chénzhōu were subordinated to it.
Táng returned Suānzǎo, Zhōngmóu, Xiāngyì, Líng, and Tàikāng five counties to their former affiliations.
Jìn promoted Biànzhōu to Dōngjīng,
and again subordinated these five counties to it.
Yōngqiū,
Jìn renamed it Shí,
Hàn restored its former name.
Chángyuán,
Táng renamed it Kuāngchéng.
Líyáng,
formerly belonged to Huázhōu,
Jìn assigned it to Wèizhōu.
Yè and Xiāngchéng,
formerly belonged to Xǔzhōu,
Táng assigned them to Rǔzhōu.
Chǔqiū,
formerly belonged to Shànzhōu,
Liáng assigned it to Sòngzhōu.
Mìzhōu Jiāoxī,
formerly called Fǔtáng,
Liáng renamed it Ānqiū,
Táng restored its former name,
Jìn renamed it Jiāoxī.
Wèinán,
formerly belonged to Jīngzhào,
Zhōu reassigned it to Huázhōu.
Tóngguān,
formerly belonged to Jīngzhào Fǔ,
Liáng assigned it to Tóngzhōu,
Táng assigned it to Yàozhōu.
Měiyuán,
formerly belonged to Tóngzhōu,
Lǐ Màozhēn established Dǐngzhōu and governed it.
Liáng renamed it Yùzhōu,
subordinate to Shùnyì Jūnjiédù.
Later, its abolition time is not seen.
In the third year of Táng Tóngguāng,
it was assigned to Yàozhōu.
In the third year of Zhōnghé,
the Táng immediately appointed Yáng Xíngmì the Cìshǐ of Lúzhōu.
Gāo Pián, the Jiédùshǐ of Huáinán, was attacked by Bì Shīduó.
Pián memorialized to appoint Xíngmì the Xíngjūn Sīmǎ.
Xíngmì led several thousand soldiers to rush there,
but upon reaching Tiāncháng,
Shīduó had already imprisoned Pián
and summoned Qín Yàn of Xuānzhōu to enter Yángzhōu.
Xíngmì was unable to enter
and pitched camp at Shǔgāng.
Shīduó's army of tens of thousands attacked Xíngmì.
Xíngmì feigned defeat,
abandoned his camp, and fled.
Shīduó’s soldiers were hungry;
taking advantage of the victory, they scrambled into the camp to seize military supplies.
Xíngmì turned his troops back and attacked them.
Shīduó was greatly defeated
and fled back into the city alone on horseback,
whereupon he killed Gāo Pián.
When Xíngmì heard of Pián’s death,
he clothed his army in white and wept toward the city for three days.
He attacked the west gate.
Yàn and Shīduó fled to Dōngtáng,
and Xíngmì subsequently entered Yángzhōu.
At this time,
the granaries in the city were empty.
The starving populace killed and ate one another.
Husbands and wives, fathers and sons, dragged one another
to the butcher to sell them.
The butchers sliced and stripped the meat as if it were sheep or swine.
Xíngmì could not hold the city
and wished to flee.
Meanwhile, Qín Zōngquán of Càizhōu sent his younger brother, Zōnghéng, to plunder the Huáinán region.
Yàn and Shīduó returned from Dōngtáng
and joined forces with Zōnghéng.
Xíngmì closed the city gates and dared not venture out.
Soon after, Zōnghéng was killed by the subordinate general Sūn Rú.
Rú attacked and captured Gāoyóu.
Xíngmì grew even more fearful.
His retainer, Yuán Xí, said:
"We are using newly assembled troops to defend an empty city,
and many of the generals are Pián's former subordinates.
They are not bound by deep favors, long-established trust, or sheer force to make them submit wholeheartedly.
Now Rú's army is flourishing;
they will certainly conquer whatever they attack.
This is the time when these generals will hold to two possibilities, relying on who is strong or weak, and choosing whom to support or abandon.
Gāo Bà, the Zhènshǐ of Hǎilíng,
is an old general of Pián's,
and will certainly not be used by us."
Xíngmì then used a military order to summon Bà.
Bà led his soldiers into Guǎnglíng.
Xíngmì intended to make Bà defend Tiāncháng.
Xí said:
"We summoned Bà because we suspected him.
How can we use him again?
Moreover, if we can defeat Rú,
we have no use for Bà;
if, unfortunately, we cannot defeat him,
how can Tiāncháng remain ours?
It is better to kill him
and incorporate his troops."
Xíngmì then held a troop review, captured Bà, and executed his clan,
gaining several thousand of his soldiers.
Soon after, Sūn Rú killed Qín Yàn and Bì Shīduó
and incorporated their troops to attack Xíngmì.
Xíngmì wished to flee to Hǎilíng.
Xí said:
"Hǎilíng is difficult to defend,
but Lúzhōu is our former base.
Its city walls and granaries are intact and substantial,
which allows for future planning."
Xíngmì then fled to Lúzhōu.
After a long time,
not knowing where to proceed,
he asked Xí:
"I wish to cover up our armor, double our pace,
and take Hóngzhōu to the west. Is this permissible?"
Xí replied:
"Zhōng Chuán recently acquired Jiāngxī,
and his position cannot yet be schemed against.
When Qín Yàn entered Guǎnglíng,
he summoned Zhào Huáng, the Cìshǐ of Chízhōu, and entrusted him with Xuānzhōu.
Now that Yàn is about to die,
Huáng has lost his reliance.
Furthermore, defending Xuānzhōu is not his original ambition,
and he is not a match for Your Lordship.
This place can be taken."
Xíngmì then led his troops to attack Huáng,
and fought him at Héshān,
inflicting a great defeat.
He advanced and besieged Xuānzhōu.
Huáng abandoned the city and fled.
Xíngmì pursued, overtook, and killed him,
and subsequently entered Xuānzhōu.
In the first year of Lóngjì,
the Táng appointed Xíngmì the Guānchásǐ of Xuānzhōu.
Xíngmì sent Tián Yūn, Ān Rényì, Lǐ Shénfú, and others to attack Zhèxī,
taking Sūzhōu, Chángzhōu, and Rùnzhōu.
In the second year,
they took Chúzhōu and Hézhōu.
In the first year of Jǐngfú,
they took Chǔzhōu.
Sūn Rú, having chased Xíngmì out,
entered Guǎnglíng.
After some time,
he also could not hold it,
so he burned the city.
He killed the elderly and the sick among the populace to feed his army,
and drove his multitude across the river,
claiming fifty thousand,
to attack Xíngmì.
Whenever his generals Tián Yūn, Liú Wēi, and others encountered Rú, they were defeated.
Xíngmì wanted to flee to Tóngguān.
His retainer, Dài Yǒuguī, said:
"Rú arrived with sharp morale and numerous troops.
His vanguard cannot be withstood but can be blunted,
and his multitude cannot be fought head-on but can be worn down over time.
If we avoid him and flee,
we will be captured."
Liú Wēi also said:
"By turning our backs to the city and strengthening the stockades,
we can exhaust him without fighting."
Xíngmì considered this correct.
After a long period,
Rú's soldiers starved
and also suffered a great plague.
Xíngmì used all his troops to attack him.
Rú was defeated
and captured.
As he was about to die,
he looked up at Wēi and said:
"I hear that you devised this plan to defeat me.
If I had a general like you,
could I have been defeated?"
Xíngmì gathered Rú’s remaining several thousand soldiers.
He clad them in black robes over their armor
and named them
"Hēiyúndū" (Black Cloud Brigade).
They served constantly as his personal army.
That year,
he re-entered Yángzhōu.
The Táng appointed Xíngmì the Jiédùshǐ of Huáinán.
In the second year of Qiánníng,
he was promoted to Jiǎnjiào Tàifù and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Xíngmì assigned Tián Yūn to guard Xuānzhōu
and Ān Rényì to guard Rùnzhōu.
Féng Hóngduó, the Cìshǐ of Shēngzhōu, came to submit.
He dispatched Yūn and others separately to attack and plunder.
All the prefectures south of the Huái River and east of the Yangtze River submitted to him.
He advanced to attack Sūzhōu
and captured its Cìshǐ, Chéng Jí.
In the fourth year,
Zhū Jǐn of Yǎnzhōu fled to Xíngmì.
Initially,
Jǐn was attacked by the Liáng
and sought aid from the Jìn.
The Jìn sent Lǐ Chéngsì to lead several thousand strong cavalry to assist Jǐn.
Jǐn was defeated
and consequently fled, together with them, to Xíngmì.
Xíngmì's soldiers were all people from the Jiāng-Huái region.
The Huái people were light and weak.
Upon gaining Jǐn's strong cavalry,
his military strength increased significantly.
That year,
Liáng Tàizǔ sent Gě Cóngzhōu and Páng Shīgǔ to attack Xíngmì’s Shòuzhōu.
Xíngmì defeated the Liáng troops at Qīngkǒu,
killing Shīgǔ.
Cóngzhōu gathered his troops and fled.
Xíngmì pursued them to the Pēi Hé
and inflicted another great defeat.
In the fifth year,
Qián Liú attacked Sūzhōu.
He and Zhōu Běn fought at Báifāng Hú.
Běn was defeated,
and Sūzhōu fell back under the control of Yuè.
In the first year of Tiānfù,
Xíngmì sent Lǐ Shénfú to attack Yuè.
They fought at Lín'ān,
inflicting a great defeat
and capturing their general Gù Quánwǔ, whom they brought back.
In the second year,
Féng Hóngduó rebelled
and attacked Xuānzhōu.
He fought Tián Yūn at Héshān.
Hóngduó was defeated
and was about to flee to the sea.
Xíngmì personally went to Dōngtáng to intercept him
and sent a messenger to Hóngduó saying:
"Victory and defeat
are ordinary matters in warfare.
Why, because of a single battle's defeat,
do you punish yourself by abandoning yourself to a sea island?
Although my administration is small,
it is still enough to accommodate you."
Hóngduó was moved to tears.
Xíngmì, accompanied by just over ten horsemen,
galloped into his camp,
appointed Hóngduó the Jiédù Fùshǐ,
and replaced Hóngduó with Lǐ Shénfú as the Cìshǐ of Shēngzhōu.
In this year,
Táng Zhāozōng was in Qí,

and sent Lǐ Yǎn, the Envoy for Pacification and Proclamation in Jiānghuái, to bestow upon Hángmì the titles of Commander-in-Chief of the Eastern Armies of All Circuits, Acting Grand Preceptor (Jiǎnjiào Tàishī), and Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and enfeoffed him as the Prince of Wú.
In the third year (906),
he appointed Lǐ Shénfú as the Grand Commander for Campaigning against È-Yuè to attack Dù Hóng.
Chéng Ruì of Jīngnán rescued Hóng,
but Shénfú defeated him at Jūnshān.
The Liáng army attacked Qīngzhōu,
and Wáng Shīfàn came to ask for aid.
He dispatched Wáng Màozhāng to rescue him,
who utterly defeated the Liáng army
and killed Zhū Yǒuníng.
Yǒuníng
was the son of Liáng Tàizǔ (Zhū Wén),
who was greatly enraged.
He personally led his forces to attack Màozhāng;
the troops were said to number 200,000,
but they were again defeated by Màozhāng.
Tián Yūn rebelled,
assaulted Shēngzhōu,
and captured Lǐ Shénfú's wife and children, returning with them to Xuānzhōu.
Hángmì summoned Shénfú to campaign against Yūn.
Yūn sent his general Wáng Tán to meet him,
and also sent a letter to Shénfú,
using his wife and children to lure him.
Shénfú said:
“I started following the Prince of Wú with a single soldier;
now I am a great general.
How can I bear to betray my virtue and care for my wife and children?”
He immediately executed the messenger to definitively cut ties,
and the soldiers, hearing this, were all moved and inspired.
When they reached Jíyáng Jī,
Yūn held Shénfú's son Chéngdǐng to tempt him.
Shénfú shouted at his attendants to shoot him,
and subsequently defeated Tán’s army at Jíyáng.
Hángmì separately dispatched Tái Méng to attack Yūn,
and Yūn was defeated and killed.
Originally,
Yūn, Ān Rènyì, Zhū Yánshòu, and others all followed Hángmì starting from humble origins.
As soon as the Jiāng and Huái regions were settled,
he wished for gradual rest and stabilization,
but these three men were fierce, violent, and difficult to control,
and he often wanted to eliminate them,
though he had no pretext to initiate it.
In the second year of Tiānfù (902),
Qián Liú was besieged by his rebellious general Xǔ Zàisī and others.
Zàisī summoned Yūn to attack Liú's Hángzhōu;
it was on the verge of capture,
but Hángmì accepted a bribe from Liú
and ordered Yūn to withdraw his troops.
Yūn resented this.
Yūn once discussed strategy at Guǎnglíng,
and many of Hángmì's generals came to Yūn seeking bribes,
and even the prison clerks made demands.
Yūn angrily said:
“The clerks wish me to be put in prison!”
He returned and then plotted rebellion.
Rènyì heard about it and also rebelled,
burning Dōngtáng and assaulting Chángzhōu.
Lǐ Yù, the Prefect of Chángzhōu, went out to fight,
and upon seeing Rènyì, he cursed him loudly.
Rènyì halted his troops and said:
“Lǐ Yù dares to insult me like this;
there must be an ambush.”
He consequently withdrew his army,
and indeed the ambush was sprung.
They pursued him to Jiágāng,
where Rènyì planted his standard, removed his armor, and ate.
Yù's soldiers did not dare pursue,
and Rènyì returned to Rùnzhōu.
Hángmì sent Wáng Màozhāng, Lǐ Déchéng, Mǐ Zhìchéng, and others to surround him.
In the Wú army, Zhū Jǐn was recognized as the best at spear fighting,
and Zhìchéng as the best archer,
both ranking first.
Rènyì, however, was confident in his own archery,
saying:
“Ten of Zhìchéng’s bows
do not equal one of Jǐn’s spears;
and ten of Jǐn’s spears
do not equal one of Rènyì’s bows.”
Whenever he fought with Màozhāng and the others,
he would always hit the target before shooting (meaning: he shot only when certain of hitting).
Because of this, the Wú army feared him
and dared not approach.
Hángmì also wanted to induce him to surrender,
but Rènyì hesitated and was undecided.
Màozhāng took advantage of his complacency,
dug a tunnel to enter,
captured Rènyì,
and executed him at Guǎnglíng.
Yánshòu
was the younger brother of Hángmì's wife, Lady Zhū.
When Yūn and Rènyì were about to rebel,
Hángmì grew suspicious of Yánshòu.
He pretended to suffer from an eye disease,
and whenever he met Yánshòu’s messengers,
he would deliberately confuse what he saw to demonstrate it.
Once, while walking,
he intentionally bumped into a pillar and fell.
Lady Zhū supported him,
and only after a long time did he regain consciousness.
He wept, saying:
“My great task is accomplished, but I have lost my sight!
This is Heaven abandoning me!
None of my sons are competent enough to take charge.
If I can entrust things to Yánshòu,
I will have no regrets.”
The Lady was delighted
and urgently summoned Yánshòu.
When Yánshòu arrived,
Hángmì welcomed him to the door of his bedchamber
and had him assassinated,
and sent Lady Zhū out to be married off.
In the second year of Tiānyòu (905),
he sent Liú Cún to attack Èzhōu
and burn its city walls.
The troops inside the city broke through the siege and escaped.
The generals requested to launch an immediate pursuit,
but Cún said:
“If we attack, they will retreat back inside,
and the city defenses will become even stronger.
If we let them leave,
the city can be taken.”
On that very day, the city fell.
Dù Hóng was captured
and executed at Guǎnglíng.
In the ninth month,
the Liáng army broke and captured Xiāngzhōu,
and Zhào Kuāngníng fled to Hángmì.
In the eleventh month,
Hángmì died
at the age of fifty-four.
He was posthumously given the title Wǔzhōng.
His son Wò succeeded him.
Pǔ usurped the imperial title,
and posthumously honored Hángmì as Grand Progenitor Emperor Wǔ (Tàizǔ Wǔ Huángdì).
His mausoleum was named Xīnglíng.
Wò, courtesy name Chéngtiān,
was Hángmì’s eldest son.
When Hángmì fell ill,
he sent Wò out to serve as the Surveillance Commissioner of Xuānzhōu.
Xú Wēn, the Commander of the Right Yamen, secretly said to Wò:
“The King is ill now and is sending out his legitimate heir;
there must be a scheme by treacherous ministers.
If he summons you another day,
you must not answer the order unless it is conveyed by my messenger.”
Wò thanked Wēn tearfully and departed.
When Hángmì's illness became severe,
he ordered the Deputy Director Zhōu Yǐn to write a summons to recall Wò.
Yǐn was concerned that Wò was young and weak and could not handle the affairs,
and advised Hángmì to appoint a veteran general with prestige to temporarily lead the military government.
He then recommended the great general Liú Wēi.
Hángmì had not yet agreed.
Wēn and Yán Kěqiú entered to inquire about his illness.
Hángmì informed them of Yǐn’s suggestion.
Wēn and the others were greatly alarmed
and hurried to Yǐn’s residence to discuss the matter.
Before Yǐn came out,
Wēn saw the recall writ that Yǐn had prepared still on the desk.
He quickly took it and dispatched it.
Wò, seeing Wēn’s messenger,
then set off.
When Hángmì died,
Wò succeeded him.
He summoned Zhōu Yǐn and cursed him, saying:
“You,
who wished to sell my state,
