what face do you have to see the Yáng family again?”
He then executed him.
He appointed Wáng Màozhāng as the Surveillance Commissioner of Xuānzhōu.
When Wò entered (Guǎnglíng),
he transported much of the property from the Xuānzhōu arsenal back to Guǎnglíng.
Màozhāng was reluctant and did not provide it.
Wò was angered,
and ordered Lǐ Jiǎn to besiege him with five thousand troops.
Màozhāng fled to Qiántáng.
In the second month of the third year of Tiānyòu (906),
Liú Cún captured Yuèzhōu.
In the fourth month,
Zhōng Chuán of Jiāngxī died.
His son Kuāngshí temporarily succeeded him.
Chuán's adopted son Yán’guī resented not being appointed
and attacked Kuāngshí with troops.
Wò sent Qín Péi to lead troops to attack them.
In the ninth month,
they captured Hóngzhōu
and arrested Kuāngshí and the Military Advisor Chén Xiàng, bringing them back.
Xiàng was executed in the marketplace,
but Kuāngshí was pardoned.
Qín Péi was appointed Commissioner for Stabilization of Jiāngxī.
replaced Táng,
changing the era name to Kāipíng.
Wò still claimed the era name Tiānyòu.
Liú Cún of Èzhōu and Chén Zhīxīn of Yuèzhōu used a naval force to attack Chǔ.
They were defeated at Liúyáng.
The Chǔ people captured Cún and Zhīxīn and returned [with them].
Mǎ Yīn, the King of Chǔ, had long heard of their reputation
and wanted to spare both of them.
Cún and the others cursed Yīn severely, saying:
"In former years, Xuānchéng escaped beneath our blades.
Our defeat today
is Heaven destroying us.
How could we serve you to beg for survival?
Are we people who would betray the Yáng family?"
Yīn knew they could not be subdued,
so he executed them.
Yuèzhōu thus fell back under the control of Chǔ.
Initially,
when Wò entered Guǎnglíng,
he left three thousand troops from his personal guard in Xuānzhōu,
putting his confidants Chén Fán and Fàn Yù in command.
After he was installed,
he disliked Xú Wēn controlling the Imperial Guard (Yá bīng),
so he summoned Fán and the others to lead the cavalry of the Eastern Quarters for his own protection.
However, Wēn and Zhāng Hào, the Commander of the Left Imperial Guard (Zuǒ Yá Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ), were both veteran generals from Xíngmì’s time,
and they also had the merit of installing Wò.
Together they resented Fán and the others encroaching upon their authority.
In the first month of the fourth year,
when Wò was attending to state affairs,
and Fán and the others were waiting by his side,
Wēn and Hào led the Imperial Guard in,
dragged Fán and the others down,
and executed them.
Wò was unable to stop them.
From this point, he lost control of the government,
but the resentment in his heart had not yet been expressed.
Wēn and the others grew increasingly uneasy.
In the fifth month of the fifth year,
Wēn and Hào jointly sent bandits into the bedchamber to kill Wò.
Wò promised the bandits that anyone who could turn against and kill Wēn and the others would be made an Inspector (Cìshǐ).
The bandits all agreed,
but only Jǐ Xiáng refused to comply.
He seized Wò and strangled him to death.
He was twenty-three years old at the time.
His posthumous title was Jǐng.
His younger brother Lóngyǎn was installed.
Pǔ, usurping the title [of emperor],
posthumously honored Wò as Emperor Jǐng, Lièzōng.
His tomb was called Shàolíng.
Lóngyǎn, courtesy name Hóngyuán,
was the second son of Xíngmì.
His original name was Yíng,
and also Wèi.
Initially,
when Wēn and Hào assassinated Wò,
they had agreed to divide his territory and submit as vassals to Lèang.
When Wò died,
Hào wanted to break the agreement and establish himself [as ruler].
Wēn was troubled by this.
He consulted his guest Yán Kěqíu.
Kěqíu said:
"Although Hào is headstrong and stubborn,
he is ignorant of how to successfully complete an undertaking.
This is easily managed."
The next day,
Hào lined up swords and halberds in the headquarters,
summoned the generals to discuss affairs.
From the great general Zhū Jǐn downwards,
they all had to dismiss their personal guards before entering.
Hào asked the generals,
"Who should we enthrone?"
None of the generals dared to answer.
Hào asked three times.
Kěqíu stepped forward and secretly advised, saying:
"Currently, our four borders are beset by many troubles.
It is not that you cannot become the ruler,
but I fear that doing so would be too quick.
Furthermore, externally we have Liú Wēi, Táo Yǎ, Lǐ Jiǎn, and Lǐ Yù, all being peers of the former King.
Even if you establish yourself,
it is unknown whether this group will willingly submit and serve you.
It would be better to assist a young master to the throne,
and gradually over time,
wait until [the generals] give their allegiance,
and then you may proceed."
Hào was unable to respond.
Kěqíu immediately rushed out,
wrote an edict and hid it in his sleeve,
and led the generals in to offer congratulations.
The generals did not know what they were doing.
When he produced the edict and proclaimed it,
it was an edict from Wò’s mother, Lady Shǐ.
It stated that the Yáng family founded their enterprise with great difficulty,
but the heir had been unfortunate.
Lóngyǎn should succeed him according to precedence,
and it instructed the generals not to fail the Yáng family but to serve him well.
The phrasing was stirring and poignant,
and those who heard it were deeply moved.
Hào’s expression was completely crestfallen.
Ultimately, he was powerless to act,
and Lóngyǎn was thus able to be installed.
Hào subsequently had a rift with Wēn.
He subtly advised Lóngyǎn to send Wēn out to Rùnzhōu.
Kěqíu said to Wēn:
"Now, abandoning the Imperial Guard and going out to an external prefecture,
disaster will soon arrive."
Wēn was worried about this.
Kěqíu then spoke to Hào, saying:
"You and Xú Wēn both received the mandate [of the former king].
Commentators say that by stripping him of the Imperial Guard,
you intend to kill him externally.
Is this true?"
Hào said:
"The action has already been taken.
How can it be stopped?"
Kěqíu said:
"It is very easy."
The next day,
he accompanied Hào and the generals to visit Wēn.
Kěqíu feigned blame toward Wēn, saying:
"The ancients did not forget the kindness of a single meal,
much less you, a general of the Yáng family for three generations.
Now that the young heir is newly installed,
in a time of great troubles,
how can you request to reside outside merely to seek temporary peace?"
Wēn also feigned thanks, saying:
"Since you gentlemen wish to keep me here,
I do not desire to leave."
Consequently, the transfer did not proceed.
Lǐ Chéngsì, the Deputy Commander of Military Affairs (Xíngjūn Fùshǐ), was friendly with Zhāng Hào.
He perceived that Kěqíu intended to attach himself to Wēn,
and hinted to Hào to hire an assassin to kill Kěqíu that night.
The assassin stabbed Kěqíu but failed to strike a fatal blow.
The next day,
Kěqíu went to Wēn,
and they plotted to kill Hào first.
He secretly sent Zhōng Zhāng to select thirty brave men,
who executed Hào in the inner court.
They then blamed him for the crime of assassinating Wò.
Wēn thus gained control of the government,
and Lóngyǎn merely occupied the throne.
In the sixth month,
Wēi Quánfěng of Fǔzhōu rebelled
and attacked Hóngzhōu.
Péng Yànzhāng of Yuánzhōu, Péng Gān of Jízhōu, and Wēi Zǐchàng of Xìnzhōu all raised troops and revolted.
Lóngyǎn summoned Yán Kěqíu and asked who was capable of handling the situation.
Kěqíu recommended Zhōu Běn.
At that time, Běn had recently returned defeated from attacking Sūzhōu,
and was ashamed and unwilling to come out.
Kěqíu strongly urged him to take the command.
Běn said:
"The defeat at Sūzhōu
was not due to cowardice,
but because the chief commander's authority was weak,
and the subordinates often acted independently.
If I must be entrusted with the task,
I request that no subcommanders or adjutants be employed."
He then requested seven thousand troops.
They fought at Xiàngyátán,
and defeated the rebels.
They captured Quánfěng and Yànzhāng,
while Gān fled to Chǔ,
and Zǐchàng fled to Qiántáng.
When Quánfěng arrived at Guǎnglíng,
the generals deliberated, saying:
"In the past, when the former King attacked Zhào Huáng,
Quánfěng repeatedly supplied rations to the Wú army."
Thus, he was released and not executed.
Originally,
when Quánfěng intended to raise troops,
Qián Líu was sending Wáng Màozhāng to Lèang.
Màozhāng passed by Quánfěng on the way
and said to him:
"I hear you wish to launch a major campaign.
I would like to see your troops,
so that I may know whether you will succeed or not."
Quánfěng arrayed his troops,
and together with Màozhāng, he ascended the city wall to view them.
Màozhāng said:
"I have long served Wú.
The Wú army has three ranks.
A force like yours
could only match their lowest rank of generals.
Unless you gain ten thousand more troops, you cannot succeed."
But Quánfěng was ultimately defeated because of this.
In the eighth year,
Xú Wēn assumed the leadership of Shēngzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Shēng Prefecture),
and organized naval forces at Jīnlíng.
Lǐ Yù of Xuānzhōu had been a great general since the time of Xíng Mì,
and his meritorious rank was already high.
He resented Wēn exercising power,
and once said:
"Who is Xú Wēn?
I still don't know him,
yet he has suddenly risen to this point."
Wēn heard this,
and was angered.
He sent Chái Zàiyòng with troops to escort Wáng Tán to replace Yù,
and also summoned Yù.
Yù was suspicious and refused the order.
Zàiyòng besieged him.
Lóngyǎn sent the guest general Hé Ráo to persuade Yù to surrender himself.
Ráo then argued, saying:
"If Your Lordship truly intends to rebel,
you may kill Ráo to show the masses.
If you originally had no such intention,
why not follow Ráo and leave?"
Yù felt that he had no intention of rebelling,
so he followed Ráo out.
Wēn secretly instructed Zàiyòng to wait for him to come out,
kill him,
and exterminate his entire family.
In the ninth year,
Wēn led the generals and officials in promoting Lóngyǎn to the positions of Tàishī (Grand Tutor), Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Central Secretariat), and King of Wú (Wú Wáng).

Wēn was made Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (Mobilization Commander), Zhènhǎijūn Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of the Zhènhǎi Circuit), and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Joint Manager of the Affairs of the Secretariats).
Chén Zhāng attacked Chǔ and captured Yuèzhōu,
seizing its Cìshǐ (Prefect) Yuàn Méi.
In the tenth year,
the Yuè people attacked Chángzhōu.
Xú Wēn defeated them at Wúxī.
Liáng sent Wáng Màozhāng to attack Shòuchūn.
Wēn defeated him at Huòqiū.
In the twelfth year, Xú Wēn was enfeoffed as the Duke of Qí (Qí Guógōng) and Chief Commander of the Two Zhè Districts (Liǎngzhè Dūzhāotǎoshǐ).
He first took up residence in Rùnzhōu.
He left his son, Zhīxùn, as Xíngjūn Fùshǐ (Deputy Mobilization Commander),
to manage the government,
but major affairs were decided remotely by Wēn.
In winter,
the Yánglín Jiāng river was dredged.
Fire came out of the water,
capable of burning.
In the thirteenth year,
the palace guards Lǐ Qiú and Mǎ Qiān coerced Lóngyǎn onto a tower,
took weapons from the armory to execute Zhīxùn,
and arrayed their forces at Mén Qiáo (Gate Bridge).
Zhīxùn fought them,
but was frequently repulsed.
Zhū Jǐn happened to arrive from outside.
He rode forward alone to observe their formation,
and said:
"This is not worth bothering with."
He then looked back and gave a single wave of his hand.
The outside troops rushed forward,
subsequently beheading Qiú and Qiān,
and the rebel soldiers all scattered.
In the fourteenth year,
Xú Wēn moved his administrative center to Jīnlíng.
In the fifteenth year,
Wēn sent Wáng Qí to gather troops from the three prefectures of Hóng, Yuán, and Xìn, to attack Qián and Sháo.
After a long time, they failed to conquer them.
Qí fell ill,
and Liú Xìn replaced him.
In the fourth month,
Deputy Commander-in-Chief Zhū Jǐn killed Xú Zhīxùn.
Jǐn then committed suicide.
Xú Zhīgào of Rùnzhōu heard of the chaos,
led troops in,
killed the Táng Envoy Lǐ Yǎn to stop the disorder,
and thereby took charge of the government.
When the Xú clan monopolized power,
Lóngyǎn was young and weak,
unable to maintain control,
and Zhīxùn especially harassed and insulted him.
Once, while drinking wine upstairs,
Lóngyǎn ordered the actor Gāo Guìqīng to serve wine.
Zhīxùn acted as a Military Advisor (Cānjūn).
Lóngyǎn wore ragged clothes and braided hair, acting as a falcon.
Zhīxùn often used the occasion of drinking to curse the assembly,
with words insulting Lóngyǎn.
Lóngyǎn felt shame, blushed, and wept,
but Zhīxùn insulted him even more severely.
Attendants helped Lóngyǎn stand up and leave.
Zhīxùn killed one official,
and then stopped.
The people of Wú all looked askance.
Zhīxùn also had a feud with Zhū Jǐn.
When Jǐn had killed Zhīxùn,
he carried his head and rushed into the government compound, showing it to Lóngyǎn and saying:
"Today, a menace has been removed for Wú."
Lóngyǎn said:
"This matter is not something I dare to know."
He immediately stood up and went inside.
Jǐn became furious,
struck the pillar with the head,
grabbed his sword, and went out.
The gate of the compound was already closed.
He climbed over the wall,
broke his leg,
and subsequently cut his own throat and died.
Mǐ Zhìchéng heard that Jǐn had killed Zhīxùn.
He put on armor and led his household troops to Tiānxīng Mén (Gate of Heavenly Prosperity) to ask where Jǐn was.
Hearing that Jǐn was dead,
he then returned.
Xú Wēn suspected Zhìchéng of assisting Jǐn,
and sent an envoy to kill him.
Yán Kěqiú feared that the action would fail,
so he had someone pretend to arrive from the border of Húnán to report a military victory.
He summoned the generals to come in and offer congratulations,
captured Zhìchéng, and beheaded him.
Liú Xìn conquered Qiánzhōu,
capturing Tán Quánbō and returning.
In the sixteenth year,
in the second month of spring,
Wēn led the generals and officials to request that Lóngyǎn assume the position of Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
He did not permit it.
In the fourth month of summer,
Wēn, presenting the jade tablet and precious seal cord, honored Lóngyǎn to ascend the position of King of Wú.
He established ancestral temples and altars to the gods of land and grain (Shèjì),
and set up the hundred officials according to the system of the Son of Heaven.
He changed the sixteenth year of Tiānyòu to the first year of Wǔyì,
and granted a great amnesty throughout the territory.
He posthumously honored Xíng Mì as King Xiàowǔ,
with the temple name Tàizǔ (Grand Progenitor),
and Wò Jǐngwáng (King Wò Jǐng),
with the temple name Lièzǔ (Illustrious Progenitor).
Wēn was appointed Dà Chéngxiàng (Grand Chancellor) and Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs Internal and External),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōnghǎi Commandery (Dōnghǎi Jùnwáng).
Xú Zhīgào was made Zuǒ Púshè (Left Executive Assistant) and Cānzhī Zhèngshì (Participant in the Administration of Government).
Yán Kěqiú was made Ménxià Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Chancellery).
Luò Zhīxiáng was made Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Secretariat).
Yīn Wénkuí and Shěn Yán were made Hànlín Xuéshì (Academicians of the Hanlin Academy).
Lú Zé was made Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel).
Lǐ Zōng and Chén Zhāng were made Left and Right Xióngwǔ Tǒngjūn (Commanders of the Valiant and Martial Forces).
Chái Zàiyòng and Qián Biāo were made Left and Right Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn (Commanders of the Dragon and Martial Forces).
Wáng Lìngmóu was made Nèi Shūmìshǐ (Internal Commissioner of Military Affairs).
Liú Xìn of Jiāngxī was made Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General Who Conquers the South).
Lǐ Jiǎn of Èzhōu was made Zhènxī Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General Who Guards the West).
Lǐ Déchéng of Fǔzhōu was made Píngnán Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General Who Pacifies the South).
Zhāng Chóng of Lúzhōu was made Ānxī Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General Who Pacifies the West).
Wáng Wǎn of Hǎizhōu was made Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General Who Guards the East).
Civil and military officials were promoted in sequence.
All members of the imperial clan were enfeoffed as Commandery Dukes (Jùngōng).
When Wēn moved his garrison to Jīnlíng,
he ordered his adopted son, Zhīgào, to guard Rùnzhōu.
Yán Kěqiú once said to Wēn:
"The second son (Zhīgào) is not a true son of the Xú clan,
yet he supports the worthy and is condescending to gentlemen,
and popular support is leaning toward him.
If you do not remove him,
I fear he will become a future danger."
Wēn was unable to adopt his advice.
When Zhīgào took charge of the government,
Kěqiú's statement was leaked.
Zhīgào dismissed Kěqiú to Chǔzhōu.
Kěqiú was afraid,
and went to Jīnlíng to see Wēn and plot, saying:
"It has been twelve years since Táng perished,
yet Wú still does not dare to change the Tiānyòu era name.
It can be said that we have not failed Táng.
However, the reason Wú conquered the four directions
and established its foundational enterprise
was always using the pretext of restoration.
Now we hear that in the battles on the river,
the Liáng forces have repeatedly lost ground.
If the Lǐ clan were to revive,
would Wú be able to yield its authority?
It is appropriate at this time to first establish our own state to secure our independence."
Wēn deeply agreed with this,
and consequently detained Kěqiú and did not dismiss him.
They were then planning to force Lóngyǎn to assume the imperial title.
In the fifth month of the second year,
Lóngyǎn died.
Lóngyǎn succeeded to the throne while still young,
and power rested with the Xú clan.
When the state was established and he assumed the imperial system,
it was against his wishes.
He was perpetually dejected,
drank heavily,
and seldom ate,
eventually leading to illness and death
at the age of twenty-four.
His posthumous title was Xuān.
His younger brother Pǔ was enthroned.
He claimed the imperial title,
and posthumously honored Lóngyǎn as Gāozǔ Xuān Huángdì (Grand Progenitor, Emperor Xuān).
His tomb was named Sùlíng.
Pǔ,
was Xíngmì’s fourth son.
When Lóngyǎn founded the state,
Pǔ was enfeoffed as the Duke of Dānyáng Commandery (Dānyáng Jùn Gōng).
When Lóngyǎn died,
his younger brother Méng, the Duke of Lújiāng, was next in line to ascend the throne.
However, the Xú clan controlled the government,
and not desiring a mature ruler,
they consequently established Pǔ.
In the seventh month,
Shēngzhōu Grand Military Governorship (Dà Dūdū Fǔ) was changed to Jīnlíng Prefecture (Fǔ).
Xú Wēn was appointed the Prefect (Yǐn) of Jīnlíng.
In the second month of the following year,
the era name was changed to Shùnyì,
and a general amnesty was granted throughout the territory.
In the winter, eleventh month,
sacrifices were offered to Heaven in the southern suburbs.
He proceeded to the Tiānxīng Tower
and granted a great amnesty.
Xú Wēn was appointed Grand Tutor (Tài Shī),
and Yán Kěqiú was appointed Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púshè).
In the third year,
Zhuāngzōng of Táng destroyed Liáng.
He dispatched Lú Píng, Minister of Agriculture (Sī Nóng Qīng), as envoy to Táng.
Yán Kěqiú secretly drew up several articles and presented them to Píng for his mission.
Píng had an audience in Luòyáng.
Zhuāngzōng questioned him,
and Píng answered him item by item,
all exactly as he had been instructed.
In the fourth year,
Pǔ went to Báishā to review the naval forces.
Xú Wēn came to meet him,
and Báishā was established as Yíngluán Garrison (Zhèn).
In the fifth year,
Táng dispatched Xuē Zhāowén, Censor-Consultant (Jiàn Yì Dà Fū), as envoy to Fúzhōu.
He borrowed a route through Jiāngxī.
Liú Xìn went out to offer greetings and comfort,
and said to him:
"Has your Sovereign (Yà Cì) heard of Xìn?"
Zhāowén replied:
"The Son of Heaven has only recently acquired Hénán,
and is not yet familiar with your name, sir."
Xìn said:
"Hàn had Hán Xìn,
Wú has Liú Xìn.
When you return,
tell your Sovereign
that I should come to compete in archery on the Huái River."
Then he poured a great goblet of wine,
facing the point of the military banner a hundred paces away.
He said to Zhāowén:
"If I hit it with one shot,
I wish to use this goblet to toast your long life.
If not, I shall use it to punish myself."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the arrow had already pierced the target.
In the sixth year,
posthumous titles were granted to Xú Wēn's ancestors for four generations, making them Grand Chancellors (Dà Chéngxiàng),
and a temple was established for them in Jīnlíng.
Xú Zhīgào, Director of the Department of State Affairs (Zuǒ Púshè), became Grand Councillor (Shìzhōng).
Yán Kěqiú, Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púshè), was granted the title Concurrent Administrator of Affairs (Tóng Píngzhāng Shì).
That year,
Zhuāngzōng died.
On the Dīngmǎo day of the fifth month,
an imperial edict decreed the suspension of court for seven days in mourning for the Sovereign of Tóngguāng.
In the seventh year,
Grand Chancellor Xú Wēn led the civil and military officials of Wú in presenting a memorial urging Pǔ to ascend the throne as Emperor.
Pǔ had not yet agreed when Wēn fell ill and died.
On the Gēngxū day of the eleventh month,
Pǔ proceeded to the Wénmíng Hall and ascended the throne as Emperor.
He changed the era name to Qiánzhēn,
and granted a great amnesty throughout the territory.
He posthumously honored Xíngmì as Emperor Wǔ;
Wòjǐng as Emperor Huángdì;
and Lóngyǎn as Emperor Xuān.
Xú Zhīgào was made Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and concurrently Grand Councillor (Shìzhōng).
Wēn’s son, Zhīxún, was appointed Grand General Who Assists the State (Fǔ Guó Dà Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of Jīnlíng (Jīnlíng Yǐn),
governing Wēn’s former garrison.
All of his sons were enfeoffed as princes (Wáng).
In the first month of the second year,
Dōng Hǎi (the East Sea) was enfeoffed as Guǎngdé Wáng,
the Jiāng Dú (River God) as Guǎngyuán Wáng,
the Huái Dú (Huai River God) as Chángyuán Wáng,
the Upper Water Residence of Mǎdāng as Níngjiāng Wáng,
the Middle Water Residence of Cǎishí as Dìngjiāng Wáng,
and the Lower Water Residence of Jīnshān as Zhènjiāng Wáng.
In the sixth month,
Gāo Jìxīng of Jīngnán came to submit,
and Jìxīng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín (Qín Wáng).
In the ninth month,
Jìxīng defeated the Chǔ army at Báitián,
capturing thirty-four of their generals and officials, whom he presented.
In the eleventh month of the third year,
Xú Zhīxún, Prefect of Jīnlíng, came to court.
Zhīgào falsely accused him of having rebellious intent,
detained him and did not let him leave.
He was made Left Commander of the Army (Zuǒ Tǒng Jūn),
and his guest general, Zhōu Tíngwàng, was executed.
Xú Zhī’è was made Prefect of Jīnlíng.
Pǔ was given the honored title of Ruìshèng Wénmíng Xiào Huángdì.
A great amnesty was granted throughout the territory,
and the era name was changed to Dàhé.
Xú Zhīgào was made Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
In the second year,
his son, Lián, the Prince of Jiāngdū, was formally designated as Crown Prince (Tài Zǐ).
In the third year,
Xú Zhīgào was made Prefect of Jīnlíng.
His son, Jǐngtōng, was made Minister of the Masses (Sītú),

and Wáng Lìngmóu, Left Director of the Department of State Affairs (Zuǒ Púshè), and Sòng Qíqiū, Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púshè), were both made Concurrent Administrators of Affairs (Píngzhāng Shì).
In the fourth year,
Zhīgào was enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōng Hǎi (Dōng Hǎi Wáng).
In the fifth year,
the capital was established at Jīnlíng.
In the intercalary first month of the sixth year,
Jīnlíng caught fire,
and the plan to establish the capital was abandoned.
Méng, the Prince of Línchuān, was deposed as the Duke of Lìyáng.
Zhīgào dispatched his trusted associate Wáng Hóng with troops to guard him.
Lìngmóu was appointed Minister of the Masses (Sītú),
and Sòng Qíqiū was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Zhīgào summoned Jǐngtōng back to Jīnlíng,
to serve as Deputy Military Commissioner (Jiédù Fùshǐ) of Zhènhǎi Army.
His son, Jǐngqiān, was made Grand Guardian (Tài Bǎo) and Concurrent Administrator of Affairs (Píngzhāng Shì),
administering the government alongside Lìngmóu and others.
In the ninth month of the seventh year,
Pǔ was given the honored title of Ruìshèng Wénmíng Guāngxiào Yìngtiān Hóngdào Guǎngdé Huángdì.
A great amnesty was granted,
and the era name was changed to Tiānzuò.
Zhīgào was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tài Shī) and Grand Marshal of the Armies of the Realm (Tiānxià Bīngmǎ Dà Yuánshuài),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng).
In the second year,
Jǐngqiān fell ill,
and his second son, Jǐngsuì, was made Vice Director of the Chancellery (Ménxià Shìláng) and granted the title Participant in Government (Cān Zhèngshì).
In the third year,
Zhīgào established the state of Qí,
setting up ancestral temples and altars to the gods of soil and grain.
He established the offices of Left and Right Chancellors (Zuǒ, Yòu Chéngxiàng) and lesser positions.
Jīnlíng was designated as the Western Capital (Xī Dū),
and Guǎnglíng as the Eastern Capital (Dōng Dū).
In the winter, tenth month,
Pǔ dispatched Lín, the Prince of Jiāngxià, to present the imperial seal and abdicate the throne to the Prince of Qí.
In the twelfth month,
Pǔ died in Dānyáng,
aged thirty-eight.
His posthumous title was Ruì.
In the sixth year of Shēngyuán,
Lǐ Jǐng moved Pǔ's descendants to Hǎilíng.
Their residence was named Yǒngníng Palace.
They were guarded strictly by troops,
and completely cut off from contact with outsiders.
After a long time, the men and women married among themselves.
The people of Wú mostly felt pity for them.
In the third year of Xiǎndé,
Shìzōng campaigned against Huáinán.
He issued an edict to comfort and settle the descendants of the Yáng clan.
When Lǐ Jǐng heard of this,
he dispatched men to kill the entire clan.
Liú Chóngjìn, the Supervisor-in-Chief of the Vanguard of Zhōu, obtained their jade inkstone, agate bowl, and kingfisher-feather vase and presented them.
Thus, the Yáng lineage was extinguished.
Xú Wēn
Xú Wēn, courtesy name Dūnměi,
was a native of Qúshān, Hǎizhōu.
When young, he was a salt smuggler and a bandit.
When Xíngmì raised forces at Héféi,
Xú Wēn joined his ranks.
The people with whom Xíngmì initially started the uprising—such as Liú Wēi and Táo Yǎ—
were called the Thirty-Six Heroes.
Wēn alone had never achieved military distinction.
When Xíngmì wished to kill Zhū Yánshòu and others,
Wēn employed the strategy of his retainer Yán Kěqiú.
He advised Xíngmì to feign an eye disease.
When the affair succeeded,
he was transferred due to this merit to Right Commander of the Palace Guard (Yòu Yá Zhǐhuī Shǐ),
and only then did he begin to participate in planning and deliberation.
When Yáng Hángmì fell ill,
his lifelong veteran generals
were all outside conducting battles and defenses,
but Wēn was residing beneath the commander's tent,
and thus participated in the merits of establishing Wò.
When Wò was assassinated,
Wēn again had a rift with Zhāng Hào,
and he had Zhōng Zhāng kill him.
Zhāng promised agreement,
selected thirty stout warriors,
slaughtered oxen to feast them,
and pricked blood to swear an alliance.
Wēn still doubted that Zhāng would carry it out,
and at midnight sent someone to probe his intentions,
falsely telling him:
“Wēn has an aged mother,
and fears the plot will not succeed;
it is better to stop for now.”
Zhāng replied:
“Words have already left the mouth;
can we stop now?”
Wēn was then relieved.
The next day,
Zhōng Zhāng killed Hào.
Wēn subsequently executed Jǐ Xiáng and others,
imputed the crime of assassinating Wò to Hào,
and entered to report the matter to Wò’s mother, Shǐshì.
Shǐshì trembled and wept, saying:
“My son was young,
and the turmoil was like this.
To be able to keep our hundred-odd people safe and return to Héféi
is due to your grace, my lord.”
When Lóngyǎn was enthroned,
Wēn then monopolized political power,
was promoted to Prefect of Shēngzhōu,
and built a naval fleet at Jīnlíng.
The great general Lǐ Yù was angered by Wēn's assumption of power
and spoke arrogant words.
Wēn had Chái Zàiyòng exterminate Yù's clan in Xuānzhōu.
Yáng Hángmì's old generals
all became suspicious of themselves.
Wēn then pretended to humble himself before them,
being respectful and cautious as if seeing Hángmì,
and the generals were then reassured.
In the eighth year [of Wǔyì],
Wēn was promoted to Army Administrator, Prefect of Rùnzhōu, Jìedùshǐ of Zhènhǎijūn, and Grand Councilor (Tóng píngzhāng shì).
In the tenth year,
he dispatched the Commander of Suppression and Pacification Lǐ Tāo to attack Yuè,
and they fought at Lín'ān.
The deputy general Cáo Jūn defected to Yuè,
and Tāo was defeated and captured.
Wēn secretly sent someone to speak to Jūn, saying:
“I employed you as a general,
and when your army had requests,
I could not supply them.
This is my fault.”
He pardoned Jūn's wife and children and did not execute them,
treating them generously.
In the autumn,
the Yuè people attacked Pílíng.
Wēn fought at Wúxī.
Jūn was moved by Wēn’s previous words,
defected back just before the battle,
and subsequently defeated the Yuè forces.
In the twelfth year,
Wēn was enfeoffed as the Duke of Qí State,
and concurrently held the title of Commander of Suppression and Pacification of the Two Zhè Regions.
He first took up residence in Rùnzhōu,
and the six prefectures of Shēng, Rùn, Xuān, Cháng, Chí, and Huáng were designated as the State of Qí.
Wēn fortified Shēngzhōu
and established a Grand Commandery Administrator's Residence (Dà Dūdū Fǔ).
In the fourteenth year,
he moved the governance there.
He had his son Zhīxùn assist Lóngyǎn in Guǎnglíng,
while Wēn remotely decided major affairs.
When Zhīxùn was killed by Zhū Jǐn,
Wēn's adopted son Zhīgào entered first from Rùnzhōu,
and subsequently obtained political power.
Although Wēn was treacherous, deceitful, and suspicious,
he was skilled at employing generals and officials.
When Liú Xìn of Jiāngxī besieged Qiánzhōu
for a long time without success,
he sent someone to persuade Tán Quánbō to surrender,
and dispatched an envoy to report to Wēn.
Wēn was angry and said:
“Xìn, with ten times the multitude,
cannot take a single city,
but instead uses a persuader to make it surrender.
How can this be used to overawe enemy states?”
He had the envoy beaten with a bamboo rod and sent him away,
saying:
“I am beating Xìn through him.”
He then ordered troops to reinforce the army,
and subsequently defeated Quánbō.
Someone falsely accused Xìn of lingering and secretly allowing Quánbō to escape,
saying that Xìn was about to rebel.
When Xìn heard this,
he personally presented the victory report and came to Jīnlíng to see Wēn.
Wēn gambled with Xìn.
Xìn collected the dice and loudly swore an oath, saying:
“If Liú Xìn wishes to betray Wú,
may I roll a wicked result;
if I have no second thoughts,
may I achieve a perfect 'flourish.'”
Wēn hastily stopped him.
With one throw,
all six dice were red.
Wēn felt ashamed.
He personally poured a cup of wine and offered it to Xìn,
but he remained suspicious of him until the end.
When the Táng army attacked Wáng Yǎn,
Wēn urgently summoned Xìn to Guǎnglíng,
made him Left Commander (Zuǒ Tǒngjūn),
on the pretext of internal defense,
and thus seized his territory.
Among Wēn's retainers who were particularly trusted by him,
there were only Luò Zhīxiáng and Yán Kěqiú.
Kěqiú was good at planning and strategy;
Zhīxiáng excelled in finance and profit.
Wēn often asked Kěqiú about military affairs,
and Zhīxiáng about state expenditure.
The people of Wú called them
“Yán and Luò.”
Wēn also took pleasure in his own ingenuity and cunning,
and particularly won the hearts of the Wú people.
When he first followed Hángmì to defeat Zhào Huáng,
the generals all scrambled for gold and silks,
but Wēn alone occupied the remaining granaries,
making congee to feed the starving.
In the sixteenth year,
Wēn requested that Lóngyǎn assume the title of Emperor,
but this was not permitted.
He then requested that he assume the title of King of Wú,
which was permitted.
Thereupon, the state was established and the era name was changed.
Wēn was appointed Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng) and Commander-in-Chief of All Military Forces (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōnghǎi Commandery.
When Lóngyǎn died,
Wēn bypassed the order of succession and enthroned his younger brother Pǔ.
In the seventh year of Shùnyì,
Wēn again requested that Pǔ assume the title of Emperor.
Pǔ had not yet consented when Wēn fell ill and died,
at the age of sixty-six.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as the King of Qí
and granted the posthumous title Wǔ.
When Lǐ Biàn usurped the title,
he posthumously honored Wēn as Yìzǔ.
Alas,
that even bandits have their Way (Dào),
is truly believable!
The writings about Yáng Xíngmì
describe Yáng Xíngmì’s character
as generous, benevolent, refined, and trustworthy,
able to win the hearts of gentlemen.
When his general Cài Chóu rebelled at Lúzhōu,
he utterly destroyed Xíngmì’s graves and tombs.
When Chóu was defeated,
all the generals requested destroying Chóu’s tomb to retaliate against him.
Xíngmì sighed, saying:
“Chóu committed this evil using this means,
how could I repeat such an action?”
He once ordered his attendant, Zhāng Hóng, to bear his sword and serve him.
Hóng drew the sword and struck Xíngmì,
but missed.
Hóng died.
He again employed Chén Shào, whom Hóng favored, to bear the sword,
without suspicion.
He also once cursed his general Liú Xìn.
Xìn became angry,
and fled to Sūn Rú.
Xíngmì warned his attendants not to pursue him,
saying:
“How could Xìn betray me?
He departed while drunk;
when sober, he will surely return.”
The next day,
he indeed returned.
Xíngmì rose up from banditry,
and his subordinates were all fierce, courageous, and violent,
yet they were happy to be used by him,
because of this.
Thus, two generations and four rulers lasted nearly fifty years.
When [Yáng] Wò took over,
governing power rested with Xú Wēn.
At this time,
the world was in great chaos,
the calamities of the Central States (Zhōngguó),
usurpation and regicide followed one after another,
yet Xú's father and son,
relying merely on schemes and force,
lingered under three rulers,
not daring to lightly seize the throne.
Why?
Could it be that his grace and might still held influence over the people?
According to the Wúlù, the Yùnlìtú, and the Jiǔguózhì, they all say that Xíngmì, in the first year of Táng Jǐngfú,
re-entered Yángzhōu,
until the second year of Jìn Tiānfú,
when he was usurped by Lǐ Dǎo,
making it actually forty-six years.
However, the Jiù Táng Shū and the Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ all say: He entered Yángzhōu in the second year of Dàshùn,
until the usurpation,
forty-seven years.
The Wúlù was compiled by Xú Xuàn and others,
the Yùnlìtú was compiled by Gōng Yǐng.
Both men were former officials of Jiāngnán,
so their records should be accurate.
But during the disturbances at the end of the Táng dynasty,
texts in the central court contained many errors,
therefore, we now take the records of Xuàn and Yǐng as definitive.
The Hereditary House of Nán Táng, Second Ruler: Lǐ Dǎo (Son Jǐng, Jǐng's Son Yù)
Lǐ Dǎo, courtesy name Zhènglún,
was a man from Xúzhōu.
His family background was originally humble.
His father, Róng,
encountered the chaos at the end of the Táng,
and his fate is unknown.
Dǎo was orphaned young,
and drifted and settled between Háozhōu and Sìzhōu.
When Yáng Xíngmì attacked Háozhōu,
he captured him,
admired his appearance,
and adopted him as a son.
However, Yáng’s other sons could not tolerate him,
so Xíngmì gifted him to Xú Wēn.
He then falsely adopted the surname Xú,
and was named Zhīgào.
When he reached adulthood,
he was seven *chǐ* tall,
with a broad forehead and a prominent nose.
As a person, he was gentle, generous, and resourceful.
He served as the Commandant of the Navy (Lóuchuán Jūnshǐ) for Wú,
stationing naval troops at Jīnlíng.
Chái Zàiyòng attacked Xuānzhōu,
using Zhīgào’s troops to kill Lǐ Yù.
Dǎo was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Shēngzhōu due to his merit.
At that time, Jiānghuái had just been settled,
and most prefectural and county officials were military men,
focused on levying taxes and maintaining battle defenses.
Dǎo alone loved learning,
treated scholars with courtesy,
disciplined himself to be diligent and frugal,
and governed with leniency and benevolence.
The people gradually praised him.
Xú Wēn was stationed at Rùnzhōu,
taking six prefectures including Shēngzhōu and Chízhōu as his dependencies.
Wēn heard that Dǎo had implemented good governance in Shēngzhōu,
and went to inspect it.
Seeing that the storehouses were full,
and the city walls were well-maintained,
he moved his headquarters there,
and transferred Dǎo to be the Prefect of Rùnzhōu.
Dǎo initially did not want to go,
repeatedly requesting Xuānzhōu,
but Wēn did not grant it.
Soon after, Xú Zhīxùn was killed by Zhū Jǐn.
Wēn was residing in Jīnlíng,
and had not yet heard the news.
Dǎo, residing in Rùnzhōu,
was close to Guǎnglíng,
and heard the news first.
That same day, he crossed the river with his prefectural troops to suppress the chaos,
and subsequently gained control of the government.
Dǎo served Xú Wēn with great filial piety and caution.
Wēn once scolded his own sons, saying they were inferior to Dǎo.
The other sons could hardly tolerate him,
and Zhīxùn was especially severe.
He once summoned Dǎo to a drinking party,
having swordsmen lying in wait to kill him.
The official serving the wine, Diāo Yànnéng, perceived this.
When the wine reached Dǎo,
he used his fingernail to pinch (Dǎo).
Dǎo realized the danger, got up and fled,
and thus escaped.
Later, Dǎo entered the capital from Rùnzhōu for an audience.
Zhīxùn drank with him at Shānguāng Sì,
and again tried to harm him.
Xú Zhījiàn informed Dǎo of the plot,
and Dǎo got up and escaped.
Zhīxùn handed a sword to Diāo Yànnéng,
ordering him to pursue and kill Dǎo.
Yànnéng reached him halfway and returned,
falsely reporting that he could not catch him.
Because of this, Dǎo escaped death.
Later, when Dǎo became powerful,
he appointed Yànnéng as Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of Fǔzhōu.
When Zhīxùn was in power,
he habitually bullied the weak Yáng clan and treated the generals arrogantly,
and was consequently killed.
When Dǎo took control of the government,
wishing to win over the people,
he relaxed the criminal laws and extended grace and trust.
He built the Yánbīntíng (Pavilion for Welcoming Guests) to receive scholars from all regions.
He invited Sòng Qíqiū, Luò Zhīxiáng, Wáng Lìngmóu, and others to be his advisors.
Any gentlemen residing as sojourners in Wú
were all given positions.
He often secretly sent people to observe the populace and check on those who lacked resources for marriages or funerals,
and frequently provided them with relief.
In the extreme heat, he never used a parasol or held a fan.
When his attendants presented a parasol,
he would surely refuse it,
saying:
"My soldiers and people are still greatly exposed (to the elements).
Why should I use this?"
Because of this, although Wēn remotely held great political power,
the people of Wú largely had already aligned themselves with Dǎo.
In the first year of Wǔyì,
he was appointed Left Vice-Director (Zuǒ Púshè),
participating in state affairs (Cānzhī Zhèngshì).
Wēn’s Army Commander (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ), Xú Jiè, repeatedly urged Wēn to replace Dǎo with his own son.
Wēn sent his son Zhīxún to enter Guǎnglíng,
plotting to replace Dǎo in controlling the government.
Just then, Wēn died from illness.
Zhīxún rushed back to Jīnlíng.
Jiè, conversely, plotted for Dǎo,
falsely accusing Zhīxún of crimes,
executing his guest general Zhōu Tíngwàng,
and appointing Zhīxún as Right Commandant (Yòu Tǒngjūn).
Yáng Pǔ usurped the title (Emperor),
and appointed Dǎo as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Director of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
In the third year of Dàhé,
he left to be stationed in Jīnlíng,
following the precedent of Wēn.
He left his son Jǐngtōng to be Minister of Education (Sītú) and Grand Councillor (Tóng Píngzhāng Shì),
and appointed Wáng Lìngmóu and Sòng Qíqiū as Left and Right Vice-Directors (Zuǒ, Yòu Púshè) and Grand Councillors (Tóng Píngzhāng Shì).
In the fourth year,
Dǎo was enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōnghǎi Commandery (Dōnghǎi Jùnwáng).
Dǎo looked in a mirror and saw white whiskers.
He turned to his official Zhōu Zōng and sighed, saying:
"My great accomplishments are already established,
yet I am old now,
what shall I do?"
Zōng knew his intent,
and immediately rode to Guǎnglíng to see Sòng Qíqiū,
plotting the abdication and succession.
Qíqiū believed it was not yet the right time,
and requested executing Zōng to apologize to the people of Wú.
Dǎo demoted Zōng to be the Prefect of Chízhōu.
Méng, Prince of Línjiāng of Wú,
resented Xú Shì abandoning him and establishing Pǔ,
his heart was constantly troubled.
When Lǐ Bǐng was about to plot usurpation of the state,
he first deposed Méng to become the Duke of Lìyáng,
ordering officials to guard him with troops.
Méng killed the guards,
fleeing to Zhōu Běn, the Jìedùshǐ of Lúzhōu.
Běn
was an old general of Wú.
Hearing Méng arrived,
he wanted to take him in,
but was prevented by his son, Zuò.
Běn said:
“This is the young master of my former lord’s house;
how can I bear to reject him!”
He hurriedly went out to welcome him,
but Zuò closed the gates, preventing Běn from leaving,
tied up Méng and sent him to Jīnlíng,
where he was killed.
In the fifth year,
Lǐ Bǐng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí.
Soon afterwards, the states of Mǐn and Yuè all sent envoys urging him to ascend the throne.
Lǐ Bǐng believed popular support had shifted to him.
In the third year of Tiānzuò,
he established the state of Qí,
set up ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
and made Sòng Qíqiū and Xú Jiè the Left and Right Chéngxiàng (Chancellors).
In the tenth month,
Pǔ sent acting Tàiwèi Yáng Lín to transmit the throne to Lǐ Bǐng.
The state was named Qí,
and the era name was changed to Shēngyuán.
Lǐ Bǐng honored Pǔ with an official decree, saying:
“I, the old minister who received the abdication, knowing the mandate,
respectfully present this official document honoring the Emperor as Gāoshàng Sīxuán Hónggǔ Ràng Huángdì.”
He posthumously honored Xú Wēn as Huángdì (Emperor) Zhōngwǔ.
He enfeoffed his son Jǐng as the Prince of Wú,
and Xú Shì’s sons Zhīzhèng as the Prince of Jiāng,
and Zhī'è as the Prince of Ráo.
Zhōu Běn and the generals went to Jīnlíng to urge Lǐ Bǐng to ascend the throne.
Returning, he sighed and said:
“I failed to execute the usurper to repay the Yáng family.
Now I am old,
how can I serve two surnames!”
He died of indignation and grief.
In the second year, fourth month,
Yáng Pǔ was relocated to the Dānyáng Palace in Rùnzhōu.
He appointed Wáng Yú as the Jìedùshǐ of Zhèxī, and Mǎ Sīràng as the Dānyáng Gōngshǐ (Palace Administrator),
and guarded him with strict forces.
The various sons of Xú Shì requested Lǐ Bǐng to revert to his surname.
Lǐ Bǐng was humble and dared not forget the kindness of the Xú family.
He submitted the discussion to the hundred officials.
After all the officials petitioned,
he then reverted to the Lǐ surname,
changing his name to Lǐ Jīng.
He claimed that Kè, Prince Jiàn, son of Emperor Xiànzōng of Táng, begot Chāo;
Chāo begot Zhì,
who served as a Judicial Administrator in Xúzhōu;
and Zhì begot Róng.
He thus claimed to be the fourth-generation descendant of Prince Jiàn,
and changed the state name to Táng.
He established temples for Emperor Gāozǔ and Emperor Tàizōng of Táng.
He posthumously honored his ancestor of the fourth generation, Kè, as Huángdì Xiàojìng,
with the temple name Dìngzōng;
his great-grandfather Chāo as Huángdì Xiàopíng,
with the temple name Chéngzōng;
his grandfather Zhì as Huángdì Xiào'ān,
with the temple name Huìzōng;
and his father Róng as Huángdì Xiàodé,
with the temple name Qìngzōng.
He treated Xú Wēn as his adoptive father.
Xú Shì's sons and grandsons were all enfeoffed as princes or dukes,
and the daughters were enfeoffed as Commandery or County Mistresses.
He appointed Zhāng Jūyǒng, Attendant Gentleman of the Ménxià; Lǐ Jiànxūn, Attendant Gentleman of the Zhōngshū; and Zhāng Yánhàn, Right Púshè, to serve as Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
In the eleventh month,
he held a military review of 80,000 infantry and cavalry at Tóngqiáo.
Yáng Pǔ died at the Dānyáng Palace.
When Pǔ’s son Liǎn was the Crown Prince of Wú,
Lǐ Jīng married his daughter to him.
When Lǐ Jīng usurped the state,
he enfeoffed his daughter as Princess Yǒngxīng.
When the daughter heard people calling her Princess,
she would sob, weep, and decline the title.
Everyone in the palace pitied her.
After Pǔ died,
Liǎn was made the Jìedùshǐ of Kānghuà Commandery,
and soon thereafter died of illness.
In the third year, fourth month,
Lǐ Jīng performed the suburban sacrifice to Hàotiān Shàngdì at the Yuánqiū (Round Mound).
When the rite was complete,
the ministers requested to bestow an honorific title.
Lǐ Jīng said:
“Honorific titles
are not the ancient way.”
He did not permit it.
The prefectures and counties reported seven households where the people practiced filial piety and fraternity, living together for five generations.
He ordered their gates and neighborhoods to be marked,
and exempted them from corvée labor.
The most distinguished of these was the Chén clan of Jiāngzhōu,
comprising seven hundred family members.
At every meal, a wide mat was set out,
and the elders and young sat in order to eat together.
They kept more than a hundred dogs,
which shared one feed trough.
If one dog failed to arrive,
the other dogs would refuse to eat for its sake.
In the fourth year, sixth month,
Lǐ Jīnquán, Jìedùshǐ of Ānzhōu of Jìn, rebelled,
offering submission to Lǐ Jīng.
Lǐ Jīng sent Lǐ Chéngyù, Commander of the Garrison Camp of Èzhōu, to welcome him.
Chéngyù fought the Jìn generals Mǎ Quánjié and Ān Shěnhuī south of Ānlù.
They lost all three battles.
Chéngyù and Brigadier General Duàn Chǔgōng both died.
The Commander Dù Guāngyè and his five hundred soldiers were captured and sent to the capital.
Emperor Gāozǔ heavily rewarded them
and sent them back.
Lǐ Jīng sent a letter to Emperor Gāozǔ,
returning Guāngyè and the others,
requesting to punish the defeated troops according to law.
Emperor Gāozǔ sent them back again,
but Lǐ Jīng used armored troops at Línhuái to refuse them,
and so they stopped.
In the sixth year,
the state of Wúyuè suffered a fire.
Its palaces and government stores were burned,
and its weapons were all destroyed.
The ministers requested to take advantage of this vulnerability and attack them,
but Lǐ Jīng refused.
He sent an envoy to offer condolences
and generously relieve their shortages.
The Qián family had long been an enemy state since the time of Wú.
Lǐ Jīng saw that the world had been in chaos for a long time
and was constantly weary of using military force.
When he was about to usurp the state,
he first negotiated peace with the Qián family,
returning the officers and soldiers he held captive.
The Qián family also returned Wú’s defeated generals,
and friendly relations were subsequently maintained without interruption.
Féng Yánjǐ, a retainer of Lǐ Jīng, liked to discuss military matters and spoke boastfully.
He once mocked Lǐ Jīng, saying:
“How can a peasant achieve great things!”
Lǐ Jīng’s ambition was merely to hold the old territory of Wú,
and he had no further strategies for expansion.
Nevertheless, the people of Wú relied on this for rest and recovery.
In the seventh year,
Lǐ Jīng died,
aged fifty-six.
His posthumous title was Huángdì Guāngwén Sùwǔ Xiàogāo,
his temple name was Lièzǔ,
and his mausoleum was called Yǒnglíng.
His son Jǐng was established.
Jǐng,
whose original name was Jǐngtōng,
was Lǐ Jīng’s eldest son.
After he was established,
he again changed his name to Jǐng.
When Xú Wēn died,
Lǐ Jīng monopolized governance
and made Jǐng Minister of War and Advisor on Governmental Affairs.
The following year,
Lǐ Jīng garrisoned Jīnlíng,
leaving Jǐng as Sītú (Minister of Education) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
residing in Guǎnglíng with Sòng Qíqiū and Wáng Lìngmóu,
to assist Yáng Pǔ.
When Lǐ Jīng was about to usurp the state,
he summoned Jǐng back to Jīnlíng as Deputy Commander-in-Chief.
When Lǐ Jīng ascended the throne,
Jǐng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí.
When Lǐ Jīng died,
Jǐng succeeded to the throne,
changing the era name to Bǎodà.
He honored his mother, née Sòng, as the Empress Dowager,
and his consort, née Zhōng, as the Empress.
He enfeoffed his younger brother Jǐngsuì, Prince of Shòu, as the Prince of Yàn;
Jǐngdá, Prince of Xuānchéng, as the Prince of È;
and Jǐngtì, who had not previously been a prince,
as the Prince of Bǎoníng.
In the autumn,
he changed Jǐngsuì’s title to Prince of Qí, Grand Marshal of All Routes, Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant), and Director of the Chancellery;
and Jǐngdá to Prince of Yàn and Deputy Marshal.
They swore an oath before Lǐ Jīng’s coffin,
promising that the brothers would succeed the throne generation after generation.
He enfeoffed his son Jì as the Prince of Nánchāng and Administrator of Jiāngdū.
Winter, the tenth month,
defeated the demon rebel Zhāng Yùxián in Qiánzhōu.
Yùxián
was a minor official in Luó Xiàn, Xúnzhōu.
Earlier,
a spirit descended upon a civilian household in Luó Xiàn,
and whenever it spoke of fortune or misfortune to people, it was accurate.
Yùxián prayed to it,
and the spirit said:
"Yùxián is an Arhat (Luóhàn);
you may stay and serve me."
At this time,
Liú Yăn of Nánhǎi died,
and his son Fēn was newly established.
Bandits arose in Língnán.
A host of over a thousand bandits
had no unified leader,
and they asked the spirit who should be their master.
The spirit named Yùxián,
so they jointly elevated him as their commander.
Yùxián titled himself the King of the Eight Central Heavenly Kingdoms (Zhōngtiān Bā Guówáng),
changed the reign title to Yǒnglè,
and established officials and subordinates.
All the rebels and bandits wore crimson robes.
They attacked and plundered outside the Ridge (Lǐngwài).
Asking the spirit where they should go,
the spirit said:
"You must cross the ridge and take Qiánzhōu."
They then raided Nánkāng,
and the Military Commissioner (Jiédù) Jiă Hào could not stop them.
Yùxián occupied Báiyún Dòng,
built palaces and residences,
and had a host of over a hundred thousand,
successively capturing various districts.
Jǐng sent Yán Sī, the Marshal (Yúhòu) of the Hóngzhōu Garrison, and Biān Hào, the Palace Attendant for Transmission (Tōngshì Shèrén), leading troops to attack them.
Yùxián consulted the spirit,
but the spirit spoke no more.
All the bandits were terrified,
and consequently captured Yùxián and surrendered.
Jǐng appointed Féng Yánsí and Cháng Mèngxī as Academicians of the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì);
Féng Yánlǔ as Palace Attendant (Shèrén) of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū);
Chén Jué as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ);
and Wèi Cén and Zhā Wénhuī as Deputy Commissioners.
Mèngxī served in the Xuānzhèng Hall,
exclusively managing confidential orders.
However, Yánsí and the others wielded power through wickedness and flattery.
The Wú people called them
"The Five Devils" (Wŭ Guǐ).
Mèngxī repeatedly stated that those five men should not be employed,
but Jǐng did not accept the advice.
In the twelfth month,
Jǐng issued an order delegating all general governmental affairs, both internal and external, to Qí Wáng Jǐngsuì for consultation and decision-making.
Only Chén Jué and Zhā Wénhuī were permitted to present memorials.
Ministers, unless summoned for an audience,
were forbidden to enter (the palace).
Xiāo Yăn, a Supervising Secretary (Jìshì Zhōng), submitted a strongly worded memorial of remonstrance,
but received no reply.
Jiă Chóng, the Chief Marshal (Dū Yúhòu) of the Imperial Guards, went to the palace gate seeking an audience with Jǐng.
He said:
"Your servant served the previous court for thirty years,
and saw that the reason the late emperor achieved success and great work
was that he utilized the plans of many worthy men.
Thus, he received those who were distant or close,
and never obstructed access.
Yet, even then, the feelings of those below still sometimes failed to reach him.
Now Your Majesty has newly ascended the throne,
and whom are you relying upon?
Why have you suddenly isolated yourself from your officials?
If this old servant were to die soon,
I fear I would never again have a glimpse of your presence."
Thereupon he wept, sobbing deeply.
Jǐng was moved by this,
invited him to sit,
granted him food, and comforted him.
Consequently, he rescinded the order that had been issued.
Originally,
Sòng Qíqiū was the most vigorous plotter for [Tài] Zǔ's seizure of the Yáng clan's power.
When the deed was accomplished,
he feigned entering Jiŭhuá Shān.
[Tài] Zǔ repeatedly called upon him,
and only then did he emerge.
After [Tài] Zǔ claimed the imperial title,
not long after,
Qíqiū was dismissed from the chancellorship due to illness,
and was sent out as the Military Commissioner of Hóngzhōu.
When Jǐng ascended,
he was recalled to be Chancellor again.
However, Chén Jué, Wèi Cén, and the others were all protégés introduced by Qíqiū.
Cén and Jué developed a rift.
Cén slandered Jué to Jǐng,
who was demoted to Deputy Director of the Imperial Treasury (Shàofŭ Jiān).
Qíqiū was also dismissed from the chancellorship and became the Military Commissioner of Zhèxī.
Qíqiū, displeased,
requested to return to Jiŭhuá Shān.
He was granted the title Master of Jiŭhuá (Jiŭhuá Xiānshēng),
enfeoffed as the Duke of Qīngyáng (Qīngyáng Gōng),
and granted the revenue of the district of Qīngyáng.
In the second year, second month,
Lián Chóngyù and Zhū Wénjìn of Mǐn assassinated their sovereign Wáng Yánxī,
and Wénjìn established himself.
At this time,
Yánxī’s younger brother Yánzhèng had also established himself in Jiànzhōu,
naming his state Yīn.
The Wáng clan brothers waged war for several years.
Mǐn was in great disorder.
Taking advantage of this chaos, Jǐng dispatched Zhā Wénhuī and Zāng Xún, a Palace Attendant (Dàizhào), raising troops to attack Jiànzhōu.
Yánzhèng, hearing that Táng was about to attack,
sent someone to deceive Fúzhōu, saying:
"The Táng army is assisting us in suppressing the rebels."
Fúzhōu believed this,
and together killed Wénjìn and others and surrendered.
Yánzhèng sent his nephew Jìchāng to guard Fúzhōu.
Wénhuī's army was garrisoned at Jiànyáng.
Lǐ Rénidá, a general from Fúzhōu, killed Wáng Jìchāng and proclaimed himself Acting Military Commissioner (Liúhòu).
Liú Cóngxiào, a general from Quánzhōu, also killed his Prefect (Cìshǐ), Huáng Shàopuǒ.
Both sent proposals of submission to Wénhuī.
In the fourth year, eighth month,
Wénhuī followed up his victory and captured the four prefectures of Jiàn, Tīng, Quán, and Zhāng.
Jǐng divided the three districts of Yánpíng, Jiànpŭ, and Fùshā
to establish Jiànzhōu.
He moved Wáng Yánzhèng's clan to Jīnlíng.
He appointed Yánzhèng as the Military Commissioner of Ráozhōu, Lǐ Rénidá as the Military Commissioner of Fúzhōu, and Liú Cóngxiào as the Military Commissioner of the Qīngyuán Army.
Jǐng consequently wished to halt the troops,
but Zhā Wénhuī, Chén Jué, and the others all argued:
"The lingering remnants (yúniè) of Rénidá and the others remain.
It is better to take advantage of the victory and seize them entirely."
Chén Jué personally claimed he could secure Rénidá and the others without using a single soldier (chĭ bīng).
Jǐng appointed Jué as Envoy of Proclamation (Xuānyù Shǐ),
summoning Rénidá to pay court at Jīnlíng.
Rénidá did not comply.
Jué was ashamed.
Returning to Jiànzhōu,
he falsely issued an order to mobilize troops from Tīng, Jiàn, Xìn, and Fŭ prefectures to attack Rénidá.
At that time, Wèi Cén was pacifying Zhāng and Quán.
Hearing that Jué had raised troops,
he also independently mobilized soldiers to join Jué.
Jǐng was greatly enraged.
Féng Yánsí and others spoke on their behalf, saying:
"Since the troops have already marched,
they cannot be stopped."
Thus, he appointed Wáng Chóngwén as the Commander of Pacification (Zhāotăo Shǐ) and Wáng Jiànfēng as the Deputy Commander,
increasing the army to join the operation.
Yánlŭ, Wèi Cén, and Chén Jué were all made Supervising Commissioners (Jiānjūn Shǐ).
Rénidá offered submission to Wúyuè.
Wúyuè responded to Rénidá with thirty thousand troops.
Jué and the others competed for merit,
their advances and retreats failing to coordinate.
Yánlŭ engaged the Wúyuè army first,
suffered a crushing defeat and fled.
All the armies dispersed and returned.
Jǐng was furious,
and sent emissaries to bind Jué and Yánlŭ and bring them to Jīnlíng.
Féng Yánsí was currently Chancellor,
and Sòng Qíqiū had been recalled from Jiŭhuá to be Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
They mitigated the situation somewhat on their behalf,
resulting in Jué being exiled to Qízhōu and Yánlŭ to Shūzhōu.
Hán Xīzài submitted a strongly worded memorial of remonstrance,
requesting the execution of Jué and the others.
Qíqiū disliked him,
and Xīzài was demoted to Administrator of Hèzhōu (Hèzhōu Sīmă).
That year,
the Qìdān captured the capital (Jīngshī).
Central China (Zhōngguó) was without a ruler,
but Jǐng was busy wearing out his troops in the southeast because of Jué and the others,
and had no time to look north.
Jiāng Wénwèi, the Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), impeached Chancellor Féng Yánsí and Remonstrance Official (Jiànyì Dàfū) Wèi Cén for disrupting governance,
arguing that they shared the same guilt as Jué and the others yet had not been demoted or dismissed.
His words were extremely sharp and direct.
Jǐng was greatly angered,
and personally replied to the memorial.
He demoted Wénwèi to Service Administrator of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Sīshì Cānjūn).
He also dismissed Yánsí, making him Junior Tutor (Shàofù), and Cén, making him Equerry to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xĭmă).
In the fifth year,
Jǐngsuì was made Imperial Younger Brother (Tàidì).
Jǐngdá was made Grand Marshal (Yuánshuài),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng).
Jì, the Prince of Nánchāng, was made Deputy Grand Marshal (Fù Yuánshuài),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Yān (Yān Wáng).
The Qìdān sent an envoy to offer a marriage proposal (or courtesy visit).
Jiă Tán, the President of the Board of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū), was dispatched in return.
In the sixth year,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn of Hàn rebelled in Hézhōng.
He sent his retainer, General Zhū Yuán, to seek aid.
Jǐng appointed Lǐ Jīnquán, the Military Commissioner of Rùnzhōu, as the Commissioner of Pacification of the Northern Campaigning Army (Běimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāofŭ Shǐ).
The army attacked Shùyáng.
Hearing that Shǒuzhēn had already been defeated,
they returned.
At this time,
Emperor Yĭndì of Hàn was young,
and Central China was weak.
Many bandit groups north of the Huái River (Huáiběi) sent submissions to Jǐng.
Jǐng dispatched Huángpŭ Huī to the prefectures of Hăi and Sì to invite and receive them.
In the eighth year,
Fúzhōu deceitfully stated,
“The Wúyuè garrison troops have rebelled,
killed Lǐ Réndá and fled,”
and sent men to invite the Jiànzhōu Jìedùshǐ, Zhā Wénhuī.
Wénhuī and Chén Huì, the Cìshǐ of Jiànzhōu, went down the Mǐnjiāng River by boat to respond.
Fúzhōu sent troops out to welcome them.
Huì said:
“The Mǐn people are often deceitful and hard to trust;
we should halt on the riverbank and plan slowly.”
Wénhuī said:
“Delay will cause trouble;
while they are unsettled,
we must take it quickly.”
He left Huì to camp at the river mouth
and advanced to the west gate.
The hidden troops emerged,
and Wénhuī was captured.
Huì fought the Yuè people
and defeated them soundly,
capturing their general Mǎ Xiānjìn.
Jǐng sent Xiānjìn back to Yuè,
and Yuè also returned Wénhuī to Jǐng.
That year,
Mǎ Xīguǎng, the King of Chǔ, was assassinated by his younger brother Xī'è,
and Xī'è enthroned himself.
In the autumn of the ninth year,
the Chǔ people imprisoned Xī'è at Héngshān
and established his younger brother Xīchóng,
who submitted to Jǐng.
The state of Chǔ fell into great chaos.
Jǐng sent Biān Hào, the Cìshǐ of Xìnzhōu, to attack Chǔ.
He defeated Tánzhōu
and completely relocated Mǎ’s clan to Jīnlíng.
Jǐng appointed Xī'è as the Jìedùshǐ of Hóngzhōu,
Xīchóng as the Jìedùshǐ of Shūzhōu,
and Biān Hào as the Jìedùshǐ of Húnán.
In the tenth year,
Gāo'ān, Qīngjiāng, Wànzǎi, and Shànggāo—four counties of Hóngzhōu—were partitioned
to establish Yúnzhōu.
Féng Yánsì and Sūn Jì were appointed Zuǒ and Yòu Púshè Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Liú Shèng of Guǎngzhōu took advantage of Chǔ’s chaos
to seize Guìguǎn.
Jǐng sent General Zhāng Luán to dispatch troops to contest it,
but they were unsuccessful.
The Chǔ territory had just been settled,
and its official treasuries were empty.
The Chief Minister Féng Yánsì claimed the conquest of Chǔ as his accomplishment
and did not wish to draw expenses from the state;
therefore, he heavily taxed the people to supply the army.
All the Chǔ people resented this and rebelled.
Their general Liú Yán attacked Biān Hào.
Hào could not hold his position
and fled back.
In the eleventh year,
a great fire in Jīnlíng lasted for more than a month.
In the twelfth year,
there was a great famine,
and many people died of pestilence.
In the eleventh month of the thirteenth year,
the Zhōu army marched south.
An imperial edict stated:
“The foolish Huáidiàn,
daring to resist the great state,
illegally occupies one region
and presumptuously adopts a false reign title.
During the ages of Jìn and Hàn,
the world was not yet peaceful,
but they instead recruited and accepted rebels who had fled,
and supported the vicious insurgents as allies.
When Jīn Quán occupied Ānlù,
and when Shǒu Zhēn rebelled at Hézhōng,
they mobilized large armies
to come and provide assistance.
They coercively seized Mǐn and Yuè,
and plunged Xiāng and Tán into misery.
Furthermore, they communicated with Mùróng
and encroached upon the Xú region.
In the battle of Shùyáng,
who was right and who was wrong is evident.
They lured the Qìdān
to enter and cause border troubles,
and allied themselves with the Bǐng camps,
truly our hereditary enemies.
Their crimes are unspeakable,
and gods and men alike are furious.”
Thus, Lǐ Gǔ was appointed Xíngyíng Dū Bùshǔ (Area Commander-in-Chief of the Expeditionary Army),
and the attack began at Shòuzhōu.
At this time,
Sòng Qīqiū was the Jìedùshǐ of Hóngzhōu.
Jǐng recalled Qīqiū to Jīnlíng,
appointed Liú Yànzhēn as Shénwǔ Tǒngjūn,
and Liú Rénshàn as the Qīnghuái Jūn Jìedùshǐ,
to resist the Zhōu army.
Lǐ Gǔ said:
“We lack the equipment for naval warfare,
and if we let the Huái troops cut off the floating bridge at Zhèngyáng,
then we will be attacked from front and back.”
So he burned their fodder and rations
and retreated to camp at Zhèngyáng.
At this time, Shìzōng personally led the expedition.
When he reached Yǔzhèn,
he heard that Gǔ had retreated with the army,
and said:
“When our army withdraws,
the Táng troops will certainly pursue them.”
He sent Lǐ Chóngjìn to rush to Zhèngyáng
and said:
“The Táng troops will soon arrive;
you must attack them quickly.”
When Liú Yànzhēn and others heard that Gǔ had retreated,
they indeed thought he was timid
and swiftly pursued him.
By the time they reached Zhèngyáng,
Chóngjìn had already arrived first.
They fought before the Táng army could eat,
and Yànzhēn and the others were consequently defeated.
Yànzhēn’s troops had affixed sharp blades to their chevaux de frise,
securing them with iron chains.
They also carved wood into animal shapes,
calling them
“Jiémǎ Pái” (Swift Horse Shields),
and scattered iron caltrops on the ground using leather bags.
The Zhōu troops saw this and knew of their timidity,
and defeated them in one drumbeat.
Shìzōng camped on the south bank of the Féishuǐ River
and moved the floating bridge to Xiàcài.
Jǐng sent Lín Rénzhào and others to contest it but could not succeed,
and the Zhōu army captured Chúzhōu.
Jǐng was afraid,
and sent Wáng Zhīlǎng, an officer of the Yájiàng rank from Sìzhōu, to Xúzhōu,
claiming that the Táng Emperor had sent a letter,
expressing willingness to pay tribute and taxes
and to observe the rites of serving him as an elder brother.
Shìzōng did not reply.
Féng Yánlǔ, Deputy Retainer of Jǐng’s Eastern Capital, Zhāng Shào, Cìshǐ of Guāngzhōu, Zhōu Zuò, Cìshǐ of Shūzhōu, and Fāng Nà, Cìshǐ of Tàizhōu, all abandoned their cities and fled;
Yánlǔ shaved his head and became a monk,
but was captured by the Zhōu army.
Lǐ Fú, a subordinate general (Bìjiàng) of Qízhōu, killed his Cìshǐ Wáng Chéngjùn and surrendered to Zhōu.
Jǐng grew even more fearful,
and first changed his name to Jǐng to avoid the taboo names of the Zhōu imperial temple.
He sent Zhōng Mó, his Hanlin Academician, and Lǐ Démíng, Academician of the Wénlǐ Yuàn, to present a memorial claiming vassalage,
offering five hundred cattle for the army, two thousand shí of wine, and several thousand pieces of gold, silver, silk gauze, and fine silk,
requesting to cede the six prefectures of Shòu, Háo, Sì, Chǔ, Guāng, and Hǎi,
in exchange for a cessation of hostilities.
Shìzōng did not respond,
but divided his troops to attack and take Yáng and Tài.
Jǐng sent a person carrying a wax-pellet letter to the Qìdān seeking aid,
but he was captured by a border general.
Zhāng Chénghàn, Cìshǐ of Guāngzhōu, surrendered to Zhōu.
In the third month of the fourteenth year,
Lǐ Jǐng again sent Sīkōng Sūn Shèng and Lǐbù Shàngshū Wáng Chóngzhì with a memorial.
The language of the apology was even humbler and more subservient.
Shìzōng still did not reply.
The previously dispatched Zhōng Mó and the others, along with Shèng and Chóngzhì, were all detained at the traveling court (Xíngzài).
However, Mó and the others requested leave to return and retrieve Jǐng’s memorial,
offering all the territory north of the Jiāng (Yangzi River).
Shìzōng permitted this.
He sent Chóngzhì, Dé Míng, and others back,
and for the first time presented a letter to Jǐng, saying:
“Since the Táng dynasty lost control,
the path of Heaven has been difficult.
Six cycles (of twelve years) have passed since then,
and the land has been split like a melon or balanced like a tripod.
You have established your own education and customs,
each monopolizing the common people (zhēng lí).
You have formed alliances with the four barbarians (Sì Yí)
and oppressed the superior state (Shàngguó).
The culture of Huá (China) is not competitive—
it is a concentration of ill fortune.
Among all those who have a heart,
who does not rise up in indignation?
I possess the wealth and resources of one hundred prefectures (Zhōu),
and I command thirty myriad armored soldiers (Jiǎ Bīng).
Agriculture and warfare are practiced together,
and the officers and troops are happy to be utilized.
If I cannot recover the inner territory
and clearly define the borders,
and simply discuss turning back the troops,
it would truly be like a theatrical farce.
As for abolishing your supreme title
and wishing to submit as a minister,
Sūn Quán served Wèi,
and Xiāo Chá served Zhōu.
Although that was the custom of antiquity,
I will not accept it now.
If you merely retain the imperial title (Dì Hào),
how will it harm the winter season (suì hán)?
If you are firm in your heart to serve the great power (shì dà zhī xīn),
I will certainly not press a person into peril.”
When Dé Míng and the others returned,
they greatly praised Shìzōng’s heroic might.
Jǐng was displeased.
Sòng Qíqiū, Chén Jué, and others all argued that ceding territory was useless,
and that Dé Míng had betrayed the country for personal gain.
Jǐng was enraged
and had Dé Míng executed.
He sent the Marshal, the Prince of Qí, Lǐ Jǐngdá, along with Chén Jué, Biān Hào, and Xǔ Wénzhěn, to lead troops quickly toward Shòuchūn.
Jǐngdá’s commander, Zhū Yuán, and others successfully recaptured the three prefectures of Shū, Qí, and Tài.
In the summer,
there was heavy rain.
The Zhōu armies stationed in Yáng, Chú, and Hé were all forced back.
The generals requested to attack them at their strategic choke points.
Sòng Qíqiū said:
“Attacking them will deepen their resentment;
it is better to let them go, thereby earning merit (Dé).”
He commanded the generals to close ranks and defend the fortresses,
forbidding them to engage in critical battles.
Consequently, the Zhōu armies all concentrated at Shòuzhōu.
Shìzōng camped at Guōkǒu,
intending to travel again to Yángzhōu.
The Chancellor Fàn Zhì wept and remonstrated, citing the army’s exhaustion.
Thereupon, Shìzōng ordered the army to withdraw,
but left Lǐ Chóngjìn to attack Lú and Shòu,
and Xiàng Xùn to guard Yángzhōu.
Xùn requested to abandon Yángzhōu
and concentrate forces to attack Shòuchūn.
He sealed the arsenal and treasury, handed them over to the principal officer,
and dispatched Jǐng’s former generals to patrol the city.
Not a single item was violated when they departed.
The people of Huái were greatly pleased
and carried provisions
to send off the Zhōu army.
In the fifteenth year,
Jǐngdá sent Zhū Yuán and others to camp at Zǐjīnshān
and built a covered pathway (Yǒngdào) to supply Shòuzhōu.
In the second month,
Shìzōng again marched south.
He moved the pontoon bridge from Xiàcài to Guōkǒu,
established it as the Zhèn Huái Army,
and built two cities to flank the Huái River.
The Zhōu army repeatedly defeated the various stockades at Zǐjīnshān.
Although Jǐngdá was the Marshal,
all military matters were decided by Chén Jué.
Juě and Zhū Yuán had previous enmity.
As Yuán was a retainer of Lǐ Shǒuzhēn,
he was considered unreliable and vacillating.
Jǐng sent the great general Yáng Shǒuzhōng to replace Yuán
and also summoned Yuán back.
Yuán was furious
and defected and surrendered to Zhōu.
All the armies collapsed.
Xǔ Wénzhěn and Biān Hào were both captured.
Jǐngdá fled back to Jīnlíng with the naval forces.
Liú Rénshàn was ill and near death.
His deputy, Sūn Yǔ, and others surrendered Shòuzhōu to Zhōu.
Shìzōng ordered the army to withdraw.
Jǐng sent people to burn Yángzhōu
and drove away its officials and common people.
In the winter, tenth month,
Shìzōng again marched south
and proceeded to besiege Háozhōu.
The Prefect Guō Tíngwèi informed Zhōu, saying:
“I cannot hold one prefecture to resist the King’s Army.
However, I wish to request permission from Táng before surrendering.”
Shìzōng delayed the attack for him.
Tíngwèi sent a person to request permission from Jǐng.
Jǐng permitted his surrender,
and he then surrendered.
Zhōu also took Sìzhōu.
The Zhōu army, tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
advanced simultaneously by water and land.
The soldiers sang the “Tán Lái” song;
its sound could be heard for several dozens of Lǐ.
In the twelfth month,
they camped at the north gate of Chǔzhōu.
In the first month of Jiāotài first year,
a general amnesty was proclaimed and the reign title was changed.
The Zhōu army attacked Chǔzhōu.
The defending generals Zhāng Yànqīng and Zhèng Zhāoyè defended the city very firmly.
The attack lasted forty days and could not break through.
Shìzōng personally supervised the troops, using covered carts (Dòngwū) to tunnel beneath the city and burn it.
The city wall broke down.
Yànqīng and Zhāoyè died in battle.
The Zhōu soldiers were extremely angry
and massacred almost everyone.
The Zhōu army then recaptured Hǎi, Tài, and Yángzhōu.
Shìzōng traveled to Yíngluán to oversee the Great River.
Jǐng knew he could not hold out,
but was ashamed to humble himself and discard his title.
He then sent Chén Jué with a memorial,
requesting to transfer the state (Guó) to his heir apparent and obey Shìzōng’s orders.
Initially,
when the Zhōu army marched south,
they lacked equipment for naval warfare.
After repeatedly defeating Jǐng’s troops,
they captured naval soldiers,
and consequently built several hundred warships.
They ordered the surrendered soldiers to teach naval warfare
and commanded Wáng Huán to lead them down the Huái River.
Most of Jǐng’s naval forces were defeated,
and the ships on the Long Huái
were all seized by the Zhōu army.
They also built several hundred Qíyún ships.
When Shìzōng reached Běishényàn in Chǔzhōu,
the Qíyún ships were too large
to pass.
He then opened the Lǎoguàn River to let them through
and thus reached the Great River.
Jǐng initially relied on his naval forces,
believing the Zhōu army was no match
and could not reach the River yet.
When Jué acted as envoy
and saw the naval fleet lined up magnificently along the River banks,
he thought they had descended from heaven.
He then requested, saying:
“Your servant wishes to return to my state to fetch Jǐng’s memorial
and offer all the prefectures north of the Jiāng,
as promised.”
Shìzōng permitted this
and for the first time presented a letter to Jǐng, saying,
“The Emperor respectfully inquires of the Lord of the Southern Land,”
only offering consolation for his hardship.
At this time, the prefectures of Yáng, Tài, Chú, Hé, Shòu, Háo, Sì, Chǔ, Guāng, and Hǎi
had already been acquired by Zhōu.
Jǐng then offered Lú, Shū, Qí, and Huáng,
making the Jiāng River the boundary.
In the fifth month,
Jǐng issued an order to abandon the imperial title,
calling himself the State Lord (Guózhǔ),
and observing the Zhōu calendar.
This was the fifth year of Xiǎndé.
Initially,
Sūn Shèng was sent as an envoy to Zhōu
and detained.
When Shìzōng asked Shèng about the reality of the south (Jiāngnán),
he did not reply.
Shìzōng was angry
and killed Shèng.
After Zhōu withdrew its forces,
Jǐng posthumously conferred the title of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī) upon Liú Rénshàn
and posthumously enfeoffed Shèng as the Duke of Lǔ State (Lǔguó Gōng).
Shìzōng sent Zhōng Mó and Féng Yánlǔ back to their state.
Jǐng again sent Mó and the others to pay tribute at the capital,
personally writing the memorial
which claimed that the kindness of Heaven and Earth and his Parents could not be repaid.
He also requested that an imperial edict be issued treating him the same as a vassal state (Fānzhèn),
and he sent Mó to personally present his wish to transfer the throne to his heir apparent.
Shìzōng sent Mó and the others back to their state,
giving gracious edicts to console and reassure him.
Jǐng appointed Mó as Lǐbù Shìláng and Yánlǔ as Hùbù Shìláng.
was the crown prince at the time,
Yán Lǔ and others all moved freely in and out of the Eastern Palace. Cháng Mèngxī,
Minister of the Board of Rites, had repeatedly stated since the time of [that reign] that Yán Lǔ and his group should not be allowed near the crown prince.
When Jǐng ascended [the throne],
Yán Lǔ gained influence.
Mèngxī constantly criticized and ostracized him.
After Jǐng had ceded territory and submitted as a vassal,
when someone spoke of the court as the "Great Court,"
Mèngxī laughed heartily and said:
"You gentlemen once wanted your lord to achieve the standards of Yáo and Shùn.
Today, you yourselves have become the 'Lesser Court,' haven't you?"
Zhōng Mó was always friendly with Lǐ Démíng.
After he returned,
he heard that Démíng had been killed by Sòng Qíqiū and others.
[Mó] wished to avenge his wrong,
but was unable to initiate it.
Chén Jué,
a member of Qíqiū's faction,
already had a feud with Yán Xù.
Jué once served as an envoy to Zhōu,
and upon returning, he claimed that the reason Shìzōng believed Jiāngnán did not immediately obey orders
was due to the schemes of Yán Xù,
and he advised Jǐng to execute Xù in order to apologize [to Zhōu].
Jǐng was suspicious of this.
Mó subsequently requested to be sent as an envoy to Zhōu
to verify the matter.
Jǐng had already ceded territory and submitted as a vassal,
so he sent Mó to the court to apologize,
stating that the failure to immediately cede the territory
was not Xù's scheme,
and requesting that Xù be pardoned.
Shìzōng was greatly surprised
and said:
"If Xù was capable of forming such a strategy,
that means he was loyal to his sovereign.
How could I execute a loyal minister?"
When Mó returned,
he reported that Jué was treacherous and deceitful.
Jǐng grew angry,
exiled Jué to Ráozhōu,
and executed him.
Sòng Qíqiū, implicated for being Jué's partisan,
was banished back to Qīngyáng
and granted death.
[Jǐng] appointed his younger brother, the Grand Younger Brother Jǐngsuì, as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Hóngzhōu,
and made Yànwáng Jì the Crown Prince.
Jǐng was distressed by the ongoing military expenditures.
Zhōng Mó requested the minting of large coins, making one coin equivalent to ten,
inscribed with the words
"Yǒngtōng Quánhuò."
Mó later incurred an offense,
and the large coins were abolished.
Hán Xīzài subsequently minted iron coins,
making one coin equivalent to two.
In the ninth month,
Crown Prince Jì died.
His second son Cóngjiā was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wú (Wúwáng)
and resided in the Eastern Palace.
Zhōng Mó stated that Cóngjiā was frivolous and unrestrained,
and requested that Jìguógōng Cóngshàn be established [as Crown Prince].
Jǐng grew angry,
demoted Mó to Libationer of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ Sīyè),
and established Cóngjiā as Crown Prince.
Shìzōng sent someone to tell Jǐng:
"The great relationship (dàyì) between me and Jiāngnán
is already settled.
However, I worry that later generations may not tolerate you.
You should, while I am alive, repair your city walls and manage strategic points as a plan for your descendants."
Jǐng subsequently set about constructing and repairing various cities,
and planned to move his capital to Hóngzhōu.
All the officials did not wish to move,
except for the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) Táng Gǎo, who endorsed it.
Thereupon, [Jǐng] raised Hóngzhōu's status to Nánchāng,
and established the Southern Capital (Nándū).
In the second year of Jiànlóng [961 CE],
[Jǐng] left Crown Prince Cóngjiā to oversee the state (jiānguó),
and Jǐng moved to the Southern Capital.
However, Hóngzhōu was constrained and narrow;
the palaces, government offices, camps, and bureaus
could not all be accommodated.
The officials thought day and night of returning,
and Jǐng regretted and raged incessantly.
Táng Gǎo, feeling shame and fear,
became ill and died.
In the sixth month,
Jǐng died,
at the age of sixty-four.
Cóngjiā succeeded him,
returned to Jīnlíng for the funeral rites,
and sent an envoy to the [Northern] court,
requesting the restoration of Jǐng's imperial title.
Emperor Tàizǔ (of Sòng) granted this,
and so the posthumous name was Míngdào Chóngdé Wénxuān Xiàohuángdì,
the temple name Yuánzōng,
and the mausoleum was named Shùnlíng.
Yù, courtesy name Chóngguāng,
whose original name was Cóngjiā,
was the sixth son of Jǐng.
Yù was benevolent and filial by nature,
skilled in literary composition,
and proficient in calligraphy and painting.
He had a broad forehead and double teeth,
and one eye had double pupils (chóngtóngzǐ).
Of the sons older than Crown Prince Jì,
five sons had all died young.
Yù was subsequently enfeoffed as the Prince of Wú (Wúwáng).
In the second year of Jiànlóng,
when Jǐng moved to the Southern Capital,
he established Yù as Crown Prince
and left him to oversee the state.
When Jǐng died,
Yù succeeded him and ascended the throne in Jīnlíng.
His mother was Lady Zhōng.
Her father's name was Tàizhāng.
Yù honored his mother by calling her Shèngzūnhòu;
he established his consort Lady Zhōu as the Queen (Guóhòu);
he enfeoffed his younger brother Cóngshàn as Prince of Hán (Hánwáng),
Cóngyì as Prince of Zhèng (Zhèngwáng),
Cóngqiān as Prince of Yíchūn (Yíchūn Wáng),
Cóngdù as Duke of Zhāopíng Commandery (Zhāopíng Jùngōng),
and Cóngxìn as Duke of Wényáng Commandery (Wényáng Jùngōng).
A general amnesty was declared within the borders.
He sent Féng Yánlǔ, Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat, to present tribute to the court.
He ordered that two officials daily, of the fourth rank and below in the various departments who had no specific duties,
should wait for appointment (dàizhì) in the Inner Palace.
In the third year,
Liú Cóngxiào of Quánzhōu died.
When Jǐng submitted as a vassal to Zhōu,
Cóngxiào also presented memorials and tribute to the capital [of Zhōu].
Shìzōng, because of Jǐng,
did not accept them.
Cóngxiào heard that Jǐng had moved to Hóngzhōu,
and feared that this move was intended to attack him.
He sent his son Shàojī to present tribute to Jīnlíng.
Subsequently, Cóngxiào died of illness.
The people of Quán [Quánzhōu] then sent his entire clan to Jīnlíng
and nominated and established Zhāng Hànsī, the deputy commissioner.
