Hànsī was old and unequal to the task.
Chén Hóngjìn, a man of the prefecture, expelled him,
and proclaimed himself Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
Yù immediately appointed Hóngjìn as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ).
In the second year of Qiándé [964 CE],
[Yù] began to use iron coins.
The common people largely hoarded and hid the old copper coins.
The old coins became increasingly scarce,
and merchants often exchanged ten iron coins for one copper coin and took [the copper] out of the territory.
The authorities could not prohibit this.
Yù then issued an order making one [iron coin] equivalent to ten.
He appointed Hán Xīzài as Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Scholar of the Qínzhèng Hall.
He enfeoffed his eldest son Zhòngyù as Duke of Qīngyuán (Qīngyuán Gōng),
and his second son Zhòngyí as Duke of Xuānchéng (Xuānchéng Gōng).
In the fifth year,

he commanded the Vice Ministers of the two Secretariats, the Supervising Secretaries (Jǐshìzhōng), the Secretaries of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén), and the Scholars of the Jíxián and Qínzhèng Halls
to take turns lodging and being on duty (sùzhí) in the Guāngzhèng Hall.
Yù brought them in to converse and discuss matters.
Yù had often considered Xīzài fully loyal
and capable of speaking frankly.
He wanted to appoint him as Chancellor,
but Xīzài had dozens of singing girls and concubines in his inner apartments.
Many were sent out to outside residences to privately serve guests.
Yù found this conduct problematic
and demoted Xīzài to Palace Assistant (Yòu Shùzǐ),
assigning him duty in the Southern Capital.
Xīzài dismissed all the singing girls,
and set out on the road in a single carriage.
Yù was pleased, kept him,
and restored his rank.
After a while, the singing girls gradually returned.
Yù said:
"I cannot do anything about him!"
In that year,
Xīzài died.
Yù sighed and said:
"In the end, I could not have Xīzài as my Chancellor."
He wished to posthumously grant him the title of Administrator (Píngzhāng Shì).
He asked if there was any precedent for this in previous generations.
The officials replied:
"In the past, Liú Mùzhī was posthumously granted Kàifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Opening the Palace with the Same Ceremonial Honors as the Three Ducal Ministers)."
Consequently, [Yù] posthumously granted Xīzài the title of Píngzhāng Shì.
Xīzài
was the son of a general from Běihǎi.
He was initially good friends with Lǐ Gǔ.
During the time of Míngzōng [of Later Táng],
Xīzài fled south to Wú.
Gǔ escorted him to Zhèngyáng.
As the wine flowed freely before their parting,
Xīzài said to Gǔ:
"If Jiāngzuǒ (Jiangnan) employs me as Chancellor,
I shall drive straight onward to settle the Central Plains."
Gǔ replied:
"If Zhōngguó (the Central Kingdom) employs me as Chancellor,
taking Jiāngnán will be as easy as reaching into a pouch to fetch something."
When the Zhōu army campaigned against the Huái River region,
Gǔ was commanded to be the general,
to capture Huáinán.
But Xīzài was unable to accomplish anything.
In the fourth year of Kāibǎo (971),
Yù sent his younger brother, the Prince of Hán, Cóngshàn, to pay court to the capital (Jīngshī).
Consequently, he was detained and not allowed to return.
Yù personally submitted a memorial requesting Cóngshàn's return to his state,
but Emperor Tàizǔ did not grant permission.
Yù often felt depressed, worrying over the reduction of his state.
Daily, he engaged in heavy drinking feasts with his officials,
his melancholic thoughts turning into unending sad songs.
In the fifth year (972),
Yù issued an order to reduce and diminish court regulations and systems.
Written edicts were termed "Instructions" (Jiào).
He changed the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng) and Chancellery (Ménxià Shěng) to the Left and Right Inner History Bureaus (Zuǒ, Yòu Nèishǐ Fǔ),
the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng) became the Bureau of Treasury (Sīhuì Fǔ),
the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái) became the Bureau of Justice (Sīxiàn Fǔ),
the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín) became the Literary College (Wén Guǎn),
the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Yuàn) became the Glorious Governance Bureau (Guāngzhèng Yuàn),
and all princes were made Dukes of the State (Guó Gōng),
in order to show respect to the Imperial Court.
Yù was naturally arrogant and extravagant,
fond of music and beautiful women,
and he also delighted in Buddhism (Fútú).
He indulged in lofty discussions,
paying no attention to governmental affairs.
In the sixth year (973),
the Palace Aide to the Inner History Bureau, Pān Yòu, submitted a severely critical memorial.
Yù had him arrested and imprisoned,
and Yòu hanged himself.
In the seventh year (974),
Emperor Tàizǔ sent an envoy to summon Yù to the palace (Què).
Yù claimed illness and did not go.
The royal army marched south.
Yù sent Xú Xuàn and Zhōu Wéijiǎn, among others, to present a memorial to the court requesting a delay in the campaign,
but received no reply.
In the twelfth month of the eighth year (975),
the royal army captured Jīnlíng.
In the ninth year (976),
Yù was taken captive to the capital (Jīngshī).
Tàizǔ pardoned him,
enfeoffed Yù as the Marquis Who Disobeyed Mandates (Wéimìng Hóu),
and appointed him General of the Left Ox Guard (Zuǒ Qiānniú Wèi Jiāngjūn).
Subsequent events are detailed in the National History (Guó Shǐ).
My family has been established in Jiāngnán for generations,
and the old people there can mostly recount events from the time of the Lǐ clan.
They say that when Emperor Tàizǔ dispatched his army for the southern campaign,
Yù sent his minister Xú Xuàn to pay court in the capital (Jīngshī).
Xuàn, residing in Jiāngnán,
considered himself a famous minister.
When he came,
he intended to use his eloquence to rush forth arguments and save his state.
He was meticulous in his planning, deliberation, speech, and response, day and night.
When he was about to have his audience,
the great ministers also entered first and requested,
saying that Xuàn was learned and skilled in rhetoric,
and that preparations should be made to handle him.
Tàizǔ laughed and said:
"Just leave;
this is not something you understand."
The next day,
Xuàn paid court in the hall,
looked up, and said:
"Lǐ Yù is guiltless,
and Your Majesty's army marches without justification."
Tàizǔ slowly summoned him forward,
allowing him to complete his argument.
Xuàn said:
"Yù serves the large state as a small state,
just as a son serves his father.
He has committed no transgression.
Why is he being attacked?"
His argument amounted to several hundred words.
Tàizǔ said:
"Do you believe that those who are father and son can constitute two separate families?"
Xuàn had nothing to reply with and withdrew.
Alas,
how great,
how concise his words were!
Truly, when a true sovereign rises,
the world must inevitably unite under one rule.
Those who can be made to come,
are brought;
those who cannot,
are attacked.
Usurpers, pretenders, and opportunistic thieves
must be utterly swept away and pacified before the effort ceases.
When I read the edict of Zhōu Shìzōng conquering Huáinán,
I find it strange that he painstakingly collected previous events,
striving to compare right and wrong as his pretext—
how petty!
However, Shìzōng’s heroic martial ability is commendable;
perhaps the fault lies with the person who drafted the edict?
According to the Record of Jiāngnán (Jiāngnán Lù) compiled by Tāng Yuè, it says:
"Jǐng, in the first month of the fifteenth year of Bǎodà,
changed the reign title to Jiāotài.
In this year, he completely ceded the fourteen prefectures of Huáinán,
making the river (Jiāng) the border."
The fifteenth year of Bǎodà,
was the fourth year of Xiǎndé of Zhōu.
Examining the Old History of the Five Dynasties and the Veritable Records of Shìzōng,
on the day Rénshēn in the tenth month of the fourth year of Xiǎndé,
Shìzōng was just resuming his southern campaign.
On the day Bǐngwǔ in the first month of the fifth year (Xiǎndé),
Chǔzhōu was first captured.
On the day Jǐhài in the second month,
Jǐng began to fully cede all prefectures of Huáinán,
making the river the border.
This should therefore be the sixteenth year of Bǎodà.
Yuè and others were former ministers of Nán Táng;
how is it that in recording events they personally witnessed,
they made such an error?
And works like the Records of the Nine States (Jiǔ Guó Zhì) and the Comprehensive Register of Chronology (Jìnián Tōng Pǔ),
merely take Yuè's book as correct,
failing to check and compare it,
resulting in all of them being off by one year.
Regarding Jǐng’s destruction of the state of Mǐn,
that was the fourth year of Bǎodà.
The Record of Jiāngnán writes it as the third year,
also being off by one year.
This has already been noted in the annotations to the Hereditary House of Mǐn (Mǐn Shìjiā).
Some may suspect that Jǐng changed his reign title in the year after his accession,
in which case the destruction of the state of Mǐn would be the third year,
and Zhōu's seizure of Huáinán would correctly be the fifteenth year, with no error.
They argue that the Record of Jiāngnán mistakenly recorded the year of Jǐng’s accession as the year Bǎodà began,
thus always causing a difference of one year.
I now know this is not the case,
because by cross-referencing various texts:
The people of Mǐn killed Wáng Yánxī,
which occurred in the first year of Kāiyùn of Jìn (944).
The Zhōu army first attacked Nán Táng in the second year of Xiǎndé (955).
If Jǐng changed the reign title in the year he first ascended,
then the first year of Kāiyùn would be the second year of Bǎodà,
and the second year of Xiǎndé would be the thirteenth year of Bǎodà.
Now, the Record of Jiāngnán records Yánxī's death in the second year (of Bǎodà),
and the Zhōu army's first attack in the thirteenth year (of Bǎodà).
Therefore, Jǐng did change the reign title in the year he ascended;
this is not an error.
Rather, Yuè and others mistakenly recorded the destruction of the Wáng clan (Mǐn) and the ceding of Huáinán, each being off by one year.
The state was established in the second year of Tiānfú of Jìn (937),
until the eighth year of Kāibǎo (975) of the Imperial Dynasty, when the state was extinguished,
covering a total of thirty-nine years.
Hereditary House of Former Shǔ, Third: Wáng Jiàn (and his son Yǎn)
Wáng Jiàn, courtesy name Guāngtú,
was a native of Wǔyáng, Xǔzhōu.
He had thick eyebrows and a broad forehead;
his appearance was imposing.
In his youth, he was a scoundrel,
making a living by slaughtering cattle, stealing donkeys, and selling illicit salt.
The villagers called him
"Wáng Bā the Thief."
Later, he became a soldier in the Zhōngwǔ Army,
gradually rising to be a company commander.
When Huáng Cháo captured Cháng'ān,
Emperor Xīzōng was in Shǔ.
Lù Yànhóng, a general of the Zhōngwǔ Army, placed eight thousand troops under Yáng Fùguāng to suppress the rebels.
When Cháo was defeated and fled,
Fùguāng organized those troops into Eight Divisions (Bā Dū),
each division having one thousand soldiers.
Jiàn and Yànhóng were both commanders (Dōutóu) of one division.
After Fùguāng died,
Yànhóng led the Eight Divisions west to welcome Xīzōng in Shǔ.
Wherever they passed, they plundered.
Upon reaching Xīngyuán,
they expelled the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) Niú Cóng,
and Yànhóng proclaimed himself Acting Commissioner (Liúhòu).
Xīzōng immediately appointed Yànhóng as Military Commissioner.
Yànhóng appointed Jiàn and the other eight division commanders to concurrently serve as prefects (Cìshǐ) of subordinate prefectures.
Soon after, Yànhóng led his troops eastward,
capturing Chén and Xǔ prefectures.
Jiàn, along with Jìn Huī, Hán Jiàn, Zhāng Zào, and Lǐ Shītài, each led one division,
fleeing west to Shǔ.
Xīzōng was greatly pleased to receive them,
naming them
the "Five Divisions Accompanying the Emperor" (Suí Jià Wǔ Dū).
He assigned them to Tián Lìngzī, the Overseer of Military Affairs for the Ten Armies (Shí Jūn Guānjūnróng Shǐ).
Lìngzī adopted Jiàn and the others as foster sons.
When Xīzōng returned to Cháng'ān,
he ordered Jiàn, Jìn Huī, and the others to command the Shéncè Army for palace guard duty.
In the first year of Guāngqǐ (885),
Wáng Chóngróng of Hézhōng contended with Lìngzī over the salt ponds.
Chóngróng summoned Jìn troops to attack the capital (Jīngshī).
Xīzōng fled to Fèngxiáng.
In the third month of the second year (886),
he moved his residence to Xīngyuán.
He appointed Jiàn as Commissioner for Clearing the Road (Qīngdào Shǐ),
carrying the Imperial Seal (Yùxǐ) and following him.
When they reached Dāngtú Post Station,
Lǐ Chāngfú set fire to the gallery road (zhàndào).
The gallery road was nearly severed.
Jiàn controlled Xīzōng's horse,
passing through the smoke and flames.
They lodged below the slope.
Xīzōng rested his head on Jiàn's knee to sleep.
When he awoke,
he wept,
took off his imperial robe, and bestowed it upon him.
Xīzōng had already reached Xīngyuán,
Lìngzī believed that the Tiānzǐ's flight and exile
was caused by himself,
and fearing punishment,
Chén Jìngxuān, the Jiédùshǐ of Xīchuān,
was Lìngzī's full younger brother.
Lìngzī therefore requested to be the Jiānjūn of Xīchuān,
and Yáng Fùgōng replaced him as the Jūnróngshǐ.
Fùgōng sent Jiàn out to be the Cìshǐ of Bìzhōu,
so Jiàn gathered fugitives and indigenous peoples from the valleys and caves,
amassing a force of eight thousand,
and therewith attacked Làngzhōu,
capturing its Cìshǐ, Yáng Xíngqiān.
He then attacked Lìzhōu.
Wáng Gǒng, the Cìshǐ of Lìzhōu, abandoned the city and fled.
Jìngxuān was troubled by this,
and asked Lìngzī about it.
Lìngzī said:
“Wáng Bā is my son.
If you summon him with a single messenger,
he can be placed under your command.”
Consequently, he sent someone to summon Jiàn.
Gù Yǎnlǎng of Dōngchuān had a prior relationship with Jiàn.
When Jiàn heard that Lìngzī had summoned him,
he was greatly pleased,
and subsequently went to Zǐzhōu.
He said to Yǎnlǎng:
“The father of the Ten Armies has summoned me.
I wish to go to Chéngdū to see Chén Gōng,
so that I may ask for a command post.”
He immediately entrusted his family members to Yǎnlǎng,
selected two thousand elite soldiers,
and rushed toward Chéngdū.
When he reached Lùtóuguān,
Jìngxuān regretted summoning Jiàn,
and sent someone to stop him.
Jiàn was furious,
attacked and destroyed Lùtóuguān,
and seized Hànzhōu.
When Yǎnlǎng heard this,
he deployed troops to aid Jiàn,
stationing them at Xuéshè.
Jìngxuān dispatched the general Gōu Wéilì to oppose Jiàn.
Jiàn attacked and defeated him,
and then proceeded to attack Péngzhōu.
Jìngxuān sent Shān Xíngzhāng, the Cìshǐ of Méizhōu, leading fifty thousand troops to garrison Xīnfán.
Jiàn defeated him again,
capturing over ten thousand men,
with corpses strewn across forty *lǐ*.
Jìngxuān dispatched seventy thousand troops to reinforce Xíngzhāng,
and they faced off against Jiàn in Méngyáng and Xīndū for over a hundred days.
Zhāozōng sent Lǐ Xún, Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left, as Commissioner to Proclaim Reconciliation and Harmony to the Two Shu Circuits (Liǎng Chuān),
ordering Yǎnlǎng and the others to cease hostilities.
Yǎnlǎng requested that a high minister be appointed to govern Shǔ,
and subsequently requested symbols of authority (banners and tallies) for Jiàn.
In the sixth month of the first year of Wéndé [888 CE],
the Chancellor Wéi Zhāodù was made Jiédùshǐ of Xīchuān.
The prefectures of Qióng, Shǔ, Lí, and Yǎ were separated to form the Yǒngpíng Army,
and Jiàn was appointed Jiédùshǐ.
Jìngxuān refused to relinquish his post.
Zhāozōng immediately ordered Zhāodù to lead the troops of Yǎnlǎng and others to suppress him.
Zhāozōng appointed Jiàn as Commander-in-Chief of the Headquarters for the Pacification Campaign.
After a long time,
they failed to overcome him.
Jiàn said to Zhāodù:
“You, sir, leading tens of thousands of troops,
have cornered the people of the two Shu circuits,
yet your army has long been without success.
What should be done?
Moreover, the Táng court faces many troubles.
The various garrisons in the east
have their forces close to the capital region.
You should return to assist the Tiānzǐ
and pacify the central plains to consolidate the foundation.
This land of barbarians
is not worth keeping you here!”
Zhāodù hesitated and could not decide.
Jiàn sent soldiers to seize Zhāodù’s personal aide at the camp gate,
cut him into pieces, and ate him.
Jiàn then entered and reported, saying:
“The soldiers were hungry,
and needed this for food!”
Zhāodù was terrified,
and immediately left the credentials and tallies with Jiàn and departed eastward.
Once Zhāodù had left,
Jiàn immediately used troops to block Jiànmén Pass.
Communication with the Liǎng Chuān was thereby cut off.
Shān Xíngzhāng was garrisoned at Guǎngdū.
Jiàn attacked and defeated him.
Xíngzhāng fled to Méizhōu,
and surrendered the prefecture to Jiàn.
Jiàn led his troops to attack Chéngdū,
while the prefectures of Zī, Jiǎn, Róng, Mào, Jiā, and Qióng all killed their Cìshǐs and surrendered to Jiàn.
Jiàn’s attack on Chéngdū was extremely fierce.
Tián Lìngzī ascended the wall and shouted to Jiàn:
“This old man has always been close to you, sir.
Why do you hold a grudge and come here?”
Jiàn replied:
“How can I forget
the kindness of the Jūnróng and the father-son relationship [with you]?
However, leading troops to punish one who refuses to relinquish his post
is the order of the Tiānzǐ.”
That night, Lìngzī entered Jiàn’s camp,
and handed over the tablets and seals of the Jiédù and Surveillance Commissioners to Jiàn.
The next day,
Jìngxuān opened the gates and welcomed Jiàn.
As Jiàn was about to enter the city,
he appointed Zhāng Qíng as Deputy Commissioner of Patrols and Arrests,
and warned his soldiers, saying:
“I have appointed Zhāng Qíng as Commissioner of Patrols.
You must not violate his orders.
If Qíng happens to arrest you and bring you to me,
I will still spare your lives.
If he kills you first and then reports it,
I will not be able to question him either.”
When Jiàn entered the city,
the soldiers began to loot.
Qíng killed a hundred men, and the looting stopped.
Later, Jiàn relocated Jìngxuān to Yǎzhōu,
and sent someone to kill him;
he reappointed Lìngzī as Jiānjūn,
but later killed him too.
In the tenth month of the second year of Dàshùn [891 CE],

The Táng [court] appointed Jiàn as Acting Minister of Works (Jiǎnjiào Sītú), Governor of Chéngdū (Chéngdū Yǐn), Deputy Grand Jiédùshǐ of Jiànnán Xīchuān with authority over Jiédù affairs, and Commissioner for Surveillance, Administration, and Pacification of the Eight Kingdoms of Yúnnán within the Circuit.
Gù Yǎnlǎng of Dōngchuān died,
and his younger brother Gù Yǎnhuī succeeded him.
The Táng [court] sent the eunuch Zōng Dàobì to grant Yǎnhuī the banners and tallies of Dōngchuān.
Cháng Hòu, the Cìshǐ of Miánzhōu, seized Dàobì and attacked Zǐzhōu.
Jiàn dispatched Lǐ Jiǎn, Wáng Zōngdí, and others to suppress Hòu.
Since Yǎnlǎng's death,
Jiàn intended to annex Dōngchuān but had not yet found an opportunity to act.
When Lǐ Jiǎn and the others were suppressing Hòu,
Jiàn warned them, saying:
“Once the army has defeated Hòu,
Yǎnhuī will certainly come out to reward the troops.
Immediately bring him back with you;
there is no need for me to mobilize again.”
Jiǎn and the others attacked Hòu,
defeating him at Zhōngyáng.
Hòu fled back to Miánzhōu,
and returned the Táng banners and tallies to Dàobì before releasing him.
Having already received the tally, Yǎnhuī
claimed illness and did not come out to reward the army.
In the second year of Qiánníng [895 CE],
Jiàn sent Wáng Zōngdí to attack him.
In the twelfth month,
Zōngdí defeated Yǎnhuī at Qiūlín,
beheading his general Luō Zhāng,
and consequently besieged Zǐzhōu.
In the fifth month of the third year [896 CE],
Zhāozōng sent the eunuch Yuán Yìjiǎn with an edict ordering Jiàn to cease hostilities.
Jiàn withdrew his troops and returned to Chéngdū.
Wáng Zhào, the Jiédùshǐ of Qiánnán, surrendered his territory to Jiàn.
In the fourth year [897 CE],
Zōngdí resumed the attack on Dōngchuān.
He separately dispatched Wáng Zōngkǎn, Zōng Ruǎn, and others to leave the gorge,
and seize Yú and Lú prefectures.
In the fifth month,
Jiàn personally led troops to attack Dōngchuān.
Zhāozōng sent Lǐ Xún, Grand Master of Remonstrance, and Wéi Zhuāng, Judicial Administrator, to proclaim an edict to the Liǎng Chuān,
ordering Jiàn to cease hostilities.
Jiàn did not obey the edict,
so [the court] demoted Jiàn to the Cìshǐ of Nánzhōu,
appointed the Prince of Tán (Tán Wáng) as Jiédùshǐ of Fèngxiáng,
and replaced Jiàn with Lǐ Màozhēn as Jiédùshǐ of Xīchuān.
Mào-zhēn refused the order.
Consequently, Jiàn’s official titles and ranks were restored.
In the winter, tenth month,
Jiàn attacked and captured Zǐzhōu,
and Yǎnhuī committed suicide.
Gù Yǎnyáo, Yǎnhuī’s general, seeing the city was already in danger,
said to the various generals and officials:
“Serving our lord means seeing this through, living or dying!”
Pointing to the dark iron sword he wore, he said:
“If, when the situation is desperate, anyone defects,
he should chew on this sword!”
When the city was about to fall,
Yǎnyáo and Yǎnhuī summoned the generals and officials to drink wine,
and consequently all died together.
Jiàn appointed Wáng Zōngdí as Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu) of Dōngchuān.
The Táng [court] immediately appointed Zōngdí as Jiédùshǐ.
Thus, [Jiàn] simultaneously possessed the territory of the Two Shu Circuits.
At this time,
Lǐ Màozhēn of Fèngxiáng concurrently held Liáng, Yáng, Qín, and Lǒng prefectures,
frequently invading Jiàn (Wáng Jiàn) with troops.
In the first year of Tiānfù (901),
Liáng Tàizǔ used troops to execute the eunuchs.
The eunuchs Hán Quánhuì and others kidnapped the Son of Heaven (Emperor Zhāozōng) and fled to Fèngxiáng.
The Liáng troops besieged them.
Màozhēn closed the city gates and resisted for over a year.
His strength exhausted,
he sought peace with Liáng.
During this interval, Jiàn sent envoys to court Màozhēn,
promising to send troops as reinforcement,
and urging him to hold the fortifications firmly and not make peace.
He sent Wáng Zōngdí to lead fifty thousand troops,
claiming openly that they were coming to escort the Emperor,
but actually to attack Xīngyuán.
He captured its Jìedùshǐ, Lǐ Jìyè,
and the Jìedùshǐ of Wǔdìng, Tuòbá Sījìng, subsequently surrendered his territory to Jiàn.
Thereupon, he also acquired the Shānnán Xīdào Circuit.
At this time,
Chéng Ruì of Jīngnán died.
Zhào Kuāngníng of Xiāngzhōu sent his younger brother, Kuāngmíng, to attack and occupy it.
Jiàn took advantage of this situation,
and attacked and captured the four prefectures of Kuí, Shī, Zhōng, and Wàn.
In the eighth month of the third year (903),
Táng enfeoffed Jiàn as the Prince of Shǔ.
In the fourth year (904),
Táng moved its capital to Luòyáng,
and changed the reign title to Tiānyòu.
Jiàn was cut off from Táng and did not know this,
so he continued to use the title Tiānfù.
In the sixth year (906),
he further captured Guī Prefecture.
Thus, he completely controlled the Three Gorges.
In the seventh year (907),
Liáng destroyed Táng.
It sent an envoy to announce this to Jiàn,
but Jiàn refused to receive the message.
Jiàn then issued a swift proclamation to all quarters,
calling for allied troops to attack Liáng.
All quarters knew he was insincere,
and none responded.
In the first month of that year,
a giant was seen on Qīngchéng Shān.
In the sixth month,
a phoenix was seen in Wànsuì County;
a yellow dragon was seen in the Jiāyáng Jiāng (River);
and all the prefectures reported auspicious signs of sweet dew, white deer, white sparrows, turtles, and dragons.
In autumn, the ninth month, on the day Jǐhài,
Jiàn thereupon ascended the throne as Emperor.
He enfeoffed his various sons as princes,
appointed Wáng Zōngjí as Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat),
Wéi Zhuāng as Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì (Left Palace Attendant) acting concurrently as the superintendent of affairs of the Chancellery and the Secretariat (Pàn Zhōngshū Ménxià zhī Shì),
Táng Xí as Shūmì Shǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs),
Zhèng Qiān as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Vice Censor-in-Chief),
Zhāng Gé and Wáng Kǎi were both appointed Hànlín Xuéshì (Academicians of the Hanlin Academy),
and Zhōu Bóyǎ as Chéngdū Yǐn (Prefect of Chéngdū).
Shǔ relied on its natural defenses and wealth.
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
many scholars desired to rely on Jiàn to escape the turmoil.
Although Jiàn rose from banditry,
he was a man of great cunning and intelligence,
and treated scholars well.
Therefore, when he usurped the title,
those he employed were all famous ministers and hereditary families of Táng: Zhuāng,
was the grandson of Jiàn Sù;
Gé,
was the son of Jùn.
Jiàn said to his attendants:
“When I was a general in the Shéncè Army,
and served as a guard in the forbidden palace,
I saw the Son of Heaven summon academicians at night,
entering and exiting without restriction,
with favor and respect as close as colleagues.
This is not comparable to how generals and chancellors are treated.”
Therefore, Jiàn treated Gé and the others with especially high favor and respect.
The remaining hundred or so people, such as Sòng Pín,
were all trusted and employed.
In the first month of the first year of Wǔchéng (908),
he sacrificed to Heaven in the Southern Suburbs,
declared a great amnesty,
and changed the reign title.
He appointed Wáng Zōngjí as Tàishī (Grand Preceptor).
Zōngjí’s original surname was Gān.
Jiàn captured him when he was a soldier in the Zhōngwǔ Army,
and raised him as his son.
Later, due to military merit, he was repeatedly promoted to Jìedùshǐ of the Wǔxìn Army.
Later, as Yuányì and other biological sons of Jiàn grew older,
Zōngjí felt uneasy due to his status as an adopted son.
He plotted with Zhèng Qiān and others,
requesting to be Dà Sīmǎ (Grand Marshal),
to command all six armies,
to establish a Grand Marshal's office,
and to handle all military matters expediently before reporting.
Jiàn considered that Zōngjí had rendered great service in founding the state,
and treated him generously.
Táng Xí originally gained Jiàn's favor as a dancing boy.
Zōngjí especially slighted him.
Even after he became Shūmì Shǐ,
he still called Xí by his personal name.
Although Xí secretly resented this,
outwardly he served Zōngjí with even greater deference.
When Jiàn heard this,
he said angrily:
“Zōngjí calls my Commissioner of Military Affairs by his personal name.
He is planning rebellion.”
Zōngjí sought the title of Grand Marshal.
His memorial was submitted three times.
Jiàn consulted Xí about it.
Xí thereupon provoked Jiàn, saying:
“Zōngjí is a meritorious minister.
His prestige and reputation are sufficient to subdue the hearts of the people.
Your Majesty should grant it to him immediately.”
Jiàn’s suspicions increased.
When Zōngjí entered to report on affairs,
and repeatedly pleaded his own case,
Jiàn shouted at the guards to bludgeon him to death,
and also ordered Qiān to commit suicide.
In the sixth month,
he appointed Wáng Zōngyì, Prince of Suì, as Crown Prince.
Jiàn added the honorary title Yīngwǔ Ruìshèng Huángdì (Brave and Sagacious Emperor).
In the seventh month,
a Zōu Yú (a benevolent beast) was seen in Wǔdìng.
In the second year (909),
the Yǒngchāng Calendar was promulgated.
In Guǎngdū, auspicious grain stalks grew with joined ears.
In the eighth month of the third year (910),
fifty dragons were seen in the waters of Xúnyáng.
In the tenth month,
a Qílín was seen in Bì Prefecture.
In the twelfth month,
a great amnesty was declared,
and the following year was designated the first year of Yǒngpíng (911).
Lǐ Màozhēn, Prince of Qí, since being besieged by Liáng,
and since Shānnán had been incorporated into Shǔ,
was restricted in territory and isolated in power.
Consequently, he made peace with Jiàn,
and had his son marry Jiàn’s daughter.
He then requested his former territory in Shānnán.
Jiàn was angered
and refused to grant it.
He appointed Wáng Zōngkǎn as Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Route,
and Zōngyòu, Zōnghè, and Táng Xí as Commanders of Three-Front Punitive Expeditions to attack Qí.
They fought at Qīngní,
but Zōngkǎn suffered a defeat,
and retreated to defend Xī County,
where he was besieged by Màozhēn’s troops.
Jiàn personally led an attack against them.
The Qí troops were defeated,
and dispersed.
Jiàn reached Xīngyuán before returning.
He added the honorary title Yīngwǔ Ruìshèng Guāngxiào Huángdì (Brave, Sagacious, Glorious, and Filial Emperor).
In the second year (912),
he further added the title Yīngwǔ Ruìshèng Shéngōng Wéndé Guāngxiào Huángdì (Brave, Sagacious, Divinely Meritorious, Cultured, Virtuous, Glorious, and Filial Emperor).
Originally,
when Tián Lìngzī was the Superintendent of the Army,
he stole the Táng imperial seal, brought it into Shǔ, and buried it.
In the second month,
Ōuyáng Róu, the Director of the Imperial Kitchen, was renovating Lìngzī’s old residence.
He dug into the ground and found it,
and presented it.
In the fifth month,
Liáng sent Lú Pín, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, to come and engage in diplomatic relations.
He referred to Jiàn as elder brother,
but the inscription on his seal read:
“Seal of Great Liáng entering Shǔ.”
The Chancellor Zhāng Gé said:
“According to Táng precedents,
when sending envoys to the four barbarian regions,
the seal read, ‘Seal of Great Táng entering [such-and-such] country.’
Now Liáng already treats Your Majesty as an elder brother,
how can they humble us like barbarians?”
Jiàn was furious,
and wanted to kill the Liáng envoy.
Gé said:
“This is merely the fault of the responsible officials in Liáng;
one should not cut off the pleasant relations between the two countries.”
Soon after, Liáng Tàizǔ died.
Jiàn sent Lǐ Hóng, the Supervisor of Imperial Construction, to offer condolences.
He then had his seal inscribed to read:
“Seal of Great Shǔ entering Liáng.”
In Jiàn Prefecture, trees grew with interlocked branches.
In the sixth month,
a Qílín was seen in Wén Prefecture.
In the twelfth month,
a yellow dragon was seen in the Fùyì Jiāng (River).
In the first month of the third year,
a Qílín was seen in Yǒngtài.
In the fifth month,
a Zōuyú was seen on Bìshān,
with two deer following it.
In the seventh month of autumn,
Crown Prince Yuán Yīng killed Tàizǐ Shàobǎo Táng Xí.
Yuán Yīng
was Jiàn’s second son.
His original name was Zōng Yì,
later changed to Zōng Tǎn.
Jiàn had obtained a copper plaque at Shífǎng,
which had more than twenty characters inscribed on it.
Jiàn considered this an auspicious omen (fúchèn),
and consequently used characters from it to name his sons.
Therefore, he changed his name again to Yuán Yīng.
Yuán Yīng had a protruding jaw and decayed teeth.
He was gifted in many arts,
able to shoot arrows through the hole of a coin.
He once held a painted ball, threw it while on horseback,
galloped away and shot it,
and never missed.
At the age of seventeen,
he was made Crown Prince,
given jurisdiction over the Six Armies,
established the Tiānwǔ Shénjī Battalion,
opened the Yǒnghé Prefecture,
and appointed officials.
Jiàn, considering Yuán Yīng young and his responsibilities heavy,
admonished him with an account,
ordering,
“In all matters, study what I have done,
and then you can preserve the state.”
He also appointed the Daoist Guǎngchéng Xiānshēng Dù Guāngtíng as his teacher.
Táng Xí
was a favorite of Jiàn.
Yuán Yīng treated him disrespectfully
and repeatedly mocked him at court.
Jiàn feared their enmity,
and thus dismissed Xí as Pīmìshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs),
sending him out to be the Jìedùshǐ of Xīngyuán.
Later, when Xí was dismissed and returned home,
Yuán Yīng detailed Xí’s faults openly at court.
Jiàn became even more displeased.
On the Qīxī festival that month,
Yuán Yīng summoned the various princes and high ministers for a feast.
However, Jí Wáng Zōng Hàn, Pīmìshǐ Pān Qiào, and Hànlín Xuéshì Máo Wénxī did not attend.
Yuán Yīng angrily said:
“Jí Wáng did not come,
it must be Qiào and Wén Xī who instructed him!”
The next day,
Yuán Yīng reported to Jiàn that Qiào and Wén Xī were sowing discord.
Jiàn grew angry
and was about to punish them.
Yuán Yīng went out, and Xí came in.
Jiàn questioned him about the matter.
Xí replied:
“The Crown Prince is plotting a rebellion.
He intends to summon the generals and princes, confine them with soldiers,
and only then launch his plot!”
Jiàn was suspicious.
Xí requested that the garrison troops be summoned for palace defense.
Yuán Yīng had initially made no preparations.
Hearing that Xí had summoned troops,
he believed he was about to be executed.
Therefore, he and the entertainer Ān Xīxiāng, along with the military commander Yù Quánshū, led the Tiānwǔ troops for self-defense.
He sent men to capture Qiào and Wén Xī and flog them,
imprisoning them in their own homes.
He summoned the great generals Xú Yáo and Cháng Qiān to lead troops out to resist Xí.
They fought Xí at the Shénwǔ Gate.
Xí was struck by a stray arrow
and fell from his horse, dying.
Jiàn sent Wáng Zōnghè with troops to suppress them.
Yuán Yīng’s forces were defeated and scattered.
Yuán Yīng hid among the railings of the Yuèlóng Pond.
The next day,
he came out to beg for food.
A man from Shǔ recognized him
and reported it.
Jiàn sent Zōng Hàn to persuade and comfort him.
Before Zōng Hàn arrived,
Yuán Yīng was killed by the imperial guards.
Jiàn then established his youngest son, Zhèng Wáng Zōng Yǎn, as Crown Prince.
A white dragon was seen in the river near Qióngzhōu.
In the fourth year,
Gāo Jìchāng of Jīngnán invaded Wūshān in Shǔ.
Jiàn sent Jiā Wáng Zōng Shòu to defeat him at Qūtáng.
In the eighth month,
the Jìedùshǐ of Qiánnán, Wáng Zōngxùn, was executed.
In winter,
the Southern Man attacked and plundered the border.
Jiàn sent Kuí Wáng Zōng Fàn to defeat them at the Dàdù River.
A Qílín was seen in Chāngzhōu.
In the fifth year,
the Shòuchāng Hall was erected in the Lóngxīng Palace,
and Jiàn’s portrait was painted on the wall.
The Fútiān Pavilion was also erected,
and portraits of various meritorious officials were painted there.
In the eleventh month,
a great fire occurred,
burning down the palace buildings.
Wáng Zōngchóu and others were sent to attack Qí,
capturing the four prefectures of Qín, Fèng, Jiē, and Chéng,
reaching Dàsànguān.
Liáng’s rebellious general Liú Zhījùn was in Qí,
and thus he specially came with his entire clan.
In the first year of Tōngzhèng,
Wáng Zōngwǎn and others were sent to lead 120,000 troops out through Dàsànguān to attack Qí,
capturing Lǒngzhōu.
In the eighth month,
the Wénsī Hall was established.
Officials of the fifth rank or higher who were honest and uncorrupted were used to procure various books to fill it.
The Internal Pīmìshǐ, Máo Wénxī, was made Grand Academician of the Wénsī Hall (Wénsīdiàn Dàxuéshì).
A yellow dragon was seen at Dàchāng Pond.
In the tenth month,
a general amnesty was declared.
The era name for the following year was changed to Tiānhàn,
and the state name was Hàn.
In the first year of Tiānhàn,
Liú Zhījùn was executed.
In the twelfth month,
a general amnesty was declared.
The era name for the following year was changed to Guāngtiān,
and the state name reverted to Shǔ.
In the sixth month of the first year of Guāngtiān,
Jiàn died,
at the age of seventy-two.
In his later years, Jiàn had many imperial favorites.
Xián Fēi Xú Shì and her sister, Shū Fēi,
both entered [the palace] because of their beauty,
dominated the inner chambers, managed affairs,
and collaborated with eunuchs like Táng Wényǐ to interfere with external politics.
Jiàn was old and senile.
Wényǐ commanded the Six Armies,
and matters, whether great or small,
were all decided by Wényǐ.
When Jiàn fell ill,
Wényǐ brought troops into the imperial guard
and planned to eliminate all of Jiàn’s former generals.
The old generals, hearing that Jiàn was sick,
were all forbidden from entering to see him.
After a long time,
Zōng Bì and others forced their way in,
stated that Wényǐ intended to stage a coup,
and then killed him.
Because Jiàn realized that many of the old generals and high ministers were former associates from Xǔchāng,
and would certainly not serve the Crown Prince,
he tried to select a suitable person, but before he could, his illness worsened rapidly.
He then appointed the eunuch Sòng Guāngsì as Pīmìshǐ and commander of the Six Armies, and then Jiàn died.
When the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
he removed
the character "Zōng"
and used the name Yǎn.
Yǎn’s courtesy name (zì) was Huàyuán.
Jiàn had eleven sons:
Wèi Wáng Zōng Rén,
Jiǎn Wáng Yuán Yīng,
Zhào Wáng Zōng Jì,
Bīn Wáng Zōng Lù,
Hán Wáng Zōng Zhì,
Jǔ Wáng Zōng Tè,
Xìn Wáng Zōng Jié,
Lǔ Wáng Zōng Dǐng,
Xīng Wáng Zōng Zé,
Xuē Wáng Zōng Píng.
Zhèng Wáng Zōng Yǎn was the youngest.
His mother was Xú Xián Fēi.
Due to his mother’s favor, he was established as Crown Prince,
the Chóngxián Prefecture was opened,
and officials were appointed.
It was later renamed Tiāncè Prefecture.
Yǎn had a square jaw and a large mouth,
his hands hung down past his knees,
and when he looked back, his eyes reached his ears.
He possessed considerable scholarly knowledge
and was capable of writing ornate and flowery prose.
After Yuán Yīng died,
Jiàn considered Bīn Wáng Zōng Lù to resemble himself in appearance,
and Xìn Wáng Zōng Jié to be the most talented and virtuous among his sons.
He intended to choose one of the two to establish.
However, Consort Xú held exclusive favor,
and Jiàn was old and senile.
The Consort and the eunuch Táng Wényǐ instructed the physiognomist to report that Yǎn had the most noble physiognomy.
They also prompted the Chancellor Zhāng Gé to endorse this,
and Yǎn was consequently made Crown Prince.
Jiàn died,
Yăn was established (as ruler).
Jiàn was posthumously titled Shénwŭ Shèngwén Xiàodé Mínghuì Huángdì,
his temple name was Gāozŭ,
and his mausoleum was called Yǒnglíng.
Jiàn's principal wife, née Zhōu, was titled Zhāoshèng Huánghòu,
but she died a few days after Jiàn.
Yăn therefore honored his mother, née Xú, as Huáng Tàihòu,
and the empress's younger sister, Shú Fēi, as Huáng Tàifēi.
The Tàihòu and Tàifēi sold offices by decree;
for positions from Cìshĭ (Prefect) downwards,
whenever an office became vacant,
several people would inevitably compete for it,
and the one who offered the most money received it.
They erected large shops and inns in major cities and settlements,
thereby seizing profits from the common people.
Yăn was young and dissolute,
entrusting his administration to the eunuchs Sòng Guāngsì, Guāngbăo, Jĭng Rùnchéng, Wáng Chéngxīu, Ōuyáng Huăng, Tián Lŭchóu, and others.
He appointed Hán Zhāo, Pān Zàiyíng, Gù Zàixún, Yán Xù, and others as his court favorites (xiákè).
He built the Xuānhuá Yuàn (Garden),
which included the halls of Chóngguāng, Tàiqīng, Yánchāng, and Huìzhēn;
the palaces of Qīnghé and Yíngxiān;
the pavilions of Jiàngzhēn, Pénglái, and Dānxiá;
the Fēiluán Pavilion;
and the Ruìshòu Gate.
He also constructed the Yíshén Tíng (Pavilion),
where he and his court favorites and women indulged in drinking day and night.
Once, on the ninth day (of the ninth lunar month), he hosted a feast in the Xuānhuá Yuàn;
Jiā Wáng Zōngshòu spoke about the state and the ancestral altars (shèjì),
and tears flowed as he spoke.
Hán Zhāo and the others said:
"Jiā Wáng is just sad from the wine!"
All the court favorites together mocked and ridiculed him with insolent language,
creating an uproar at the feast.
Yăn paid no heed to this.
The people of Shŭ were wealthy and loved to wander.
In the later years of the Wáng clan (reign),
it was customary to compete in wearing small caps
that barely covered the crown of the head;
if one bowed the head, they immediately fell off.
These were called
"Wēinăomào" (Precarious Brain Caps).
Yăn deemed them inauspicious
and forbade them.
However, Yăn loved to wear large caps.
Whenever he traveled among the common people in disguise,
the common people recognized him by his large cap,
so he ordered everyone in the state to wear large caps.
He also liked to wrap pointed scarves,
whose shape resembled an awl.
Furthermore, the women of the inner palace all wore golden lotus flower crowns
and dressed in Daoist robes.
When deeply drunk, they would remove their crowns;
their hair knots were messy,
and they would reapply vermillion and powder.
This style was called
"Zuìzàng" (Drunk Burial),
and the people throughout the state imitated it.
He once traveled with the Tàihòu and Tàifēi to Qīngchéng Shān.
The palace women's clothes
were all painted with clouds and rosy mist,
so that when viewed from afar, they seemed to float like immortals.
Yăn personally composed the Gānzhōu Qŭ,
describing their immortal appearance.
While moving up and down the mountains and valleys,
Yăn often sang it himself,
and he made the palace women harmonize with him.
The year after Yăn was established,
he changed the reign title to Qiándé.
In the first month of Qiándé first year (919 CE),
he performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven in the south,
granted a general amnesty,
and was given the elevated title Shèngdé Míngxiào Huángdì.
In the winter of the second year (920 CE),
he made a northern inspection tour,
reaching Xī Xiàn.
His banners, flags, spears, and armor
stretched continuously for more than a hundred *lĭ*.
On his return,
he sailed up the river from Làng Zhōu.
His dragon boats and decorated barges
illuminated the river water.
The expenses demanded from the localities
were unbearable for the people.
In the first month of the third year (921 CE),
he returned to Chéngdū.
In the fifth year (923 CE),
he erected the Shàngqīng Gōng (Palace),
molded a statue of Wáng Zĭjìn,
and honored him as Shèngzŭ Zhìdào Yùchén Huángdì.
He also molded statues of Jiàn and Yăn
to stand attendant at his left and right.
Furthermore, in the main hall, he molded statues of Xuányuán Huángdì and the various emperors of Táng,
and performed imperial sacrifices (cháo) to them using the full ritual chariots and regalia (făjià).
In the sixth year (924 CE),
he appointed Wáng Chéngxīu as the Tiānxíong Jiédùshĭ (Military Governor).
The Tiānxíong Commandery
was Qín Zhōu.
Chéngxīu, being a eunuch, was favored
and held the post of Xuānhuī Shĭ.
Chéngxīu’s wife, née Yán,
was exceptionally beautiful,
and Yăn had relations with her.
At this time,
Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
and all the people of Shŭ were afraid.
Zhuāngzōng sent Lĭ Yán to conduct an interview mission to Shŭ.
Yăn took him along to pay respects at the Shàngqīng Palace,
and the officials and commoners of the Shŭ capital,
with curtains, drapes, pearls, and jade ornaments,
lined the road without end.
Yán saw that the people were wealthy and prosperous,
but Yăn was arrogant and debauched.
Upon returning, he presented a strategy to attack Shŭ.
The following year,
Táng Wèi Wáng Jìjí and Guō Chóngtāo attacked Shŭ.
That same year,
Yăn changed the reign title to Xiánkāng.
Since Yăn had ascended the throne,
he regularly hunted yearly at Zĭlái Shān.
This year,
he also toured Yángpíng Huà in Péng Zhōu and Sānxué Shān in Hàn Zhōu.
Because of Wáng Chéngxīu’s wife, née Yán,
in the tenth month,
he toured Qín Zhōu.
His officials remonstrated sharply,
but Yăn did not listen.
Traveling to Zĭtóng,
a great wind ripped off roofs and uprooted trees.
The Grand Astrologer said:
"This is the Greedy Wolf Wind (Tānláng Fēng);
there will be a defeat of the army and the killing of generals."
Yăn paid no attention.
When Yăn reached Miángŭ, the Táng army entered his territory.
Yăn was afraid
and immediately returned.
Wherever the Táng army arrived,
the prefectures and counties welcomed them and surrendered.
Yăn left Wáng Zōngbì to guard Miángŭ,
and sent Wáng Zōngxūn, Zōngyăn, and Zōngyù to lead troops to resist the Táng army.
When Zōngxūn and the others reached Sānquán,
they fled upon seeing the enemy forces.
Yăn ordered Zōngbì to execute Zōngxūn and the others,
but Zōngbì, conversely, conspired with Zōngxūn and the others
and surrendered terms (sòngkuăn) to the Táng army.
Yăn returned to Chéngdū from Miángŭ.
Officials and the women of the inner palace met him at Qīlĭ Tíng (Seven Mile Pavilion).
Yăn, mixed with the palace women, formed a Huíhú (Uygur) troupe to enter the city.
The next day,
he held court in the Wénmíng Diàn (Hall),
weeping opposite his assembled officials.
Zōngbì also rushed back from Miángŭ,
entered the Tàixuán Mén (Gate),
arrested Hán Zhāo, the Mayor of Chéngdū, and the eunuchs Sòng Guāngsì, Jĭng Rùnchéng, Ōuyáng Huăng, and others, killing them,
and sent their severed heads in a box to Jìjí.
Yăn immediately submitted a memorial requesting surrender.
Zōngbì moved Yăn to the Tiānqĭ Gōng (Palace).
When Wèi Wáng Jìjí arrived at Chéngdū,
Yăn, along with his ministers, presented themselves with their faces bound and carrying coffins (a gesture of extreme submission),
and formally surrendered at Qīlĭ Tíng.
Zhuāngzōng summoned Yăn to enter Luò (Luòyáng),
and bestowed an imperial edict upon Yăn, saying:
"You certainly deserve to be granted territory and enfeoffed.
I surely will not treat a person harshly in a difficult time.
The Three Luminaries (Sun, Moon, Stars) are above,
and my word shall not deceive!"
Yăn, holding the edict, joyfully set out on the road,
leading his relatives, the former chancellors Wáng Kăi, Zhāng Gé, Yŭ Chuánsù, Xŭ Jì, the Hanlin Academician Lĭ Mín, and others,
along with the families of several thousand officers and subordinates, toward the east.
In the fourth month of Tóngguāng fourth year (926 CE),
when they reached Qínchuān Yì (Post Station),
Zhuāngzōng, employing the scheme of the performer Jĭng Jìn,
sent the eunuch Xiàng Yánsì to execute Yăn's family clan.
Yăn’s mother, née Xú, cried out before the execution:
"My son surrendered with an entire state,
but instead he is being executed!
Trustworthiness and righteousness have both been abandoned.
I know that disaster for them is imminent!"
Yăn’s concubine, née Líu,
had hair as black as clouds and was beautiful.
The executioner intended to spare her,
but Madame Líu said:
"My family and state are lost;
it is against righteousness to accept humiliation!"
She then proceeded to her death.
Zōngbì,
whose original surname was Wèi,
was named Hóngfū.
Wáng Jiàn adopted him as a son.
When Jiàn attacked Gù Yànhuī,
Zōngbì often leaked Jiàn's plans to Yànhuī.
After Yànhuī was defeated,
Jiàn treated him as before.
When Jiàn fell ill and was about to die,
Zōngbì held the positions of Grand Preceptor (tàishī) and concurrent Director of the Central Secretariat (zhōngshūlìng), and Administrator of the Six Armies (pàn liùjūn),
assisting in governance.
After Wáng Yǎn had surrendered,
Zōngbì offered the treasures of Shǔ to Wèi Wáng and Guō Chóngtāo,
requesting to be appointed Military Governor of Xīchuān (Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ).
Wèi Wáng said:
“These are my family's possessions,
why present them as offerings?”
A few days later,
he was killed by Chóngtāo.
Zōngshòu
was a commoner from Xǔzhōu.
Jiàn adopted him as a son
because they shared the same surname.
Zōngshòu was fond of learning,
skilled in playing the qín and in chess,
and was quiet and retiring by nature.
He enjoyed Daoist arts.
When he served Jiàn, he was the Military Governor of Zhènjiāng Commandery (Zhènjiāngjūn Jiédùshǐ).
After Yǎn was enthroned,
Zōngshòu became Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (tàizǐtàibǎo) and attended court (fèng cháoqǐng),
amusing himself with alchemy and nurturing his vital energy.
Yǎn engaged in lewd and disorderly conduct,
and Zōngshòu alone often remonstrated with him sharply.
Later he became Military Governor of Wǔxìn Commandery (Wǔxìnjūn Jiédùshǐ).
When the Táng army attacked Shǔ,
local areas surrendered upon their arrival,
and Wèi Wáng even sent letters to invite him to surrender.
Only Zōngshòu refused to surrender.
When he heard that Yǎn had already surrendered with the jade disk in his mouth (xiánbì),
he wept greatly.
He followed Yǎn on his eastward migration.
Upon reaching Qíyáng,
he bribed the guards
and was able to see Yǎn.
Yǎn cried until his lap was soaked,
saying:
“If I had listened to your words earlier,
how could I have come to this today!”
After Yǎn died,
Zōngshòu fled to Miǎnchí.
When he heard that Zhuāngzōng had been assassinated,
he disappeared into Mount Xióng'ěr.
In the second year of Tiānchéng (927 CE),
he emerged and went to the capital,
submitting a memorial to request burial for Yǎn's clan.
Míngzōng praised his loyalty
and appointed him as Assistant Military Administrator (xíngjūn sīmǎ) of Bǎoyì Commandery (Bǎoyìjūn),
enfeoffed Yǎn as Shùnzhèng Gōng,
and permitted him to be buried with the rites of a feudal lord.
Zōngshòu obtained the coffins of eighteen members of the Wáng family
and buried them in Sānzhào Village, south of Cháng'ān.
Alas!
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
scholars have largely spoken of auspicious omens (xiángruì).
Even those skilled in discernment
could not dispel their delusion!
When I read the History of Shǔ,
regarding turtles, dragons, qílín, phoenixes, and zōuyú – what the world calls the auspicious omens of a king –
none failed to appear in their state.
How extraordinary!
However, by examining why the Wáng family rose and fell, succeeded and failed,
one can understand it.
Some might think that a single Wáng family is insufficient to account for this;
then by observing the order and disorder of the world at that time,
one can understand it.
As for the dragon,
it is considered divine by not being seen,
and by ascending into the clouds and traveling through the heavens it achieves its ambition.
Now, it lies prone, its form exposed –
this is not divine;
it does not ascend to heaven but appears below in the water –
this is a dereliction of duty.
Yet, how numerous they were!
They can be considered omens of disaster!
The phoenix
is a bird that stays far from humans.
In ancient times, when Shùn governed the world,
his administration was perfected and the people were pleased.
He ordered Kuí to compose music.
When the music was harmonious,
birds and beasts all danced upon hearing it.
At that time,
a phoenix happened to arrive.
Shùn's historian consequently recorded it as a marvel,
and later generations therefore took the arrival of a phoenix as a sign of a virtuous reign.
Thereafter, phoenixes appeared many times,
sometimes during the reigns of mediocre rulers and misguided policies,
sometimes during periods of peril, destruction, and great chaos.
Are these truly auspicious omens?
The qílín
is a beast that stays far from humans.
In ancient times, when Lǔ Āigōng went hunting,
he caught one but did not recognize it.
It was sought out and captured,
not something that appeared on its own.
Therefore, Confucius wrote in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū),
“Westward hunt and captured a qílín” –
this
was a criticism.
“Westward hunt”
means it was not far;
“captured a qílín”
means he disliked his exhaustive taking.
A hunt must record the place,
but Āigōng traversed many places during his pursuit,
so they could not all be named individually.
Therefore,
“west”
was written to encompass all the lands,
meaning he reached everywhere west of his state.
The qílín
is a beast rarely recognized by humans.
Its appearance shows that the Duke exhausted mountains and drained marshes to take everything,
even to the point of searching for and capturing
beasts he did not recognize.
Thus, it is said
“this was a criticism.”
After the Sages passed away,
heterodox theories arose,
and then the qílín was taken as an omen of a king,
and attached to it were portents, prophecies, and strange, bizarre sayings.
A phoenix once appeared during Shùn's time
and was considered an omen,
which still makes some sense.
But when it later appeared in times of chaos,
then one can know it was not an omen.
As for the qílín,
in previous well-governed eras like those of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Zhōugōng,
it never once appeared.
Its single appearance occurred during a chaotic era.
Therefore, who knows if it was an omen?
The turtle
is a creature of mystery.
In muddy rivers and marshes,
they are countless.
Its value to diviners after its death
is simply due to its suitability for that purpose.
But in Dài's Rites (Dài Lǐ), its presence in palace ponds is considered a rare omen for a king,
and Dài Lǐ contains various contributions from different schools,
so its errors are also numerous!
As for the zōuyú,
I do not know what kind of creature it is.
The Shījīng says:
“Alas for the zōuyú!”
Jiǎ Yì believed that zōu
referred to Wénwáng's park,
and yú
referred to the park official (yúguān).
At the time of Yì,
this explanation was current.
Then, to consider it a beast –
did that explanation originate in recent times?
Indeed, dispelling people's delusions
is difficult to debate during times of strong belief.
One must wait until they harbor some doubt,
and then one can proceed to attack it.
The qílín, phoenix, turtle, and dragon,
considered omens of a king,
appeared during the period of the Five Dynasties,
and moreover were all concentrated in Shǔ.
Even those who are fond of speaking of auspicious omens should find this questionable.
By attacking what is questionable,
perhaps the deluded will be prompted to think.

According to the Former Shǔ History (Qián Shǔ Shū), the Yùnlì Tú, and the Jiǔ Guó Zhì, all state that Jiàn entered Chéngdū in the second year of Dàshùn of Táng and became Military Governor of Xīchuān,
and in the seventh year of Tiānfù, in the ninth month, he proclaimed himself emperor,
and in the first month of the following year, he changed the era name to Wǔchéng.
This is now taken as definite.
Only the Old History of the Five Dynasties (Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ) states,
“He entered Chéngdū in the first year of Lóngjì,
and proclaimed himself emperor and changed the era name in the fifth year of Tiānyòu,”
which is erroneous.
Regarding the fall of Shǔ in the third year of Tóngguāng of Later Táng,
all records agree.
From the second year of Dàshùn to the third year of Tóngguāng,
there were thirty-five years in total.
Collations and Notes
Fourth Chapter on the Later Shǔ Imperial Family: Mèng Zhīxiáng (and his son Mèng Chǎng)
Mèng Zhīxiáng, courtesy name Bǎoyìn,
was a man from Lónggāng in Xīngzhōu.
His uncle, Qiān,
during the end of the Táng dynasty,
occupied the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí,
and was captured by Jìn.
The King of Jìn made Qiān the governor of Zélù.
When Liáng troops attacked Jìn,
Qiān used Zélù to surrender to Liáng.
Zhīxiáng's father, Dào,
remained alone serving Jìn but was not prominent.
When Zhīxiáng came of age,
the King of Jìn gave him his younger brother Kèràng's daughter in marriage,
and appointed him Zǔo Jiàoliàn Shǐ (Commander of the Left Training).
When Zhuāngzōng was the King of Jìn,
he made Zhīxiáng the Zhōngmén Shǐ (Court Gate Commissioner).
Previously, many who served as Zhōngmén Shǐ had been executed for crimes.
Zhīxiáng was afraid,
and sought another post.
Zhuāngzōng ordered Zhīxiáng to recommend someone who could replace him.
Zhīxiáng consequently recommended Guō Chóngtāo to take his place.
Chóngtāo was grateful for this,
and Zhīxiáng was promoted to Mǎbù Jūn Dū Yúhòu (Commissioner of Military Supplies for the Cavalry and Infantry).
When Zhuāngzōng established his reign title (as Emperor),
he designated Tàiyuán as Běijīng (the Northern Capital),
and appointed Zhīxiáng as the Prefect of Tàiyuán and Běijīng Liúshǒu (Resident Retainer).
When Wèi Wáng Jìjí attacked Shǔ,
Guō Chóngtāo was the Zhāotǎo Shǐ (Commander of Pacification).
When Chóngtāo was about to leave,
he reported (to the Emperor) saying:
"If your subjects succeed in conquering Shǔ,
Your Majesty must select a marshal to guard Xīchuān.
There is none better than Mèng Zhīxiáng."
Not long after, Táng forces defeated Shǔ,
and Zhuāngzōng consequently appointed Zhīxiáng as Chéngdū Yǐn (Prefect of Chéngdū) and Jiànnán Xīchuān Jiédù Fù Dàshǐ (Deputy Grand Military Commissioner of Xīchuān, Jiànnán).
Zhīxiáng hastened to the capital.
Zhuāngzōng ordered the relevant authorities to set up grand provisions and tents,
and brought forth many rare treasures from the imperial treasury to feast and reward him.
In the midst of the drinking,
they spoke of old times,
finding amusement and joy in the reminiscence.
(Zhuāngzōng) sighed, saying:
"Jìjí was just an inexperienced youth (lit. suckling child) a few days ago,
yet he was able to pacify the Two Chuān regions for me!
We companions are growing old.
This young man is admirable,
but it makes one even sadder!
I recall when the late Emperor passed away,
our territory was encroached upon and chipped away,
we barely held onto a single corner.
How could we have known that today we would suddenly possess the world,
the Nine Provinces and the Four Seas?
Rare treasures and exotic products
fill my treasury!"
He then pointed them out to show Zhīxiáng,
and said:
"I hear that the wealth of the land of Shǔ
is no different from this.
Since you are a loyal relative and worthy,
I entrust it to you."
On the *wùchén* day of the first month of the fourth year of Tóngguāng (926 CE),
Zhīxiáng arrived in Chéngdū.
However, Chóngtāo had already died.
Wèi Wáng Jìjí led his army back east.
The vanguard commander Kāng Yánxiào rebelled
and captured Hànzhōu.
Zhīxiáng dispatched the great general Lǐ Rěnhǎn to join forces with Rén Yuán and Dǒng Zhāng to defeat Yánxiào.
Zhīxiáng gained possession of Yánxiào's generals, Lǐ Zhào and Hóu Hóngshí, and several thousand of their soldiers, whom he brought back.
Then Zhuāngzōng died,
Wèi Wáng Jìjí died,
and Míngzōng ascended the throne.
Zhīxiáng immediately trained his troops and armor,
secretly harboring the ambition to rule Shǔ.
He further established the Yìshèng, Dìngyuǎn, Xiāoruì, Yìníng, and Fēizhào armies, totaling more than seventy thousand men.
He ordered Lǐ Rěnhǎn, Zhào Tíngyǐn, Zhāng Yè, and others to command them separately.
Initially,
when the Wèi Wáng's army returned to the capital,
Zhīxiáng levied money from the wealthy residents of Chéngdū and the families of the former officials of the Wáng clan (of Former Shǔ),
obtaining six million *mín* of cash to reward the troops.
The remainder was still two million.
Rén Yuán, having returned from Shǔ, became Chancellor,
and also supervised the Three Departments (Sān Sī).
He had long known about the remaining money in Shǔ.
That winter,
Zhīxiáng was appointed Shìzhōng (Chamberlain),
and (Míngzōng) then sent the certificate of appointment via Zhào Jìliáng, the Tàipú Qīng (Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud),
and simultaneously made him Sānchuān Zhìzhì Shǐ (Commissioner for Administration of the Three Chuān regions),
ordering him to supervise the remaining reward money in Shǔ and send it to the capital,
and also to manage the taxes and levies in the Two Chuān regions.
Zhīxiáng was enraged
and refused to accept the edict.
However, Zhīxiáng had an old acquaintance with Jìliáng,
so he detained him.
Ān Chónghuǐ, the Shūmì Shǐ (Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs), highly suspected that Zhīxiáng harbored rebellious intentions
and sought a means to control him.
Originally,
when Zhīxiáng governed Shǔ,
Zhuāngzōng had appointed the eunuch Jiāo Yànbīn as Jiānjūn (Army Supervisor).
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he executed all the eunuchs
and abolished the Army Supervisors in all circuits.
Although Yànbīn had been dismissed,
Chónghuǐ again appointed Lǐ Yán, the Kèshěng Shǐ (Reception Commissioner), as Army Supervisor.
Yán had previously been sent to Shǔ.
After returning, he had presented a strategy to attack Shǔ,
and the people of Shǔ all hated him.
Zhīxiáng was also angry and said:
"Jiāo Yànbīn was dismissed by precedent,
and all other circuits have abolished the position of Army Supervisor.
Only my army has one appointed.
This means Yán intends to gain merit by conquering Shǔ again."
Mú Zhāoyì, the Clerk, and all the generals and officials requested that Yán be stopped and not allowed entry.
Zhīxiáng said:
"I will have a way to await his arrival!"
When Yán reached the border,
he sent someone bearing a letter to wait upon Zhīxiáng.
Zhīxiáng displayed his troops when receiving the envoy,
hoping Yán would be afraid and not come.
Yán heard of this but remained composed.
In the first month of the second year of Tiānchéng (927 CE),
Yán arrived in Chéngdū.
Zhīxiáng set up a feast and summoned Yán.
At that time,
although Jiāo Yànbīn had been dismissed,
he was still in Shǔ.
Yán pulled an edict from his bosom and showed it to Zhīxiáng, ordering the execution of Yànbīn.
Zhīxiáng refused to listen.
He then interrogated Yán, saying:
"All the regional governors have now dismissed their Army Supervisors.
How dare you come here?"
He signaled his guest general Wáng Yànzhū to seize Yán and take him away,
and execute him.
Míngzōng was unable to punish (Zhīxiáng).
Earlier,
when Zhīxiáng governed Shǔ,
he had sent men to bring his family from Tàiyuán.
When they reached Fèngxiáng,
Lǐ Cóngyǎn, the Jiédù Shǐ of Fèngxiáng, heard that Zhīxiáng had killed Lǐ Yán,
and believed Zhīxiáng had rebelled.
He consequently detained the family.
Since Míngzōng could not punish him,
and wished instead to win him over with grace and trust,
he dispatched the Kèshěng Shǐ, Lǐ Rěnjǔ, to convey comfort and instructions to Zhīxiáng,
and also sent Princess Qiónghuá and his son Chǎng, among others, back to him.
Zhīxiáng then requested that Zhào Jìliáng be made Jiédù Fùshǐ (Deputy Military Commissioner).
Regardless of the importance of the matter,
he consulted with Jìliáng and let him participate in the decisions.
In the third year (of Tiānchéng, 928 CE),
the Táng court transferred Jìliáng to be the Tuánliàn Shǐ (Militia Commissioner) of Guǒzhōu,
and appointed Hé Zàn as the Deputy Military Commissioner.
Zhīxiáng received the imperial order but concealed it,
and submitted a memorial requesting that Jìliáng be retained.
This was not granted.
He then sent his general Léi Tínglǔ to the capital to argue and plead for the retention.
Míngzōng, having no choice, complied.
At this time,
Zàn had traveled as far as Miángǔ.
He was afraid and dared not proceed further.
Zhīxiáng therefore memorialized that Zàn be appointed Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (Field Marshal).
That same year,
the Táng army attacked Jīngnán.
An edict ordered Zhīxiáng to send troops down the gorges.
Zhīxiáng dispatched Máo Chóngwēi to lead three thousand troops to garrison Kuízhōu.
Not long after, Gāo Jìxīng of Jīngnán died,
and his son Cónghuǐ requested amnesty.
Zhīxiáng requested the dismissal of the garrison troops,
but it was not granted.
Zhīxiáng secretly instructed Chóngwēi to make a clamor with his troops and drums,
and disperse and return (home).
The Táng court impeached Chóngwēi via imperial edict.
Zhīxiáng memorialized, requesting that the impeachment be dropped.
Because of this, the Táng ministers increasingly believed that Zhīxiáng would definitely rebel.
In the fourth year,
Míngzōng was preparing for the ritual at the Southern Suburbs [of the capital].
He sent Lǐ Rénjǔ to demand 1,000,000 mín in funds from Zhīxiáng for the ceremony.
Zhīxiáng suspected that the Táng plot was intended to wear him down,
and he refused, declining to provide it.
After a long delay,
he requested permission to offer only 500,000 mín.
Previously,
when the Prince of Wèi, Jìjí, returned eastward,
he left 5,000 elite troops to garrison Shǔ.
Since Ān Chónghuǐ suspected Zhīxiáng of harboring disloyalty,
he listened to those who offered advice [against Zhīxiáng],
and used his trusted confidants to take control of the various prefectures within the jurisdiction of the two Chuan circuits.
Every time a governor or general was appointed,
they were provided with elite troops as their personal guard unit,
some having two or three thousand,
and the fewest having no less than five hundred men,
in preparation for emergencies.
In this year,
Xià Lǔqí was appointed Military Governor of Wǔxìn Command;
Lǎng Prefecture of Dōngchuān was separated and established as Bǎoníng Command,
with Lǐ Rénjǔ appointed as Military Governor;
Wǔ Qiányù was also appointed Prefect of Mián Prefecture.
Rénjǔ had a feud with Dǒng Zhāng of Dōngchuān,
and Qiányù
was Chónghuǐ's maternal cousin.
Due to this, both Zhāng and Zhīxiáng became afraid,
believing that the Táng was preparing to launch an expedition against them.
Since Zhāng had been garrisoned in Dōngchuān,
he had never communicated with Zhīxiáng.
Thereupon, Zhāng first sent someone to propose a marriage alliance to secure his relationship [with Zhīxiáng].
But Zhīxiáng harbored resentment toward Zhāng [in his heart],
and wished not to agree.
He consulted Zhào Jìliáng about this.
Jìliáng believed they should form an alliance to resist the Táng,
and Zhīxiáng subsequently agreed.
Therefore, they jointly submitted memorials requesting the removal and return of the Military Governors and Prefects sent by the Táng.
Míngzōng issued gracious edicts to console and reassure them.
In the second month of Chángxīng First Year (930),
Míngzōng performed the ritual at the Southern Suburbs,
and bestowed upon Zhīxiáng the added title of Grand Councillor.
Initially,
both Zhīxiáng and Zhāng harbored intentions of disloyalty,
but Chónghuǐ trusted those who spoke [favorably of Zhāng],
believing that Zhāng was completely loyal to the state,
and that only Zhīxiáng was suspect.
Chónghuǐ still intended to rely on Zhāng to deal with Zhīxiáng.
In the ninth month of this year,
Dǒng Zhāng rebelled first,
attacking and breaking into Lǎng Prefecture,
capturing and killing Lǐ Rénjǔ.
In the same month, for the Emperor's birthday festival (Yìng Shèng Jié),
Zhīxiáng held a banquet.
He bowed twice toward the northeast,
prostrated himself, and sobbed,
tears streaming down, wetting his lapels.
The officers and soldiers all sighed in sorrow for him.
The next day, he subsequently raised his army and rebelled.
In this autumn,
Míngzōng changed the title of Princess Qiónghuá to Senior Princess Fúqìng.
The relevant officials reported that in previous generations, when princesses received their titles,
they had not yet been married off,
and there was no ceremony for sending envoys to their vassal states to invest them.
An imperial decree ordered the relevant officials to draft new ceremonies.
Then, they sent the Director of the Palace Library, Liú Yuè, as the investing envoy.
When Yuè reached Fèngxiáng,
he heard that Zhīxiáng had rebelled,
and consequently returned.
Míngzōng issued an edict stripping Zhīxiáng of his offices and titles,
and appointed Shí Jìngtáng, Military Governor of Tiānxíong Command, as Commander-in-Chief of the Expeditionary Forces,
with Xià Lǔqí as his deputy.
Zhīxiáng sent Lǐ Rěnhǎn, Zhāng Yè, and Zhào Tíngyǐn to lead 30,000 troops to join Zhāng in attacking Suí Prefecture.
Separately, he sent Hóu Hóngshí to lead 4,000 men to assist Zhāng in defending Dōngchuān,
and also sent Zhāng Wǔ down the gorges to take Yú Prefecture.
The Táng army attacked Jiàn Gate,
killed 3,000 of Zhāng's defending troops,
and subsequently entered Jiàn Gate.
Zhāng came to report the emergency.
Zhīxiáng was greatly alarmed
and sent Tíngyǐn to divide 10,000 troops and move them eastward.
But later, he heard that the Táng army halted at Jiàn Prefecture and did not advance,
and he rejoiced, saying:
"If the Táng army had swiftly rushed toward Dōngchuān,
Suí Prefecture's siege would have been lifted,
our momentum would be frustrated, and the two Chuan circuits would waver.
Now that they are not advancing,
I know they will be easy to deal with."
In the twelfth month,
Jìngtáng and Tíngyǐn fought at Jiàn Gate,
and the Táng army was severely defeated.
Zhāng Wǔ had already captured Yú Prefecture.
Wǔ became ill and died,
and his deputy, Yuán Yànchāo, took command of his troops,
and subsequently captured Qián Prefecture.
In the first month of the second year (931),
Lǐ Rěnhǎn conquered Suí Prefecture,
and Xià Lǔqí died there.
Zhīxiáng appointed Rěnhǎn as Acting Military Governor of Wǔxìn Command.
He sent someone to speedily deliver Lǔqí's head to show the army of Jìngtáng,
whereupon Jìngtáng withdrew his forces.
Lǐ Yànkē of Lì Prefecture, hearing that the Táng army was defeated and returning east,
abandoned the city and fled.
Zhīxiáng appointed Zhào Tíngyǐn as Acting Military Governor of Zhāowǔ Command.
Lǐ Rěnhǎn advanced to attack Kuí Prefecture.
The Prefect, Ān Chóngruǎn, abandoned the city and fled.
Zhīxiáng appointed Zhào Jìliáng as Acting Military Governor.
At this time,
the Táng army was traversing perilous terrain,
facing difficulty with the supply route.
West of Tóng Gate,
the populace suffered from transporting provisions;
for every stone [of grain] expended, less than one dou could be delivered.
Lamentation filled the roads,
and Jìngtáng's army also returned.
The local garrison commanders everywhere also abandoned their cities and fled.
Míngzōng was worried about this
and criticized Ān Chónghuǐ for it.
Chónghuǐ, afraid,
hastily requested permission to go himself.
However, Chónghuǐ was also condemned due to slander and died.
Míngzōng believed that the rebellion of Zhīxiáng and others
was due to Chónghuǐ's poor strategy.
When Chónghuǐ died,
he sent Sū Yuàn, the Presenting Official of Xīchuān, and Dù Shàoběn, the Military Commander of the Offering Troops, to return west and attempt to persuade Zhīxiáng to submit.
They fully explained that Zhīxiáng's family members in the capital were all safe.
Zhīxiáng, hearing that Chónghuǐ had been executed,
and that the Táng was treating his family well,
invited Zhāng, intending to jointly apologize for their crimes.
Zhāng said:
"Mèng Gōng's family members are all alive,
but my sons and grandsons alone were killed.
What am I apologizing for!"
Zhīxiáng sent three envoys to meet Zhāng,
but Zhāng did not listen.
Zhīxiáng then sent the Observing Commissioner's Consultant, Lǐ Hào, to persuade Zhāng.
Zhāng became even more suspicious that Zhīxiáng was betraying him,
and consequently became angry,
using his words to insult Hào.
Hào then advised Zhīxiáng to attack Zhāng.
Zhāng, however, first launched a surprise attack and captured Zhīxiáng's Hàn Prefecture.
Zhīxiáng sent Zhào Tíngyǐn to lead 30,000 troops,
and personally attacked him,
arraying his forces at Jījù Bridge.
Zhīxiáng obtained a surrendered soldier from Zhāng's army,
dressed him in a brocade robe,
and had him carry a letter to recruit Zhāng to surrender.
Zhāng said:
"Matters have reached this point;
there is no regretting it!"
Zhāng's soldiers all shouted, saying:
"You only expose us to the sun;
why not fight quickly?"
Zhāng immediately waved his army to engage in battle.
As soon as the armies clashed,
Zhāng's brigade general, Zhāng Shǒujìn, came over and surrendered.
Zhīxiáng capitalized on this,
and Zhāng was consequently greatly defeated
and fled.
Passing over Jīnyàn Bridge,
he waved at his son, Guāngsì, instructing him to surrender
to preserve the family.
Guāngsì wept, saying:
"Since ancient times, how could there be anyone who kills his father to seek life!
I would rather die together with you."
Consequently, he fled along with Zhāng.
Zhīxiáng sent Zhào Tíngyǐn to pursue them.
They did not catch them.
Zhāng fled to Zǐ Prefecture, where he was killed.
Guāngsì hanged himself and died.
Zhīxiáng consequently incorporated Dōngchuān.
However, since Zhāng's death,
Zhīxiáng ultimately did not send an envoy to apologize to the Táng.
Fàn Yán'guāng (范延光), the Táng (唐) Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ), said:
“Although Zhīxiáng (知祥) has already defeated Zhāng (璋),
he will certainly borrow the power of the Imperial Court
to give weight to the Two Chuān (Liǎng Chuān).
Unless we condescend to invite him,
he will not be able to return of his own accord.”
Míngzōng (明宗) said:
“Zhīxiáng
is my old friend.
It was originally due to spies that this dangerous doubt arose.
In comforting my old friend,
why should there be any condescension?”
Before this,
Kèníng's (克寧) wife, Madam Mèng (孟氏),
was Zhīxiáng’s younger sister.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) killed Kèníng,
Madam Mèng returned to Zhīxiáng.
Her son, Guī (瓌),
remained to serve Táng as an Official of the Palace Service (Gōngfèng Guān).
Míngzōng immediately dispatched Guī to return and visit his mother,
and consequently bestowed an imperial edict upon Zhīxiáng to invite and comfort him.
Zhīxiáng concurrently occupied the Two Chuān (Liǎng Chuān).

He made Zhào Jìliáng (趙季良) Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu) of the Wǔtài (武泰) Army, Lǐ Rěnhǎn (李仁罕) Acting Military Governor of the Wǔxìn (武信) Army, Zhào Tíngyǐn (趙廷隱) Acting Military Governor of the Bǎoníng (保寧) Army, Zhāng Yè (張業) Acting Military Governor of the Níngjiāng (寧江) Army, and Lǐ Zhào (李肇) Acting Military Governor of the Zhāowǔ (昭武) Army.
Jìliáng and the others subsequently requested that Zhīxiáng declare himself King,
and handle affairs using unofficial, black-inked orders (mò zhì).
While the deliberation was still undecided, Guī arrived in Shǔ (蜀).
Zhīxiáng treated Guī with arrogance and disrespect.
In the ninth month,
Guī returned from Shǔ,
bringing a memorial from Zhīxiáng,
requesting that Zhào Jìliáng and the others be appointed as Military Governors (Jiédù) of the Five Garrisons,
and that all officials below the rank of Prefect (Cìshǐ)
could be appointed by him personally.
He also requested to be enfeoffed as the King of Shǔ (Shǔ Wáng),
and moreover stated that Princess Fúqìng (福慶公主) had died.
Míngzōng mourned for this,
and dispatched the Palace Gate Commissioner (Gémén Shǐ), Liú Zhèng'ēn (劉政恩), as Envoy of Pacification (Xuānyù Shǐ).
When Zhèng'ēn returned from his mission,
Zhīxiáng finally dispatched his general Zhū Huàng (朱滉) to come to the court.
In the second month of the fourth year, on the day Guǐhài (癸亥),
an edict was issued appointing Zhīxiáng as Acting Grand Commandant (Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi) and concurrently Grand Secretary (Zhōngshū Lìng),
with the status of Administrator of Chéngdū (Chéngdū Yǐn), Military Governor of Jiànnán East and West Chuān (Jiànnán Dōngxī Liǎng Chuān Jiédù),
Commissioner of Observation and Management within his jurisdiction, Superintendent of all the neighboring barbarians,
and concurrently Commissioner for Pacification and Management of the Eight States of Xīshān (西山) and Yúnnán (雲南).
He sent Lú Wénjì (盧文紀), President of the Board of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū), to perform the ceremony of enfeoffing Zhīxiáng as the King of Shǔ,
and Zhào Jìliáng and the other five men were all appointed Military Governors.
The Táng troops previously stationed in Shǔ numbered tens of thousands.
Zhīxiáng generously provided them all with clothing and food,
and consequently requested that their families be sent [to Shǔ].
Míngzōng issued an imperial decree refusing this request.
In the eleventh month,
Míngzōng died.
In the intercalary first month of the following year,
Zhīxiáng then ascended the imperial throne,
naming his state Shǔ.
He appointed Zhào Jìliáng as Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
He appointed Wáng Chùhuí (王處回), the Palace Gate Commissioner (Zhōngmén Shǐ), as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ),
and Lǐ Hào (李昊) as Academician of the Hànlín Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì).
In the third month,
Lù Wáng (潞王) of Táng raised troops at Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
Mǐndì (愍帝) dispatched Wáng Sītóng (王思同) and others to suppress him.
Sītóng’s forces collapsed.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo (張虔釗), the Military Governor of Shānnán West Circuit (Shānnán Xīdào), and Sūn Hànsháo (孫漢韶), the Military Governor of the Wǔdìng (武定) Army, both attached their territories to Shǔ.
In the fourth month,
Zhīxiáng changed the era name to Míngdé (明德).
In the sixth month,
Qiánzhāo and the others arrived in Chéngdū (成都).
Zhīxiáng hosted a banquet to reward them.
When Qiánzhāo offered a cup and rose to propose a toast,
Zhīxiáng’s hand became weak and he could not lift the cup.
He subsequently fell ill,
and appointed his son, Chǎng (昶), as Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) to supervise the state (jiān guó).
Zhīxiáng died.
His posthumous title was Emperor Wénwǔ Shèngdé Yīngliè Míngxiào (文武聖德英烈明孝 Huángdì),
his temple name was Gāozǔ (高祖),
and his tomb was called Hé Líng (和陵).
Chǎng
was the third son of Zhīxiáng.
When Zhīxiáng was Military Governor of the Two Chuān,
Chǎng served as General Manager of Military Affairs (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
When Zhīxiáng usurped the title [of Emperor],
he made Chǎng Military Governor of Dōngchuān (東川) and Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì).
When Zhīxiáng was ill,
Chǎng supervised the state.
Zhīxiáng had already died, but the news was kept secret.
Wáng Chùhuí visited Zhào Jìliáng late at night.
They wept and cried continuously facing each other.
Jìliáng said sternly:
“Now, powerful marquises (jiāng hóu) hold military power
and are solely watching for changes in the situation.
We must quickly establish the successor ruler to preempt unwarranted ambitions.
Weeping is useless.”
Chùhuí subsequently established Chǎng with Jìliáng,
and only then announced the death.
When Chǎng ascended the throne,
he did not change the era name,
still calling it Míngdé.
It was not until the fifth year that the era name was changed to Guǎngzhèng (廣政).
In the third month of the third year of Míngdé,
Yínghuò (Mars) violated Jīshī (the stellar station),
Chǎng believed that Jīshī corresponded to the Shǔ territory,
and being afraid,
he wanted to perform a ritual sacrifice (ráng) to avert misfortune.
He asked Hú Yùn (胡韞), the Vice Supervising Secretary of Astronomy (Sītiān Shàojiān).
Yùn said:
“According to the Twelve Divisions (Shí'èr Cì),
starting from five degrees of Jǐng (井) up to eight degrees of Liǔ (柳),
it constitutes the division of Chúnshǒu (鶉首).
Chúnshǒu
is the territory of Qín (秦).
Although Shǔ belongs to Qín,
it is only the extreme southern boundary.
In previous ages, when Huǒ (Mars) entered Guǐ (the Ghost stellar mansion),
its corresponding effect was in Qín.
In the third month of the ninth year of Xiánhé (咸和) during the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
Huǒ violated Jīshī,
and in the fourth month,
Guō Quán (郭權), the Prefect of Yōngzhōu (雍州), was killed.
In the fourth year of Yìxī (義熙),
Huǒ violated Guǐ.
The following year,
Zhū Língshí (朱齡石), the Prefect of Yōngzhōu, was killed.
But Shǔ was entirely unaffected.”
Thereupon, [Chǎng] stopped [the ritual plan].
Chǎng was fond of polo (dǎ qiú) and riding horses,
and also practiced the inner chamber arts (fáng zhōng zhī shù) of the Daoist masters (fāngshì).
He frequently selected daughters from respectable families to fill his inner palace.
Hán Bǎozhēn (韓保貞), the Deputy Commissioner of Military Affairs, remonstrated sharply.
Chǎng was greatly enlightened [by the advice].
That very day, he released them [the women],
and bestowed several pounds of gold upon Bǎozhēn.
Someone presented a memorial [to the throne],
stating that officials in the Censorate and ministries (tái shěng guān) should be chosen from the “Pure Stream” (qīng liú).
Chǎng sighed, saying:
“Why did he not say, ‘Choose the right people and employ them’?”
His attendants requested permission to question the memorialist about his statement.
Chǎng said:
“I saw that when Táng Tàizōng (唐太宗) first ascended the throne,
Sūn Fúgā (孫伏伽), a prison clerk, presented a memorial concerning affairs,
and his advice was all accepted with approval.
How can you urge me to reject remonstrance!”
However, Chǎng was young and did not personally attend to state affairs,
and the generals, chancellors, and great ministers were all old acquaintances of Zhīxiáng.
Zhīxiáng was generous and tolerant,
often treating them with excessive leniency.
When they came to serve Chǎng,
they became increasingly arrogant and unruly,
often exceeding legal limits.
They focused on expanding their residences,
seizing good farmland from the people,
and even disturbing their graves.
Lǐ Rěnhǎn and Zhāng Yè were especially extreme in this regard.
A few months after Chǎng ascended the throne,
he arrested Rěnhǎn and executed him,
and exterminated his entire clan.
At this time,
Lǐ Zhào came to court from his garrison.
He entered the audience supported by a staff,
claiming illness and refusing to bow.
When he heard of Rěnhǎn’s death,
he immediately dropped his staff and performed the kowtow.
In the ninth year of Guǎngzhèng,
Zhào Jìliáng died.
Zhāng Yè became increasingly powerful in managing affairs.
Yè
