was Rěnhǎn’s nephew.
When Rěnhǎn was executed,
Yè was in charge of the palace guards (jìn bīng).
Chǎng feared that he might rebel,
so he appointed him as Chancellor (xiàng).
Yè concurrently managed the Finance Commission (dù zhī).
He established a prison in his own residence,
and strove to heavily tax the people of Shǔ using cruel laws.
The people of Shǔ greatly resented him.
In the eleventh year,
Chǎng conspired with Ān Sīqiān (安思謙), the Commander of the Kuāngshèng (匡聖) Guard,
to arrest and execute him.
Wáng Chùhuí and Zhào Tíngyǐn subsequently retired from office.
Consequently, the old generals and former ministers were nearly all gone.
Chǎng began to personally attend to state affairs,
and established a suggestion box (kuǐ) in the court hall to communicate with the populace.
At this time,
the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
Hàn Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán,
and the Central Plains suffered much turmoil.
Hé Jiàn, the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) of the Xióngwǔ Army, attached the three prefectures of Qín, Chéng, and Jiē to Shǔ.
Chǎng thereupon sent Sūn Hànsháo to attack and conquer Fèngzhōu,
thus possessing all the former territory of Wáng Yǎn.
The Hàn generals Zhào Sīwǎn, holding Yǒngxīng, and Wáng Jǐngchóng, holding Fèngxiáng, rebelled,
and both sent allegiance to Chǎng.
Chǎng sent Zhāng Qiánzhāo out through Dàsànguān,
Hé Jiàn out through Lǒngyòu,
and Lǐ Tíngguī out through Zǐwǔgǔ,
to support Sīwǎn.
Chǎng’s Chancellor, Wú Zhāoyì, earnestly remonstrated,
believing this action was improper,
but Chǎng’s ambition to spy upon Guānzhōng was very strong,
so he dispatched Ān Sīqiān with additional troops eastward.
Subsequently, Hàn executed Sīwǎn and Jǐngchóng,
and Qiánzhāo and the others were all ordered back.
Sīqiān, ashamed of having achieved nothing,
killed many soldiers to intimidate the populace.
Chǎng planned with the Academician-in-Waiting (Hànlín Shǐ), Wáng Zǎo, to kill Sīqiān,
but when a border official had an urgent memorial,
Zǎo failed to report it immediately
and arbitrarily broke the seal on it.
Chǎng grew angry at him.
When Sīqiān was killed,
Zǎo happened to be attending nearby,
and so he was seized along with Sīqiān and executed.
In the twelfth year (of his reign),
he established the Three Evaluations (Sān Quán) in the Ministry of Personnel and the Tribute Examination (Gòngjǔ) in the Ministry of Rites.
In the thirteenth year,
Chǎng adopted the augmented title Ruìwén Yīngwǔ Rénshèng Míngxiào Huángdì.
He enfeoffed his son Xuánzhé as Prince of Qín,
who was put in charge of the Six Armies;
his second son Xuányù as Prince of Bāo;
his younger brother Rén'yì as Prince of Kuí;
Rénzhì as Prince of Yǎ;
and Rén'yù as Prince of Jiā.
In the eighteenth year,
Zhōu Shìzōng attacked Shǔ,
launching the assault from Qínzhōu.
Chǎng appointed Hán Jìxūn as Military Commissioner of the Xióngwǔ Army,
but when he heard the Zhōu forces were coming to attack,
he sighed, saying:
“How can Jìxūn possibly withstand the Zhōu army!”
Zhào Jìzhá, the Director of the Guest Department (Kèshěng Shǐ), requested permission to go,
so Chǎng appointed Jìzhá as Monitor of the Army (Jiānjūn Shǐ) for Qínzhōu.
Jìzhá traveled until he reached Déyáng,
but when he heard the Zhōu army had arrived,
he immediately galloped back to report the matter.
Chǎng questioned him,
but Jìzhá was so frightened that he could not utter a single word.
Chǎng angrily executed him.
Then he dispatched Gāo Yànchóu and Lǐ Tíngguī to leave Tángcāng to resist the Zhōu forces.
Yànchóu suffered a great defeat
and fled to Qīngní.
Thus, Qín, Chéng, Jiē, and Fèng prefectures returned to Zhōu control.
Chǎng was afraid,
and sent out envoys separately to court Nán Táng and Dōng Hàn
to bolster his strategic position.
In the twentieth year,
Shìzōng returned the Shǔ captives he had taken.
Chǎng also returned the captured Zhōu general, Hú Lì, to the capital (Jīngshī),
and thereupon enclosed a letter to Shìzōng.
Shìzōng was angered that Chǎng had failed to observe the etiquette due to a subject,
and did not reply.
In the twenty-first year,
the Zhōu army attacked Nán Táng,
capturing fourteen prefectures in Huáinán.
All the various states became fearful.
Gāo Bǎoróng of Jīngnán invited Chǎng by letter to submit to Zhōu,
but because Chǎng had previously sent a letter to Shìzōng and received no reply,
he ceased the effort.
Chǎng’s youngest son, Xuánbǎo,
died at the age of seven.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) stated that a child who died before the age for wearing mourning clothes should not be given posthumous honors.
Chǎng asked Lǐ Hào,
and Hào replied:
“In the past, Píng, the son of Emperor Dézōng of Táng,
died at the age of four,
and was posthumously granted the title Grand Governor of Yángzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Sù.
This is a precedent.”
Chǎng then posthumously granted Xuánbǎo the title Grand Governor of Qīngzhōu
and retroactively enfeoffed him as Prince of Suì.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he established the Prince of Qín, Xuánzhé, as the Crown Prince.
Chǎng, taking advantage of the period between Jìn and Hàn,
when the Central Plains suffered much turmoil,
occupied a strategic and secluded region.
The ruler and his ministers dedicated themselves to extravagance for self-amusement.
Even chamber pots
were decorated with the Seven Treasures.
When Sòng arose,
and had already captured Jīng and Tán (prefectures),
Chǎng became increasingly fearful.
He sent the Grand Recorder (Dàchéng Guān), Sūn Yù, with a secret letter concealed in a wax pellet, to travel covertly to Dōng Hàn,
proposing they mobilize troops to disrupt the Central Plains.
Yù was captured by border officials.
Emperor Tàizǔ consequently issued an edict to attack Shǔ,
sending Wáng Quánbīn, Cuī Yànjìn, and others out from Fèngzhōu,
and Liú Guāngyì, Cáo Bīn, and others out from Guīzhōu.
An imperial edict instructed the Eight Workshops Department (Bāzuò Sī) to measure a site south of the Right Flanking Gate (Yòuyèmén),
adjoining the Biàn River, and construct a first-class residence for Chǎng,
totaling over five hundred bays.
All the furnishings, tents, and assorted articles were prepared
to await Chǎng.
Chǎng sent Wáng Zhāoyuǎn, Zhào Yàntāo, and others to resist the command.
Zhāoyuǎn
was a native of Chéngdū.
At thirteen,
he served the Chan Master (Chánshī) Zhìyīn of Dōngguō as a page boy.
Zhīxiáng once hosted a meal for monks at the governor’s residence.
Zhāoyuǎn, holding Zhìyīn’s cap and shoes, followed him inside.
Zhīxiáng saw him
and loved his intelligence and shrewdness.
Since Chǎng was then commencing his studies,
Zhīxiáng immediately ordered Zhāoyuǎn to attend upon him,
and he became familiar and intimate with Chǎng.
When Chǎng ascended the throne,
he made him Kònglián Shǐ (Curtain-Rolling Envoy).
When Wáng Chǔhuí, the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ), retired,
Chǎng, believing the power of the Shūmì Shǐ was too great and difficult to control,
appointed Zhāoyuǎn as Tōngzòu Shǐ and Acting Commissioner of Military Affairs (Zhī Shūmì Shǐ Shì).
However, regardless of the importance of the matter,
he entrusted everything to him,
and Zhāoyuǎn was allowed to take gold and silk from the palace treasury as he pleased without question.
Chǎng’s mother, Empress Dowager Lǐ, often told Chǎng that Zhāoyuǎn should not be employed,
but Chǎng refused to listen.
Zhāoyuǎn enjoyed reading military texts
and regarded himself highly for his strategy.
When the troops first departed Chéngdū,
Chǎng sent Lǐ Hào and others to send them off.
Zhāoyuǎn held an iron Rúyì in his hand,
directing military affairs,
and compared himself to Zhūgě Liàng.
When the drinking was well underway,
he said to Hào:
“My purpose in this campaign
is not merely to overcome the enemy;
leading these twenty or thirty thousand tattooed, vicious youths,
taking the Central Plains will be as easy as turning over my palm!”
Chǎng also sent his son Xuánzhé to lead tens of thousands of elite troops to guard Jiànmén.
Xuánzhé traveled in a carriage with his favorite concubine,
bringing along musical instruments and dozens of entertainers.
All the Shǔ people who saw this secretly laughed.
Quánbīn arrived at Sānquán,
encountered Zhāoyuǎn,
and defeated him.
Zhāoyuǎn burned the pontoon bridge at Jíbǎijiāng
and retreated to defend Jiànmén.
Xiàng Tāo, the Army Commander (Jūntóu), learned from a surrendered Shǔ soldier:
“The path of Láisū
exits south of Jiànmén at Qīngqiángdiàn
and rejoins the main road.”
Quánbīn sent the subordinate general Shǐ Yándé to lead a detachment out via Láisū,
attacking Jiànmén from the north.
Together with Quánbīn, they launched a pincer attack.
Zhāoyuǎn and Yàntāo were defeated and fled,
and both were captured.
Xuánzhé, hearing of the defeat of Zhāoyuǎn and the others,
also fled home.
Liú Guāngyì attacked Kuízhōu.
The defending general, Gāo Yànchóu, was defeated in battle.
He closed the inner city and refused to surrender.
The judicial administrator, Luó Jì, advised him to flee.
Yànchóu said:
“In the past, I could not hold Qínchuān.
If I now flee again,
even if the sovereign does not kill me,
what face will I have to see the people of Shǔ?”
He also advised him to surrender.
Yànchóu did not consent
and subsequently burned himself to death.
Meanwhile, the Shǔ troops everywhere scattered and collapsed,
and most of the commanders and generals were captured.
Chǎng asked his attendants for a plan.
The veteran general Shí Yūn believed that since the Eastern troops had come from afar,
their momentum could not last long.
They should gather their troops and hold fast defensively to wear them out.
Chǎng sighed and said:
“My late sovereign and I nurtured these soldiers with warm clothing and fine food for forty years.
Now facing the enemy,
they cannot shoot a single arrow facing East for me.
Although I wish to strengthen the walls,
who will guard them with me?”
He then ordered Lǐ Hào to draft the memorial of surrender.
This was the first month of Qiándé 3rd Year.
From the start of the campaign until Chǎng surrendered,
it totaled sixty-six days.
Previously,
Hào had served Wáng Yǎn as a Hanlin Scholar (Hànlín Xuéshì).
When Yǎn perished,
Hào drafted the memorial of surrender for him.
Now, he drafted one again.
The Shǔ people secretly marked his gate at night, saying,
“The Lǐ family, generations of drafters of surrender memorials.”
This anecdote was widely circulated as a joke at the time.
When Chǎng arrived at the capital (Jīngshī),
he was appointed Investigating Grand Preceptor (Jiǎnxiào Tàishī) concurrently with Grand Councilor (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Qín (Qínguó Gōng).
He died seven days later.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Chǔ (Chǔ Wáng).
His mother, Lady Lǐ,
was intelligent and articulate.
She was treated with great courtesy.
Imperial decrees referred to her as
“Guómǔ” (Mother of the State).
Tàizǔ once summoned her and consoled her, saying:
“Mother, please take good care of yourself.
Do not worry constantly about Shǔ.
At a later date, I shall send Mother back home.”
Lady Lǐ said:
“My family originally comes from Tàiyuán.
If I could return to my old hometown to live out my final years,
that would be my greatest wish.”
At this time, Liú Jūn was still alive.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased and said:
“Once Liú Jūn is pacified,
I will fulfill Mother's wish.”
When Chǎng died,
Lady Lǐ did not weep.
She poured wine upon the ground and prayed, saying:
“You were unable to die for your state (shèjì),
but lived shamelessly instead.
The reason I tolerated life
was because you were still here.
Now, what use is there for me to live?”
Consequently, she refused to eat and died.
The rest of the matters are detailed in the National History (Guó Shǐ).
The year count for the rise and fall [of Shǔ] is very clear,
and all records agree.
It began when [Wáng Yǎn] entered Shǔ in Tóngguāng 3rd Year (Yǐyǒu, 923 CE),
until the state perished in Huángcháo Qiándé 3rd Year (Yǐchǒu, 965 CE).
This totals forty-one years.
Only the *Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ* (Old History of the Five Dynasties) states
Tóngguāng 3rd Year (Bǐngxū),
until Qiándé 3rd Year (Yǐchǒu),
a period of forty years—
this is erroneous.
Hereditary House of Nán Hàn, Fifth: Liú Yǐn (younger brother Yǎn; Yǎn's son Fēn; Fēn's younger brother Shèng; Shèng's son Chǎng)
Liú Yǐn.
His ancestor, Ānrén,
was a native of Shàngcài.
Later, [his family] moved to Mǐnzhōng.
They traded in Nánhǎi,
and thus settled there.
His father, Qiān,
served as a staff officer (yájiàng) in Guǎngzhōu.
In the 5th year of Táng Qiánfú (878 CE),
Huáng Cháo attacked and breached Guǎngzhōu.
When [Huáng Cháo] left to campaign between Hú and Xiāng,
Guǎngzhōu appointed Qiān as the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Fēngzhōu and Suppression Commissioner (Zhènè Shǐ) of Héjiāng,
to guard against the regions west of Wú and Guì.
After more than a year,
he commanded ten thousand troops
and over a hundred warships.
Qiān had three sons:
Yǐn, Tái, and Yán.
When Qiān died,
Guǎngzhōu appointed Yǐn to succeed Qiān as Prefect of Fēngzhōu.
During the Qiánníng period,
the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) Liú Chóngguī died.
Xūe Wáng Zhīróu was appointed to replace him as the commander.
When [Zhīróu] traveled to Húnán,
the Guǎngzhōu generals Lú Jū and Tán rebelled.
Zhīróu dared not advance.
Yǐn used the Fēngzhōu troops to attack and kill Jū and Tán,
and welcomed Zhīróu.
Zhīróu appointed Yǐn as Commissioner of Military Affairs (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
Afterwards, Xú Yànruò replaced Zhīróu.
He appointed Yǐn as Deputy Military Commissioner (Jiédù Fùshǐ),
entrusting him with military and governmental affairs.
When Yànruò died,
the army promoted Yǐn to Acting Commissioner (Liúhòu).
In Tiānyòu 2nd Year (905 CE),
Yǐn was appointed Military Commissioner.
In Liáng Kāipíng 1st Year (907 CE),
he was promoted to Investigating Grand Commandant (Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi) concurrently with Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the 2nd Year,
he was concurrently made Military Commissioner of Jìnghǎi Circuit and Protector-General of Ānnán (Ānnán Dūhù).
In the 3rd Year,
he was promoted to Investigating Grand Preceptor concurrently with Grand Councilor,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánpíng (Nánpíng Wáng).
Yǐn and his father rose up from Fēngzhōu.
Encountering many troubles in the world,
they repeatedly achieved merit in Língnán,
thus possessing Nánhǎi.
Furthermore, Yǐn liked worthy scholars.
At this time,
the realm was already in chaos.
Scholars and officials of the central court considered the region beyond the ridge (Lǐngwài) the farthest,
and a good place to escape to,
so many traveled there.
Famous officials of the Táng dynasty who had died in banishment in the South often had descendants there,
or officials who were serving there at the time and could not return due to the turmoil,
all became sojourners in Língbiǎo.
People such as Wáng Dìngbǎo, Ní Shǔ, Liú Jùn, Lǐ Héng, Zhōu Jié, Yáng Dòngqián, and Zhào Guāngyì,
Yǐn summoned and treated with courtesy.
Dìngbǎo was a Patrol Officer (Xúnguān) of Róngguǎn.
Shǔ was a Táng Imperial University Erudite (Tàixué Bóshì).
Jùn was the son of Chóngwàng,
and went there to escape the chaos.
Héng was the grandson of Déyù,
a Táng Right Reminder (Yòu Bǔquē),
and had gone there on an official mission.
All were appointed to his headquarters (mùfǔ),
and treated as honored guests.
Jié was skilled in astronomy and calendrical calculations.
He had been a Táng Vice Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Shàoqīng).
He went there escaping the chaos.
Yǐn frequently consulted him about portents and disasters.
Jié felt ashamed of serving others using astrology.
He often claimed illness and did not rise [to serve],
but Yǐn still treated him as a guest.
Dòngqián was initially a Patrol Officer in Yōngguǎn.
After his term ended, he became a sojourner in Nánhǎi.
Yǐn always treated him as a mentor.
Later, he made him Deputy Military Commissioner.
When Yǎn claimed the imperial title (jiànhào),
Dòngqián explained the rules of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, and ritual law.
The national systems and regulations,
which were generally organized,
were all implemented using these several men.
In Qiānhuà 1st Year (911 CE),
Yǐn was promoted and enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánhǎi (Nánhǎi Wáng).
He died that same year,
aged thirty-eight.
His younger brother Yǎn succeeded him.
Yǎn
was originally named Yán.
He was Qiān’s illegitimate son.
His mother, Lady Duàn, gave birth to Yǎn in an outside residence.
Qiān’s wife, Lady Wéi, was naturally jealous.
Hearing this, she became angry.
She drew her sword and went out.
She ordered that Yǎn be brought to her,
intending to kill him.
When she saw him, she was startled,
and the sword immediately fell to the ground.
After a long time, she said:
“This is no ordinary child!”
Three days later,
she nevertheless killed Lady Duàn,
and raised Yǎn as her own son.
When he grew up,
he was skilled in riding and archery.
He was seven *chǐ* tall,
his hands hanging past his knees.
Yǐn was made Commander of the Army (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
Yǎn was also appointed Policy Consultant and Participant in Military Affairs of the Prince of Xuē’s court (Xuē Wáng Fǔ Zīyì Cānjūn).
Yǐn was stationed at Nánhǎi,
and Yǎn served as his Deputy Envoy.
When Yǐn died,
Yǎn succeeded him.
In the second year of Qiānhuà (912 CE),
he was appointed Jiedushi of Qīnghǎi,
and acting Grand Tutor (Jiǎnjiào Tàibǎo) and Executive in Charge of Affairs (Tóng Píngzhāngshì).
In the third year (913 CE),
he was promoted to acting Grand Preceptor (Jiǎnjiào Tàifù).
When Emperor Mòdì ascended the throne,
he conferred all of Yǐn’s official ranks and titles upon Yǎn.
Yǎn was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánhǎi.
Toward the end of the Táng Dynasty,
Nánhǎi was the last to fall into disorder.
After Emperor Xīzōng,
ministers who were sent out to govern provinces
found that all under heaven was in chaos,
and had nowhere to go,
except only Nánhǎi.
It was starting with Yǐn that they also established themselves autonomously.
At this time,
Qū Hào of Jiāozhōu, Líu Shìzhèng of Guìzhōu, Yè Guǎnglǜe of Yōngzhōu, and Páng Jùzhāo of Róngzhōu
each held separate control over various districts.
Lú Guāngchóu occupied Qiánzhōu and used it to attack the regions north of the ridges (Lǐngshàng);
his younger brother, Guāngmù, held Cháozhōu;
and his son, Yánchāng, held Sháozhōu.
Líu Chānglǔ, the Prefect of Gāozhōu, Líu Qián, the Prefect of Xīnzhōu, and over seventy strongholds east of the River (Jiāngdōng)
could not be controlled.
Yǐn attacked Sháozhōu.
Yǎn said:
“Sháozhōu relies on Guāngchóu.
If we attack it,
the people of Qiánzhōu will certainly respond.
If they respond, we will be exposed to enemies on both front and rear.
It is not advisable to attack directly; we should take it by stratagem.”
Yǐn did not listen,
and indeed was defeated and returned.
Thereupon, he fully entrusted all military affairs to Yǎn.
Yǎn pacified all the strongholds,
and then killed Chānglǔ and others,
and appointed new Prefects.
Finally, he led troops to attack and defeat the Lú clan,
and seized Cháo and Sháo.
He also fought with Mǎ Yīn in the west over Róng and Guì.
Yīn took the Guì region,
and captured Shìzhèng.
Yǎn took the Róng region,
drove out Jùzhāo,
and also took the Yōng region.
Yǐn and Yǎn only received their enfeoffments and titles from the Liáng Dynasty in the beginning
and merely accepted their calendar (zhèngshuò).
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (917 CE),
Yǎn ascended the throne as Emperor.
The state was named Dàyuè,
and the era name was changed to Qiānhēng.
He posthumously honored Ānrén Wén Huángdì,
Qiānshèng Wǔ Huángdì,
and Yǐn Xiāng Huángdì,
and established three ancestral temples.
He set up various official positions.
Yáng Dòngqián was made Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng),
Lǐ Héng Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng),
Ní Shǔ Vice Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shìláng),
and Zhào Guāngyìn Minister of War (Bīngbù Shàngshū),
all with the title Executive in Charge of Affairs (Píngzhāngshì).
Guāngyìn considered himself a scion of an eminent Táng clan,
and felt ashamed to serve a pseudo-state.
He was often discontented and longed to return home.
Yǎn then practiced forging a handwritten letter by Guāngyìn,
and sent an envoy through a secret route to Luòyáng,
summoning his two sons, Sǔn and Yì, along with their family members, to come.
Guāngyìn was surprised and delighted,
and thereafter served wholeheartedly.
Yǎn was intelligent and perceptive but harsh and cruel.
He employed punishments involving knives, saws, dismemberment, and evisceration.
Whenever he watched people being killed,
he could not contain his joy,
and would unconsciously drop his jaw (duǒyí),
saliva dripping, gulping with his mouth wide open (yāxiā).
People believed him to be a real dragon-serpent (jiāoshèn).
He also loved luxury
and gathered all the treasures of Nánhǎi
to build his Jade Hall and Pearl Palace.
In the second year (918 CE),
he performed the Sacrifice to Heaven in the southern suburbs,
granted a general amnesty within the borders,
and changed the state name to Hàn.
When Yǎn first intended to assume the imperial title,
he feared that Wáng Dìngbǎo would not comply.
He sent Dìngbǎo as an envoy to Jīngnán.
When Dìngbǎo returned,
Yǎn, fearing his disapproval,
sent Ní Shǔ to comfort him
and inform him of the state’s establishment.
Dìngbǎo said:
“The establishment of a state must involve proper regulations.
When I entered the southern gate,
the plaque of the Qīnghǎi Army was still there.
Will the four directions not ridicule us?”
Yǎn laughed and said:
“I have prepared for Dìngbǎo for a long time,
but did not consider this point.
It is fitting that he criticizes it!”
In the third year (919 CE),
he conferred the title of Empress upon Lady Mǎ, the Lady of Yuè State.
Lady Mǎ
was the daughter of Mǎ Yīn, the Prince of Chǔ.
In the spring of the fourth year (920 CE),
he established the Bureau of Selection (Xuǎnbù) for the tribute examinations,
and graduated over ten successful candidates (Jìnshì) and those proficient in the classics (Míngjīng),
following the Táng precedent.
This became an annual custom.
In the seventh year (923 CE),
Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng entered Biàn.
Yǎn was afraid,
and sent Hè Cí, the Palace Park Official (Gōngyuàn Shǐ), to inquire about the true situation in the Central Plains,
presenting a letter from the ‘Lord of the Great Hàn State’ to the ‘Emperor of the Great Táng.’
When Cí returned,
he reported that Táng was certainly heading for disorder
and was not worth worrying about.
Yǎn was greatly pleased.
He was also fond of boasting and extravagance.
He frequently summoned merchants from north of the ridges (Lǐngběi) who reached Nánhǎi,
and invited many of them
to ascend the palace halls,
showing them the extent of his wealth in pearls and jade.
He claimed his family originally hailed from Xián and Qín (the heartland of China)
and was ashamed to rule over barbarians.
He referred to the Táng Son of Heaven
as the ‘Prefect of Luòzhōu.’
In the same year,
Zhèng Mín, the King (Piàoxìn) of Yúnnán, sent an envoy bearing a white horse with a red mane to seek marriage.

The envoy called himself Zhèng Zhāochún, a close relative of the Emperor, the maternal younger brother, Minister of the Right and General Administrator (Qīngróng Bùxiè Jiān Lǐ), bestowed a gold brocade robe and a tiger-striped silk brocade belt with a gold-mounted sword, enfeoffed as the Marquis of Guīrén Qìng, granted a stipend of one thousand households, and holding the credentials (chíjié).
Zhāochún was fond of learning and possessed literary talent.
Yǎn often hosted feasts and composed poetry with him.
Yǎn and his officials could not match him.
Consequently, Yǎn gave his daughter, the District Princess of Zēngchéng (Zēngchéng Xiànzhǔ), in marriage to Mín.
In the eighth year (924 CE),
he constructed the Southern Palace (Nángōng).
Wáng Dìngbǎo presented the Rhapsody on the Seven Wonders of the Southern Palace (Nángōng Qī Qí Fù) to praise it.
Yǎn was originally named Yán,
and later changed it to Zhì.
In the ninth year (925 CE),
a white dragon was seen at the Sānqīng Hall in the Southern Palace.
He changed the era name to Báilóng (White Dragon),
and further changed his personal name to Gōng,
to accord with the auspicious sighting of the dragon.
A Hu (Central Asian) monk said:
“The prophecy states: ‘The one who destroys the Líu clan is Gōng.’”
Yǎn then selected the meaning from the *Zhouyi* (Book of Changes):
“The flying dragon is in the sky”
to create the character
“Yǎn,”
which is pronounced
“Yǎn,”
and adopted it as his name.
In the fourth year (938 CE),
the people of Chǔ attacked Fēngzhōu with a naval force.
The Fēngzhōu troops were defeated at the Hè River.
Yǎn was afraid.
He consulted the *Zhouyi* by divination,
and obtained the hexagram Dàyǒu (Great Possession).
Consequently, he granted an amnesty within his borders
and changed the era name to Dàyǒu (Great Possession).
He dispatched General Sū Zhāng with three thousand troops of the Divine Crossbow Army (Shénnǔ Jūn) to relieve Fēngzhōu.
Zhāng sank two iron chains into the Hè River.
He constructed a massive winch (jùlún) on the bank,
and built a dike to conceal it.
Then, he engaged the enemy with light boats,
feigning defeat and fleeing.
When the Chǔ forces pursued them,
Zhāng raised the giant winch and pulled the chains, locking the Chǔ boats.
He then shot at them from the banks with strong crossbows
and killed all the Chǔ people.
In the third year (936 CE),
he sent Generals Lǐ Shǒuyōng and Liáng Kèzhēn to attack Jiāozhǐ,
and captured Qū Chéngměi and others.
When Chéngměi arrived at Nánhǎi,
Yǎn ascended the Yìfèng Tower to receive the prisoners.
He said to Chéngměi:
“You always regarded me as a false court.
Why are you now bound, facing me?”
Chéngměi kowtowed and confessed his crime.
Thereupon, Yǎn pardoned him.
Chéngměi
was Hào’s son.
Kèzhēn also attacked Zhànchéng,
plundering its treasures and returning.
In the fourth year (937 CE),
Yáng Tíngyì of Àizhōu rebelled
and attacked Lǐ Jìn, the Prefect of Jiāozhōu.
Jìn fled and returned.
Yǎn sent Executive Official Chéng Bǎo to attack Tíngyì.
Bǎo was killed in battle.
In the fifth year,
he enfeoffed his son Yàoshū as the Prince of Yōng,
Guītú as the Prince of Kāng,
Hóngdù as the Prince of Qín,
Hóngxī as the Prince of Jìn,
Hóngchāng as the Prince of Yuè,
Hóngbì as the Prince of Qí,
Hóngyǎ as the Prince of Sháo,
Hóngzé as the Prince of Zhèn,
Hóngcāo as the Prince of Wàn,
Hónggǎo as the Prince of Xún,
Hóngwěi as the Prince of Xī,
Hóngmiǎo as the Prince of Gāo,
Hóngjiǎn as the Prince of Tóng,
Hóngjiàn as the Prince of Yì,
Hóngjì as the Prince of Biàn,
Hóngdào as the Prince of Guì,
Hóngzhāo as the Prince of Xuān,
Hóngzhèng as the Prince of Tōng,
and Hóngyì as the Prince of Dìng.
In the ninth year,
he dispatched General Sūn Déshèng to attack Xiàngzhōu,
but failed.
In the tenth year,
Jiǎo Gōngxiàn, a patrol general of Jiāozhōu, killed Yáng Tíngyì and established himself.
Wú Quán, a former general of Tíngyì, attacked Jiāozhōu,
and Gōngxiàn came to request military aid.
Yǎn enfeoffed Hóngcāo as the Prince of Jiāo,
and sent troops out via Báiténg to attack Wú Quán.
Yǎn stationed his forces at Hǎimén.
Quán had already killed Gōngxiàn,
and met the opposing army at the estuary,
planting iron stakes in the sea.
Quán’s forces advanced with the tide.
Hóngcāo pursued them.
When the tide receded and the ships retreated,
all those who struck the stakes capsized.
Hóngcāo died in battle.
Yǎn gathered the remaining troops and returned.
In the fifteenth year,
Yǎn died,
aged fifty-four.
His posthumous title was Tiānhuáng Dàdì,
his temple name was Gāozǔ,
and his mausoleum was called Kānglíng.
His son Bīn succeeded him.
Bīn,
whose initial name was Hóngdù,
had been enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín.
Since Yǎn’s sons Yàoshū
and Guītú had both died early,
Bīn was next in line to succeed.
When Yǎn was ill and confined to his bedchamber,
he summoned Wáng Fān, the Right Púshè (Minister), and spoke with him.
Calling Hóngdù and Hóngxī by their courtesy names, he said:
“Shòu and Jùn are older,
but neither is fit to handle my affairs.
Only Hóngchāng resembles me.
I wish to establish him.
Alas, my descendants are unworthy!
In later generations, they will be like a mouse entering an ox horn—
their power will inevitably diminish!”
He then wept and sighed mournfully.
Fān planned for Yǎn,
proposing to send Hóngdù out to Yōngzhōu,
and Hóngxī to Róngzhōu,
and then establish Hóngchāng as the Crown Prince.
Once the plan was settled,
Xiāo Yì, the Envoy of Literary Affairs, entered to inquire about the illness.
Yǎn informed him of the plan.
Yì advised against it, saying:
“If the younger son is established,
the older sons will fight for the succession.
Disaster will begin here!”
Because of this, Hóngdù was eventually established.
He changed his name to Bīn,
changed the era name to Guāngtiān,
honored his mother, Zhào Zhāoyí, as the Grand Imperial Consort,
and made Hóngxī, the Prince of Jìn, assist in governance.
Once Bīn ascended the throne,
he indeed proved incapable of handling affairs.
While Yǎn was lying in state,
Bīn summoned performers to make music,
drank wine in the palace,
and had naked men and women entertain him.
Sometimes he wore black mourning clothes and traveled at night with singing girls,
entering and exiting common households.
Because of this, bandits and thieves arose competitively between the mountains and the sea.
The seditious person Zhāng Yùxián,
who called himself the King of the Eight Central Heavenly States,
attacked and captured Xúnzhōu.
Bīn dispatched Hóngchāng, the Prince of Yuè, and Hónggǎo, the Prince of Xún, to attack Yùxián.
Yùxián besieged Hóngchāng and others at Qiánbáiguǎn.
Vanguards Wàn Jǐngxīn and Chén Dàoxiáng fought vigorously,
accompanying the two princes as they broke through the siege and fled.
Bīn was unable to take notice of the situation,
and Lǐngdōng fell entirely into chaos.
Hóngxī daily supplied Bīn with musicians and courtesans, tempting him toward even greater profligacy.
Bīn also grew suspicious that his various younger brothers were plotting against him.
He ordered eunuchs to guard the palace gates,
and everyone who entered was subjected to a body search.
Hóngxī, Hónggǎo, and Hóngchāng secretly sent Chén Dàoxiáng to foster brave warriors Líu Sīcháo, Tán Língyīn, Lín Shàoqiáng, Shàoliáng, Hé Chāngtíng, and others.
They trained them in wrestling to be presented to Bīn.
Bīn held a banquet in the Chángchūn Palace to watch them perform.
Bīn became drunk and stood up.
Dàoxiáng and Sīcháo immediately followed him to the door of the bedchamber and strangled him.
They killed all his attendants.
Bīn reigned for two years,
aged twenty-four.
His posthumous title was Shāng.
His younger brother Shèng succeeded him.
Shèng,
whose initial name was Hóngxī,
had been enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìn.
Having assassinated Bīn,
he immediately established himself,
changing the era name to Yìngqián.
He made Hóngchāng the Grand Marshal of Cavalry and Infantry,
administering political affairs,
and Hónggǎo the Vice Marshal.
Líu Sīcháo and the others were rewarded as meritorious officials.
Since Shèng had killed his elder brother,
his ascension was unpopular.
Fearing that the populace would not submit,
he greatly increased the severity of the laws and punishments to intimidate the masses.
Afterwards, Hónggǎo repeatedly requested permission to eliminate the bandits,
and secretly advised Shèng to execute Sīcháo and the others in order to quiet outside criticism.
Shèng was greatly angered,
and sent an envoy to summon Hónggǎo by night.
Hónggǎo knew he would not escape.
He detained the envoy,
went inside to prepare for a ritual bath,
and prayed before the Buddha, saying:
“Hónggǎo wrongly wished
to be born in the imperial palace in his next life.
Now I am to be killed!
In future lives, I must be born into a common household,
to avoid slaughter and harm.”
Weeping, he bade farewell to his family,
and only then answered the summons.
Upon arrival, he was killed.
That winter,
Shèng performed the sacrifice to Heaven in the Southern Suburbs.
He changed the era name to Qiánhé.
His officials presented him with the honorary title Dàshèng Wénwǔ Dàmíng Zhìdào Dàguāngxiào Huángdì.
In the summer of the second year,
he sent Hóngchāng to sacrifice at the mausoleum of Xiāngdì at Hǎiqǔ.
When Hóngchāng reached the Chānghuá Palace,
Shèng sent assassins to stab and kill him.
After Shèng had killed Hónggǎo,
he developed rifts with his younger brothers.
Hóngchāng was the most virtuous,
and was the one Yǎn had originally wished to establish.
Shèng was especially jealous of him,
and thus caused him harm first.
Hóngzé, the Prince of Zhèn, resided in Yōngzhōu,
and governed well.
That year, a phoenix was seen in Yōngzhōu.
Shèng was enraged,
and sent someone to poison him.
Thereafter, his younger brothers were killed one after another.
In the third year,
he killed his younger brother Hóngyǎ,
and also killed Líu Sīcháo and five others.
After Sīcháo and the others died,
Chén Dàoxiáng was afraid,
and felt insecure.
His friend Dèng Shēn presented him with Xún Yuè’s *Hàn Jì* (Records of the Hàn).
Dàoxiáng was unable to understand it.
Shēn cursed him, saying:
“You hateful bumpkin!
Hán Xìn was executed and Péng Yuè was minced—
it is all in this book!”
Dàoxiáng understood,
and grew even more fearful.
Shèng heard of this and was greatly enraged.
He had Dàoxiáng and Shēn thrown into prison,
and both were executed in the marketplace,
and their clans exterminated.
He appointed Wáng Fān, the Right Púshè, as the Inspector of Yīngzhōu,
and sent men to kill him on the road.
In the fifth year,
Shèng’s younger brothers Hóngbì, Hóngdào, Hóngyì, Hóngjì, Hóngjiǎn, Hóngjiàn, Hóngwěi, and Hóngzhāo,
were all killed on the same day.
In the sixth year,
he dispatched Zhōng Yǔnzhāng (Langzhong of the Ministry of Works and Director of the Drafting Office) to Chǔ (State) as an envoy to seek marriage.
Chǔ did not permit it.
When Yǔnzhāng returned,
Shèng said:
"Can Duke Mǎ strategize again regarding the southern lands?"
At this time,
Mǎ Xīguǎng had just been enthroned,
Xī’è raised troops in Wǔlíng,
and Húnán was in great chaos.
Yǔnzhāng detailed the situation indicating that Chǔ could be attacked.
Shèng then dispatched the Commander of the Giant Elephants, Wú Xún, and Palace Attendant Wú Huái’ēn to attack Hèzhōu.
They already conquered it,
but the Chǔ people came to rescue it.
Xún dug a large pit below the city walls,
covered it with mats above,
and spread earth over them.
When the Chǔ soldiers approached the city,
they all fell into the pits;
several thousand died,
and the Chǔ people all fled.
Xún and others attacked Guìzhōu and the five prefectures of Lián, Yí, Yán, Wú, and Méng,
conquering them all.
They plundered Quánzhōu and returned.
In the winter of the ninth year,
he again dispatched Palace Attendant Pān Chóngchè to attack Chēnzhōu.
Lǐ Jǐng’s troops were also present,
and they met Chóngchè.
They fought,
greatly defeating Jǐng’s troops at Yízhāng,
and subsequently seizing Chēnzhōu.
Shèng became even more complacent.
He dispatched the Commander of the Giant Warships, Jì Yànxūn, with troops to enter the sea.
He plundered gold and silk from merchants to construct detached palaces for hunting and recreation.
Therefore, at that time, the Liú clan possessed the Nángōng, Dàmíng, Chānghuá, Gānquán, Wánhuá, Xiùhuá, Yùqīng, and Tàiwēi Palaces,
numbering several hundred in total,
which cannot all be recorded.
The eunuch Lín Yányù and the palace woman Lú Qióngxiān
held exclusive sway inside and outside the court, carrying out killings indiscriminately.
Shèng no longer supervised them.
He often drank heavily at night until completely intoxicated.
He would place a melon on the neck of the entertainer Shàng Yùlóu,
draw his sword and cut it to test the blade,
and in the process, cut off the head as well.
The next day, when he sobered up,
he again summoned Yùlóu to attend him while drinking.
His attendants informed him that he had already killed him,
and Shèng merely sighed.
In the tenth year,
Wáng Jìnkuí of Húnán led 50,000 troops, consisting of the barbarians from the ravines and caves, to attack Chēnzhōu.
Pān Chóngchè defeated Jìnkuí at Háoshí,
decapitating over ten thousand heads.
In the eleventh year,
Shèng became gravely ill.
He enfeoffed his son Jìxīng as Prince Wèi,
Xuánxīng as Prince Guì,
Qìngxīng as Prince Jīng,
Bǎoxīng as Prince Xiáng,
and Chóngxīng as Prince Méi.
In the twelfth year,
Shèng personally ploughed the ceremonial field.
Wú Chāngjùn of Jiāozhōu sent an envoy to declare submission
and request the credentials of authority (staff and battle-ax).
Chāngjùn
was the son of Quán.
Quán had held Jiāozhōu since Yǎn’s time.
Yǎn dispatched Hóng Cāo to attack him,
but Hóng Cāo died in battle,
so they abandoned the campaign and did not attack again.
When Quán died,
his son Chāngjí was enthroned.
When Chāngjí died,
his younger brother Chāngjùn was enthroned,
and he first declared submission to Shèng.
Shèng sent Lǐ Yú (Attendant Official) with the ceremonial banner and credentials to summon him.
When Yú arrived at Báizhōu,
Jùn sent men to stop Yú, saying:
"Sea bandits are causing chaos,
and the roads are impassable."
Yú was consequently unable to proceed.
Shèng killed his younger brother Hóng Miǎo.
In the thirteenth year,
he also killed his younger brother Hóng Zhèng.
Thereupon, all of Yǎn’s sons were extinguished!
In the third year of Xiǎndé,
when Shìzōng pacified the regions north of the Yangtze River,
Shèng first became alarmed and apprehensive.
He sent envoys to present tribute to the capital,
but they were obstructed by the Chǔ people,
and the envoys could not proceed.
Shèng’s worry was apparent in his expression.
He also once claimed to understand astrology.
In his final years,
when the moon eclipsed between the Ox and Maiden constellations (Niú-Nǚ),
he took out a book to divine the omen,
and sighed:
"This refers to me!"
He then indulged in continuous nightly drinking.
In the sixteenth year,
he divined the burial ground north of the city,
transporting bricks to construct the tomb.
Shèng personally oversaw it.
That autumn, he died.
He was thirty-nine years old.
His posthumous title was Emperor Wénwǔ Guāngshèng Míngxiào;
his temple name was Zhōngzōng;
and his mausoleum was called Zhāolíng.
His son Chǎng was enthroned.
Chǎng’s
initial name was Jìxīng,
and he was enfeoffed as Prince Wèi.
When Shèng died,
he was enthroned as the eldest son,
and the era name was changed to Dàbǎo.
Shèng was naturally resolute and jealous,
unable to trust his subordinates,
relying only on his favored eunuchs and palace women, such as Yányù and Qióngxiān.
Chǎng was even more foolish.
He believed that all officials had their own families
and cared for their descendants,
thus unable to be completely loyal.
Only the eunuchs, being close and intimate, could be trusted.
Consequently, he handed over governance to the eunuchs Gōng Chéngshū, Chén Yánshòu, and others.
Furthermore, any official he wished to employ
was castrated before being used.
Once Chéngshū and the others controlled the government exclusively,
Chǎng indulged in licentious games in the inner palace with palace women and Persian maids,
and no longer came out to attend to affairs.
Yánshòu also introduced the female shaman Fán Húzi,
who claimed that the Jade Emperor (Yùhuáng) had descended into her body.
Chǎng set up curtains and tents in the inner hall
and displayed treasures.
Húzi wore the Yuǎnyóu Crown
and robes of purple mist and streamers (Zǐxiá jū).
She sat inside the tent proclaiming good and ill fortune,
calling Chǎng the Crown Prince Emperor (Tàizǐ Huángdì).
All state affairs were decided by Húzi,
and Lú Qióngxiān, Gōng Chéngshū, and others competed to attach themselves to her.
Húzi then spoke to Chǎng, saying:
"Chéngshū and the others are all heavenly messengers sent by the Supreme to assist the Crown Prince.
Their offenses must not be questioned."
Zhōng Yǔnzhāng (Junior Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs) participated in governance,
greatly hated this situation,
and repeatedly requested the execution of the eunuchs.
The eunuchs all looked askance at him.
In the second year,
Liú Chǎng (鋹) sacrificed to Heaven at the southern suburb.
Three days prior,
Zhōng Yǔnzhāng (鍾允章) and the ritual officials ascended the altar,
looking around and issuing commands.
The eunuch Xǔ Yànzhēn (許彥真) saw this from afar and said:
"This is plotting rebellion!"
He then drew his sword and climbed the altar.
Yǔnzhāng met him and shouted at him.
Yànzhēn fled quickly,
and accused Yǔnzhāng of rebellion.
Chǎng imprisoned Yǔnzhāng,
and sent Xuē Yòngpī (薛用丕), Minister of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū), to supervise the investigation.
Yǔnzhāng had a prior acquaintance with Yòngpī,
and thus wept, saying:
"I am currently innocent.
If I falsely incriminate myself and die, I have no regrets.
However, my two sons are both young
and do not know their father's grievance.
Wait until they are grown,
and you may tell them."
Yànzhēn heard this,
and cursed, saying:
"The rebel thief wants his sons to seek revenge, does he?"
He re-entered to inform Chǎng,
and simultaneously arrested the two sons and imprisoned them.
Consequently, Yǔnzhāng and his entire clan were executed.
Chén Yánshòu (陳延壽) said to Chǎng:
"The reason the former emperor was able to pass the throne to Your Majesty
was because he executed all his younger brothers."
He advised Chǎng to gradually execute and remove the various princes (zhū wáng).
Chǎng thought this was correct,
and killed his younger brother, Xuánxīng (璇興), the Prince of Guì (Guì Wáng).
This year
was the first year of Jiànlóng (Jiànlóng Yuánnián).
Chǎng's general Shào Tíngxuán (邵廷琄) spoke to Chǎng, saying:
"The Hàn took advantage of the chaos of the Táng,
residing here for fifty years.
Fortunately, due to issues in the Central Plains (Zhōngguó),
weapons of war have not reached us,
and the Hàn has become increasingly arrogant due to the lack of conflict.
Now the troops do not know the standards or drums (i.e., battle signals),
and the ruler does not consider survival or ruin.
Indeed, the realm has been in chaos for a long time.
After long chaos comes order;
this is the natural course of events.
Now we hear that the True Lord has emerged,
and he will certainly possess the entire land within the seas (hǎinèi).
His momentum cannot be stopped until he unifies the realm."
He advised Chǎng to repair the military and prepare,
or failing that,
to offer all treasures to the Central Plains,
sending envoys to establish friendly relations.
Chǎng was oblivious and gave it no thought,
disliking Tíngxuán's straightforward words,
and deeply resented him.
In the fourth year,
auspicious mushrooms (zhī) grew within the palace,
a wild animal struck the sleeping chamber gate,
a sheep in the imperial park spat pearls,
and a rock beside a well stood up by itself,
traveled over a hundred paces, and then fell over.
Fán Húzi (樊胡子) interpreted all these signs as auspicious omens and instructed the officials to enter and offer congratulations.
In the fifth year,
Chǎng made the adopted daughter of the eunuch Lǐ Tuō (李托) a Noble Consort (Guì Fēi),
favoring her exclusively.
Tuō was made Grand Tutor of the Interior (Nèi Tàishī),
residing in the palace and monopolizing governance.
Xǔ Yànzhēn, having already killed Zhōng Yǔnzhāng,
disliked that Gōng Chéngshū (龔澄樞) and others held positions superior to his own,
and plotted to kill them.
Chéngshū sent someone to accuse Yànzhēn of rebellion,
and he was executed along with his clan.
In the seventh year,
the royal army campaigned south,
conquering Chén Zhōu (郴州).
The general Jì Yànwēn (暨彥贇) and the Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ) Lù Guāngtú (陸光圖), sent by Mǎ Shèng (晟), both died in battle.
The remaining troops retreated and defended Sháo Zhōu (韶州).
Chǎng first thought of Tíngxuán's words,
and sent Tíngxuán with naval forces to exit Guāngkǒu (洸口) to resist the royal army.
It happened that the royal army withdrew its forces.
Tíngxuán trained his soldiers,
and repaired the military equipment.
The people of the Ridge (Lǐng rén) relied on him as a good general.
There was an informer who submitted an anonymous letter alleging Tíngxuán was rebelling.
Chǎng sent an envoy to grant him death.
The officers and soldiers forced open the military gate to see the envoy
and pleaded that Tíngxuán showed no signs of rebellion,
but they could not save him.
A shrine was erected for him at Guāngkǒu.
In the eighth year,
Wú Chāngwén (吳昌文) of Jiāozhōu (交州) died.
His assistant Lǚ Chùpíng (呂處玶) contended for the succession with Qiáo Zhīyòu (喬知祐), the Regional Inspector of Fēngzhōu (峯州).
Jiāozhǐ (交趾) fell into great chaos.
Dīng Liǎn (丁璉) of Huānzhōu (驩州) raised troops and defeated them.
Chǎng granted Liǎn the position of Military Commissioner (Jiéduò) of Jiāozhōu.
In the ninth year,
the wife of a resident of Nánhǎi (南海) gave birth to a child with two heads and four arms.
At this time,
Emperor Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ Huángdì) commanded Lǐ Yù (李煜) to instruct Chǎng to declare himself a subject.
Chǎng became angry
and imprisoned Gōng Shènyí (龔慎儀), Yù's envoy.
In the thirteenth year,
an imperial edict commanded Pān Měi (潘美), the Defender-in-Chief (Fángyùshǐ) of Tánzhōu (潭州), to mobilize troops.
The army reached Báixiá (白霞).
Chǎng sent Gōng Chéngshū to defend Hè Zhōu (賀州), Guō Chóngyuè (郭崇岳) to defend Guì Zhōu (桂州), and Lǐ Tuō to defend Sháo Zhōu, as preparation.
In the autumn of that year,
Pān Měi pacified Hè Zhōu.
In the tenth month, he pacified Zhāo Zhōu (昭州).
He also pacified Guì Zhōu,
and in the eleventh month, he pacified Lián Zhōu (連州).
Chǎng rejoiced, saying:
"Zhāo, Guì, Lián, and Hè
originally belonged to Húnán.
Now the Northern Army has taken them,
which is enough.
They will not proceed further south."
His folly was thus!
In the twelfth month, Sháo Zhōu was pacified.
In the first month of Kāibǎo (開寶) fourth year,
Yīng (英) and Xióng (雄) two prefectures were pacified.
Chǎng's general Pān Chóngchè (潘崇徹) surrendered first.
The army reached Lóngtóu (瀧頭).
Chǎng sent an envoy to request peace,
asking the army to delay its advance.
In the second month,
the army crossed Mǎjìng (馬逕).
Chǎng sent his Right Director of the Affairs of the Secretariat (Yòu Púshè), Xiāo Cuǐ (蕭漼), to present a memorial of surrender.
After Cuǐ left,
Chǎng was panicked and pressured,
and again ordered the troops to be mustered to resist the imperial command.
Měi and the others advanced their army.
Chǎng sent his younger brother, Bǎoxīng (保興), the Prince of Xiáng (Xiáng Wáng), leading civil and military officials to Měi's camp to surrender,
but they were not accepted.
Gōng Chéngshū, Lǐ Tuō, and others plotted, saying:
"The Northern Army came
only to covet our nation's treasures and goods.
If we burn it into an empty city,
the army will not be able to remain,
and will naturally return."
They then completely burned the treasuries, armories, and palaces.
Chǎng took more than ten sea vessels,
loaded entirely with treasures and imperial consorts (pínyù),
intending to enter the sea.
The eunuch Yuè Fàn (樂範) stole his boat and fled home.
The army reached Báitián (白田).
Chǎng, dressed in plain white clothing and riding a white horse, surrendered.
The captives were presented at the capital.
Chǎng was pardoned and made Grand General of the Left Ox Cavalry Guard (Zuǒ Qiānniú Wèi Dà Jiàngjūn),
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Enshè (Ēnshè Hóu).
His subsequent affairs are fully recorded in the National History (Guó Shǐ).
The years of Yǐn's (隱) rise and ruin
are consistent across all records.
From the second year of Tiānyòu (天祐) of the Táng dynasty, when Yǐn became the Military Commissioner of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Jiéduòshǐ),
until the fourth year of Kāibǎo (開寶) of the reigning dynasty (Huángcháo) when the state was extinguished,
it totaled sixty-seven years.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties (Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ) uses the third year of Zhēnmíng (貞明) of the Liáng, when Yǎn (龑) claimed the title, as the starting point,
hence it states fifty-five years.
Hereditary House of Chǔ (Chǔ Shìjiā) Sixth: Mǎ Yīn (馬殷) (Sons: Xīshēng 希聲, Xīfàn 希範, Xīguǎng 希廣)
Mǎ Yīn, courtesy name Bàtú,
was a man from Yānlíng, Xǔzhōu.
In the third year of Zhōnghé of the Táng dynasty (883 CE),
Qín Zōngquán of Cáizhōu sent Sūn Rú and Liú Jiànfēng with ten thousand soldiers to join his younger brother, Qín Zōnghéng,
to seize territory in Huáinán.
Yīn initially served as a minor general under Rú.
Zōnghéng and the others attacked Yáng Xíngmì at Yángzhōu,
but failed to conquer it.
As the Liáng forces urgently attacked Qín Zōngquán,
Zōngquán repeatedly summoned Rú and the others.
Rú did not wish to return.
Zōnghéng repeatedly urged him,
Rú grew angry,
and killed Zōnghéng.
He personally led the troops to capture Gāoyóu,
and then pursued Xíngmì.
Xíngmì occupied Xuānzhōu,
and Rú surrounded it with his forces.
After a long siege without success,
he sent Yīn and Jiànfēng to plunder surrounding counties for provisions.
Rú was defeated in battle and died.
Yīn and the others had nowhere to return,
so they nominated Jiànfēng as their commander.
Yīn was made the vanguard.
They turned to attack Yùzhāng,
and seized Qián and Jí prefectures,
amassing tens of thousands of followers.
In the first year of Qiánníng (894 CE),
they entered Húnán,
and stopped at Lǐlíng.
Dèng Chùnè, the Governor of Tánzhōu, mobilized Shàozhōu troops to garrison Lónghuí Pass.
When Jiànfēng and the others reached the pass,
they secured the surrender of its garrison commander, Jiǎng Xūn.
Jiànfēng took Xūn’s armor and equipped his vanguard troops with it,
unfurled their banners and flags,
and headed straight for Tánzhōu.
When they reached the East Gate,
the defenders of the East Gate thought they were the garrison troops returning from the pass,
and opened the gate to let them in.
They immediately killed Chùnè.
Jiànfēng proclaimed himself the Acting Military Governor (Liúhòu).
Emperor Xīzōng appointed Jiànfēng as the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Húnán
and Yīn as the Grand Commander of Cavalry and Infantry (Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ).
Jiǎng Xūn requested to be the Governor of Shàozhōu,
but Jiànfēng refused him.
Xūn led his troops to attack Xiāngxiāng.
Jiànfēng sent Yīn to attack Xūn at Shàozhōu.
Jiànfēng was a mediocre person,
and unable to command his subordinates well.
He often drank and caroused with his retainers.
An army soldier named Chén Shàn had a wife of beautiful appearance.
Jiànfēng had a private affair with her.
Shàn was enraged,
and killed Jiànfēng by striking him with an iron bludgeon.
The army leaders nominated Zhāng Jí, the Provisional Military Administrator (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ), as their commander.
When Jí was about to enter the government office,
the horse he rode suddenly kicked and bit,
injuring Jí’s thigh.
Jí lay ill,
and addressed the generals, saying:
“I am not your master.
Lord Mǎ is heroic and courageous;
you should jointly elevate him.”
The generals then jointly killed Shàn,
mutilated his corpse,
and sent Yáo Yànzhāng to welcome Yīn back from Shàozhōu.
When Yīn arrived,
Jí was carried into the office on a shoulder litter.
Yīn performed the ceremony of greeting and reverence in the courtyard.
Jí called Yīn up.
Then he led the generals and officials down,
bowed twice facing north,
and handed the position over to him.
This was in the third year of Qiánníng (896 CE).
The Táng court appointed Yīn as the Governor of Tánzhōu.
Yīn sent his generals Qín Yànhuī and Lǐ Qióng to attack the six prefectures of Lián, Shào, Chēn, Héng, Dào, and Yǒng.
They all surrendered.
Liú Shìzhèng of Guìguǎn was afraid,
and sent his generals Chén Kěfán and Wáng Jiànwǔ with troops to guard Quányì Ridge.
Yīn sent an envoy to confer with Shìzhèng,
but when the envoy reached the border,
Kěfán and the others refused to admit him.
Yīn was angered,
and sent Qióng and the others with seven thousand troops to attack them.
They captured Kěfán and the others, along with over two thousand of their soldiers,
and buried all of them alive.
They then besieged Guìguǎn,
captured Shìzhèng,
and took all his subordinate prefectures.
Yīn memorialized to have Qióng appointed as the Surveillance Commissioner (Guānchásǐ) of Guìguǎn.
In the fourth year (897 CE),
Yīn was appointed Military Governor of Wǔ'ān Circuit (Wǔ'ānjūn Jiédùshǐ).
Previously,
when Sūn Rú was defeated at Xuānzhōu,
Yīn’s younger brother, Mǎ Cóng, was captured by Yáng Xíngmì.
Xíngmì absorbed Rú’s remaining soldiers into the
“Black Cloud Corps” (Hēiyúndū),
and made Cóng its commander.
Cóng followed Xíngmì in campaigns and battles,
and frequently achieved merit.
He was dignified and steady,
never boasting about himself.
Xíngmì favored him,
and asked Cóng whose son he was.
Cóng replied:
“I am Mǎ Yīn’s younger brother.”
Xíngmì was greatly surprised and said:
“Your elder brother is noble now.
Would it be permissible for me to send you back now?”
Cóng did not answer.
On another day, he asked him again.
Cóng apologized, saying:
“I
am a defeated soldier of Sūn Rú.
I am fortunate that you allow me to live;
nothing short of risking my life is sufficient repayment.
Húnán is a neighboring territory,
and hearing the news of Yīn’s activities morning and night is enough for me.
I do not wish to leave.”
Xíngmì sighed and said:
“In the past, I loved your appearance,
but now I have gained your heart.
Nevertheless, strive to forge harmony between our two states,
allowing merchants to trade and exchanging surpluses for shortages to support each other.
That will also be a way of repaying me!”
Then, he treated Cóng generously and sent him back.
Yīn was overjoyed,
and memorialized to have Cóng appointed as Deputy Military Governor (Jiédù Fùshǐ).
Xíngmì sent generals Liú Cún and others to attack Dù Hóng,
and besiege Èzhōu.
Yīn sent Qín Yànhuī and Xǔ Déxūn with naval forces to relieve them.
Soon after, Dù Hóng was defeated and died.
Cún and the others then attacked Yīn.
Yīn sent Yànhuī to resist them upriver.
His subordinate general, Huáng Fán, ambushed them with three hundred boats at the mouth of the Liúyáng River.
Cún and the others repeatedly fought without success,
so they sent a letter to Yīn requesting peace.
Yīn intended to agree to it.
Yànhuī said:
“The Huái people are deceitful;
they want to weaken our army.
They cannot be trusted.”
He immediately attacked them.
Cún and the others retreated and fled.
Huáng Fán, with the Liúyáng boats, intercepted the river and launched a joint attack,
thoroughly defeating them.
Liú Cún and Chén Zhīxīn were killed in battle.
Yànhuī captured Yuèzhōu.
When the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) of Liáng ascended the throne,
Yīn sent envoys to present tribute.
Tàizǔ appointed Yīn as Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng) concurrently Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and enfeoffed him as the Prince of Chǔ.
Gāo Jìchāng of Jīngnán used troops to block the mouth of the Hàn River,
intercepting Yīn’s tribute envoys.
Yīn sent Xǔ Déxūn to attack his position at Shātóu.
Jìchāng sought peace,
and so the attack stopped.
Lǚ Shīzhōu, the Governor of Yuánzhōu under Yáng Xíngmì, defected.
Shīzhōu
was brave, robust, and heroic.
He was quite conversant with divination, calendrics, and military texts.
He claimed his family had been generals for five generations.
Fearing he could not escape trouble,
he often gathered with his drinking companions,
and when drunk, he would stand up and dance,
singing mournfully and passionately, often weeping.
Xíngmì heard of this,
suspected he had rebellious intentions,
and sent people to observe his movements.
Shīzhōu grew even more afraid.
He said to his subordinate general, Qíwú Zhāng:
“We are enemies of the Chǔ people on the border.
I often observe that the ethereal vapors above their camp are excellent;
they are not easily defeated.
I hear that Lord Mǎ is benevolent,
and treats scholars with courtesy.
May I seek refuge from death in Chǔ?”
Zhāng replied:
“You must plan this yourself.
My tongue may be cut off,
but the words will not leak out.”
Shīzhōu led troops to hunt near the border,
and then defected to Chǔ.
Qíwú Zhāng allowed his family members to follow him.
Yīn was greatly pleased when he heard Shīzhōu had arrived,
saying:
“I was planning to conquer the area south of the ridges (Lǐngbiǎo),
and having this man is sufficient.”
He made him the Grand Commander of Cavalry and Infantry,
and sent him with troops to attack Lǐngnán,
capturing Zhāo, Hè, Wú, Méng, Gōng, and Fù prefectures.
Yīn memorialized to have Shīzhōu appointed as the Governor of Zhāozhōu.
Léi Yàngōng of Lǎngzhōu summoned the Wú forces to attack Píngjiāng,
Xǔ Déxūn defeated them.
Mǎ Yīn sent Qín Yànhuī to attack Lǎngzhōu,
Yàngōng fled to Wú,
and seven people, including his younger brother Yànxióng, were captured and sent to Liáng.
Thereupon, Xiàng Guī of Lǐzhōu, Sòng Yè of Chénzhōu, Chāng Shīyì of Xùzhōu, and others led the various Mán tribes of Xīdòng, all submitting to Mǎ Yīn.
Mǎ Yīn requested that Lǎngzhōu be promoted to Yǒngshùn Jūn,
and nominated Zhāng Jí as Jieduōshǐ.
Mǎ Yīn then requested permission to follow the precedent of Táng Tàizōng,
to establish the Tiāncè Fǔ (Heavenly Book Administration),
and appoint officials.
Tàizǔ appointed Mǎ Yīn as Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn,
Mǎ Yīn made his younger brother Cóng the Left Chancellor (Zuǒxiàng),
and Cún the Right Chancellor (Yòuxiàng).
Liào Guāngtú and eighteen others were appointed as Scholars (Xuéshì).
During the reign of Emperor Mòdì,
Mǎ Yīn was additionally granted the posts of Jieduōshǐ for the armies of Wǔchāng, Jìngjiāng, Níngyuǎn, and others,
and Commander-in-Chief (Dūtǒng) of the campaigning armies on all four sides of Hóng and È.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
Mǎ Yīn sent his son Xīfàn to present tribute to the capital,
and surrendered the Commander-in-Chief seal (Dūtǒng Yìn) granted by Liáng.
Zhuāngzōng asked about the size of Dòngtíng Lake,
and Xīfàn replied:
“When the imperial carriage travels south,
it is barely large enough to water the horses.”
Zhuāngzōng praised this.
When Zhuāngzōng pacified Shǔ,
Mǎ Yīn was greatly alarmed,
and formally requested retirement (zhìshì).
Zhuāngzōng issued an imperial letter (xǐshū) to comfort and reassure him.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
Mǎ Yīn sent an envoy to present tribute,
and also to congratulate him for the first month of the coming year.
Gāo Jìchāng of Jīngnán seized his tribute envoy, Shǐ Guāngxiàn.
Mǎ Yīn sent Yuán Quán, Wáng Huán, and others to attack him.
When they reached his city walls,
Jìchāng sued for peace,
and the attack stopped.
In the beginning, Mǎ Yīn’s military strength was still meager,
and he had hostile relations with Yáng Xíngmì, Chéng Ruì, Liú Yǎn, and others.
Mǎ Yīn was worried about this,
and asked his general Gāo Yù for advice.
Yù said:
“Chéng Ruì’s territory is narrow and his troops are few;
he is not enough of a threat to us.
Liú Yǎn’s ambition is limited to Wǔguǎn.
As for Yáng Xíngmì,
he is the enemy of Sūn Rú;
even if you try to make peace with him using ten thousand pieces of gold,
you cannot win his sincere goodwill.
However, honoring the sovereign and upholding legitimacy
is the enterprise of a Hegemon.
Now, you should internally serve the Imperial Court to seek titles and externally impress your neighbors and enemies.
After that, withdraw and focus on military affairs and agriculture,
accumulating strength and awaiting the opportunity.”
Thereupon, Mǎ Yīn began presenting tribute to the capital,
although the annual tribute consisted of nothing more than the tea produced in his region.
He then established commercial bureaus (dǐwù) for selling tea in prefectures such as Xiāng, Táng, Yǐng, and Fù, extending from the capital,
the profit from which was tenfold.
Yù also persuaded Mǎ Yīn to mint lead and iron coins,
making ten pieces equal to one copper coin.
He also ordered the people to manufacture their own tea for trade,
and collected taxes (suàn) on it,
the annual revenue amounting to tens of thousands.
Because of this, his territory became strong and his strength complete,
and he frequently sought high titles.
In the second year of Tiānchéng,
he requested the establishment of a Branch Department (Xíngtái).
Míngzōng enfeoffed Mǎ Yīn as the Prince of Chǔ (Chǔ Guó Wáng).
The relevant authorities stated there was no precedent for the ceremony of enfeoffing a prince,
and requested that the bamboo tablet used for the Three Dukes be utilized.
Therefore, Lǐ Xù, the Assistant Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòuchéng), was sent with the imperial insignia to enfeoff him using the bamboo tablet.
Mǎ Yīn designated Tánzhōu as Chángshā Prefecture (Chángshā Fǔ),
established his state, acted as an autonomous power (chéngzhì),
and appointed his own officials.
He made his younger brother Cóng the Jieduōshǐ of Jìngjiāng Army (Jìngjiāng Jūn Jiéduōshǐ),
his son Xīzhèn the Jieduōshǐ of Wǔshùn Army (Wǔshùn Jūn Jiéduōshǐ),
his second son Xīshēng as acting supervisor of all military affairs internal and external (pàn nèiwài zhū jūnshì),
Yáo Yànzhāng as Left Chancellor (Zuǒxiàng),
Xǔ Déxūn as Right Chancellor (Yòuxiàng),
Lǐ Duó as Minister of Education (Sītú),
Cuī Yǐng as Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
Tuòbá Cháng as Executive (Púyè),
and Mǎ Gǒng as Director (Shàngshū).
Both civil and military officials were promoted in rank.
He granted posthumous titles to his great-grandfather Yún as Wénsù, his grandfather Zhèng as Zhuāngmù, and his father Yuánfēng as Jǐngzhuāng,
and established the Three Ancestral Temples (Sān Miào) in Chángshā.
In the first year of Chángxīng,
Mǎ Yīn died,
at the age of seventy-nine.
The imperial edict stated:
“Mǎ Yīn’s official rank and titles were already high;
there is nothing higher to confer posthumously.
His posthumous name shall be Wǔmù,”
and that was all.
His son Xīshēng succeeded him.
Xīshēng, courtesy name Ruònè,
was Mǎ Yīn’s second son.
When Mǎ Yīn established his state,
he made Xīshēng acting supervisor of all military affairs internal and external (pàn nèiwài zhū jūnshì).
Gāo Jìchāng of Jīngnán heard that Mǎ Yīn’s general Gāo Yù had always instructed Mǎ Yīn in strategy, which was why Chǔ was strong,
and worried about it.
He once sent a spy to sow discord against Mǎ Yīn,
but Mǎ Yīn did not listen.
When Xīshēng was in power,
the spy spoke to Xīshēng, saying:
“Jìchāng heard that Chǔ employed Gāo Yù,
and was greatly pleased,
believing that the person who would destroy the Mǎ family must be Yù.”
Xīshēng was naturally foolish,
and believed this to be true.
He immediately stripped Yù of his military command.
Yù angrily said:
“I have served the Prince for a long time.
I have hurried to prepare Xīshān (West Mountain),
intending to spend my old age there.
The puppy is getting bigger,
and now it can bite people!”
When Xīshēng heard this,
he forged Mǎ Yīn’s order and had Yù killed.
Mǎ Yīn was old and no longer managed affairs,
and did not know Yù had died.
On that day, a thick fog covered everything.
Mǎ Yīn found it strange,
and said to his attendants:
“I once followed Sūn Rú;
whenever Rú killed an innocent person,
Heaven would certainly send a great fog.
Did someone perhaps die unjustly in the Mǎ Bù prison?”
The next day,
an official reported the facts.
Mǎ Yīn beat his chest and cried loudly, saying:
“I am so senile
that I have killed my meritorious veteran!”
He looked at his attendants and said:
“I, too, will not be here much longer!”
The following year, Mǎ Yīn passed away.
Xīshēng ascended the throne,
and was granted the title of Jieduōshǐ for the Wǔ'ān, Jìngjiāng, and other armies.
Xīshēng had heard that Liáng Tàizǔ liked to eat chicken,
and admired this.
He therefore had fifty chickens cooked daily for his meals.
When Mǎ Yīn was buried at Shàng Huáng,
Xīshēng did not weep;
he immediately ate several bowls of chicken meat and stood up.
His Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng), Pān Qǐ, mocked him, saying:
“In the past, Ruǎn Jí ate roasted suckling pig while in mourning;
how can this generation lack such a worthy man!”
In the third year of Chángxīng,
Xīshēng died,
and was posthumously granted the title Prince of Héngyáng (Héngyáng Wáng).
His younger brother Xīfàn succeeded him.
Xīfàn, courtesy name Bǎoguī,
was Mǎ Yīn’s fourth son.
Mǎ Yīn had more than ten sons.
The primary son, Xīzhèn, was the eldest and worthy,
while the next two, Xīshēng and Xīfàn, were born on the same day.
But Xīshēng’s mother, Lady Yuán (Yuán Fūrén), was beautiful,
and Xīshēng was able to succeed due to his mother’s favor.
Xīzhèn abandoned his office to become a Daoist priest (dàoshì),
living at home.
When Xīshēng died,
Xīfàn succeeded according to seniority (by age),
inheriting Mǎ Yīn’s offices and titles,
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chǔ (Chǔ Wáng).
In the second year of Qīngtài,
he was bestowed with a bow, arrows, a crown, and a sword.
In the fourth year of Tiānfú,
Xīfàn was granted the additional title of Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn,
and permitted to establish a chancery and act autonomously (kāifǔ chéngzhì), following Mǎ Yīn’s precedent.
Xīfàn loved learning
and was skilled in poetry.
The literary figures Liào Guāngtú, Xú Zhòngyǎ, Lǐ Gāo, Tuòbá Cháng, and eighteen others were all scholars (xuéshì) from the time of the late Mǎ Yīn.
Xīfàn was naturally extravagant;
Guāngtú and the others were all disreputable fellows.
They drank, gambled, and shouted boisterously.
Only Cháng was reserved, dignified, and a senior figure.
He submitted memorials with sharp remonstrance,
which Guāngtú and the others resented.
When Ān Cóngjìn of Xiāngzhōu and Lǐ Jīnquán of Ānzhōu rebelled,
Jìn Gāozǔ ordered Xīfàn to dispatch troops.
Xīfàn sent Zhāng Shàodí with naval forces towards Hàn Yáng,
transporting fifty thousand *hú* of rice to provision the army.
When Jīnquán and the others were defeated,
Shàodí returned.
Péng Shìchóu, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Xīzhōu, led the various Mán tribes of Jǐn and Jiǎng to attack Lǐzhōu.
Xīfàn sent Liú Qíng, Liú Quánmíng, and others with five thousand infantry to attack them.
Shìchóu was soundly defeated.
Qíng and the others attacked Xīzhōu;
Shìchóu fled to Jiǎngzhōu,
and sent his son Shī Gǎo, leading the various Mán chiefs, to surrender to Qíng.
Xīzhōu bordered Zāngkē and Liǎnglín to the west,
and communicated with Guìlín and Xiàngjùn to the south.
Xīfàn therefore erected a Bronze Pillar (tóngzhù) as a landmark,
and ordered the scholar Lǐ Gāo to engrave an inscription upon it.
Subsequently,

the chief (qiúzhǎng) Mò Yànshū of Nánníngzhōu led his original eighteen prefectures, the chief (qiúzhǎng) Yǐn Huáichāng of Dōuyún led his twelve tribes including Kūnmíng, and Zhāng Wànjùn of Zāngkē led his seven prefectures including Yí and Bō, all submitting to Xīfàn.
Mǎ Xī Fàn built the Huìchūnyuán (Garden of Gathering Spring) and the Jiāyàntáng (Hall of Grand Feasts).
The cost was enormous,
and he began imposing additional taxes within the state.
Tuòbá Cháng earnestly remonstrated, believing this was unacceptable.
Xī Fàn also built the Jiǔlóngdiàn (Nine Dragons Palace),
using eight dragons wrapping the pillars.
He proclaimed himself to be the ninth dragon.
At this time,
the Qìdān destroyed Jìn,
and the Central Plains were in great disorder.
Xī Fàn's general, Dīng Sījìn, offered a court remonstrance to Xī Fàn, saying:
“The former king rose from the ranks of the common soldiers,
and obtained this prefecture through assault and combat.
He relied on the Imperial Court to restrain neighboring enemies.
The state has been passed down for three generations,
possessing territory thousands of lǐ wide,
and maintaining an army of one hundred thousand men.
Today, the Son of Heaven is imprisoned and humiliated,
the Central Plains lack a ruler.
This is truly the time for an Hegemon to establish great achievements.
If you could truly dispatch all the state's troops, exiting through Jīng and Xiāng to advance rapidly toward the Capital,
and champion righteousness throughout the world,
this would be the achievement of Huán and Wén.
Why, instead, waste national resources and exhaust efforts on construction,
for the pleasures of children?”
Xī Fàn apologized to him.
Sījìn glared at Xī Fàn and said:
“This child is ultimately beyond teaching!”
He then choked himself and died.
In the fourth year of Kāiyùn (947 CE),
Xī Fàn died.
He was forty-nine years old.
His posthumous title was Wénzhāo.
Mǎ Xī Guǎng succeeded him.
Xī Guǎng's courtesy name was Dépī.
He was Xī Fàn's younger brother by the same mother.
Throughout his life, Xī Fàn disliked Tuòbá Cháng's remonstrances.
When Cháng regularly came to visit and report,
Xī Fàn called the gatekeeper, pointed at Cháng, and said:
“I do not wish to see this person.
Do not allow him inside again.”
Thus, he severed contact with him.
When he became bedridden,
he first began to reflect on Cháng's words,
considering them loyal.
He summoned him and entrusted Xī Guǎng to his care.
After Xī Fàn's death,
Cháng repeatedly urged Xī Guǎng to yield his position to his elder brother, Xī È.
Xī Guǎng did not comply.
Xī È was the Military Governor of Lǎngzhōu.
Upon Xī Fàn's death,
Xī È came from Lǎngzhōu to rush to the funeral.
Xī Guǎng's general, Liú Yànxú, deliberated, saying:
“The arrival of Wǔlíng,
his intentions are not good.
We should dispatch troops to meet him,
to guard against the unexpected,
and only allow him entry after he has removed his armor and laid down his weapons.”
Zhāng Shàodí and Zhōu Tínghuì said:
“If the King can share the rule with him, so be it;
otherwise, he should be eliminated quickly.”
Xī Guǎng wept and said:
“He is my elder brother.
How could I bear to kill him?
It is acceptable to divide the state and rule.”
Thus, he sent troops to welcome Xī È at Púshí,
housed him at the Bìxiānggōng Palace,
and dispatched him with lavish gifts.
Xī È departed in indignation.
He then sent an envoy to the Capital requesting enfeoffment and titles,
and asking to establish an official residence and declare vassalage.
Emperor Yǐn of the Hàn did not permit it.
He instead issued an imperial edict to comfort him and explain the situation.
Xī È grew angry.
He sent overtures of submission to Lǐ Jǐng,
and raised an army to attack Chángshā.
Xī Guǎng sent Liú Yànxú and Xǔ Kěqióng (and others) to resist him.
Yànxú defeated Xī È at Púshèzhōu.
Xī È departed.
He lured various barbarian tribes from the river valleys and caves to raid Yìyáng.
Xī Guǎng sent Cuī Gǒngliǎn with seven thousand infantry to garrison Xiāngxiāng's Yùtán to block the various barbarians.
Liú Yànxú led naval forces toward Wǔlíng,
to attack Xī È.
Yànxú was defeated at Méizhōu.
Xī Guǎng became greatly frightened.
He sent an envoy to request troops from the Capital.
Emperor Yǐn of the Hàn was unable to dispatch an army.
Xī È's naval forces sailed up the river.
He declared himself
“General Submitting to Heaven” (Shùntiān Jiāngjūn).
He attacked Yuèzhōu.
The prefect, Wáng Yūn, held the city securely and refused to fight.
Xī È called out to Yūn, saying:
“I formerly pledged with you to act together.
Why do you now harbor different intentions?”
Yūn replied:
“The princely brothers cannot tolerate each other,
yet you blame generals and officials for having different intentions?
I pray that Your Highness, upon entering Chángshā,
does not harm your kin.
Your servant will then not dare fail to exert loyalty.”
Xī È led his troops away.
He descended upon Xiāngxiāng,
and halted at Chángshā,
camping at the west of the river.
Liú Yànxú and Xǔ Kěqióng camped at the east of the river.
Péng Shīgǎo ascended the city wall to view the army west of the river.
He entered and reported to Xī Guǎng, saying:
“The Wǔlíng troops are arrogant,
mixed with barbarians and river dwellers.
Their position is easy to break.
I request that you order Kěqióng and others to array themselves in front of the mountain.
Your servant, with three thousand infantry, will cross the river from Bāxī and advance rapidly toward Yuèlù.
We will wait for nightfall and then strike them.”
Xī Guǎng thought this was viable,
but Kěqióng had already secretly sent overtures of submission to Xī È.
He therefore obstructed the plan.
The next day,
Shīgǎo went to Kěqióng to discuss matters.
He glared and angrily scolded him, saying:
“I see the mark of rebellion upon your face!
Do you intend to defect to the rebels?”
He tossed his sleeves and departed.
He quickly reported to Xī Guǎng,
requesting that Kěqióng be executed.
Xī Guǎng refused to listen.
Xī È attacked the Chánglèmén Gate.
The generals Wú Hóng and Yáng Dí fought within the gate.
Xī È suffered a minor setback.
Soon afterward, Xǔ Kěqióng defected to Xī È.
Hóng and Dí, hearing this, both scattered.
Xī Guǎng led his wife and children to hide in the Cítáng (Hall of Compassion).
The next day, he was captured.
Xī È saw him and said sorrowfully:
“This man is dull-witted.
How could he commit evil?
He was merely misled by his attendants.”
He looked at his subordinates and said:
“I wish to spare him.
What should be done?”
His subordinates all remained silent.
Consequently, he was strangled to death.
In the third year of Qiányòu (950 CE),
Xī È established himself as ruler.
The following year,
Emperor Yǐn of the Hàn died.
The Capital fell into great chaos.
Xī È then submitted as a vassal to Lǐ Jǐng.
Jǐng conferred upon Xī È the title of Prince of Chǔ.
Xī È entrusted all military and administrative affairs to his younger brother, Xī Chóng.
Xī Chóng conspired to rebel with the former Chǔ generals Xú Wēi, Lù Mèngjùn, and Lǔ Wǎn.
Xī È hosted a banquet at the Duānyángmén Gate.
Xī Chóng declined, citing illness.
Wēi and the others released more than ten wild horses,
accompanied by strong warriors carrying cudgels.
They burst into his residence,
seized the weapons from the armory,
bound Xī È,
and welcomed Xī Chóng to take the throne.
Xī Chóng sent Péng Shīgǎo and Liào Yǎn to imprison Xī È at Héngshān.
Shīgǎo supported Xī È as the Prince of Héngshān,
and submitted him as a vassal to Lǐ Jǐng.
Xī Chóng became afraid,
and also sought recognition from Jǐng.
Jǐng sent Biān Hào to enter Chǔ,
and entirely relocated the Mǎ clan to Jīnlíng.
This was during the first year of Guǎngshùn of the Zhōu (951 CE).
Xī È was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chǔ,
residing in Hóngzhōu.
Xī Chóng was given the title of Military Governor of Shūzhōu,
residing in Yángzhōu.
In the third year of Xiǎndé (956 CE),
Emperor Shìzōng campaigned against Huái.
He captured Yángzhōu.
He issued an edict to pacify and comfort the descendants of the Mǎ clan.
Soon thereafter, Yángzhōu fell back under the control of Jǐng.
Xī Chóng led his seventeen brothers back to the Capital.
He was appointed Commander of the Right Yǔlín Guards.
Xī Néng was appointed Grand General of the Left Túnwèi Guards.
Xī Guàn was appointed Grand General of the Right Qiānniúwèi Guards.
Xī Yǐn, Xī Jùn, Xī Zhī, and Xī Lǎng were all made Military Commanders under a Military Governor.
Liú Yán.
Liú Yán
was a native of Lúlíng in Jízhōu.
Wáng Jìnkuí
was a native of Wǔlíng.
Yán
initially served the prefect Péng Gān.
He followed Gān when he defected to Chǔ.
Yán served Xī Fàn as the Prefect of Chénzhōu.
Jìnkuí, when young, was a soldier of the Jìngjiāng Army.
He served Xī È as a Commander.
attacked Xīguǎng,
using Wáng Jìnkuí as vanguard,
and captured Chángshā.
Chángshā had been devastated and ruined by the conflict.
Xī'è ordered Jìnkuí to use the Jìngjiāng troops to encamp and restore it.
All the soldiers were distressed and resentful.
Jìnkuí, consequently, gathered them,
and at night used long-handled great axes to chop down the gate,
fleeing back to Wǔlíng.
Xī'è was currently drunk
and could not comprehend the situation.
The next day, he sent the general Táng Zhù to pursue him.
Upon reaching Wǔlíng,
Zhù suffered a major defeat in battle and returned.
Jìnkuí then drove out the acting military governor (Liúhòu), Mǎ Guānghuì,
welcomed Yán from Chénzhōu and established him as the commander (Shuài),
while Jìnkuí served as the deputy.
Soon after, Xī'è's general Xú Wēi and others initiated a rebellion,
captured Xī'è,
and installed Xīchóng.
Húnán fell into great chaos.
Lǐ Jǐng sent Biān Hào into Chǔ,
relocated the Mǎ family to Jīnlíng,
and also summoned Yán.
Yán refused to comply.
He sent Jìnkuí and the Commandant of the Moving Army (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ) Hé Jǐngzhēn, among others, to attack Hào at Chángshā.
Hào was defeated and fled.
In the third year of Zhōu Guǎngshùn (953 CE),
Yán presented a memorial to the Capital,
requesting an enfeoffment and title.
He also stated that Chángshā was ruined
and uninhabitable,
requesting the transfer of the administrative seat to Wǔlíng.
Zhōu Tàizǔ granted all his requests.
Accordingly, Lǎngzhōu was elevated to Wǔpíng Commandery (Wǔpíng Jūn),
superior to Wǔ'ān Commandery (Wǔ'ān Jūn).
Yán was appointed Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ),
and Wǔ'ān was subsequently conferred upon Jìnkuí.
Jìnkuí considered that Yán had been installed by himself,
and refused to submit to him.
Yán worried about this,
and the two men began to have a rift,
intending to plot against each other.
Jìnkuí planned, saying:
"Yán's serviceable generals are none other than Hé Jǐngzhēn and Zhū Quánxiù.
If we summon and kill them,
Yán can be taken."
At this time,
Liú Shèng had captured Chǔwú, Guì, Yí, Méng, and other prefectures in Chǔ.
Jìnkuí therefore reported to Yán, suggesting they summon Jǐngzhēn and the others to gather troops and attack Shèng.
Yán believed him,
and sent Jǐngzhēn and Quánxiù.
Upon arrival, they were all killed.
Jìnkuí then raised troops and attacked Wǔlíng,
captured Yán and killed him.
He presented a memorial to the Capital,
and Zhōu Tàizǔ immediately appointed Jìnkuí as the Military Commissioner of Wǔpíng Commandery.
Shìzōng campaigned against Huáinán,
and appointed Jìnkuí as Commander-in-Chief of the Southern Campaign (Nánmiàn Xíngyíng Dūtǒng).
Jìnkuí attacked Èzhōu,
passing through Yuèzhōu.
Pān Shūsì, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yuèzhōu,
was an old comrade of Jìnkuí,
and treated Jìnkuí with extreme deference.
Jìnkuí’s attendants sought bribes from Shūsì.
Shūsì refused to give them.
The attendants slandered him.
Jìnkuí berated him face-to-face.
Shūsì felt shame and resentment,
and told his subordinates:
"If Jìnkuí returns victorious,
none of us will be left alive."
Jìnkuí entered Èzhōu
and was currently attacking and subduing Chángshān.
Shūsì used his troops to launch a surprise attack on Wǔlíng.
Jìnkuí heard of this,
returned by light boat,
and fought Shūsì outside the walls of Wǔlíng.
Jìnkuí was defeated
and killed.
Zhōu Xíngféng (whose son was Bǎoquán).
Zhōu Xíngféng
was a native of Wǔlíng.
He and Wáng Jìnkuí were both soldiers in the Jìngjiāng Army,
and served Xī'è as military officers (Jūn Xiào).
When Jìnkuí attacked Biān Hào,
Xíngféng separately defeated Yìyáng,
killed more than two thousand of Lǐ Jǐng’s soldiers,
and captured his general Lǐ Jiànqī.
When Jìnkuí became the Military Commissioner of Wǔ'ān Commandery,
he appointed Xíngféng as Prefect of Jízhōu,
making him Jìnkuí’s Commandant of the Moving Army.
Jìnkuí and Liú Yán had a falling out,
and Xíngféng devised the plan to launch a surprise attack and kill Yán.
Jìnkuí occupied Wǔlíng,
and Xíngféng occupied Tánzhōu.
In the first year of Xiǎndé (954 CE),
Xíngféng was appointed Military Commissioner of Wǔqīng Commandery,
provisionally governing the affairs of the Tánzhōu military administration.
Pān Shūsì killed Jìnkuí.
Someone advised him to enter Wǔlíng,
but Shūsì replied:
"I killed Jìnkuí
merely to save myself from death.
Wǔlíng is not to my advantage."
He then returned to Yuèzhōu
and sent his guest general Lǐ Jiǎn to lead the Wǔlíng residents to welcome Xíngféng from Tánzhōu.
Xíngféng entered Wǔlíng.
Someone requested that Tánzhōu be given to Shūsì.
Xíngféng said:
"Shūsì killed his commander;
his crime warrants death.
Since he welcomed me,
I cannot bear to kill him yet.
If I were to give him Wǔ'ān,
it would be equivalent to me ordering him to kill Lord Wáng."
He summoned him and made him the Commandant of the Moving Army.
Shūsì was angered
and claimed illness, refusing to come.
Xíngféng angrily exclaimed:
"He wants to kill me again!"
He then pretended to grant him Wǔ'ān,
summoning him to the headquarters to receive the commission.
When he arrived, he was killed.
Xíngféng
was formerly the son of a Wǔlíng farmer.
In his youth, he was poor and humble,
lacked discipline,
