but often spoke with grand passion.
When he came to reside in Wǔlíng,
he was able to be frugal and discipline himself,
but his nature was brave and fierce,
and he was decisive in execution.
Those officers and officials under his command who traditionally relied on their merit to be arrogant and contemptuous
were all held accountable by the law.
Over ten high-ranking generals conspired to rebel.
Xíngféng summoned all the generals for a feast.
Halfway through the drinking,
he ordered strong men to capture and execute them.
The entire territory was thereafter intimidated and obeyed him.
For the common people, crimes, regardless of severity, resulted in death.
His wife, Madame Yán, remonstrated, saying:
"Human nature includes both good and evil.
How can you kill everyone without distinction?"
Xíngféng angrily replied:
"These are external matters;
what does a woman know about them!"
Madame Yán was displeased
and pretended to say:
"The tenants on our family land,
relying on your high status,
are generally not working diligently
and often exploit their power to infringe upon the populace.
Please allow me to go and inspect them."
When she arrived, she built a residence and lived there permanently.
Annually, she would wear a blue skirt, overseeing the tenants delivering the rent into the city.
Xíngféng went to visit her
and consoled her, saying:
"I am now of high rank.
Why must you, Madame, subject yourself to such hardship?"
Madame Yán said:
"Do you recall when you served as the Village Head (Hù Zhǎng)?
If the tenants' rent was late,
you always suffered lashing and beating.
Now that you are esteemed,
you ought to lead the populace by meeting deadlines early.
How can you completely forget the affairs of the fields and ridges?"
Xíngféng tried forcibly to invite her back,
using a retinue of concubines to escort her onto a shoulder sedan.
Madame Yán ultimately showed no intention of staying
and therefore said:
"Your application of the law is too severe and you are losing the hearts of the people.
The reason I do not wish to remain here
is that should disaster arise suddenly,
it will be easier to escape death in the countryside."
Xíngféng consequently moderated his methods slightly.
In the third year of Jiànlóng (962 CE),
Xíngféng fell ill.
He summoned his officers and officials
and entrusted his son Bǎoquán to them, saying:
"I rose from the fields to lead local militia (Tuán Bīng).
Ten people who started with me
have all been executed,
only the Prefect of Héngzhōu, Zhāng Wénbiǎo, survives.
However, he is constantly discontented for not having received the rank of Commandant of the Moving Army.
If I die,
Wénbiǎo will certainly rebel.
You must use Yáng Shīfán to suppress him.
If he is unsuccessful,
then blockade the city and do not fight,
but surrender directly to the imperial court."
Xínɡ Fénɡ died,
his son Bǎoquán was established.
Wén Biǎo heard of this
and angrily said:
"Xínɡ Fénɡ and I rose from humble origins and established fame and merit.
How can I today face north and serve a little child!"
He subsequently raised troops in rebellion
and attacked and captured Tánzhōu.
Bǎoquán begged the imperial court for military aid,
which then ordered Yánɡ Shīfán to suppress Wén Biǎo.
Bǎoquán informed him of the words of his late father,
deeply moving him to tears.
Shīfán also wept,
and looking back at his troops, said:
"Have you seen the young lord?
He is not yet an adult, yet he is this worthy."
The soldiers were invigorated
and all wished to prove their service.
Shīfán reached Pínɡjīn Tínɡ (Pavilion).
Wén Biǎo came out to fight
and was greatly defeated.
Originally,
when Bǎoquán had requested military aid,
Emperor Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ Huánɡdì) had sent Mùrónɡ Yánzhāo to suppress Wén Biǎo.
Before he arrived, Wén Biǎo was captured by Shīfán.
Yánzhāo’s army entered Lǎnɡzhōu.
Bǎoquán, with his whole clan, paid court in the capital (Jīnɡshī).
The subsequent events are detailed in the National History (Guóshǐ).
Yīn, having entered Húnán in the third year of Qiánnínɡ of Tánɡ,
until the first year of Guǎnɡshùn of Zhōu,
was altogether fifty-seven years.
The remainder is detailed in the chronological biography notes (Niánpǔ zhù).
Hereditary House of Wúyuè, Section Seven: Qián Liú (Son Yuánɡuàn; Yuánɡuàn’s son Zuǒ; Zuǒ’s younger brother Chù)
Qián Liú, courtesy name Jùměi,
was a native of Lín'ān, Hánɡzhōu.
In the village of Lín'ān there was a large tree.
When Liú was young, he played with a group of boys beneath the tree.
Liú sat upon a large rock and commanded the boys to form ranks and files.
His orders and signals were quite disciplined,
and all the boys feared him.
When he grew up,
he was dissolute,
not liking to engage in productive livelihoods,
and became a bandit by selling salt illegally.
Zhōnɡ Qǐ, the county Registrar, had several sons
who drank and gambled with Liú.
Qǐ had often forbidden his sons
from associating with him, but many of the sons secretly continued their fellowship.
There was a soothsayer from Yùzhānɡ
who observed the aura of a future king between the constellations Ox and Dipper (Niúdǒu).
Niúdǒu
was the section corresponding to Qiántánɡ.
He therefore traveled to Qiántánɡ.
His divination placed the aura in Lín'ān,
so he went to Lín'ān.
He concealed himself in the market, using the art of physiognomy,
secretly seeking the person.
Qǐ was friendly with the soothsayer.
The soothsayer privately said to Qǐ:
"My divination shows there is a nobleman in your county.
I cannot find him by seeking him in the market.
Judging by your appearance, you are noble,
but you are not worthy enough to be that person."
Qǐ then arranged a feast,
calling together all the worthy and prominent men for the gathering.
He secretly allowed the soothsayer to examine them all,
but none were deemed worthy.
The soothsayer stopped by Qǐ’s house.
Liú happened to be coming in from outside.
Seeing Qǐ,
he turned and ran away.
The soothsayer caught sight of him
and greatly exclaimed:
"This is truly the nobleman!"
Qǐ laughed and said:
"That is just Qián Shēnɡ, my neighbor."
The soothsayer summoned Liú to come forward
and examined him closely.
He looked at Qǐ and said:
"Your nobility
comes through this man."
He then consoled Liú, saying:
"Your bone structure is extraordinary.
Please take care of yourself!"
He then bade farewell to Qǐ, saying:
"The reason I sought this man
was not that I desired anything,
but merely to verify my divination technique."
The next day, he departed.
Qǐ thereupon allowed his sons to associate freely with Liú
and occasionally lent him money when he was in want.
Liú excelled at archery and using the spear,
and became somewhat versed in the various works on prognostication (túwěi).
In the second year of Qiánfú of Tánɡ,
Wánɡ Yǐnɡ, a deputy general of Zhèxī, started a rebellion.
Dǒnɡ Chānɡ, the garrison commander of Shíjiàn, recruited local troops to suppress the bandits.
He appointed Liú as a lieutenant general
and attacked and defeated Yǐnɡ.
At this time,
Huánɡ Cháo’s forces already numbered several thousand.
They attacked and plundered Zhèdōnɡ
and reached Lín'ān.
Liú said:
"Now the garrison troops are few while the bandit troops are numerous.
It is difficult to resist them by brute force.
We should dispatch surprise forces to intercept them."
He then, with twenty elite soldiers, lay in ambush in the valleys.
Cháo's vanguard, crossing the perilous area, were all on single horses.
Liú used hidden crossbows to shoot and kill their general.
Cháo's soldiers fell into chaos.
Liú led his elite troops to overrun them,
decapitating several hundred men.
Liú said:
"This strategy can be used once,
but how can we resist them when the main force arrives!"
He then led his troops toward Bābǎilǐ.
Bābǎilǐ
is a place name.
He told an old woman by the roadside:
"If anyone later asks,
tell them: 'The Lín'ān troops are garrisoned at Bābǎilǐ.'"
When Cháo’s forces arrived
and heard the old woman’s words,
they did not realize it was a place name,
and said:
"If ten or so soldiers earlier could not be resisted,
how much more so 'eight hundred li'!?"
They immediately led their troops past in haste.
Gāo Pián, the Supreme Commander (Dū Tǒnɡ), heard that Cháo dared not encroach upon Lín'ān.
He admired this feat
and summoned Dǒnɡ Chānɡ and Liú to both come to Guǎnɡlínɡ.
After a long time,
Pián showed no intention of suppressing the bandits.
Chānɡ and the others were not employed,
so they resigned and returned.
Pián recommended Chānɡ as Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Hánɡzhōu.
At this time,
the world was already in chaos.
Chānɡ then grouped the troops of the various counties into Eight Divisions (Bādū).
He made Liú the Commander-in-Chief (Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ),
and Chénɡ Jí the General of Jìnɡjiānɡ Division.
In the second year of Zhōnɡhé,
Liú Hàn hónɡ, the Surveillance Commissioner (Guānchá Shǐ) of Yuèzhōu, had a feud with Chānɡ.
Hàn hónɡ sent his younger brother Hàn Yòu and the Grand Usher (Dū Yúhòu), Xīn Yuē,
to station troops at Xīlínɡ.
Liú led the troops of the Eight Divisions across the river.
He secretly adopted their military designations,
attacked their camp,
and threw the camp into panic.
He then set fire to it,
and Hàn Yòu and the others all fled.
Hàn hónɡ again sent the generals Huánɡ Guī and Hé Sù to garrison Zhūjì and Xiāoshān.
Liú attacked and defeated them all.
Meeting Hàn hónɡ,
they fought
and inflicted a great defeat,
killing Hé Sù and Xīn Yuē.
Hàn hónɡ changed his clothes and carried a carving knife to escape.
The pursuers caught up with him.
Hàn hónɡ said:
"I am a butcher."
He raised the knife to show them,
and was thus spared.
In the fourth year,
Emperor Xīzōnɡ sent the palace envoy (Zhōnɡ Shǐ), Jiāo Jūfán, to serve as the Peace Envoy (Tōnɡhé Shǐ) for Hánɡzhōu and Yuèzhōu.
An edict commanded Chānɡ and Hàn hónɡ to cease hostilities,
but neither obeyed the edict.
Hàn hónɡ sent his generals Zhū Bāo, Hán Gōnɡméi, Shī Jiānshí, and others with naval forces to garrison Wànɡhǎi.
Liú marched out to Pínɡshuǐ.
Chénɡ Jí led surprise troops at night and defeated Bāo and the others at Cáowěi Dài.
He then advanced and garrisoned Fēnɡshān.
Shī Jiānshí and the others surrendered,
and subsequently, Yuèzhōu was attacked and defeated.
Hàn hónɡ fled to Táizhōu.
The Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Táizhōu captured Hàn hónɡ and delivered him to Liú,
who executed him at Kuàijī
and exterminated his clan.
Liú then memorialized that Chānɡ should replace Hàn hónɡ,
while he himself resided in Hánɡzhōu.
In the third year of Guāngqǐ (887),
Liú was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Left Guard, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Hángzhōu,
and Chāng was appointed Surveillance Commissioner (Guāncháshǐ) of Yuèzhōu.
In this year,
Bì Shīduó imprisoned Gāo Pián,
Huáinán fell into great chaos,
and Xú Yuē, the garrison commander of Liùhé, attacked and seized Sūzhōu.
Liú Hào, an aide-de-camp in Rùnzhōu, drove out their commander Zhōu Bǎo.
Bǎo fled to Chángzhōu.
Hào nominated Xuē Lǎng, the Director of Financial Scrutiny, to be the commander.
Liú dispatched his supreme generals Chéng Jí and Dù Léng, among others, to attack Chángzhōu,
brought Zhōu Bǎo back,
and Liú received him with a full military ceremony outside the city.
He housed Bǎo at Zhāngtíng,
where Bǎo died of illness.
Léng and his troops then advanced to attack Rùnzhōu,
drove out Liú Hào,
captured Xuē Lǎng,
and cut out his heart to sacrifice to Bǎo.
Following this, he sent his younger brother Qiú to attack Xú Yuē.
Yuē was defeated and fled into the sea,
and (they) pursued and killed him.
Emperor Zhāozōng appointed Liú as the Defense Commissioner (Fángyùshǐ) of Hángzhōu.
At this time,
Yáng Xíngmì and Sūn Rú were fighting over Huáinán,
and battled Liú between Sūzhōu and Chángzhōu.
After a long time,
Rú was killed by Xíngmì.
Xíngmì occupied Huáinán,
and took Rùnzhōu.
Liú also took Sūzhōu and Chángzhōu.
The Táng elevated Yuèzhōu to the Wēishèng Command,
appointing Dǒng Chāng as the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ),
and enfeoffing him as the Prince of Lǒngxī Commandery.
Hángzhōu was established as the Wǔshèng Command,
and Liú was appointed Director of Military Training (Dū Tuánliànshǐ),
with Chéng Jí as his Deputy Commissioner (Fùshǐ).
Jí, courtesy name Hóngjì,
worked alongside Liú in campaigns and suppressions.
Many strategies originated from Jí,
and Liú gave his daughter in marriage to Jí's son, Rénxiù.
Liú then appointed Dù Léng, Ruǎn Jié, Gù Quánwǔ, and others as his officers,
and Shěn Sōng, Pí Guāngyè, Lín Dǐng, and Luó Yǐn as his advisors.
In the second year of Jǐngfú (893),
Liú was appointed Military Commissioner of the Zhènhǎi Command and Governor of Rùnzhōu.
In the first year of Qiánníng (894),
he was given the title Associate Administrator (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
In the second year (895),
Dǒng Chāng of Yuèzhōu rebelled.
Chāng was inherently foolish,
unable to make decisions.
When presiding over civil disputes,
he would throw dice,
and the winner would be judged correct.
Sorcerers like Yìng Zhì Wáng Wēn and the shaman Hán Ǎo,
confused Chāng with ominous prophecies,
and presented birds and beasts as auspicious omens.
Ní Dérú, an aide-de-camp, told Chāng:
"In earlier times, a folk rhyme claimed that the Luópíng Bird governed the fortunes of the Yuè people.
Many people drew its likeness and prayed to it.
We see that the written characters of your princely title resemble the drawing."
He then showed the drawing to Chāng.
Chāng was greatly pleased.
He then proclaimed himself Emperor,
named his state Luópíng,
and changed his reign title to Shùntiān.
He divided his troops into two armies:
the central army wore yellow,
the outer army wore white,
and inscribed their clothing with the characters
"Guīyì."
His Deputy Commissioner Huáng Jié strongly admonished Chāng that this was unacceptable.
Chāng became furious.
He ordered men to decapitate Jié,
and when the head was brought,
he cursed, saying:
"This villain failed to support my desire to be a sage!
In a clear age, he refused to serve as one of the Three Dukes,
but instead sought his own death!"
He threw the head into a latrine.
Chāng then sent a letter informing Liú.
Liú reported Chāng's rebellion to the imperial court.
Emperor Zhāozōng issued an edict stripping Chāng of his titles and ranks,
enfeoffing Liú as the Prince of Péngchéng Commandery,
and making him Pacification Commissioner of the Eastern Circuit of Zhèjiāng.
Liú said:
"The Dǒng clan showed me kindness.
We cannot rush to attack him."
He stationed thirty thousand troops at Yíng'ēnmén (Gate of Receiving Grace),
and sent his advisor Shěn Pāng to persuade Chāng to reform.
Chāng gave two million coins to reward the army,
captured Yìng Zhì and others and sent them to the army camp,
and requested to await punishment.
Liú then withdrew his troops.
Chāng subsequently refused the order again,
and sent his generals Chén Yù and Cuī Wēn, among others, to garrison Xiāngyán and Shíhóu.
He begged Yáng Xíngmì for aid.
Xíngmì dispatched Ān Rényì to rescue Chāng.
Liú sent Gù Quánwǔ to attack Chāng,
and Cuī Wēn was beheaded.
The various generals Chāng employed—Xú Xún, Tāng Jiù, and Yuán Bīn—were all mediocrities,
ignorant of warfare.
Whenever they met Quánwǔ, they were defeated.
Chāng's nephew, Zhēn,
was fierce, brave, and good at fighting.
Quánwǔ and his forces attacked him,
but could not overcome him for over a year.
Zhēn had a falling out with his subordinate general, Cì Yǔ.
Yǔ slandered him,
and Chāng killed Zhēn.
The army was then defeated.
Quánwǔ captured Chāng and returned toward Hángzhōu.
When they reached Xī Xiǎojiāng,
Chāng looked at his attendants and said:
"Lord Qián and I both rose from the countryside.
I once served as a supreme general.
How can I now face him again!"
His attendants wept in response.
He then stared wide-eyed, shouted loudly,
and drowned himself in the water.
Emperor Zhāozōng tasked Chancellor Wáng Pǔ with governing Yuèzhōu.
Pǔ requested that the post be given to Liú.
Consequently, the Wēishèng Command was renamed the Zhèndōng Command,

and Liú was appointed Military Commissioner of the Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng Commands, given the additional titles Grand Commandant (Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi), and Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
He was granted an Iron Certificate,
guaranteeing pardon for nine death offenses.
Liú went to Yuèzhōu to accept the commission,
then returned to govern Qiántáng.
He designated Yuèzhōu as
the "Eastern Prefecture" (Dōng Fǔ).
In the first year of Guānghuà (898),
the Zhènhǎi Command was moved to Hángzhōu.
Liú was further promoted to Grand Preceptor (Jiǎnxiào Tàishī).
Liú’s home village was renamed Guǎngyì Township, Xūn Guì Hamlet,
and the camp where Liú had always lived was named Yìjǐn Camp.
Wáng Tán, the Governor of Wùzhōu, rebelled and defected to Huáinán.
Yáng Xíngmì sent his general Kāng Rú to assist Tán,
and consequently attacked Mùzhōu.
Liú dispatched his younger brother Qiú, who defeated Rú at Xuānzhǔ.
Tán fled to Xuānzhōu.
Emperor Zhāozōng decreed that Liú’s portrait be painted in the Língyān Pavilion.
Yìjǐn Camp was elevated to Yìjǐn City.
Shíjiàn Mountain was named Yìjǐn Mountain.
Dàguān Mountain was named Gōngchén Mountain. When Liú toured Yìjǐn City,
and hosted a banquet for the elders,
the mountains and forests were all covered with brocade.
The large tree he used to play near in his youth was named
"Brocade-Clad General" (Yìjǐn Jiāngjūn).
In the second year of Tiānfù (902),
Liú was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yuè (Yuè Wáng).
While Liú was inspecting Yìjǐn City,
Xú Wǎn, Commander-in-Chief of the Right Division of the Martial Braves, and Xǔ Zàisī, Commander-in-Chief of the Left Division, rebelled.
They burned and looted the city and suburbs,
and attacked the inner city.
Liú’s son, Chuán'īng, and his generals Mǎ Chuò and Chén Wéi, closed the gates and resisted them.
When Liú returned,
he reached the Northern Outer Gate but could not enter.
Chéng Jí fought Wǎn on Liú’s behalf,
beheading over a hundred people.
Wǎn stationed his troops at Lóngxīng Temple.
Liú entered the city secretly in disguise by climbing over the wall.
He sent Mǎ Chuò, Wáng Róng, and Dù Jiànhuī, among others, to garrison the various gates.
He ordered Gù Quánwǔ to secure the Eastern Prefecture.
Quánwǔ said:
"The Eastern Prefecture is not a concern;
what is concerning is Huáinán.
If Wǎn is desperate,
he will definitely summon the Huái troops to come,
and the trouble will be significant.
Lord Yáng is a true hero.
If we inform him of our difficulty now,
he will surely pity us."
Liú agreed.
Quánwǔ said:
"If I go alone,
the mission will certainly fail.
Please choose one of your sons who can go."
Liú said:
"I have long wished to marry Yuánfán into the Yáng clan."
So he sent him to accompany Quánwǔ to Guǎnglíng.
Wǎn indeed summoned Tián Yūn from Xuānzhōu.
When Quánwǔ and the others arrived at Guǎnglíng,
Xíngmì gave his daughter in marriage to Yuánfán,
and immediately recalled Yūn.
Yūn took one million coins from Liú,
held Liú’s son Yuánguàn as collateral, and returned.
In the first year of Tiānyòu (904),
Liú was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wú (Wú Wáng).
Liú established the Hall of Meritorious Officials (Gōngchén Táng),
erected a stele to record their achievements,
listing five hundred names of his advisors, staff, and military officers on the back of the stele.
In the fourth year (907),
Yìjǐn City was elevated to the Ānguó Yìjǐn Command.
Liáng Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
and enfeoffed Qián Liú as King of Wúyuè and concurrent Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Huáinán.
There was a guest who urged Qián Liú to refuse the command from the Liáng,
but Qián Liú laughed and said:
"How could I fail to be like Sūn Zhòngmóu!"
Thereupon, he accepted it.
Tàizǔ once asked the official reporting from Wúyuè:
"Does Qián Liú have any hobbies in his life?"
The official replied:
"He likes jade belts and famous horses."
Tàizǔ laughed and said:
"A true hero, indeed."
He then bestowed upon him a casket of jade belts and ten imperial polo horses.
Wēi Quánfěng (and others) from Jiāngxī were defeated by Yáng Wò.
Wēi Zǐchàng of Xìn Zhōu defected to Qián Liú.
Qián Liú disliked his surname,
and changed it to Yuán.
In the second year of Kāipíng (908),
he was promoted to acting Minister of the Central Secretariat (Shǒu Zhōngshū Lìng).
He changed Lín'ān County (Xiàn) to Ānguó County,
and Guǎngyì Township (Xiāng) to Yījǐn Township.
In the third year (909),
he was promoted to acting Grand Guardian (Shǒu Tàibǎo).
Zhōu Běn and Chén Zhāng, generals under Yáng Wò, besieged Sūzhōu.
Qián Liú sent his younger brothers Qián Jù and Qián Biāo to relieve it.
The Huái troops surrounded the city with water barriers,
tying copper bells to nets submerged in the water,
to intercept those trying to sneak through.
The naval soldier Sīmǎ Fú,
who was highly resourceful and skilled in swimming underwater,
first used a massive bamboo pole to hit the net.
When the Huái men heard the bell sound, they immediately raised the net,
and Fú was able to pass.
When entering the city,
his method for exiting was also the same.
He then took their military signals,
and they attacked from both inside and outside simultaneously.
The signals and commands matched,
which the Huái men mistook for divine intervention,
and consequently they suffered a great defeat.
Zhōu Běn and the others fled,
and their generals Lǘqiū Zhí and Hé Míng (and others) were captured.
In the fourth year (910),
Qián Liú toured Yījǐn Commandery (Jūn),
and composed the "Returning Home Song," which said:
"With three credentials I return home, displaying brocade robes,
The elders travel far to attend and follow me.
The Ox and Dipper constellations are stable, people are honest,
The single King of Wúyuè returns with a four-horse chariot."
In the first year of Qiànhuà (911),
Qián Liú was promoted to acting Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shǒu Shàngshū Lìng),
concurrently serving as Commander-in-Chief of the Four Sides Mobile Army (Sìmiàn Xíngyíng Dūtǒng) for the Huáinán and Xuānrùn circuits (Dào).
He established a shrine for himself while living (Shēngcí) in Yījǐn Commandery.
Qián Biāo, Qián Liú’s younger brother, residing in Húzhōu,
illegally killed the garrison commander Pān Cháng.
Fearing punishment, he fled to Huáinán.
In the second year (912),
Yǐng Wáng Zhū Yǒuguì of Liáng ascended the throne,
and conferred upon Qián Liú the respected title of Shàngfǔ (Father of the Nation).
In the third year of Zhēnmíng (917), under the Last Emperor (Mòdì),
Qián Liú was granted the title Grand Marshal of the Armies of the Realm (Tiānxià Bīngmǎ Dū Yuánshuài),
and permitted to establish a staff and administration (Kāifǔ Zhì Guānshǔ).
In the fourth year (918),
Yáng Lóngyǎn seized Qiánzhōu,
and Qián Liú began submitting tribute to the capital (Jīngshī) via the sea route.
In the first year of Lóngdé (921),
Qián Liú was given imperial edicts that did not address him by name.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng entered Luòyáng,
Qián Liú sent envoys to offer tribute,
and requested a jade charter (Yùcè).
Zhuāngzōng submitted the proposal to the relevant authorities.
All the officials believed that only the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) could use a jade charter,
with Guō Chóngtāo being particularly opposed.
Eventually, however, it was granted,
and Qián Liú was bestowed a jade charter and a gold seal.
Qián Liú then conferred the Military Governorship (Jiédù) of the Zhènhǎi Commandery (and others) upon his son Qián Yuánguàn,
and declared himself King of the State of Wúyuè (Wúyuè Guówáng).
He renamed his residence "Palace" (Gōngdiàn) and his administrative office "Court" (Cháo).
All his officials referred to themselves as subjects (Chén).
He built three towers—for the jade charter, the gold covenant, and the imperial edicts—in Yījǐn Commandery.
He sent envoys to invest the Kings of Sīllá (Xīnluó) and Bóhǎi.
He also enfeoffed and appointed
the rulers of various maritime states.
Míngzōng ascended the throne,
and Ān Zhònghuǐ handled governmental affairs.
Qián Liú sent a letter to Zhònghuǐ;
the language of the letter was disrespectful,
and Zhònghuǐ became furious.
At this time,
the officials of the Palace Supply Office, Wū Zhāoyù and Hán Méi, were envoys to Wúyuè.
After their return,
Hán Méi falsely accused Wū Zhāoyù of proclaiming himself a subject and performing the ceremonial dance.
Zhònghuǐ subsequently memorialized to strip Qián Liú of his princely title, Grand Marshal, and Father of the Nation,
forcing him into retirement as a Grand Commander (Tàishuài).
Yuánguàn and others sent a person to submit a memorial written on silk via secret paths to explain their case.
When Ān Zhònghuǐ died,
Míngzōng restored Qián Liú's titles and official ranks.
In the third year of Chángxīng (932),
Qián Liú died,
aged eighty-one.
His posthumous title was Wǔsù.
His son, Qián Yuánguàn, succeeded him.
Qián Yuánguàn, courtesy name Míngbǎo,
was taken hostage by Tián Yūn when he was young.
When Tián Yūn rebelled against Wú,
Yáng Xíngmì gathered the Yuè forces and attacked him.
Whenever Tián Yūn returned defeated from battle,
he immediately wanted to kill Yuánguàn,
but Tián Yūn's mother always protected him.
Later, when Tián Yūn was about to leave,
he told his attendants:
"If I don't win today,
I will surely execute Master Qián (Qián Láng)."
That same day, Tián Yūn was killed in battle,
and Yuánguàn was able to return home.
When Qián Liú was confined by illness,
he summoned all the major generals and told them:
"My sons are all foolish and weak,
unfit to handle the affairs after my death.
After I die,
you gentlemen must choose [a successor] yourselves."
The generals wept,
and all said:
"Yuánguàn has accomplished the most merit following the King in campaigns and expeditions.
None of the other sons can compare.
We request that he be installed."
Qián Liú then produced several boxes of seals and keys,
summoned Yuánguàn, and gave them to him, saying:
"The generals have agreed upon you."
Qián Liú died,
Yuánguàn was installed,
succeeding to the title King of Wúyuè (Wúyuè Guówáng).
The jade charter and gold seal
were all handled according to Qián Liú’s precedent.
Wáng Yánzhèng established himself in Jiànzhōu,
causing great chaos in Mǐn (Fújiàn).
Yuánguàn dispatched his generals Yǎng Quán and Xuē Wànzhōng (and others) to attack him.
After more than a year,
they returned in great defeat.
Yuánguàn was also skilled at treating his officers and soldiers kindly,
he favored Confucian studies,
and was good at writing poetry.
He instructed his State Chancellor Shěn Sōng to establish the Academy for Selecting Talent (Zé Nénɡ Yuàn),
to select and employ literary scholars from the Wú region.
However, his nature was especially extravagant and presumptuous;
he loved constructing palaces and residences.
In the sixth year of Tiānfú (941),
Hángzhōu suffered a massive fire,
burning nearly all his palaces and residences.
When Yuánguàn fled,
the fire always followed and broke out again.
Yuánguàn was greatly terrified,
and consequently suffered from madness.
He died that year,
aged fifty-five.
His posthumous title was Wénmù.
His son, Qián Zuǒ, succeeded him.
Qián Zuǒ, courtesy name Yòu,
was thirteen years old when he ascended.
All the generals looked down on Qián Zuǒ.
Qián Zuǒ initially treated them leniently,
but when the generals gradually acted unlawfully,
Qián Zuǒ then dismissed his major generals Zhāng Dé'ān to Míngzhōu and Lǐ Wénqìng to Mùzhōu,
and executed the Internal Chief Supervisor Dù Zhāodá and the Commander-in-Chief Kàn Fán.
Because of this, everyone in the state feared him.
Wáng Yánxī and Wáng Yánzhèng, brothers, attacked each other.
Zhuō Yǎnmíng, Zhū Wénjìn, Lǐ Réndá (and others) usurped and killed each other.
The warfare did not cease for several years.
Lǐ Réndá attached himself to Lǐ Jǐng,
but later rebelled again.
Lǐ Jǐng’s forces attacked him,
and Lǐ Réndá sought aid from Qián Zuǒ.
Qián Zuǒ summoned the generals to discuss the matter.
The generals all were unwilling to go.
Qián Zuǒ furiously said:
"I am the Marshal,
yet am I unable to raise troops?
My family has always sustained and trained you generals.
Will you alone not put yourselves forward for me?
Anyone who disagrees with my plan will be executed!"
He then dispatched his commanders Zhāng Jūn and Zhào Chéngtài (and others) leading thirty thousand troops,
to proceed there by land and sea.
He sent generals to swear in the army,
and the orders were strict and uniform.
Zhāng Jūn and the others heavily defeated Lǐ Jǐng's forces,
capturing and executing tens of thousands.
They captured his generals Yáng Yè and Cài Yù (and others),
and consequently took Fúzhōu before returning.
Due to this, all the generals submitted to him.
Qián Zuǒ reigned for seven years,
succeeding to the title King of Wúyuè (Wúyuè Guówáng).
The jade charter and gold seal
were all as in the case of Qián Yuánguàn.
In the fourth year of Kāiyùn (947),
Qián Zuǒ died,
aged twenty.
His posthumous title was Zhōngxiàn.
His younger brother, Qián Chù, succeeded him.
Jiāo (椒), courtesy name Wéndé (文德).
Zuǒ (佐) died.
His younger brother, Zōng (倧), succeeded him in sequence.
Originally,
Yuánguàn (元瓘) had been held as a hostage in Xuānzhōu (宣州).
He took Hú Jìnsī (胡進思), Dài Yùn (戴惲), and others with him.
When Yuánguàn was established [as ruler],
he employed Jìnsī and others as high generals.
When Zuǒ was still young,
Jìnsī treated himself as an old general
and was greatly respected and honored [by Zuǒ].
However, when Zōng succeeded,
he somewhat treated Jìnsī with contempt and insult.
Jìnsī could not accept this.
Zōng held a grand troop review at Bìbō Tíng (碧波亭).
When he was grading and giving rewards,
Jìnsī stepped forward and remonstrated, saying the rewards were too generous.
Zōng angrily threw his writing brush into the water and said:
“These things are given to the soldiers;
how could I be doing this for selfish reasons?
Why do you criticize me?”
Jìnsī became extremely fearful.
On New Year's Eve,
a painter presented a depiction of Zhōng Kuí (鍾馗) striking down demons.
Zōng inscribed a poem onto the painting.
When Jìnsī saw it, he was greatly startled,
knowing that Zōng intended to kill him.
That night, gathering the guard troops, he deposed Zōng,
imprisoning him in Yìhé Yuàn (義和院).
He welcomed Chù (俶) and installed him [as ruler],
moving Zōng to the Eastern Residence (Dōngfǔ, 東府).
Chù served consecutively through the Hàn (漢) and Zhōu (周) dynasties,
succeeding to the title King of Wúyuè (吳越 Guówáng).
He was granted a jade mandate tablet and a gold seal.
When Shìzōng (世宗) campaigned against Huáinán (淮南),
he decreed that Chù should attack Chángzhōu (常州) and Xuānzhōu (宣州) to distract Lǐ Jǐng (李景).
Chù organized the troops within his state and waited.
Jǐng heard that the Zhōu army was about to launch a large-scale invasion,
so he sent envoys to pacify the border.
The border regions were all on high alert.
Chén Mǎn (陳滿), a watch official in Sūzhōu (蘇州), unaware of Jǐng’s envoys,
believed that the Imperial Court had already conquered all the prefectures,
and that envoys were sent for pacification.
He urgently reported to Chù,
requesting to mobilize troops in response.
Chù’s Chancellor Wú Chéng (吳程) hastily deployed troops to march out.
Chancellor Yuán Dézhāo (元德昭) believed the King’s army had surely not yet crossed the Huai River (Huái),
and argued with Chéng before Chù,
but could not persuade him otherwise.
Chéng and his men attacked Chángzhōu,
and were indeed defeated by Jǐng’s general Chái Kèhóng (柴克宏).
Chéng’s subordinate general Shào Kěqiān (邵可遷) fought fiercely;
Kěqiān’s son died before his horse,
but he continued fighting without looking back.
Chéng and his men barely escaped with their lives.
When the Zhōu army crossed the Huai,
Chù then mobilized all adult men (dīngmín) in his state to augment his forces,
sending Shào Kěqiān and others with four hundred battleships and seventeen thousand naval troops to Tōngzhōu (通州) to meet the deadline.
Wúyuè had possessed a state since the end of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
while Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) and Lǐ Biàn (李昪) occupied Jiānghuái (江淮).
When Wúyuè presented tributes,
and when the Imperial Court dispatched envoys,
they all sailed across the sea from Dēng (登) and Lái (萊) [prefectures].
Every year, envoys were often lost at sea.
In the fourth year of Xiǎndé (顯德) [957 CE],
an edict was issued, sending Yǐn Rìjiù (尹日就), Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left, and Cuī Sòng (崔頌), Director of the Ministry of Personnel, and others as envoys to Chù.
Shìzōng instructed them, saying:
“In this campaign, We are determined to pacify the north bank of the Yangzi (Jiāngběi).
When you return, you should come by land.”
In the fifth year [958 CE],
the King’s army campaigned against the Huai region.
In the first month, Jìnghǎi Jūn (靜海軍) was captured,
and Rìjiù and the others indeed returned by land.
After Shìzōng had pacified Huáinán,
he sent envoys to grant Chù weapons, armor, flags, banners, camels, sheep, and horses.
The Qián clan (Qián Shì) governed the Two Zhè (Liǎngzhè, 兩浙) regions for nearly a hundred years.
Compared to other states, their people were reputed to be timid and weak,
but their customs favored extravagance and luxury,
they indulged in easy living and excelled in craftsmanship.
Starting from the time of Liú (鏐), heavy taxes were constantly levied upon the people to support extravagance and unauthorized imperial ceremonies.
Even down to chickens, fish, eggs, and nestlings,
they were taken from every household daily.
Whenever someone was flogged to extract payment of their debt,
the various clerks (ànshǐ) would each hold their ledger and stand arrayed in the court.
For every debt listed in a ledger,
the amount was announced,
and the number of strokes was determined accordingly.
They were announced and flogged one after another.
The minimum accumulated dozens of strokes,
and the maximum reached over a hundred strokes.
The people particularly could not bear this suffering.
They also frequently seized precious goods from merchants from the Southern Mountains (Lǐng) and the coastal regions (Hǎi).
During the period of the Five Dynasties (Wǔdài),
they constantly offered tribute to the Middle Kingdom without fail.
When Shìzōng pacified Huáinán,
and the Sòng (宋) dynasty arose,
the states of Jīng (荊) and Chǔ (楚) submitted one after another.
Chù's position became increasingly isolated.
He began to exhaust his state's wealth to offer gifts and tribute.
During the reign of Emperor Tàizǔ (太祖 Huángdì),
Chù once came to court.
He was treated with great courtesy and sent back to his state.
Chù was pleased,
and increasingly presented rare and precious objects, vessels, and clothing as tribute,
more than could be counted.
Tàizǔ said:
“These are merely things from Our own treasury.
Why bother presenting them!”
In the third year of Tàipíng Xīngguó (太平興國) [978 CE],
an edict summoned Chù to court.
Chù led his entire clan to the capital (Jīngshī),
and his state was abolished.
The subsequent events are detailed in the National History (Guóshǐ).
Alas!
The connection between Heaven and man
is difficult to explain.
It is not merely that ancient diviners, seeking the extraordinary, sometimes fortunately hit the mark,
but even heroes and opportunistic bandits often claim association with portents and omens.
Could it be that they deceive and mislead the ignorant masses,
and thus use them?
If they rise up,
and do not rely on diligently accumulating meritorious deeds and virtue,
yet tattooed, shaved, thieving peddlers
stubbornly rise to the rank of princes and marquises,
is it also because people happily transmit such stories?
Considering the beginning and end of the Qián clan,
they did not bestow virtue or kindness upon their region.
Over the course of a hundred years,
they severely abused their people.
Did the forces that moved in the atmospheric signs
not stem from their own evil karma?
At that time, the four seas (the entire realm) were divided,
and the violence was unbearable.
But were all cases like this?
Or is it that we can deduce nothing at all from this?
The words of the diviners:
those that miss the mark are many,
while those that hit the mark are few.
Yet people especially like to speak of those that hit the mark?
The rise and fall of the house of Liú,
is consistently recorded in various texts.
It began in the second year of Qiánníng (乾寧) of the Táng dynasty [895 CE], when he became Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Zhènhǎi (鎮海) and Zhèndōng (鎮東) commands, simultaneously holding Liǎngzhè.
It ended in the third year of Tàipíng Xīngguó of the reigning dynasty [978 CE], when the state was abolished.
In total, eighty-four years.
Hereditary House of Mǐn (Mǐn Shìjiā) VIII: Wáng Shěnzhī (王審知) (Son Yánhàn, 延翰; Son Lín, 鏻; Lín’s son Jìpéng, 繼鵬; Yánxī, 延羲; Yánzhèng, 延政).
Wáng Shěnzhī, courtesy name Xìntōng (信通),
was a native of Gùshǐ (固始) in Guāngzhōu (光州).
His father, Nèn (恁),
had been a farmer for generations.
His elder brother, Cháo (潮),
was a county clerk.
Toward the end of the Táng dynasty, when bandits arose,
Wáng Xù (王緒) of Shòuzhōu (壽州) attacked and captured Gùshǐ.
Xù heard that Cháo and his brothers were capable and brave,
and summoned them to his army,
making Cháo a military officer (jūnxiào).
At that time,
Qín Zōngquán (秦宗權) of Càizhōu (蔡州) was recruiting soldiers to augment his forces.
He thus appointed Xù as Prefect (Cǐshǐ) of Guāngzhōu,
and summoned his troops to join the attack on Huáng Cháo (黃巢).
Xù procrastinated and failed to march.
Zōngquán mobilized troops and attacked Xù.
Xù led his multitude and fled south,
plundering wherever they went.
They entered Líntīng (臨汀) from Nánkāng (南康),
and captured Zhāngpǔ (漳浦).
They had tens of thousands of followers.
Xù was naturally suspicious and jealous.
If his subordinate generals were capable,
he often used some pretext to kill them.
Cháo became quite afraid for himself.
When the army reached Nán'ān (南安),
Cháo spoke to his vanguard general, saying:
“We who abandoned our ancestors’ tombs and our wives and children to become bandits,
were merely coerced by Xù.
How could this be our original intention?
Now Xù is arrogant and suspicious.
Those generals and officers who possess ability will surely die.
We cannot guarantee our safety from morning till night,
much less plan to achieve great things!”
The vanguard general was greatly enlightened,
and held Cháo, weeping together.
They then selected several dozen strong men,
hid them among the thick bamboo,
waited for Xù to arrive,
leapt out and captured him,
and imprisoned him within the army camp.
Xù subsequently committed suicide.
Xù had already been deposed.
The general of the vanguard said:
“The one who saved us is Cháo.”
Thereupon, they promoted Cháo to be their leader.
At this time,
Liào Yànruò, the Cìshǐ (Prefect) of Quánzhōu, governed with greed and tyranny.
The people of Quán suffered because of him.
Hearing that Cháo was seizing territory and approaching their border,
and that his army maintained strict discipline,
their elders led one another to block the road and urge him to stay.
Cháo immediately led his troops to besiege Yànruò.
After more than a year, they overcame him.
In the second year of Guāngqǐ (886 CE),
Chén Yán, the Guānchásǐ (Regional Governor) of Fújiàn, memorialized the throne recommending Cháo as the Cìshǐ of Quánzhōu.
Chén Yán died in the first year of Jǐngfú (892 CE).
His son-in-law, Fàn Huī, proclaimed himself Liúhòu (Acting Regional Governor).
Cháo sent Shěnzhī to attack Huī.
After a long time, they could not overcome him.
The officers and soldiers who were wounded or killed were very numerous.
Shěnzhī requested permission to return the troops.
Cháo did not permit it.
He further requested that Cháo personally oversee the army,
and also increase the troops.
Cháo replied:
“If both the soldiers and generals are entirely exhausted,
I will go myself.”
Shěnzhī then personally directed the officers and soldiers to attack and defeat him.
Huī was killed.
The Táng dynasty immediately appointed Cháo as the Guānchásǐ of Fújiàn.
Cháo made Shěnzhī the Fùshǐ (Deputy Governor).
Shěnzhī was a person of imposing appearance,
with a high nose bridge and a square mouth.
He always rode a white horse.
In the army, he was called
“Báimǎ Sānláng” (Third Gentleman on the White Horse).
In the fourth year of Qiánníng (897 CE),
Cháo died.
Shěnzhī succeeded him.
The Táng dynasty designated Fúzhōu as Wēiwǔ Jūn,
and appointed Shěnzhī as Jiédùshǐ (Military Commissioner).
He was successively promoted to Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (Chancellor),
and granted the title Lángyá Wáng (Prince of Lángyá).
When Táng perished,
Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng additionally appointed Shěnzhī as Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Imperial Chancellery),
granted him the title Mǐn Wáng (Prince of Mǐn),
and elevated Fúzhōu to Dà Dūdū Fǔ (Grand Military Governorship).
At this time,
Yáng Xíngmì occupied Jiānghuái.
Every year, Shěnzhī sent envoys across the sea,
traveling from Dēng and Lái to pay tribute at the Liáng court.
When the envoys entered the sea,
a frequent loss of one third or one fourth [of the travelers] by capsizing and drowning.
Although Shěnzhī had risen from a band of bandits,
he was personally frugal and temperate,
fond of propriety, and respected scholars.
Wáng Dàn,
the son of Táng Chancellor Pǔ;
Yáng Yí,
the cousin of Táng Chancellor Shè;
Xú Yín,
a well-known Jìnshì (advanced scholar) during the Táng era,
all served under Shěnzhī.
He also established schools for the Four Gates (Sìmén),
to educate the most excellent scholars of Mǐn.
He attracted foreign traders and merchants from across the sea.
At Huáng Qí on the sea,
the waves and tides formed a barrier.
One night, wind, rain, thunder, and lightning struck and cracked the area,
opening it up to become a harbor.
The people of Mǐn believed this was brought about by Shěnzhī's virtuous governance.
They named it Gāntáng Gǎng (Sweet Pear Harbor).
Shěnzhī died in the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE),
at the age of sixty-four.
His posthumous title was Zhōngyì.
His son, Yánhàn, succeeded him.
Yánhàn, courtesy name Zǐyì,
was Shěnzhī’s eldest son.
In the fourth year of Tóngguāng (926 CE),
the Táng court appointed Yánhàn as Jiédùshǐ.
That same year,
Zhuāngzōng was assassinated,
and the Central Plains faced many troubles.
Yánhàn therefore took the Biography of Wúzhū, King of Mǐnyuè, from Sīmǎ Qiān’s Shǐjì and showed it to his generals and officials, saying:
“Mǐn,
has been a kingdom since ancient times.
If I do not become king now,
what else should I wait for?”
Thereupon, the generals and officials of the Military Governorship submitted memorials urging him to assume the title.
In the tenth month,
Yánhàn established his state and proclaimed himself King,
yet he still maintained the calendar of the Táng dynasty.
Yánhàn was a tall person,
and beautiful as jade.
His wife, Lady Cuī, was ugly and promiscuous.
Yánhàn was unable to restrain her.
Before the mourning period for Shěnzhī was complete,
he removed the offering tables and mats.
He also selected many daughters from good families to be his concubines.
Lady Cuī was extremely jealous by nature.
Any of the daughters from good families who were beautiful,
she would immediately confine in a separate room,
bind them with heavy fetters,
carve a wooden hand to slap their cheeks,
and also stab them with an iron awl.
Eighty-four people died within one year.
Later, Lady Cuī fell ill.
She saw ghosts (or felt haunted by the spirits) and died.
Yánbǐng, the adopted son of Shěnzhī and Cìshǐ of Jiànzhōu,
whose original surname was Zhōu,
had been in discord with Yánhàn since Shěnzhī's time.
When Yánhàn succeeded to the throne,
he made his younger brother, Yánjūn, the Cìshǐ of Quánzhōu.
Yánjūn was angered by this appointment.
The two men consequently plotted a rebellion.
In the twelfth month,
Yánbǐng and Yánjūn both entered with their troops.
They captured Yánhàn and killed him.
Then Yánjūn succeeded to the throne.
He changed his name to Lín.
Lín,
was Shěnzhī’s second son.
The Táng court immediately appointed Lín as Jiédùshǐ,
and successively promoted him to Jiǎnxiào Tàishī (Acting Grand Preceptor) and Zhōngshū Lìng,
granting him the title Mǐn Wáng.
Originally,
when Yánbǐng and Lín plotted to kill Yánhàn,
Yánbǐng’s troops arrived first.
He had already captured and killed Yánhàn.
Lín’s troops only arrived the next day.
Yánbǐng, considering himself the adopted son,
deferred to Lín and had him installed.
When Yánbǐng returned to Jiànzhōu,
Lín saw him off in the suburbs.
As Yánbǐng was about to depart, he said to Lín:
“Carefully continue the aspirations of our predecessor,
and do not trouble your Elder Brother to come again!”
Lín resented this remark.
In the second year of Chángxīng (931 CE),
Yánbǐng led troops to attack Lín,
attacking the west gate.
He ordered his son, Jìxióng, to travel by sea and attack the south gate.
Lín sent Wáng Réndá to resist them.
Réndá concealed armored men inside the boats,
falsely raising white banners to request surrender.
Jìxióng believed him.
When he boarded the boat,
the hidden troops sprang out,
stabbed him to death,
and displayed his head at the west gate.
When the [remaining] troops saw this, they all scattered and fled.
Yánbǐng was captured.
Lín reproached him, saying:
“I could not continue the aspirations of our predecessor;
indeed, I have troubled Elder Brother to come again!”
Yánbǐng could not reply,
and subsequently Lín killed him.
Yánbǐng's son, Jìshēng, who was defending Jiànzhōu,
heard of the defeat,
and fled to Qiántáng.
In the third year of Chángxīng (932 CE),
Lín submitted a memorial stating:
“Mǎ Yīn, Prince of Chǔ, and Qián Liú, Prince of Wúyuè, were both Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs).
Both have now passed away.
I request that I be conferred the title of Shàngshū Lìng.”
The Táng court did not respond.
Lín subsequently severed tributary relations.
was fond of the theories of ghosts, spirits, and the Daoist school.
The Daoist Chén Shǒuyuán (陳守元) gained his trust by means of heterodox methods (zuǒdào),
and established the Bǎohuáng Gōng (寶皇宮) for him to reside in.
Shǒuyuán said to Wáng Lín:
"Bǎohuáng (寶皇) commands Your Majesty to temporarily withdraw from your position,
and later you will be Son of Heaven for sixty years."
Wáng Lín happily abdicated his throne,
ordering his son, Jìpéng (繼鵬), to provisionally manage the affairs of the government.
Afterwards, he returned to his position,
and dispatched Shǒuyuán to ask Bǎohuáng:
"Where will I go after the sixty years?"
Shǒuyuán conveyed Bǎohuáng's message, saying:
"After sixty years,
you shall become a Dàluó Xiānrén (大羅仙人, Grand Golden Immortal)."
Wáng Lín then immediately ascended the Imperial throne,
receiving the investiture mandate from Bǎohuáng.
Using the auspicious sight of a yellow dragon (huánglóng jiànzhēn) as a sign for the imperial domain,
he changed the reign title to Lóngqǐ (龍啟),
and named his state Mǐn (閩).
He posthumously granted Shěnzhī (審知) the title Zhāowǔ Xiàohuángdì (昭武孝皇帝),
with the temple name Tàizǔ (太祖).
He established five ancestral temples (wǔmiào),
set up a hundred officials,
and designated Fúzhōu (福州) as Chánglè Fǔ (長樂府).
However, the Mǐn territory was narrow,
and state revenue was insufficient.
He appointed Xuē Wénjié (薛文傑), the Commander of the Central Army, as Commissioner of National Finance (Guójì Shǐ).
Wénjié often investigated private, hidden affairs among the populace,
bringing charges against wealthy people,
and confiscating their assets to support state expenditures.
All the people of Mǐn resented him.
He further recommended the sorcerer Xú Yàn (徐彥),
saying:
"Your Majesty has many treacherous ministers around you,
if you do not submit them to judgment by the ghosts and spirits,
chaos will ensue."
Wáng Lín commanded Yàn to perceive ghosts within the palace.
Wénjié had a grudge against Wú Yīng (吳英), the Inner Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Yīng was ill and on leave.
Wénjié said to Yīng:
"The Emperor finds that since you hold a close, sensitive post,
yet repeatedly request leave due to illness,
he intends to dismiss you."
Yīng asked:
"What should I do?"
Wénjié consequently instructed Yīng, saying:
"If the Emperor sends someone to inquire about your illness,
you must say, 'It is merely a headache,
there is no other suffering.'"
Yīng believed this to be true.
The next day,
Wénjié subtly encouraged Wáng Lín to have the sorcerer examine Yīng's illness.
The sorcerer reported:
"I entered the Northern Temple
and saw Yīng being interrogated by Chóngshùn Wáng (崇順王).
He said: 'How dare you plot rebellion?'
and struck his head with a golden mallet."
Wáng Lín told this to Wénjié.
Wénjié said:
"This cannot yet be believed.
We ought to ask how his sickness is."
Wáng Lín sent someone to ask him.
Yīng replied:
"Headache."
Wáng Lín considered the evidence corroborating the sorcerer's words.
He immediately put Yīng in prison
and ordered Wénjié to impeach him.
Yīng falsely confessed,
and was executed.
Yīng had previously commanded the Mǐn troops
and had earned the loyalty of the soldiers.
When the soldiers heard of Yīng's death,
they were all enraged.
That year,
the people of Wú (吳) attacked Jiànzhōu (建州).
Wáng Lín sent his general Wáng Yánzōng (王延宗) to relieve the city,
but the soldiers on the road refused to advance,
saying:
"Only if we get Wénjié will we advance."
Wáng Lín valued Wénjié and refused to surrender him.
His son Jìpéng pleaded that Wénjié be surrendered to alleviate the crisis.
So, Wáng Lín sent Wénjié to the army in a cage cart (jiànchē).
Wénjié was skilled in prognostication.
He calculated for himself, saying:
"If I survive three days, I will be free from harm."
Those escorting him heard this
and rushed quickly, arriving in two days.
The soldiers were jubilant.
They mutilated Wénjié in the marketplace.
The people of Mǐn scrambled to throw tiles and stones at him,
and his body was instantly devoured, piece by piece.
The next day,
Wáng Lín's envoy arrived
to pardon him,
but it was already too late.
Previously,
Wénjié had designed a cage cart for Wáng Lín.
Thinking the ancient design was too loose and spacious,
he changed the design,
making it pass right through from top to bottom,
and lining the inside with iron spikes pointing inward,
so that movement would constantly cause injury.
Once completed,
he was the first to suffer its torment.
In the third year of Lóngqǐ (935 CE),
the reign title was changed to Yǒnghé (永和).
Wáng Rén-dá (王仁達) had rendered merit to Wáng Lín by killing Yánbǐng,
and he commanded the Emperor's personal guard.
Wáng Lín was inwardly jealous of him.
He once asked Rén-dá:
"Did Zhào Gāo (趙高) truly point to a deer and call it a horse
in order to deceive the Second Emperor (Èr Shì)?
Did this really happen?"
Rén-dá replied:
"The Second Emperor of Qín (Qín Èr Shì) was foolish;
thus, Gāo could point to a deer and call it a horse.
It was not that Gāo was capable of deceiving the Second Emperor.
Now, Your Majesty is wise and intelligent,
and the court officials number less than one hundred.
Their daily movements and activities
are all known to Your Majesty.
Should anyone dare to seize undue authority or power,
they would simply be exterminated along with their clan."
Wáng Lín was ashamed,
and rewarded him with gold and silk to comfort and pacify him.
After Rén-dá withdrew, Wáng Lín said to others:
"Rén-dá’s intelligence and strategy
are useful during my reign,
but I cannot leave him as a danger to future generations."
Eventually, he fabricated a charge and had him executed.
Wáng Lín’s wife died early.
His second wife, of the Jīn (金) clan, was virtuous but was not favored.
There was a maid of Shěnzhī named Jīnfèng (金鳳),
whose surname was Chén (陳).
Wáng Lín favored her,
and subsequently established her as Empress.
Earlier,
Wáng Lín had a favorite official named Guī Shǒumíng (歸守明).
He gained favor through his looks
and was nicknamed Guī Láng (歸郎, Gentleman Guī).
Later, Wáng Lín suffered a wind-illness.
Empress Chén committed adultery with Guī Láng.
There was also Lǐ Kěyīn (李可殷), the Director of the Bureau of Works,
who used Guī Láng as an intermediary to sleep with Empress Chén.
Wáng Lín ordered the brocade weavers to make a Nine-Dragon Curtain (Jiǔlóng Zhàng).
The people of the state sang:
"Who says the Nine-Dragon Curtain
only harbors one Guī Láng?"
Wáng Lín had a beautiful maid named Chūnyàn (春鷰).
His son Jìpéng had incestuous relations with her.
As Wáng Lín was already ill,
Jìpéng used Empress Chén as a means to ask for Chūnyàn.
Wáng Lín reluctantly gave her up.
His second son, Jìtāo (繼韜), became angry
and plotted to kill Jìpéng.
Jìpéng was fearful,
and conspired with Lǐ Fǎng (李倣), the Imperial City Commissioner.
In the tenth month of that year,
Wáng Lín hosted a feast for the army in the Dàpú Diàn (大酺殿).
While seated, he became delirious
and claimed to see Yánbǐng arriving.
Fǎng believed Wáng Lín's illness had become severe,
and immediately ordered strong men to first kill Lǐ Kěyīn at his home.
The next day, at morning court,
Wáng Lín was well
and asked Fǎng what crime Kěyīn had committed to warrant his death.
Fǎng, terrified, left
and, along with Jìpéng, led the Imperial City Guards to enter the palace.
Wáng Lín heard the sound of drums and shouts
and ran to hide inside the Nine-Dragon Curtain.
The guards stabbed him but could not kill him completely.
The palace women, unable to bear his suffering,
finished him off.
Jìtāo, Empress Chén, and Guī Láng were all killed by Fǎng.
Wáng Lín ruled for ten years before being killed.
He was posthumously named Huì Huángdì (惠皇帝),
with the temple name Tàizōng (太宗).
Jìpéng
was Wáng Lín's eldest son.
Once established on the throne,
he changed his name to Chǎng (昶).
He changed the reign title to Tōngwén (通文),
and appointed Lǐ Fǎng as Acting Manager of the Affairs of the Six Armies and Various Guards.
Since Fǎng had committed the crime of regicide,
even after establishing Chǎng,
he was always suspicious in his heart.
He recruited many sworn retainers (sǐshì) as a precaution.
Chǎng worried about this.
He subsequently held a great banquet for the army,
concealed armored troops, captured Fǎng, and executed him,
hanging his head in the marketplace.
A thousand men from Fǎng's personal contingent rebelled,
burned the Qǐshèng Mén (啟聖門),
seized Fǎng's head,
and fled to Qiántáng (錢塘).
Chǎng sent envoys to offer tribute at the capital (Jīngshī).
Gāozǔ sent the Sanqí Chángshì, Lú Sǔn, to enfeoff Chǎng as King of Mǐn,
and appointed his son Jìgōng as Prince of Línghǎi Commandery.
When Sǔn arrived in Mǐn,
Chǎng claimed illness and did not appear,
ordering Jìgōng to manage the reception.
He also sent the Zhōngshū Shèrén, Liú Yǐ, to present comfort gifts to Sǔn at the residence.
Yǐ’s clothing and cap were impressive,
and his retinue of grooms and servants was very grand.
On another day, Sǔn encountered Yǐ on the road,
but he was only in plain cloth clothes and straw sandals.
Sǔn sent someone to mock him, saying:
"You are the Fènggé Shèrén,
why are you so extremely debasing yourself!"
Yǐ was ashamed and embarrassed,
covering his face with his hand and fleeing.
When Chǎng heard of this,
he was angered that Sǔn had subjected him to insult and humiliation.
When Sǔn returned,
Chǎng gave no reply.
However, his son Jìgōng sent his aide, Zhèng Yuánbì, to accompany Sǔn to the capital to offer regional goods.
He sent a letter to the high ministers of Jìn,
stating Chǎng’s desire to interact using the rites of an equal state.
Gāozǔ was angered by his lack of deference,
and issued an edict exposing his offenses.
He returned the tribute items, refusing to accept them.
Lǐ Zhīsǔn, the Bīngbù Yúanwàiláng, submitted a memorial requesting that the goods be confiscated and the envoy imprisoned.
Thereupon, Yuánbì was put into prison.
When the case was ready, he was brought forth for an audience.
Yuánbì prostrated himself and said:
"Chǎng,
is a ruler of the Yímò,
unaware of rites and righteousness.
Your Majesty is currently demonstrating great sincerity,
to draw in people from distant lands.
I, your servant, executed my mission improperly;
I wish to submit to the axe and the execution block,
in order to redeem Chǎng’s crime."
Gāozǔ then pardoned Yuánbì
and sent him back.
Chǎng also loved sorcery.
He appointed the Daoist priest Tán Zǐxiāo as Zhèngyī Xiānshēng.
He also appointed Chén Shǒuyuán as Tiānshī.
Moreover, the wicked man Lín Xīng gained favor through sorcery.
Regardless of the importance of the matter,
Xīng invariably issued commands in the name of the Bǎohuáng before it was carried out.
Shǒuyuán instructed Chǎng to build the Sānqīng Terrace in three stories.
Using several thousand catties of gold to cast images of the Bǎohuáng, Yuánshǐ Tiānzūn, and Tàishàng Lǎojūn.
Daily, several catties of lóngnǎo, xūnlù, and other perfumes were burned.
Music was performed beneath the terrace,
the sound never stopping day or night.
It was said that through this, the Dà Huándān could be sought.
In the summer of the third year,
a rainbow appeared inside his palace.
Lín Xīng transmitted the divine message:
"This is an omen that the imperial clan is about to cause disorder."
He then commanded Xīng to lead strong men to kill Shěnzhī’s sons, Yánwǔ and Yánwàng, and their five sons.
Later, Xīng’s plans failed,
and he too was killed.
Chǎng, however, became increasingly deluded and erratic.
He established Chūn Yàn, his father’s maidservant, as Shūfēi.
Later, he established her as Empress.
He also sent the physician Chén Jiū to sell official positions using blank tángdié.
Chǎng’s younger brother, Jìyán, oversaw the affairs of the Six Armies and all the Guards.
Chǎng grew suspicious and dismissed him,
replacing him with his youngest brother, Jìyōng.
Furthermore, he recruited brave soldiers to form the Chénwèi Dū for his personal defense.
The grants and rewards he bestowed upon them
were uniquely generous compared to the other armies.
Lián Chóngyù, the Kònghè Dūjiàng, and Zhū Wénjìn, the Gǒngchén Dūjiàng,
were both provoked to anger by this, rousing their troops.
In the summer of that year,
diviners said that disaster was due to occur in Chǎng’s palace.
Chǎng moved to the Nángōng to evade the disaster,
but a fire broke out in the palace.
Chǎng suspected Chóngyù’s soldiers of starting the fire.
The Nèixuéshì Chén Tán was usually trusted and favored by Chǎng for his clever flattery.
Chǎng spoke to him about the fire incident.
Tán, instead, reported it to Chóngyù.
Chóngyù was fearful,
and that night led the Guards to set fire to the Nángōng.
Chǎng, grasping his beloved concubines, sons, younger brothers, huángmén, and guards, cut open the gate and fled,
lodging in the open countryside.
Chóngyù welcomed Yánxī and installed him.
Yánxī ordered his son Jìyè to lead troops to attack Chǎng.
They caught up to him;
they shot and killed several people.
Chǎng knew he could not escape,
threw his bow onto the ground.
Jìyè seized and killed him,
and his wife and sons all died, leaving no survivors.
When Yánxī was established,
he gave Chǎng the posthumous title Kāngzōng.
Yánxī
was Shěnzhī’s youngest son.
Once established,
he changed his name to Xī.
He sent envoys to offer tribute to Jìn,
and changed the era name to Yǒnglóng.
He cast large iron coins,
with one being equivalent to ten.
Since Chǎng’s reign, Xī had been stubborn and difficult to control.
Chǎng’s Chancellor, Wáng Tán, always suppressed and checked him.
Xī also feared Tán,
and dared not let his feelings show.
Sillá sent an envoy to Mǐn with a precious sword.
Chǎng held it up and showed it to Tán, saying:
"What is this intended for?"
Tán replied:
"He who is disloyal or unfilial
shall be executed."
Xī, who was nearby, changed color.
Once Xī was established,
and Sillá again presented a sword,
Xī recalled Tán’s previous words.
Although Tán was already dead,
he commanded that the tomb be opened and the corpse mutilated.
Tán’s face looked lifelike,
and blood flowed over his body.
Yú Tíngyīng, the Cìshǐ of Quánzhōu, had once falsely used Xī’s command to seize children from respectable families.
Xī was angered,
and summoned the Yùshǐ to impeach him.
Tíngyīng offered ten million cash as ‘banquet money.’
Xī said:
"Where is the Empress’s local tribute?"
Tíngyīng then offered another ten million cash to the Empress,
and only then escaped impeachment.
Xī once married off a daughter.
Any court official who failed to offer congratulations was flogged.
Liú Zàn, the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, was charged for failing to investigate and report the offenses.
When he was about to be flogged,
the Jiànyì Dàfū Zhèng Yuánbì remonstrated sharply.
Xī said to Yuánbì:
"How do you compare to Wèi Zhènggōng,
that you dare to remonstrate so forcefully!"
Yuánbì replied:
"Since Your Majesty resembles Emperor Tàizōng of Táng,
it is acceptable for your servant to be Wèi Zhènggōng."
Xī was pleased,
and thereupon released Zàn and did not flog him.
Xī’s younger brother, Yánzhèng, was the Jiédùshǐ of Jiànzhōu,
and enfeoffed as the King of Fùshā.
Since Xī was established,
they were incompatible.
They frequently raised troops to attack each other.
Xī, due to this, hated the Zōngshì,
and often had many of them executed on pretexts.
The Jiànyì Dàfū Huáng Jùn carried a coffin and went to the court hall to remonstrate extremely urgently.
Xī was angered,
and demoted Jùn to Sīhù Cānjūn of Zhāngzhōu.
The Jiàoshū Láng Chén Guāngyì submitted a memorial listing over fifty faults and wicked deeds of Xī.
Xī ordered the guards to flog him one hundred times, but he did not die.
(Then he had) a rope tied around his neck,
and hung him from a tree.
Only after a long time did he expire.
Chén Kuāngfàn, the Guójì Shǐ, presented a method for increasing the calculation of taxes on merchants.
Xī said:
"Kuāngfàn is a jewel among men."
Soon thereafter, the annual revenue did not meet the projected amount.
He then borrowed from the people to make up the shortfall.
Kuāngfàn died of worry.
Afterward, when Xī learned that Kuāngfàn had borrowed from the people,
he opened the coffin, severed the corpse,
and abandoned it in the water.
Xī’s nature was already licentious and cruel,
and his wife, Lady Lǐ, was fierce and addicted to alcohol.
The Xiánfēi Lady Shàng was beautiful and favored.
Lǐ Rén Yù was Xī’s nephew,
who was favored by him sexually,
and was used by him as Chancellor.
Xī often drank excessively.
When the officials attended him while drinking,
if they became drunk and could not handle it,
anyone who was reported or accused of secretly discarding wine was immediately killed.
His son Jìróu discarded wine.
and he killed him along with one attendant.
Lián Chóngyù, having killed Chǎng,
feared being punished by the people of the state.
He established marriage ties with Zhū Wénjìn to secure his position.
Xī was suspicious of them in his heart,
and often used words to reproach Chóngyù and the others.
Chóngyù and the others wept and defended themselves.
Lady Lǐ was jealous of Consort Shàng’s favor,
and planned to murder Xī and establish her son Yàchéng.
She then sent someone to tell Chóngyù and the others:
"The Emperor's heart is unsettled concerning you two gentlemen.
What are you going to do?"
Chóngyù and the others were frightened.
In the third month of the sixth year,
Xī went out touring.
Returning drunk,
Chóngyù and the others sent strong men to pull him from his horse and kill him.
He was given the posthumous title Jǐngzōng.
Yánzhèng
was the son of Shěnzhī.
When Xī
was established, he practiced debauchery and cruelty.
Yánzhèng repeatedly sent letters to admonish him.
Xī was angry,
and sent Dù Jiànchóng to supervise his army.
Yánzhèng drove him out.
Xī then raised troops to attack Yánzhèng,
but was defeated by Yánzhèng.
Yánzhèng then established a state in Jiànzhōu, proclaimed himself Yīn,
and changed the reign title to Tiāndé.
The following year,
Lián Chóngyù had already killed Xī,
and gathered the officials of Mǐn, declaring:
“In the past, Tàizǔ Wǔ Huángdì personally braved arrows and stones,
thereby establishing Mǐn.
But his descendants
have been depraved, cruel, and without principle.
Now Heaven rejects the Wáng clan,
and the common people support change.
We must seek a virtuous person
to bring peace to this land.”
None of the officials dared to debate the matter.
Thus, they escorted Zhū Wénjìn up to the throne hall,
and led all the officials to face north and submit to him as subjects.
Wénjìn appointed Chóngyù to administer the affairs of the Six Armies and all Guards.
All male descendants of the Wáng clan residing in Fúzhōu, regardless of age, were executed.
He assigned Huáng Shàopǒ to govern Quánzhōu,
Chéng Yūn to govern Zhāngzhōu,
Xǔ Wénzhěn to govern Tīngzhōu,
and adopted the Jìn reign title.
This was the first year of Kāiyùn (944).
Liú Cóngxiào, a general of the Quánzhōu army, deceived the people of the prefecture, saying:
“The army of the Prince of Fùshā has recaptured Fúzhōu!
Our families have served the Wáng clan for generations;
how can we stand idly by and serve bandits?”
The people of the prefecture jointly killed Shàopǒ,
and welcomed Wáng Jìxūn as Administrator (Cìshǐ).
When Zhāngzhōu heard of this,
they also killed Yūn,
and welcomed Wáng Jìchéng as Administrator.
Both were cousins/nephews of the Wáng clan.
Wénzhěn was fearful,
and surrendered Tīngzhōu to Yánzhèng.
Yánzhèng had now acquired the three prefectures.
Chóngyù also killed Wénjìn,
sent his head to Jiànzhōu, and submitted himself.
Lín Rénhàn, a deputy general in Fúzhōu, then killed Chóngyù,
planning to welcome Yánzhèng to establish his capital in Fúzhōu.
At this time,
Lǐ Jǐng of Nán Táng heard of the chaos in Mǐn,
and dispatched troops to attack it.
Yánzhèng sent his nephew Jìchāng to guard Fúzhōu.
However, the Nán Táng forces were fiercely attacking Yánzhèng.
Lǐ Réndá, a Fúzhōu general, said to his followers:
“The Táng army is attacking Jiànzhōu.
The Prince of Fùshā cannot even protect himself,
how can he hold onto this territory?”
He then captured and killed Jìchāng.
He wished to establish himself,
but feared the populace would not support him.
He used Zhuó Yǎnmíng, a monk from Xuěfēng Temple, presenting him to the crowds and saying:
“This is no ordinary man.”
He dressed him in imperial robes and a crown,
and led all the generals and officials to face north and submit to him as subjects.
Soon after, he again killed Yǎnmíng,
then established himself,
and sent assurances of submission to Lǐ Jǐng.
Jǐng appointed Réndá as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Wēiwǔ Army,
and changed his name to Hóngyì.
Meanwhile, Jǐng’s forces attacked and captured Jiànzhōu,
moved Yánzhèng’s clan to Jīnlíng,
and enfeoffed him as the Prince of Póyáng.
This year
was the fourth year of Bǎodà of Jǐng (946).
Liú Cóngxiào heard that Yánzhèng had surrendered to Táng,
so he seized Wáng Jìxūn and sent him to Jīnlíng.
Lǐ Jǐng renamed Quánzhōu the Qīngyuán Army,
and made Cóngxiào its Military Governor.
After Jǐng defeated Yánzhèng,
he sent messengers to summon Lǐ Réndá to court.
Réndá refused to comply,
and consequently surrendered to Wúyuè.
Liú Cóngxiào also expelled Jǐng’s garrison troops,
occupying Quán and Zhāng prefectures.
Jǐng nevertheless enfeoffed Cóngxiào as the Prince of Jìnjiāng.
During the time of Zhōu Shìzōng,
Cóngxiào sent his staff officer Cài Zhòngxīng disguised as a merchant,
traveling by secret routes to the capital (Jīngshī),
seeking to establish a residence and submit to the court.
At this time,
Shìzōng had agreed with Lǐ Jǐng to use the river as the boundary,
and therefore did not accept the submission.
Cóngxiào remained a subject of Nán Táng.
Subsequent events are detailed in the National History.
The third year of Kāiyùn of Jìn, the year Bǐngwǔ (946),
was also the fourth year of Bǎodà of Nán Táng.
In this year,
Lǐ Jǐng’s forces destroyed Jiànzhōu,
and the Wáng clan was extinguished.
The *Jiāngnán Lù* states:
“In the third year of Bǎodà (945),
the Wáng clan was captured
and moved to Jīnlíng.”
This is erroneous.
Based on the fact that Wáng Cháo entered Fúzhōu in the first year of Jǐngfú of Táng (892)
and was appointed Surveillance Commissioner (Guānchá Shǐ),
those who recorded history later
used
the prophecy of "coming on horseback, going on horseback"
as their basis.
Thus, they took the second year of Guāngqǐ (886), the year Bǐngwǔ, when Wáng Cháo was appointed Administrator of Quánzhōu, as the starting year.
Extending to the fourth year of Bǎodà (946),
which was again the year Bǐngwǔ when they were extinguished,
makes the duration sixty-one years.
However, their complete possession of the state of Mǐn
should properly start from the first year of Jǐngfú (892),
making the actual duration fifty-five years.
Although all historians correctly record the state's destruction in the year Bǐngwǔ,
their starting year is bound by the prophetic text
and is erroneous.
Moreover, the *Jiāngnán Lù* is also incorrect regarding the final year.
Hereditary House of Nánpíng, Ninth [House]: Gāo Jìxīng (Son: Cónghuǐ. Sons of Cónghuǐ: Bǎoróng, Bǎoxù. Son of Bǎoróng: Jìchōng)
Gāo Jìxīng, courtesy name Yísūn,
was a native of Xiáshí in Shǎnzhōu.
His original name was Jìchāng.
To avoid the personal taboo name of Hòutáng Xiànzǔ (Li Kejing),
he changed his name to Jìxīng.
In his youth, Jìxīng was a household servant of the wealthy Lǐ Ràng of Biànzhōu.
When Liáng Tàizǔ first garrisoned Xuānwǔ,
Ràng gained favor by contributing wealth,
was adopted as a son,
and his name was changed to Zhū Yǒuràng.
Because of Yǒuràng, Jìxīng gained an audience.
Tàizǔ admired his talent
and ordered Yǒuràng to raise him as a son.
Consequently, he falsely adopted the family name Zhū,
and was appointed Commander of the Zhìshèng Army,
later promoted to Commander of the Yìyǒng (Brave and Valiant) Forces.
In the second year of Tiānfù (902),
the Liáng army attacked Fèngxiáng,
but Lǐ Màozhēn held firmly within the walls and did not come out.
Tàizǔ considered withdrawing his army and returning to Hézhōng.
Jìxīng alone stepped forward and said:
“The heroes of the realm have been watching this maneuver for a year.
Now the Qí people are exhausted,
and defeat is imminent.
What Your Highness worries about
is that they are closing the walls to wear out our army.
This can be overcome by luring them out.”
Tàizǔ praised his suggestion
and ordered Jìxīng to recruit brave and capable warriors.
He found the cavalryman Mǎ Jǐng.
Jìxīng gave him the plan
and introduced him to Tàizǔ.
Jǐng said:
“There is no chance of returning from this mission.
I hope my descendants will be taken care of.”
Tàizǔ felt compassion and tried to stop him,
but Jǐng insisted.
He then departed.
Jǐng, with a few horsemen, rode swiftly and knocked on the city gate, announcing:
“The Liáng forces are heading east,
the vanguard has already left!”
The Qí people believed him,
opened the gates, and came out to pursue the Liáng army.
The Liáng troops followed immediately behind Jǐng and advanced,
killing more than nine thousand of the enemy.
Jǐng died in the effort.
Later, when Màozhēn made peace with Liáng
and Zhāozōng returned [to the capital],
Jǐng was posthumously honored with an official rank
and given the posthumous title Zhōngzhuàng.
Jìxīng became famous because of this incident.
The following year,
he was appointed Administrator of Sòngzhōu.
He participated in the defeat of Qīngzhōu,
was transferred to be Defense Commissioner (Fángyù Shǐ) of Yǐngzhōu,
and reverted to the family name Gāo.
At the end of the Táng,
Zhào Kuāngníng of Xiāngzhōu attacked and defeated Léi Yàngōng at Jīngnán,
and made his younger brother, Kuāngmíng, acting military commissioner (Liúhòu).
Liáng forces attacked and conquered Xiāngzhōu.
Kuāngníng fled to Wú,
and Kuāngmíng fled to Shǔ.
Subsequently, Jìxīng was appointed acting Regional Governor (Jiédù Guānchá Liúhòu) of Jīngnán.
In the first year of Kāipíng [907 CE],
Jìxīng was appointed Regional Governor (Jiédùshǐ).
In the second year [908 CE],
he was granted the additional title of Grand Councillor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
The Jīngnán commandery consisted of ten prefectures.
At the end of the Táng,
it had been invaded by various circuits.
When Jìxīng first arrived,
Jīnglíng was but a single city.
After the devastation of war and fire,
the communities were desolate and sparse.
Jìxīng recruited, organized, and pacified the populace,
and scholars and people returned to him.
He appointed Ní Kěfú and Bāo Táng as generals and commanders,
and Liáng Zhèn, Sīkōng Xūn, Wáng Bǎoyì, and others as counselors.
When Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) died,
Jìxīng saw that Liáng was weakening day by day,
and planned to resist [orders] with his troops to secure himself.
He restored the city walls and moats,
and erected defense towers and barricades.
He sent troops to attack Guī and Xiá,
but was defeated by the Shǔ general Wáng Zōngshòu.
He again dispatched troops, claiming to aid Liáng in attacking Jìn,
but used them to invade Xiāngzhōu.
He was defeated by Kǒng Qíng,
and consequently ceased paying tribute and taxes for several years.
The Last Emperor (Mòdì) of Liáng treated him leniently,
conferring upon Jìxīng the title Prince of Bóhǎi (Bóhǎiwáng),
and granting him imperial robes, crowns, swords, and jade pendants.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng [917 CE],
he resumed paying tribute.
When Liáng fell,
Táng Zhuāngzōng entered Luò,
and issued an edict reassuring and comforting Jìxīng.
Sīkōng Xūn and others all urged Jìxīng to attend the imperial court in the capital.
Liáng Zhèn believed it was unwise,
saying:
"Liáng and Táng were enemies for generations,
battling fiercely along the Yellow River for nearly twenty years.
Now the Sovereign has newly destroyed Liáng,
and Your Highness is a former official of the Liáng court.
You command powerful troops
and occupy a major garrison.
If you go to court in person,
you will surely be held captive."
Jìxīng did not listen.
He left his two sons [in charge],
and, escorted by three hundred cavalrymen,
went to court in Luòyáng.
Zhuāngzōng indeed wanted to detain him.
Guō Chóngtāo remonstrated, saying:
"Táng has just conquered Liáng and gained the empire.
We should now display great trustworthiness to the world.
Currently, the regional lords from all directions are successively coming to pay tribute,
sending only their sons, younger brothers, generals, and officials.
But Jìxīng has personally come to report his duty,
setting an example for the regional lords.
We should treat him with special kindness and ceremony,
to encourage those who may come later.
If, instead, we restrain him,
it will show the world that our tolerance is limited,
and will cut off the intent of the four quarters to turn inward towards us.
This is unacceptable."
Zhuāngzōng then stopped the plan,
and treated him with generous ceremony before sending him away.
Zhuāngzōng once asked Jìxīng:
"I have already destroyed Liáng.
If I want to conquer Wú and Shǔ, which should I do first?"
Jìxīng replied:
"Shǔ should be prioritized.
Your subject requests to lead the troops from my own circuit to advance first."
Zhuāngzōng was greatly pleased
and patted his back with his hand.
Jìxīng subsequently ordered artisans to embroider the imprint of the hand on his robe,
taking it home as an honor.
After Jìxīng had departed,
Zhuāngzōng regretted having let him go
and secretly ordered Liú Xùn of Xiāngzhōu to scheme against him.
When Jìxīng traveled to Xiāngzhōu,
his heart was troubled.
He cut through the gate at night and left.
Just after he left,
the imperial edict arrived late that night.
Upon returning, Jìxīng said to Liáng Zhèn:
"If I had not disregarded your words,
I would almost not have escaped."
He then said:
"My journey had two flaws: coming to court was one flaw,
and being released and allowed to return was the other flaw.
Moreover, the Sovereign fought a hundred battles to capture Hénán,
and boasts to his meritorious officials that he personally transcribed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
He also said: 'I gained the empire on the tip of my finger.'
His self-congratulation is like this.
But he is excessively devoted to hunting,
and many government affairs are neglected.
I have nothing to worry about now."
In the third year of Tóngguāng [925 CE],
he was invested as the Prince of Nánpíng (Nánpíngwáng).
Wèi Wáng Jìjí had already defeated Shǔ
and obtained over 400,000 [units] of gold and silk from Shǔ.
As he descended through the gorges (Xiá),
the disaster concerning Zhuāngzōng occurred.
Hearing that there was a change in the capital,
Jìxīng confiscated all the Shǔ goods
and killed their envoys, Hán Gǒng and over ten others.
Initially,
when the Táng forces attacked Shǔ,
Jìxīng requested to personally take Kuí, Zhōng, Wàn, Guī, and Xiá prefectures using the troops of his own circuit.
Jìxīng was appointed Pacification Commissioner for the Southeast Route of the Gorges (Xiálù Dōngnánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ).
However, Jìxīng never dispatched any troops.
After Wèi Wáng had defeated Shǔ,
and Míngzōng ascended the throne,
Jìxīng consequently requested that Kuí, Zhōng, and the other prefectures be attached to his commandery.
The Táng ministers believed that Jìxīng had requested to take them himself,
but his troops had been deployed without success,
so they refused.
Jìxīng repeatedly requested them.
Although Táng eventually granted them reluctantly,
Táng still appointed the prefects (Cǐshǐ) themselves.
Jìxīng refused to accept them.
Míngzōng then appointed Liú Xùn of Xiāngzhōu as Pacification Commissioner
to attack him,
but he failed to conquer [Jīngnán].
However, Táng's separate general, Xīfāng Yè, captured Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn prefectures.
Jìxīng then submitted Jīng, Guī, and Xiá prefectures to Wú.
Wú enfeoffed Jìxīng as the Prince of Qín (Qínwáng).
He died in the winter of the third year of Tiānchéng [928 CE]
at the age of seventy-one,
and was posthumously named Wǔxìn.
Jìxīng had nine sons.
His eldest son, Cónghuì, succeeded him.
Cónghuì’s courtesy name was Zūnshèng.
During Jìxīng’s time,
he served in Liáng as an Official of Imperial Service (Gōngfèngguān),
and was successively promoted to Prefect of the Saddle and Bridle Repository (Ānpèikù Shǐ).
He was granted leave to return home.
Jìxīng then detained him and made him Commander-in-Chief of the Infantry and Cavalry (Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ) and Administrative Assistant to the Field Marshal (Xíngjūn Sīmǎ).
When Jìxīng died,
Wú appointed Cónghuì as Regional Governor of Jīngnán (Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ).
Since his father had severed ties with Táng,
Cónghuì feared he might be attacked again.
He sent an envoy to Chǔ.
Mǎ Yīn, the King of Chǔ, petitioned Táng on his behalf,
and Cónghuì also dispatched the Commandant (Yāyá) Liú Zhīqiān to present a memorial, submitting himself [to Táng].
He presented three thousand *liǎng* of silver as an indemnity for past crimes.
Míngzōng accepted it.
In the first month of the first year of Chángxīng [930 CE],
Cónghuì was appointed Regional Governor,
and Jìxīng was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Chǔ (Chǔwáng),
with the posthumous name Wǔxìn.
In the third year [932 CE],
Cónghuì was enfeoffed as the Prince of Bóhǎi.
In the first year of Yìngshùn [934 CE],
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánpíng.
Cónghuì was astute and resourceful
and possessed much cunning and deceit.
Gāo Zǔ of Jìn sent Táo Gǔ, a scholar of the Hanlin Academy, as the envoy bearing national credentials for Cónghuì’s birthday.
Cónghuì hosted a banquet for Gǔ at the Wàngshā Tower,
where he displayed a large array of warships beneath the tower.
He said to Gǔ:
"Wú and Shǔ have been insubordinate for a long time.
I wish to restore military preparations
and practice naval warfare,
to await the time for the imperial army."
When Gǔ returned,
he reported his words in detail.
Gāo Zǔ of Jìn was delighted,
and again sent an envoy to bestow upon him a hundred armored horses.
When Ān Cóngjìn of Xiāngzhōu rebelled,
he attempted to ally with Cónghuì for support.
Cónghuì outwardly rejected him
but secretly maintained communication.
When the Jìn army launched its punitive campaign,
Cónghuì dispatched his general Lǐ Duān with a naval force to respond [to Ān Cóngjìn].
When Cóngjìn was executed,
Cónghuì requested Yǐngzhōu to be attached to his commandery.
Gāo Zǔ did not permit it.
Hàn Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán.
Cónghuì sent a messenger via an unofficial path to present a memorial urging him to ascend the throne,
