and further stated that if Hàn gained the realm,
he wished to beg for Yǐngzhōu to be his dependency.
Hàn Gāozǔ outwardly consented to this.
When Gāozǔ entered Biàn,
Cónghuì sent an envoy to pay tribute,
and consequently requested Yǐngzhōu.
Gāozǔ did not grant it.
Cónghuì was angered,
dispatched troops to attack Yǐngzhōu,
but was defeated by the Prefect Yǐn Shí.
Hàn sent the Libationer of the Directorate of Education, Tián Mǐn, as an envoy to Chǔ,
borrowing passage through Jīngnán.
Cónghuì asked Mǐn about the strength and weakness of the Central State,
thinking that after Qìdān's time,
both armies and supplies were exhausted,
intending to use this idea to reproach Mǐn.
Mǐn spoke on the matter:
“Dù Chóngwēi completely surrendered the Jìn armor and weapons to the captives,
who placed them in Zhènzhōu
and never moved them north.
Therefore, the Jìn troops are all possessed by Hàn.”
Cónghuì was displeased.
Mǐn presented Cónghuì with the printed version of the Five Classics.
Cónghuì declined, saying:
“What I know does not exceed the eighteen chapters of the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety).”
Mǐn said:
“The essential way of ultimate virtue,
is sufficient in this.”
Mǐn then recited the Chapter on Feudal Lords:
“When in high position, he is not arrogant;
though lofty, he is not endangered.
He restrains excess and is cautious in measures,
so though full, he does not overflow.”
Cónghuì thought this was mocking himself,
and immediately punished Mǐn with a large wine cup [of drink].
Jīngnán’s territory was narrow and its army weak,
situated between Wú and Chǔ, it was a small state.
Since Wú proclaimed itself emperor,
Nán Hàn, Mǐn, and Chǔ all honored the established calendar of Liáng,
presenting tribute yearly and seasonally,
and all borrowed passage through Jīngnán.
Jìxīng and Cónghuì constantly intercepted and detained their envoys,
seizing their possessions.
Although the various domains reproached and criticized them in writing,
or sometimes dispatched troops to launch punitive campaigns,
they would simply return the goods without shame.
After this, Nán Hàn, Mǐn, and Shǔ all proclaimed themselves emperors.
Cónghuì declared himself a subject to whichever state he faced,
mostly because he profited from their gifts.
The local slang called those who seized, plundered, and acquired things shamelessly "Làizi,"
meaning a rascal or scoundrel.
Therefore, all the states referred to him as
“Gāo Làizi.”
Since Cónghuì failed to obtain Yǐngzhōu,
he consequently severed ties with Hàn.
After a year passed,
tribute relations were resumed.
He died in the tenth month of Qiányòu First Year,
aged fifty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title Shàngshū Lìng,
with the posthumous name Wénxiàn.
His son, Bǎoróng, succeeded him.
Cónghuì had fifteen sons.
The eldest was Bǎoxūn,
the next was Bǎozhèng.
Bǎoróng was the third son.
The reason he succeeded is unknown.
Bǎoróng’s courtesy name was Décháng.
During Cónghuì’s time,
he served as the Deputy Military Commissioner,
concurrently serving as the Prefect of Xiázhōu.
When Cónghuì died,
he was appointed Military Commissioner.
In Guǎngshùn First Year,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Bóhǎi Commandery.
In Xiǎndé First Year,
he was promoted to be the Prince of Nánpíng.
When Shìzōng campaigned against Huái,
Bǎoróng sent Commander Wèi Lín to lead three thousand troops,
marching out of Xiàkǒu to act as support.
He also sent Guest General Liú Fú to deliver a memorial to Nán Táng,
urging them to submit.
Lǐ Jǐng declared himself a subject,
and Shìzōng obtained the memorial Bǎoróng had presented.
He was greatly pleased,
and rewarded him with one hundred bolts of silk.
Since the time of Hòu Táng, Jīngnán
usually paid tribute to the capital once every few years,
but relations were broken twice in between.
By the time of Shìzōng,
there was no year without tribute.
Bǎoróng believed that weapons, gold, and silk
were merely ordinary products of the land,
insufficient to demonstrate sincere loyalty.
Therefore, he sent his younger brother Bǎoshēn to pay court.
Shìzōng praised him even more.
Initially,
when Jìxīng governed the region,
Liáng had granted five thousand troops as his garrison army.
Their clothing and food were all supplied by Liáng.
By the time of Míngzōng,
thirteen thousand *shí* of salt were supplied annually.
Later, the supply ceased.
When Shìzōng pacified Huái,
he therefore ordered Tàizhōu to supply it.
Bǎoróng was slow-witted and indecisive by nature,
lacking talent or ability.
All matters, regardless of size,
he entrusted to his younger brother Bǎoxù.
His paternal cousin Cóngyì plotted rebellion,
but was reported by his adherent Gāo Zhīxùn.
He was banished to Sōngzī and killed there.
When Sòng arose,
Bǎoróng grew afraid,
and presented tribute three times within a single year.
In Jiànlóng First Year,
he died of illness,
aged forty-one.
He was posthumously granted the title Tàiwèi,
with the posthumous name Zhēnyì.
His younger brother Bǎoxù succeeded him.
Bǎoxù’s courtesy name was Xǐnggōng.
He was Cónghuì’s tenth son.
When Bǎoróng died,
he was appointed Military Commissioner.
In the third year [of Jiànlóng],
Bǎoxù fell ill
and said to his general, Liáng Yánsì:
“If I do not recover from this sickness,
which of my brothers should I entrust with the future affairs?”
Yánsì said:
“Does Your Excellency not recall Prince Zhēnyì?
When the former Prince was confined by illness,
he entrusted the military administration to Your Excellency.
Now, the former Prince’s son, Jìchōng, is grown up.”
Bǎoxù said:
“What you say is correct.”
He immediately appointed Jìchōng to manage the internal and external military forces.
In the eleventh month,
Bǎoxù died,
aged thirty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the title Shìzhōng.
Bǎoróng’s son, Jìchōng, succeeded him.
Jìchōng’s courtesy name was Chénghé.
When Bǎoxù died,
he was appointed Military Commissioner.
In Húnán, Zhōu Xíngféng died,
and his son Bǎoquán succeeded him.
His general Zhāng Wénbiǎo launched a rebellion.
In Jiànlóng Fourth Year,
Tàizǔ ordered Mùróng Yánzhāo and others to subdue him.
Yánzhāo borrowed passage through Jīngnán,
agreeing that the troops would pass outside the city walls.
Jìchōng’s senior general, Lǐ Jǐngwēi, said:
“Military matters emphasize strategy and deception.
The agreement to stay outside the city
cannot be trusted.
We should strictly prepare our forces to wait for them!”
The Aide, Sūn Guāngxiàn, rebuked him, saying:
“You are merely a common person from the Xiájiāng area!
How can you know success or failure?
Moreover, since the time of Zhōu Shìzōng, the Central State
already possessed the ambition to unify the realm.
How much more so now that the Sacred Sòng has received the Mandate,
and the true Lord has appeared!
How can the King’s army be easily resisted?”
He then persuaded Jìchōng to dismiss the scouts
and seal the treasuries to await them.
Jìchōng thought this was correct.
Jǐngwēi left and sighed, saying:
“My words are not used.
The great enterprise is lost!
Why should I remain alive?”
He consequently choked himself to death.
Yánzhāo’s army arrived.
Jìchōng went out to meet them in the suburbs,
but the vanguard immediately entered his city.
Jìchōng urgently returned [to the city],
saw banners, flags, armored soldiers, and horses
arrayed throughout the streets and alleys,
and was greatly terrified.
He immediately went to Yánzhāo and surrendered his credentials and seal.
Tàizǔ issued a lenient edict, restoring Jìchōng as Military Commissioner.
In the first year of Qiándé (963),
when there were rites performed at the Southern Suburb,
Jì Chōng submitted a memorial wishing to attend the sacrifice.
In the ninth month,
he prepared documents announcing the situation to the Three Shrines (Miào),
leading his officers, subordinates, and clan members, over five hundred people, to pay court in the Capital (Jīngshī).
He was appointed Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of the Wǔníng Army, and then died.
Guāngxiàn was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Huángzhōu.
Subsequent events concerning him are fully recorded in the National History (Guóshǐ).
The years and times of Jìxīng's rise and demise are very clear,
all books concur,
spanning from the first year of Kāipíng of the Liáng (907), when he was stationed in Jīngnán,
until the first year of Qiándé (963) of the Imperial Dynasty (Huángcháo), when his state was abolished,
totaling fifty-seven years.
Hereditary House of the Southern Hàn, Chapter 10: Liú Mín (Son Chéngjūn, Chéngjūn's sons Jì'ēn, Jìyuán)
Liú Mín,
was the full younger brother of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Hàn.
His original name was Chóng.
He possessed a beautiful beard and whiskers,
and his eyes had double pupils.
When young, he was shiftless,
addicted to wine and fond of gambling,
and was once tattooed and made a soldier.
When Gāozǔ served the Jìn dynasty as Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Hédōng,
he appointed Mín as Commander-in-Chief (Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Administrator (Yǐn) of Tàiyuán, Resident Governor (Liúshǒu) of the Northern Capital (Běijīng), and Chancellor (Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì).
During the reign of Emperor Yǐndì,
he was repeatedly promoted to Director of the Chancellery (Zhōngshū Lìng).
Emperor Yǐndì was young,
and governance rested with the high ministers.
Emperor Tàizǔ of the Zhōu dynasty (Guō Wēi) was Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ),
having recently quelled the Three Rebellions (Sān Pàn),
and had established great merit.
However, he and Mín had long had a rift.
Mín felt quite uneasy
and said to Judge (Pànguān) Zhèng Gǒng:
“The sovereign is young and weak,
governance rests with powerful ministers,
and I am not in harmony with Duke Guō (Guō Wēi).
What should we do about the current situation?”
Gǒng replied:
“The Hàn government is about to collapse!
The military forces in Jìnyáng are the strongest in the world,
and the terrain is dangerous and secure.
The taxes levied from ten prefectures are sufficient to sustain ourselves.
You are a member of the imperial clan;
if you do not make plans at this time,
you will certainly be controlled by others later.”
Mín said:
“Your words
are precisely my intention.”
Thereupon he ceased sending tax levies to the central government,
recruited local heroes,
and registered adult males to augment his army.
In the third year (of Qiányòu, 950),
Emperor Tàizǔ of the Zhōu rose up in Wèi,
and Emperor Yǐndì was assassinated.
Mín then plotted to raise troops.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of the Zhōu entered the capital from Wèi,
his intention to rebel was already clear,
but the high ministers of the Hàn did not immediately elevate him,
so he did not dare immediately establish himself.
Instead, he informed the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) of the Hàn
that Mín’s son, Yūn, should be established as the heir of Hàn,
and dispatched Chancellor Féng Dào to escort Yūn from Xúzhōu.
At that time,
everyone knew that this was not the true intention of Tàizǔ,
but Mín alone was pleased and said:
“My son is going to be emperor!
What trouble is there to fear?”
Thereupon he disbanded his troops
and sent an envoy to the Capital (Jīngshī).
Emperor Tàizǔ of the Zhōu had been lowly in his youth,
and had a flying sparrow tattooed on his neck.
People of the time called him Guō Què'ér (Guō the Sparrow).
Tàizǔ met Mín’s envoy,
fully explained his reasons for establishing Yūn,
and then pointed to his own neck, showing the envoy, saying:
“Since ancient times, how could there be a Son of Heaven with etched blue marks (tattoos)?
I hope you (the duke) do not suspect me.”
Mín was delighted,
and became even more convinced that this was true.
Lǐ Xiāng, Assistant Administrator (Shǎoyǐn) of Tàiyuán, said:
“Duke Guō raised troops and violated imperial authority;
given the circumstances, he cannot remain a Hàn subject,
and he will certainly not establish an heir for the Liú clan.”
He thus advised Mín to lead troops down the Tàiháng Mountains,
control Mèngjīn, and wait for the inevitable change.
“If Yūn should fortunately be established,
then you can disband your troops.”
Mín cursed loudly, saying:
“Xiāng is a rotten scholar!
He wants to sow discord between me and my son!”
He ordered his attendants to drag him out and execute him.
Xiāng sighed at the execution block, saying:
“I made plans for a fool;
my death is truly fitting!
However, my wife is ill
and cannot survive alone.
I wish to die together with her.”
When Mín heard this,
he immediately executed his wife along with him in the marketplace,
and reported the incident to the Hàn court
to show that he had no other intentions.
Soon after, Emperor Tàizǔ of the Zhōu indeed replaced the Hàn dynasty,
demoting Yūn to Duke of Xiāngyīn.
Mín sent Garrison Commander (Yájiàng) Lǐ Mǒu with a letter to Emperor Tàizǔ of the Zhōu,
requesting Yūn be returned to Tàiyuán,
but Yūn had already died.
Mín cried bitterly,
established a shrine for Lǐ Xiāng,
and offered sacrifices there annually.
Thereupon, on the day Wùyín in the first month of the first year of Guǎngshùn of the Zhōu (951), he ascended the imperial throne in Tàiyuán,
appointing his son Chéngjūn as Administrator (Yǐn) of Tàiyuán,
and Judges (Pànguān) Zhèng Gǒng and Zhào Huá as Chancellors (Zǎixiàng),
and Commander of the Palace Guards (Dū Yāyá) Chén Guāngyù as Commissioner of Palace Affairs (Xuānhuīshǐ).
He dispatched Vice Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (Tōngshì Shèrén) Lǐ Mǒu to travel secretly as an envoy to the Qìdān.
Yǒngkāng Wáng Wùyù of the Qìdān agreed with Mín to establish a relationship as a father state and a son state.
Mín then sent Chancellor Zhèng Gǒng with a letter to Wùyù,
referring to himself as the “Nephew Emperor” (Zhí Huángdì),
treating him merely as an uncle.
Wùyù dispatched Yān Wáng Shùzhá and Administrator (Zhèngshì Lìng) Gāo Xūn with a formal document honoring Mín as Emperor Shénwǔ of Great Hàn (Dà Hàn Shénwǔ Huángdì),
and also confirming Mín’s wife as Empress (Huánghòu).
Wùyù was by nature magnificent and vigorous;
whenever a Hàn envoy arrived,
he invariably overwhelmed them with wine and meat.
Gǒng was already ill,
but Wùyù forced him to drink,
and he died of intoxication in a single night.
However, when Wùyù heard that Mín had established himself,
he was rather pleased that the Central Plains (Zhōngguó) had so many troubles.
He thus sent his noble ministers Shùzhá and Gāo Xūn to return the courtesy with a beloved yellow-red steed and a jade belt adorned with nine dragons and twelve rice grains.
Shortly thereafter, Wùyù was assassinated by Shùzhá,
and Shùlǜ succeeded him.
Mín dispatched Academian-in-Waiting of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmì Zhí Xuéshì) Wáng Dézhōng as an envoy to Shùlǜ,
requesting troops to attack the Zhōu.
Shùlǜ sent Xiāo Yǔjué to lead fifty thousand troops to assist Mín.
Mín marched out through Yīndì to attack Jìnzhōu,
but was defeated by Wáng Jùn.
That year there was intense cold;
Mín’s army suffered from freezing and starvation,
losing more than half its number.
The following year,
he again attacked Fǔzhōu,
but was defeated by Shé Déyǐ.
Déyǐ subsequently seized Kělán Commandery (Jūn).
When Emperor Tàizǔ of the Zhōu died,
Mín was delighted to hear it.
He dispatched an envoy to request troops from the Qìdān.

The Qìdān sent Yáng Gǔn to lead ten thousand cavalry of armored horses and five or six tens of thousands of troops from the Xī and other tribes, claiming a strength of one hundred thousand, to assist Mín.
Mín appointed Zhāng Yuánkuī as the vanguard,
and personally led thirty thousand cavalry to attack Lùzhōu.
Lǐ Jūn of Lùzhōu sent Mù Lìngjūn with three thousand infantry and cavalry to resist Yuánkuī at Tàipíng Post Station (Yì).
Yuánkuī defeated them,
and subsequently besieged Lùzhōu.
At this time,
Shìzōng had newly ascended the throne,
and believed Mín would rely on the fact that Zhōu had suffered a great loss (a period of mourning)
and that the Son of Heaven was newly established,
and certainly would not be able to dispatch troops.
Therefore, it was advisable to lead the troops himself and strike unexpectedly.
Although Chancellor Féng Dào and many others argued strongly against it,
Shìzōng’s resolve was very sharp.
In the third month of Xiǎndé Yuánnián (954 CE), he personally led the campaign.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
they battled at Gāopíng.
Lǐ Chóngjìn and Bái Chóngzàn commanded the left flank;
Fán Àinéng and Hé Huī commanded the right flank;
Xiàng Xùn and Shǐ Yànchāo occupied the center army;
Zhāng Yǒngdé protected the imperial carriage with the forbidden troops.
Mín also arrayed his troops into three formations.
Zhāng Yuánhuī occupied the eastern wing,
Yáng Gǔn occupied the western wing,
and Mín occupied the center.
Gǔn, looking at the Zhōu army, said to Mín:
“They are powerful enemies.
We cannot move lightly!”
Mín bristled his beard and replied:
“The opportunity must not be lost.
Do not speak recklessly!”
Gǔn became angry and left.
Mín commanded the eastern wing to advance first.
Wáng Dézhōng halted his horse and admonished him, saying:
“The south wind is very fierce.
This is not advantageous for the northern army.
It is advisable to wait a little.”
Mín angrily said:
“You old boor,
do not recklessly obstruct my army!”
He immediately waved Zhāng Yuánhuī forward.
Yuánhuī attacked the Zhōu right army.
As soon as the troops engaged,
Àinéng and Huī retreated and fled.
Their cavalry became disordered,
and several thousand infantry soldiers abandoned their armor and defected, surrendering to Yuánhuī.
The shouts of “Long Live!” shook the valleys.
Shìzōng was greatly alarmed.
He personally oversaw the fighting troops.
All the soldiers fought desperately to take the lead,
and the wind grew fiercer.
Mín personally waved the red banner to recall his troops,
but the army could not be checked,
and Mín was consequently defeated.
As night fell,
Mín gathered his remaining troops, about ten thousand men, and stopped behind a ravine.
At this time,
the Zhōu rear army,
commanded by Liú Cí,
was following behind and had not yet arrived.
But Shìzōng was keen on quick victory,
and once the battle was won,
Cí's army arrived shortly after.
They then seized the momentum and pursued the attack.
Mín was again greatly defeated,
and all his supplies, equipment, armor, carriages, and personal objects were captured by the Zhōu army.
Mín alone rode his Qìdān bay horse,
and fled by a secluded path from Diāokē Lǐng.
At night, he lost his way in the mountains and valleys.
He obtained a villager to act as a local guide.
Mistakenly heading towards Píngyáng,
he eventually found another route to return.
Meanwhile, Zhāng Yuánhuī died in battle on the field.
Yáng Gǔn was angry at Mín,
and held back his troops on the western wing without engaging in battle,
thus he alone returned with his entire army intact.
When Mín returned,
he prepared stables for the bay horse,
decorated it with gold and silver,
fed it with rations suitable for the third rank,
and nicknamed it
“Zìzài Jiāngjūn” (The General of Freedom).
Shìzōng rested his army at Lùzhōu,
held a great feast for the officers and men,
and executed the defeated generals Fán Àinéng, Hé Huī, and over seventy others.
The army’s morale and prestige greatly increased.
He advanced to attack Tàiyuán,
and dispatched Fú Yànqīng and Shǐ Yànchāo north to control Xīnkǒu,
in order to cut off the Qìdān reinforcement route.
The city of Tàiyuán was forty *lǐ* square.
The Zhōu army advanced three hundred paces from the city walls
and completely surrounded it.
From the fourth month until the sixth month,
they attacked but could not conquer it.
Furthermore, Yànqīng and his forces were defeated by the Qìdān,
and Yànchāo died in battle.
Shìzōng immediately ordered the troops to return.
Earlier,
when the Zhōu army was besieging the city,
Mín had sent Wáng Dézhōng to escort Yáng Gǔn home,
and then sought reinforcements from the Qìdān.
The Qìdān dispatched several tens of thousands of cavalry to aid Mín,
and ordered Dézhōng to return first.
Upon reaching Dàizhōu,
Sāng Guī, the general of Dàizhōu, killed Zhèng Chǔqiān, the Defense Commissioner,
and surrendered the city to Zhōu,
and also delivered Dézhōng to Zhōu.
Shìzōng summoned Dézhōng and asked how many troops the barbarians (Qìdān) were sending to help.
Dézhōng claimed he was only escorting Gǔn home
and was not seeking anything.
Shìzōng believed him.
Soon after, the Qìdān defeated Fú Yànqīng at Xīnkǒu,
and Dézhōng was consequently executed.
After Mín’s defeat at Gāopíng,
and subsequently being besieged,
he fell ill from worry.
He died in the eleventh month of the following year,
at the age of sixty.
His son, Chéngjūn, was established (as ruler).
Chéngjūn
was Mín's second son.
When young, he was quite fond of learning
and skilled in calligraphy.
When Mín died,
Chéngjūn sent someone to present a memorial to the Qìdān,
referring to himself as their son.
Shùlǜ replied to him with an imperial edict,
calling Chéngjūn “my child,”
and permitting him to succeed to the throne.
Originally,
Mín often said to Zhāng Yuánhuī and others:
“Because of the inheritance of Gāozǔ [Liú Zhìyuǎn]
and the injustice suffered by Yūn [Liú Yūn],
I am morally bound not to submit to Lord Guō [Guō Wēi].
I hope to strive with you all to avenge the hatred of our family and state.
As for claiming the title of Emperor in one region,
how can I help but do so?
But what sort of Son of Heaven am I,
and what sort of military governors (*jiédùshǐ*) are you?”
Therefore, when he usurped the title, he still used the era name Qiányòu,
did not change the reign title,
and did not establish an Imperial Ancestral Temple.
The seasonal sacrifices
were conducted using family rituals.
Once Chéngjūn was established,
he first granted a general amnesty within his borders,
changed Qiányòu Shínián (the tenth year of Qiányòu) to Tiānhuì Yuánnián,
and established seven ancestral temples in Xiǎnshèng Gōng.
The Qìdān dispatched Gāo Xūn to assist Chéngjūn.
Chéngjūn sent Lǐ Cúnguī to attack Shàngdǎng with Xūn,
but they gained nothing and returned.
The following year,
Shìzōng campaigned north against the Qìdān,
and captured the Three Passes.
A Qìdān envoy arrived to report the emergency.
Chéngjūn was about to dispatch troops,
but Shìzōng returned his army,
so the matter ceased.
When Sòng arose,
Lǐ Jūn, the Military Governor of Zhāoyì, rebelled against the mandate.
He sent his general Liú Jìchōng and Administrator Sūn Fú to present a memorial declaring submission (as a vassal).
He seized the supervising officers Zhōu Guāngxùn and Lǐ Tíngyù and sent them to Tàiyuán,
begging for troops as reinforcement.
Chéngjūn wanted to consult the Qìdān,
but Jìchōng conveyed Jūn's intent,
asking that Qìdān troops not be used.
Chéngjūn immediately led his own national army personally and marched out via Tuánbǎigǔ.
The assembled officials saw him off at Fénshuǐ.
Púyè Zhào Huá said:
“Lǐ Jūn undertakes matters lightly and easily.
If Your Majesty does not plan for success or failure,
but raises an army that empties the state,
I am truly worried about it.”
Chéngjūn arrived at Tàipíng Yì [Post Station],
and enfeoffed Jūn as the Prince of Lǒngxī Commandery.
Jūn saw that Chéngjūn’s ceremonial guard was incomplete
and not like that of a true king,
and regretted having submitted to him as a vassal.
Jūn then personally stated that he had received kindness from the Zhōu clan
and could not bear to betray that virtue.
However, Chéngjūn and Zhōu were enemies for generations,
and upon hearing Jūn's words, he was also displeased.
He sent the Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Lú Zàn, to supervise Jūn’s army.
Jūn became increasingly resentful in his heart
and was often uncooperative with Zàn.
Chéngjūn dispatched Chancellor Wèi Róng to mediate between them.
was defeated and died. Wèi Róng
was captured and brought to the capital. Emperor Tàizǔ
asked Róng concerning Chéngjūn's reasons for assisting Lǐ Yún's rebellion. Róng's
words were defiant. Tàizǔ
ordered that his head be struck with an iron mace. Blood
streamed down his face. Róng
cried out: "Your subject
has found a worthy place to die!" Tàizǔ
looked at those attending him and said: "This
is a loyal minister." He
released him, and ordered good
medicine to be applied to his wounds. He sent Róng
to deliver a letter to Chéngjūn, asking for Zhōu Guāngxùn
and others. He promised
to return Róng to Tàiyuán as well. Chéngjūn
did not reply, so Róng
subsequently remained in the capital. Chéngjūn
said to Zhào Huá: "Not
listening to your words nearly
led to defeat. However,
losing Wèi Róng and Lú Zàn is what
I regard as a deep regret." Chéngjūn
henceforth valued scholars even more, and included Guō Wúwéi,
the recluse of Bàofù Shān, in discussions of state policy. Wúwéi
was a native
of Dìzhōu. He had
a square forehead and a sharp, projecting mouth, loved
learning, was widely informed, and was good
at discussion and debate. He once
wore coarse clothes and was a Daoist priest, residing
on Wǔdāng Shān. When Zhōu Tàizǔ
campaigned against Lǐ Shǒuzhēn in Hézhōng, Wúwéi
went to the camp gate to request an audience. He was asked
about the affairs of the present age, and Tàizǔ
was greatly impressed. Someone
said to Tàizǔ: "You,
Sir, are a great minister of Hàn, holding
heavy military power and residing far away. To welcome
strategists and persuaders is not the
way to guard against the subtle beginnings [of trouble] and plan for the distant future." For this
reason, Tàizǔ did not retain him. Wúwéi
departed and lived
hidden on Bàofù Shān. Duàn Cháng,
Chéngjūn's Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, recognized him, and recommended
his talent. Chéngjūn
summoned him as Grand Master of Remonstrance, and subsequently
made him Chancellor. In the fifth
year, Wáng Yǐn,
Liú Shào, Zhào Luán, and others, who were leaders among the Palace Attendants and Guards, plotted rebellion. The plot
was discovered and they were executed. Their confessions
implicated Duàn Cháng, so [Chéngjūn] dismissed
Cháng from the Bureau of Military Affairs, made him Prefect of Fénzhōu, and had
him strangled to death. Since
the reign of Liú Mín, every action undertaken had to be reported to Qìdān. However, Chéngjūn's
ascension involved many omissions. Qìdān
sent an envoy to reproach Chéngjūn for changing his reign title, aiding Lǐ Yún, and executing Duàn Cháng without notification. Chéngjūn
was terrified and apologized for his faults. Whenever
his envoys reached Qìdān, they were immediately detained. Chéngjūn
served them with increasing caution, while Qìdān
treated Chéngjūn with greater contempt. Since
Lǐ Yún’s defeat, Chéngjūn lost Qìdān’s support, and had
no further desire to invade the south. The land
was narrow and resources were meager. Because
of the annual tribute paid to Qìdān, state
funds were diminished daily. Therefore,
he appointed the monk Jì Yóng of Wǔtái Shān as Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials. Jì Yóng
was the son
of the former Prince of Yān, Liú Shǒuguāng. When
Shǒuguāng died, he was spared
execution because he was a bastard son. He shaved
his head and became a Buddhist monk. Later,
he resided on Wǔtái Shān. He was
very clever, and good
at dealing in trade and profit. Since
Mín’s reign, the state had relied on him heavily. Jì Yóng
was able to lecture on the Huáyán Jīng. People
from all directions offered tribute and donations. He accumulated
much wealth to supplement state expenses. Wǔtái
was situated on the Qìdān frontier. Jì Yóng
often obtained Qìdān horses to present [to the court], which
were known
as "Tiāndū Mǎ" (Horses Supplied by the Capital/Court). The annual
rate was several hundred steeds. He also
established a silver refinery at Bǎigǔ, recruited
people to dig into the mountains and extract ore, refining
the silver for contribution. The Liú Shì
relied on this to supplement their expenses. They then
established Bǎoxīng Jūn at the site of the refinery. Jì Yóng
was later promoted through various offices to Grand Preceptor and Director of the Secretariat. He
died of old age and sickness, and was
posthumously enfeoffed as Prince Dìng. Emperor Tàizǔ
once used a border spy to relay a message to Chéngjūn: "Your
house and the Zhōu clan are hereditary enemies; it is
proper that you do not submit. Now,
there is no separation between me and you. Why do
you inflict hardship upon the people of this single region? If
you aspire to the Central Plains, you should
descend the Tài Háng Mountains to settle the matter." Chéngjūn
sent the spy back with a reply, saying: "The land
and armed forces of Hédōng are not
sufficient to match one-tenth of the Central Plains. However,
Chéngjūn’s family has never been rebellious. Our humble
preservation of this territory is likely
due to fear that the Hàn Shì will lose their ancestral sacrifices." Tàizǔ
sympathized with his words, and, laughing,
said to the spy: "Tell
Chéngjūn for me, 'I will
open a path for you to survive.' " Thus, throughout
his lifetime, he did not launch an attack. Chéngjūn
reigned for thirteen years and died of sickness. His adopted
son, Jì'ēn, succeeded him. Jì'ēn's
original surname was Xuē. His
father, Zhāo, was a common soldier. Liú Mín
married his daughter to him. They gave
birth to Jì'ēn. Hàn Gāozǔ,
because Zhāo was his son-in-law, removed
his military registration, and placed
him under his personal care. Zhāo
had no talent or ability. Gāozǔ
clothed and fed him but found no use for him. Since his
wife, Mín's daughter, constantly resided in the inner apartments, Zhāo
seldom got to see her. Zhāo
was constantly miserable. He became
drunk, drew his waist knife, and stabbed her. She was
wounded but did not die. Zhāo
immediately committed suicide. Mín’s daughter
later married a man of the Hé Shì, and gave
birth to a son, Jìyuán. Subsequently,
both the Hé man and Mín's daughter died. Mín,
because his son Chéngjūn had no sons, commanded
Chéngjūn to adopt the two boys as his sons. When
Chéngjūn ascended the throne, he made
Jì'ēn the Governor of Tàiyuán. Chéngjūn
once said to Guō Wúwéi: "Jì'ēn
is truly filial, but he
does not possess the talent to govern the realm. I fear
he will not be able to finish my family's affairs." Wúwéi
did not respond. Chéngjūn
lay sick in the Qínzhèng Gé. He summoned
Wúwéi, held
his hand, and entrusted him with his posthumous affairs. When Chéngjūn
died, Jì'ēn
announced the mourning to Qìdān before he was enthroned. Jì'ēn
wore sackcloth mourning robes while handling state affairs. He
resided and slept entirely in the Qínzhèng Gé, while Chéngjūn's
former attendants, officials of the various bureaus, and palace guards were all lodged in the Tàiyuán Prefectural Office. In the
ninth month, Jì'ēn
hosted a wine party for the ministers and imperial relatives. When the
drinking ended, he lay
down inside the Hall. Hóu Bàróng,
an Attendant Official, led more than ten men, drew their blades, and entered the Hall, closed
the door, and murdered him. Guō Wúwéi
sent men who used a ladder to climb onto the roof and enter. They killed
Bàróng and his entire faction. Originally,
when Chéngjūn
spoke to Guō Wúwéi, Jì'ēn
resented Wúwéi for not supporting him. When
he was enthroned, he wished
to drive him out, but had not yet done so. Therefore,
at the time of Bàróng’s revolt, everyone
thought it was Wúwéi's plan. When Bàróng
died, the evidence
was destroyed and no one knew the truth. Wúwéi
welcomed Jìyuán and established him on the throne. Jìyuán
was a cruel person. Liú Mín
had more than ten sons, none
of whom were noteworthy. During
Jìyuán’s time, there were
Gǎo, Kǎi, Qí, Xī, and Xiǎn. To Jìyuán,
they were paternal uncles. They were
all killed by Jìyuán. Only
Xiǎn escaped by feigning idiocy. Chéngjūn's
wife was the Guō Shì. Jìyuán
and his brother had been mothered by her since they were young. Jìyuán's
wife was the Duàn Shì. She had
once been scolded by the Guō Shì for a minor transgression. Not long
after, she died of a different illness. Jìyuán
suspected that she had been murdered by her. When
he ascended the throne, he sent
his favorite retainer Fàn Chāo to arrange the murder of the Guō Shì. The Guō Shì
was wearing sackcloth mourning robes, weeping for Chéngjūn before his coffin. Chāo
seized and strangled her to death. At
this point, there were no surviving descendants of the Liú clan left.
Jìyuán was enthroned,
and changed the reign title to Guǎngyùn.
The royal army campaigned in the north.
Jìyuán closed the city gates and resisted
. Emperor Tàizǔ Huángdì used an imperial edict to summon Jìyuán to surrender,
promising him the position of Military Commissioner (Jiédu Shǐ) of Pínglú Command,
and Guō Wúwéi that of Military Commissioner of Ānguó Command.
Wúwéi received the edict, his expression moved,
but the people of Bīng and those close to Jìyuán all desired to hold fast and refuse the command.
Wúwéi looked up to heaven and wailed loudly.
He drew the sabre he wore, intending to kill himself,
but was restrained by his attendants.
Jìyuán came down, held his hands,
and invited him to the seat of honor.
Wúwéi said:
"How can we use a solitary city to resist the royal army of a million men?"
He was probably intending to sway the people of Bīng,
but the people of Bīng’s resolve to defend only grew firmer.
The eunuch Wèi Déguì observed that Wúwéi harbored dissenting intentions,
and informed Jìyuán.
Jìyuán sent men to strangle him.
Initially,
Emperor Tàizǔ Huángdì ordered the waters of the Fén River to be diverted to flood the city.
The water entered through the city gates,
but accumulated grass floated out from within the city and blocked the flow.
At this time,
the royal army was encamped on the ground of Gāncǎo.
Coincidentally, it was the season of summer heat and rain,
and many soldiers became ill,
so they withdrew the army.
After the royal army had departed,
Jìyuán released the water beneath the city, directing it into Tái Dài Zé (Marsh of Tái Dài).
Once the water subsided, much of the city wall was destroyed and ruined.
Hán Zhīfán, an envoy from the Qìdān, was in Tàiyuán at the time,
and he sighed, saying:
"When the royal army diverted water to flood the city,
they knew the first point but not the second.
If they had first flooded it and then allowed it to dry out,
the people of Bīng would have been utterly ruined!"
In the fourth year of Tàipíng Xīngguó,
the royal army campaigned north again.
Jìyuán was exhausted and desperate,
but the people of Bīng still wanted to hold fast.
Mǎ Fēng, the Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs, was old and ill, staying at home.
He was carried in to see Jìyuán.
Weeping, he explained the principles of survival and downfall to him,
and Jìyuán then surrendered.
Emperor Tàizōng Huángdì presided over the surrender ceremony atop a high terrace north of the city.
He appointed Jìyuán as Superior General of the Right Guard,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Péngchéng.
His later affairs are fully recorded in the National History.
The years, generations, rise, and fall of Mín
are consistent across various records.
From the establishment of the designation in the first year of Guǎngshùn of the Zhōu dynasty,
until its destruction in the fourth year of Tàipíng Xīngguó of the Imperial Dynasty (Huángcháo),
it lasted twenty-eight years in total.
The remainder is detailed in the annotations to the Chronological Table (Niánpǔ).
Chronological Table of the Hereditary Houses of the Ten Kingdoms, Chapter Eleven
Alas!
Yáo and Shùn were glorious indeed!
The kings of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
though successful in achievement, lacked sufficient Virtue (Dé).
Therefore, they all made a fresh start to renew themselves,
and consequently, they rectified the calendar (zhèng shuò).
Coming to later generations,
they established reign titles (jiànyuán) by naming the years.
When usurpations arose simultaneously,
and the titles and designations became confused and numerous,
it became necessary to distinguish between them.
Among the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms (Shíguó),
seven states declared themselves emperors and changed reign titles.
Wúyuè, Jīng, and Chǔ
regularly used the reign titles of the Central Kingdom (Zhōngguó).
However, I heard from old elders
that Wúyuè had also proclaimed itself emperor and changed its reign title,
but the records of this event are unobtainable.
I rather suspect that Wúyuè later concealed this history.
Furthermore, gathering information from the records of Mǐn, Chǔ, and Nán Hàn and other states,
there are many accounts of interaction with Wúyuè.
None contain mention of Wúyuè proclaiming itself emperor.
I only found an imperial decree regarding the enfeoffment of the Star-Falling Stone (Luòxīng Shí) as Precious Stone Mountain (Bǎoshí Shān),
which mentions Bǎozhèng year six, xīnmǎo.
Thus, we know that they had once changed the reign title.
Xīnmǎo
was the second year of Chángxīng,
which was the last generation (period) of Liú.
However, we cannot see the reasons for its beginning and end,
and thus we cannot list it completely.
The Qián clan, throughout the Five Dynasties,
consistently showed outward respect to the Central Kingdom.
How could they be compared to Zhāng Guǐ?
The Ten Kingdoms were all outside the possession of the Central Kingdom.
Whether they proclaimed themselves emperors and changed reign titles or not
is insufficient to judge their success or failure,
thus we list them together.
This forms the Chronological Table of the Hereditary Houses of the Ten Kingdoms.
Someone asked: "The Ten Kingdoms were certainly not possessed by the Central Kingdom,
yet they were still bestowed with titles and ranks,
and there were those who used the Central Kingdom's reign titles to come and pay tribute.
Why are these not recorded in the Basic Annals (Běnjì)
I reply: The reason for not recording the enfeoffment and titles
is to show that they were not possessed by the Central Kingdom.
Their coming to pay tribute was like the Yídí (Barbarians).
To record them as Yídí
would be excessive.
The questioner said: "The Four Yí (Sì Yí) and the Ten Kingdoms
were all outside the possession of the Central Kingdom.
Yet, the enfeoffment and tribute of the Four Yí are recorded.
Why are those of the Ten Kingdoms not recorded?"
I reply: To treat the Yídí as Yídí,
when viewed from the perspective of the Central Kingdom, is acceptable.
But for the rulers of the Five Dynasties to treat the Ten Kingdoms
as Yídí is not acceptable.
Therefore, if the enfeoffment and tribute of the Ten Kingdoms
are not treated like that of the Yídí,
there is no basis to record them.
If they were recorded like the Yídí,
then the rulers of the Five Dynasties should not have treated them as such.
That is why we exclude them and do not record them,
showing that they had naturally severed themselves from the Central Kingdom.
The questioner asked: "If you exclude them and do not record them,
then why is the establishment of the Eastern Hàn (Dōng Hàn) recorded?"
I reply: Regarding Dōng Hàn,
I always use different terminology than for the Nine Kingdoms.
The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) established laws of governance based on an age of disorder.
The Basic Annals use these laws of governance to rectify the disorderly rulers.
When the age is chaotic, there are many doubtful and difficult matters.
When rectifying the doubtful and handling the difficult,
how dare one not be cautious?
The affairs concerning Zhōu and Hàn
can indeed be called difficult!
Someone claimed: Liú Mín once sent a letter to Zhōu,
asking for his son Yūn, and only after failing to get him back did he establish himself.
If so, Mín’s intention was not to treat the forgetting of Hàn as an enemy,
but to treat the loss of his son as an enemy.
I reply: Hàn had previously decreed Yūn established as heir.
Therefore, Yūn was the sovereign of the state of Hàn,
not merely Mín’s son.
Based on Mín’s great principle (Dàyì),
he should not have submitted to Zhōu.
Although his establishment [of his state] might not have been entirely correct,
it was proper by principle that he did not yield to Zhōu.
This is why he can be treated differently from the Nine Kingdoms.
Throughout Mín’s life,
he still used the Qianyòu reign title.
It was only when Chéngjūn was enthroned
that the reign title was changed.
Thus, how sorrowful must Mín’s ambition have been!
Regarding the years and generations of the Ten Kingdoms,
only the three states of Chǔ, Mǐn, and Dōng Hàn
have differing accounts among various scholars.
They each have points of accuracy and error,
making them the most difficult to verify and correct.
Now, I omit the various theories and correct those that are right,
hoping that wide readers will not be confused,
and will uniformly regard the Chronological Table (Niánpǔ) as the standard.
The Mǎ clan (of Chǔ),
according to the Húxiāng Gùshì, Jiǔguó Zhì, and Yùnlì Tú, all state
that Yīn died in the first year of Chángxīng.
In that year,
his son Xīshēng was enthroned,
and he died in the third year of Chángxīng.
However,
the biography of Yīn in the Old History of the Five Dynasties (Wǔdài Jiù Shǐ) states
that Yīn died in the second year of Chángxīng,
having lived seventy-eight years.
His son Xīshēng was enthroned,
and died within a year.
The Basic Annals of Míngzōng, in the first year of Chángxīng,
records that Xīshēng was appointed Military Commissioner (Jiédu Shǐ)
and restored to office.
In the eighth month of the third year,
it again records Xīshēng’s death.
Now, according to the Jiǔguó Zhì, Yīn was born in the year Rénshēn
, the sixth year of Dàzhōng, having lived seventy-nine years.
From Rénshēn (Dàzhōng) until Gēngyín (the first year of Chángxīng),
it is actually seventy-nine years.
This is the factual record.
As for Xīshēng,
the Húxiāng Gùshì, Jiǔguó Zhì, and Yùnlì Tú all record his death in the third year.
This aligns with the Basic Annals of Míngzōng,
leaving no doubt.
Only the Old History recording Yīn’s death in the second
year,
and his age as seventy-eight,
and Xīshēng dying within a year of his enthronement, are errors.
During the revolt of Xī’è and Xīchóng,
Nán Táng moved all members of the Mǎ clan back to Jīnlíng.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties says
that at that time, it was the first year of Guǎngshùn.
(is correct).
However, the *Yùnlì Tú* states that the Mǎ Shì were destroyed in the second year of Qián Yòu,
which is mistaken.
Initially, when Yīn
entered Húnán,
he dug the ground and obtained a stone,
which bore a prophecy saying:
"The Dragon raises its head,
the Pig drops its tail."
Generally, Yīn established himself in Húnán
in the third year of Qiánníng, which was the *bǐngchén* year,
and was destroyed
in the first year of Guǎngshùn, the *xīnhài* year.
The *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* takes the third year of Qián Yòu as the *xīnhài* year,
and the *Hú Xiāng Gùshì* takes the first year of Xiǎndé as the *xīnhài* year;
both are mistaken.
Only the *Wǔ Dài Jiù Shǐ* (Old History of the Five Dynasties) gets the facts correct.
The generational sequence of the Wáng Shì
is: Cháo, Shěnzhī, Yánhàn, Lín, Chǎng, Xī, and Yánzhèng,
totaling seven rulers.
And Cháo first entered Fúzhōu
in the first year of Jǐngfú of Táng, which was the *rénzǐ* year,
and they were destroyed in the third year of Kāiyùn, the *bǐngwǔ* year.
This was exactly fifty-five years.
It ought to be stated as seven rulers and fifty-five years,
which is the correct fact.
But the *Yùnlì Tú* states fifty-six years,
and the *Jiǔ Guó*
*Zhì*, the *Wǔ Dài Jiù Shǐ*, the *Jì Nián Tōng Pǔ*, the *Mǐn Zhōng Shílù*, and the *Mǐn Wáng Lièzhuàn* all state seven rulers and sixty years;
these are all mistaken.
Regarding Shěnzhī,
the main biography in the *Wǔ Dài Jiù Shǐ* states that
he died in the twelfth
month of the first year of Tóngguāng.
The *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* also says he died in the first year of Tóngguāng.
The *Yùnlì Tú* says he died in the third year of Tóngguāng.
Now, upon checking the Basic Annals of Zhuāng Zōng in the *Wǔ Dài Jiù Shǐ*,
on the *bǐngwǔ* day of the fifth month of the second year of Tóngguāng,
Shěnzhī was promoted to acting
Grand Preceptor and serving as Director of the Central Secretariat.
How could he have died in the first year?
Furthermore, on the *gēngzǐ* day of the second month of the fourth year,
Wáng Yánhàn, the Deputy Envoy of Fújiàn, submitted a memorial stating he was provisionally managing the affairs of the military headquarters.
On the *xīnhài* day of the third month,
Yánhàn was consequently appointed Wēiwǔ
Circuit Military Governor (*Jiédù Shǐ*).
Based on this deduction,
Shěnzhī’s death must have occurred in the twelfth month of the third year of Tóngguāng.
Since Mǐn was far from the capital,
Yánhàn’s memorial only reached the capital in the second month of the following year.
This is naturally the case.
Furthermore, according to
the *Mǐn Wáng Lièzhuàn* and the *Jiǔ Guó Zhì*, both state that
Shěnzhī was on the throne for twenty-nine years.
Shěnzhī succeeded to the throne in the fourth year of Qiánníng of Táng,
which was the *dīngsì* year,
until the third year of Tóngguāng, the *yǐyǒu* year,
which is exactly twenty-nine years.
Thus the *Yùnlì Tú* is correct,
and the *Jiù Shǐ* and the *Jiǔ Guó Zhì*, which say he died in the first year,
are mistaken.
Lín's original name was Yánjūn.
The main biography in the *Wǔ Dài Jiù Shǐ* states
he was on the throne for twelve years.
The *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* states
he was on the
throne for eleven years.
The *Mǐn Wáng Lièzhuàn* and the *Jì Nián Tōng Pǔ* both state he was on the throne for ten years.
Lín killed Yánhàn and established himself in the first year of Tiānchéng,
which was the *bǐngxū* year,
and died in the second year of Qīngtài, the *yǐwèi* year,
which was truly ten years.
He died,
which aligns with the *Mǐn Wáng Lièzhuàn*,
but the *Jiù Shǐ* and the *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* are both mistaken.
In the second year of Qīngtài, Lín changed his reign title to Yǒnghé,
and was killed that very year.
However, the *Jiù Shǐ*, the *Jiǔ Guó Zhì*, and the *Yùnlì Tú* all lack the reign title of Yǒng
Hé.
Furthermore, the *Yùnlì Tú* records Lín being killed in the first year of Tiānfú, the *bǐngshēn* year;
this is also mistaken.
Regarding Liú Mín,
the *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* states that
Mín died in the eleventh month of the seventh year of Qián Yòu,
having enjoyed the age of sixty.
His son Chéng
Jūn succeeded,
at the age of twenty-nine.
The seventh year of Qián Yòu
was the first year of Xiǎndé.
However, the *Wǔ Dài Jiù Shǐ*, the *Zhōu Shì Zōng Shílù*, the *Yùnlì Tú*, and the *Jì Nián Tōng Pǔ* all state that Mín
died in the winter of the second year of Xiǎndé.
Furthermore, Wáng Bǎohéng, Mín's self-appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Central Secretariat, states in the *Jìnyáng Jiànwén Yàolù* (Essential Records of Observations in Jìnyáng) that
Mín was born in the *yǐmǎo* year,
died at the age of sixty-one,
and his son Chéngjūn succeeded him.
Chéngjūn was born in the *bǐngxū* year,
and was twenty-nine years old when he succeeded.
Bǎohéng
was Mín's minister;
what he personally saw and heard
should be the most reliable facts,
but perhaps there were errors in transcription.
Examining Bǎohéng’s record that Mín was born in the *yǐmǎo* year:
if he enjoyed the age of sixty-one,
he should have died in the *yǐmǎo* year,
which
is the second year of Xiǎndé.
Furthermore, he recorded that Chéngjūn was born in the *bǐngxū* year,
and was twenty-nine years old when he succeeded,
which means that year must have been the first year of Xiǎndé, the *jiǎyín* year.
How could Mín die in the second year,
while Chéngjūn succeeded in the first year?
Logically,
this is impossible.
Comparing this with the *Jiǔ Guó Zhì*:
Mín enjoyed the age of sixty,
died in the first year of Xiǎndé,
and Chéngjūn succeeded in that same year,
at the age of twenty-nine.
This is the correct fact,
only the *Jiànwén Yàolù* redundantly added
the character "one"
(after sixty).
Those who say he died in the second year
are all mistaken.
The *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* further states that
Chéngjūn succeeded,
observed mourning for three years,
and the mourning ended in the ninth year of Qián Yòu.
He changed the tenth year to the first year of Tiānhuì,
which should correspond to the fourth
year of Xiǎndé.
Therefore, the *Jì Nián Tōng Pǔ*, which takes the third year of Xiǎndé as the first year of Tiānhuì,
is mistaken.
Jìn and Liáng were enemy states.
Jìn titled itself Tiānyòu for twenty years,
thus it is listed first in the Chronological Tables (*Nián Pǔ*).
Subsequently, Jìn destroyed Liáng and became Táng,
therefore it is not listed in the Hereditary Houses (*Shì Jiā*).
Appendix on the Four Barbarian Tribes, Part One
Alas!
The Yí Dí (Barbarian tribes), in their habitation and sustenance,
migrate following water, grass, cold, and heat.
They have chiefs and tribal names but lack hereditary lineage records or writing systems for distinction.
They rely on strung bows and poisoned arrows,
the strong annexing the weak.
The size of their territories,
their rise and fall are not constant.
How can one possibly investigate and narrate all of these matters!
Only those tribes whose submission, rebellion, departure, or arrival
affect the interests or harms of the Central State (*Zhōngguó*)—
these things cannot be left unknown.
Since antiquity, regarding the Yí Dí and the Central State (*Zhōngguó*):
if the state possesses the Way, the tribes do not necessarily submit;
if the state lacks the Way, the tribes do not necessarily refrain from coming.
It is generally due to their own rise and decline.
Although they have often been placed outside of proper governance,
the balance of gentle control, firm restraint, kindness, and might
must not be lost.
Gaining them does not necessarily bring advantage,
but losing them is sufficient to cause trouble.
How can we not be cautious!
I compile the *Sì Yí Fù Lù*.
There are
many names and types of Yí Dí.
The major ones
communicate their names to the Central State (*Zhōngguó*);
the smaller and more distant ones are mentioned in appendices;
and those that are too insignificant to record
are countless.
Their territories encircle the area outside of the Nine Provinces (*Jiǔ Zhōu*),
and the Northwest is constantly strong,
causing trouble for the Central State (*Zhōngguó*).
The Xiǎnyǔn of the Three Dynasties
are seen in the *Shī* (Odes) and the *Shū* (Documents).
Since the Qín and Hàn Dynasties,
the Xiōngnú have been prominent.
During the Suí and Táng Dynasties,
the Tūjué were powerful.
After that, the Tǔbō and the Huíhú were strong.
During the period of the Five Dynasties (*Wǔ Dài*),
those known by name to the Central State (*Zhōngguó*) were seventeen or eighteen [groups],
but the Qìdān were the most dominant.
have been named in Zhōngguó records.
Some say they are of the same genus as the Kùmò Xī but a different species.
Their habitation is called Xiāoluó Gèmòlǐ.
Mòlǐ
means river.
This refers to the south of the Yellow River (Huáng Shuǐ),
north of the Yellow Dragon (Huáng Lóng),
occupying the former territory of the Xiānbēi;
thus, they are also considered a remnant branch of the Xiānbēi.
During the age of the Táng,
their land bordered the Shìwéi to the north,
adjoined Gāolì to the east,
was delimited by the Xī Guó to the west,
and extended south to Yíngzhōu.
The largest of their clans was called the Dàhè Shì.
Later, they split into eight tribes (bù):
the first was called the Kū Jiēlì Bù,
the second the Yǐshìhuó Bù,
the third the Shíhuó Bù,
the fourth the Nàwěi Bù,
the fifth the Pínmò Bù,
the sixth the Nèihuìjī Bù,
the seventh the Jíjiě Bù,
and the eighth the Xīwà Bù.
The chief of a tribe was titled Dàrén (Great Man),
and customarily they elected one Dàrén to establish the banner and drum (qi-gǔ) to govern the eight tribes.
When a long time passed,
or if their state suffered calamity or sickness and livestock declined,
the eight tribes would gather for consultation,
and install the next person in line, replacing the current leader with the banner and drum.
The one being replaced believed that the agreement was originally thus,
and dared not contest it.
Yáoliǎn, the Dàrén of a certain tribe, was next in line and installed.
At that time, Liú Rén-gōng held Yōuzhōu,
and repeatedly sent troops to Zhāixīng Lǐng to attack them.
Every year when the autumn frost fell,
he would burn their wild grass.
Many Qìdān horses starved to death,
so they immediately used good horses to bribe Rén-gōng, asking to buy grazing land,
and asked to observe the covenant very carefully.
The people of the eight tribes believed that Yáoliǎn was incapable of governing,
so they selected from among their multitudes,
and replaced him with Ābǎojī.
Ābǎojī—
it is also unknown which tribe he belonged to—
was a man of great intelligence and courage, skilled in horsemanship and archery.
At this time,
Liú Shǒu-guāng was tyrannical,
and many people from Yōu and Zhuō fled and defected to the Qìdān.
Ābǎojī seized the opportunity to enter the frontier,
attacking and capturing cities and towns,
taking their inhabitants captive,
and establishing cities based on the Táng prefectural and county models to settle them.
The Hàn people taught Ābǎojī, saying:
“Kings in Zhōngguó are not replaced.”
Consequently, Ābǎojī increasingly used his authority to control the various tribes and refused to step down.
After he had been established for nine years,
the various tribes, because he had long refused replacement,
jointly criticized and reprimanded him.
Ābǎojī had no choice;
he handed over his banner and drum,
and said to the various tribes:
“I have been established for nine years,
and I have acquired many Hàn people.
I wish to form my own tribe to govern the Hàn cities;
is this permissible?”
The various tribes permitted it.
The Hàn city was situated on the Luán Hé, southeast of Tàn Shān.
It possessed the profit of salt and iron,
and was the Huáyán Xiàn of the Hòu Wèi dynasty.
The land was suitable for planting five grains.
Ābǎojī led the Hàn people in cultivation,
building city walls, inner cities, settlements, houses, markets, and shops modeled after the system of Yōuzhōu.
The Hàn people felt secure there
and no longer thought of returning home.
Ābǎojī knew his followers were usable.
Employing the strategy of his wife, Shùlǜ,
he sent someone to inform the Dàrén of the various tribes, saying:
“I have a salt pond,
from which the various tribes consume salt.
However, while the various tribes know the benefit of eating salt,
they do not know that the salt has a master.
Is this acceptable?
You should come and offer me provisions.”
The various tribes believed this was reasonable,
and gathered at the salt pond with oxen and wine.
Ābǎojī positioned ambush troops nearby.
When the drinking was well underway, the ambush was sprung,
killing all the Dàrén of the various tribes.
He thus established himself
and was no longer replaced.
When the Liáng were about to usurp the Táng,
the Jìn Wáng, Lǐ Kè-yòng, sent an envoy to the Qìdān.
Ābǎojī brought 300,000 troops to meet Kè-yòng at the eastern city of Yúnzhōu.
They set out wine,
and when the drinking was enjoyable,
they clasped hands and swore to be brothers.
Kè-yòng gave him extremely generous gifts of gold and silk,
promising to jointly raise troops to attack the Liáng.
Ābǎojī presented Jìn with a thousand horses.
After returning, however, he broke the covenant,
and dispatched the envoy Páohù Méilǎo to send greetings to the Liáng.
The Liáng sent the Tàifǔ Qīng Gāo Qǐng and the military commander Láng Gōng-yuǎn, among others, to return the visit.
After more than a year,
Qǐng returned,
and Ābǎojī sent the envoy Xièlǐ to accompany Qǐng,
offering good horses, sable furs, and ‘Morning Glow’ brocade to send greetings to the Liáng,
presenting a memorial to declare himself a vassal (chēng chén),
seeking official investiture (fēng cè).
The Liáng subsequently sent Gōng-yuǎn again, along with the Sīnóng Qīng Húntè, bearing an imperial edict to reward him,
and separately bestowed an annotated document upon him,
covenanting that they would jointly raise troops to destroy Jìn,
and only then would Ābǎojī be invested and named a state of “nephew and uncle.”
They also arranged for 300 cavalry troops composed of his sons and younger brothers to enter the capital to serve as guards.
Kè-yòng heard of this
and felt deep resentment.
That year, Kè-yòng fell ill,
and before his death,
he entrusted one arrow to Zhuāng Zōng,
mandating that he must destroy the Qìdān.
Húntè and the others arrived in Qìdān,
but Ābǎojī was unable to fulfill the agreement,
nor did the Liáng ever officially grant the investiture.
Yet, throughout the Liáng dynasty,
Qìdān envoys visited four times.
In the thirteenth year of the Tiānyòu era of Zhuāng Zōng (916 CE),
Ābǎojī attacked Jìn’s Wèizhōu,
capturing Lǐ Sì-běn, the Zhènwǔ Jiédùshǐ.
At this time,
Zhuāng Zōng had already gained Wèibó,
and was turning south to contest the empire with the Liáng.
He dispatched Lǐ Cún-jǔ to mobilize the Shānběi troops.
When Cún-jǔ reached Qígōu Guān,
the troops rebelled,
supporting the subordinate general Lú Wén-jìn, who attacked and killed Cún-jǔ,
and then fled into the Qìdān territory.
The Qìdān attacked and destroyed Xīnzhōu,
and installed Wén-jìn's divisional commander, Liú Yīn, to defend it.
Zhuāng Zōng sent Zhōu Dé-wēi to attack Yīn,
but Wén-jìn led hundreds of thousands of Qìdān troops who arrived en masse.
Dé-wēi was fearful
and led his army away,
but was overtaken by the pursuing Qìdān
and utterly defeated.
Dé-wēi fled to Yōuzhōu,
and the Qìdān besieged it.
Between Yōu and Jì,
enemy cavalry filled the mountains and valleys.
The Hàn people they captured
were tied together by the head with long ropes attached to trees.
Many of the Hàn people managed to untie themselves and escape at night.
Wén-jìn also taught the Qìdān how to build fire chariots, tunnels, and earthen mounds to assault the city.
From within the city, they hurled molten copper and iron liquid,
and those struck by it immediately rotted and fell.
Dé-wēi resisted the siege for over a hundred days.
Zhuāng Zōng sent Lǐ Sì-yuán, Yán Bǎo, and Lǐ Cún-shěn, among others, to relieve the city.
The Qìdān were defeated several times by Sì-yuán and the others,
and subsequently withdrew.
The Qìdān were especially stubborn and arrogant compared to other barbarians (tuó Yídí).
When a parent died,
they considered not crying a mark of bravery.
They carried the corpse into the deep mountains
and placed it upon a large tree.
After three years, they went to retrieve the bones and burn them,
pouring a libation and uttering an incantation, saying:
“In summer, eat toward the sun;
in winter, eat toward the shade.
Grant that my hunting
yields many pigs and deer.”
Their customs were quite similar to those of the Xī and the Mòhé.
When it came to Ābǎojī,
he gradually annexed and subdued the various small neighboring states,
and utilized many Hàn people.
The Hàn people taught them to modify the standard script (Lìshū) by reducing and adding parts,
creating several thousand characters,
which replaced the custom of carving notches in wood for agreements.
He also regulated marriages
and established official titles.
Subsequently, he presumptuously claimed the title of Huángdì (Emperor),
and styled himself Tiānhuáng Wáng (Heavenly Imperial King).
He took the place name of his mobile tent (héng zhàng) residence as his surname,
calling it Shìlǐ.
Shìlǐ,
translators referred to as Yēlǜ.
He named his reign year Tiānzàn.
He designated his residence as Shàngjīng (Supreme Capital),
building towers within it,
which he called the Xī Lóu (Western Tower).
A thousand *lǐ* to the east, he built the Dōng Lóu (Eastern Tower);
three hundred *lǐ* to the north, he built the Běi Lóu (Northern Tower);
and to the south, at Mùyè Shān, he built the Nán Lóu (Southern Tower).
He traveled between these four towers for hunting.
The Qìdān liked ghosts and honored the sun.
On the first morning of every month,
they faced east and bowed to the sun.
When holding great assemblies or conducting state affairs,
they always considered facing east to be the position of honor.
The gates and houses of the four towers all faced east.
Zhuāng Zōng (莊宗) attacked Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮),
and besieged Zhèn Zhōu (鎮州).
Wáng Chǔzhí (王處直) of Dìng Zhōu (定州) feared that Zhèn (鎮) was about to fall,
and that the Jìn (晉) forces would inevitably attack him concurrently.
He dispatched his son, Yù (郁), to persuade the Qìdān (契丹),
making them enter the frontier to restrain the Jìn forces.
Yù said to Ābǎojī (阿保機):
"My father, Chǔzhí, sends this humble message: The late King of Zhào (趙), Wáng Róng (王鎔),
ruled Zhào for six generations.
Zhèn Zhōu possesses walls of metal and moats of boiling water,
gold and silk piled up like mountains,
Yan concubines and Zhao maidens,
and fine silks filling the court.
Zhāng Wénlǐ seized these, but is now being attacked by Jìn.
He is too fearful of death to attend to anything else.
Therefore, all these things are being reserved to await the Emperor."
Ābǎojī was greatly pleased.
His wife, Shùlǜ (述律), was unwilling,
saying:
"We possess riches in sheep and horses,
and the West Tower (Xī Lóu) is sufficient for enjoyment.
Now, abandoning this, we rush far away to meet another's emergency.
I hear that the Jìn forces are the strongest in the world,
and in battle there are victories and defeats.
What remedy will there be for regret?"
Ābǎojī leapt up and said happily:
"Zhāng Wénlǐ has a million in gold and jade.
It is being reserved to await the Empress;
we can go together and seize it."
Thereupon, he emptied the nation (of troops) and entered the border to raid.
When Yù summoned the Qìdān,
all the people of Dìng believed that they should not be summoned, fearing future trouble,
but Chǔzhí did not listen.
After Yù had departed,
Chǔzhí was deposed by his son, Dū (都).
Ābǎojī attacked Yōu Zhōu (幽州) but did not conquer it.
He then attacked Zhuō Zhōu (涿州),
and captured it.
Hearing that Chǔzhí had been deposed and Dū installed,
he immediately attacked Zhōngshān (中山),
crossing the Shā Hé (沙河).
Dū reported the emergency to Zhuāng Zōng.
Zhuāng Zōng personally led five thousand iron cavalry,
and encountered the Qìdān vanguard at Xīn Chéng (新城).
The Jìn forces galloped out from Sāng Lín (桑林).
The men and horses wore excellent armor,
shining brightly and illuminating the sun.
The barbarian cavalry were astonished,
and slowly retreated.
The Jìn army capitalized on this,
and the barbarians scattered and fled.
Because the ice on the Shā Hé was thin,
the barbarians all fell through and perished.
Ābǎojī retreated and secured Wàng Dū (望都).
Coincidentally, there was a heavy snow.
The Qìdān people and horses suffered from hunger and cold,
and many died.
Ābǎojī looked at Lú Wénjìn (盧文進) and pointed to the sky, saying:
"Heaven has not allowed me to reach this point."
Then he led his troops away.
Zhuāng Zōng pursued closely behind them.
He saw their encampment,
where bundles of straw were spread around the ground,
and the corners and layout were orderly.
Although they had left, there was no mess.
He sighed and said:
"The barbarian laws and discipline are strict,
truly like this!"
Although the Qìdān returned without gaining anything,
from this time on, they harbored intentions of spying on Zhōng Guó (中國, China).
Concerned that the Nǚzhēn (女真) and Bóhǎi (渤海) peoples were behind them,
and wanting to attack Bóhǎi,
they feared that Zhōng Guó would take advantage of their vulnerability.
So they sent envoys to court the Táng (唐) and establish friendly relations.
Between the Tóngguāng (同光) years,
envoys arrived twice.
When Zhuāng Zōng died,
Míng Zōng (明宗) dispatched the Palace Attendant, Yáo Kūn (姚坤), to report the mourning to the Qìdān.
Kūn arrived at Xī Lóu, but Ābǎojī was currently attacking Bóhǎi to the east.
Kūn pursued him and met him at Shèn Zhōu (慎州).
Ābǎojī wore a brocade robe and a large sash trailing behind him,
sitting opposite his wife inside a felt tent (qióng lú).
He invited Kūn to enter and pay his respects.
Ābǎojī asked:
"I heard that you have two Sons of Heaven (Emperors) in Hé Nán (河南) and Hé Běi (河北).
Is this true?"
Kūn replied:
"The Son of Heaven, due to the military uprising in Wèi Zhōu (魏州),
ordered the Grand Commandant (Zǒng Guǎn Lìng Gōng) to lead troops to suppress it.
However, the crisis arose in Luò Yáng (洛陽),
and the news of the tragedy has now arrived.
The Grand Commandant led his troops back to Hé Běi,
and hurried to the capital to face the emergency.
He was supported by the masses
and already fulfills the people's expectations."
Ābǎojī looked up at the sky and wept loudly, saying:
"The King of Jìn (Zhuāng Zōng) and I agreed to be brothers.
The Son of Heaven in Hé Nán,
he was my son.
Yesterday, when I heard Zhōng Guó was in chaos,
I wished to take fifty thousand armored men and horses to assist my son,
but Bóhǎi has not yet been eliminated,
and so my intention could not be realized."
He also said:
"Now that my son has perished,
logically, they should have consulted me.
How dare the new Son of Heaven establish himself independently?"
Kūn replied:
"The new Son of Heaven has commanded troops for twenty years.
His rank reached that of Grand Commandant.
He commands three hundred thousand elite soldiers.
Heaven's timing and human affairs—
how can they be resisted?"
His son, Tūyù (突欲), who was at his side, said:
"Envoy, speak no further!
To cut across the field and seize an ox—
how can that not be considered a transgression!"
Kūn replied:
"Responding to Heaven and obeying the people
is not comparable to the actions of a common man.
For instance, when the Emperor King (Tiānhuáng Wáng, referring to Ābǎojī) obtained his state but did not replace it,
did he forcibly seize it?"
Ābǎojī immediately comforted Kūn and said:
"The principle is exactly as you state!"
He further said:
"I heard that this son had two thousand palace maids,
one thousand musicians,
indulged in releasing falcons and chasing dogs,
was fond of drinking and lust,
employed the unworthy,
and did not cherish the populace.
This is why he failed.
Since I heard of his misfortune,
I immediately had my whole family stop drinking alcohol,
released the falcons and dogs,
and disbanded the musicians.
I also have a thousand musicians from various tribes,
but they are only used for official feasts.
If my actions resembled those of my son,
how could I last long either?"
He also said to Kūn:
"I can speak the Hàn (漢) language,
but I never speak it to my tribal people,
fearing that they would imitate the Hàn and become timid and weak."
Thereupon he instructed Kūn, saying:
"You should return first.
I will meet the new Son of Heaven with thirty thousand armored men and horses between Yōu and Zhèn (Yōu Zhōu and Zhèn Zhōu),
and together we shall form an alliance.
If you give me Yōu Zhōu,
I will never invade your territory again."
Ābǎojī attacked Bóhǎi,
and captured the city of Fúyú (扶餘) from them.
He established it as the Kingdom of Dōng Dān (東丹 Guó),
and made his eldest son, Rén Huáng Wáng (人皇王) Tūyù, the King of Dōng Dān.
Soon after, Ābǎojī died of illness.
Shùlǜ guarded his coffin and returned to Xī Lóu,
and installed his second son, Commander-in-Chief Prince Yàoqūzhī (耀屈之).
Kūn followed them to Xī Lóu and then returned.
When Ābǎojī was in power,
there was a man named Hán Yánhuī,
who was from Yōuzhōu.
He served as a staff officer for Liú Shǒuguāng.
Shǒuguāng sent Yánhuī on a mission to Qìdān.
When Yánhuī met Ābǎojī, he did not bow.
Ābǎojī was furious,
detained him and refused to send him back,
making him herd sheep and horses.
After a long time,
he recognized his talent,
summoned him to speak,
found him exceptional,
and subsequently employed him as his chief strategist.
Ābǎojī’s attacks on the Dǎngxiàng and Shìwéi,
and the submission of various small states,
were all due to Yánhuī’s planning.
Yánhuī later fled back [to China]
and served Zhuāngzōng.
Wáng Jiān, a guest general of Zhuāngzōng, slandered him.
Yánhuī became afraid,
and requested permission to return to Yōuzhōu to visit his mother.
Traveling past Chángshān,
he hid at Wáng Démíng’s house.
After staying for several months,
Démíng asked him where he intended to go.
Yánhuī replied:
"I want to flee back to Qìdān again."
Démíng believed this was impossible,
but Yánhuī said:
"When Ābǎojī lost me,
it was like losing both eyes and breaking his hands and feet.
If he gets me back now,
he will surely be delighted."
Thereupon, he fled back to Qìdān.
When Ābǎojī saw him,
he was indeed greatly pleased,
believing he had descended from heaven.
When Ābǎojī assumed the title [of emperor],
he made Yánhuī his chancellor,
giving him the title
"Zhèngshì Lìng."
The Qìdān called him
"Chóngwén Lìnggōng."
He later died among the captives (the Qìdān).
Yàoqū later changed his name to Déguāng.
Ābǎojī was buried at Mùyè Shān,
and given the posthumous title Dàshèng Huángdì.
Later, his personal name was changed to Yì.
Déguāng reigned for three years,
changed the reign title to Tiānxiǎn,
and sent envoys with famous horses to seek alliance with Táng (Later Táng),
and also requested memorial stone to engrave an inscription for Ābǎojī.
Míngzōng treated them generously,
and sent Ān Niàndé, the Commander of the Fēishèng contingent, to return the visit.
Wáng Dū of Dìngzhōu rebelled.
Táng sent Wáng Yànqiú to suppress him.
Dū used a wax-sealed letter to flee to Qìdān seeking aid.
Déguāng sent Tūněi, Cèlà, and others with five thousand cavalry to rescue Dū.
Dū and Tūněi attacked Yànqiú at Qǔyáng,
but were defeated by Yànqiú.
Déguāng again sent the Tìyǐn Hè Miǎo to reinforce Tūněi with seven thousand cavalry.
Yànqiú again defeated them at Táng Hé.
Hè Miǎo fled back with a few riders,
arriving at Yōuzhōu,
where he was captured by Zhào Déjūn.
Meanwhile, Yànqiú attacked and broke Dìngzhōu,
capturing Tūněi and Cèlà,
and sending them all to the capital.
Míngzōng executed Tūněi and more than six hundred others,
but pardoned Hè Miǎo,
and selected fifty or so of the strongest men to serve in the
"Qìdān Zhí" (Qìdān Guard).
Initially,
when Ābǎojī died,
his eldest son, Tūyù, Prince of Dōngdān, ought to have been established [as successor].
However, his mother Shùlǜ sent her younger son, Ānduān Shàojūn, to Fúyú to replace him,
intending to install him as heir.
Nevertheless, Shùlǜ especially loved Déguāng.
Déguāng possessed wisdom and courage,
and had already subjugated the various tribes.
Since Ānduān had already left,
the various tribes sought to satisfy Shùlǜ’s wishes
and jointly established Déguāng.
Tūyù was therefore not established.
In the first year of Chángxīng (930 CE),
he traveled by sea from Fúyú and fled to Táng.
Míngzōng consequently bestowed upon him the surname Dōngdān,
and changed his personal name to Mùhuá.
Because he came from Liáodōng,
he designated Ruìzhōu as Huáihuà Jūn (Huáihuà Military Prefecture).
He appointed Mùhuá as Military Commissioner (Jiédù Shǐ) of Huáihuà Jūn, and Commissioner of Observation and Management for Ruìzhōu, Shènzhōu, and other prefectures.
His five subordinates were all granted Chinese names and surnames:
Hǎnzhǐ was named Hǎn Yǒutōng;
Mùgě was named Mù Shùnyì;
Sāluó was named Luó Bīndé;
Yìmì was named Yì Shīrén;
and Gàilǐ was named Gài Láibīn.
They were made Generals (Jiāngjūn) and Palace Assistants (Lángjiàng) of Guīhuà and Guīdé.
Furthermore, Hè Miǎo, whom they had previously captured, was given the name Dí Huáihuì;
Zhǎliè was named Liè Zhīēn;
Cèlà was named Yuán Zhīgǎn;
Fúláng was named Fú Huáizào;
and Jiéshījì was named Yǐ Huáiyòu.
The rest who were
"Qìdān Zhí"
were
all granted Chinese names and surnames.
In the second year (931 CE),
Tūyù was again granted the surname Lǐ,
and his name was changed to Zànhuá.
In the third year (932 CE),
Zànhuá was made Military Commissioner of Yìchéng Jūn.
Since the time of Ābǎojī, Qìdān had invaded and destroyed various nations,
claiming dominance in the north.
However, when they went to rescue Wáng Dū,
they were defeated by Wáng Yànqiú,
losing ten thousand cavalry,
and also losing Hè Miǎo and others,
all of whom were famous generals.
Furthermore, Shùlǜ especially missed Tūyù.
Because of this, [Qìdān] frequently sent envoys with humble words and rich tributes to seek alliance with Zhōngguó (China),
subsequently requesting the return of Hè Miǎo, Cèlà, and others.
Táng summarily executed their envoys and did not reply.
At this time,
the prestige of Zhōngguó was nearly revived.
Seven hundred *lǐ* north of Yōuzhōu was Yú Guān.
To its east, it bordered the sea,
and to the north lay Tùěr Shān and Fùzhōu Shān.
All the mountains were precipitous and rugged.
The path ran along the sea to the northeast,
barely wide enough for carts to pass.
The land beside it was suitable for farming and planting.
During the Táng era, garrisons such as Dōngxī Xiáshí, Lùchóu, Mǐzhuān, Chángyáng
, Huánghuā, Zǐméng, and Báiláng were established,
in order to block Qìdān here.
The garrison soldiers usually farmed for their own food.
Only their padded clothes were supplied annually by Yōuzhōu.
After a long time, they all acquired fields and houses,
raised children and grandchildren,
and considered staunch defense to be in their own interest.
Since the end of the Táng dynasty, when Yōu and Jì prefectures became fragmented territories,
the garrison soldiers were disbanded.
Qìdān was therefore able to invade and occupy Píngzhōu and Yíngzhōu,
and the people of Yōu and Jì suffered annual bandit raids.
For the hundred *lǐ* stretch from Zhuōzhōu to Yōuzhōu,
human tracks ceased.
Supplies were usually transported under military escort,
and Qìdān often ambushed them at Yángōu (Salt Trench) to attack and seize them.
At the end of Zhuāngzōng's reign,
Zhào Déjūn governed Yōuzhōu.
He established Liángxiāng Xiàn (Liángxiāng County) at Yángōu,
and also built a city fifty *lǐ* east of Yōuzhōu.
Both were garrisoned with troops.
After defeating Hè Miǎo and the others,
he further established Sānhé Xiàn (Sānhé County) to the east of that city.
Following this, the people of Yōu and Jì
were finally able to farm and herd,
and the transport of supplies was made possible.
Déguāng then moved his mobile imperial camp (Héng Zhàng) west to Kuílào Pō,
and launched raids between Yúnzhōu and Shuòzhōu.
Míngzōng worried about this,
and appointed Shí Jìngtáng to govern Hédōng,
placing him in command of the armies of Dàtóng, Zhāngguó, Zhènwǔ, and Wēisài to defend against them.
Between the Yìngshùn and Qīngtài eras,
the mobilization of troops and delivery of supplies
exhausted those both near and far.
Dégūang served his mother with extreme attentiveness;
he constantly stood in attendance by her side,
and national affairs were always announced to her before being carried out.
When Shí Jìngtáng rebelled,
Táng sent Zhāng Jìngdá and others to suppress him.
Shí Jìngtáng dispatched an envoy to Dégūang to request aid.
Dégūang reported to his mother, saying:
“I once dreamed that Lord Shí summoned me,
and now an envoy has truly arrived—
is this not Heaven’s will!”
His mother summoned a Hu (shaman) to ask about the fortune,
and the shaman pronounced it auspicious.
Thereupon, they agreed.
In the ninth month of that year,
the Qìdān emerged from Yànmén,
their chariots and cavalry stretching continuously for dozens of *lǐ*.
As they were about to reach Tàiyuán,
they sent a person to tell Jìngtáng:
“Would it be acceptable for me to break the enemy for you today?”
Jìngtáng replied, saying:
“The Emperor (referring to himself, the newly established Jìn emperor) is attending to this difficulty;
the essential thing is success,
not speed.
Your great army has come a long distance,
and the Táng army is very strong.
Please wait for a little while.”
Before the envoy arrived back,
battle had already been joined.
Jìngdá was greatly defeated.
Jìngtáng emerged from the North Gate during the night to meet Dégūang,
and they pledged to be father and son.
He asked:
“Your great army came a long distance,
yet you fought swiftly and won.
Why was this?”
Dégūang replied:
“I had thought that if the Táng troops could defend Yànmén and block the various strategic passes,
then the outcome might have been uncertain.
Now, the army drove deep without resistance;
I knew that the great undertaking was certain to succeed.
Furthermore, our troops have suffered many hardships for a long time;
it was proper to break them with divine speed.
This is why we won.”
Jìngdá, having been defeated,
retreated and secured the Jìn'ān Stockade.
Dégūang besieged it.
Táng sent Zhào Déjūn and Yánshòu to rescue Jìngdá,
but Déjūn and his son halted their troops at Tuánbǎigǔ and did not provide rescue.
Dégūang said to Jìngtáng:
“I traveled three thousand *lǐ* to fulfill this commitment to righteousness (Yì);
it is proper that this righteousness be fulfilled completely.”
Thereupon, he constructed an altar south of the Jìn city
and enthroned Jìngtáng as Emperor.
He personally took off his own clothes and cap and presented them to him.
The edict stated:
“Alas, you, the Jìn Prince, my son!
I regard you as my son,
and you shall regard me as your father.”
Shortly thereafter,
Yáng Gūangyuǎn killed Zhāng Jìngdá and surrendered to Jìn.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn entered Luòyáng from Tàiyuán.
Dégūang escorted him to Lùzhōu.
Zhào Déjūn and Yánshòu came out and surrendered.
Dégūang said to Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn:
“The great matter is now complete.
I shall order the Grand Minister Wēn to cross the river with you,
and I shall remain here
and only head north after you have entered Luòyáng.”
When they bid farewell,
they grasped hands and sighed in emotion.
Dégūang took off his white sable fur coat and presented it to Gāozǔ,
and sent him twenty fine horses
and one thousand two hundred war horses.
He cautioned him, saying:
“May our descendants never forget each other!”
This was the ninth year of Tiānxiǎn.
After Gāozǔ had entered Luòyáng,
Dégūang then went north,
taking Zhào Déjūn and Yánshòu captive back with him.
Déjūn
was a person from Yōuzhōu,
who had served Líu Shǒugūang and Shǒuwén as an army officer.
Zhuāngzōng captured him when attacking Yān
and granted him the surname and given name Lǐ Shàobīn.
His son Yánshòu,
whose original surname was Líu,
was a person from Chángshān.
His father Yuán was the magistrate of Tiáoxiàn.
When Líu Shǒuwén attacked and breached Tiáoxiàn,
Déjūn acquired Yánshòu and his mother, Lady Zhǒng, and took them in.
Consequently, he adopted Yánshòu as his son.
Yánshòu, as a person,
had a charming and gentle appearance,
and had some exposure to classical texts and history.
Míngzōng married his daughter to him,
and she was titled Princess Xīngpíng.
During the reigns of Zhuāngzōng and Míngzōng,
Déjūn governed Yōuzhōu for more than ten years,
and was particularly trusted because of Yánshòu.
Yánshòu served as Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs (*Shūmìshǐ*) during the time of Míngzōng,
but was later dismissed.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) ascended the throne,
he was reinstated as Chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn rose up in Tàiyuán,
Fèidì sent Yánshòu to command troops to suppress him.
And Déjūn also requested to use his garrison troops to suppress the rebels.
Fèidì perceived that he harbored divergent intentions,
and ordered him to exit from Fēihú to strike their rear.
However, Déjūn moved south, exiting at Wú’ér,
and met Yánshòu at Xītáng.
Yánshòu consequently submitted his troops to him.
Fèidì appointed Déjūn as Supreme Commander of all Circuit Expeditionary Forces (*Zhū Dào Xíngyíng Dū Tǒng*),
and Yánshòu as Pacification Commissioner of the Southern Front in Tàiyuán (*Tàiyuán Nánmiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ*).
Déjūn requested the Military Governorship (*Jiédùshǐ*) of Zhènzhōu for Yánshòu.
Fèidì angrily said:
“Déjūn and his son wield strong troops
and seek a major governorship.
If they can truly defeat the Qìdān and break Tàiyuán,
even replacing me would be acceptable.
If they instead play with the enemy and coerce the sovereign,
I fear that both the dog and the rabbit will perish.”
Consequently, he sent an envoy to urge Déjūn and the others to advance their troops.
Déjūn secretly sent men to seek alliance with Dégūang,
requesting to be established as Emperor.
Dégūang pointed to a huge rock in front of his yurt and said to Déjūn’s envoy:
“I have already promised Lord Shí.
When the rock rots,
then a change can be made.”
When Dégūang arrived at Lùzhōu,
he shackled Déjūn and his son and departed.
Dégūang’s mother, Shùlǜ, saw them
and asked:
“Why did you and your son seek to become the Son of Heaven?”
