Déjūn was ashamed and unable to reply,
so he presented all the registers of his fields and residences.
Shùlǜ asked where they were located.
He replied:
“Yōuzhōu.”
Shùlǜ said:
“Yōuzhōu already belongs to me;
why offer it?”
The following year,
Déjūn died.
Dégūang appointed Yánshòu as the Military Governor of Yōuzhōu
and enfeoffed him as the Prince of Yān.
When Qìdān was fighting during the reigns of Zhuāngzōng and Míngzōng, they captured Yíng and Píng prefectures.
After establishing Jìn,
they further gained the territory north of Yànmén within the jurisdiction of the Yōuzhōu Military Governorship,
totaling sixteen prefectures.
They then designated Yōuzhōu as Yànjīng,
changed the eleventh year of Tiānxiǎn to the first year of Huìtóng,
renamed their state Dà Liáo,
established a bureaucracy,
and modeled everything upon the Chinese system,
making joint use of Chinese people.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn frequently sent envoys to pay visits and ask after him,
presented memorials addressing him as a subject,
and annually delivered three hundred thousand bolts of silk.
Regarding other precious jade and rare items,
down to Chinese foods and various goods,
envoys followed one another along the road,
without a single empty day.
Dégūang had stipulated that Gāozǔ not refer to himself as a subject,
but instead re-write his memorial as a letter,
addressing himself as
“Imperial Son,”
following the etiquette for family members.
Dégūang sent Hán Jǐng, Minister of the Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Lìng*), to present the imperial edict establishing Gāozǔ as Emperor Yīngwǔ Míngyì.

Gāozǔ in turn sent Zhào Yǐng, Fény Dào, and others with the insignia and retinues of the Grand Court of Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Lǔbù*) to present imperial edicts conferring honorary titles upon Dégūang and his mother.
Throughout his lifetime,
Gāozǔ served them with great deference.
Gāozǔ died,
Chūdì ascended the throne.
Déguāng was angry that he had not informed him first,
and furthermore did not present a memorial,
did not declare himself a subject but called himself a grandson.
He repeatedly sent envoys to reprimand Jìn.
All the great ministers of Jìn were afraid,
but Jǐng Yán'guǎng, speaking to the Qìdān envoys,
was uniquely defiant.
Déguāng became even angrier.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn rebelled in Qīngzhōu,
and (Déguāng) invited him (to join).
In the spring of the first year of Kāiyùn,
Déguāng mobilized the entire state to invade the south,
dividing his troops into three: the western group exited Yànmén,
and attacked Bīng and Dài.
Liú Zhǐyuǎn defeated them at Xiùróng.
The eastern group reached the River,
and captured Bózhōu,
to support Guāngyuǎn.
Déguāng and Yánshòu headed south,
and attacked and captured Bèizhōu.
Déguāng camped at Yuánchéng,
and his troops reached Líyáng.
Jìn Chūdì personally led the campaign,
sending Lǐ Shǒuzhēn and others eastward to rush to Mǎjiādù,
and defeat the Qìdān.
Meanwhile, Déguāng and Jìn faced each other across the River
for over a month.
Hearing that the troops at Mǎjiādù had been defeated,
he then led his masses to attack Jìn,
fighting at Qīchéng.
When Déguāng arrived at the battle formation,
he looked out and saw the Jìn army’s banners shining brightly,
and the soldiers and horses were well-ordered and disciplined.
He showed a look of fear,
and said to his attendants:
“Yáng Guāngyuǎn said that half of the Jìn household’s troops had already starved to death,
How can they be so strong!”
Once the armies engaged,
the casualties were roughly equal,
and between the formations, broken arrows and scattered arrowheads
were spread to a depth of more than an inch.
As night fell,
Déguāng withdrew,
dividing his army into two groups:
one exited via Cāngzhōu,
the other exited via Shēnzhōu to return home.
In the first month of the second year,
Déguāng once again mobilized the entire state to invade,
besieging Zhènzhōu,
and dividing his troops to attack and seize Gǔchéng and nine other counties.
Dù Chóngwēi defended Zhènzhōu,
keeping the defenses shut and daring not to sortie.
The Qìdān plundered south through Xíng, Míng, and Cí,
reaching Ānyánghé.
Within a thousand *lǐ*,
everything was burned and pillaged almost completely.
The Qìdān saw a large mulberry tree,
and cursed it, saying:
“I know the purple-robed officials originated from your essence,
How can I allow you to live!”
They stacked firewood around the tree and burned it.
At this time,
Chūdì was ill,
and unable to lead the campaign.
He sent Zhāng Cóng'ēn, Ān Shěnqí, Huángfǔ Yù, and others to resist them.
Yù advanced and crossed the Zhāngshuǐ,
where he encountered the Qìdān.
They fought at Yúlín,
and he was almost captured.
Shěnqí came from the rear to rescue him.
The Qìdān looked out and saw dust rising,
believing that reinforcements had arrived,
and they withdrew.
Cóng'ēn, however, was fearful and timid,
and dared not pursue them.
He also led his troops south toward Líyáng.
The Qìdān had already headed north,
and Chūdì's illness had slightly abated.
He then issued an edict to personally lead the campaign,
and stationed his army at Chénzhōu.
He sent Dù Chóngwēi and others to campaign north.
The Qìdān, returning, reached Gǔběi,
but hearing that the Jìn army was about to arrive,
they immediately led their forces south again,
and fought Chóngwēi at Yángchéng and Wèicūn.
The Jìn army was hungry and thirsty.
Whenever they dug wells, they immediately collapsed,
so they squeezed the mud juice and drank it.
Déguāng sat inside a Xī cart,
and called out to his masses:
“The entire Jìn army is here!
We can capture them alive,
and then pacify the world.”
Just then, a great wind arose,
and the Jìn army fought fiercely and attacked them.
The Qìdān suffered a major defeat.
Déguāng lost his cart,
and rode away on a white camel.
When he arrived at Yōuzhōu,
their leaders and great generals were each flogged several hundred times.
Only Zhào Yánshòu was exempted.
At this time,
the realm suffered from drought and locusts,
and the Jìn people were exhausted by warfare.
Jìn therefore sent Zhāng Huī, a military general from Kāifēngfǔ, pretending to be an Official of the Palace Guard, to sue for peace with the Qìdān,
presenting a memorial and declaring themselves subjects,
in order to restore friendly relations.
Déguāng spoke discourteously.
However, the Qìdān themselves were also weary of war.
Déguāng's mother, Shùlǜ, once said to the Jìn envoys:
“How can the Hàn children of the Southern Court afford to remain inactive?
Since antiquity, we have heard of Hàn coming to seek peace with the barbarians,
but we have never heard of barbarians going to seek peace with Hàn.
If the Hàn children truly have a change of heart,
then why should I hesitate to establish good relations!”
Jìn did not send envoys again,
but repeatedly sent letters to entice Zhào Yánshòu.
saw that the *Jìn* was declining and the world was in chaos,
and he once had the intention of seeking to control the *Zhōngguó*.
Yēlǜ Déguāng had also once promised *Yánshòu* that if he destroyed *Jìn*, he would install him as ruler.
*Yánshòu* obtained a letter from *Jìn*,
and fabricated favorable words in reply to *Jìn*,
saying that he was trapped among the captives and longed to return,
promising that if *Jìn* dispatched troops, he would respond in kind.
Furthermore, *Déguāng*'s general, Gāo Móuhàn, also fraudulently offered *Yíngzhōu* to surrender to *Jìn*.
The ruler and ministers of *Jìn* were all delighted.
In the seventh month of the third year (of *Kāiyùn*),
they dispatched Dù Zhòngwēi, Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, Zhāng Yànzé, and others to march out with troops
to respond to *Yánshòu*.
The forces advanced rapidly toward *Yíngzhōu*.
*Móuhàn* abandoned the empty city and departed.
When the *Jìn* army arrived beneath the city walls,
they saw that all the city gates were open.
Suspecting an ambush,
they dared not enter.
They dispatched Liáng Hànzhāng to pursue *Móuhàn* and caught up with him,
but *Hànzhāng* died in battle.
*Zhòngwēi*'s army and the others were garrisoned at *Wǔqiáng*.
*Déguāng*, upon hearing that *Jìn* had mobilized troops,
then invaded *Zhènzhōu*.
*Zhòngwēi* garrisoned westwards at *Zhōngdù*,
camping across the water from *Déguāng*.
*Déguāng* divided his forces,
and emerged behind the *Jìn* army by following the Western Mountains,
attacking and defeating *Luánchéng Xiàn*.
The county had a thousand cavalry troops,
all of whom surrendered to the captives.
Whenever *Déguāng* captured *Jìn* people,
he tattooed their faces,
the inscription reading
"By Imperial Edict, Do Not Kill,"
and released them to return south.
*Zhòngwēi* and the others were besieged and ran out of provisions,
so they surrendered their entire army.
*Déguāng* was delighted,
and said to Zhào Yánshòu:
"All the Han people captured are given to you."
He consequently bestowed upon him a reddish-brown robe decorated with dragons and phoenixes,
making him wear it to reassure the *Jìn* troops.
He also bestowed a reddish-brown robe upon *Zhòngwēi*.
He dispatched Fù Zhù'ér to supervise Zhāng Yànzé, commanding two thousand cavalry,
to enter the capital first.
The Displaced Emperor of *Jìn* and the Empress Dowager prepared a memorial of surrender,
stating their faults and transgressions.
*Déguāng* sent Xièlǐ with a handwritten decree, which he bestowed upon the Emperor, saying:
"Grandson, just don't worry,
I guarantee you a place to eat your rice."
When *Déguāng* was about to arrive at the capital,
the relevant authorities requested to use the ceremonial imperial carriage for the welcome procession.
*Déguāng* said:
"I personally donned armor and helmet
in order to pacify the Central Plains.
The rites of the Grand Master of Ceremonies
I have no time to attend to."
He stopped them and did not use it.
The Displaced Emperor and the Empress Dowager went out to the suburb to welcome him,
but *Déguāng* declined to meet them,
saying:
"How can two Sons of Heaven meet on the road!"
On the morning of *Dīnghài*, the first day of the first month of the fourth year (of *Kāiyùn*),
the civil and military officials of *Jìn*,
lined up north of the capital city,
paying respects and bidding farewell to the Emperor,
and waited wearing plain clothes and gauze caps.
*Déguāng* wore armor, donned a sable fur coat and cap,
and stood his horse upon a high ridge.
The hundred officials prostrated themselves, awaiting their judgment.
*Déguāng* entered through the *Fēngqiūmén*,
ascended the city tower,
and sent an interpreter to publicly address the populace, saying:
"I am also a person;
there is no need to fear.
I originally had no intention of coming here;
the Han troops brought me here."
He then entered the *Jìn* Palace.
The palace concubines and entertainers came forward to pay respects,
but he disregarded them all.
That evening he left and lodged at *Chìgāng*.
He enfeoffed the Displaced Emperor as the Marquis of Faithlessness,
and relocated him to *Huánglóng Fǔ*.
On *Guǐsì*,
he entered and resided in the *Jìn* Palace.
He had *Qìdān* guard the various gates.
At the gates, corridors, and palace courts, dogs were impaled and skins were hung,
as a form of superstitious exorcism.
On *Jiǎwǔ*,
*Déguāng*, in barbarian clothing, held court at *Guǎngzhèng Diàn*.
On *Yǐwèi*,
he wore the caps and robes of the Central Lands,
and the hundred officials paid routine attendance.
His daily routines followed the *Jìn* rites,
but felt furs and garments fastening on the left—
barbarian horses and *Xī* carriages—
were arrayed along the steps of the palace.
The *Jìn* people bowed their heads and dared not look up.
On *Dīngsì Shuò*, the first day of the second month,
the Golden Guard Six Armies, the guards of the Palace Supervisory Bureau, and the music and dance of the Grand Master of Ceremonies were displayed in the court.
*Déguāng* wore the Heaven-Reaching Cap,
wore a crimson gauze robe,
and held the Great Jade Tablet while holding court.
He proclaimed a general amnesty,
changing the state of *Jìn* to the state of *Dàliáo*,
and changing the fourth year of *Kāiyùn* to the tenth year of *Huìtóng*.
*Déguāng* had previously promised Zhào Yánshòu that if he destroyed *Jìn*, he would enthrone him as Emperor.
Therefore, when the *Qìdān* attacked *Jìn*,
*Yánshòu* always served as the vanguard.
All that he captured and plundered,
he offered entirely to *Déguāng* and his mother, Shùlǜ.
*Déguāng* had already destroyed *Jìn* but had no intention of enthroning *Yánshòu*.
*Yánshòu* dared not mention it himself,
so he used Lǐ Sōng to request to be made Crown Prince.
*Déguāng* said:
"I spare nothing for the King of *Yān*.
Even my own flesh and skin—
if it can be useful to the King of *Yān*,
I would cut it off.
I have heard that the Crown Prince must be the Son of the Son of Heaven.
How can the King of *Yān* become one?"
He then ordered that *Yánshòu*'s rank be promoted.

The Hanlin Academician Zhāng Lì proposed appointing *Yánshòu* as Resident of the Central Capital, Grand Chancellor, Superintendent of Affairs of the Secretariat, and Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital.
*Déguāng* asked for a brush,
and struck out the titles Superintendent of Affairs of the Secretariat and Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital,
keeping only Resident of the Central Capital and Grand Chancellor.
However, *Yánshòu*'s previous titles as Commissioner of Military Affairs and the enfeoffment as King of *Yān* remained unchanged.
He also appointed *Lì* as Right Executive Assistant, concurrently Vice Director of the Chancellery, and Chief Minister.
He served as Chancellor alongside Hè Níng, the former *Jìn* Chancellor.
*Lì*
was a Hanlin Academician during the time of Míngzōng.
When Gāozǔ of *Jìn* rose up at *Tàiyuán*,
the Deposed Emperor of *Táng* sent *Lì* to supervise Zhào Yánshòu as he advanced his troops at *Tuánbǎigǔ*.
Later, *Yánshòu* was captured by *Déguāng*,
and *Lì* was also relocated to *Qìdān*.
*Déguāng* valued his literary scholarship,
and retained him as Hanlin Academician.
*Lì* constantly longed to return home.
He fled and reached the border,
but was captured by those pursuing him.
*Déguāng* reprimanded him,
and *Lì* said:
"Your servant is fundamentally a Han person.
My clothes, food, drink, and language are different.
Now I long to return home but cannot;
it is better to die than to live."
*Déguāng* looked at his interpreter, Gāo Tángyīng, and said:
"I warned you all to treat this man well.
The fact that he was caused to flee
is your fault."
Consequently, he had *Tángyīng* flogged a hundred times, but treated *Lì* as before.
His affection for him was thus.
When *Déguāng* was about to hold court,
the authorities issued *Yánshòu* the sable-cicada cap,
and *Lì* the cap and robes of the third rank.
Both *Yánshòu* and *Lì* refused to wear them.
*Yánshòu*, however, made a separate king's cap to distinguish himself.
*Lì* said:
"When I was in the Upper Kingdom (the *Qìdān* court),
*Jìn* sent Féng Dào to present the imperial documents to the Northern Court.
*Dào* carried two sable caps.
One of them Chancellor Hán Yánhuī wore,
and the other he ordered me to wear.
How can I now submit and change my attire!"
In the end, he wore the sable-cicada cap to court.
On *Bǐngxū Shuò*, the first day of the third month,
*Déguāng* wore boots and a robe,
and presided over the *Chóngyuán Diàn*.
The hundred officials entered the pavilion.
*Déguāng* was greatly pleased,
and looked at his attendants, saying:
"The ceremonial objects and institutions of the Han house
are magnificent to this extent!
That I am able to sit in this palace hall—
am I not truly the Son of Heaven!"
His mother, Shùlǜ, sent a messenger carrying a letter and a document from Ābǎojī's *Míngdiàn* to bestow upon *Déguāng*.
The *Míngdiàn*
is similar to the system of the auxiliary palace beneath an imperial mausoleum in the Central Lands.
When the ruler of their state dies,
and is buried,
they erect a structure beside his tomb,
which is called the *Míngdiàn*.
Officials and staff are appointed to hold duties,
and memorials are presented annually and seasonally, reporting on activities as if serving the living.
One *Míngdiàn* Academician is appointed to manage replies to correspondence and edicts.
Whenever the state has a great celebration or mourning event,
the Academician writes a letter in the name of the previous ruler to bestow upon the current ruler.
This letter invariably says, "In reply to the Son-Emperor."
had already destroyed Jìn,
and sent the tribal chieftains and their interpreters to be Cìshǐ and Jiédùshǐ for the various prefectures and garrisons (zhōuzhèn),
gathering (extorting) money and silk from all under Heaven to reward the army.
Since the Hu soldiers and horses were not provided with grain and fodder,
Deguāng sent several thousand cavalrymen to disperse into the four wilds,
robbing and plundering the people.
This was referred to
as "Dǎ Cǎogǔ" (Beating/Gathering Grass and Grain).
Between two and three thousand *lǐ* east and west,
the populace suffered their cruelty,
and people near and far groaned with resentment.
Hàn Gāozǔ rose up at Tàiyuán,
and many of the prefectures and garrisons where Kìdān commanders were stationed killed them and submitted to Hàn.
Deguāng was greatly terrified.
Furthermore, the weather was already hot.
Thereupon, he appointed Xiāo Hàn as the Jiédùshǐ of the Xuānwǔ Army.
Hàn
was from a great Kìdān clan;
his title was Ābō.
Hàn's younger sister was also married to Deguāng,
but Ābō originally had no surname (xìngshì).
The Kìdān called Hàn "Guójìu" (Imperial Maternal Uncle).
When Deguāng was about to make him a Jiédùshǐ,
Lǐ Sōng fabricated a name for him, calling him Xiāo Hàn.
He thus began to bear the surname Xiāo.
Having left Hàn to guard Biàn,
Deguāng then returned north,
taking with him several thousand men—artisans from the various bureaus (sī) within Jìn, palace women, officers, and soldiers from the various armies.
He crossed the river (Hé) from Líyáng,
traveled until he reached Tāngyīn,
and ascended Chóusǐ Gāng (Sorrow-to-Death Ridge).
He said to his Xuānhuī Envoy Gāo Xūn:
"When I was in the Upper Kingdom (Kìdān),
I took pleasure in hunting and eating meat.
Since entering the Central States (Zhōngguó),
my heart has always been unhappy.
If I could return to my native land,
I would have no regrets, even if I were to die."
Xūn withdrew and said to others:
"The captive (Lǔ) is about to die."
Liáng Huī of Xiàngzhōu killed the Kìdān garrison commander,
shut the city gates, and resisted the occupation.
Deguāng led his troops and defeated them.
All the men in the city, regardless of age, were slaughtered,
and all the women were driven north.
Later, the Hòu Hàn appointed Wáng Jìhóng to govern Xiàngzhōu,
and he recovered tens of thousands of skulls,
which he buried in a great mound.
Deguāng arrived at Línmíng,
and seeing that the towns and villages were desolate and ruined,
he smiled and said to the Jìn people:
"The reason the Central States have reached this point
is entirely because the King of Yān (Yānwáng) was the chief culprit."
He then looked at Zhāng Lì and said:
"You also played a role in this."
Deguāng traveled until he reached Luánchéng,
where he contracted an illness
and died in Shāhú Lín (Slaughter-Hu Forest).
The Kìdān cut open his abdomen,
removed his intestines and stomach,
packed the cavity with salt,
and carried him north.
The Jìn people called this
"The [Salty] Emperor"
Yǒngkāng Wáng Wùyù was established (as ruler).
He gave Deguāng the posthumous title Sìshèng Huángdì,
naming Ābǎojī Tàizǔ,
and Deguāng Tàizōng.
Appendix on the Four Barbarians, Part Two.
Wùyù
was the son of Dōngdān Wáng Tūyù.
Tūyù fled to Táng,
but Wùyù remained behind and did not follow,
receiving the title Yǒngkāng Wáng.
The Kìdān enjoyed drinking human blood.
Tūyù's attendants and concubines
often had their arms pierced so that Tūyù could suck the blood.
For minor faults, he would immediately gouge out their eyes or brand them with cautery,
causing unbearable cruelty.
However, he liked guests,
enjoyed drinking wine,
was skilled in painting,
and was somewhat knowledgeable in literature.
When he returned to the Central States from Kìdān,
he brought several thousand scrolls of books.
Zhào Yánshòu, the Shūmì Envoy, often borrowed his rare books and medical classics,
all of which were unavailable in the Central States.
During the reign of Míngzōng,
Tūyù traveled from Huázhōu to the capital to attend court.
He was nominally appointed Jiédùshǐ of the Wǔxìn Army,
received its emoluments,
and was granted a mansion
and several palace women.
When Kìdān troops aided Jìn at Tàiyuán,
the deposed Emperor of Táng sent the eunuch Qín Jìmín and the Imperial City Envoy Lǐ Yànshēn to kill Tūyù at his residence.
Jìn Gāozǔ posthumously enfeoffed Tūyù as Yān Wáng.
When Deguāng destroyed Jìn,
Wùyù followed him to the capital.
Deguāng killed Jìmín and Yànshēn,
confiscated their household wealth,
and bestowed it all upon Wùyù.
When Deguāng died at Luánchéng,
Wùyù, along with Zhào Yánshòu and the various great generals, all entered Zhènzhōu.
Yánshòu declared himself Acting Manager of Military and State Affairs (Quán Zhī Jūnguó Shì),
and sent someone to request the keys to Zhènzhōu from Wùyù,
but Wùyù did not give them.
Yánshòu's attendants said:
"The Kìdān notables are gathering and plotting noisily (xiōngxiōng).
There will certainly be trouble;
you ought to prepare for it.
Now, the troops of the Central States
still number ten thousand men.
We can strike the Lǔ (barbarians);
otherwise,
the matter will surely fail."
Yánshòu was hesitant and undecided.
Wùyù's wife
was recognized by Yánshòu as his younger sister (by marriage).
On the first day of the fifth month,
Wùyù summoned Yánshòu, along with Zhāng Lì, Lǐ Sōng, Féng Dào, and others, and set out wine.
After several rounds of wine,
Wùyù said to Yánshòu:
"Since my sister came from the Upper Kingdom,
you should meet her once."
Yánshòu happily entered with Wùyù.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
Wùyù came out and sat down.
Smiling, he said to Lì and the others:
"The King of Yān (Yánshòu) was plotting rebellion,
and I have locked him up.
Gentlemen, you need not worry."
He further said:
"When the late Emperor (Deguāng) was in Biànzhōu, he gave me one counting rod,
promising me the management of the military and state affairs of the Southern Court (Náncháo).
Although I heard yesterday that he was ill,
there was no dying instruction.
How could the King of Yān presume to act on his own?"
Lì and the others dispersed.
Wùyù summoned Yánshòu, made him stand in the court, and interrogated him.
Yánshòu was unable to reply.
Wùyù then sent men to guard him
and confiscated his household wealth.
Wùyù then proclaimed Deguāng's dying edict, which read:
"Yǒngkāng Wáng,
the legitimate grandson of Dàshèng Huángdì,
and the eldest son of Rén Huáng Wáng,
may immediately ascend the Imperial throne at Zhōngjīng."
Zhōngjīng
was what the Kìdān called Zhènzhōu.
He sent envoys to announce the mourning to the various garrisons.
Xiāo Hàn heard that Deguāng had died,
abandoned Biànzhōu and headed north.
When he reached Zhènzhōu,
Wùyù had already departed.
Hàn surrounded Zhāng Lì's residence with cavalry,
seized Lì, and rebuked him, saying:
"You advised the late Emperor not to use Hu (barbarians) as Jiédùshǐ.
Why did you do this?"
Lì answered defiantly (did not yield).
Hàn imprisoned him in chains.
That night,
Lì died.
Wùyù was a man of outstanding greatness,
also skilled in painting,
able to drink wine,
and fond of showing respect to scholars.
Deguāng once bestowed upon him several thousand bolts of silk.
Wùyù distributed it
and used it all up within a single day.
After Wùyù was established (as ruler),
he first sent a messenger to inform his grandmother, Shùlǜ.
Shùlǜ angrily said:
"My son pacified Jìn and seized the empire.
He had great achievements and accomplishments.
His son who is here by my side should be established.
Since Rén Huáng Wáng betrayed me and returned to the Central States,
how can his son be established?"
Thereupon, she led troops to meet Wùyù,
intending to depose him.
Wùyù left his general Mádá to guard Zhènzhōu,
and all the Jìn generals who had followed Deguāng to Zhènzhōu were left behind as he departed.
He took the Hànlín Academicians Xú Táifú and Lǐ Huǎn with him,
and they confronted his grandmother Shùlǜ at Shíqiáo.
Most of the troops led by Shùlǜ deserted and returned to Wùyù.
Wùyù then confined Shùlǜ at Zǔzhōu.
Zǔzhōu
was the location of Ābǎojī’s tomb.
Shùlǜ was intelligent and patient.
When Ābǎojī died,
she summoned all the wives of the generals who had accompanied him,
and said to them:
"I am now a widow;
how can you all still have husbands?"
She then killed over a hundred of his generals,
saying:
"You may go and attend the late emperor."
If any of her attendants erred,
many were sent to Mùyè Shān,
and killed in Ābǎojī's tomb passage,
saying:
"Go see the late emperor for me in the underworld."
General Zhào Sīwēn
was originally a man from Zhōngguó,
and was favored by Ābǎojī for his talent and bravery.
Later, Shùlǜ became angry with him over an issue,
and ordered him to be sent to Mùyè Shān.
Sīwēn refused to go,
whereupon Shùlǜ said:
"You,
a trusted confidant of the late emperor,
how can you not go to see him?"
Sīwēn replied:
"No one is closer than Your Majesty the Empress Dowager;
why do you not go?"
Shùlǜ said:
"I originally intended to follow the late emperor to the underworld,
but because my son is young
and there are many troubles in the state,
I have not been able to.
However, I can cut off one of my arms and send it."
Her attendants earnestly remonstrated,
so she cut off one of her wrists,
and released Sīwēn, not killing him.
Initially,
when Déguāng attacked Jìn,
Shùlǜ often disapproved,
saying:
"Is it acceptable for our country to have a Hàn person as its ruler?"
Déguāng said:
"No, it is not."
Shùlǜ said:
"If so, then you, having gained Zhōngguó, cannot hold it.
Later there will certainly be disaster,
and regret will be too late."
When Déguāng died,
his body was transported back.
Shùlǜ did not weep but stroked his corpse and said:
"Wait until my people and livestock in the country are as before,
then I will bury you."
Later,
Wùyù imprisoned her,
and she later died at Mùyè Shān.
Wùyù changed his name to Ruǎn,
and was styled Tiānshòu Huángdì,
changing the era name to Tiānlù.
In the eighth month of that year,
Déguāng was buried at Mùyè Shān.
Envoys were sent to Zhènzhōu to summon FÉNG Dào, Hé Níng, and others to attend the funeral.
When the envoys reached Zhènzhōu,
the Zhènzhōu army mutinied,
and General Bái Zàiróng and others expelled Má Dá.
They occupied Dìngzhōu,
and later led all their forces northward.
Má Dá
was Déguāng's cousin.
When Déguāng destroyed Jìn,
he appointed him as the military governor of Xíngzhōu.
When Yuányù was about to ascend,
he ordered him to guard Zhènzhōu.
Má Dá was exceptionally cruel and tyrannical,
often capturing Zhōngguó people,
skinning their faces,
gouging out their eyes,
pulling out their hair,
and severing their wrists before killing them.
When going out or coming in, he always carried tools for pinching, chiseling, gouging, and cutting.
Around his sleeping quarters, human livers, shins, hands, and feet were hung,
yet he spoke and laughed as usual.
The people of Zhèn and Dìng could not endure his poison.
After Má Dá left,
FÉNG Dào and others then returned south.
In the first year of Gānyòu of Hàn,
Wùyù led ten thousand cavalry to attack Xíngzhōu,
capturing Nèiqiū.
When the Qìdān invaded,
they always used horse neighing as a signal.
When they came,
the horses did not neigh,
but spears and halberds shone at night,
and there was also a lunar eclipse.
The barbarian masses were all fearful,
considering it an ill omen.
Although they broke Nèiqiū, more than half of their men and horses were injured or died.
Wùyù reigned for five years.
He convened the chieftains of various tribes
and again plotted an invasion.
The leaders of all tribes were unwilling,
but Wùyù forced them.
Yān Wáng Shùyà and Tàiníng Wáng Òulǐsēng and others led troops to kill Wùyù at Dàshéndiàn.
Déguāng's son, Qí Wáng Shùlǜ, heard of the uprising
and fled to Nánshān.
The Qìdān attacked and killed Shùyà and Òulǐsēng,
and then welcomed Shùlǜ to be enthroned.
Upon Shùlǜ's ascension,
he changed the era name to Yìnglì,
and was styled Tiānshùn Huángdì,
later changing his name to Jǐng.
Shùlǜ suffered from an illness
that prevented him from being intimate with women;
many of his attendants
were eunuchs.
However, he enjoyed hunting and drinking,
and neglected state affairs.
Whenever he drank heavily,
from night until dawn,
he would usually sleep during the day.
The people of the country called him
"the Sleeping King."
Initially,
Wùyù often sent envoys to Hàn.
When the envoy reached Zhōngguó, Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne.
Tàizǔ then sent General Zhū Xiàn to return the diplomatic visit;
Xiàn returned after Wùyù had died.
Upon Shùlǜ's ascension,
he ceased to raid the south.
In the summer of the sixth year of Xiǎndé,
Shìzōng campaigned northward,
appointing Tián Jǐngxián, Military Governor of Bǎodà Commandery, as commander of Yúkǒuguān,
Lǐ Hóngxìn, Right Commander-in-Chief of Shénwǔ, as commander of Héliúkǒu,
Wáng Yàn, former Military Governor of Fèngxiáng, as commander of Yìjīnguān,
and Hán Tōng, Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards for Cavalry and Infantry, as overall land forces commander.
Shìzōng himself took a dragon boat from Gānníngjūn,
with a continuous line of covered boats and warships
stretching for dozens of *lǐ* from end to end.
Upon reaching Yìjīnguān,
its defending general surrendered.
As the river path gradually narrowed,
the boats could not proceed,
so he abandoned the boats and traveled by land.
The defending generals of Wǎqiáo Yúkǒuguān, Yíngzhōu, and Mòzhōu
all came forward to surrender.
Just as he was about to order an advance on Yōuzhōu,
Shìzōng fell ill,
so he established Xióngzhōu at Wǎqiáoguān and Bàzhōu at Yìjīnguān, and returned.
The Zhōu army conquered the Three Passes, Yíngzhōu, and Mòzhōu
without bloodshed.
Upon hearing this, Shùlǜ
said to his countrymen:
"These were originally Hàn lands;
now they are returned to Hàn,
so what is there to regret?"
Later, Shùlǜ was killed by a cook during his drunken state.
Alas!
Since ancient times, though the submission and rebellion of the barbarians
did not depend on the rise and fall of Zhōngguó,
Zhōngguó's control over the barbarians invariably depended on its strength or weakness.
I read the Zhōu diary,
and saw Shìzōng take Yíngzhōu and Mòzhōu,
and secure the Three Passes,
without bloodshed.
Yet the historians criticized him for, as a king's army,
rushing a thousand *lǐ* to attack others,
and risking the prestige of the Son of Heaven among reeds and rushes,
in pursuit of a single victory.
Indeed, military strategy
involves seizing opportunities and adapting to circumstances;
there are times that must not be missed.
Shìzōng pacified Huáidiàn in the south,
and campaigned against Qìdān in the north,
capitalizing on his victorious might
to strike when they were bewildered and dispirited.
People only saw how swiftly the Zhōu army moved out,
but did not know that Shùlǜ presented an opportunity that could be seized.
At that time,
Shùlǜ believed that what Zhōu had taken
were all former Hàn territories,
and not worth bothering about.
If so, then the former territories of the Fourteen Prefectures
could all have been commanded and taken.
Unfortunately, Shìzōng fell ill,
and his great ambition was not realized.
However, Yíngzhōu, Mòzhōu, and the Three Passes
were thus able to become people of Zhōngguó again,
while the customs of the Fourteen Prefectures
remain entangled with the barbarians to this day.
How regrettable was his ambition not to be fully achieved,
yet his achievement was not magnificent?
Indeed, the permutations and adaptations of warfare,
how could they be understood by those who rigidly adhere to conventional wisdom!
Initially,
Xiāo Hàn (蕭翰), hearing of Déguāng’s (德光) death,
returned north.
Hú Qiáo (胡嶠), the magistrate of Héyáng (郃陽) County in Tóngzhōu (同州), served as Hàn’s (翰) secretary,
and thus followed him into Qìdān (契丹).
However, Hàn’s (翰) wife, out of jealousy,
accused Hàn (翰) of plotting rebellion.
Hàn (翰) was executed.
Qiáo (嶠), with no one to rely on,
remained among the captives for seven years.
In the third year of Guǎngshùn (廣順) of the Zhōu (周) dynasty,
he escaped and returned to Zhōngguó (中國),
able to relate some of what he had seen.
He said:
“From Yōuzhōu (幽州), heading northwest, one enters Jūyōng Guān (居庸關).
The next day,
again northwest, one enters Shímén Guān (石門關).
The pass road is narrow and steep;
one man can hold off a hundred.
This is the strategic point by which Zhōngguó (中國) controls Qìdān (契丹).
After another three days,
we reached Kèhán Zhōu (可汗州).
To the south, one can see Wǔtái Shān (五臺山);
the highest peak among them
is the East Terrace (Dōngtái 東臺).
After another three days,
we reached Xīnwǔ Zhōu (新武州).
Fifty *lǐ* (里) to the northwest is Jīmíng Shān (雞鳴山).
It is said that Táng (唐) Tàizōng (太宗) heard a rooster crowing here during his northern campaign,
and thus the mountain was named.
The next day,
we entered Yǒngdìng Guān (永定關),
which was an old pass of the Táng (唐) dynasty.
After another four days,
we reached Guīhuà Zhōu (歸化州).
After another three days,
we ascended Tiānlǐng (天嶺).
The ridge stretched continuously east and west.
There was a road leading north down the ridge.
Looking in all four directions, it was a desolate expanse,
with yellow clouds and white grass,
seemingly without end.
The Qìdān (契丹) people said to Qiáo (嶠): ‘This is Cíxiāng Lǐng (辭鄉嶺) [the Ridge of Bidding Farewell to Home];
you may cast one last glance south and say an eternal farewell.’
All those traveling with us wept bitterly,
often fainting and then reviving.
After traveling another three or four days,
we reached Hēiyúlín (黑榆林).
It was July,
but the cold was like deep winter.
The next day,
we entered Xié Gǔ (斜谷).
The valley was fifty *lǐ* (里) long,
with high cliffs and steep gorges.
Looking up, one could not see the sun,
and the cold was even more intense.
After exiting the valley,
we reached flat ground,
and the air became slightly warmer.
After another two days of travel,
we crossed the Huáng Shuǐ (湟水).
The next day,
we crossed the Hēi Shuǐ (黑水).
After another two days,
we reached Tāngchéng Diàn (湯城淀).
The climate there was the warmest.
If the Qìdān (契丹) experienced severe cold,
they would come here for warmth.
Its spring water was clear and cold,
and the grass was soft as down,
suitable for bedding.
There were many exotic flowers;
I recall two types: one called Hàngjīn (旱金),
as large as a palm,
its golden color dazzling;
the other called Qīngnáng (青囊),
like Zhōngguó’s (中國) Golden Lantern (Jīndēng 金燈),
but its color was a lovely blue.
After another two days,
we reached Yíkūn Zhōu (儀坤州) [or Yíkūn Prefecture (儀坤州)],
and crossed the Shèxiāng Hé (麝香河).
From Yōuzhōu (幽州) to this point, there were no distance markers,
and we did not know whether we were heading north or south.
After another two days,
we reached Chìyá (赤崖).
Hàn (翰) and Wùyù (兀欲) caught up with each other,
and then engaged Shùlǜ (述律) in battle at the Shāhé (沙河).
Shùlǜ’s (述律) troops were defeated and fled north.
Wùyù (兀欲) pursued them to Dúshù Dù (獨樹渡),
and then imprisoned Shùlǜ (述律) on Pūmǎ Shān (撲馬山).
After another three days of travel, we reached Shàngjīng (上京),
which was called Xīlóu (西樓).
Xīlóu (西樓) had towns and markets.
Transactions used cloth instead of money.
There were workshops for silk and brocade, eunuchs, Hanlin (Hànlín 翰林) scholars, artisans, performers, wrestlers, scholars, monks, nuns, and Daoist (Dàoshì 道士) priests,
all of whom were Zhōngguó (中國) people,
with those from Bìng (幷), Fén (汾), Yōu (幽), and Jì (薊) being particularly numerous.
Forty *lǐ* (里) east of Shàngjīng (上京),
we reached Zhēnhū Zhài (真珠寨),
where we first ate vegetables.
The next day,
traveling east, the terrain gradually rose.
Looking west, flat pine forests stretched for dozens of *lǐ* (里).
Then we entered a plain,
rich in vegetation.
We first ate watermelons.
It was said that the Qìdān (契丹) obtained these seeds when they defeated the Huíhél (回紇).
They were grown by covering sheds with cow dung,
and were as large as Zhōngguó’s (中國) winter melons but tasted sweet.
Continuing east,
we reached Niǎotán (褭潭).
Willows first appeared here,
and the water and grass were lush and beautiful.
There was a particularly beautiful type of grass called Xījī Cǎo (息雞草).
Its stalks were large;
a horse would be full after eating no more than ten stalks.
From Niǎotán (褭潭), we entered a large mountain range,
traveled for more than ten days, and then exited.
We passed a large forest,
two or three *lǐ* (里) long,
all covered with Wúyí (蕪荑) trees.
Their branches and leaves had thorns like arrow feathers,
and there was no grass on the ground there.
Wùyù (兀欲) set up his tent here at the time,
and assembled the various tribes to bury Déguāng (德光).
From here, we traveled southwest,
sixty *lǐ* (里) a day.
After seven days of travel,
we reached Dàshānmén (大山門).
Two high mountains were about one *lǐ* (里) apart.
There were tall pines and abundant grass,
rare birds and wild flowers.
There were also houses and stone tablets,
which read: ‘This is the imperial tomb.’
Wùyù (兀欲) entered to make offerings.
Among the chieftains of the various tribes, only those carrying sacrificial vessels were allowed to enter.
After they entered, the gate was closed.
The next day the gate was opened,
and they said ‘pāozhǎn’ (拋盞) [throwing cups],
signifying the completion of the ritual.
When asked about the ritual,
they all kept it secret and refused to speak.”
The events Qiáo (嶠) witnessed, such as the imprisonment of Shùlǜ (述律) and the burial of Déguāng (德光),
differ from what is recorded in Zhōngguó (中國) historical accounts.
Subsequently,
Hàn incurred guilt and was locked up.
Qiáo and his retainers traveled east to Fúzhōu.
Fúzhōu
was where Hàn governed.
Qiáo and his company traveled east,
passing a mountain
named Shísānshān.
It was said that this place was two thousand *lǐ* southwest of Yōuzhōu.
Traveling further east,
after several days,
they passed Wèizhōu.
There were more than thirty resident families,
who were reportedly Wèizhōu people from the Central Plains captured by the Qìdān,
and they built a walled city to live in.
When Qiáo arrived in Fúzhōu, the Qìdān often showed pity for Qiáo
and advised him to escape and return.
Consequently, Qiáo learned about the distant and neighboring states, their tribes, and their extent.
He reported:
“East from the state of Qìdān, reaching the sea,
there is Tiědiàn.
Their tribe lives wildly in hide tents,
and the people are fierce and brave.
Their land has few plants and trees;
the water is salty and murky,
the color of blood.
It can only be drunk after it has settled for a long time.
Further east is
Nǚzhēn,
skilled in archery,
and rich in oxen, deer, and wild dogs.
Their people have no fixed residence;
when traveling, they use oxen to carry burdens,
and when they encounter rain, they stretch hides to form a dwelling.
They constantly imitate the cry of deer,
call the deer, and shoot them,
eating their raw flesh.
They can brew millet into alcohol.
When drunk, they must be tied up to sleep,
and only untied after they awaken;
otherwise,
they will kill people.
Further southeast is
Bóhǎi.
Further east is
Liáoguó.
All are generally similar to the Qìdān.
In the southern curve of the sea,
they have the benefit of fish and salt.
Further south is
Xī,
generally similar to the Qìdān,
but the people are fond of slaughter.
Further south,
one reaches Yúguān.
Southwest reaches Rúzhōu.
These are all former Hàn territories.
To the west are the Tūjué and the Huíhé.
Northwest reaches Yūjuélǜ.
Their people are tall,
with shaggy hair.
The chieftains preserve all their hair,
putting it into purple pouches.
The land is extremely cold.
The waters produce large fish,
on which the Qìdān rely for food.
It also has many black, white, and yellow sable furs,
which all the northern states depend on for sufficiency.
Their people are the bravest;
neighboring states dare not invade them.
Further to their west is
Xiágá.
Further to their north is
Chányú Tūjué.
All are generally similar to Yūjuélǜ.
Further north is
Hēichēzi,
skilled at making cart-tents.
Their people understand filial piety and righteousness,
but the land is barren and produces nothing.
It is said that the ancestors of the Qìdān
were often subjected to service by the Huíhé.
Later, they abandoned them and fled to the Hēichēzi,
and only then began to learn how to make cart-tents.
Further north is
Niútí Tūjué (Ox-Hoof Tūjué).
They have human bodies and ox feet.
Their land is especially cold.
The water is called the Hù[●]hé.
In summer and autumn, the ice is two *chǐ* thick;
in spring and winter, the ice reaches the bottom.
They must always burn vessels to melt the ice before they can drink it.
To the northeast,
one reaches Mòjiézi.
Their people have shaggy hair
and wear draped cloth as clothing.
They ride without saddles,
use great bows and long arrows,
and are particularly skilled in archery.
When they encounter people, they immediately kill them and eat their raw flesh.
Qìdān and other states all fear them.
If five Qìdān riders meet one Mòjiézi,
they all scatter and flee.
Their country is surrounded on three sides by Shìwéi:
The first is Shìwéi,
the second is Huángtóu Shìwéi,
and the third is Shòu Shìwéi.
Their land is rich in copper, iron, gold, and silver.
Their craftsmen are skillful;
all their copper and iron vessels are refined and excellent,
and they are skilled at weaving woolen brocade.
The land is extremely cold;
horse urine freezes into piles of ice upon hitting the ground.
Further north is
Gǒuguó (Dog State).
They have human bodies and dog heads,
are long-haired, and wear no clothes.
They fight fierce beasts with their bare hands,
and their speech is the howling of dogs.
Their wives are all human
and can speak Hànyǔ (Chinese language).
If they bear a son, he is a dog;
if they bear a daughter, she is human.
They marry amongst themselves.
They live in caves and eat raw food,
but the wives and daughters eat cooked food.
It is said that a man from the Central Plains once arrived in their country,
and the wife pitied him and helped him escape home.
She gave him more than ten pairs of chopsticks
and taught him to drop one pair every ten *lǐ* he ran.
When the dog-husband chased him,
if he saw an object belonging to his home,
he would surely pick it up in his mouth and return home,
and thus would be unable to continue the chase.”
This account is thus.
It also said:
“The Qìdān once selected twenty horses capable of traveling a hundred *lǐ* a day,
and sent ten men carrying dry provisions north,
to fully investigate what they saw.
The men traveled from Hēichēzi,
passing north of Niútí Guó.
They traveled for one year,
passing through forty-three walled cities.
The inhabitants mostly used tree bark for houses.
There was no one to translate their language,
so they did not know the names of their lands, mountains, rivers, tribes, or titles.
Regarding the climate of the land,
when they encountered flat ground, it was warm and mild,
but in the mountains and forests, it was bitterly cold.
Upon reaching the thirty-third city,
they found one person
who could speak the Tiědiàn language.
His words were somewhat understandable.
He said the place name was Xiélìwūyúyéyàn.
He said, ‘Northward from here,
dragons, snakes, fierce beasts, and *chīmèi* travel in groups,
and it is impossible to proceed.’
The men then returned.
This was the limit of the northern wilderness.”
The Qìdān said to Jiào:
“How can the people of the barbarians defeat the Central States (Zhōngguó)?
However, the reason Jìn was defeated
was that its lord was ignorant and its ministers were disloyal.”
They then fully described the affairs of the various states,
saying:
“When you return, tell everything to the Hàn people,
and make the Hàn people exert themselves in serving their lord,
so they are not captured by the barbarians.
Our country is not a place for humans.”
When Jiào returned,
he recorded this as the Jìn Lǔ Jì (Record of Being Captured) (or Xiàn Lǔ Jì).
The Qìdān era names,
as recorded by various sources,
contain multiple errors and discrepancies,
making it impossible to verify them accurately.
Only those that appeared in the Central States can be relied upon.
According to the document of investiture of Jìn Gāozǔ by Yēlǜ Déguāng, it states:
“It is Tiānxiǎn Ninth Year,
in the cyclic year Bǐngshēn.”
This year
was exactly the first year of Jìn Tiānfú (Tiānfú Yuánnián).
Extrapolating backwards from this,
we find that the third year of Táng Tiānchéng (Tiānchéng Sānnián), which was Wùzǐ,
was Tiānxiǎn First Year (Tiānxiǎn Yuánnián).
Consulting the “Appendix on Qìdān,”
Déguāng ascended the throne in the same year as Táng Míngzōng,
and after three years on the throne, he changed the era name to Tiānxiǎn,
which matches this precisely.
Furthermore, based on the fact that in Kāiyùn Fourth Year, Déguāng destroyed Jìn and entered Biàn,
issued a great amnesty,
and named the era Huìtóng Tenth Year,
extrapolating backwards from this,
we find that Tiānfú Third Year was Huìtóng First Year (Huìtóng Yuánnián).
This means that Tiānxiǎn lasted exactly ten years,
and in the eleventh year, it was changed to Huìtóng.
Only these two points
are based on very clear evidence.
All others are insufficient for verification.
The barbarian era names recorded in the Appendix
are often abbreviated or omitted,
as they are largely useless,
and therefore need not be exhaustively listed.
Appendix on the Four Barbarians III
The Xī,
were originally a separate branch of the Xiōngnú.
Toward the end of the Táng dynasty,
they resided in Yīnliáng Chuān,
west of Yíng Fǔ,
and southwest of Yōuzhōu,
all several hundred *lǐ* away.
They had two thousand cavalrymen and horses.
They were divided into five tribes: the first was called Āhuì Bù,
the second Chuò Mǐ Bù,
the third Yuè Zhì Bù,
the fourth Nú Jiē Bù,
and the fifth Hēi Qǐ Zhī Bù.
Later, they migrated to Pípá Chuān,
several hundred *lǐ* northeast of Yōuzhōu.
The land produced many black sheep,
and the horses’ front hooves were strong and they ran well.
When climbing mountains to hunt beasts,
they ascended and descended like flying.
When the Qìdān Ābǎojī became powerful,
the Shìwěi, Xī, and Xī all submitted to him.
The Xī people frequently guarded the borders for the Qìdān,
but suffered from their harsh oppression.
The Xī King Qùzhū resented this and rebelled,
moving west with his separate tribe to Guīzhōu,
relying on the Northern Mountains for hunting.
He regularly collected musk and ginseng from the Northern Mountains to bribe Liú Shǒuguāng in order to secure his position.
His tribe eventually grew to several thousand tents,
and they began to be divided into the Eastern Xī and Western Xī.
The tribe of Qùzhū
knew how to farm to some extent.
Each year, they borrowed fallow land from the border populace to plant millet (jì),
and when it ripened in the autumn, they came to harvest it,
storing it in pits beneath the mountains,
the location of which no one knew.
They cooked using flat-bottomed earthenware cauldrons (wǎ dǐng),
boiling millet to make porridge,
which they diluted with cold water before drinking.
When Qùzhū died,
his son Sǎolà was enthroned.
When Zhuāngzōng defeated Liú Shǒuguāng,
he bestowed the surname Lǐ upon Sǎolà,
and changed his given name to Shàowēi.
When Shàowēi died,
his son Zhuàilà was enthroned.
After Tóngguāng,
Shàowēi and his son frequently sent envoys to pay tribute.
Originally,
Shàowēi married the elder sister of the Qìdān woman Shèlì Zhúbùlǔ.
Later, Zhúbùlǔ rebelled and fled into the Western Xī,
and Shàowēi received him.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he ceded Yōuzhōu and north of Yànmén to the Qìdān.
At this time, both Shàowēi and Zhúbùlǔ had already died.
When Yēlǜ Déguāng, having enthroned Jìn, returned north,
Zhuàilà went to pay respects before his horse.
Déguāng said:
“The fault is not yours.
Those who wronged me
were Sǎolà and Zhúbùlǔ.”
He then opened their tombs,
pulverized their bones, and scattered them.
Later, when Déguāng destroyed Jìn,
Zhuàilà constantly followed him with his troops.
After that, they were no longer seen in the Central States.
Since Qùzhū migrated to Guīzhōu,
setting himself apart as the Western Xī,
the Eastern Xī, who remained in Pípá Chuān,
were also absorbed by the Qìdān,
and were no longer able to establish themselves separately.
The Tǔhùn,
originally named Tǔyùhùn,
were perhaps the descendants of Qǐfú Gān Guī.
Since the Latter Wèi (Hòu Wèi) period,
their name appeared in the Central States,
residing on the shores of Qīnghǎi.
During the Zhìdé reign of Táng,
they were attacked by the Tǔbō,
and their tribes scattered.
Those who submitted internally
were settled by Táng west of the Yellow River (Héxī).
Their major clans included Mùróng, Tuòbá, Hèlián, and others.
During the time of Yìzōng,
their leader Hèlián Duó was the Regional Commander (Dūdū) of Yīnshān Fǔ.
He participated in the campaign against Páng Xūn,
and for his merit was appointed Military Governor (Jiédù Shǐ) of Dàtóng Army.
He was later defeated by the Prince of Jìn (Jìn Wáng),
and his tribe became even weaker,
scattering throughout the borders of Wèizhōu.
During the time of Zhuāngzōng,
there was a leader named Bái Chéngfú,
who established a stockade near Shímén, north of Zhōngshān.
Zhuāngzōng established the two prefectures, Níngshuò and Fènghuà, for them,
making Chéngfú the Regional Commander (Dūdū),
and bestowed upon him the surname and given name Lǐ Shàolǔ.
Throughout the Táng period,
he constantly sent envoys to pay tribute to the Central States.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he ceded the land north of Yànmén to the Qìdān.
Consequently, the Tǔhùn were subjected to the labor of the Qìdān,
and suffered from their cruel oppression.
At this time,
Ān Chóngróng was stationed at Chéngdé,
harboring rebellious intentions.
He secretly sent men to recruit the Tǔhùn to enter the pass.
Chéngfú and others thus entered the Central States via Wǔtái.
Yēlǜ Déguāng of the Qìdān was greatly angered
and sent an envoy to rebuke Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ, seized by fear,
sent the palace attendant Zhāng Chéng to lead troops to search for the Tǔhùn in the mountain valleys of Bìng, Zhèn, Xīn, Dài, and other prefectures, and drive them out.
However, Jìn also suffered under the Qìdān,
and desired to have the Tǔhùn for use in emergencies.
They secretly sent Liú Zhīyuǎn to Taiyuan to comfort and placate them.
Throughout Gāozǔ’s reign,
Chéngfú frequently sent envoys to pay tribute.
Later, the Last Emperor (Chū Dì) severed ties with the Qìdān,
summoned Chéngfú to court,
appointed him Military Governor of Dàtóng Army,
and treated him very generously.
When the Qìdān and Jìn confronted each other across the River,
Chéngfú led his troops to follow the Last Emperor in resisting the barbarians.
That year was extremely hot,
and many Tǔhùn died of illness.
Chéngfú was then sent back to Tàiyuán,
and settled between Lán and Shí.
Liú Zhīyuǎn gradually encroached upon and insulted him.
Chéngfú planned to flee back out of the pass,
but Zhīyuǎn surrounded his tribe with soldiers,
killing Chéngfú and his major clan leaders Hèlián Hǎilóng, Bái Kějiǔ, Bái Tiěkuì, and others.
Their sheep, horses, and wealth, which amounted to tens of thousands,
were all confiscated.
The remaining populace was placed under the leadership of their separate tribal king Yìzōng.
The Tǔhùn subsequently declined,
and were no longer seen.
Initially,
Táng referred to Chéngfú’s tribe as the Acculturated Tǔhùn (Shú Tǔhùn).
During the Chángxīng reign,
there was also Dù Měi’ér of the Unacculturated Tǔhùn (Shēng Tǔhùn) who came to pay tribute.
The location of Měi’ér’s
country and his tribe are unknown.
By the second year of Hàn Qiányòu (Qiányòu Èrnián),
another Tǔhùn named Hé Gārà came to pay tribute.
It is unknown if he belonged to the Acculturated or Unacculturated Tǔhùn.
They had presumably all diminished
and were not worth investigating and recording.
are
the residual lineage of the Mòhé.
Originally, they lived northeast of the Xī and the Qìdān.
Later, they were attacked by the Qìdān,
and their tribes dispersed.
Some belonged to the Qìdān,
some belonged to Bóhǎi.
A separate branch that scattered and lived in the Yīnshān
called themselves Dádá.
During the end of the Táng dynasty,
they appeared by name in the Central Kingdom (China).
There were Měi Xiāngwēn and Yúyuè Xiāngwēn.
During the Xiántōng era,
they followed Zhūyé Chìxīn in suppressing Páng Xūn.
Afterwards, Lǐ Guóchāng and his son, Kèyòng, were defeated by Hèlián Duó and others,
and once fled to the Dádá.
Later, they followed Kèyòng into the pass and defeated Huáng Cháo,
and thus resided between Yúnzhōu and Dàizhōu.
Their customs involved skill in horsemanship and archery,
and their livestock included many camels and horses.
The names of their chieftains and tribes
cannot be fully ascertained;
only those who frequently communicated with the Central Kingdom are known.
During the Tóngguāng era,
Dūdu Zhé Wénbū
frequently came from Héxī to present camels and horses as tribute.
When Míngzōng campaigned against Wáng Dū at Dìngzhōu,
Wáng Dū enticed the Qìdān to invade.
Míngzōng ordered the Dádá to enter the Qìdān territory
to bolster his military presence.
He dispatched Xuē Jìngzhōng, the Cìshǐ of Sùzhōu, to bestow 250 captured Qìdān round shields and several hundred bows and arrows upon the Dádá residing in the borderlands of Yúnzhōu.
The Táng dynasty had habitually kept them in service.
In the third year of Chángxīng (932 CE),
chieftain Jiégē led his tribe of over four hundred people to submit.
Ending in the Xiǎndé era,
they came constantly without interruption.
The Dǎngxiàng,
are the residual lineage of the Western Qiāng.
Their territory is in the land of Xīzhī mentioned in the Yǔ Gòng,
extending east to Sōngzhōu,
west connecting to Yèhù,
bounded south by Chūnsāng,
and bordering Tǔhún in the north,
covering over three thousand *lǐ* of land.
They have no walled cities but possess dwelling houses,
covered with wool blankets.
Their people are fond of thievery but are long-lived,
often reaching 150 or 160 years of age.
Their prominent clans include the Xìfēng family, the Fèitīng family, the Zhé family, and the Yělì family,
with the Tuòbá family being the strongest.
During the reign of Táng Dézōng,
the various Dǎngxiàng tribes led each other to submit internally.
Those residing in Qìngzhōu were called the Dōngshān Tribe,
and those residing in Xiàzhōu were called the Píngxià Tribe.
The tribes had prominent families but no unified ruler;
they were not centrally organized,
scattered throughout Bīnníng, Fūyán, Língwǔ, Héxī,
extending east to the area between Línzhōu and Fǔzhōu.
Since the Tóngguāng era,
the stronger members of the prominent families independently came to court to offer tribute.
During the time of Míngzōng,
an edict ordered that markets be established along the border for trading horses.
All the foreign tribes came to trade with the Central Kingdom,
and the Huíhú (Uighurs) and Dǎngxiàng supplied the most horses.
Míngzōng welcomed and soothed people from distant lands,
and regardless of whether the horses presented were inferior or strong, they were all purchased.
The price paid often exceeded their actual value,
and for their accommodations during arrival and departure,
the expenses incurred on the road were doubled.
Whenever they reached the capital,
Míngzōng would meet them in the imperial hall,
rewarding them with wine and food.
Once drunk,
they would link arms, singing and shouting,
expressing their regional customs for enjoyment.
When they departed, they were again heavily rewarded with gifts,
costing millions annually.
The Táng ministers all worried about this
and frequently spoke against it.
Consequently, an edict ordered officials to purchase the horses and pay the value at the border markets,
thus curbing their visits to court.
However, the Dǎngxiàng profited greatly from the transaction,
and their arrival could not be stopped.
Those who resided between Língzhōu and Qìngzhōu
frequently violated the border and committed robbery.
When the Huíhú of Héxī came to pay tribute to the Central Kingdom,
passing through their tribes' territory,
they would immediately intercept and rob them,
capturing the envoys
and selling them to other tribes
in exchange for cattle and horses.
Míngzōng dispatched Kāng Fú of Língwǔ, Yào Yànchóu of Bīnzhōu, and others to lead troops to suppress them.
Kāng Fú and the others defeated the tribes of Āmái Wéixībāolè Qiánglàimáisīgǔwěi and their great chieftains Liánxiāng Lǐbāsà Wáng, Dūtǒng Xīnàmáimó, Shìyù Qǐmáiwéixībū, and others.
They killed several thousand people,
captured tens of thousands of their cattle and sheep,
along with the precious jewels and jades they had stolen from foreign nations,
all of which were bestowed upon the soldiers.
Because of this, the trouble caused by the Dǎngxiàng slightly ceased.
When it reached the time of Zhōu Tàizǔ,
the Dǎngxiàng Níyělìuníxiāng Wángzǐ and Tuòbá Shān of Fǔzhōu all came to court to pay tribute.
In the third year of Guǎngshùn (953 CE),
Guō Yànqīn, the Cìshǐ of Qìngzhōu, coveted their sheep and horses
and harassed the various tribes.
Only the Yějī Tribe was too strong to approach,
so he falsely accused their tribe of violating the border.
Tàizǔ sent an envoy to recruit and appease them.
The Yějī Tribe suffered due to Yànqīn
and refused to comply with the order.
Tàizǔ dispatched Zhé Cóngruǎn of Bīnzhōu and Zhāng Jiànwǔ, the Cìshǐ of Níngzhōu, and others to suppress them.
Zhāng Jiànwǔ was eager to achieve merit,
but he could not understand the customs of the foreign tribes.
He rapidly marched his troops to attack the Yějī Tribe,
killing several hundred people.
When the Xǐyù, Zhésī, and Shāniú three tribes heard that Jiànwǔ had defeated the Yějī Tribe,
they each presented cattle and wine to reward the army.
The soldiers coveted their possessions
and instead robbed and plundered them.
The three tribes collectively lured Jiànwǔ’s army to Bāoshān,
and when they crossed the dangerous terrain,
the three tribes attacked them together.
The army fled into the ravines and valleys,
and the dead and wounded were numerous.
Tàizǔ was enraged,
punished Jiànwǔ and the others,
and selected worthy officials to serve as Cìshǐ of Qìngzhōu to recruit and pacify them.
As for the other tribes,
there were many scattered along the borderlands.
However, as they had no state territory or unified ruler,
they could not be fully recorded or ordered.
Regarding the Tūjué,
their territory, ruling dynasties, tribes, titles, and customs
are already documented in Táng records.
By the end of the Táng dynasty,
they were attacked by various foreign groups,
and their tribes became sparse and dispersed.
During the period of the Five Dynasties,
they occasionally came to court to pay tribute.
In the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE),
Hún Jiělóu came.
In the second year of Tiānchéng (927 CE),
chieftain Zhāng Mùjìn came.
In the second year of Chángxīng (931 CE),
chieftain Dù Āshú came.
In the sixth year of Tiānfú (941 CE),
they sent envoys such as Xuē Tónghǎi.
They came four times in total,
but did not come again afterward.
However, the Tūjué were extremely weak at that time,
and their visits were infrequent,
thus the records of their chieftains and history are incomplete.
Regarding the Tǔbō,
their territory, ruling dynasties, tribes, titles, and customs
are already documented in Táng records.
During the prosperity of the Táng dynasty,
in the thirty-three prefectures of Héxī and Lǒngyòu,
Liángzhōu was the largest.
The soil was fertile, resources abundant, and the people prosperous and happy.
The land was suitable for horses;
the Táng established eight directorates
and pastured 300,000 horses.
Using the Ānxī Dūhùfǔ (Protectorate-General of Ānxī), they maintained loose control over the thirty-six kingdoms of the Western Regions.
In the Táng armies, garrisons, directorates, and bureaus,
spanning over three hundred cities,
Chinese troops were routinely rotated for defense,
and an envoy was established in Liángzhōu to oversee them as a Jìedùshǐ (Military Governor).
During the rebellion of Ān Lùshān,
Sùzōng arose at Língwǔ
and summoned all the Héxī troops to meet the crisis.
The Tǔbō took advantage of the vulnerability and attacked and captured Héxī and Lǒngyòu.
A million Chinese people all fell captive.
During the time of Wénzōng,
an envoy was once sent to the Western Regions,
who saw that the walled cities and towns of Gānzhōu, Liángzhōu, Guāzhōu, Shāzhōu, and other prefectures were as they had been,
and the captive people, upon seeing the Táng envoy,
lined the roads, welcoming and shouting.
They wept and said:
“Does the Emperor still think of us, the people captured by the Fān (Tibetans)?”
These people were all descendants of those captured during the Tiānbǎo era.
Their language had slightly changed,
but their clothing remained unaltered.
By the time of the Wǔdài period,
the Tǔfān (Tibetans) were already weak.
The Huíhú (Uyghurs), Dǎngxiàng (Tanguts), and various Qiāng barbarians divided and encroached upon their territory,
but did not possess their people.
As Zhōngguó (China) was suffering decline and chaos,
it was unable to maintain control.
Only the four prefectures of Gānzhōu, Liángzhōu, Guāzhōu, and Shāzhōu regularly maintained contact with Zhōngguó.
Gānzhōu was the headquarters (yá) of the Huíhú,
while the generals and officials of the three prefectures of Liángzhōu, Guāzhōu, and Shāzhōu
still claimed to be Táng (Tang Dynasty) officials.
They frequently came to request appointments.
Starting from the time of Liáng Tàizǔ,
it was common practice to appoint the Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Língwǔ to concurrently lead the Military Governorship of Héxī,
and to oversee Gānzhōu, Sùzhōu, Wēizhōu, and other prefectures.
However, although the title existed,
Liángzhōu established its own defending generals.
In the fourth year of Táng Chángxīng (933 CE),

Sūn Chāo, the acting Military Governor (Liúhòu) of Liángzhōu, sent the great general Tuòbá Chéngqiān, along with monks, Daoist priests, and elders like Yáng Tōngxìn, to the capital (Jīngshī) to request insignia (jīngjié).
Míngzōng asked about the ancestry of Sūn Chāo and others.
Chéngqiān replied:
“When the Tǔfān occupied Liángzhōu,
Zhāng Yìcháo, a native of Zhāngyè, raised troops and drove the Tǔfān away.
The Táng then appointed Yìcháo as Military Governor
and dispatched 2,500 soldiers from Yùnzhōu to garrison the area.
When the Táng fell
and the realm was in chaos,
the area east of Liángzhōu was cut off by the Tūjué and the Dǎngxiàng.
The Yùnzhōu soldiers thus stayed and could not return.
The Hàn people in Liángzhōu today are all descendants of those garrisoned soldiers.”
Míngzōng then appointed Sūn Chāo as Military Governor.
In the first year of Qīngtài (934 CE),
Lǐ Wénqiān, the acting Military Governor, came to request an appointment.
A few years later,
the people of Liángzhōu drove Wénqiān out.
Féng Huī of Língwǔ sent his adjutant Wú Jìxūn to replace Wénqiān as acting Military Governor.
This was in the seventh year of Tiānfú (942 CE).
The following year,
Jìn Gāozǔ sent Chén Yánhuī, the staff officer (Yāyá) of Jīngzhōu, carrying an imperial edict to pacify Liángzhōu.
The people of Liángzhōu jointly detained Yánhuī
and established him as Prefect (Cìshǐ).
When it reached the time of Hàn Yǐndì,
Zhébū Jiāshī, the acting Military Governor of Liángzhōu, came to request an appointment.
The Hàn Dynasty immediately appointed him Military Governor.
Jiāshī
was a local strongman (tǔháo).
In the second year of Zhōu Guǎngshùn (952 CE),
Jiāshī sent someone to trade horses in the capital (Jīngshī),
and subsequently requested the appointment of a commander.
At this time,
Wáng Jùn, the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ), was influential.
Shēn Shīhòu was an old acquaintance of Jùn.
He had started out as a bandit in his youth,
and became a staff officer (yájiàng) in Yǎnzhōu.
He and Jùn were good friends.
Later, when Jùn achieved prominence,
Shīhòu, in tattered clothes and with disheveled hair,
waited daily for Jùn to emerge,
bowed before his horse,
and complained of hunger and cold.
Jùn had not yet found an opportunity to promote him.
When Jiāshī and others came requesting a commander,
Jùn immediately proposed:
“Liángzhōu is deep within barbarian territory,
and Zhōngguó has never appointed an official there.
I request recruiting guards (shuàifǔ shuài) or palace attendants (gòngfèng guān) who are willing to go.”
A month later,
no one responded to the recruitment call.
Jùn then memorialized to appoint Shīhòu as General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn),
and soon after appointed him Military Governor of Héxī.
When Shīhòu arrived in Liángzhōu,

he memorialized recommending the Deputy Staff Officer (Yāyá Fùshǐ) Cuī Hǔxīn, the chieftain of Yángfēi Gǔ, Shěn Niànbān, and descendants of Chinese residents, such as Wáng Tínghàn, Wēn Chónglè, and Liú Shàoyīng, to serve as generals and officials.
Furthermore, from Ānguó Zhèn to Liángzhōu,
he established three prefectures to control and restrain the various Qiāng tribes,
using their chieftains and strongmen as Prefects.
However, in Liángzhōu, the barbarians and the Chinese lived intermingled,
and Shīhòu was an ignoble person
who was unable to maintain control.
By the time of Shìzōng,
Shīhòu abandoned his son and fled back,
and Liángzhōu was subsequently cut off from Zhōngguó.
Only the two prefectures of Guāzhōu and Shāzhōu
maintained regular contact throughout the Wǔdài period.
In Shāzhōu,
during the Kāipíng era of the Liáng Dynasty, there was a Military Governor, Zhāng Fèng,
who proclaimed himself
“The White-Robed Son of Heaven of Jīnshān.”
When it reached the time of Táng Zhuāngzōng,
the Huíhú came to court.
Cáo Yìjīn, the acting Military Governor of Shāzhōu, also sent envoys who attached themselves to the Huíhú and came.
Zhuāngzōng appointed Yìjīn as Military Governor of the Guīyì Army and Commissioner for Observation and Administration of Guāzhōu, Shāzhōu, and other prefectures.
In the fifth year of Jìn Tiānfú (940 CE),
Yìjīn died,
and his son Yuándé succeeded him.
By the seventh year,
Cáo Yuánzhōng of Shāzhōu and Cáo Yuánshēn of Guāzhōu both sent envoys.
During the time of Zhōu Shìzōng,
Yuánzhōng was again appointed Military Governor of the Guīyì Army,
and Yuángōng was appointed Garrison Commander (Tuánliànshǐ) of Guāzhōu.

The tribute they offered included: shā, antelope horn (língyáng jiǎo), Persian brocade (bōsī jǐn), Ānxī white bó, gold-star alum (jīnxīng fán), hútóng lǜ, dàpěng shā, ruòhè, and jade spheres (yùtuán).
These items were all named as they were brought by the envoys.
However, the details of when they died, succeeded, or the order of their generations,
the historians have all failed to record.
The Tǔfān did not appear during the Liáng Dynasty period.
In the third year of Táng Tiānchéng (928 CE),
Rén Yù, the King of the Huíhú, came to court.
The Tǔfān also sent envoys who attached themselves to the mission and came.
From then on, they frequently visited Zhōngguó.
Míngzōng once attended the Duānmíng Hall and met their envoys.
He asked where their headquarters (yázhàng) were located.
They replied:
“Two thousand *lǐ* west of Jīngzhōu.”
Míngzōng bestowed tiger hides upon them,
one hide per person.
They all donned them to perform the ritual bow,
twisting and turning their bodies.
Their felt caps fell off,
and their messy hair resembled mugwort (péng).
Míngzōng and his attendants all burst into laughter.
They continued to come to court until the time of Hàn Yǐndì.
After that, they stopped coming.
Historians have also lost the record of their rulers and generations.
The Huíhú
had been a particularly severe plague upon the Táng Dynasty.
Their territory, the generations of their rulers, and their customs
are recorded in Táng writings.
The Táng frequently gave their daughters to marry them,
so they traditionally regarded Zhōngguó as their uncle (jiù).
Their original state was located along the Suōlíng River. Later, they were invaded by the Xiájiásī,
and migrated to the area between Tiāndé and Zhènnǔ.
They were again defeated by Shí Xióng and Zhāng Zhòngwǔ.
The remaining population moved west
and were subjugated by the Tǔfān.
At this time, the Tǔfān had already occupied Héxī and Lǒngyòu,
and they used the scattered Huíhú to settle the area.
During the Wǔdài period,
those Huíhú residing in Gānzhōu and Xīzhōu regularly visited Zhōngguó.
The Gānzhōu Huíhú frequently arrived,
still calling Zhōngguó their uncle (jiù),
and Zhōngguó, responding in imperial edicts, also called them nephew (shēng).
In the first year of Liáng Qiánhuà (911 CE),
they sent the Commandant (Dūdū) Zhōu Yìyán and others to visit.
Historians, however, do not record the name or title of their ruler.
The Liáng Dynasty conferred official titles upon Yìyán and the others,
and sent the Supreme General of the Left Gate Guard (Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Shàng Jiāngjūn), Yáng Zhǎo, to escort them back to their territory (Fān).
When it reached the time of Táng Zhuāngzōng,
Wáng Rénměi sent envoys,
offering tribute of jade and horses.
He styled himself
“Provisional Khaghan (Quán Zhī Kèhán).”
Zhuāngzōng sent Zhèng Xù, the Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng), bearing insignia, to officially appoint Rénměi as the Khaghan Yīngyì.
That year,
Rénměi died.
His younger brother, Dí Yín, succeeded him
and sent the Commandant Ān Qiānxiǎng and others.
In the fourth year of Tóngguāng (926 CE),
Dí Yín died,
and Āduōyù succeeded him.
In the second year of Tiānchéng (927 CE),
Wáng Rén Yù, who provisionally managed state affairs, sent Lǐ Āshān and others to court.
Míngzōng sent envoys to appoint Rén Yù as the Khaghan Shùnhuà.
During the time of Jìn Gāozǔ, he was again appointed as the Khaghan Fènghuà.
As for Āduōyù,
it is unknown whether he was related closely or distantly to Dí Yín,
nor is it known when he succeeded or died.
However, Rén Yù
came to pay tribute constantly throughout the Wǔdài period,
and the historians have also lost his records.

Their land produces jade (yù), yaks (lí), green wild horses (lǜyě mǎ), single-humped camels (dúfēng tuó), white sables (báidiāo shǔ), antelope horn (língyáng jiǎo), cǐ shā, seals’ penises (wò nà qí), diamonds (jīngāng zuàn), red salt (hóng yán), felt rugs (jì), and the hides of táotú.
Their land is suitable for white wheat (bái mài), blue (qīng) mài, hemp (huángmá), onions and leeks (cōng jiǔ), and coriander (hú suī).
They use camels to plow and sow.
Their Khaghan usually resides in a storied building.
His wife is titled Tiān Gōngzhǔ (Heavenly Princess).
Their chief minister (guóxiàng) is titled Mèilù Dūdū (Mèilù Commandant).
When meeting the Khaghan,
it is customary to remove the hat and enter with unbound hair.
Women gather their hair into a chignon (jì),
five or six inches high,
and cover it with a red silk bag.
After marriage,
they add a felt cap.
There is also another tribe called the Lóng Jiā (Dragon Family).
Their customs differ slightly from the Huíhé.
In the fourth year of Chángxīng (933 CE),
the Huíhú came and presented a pair of white gyrfalcons (bái hú).
Míngzōng ordered them to be untied and released.
Starting from the time of Míngzōng,
they often traded horses with Zhōngguó.
The precious jade they carried all belonged to the government (xuàn guān),
and commoners who violated the prohibition by trading privately were punished.
During the time of Zhōu Tàizǔ, this prohibition was abolished.
The common people were allowed to trade privately with the Huíhú,
and consequently, the price of jade became doubly cheap.
During the Xiǎndé era,
they came offering jade.
Shìzōng said:
“Although jade is precious, it is useless.”
He refused it.
Yútián,
the territory of the state, the lineage of its rulers, and its customs were recorded during the Táng Dynasty.
During the chaotic period of the Five Dynasties,
China experienced many troubles,
and was unable to manage the outlying border regions (Sìyí).
Those who had previously maintained contact with China are merely recorded by name;
the lineage of their rulers,
or their complete history, is unknown.
And Yútián was especially distant,
located ten thousand *lǐ* outside the capital (Jīngshī).
Its kingdom,
to the southwest, was close to the Cōnglǐng (Pamir Mountains),
and was a neighboring state to Póluómén (Brahman/India),
though separated by still more than three thousand *lǐ*.
To the south, it bordered Tǔbō (Tibet).
To the northwest, it was over two thousand *lǐ* to Shūlè (Kashgar).
In the third year of Tiānfú of Jìn [938 CE],
Lǐ Shèngtiān, the king of the state of Yútián, sent the envoy Mǎ Jìróng to offer tribute, including red salt, turmeric (*yùjīn*), yak tails, and jade.
Jìn dispatched the Attendant Official (Gōngfèng Guān) Zhāng Kuāngyè, provisionally appointed as Grand Master of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglú Qīng),
and Gāo Jūhuì, the Adjudicant (Pànguān) of the Military Governor (Jiédù) of Zhāngwǔ Command, as Adjudicant,
to confer upon Shèngtiān the title "Great Treasure King of the State of Yútián" (Dàbǎo Yútián Guówáng).
In the twelfth month of winter that year,
Kuāngyè and the others departed from Língzhōu and traveled for two years until they reached Yútián,
only returning in the winter of the seventh year [942 CE].
Jūhuì recorded in some detail the mountains, rivers, and various states he saw during his outward and return journeys,
but he was unable to state the sequence of generations of Shèngtiān.
Jūhuì recorded:
"From Língzhōu, we crossed the Yellow River,
and traveled thirty *lǐ*,
where we first crossed the sand and entered the territory of the Dǎngxiàng,
called Xìyāo Shā (Slender Waist Sands) and Shéndiǎn Shā (Spirit Spot Sands).
We reached Sāngōng Shā (Three Dukes Sands),
and lodged in the tent of the Governor-General (Dūdū) of Yuèzhī.
From here, we traveled over four hundred *lǐ* through the sand,
reaching Hēibǎo Shā (Black Fortress Sands),
where the sands were especially vast.
We then ascended the Shā Líng (Sand Ridge).
Shā Líng
was the headquarters (*yá*) of the Dǎngxiàng.
Their chieftain was called Niǎnyá Tiānzǐ.
We crossed the Báitíng Hé (White Pavilion River) and reached Liángzhōu.
From Liángzhōu, we traveled five hundred *lǐ* west to Gānzhōu.
Gānzhōu
was the headquarters of the Huíhú (Uighurs).
To its south,
for over a hundred *lǐ* across the mountains,
was the former territory of the Lesser Yuèzhī (Xiǎo Yuèzhī) during the Hàn Dynasty.
There was a separate tribe called the Lùjiǎoshān Shātuó (Shatuo of Deer Horn Mountain),
who claimed to be descendants of the Zhūyé clan.
West of Gānzhōu,
we began to cross the *qì* (gravel desert).
The *qì* had no water,
so we carried water as we traveled.
The people of Gānzhōu taught the Jìn envoys to make wooden horse-hoof shoes (*mù sè*).
The wooden shoes had four holes,
and four holes were drilled into the horse's hooves to attach them.
Camel hooves were wrapped in yak hide before they could proceed.
Five hundred *lǐ* northwest, we reached Sùzhōu.
We crossed the Jīn Hé (Gold River),
and a hundred *lǐ* west, we exited the Tiānmén Guān (Heavenly Gate Pass).
Another hundred *lǐ* west, we exited the Yùmén Guān (Jade Gate Pass),
passing through the territory of Tǔbō.
Tǔbō men wore Chinese caps,
while the women braided their hair
and wore *sèsè* pearls.
It was said that for the finest pearls,
one pearl could be exchanged for one excellent horse.
West, we reached Guāzhōu and Shāzhōu.
These two prefectures had many Chinese people.
Hearing that the Jìn envoys were coming,
their regional inspector Cáo Yuánshēn and others welcomed us outside the city
and asked about the health of the Son of Heaven.
Ten *lǐ* south of Guāzhōu is Míngshā Shān (Singing Sand Mountain).
It is said that in winter and summer, it constantly makes a booming sound like thunder,
and that this is the Liúshā (Flowing Sands) mentioned in the *Yǔ Gòng*.
Another ten *lǐ* southeast is Sānwēi Shān (Three Perils Mountain),
said to be where the Sānxū (Sān Miáo) were banished.
To its west,
after crossing the Dūxiāng Hé (Capital Town River), is Yáng Guān.
West of Shāzhōu is Zhòngyún,
whose royal tent (*yázhàng*) resided in Húlú Qì.
It is said that the Zhòngyún
are the descendants of the Xiǎo Yuèzhī.
Their people are brave and fond of fighting;
the people of Guā and Shā fear them all.
Húlú Qì,
during the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn, when troops were levied against the Xiōngnú,
military agricultural colonies were established at Wúlú;
this is likely that territory.
The land has no water and is often cold with much snow.
Whenever the weather warms and the snow melts,
water becomes available.
Kuāngyè and the others traveled west, entering the territory of Zhòngyún.
Upon reaching Dàtún Chéng (Great Garrison City),
Zhòngyún sent four prime ministers and thirty-seven governors-general to wait upon the Jìn envoys.
Kuāngyè and the others comforted and instructed them with the imperial edict,
and they all bowed facing east.
West of the Zhòngyún territory,
we began to cross the *míng* *qì* (dark gravel desert).
There was no water.
Digging into the ground yielded wet sand,
which people placed on their chests to quench their thirst.
Further west,
we crossed the Xiàn Hé (Trapping River).
We had to cut down tamarisks (*chēng*) and place them in the water to cross,
otherwise one would sink.
Further west,
we reached Gànzhōu.
Gànzhōu
was established by Yútián.
It is southwest of Shāzhōu,
and it was said to be nine thousand five hundred *lǐ* from the capital.
After traveling two more days, we reached Ānjūn Zhōu,
and then arrived at Yútián.
Shèngtiān's attire was like that of China.
His halls all faced east,
called the Jīncè Diàn (Gold Scroll Hall).
There was a tower called Qīfèng Lóu (Seven Phoenix Tower).
They made wine from grapes (pútao),
and also had purple wine and green wine;
how they were brewed is unknown,
but the taste was exceptionally good.
For food,
polished rice (*jīng*) was soaked in honey,
and millet (*sù*) was soaked in yogurt (*lào*).
For clothing,
they used cotton and silk.
They had gardens with flowers and trees.
The custom was to honor ghosts and spirits and to favor Buddhism.
When Shèngtiān resided in his palace,
he always had fifty purple-robed monks arrayed to attend him.
His reign title was Tóngqìng, and this was the twenty-ninth year [of his reign].
To the southeast of his state were Yínzhōu, Lúzhōu, and Méizhōu.
Thirteen hundred *lǐ* to the south was Yùzhōu (Jade Prefecture).
It was said that the source of the river that Zhāng Qiān of Hàn traced originated in Yútián,
and the mountains rich in jade are these mountains."
The source of that river,
upon reaching Yútián, divides into three: the eastern one is called Báiyù Hé (White Jade River);
the western one is called Lǜyù Hé (Green Jade River);
and further west is the Wūyù Hé (Black Jade River).
All three rivers have jade, but the colors differ.
Each year when the autumn water subsides,
the king first dredges the jade from the river,
and only then are the people of the state allowed to dredge for jade.
From Língzhōu, crossing the Yellow River to Yútián,
Tǔbō tribal tents were frequently seen,
and Yútián constantly engaged in mutual attacks and raids with Tǔbō.
When Kuāngyè and the others reached Yútián,
Shèngtiān slightly reproached them
in order to exact an oath and covenant.
When Kuāngyè and the others returned,
Shèngtiān again dispatched the Governor-General Liú Zàishēng to present a thousand *jīn* of jade, along with a jade seal and a *jiàngmóchǔ* (vajra), etc.
In the first year of Qiányòu of Hàn [948 CE],
he again sent the envoy Wáng Zhíduó to come [to court].
Gāolì
was originally a separate branch of the Fúyú rén people.
Its territory and the lineage of its rulers were known during the Táng dynasty.
Compared to other barbarian tribes, they had family names,
and the meaning of their official titles could be generally understood.
Toward the end of the Táng dynasty,
