their king's surname was Gāo.
In the first year of Tóngguāng (923 CE),
they sent the envoy, Grand Criticizing Court Gentleman (Guǎngpíng Shìláng) Hán Shēnyī, and the deputy envoy, Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Spring (Chūnbù Shàoqīng) Piáo Yán.
However, the name of their king
was lost and not recorded by the historians.
In the third year of Chángxīng (932 CE),
Wáng Jiàn, acting as regent (Quán Zhī Guóshì), sent an envoy.
Míngzōng then appointed Jiàn as the Commandant-Governor (Dūdu) of Xuántǔ Zhōu,
concurrently serving as the Commissioner of the Great Righteous Army (Dàyì Jūnshǐ),
and enfeoffed him as the King of the State of Gāolì.
Jiàn
was from a great Gāolì clan.
In the second year of Kāiyùn (945 CE),
Jiàn died,
and his son Wǔ succeeded him.
In the fourth year of Qiányòu (951 CE),
Wǔ died,
and his son Zhāo succeeded him.
The Wáng lineage, spanning three generations,
regularly came to pay tribute throughout the Wǔdài (Five Dynasties) period.
When a new ruler ascended, he always requested appointment from Zhōngguó,
and Zhōngguó always replied favorably.
Their land produced copper and silver.
During the reign of Zhōu Shìzōng,
the Emperor sent Hán Yànqīng, Vice-Director of the Bureau of Waterways (Shàngshū Shuǐbù Yuánwailáng), with several thousand bolts of silk to Gāolì to purchase copper for minting coins.
Six years later,
Zhāo sent an envoy to present fifty thousand catties of yellow copper as tribute.
The Gāolì people were customarily literate,
and fond of reading.

Zhāo presented: one scroll of the *Bié Xiàojīng* (Separate Classic of Filial Piety), eight scrolls of the *Yuè Wáng Xīnyì* (New Interpretations of the King of Yuè), one scroll of the *Huánglíng Xiàojīng* (Imperial Spirit Classic of Filial Piety), and one scroll of the *Xiàojīng Cītú* (Female Chart of the Classic of Filial Piety).
The *Bié* (Separate)
records the birth of Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) and the deeds of his disciples.
The *Yuè Wáng Xīnyì* (New Interpretations of the King of Yuè)
uses
"King of Yuè"
as the topic of inquiry,
similar to the modern
*Zhèngyì* (Correct Meaning).
The *Huánglíng* (Imperial Spirit)
discusses prolonging life and avoiding grain consumption (*bìgǔ*).
The *Cītú* (Female Chart)
records solar eclipses and stellar anomalies.
All these are unconventional theories.
Bóhǎi
was originally called Mòhé,
a separate branch of Gāolì.
When Táng Gāozōng destroyed Gāolì,
he relocated its people to be scattered across Zhōngguó,
and established the Āndōng Dūhù Fǔ (Protectorate General to Pacify the East) at Píngrǎng to govern them.
During the time of Wǔ Hòu (Empress Wǔ Zétiān),
the Qìdān attacked the northern border.
Dà Qǐqǐ Zhòngxiàng, a separate branch of Gāolì, and Qǐ Sībǐyǔ, a Mòhé chieftain, fled to Liáodōng.
They divided and ruled the former territory of Gāolì.
Wǔ Hòu sent a general who attacked and killed Qǐ Sībǐyǔ,
and Qǐqǐ Zhòngxiàng also died of illness.
Zhòngxiàng’s son Zuòróng succeeded him,
and consequently incorporated Sǐbǐyǔ’s followers.
His followers numbered four hundred thousand people.
They occupied Yìlǒu,
and submitted to Táng.
During the time of Zhōngzōng,
Hūhàn Zhōu was established,
and Zuòróng was appointed as its Commandant-Governor (Dūdu),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Bóhǎi Commandery (Bóhǎi Jùnwáng).
His descendants subsequently referred to their state as Bóhǎi.
Their nobles bore the surname Dà.
In the first year of Kāipíng (907 CE),
King Dà Yīnzuàn sent an envoy,
and they continued to come and pay tribute until the Xiǎndé era.
The land and products of their state
were the same as those of Gāolì.
The generational lineage, succession, and death of Yīnzuàn
were lost and not recorded by the historians.
Xīnluó
was a remnant branch of Biànhán.
Its territory, the lineage of its rulers, and its customs were known during the Táng dynasty.
Their great clans were named Jīn and Piáo.
Since the time Táng Gāozǔ enfeoffed Jīn Zhēn as the Prince of Lèlàng Commandery (Lèlàng Jùnwáng),
his descendants habitually served as rulers.
In the first year of Tóngguāng (923 CE),
Jīn Piáoyīng, the King of the State of Xīnluó, sent an envoy to pay tribute.
In the fourth year of Chángxīng (933 CE),
Jīn Pǔ, acting as regent (Quán Zhī Guóshì), sent an envoy.
The generational lineage, death, and succession of Piáoyīng and Pǔ
were all lost and not recorded by the historians.
After the Jìn dynasty (Later Jìn), they never came again.
Hēishuǐ Mòhé
was originally named Wùjí.
They appeared in Zhōngguó during the Hòu Wèi (Later Wèi) period.
Their state
reached the sea in the east,
bordered Gāolì in the south,
touched the Tūjué in the west,
and neighbored the Shìwéi in the north.
This was likely the land of the Sùshèn clan.
Their population was divided into several tens of tribes,
and the Hēishuǐ Mòhé resided furthest north,
being particularly strong and fierce,
and having no written records.
Their weapons were
horn bows and arrows made of *hù* wood.
In the second year of Tóngguāng (924 CE),
Wù'ér of Hēishuǐ sent an envoy.
Thereafter, they regularly came to pay tribute,
crossing the sea from Dēng Zhōu and emerging at Qīng Zhōu.
The following year,
Hú Dúlù of Hēishuǐ also sent an envoy.
Wù'ér and Hú Dúlù were likely chieftains of two different tribes,
each sending their own envoy.
However, the records of their tribes, generational lineage, succession, and death
were all lost and not recorded by the historians.
In the third year of Chángxīng (932 CE),
Hú Dúlù died,
and his son Táo Lǐhuā succeeded him.
He once requested appointment from Zhōngguó,
but thereafter, they are said to have been seen no more.
The Southern Zhào Man (Nánzhào Mán)
were known during the Táng dynasty.
Their state was located east of the former Hàn Yǒngchāng Commandery and west of Yáo Zhōu.
When Xīzōng fled to Shǔ,
he sought men capable of serving as envoys to Nánzhào.
He obtained Lǐ Guīnián, a son of the imperial clan, as well as Xú Hǔ and Hǔ’s nephew Xú Ài.
Consequently, Guīnián was made the envoy,
Hǔ the deputy,
and Ài the secretary (Pànguān),
and they were sent to Nánzhào.
The place where the Nánzhào resided was called Jūpán Chéng.
Guīnián and the others did not reach Jūpán,
but went to Shànchǎn.
They obtained a crucial agreement for Táng and Nánzhào to become uncle and nephew (a diplomatic kinship relationship).
Xīzōng promised to give them Princess Ānhuà in marriage.
Nánzhào was greatly pleased,
and sent people to follow Guīnián back to request the Princess.
Soon after,
Huáng Cháo was defeated,
Cháng'ān was recovered,
and Xīzōng returned east, whereupon the marriage plan was halted.
In the third year of Tóngguāng (925 CE),
when Wèi Wáng Jìjí and Guō Chóngtāo defeated Shǔ,
they captured several tens of Nánzhào Mán who had been taken prisoner during Wáng Yǎn's time.
They also found Xú Ài,
who claimed he had previously served as an envoy to Nánzhào.
They then issued a false edict, returning the captives,
and sent Ài and others carrying gold and silk to recruit and pacify Nánzhào,
instructing them through might and virtue.
Nánzhào did not accept this.
During the time of Míngzōng,
Lǐ Bēiwǎn, the Supreme Ghost Chief (Dū Guǐzhǔ) of the Bǎimán (Hundred Barbarians) of Liǎnglín behind the mountains of Kuí Zhōu, and Grand General of the Right Martial Guard (Yòu Wǔwèi Dà Jiāngjūn),
sent the Great Ghost Chief (Dà Guǐzhǔ) Fù Néng Héhuá to pay tribute.
Míngzōng appointed Bēiwǎn as General Who Pacifies Afar (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn).

He also appointed Wùdìng Biāoshā, the Prince of Huái'ān Commandery (Huái'ān Jùnwáng) and Supreme Ghost Chief of the Six Surnames of Qióng Zhōu in front of the mountains south of the Dàdù River, as General Who Determines Afar (Dìngyuǎn Jiāngjūn).
The following year, the General of the Left Imperial Insignia Guard (Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi Jiāngjūn), Wū Zhāoyuǎn, was sent as the Diplomatic Envoy to the Mán States (Rùmán Guó Xìnshǐ).
Zhāoyuǎn was unable to reach them and returned.
The Qiáo Mán
were located one thousand five hundred *lǐ* west of Chén Zhōu.
They lived by farming and planting,
but had no city walls or permanent settlements.
When they needed to launch an attack,
they would gather and encamp together.
They used notched wood for contracts.
Their leaders bore the surname Xiè,
and their names were known during the Táng dynasty.
They came once in the second year of Tiānchéng (927 CE).
Their envoy was Sòng Cháohuà, Prefect (Cìshǐ) of the Eight Commanderies of Qīng Zhōu.
He wore the cap and belt typical of Zhōngguó.
He presented twenty thousand pieces of grass cardamom, five hundred taels of cinnabar, and two hundred catties of wax as tribute.
Kūnmíng
was located three thousand *lǐ* southwest of Qián Zhōu.
The land produced sheep and horses.
The people wore hair coiled on the head (*chuī jì*), were barefoot, and wore felt wraps.
Their leaders wore tiger skins.
In the second year of Tiānchéng (927 CE),
they came once.
Their leaders were titled the Supreme Ghost Chief of Kūnmíng (Kūnmíng Dà Guǐzhǔ),
the King of Luódiàn, and the King of Pǔlùjìng of the Nine Tribes.
Each sent an envoy,
whose title was Ruòtǔ,
accompanying the Qiáo Mán on their arrival.
Zhànchéng
is located in the southwestern sea.
Its territory spans a thousand *lǐ*.
To the east it reaches the sea,
to the west it reaches Yúnnán,
to the south it neighbors Zhēnlà,
and to the north it extends to Huānzhōu.
Its people,
their customs are the same as Dàshí.
Their transport
includes elephants and horses.
Their food
includes rice, water rhinoceros (or water buffalo), and goats.
Remarkable birds and beasts
are the rhinoceros and the peacock.
Since former ages, they had never communicated with Zhōngguó.
In the fifth year of Xiǎndé,
its king, Yīndémàn, dispatched the envoy Púhēsàn to come.
He offered tribute of eighty-four bottles of fierce fire oil and fifteen bottles of rose water.
His memorial was written on *bèiduō* leaves,
enclosed in a case made of fragrant wood.
The fierce fire oil, when sprinkled on things,
if it encounters water, fire bursts forth.
The rose water,
is said to have been obtained from Xīyù (Western Regions),
used to sprinkle on clothes;
although the clothes are worn out, the fragrance does not fade.
During the Wǔdài (Five Dynasties) period,
among the surrounding foreign nations who had appeared before Zhōngguó,
the farthest did not exceed Yútián and Zhànchéng.
In the records of the historians,
the northwest is quite detailed,
but the southeast is especially brief.
This is probably because they are distant and rarely reached,
and moreover, they are not a matter of advantage or harm to Zhōngguó, it is said.
